en: Salutations to the Lord of the Gaṇas. Salutations to Sarasvatī. Now begins the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa; therein, first, the Pūrvakhaṇḍa, known as the Karmakāṇḍa, is commenced. Om! Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa, and to Nara, the best of men, and to the Goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Jaya."

Oṃ! I bow to that one Hari, who is unborn, undecaying, infinite, whose nature is knowledge, great, auspicious, stainless, and without beginning; who is devoid of a body composed of elements, free from all sense organs, abiding within all beings, pure, free from illusion, and omnipresent.
I perpetually pay homage with mind, speech, and action to Hari, Rudra, Brahmā, the Lord of the Gaṇas, and the Goddess Sarasvatī.
To the Sūta, a reciter of the Purāṇas, who was tranquil, learned in all the scriptures, a devotee of Viṣṇu, and a high-souled being who had arrived at the Naimiṣa forest.
While the sinless sage was seated upon an auspicious seat in the course of a pilgrimage to holy places, meditating upon Viṣṇu, they honored and praised that seer.
The highly fortunate Śaunaka and others, the ascetics of Naimiṣa whose wealth is their austerity, were sages resplendent like the sun, peaceful, and devoted to sacrifice.
The sages said: "O Sūta, you know everything; therefore we ask you this: among the deities, who indeed is the god who is the Lord, and who is truly worthy of worship?"
Who is to be meditated upon? Who is the creator of the world, and who protects and destroys it? From what does Dharma proceed, and who is remembered as the slayer of the wicked?
What is the form of that god? How is the creation of the world considered by him? By what vows is he pleased, or by what yoga is he attained?
Who are his incarnations, and how did the lineage and so forth originate? Who is the protector of the duties of the castes and stages of life, and who is their promulgator?
O Sūta of great intelligence, tell us all of this and whatever else there may be; relate to us all the most excellent accounts concerning Nārāyaṇa.
Sūta said: I shall proclaim the Gāruḍa Purāṇa, which is the essence based on the narratives of Viṣṇu; it was spoken by Garuḍa to Kaśyapa in ancient times, and I have heard it from Vyāsa.
The one god Nārāyaṇa is the Lord of the lords of gods; he is the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, from whom the birth and so forth of this universe proceed.
For the sake of protecting the world, Vāsudeva—the unborn, undecaying, and immortal—manifests incarnations in the form of Kumāra and others.
O Brahmin, that Lord Hari, having first established the Kaumāra creation, practiced difficult and unbroken celibacy.
But for the sake of his second birth, the Lord of Sacrifice assumes the form of a boar, intending to lift up the earth that has sunk into the netherworld.

In the third creation, that of the sages, having attained the status of a divine sage (devarṣi), he expounds the Sātvata system, because therein the cessation of karmic action is achieved through action itself.
Having become Nara and Nārāyaṇa, Hari performed austerities in the fourth age for the sake of protecting dharma; he was worshipped by both gods and asuras.
The fifth, the lord of perfected beings named Kapila, proclaimed to Sūri the Sāṅkhya system—which determines the collection of principles—after it had been obscured by time.
He became the sixth son of Atri, having been granted by Anasūyā; he taught the science of logic (ānvīkṣikī) to Alarka, Prahlāda, and others.
Then, during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, after the gods led by Sutrāman had performed sacrifices, Yajña was born from Ruci through Ākūti.
In the eighth [birth], Urukrama was born to Nābhi from Merudevī, demonstrating the path for women that is honored by all stages of life.
Entreated by the sages, he assumed a ninth earthly form; by means of the great medicinal herbs milked from him, O brahmins, the subjects were restored to life.
During the dissolution at the end of the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara, he assumed the form of a fish and, having placed Vaivasvata Manu upon a boat made of earth, rescued him.
In the eleventh [incarnation], the Lord, in the form of a tortoise, supported on his back Mount Mandara as the gods and demons churned the ocean.
The twelfth was Dhānvantara, and the thirteenth was indeed Āpyāyan; he deluded other gods with the woman Mohinī.
And in the fourteenth [incarnation], as the Nārasiṃha Caitya,
he tore apart the powerful lord of the Daityas with his fierce claws, just as one might split a reed-stalk with a bamboo thorn.
On the fifteenth day, having become a dwarf, he went to the sacrifice of Bali, requesting three paces of land while intending to reclaim the triple heaven.
In his sixteenth incarnation, seeing kings who were enemies of Brahman, he became enraged and thrice seven times rid the earth of the Kṣatriya caste.
Then, born of Satyavatī from Parāśara in the seventeenth [generation], he saw that men possessed but little intelligence and thus divided the branches of the tree of the Veda.
Having attained the status of a god among men out of a desire to accomplish the work of the gods, he thereafter performed deeds such as the subduing of the ocean.
Having taken birth among the Vṛṣṇis in his nineteenth and twentieth incarnations as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, the Blessed One removed the burden of the earth.
Then, at the end of the twilight of the Kali age, for the sake of deluding the enemies of the gods, a son of the Jina named Buddha will appear among the Kīkaṭas.
Then, at the eighth twilight, when the kings have almost perished, Viṣṇuyaśas will become the Lord of the World by the name of Kalki.
O twice-born ones, the incarnations of Hari, the treasury of being, are indeed innumerable; for all those who know the Manu-veda are remembered as portions of Viṣṇu from the beginning.
Therefore, the creations and other [topics] have arisen; they should be honored through vows and other observances. Vyāsa previously told this Garuḍa Purāṇa to me.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Cause for the Commencement of this Purāṇa," in the Karmakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. The Sages said: "How was the Garuḍa Purāṇa told to you by Vyāsa? Explain all of this in detail, for it is supremely based upon the narrations of Viṣṇu."
Sūta said: "Indeed, I went to Badarikāśrama together with the sages; there I saw Vyāsa absorbed in meditation upon the Supreme Lord."
Having bowed to him, I sat down and questioned the lord of sages. Sūta said: "O Vyāsa, tell me now of the form of Hari and the creation of the world and so forth."
"I think you meditate upon him; therefore, you know that all-pervading Lord. O brahmins, listen to how he spoke when thus questioned.
Vyāsa said: Listen, O Sūta; I shall proclaim to you the Gāruḍa Purāṇa, just as Brahmā spoke it to me in the past along with Nārada, Dakṣa, and others.
Sūta said: How did Brahmā speak to you—when you were joined by Dakṣa, Nārada, and other leaders—regarding the meritorious Śrī-Gāruḍa Purāṇa, which expresses the very essence?
Vyāsa said: Indeed, I, Nārada, Dakṣa, Bhṛgu, and others, having prostrated before Brahmā while he was in the world of Brahmā, asked him, "Tell us the essence."
Brahmā said: "O Vyāsa, just as Viṣṇu formerly spoke to me—the essence of the Gāruḍa Purāṇa and the Rudra Purāṇa—along with the gods, so shall I speak it."
Vyāsa said: How did Hari formerly speak with the gods regarding Rudra? O Brahmin, tell me the essence of the ancient Gāruḍa Purāṇa, which is of great significance.
Brahmā said: I went to Mount Kailāsa together with Indra and the other deities; there I beheld Rudra meditating upon the supreme state.
"O Śaṅkara, when questioned and saluted, what god do you meditate upon? I know no supreme god other than you; therefore, tell me."
Desiring to hear the reality that is the most essential of all essences, Rudra, together with the gods, said: "I meditate upon that Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, the Lord."
He is the giver of all, the all-pervading, the All, residing in the hearts of all living beings; his body is smeared with ashes, and he is adorned with a mass of matted hair.
"O Grandfather, for the sake of propitiating Viṣṇu, I am engaged in the practice of a vow; let us go to him and ask about that very essence which I am contemplating."
Viṣṇu, the Victorious One, Padmanābha, Hari, who is devoid of a body; the Pure One, dwelling in purity, the Swan, that state, the Supreme Lord.
With my whole being, I meditate upon that God, the Self, in whom all beings abide and into whom they enter.
In the Lord of Beings, all qualities are subordinate, like clusters of gems upon a thread; he who has a thousand eyes, a thousand feet, a thousand thighs, and a beautiful face.
The most minute among the minute, the largest among the large, the heaviest among the heavy, and the best even among the excellent.
Him who is of true deeds, the True One, whom they praise in the *vākya*s, the *anuvākya*s, the *niṣat*s, and the *upaniṣat*s, and in the true *sāman* chants.
He is declared the Ancient Puruṣa; among the twice-born, he is declared Brahmā; at the time of dissolution, he is declared Saṅkarṣaṇa—we worship him who is worthy of worship.
In which these worlds flutter like birds upon the water—that single-syllabled Brahman, the Truth (Ṛta), which is beyond both being and non-being.
The gods, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas worship him, whose mouth is fire, whose head is the sky, whose navel is space, and whose feet are the earth.
I meditate upon that God whose eyes are the moon and the sun, within whose belly are the three worlds, and whose arms are the quarters of space.
I meditate upon that God whose breath is the wind, in whose hair are the clouds, and in the joints of whose limbs are all the rivers.
Within his belly are the four oceans; I meditate upon that God who is beyond time, beyond sacrifice, and beyond both being and non-being.
I meditate upon that God who is the beginningless origin of the universe, whose mind is the moon and whose eyes are the sun.
From his mouth fire was born; I meditate upon that god from whose feet the earth arose, and from whose two ears the directions likewise emerged.
I meditate upon that God whose summit reaches to heaven; [I meditate upon] primary creation, secondary creation, the lineages, and the periods of the Manus.
Since I am contemplating that deity through the history of his lineage, I shall therefore proceed to examine the essence of what I am meditating upon.
Brahmā said: Having been addressed thus in the past, Rudra, together with the gods, stood desiring to hear, after having praised and bowed down to that Viṣṇu who dwells in Śvetadvīpa.
From among us, Rudra, having prostrated before that Supreme Lord Viṣṇu—the essence of all essences—indeed questioned him.
Brahmā said: Just as Vyāsa questioned me, so did that blessed Lord Bhava question Viṣṇu while the gods and other immortals listened together.
Rudra said: O Hari, tell me, O Lord of Gods—Who is the God of gods? Who is the Sovereign? Who is to be meditated upon? And who indeed is to be worshipped? By what vows is the Supreme One pleased?
By what qualities, by what observances, or by what worship of the Dharma, and by what conduct would he be pleased? And what indeed is his form?
From which god was the world born, and who protects the world? By what kinds of incarnations does he do so, and into whom does the world go for dissolution?
From which deity do primary creation, secondary creation, the lineages, and the periods of the Manvantaras proceed? Upon what is all this established?
O Hari, tell me all of this, as well as anything else whatsoever—the majesty of the Supreme Lord, as well as yoga, reasoning, and so forth.
Likewise, [the eighteen branches of] knowledge and Hari spoke to Rudra. Hari said: "Listen, O Rudra! I shall proclaim [this], together with Brahmā and the gods."
For I am the god of gods, the Lord of the lords of all worlds; I am to be meditated upon and worshipped, and I am to be praised by the gods with hymns of praise.
O Rudra, when I am honored by men through their observances, vows, and conduct, I grant them the supreme goal.
O Śiva, I am the seed of the world’s existence and I am the creator of the world; O Hara, I am indeed the subduer of the wicked and the protector of Dharma.
Through incarnations such as the Fish and others, I protect the entire world; I am the mantras, the meaning of the mantras, and indeed I am devoted to worship and meditation.
I am the creator of heaven and the like, and I alone am heaven and the like; I am the primordial yoga, and I alone am the ancient scriptures.
The knower, the hearer, as well as the thinker, the speaker, and that which is to be spoken—all this is the God who is the self of all, the supreme bestower of enjoyment and liberation.
I am meditation and the offering of worship; I alone am the mandalas. O Rudra, I am the ancient histories; indeed, O Śiva, I am all the Vedas.
O Śambhu, I am all-knowing; I am the Self that is Brahman, I am Śiva. I am Brahmā, the entire world, for I am indeed the self of all the gods.
I am the personified practice of right conduct; I am indeed Dharma; I am the Vaiṣṇava; likewise, I am the castes and stages of life, and I am their ancient duty.
I am Yama, I am Niyama, O Rudra, and the various Vratas; I am likewise the Sun, the Moon, and Maṅgala and the other planets.
In former times, the bird Garuḍa propitiated me on earth through ascetic penance; being pleased, I said, "Choose a boon from me," and he chose a boon from me.
Garuḍa said: "O Hari, my mother Vinatā has been made a slave by the Nāgas; O Lord, therefore I shall conquer them and bring back that nectar."
I shall liberate you from slavery, just as I am your vehicle—possessing great strength and great heroism, omniscient, and the subduer of the Nāgas.
"Act in such a way that I may become the compiler of the Purāṇa-saṃhitā. Viṣṇu said: "O Garuḍa, everything shall happen exactly as you have spoken."
Through the gift of the Naga, you shall liberate your mother Vinatā; and having conquered all the gods and others, you shall indeed bring back the nectar of immortality.
"You shall become a mighty vehicle, a destroyer of poison; and by my grace, you shall proclaim my greatness through this ancient [text]."
"That which was spoken regarding my own nature shall manifest within you; that Gāruḍa [Purāṇa] shall attain renown in the world under your name."
Just as I am known as the glory of the gods of gods, O son of Vinatā, so shall the Gāruḍa Purāṇa attain renown in the Purāṇas as "Gāruḍa."
Just as I am to be glorified, so too are you in your form as Garuḍa; O chief of birds, meditating upon me, proclaim this Purāṇa, the Gāruḍa.
Thus addressed by Rudra, Garuḍa spoke to the inquiring Kaśyapa; having heard the Gāruḍa [teachings], Kaśyapa restored a burnt tree to life.

And having yourself become single-minded, you shall revive others by means of this knowledge. O Yakṣiṇī, one who recites "Oṃ uṃ svāhā" possesses this supreme Gāruḍī vidyā. Indeed, O Rudra, hear now the Gāruḍa taught by Garuḍa, which is identical with my own self.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Description of the Origin of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa," in the Ācāra-kāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrva-khaṇḍa within the glorious Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

The Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 3. Sūta said: In this manner, the sage Vyāsa heard it from Brahmā, who was born from the lotus of Viṣṇu and himself from Rudra; and I shall now relate it to you, O Śaunaka, at Naimiṣa.

In the midst of the sages who were listening, [the following] was spoken here: the creation and so forth, the worship of the gods, the sacred fords, the structure of the universe, and the periods of the Manvantaras.
The duties of the castes and stages of life, as well as the duties such as giving and kingship; legal procedure, religious observances, genealogies, and medicine together with its pathology.

The limbs, dissolution, and the supreme knowledge of dharma, desire, and wealth—whether with conceptual elaboration (*saprapañca*) or without conceptual elaboration (*niṣprapañca*)—are declared to be the deeds of Viṣṇu.
In the Gāruḍa Purāṇa, the Lord Garuḍa is described as being endowed with an excellence of power through the grace of Vāsudeva.
Having become the vehicle of Hari and the cause of creation and the other cosmic processes, Garuḍa indeed conquered the gods and likewise performed the bringing of the nectar of immortality.
Within whose belly Hari held the universe swallowed by hunger; upon seeing whom, and merely by remembering him, there is the destruction of the serpents and the demons.
Since Kaśyapa restored to life the tree burnt by Garuḍa, he is called Garuḍa; and because he is Hari, it was said to the illustrious Kaśyapa: "He is Garuḍa."
Having bowed to Vyāsa, I shall speak that auspicious and merit-bestowing *Raurava*, which grants all things to you who recite it; listen, O Śaunaka, to how it is so.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Description of the Subjects," in the section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa) within the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 4.

Rudra said: "O Janārdana, please describe the primary creation (Sarga), the secondary creation (Pratisarga), the genealogies (Vaṃśa), the periods of the Manus (Manvantaras), and the history of the dynasties (Vaṃśānucarita)."
Hari said: Listen, O Rudra, I shall proclaim that ancient sport of Viṣṇu, which destroys sins and encompasses the beginning of creation, its maintenance, and its dissolution.
The Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, the stainless one, the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, is the author of the creation, dissolution, and other states of the universe.
All this, indeed, exists in the form of both the manifest and the unmanifest; likewise, it exists in the form of the Puruṣa and in the form of Time.
The manifest, as well as the unmanifest, the Puruṣa, and even Time—behold his activity, which is like that of a playing child.
The Sustainer is without beginning or end, infinite, and the Supreme Person; from him arises the Unmanifest, and from that, the Self is also born.
From that [the Self] arose the intellect, from that the mind, from that the ether, from that the wind; from that arose fire, from that the waters, and from those the earth came into being.
O Rudra, that golden egg indeed exists by itself within; the Lord himself first assumes a body for the sake of creation.
Brahmā, having become four-faced and always possessing an excess of the quality of rajas, assumed a physical body and created this world of moving and non-moving beings.
Within the cosmic egg is the entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans; Viṣṇu, the creator, creates himself, and he protects that which is to be protected.
At the end, O Hara, he is withdrawn and you yourself are the withdrawer; having become Brahmā, you created, and Hari himself, as Viṣṇu, protects the world.
In the form of Rudra, he destroys the entire universe at the end of the kalpa; but as Brahmā, at the time of creation, [he supports] the earth situated within the midst of the waters.
Having assumed the body of a boar and knowing [the truth], he raised it up with his tusk; O Śaṅkara, listen as I shall describe the creation of the gods and others in brief.

(1) The first creation is that of Mahat, which is indeed the formless [creation] of Brahmā; (2) the second, however, is the creation of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), which is known as the creation of the gross elements (*bhūtasarga*).
(3) But the third creation is that of the vaikārika [gods], which is known as the creation of the senses; thus this is the primary (prākṛta) creation, which arose preceded by intelligence.

The fourth is the primary creation (*mukhyasarga*), and the primary beings are indeed remembered as the immobile (*sthāvara*). That which is called the "sideways-streamed" (*tiryaksrotas*) is said to be the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*).

(6) That which follows [the upward-streaming beings] is known as the sixth creation, that of the gods; (7) thereafter, the seventh creation is that of the downward-streaming beings, which is the human creation.

The eighth is the creation of grace; that [creation] is both characterized by goodness (*sāttvika*) and characterized by darkness (*tāmasa*). These five are known as the secondary creations (*vaikṛta-sarga*), while three are known as the primary creations (*prākṛta-sarga*).

The natural (prākṛta), the modified (vaikṛta), and the youthful (kaumāra) are recorded as the ninth; O Rudra, the fourfold progeny, beginning with the gods and ending with the stationary beings, are thus established.
As Brahmā was performing the act of creation, mind-born sons were born to him; from them arose the fourfold classes: gods, asuras, ancestors, and humans.
Desiring to emit these waters, Prajāpati joined his own self; from his manifest self, the quality of darkness (tamas) was intensified.
From the loins of Him desiring to create, the Asuras were first born; thereafter, He cast off that body which consisted of the quality of darkness (tamas).
The subtle body consisting of pure darkness was cast off and became Śaṅkara, the Night; then the Yakṣas, Upakṣas, and Rākṣasas found delight in that body, and from them the gods were born.
But those characterized by an abundance of *sattva* were produced from the mouth of Brahmā, O Hara; that body, consisting mostly of *sattva*, was cast off by him and became the day.
For from that [creation], the Asuras were strong by night and the deities by day; and from that, the Pitṛs came into being, having assumed bodies consisting of pure sattva.
And that twilight, which exists as the interval between day and night, having assumed a subtle body consisting of the quality of passion (rajas), then became human beings.
That moonlight which was previously called the morning twilight became abandoned; indeed, moonlight, night, day, and twilight were his very bodies.
Having taken up a minute particle of dust, hunger and anger arose; those who were called Rākṣasas because they protected (rakṣaṇāt) became emaciated by hunger and thirst and subsisted on raw flesh.

They are to be known as Yakṣas because of their devouring (jakṣaṇa); they are indeed serpents (sarpa) because of the gliding (sarpaṇa) of their hair. Those beings were born from anger, and from that, the Gandharvas were produced.
Singing, the Gandharvas and Apsarases brought forth speech; Dyaus made heaven his breast, and the Unborn One (Aja) was well-pleased by that sacrifice.
From his belly and from his two sides Prajāpati created [beings], and from his feet he likewise created the lowest elephants, as well as buffaloes, camels, and sheep.
From his body hairs were born medicinal herbs bearing fruits and roots; likewise, the cow, the goat, the man fit for sacrifice, as well as the horse, the mule, and the donkey were produced.
These they call domestic animals; now learn from me the wild ones: beasts of prey, cloven-hoofed animals, elephants, monkeys, and birds as the fifth.
Aquatic animals were born from the sixth [mouth], and reptiles from the seventh; from the eastern and other mouths, the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas were produced.
From his mouth, indeed, the Brāhmaṇas were born; from his two arms, the Kṣatriyas are remembered [to have been born]; from his thighs, the Vaiśyas were created; and from his feet, the Śūdra was born.
The world of Brahmā belongs to the Brāhmaṇas; that of Śakra to those born as Kṣatriyas; the station of the Maruts to the Vaiśyas; and the world of the Gandharvas to those born as Śūdras.
For those established in the vow of celibacy, the world of Brahmā arises; for householders who act according to the prescribed rules, the world of Prajāpati arises.
There is the abode of the seven sages, and likewise that of the forest-dwellers; and there is the imperishable station for ascetics who always travel according to their own will.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "Description of Creation," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Śrī Hari said: Having established his residence in this world and the next, and having performed the mental creation of progeny, the Lord then created the mind-born sons who were the progenitors of creatures.
Dharma, Rudra, Manu, Sanaka, Sanātana, Bhṛgu, Sanatkumāra, as well as Ruci and Śraddhā.
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, and likewise the Barhiṣat Pitṛs.
The Agniṣvātta, the Kavyāda, the Ājyapa, and the Sukālins; likewise the Upahūta, the Dīpya, and the three who are devoid of physical form.
The Lotus-born [Brahmā] created the four [sages] endowed with forms; from his right thumb he created the Lord Īśvara, and from his left thumb he created his wife.
Upon her, Dakṣa begot auspicious daughters; he gave those to the sons of Brahmā, but gave Satī to Rudra.
Indeed, Rudra had countless sons of great strength; and he gave Khyāti, who was auspicious and peerless in beauty, to Bhṛgu.
That auspicious woman gave birth to Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ for Bhṛgu, and she also gave birth to Śrī, who is the wife of Nārāyaṇa.
Upon her, Hari himself begot Balonmada and Āyati and Niyati, the two daughters of the high-souled Manu.
Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ had two wives, and from them were born two sons, Prāṇa and Mṛkaṇḍu; and from Mṛkaṇḍu was born Mārkaṇḍeya.
Marīci’s wife Sambhūti gave birth to Paurṇamāsa; Virajas and Sarvaga were the two sons of that high-souled one.
And from Smṛti were born the sons of Aṅgiras, as well as daughters: Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, and Anumati.
In the same manner, Anasūyā bore to Atri three stainless sons: Soma, Durvāsas, and the yogi Dattātreya.
From Prīti, the wife of Pulastya, Dattoli was born as their son; he had three sons: Karṇaśa, Arthavīra, and Sahiṣṇu.
Kṣamā, the wife of the progenitor Pulaha, gave birth [to the Kṣamācyas], and Sumati, the wife of Kratu, gave birth to the Bālakhilyas.
There were sixty thousand sages of perpetual celibacy, the size of a thumb’s joint, possessing a radiance like that of the blazing sun.
To Ūrjā, however, seven sons were born to Vasiṣṭha: Rajas, Gātra, Urdhvabāhu, Śaraṇa, and likewise Anagha.
Sutapās and Śukra—these were all the stainless Seven Sages; Dakṣa also gave Svāhā to the Fire-god, who was bodiless.
Therefore, O Hara, Svāhā obtained three sons of noble vigor: Phāvaka, Pavamāna, and Śuci, who subsist on water.
From the Pitṛs, Svadhā gave birth to Menā and likewise Vaitaraṇī; both of them were exponents of the Veda, and Himācala begot [children] upon Menā.
The Lord first begot Maināka and Gaurī, who was formerly Satī; thereafter, he first produced from his own self the Svāyambhuva Brahmā, the sovereign.
O Hara, you made Manu himself the protector of creatures, and Śatarūpā that woman whose impurities were destroyed by asceticism.
The divine and all-pervading Manu Svāyambhuva took her as his wife; and from that Puruṣa, the goddess Śatarūpā was born.
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were born [of them], along with those named Prasūti and Ākūti; among them, Manu gave Devahūti to Ruci and Ākūti to Dakṣa.
He gave Prasūti to Dakṣa and Dahanūti to Kardama; from Ruci, Yajña was born, and from Yajña, Dakṣiṇā was born.
There were twelve sons named Yāmas of great strength, and Dakṣa also created twenty-four excellent daughters.
Faith, activity, fortitude, contentment, nourishment, intelligence, action, as well as understanding, modesty, form, tranquility, prosperity, and fame as the thirteenth.
The lord Dharma, the son of Dakṣa, accepted them as his wives: Khyāti, Satī, Sambhūti, Smṛti, Prīti, and likewise Kṣamā.
Sannati, Anasūyā, Ūrjā, Svāhā, and likewise Svadhā; as well as Bhṛgu, Bhava, Marīci, and the sage Aṅgiras.
Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and likewise Atri, the best of sages; Vasiṣṭha, Vahni, and the Pitṛs, in their proper order.
The sages, the best of ascetics, took these daughters: Khyāti took Kāma, Calā took Darpa, and Dhṛti took her son Niyama.
Contentment gave birth to satisfaction, and nourishment gave birth to greed; likewise, intelligence gave birth to sacred learning, action to punishment, dissolution to discipline, and so forth.
Buddhi gave birth to Bodha, as well as Lajjā, Vinaya, Vapus, and Ātmaja; Śānti indeed gave birth to Vyavasāya and Kṣema.
Happiness, prosperity, fame, and renown—these are the sons of Dharma; and Rati is the wife of Kāma, and their son is said to be Harṣa (Joy).
Once, Dakṣa performed a horse sacrifice; all his sons-in-law, having been invited, went to that sacrifice.
All were accompanied by their wives, except for the goddess Satī and Rudra; Satī arrived uninvited and was indeed insulted by Dakṣa.
Having cast off her body, she was born again from Himālaya as Menā; she became the wife of Śambhu as Raurī, and from her Vināyaka was born.
And the powerful Kumāra Bhṛṅgīśa, the wrathful Rudra, the wielder of the Pināka bow, having destroyed the sacrifice, cursed Dakṣa: "You shall become a human being born in the lineage of Dhruva."
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Creation of the Progenitor and Others," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 6—Hari said: From Uttānapāda and Suruci was born a son named Uttama; from Sunīti, however, was born the son Dhruva, who attained the highest station.
Through the grace of the Sage, having propitiated Janārdana, the god of gods, Śliṣṭi—the son of Dhruva—possessed great strength and prowess.
His son was Prācīnavarhis; his son was Udāradhī; his son was Divañjaya; and his son is recorded as Ripu.
Likewise, the illustrious Cākṣuṣa is celebrated as the son of Ripu; his son was the illustrious Ruru, and Aṅga was his offspring.
The son of Aṅga was Veṇa, who was an atheist, devoid of dharma, and a doer of unrighteousness;
he was slain by the sages with blades of kusha grass.
They churned his thigh for the sake of a son; from that, a son was born who was exceedingly short and dark-limbed, whereupon they said, "Let him sit down (niṣīda)."
From that [act], he was indeed born as a Niṣāda who dwelt on the Vindhya mountain; thereafter, the twice-born ones suddenly churned his right hand.
Therefore, a son was born to him who bore the mental form of Viṣṇu; that son of Veṇa, named Pṛthu, ascended to heaven.
Indeed, King Antardhāna milked the earth for the livelihood of his subjects; his son was Pṛthu, and Havidhāna was the son of Pṛthu.
His son, Prācīnabarhis, shone as the sole sovereign of the earth; he indeed married the daughter of the salt ocean.
Therefore, Sāmudrī bore ten sons to Prācīnabarhis; all were named Prācetasas and were masters of the science of archery.
Practicing their dharma without separation, they performed great asceticism for ten thousand years, dwelling within the waters of the ocean.
O noble one, having attained the status of Prajāpati, he took them as his wives; and by the curse of Bhava, Dakṣa was subsequently born from her.
In the beginning, Dakṣa created beings of four classes by means of his mind; however, they did not multiply because they were cursed by Hara.
Then Prajāpati desired to effect creation through sexual union; he took Asiknī, the daughter of the Prajāpati Vīraṇa, as his wife.
He had a thousand sons born of Vairaṇī; they went to the end of the earth as directed by Nārada, but they did not return.
And when they had perished, he created the thousand sons of Dakṣa; O Hara, those Śabalāśvas also followed the path of their brothers.
Then Dakṣa, enraged, cursed Nārada, saying, "You shall undergo birth"; and so Nārada was born again as the son of the sage Kaśyapa.
When the sacrifice has been destroyed, Dakṣa too shall curse Maheśvara with fierce words; but after praising you and worshipping you with ritual offerings, O Śaṅkara, they will honor you.
"O Śaṅkara, even in another birth they will perish through enmity; therefore, one should never harbor enmity toward anyone. Then Dakṣa begot daughters upon his queen, Asiknī.
He gave sixty beautiful maidens and two to Aṅgiras; he gave two to Kṛśāśva and ten to Dharma.
He gave Suprabhā, that beautiful woman, to Kaśyapa as his fourteenth wife, and likewise to Indu, the father of many sons, as his twenty-eighth.
O Mahādeva, Dakṣa gave four daughters—Manoramā, Bhānumatī, Viśālā, and Bahudāmā—to Ariṣṭanemi.
He gave Suprajā and likewise Jayā to Kṛśāśva; [and he gave] Arundhatī, Vasu, Yāmī, Lambā, Bhānu, and Marudvatī.
Saṅkalpā, Muhūrtā, Sādhyā, and Viśvā—these ten are declared to be the wives of Dharma; now I shall speak of the wives of Kaśyapa.
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kālā, Anāyuḥ, Siṃhikā, Muni, Kadrū, Sādhyā, Harā, Krodhā, Vinatā, Surabhi, and Khagā.
From Viśvā were born the Viśvedevas; Sādhyā gave birth to the Sādhyas; from Marutvatī came the Marutvats, and likewise the Vasus from Vasu.
O Rudra, the rays belong to Bhānu, and the Muhūrtas are born from Muhūrta; from Lambā comes Ghoṣa, and from Yāmitā comes Nāgavīthi.
The entire realm of the earth was born from Marutvatī; and from Saṅkalpā was born Saṅkalpa himself, the soul of all.
Āpa, Dhruva, Soma, Dhara, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are remembered as the Vasus by their names.
Āpasya’s sons were Vetuṇḍi (or Veṇḍa), Śrama, Śrānta, and Dhvani; and the son of Dhruva was the blessed Kāla, the destroyer of the worlds.
The venerable Varcas was born from Soma, by whom one becomes radiant; likewise, Druhiṇa and Hutahavyavaha were the sons of Dhara.
From Manoharā were born Śiśira, Prāṇa, and likewise Ramaṇa. Anila’s wife was Śivā, and her son was Pulomaja.
Avijñātagati was the second; these were the two sons of Anila. As for Kumāra, the son of Agni, he was born within a clump of *śara* reeds.
His sons were Śākha, Viśākha, and Naigameya, born after him; and because he was the offspring of the Kṛttikās, he is known as Kārttikeya.
They know Pratyūṣa’s son to be the ṛṣi named Devala; Viśvakarman is the renowned divine architect of Prabhāsa.
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Tvaṣṭṛ, and the heroic Rudra; and also the son born of Tvaṣṭṛ, Viśvarūpa, who was possessed of great ascetic power.
Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, Aparājita, Vṛṣākapi, Śambhu, Kapardin, and likewise Raivata.
Mṛgavyādha, Śarva, and Kapālī, O great sage—these eleven are declared to be the Rudras, the lords of the three worlds.
From Kaśyapa and Aditi, twelve sons were born to Sūryā: Viṣṇu, Śakra, Aryaman, Dhātṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, and likewise Pūṣan.
Vivasvat, Savitṛ, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśumat, and Bhaga—these are remembered as the twelve Ādityas.
There were twenty-seven wives of Soma, known as the lunar mansions (nakṣatras). At that time, Hiraṇyākṣa was born to Diti from Hiraṇyakaśipu.
And Siṃhikā became the daughter who was wedded to Vipracitti; Hiraṇyakaśipu had four sons of immense power.
Anuhrāda, Hrāda, the heroic Prahrāda, and Saṃhrāda were their youngest; among them, Prahrāda was devoted to Viṣṇu.
The venerable Śibi Vāṣkala was born as the son of Saṃhrāda; Virocana was the son of Prahrādi, and from Virocana, Bali was born.
O bull-bannered one, Bali had a hundred sons with Bāṇa as the eldest; and all the sons of Hiraṇyākṣa were likewise possessed of great strength.
Utkura and Śakuni, as well as Bhūtasaṃtāpana; Mahānāga, Mahābāhu, and another, Kālanābha.
And the sons of Anubhava were Dvimūrdhan, Śaṅkara, Ayomukha, Śaṅkuśiras, Kapila, and Śambara.
Ekacakra, the long-armed Tāraka of great strength, Svarbhānu, Vṛṣaparvan, and the great Asura Puloman.
These are known as the sons of Danu, along with the powerful Vipracitti; Svarbhānu’s daughter was Suprabhā, and Śarmiṣṭhā was the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan.
Upadanavi and Hayashira were two renowned and excellent daughters; both Puloma and Kalaka were the daughters of Vaiśvānara.
Both of those illustrious women were the wives of Mārīca; from them were born sixty thousand sons, the most excellent of the Dānavas.
The Paulomas and Kālakañjas are known as the sons of Mārīca; likewise, those born of Siṃhikā are the sons of Vipracitti.
Vyaṃśa, Śalya, the powerful Nabhas, the exceedingly mighty Mahābala, Vātāpi, Namuci, Ilvala, and likewise Khasṛmān.
Añjika, Narakas, Kālanābha, and likewise the Nivātakavacas—these Daityas were born in the lineage of Prahlāda.
And six sons, who were great beings, are proclaimed as the offspring of Tāmrā: Śukī, Śyenī, Bhāsī, Sugrīvī, Śuci, and Gṛdhrikā.
Śukī gave birth to parrots, Ulūkī to owls, Śyenī to hawks, Bhāsī to vultures, and Gṛdhri to eagles.
Sugrīvī gave birth to flocks of parrots and water-birds; the lineage of Tāmrā is proclaimed to consist of horses, mules, and donkeys.
Vinatā had two famous sons, Garuḍa and Aruṇa; and Surasā had a thousand sons, serpents of immeasurable power.
And there were a thousand hooded serpents of immeasurable power, the offspring of Kadrū; among them, O Lord of Beings, the foremost were Śeṣa, Vāsuki, and Takṣaka.
Śaṅkha, Śveta, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkha, Kambala and Aśvatara, as well as the nāga Elāpatra, Karkoṭaka, and Dhanañjaya.
Know that the Gaṇa is Krodhavaśa, and all of them are fanged; moreover, Krodhā gave birth to the Piśācas of great strength.
Surabhi gave birth to cows and likewise to buffaloes; Irā produced trees, creepers, climbing plants, and all varieties of grasses.
Khagā gave birth to the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, while Muni gave birth to the Apsarases; Ariṣṭā, however, gave birth to the Gandharvas of great being.
The gods were indeed the forty-nine Maruts; likewise, there were those with one light, two lights, and four lights.
Ekaśukra, Dviśukra, and the mighty Triśukra; likewise Īdṛk, Sadṛk, Anyādṛk, and Pratisadṛk.
Mita, Samita, and the mighty Sumita; likewise Ṛtajit, Satyajit, Suṣeṇa, and Senajit.
Atimitra, Amitra, Dūramitra, Ajita, Ṛta, Ṛtadharmā, Vihartṛ, Varuṇa, Camasa, and Dhruva.
Vidhāraṇa, Durmedhas—this is known as one group; likewise, Īdṛśa, Sadṛkṣa, Etādṛkṣa, and Mitāśana.
By him were born Prasadṛśa, Surata, Mahātapa, Hetumat, Prasava, and likewise Surabha of great renown.
Nādi, Rugra, Dhvani, Bhāsa, Vimukta, Vikṣipa, Saha, Dyuti, Vasu, Anādhṛṣya, Lābha, Kāma, Jayin, and Virāj.
The group known as Udveṣaṇa is in the seventh layer of wind; all this is the form of Hari—the kings, the Dānavas, and the gods.
Together with their retinues of the Sun and other deities, Manu and the others worshipped Hari.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Lineage of Uttānapāda and Others," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 7.
Rudra said: "O Vyāsa, tell me in brief the supreme essence of the worship of the Sun and other deities as performed by Svāyambhuva Manu and others; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
Hari said: I shall describe the worship of the Sun and other deities, which brings about merit, desire, and the other aims of human life.
Oṃ, homage to the seat of the Sun. Oṃ, homage to the form of the Sun. Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ, homage to the Sun. Oṃ, homage to Soma. Oṃ, homage to Maṅgala. Oṃ, homage to Budha.
Oṃ, homage to Bṛhaspati. Oṃ, homage to Śukra. Oṃ, homage to Śanaiścara. Oṃ, homage to Rāhu. Oṃ, homage to Ketu. Oṃ, homage to Tejaścaṇḍa.
The seat, the invitation, water for the feet, the respectful offering, water for sipping, as well as the bath, clothing, the sacred thread, fragrance, flowers, and incense.
O Bull-bannered One, one should always perform the offering of lamps, prostrations, circumambulations, and the ritual dismissal for the Sun and other deities using these mantras.

Oṃ hrāṃ, obeisance to Śiva. Oṃ hrāṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the embodiment of auspiciousness. Oṃ hrāṃ, obeisance to the Heart. Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the Head. Oṃ hrūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the Tuft of Hair (Śikhā). Oṃ hrai, huṃ to the Armor (Kavaca). Oṃ hrauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the Three Eyes. Oṃ hraḥ, obeisance to the Weapon (Astra). Oṃ hrāṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva. Oṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to Aghora. Oṃ hraiṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa. Oṃ hrauṃ, obeisance to Īśāna. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Gaurī. Oṃ hrauṃ, obeisance to the Gurus. Oṃ hrauṃ, obeisance to Indra. Oṃ hrauṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍa. Oṃ hrāṃ, obeisance to Aghora. Oṃ, obeisance to the seat of Vāsudeva. Oṃ, obeisance to the form of Vāsudeva. Oṃ aṃ oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva. Oṃ āṃ oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa. Oṃ aṃ oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Lord Pradyumna. Oṃ aḥ oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Lord Aniruddha. Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa. Oṃ, obeisance to that Brahman. Oṃ hrāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu. Oṃ kṣauṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Lord Narasiṃha. Oṃ bhūḥ oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Lord Varāha. Oṃ kaṃ ṭaṃ paṃ śaṃ, obeisance to Vainateya (Garuḍa). Oṃ jaṃ khaṃ raṃ, obeisance to Sudarśana (the Discus). Oṃ khaṃ ṭhaṃ phaṃ ṣaṃ, obeisance to the Mace. Oṃ vaṃ laṃ maṃ kṣaṃ, obeisance to Pāñcajanya (the Conch). Oṃ ghaṃ ḍhaṃ bhaṃ haṃ, obeisance to Śrī. Oṃ gaṃ ḍaṃ vaṃ saṃ, obeisance to Puṣṭi. Oṃ dhaṃ ṣaṃ vaṃ saṃ, obeisance to the Forest Garland. Oṃ saṃ daṃ laṃ, obeisance to the Śrīvatsa mark. Oṃ ṭhaṃ caṃ bhaṃ yaṃ, obeisance to the Kaustubha gem. Oṃ, obeisance to the Gurus. Oṃ, obeisance to the Guardians of the Quarters beginning with Indra. O
O bull-bannered one, one should offer the seat and other articles to Hari with these mantras; now hear the auspicious worship of Viṣṇu’s Śakti, Sarasvatī.

Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī. Oṃ hrāṃ, salutation to the heart. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the head. Oṃ hrūṃ, salutation to the crest-lock. Oṃ hraiṃ, salutation to the armor. Oṃ hrauṃ, salutation to the three eyes. Oṃ hraḥ, salutation to the weapon.
Śraddhā, Ṛddhi, Kalā, Medhā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Prabhā, Mati, and Oṃ Hrīṅkārā—these are the powers (śaktis) of Sarasvatī, beginning with "Oṃ Hrīṃ" and ending with "Namaḥ."
Homage to the Guardian of the Field. Oṃ, homage to the Gurus. Oṃ, homage to the Supreme Gurus.

One should arrange the seat and other offerings for Sarasvatī, who resides upon a lotus; likewise, one should perform the investiture of the sacred thread for the Sun and the others with their respective mantras.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Worship of the Sun and Others as well as Sarasvatī," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Hari said: Having bathed in a pavilion situated on the ground, one should worship Viṣṇu within a mandala; the mandala should be a Vajranābha design made with powder of five colors.
O Rudra, one should have it constructed there with sixteen squares; one should then cause the laying of the lines in the fourth and fifth corners.
The wise one should cast the lines upon those corners situated there on both sides of the diagonal line.
In the corners immediately following that, one should likewise cause [the lines] to be made; the first navel is thus designated at the intersection of the central lines.
And in all the intermediate spaces, there are eight navel-points; one should then rotate the thread from the eastern and central navel-points.
In the interval, O Hara, that best of the twice-born should rotate [the circle] by three-quarters; by this, O Śiva, he should rotate the pericarp of the navel-line.
The wise one should draw the filaments with two parts of the pericarp; at their tips, the learned one should always paint the petals.
O observer of excellent vows, the teacher who knows the ultimate truth should fashion those lotuses in all the navel-fields according to this measurement.
One should design the doors by means of the division of the initial sūtra; likewise, one should design the beauty of the doors there with half of that measure.
The pericarp is yellow in color, with filaments that are white, red, and so forth; the interior is blue in color, and the petals are black.
One should fill the square with black-colored powder; the doors and the five lines in the mandala should be white-colored.
White, red, yellow, and black, respectively; having first prepared the mandala and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should worship Hari.
One should place Viṣṇu in the center of the heart, and likewise Saṅkarṣaṇa in the throat; having placed Pradyumna on the head, one should place Aniruddha at the crest-lock.
Having meditated on Brahmā in all the limbs and likewise Śrīdhara in the two hands, one should place Hari in the pericarp, thinking, "I am Viṣṇu."
One should place Saṅkarṣaṇa in the east, Pradyumna in the south, Aniruddha in the west, and Brahmā in the north.

One should place Śrīdhara in the corners of Rudra (the northeast) and Indra and the others in the cardinal directions; then, having worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings, one shall attain the supreme state.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Vajranābha Maṇḍala Useful for the Worship of Viṣṇu," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter Nine.
Hari said: At the proper time, the initiated disciple, with his eyes bound by a cloth, [the preceptor] should perform one hundred and eight oblations for him with the root mantra.

O Rudra, for a *putraka* initiate, the fire offering (*homa*) is considered to be twofold; for a *sādhaka*, it is held to be threefold; and for one who is an instructor in the state of *nirvāṇa*, it is declared to be fourfold.
One who kills a guru, Viṣṇu, a twice-born, or a woman is to be bound by those who are uninitiated. Now, I shall explain initiation, which brings about the destruction of both merit and demerit.
Having seated the disciples outside, one should cause them to perform dhāraṇā; O Rudra, one should contemplate them being dried up by the Vāyavyā kalā.
Having unified those fiery elements—both those being consumed by fire and those drenched by water—with that living soul (jīva), one should cast them together.

One should contemplate the *prāṇava* in the sky [of the heart] within the body; however, there is another cause. He who would conquer each one therein [must do so] by means of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) as the cause of the body.

O Bull-bannered One, having first generated each [deity] one by one, he should subsequently join them; however, one who is incapable regarding the mandalas and other rites should worship Hari after merely visualizing Him.
It should have four gates in sequence starting from the Brahma-tīrtha; the hand is declared to be a lotus, and its fingers are known as the petals.
The palm of the hand is the pericarp, and its nails are the filaments; having meditated upon Hari there as being between the sun and the fire, one should worship him.

Being composed, he should place that hand upon the head of the disciple; because Viṣṇu resides in the hand, it is therefore called the "Viṣṇu-hand. By the touch of it, all sins whatsoever are destroyed.

The Guru, having honored the disciple and bound his eyes with a cloth, should then cause him to offer a flower before the presence of the God; wherever that flower falls upon the head of the Lord who bears the Śārṅga bow.
The wise man himself should cause a name to be given to him marked with the names of women; for Śūdras, however, he should cause a name joined with the word "dāsa" (servant) to be made.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Viṣṇu-initiation," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Hari said: I shall now describe the worship of Śrī and others upon the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) and other sites for the sake of accomplishment. *Śrīṃ hrīṃ mahālakṣmyai namaḥ.* One should worship, in sequence, the heart, the head, the crest (*śikhā*), the armor (*kavaca*), the eyes, the weapon (*astra*), the seat (*āsana*), and the form (*mūrti*) with the syllables *śrāṃ*, *śrīṃ*, *śrūṃ*, *śraiṃ*, *śrauṃ*, and *śraḥ*.

In the mandala, within the center of a lotus, with four gates and marked by colored powders, the mandala consists of sixty-four [squares] down to eight, and from thirty-six up to one hundred and eight.

Everything [is placed] according to the sky (0), eyes (2), moon (1), and sun (12), by means of the progression of sky (0), etc., Vedas (4), and moon (1); [one places] Lakṣmī and the limbs in one corner, as well as Durgā, Gaṇa, and the Guru.
Then, desiring his desires, he offered oblations into the fire and other elements for the protector of the field (kṣetrapāla), reciting: "Oṃ ghaṃ ṭaṃ ḍaṃ haṃ, obeisance to Śrī Mahālakṣmī."
With this, one should worship Lakṣmī along with the previously mentioned retinue: *Oṃ saiṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī*. *Oṃ hrīṃ saiṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī*.
Oṃ hrīṃ vadavada vāgvādini svāhā. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of Lakṣmī," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Hari said: I shall now describe the worship of the nine manifestations (Navavyūha), as it was indeed told to Kaśyapa. Having drawn the individual soul (jīva) up to the head, one should establish it in the space of the navel.
Then, one should burn the body composed of the elements with the seed-syllable *raṃ*; and with the seed-syllable *yaṃ*, one should cause all of that to perish.
One should inundate all that is moving and unmoving with this seed-syllable *laṃ*; thereafter, one should contemplate nectar with this seed-syllable *vaṃ*.
Then, in the center of that bubble, one should contemplate oneself through meditation as being four-armed and clad in yellow garments—thus I am considered to be.
Then one should perform the threefold mantra-installation (nyāsa) on the hands and the body, using the twelve-syllable seed-mantra and subsequently with the aforementioned seed-mantras.
Then, one should perform the six-limbed rite by which Hari becomes manifest; beginning from the right thumb, one should place [the syllables] upon the petals up to the middle finger.
Having placed the two seed-syllables in the center, one should then place them on the limbs: on the heart, the head, the crest, the armor, the face, the eyes, the water, and the back.
One should place [the hands] on the arms, the wrists, the knees, and also the feet; having formed the hands into the shape of a lotus, one should place the thumbs in the middle.
There, one should contemplate the supreme, stainless reality, the Lord of All; then, one should gradually place these seed-syllables upon the forefinger and the other fingers.
Then, one should place [the mantras] in sequence upon the head, eyes, face, throat, heart, navel, secret place, knees, and feet.
Having assigned the six seed-syllables of the limbs to the two hands, one should then assign them to the body; one should assign the five seed-syllables from the thumb to the little finger.

The seed-syllable of the eye is in the middle of the hand; this same sequence applies to the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa): having placed the heart at the heart, one should place the head upon the head.
Having placed the *śikhā* on the crest, one should place the *kavaca* all over the body; the *netra* should be applied to the two eyes, and the *astra* to both hands.
Having secured the directions with that very [mantra], one should then perform the ritual of worship; first, being composed, one should contemplate the yoga-throne within the heart.

One should likewise assign Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya in their proper order; and in the directions starting from the southeast (Āgneya) and the east (Pūrva), one should assign Adharma and the others.

Then, one should visualize the infinite [deity] whose body is enveloped by these [elements], who serves as the foundation (pīṭha) and consists of that very essence; subsequently, one should visualize him standing with the front part elevated.
Then one should know the lotus born of knowledge, with eight petals corresponding to the cardinal directions, a white lotus rich with a hundred petals, and its pericarp spread upwards.
Having meditated with the *veda* mantra and others, one should subsequently contemplate the mandalas of the sun, moon, and fire in this manner, one above the other, in their proper sequence.
Then, one should assign the eight Śaktis beginning with Vimalā, who reside in the directions starting from the east and are within the domain of Keśava, and the ninth, located in the pericarp.
Having meditated thus and worshipped the Yoga-pīṭha immediately thereafter, one should mentally invoke the Lord Hari there and again install the Śārṅga bow.
One should then place the heart-mantra and the others in the petals of the four directions starting from the east, the eye-mantra in the center, and the weapon-mantra in the corners.
One should place the seed-syllables of Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others in order starting from the east; furthermore, one should install Vainateya at both the eastern and western doors.
One should place the Sudarśana disc with its thousand spokes at the southern gate; having placed Śrī to the south, one should likewise place Lakṣmī to the north.
Having placed the mace at the inner door, one should place the conch in the corners; the wise man should place the Śārṅga bow to the right of the deity and likewise on the left.
In the same manner, one should place a sword and likewise a discus, two on each of the two sides; thereafter, one should install the inner world-protectors according to their respective directions.
One should likewise position the weapons, such as the vajra and others; one should likewise contemplate Brahmā above and Ananta below.
Having meditated on all this and performed worship, one should then display the mudrās. The first mudrā is the añjali; it quickly propitiates the deity.
The *vandanī* [mudrā] has the right thumb raised while attached to the heart; it consists of the left fist with the right thumb bound within it.
The thumb of that left hand is proclaimed as the upward-facing one; these three are indeed common, though conceived through the differentiation of forms.
By releasing [the fingers] starting from the little finger, one should understand the eight mudrās in their proper sequence, corresponding respectively to the eight preceding seed-syllables.
Having bent the three fingers from the thumb to the little finger, and having placed both hands face down, this is the mudrā of Narasiṃha.
Having likewise turned the left hand upward, one should slowly rotate it above; this is remembered as the ninth mudrā, always favored by Varāha.
Then, with both hands turned upward, one should release them one by one straight; having released everything, one should contract [the fingers]—this is called the limb-mudrā (aṅgamudrā).
Then, having likewise bound the two fists in this same sequential order, one should perform the mudrās of the ten world-protectors according to their proper sequence.
Suramādyam is the second, upāntya is the penultimate, and antya is the last; these correspond respectively to Vāsudeva, Bala, Kāma, and Aniruddha.
The Praṇava, "Tat-sat," "Huṃ," "Kṣaiṃ," and "Bhūḥ" are the mantras; likewise are Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Siṃha, and the sovereign Varāha.
White, reddish, yellow, blue, dark, red, cloud-colored, fire-colored, and tawny—these are the nine names according to their colors.
Kaṃ, ṭaṃ, paṃ, and śaṃ are Garuḍa; jaṃ, khaṃ, and vaṃ are Sudarśana; ṣaṃ, caṃ, phaṃ, and ṣaṃ are the goddess Gadā; and vaṃ, laṃ, maṃ, and kṣaṃ are the Śaṅkha.
Ghaṃ, ḍhaṃ, bhaṃ, and haṃ constitute Śrī; gaṃ, jaṃ, vaṃ, and śaṃ constitute Puṣṭikā; ghaṃ and vaṃ constitute Vanamālā; and daṃ and saṃ constitute Śrīvatsa.
"Chaṃ, ḍaṃ, paṃ, yaṃ, the Kaustubha gem, and indeed I myself as Ananta—these are the ten limbs of the God of gods, to be applied according to their respective positions."
Garuḍa resembles a lotus; the mace is black in form; Puṣṭi has the luster of a śirīṣa flower; and Lakṣmī is like gold.
The conch resembles the full moon; the Kaustubha gem possesses a reddish luster; the discus has the brilliance of a thousand suns; and the Śrīvatsa mark is like a jasmine flower.
The garland indeed has the appearance of five colors, and Ananta is like a cloud; the weapons, which are of the nature of lightning, are those whose colors have not been mentioned.
One should indeed offer the water for honor (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), and so forth, with the Puṇḍarīkākṣa mantra.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Worship of the Nine Vyūhas," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 12.

Hari said: For the sake of establishing the sequence of worship, the order of worship is now declared. At the beginning, with the words "Oṃ Namaḥ" and so forth, there is the remembrance of the Supreme Self.
Yaṃ raṃ vaṃ laṃ constitutes the purification of the body; Oṃ namaḥ constitutes the self-manifestation as the four-armed deity.

Then follows the threefold placement (*nyāsa*) of the hand-gestures (*karakāya*). Then comes the worship of the Yoga-pīṭha situated within the heart: Oṃ *anantāya* namaḥ / Oṃ *dharmāya* namaḥ / Oṃ *jñānāya* namaḥ / Oṃ *vairāgyāya* namaḥ / Oṃ *aiśvaryāya* namaḥ / Oṃ *adharṃmāya* namaḥ / Oṃ *ajñānāya* namaḥ / Oṃ *avairāgyāya* namaḥ / Oṃ *anaiśvaryāya* namaḥ / Oṃ *padmāya* namaḥ / Oṃ *ādityamaṇḍalāya* namaḥ / Oṃ *candramaṇḍalāya* namaḥ / Oṃ *vahnimaṇḍalāya* namaḥ / Oṃ *vimalāyai* namaḥ / Oṃ *utkarṣiṇyai* namaḥ / Oṃ *jñānāyai* namaḥ / Oṃ *kriyāyai* namaḥ / Oṃ *yogāyai* namaḥ / Oṃ *prahvyai* namaḥ / Oṃ *satyāyai* namaḥ / Oṃ *īśānāyai* namaḥ / Oṃ *sarvatomukhyai* namaḥ / Oṃ *saṃgopāṅgāya harerāsanāya* namaḥ. Then, upon the pericarp (*karṇikā*): Aṃ *vāsudevāya* namaḥ / Āṃ *hṛdayāya* namaḥ / Īṃ *śirase* namaḥ / Ūṃ *śikhāyai* namaḥ / Aiṃ *kavacāya* namaḥ / Auṃ *netratrayāya* namaḥ / Aḥ *phaṭ* *astrāya* namaḥ / Āṃ *saṅkarṣaṇāya* namaḥ / Aṃ *pradyumnāya* namaḥ / Aḥ *aniruddhāya* namaḥ / Oṃ Aḥ *nārāyaṇāya* namaḥ / Oṃ *tatsadbrahmaṇe* namaḥ / Oṃ Huṃ *viṣṇave* namaḥ / Kṣaiṃ *narasiṃhāya* bhūrvarāhya / Kaṃ *vainateyāya* / Jaṃ Khaṃ Vaṃ *sudarśanāya* / Khaṃ Caṃ Phaṃ.

*Ṣaṃ* to the mace; *vaṃ laṃ maṃ kṣaṃ* to the Pāñcajanya conch; *ghaṃ ḍhaṃ bhaṃ haṃ* to Śrī; *gaṃ ḍaṃ vaṃ śaṃ* to Puṣṭi; *dhaṃ vaṃ* to the forest garland (*vanamālā*); *daṃ śaṃ* to the Śrīvatsa mark; *chaṃ ḍaṃ yaṃ* to the Kaustubha gem; *śaṃ* to the Śārṅga bow; *iṃ* to the two quivers; *caṃ* to the shield; *khaṃ* to the sword; to Indra, the lord of the gods; to Yama, the lord of splendor; to Varuṇa, the lord of Dharma; to Kṣaṃ, the lord of the Rākṣasas.

*Yaṃ* to Varuṇa, lord of the waters; *vaṃ* to Vāyu, lord of the vital breaths; *dhāṃ* to Dhanada, lord of wealth; *hāṃ* to Īśāna, lord of knowledge; *oṃ* to the Vajra, to Śakti; *oṃ* to Daṇḍa, to Khaḍga;
*oṃ* to Pāśa, to Dhvaja, to Gadā, to Triśūla; *laṃ* to Ananta, lord of the netherworlds; *khaṃ* to Brahmā, lord of all worlds; *oṃ*.

Homage to the Blessed One Vāsudeva! Homage! Oṃ oṃ, homage! Oṃ naṃ, homage! Oṃ moṃ, homage! Oṃ oṃ bhaṃ, homage! Oṃ gaṃ, homage! Oṃ vaṃ, homage! Oṃ teṃ, homage! Oṃ vāṃ, homage! Oṃ suṃ, homage! Oṃ deṃ, homage! Oṃ vāṃ, homage! Oṃ yaṃ, homage! Oṃ oṃ, homage! Oṃ naṃ, homage! Oṃ moṃ, homage! Oṃ nāṃ, homage! Oṃ rāṃ, homage! Oṃ ṇāṃ, homage! Oṃ yaṃ, homage! Oṃ naṃnoṃ bhagavate vāṃsuṃdevāya oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya namaḥ! Oṃ, homage to Puruṣottama! Homage!
Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe. Salutations be to you, O Subrahmaṇya, O Great Being, O Primordial One.
And for these, one should provide the oblation with the word "svāhā" at the end; having thus recited [the mantra] according to the rule one hundred and eight times.
Having offered the *argha* and prostrated again and again, saying "Victory to Him!", one should then worship and sacrifice to Him in the fire according to the prescribed ritual.

Then, the knower of mantras, having first inscribed the God of gods, Acyuta, with his own seed-syllable and with the limbs (aṅgas) and so forth, should sprinkle him with water while reciting the Praṇava.
Having whirled the fire over the sacrificial pit, one should worship it with auspicious fruits; having first meditated upon that entire [deity] in the mandala, one should mentally place it there.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the principle known as Vāsudeva, one should likewise worship the group of six with the seed-syllables of Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others.
Likewise, one should offer three sets of three limbs, as well as the lords of each of the directions, and finally, standing properly composed, one should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
One should lead the self into dissolution within the supreme reality that transcends speech; then, having sat down again and displayed the mudrā, one should bow once more.
Such a fire-oblation (homa) should be performed constantly; on an occasional occasion (naimitta), it should be doubled. Go, go to the supreme abode where the stainless God resides.
May all the deities depart for the sake of remaining in their own abodes: Sudarśana, Śrī Hari, Acyuta, and Trivikrama.
Vāsudeva with four arms is the sixth, and Pradyumna as well; then Saṃkarṣaṇa, the Puruṣa, who is the ninefold manifestation and consists of ten aspects.
Aniruddha consists of twelve aspects, and then there is Anantaka above; these gods are to be recognized and characterized by wheels numbering one and so forth.
One shall be honored by those marked with the wheel-signs, and one’s household shall always be protected by men. *Oṃ cakrāya svāhā*,
*oṃ vicakrāya svāhā*,
*oṃ sucakrāya svāhā*.
Oṃ mahācakrāya svāhā; Oṃ mahācakrāya asurāntakṛt hūṃ phaṭ; Oṃ hūṃ sahasrāra hūṃ phaṭ.
This worship of the Dvārakā-cakra is auspicious and provides protection within the home.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Sequence of Worship," in the section on Conduct (*ācārakāṇḍa*) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Lord Hari said: I shall now proclaim this auspicious Vaiṣṇava armor (*pañjara*). [The mantra is: "Salutations, salutations to You, O Knower of All! Having taken up the Sudarśana discus.
Protect me in the east, O Viṣṇu; I have come to you for refuge. Take up your mace Kaumodakī, O Padmanābha; salutations be unto you!
O Viṣṇu, protect me from the south; I have come to you for refuge. O Puruṣottama, salutations to you who hold the Saunanda plow!
In the western direction, protect me, O Viṣṇu! I have come to you for refuge. Grasping the club that shatters [enemies], O lotus-eyed one, protect me!
O Lord of the World, I have come to you for refuge from the north; O Hare, take up your sword, shield, and other weapons and missiles.
Salutations to you, O destroyer of Rākṣasas, protect me! I have come for refuge in the northeast. [I salute] the great conch Pāñcajanya and the lotus that resounds.
O Viṣṇu, grasping [the weapon], protect me; O Sūkara, protect me in the south-eastern quarter! Likewise, having grasped the moon and sun, as well as the lunar sword, [protect me].
O divine-formed one, O man-lion, protect me in the southwest; hold fast to the Vaijayantī garland and the Śrīvatsa mark as your neck-ornament.
O God Hayagrīva, protect me in the northwest; salutations be unto you! O Janārdana, having mounted Vainateya, [protect me] in the intermediate space.
Protect me always, O Unconquered One; homage be to you, O Invincible One! Having mounted Viśālākṣa, protect me in the netherworld (rasātala).
O Akūpāra, homage to you; O Mahāmīna, homage be to you! You are truth in the hands, head, and fingers, and you are the cage of the arms.
"Having performed this, protect me, O Viṣṇu; salutations to you, O Supreme Person. Thus was this great Vaiṣṇava armor spoken to Śaṅkara.
O Bull-bannered Lord, in ancient times, for the sake of protecting Īśānī Kātyāyanī, she brought about the destruction of the demon Mahiṣāsura and his immortals.
A person who recites this with devotion always conquers their enemies, including Dānava, Raktabīja, and other thorns of the gods.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Hymn of the Viṣṇu-Armor," in the section on Conduct within the first part of the glorious *Garuḍa Purāṇa*.

Hari said: Now I shall proclaim the supreme Yoga, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Lord Hari is the object of meditation proclaimed by those who meditate; He is attained through meditation.
Listen to that, O Maheśāna, which destroys all sins: Viṣṇu is the Lord of All, the Infinite, devoid of the six states of worldly existence.
I am indeed Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, the Self of Brahman; I abide eternally within the bodies of embodied beings, yet am forever free from all bodies.
Devoid of bodily attributes and free from the perishable and the imperishable, he is the seer, the hearer, and the smeller who abides within the sixfold [senses], yet transcends the senses.
Devoid of that dharma, the Creator is free from name and lineage; he is the thinker, abiding in the mind, yet the God is entirely devoid of the mind.
Devoid of mind and mental objects, it is both consciousness and gnosis; it is the knower, established in awakening, the witness, the omniscient one, yet free from the intellect.
Devoid of the attributes of the intellect, all-pervading, the mind is entirely free from living beings and divested of the attributes of vital breath.
The life-force of the life-force is the great peace, entirely free from fear; it is devoid of egoism and the like, and is likewise free from that [notion of] "dharma."
The witness of that, its controller, whose nature is supreme bliss, abides in waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; it is the witness of those states, yet remains free from them.
I am Śiva, the Self—the Fourth state, the supreme sustainer, whose form is pure consciousness, devoid of qualities, liberated, awakened, undecaying, all-pervading, and the Truth.
Thus, those wise men who meditate upon the Lord, the supreme state, shall attain His very form; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Thus has meditation been fully explained to you, O Śaṅkara of noble vows; he who constantly recites this goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Meditation," in the section on Conduct within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Rudra said: "O Lord Janārdana, what should a man recite so that he is liberated from the terrible ocean of worldly existence? Please instruct me in that supreme mantra for recitation."
Hari said: By praising Viṣṇu—the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Brahman, the Imperishable Supreme Self—with His thousand names, a person shall become liberated.
O Bull-bannered One, listen attentively as I declare that supreme Vidyā which is to be recited, which destroys all sins.
Oṃ! Vāsudeva, Mahāviṣṇu, Vāmana, Vāsava, Vasu; the youth resembling the crescent moon, Balabhadra, the lord of strength.
The creator who bound Bali, the most excellent one, the knower of the Vedas, the wise one; the author of the Vedas, whose form is the Veda, the one to be known, and he who is immersed in the Vedas.
He is the knower of the Vedāṅgas, the Lord of the Vedas, the bestower of strength, and the subduer of Bala; he is the immutable one, the Lord of boons, Varuṇa, and the sovereign of Varuṇa.
The slayer of heroes, the great hero, the praised Supreme Lord; the Self, the Supreme Self, the innermost Self, and that which is beyond the ether. (30)
Padmanābha, Padmanidhi, Padmahasta, Gadādhara, Parama, Parabhūta, Puruṣottama, and Īśvara.
Padmajangha, Puṇḍarīka, Padmamālādhara, Priya, Padmākṣa, Padmagarbha, Parjanya, and Padmasaṃsthita. (50)
He is the shoreless ultimate reality, the supreme lord of the highest beings, the wise one worthy of worship by the wise, the purifier, and the crusher of evil.
He is pure, (60) luminous by nature, holy, and a protector; he is free from thirst, worthy of worship, the Supreme Person, and likewise primordial nature.
He is the primordial matter, the lotus of the earth, the one with a lotus-navel,
the bestower of what is dear, the Lord of all, the omnipresent, the All, the knower of all, the giver of all, and the divine being.
The abode of the entire world, all-seeing and the sustainer of all, the God who bestows grace upon everyone, he dwells in the heart of every being. (80)
He is worthy of worship by all, the primordial source of all, and saluted by all the gods; he is the root of the entire world, both with parts and without parts, and free from passion. (90)
The protector of all, the ultimate refuge of all, the cause of all causes; the object of meditation for all, the friend of all, who assumes the form of the sovereign of all lands.
The presiding lord of all, the presiding lord of the gods, saluted by both gods and asuras; he is the eternal destroyer and the end-maker of wicked gods. (101)
Satyapāla, Sannābha, Siddheśa, Siddhavandita, Siddhasādhya, Siddhasiddha, Sādhyasiddha,
and Hṛdīśvara.
He is the refuge of the world, as well as its welfare and security; he is the doer of good, the beautiful, the gentle, the truthful, and one whose prowess is truth.
Established in truth, with true resolve, the knower of truth, and likewise the bestower of truth; he is Dharma, the upholder of Dharma, and Karma, yet he is entirely free from all karma.
He is the agent of action and action itself, as well as the performance and the effect; he is the Lord of Śrī, the sovereign, the illustrious one, the powerful master of all.
He is the Lord of the gods, the praised Lord of the Vṛṣṇis, the Lord of Hiraṇyagarbha, and likewise the Lord who brings an end to Tripura.
He is generally the lord of cattle, the lord of the Vasus, the lord of Indra, and likewise the lord of Varuṇa. (140)
He is the lord of the trees, as well as the lord of the wind; he is indeed the lord of fire and the lord of Yama.
He is the lord of Kubera, as well as the lord of the constellations; he is the lord of medicinal herbs and likewise the lord of trees. (150)
He is the lord of the Nāgas, the lord of Arka, and indeed the lord of Dakṣa; he is the lord of friends and likewise the lord of kings.
He is the lord of the Gandharvas, the supreme lord of the vital breaths, the lord of the mountains, and likewise the lord of the rivers.
He is the most excellent lord of the gods (160), likewise the lord of Kapila; he is the lord of creepers and the lord of climbing plants as well.
He is the lord of the sages, the supreme lord of the sun, the most excellent lord of the moon, and indeed the lord of Sukra.
He is the lord of the planets and likewise the lord of the rākṣasas; he is the lord of the kinnaras and the supreme lord of the twice-born.
He is the lord of rivers and likewise the lord of oceans; he is the lord of lakes and likewise the lord of all beings.
He is the lord of the Vetālas and likewise the lord of the Kūṣmāṇḍas; he is the supreme lord of birds and indeed the lord of beasts.
The Great Soul, the Auspicious One, the Measurable, Mandara, the Lord of Mandara, Meru, the Mother, the Standard of Measure, Mādhava, and the One Free from Impurity.
Mālādhara, Mahādeva—who is worshipped by Mahādeva—Mahāśānta, Mahābhāga, and Madhusūdana.
Possessing great heroism and great vital power, he is praised by the sage Mārkaṇḍeya; his nature is illusion, yet he is bound by illusion and also liberated from illusion.
The Sage praised by sages,
the Benevolent One, the Great Hero, the one with great jaws, the long-armed one, the greatly self-controlled, who is utterly free from death.
He has great arms, a great soul, a great body, and a great belly; he has great feet, a great neck, great pride, and a great mind.
He of the great course, the one of great fame, the one of great form, the great Asura; he who is Madhu and Mādhava, the Great God, the Supreme Lord.
He is the sacrifice, the one in the form of the sacrifice, and the one worthy of honor;
he is the Lord of Sacrifice, the great wind, the highly fortunate one, the Great Lord who transcends humanity.
He is Mānava and Manu, the bringer of joy to human beings; he is Mṛga and Mṛgapūjya, as well as the lord of the deer.
He is the lord of Mercury, the lord of Jupiter, the lord of Saturn, and likewise the lord of Rāhu and Ketu.
Lakṣmaṇa, Lakṣaṇa, Lambauṣṭha, and Lalita likewise, adorned with various ornaments and anointed with various kinds of sandalwood paste.
Rāma, the Lord of Ramā and Supreme Sovereign, together with his wife, has faces resplendent with various expressions and is adorned with diverse flowers.
The jewel among jewels and the stealer of jewels; possessing form and yet devoid of form; of great form and of fierce form, and likewise of gentle form.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, pure, and likewise resembling a sala-tree cloud; smoke-colored, the color of a leaf, possessing various forms, and indeed colorless.
He is the deformed and the beautiful, as well as the white-colored; he is all colors, the great yogi, the sacrifice, the one to be sacrificed for, and the performer of the sacrifice.
Suvarṇavarṇavān, Suvarṇākhya, Suvarṇāvayava, Suvarṇa, and Svarṇamekhala; (280) [these are the names].
He is the giver of gold, the lord of gold, the beloved of gold,
and likewise one who is rich in gold.
Suparṇa, Mahāparṇa, and the cause of Suparṇa; likewise Vainateya, Āditya, the primordial originator, and Śiva.
It is the cause of the Great One (mahat) and the cause of primordial matter (pradhāna); it is the cause of the intellects (buddhi) and likewise the cause of the mind (manas).
It is the cause of the mind and the cause of the ego; likewise, it is the cause of the elements and the cause of fire.
In that same way, it is the cause of space, the supreme cause of the earth, the cause of the cosmic egg, and likewise the cause of primordial nature (prakṛti).
The cause of the body, as well as the cause of the eye, the cause of the ear,
and likewise the cause of the skin;
The cause of the tongue, as well as the cause of the vital breath, the cause of the two hands, and likewise the cause of the two feet.
Likewise, it is the cause of speech and the cause of the anus; it is the cause of Indra and the cause of Kubera.
The cause of Yama, the cause of Īśāna, the cause of the Yakṣas, and the supreme cause of the Rākṣasas.
It is the supreme cause for kings, the very cause of dharma, the cause of living beings, and the highest cause of wealth.
He is the cause of the Manus, the supreme cause of the birds, the most excellent cause of the sages,
and the supreme cause of the yogis.
It is the cause of the Siddhas, the supreme cause of the Yakṣas, the cause of the Kinnaras,
and the cause of the Gandharvas.
The cause of the male rivers, the supreme cause of the female rivers, the cause of the oceans, and likewise the cause of the trees.
He is the cause of the plants and likewise the cause of the worlds; he is the cause of the netherworld (pātāla) and likewise the cause of the gods.
It is the cause of serpents, and likewise the cause of blessings; it is the cause of cities, and likewise the cause of all things.
The self of the body, the self of the senses, the self of the intellect, as well as the self of the mind, and the self of the ego-consciousness and the heart.
The Self of the waking state and the sleeping state,
the Great Self (Mahadātman), the Supreme Self (Parātman), the Self beyond primordial matter (Pradhāna), the Self of space, and likewise the Self of the waters.
He is the supreme self of the earth and likewise the self of taste; he is the supreme self of smell and likewise the transcendent self of form.

He is the essence of sound and the essence of speech; likewise, he is the essence of touch and the Person; he is the essence of hearing and the essence of the skin, as well as that which is beyond the tongue.
The self of the nose, the self of the hands, and likewise the supreme self of the feet; likewise the self of the genitals, and the supreme self of the anus.
The self of Indra, the self of Brahmā, the self of Rudra, and likewise that of Manu; the self of Dakṣa Prajāpati, the self of Satya, the self of the Creator,
and likewise the Supreme Self.
Īśātmā, Paramātmā, Raudrātmā, Mokṣavidyati, Yatnavān, as well as Yatna, Carma, Khaḍgin, and Murāntaka.
He is the one whose nature is to promote modesty, who is devoted to the welfare of ascetics, who takes the form of an ascetic,
who is a yogi, who is the object of meditation for yogis, and who is Hari, the dark-hued one.
Consciousness, intelligence, time, heat, the rainy season, and likewise mind; the year, the bringer of liberation, and likewise the destroyer of delusion.
The creator of delusion for the wicked is Māṇḍavya, as is Vaḍavāmukha; Saṃvarta is the ender of time, as are Gautama, Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras. (420)
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Pulaha, Pulastya, and Kutsa; Yājñavalkya, Devala, Vyāsa, and Parāśara.
Gāṅgeya, Hṛṣīkeśa, Bṛhacchravas; Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, Sukarṇa, and Karṇavarjita.
The highly fortunate Nārāyaṇa is indeed the lord of prāṇa, as well as the lord of apāna and the lord of vyāna. (440)
He is the supreme lord of the udāna breath, and likewise the lord of the samāna breath; he is the supreme lord of sound and indeed the lord of touch as well.
And he is the primordial Lord of forms, sword in hand, with a plow for his weapon; he holds the discus in his hand, wears earrings, and likewise bears the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest.
Prakṛti, Kaustubhagrīva, and likewise Pītāmbaradhara; Sumukha and Durmukha, who was indeed devoid of a mouth.
Ananta, Anantarūpa,
Sunakha, Suramandara, Sukapola, Vibhu, Jiṣṇu, Bhrājiṣṇu, and likewise Eṣudhi.
The slayer of Hiraṇyakaśipu, the crusher of Hiraṇyākṣa, the destroyer of Pūtanā, and the annihilator of the Sun at the end of time.
The crusher of Keśin, the destroyer of Muṣṭika, the breaker of the Dānava Kaṃsa, and the subduer of Cāṇūra.
The destroyer of misfortune and the beloved of Akrūra; he who is Akrūra yet possesses a fierce form, and is praised by those dear to Akrūra.

The Blessed One is the destroyer of fortune, the sun, and likewise the devotee of the Lord; he is himself possessed of his own cows, and Uddhava is his servant, for the Lord of Uddhava is meditated upon through sport.
The bearer of the wheel, the restless, and indeed that which is free from moving and unmoving; the mind, space, earth, and water are like the notion of "I."
Wind, the eye, as well as the ear, the tongue, and the nose; speech, the hands, the feet, the organ of generation, and likewise the anus and the organ of excretion.
Śaṅkara, Sarva, the giver of patience, the man who practices patience, the lover of devotion, the sustainer, the devoted one, and the increaser of devotion. (511)
Praised by devotees, devoted to devotees, bestower of fame, increaser of fame, fame itself, splendor,
forgiveness, beauty, a devotee, and supreme compassion.

He is charity, the giver, and the agent; he is dear to the God of gods, the pure one, the possessor of purity, the bestower of happiness, liberation, desire, and wealth; he is the thousand-footed one.
Sahasraśīrṣā, Vaidya, and likewise Mokṣadvāra; Prajādvāra, Sahasrākṣa, and indeed Sahasrakara. (540)
Śukra, Sukirīṭin, Sugrīva, and Kaustubha; likewise Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Hayagrīva, and Sūkara.
Matsya, Paraśurāma, Prahlāda, and Bali; Śaraṇya, Nitya, Buddha, and Mukta—these are the embodied beings.
The slayer of Khara and Dūṣaṇa, the crusher of Rāvaṇa, the husband of Sītā,
the ever-prospering one, and likewise Bharata.
The slayer of Kumbha and Indrajit, the crusher of Kumbhakarna, the ender of Narāntaka, and the destroyer of Devāntaka.
He is the slayer of the wicked asuras and likewise the enemy of Śambara; he is the destroyer of Naraka and the annihilator of Triśīrṣa. (570)
The shatterer of Yama and Arjuna, as well as the one who bestows the fruit of asceticism; the musical instrument and the music itself, and the Buddha who grants boons.
Sāra, Sārapriya, Saura, Kālahantṛnikṛntana (580), Agastya, Devala, Nārada, and Nāradapriya.
