Prāṇa, apāna, and likewise vyāna; rajas, sattva, and tamas; śarad; udāna and samāna; as well as the medicine and the physician.
He is immutable, of pure nature, and devoid of all bodies; he is without the faculty of sight and is bereft of the faculty of speech.
He was deprived of the faculty of the hands and devoid of feet; he was also lacking the organs of excretion and procreation, and was bereft of vital breath.
Devoid of awakening and indeed bereft of intellect, he is likewise devoid of consciousness and bereft of vital breath.
Deprived of apāna and devoid of vyāna, deprived of udāna and devoid of samāna.
Devoid of space and entirely lacking wind, devoid of fire and bereft of water.
Devoid of earth and devoid of sound, devoid of touch and devoid of all forms. (620)
He is indeed free from passion, entirely devoid of evil, liberated from sorrow, and released from [the bonds of] speech.
He is indeed free from passion and the six transformations; he is devoid of desire and completely abandoned by anger.
Free from greed and likewise devoid of hypocrisy, he is subtle and exceedingly subtle,
as well as more gross than the gross.
He is the fearless one, the commander of the forces, and likewise the agitator of all; he is the agitator of primordial nature (prakṛti) and the agitator of the great principle (mahat).
He is the agitator of the elements and likewise the agitator of the intellect; he is the agitator of the sense faculties and likewise the agitator of the objects of the senses.
He is the agitator of Brahmā and likewise the agitator of Rudra; he is inaccessible to sight and the other senses, and similarly inaccessible to hearing.
The tortoise cannot be reached by the skin, nor likewise can it be grasped by the tip of the tongue; it is beyond the reach of the sense of smell, and likewise cannot be grasped by speech. (650)
Hari is indeed unapproachable by the hands and likewise unapproachable by the feet; he is ungraspable by the mind and likewise ungraspable by the intellect.
I am to be grasped by the intellect and likewise to be grasped by the mind; I am Śaṅkhapāṇi, the Imperishable, and likewise Gadāpāṇi. (660)

The wielder of the Śārṅga bow, Kṛṣṇa, the embodiment of knowledge, the scorcher of foes; he is indeed an ascetic, accessible through knowledge, the knower, and the one who knows all that is to be known.

He is the object of knowledge and devoid of objects of knowledge; he is cognition and the embodiment of consciousness; he is existence, that which is to be meditated upon, the creator of existence, the meditator, and the destroyer of existence.

He who has come as the protector of cows (*gopati*), the cowherd (*gopa*) who bestows happiness upon all the cowherdesses (*gopī*); he who is the lord of cows (*gopāla*), the goal of the cows (*gogati*), the one whose intellect is the cows (*gomati*), and likewise the one who sustains the cows (*godhara*).
Upendra, Nṛsiṃha, Śauri, Janārdana, Āraṇeya, Bṛhadbhānu, and likewise Bṛhaddīpti.
Dāmodara, the three times, the knower of time, and he who is beyond time; the three junctions, the Dvāpara age, the Tretā age, the gateway for progeny, and Trivikrama.

He is valorous, he holds the staff of punishment in his hand, he is the single-staffed ascetic and the bearer of the triple-staff; he is the means of conciliation and sowing dissension, he is the embodiment of diplomacy, and he is the singer of the Sāman hymns.
The Sāmaveda, the Atharvaveda, the well-performed [ritual], and the beautiful form; as well as one who is a knower of the Atharvaveda and indeed an ācārya of the Atharvaveda.

He is the form of the *Ṛk* and the *Ṛgveda*, established within the *Ṛgvedas*. He is the many-footed, the well-footed, and likewise the thousand-footed; he is the four-footed and the two-footed, as well as Memory, Logic, Yama, and the Mighty One.
Renunciation, the act of renouncing, and the four stages of life as well: the student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant.
A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, and likewise a Śūdra caste; one who possesses virtuous conduct, endowed with morality, and who has abandoned immoral conduct.
Liberation is entered into within the self; likewise, the praise, the praiser, and the worshiper; the object of worship, the organ of speech, that which is spoken, and the speaker.
He is the knower, and indeed grammar itself; he is the sentence, and the knower of sentences. He is the ford, the one who leads to the ford, and the knower of the ford.
He is the source of sacred fords and the like, the Sāṃkhya, and the Nirukta as the presiding deity; he is the Praṇava, the Lord of the Praṇava, and is praised by means of the Praṇava. (770)
The Praṇava is indeed to be known as Gāyatrī and Gadādhara; likewise, he is the dweller of Śālagrāma and is Śālagrāma itself.
He who reclines upon the waters, who reclines in yoga, who reclines upon Śeṣa, and who reclines on a lotus;
he who is the supporter of the earth, the effect, the cause, and the upholder of the world.
Prajāpati, the eternal, the desirable, the desirer, the Virāj, the sovereign (Samrāj), Pūṣan,
as well as heaven, the one standing on the chariot, the charioteer, and strength.
He is wealthy, a bestower of wealth, blessed, and devoted to the welfare of the Yādavas; he is dear to Arjuna, as indeed are Arjuna and Bhīma. (810)
Parākrama, Durviṣaha, Sarvaśāstraviśārada, Sārasvata, Mahābhīṣma, and likewise Pārijātahara.
He is the giver of nectar, the ocean of milk, and the milk itself; he is the son of Indra, its protector, and likewise the upholder of Govardhana.
The destroyer of Kaṃsa, likewise the elephant-driver who destroyed the elephant, Śipiviṣṭa, the gracious one, and the destroyer of the suffering of all the worlds.
He is the seal (mudra) and the hand that forms the seal, yet he is devoid of all seals; he is the embodied soul, residing within the body, and the controller of the body.
The hearer and the controller of hearing, as well as that which is to be heard and the act of hearing; likewise, having touched the toucher, the object to be touched, and the act of touching.
The seer of forms resides in the eye and is likewise the controller of the eye; and the knower of tastes, who is the object of sight, resides in the tongue as the regulator. (850)

Abiding in the nose, he is the maker of the nose, the smeller, and the controller of the olfactory faculty; abiding in speech, he is the speaker, that which is spoken, the speech itself, and the controller of speech.
Residing in a living being, it is the artisan who performs the craft, and it is the regulator of the two hands; likewise, it is the path, the goer, the place to be gone to, and the act of going.

The controller of the feet is indeed the recipient of the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) and the performer of emission; likewise, that which resides in the generative organ (*upastha*) is the controller of emission and pleasure.
And the restrainer of Upastha, as well as the one who brings him bliss; likewise Śatrughna, Kārtavīrya, and Dattātreya.
He who is beneficial to Alarka, the slayer of Kārtavīrya, Kālanemi, Mahānemi, Megha, and likewise Meghapati.
The giver of food, the one whose form is food, the eater of food, and the promoter of food—he is the supreme Son of Devakī.
He is the delight of Devakī, the joy of Rohiṇī, the beloved of Vasudeva, and likewise the son of Vasudeva.
Dundubhi, Hāsarūpa, and likewise Puṣpahāsa; Aṭṭahāsapriya, Sarvādhyakṣa, Kṣara, and Akṣara. (900)
He is indeed Acyuta, the Lord of Truth, the beloved and excellent husband of Satyā; he is the husband of Rukmiṇī and likewise the dear one of Rukmiṇī.
He is the beloved of the gopīs (910), the one of meritorious fame, and the renowned; he is Vṛṣākapi, Yama, Guhya, Makula, and likewise Budha.
Rāhu, Ketu,
the planet, the grasper, he whose face is joined with the king of elephants, the destroyer of the grasper, and likewise the village protector.
Kinnara, Siddha, Chanda, Svacchanda, Viśvarūpa, Viśālākṣa,
and Daityasūdana.
He is of infinite form, abiding in the elements, established as gods and dānavas; he is situated in deep sleep and is deep sleep itself, the locus and the very end of all loci.

Abiding in the waking state, one is awake; likewise, the waking state is its locus. Abiding in the dream state, one knows the dream; the dream state is its locus, and the dream is likewise [the object]. (940)
Devoid of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, it is indeed the fourth state; it is consciousness and the form of the object to be known, as well as the individual soul and the animator of life. (950)
He is the lord of the worlds and the regulator of the worlds; he dwells in the netherworld (pātāla) and is the destroyer of all fevers.
He is of the nature of supreme bliss and the promoter of all phenomena; he is both easily attained and difficult to attain, and likewise devoted to the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma). (960)
Pratyāhāra, Dhāraka, and likewise Pratyāhārakara; Prabhā, Kānti, and Arcis, which resembles pure crystal.
Agrāha, Gaura, Sarva,
Śuci, Abhiṣṭuta, Vaṣaṭkāra, Vaṣat, Vauṣaṭ, Svadhā, Svāhā, and likewise Rati.
The cooker, the delighter,
the enjoyer, the knower, and likewise the one who brings about existence; the self of knowledge and the self of the body— O Earth, he is the Lord of all lords.
Nadī, Nandī, Nandīśa,
Bhārata, Tarunāśana, Cakrapa, and Śrīpati— these belong to the universal monarchs among kings.
And Īśa, the lord of all the gods, likewise resides in Dvārakā; Puṣkara is the presiding deity of Puṣkara and is indeed Puṣkaradvīpa itself. (1000)
Bharata, Janaka, and Janya are devoid of all forms; they are formless, signless, free from affliction, and without support. (1008)
Thus, O Lord whose banner bears the bull, this thousand names of the divine Viṣṇu, the Sovereign, has been proclaimed; it is the destroyer of all sins.
By reciting this, a twice-born man attains the state of Viṣṇu; a Kṣatriya obtains victory; a Vaiśya gains wealth and happiness; and a Śūdra, endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu, likewise attains these.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Hymn of the Thousand Names of Śrī Viṣṇu," in the section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa) within the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 16. Rudra said: O wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, please explain once more the meditation upon Viṣṇu, the Lord, the Divine, the Pure, and the Supreme Self.
Hari said: Listen, O Rudra, to the meditation on Hari, which destroys the tree of saṃsāra—He who is of the nature of pure vision, infinite, all-pervading, unborn, and immutable.
The imperishable, all-pervading, eternal, and absolute Great Brahman exists; it is the root of the entire world, omnipresent, and the supreme Lord.
He who dwells in the hearts of all beings, the great lord of all beings, the support of all yet himself without support, the cause of all causes.
It is unanointed, likewise liberated, contemplated by liberated yogis, devoid of the gross body, and bereft of the eyes.

Devoid of the faculty of speech and lacking the dharma of vital breath; devoid of the faculty of feet and bereft of the dharma of speech; devoid of the faculties of excretion and procreation, and stripped of all sensory faculties.
Likewise, he is devoid of mind and free from mental phenomena; the Lord of Gods is destitute of intellect and utterly abandoned by consciousness.
Indeed, it is devoid of egoism, free from the attributes of the intellect, and truly bereft of both prāṇa and apāna.
"Indeed, [the body] is devoid of the wind called vyāna and is bereft of the function of prāṇa. Hari said: "I shall again describe the worship of the Sun, as it was told to Bhṛgu in the past."
Oṃ, salutation to Khakholka. This is the root mantra of Sūrya, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Oṃ, homage to Khakholka, the thirty-fold one; Oṃ vici ṭhaṭha, homage to the head; Oṃ, homage to Jñānin, ṭhaṭha, to the crest-lock; Oṃ, homage to Sahasraraśmi, ṭhaṭha, to the armor.
Oṃ, to the Lord of all splendor, ṭhaṭha, homage to the weapon! Oṃ, blaze, blaze! Blazingly, blazingly! ṭhaṭha, homage!
This is the mantra for the fire-rampart, which destroys the sins of the sun: *Oṃ, may we know Āditya;
may we meditate upon the illuminator of the universe; may that Sūrya inspire us.*
One should perform the sakalīkaraṇa (the ritual of bestowing limbs) for Rātri and Bhāskara; [one should place] "to the Self of Dharma" in the east and "yamāya" in the south.
Then, one should worship Daṇḍanāyaka and Daivatāya in the north; one should worship Śyāma and Piṅgala in the northeast, and the initiated one in the southeast.

And Vajrapāṇi in the southwest; Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ in the northwest. Oṃ, homage to Candra, the lord of the constellations. Oṃ, homage to Aṅgāraka, the son of the Earth. Oṃ, homage to Budha, the son of Soma. Oṃ, homage to Vāgīśvara, the lord of all sciences. Oṃ, homage to Śukra, the great seer, the son of Bhṛgu. Oṃ, homage to Śanaiścara, the son of the Sun. Oṃ, homage to Rāhu. Oṃ, homage to Ketu.
O Bull-bannered One, these should be worshipped starting from the east and extending to the northeast: *oṃ anūkāya namaḥ*, *oṃ prathamanāthāya namaḥ*, *oṃ buddhāya namaḥ*.

Oṃ, Blessed One, garlanded with immeasurable rays of light, Lord of the entire world, whose vehicle is the seven horses, four-armed one, bestower of supreme accomplishment, tawny with sparks of fire! Come, come hither! Accept, accept this *arghya* which has reached my head, O you of fierce radiant form, free from nakedness! Blaze, blaze! Ṭhaṭha! Homage!
Having invoked with this mantra, one should then dismiss the Sun: "Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Āditya, the thousand-rayed; go in happiness, for the sake of returning again."
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of Meditation on Hari and Worship of the Sun," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious *Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*.
The Glorious Hari said: I shall again describe the worship of the Sun as it was indeed told to Dhanada (Kubera). One should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp in a clean place.
Then, having formed the invocation mudrā, one should invoke the Sun; having established the Khakholka mudrā, one should establish the mantra-form.
O Śiva, one should place the heart of the deity in the southeastern direction; the head should be placed in the northeast, and one should install the crest-lock in the southwest.
With a mind fixed in one-pointed concentration, one should place Dharma in the northeast (paurandaryāṃ), Netra in the northwest (vāyavyāṃ), and Astra in the west (vāruṇyām).
One should place Soma in the northeast, Lohita in the east, the son of Soma (Budha) in the southeast, and Bṛhaspati in the south.
In the southwest, [he placed] the preceptor of the Dānavas; in the west, Śanaiścara; likewise in the northwest, Ketu; and in the north, Rāhu.
In the second enclosure, however, one should worship twelve Suns: Bhaga, Sūrya, Aryaman, Mitra, and Varuṇa; likewise, [Aṃśu, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, Parjanya, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Savitṛ].
Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, and Vivasvat of great strength, Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, as well as Indra—the twelfth is said to be Viṣṇu.
A person should worship with faith the gods beginning with Indra in the east; likewise, one should worship Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, Aparājitā, Śeṣa, Vāsuki, and the other Nāgas, and so forth.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Worship of the Sun," in the section on Conduct (*ācārakāṇḍa*) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Sūta said: I shall now declare to you the worship of Mṛtyuñjaya as spoken by Garuḍa to Kaśyapa. This meritorious rite, preceded by its ritual extraction (*uddhāra*), is considered to embody all the gods.
Having first extracted the syllable Oṃ, and immediately after that the syllable Huṃ, the third should be with the Visarga; this [mantra] crushes death and poverty.

The armor-mantra (*kavaca*) of Īśa, Viṣṇu, Arka, Devī, and others accomplishes all goals; the great mantra of Amṛteśa consists of three syllables, and its worship is equal [in power]. Through its recitation, one becomes free from death and liberated from all sins.

By reciting it one hundred times, one obtains the fruit of the Vedas and the fruit of sacrifices and sacred fords; by reciting it one hundred and eight times at the three junctions of the day, one conquers death and the enemy.

And one should meditate upon Amṛteśvara, seated upon a white lotus, with his two hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, while his other two hands hold a jar of nectar. One should thus contemplate him.
One should visualize the goddess Amṛtāmṛtabhāṣiṇī as being situated upon his body, holding a flask in her right hand and a lotus in her left hand.
One should indeed recite it eight thousand times at the three junctions of the day for one month; this bestows peace from the enemies of old age, death, and great diseases.
Invoking, establishing, obstructing, bringing near, and causing to enter; the water for the feet, the water for sipping, the bath, the respectful offering, the garland, and the unguent.
The lamp, the garment, the ornament, the food offering, the drink, the fan, the measure, the mudrā, the recitation, the meditation, the sacrificial fee, the oblation, and the hymn of praise.
Musical instruments, movement, dance, the application of placement, circumambulation, prostration, mantra, the bed, salutation, and dismissal.
The worship according to the sequence of the six limbs and so forth has been proclaimed from the mouth of the Supreme Lord; he who knows this is a true worshiper.

First, one should perform the worship of the *arghyapātra* (offering vessel), then strike it with the Astra-mantra, purify it with the Kavaca-mantra, and thereafter render it nectar-like (*amṛtīkaraṇa*).

One should perform the worship of the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) and so forth, as well as breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the seat (āsana); thereafter, one should perform the purification of the pedestal (pīṭhaśuddhi) by means of drying and other rites, and then one should meditate.

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the hands and limbs upon oneself as having the form of the deity; thereafter, one should worship oneself in the form of light arising from the lotus of the heart.

One should cast a radiant flower either upon an image or even on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) for the purpose of the invocation and the worship of the gateway; and the worship begins from the foundational power (ādhāraśakti).
The wise should perform the invocation of the deity's presence, the worship of the retinue, and indeed the worship of the six limbs.
Dharma and the others, Śakra and the rest, along with their weapons and retinues, as well as the Yugas, Vedas, and Muhūrtas—this worship brings about both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
First, one should worship the Mātṛkās and the Gaṇas, as well as Nandin and Gaṅgā; and previously, one should worship Mahākāla and Yamunā at the threshold.
Oṃ amṛteśvara oṃ bhairavāya namaḥ. Likewise, oṃ juṃ haṃsaḥ sūryāya namaḥ.
In this manner, one should worship Śiva, Kṛṣṇa, Brahmā, Gaṇa, Caṇḍikā, Sarasvatī, Mahālakṣmī, and the others.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Worship of Amṛteśa and Mṛtyuñjaya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Sūta said: I shall now proclaim the Prāṇeśvara and Garuḍa [mantras] as spoken by Śiva. First, I will describe the locations where one bitten by a snake does not survive.
He on whose body three lines appear hidden—whether on a funeral pyre, an anthill, a mountain, and so forth; or on a monkey, a hole, or a tree; or on a bite—is not destined to live.
On the sixth lunar day, in Cancer, Aries, and under the asterisms of Mūla, Āśleṣā, Maghā, and others, [afflictions occur] in the armpits, hips, throat, joints, temples, ears, abdomen, and so forth.

A mendicant carrying a staff and bearing weapons, or one who is not a monk but acts as a messenger of Death—when bitten by such a person on the arm, the mouth, or the neck, one certainly does not survive.
First, the Sun enjoys [the day] for half a watch; thereafter, the remaining six planets take their turns each day in succession.
The coils of the Nāgas are to be known in sequence by the revolutions of the arrows at night: Śeṣa is the Sun, Phaṇīpa is the Moon, and Takṣaka is said to be Mars.
Karkoṭa is Mercury, Padma is Jupiter, Mahāpadma is Venus, Śaṅkha is Saturn, Rāhu is Kulika, and Āhi is Mars—these are the planets.
During the day, Amarāntaka shall be in the portion of the Preceptor of the Gods (Bṛhaspati); at night, Rāhu remains together with Kulika in the time of the Lame One (Śani).

One should observe the time-period (velā) lasting for half a watch (yāmārdha) at the junctions, according to the sequence of the divisions [of the day] as five, six, three, seven, two, four, one, and one.

During the day, [the breath flows] through six, three, two, one, zero, seven, five, three, and one human parts respectively in the big toe, the back of the foot, the ankle, the knee, and the genitals.
At the navel, heart, the slope of the breasts, throat, nostrils, eyes, ears, the two eyebrows, the temples, and the head—in this sequence, one by one.
The moon should remain and the life-force (jīva) should reside in the right side of a man's body, while in the case of a woman, it is on the left side of the body from the hand that carries the wind.
The delusion produced by that [ignorance] shall cease through this crushing; it is the supreme seed of the Self, called Haṃsa, as pure as crystal.

The fourfold seed-syllable that destroys poison and sin must be given: the first is said to be joined with the *bindu* and the fifth vowel; the second is mounted on the sixth [consonant]; the third shall have the *visarga*; and the fourth is *oṃ kuru kule svāhā*.
In ancient times, this Vidyā was held by Garuḍa for the sake of protecting the three worlds; desiring the slaughter of the Nāgas and their offspring, one should then place the Praṇava in his mouth.
The wise one should place *gale* on the throat; *kule* is prescribed for the two ankles. *Svāhā* is for the pair of feet, and this is declared to be the *yugahā* placement.
Wherever [the mantra] is inscribed in the house, the nāgas abandon it; likewise, having recited the thousand-fold mantra, a thread is worn upon the ear.

If sand from one's house is consecrated with this mantra and thrown [into the water], the *nāgas* will abandon that place; indeed, by reciting it seven hundred thousand times, even the gods and asuras attained perfection.
Oṃ suvarṇarekhe kukkuṭavigraharūpiṇi svāhā! Thus, one should write two syllables on each petal of the eight-petaled lotus.
One bathed with streams of water while reciting this name shall cast off the poison when bitten. Oṃ pakṣi svāhā!

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hand from the thumb to the little finger, one should then perform it upon the body of Garuḍa: [the syllables] *ke* (or *kai*) on the mouth, the heart, the *liṅga*, and the two feet.
Even poisonous serpents do not step upon its shadow even in a dream; moreover, whoever should recite its mantra one hundred thousand times can destroy poison merely by looking at it.
Oṃ hrī hrau hrīṃ bhīruṇḍāyai svāhā. This vidyā, when whispered into the ear, shall remove the poison of one who has been bitten.
One should place *a* on the tips of the feet, *i* and *ī* on the ankles, then *u* and *ū* on the knees; *e* and *ai* on the surface of the hips, *o* on the navel, and *au* on the heart.
One should indeed place the syllable *aḥ* joined with *haṃsa* on the crooked and unreleased limbs; when chanted, meditated upon, and worshipped, this *haṃsa* removes poison and other afflictions.
Having meditated, "I am Garuḍa," one should perform the rite that removes poison; the *haṃ* mantra, when applied to the limbs of the body, is said to remove poison and other afflictions.

Having placed the *haṃsa* mantra on the left hand and blocking the nostrils and mouth, the mantra shall remove the poison located in the skin, flesh, and other parts of the victim who has been bitten.
Drawing it out with the breath, he should remove the venom of those who have been bitten; he should place [the mantra] upon the body of the victim and meditate upon Nīlakaṇṭha and the others.
The root of *pratyaṅgirā* drunk with rice-water destroys poison; likewise, the root of *punarnavā* and *phalinī*, or that produced from the mouth [of a deity], is of this same nature.
The root of white bṛhatī, karkoṭī, and gairikarṇika, rubbed with water and applied as a plaster mixed with ghee, destroys poison.
One who drinks hot clarified butter with the five parts of the *śirīṣa* tree as well as that produced from *gṛñjana* shall not suffer the increase of poison.
By smearing it on all the limbs or by drinking it, one becomes a destroyer of poison: *hrīṃ*, the remover of the poison of the *gonasā* snake and others.

Meditated upon from the heart to the forehead, ending at the visarga, it brings about subjugation and other effects; when placed in the womb [of the yoni-mudrā], it subdues a maiden and makes her drenched with the water of passion.

Having recited it seven or eight thousand times, one becomes all-pervading like Garuḍa; one becomes a poet and a possessor of a retentive memory, women become submissive, and one attains long life. It destroys poison; likewise, O Vyāsa, this mantra is certainly remembered as a jewel.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Means for Removing Snake Poison (the Prāṇeśvara-vidyā)," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter Twenty] of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: I shall declare that supreme secret, the collection of mantras spoken by Śiva: the noose, the bow, the discus, the mallet, the trident, and the sharp-edged spear.
With these very weapons and mantras, the king shall conquer his enemies in battle. Regarding the extraction of the mantras: one should write them starting from the east upon a lotus-leaf.
The eightfold group and the eighth are renowned on the leaf of Īśāna; the syllable Oṃ is the seed-syllable of Brahmā, and the syllable Hrīṃ is indeed Viṣṇu.
One should place the syllable *hrīṃ* and Śiva upon the three-pronged trident in sequence: *oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ*.
Taking up a trident and whirling it with his hand toward the sky, by the mere sight of it, the gods and the nāgas would meet their destruction.
Having meditated on a hand, smoke-colored and reddish, in the center of the sky, a person should contemplate it; then wicked nāgas, planets, clouds, and rākṣasas are destroyed.
This mantra protects the three worlds; what need is there to mention the world of mortals? Oṃ jūṃ sūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Having consecrated eight stakes made of *khadira* wood with mantras, one should plant them within the sacred field; there, no calamity such as a lightning strike or a thunderclap shall occur.
One should consecrate eight stakes with the great mantras spoken by Garuḍa twenty-one times, and bury them in the field at night.
There are also calamities such as lightning, rats, and thunderbolts; and Sadāśiva is *harakṣamalavarayū* joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*).
Oṃ hrāṃ, salutation to Sadāśiva; one should place the seed-syllable, which has the luster of a pomegranate flower, upon the index finger.
By the mere sight of him, the wicked clouds, lightning, and so forth, as well as the rākṣasas, bhūtas, and ḍākinīs, flee in the ten directions.
Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Gaṇeśa. (Oṃ hrīṃ), salutation to the Stambhana-cakra and the others. Oṃ aiṃ, salutation to the Brahma-yamāntaka-lokyaḍāmara.
The Bhairava-piṇḍa has been declared to be the remover of poison, sin, and malevolent planets; it provides protection for the sacred field and the crushing of spirits, rākṣasas, and the like.
Oṃ, homage! Having visualized Indra’s thunderbolt in one's hand as a protection against evil clouds and the like, poisons, hosts of enemies, and spirits are destroyed by the thunderbolt mudrā.

Oṃ kṣuṃ (kṣa) namaḥ. One should visualize a noose in the left hand; by this, poison, malevolent spirits, and the like are destroyed. Oṃ hrāṃ (hro) namaḥ. By the recitation of this mantra, one removes poisons, clouds, planetary afflictions, and so forth.

Having meditated upon Kṛtānta, one should indeed burn the world with the weapon-mantra of cutting: *oṃ kṣṇaṃ (kṣma) namaḥ*. Having meditated upon Bhairava, one should perform [the rite] that removes the poison of spirits and living beings.
Oṃ lasaddvijihvākṣa svāhā! This wards off malevolent planets, spirits, and the like, as well as poisons and venomous birds, in fields and other locations.
Oṃ kṣva (kṣṇaṃ) namaḥ. Having written [this] with blood upon a drum, the spirits, grahas, and others will be struck by sound. Oṃ mara mara māraya māraya svāhā. Oṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā.

Having consecrated the trident with one hundred and eight recitations, it draws out the multitude of enemies by its whirling; by the downward fall of the upper power, one should contract the lower power.

Mantras filled during *pūraka* (inhalation) and well-consecrated during *kumbhaka* (retention), when further nourished by the *praṇava*, become the very thoughts uttered therein; thus nourished, these mantras bestow fruits like devoted servants.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "Description of the Collection of Mantras for Removing Poison and Other Evils," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 21.

Sūta said: I shall now describe the worship of Pañcavaktra (the Five-faced One), which separately bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Oṃ bhūḥ! To Viṣṇu, the primordial being, the support of all, the embodied one; Svāhā!
First, one should perform the invocation of Sadyojāta with this [mantra]: "Oṃ hāṃ, to Sadyojāta indeed; for eight kalās are proclaimed [for him]."
Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Dhṛti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti, Svadhā, and Sthiti (8)—Oṃ Hīṃ, these are the thirteen digits (kalās) belonging to Vāmadeva.
Rajā, Rakṣā, Rati, Pālyā, Kānti, Tṛṣṇā, Mati, Kriyā, Kāmā, Buddhi, Rātri, Trāsanī, and Mohinī. (13)
Manonmanī, Aghorā, Mohā, Kṣudhā, Nidrā, Mṛtyu, and Māyā— these eight terrifying kalās are [the powers] of Bhayaṅkara.
Oṃ Haiṃ! To Tatpuruṣa belong Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti, not alone.
Oṃ hauṃ! Homage to Īśāna; Niścalā, Nirañjanā, Śaśinī, Aṅganā, Marīci, and likewise Jvālinī.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Five-Faced Worship," in the section on Conduct within the first part of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
The Glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*—Chapter 22.

Sūta said: I shall now proclaim the supreme worship of Śiva, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. He is peaceful, omnipresent, void, and established within the twelve measures (*mātrās*).
The five crooks are short, and the limbs are long with the *bindu*; one should utter the weapon-mantra (*astra*) together with the *visarga*, and likewise Śiva above, and again [the same].
With the sixth [syllable], the great mantra *haum*, which grants all aims, one should touch the feet with both hands; from the feet upwards, one should touch the head.
One should indeed perform the placement of hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa) for all [deities] with the Mahāmudrā; one should purify the back with the palm of the hand using the Astra-mantra.
Beginning with the little finger, one should assign the fingers as the limbs; I shall now fully explain the worship within the heart-lotus at the center.

One should worship Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, Aiśvarya, and the others with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya). One should offer the invocation (āvāhana), the installation (sthāpana), the water for the feet (pādya), and the respectful offering (arghya) with the heart-mantra.

The rinsing, the bathing, and the worship are equal when performed with a single vessel; I shall now describe the procedure for the fire-rite (agnikārya), beginning with the ritual tracing (ullekhana) using the weapon-mantra (astra).

One should perform the sprinkling with the *varman* mantra and carry out the placement of the *śakti* with the *hṛdaya* mantra; or one should cast the fire (*jātavedas*) into the heart or into the cavity of the *śakti*.

Having performed the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* and the final expiation (*niṣkṛti*) for the movement, and having performed all the ritual actions with the Heart-mantra, one should offer the auspicious oblation (*homa*) together with its constituent parts.

One should worship Śambhu in the maṇḍala within the center of a lotus, marked with the syllable *ga*; [the maṇḍalas] beginning with eight and ending with sixty-four, starting from the space-eye (khākṣi) and the space-eater (khādya).
One should cause an auspicious, half-moon-shaped sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) to be made in the southeast, measuring thirty-eight [units] by forty-one [units].

The fire-mantra is situated at the end of the life-span; the group beginning with the heart-mantra is thus described. The weapon-mantra belongs to the directions, while Sadāśiva resides in the pericarp of the beautiful lotus.

I shall describe initiation (dīkṣā), which resides within the five principles (pañcatattva) beginning with earth and culminating in the Supreme. Nivṛtti corresponds to earth, Pratiṣṭhā and the others [to water, fire, air, and ether]; Vidyā is fire, and Śānti is one's own [self].
Beyond Śānti is the sky; that is the supreme, peaceful, and imperishable. One should thus perform five hundred oblations for each [of the preceding stages].
Afterward, having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should remember Śiva with joy; for the sake of purification through expiation, one should offer eight oblations each in sequence.
One should perform the oblation with the seed-syllable of the weapon (astra-bīja) and thus complete the initiation; this supreme consecration is to be kept secret apart from the sacrificial rite.
Thus, for one whose formative impressions (saṃskāra) are purified, the state of Śiva arises with certainty.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Method of Worshipping Śiva," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Sūta said: I shall now describe the worship of Śiva, which is the means for attaining virtue, desire, and other goals. One should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with three mantras that begin with the Praṇava (Oṃ) and end with Svāhā.

Oṃ hāṃ, for the principle of the self (ātmatattva); hīṃ, likewise for the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva); oṃ hūṃ, for the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) svāhā—this [mantra] with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) shall be the salutation to the ears.

The ash-bath and the libation are performed with "Oṃ hāṃ svāhā," which serves as the mantra for all [rites]. All deities and all sages [are invoked] with mantras ending in "namaḥ" or ending in "vauṣaṭ."
All the ancestors end with *svadhā*, as do the grandfathers; likewise, *oṃ hāṃ* is for the great-grandfathers, as well as the maternal grandfathers and others.

"Hāṃ, obeisance to all the Mothers"—after this, there should be the restraint of breath (prāṇāyāma), followed by sipping water (ācamana), sprinkling (mārjana), and then one should mutter the Gāyatrī mantra.
Oṃ hāṃ! Let us know that Great Lord; let us meditate upon Him whose speech is pure;
may that Rudra inspire us.

Having performed the ritual attendance upon the Sun, one should worship him with the solar mantras: Oṃ hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ haiṃ hauṃ haḥ, obeisance to Śiva-Sūrya. Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to Khakholka, the embodiment of the Sun. Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ, obeisance to Sūrya.
Then one should remember Daṇḍin, Piṅgala, and the spirits (bhūtas); having worshipped Vimaleśāna in the southeast and other directions, one attains supreme bliss.
One should worship Padmā with *rāṃ*, Dīptā with *rīṃ*, Sūkṣmā with *rūṃ*, Jayā with *reṃ*, Bhadrā with *raiṃ*, Vibhūti with *roṃ*, Vimalā with *rauṃ*, and Amoghā with *raḥ*.

One should worship the lightning with *raṃ* in the east and other directions, and with *raṃ* in the center for the one facing all directions; then one should worship the Sun, whose form is the Sun, seated upon a solar throne, with the syllables *hrāṃ*, *hrūṃ* (*hrīṃ*), and *saḥ*.
Oṃ Āṃ, for the heart-core; and for the head and the crest-lock: Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ Oṃ. Jvālinī Hraṃ, for the armor and the weapon, and for the consecrated queens.
One should worship all [the planets] with the heart-mantra of the Sun: *soṃ* for Soma, *maṃ* for Maṅgala, *baṃ* for Budha, *bṛṃ* for Bṛhaspati, *bhaṃ* for Bhārgava, and *śaṃ* for Śanaiścara.

One should worship Raṃ Rāhu and Kaṃ Ketu; one should worship Oṃ Tejaścaṇḍa. Having worshipped the Sun and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should assign the limbs beginning with the little finger.

HĀṂ for the heart, HŪṂ for the head, HEṂ for the crest-lock, VAṂ for the armor, and HAUṂ for the eyes; HOḤ for the weapon. Having established the abiding power (śakti), one should again perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Then, having prepared the vessel for the *arghya* offering, one should sprinkle it with those waters and perform the worship.

One should visualize oneself seated upon a lotus with the syllable *hauṃ* for Śiva; then, outside of that, at the door, [one should place] Nandin and Mahākāla, as well as Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and the Earth.
One should worship Śrī, Astra, Vāstvadhipati, Brahmā, Gaṇa, and Guru; then, in the center, Śakti and Ananta, and in the east and other directions, Dharma and the others.
Adharmā and the others are in the fire and other directions; Vāmā and Jyeṣṭhā are in the pericarp of the lotus in the center; and Raudrī and Kālī are in the eastern and other directions.
Oṃ hauṃ, [salutation] to Kalavikariṇī; then to Balavikariṇī; then to Balapramathinī, the subduer of all beings.

One should worship these [energies] as Manonmanī in the middle of the recitation, before Śiva; and one should worship the seat of Śiva (śivāsana) and the Great Form (mahāmūrti) in the midst of the forms for the sake of Śiva.
Invocation, installation, bringing near, confinement, the rite of making the deity whole, the display of mudrās, and the offering of arghya and pādya.

One should perform the rinsing of the mouth, the anointing with oil, the rubbing with unguents, the bathing, and the massaging; one should offer clothing, ointment, flowers, incense, a lamp, and the sacrificial oblation (caru).
One should perform the rinsing of the mouth, the scent for the mouth, the betel leaf for cleansing the hands, the purification with the parasol and fly-whisk, and the act of supreme transformation.

The offering of the recitation consists of the recitation of the mantra for one day with the visualization of the form; the worship of the limbs of the name should be understood as praise and prostration performed with the heart-mantra and the others.

One should worship Agni, Śara, Rakṣas, and Vāyu in the intermediate directions, and Indra and the others starting from the east in the center according to the Tantra; one should also worship Caṇḍa and offer him the remains of the offerings (nirmālya).
O protector of the most secret within the cave [of the heart], accept this recitation performed by us; O God, may there be success for me through your grace, and may my abiding be in you.
Whatever action is performed, whether always good or evil, O Rudra, O Śaṅkara, destroy that for me who am established in the state of Śiva.
Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer, and Śiva is this entire world; Śiva is victorious everywhere, and he who is Śiva, I am indeed that very one.
Whatever has been done by me and whatever I shall do—all that is your well-done deed (your work). You are my protector and the leader of the universe; O Śiva, I have no other lord.
Now, I shall describe the worship of Śiva in another manner: [the worship of] Gaṇa, Sarasvatī, Nandin, Mahākāla, and then Gaṅgā.

The Wind-weapon (Pavanāstra) and the Lord of the Site (Vāstvadhipa) are at the door; furthermore, Indra and the others are to be worshipped starting from the east, as are the principles (tattvas): earth and water.
Fire, air, space, smell, taste, form, and sound; touch, speech, hands, feet, the anus, the generative organ, hearing, and the skin.

I am the eye, the tongue, the nose, the mind, and the intellect, as well as primordial nature (prakṛti). I am the person (puruṣa), the serpent (nāga), the intellect (buddhi), knowledge (vidyā), the constituent powers (kalā), time (kāla), and necessity (niyati) as well.
Māyā, Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, Śakti, and Śiva—one who knows them becomes a liberated knower and shall become Śiva.
He who is Śiva is Hari and Brahmā; he is I, O Śaṅkara, and I am Brahman.
I shall now describe the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), by which one who is purified becomes Śiva. In the heart-lotus resides the Sadyojāta mantra, the Nivṛtti-kalā, and the Iḍā nāḍī.
The two channels are Piṅgalā and [Iḍā], while the vital winds are Prāṇa and Apāna; Indra is the body, Brahmā is the cause, and the mandala is a square.

The arrows, possessing the quality of being drawn back with a single upward pull, marked the wind with their mouths; their sound, resembling the resonance of the *ṛṣabha* note, extended for a hundred *koṭis*.
Oṃ hrīṃ pratiṣṭhāyai hrūṃ hraḥ phaṭ / Oṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ vidyāyai hraṃ hraḥ phaṭ / The extent of the ground-tantra is eighty-four million [verses].
In the center of that, one should contemplate the tree of existence and oneself; then, by visualizing the earth as facing downward, that very element will certainly become purified.
The goddess Vāmā is Pratiṣṭhā, and likewise Suṣumnā is Dhārikā; Samāna, Udāna, and Varuṇa are the deities, and Viṣṇu is the cause.
The Vedas are the qualities of the path, as is white meditation; in this manner, one should form the throat-lotus, the maṇḍala known as the half-moon.
One should meditate upon oneself as being marked with a lotus, twenty-two koṭis in extent, ninety-four [yojanas] in height, and facing downwards.
The palate is the location, and the lotus is accompanied by the Aghora mantra; from the navel to the lips, one should meditate on Hastijihvā, whose deity is the serpent Agni.
The cause of Rudra is the threefold obstructor, possessing the three qualities and red in color; it is a triangle in the form of a flame, measuring four hundred million [yojanas].
One should contemplate the Rudra-tattva as extensive and elevated; on the forehead is Tatpuruṣa, while Śānti, O wise ones, is the green grass (or the bull).
The tortoise, the lizard, the wind, and the god Īśvara as the cause; the two opposing elements, the two qualities, and the smoky hexagonal mandala.
One should contemplate the Vāyu-tattva, marked by the bindu, extending eighty million [yojanas] and likewise rising for one hundred and fourteen million [yojanas].
In the twelve lotuses are the Śāntātītas and likewise the Īśvaras; the channels (nāḍīs) are Kuhū and Śaṅkhinī, and the vital breaths are Devadatta and Dhanañjaya.
The cause of the Śikhā and the Īśāna [mantras] is known as Sadāśiva; one should meditate upon this single quality as an exhalation (uddhāta), like pure crystal.
One should contemplate the sky as being sixteen crores [yojanas] in width and twenty-five [crores] in height, and circular; this is declared to be the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Guṇa, Guru, Bījaguru, Śakti, Ananta, and Dharmaka [are located] with Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya on the petals starting from the east.

One should always meditate upon that which is called Śiva, consisting of two faces—one downward and one upward—the pericarp and filaments of a lotus, and the Self-knowledge beginning with the left [channel].
The reality is the form on the seat of Śiva; *he hauṃ*, salutation to the body of knowledge. Seated in the bound lotus posture, white, sixteen years of age.
The Lord has five faces and, with his ten hands, holds the gestures of fearlessness and grace, as well as a spear, a trident, and a skull-topped staff.
With his right hands he holds a serpent and a rosary, and with his left hands a hand-drum, a blue lotus, and an excellent citron fruit.
Indeed, Sadāśiva possesses the three eyes of the powers of will, knowledge, and action; likewise, one who meditates on the worship of Śiva is forever free from time.
In this case, by the movement for one day and night, a person lives for three years; by the movement for two days, a man would live for two years.
By the movement [of the breath] for three days, he lives for one year; there is no untimely death, whether the *śītala* or the *uṣṇa* is the operative [wind].
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of Śiva," in the section on Conduct (*Ācārakāṇḍa*) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

(Herein concludes the worship of Śiva and others. **The Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 24** Sūta said: I shall describe the supreme worships of Gaṇeśa and others, which always bestow heaven. One should worship the seat of Gaṇeśa, the form of Gaṇeśa, and the Lord of Gaṇas.
The limbs such as the heart-mantra beginning with *gām* for Durgā, the sandals of the Guru, the seat of Durgā, her form, and [the mantra] *hrīṃ durge rakṣaṇī*.
The nine powers beginning with Tṛṭ are Rudracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍogrā, Caṇḍanāyikā, Caṇḍā, and Caṇḍavatī, in sequence.
Caṇārūpā, she known as Caṇḍikā, Durgā, and Durgā-rakṣiṇī; the mudrās such as the vajra and sword, and Śivā and the others, starting from the southeast.

Or likewise, [one may worship] Sadāśiva as the Great Preta upon a lotus seat. *Aiṃ Klīṃ (Hrīṃ) Sauḥ*—salutation to Tripurā. *Oṃ Hrāṃ Hrīṃ Kṣeṃ Kṣaiṃ Strīṃ Skīṃ Roṃ Spheṃ Sphīṃ Śāṃ*. [One should worship] the lotus seat, the form, and the heart-mantra and other limbs of Tripurā.
Upon the lotus of the seat, Brāhmī and Maheśvarī, Kaumārī and Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī and Indradevatā are to be worshipped.
Cāmuṇḍā and Caṇḍikā are to be worshipped; thereafter, one should sacrifice to those known as the Bhairavas: Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, and Unmattabhairava.
Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra are the eight Bhairavas; Rati, Prīti, Kāmadeva, the five arrows, and Yoginī [are the others].
One should contemplate Vaṭuka, Durgā, Vighnarāja, the Guru, and the Kṣetrapāla within the heart, in the lotus-womb, the mandala, and the triangle.

White in color, endowed with the gestures of granting boons, holding a rosary and a book, and displaying the gesture of fearlessness—Tripura shall become the bestower of success through one hundred thousand recitations and fire offerings.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of Tripura and Others," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Sūta said: Aiṃ Krīṃ Śrīṃ Spheṃ Kṣaiṃ, I worship the sandals of Anantaśakti; obeisance!
Aiṃ Śrīṃ Phraiṃ Kṣaiṃ, I worship the sandals of Ādhāraśakti; obeisance! Oṃ Hraṃ, I worship the sandals of Kālāgnirudra; obeisance!
Oṃ hrīṃ huṃ, I worship the sandals of the god Hāṭakeśvara; obeisance! Oṃ hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the venerable Śeṣa; obeisance!
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, I worship and pay homage to the seat called Ananta—the earth, its corresponding worlds, continents, oceans, and directions—and to the lotus seat (padmāsana).

*Hrīṃ śrīṃ*. The *kalās* beginning with Nivṛtti; the *tattvas* beginning with Earth; the worlds (*bhuvanas*) beginning with Ananta; the phonemes (*varṇas*) beginning with the syllable *Oṃ*; the nine-fold words (*padāni*) beginning with the letter *Ha*; the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta; the limbs (*aṅgas*) beginning with the Heart starting with *hrāṃ*: thus, O Great Lord of Mantras, you are the essence of the perfected Vidyās, an ocean of supreme nectar, the being of all things, and the six limbs present in every direction.

I worship and pay homage to the sandals upon the lotus seat, which has arisen from the earth-nature of the three root-mandalas together with the nine powers, Śiva, and the rest; which is the abode of the glorious Māna, the half-moon, and the full ocean of the waters of Sadāśiva; and whose pericarp consists of the power of Rudra in the Jyeṣṭhā-cakra, characterized by the full knowledge and agency of Vidyā and Umā.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of the Seat," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 26 of the Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇa]

Sūta said: Immediately thereafter follows the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*). One should perform the purification that brings about knowledge (*vidyākarī śuddhi*). Having formed the lotus gesture (*padmamudrā*), one should perform the ritual placement of the mantra (*mantranyāsa*): *kaiṃ* to the little finger, *namaḥ*; *naiṃ* to the ring finger, *namaḥ*; *maiṃ* to the middle finger, *namaḥ*; *taiṃ* to the forefinger, *namaḥ*; *aṃ* to the thumb, *namaḥ*; *lāṃ* to the palm, *namaḥ*; *vāṃ* to the back of the hand, *namaḥ*.

Now, the placement upon the body (*dehanyāsa*): *Smaṃ smaṃ*, salutation to the wrists (*maṇibandha*). *Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*, salutation to the clapping of the hands. One should perform the clapping of the hands with the sound *huṃ huṃ*, which is the form of great splendor (*mahātejas*).

Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Sphaiṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, salutation to Kubjikā; Hraṃ Hrīṃ Hrauṃ Ṅa-ña-ṇa-na-me, O Aghorāmukhī! Hrāṃ Hrīṃ Kilikili Vicce, O Sthaulyakrośī! Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aiṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, salutation to the Upper Face. Sphaiṃ, salutation to Kubjikā, the Eastern Face. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Ṅa-ā-ña-ṇa-na-me, salutation to the Southern Face. Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Kilikili, salutation to the Western Face. Oṃ Aghoramukhi, salutation to the Northern Face. Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, salutation to the Heart; Kṣaiṃ (Kṣeṃ Aiṃ).

To Kubjikā, for the head, svāhā! Hrīṃ krīṃ hrīṃ āṃ ṅa ña ṇa name, for the crest-lock, vaṣaṭ! O Aghorāmukhī, for the armor, huṃ! Haiṃ haiṃ īṃ, for the three eyes, vauṣaṭ! Kili kili vicce, for the weapon, phaṭ!

(1) Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to the great trident-maṇḍala whose form is an unbroken circle. (2) Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to the wind-maṇḍala. (3) Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to the moon-maṇḍala. (4) Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to the maṇḍala of the lineage of the great family of awakening. (5) Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to the great Kaula-maṇḍala. (6) Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to the guru-maṇḍala. (7)
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to the Sāma-maṇḍala (8);
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, [to] Samagra (9), [and] Siddha (10).
Salutation to the great lineage-maṇḍala of the Yoginī-pīṭhas, upapīṭhas, kṣetras, upakṣetras, and [others]. In this manner, the twelve maṇḍalas are to be worshipped in sequence.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of Karanyāsa and Other Rituals," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 27.
Sūta said: Oṃ kaṇi cikiṇika krāṇī carvāṇī bhūtahāriṇi phaṇiviṣiṇi virathanārāyaṇi ume daha daha!

O Caṇḍā, Raudrī, Māheśvarī, Mahāmukhī, Jvālāmukhī, Śaṅkukarṇī, Śukamuṇḍā, O destroyer of all! Strike, strike the enemy, O annihilator of all! Sweat his every limb with blood! O Goddess, look upon him with your mind and utterly delude him, utterly delude him! Born from the heart of Rudra, abiding in the heart of Rudra—O Goddess, you who are Rudra in your fierce form, protect, protect me! Hrūṃ! Hrūṃ! Phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ! Thaṭha thaṭha! You are the remover of Skanda, the girdle, childhood seizures, enemies, and poison.
Oṃ śāle māle, remove, remove! O you who possess the power of the syllable *oṃ* against poison! Hāṃ hāṃ Śavari! Huṃ Śavari! O Mistress of the Ākaula-velocity!
O Sarve-viñca-meghamālā! This is the remover of all poisons, such as those of the nāgas and others.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of Mantras for Removing Various Poisons such as those of Serpents," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Sūta said: I shall now describe the worship of Gopāla, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. At the entrance are Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, along with the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Śaṅkha and Padma are the two treasures (nidhi), while Sāraṅga and Śarabha are endowed with splendor; on the east are Bhadra and Subhadra, and on the south are Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍaka.
In the west, one should worship Bala, Prabala, Jaya, and Vijaya; in the north, Śrī; and at the four gates, Gaṇa, Durgā, and Sarasvatī.

In the corners of the field, starting from the southeast and proceeding through the cardinal directions, one should worship Nārada and the others; in the corner, one should worship the Siddha Guru, Nalakūbara, and the Blessed One.
First, one should worship Viṣṇu, the austerity of Viṣṇu (viṣṇutapas), and the power of Viṣṇu (viṣṇuśakti); then the retinue of Viṣṇu, and in the center, Śakti and Kūrma.
In the east is Ananta, Earth, Dharma, and Knowledge; in the southeast, Dispassion and Fire; in the west, Sovereignty and Air; and in the north, the Self of Light.

One should worship Kaṃ, the principle of the crow (kākatattva), as the lotus-bulb of the quality of passion (rajas) which is delusive in nature, and of the quality of darkness (tamas) which is the self-nature of beings (sattva).
One should worship the supreme principle of Vidyā, the solar, lunar, and fiery mandalas, and the seats beginning with Vimalā in the east, [uttering] "Śrīṃ Hrīṃ."
The mantra is said to end with "svāhā" followed by "gopījanavallabhāya. The limbs [of the ritual] are as follows: ĀCA, KRAṂ, SUCAKRA, and likewise VICAKRA.

The Sudarśana discus, the enemy of the asuras and protector of the three worlds, [is placed] in the eastern corner starting from the heart-mantra; the weapon (astra) and the spear (śakti) are likewise in the east.
Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Sunandā, Nāgnajitī, Lakṣmaṇā, Mitravindā, Jāmbavatī, and Śuśīlā.
One should worship the conch, discus, mace, lotus, pestle, and Śārṅga bow; one should worship the sword, noose, and goad in the east, as well as the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha gem.

One should worship the crown, the garland of sylvan flowers, the principal banners beginning with that of Indra, Kumuda and the others, Viṣvaksena, and Kṛṣṇa along with Śrī. Through recitation, meditation, and worship, one shall attain all desires. Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of Śrī Gopāla," in the Ācāra-kāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrva-khaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 29. Hari said: I shall describe the Trailokyamohinī [mantra], the foremost of those dedicated to Puruṣottama, as well as the mantras for the worship of Śrīdhara and others, which bestow dharma, desire, and the other goals of life.

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ hrūṃ oṃ namaḥ! O Puruṣottama, O peerless one, O abode of Lakṣmī, O agitator of the world, O piercer of the hearts of all women, O you who cause intoxication and madness in the three worlds, burn, burn the minds of the beautiful women among gods, asuras, and humans; dry them up, dry them up; kill them, kill them; paralyze them, paralyze them;
melt them, melt them; draw them in, draw them in.

O most auspicious one, O bestower of all good fortune, O granter of all desires! Slay, slay so-and-so with the discus, the mace, the sword, and with all arrows; pierce, pierce with the noose; crush, crush with the goad; strike, strike! Hurry, hurry! Why do you stand still? Deliver, deliver until my desire is accomplished! Hrīṃ (Hrūṃ)!
Phaṭ! Homage!
Oṃ śrīṃ (śrīḥ), obeisance to Śrīdhara, the Enchanter of the Three Worlds; klīṃ, obeisance to Puruṣottama, the Enchanter of the Three Worlds.
Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the Enchanter of the Three Worlds. Oṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the Enchanter of the Three Worlds.
All mantras that enchant the three worlds accomplish every purpose; they may all be contemplated either individually or collectively, whether in detail or in brief.
The seat, the form-mantra, and the six ancillaries beginning with the fire-oblation; the discus, the mace, the sword, the pestle, the conch, and the horn-bow.
By drawing an arrow, a noose, and a goad, together with Lakṣmī and Garuḍa, and Viṣvaksena in detail, a monkey shall obtain everything.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Worship of Trailokyamohinī (Śrīdhara)," in the Ācāra-kāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 30.
Sūta said: I shall describe in detail the auspicious worship of Śrīdhara; indeed, the retinue of all [deities] should be understood as identical by the wise.
Oṃ śrāṃ, homage to the heart; Oṃ śrīṃ, svāhā to the head; Oṃ śrū, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock; Oṃ śraiṃ, huṃ to the armor; Oṃ śrauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes; Oṃ śraḥ, phaṭ to the weapon. Thus.
One should display one's own mudrās, such as the conch, discus, and mace; having meditated upon oneself as the one named Śrīdhara, the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace.

Then one should worship that deity in a mandala such as a svastika; first, O Mahādeva, one should worship the seat of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow. Listen, O Śaṅkara, to those mantras.
Oṃ, deities of the seat of Śrīdhara, come! Oṃ, homage to the entire retinue of the Immovable Seat (Acyutāsana)!

Oṃ, salutation to Dhātṛ. Oṃ, salutation to Vidhātṛ. Oṃ, salutation to Gaṅgā. Oṃ, salutation to Yamunā. Oṃ, salutation to Ādhāraśakti. Oṃ, salutation to Kūrma. Oṃ, salutation to Ananta. Oṃ, salutation to Pṛthivī. Oṃ, salutation to Dharma. Oṃ, salutation to Jñāna. Oṃ, salutation to Vairāgya. Oṃ, salutation to Aiśvarya. Oṃ, salutation to Adharma. Oṃ, salutation to Ajñāna. Oṃ, salutation to Avairāgya. Oṃ, salutation to Anaiśvarya. Oṃ, salutation to Kanda. Oṃ, salutation to Nāla. Oṃ, salutation to Padma. Oṃ, salutation to Vimalā. Oṃ, salutation to Utkarṣiṇī. Oṃ, salutation to Jñānā. Oṃ, salutation to Kriyā. Oṃ, salutation to Yogā. Oṃ, salutation to Prahvī. Oṃ, salutation to Satyā. Oṃ, salutation to Īśānā. Oṃ, salutation to Anugrahā.
O Rudra, having worshipped them equally and having invoked Hari, the one of great wisdom should perform the sacrifice with these mantras that destroy all sins.
Oṃ hrīṃ! Salutation to Śrīdhara, to Viṣṇu, the Enchanter of the Three Worlds; come hither!

Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī. Oṃ śrāṃ, obeisance to the heart. Oṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to the head. Oṃ śrūṃ, obeisance to the crest-lock. Oṃ śraiṃ, obeisance to the armor. Oṃ śrauṃ, obeisance to the three eyes. Oṃ śraḥ, obeisance to the weapon. Oṃ, obeisance to the conch. Oṃ, obeisance to the lotus. Oṃ, obeisance to the discus. Oṃ, obeisance to the mace. Oṃ, obeisance to the *śrīvatsa*. Oṃ, obeisance to the Kaustubha gem. Oṃ, obeisance to the forest garland. Oṃ, obeisance to the yellow garment. Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā. Oṃ, obeisance to Nārada. Oṃ, obeisance to the gurus. Oṃ, obeisance to Indra. Oṃ, obeisance to Agni. Oṃ, obeisance to Yama. Oṃ, obeisance to Nirṛti. Oṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa. Oṃ, obeisance to Vāyu. Oṃ, obeisance to Soma. Oṃ, obeisance to Īśāna. Oṃ, obeisance to Ananta. Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā. Oṃ, obeisance to Sattva. Oṃ, obeisance to Rajas. Oṃ, obeisance to Tamas. Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣvaksena.
Then [he should offer] the consecration, as well as clothing, a sacred thread, perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, food, and circumambulation.

One should offer [the oblation] with these great mantras; having completed the offering, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times, and having thus recited it, one should then present the dedication.
Then, for a moment, one should meditate single-mindedly on the God residing in the heart, who resembles pure crystal and possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns.
With a serene countenance and gentle mien, adorned with shimmering shark-shaped earrings, wearing a crown, possessing noble limbs, and graced with a forest garland.
The wise person should meditate upon Śrīdhara, whose nature is that of the Supreme Brahman, and should praise the Supreme Lord with this very hymn.
Salutations to the divine Śrīnivāsa; salutations to the Lord of Śrī; repeated salutations to the bearer of Śrī, who holds the Śārṅga bow and bestows prosperity.
Salutations again and again to the illustrious Vallabha, the peaceful one, and to the glorious one; salutations to the dweller on Śrīparvata and to the bestower of welfare.

Salutations again and again to the Lord of all that is auspicious, and to the very embodiment of the stages of life; salutations again and again to Him whose nature is supreme bliss and who bestows prosperity.
"Salutations again and again to the one worthy of refuge, the most excellent; having offered praise and having paid homage to the God of gods, one should dismiss him."
Thus, O Rudra, has been fully described the worship of the high-souled Viṣṇu; he who performs it with great devotion goes to the supreme abode.
Whoever recites this chapter, which illuminates the method of worshiping Viṣṇu, shakes off all sins in this world and goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Worship of Śrīdhara (Viṣṇu)," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 31]
Rudra said: "O Lord of the World, O Master, please describe to me once more the mode of worship by which I may cross this most difficult ocean of worldly existence."
Hari said: O bull-bannered one, I shall describe the worship of Lord Viṣṇu; listen to that, O highly fortunate one, for it is auspicious and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Having performed his bath and then the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), he should then proceed to the sacrificial hall; having washed his hands and feet, and especially having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
One should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) of the entire root mantra upon both hands. Listen, O Rudra, as I tell you the root mantra of the deity.
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Śrīdhara Viṣṇu. This mantra is the designator of Viṣṇu, the Lord of the gods and the Sovereign.
It removes all diseases and likewise removes all planetary afflictions; it removes all sins and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Then the wise practitioner should perform the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) with these mantras: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the heart; Oṃ hīṃ, svāhā to the head; Oṃ hūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (*śikhā*); Oṃ haiṃ, huṃ to the armor (*kavaca*); Oṃ hauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes; Oṃ haḥ, phaṭ to the weapon (*astra*).
Thus has this mantra been fully declared to you by me, the powerful one; having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon oneself, the one who has conquered the self should display the mudrā.
Then one should meditate upon the supreme Viṣṇu, Hari, who resides within the hollow of the heart, endowed with the conch and the discus, and white as a kunda flower or the moon.
The Supreme Lord is endowed with the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, adorned with a forest garland, and joined with a jeweled necklace and crown.
Having meditated, "I am Viṣṇu," and having performed the purification and other rites, one should solidify [the object] with the seed-syllables *yaṃ*, *kṣaiṃ*, and *raṃ*, and with the [divine] names.
Having produced the egg, one should then pierce it with the *praṇava* alone; there, O Bull-bannered One, one should meditate upon the form previously described.
Then one should perform self-worship with auspicious offerings such as incense and flowers; having invoked them, one should worship all the deities belonging to the seat.
O Mahādeva, O Śaṅkara, listen to that mantra through these mantras: "O deities residing in Viṣṇu, come hither!"

Oṃ, homage to the one with his entire retinue, the Imperishable. Oṃ, homage to Dhātṛ. Oṃ, homage to Vidhātṛ. Oṃ, homage to Gaṅgā. Oṃ, homage to Yamunā. Oṃ, homage to Śaṅkhanidhi. Oṃ, homage to Padmanidhi. Oṃ, homage to Caṇḍa. Oṃ, homage to Pracaṇḍa. Oṃ, homage to Dvāraśrī. Oṃ, homage to Ādhāraśakti. Oṃ, homage to Kūrma. Oṃ, homage to Ananta. Oṃ, homage to Śrī. Oṃ, homage to Dharma. Oṃ, homage to Jñāna. Oṃ, homage to Vairāgya. Oṃ, homage to Aiśvarya. Oṃ, homage to Adharma. Oṃ, homage to Ajñāna. Oṃ, homage to Avairāgya. Oṃ, homage to Anaiśvarya. Oṃ Saṃ, homage to Sattva. Oṃ Raṃ, homage to Rajas. Oṃ Taṃ, homage to Tamas. Oṃ Kaṃ, homage to the Bulb (Kanda). Oṃ Naṃ, homage to the Stem (Nāla). Oṃ Lāṃ, homage to the Lotus (Padma). Oṃ Aṃ, homage to the Solar Orb (Arka-maṇḍala). Oṃ Soṃ, homage to the Lunar Orb (Soma-maṇḍala). Oṃ Vaṃ, homage to the Fire Orb (Vahni-maṇḍala). Oṃ, homage to Vimalā. Oṃ, homage to Utkarṣiṇī. Oṃ, homage to Jñānā. Oṃ, homage to Kriyā. Oṃ, homage to Yogā. Oṃ, homage to Prahvī. Oṃ, homage to Satyā. Oṃ, homage to Īśānā. Oṃ, homage to Anugrahā.
One should worship these [deities] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using these mantras; having thus worshipped Viṣṇu, the agent of creation and destruction.
O Rudra, having invoked the Supreme Lord within the mandala, one should worship him according to this supreme rite, which removes all sins.

Just as one does for oneself, so should one first perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the deity; thereafter, one should display the mudrās and then offer the water for honor (*arghya*) and the other oblations.

Then one should perform the ritual bathing, after which one should offer a garment and water for sipping; likewise, one should offer perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, and then the sacrificial oblation (caru).
Then, having performed circumambulation and recitation, the practitioner should offer worship to that [deity] and to the limbs and other parts with their respective mantras.
"Know this, O Bull-bannered One, to be the root-mantra of the God; now listen, O Three-eyed One, to the mantras being recited by me."

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the heart. Oṃ hīṃ, salutation to the head. Oṃ hūṃ, salutation to the crest-lock (śikhā). Oṃ haiṃ, salutation to the armor (kavaca). Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to the three eyes. Oṃ haḥ, salutation to the weapon (astra). Oṃ, salutation to Śrī. Oṃ, salutation to the conch. Oṃ, salutation to the lotus. Oṃ, salutation to the discus. Oṃ, salutation to the mace. Oṃ, salutation to the Śrīvatsa mark. Oṃ, salutation to the Kaustubha gem. Oṃ, salutation to the forest garland. Oṃ, salutation to the yellow garment. Oṃ, salutation to the sword. Oṃ, salutation to the club. Oṃ, salutation to the noose. Oṃ, salutation to the goad. Oṃ, salutation to the Śārṅga bow. Oṃ, salutation to the arrows. Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā. Oṃ, salutation to Nārada. Oṃ, salutation to the ancient Siddhas. Oṃ, salutation to the Bhāgavatas. Oṃ, salutation to the Gurus. Oṃ, salutation to the Paramagurus. Oṃ, salutation to Indra, lord of the gods, together with his vehicle and retinue. Oṃ, salutation to Agni, lord of fire, together with his vehicle and retinue. Oṃ, salutation to Yama, lord of the departed spirits, together with his vehicle and retinue. Oṃ, salutation to Nirṛti, lord of the Rākṣasas, together with his vehicle and retinue. Oṃ, salutation to Varuṇa, lord of the waters, together with his vehicle and retinue. Oṃ, salutation to Vāyu, lord of the vital breaths, together with his vehicle and retinue. Oṃ, salutation to Soma, lord of the constellations, together with his vehicle and retinue. Oṃ, salutation to Īśāna, lord of knowledge, together with his vehicle and retinue. Oṃ, salutation to Ananta, lord of the Nāgas, together with his vehicle and retinue. Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā, lord of the worlds, together with his vehicle and retinue. Oṃ vajrāya huṃ phaṭ, salutation. Oṃ śaktyai huṃ phaṭ, salutation. Oṃ daṇḍāya huṃ phaṭ, salutation. Oṃ khaḍgāya huṃ phaṭ, salutation. Oṃ pāśāya huṃ phaṭ, salutation. Oṃ dhvajāya huṃ phaṭ, salutation. Oṃ gadāyai huṃ phaṭ, salutation. Oṃ triśūlāya huṃ phaṭ, salutation. Oṃ cakrāya huṃ phaṭ, salutation. Oṃ padmāya huṃ phaṭ, salutation. Oṃ vaiṃ, salutation to Viṣvaksena.
O Mahādeva, by means of these mantras, the limbs and other parts are to be worshipped by men; having thus worshipped the high-souled Viṣṇu, whose nature is that of Brahman.
One should praise the imperishable Supreme Self with this hymn: "Obeisance indeed to Viṣṇu, the God of gods, the all-powerful Lord."
Salutation to Viṣṇu, to Vāsudeva, and to the one who maintains the world; salutation indeed to the devourer, and salutation to the one who reclines during the dissolution.
Homage to the source of the gods, homage to the source of sacrifices; perpetual homage to the source of the sages and the sovereign lord of the yakṣas.
Salutations again and again to the Victorious One, the Great Soul who pervades all, who is worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, and Rudra, and who is the Lord of All.
Salutations indeed to the Overseer of the World for the sake of the welfare of all worlds; to the Protector of All, the Creator of All, and the Destroyer of All that is Evil.
Homage again and again to the giver of boons, the peaceful one, the most excellent; to the refuge, the one of beautiful form, the bestower of dharma, desire, and wealth.
Having offered praise, one should meditate upon the imperishable one in the form of Brahman within one's own heart; O Śaṅkara, one should thus worship Viṣṇu with the root mantra.
Or even he who mutters the root mantra, that man goes to Hari. This, O Rudra, has been told to you—the supreme worship of Viṣṇu.

O Hara, this is the supreme secret, the ultimate mystery, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Whatever learned man, a devotee of Viṣṇu, recites this, or hears it, or causes it to be heard, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Worship of Viṣṇu," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 32.
Maheśvara said: O wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, please describe the worship of the five principles (pañcatattva), by the mere knowledge of which a person attains the supreme state.

Hari said: "O Śaṅkara of noble vows, I shall describe to you the worship of the five principles (pañcatattva)—which is auspicious, the source of auspiciousness, divine, secret, and the supreme granter of desires."
Listen to that, O Mahādeva, which is purifying and the destroyer of the Kali age: the one, immutable, peaceful, eternal Supreme Self.
Vāsudeva is eternal, pure, all-pervading, and untainted; that very Lord Hari, O deity, exists as fivefold through his māyā.
Viṣṇu, who bestows grace upon the worlds and destroys all that is wicked, exists in the form of Vāsudeva as well as in the form of Saṅkarṣaṇa.
Likewise, he exists in the form of Pradyumna and as the one named Aniruddha; indeed, though non-dual, he exists in five ways through the essential nature of Nārāyaṇa.

O Bull-bannered One, listen to these mantras that express them: Oṃ Aṃ, obeisance to Vāsudeva; Oṃ Āṃ, obeisance to Saṃkarṣaṇa; Oṃ Aṃ, obeisance to Pradyumna; Oṃ, obeisance to Aniruddha; Oṃ Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa.
Five mantras have been declared to you as the designators of the deities; they are meritorious, destroyers of all sins, and eradicators of all diseases.
Now, O Śaṅkara, I shall fully explain the auspicious worship of the five principles (pañcatattva), the procedure by which it should be performed, and the mantras that are to be used.

First, one should perform the ritual bath; having bathed, one should perform the twilight devotions (sandhyā). Then, having entered the sanctuary for worship, one should likewise wash the feet and other limbs.

Having sipped water (ācamana), the wise one should sit in the desired bound posture (baddhāsana); thereafter, he should perform the rites of drying and so forth with the mantras "Aṃ," "Kṣaiṃ," and "Raṃ."
Having made the universal principle firm, one should then produce the cosmic egg; having then split the egg, one should meditate upon the Supreme Lord within that egg.
Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, clad in yellow silk garments, resplendent like a thousand suns, with shimmering makara-shaped earrings.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Lord within the lotus of one's own heart; thereafter, one should contemplate the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa as one's own self.
Then [he saw] Pradyumna and Aniruddha, and thereafter the glorious Nārāyaṇa, as well as Indra and the other gods who had arisen from that God of Gods.

Then one should contemplate the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the two hands; thereafter, one should perform the pervasive placement with the root mantra, and after that, the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa).

O Mahādeva, O observer of noble vows, listen to those mantras of the limbs: *oṃ āṃ* homage to the heart; *oṃ īṃ* homage to the head; *oṃ ūṃ* homage to the crest-lock; *oṃ aiṃ* homage to the armor; *oṃ auṃ* homage to the three eyes; *oṃ aḥ* *phaṭ* homage to the weapon.

Oṃ, salutation to the one with his entire retinue, the Imperishable (Acyuta). Oṃ, salutation to Dhātṛ. Oṃ, salutation to Vidhātṛ. Oṃ, salutation to Ādhāraśakti. Oṃ, salutation to Kūrma. Oṃ, salutation to Ananta. Oṃ, salutation to Pṛthivī. Oṃ, salutation to Dharma. Oṃ, salutation to Dharma. Oṃ, salutation to Jñāna. Oṃ, salutation to Vairāgya. Oṃ, salutation to Aiśvarya. Oṃ, salutation to Ajñāna. Oṃ, salutation to Anaiśvarya. Oṃ Aṃ, salutation to the Solar Orb (Arka-maṇḍala). Oṃ Soṃ, salutation to the Lunar Orb (Soma-maṇḍala). Oṃ Vaṃ, salutation to the Fire Orb (Vahni-maṇḍala). Oṃ Vaṃ, salutation to Vāsudeva, the Supreme Brahman, Śiva, whose form is light, the all-pervading, the God above all gods. Oṃ, salutation to Pāñcajanya. Oṃ, salutation to Sudarśana. Oṃ, salutation to the Mace (Gadā). Oṃ, salutation to the Lotus (Padma). Oṃ, salutation to Śrī. Oṃ, salutation to Hrī. Oṃ, salutation to Puṣṭi. Oṃ, salutation to Gīti. Oṃ, salutation to Śakti. Oṃ, salutation to Prīti. Oṃ, salutation to Indra. Oṃ, salutation to Agni. Oṃ, salutation to Yama. Oṃ, salutation to Nirṛti. Oṃ, salutation to Varuṇa. Oṃ, salutation to Vāyu. Oṃ, salutation to Soma. Oṃ, salutation to Īśāna. Oṃ, salutation to Ananta. Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā. Oṃ, salutation to Viṣvaksena.
These mantras have been fully explained to you, O Rudra, in brief; and worship should indeed be performed in a mandala such as the svastika and others.
Oṃ, salutation to Padma. Having performed the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and displayed all the mudrās, one should meditate upon oneself as Vāsudeva, the Supreme Lord.
Afterwards, O bull-bannered one, a person should worship the seat and, having invoked [the deity] according to the rules, perform the worship of Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ at the door.
O Śaṅkara, one should worship Garuḍa first in front of Vāsudeva; from the conch up to the lotus, one should worship them in the central region.
One should worship Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya in the eastern direction, and Adharma and the other four [opposites] in the southeast and the subsequent directions.
Indeed, the seatless posture is proclaimed to be in the center of the three mandalas; Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others are to be worshipped on the lotus petals starting from the east.
One should worship Vāsudeva, the Supreme Lord, in the pericarp; Pāñcajanya and the others, stationed in the northeast and the other directions, are to be worshipped as well.
And the Śaktis of the God of gods, O Śaṅkara, as well as Indra and the other world-protectors situated in the east and the other directions, are to be worshipped.
"O Nāga, below and above him, the wise one should worship Brahmā; O Śaṅkara, this sequence of positions within the maṇḍala should be understood by you."

O Śaṅkara, having invoked the deity into the maṇḍala and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon him, one should display the mudrās and offer water for the feet and other offerings with the root mantra.

One should perform the bathing, the offering of cloth, the sipping of water (ācamana), the fragrance, the flower, the incense, the lamp, the food offering, the subsequent sipping of water, the prostration, and the circumambulation using the root mantra of Śaṅkara; one should also offer the recitation (japa) in the same manner.
Afterwards, one should recite this hymn while recollecting Vāsudeva: "Oṃ, salutations to Vāsudeva, and salutations to Saṅkarṣaṇa."
Salutations again and again to Pradyumna, the primordial god, and to Aniruddha; salutations to Nārāyaṇa alone, and salutations to the Lord of men.

Salutations again and again to the one worthy of worship by men, to the one of glorious fame, to the one worthy of praise, to the giver of boons, and indeed to the ancient one who is without beginning or end.
Salutation to the creator and destroyer, the Lord of Brahmā; salutation to the one who is indeed known through the Vedas, the bearer of the conch and the discus.

Salutations again and again to the Lord of the Gods, the remover of the impurities of the Kali age; salutations again and again to the cutter down of the tree of worldly existence and the piercer of illusion.

Salutations again and again to the one of many forms, the sacred ford, who possesses the three qualities yet is devoid of qualities, who assumes the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa, and who bestows liberation.
Salutations again and again to the Dharma, the door to liberation, the source of emanations; salutations to the one who grants all desires and whose very nature is the Supreme Brahman.
Rescue me, who am submerged in the terrible ocean of saṃsāra; O Lord of Gods, there is no one other than you, and there is no protector, O Lord of the World.
I have come to you for refuge; protect me, O all-pervading Viṣṇu! By granting the lamp of knowledge, illuminate me so that I am freed from darkness.
Thus one should praise the Lord of Gods, the destroyer of all afflictions; having praised Nīlalohita with these and other hymns of praise.
A person should meditate on Viṣṇu in the heart as conjoined with the five tattvas; then, by dismissing the deity, this is proclaimed as worship (pūjā).
O Śaṅkara, she is the most excellent bestower of all desires belonging to Vāsudeva; by the mere act of worshipping her, a man becomes one who has accomplished his purpose.
O Rudra, that man who recites this worship of the five principles (pañcatattva), or hears it, or causes others to hear it, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Five Principles (the Five Forms of Viṣṇu)," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 33.
Rudra said: O wielder of the conch and mace, tell me the worship of Sudarśana, by performing which all afflictions such as planetary influences and diseases truly go to destruction.
Hari said: O bull-bannered one, hear now the worship of the Sudarśana discus. One should first perform the ritual bath and thereafter worship Hari.
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the root mantra; now hear the root mantra: preceded by the *praṇava* (OM), the mantra is "Sahasrāraṃ huṃ phaṭ namaḥ."
The destroyer of all wicked ones and the breaker of [adversarial] mantras has been described; one should meditate upon the god Sudarśana in the pure and auspicious lotus of the heart.
O Hara, having invoked the gentle deity, who bears the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and wears a crown, into the mandala according to the previously mentioned procedure.
