O Maheśvara, one should worship with offerings such as incense and flowers; having worshipped, a person should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
O Rudra, he who thus performs this supreme worship of the discus shall be liberated from all diseases and attain the world of Viṣṇu.
Afterward, one should recite this hymn, which destroys all diseases: "Homage to Sudarśana, who possesses the splendor of a thousand suns."
To the one ablaze with garlands of flames, to the thousand-spoked eye, to the destroyer of all the wicked, and to the crusher of all transgressions.
Homage to the one with the excellent wheel, to the one with the manifold wheels, to the divider of all mantras, to the progenitor, to the sustainer of the world, and to the destroyer of the world.
Salutations again and again to the one who exists for the protection of the worlds, to the destroyer of wicked asuras, to the fierce and the gentle, and to the wrathful.
Salutations to the Eye, whose form is the syllable *kva*, the destroyer of the fear of saṃsāra; salutations again and again to Śiva, the shatterer of the cage of illusion.
Salutations to the one whose form consists of the seizers and the over-seizers, the lord of the seizers; salutations again and again to Time, to Death, and to the Terrifying One.
Salutations again and again to the giver of grace to devotees, the protector of devotees, to the one who has the form of Viṣṇu, the peaceful one, and the wielder of weapons.
"Obeisance to the discus, the weapon of Viṣṇu; obeisance again and again. Thus has this highly meritorious hymn to your discus been proclaimed.

He who recites this with supreme devotion goes to the world of Viṣṇu; and he who, having conquered his senses, O Rudra, recites the ritual procedure for the worship of the Discus, reduces his sin to ashes and becomes fit for the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Worship of Sudarśana," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 34.
Rudra said: O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Gadādhara, speak again of the worship of the Deity; there is no satiety for me as I listen to Your description of the ritual of worship.
Hari said: I shall describe to you the worship of the god Hayagrīva; listen to that, by which Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, is well-pleased.
O Mahādeva, I shall proclaim the root mantra that expresses Hayagrīva, which is supremely meritorious; listen first to it, O Śaṅkara.
Oṃ saiṃ kṣaiṃ, "Salutation to the head," joined with the Praṇava—this nine-syllable mantra bestows all forms of knowledge.
O Mahādeva, O Bull-bannered One, hear now its limbs: *oṃ kṣāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *oṃ kṣīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*—thus the head is declared; likewise, *kṣūṃ* with *vaṣaṭ*.
O Bull-bannered One, the crest-lock (śikhā) of the deity should be known as joined with *oṃ kāra*; *oṃ kṣaiṃ kavacāya huṃ* is indeed proclaimed as the armor (kavaca).
Oṃ kṣaiṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes; thus the eye of the deity is proclaimed. Oṃ haḥ, phaṭ to the weapon; thus the weapon of the deity is proclaimed.

I shall proclaim the ritual procedure for worship; listen as I speak it. First, having bathed and likewise performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should then proceed to the sacrificial hall.
Then, having entered [the mandala], one should duly perform the drying and other rites; and having solidified it with the seed-syllables *yaṃ*, *kṣaiṃ*, and *raṃ*, and with *laṃ*.
Having produced the egg, one should then split it with the syllable *oṃ* alone; within the center of the egg, one should contemplate oneself as Hayagrīva.

White as a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon, with the luster of a lotus stalk or silver, resembling cow’s milk and possessing a brilliance equal to ten million suns; he has four arms, holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus.
The Lord wears a crown and earrings, is adorned with a forest garland, possesses beautiful wheels and handsome cheeks, and is clothed in blue garments.
Having meditated upon the Great-Souled One accompanied by all the gods, one should then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the limb-mantras as well as with the root-mantra.
Then, O Śaṅkara, one should display auspicious mudrās such as the conch and the lotus; having meditated, one should worship Viṣṇu with the root mantra.
Then one should invoke the deities of the seat of Rudra: "Oṃ, deities of the Hayagrīva seat, please come!"
Having invoked them into the mandala, one should worship them in a svastika or similar design; O Bull-bannered One, the worship of Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ should be performed at the door.
"Salutation to the one with his entire retinue, the infallible one"—with this [mantra], worship should be performed in the center, and one should also worship Gaṅgā at the door.
One should worship the great goddess Yamunā, as well as the two treasures Śaṅkha and Padma, and Garuḍa in front; one should worship Śakti in the center.
O Mahādeva, one should then worship the one called Ādhāra, followed by Kūrma; thereafter, one should worship Ananta and Pṛthivī, and then Dharmajñāna.

One should worship detachment and sovereignty in the Āgneya and other directions; however, one should worship unrighteousness, ignorance, non-detachment, and lack of sovereignty in the eastern directions.
One should worship Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas in the middle region; one should also worship the bulb, the stalk, and the lotus in the center.
O Rudra, it is proclaimed that the worship of the mandalas known as Arka (Sun), Soma (Moon), and Agni (Fire) must be performed in the central region.
O Bull-bannered One, these are indeed the powers (śaktis) in the yoga of action: Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, Prahvī, Satyā, and likewise Īśānā and Anugrahā.
And on the petals starting from the east, Vimala and the others are to be worshipped; by men seeking the highest good, Anugrahā should be worshipped in the pericarp.
O Mahādeva, one should worship the seat with these mantras consisting of the names preceded by the syllable *praṇava*, ending in *namaḥ*, and in the dative case.
Through the offering of water for bathing and fragrances, through the offering of flowers and incense, and through the offering of lamps and food, the worship of the seat is auspicious.
"O Hara, it has been proclaimed to you that this must be performed according to this rite; thereafter, one should invoke the god Hayagrīva, the lord of the gods."
One should visualize him as arriving through the left nostril; O Śaṅkara, he arrives by means of the application of the root mantra.
The invocation of the God of gods, the wielder of the conch, should be performed; having invoked him into the mandala, one should unweariedly carry out the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon it.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should meditate upon the Supreme Lord Hayagrīva, the Great God who is saluted by gods and asuras, residing therein.
Having visualized the imperishable Viṣṇu joined by the world-protectors such as Indra, one should display the auspicious mudrās, beginning with those of the conch and the discus.
Then one should offer water for the feet, the respectful oblation, and water for sipping to Viṣṇu; thereafter, one should bathe the Lord Padmanābha, who is free from ailment.

Having installed the deity according to the prescribed rite, O bull-bannered one, one should offer a garment; then indeed one should offer water for sipping (ācamana), and thereafter a beautiful sacred thread (upavīta).
Then, O Rudra, one should meditate upon the Supreme Lord, the God, within the mandala; having meditated, O Śaṅkara, one should again offer water for the feet and other articles to the God.
O Śaṅkara, one should offer [oblations] to the god Bhairava with the root mantra: "Oṃ kṣāṃ, salutation to the heart. With this, one should worship the heart.
Oṃ kṣīṃ, obeisance to the head; thus there shall be the worship of the head. Oṃ kṣūṃ, obeisance to the crest-lock; with this one should worship the crest-lock.
Oṃ kṣaiṃ, obeisance to the armor; one should worship the armor. Oṃ kṣaiṃ, obeisance to the eyes; with this mantra, one should worship the eyes.
With "Oṃ kṣaḥ, obeisance to the weapon," one should worship the weapon with this; likewise, the heart, the head, the crest-lock, and the armor.
One should worship these in the directions starting from the east; O Rudra, one should worship the Weapon-mantra in the corners and worship the Eye-mantra in the center.
One should worship the supreme goddess Lakṣmī, the auspicious bestower of fortune; one should worship the conch, the lotus, the discus, and the mace, starting from the east.
O Rudra, one should worship the sword, the mace, the noose, the goad, and the bow with arrow in the east, using these mantras consisting of their own names.
O Rudra, one should worship from the east the Śrīvatsa, the Kaustubha gem, the garland, and the auspicious yellow garment, as well as the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace.
[One should worship] Brahmā, Nārada, the Siddha, the Guru, and likewise the Paraguru; and similarly the sandals of the Guru and those of the Paramaguru.
Then [he should worship] Indra with his vehicle and likewise accompanied by his retinue, as well as Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, and Vāyu.
O Bull-bannered One, one should thus worship Soma, Īśāna, and Brahmā; one should worship them starting from the east and extending upward to the zenith.
Then one should worship the weapons: the vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, the banner, the mace, the trident, and the wheel and lotus.
Then, O bull-bannered one, one should worship the god Viṣvaksena in the northeastern direction with these mantras, preceded by the syllable *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*.
O Mahādeva, O Bull-bannered One, worship must be performed for Ananta; O Bull-bannered One, worship of the Lord must be performed with the root mantra.
One should offer him perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food offerings, as well as circumambulation, prostration, and the recitation of mantras.
O Bull-bannered One, one should also praise with other hymns beginning with the *praṇava*: "Om, salutation to Hayaśiras; salutation indeed to the Overseer of Knowledge."
Homage to the one whose very nature is knowledge, homage again and again to the giver of knowledge; homage to the peaceful deity, homage to the self consisting of the three qualities.
Salutations indeed to the slayer of gods and asuras, to the destroyer of all the wicked, to the sovereign of all worlds, who possesses the form of Brahmā.
Homage to the one worthy of worship by the lords, who bears the conch and the discus; homage to the primordial one, the self-controlled, and the benefactor of all sentient beings.

Salutations again and again to the one who possesses the three qualities and yet is devoid of qualities, whose nature is that of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the creator, the destroyer, the lord of gods, and the all-pervading one.
Having thus performed this praise, O Rudra, one should meditate upon the God of gods within the stainless lotus of the heart, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Resembling ten million suns, beautiful in every limb, Hayagrīva, the Lord of the Great Earth, the Supreme Self, the Imperishable.
Thus, O Śaṅkara, the worship of Hayagrīva has been described to you; whoever recites this with supreme devotion shall go to the highest state.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Worship of Hayagrīva," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 35—Hari said: "O Śaṅkara, listen as I shall explain the ritual placement (nyāsa) and other rites of the Gāyatrī. Viśvāmitra is its seer (ṛṣi), and Savitṛ is its deity."
Brahmaśīrṣā has Rudra as her crest-lock; she resides in the heart of Viṣṇu; she has Viniyoga as her sole eye; and she is born of the Kātyāyana lineage.
She who moves through the three worlds should be known as residing within the womb of the earth; having understood Gāyatrī thus, one should recite her twelve hundred thousand times.

It should be known that [the mantra] consists of three quarters with eight syllables each, or four quarters with six syllables each; for recitation it is said to be three-quartered, and for worship it is four-quartered.

In the ritual placement (nyāsa), in recitation (japa), as well as in meditation (dhyāna), in the fire-ritual (agnikārya), and likewise in worship (arcana), one should constantly perform the placement of the Gāyatrī, which destroys all sins.
Know [the sequence] to be at the toes, the middle of the ankles, the calves, the knees, the thighs, the private parts, the scrotum, the channel, the navel, and the slender belly.
On the two breasts, the heart, the throat, the lips, the mouth, the palate, the two shoulders, the eyes, the eyebrows, and the forehead—[these are the locations] in the east, south, and north.
One should place the letter Ā on the fifth head; I shall now describe the colors: sapphire-blue, fire-colored (red), yellow, dark-green, and tawny like a Kapila bull.
White, with the luster of lightning, star-like, black, and red—in that sequence; then dark-blue, white, yellow, and indeed white like a ruby.
The color of a conch shell, pale white, red like wine, equal to the color of the sun, gentle, resembling a conch, and pure white.
Whatever one touches with the hand and whatever one sees with the eye, all that becomes purified; they know nothing superior to the Gāyatrī.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Gāyatrī Nyāsa," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 36—Hari said: "I shall proclaim the ritual for the Sandhyā, which destroys sins such as those of Rudra; listen! Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), one should commence the Sandhyā bath."
One should recite the Gāyatrī, together with the Praṇava, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Śiras, three times while restraining the breath; that is called prāṇāyāma.
A twice-born person should burn away the defects born of mind, speech, and body through breath-control (prāṇāyāma); therefore, at all times, he should be devoted to prāṇāyāma.

Having recited "Agniś ca mā" in the evening, one should drink water in the morning with the mantra "Sūryo mā"; and at midday, having touched water according to the rule, one should drink with the mantra "Āpaḥ punantu."
One should perform the sprinkling (mārjana) with water from *kuśa* grass using the verse beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā"; or one may sprinkle water at every step while reciting the *praṇava*.

One should burn away these nine defects—arising from passion (rajas), darkness (tamas), and one's own delusion (moha); born of the waking, dreaming, and deep-sleep states; and produced by speech, mind, and action—by means of the nine [breaths].
Having drawn up water into his hand and recited the *drupadā* verse, he should pour it out; he should perform the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite three, six, eight, or twelve times.
One should worship the Sun with the two verses beginning with "ud u tyam" and "citram"; whatever sin has been committed by day or by night, all of it perishes instantly.
One should remain standing while reciting during the morning twilight, and seated during the evening twilight, chanting the Gāyatrī together with the Mahāvyāhṛtis and accompanied by the Praṇava.
The Gāyatrī destroys the evil deeds committed in ten lifetimes by [recitation] a hundred times, those committed in the past by a thousand times, and even those from three ages by a thousand times.
Gāyatrī is red, Sāvitrī is white in color, and Sarasvatī is to be known as black; thus the triad of junctions (saṃdhyā) is described.
Having assigned *oṃ bhūḥ* to the heart, one should assign *oṃ bhuvaḥ* to the head; and *oṃ svar*, the first foot of the Gāyatrī, to the crest-lock.
The wise one should perform the placement for the armor; he should place the second [mantra] on the eyes, the third for the placement of the limbs, and the fourth everywhere.

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) at the time of twilight, one should indeed recite the Mother of the Vedas; may there be auspiciousness for him throughout the entire day, as he remains intent upon breath control (prāṇāyāma).
The three-footed Gāyatrī is indeed Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; having understood its application, seer, and meter, one should begin the recitation.
Completely liberated from all evil, one shall attain the world of Brahmā; that which is beyond the dust [of passion], accompanied by "Sāvada" and "Oṃ," is declared to be the fourth state.
The Sun strikes down that person who does not perform the twilight worship; even the seer of the fourth state is indeed stainless [only] when he does so.
The meter is the goddess Gāyatrī, and the deity is the Supreme Self.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Sandhyā," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 37—Hari said: Gāyatrī is the supreme goddess, the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. For one who recites her mantra, even the greatest sins are destroyed.
I shall now describe the Gāyatrī-kalpa, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; one should recite it one thousand and eight times, or otherwise, one hundred and eight times.

Having recited [the mantra] one hundred times at the three junctions of the day, one shall become an inhabitant of the world of Brahmā; at the time of the twilight devotion (saṃdhyā), one should invoke and worship the Goddess who destroys all sins.
Accompanied by the mantra "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ" and the twelve names, [one should offer salutations]: "Obeisance to Gāyatrī; obeisance again and again to Sāvitrī and Sarasvatī."
And to Vedamātrā, Sāṃkṛtyā, Brahmāṇī, and Kauśikī in sequence; to Sādhvī, Sarvārthasādhinī, Sahasrākṣī, and Bhūrbhuvaḥ.
One should thus offer into the fire sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and oblation-grain; either one thousand and eight times, or alternatively, eight hundred times, with ghee.
For the sake of accomplishing desires for the Dharma and other goals, one should perform oblations in all rites after having worshipped an image fashioned from sandalwood or gold.
Just as one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while subsisting on milk, roots, and fruits, by performing twenty thousand fire-offerings, one shall attain all desires.
Born on the northern peak, dwelling upon the earth and the mountains, you who are authorized by Brahmā—go, O Goddess, as you please.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Gāyatrī-kalpa," in the Ācāra-kāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

The Lord Hari said: On the ninth day and other such occasions, one should worship Durgā with the mantra: *hrīṃ durge rakṣiṇī* (Oṃ Hrīṃ, O Protectress Durgā), and: *mātarmātarvare durge sarvakāmārthasādhani* (O Mother, O Mother, O Excellent Durgā, O Fulfiller of all desires and purposes).
By this offering of oblation, grant me all my desires: Gaurī, Kālī, Umā, Durgā, Bhadrā, Kānti, and Sarasvatī.
Maṅgalā, Vijayā, Lakṣmī, Śivā, and Nārāyaṇī, in this order; beginning from the third lunar day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one who worships them shall not suffer separation.
She has eighteen arms, holding a shield, a bell, a mirror, and a threatening gesture; a bow, a banner, a hand-drum, an axe, and a noose.
One should visualize her with eighteen arms, holding a spear, a mace, a trident, a skull-cup, an arrow, a goad, a vajra, a wheel, and a probe.
I shall now proclaim the mantra of the Blessed Lady, as well as the procedure for its recitation and other rites.

Oṃ! Homage to the Blessed One, Cāmuṇḍā, dweller in the cremation ground, holding a skull in hand, mounted upon a great *preta*, surrounded by a multitude of great celestial palaces, O Night of Doom, encircled by many hosts, with a great mouth and many arms, adorned with beautiful bells, *ḍamaru* drums, and tinkling bells, laughing with loud *aṭṭāṭṭa* roars,
uttering *kilikili* and *huṃ*, abounding in all kinds of sounds and noises, her body clothed in elephant hide, smeared with blood and flesh, with a flickering, protruding tongue.
O Great Rākṣasī, with fierce fangs and terrifying form, with a formidable and loud *aṭṭahāsa* laugh, with a radiance like flashing lightning; move, move!

O you with wide-open eyes, *hili hili*, O you with a quivering tongue, *hrauṃ hrīṃ*, O you whose face is knit with a frown, O you seated upon the auspicious *oṃ*-syllable throne, encircled by a garland of skulls, wearing a crown of matted hair and the moon; O you with the *aṭṭahāsa* laugh, *kilikili*, *huṃ huṃ*, O you who create a terrible darkness with your fangs, O destroyer of all obstacles!

Accomplish this rite! Accomplish it quickly! Act, act! Ka-ha-ka-ha! Cause [them] to enter the goad! Group by group, tremble, tremble! Move, move! Cause to move, cause to move! O you who delight in blood, flesh, and wine! Strike, strike! Pound, pound! Cut, cut!
Kill, kill! Anubūma, anubūma! Accomplish the adamantine body! Accomplish it even if it be a wicked one, whether it has gone to the three worlds or not!
Whether seized or unseized, cause them to enter, cause them to enter! Cause them to step forward, cause them to step forward! Dance, dance! Bind, bind! Leap, leap!
O you with hollow eyes, O you with hair standing on end, O you with the face of an owl, O you who wear hand-bells and a garland of skulls! Burn, burn! Cook, cook!
Seize, seize! Cause them to enter into the center of the mandala! Why do you delay? By the truth of Brahmā, by the truth of Viṣṇu!

By the truth of the Ṛṣis, by the truth of Rudra, cause [them] to enter, cause [them] to enter! Kilikili khilikhili milimili cilicili! O you who assume a deformed shape; O you whose body is entwined by black serpents; O you who cause all seizing spirits to enter; O you with protruding lips; O you whose nose is sunk between your brows; O you with a hideous face;
O you with tawny matted hair; O Brāhmī! Break, break! Blaze, blaze! O you with a dark face! Khalakhala kharakharaḥ! Cause [them] to fall, cause [them] to fall!
O Raktākṣī! Shake it, shake it! Cast it to the ground, cast it to the ground! Seize the head, seize it! Close the eyes, close them!
Break, break the feet! Seize them, seize them! Shatter the seal, shatter it! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Tear asunder, tear asunder!
Pierce with the trident, pierce it! Strike with the vajra, strike it! Beat with the staff, beat it! Cut with the discus, cut it!
Pierce, pierce with the spear!

Bite, bite with the fangs! Stake, stake with the stake! Split, split with the knife! Seize, seize with the goad! O Brahmāṇī, come, come! O Māheśvarī, come, come! O Kaumārī, come, come! O Vārāhī, come, come!
Aindri, come, come! Cāmuṇḍā, come, come! Vaiṣṇavī, come, come! O you who roam the Himavat, come, come! O you who dwell on Kailāsa, come, come!
Cut, cut the spells of others! Kilikili! O Bimbā, O Aghorā, O you of terrible form! O Cāmuṇḍā, O you who have emerged from the darkness of Ruru’s wrath!
O destroyer of Asuras! O you who move through the sky! Bind, bind with the noose! Stay, stay at the moment of the commitment! [Enter] the maṇḍala!

Enter, enter! Fall, fall! Seize, seize! Bind the mouth, bind, bind! Bind the eyes, bind, bind! Bind the heart, bind, bind! Bind the hands and feet, bind, bind! Bind all evil grahas, bind, bind! Bind the cardinal directions, bind, bind! Bind the intermediate directions, bind, bind! Bind above, bind, bind! Bind below with ashes, bind, bind!
With water, clay, or mustard seeds, cause [him] to enter, cause [him] to enter! Cause [him] to fall, cause [him] to fall! O Cāmuṇḍā, kilikili, vicche hrīṃ (huṃ) phaṭ svāhā!
The recitation consists of a garland of one hundred and eight mantra-words; for each individual word, there is an offering of eight thousand sesame seeds smeared with the three sweets.

With human flesh smeared with the three sweets, one should perform one thousand and eight offerings for each individual verse; and one should likewise offer one thousand and eight oblations of sesame seeds smeared with the three sweets.
Alternatively, human flesh combined with the three sweets accomplishes all rites; by casting water, mustard seeds, ashes, and so forth, one achieves victory in battle and other such contests.
She should be meditated upon as having twenty-eight arms, or eighteen arms, or twelve or eight arms, or even four arms.
Two hands are equipped with sword and shield, the next two are joined with mace and staff, another pair are endowed with arrow and bow, and [the final two] are united with sword and mallet.
Two others hold a sword and a bell; two others are joined with a banner-staff; two others are enriched with an axe and a discus; and two others hold a hand-drum and a mirror.
And two others rest upon their hands holding spears, while others are equipped with clubs; some are joined with nooses and tomara-lances, and others with ḍhakkās and paṇavas.
Threatening others with her supreme [weapon], she makes a clamorous sound; she holds the *abhaya* and *svastika* gestures and so forth, is the slayer of Mahiṣa, and rides upon a lion.
Victory to you, O Mistress of Beings, surrounded by all beings! Protect me from your own attendants; accept this offering; salutations be unto you!

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Mantras for the Worship, Recitation, and Offerings to Durgā," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 39.
Rudra said: O Janārdana, please describe again in brief the worship of the Sun, who is a form of Viṣṇu, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Vāsudeva said: Listen, O Rudra, I shall speak again of the worship of the Sun. "Oṃ, obeisance to Uccaiḥśravas; Oṃ, obeisance to Aruṇa; Oṃ, obeisance to Daṇḍin; Oṃ, obeisance to Piṅgala. O Bull-bannered One, these indeed should be worshipped at the door with these mantras.

Oṃ aṃ, homage to Prabhūta! One should worship this one named Prabhūta-āmala in the center. Oṃ aṃ, homage to Vimala; oṃ aṃ, homage to Sāra; oṃ aṃ, homage to Ādhāra; oṃ aṃ, homage to Paramamukha. Thus, Vimala and the others are indeed to be worshipped in the corners beginning with the southeast.

Oṃ, homage to the lotus. Oṃ, homage to the pericarp. O Rudra, one should worship [the goddesses] in the center, and likewise in the directions beginning with the east. One should worship Dīptā and the others in the center, and worship those who face in all directions. Oṃ vāṃ (rāṃ), homage to Dīptā. Oṃ vīṃ (rīṃ), homage to Sūkṣmā. Oṃ vūṃ (rūṃ), homage to Bhadrā. Oṃ vaiṃ (raiṃ), homage to Jayā. Oṃ vauṃ (rauṃ).
Oṃ, vaṃ (raṃ), salutation to Vibhūti; oṃ, vaṃ (raṃ), salutation to Adhorā; oṃ, vaṃ (raṃ), salutation to Vaidyutā; oṃ, vaḥ (raḥ), salutation to Vijayā; oṃ, ro, salutation to Sarvatomukhī.

Oṃ, homage to the seat of the Sun (arkāsana). Oṃ hrāṃ, homage to the form of the Sun (sūryamūrti). One should worship these in the center; now hear the *hran* mantras, O Śaṅkara. Oṃ haṃ saṃ khaṃ, homage to Khakholka; krāṃ krīṃ saḥ svāhā, homage to the form of the Sun. With this [mantra], one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*), the installation (*sthāpana*), the bringing into proximity (*sannidhāpana*), and likewise the ritual of making [the deity] complete (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the mantra for binding [the deity] (*sanniropana*).

O Rudra, O Hara, perform the visualization of the mudrā either with the root mantra or by itself: [he is] of the nature of radiant energy, red in color, seated upon a white lotus, mounted on a chariot with a single wheel, two-armed, and holding a lotus.
One should thus always meditate upon the Sun; now hear the root mantra: Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ sūryāya namaḥ.

Three times he should display the lotus mudrā and the image mudrā. [He should recite: Oṃ āṃ, homage to the heart; Oṃ arkāya, svāhā to the head; Oṃ aḥ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ jvālini, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock; Oṃ huṃ, huṃ to the armor; Oṃ bhāṃ, vauṣaṭ to the two eyes; Oṃ vaḥ, phaṭ to the weapon.
One should worship Hara in the southeast, the northeast, or the southwest; one should worship the heart and so forth in the northwest, and worship the eye within.
O Rudra, one should worship Soma, who is clothed in bark and white in color; O Rudra, on the eastern petal, one should worship Budha, who has the luster of gold.
One should worship Rudra in the south and honor the Guru; likewise, one should worship Bhūteśa in the west and the white Bhārgava in the north.
O Hara, one should worship the red Aṅgāraka in the southeast; one should worship the black-colored Śanaiścara in the southwestern direction.
O Hara, one should worship Rāhu, who resembles a *nandyāvarta* flower, in the northwest; and one should fully worship Ketu, who is smoke-colored, in the northeast.
O Mahādeva, O Śaṅkara, listen now to these mantras.

Oṃ soṃ, homage to Soma; Oṃ buṃ, homage to Budha; Oṃ bṛṃ, homage to Bṛhaspati; Oṃ bhaṃ, homage to Bhārgava; Oṃ aṃ, homage to Aṅgāraka; Oṃ śaṃ, homage to Śanaiścara; Oṃ raṃ, homage to Rāhu; Oṃ kaṃ, homage to Ketu. Thus it is said.
O Śaṅkara, having offered the water for the feet and other items with the root mantra to the Sun, the best of practitioners should display the dhenu-mudrā at the conclusion of the food offering.
Having recited that [mantra] eight thousand times, one should offer it to him; then, in the northeastern direction, one should worship Tejaścaṇḍa, the Lord of Beings.
Oṃ tejaścaṇḍāya huṃ phaṭ svadhā svāhā pauṣaṭ. One should offer the remains of the flowers (*nirmālya*) to him, and then, O Hara, one should present the water of honor (*arghya*).
Combined with sesame seeds and rice, anointed with red sandalwood, mixed with scented water, and provided with flowers and incense.
O bull-bannered one, having placed that vessel upon his head and knelt upon the ground, he should offer the arghya to the Sun with the heart-mantra.
Having first worshipped Gaṇeśa and all the gurus, one should then worship all the deities: Oṃ Gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati; Oṃ Aṃ, obeisance to the gurus.
The worship of the Sun has been described; by performing this, one becomes a partaker of the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Method of Worshipping the Sun," in the section on Conduct within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 40.
Śaṅkara said: "O wielder of the conch and mace, tell me of the worship of Maheśvarī, by knowing which human beings attain perfection, O Supreme Lord."
Hari said: Listen, O bull-bannered one, as the worship of Maheśvara is being told. Having first bathed, performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and sat down upon a seat;
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the mandala, one should indeed worship Maheśvara, O Great Lord, [namely] Hara together with his retinue, using these mantras.
Oṃ hāṃ, O deities of Śiva’s throne, come! With this [mantra], one should invoke those deities of Rudra who belong to the throne.

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Gaṇapati. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Sarasvatī. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Nandin. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mahākāla. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Gaṅgā. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Lakṣmī. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mahākalā. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Weapon (astra). Thus it is said.

O Hara, these indeed should be worshipped at the gateway with baths, perfumes, and other offerings: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the site (vāstvadhipati).* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Gurus.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ananta.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Dharma.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Jñāna.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vairāgya.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Aiśvarya.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Adharma.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ajñāna.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Avairāgya.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Anaiśvarya.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Urdhvacchanda.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Adhaśchanda.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Padma.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Karṇikā.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāmā.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Jyeṣṭhā.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Raudrī.* *Oṃ, obeisance to Kālī.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kalavikaraṇī.* *Oṃ, obeisance to Balapramathinī.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sarvabhūtadamanī.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Manonmanī.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the three circles (maṇḍalatritaya).* *Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ haṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva (śivamūrti).* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vidyeśvara, the lord of knowledge.* *Oṃ hāṃ hīṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Heart.* *Oṃ, obeisance to the Head.* *Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the Tuft (śikhā).* *Oṃ haiṃ, obeisance to the Armor (kavaca).* *Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the Three Eyes.* *Oṃ haḥ, obeisance to the Weapon (astra).* *Oṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta.*

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Siddhi! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Ṛddhi! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vidyutā! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Lakṣmī! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Bodhā! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kālī! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Svadhā! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Prabhā!
The eight digits of Truth (satya) should be known; they are to be worshipped, situated in the directions starting from the east.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rajas; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rakṣā; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rati; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kanyā; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kāmā; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Jananī; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kriyā; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vṛddhi; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kāryā; oṃ [rā]dhātryai, salutation; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Bhrāmaṇī; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mohinī; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kṣavarā. O Bull-bannered One, these thirteen should be known as the digits (kalās) of Vāmadeva.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nivṛtti; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Pratiṣṭhā; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vidyā; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śānti. O Bull-bannered Lord, these four are to be known as belonging to Tatpuruṣa alone.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Tṛṣṇā. O Hara, the six parts (kalās) of Akhora are indeed to be known as Bhairava.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Īśāna. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Samiti. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Aṅgadā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kṛṣṇā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Marīci. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Jvālā. Know these to be the five digits (kalās) of Īśāna, O Bull-bannered One.

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the retinue of Śiva. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Indra, the lord of the gods. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Agni, the lord of fire. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Yama, the lord of the pretas. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Nirṛti, the lord of the rākṣasas. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Varuṇa, the lord of the waters. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāyu, the lord of the vital breaths. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Soma, the lord of the eyes. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Īśāna, the lord of all vidyās. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Ananta, the lord of the nāgas. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Brahmā, the lord of all worlds. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Dhūlicaṇḍeśvara.

O Śaṅkara, one should perform the invocation (āvāhana), the installation (sthāpana), the bringing near (sannidhāna), as well as the confinement (sannirodha) and the ritual of making the deity manifest with all its limbs (sakalīkaraṇa).

One should perform the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa), the display of the mudrās, and meditation; as well as the offering of water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), the respectful oblation (arghya), flowers, and the application of unguents (abhyaṅga).
Then [one should perform] the rubbing with unguents, bathing, fragrant ointment, clothing, ornaments, enjoyments, the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa), and incense.

The offering of a lamp, the gift of food, the rubbing of the hands, as well as water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamana), fragrance, betel, song, and instrumental music.
Dancing, the making of parasols and other objects, the display of mudrās, as well as form, meditation, recitation, and the state of oneness.
One should indeed perform the recitation, worship, and offering with the root mantra; O Rudra, this worship of Māheśī has been described as the destroyer of sins.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Worship of Maheśvara," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Vāsudeva said: "Oṃ! I am the Gandharva named Viśvāvasu, the lord of maidens; having produced a maiden for you, I grant her to that Viśvāvasu—*svāhā*! Through the recitation of this mantra, one obtains a woman. Now I shall declare the *Kālarātri* [mantra]."
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, O Ṛkṣakarṇī, four-armed one, with hair standing erect, three-eyed one, O Kālarātri, you who feed on the fat and blood of human beings!

Grant death to [name], whose time has come! Huṃ phaṭ! Slay, slay! Burn, burn! Cook, cook the flesh and blood! O wife of the bear, svāhā! Neither a lunar day, nor a constellation, nor fasting is prescribed for this rite.

Enraged, having wiped his hands with blood and grasping them with both [hands], one should recite the mantra over the *liṅga* at dusk; an unbaked earthen vessel (*āmapātra*) shall cause death. Oṃ namaḥ sarvatoyantrāṇi! Just as: O Jambhani! O Mohani! O Destroyer of all enemies! Protect, protect me, [Name], from all fears and calamities! Svāhā! O Mahādeva, when semen is lost, I shall here declare the procedure for the twice-born.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "Description of Mantras for Accomplishing Subjugation and Other Rites," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 42.

Hari said: I shall describe the Pavitrāropaṇa (the rite of offering the sacred thread), which destroys the inauspiciousness of Śiva. O Hara, the Ācārya, the Sādhaka, the Putraka, and the Samayī should perform it.
Otherwise, Vighneśa takes away the worship performed throughout the year; one should perform it in the months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, Māgha, or Bhādrapada.
The threads for the [mandala] lines should be known, in order, as being made of gold, silver, copper, and cotton; they should be collected starting from Tuesday and spun by a virgin.
Having tripled the thread three times, one should then fashion the *pavitraka*. O Śiva, one should tie the knots with the *Vāmadeva* mantra and wash it with the *Satya* mantra.
Having purified it with the Aghora mantra, it should be bound with the Tatpuruṣa mantra; one should fumigate it with the Īśāna mantra—thus are the deities of the thread remembered by me.
Oṃkāra, Candramas, Vahni, Brahmā, Nāga, Śikhidhvaja, Ravi, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are declared to be the deities in the threads in successive order.
One should perform one hundred and eight, fifty, or twenty-five [recitations]; Rudra is to be known as the best and so forth, and the measurements and knots are ten.
The intervals between the knots should be four finger-breadths wide, and their names are, in order: Prakṛti, Pauruṣī, Vīrā, and the fourth is Aparājitā.
Jayā, Vijayā, Rudrā, Ajitā, Sadāśivā, Manonmanī, and Sarvamukhī [are worshipped] at intervals of two finger-breadths or one finger-breadth.

One should dye [the threads] with saffron and other substances and fashion the *pavitraka* from nine strands; this should be done on the seventh or the thirteenth day of either the bright or the dark fortnight.

Having bathed the Liṅga with milk and other substances, one should worship it with perfumes and other offerings; O Hara, one should then present a fragrant purifier (pavitra) to oneself and to Brahmā.
One should offer a flower endowed with fragrance in the northeast using the root mantra; likewise, one should offer a staff of wood in the east and the fruit of the *āmalakī* tree in the north.
The knower of mantras should offer earth in the west, ashes for prosperity in the south, and aloe-wood in the southwest, using the *śikhā* mantra.
O Bull-bannered One, one should offer mustard seeds in the northwest with the Kavaca mantra; having encircled the house with a thread, one should offer a fragrant purifier.

Having performed the fire sacrifice and offered the oblation to Agni, one should likewise give the bali-offering to the spirits: "O Maheśvara, Lord of Gods, you are invited together with your attendants."
"I shall worship you in the morning; remain present here. Having invited him with this, he should stay there through the night, performing songs and other such acts.
One should place the consecrated purifiers beside the deity; having bathed on the fourteenth day, one should first worship the Sun and then Rudra.

Having meditated upon the Self as the Universal Form situated on the forehead, one should worship it; thus, having sprinkled [the offerings] with the Astra-mantra, they are then honored with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
One should offer those very [substances] consecrated with mantras and perfumed; first that which consists of the Śiva-tattva, and thereafter that which consists of the Vidyā-tattva.

Thereafter, one should worship that which consists of the principle of the Self (ātmatattva), known as Devakā; then [one should worship] with: "Oṃ hauṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the Śiva-principle (śivatattva); Oṃ hīṃ (or hīḥ), obeisance to the Knowledge-principle (vidyātattva)."

Oṃ hāṃ (hauḥ), homage to the principle of the self (ātmatattva). Oṃ hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ kṣaiṃ, homage to the universal principle (sarvatattva). O God, whatever has been seen by you, whose nature is Time, within my ritual procedure—

O Śambhu, whatever has been done—whether afflicted, abandoned, offered as an oblation, or kept secret—I have performed it with my whole being, through myself, by means of the purifier that is Your will.
Fulfill, fulfill that vow of sacrifice for the Lord of Restraints, who is the essence of all principles and the protector of all causes; Oṃ hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ haiṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva!
Whoever offers four sacred threads (*pavitra*) as prescribed by the ancients, having offered a sacred thread to the fire,
he should then bestow a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) upon the preceptor.
Having offered the bali-oblation and fed the twice-born, one should dismiss Caṇḍa toward the east.

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Installation of the Sacred Thread for Śiva," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Hari said: I shall describe the installation of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) for Hari, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Formerly, during the war between the gods and the asuras, Brahmā and the other deities went to him for refuge.
And Viṣṇu gave those gods a banner and a neck-ornament; seeing these two, the Dānavas will perish—so Hari said.
When Viṣṇu had spoken thus, the Naga, the younger brother of Vāsuki, then said: "O Bull-bannered One, let him choose this boon known as 'the Sacrificer' (vapitrākhya)."
"The necklace given by Hari shall become famous by my name," he said; when this was spoken by him, those gods understood that boon to be known by his name.
But those mortals who do not worship with purificatory blades during the rainy season—their worship throughout the entire year shall become fruitless.

Therefore, for all the deities, the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) should be performed in sequence; whichever lunar day (tithi) is prescribed for each, beginning from the first day (pratipad) and ending with the full moon (paurṇamāsī).

O Hara, O Śiva, on the twelfth day of either the bright or the dark fortnight, or during a Vyatīpāta yoga, at the solstices, or during an eclipse of the moon or sun, an offering should be made to Viṣṇu.
It is prescribed as a constant purifier for Viṣṇu, for rites of prosperity, and likewise upon the arrival of a guru; however, it is mandatory during the rainy season.
Silk thread, or cotton thread, or linen thread, or even thread made of kuśa grass should be used for the twice-born; for kings, however, it should be silk or woven cloth.
O Lord, for Vaiśyas, bark cloth or linen is prescribed; for Śūdras, that made from hemp or bark; and cotton or lotus-fiber is recommended for all.
The thread spun by the Brahmin woman is tripled and then tripled again; it consists of Oṃkāra, Śiva, Soma, Agni, Brahmā, Phaṇī, and Ravi.
Vighneśa and Viṣṇu—these deities reside in the threads; Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are remembered as the deities in the triple thread.
One should place [the vessel] made of gold, silver, copper, bamboo, or clay; sixty-four finger-breadths is the best size, and half of that is the middling.
Half of that shall be the smallest; the thread should be one hundred and eight [units] long, according to the sequence of best, middling, and smallest as before.
The knots are prescribed as being the size of the thumb for the best [type of rosary], the middle finger for the middling, and the little finger for the inferior.
Whether on a celestial chariot or upon a sacrificial mound, this is the general characteristic; one should likewise cause the purifying thread extracted by Śiva to be placed upon an image.
It reaches the heart, the navel, and the thighs, and hangs down to the knees; four knots are traditionally taught for the one thousand and eight [beads].

Alternatively, the sacred thread (*pavitraka*) should be known to have thirty-six, twenty-four, or twelve knots, according to whether it is for the highest, middle, or lowest [grade], or else according to its sections (*parvan*).
Anointed with saffron or with turmeric and sandalwood paste, one who observes a fast should consecrate the sacred thread placed within a vessel.
A staff made of wood and the tip of a *kuśa* blade are placed in the eight directions within a vessel made from the leaf of an *aśvattha* tree; in the east, they are placed by Saṅkarṣaṇa.
With yellow pigment and saffron on the right for the sake of victory in battle, and with Pradyumna on the west for the sake of accomplishing one's goals, [one should worship] with Aniruddha.
One should place sandalwood mixed with blue [pigment], sesame ashes, and unbroken rice grains in the corners starting from the southeast, in sequence for Śyāmā and the others.
Having consecrated the purifier with Vāsudeva’s mantra once, and having looked upon it and worshipped it again, one should then carefully cover it with a cloth.
It should be placed before the deity, or within the maṇḍala of the images, in the west, south, and north, respectively, following the same sequence as previously described.
Having also established the Brahma and other deities, one should worship the water-pot; having delineated the mandala with the weapon-mantra (astra), one should offer the food oblation (naivedya).
Having consecrated the purifier with three strands or a new one, and having encircled the altar, as well as oneself, the vessel, and the clarified butter;
Having taken a single thread, one should place it upon the head of the deity, [representing] the fire-pit, the celestial chariot, the pavilion, and the house itself.
Having made the offering and worshipped Maheśvara, one should recite this mantra: "O Lord of Gods, O Supreme Lord, you have been invoked for the sake of worship."
"I shall worship it at dawn; be present in the vicinity of the ritual materials. Having consecrated the *pavitraka* for one night or three nights, [one should proceed].
Having kept a vigil at night and having worshipped Keśava in the morning, one should install [the images] in order: the eldest, the middle, and the youngest.
Having fumigated the purifier (pavitra), one should consecrate it with the mantra itself; having tied a knot while reciting the mantra, one should worship it with flowers and other offerings.
Having worshipped the deity honored with the Gāyatrī mantra, one should cause [the disciple] to offer it; then, together with his sons, wife, and others, he should wear the thread and the tail.
O Lord, I wear before you this beautiful rosary with pure knots, which destroys great sins and brings about the exhaustion of all evils.
Having thus worshipped with incense and other offerings, one should present the central and other [vessels], which are the Vaiṣṇava purifier, a splendor that destroys all sins.
For the sake of accomplishing the goals of Dharma, Kama, and Artha, I wear this upon my own neck; having worshipped it, one should cause it to be given with its own mantra.

Having offered various kinds of food offerings (naivedya), one should present an oblation (bali) of flowers and other items; there, one should also satisfy the fire with a measure of twelve finger-breadths.
One should offer one hundred and eight single-strand purifiers; having first offered the *arghya* water to the Sun, one should place a single purifier there as well.
Then, having worshipped Viṣvaksena with water for the feet, arghya, and other offerings, O Hara, one should stand before the deity with palms joined in reverence and recite the mantra.
Whether performed with knowledge or without knowledge, whatever worship and other rites have been performed by me—may all that become complete through your grace, O Lord of the Gods.
O you whose banner is Garuḍa, may this annual worship with garlands of jewels and coral, and with mandāraka flowers and the like, be yours.
O Lord, just as you always bear the Kaustubha gem upon your heart, so too should you wear this sacred garland of threads upon your breast.
Having thus made this request, fed the twice-born, and given them their sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), he should dismiss them on that very same evening or on the following day.
Having duly performed this annual worship by me, O Pavitra, you shall now depart for the realm of Viṣṇu, having been dismissed.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Installation of the Sacred Thread for Viṣṇu," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Hari said: "Having worshipped with the sacred thread and other offerings, and having meditated upon Brahman, one becomes Hari. I shall now describe the meditation on Brahman, which crushes the machine of Māyā."
The wise man who desires knowledge should restrain speech and mind, and offer them into the self; he who desires knowledge within the self should restrain that knowledge within the Great (Mahat).
It is devoid of body, senses, mind, intellect, vital breath, and ego; it is free from the gross elements and subtle essences, as well as from the qualities (guṇas), birth, eating, and so forth.
Self-luminous, formless, eternally blissful, and free from disease and so forth; it is eternal, pure, awakened, sovereign, true, blissful, and non-dual.
I am the fourth syllable, Brahman, the supreme state; this abiding in the realization "I am Brahman" is also called samādhi.

Know the self as the rider in the chariot, and the body as the chariot itself. Know the intellect as the charioteer, and the mind as the reins. They say the senses are the horses, and the sense-objects are their range.
The wise declare that the self, when joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer; for he who is always joined with the external consciousness through the mind.
But he attains that state, for he is not born again—the man who has discernment as his charioteer and holds the reins of the mind.
One reaches the further shore of the celestial river; that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. Non-violence and the like are declared to be *yama*, while purity and the like are remembered as *niyama*.

The posture is said to be the lotus and others; breath control is the mastery over the vital winds; withdrawal of the senses is declared to be mastery [over the objects]; and meditation is the contemplation of the Lord.
Mental retention is dhāraṇā, and samādhi is abiding in Brahman. First, the mind must not be steady; thereafter, one should contemplate the form.

In the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus, he holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus; he is endowed with the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, and is graced by the beauty of a forest garland.
I am the Self, eternal, pure, endowed with prosperity, called truth and bliss, supreme; I am indeed the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Light itself.

He who exists in the form of the twenty-four manifestations residing in the Śālagrāma stone, and who resides in the stones of Dvārakā and other sacred sites—he is I, and he is to be meditated upon and worshipped.

Having obtained whatever is desired by the mind, one becomes a deity traveling in a celestial vehicle; being free from desire, while meditating upon, praising, and reciting [the mantra], one attains liberation.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Meditation on the Form of Brahmā," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 45. Hari said: "In this context, I shall describe the characteristics of the Śālagrāma. By the touch of a Śālagrāma stone, the sins of ten million births are destroyed."
The one called Keśava has the conch, discus, mace, and lotus in his hands;
the all-pervading Nārāyaṇa holds the mace, the Śārṅga bow, the Kaumodakī mace, the discus, and the conch.

Mādhava, the bearer of the mace, should be worshipped as Gadādhara, holding the discus, conch, lotus, and mace; or alternatively, Govinda, the bearer of the mace, should be worshipped as possessing the mace, lotus, conch, and discus.
Salutation to you who bear the lotus, conch, sword, and mace (in the form of Viṣṇu); salutation to the form of Madhusūdana who holds the conch, lotus, mace, and discus.
Homage to the one who possesses the mace, discus, conch, and lotus (the Traivikrama form), and to the Vāmana form who possesses the śārṅga bow, kaumodakī mace, lotus, and conch.
Salutation to the one who holds the discus, lotus, conch, and mace (the form of Śrīdhara); salutation to Hṛṣīkeśa, who holds the lotus, mace, and conch, and wields the discus.
Obeisance to Dāmodara, who possesses the lotus, discus, mace, and conch (in the form of Padmanābha), and who holds the conch, discus, mace,
and lotus.
Salutation indeed to Vāsudeva, who holds the sword, conch, mace, and lotus; and salutation to Saṅkarṣaṇa, who wields the conch, lotus, discus, and mace.
Salutations to Pradyumna, who holds a beautiful conch, a beautiful mace, and a lotus; salutations to Aniruddha, who bears a mace, a conch, a lotus, and an enemy.
Salutations to the form of Puruṣottama, who holds the lotus, conch, mace, and discus; salutations to the form of Adhokṣaja, who bears the mace, conch, discus, and lotus.
Salutation to the form of Nṛsiṃha; salutation to the form of Acyuta, who bears the lotus, mace, conch, and discus, and who holds the lotus, discus, conch, and mace.
I invoke Janārdana here, who holds the conch, discus, lotus, and mace; salutations to Upendra, who possesses the mace, the arrow, the lotus, and the conch.
Salutation to the form of Hari, who possesses a beautiful discus, lotus, mace, and conch; salutation to the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who holds a mace, lotus, discus, and conch.
May that Śrī Gadādhara, who bears two wheels fixed upon the surface of the entrance of a Śālagrāma stone and possesses a white luster (known as Vāsudeva), protect you.
The one with two wheels fixed [to it], red in appearance, and with its front portion fully developed, is Saṃkarṣaṇa; then Pradyumna has a subtle wheel and is yellowish.
That which is long with a hole at the top is [the *aniruddha*]; that which is circular, blue, with three lines at the opening, is [the *nārāyaṇa*], which is black.
May the tawny Nṛsiṃha, whose belly is marked with lines, whose navel-center is deeply elevated, who possesses a broad chest,
and who bears three dots, protect you!
Alternatively, for a celibate student, there is the worship of the five drops; may the Śakti-liṅga, which possesses two unequal wheels, protect you. (Varāha)
May he who is dark blue, marked with three lines, thick, possessing the form of a tortoise and a dot, circular in his coils, and with a curved back, protect you.
(Śrīdhara) has five lines; (Dvanamālī) is marked by a goad; (Vāmana) is circular or short;
(Rāmacakra) is the Lord of the Gods.
Nānāvarṇa, Anekamūrti, Nāgabhogin (Anantaka), Sthūla (Dāmodara),
Nīla, Madhyevakra, and Sunīlaka.
May he whose door is crowded protect you—he who is dark-red like refined copper, possessing long lines, hollow, with a single wheel and lotus, and broad.
Pṛthucchidra has a broad disc; Kṛṣṇa and Viṣṇu are like the bilva fruit; Hayagrīva is shaped like a goad and possesses five lines along with the kaustubha gem.
May Vaikuṇṭha—resembling a jewel of gems, possessing a single wheel and a lotus, dark-hued, long, shaped like a lotus, and marked with lines at the gates—protect you all. (Matsya).
May the dark-complexioned Trivikrama, who possesses the Rāmacakra and the right-line [mark], protect me; salutations to the mace-bearer residing in Śālagrāma and Dvārakā.
It has one opening and four wheels, is adorned with a garland of forest flowers, is joined by a golden line, and is distinguished by a "cow's footprint."
May Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, who has the form of a kadamba flower, protect us; may Sudarśana, who bears teeth and is marked by the single [disc], extend his protection.
With two [forms] he is Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa; with three, Trivikrama; with four, Caturvyūha and Vāsudeva.
By means of five.
Pradyumna should consist of six [forms], Saṃkarṣaṇa of eight, Puruṣottama of eight, and Navavyūha of nine.
Marked with the number nine.
May Aniruddha protect us with the ten incarnations; then may the twelve-fold one protect us from above, and thereafter the infinite one.
Whoever recites this hymn consisting of the forms of Viṣṇu shall go to heaven; [he beholds] Brahmā, four-faced, holding a staff and accompanied by a water-pot.
(Maheśvara is) five-faced, ten-armed, and has the bull as his emblem; Gaurī, Caṇḍikā, and Sarasvatī likewise possess the same weapons.
Mahālakṣmī, the Mothers, the lotus-handed [Viṣṇu], the Sun, the elephant-faced Gaṇeśa, Skanda, the six-faced one, and manifold virtues.
When these [deities] are honored and installed in a temple where the site has been consecrated, a person attains virtue, wealth, desire, liberation, and other goals.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Śālagrāma Image," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Hari said: I shall briefly describe the Vāstu ritual, which destroys obstacles in the construction of houses and other structures. One should perform the worship on a grid of eighty-one squares, beginning from the northeast corner (Īśāna).

The head is in the northeast and the feet in the southwest; the hands are in the southeast and northwest. [This applies] in dwellings, houses, and the like, as well as in cities, villages, and merchant routes.
In palaces, gardens, fortresses, temples, and monasteries, one should worship twenty-two deities on the exterior and thirteen within.
Īśa, Parjanya, Jayanta, the wielder of the thunderbolt (Kuliśāyudha), Sūrya, Satya, Bhṛgu, Ākāśa, and Vāyu.
Pūṣan and Vitatha, both the planet and the field, Yamau, Gandharva, Bhṛgurāja, Mṛga, and likewise the Pitṛgaṇa.
Then there are the gatekeepers Sugrīva and Puṣpadanta, the leader of the Gaṇas; the Asuras Śeṣa and Pāpa, as well as Roga and the one known as Ḍahimukha.
Bhallāṭa, Soma, Sarpa, Aditi, and likewise Diti—these thirty-two are on the outside; now hear of the four within them.
The wise one should worship those situated in the four corners beginning with Īśāna: Āpa, Sāvitrī, Jaya, and likewise Rudra.
In the center of the nine squares is Brahmā; now hear by name these eight deities situated near him, starting from the east and proceeding in order.
Aryaman, Savitṛ, Vivasvat the lord of the gods, Mitra, Rājayakṣman, and likewise Pṛthvīdhara follow in sequence.
Aṣṭama and Apavatsa are recorded as being around Brahmā; beginning from the northeast corner (īśānakoṇa), that which is known as the lineage (vaṃśa) is said to be located in Durgā.
Starting from the southeast corner, there is the lineage of Durdhara; these three are Aditi, Himavat, and Jayanta.
Furthermore, having worshipped the presiding deities (Vāstudevas) starting from Indra, the leader named Kālikā, and the Gandharvas, one may become the builder of houses and palaces.
The preceptor should be stationed in front, the kitchen in the southeast, the monkey-entrance in the south,
and the sacrificial pavilion in the east.
A house for perfumes and flowers, provided with silk hangings, should be constructed in the northeast; a treasury in the north, and a stable for cattle in the northwest.
In the southwest, there should be a bright dwelling provided with a window; in the northwest, a place for fuel such as sacrificial wood and *kuśa* grass, and for weapons.
The guest chamber, provided with delightful beds, seats, and footstools, and equipped with water, fire, lamps, and excellent servants, should be situated to the south.
One should arrange all the interior spaces of the houses so that they are beautified by water-filled plantain groves and flowers of five colors.
One should provide a wall outside that, measuring five cubits in height; thus one should construct the hermitage of Viṣṇu, endowed with forests and groves.
The sixty-four-pada site-plan is worshipped in temples and other such structures; in the center is the four-pada Brahmā, while Aryaman and the others occupy two-pada squares.
Karna, Śikhin, and other gods are likewise proclaimed; from them, on both sides, there are also other bipedal deities along with their attendants.
The gods are thus proclaimed to be sixty-four in number: Carakī, Vidārī, Pūtanā, and Pāparākṣasī;
Then, on the exterior, starting from Īśāna, are Deva and the others, as well as Hetuka and the rest; [these are] Hetuka, Tripurāntaka, Agni, Vetālaka, and Yama.
Agnijihva, Kālaka, Karāla, and Akapādaka are in the northeast; Bhīmarūpa is in the netherworld (pātāla) as the leader of the pretas.
In the space [of the diagram], there should be a fragrant garland; then one should worship the Kṣetrapālas. One should calculate the total of the Vāstu by multiplying its length by its width.
Having made a division by the Vasus (eight), one should bind the remainder and indicate the Yama; then, having multiplied again by eight, one should divide by the Ṛtus (six).

Whatever remains shall be the asterism; having divided by the [stellar] portions, the remainder becomes the *avyaya*. Having multiplied the asterism by four and divided it by nine, [the result is the *tithi*].
One should understand the remaining portion according to the opinion of Devala: the *piṇḍa* multiplied by eight, divided by sixty.
Whatever remains shall be the living space, while death is that which has been taken by the Bhata. A man should always build his house within the belly of the Vastu, never upon its back.
One should sleep on one's left side; there is no need for deliberation on this point. Furthermore, during the zodiacal signs of Leo, Virgo, and Libra, the northern door shall be purified.
And thus, in the case of the scorpion and other [signs], there should be doors in the east, south, and west; the width of each door is half its length, and eight such doors are traditionally taught.
Through Raudra, there is lowliness as a servant in one's lineage, a personal vehicle, and golden ornaments; yet it is devoid of sons. Likewise, through Dakṣiṇa, there is the destruction of virility.

In the southeast (Agni), there is imprisonment, yet it bestows longevity, the gain of sons, and great satisfaction; in the north (Dhanada), it causes affliction from kings, yet destroys calamities; in the north-west (Jala), it brings disease.

A son born under Nṛpabhīti causes the death of one's offspring; being childless himself, he does not grant enmity. He bestows wealth but leads to the loss of that wealth, and being a source of faults, he brings about the death of his children.
I shall now describe the eastern doors, which are known as the "northern" ones: there is fear of fire, many daughters, wealth, and a source of honor.

The eastern gate is said to be destructive of kings and a source of anger by its fruit; the eastern [gate] should be in the northeast and so forth, while the southern [gate] should be in the southeast and so forth.

In the case of the southwest and other directions, the western door should be placed; in the case of the northwest and other directions, the northern door should be placed. When the area is divided into eight parts, the results—both favorable and unfavorable—depend upon the location of the doors within those divisions.

The *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, and *nyagrodha* should be planted in the east and other directions, while the *udumbara* is said to be auspicious for a house; furthermore, the *sālmali* tree, when worshipped in the northeast, removes obstacles for both a temple and a residence.

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Measurement of the Vāstu," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious *Śrī-Gāruḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*. Sūta said: O Śaunaka, listen as I describe the characteristics of temples (prāsādas). Having divided the ground into sixty-four squares, marked out by the cardinal and intermediate directions—
It is quadrangular with four doors numbering twelve (the sun), and the arrangement of the walls consists of forty-eight.

The shank should be equal in measure to the upper part of the body (ūrdhvakṣetra); the width of the Śukāṅghri base should be twice the half-measure of the shank and as wide as the interior width of the shrine.
The projection of the parrot-foot should be made as one-third or again as one-fifth [of the base]; its height should reach half of the pinnacle.

Having divided the pinnacle into four parts, the construction of the altar-base (vedī) is in the third part; furthermore, in the fourth part of this very [pinnacle], the neck (kaṇṭha) is established from its base.
Alternatively, having made the site level and divided it into sixteen parts, one should first construct the inner sanctum (*garbha*) in the center, occupying four parts.
The height of the walls should be one-fourth of the [overall] measurement.

The height of the spire (śikhara) should be double the height of the wall in measurement; and the circumambulatory paths (pradakṣiṇā) should be made with a width equal to half the height of the spire.
The wise should likewise understand the exit in the four directions by dividing the measurement of the inner sanctum (garbha) into five parts.
Having taken one part, one should again fashion the exit; the front portico (mukhamaṇḍapa) shall be equal to the central axis (garbhasūtra) from the [first] part forward.
This indeed has been declared as the general characteristic of the temple; now I shall describe the measurement of the *liṅga*, wherein the pedestal (*pīṭha*) should be equal in size to the *liṅga*.
O Śaunaka, the womb (garbha) is certainly twice as large on all sides; twice that again is the height of the wall (bhīti), and the plinth (jaṅghā) extends to half that width.

O Śaunaka, the pinnacle (śikhara) is said to be twice the height of the pillar-shaft (jaṅghā); the work of the pedestal and the inner sanctum (garbhāvara) is to be executed according to that same measurement, as is the "parrot-foot" (śukāṅghrika).

The exit is declared to be the same as before; the remaining details are indeed as previously stated. This has been remembered as the measurement of the linga; now the measurement of the door is described.
Having made the tip of the hand like a Veda (four units), the door shall be one-eighth of that; its width has been fully described, and it may be doubled according to one's own desire.
In the middle of the Dvāravat-pīṭha, there should be a hollow space for Śeṣa; the remaining portion for the base and the wall should be taken up by half the width of the door.

The shank should be equal in width to that [base]; the pinnacle (śikhara) should be twice that; and the parrot-foot (śukāṅghri) should be understood as before, with its projection and height being the same.
This is the measurement for the pavilion; now I shall describe its other essential form: one should cause the sacred field (*kṣetra*) to be made threefold, wherein the deities reside.
By means of the measurement thus performed, the rim of the palace is extended all around by one quarter on the outer side.
One should make the *garbha* twice the measurement of the *nemi*; that same measurement shall be the height of the wall here, and the *śikhara* is considered to be twice that.
And I shall describe the measurement and the origin of palaces according to their proportions: the Vairāja, the one called Puṣpaka, Kailāsa, and the one named Mālikā.
And these five palaces, which are the source of all [architectural] forms, constitute Triviṣṭapa; for the first is square, while the second is rectangular.
There is the circular, the oblong, another which is octagonal, and here the fifth; from these very forms are produced the most beautiful palaces.
Likewise, from all the primary elements, there are forty; and also Meru, Mandara, and another celestial palace (vimāna).
Bhadraka, Sarvabhadra, Rucaka, Nandana, the one named Nandivardhana, and Śrīvatsa—these are the nine.
It should be understood that these square structures arose from Vairāja; namely, the *valabhī*, the *gṛharāja*, the *śālāgṛha*, and the *mandira*.
The celestial chariot (vimāna), the Brahma-palace, the mansion (bhavana), the pillar (uttambha), the palanquin (śibikā), and the house (veśma)—these nine are produced from the Puṣpaka.
Valaya, Dundubhi, Padma, Mahāpadma, as well as another, Mukuli, Uṣṇīṣin, Śaṅkha, and likewise Kalaśa.
The Guvā tree and others, as well as round trees originating from Kailāsa; then the elephant, the bull, the swan, Garuḍa, and the one named Siṃha.
Bhūmukha, Bhūdhara, Śrījaya, and Pṛthivīdhara—these nine, who were round and tall, were born from the one named Maṇika.
The vajra, the cakra, and likewise another called the muṣṭika and the vabhru; the vakra, the svastika, the khaḍga, the gadā, and the śrīvṛkṣa as well.
Vijaya by name is white and originates from Triviṣṭapa; [the shapes are] a triangle, a lotus, a half-moon, a quadrangle, and two octagons.
The configuration of the pavilion should be arranged here or there, for it leads to sovereignty, prosperity, and indeed the increase of longevity.

The acquisition of a son, prosperity for women, and so forth shall occur according to the sequence beginning from the trines (tri-koṇa). One should construct the main hall (dhvaja) and other structures, as well as the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), at the renowned entrance.

The jeweled pavilion (maṇāḍapa) is multiplied by an equal number [of units], and the cord (sūtraka) is likewise; the wise one should construct the auspicious hall (bhadra) from one-fourth of the pavilion's dimension.
It may be provided with windows for competition, or it may be without windows; furthermore, it may have a height equal to half the thickness of the wall, or equal to the full thickness of the wall.
Alternatively, pavilions may sometimes be constructed with twice the number of bays; in the temple, a multi-colored gallery with uneven floors should be made.
Adorned with irregular lines due to contradictions in measurement, the base, however, has four drains and is beautified by four pavilions.
Meru is the supreme temple, endowed with a hundred peaks; its pavilions should be constructed, adorned with three auspicious features.
Those who measure by means of words are divided into those who are distinct and those who are non-distinct; among them, some have supports while others are without support.
Those palaces come into being through the differentiation of individual desires; they do not intermingle with one another because there is no distinction among those constructions.
Many temples are prescribed for the sake of specific deities; however, there is no restrictive rule regarding temples for self-manifested (svayambhu) deities.
One should first have those very [structures] made according to the measurement of the deities; they should be rectangular there, provided with four corners.
It should be provided with a moon-chamber (candraśālā) and joined with a pinnacle (bherīśikhara); and in front of the mounts, pavilions for the auspicious moment (lagnamaṇḍapa) should be constructed.
A dance hall should be constructed adjacent to the gateway; and in the case of palaces for deities, it should be built in the cardinal and intermediate directions as well.
The principal gatekeepers should be appointed individually at separate locations; monasteries for those who depend on them should be established not far from there.

The courtyard should be covered and provided with fruits, flowers, and water; having installed the gods in the pavilions, a person should worship them with offerings. Vāsudeva is the god of all gods, the partaker of all, and the creator of those houses and other structures.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Temples, Liṅgas, Pavilions, and so forth," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 48.

Sūta said: I shall now describe briefly the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of all the deities. On an auspicious lunar day and other favorable times, the preceptor (guru) should perform the beautiful rite of consecration.
Together with the officiating priests, one should choose a preceptor from the Middle Country according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Vedic branch, or else by means of the *praṇava*.
One should offer water for the feet and the respectful oblation (arghya) with five or many items, as well as with finger-rings, garments, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
Having performed the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa), the Guru should then commence the rite; he should construct a pavilion ten cubits in size in front of the temple.
One should construct a pavilion twelve cubits in size, provided with sixteen pillars, and one should have an altar four cubits square made in the center, adorned with eight banners.
One should cause sand to be placed there from the bank at the confluence of rivers; it may be square, bow-shaped, circular, or lotus-shaped.
Starting from the east and proceeding in order, one should construct five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas); or alternatively, one may have all of these made square.
For the accomplishment of all desired aims through the performance of pacifying rites (*śāntikarma*), the preceptor (*ācārya*) should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) at the head of the deity.
Some desire [the mandala] in the northeast; having smeared the auspicious ground and having made four doors near the archways.
The archways, made of *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *bilva*, *pālāśa*, and *khadira* wood, shall be five cubits in height and adorned with cloth, flowers, and other ornaments.
One should bury one [image] in each of the four directions; at the eastern gate, however, [one should place] the lion-king, and at the southern [gate], the king of horses.
In the west, one named Gopati, and in the north, a tiger among gods; first, one should place [the deity] in the east with the mantra "agnim īle."
With the mantra "Īṣe tvā," he places the second [brick] in the south; with the mantra "Agnāyi," he places the third in the west.
With the mantra "śanno devī," one should place the fourth [offering] in the north; in the east it should be like a cloud, and in the southeast it should have the form of smoke.

In the southern direction she is indeed black in form, while in the southwestern direction she should be dark gray; in the western direction she is to be known as pale white, and in the northwestern direction she is yellow in color.
In the north, however, there is a banner of red color and Śukleśī; likewise, Bahurūpā is in the center, while Indravidyā is in the east.
One should worship Agni with the *saṃsupti* mantra, Yama with *yamonāga*, in the south; and with *rakṣohano vā* in the west and the north as well.
Then, having consecrated him with "Vāta," and with "Āpyāyasva" on the northern [side], and likewise with "Tam īśānam" on the southern, and with "Viṣṇornuka" in the center.
Then, two water-pots each should be placed near the arches, well-adorned with pairs of cloths and sandalwood paste and other offerings.

Then the guardians of the directions (dikpālas), consecrated with mantras of the primary colors and [offered] abundant flowers and canopies, are to be worshipped according to the ritual procedure seen in the scriptures.
One should recite "trātāram indra" with the *bhṛhat* meter, and "agnir mūrdhā" as another; "asmin vṛkṣe" and "itaḥ" are likewise prescribed, while "pracārī" is remembered as the final one.
Furthermore, having worshipped the directions with the mantras "kiṃcedadhātu," "ācatvābhitvā," and "eti ca," as well as with "imā rudra," the wise practitioner [should proceed].
The preceptor should place the materials for the fire sacrifice, along with their accessories, in the northwest; he should then install white conches prescribed by the scriptures upon his two eyes.
Objects attain purity through inspection; there is no doubt. Likewise, the heart and other limbs [of the ritual] are purified by the *vyāhṛtis* and the *praṇava*.
This is the ritual placement (nyāsa) for all weapons, which fulfills all desires; one should likewise prepare unbroken grains and a seat, consecrated with the weapon-mantra itself.

One should touch the articles prepared for the sacrificial pavilion with the *viṣṭara* [grass-bundle]; thereafter, one should scatter unbroken rice (*akṣata*) purified by the *astra-mantra* all around.
Then, starting from the direction of Śakra (the east) and extending as far as the domain of Īśāna (the northeast), he should scatter unbroken grains of rice and subsequently smear the pavilion.

The Guru should place the collection of mantras upon the arghya vessel along with perfumes and other offerings; he should then sprinkle the sacrificial pavilion with that water from the arghya vessel.
One should place the jar named after whichever deity’s consecration it is; one should worship it in the northeast, and the *vardhanī* vessel in the south with the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
The Guru should recite the Praṇava over all these—the *kalaśa*, the *vardhanī*, the planets, and likewise Vāstoṣpati—while they are upon their seats.
The preceptor should worship the flask, which has a neck adorned with thread, contains the essence of jewels, is wrapped in a pair of cloths, and is smeared with all medicinal herbs and fragrances.
The deity is to be worshipped in the water-pot (kalaśa), and the supreme cloth in the *vardhanī* vessel; one should then cause the water-pot, joined with the *vardhanī*, to be circumambulated.
Then, sprinkling with a stream from the *vardhanī* while holding it in front, one should worship the *vardhanī* jar and worship the deity upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
Having invoked the jar in the northwest with the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā," and having [invoked] Sadgaṇa, the wise man should recite the Vāstoṣpati hymn in the northeast corner for the deity.
With the mantra "vāstoṣpate," for the pacification of defects in the site, one should offer a bali-oblation to the deity Gaṇa, who is present to the east of the water-pot.
The wise man should recite the Vidyās and perform the touching [of the site], and he should spread out a covering of green grass and *kuśa* grass with the mantra "yoge-yoge."

Then the preceptor, acting as the guru, together with the officiating priests, [performed the rite] upon the bathing throne amidst various Vedic chants and auspicious proclamations of "Punyaham" and "Jaya."
