Having placed the deity upon the Brahma-chariot, the twice-born ones then install it; the Guru should bring the pedestal from the northeast and set it down within the pavilion.

Then, having bathed with water made from threads and bark, he should perform the extraction of the marks after bathing [the image] while accompanied by the sounding of musical instruments and the like.
One should apply honey and ghee mixed together to his eyes using a golden probe, either in a bronze or copper vessel.
One should perform the opening of the eyes with the mantra "agnir jyotiḥ"; while the ritual characteristics are being performed, the consecrator (sthāpaka) should utter a single name.
One should perform a cooling treatment on the eyes with this mantra, "imaṃ me gaṅge"; one should apply earth from an anthill with the mantra, "agnirmūrdhā".
One should offer the five decoctions of bilva, udumbara, aśvattha, vaṭa, and palāśa with the mantra "yajñā yajñā."
Then one should bathe [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and with [herbs] such as sahadevī; namely, sahadevī, balā, śatamūlī, and śatāvarī.
With the mantra "yā oṣadhī," one should perform a bath with water and medicinal herbs, including *kumārī*, *guḍūcī*, *siṃhī*, and likewise *vyāghrī*.
The ritual bath with fruits is prescribed by means of the mantra "yāḥ phalinī," and the wise should perform the application of unguents by means of the mantra "drupadādiva."
And having placed [the substances] in the jars in sequence, beginning from the north, [one should place] gems, grains, and the herb śatapuṣpikā.
And having placed the four oceans in the four directions—milk, curd, the ocean of milk, and likewise the ocean of clarified butter.
One should consecrate the water-pot with the mantras "āpyāyasva," "dadhikrāvṇaḥ," "yā oṣadhīḥ," and "tejo 'si."
One should bathe [the deity] again with four jars known as "oceans"; once bathed and well-attired, incense of guggulu should be offered.
For the consecration, one should place the various sacred fords (tīrthas) within the jars—those sacred fords which exist upon the earth, as well as the rivers and the oceans.
One should consecrate the water-jar with the mantra beginning "yā oṣadhī"; whoever bathes with that water shall be liberated from all sins.

Having consecrated [the image] with the oceans, one should then again offer the arghya; and with the mantra "Gandhadvārām," one should apply fragrance and perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with Vedic mantras.
Having obtained garments prescribed by one's own scriptures, he should lead [the bride] to the auspicious pavilion with the mantra beginning "yuvam vastra" and "kavihāva."
One should settle [the deity] upon the bed with the mantra *śambhavāya*, and one should perform the rite of the manifest and the unmanifest with the mantra *viśvataścakṣuḥ*.

Having established oneself in the supreme reality, one should perform the ritual placement of the mantra (*mantranyāsa*); the mantra and its placement prescribed by one's own scripture are thus declared for that occasion.
Having covered [the image] with a cloth, it should be worshipped according to its own nature; one should cause the offerings to be presented at the base of the feet in accordance with the scriptures.
Then, one should place the water-pot, accompanied by the syllable Om (praṇava), wrapped in a pair of cloths and containing gold, upon the head.
Then, having stood near the sacrificial pit, the preceptor should perform the installation of the fire with mantras prescribed in his own scripture or those declared in the Vedas.
The reciter of the Bahvṛca-veda should first mutter the Śrīsūkta, the Pāvamānī hymns, the Vāsadāmya, the Savājin, the Vṛṣākapi, and the Mitra hymns from the east.
The Adhvaryu priest should mutter, on the southern side, the Rudra-hymn, the Puruṣasūkta, the Ślokādhyāya, the Śukriya, the Brahmāṇa, and the Pitṛmaitra.
A Chāndoga should mutter in the west the Veda-vrata, the Vāmadevya, the Jyeṣṭhasāman, the Rathantara, and the Bheruṇḍa Sāmans.
One should recite the Atharvaśiras, the Kumbhasūkta of the Atharvans, the Nīlarudras, the Maitra, and the Atharva-uttara.
The preceptor, having especially sprinkled the sacrificial pit with the Astra-mantra, [should place the offering] in a copper vessel, a clay bowl, or even according to his means.
Having brought Jātavedas, one should seat him in front; one should kindle the fire with the Astra-mantra and encircle it with the Kavaca-mantra.
After consecrating that [substance] as nectar with all the mantras, the preceptor should then take the vessel with both hands and whirl it around the sacrificial pit.
One should project the supreme splendor by means of the Vaiṣṇava yoga; one should place the Brahman priest to the south and the Praṇītā vessel to the north.
Then, with either a common mantra or one prescribed in his own Sūtra, he should place the enclosing sticks together with the grass seats in each of the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and Īśāna are to be worshipped with common offerings; one should place the fire upon darbha grass and encircle it with darbha grass.
Touched with water from *darbha* grass, one is purified even if devoid of mantras; [the grass should be] unbroken, with tips pointing eastward, northward, and westward.
Fire, when encircled by expanded [mantras], will itself come into presence; this is the rite prescribed for the protection of the fire by one who knows the mantras.

Some teachers maintain that immediately after the birth-rite (jātakarman) and other ceremonies, one should prepare the purifier (pavitra) and then perform the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya).

Then the preceptor, having gazed upon the consecrated clarified butter used for the lustration rite, should observe the procedure up to the portioning and sprinkling of the *ājya* for the sake of its successful accomplishment.

Immediately thereafter, having offered five sets of five oblations of clarified butter, [he should perform the rites] beginning with the impregnation ceremony (garbhādhāna) up until the tonsure ceremony (godānika).

One should perform the oblation with the mantras prescribed by one's own scripture and with the *praṇava*; then, having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should proceed from the full to the full.
Thus kindled, the fire grants success in all ritual actions; having worshipped the fire, one should then cause it to dwell within the sacrificial pits.

With the respective mantras of Indra and the others, one should likewise offer a hundred oblations for each; at the end of the hundred [oblations], one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for all of them.
Then the Hotṛ priest should place his own oblation into the clarified butter within that jar, as well as the deities, the mantras, and likewise Jātavedas.
Having placed oneself on one side, one should then cause the full [offering] to be given; having drawn it out, the preceptor should offer the bali-oblation to the guardians of the directions.
Through the application of spirits, gods, and nāgas, sesame seeds and sacrificial fuel are known as the two types of substances for the fire oblation (homa).
Clarified butter (ājya) is the auxiliary for those two; it is primary in the case of the two eyes. The Puruṣasūkta is used on the left, while the Rudra-hymn is used on the right.
The Jyeṣṭhasāman and the Bhāruṇḍa [are recited] in the west with "I lead him away"; the great mantra of Nīlarudra and the Kumbhasūkta of the Atharvans [are used].
Having offered one thousand oblations for each, one should assign a deity to the head; likewise in the middle and in the feet, and again with the final full oblation.
One should offer oblations at the locations of the head and enter [the body] in due order, either with the initial mantras of the Vedas, or with mantras consisting of the names of the deities.
Or those twice-born ones may perform it with the mantras prescribed in their own scriptures, or with the Gāyatrī; or the preceptor may do so with the Gāyatrī, or with the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava.
Having thus performed the rite of fire-offering (homa), the preceptor should place the mantras: "agnim īḷe" at the two feet, and "iṣetvaḥ" situated at the two ankles.

One should place [the mantra] "O Agni, come hither" on the two shanks; "May the goddesses be gracious to us" on the two knees; the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] on the two thighs; and the Svātina [mantra] on the bellies.
One should place "For long life" (dīrghāyuṣṭvāya) in the heart, "Obeisance to Śrī" (śrīśca te) on the throat, "Indra the protector" (trātāram indram) on the chest, and "Tryambaka" with the two eyes.

Likewise, when [the mark] reaches the crown of the head, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa); then one should cause the deity to rise with [the mantra]: "Arise, O Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati)!"

Having performed the circumambulation of the temples with the sounds of the Vedas and the *puṇyāha* proclamation, and having touched the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), the knower of mantras [should recite] the mantra "devasya tvā."
Then, together with the guardians of the directions, gems, minerals, medicinal herbs, and perfected metals and seeds, one should subsequently install the deity.
One should not place the deity within the womb, nor should one abandon the womb; rather, by avoiding the slight and the middle [extremes], that [placement] removes all defects.
One should bring a little more, even just the size of a sesame husk, with the mantra: "Oṃ, be firm, be auspicious; salutations, salutations to the progeny."
O daughter of Prajāpati, the Guru should place [the mantra] "devasya tvā savituḥ vaḥ" upon the six [fingers], consisting of the principles (tattva), letters (varṇa), and measures (kalā).

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the six [limbs], one should consecrate the *siddhārtha* [grains] with the *dhruva-mantras*; then, one should bathe the well-established [deity] with the *sampāta* water from the jar.
One should worship with lamps, incense, fragrant scents, and food offerings; having offered the *arghya* and paid homage, one should then ask the deity for forgiveness.
A bowl, a pair of garments, an umbrella, as well as a divine ring, and likewise a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's capacity, should be given to the officiating priests.
Thereafter, the sacrificer, being composed in mind, should offer the fourth oblation; having offered one hundred oblations, he should then cause the final full-oblation (pūrṇāhuti) to be presented.
Having gone outside, the preceptor should offer an oblation to the guardians of the directions; with flowers in hand, the preceptor should dismiss them, saying, "Forgive me."
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, one should give a tawny cow to the preceptor, as well as a fly-whisk, a crown, earrings, an umbrella, armlets, and a waist-belt.

One should provide a fan, village-cloths and the like, along with furnishings, a well-adorned pavilion, and a grand feast; by doing so, the patron becomes one who has fulfilled his duty and shall be liberated through the grace of the consecrator.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Installation of Deities and Other Rites," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

The section on installation is complete. Brahmā said: Hari, the creator of the primary creation and so forth, is to be worshipped by Svāyambhuva Manu and others, as well as by Brahmins and the other castes, each according to their own duty (*svadharma*). O Vyāsa, listen now to that dharma.
Sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, receiving gifts, teaching, and studying—these are the six duties of the best of the twice-born.
Giving, study, and sacrifice are the duties of the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya; for the Vaiśya, the duty of agriculture is likewise commended.

For Śūdras, the means of accomplishing dharma is solely the service of the twice-born; likewise, their livelihood consists of manual crafts, and according to dharma, they may also perform the *pākayajña* sacrifice.
Begging for alms, service to the teacher, Vedic study, the performance of twilight rituals, and the tending of the sacred fire—this is the duty of the religious student (brahmacārin).

Furthermore, all the stages of life (āśramas) are twofold and fourfold: the student (brahmacārin) is either the temporary student (upakurvāṇa) or the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) who is intent upon Brahman.
He who, having studied the Vedas according to the prescribed rules, enters the stage of the householder, is to be known as an *upakurvāṇaka*; he who remains until death is a *naiṣṭhika*.
Tending the sacred fires, service to guests, sacrifice, charity, and worship of the gods—this, O best of the twice-born, is the duty of the householder in brief.
The householder is of two kinds: the indifferent and the practitioner. That householder who is engaged in the maintenance of his family is the practitioner.
Having discharged the three debts and renounced wife, wealth, and the like, he who wanders alone and indifferent is one intent on liberation (maukṣika).
Subsisting on roots and fruits on the ground, the study of sacred texts, austerity, and the equitable distribution [of what one has]—this is the dharma of those dwelling in the forest.
He who performs austerity in the forest, sacrifices to the gods, offers oblations, and is devoted to the study of the Vedas is a forest-dweller, the best among ascetics.
He who, emaciated by austerity, becomes intent upon meditation, should indeed be known as a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) established in the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha).
One who is constantly devoted to the practice of yoga, desiring to ascend, with senses conquered, and who lives for the sake of knowledge while subsisting on alms, is called a *pārameṣṭhika*.
But he who delights only in the Self, who is eternally contented, a great sage, and perfectly endowed with self-control—he is called a yogi, a mendicant.
Alms-gathering, sacred learning, silence, austerity, and especially meditation, along with perfect knowledge and dispassion—this is considered the duty of a mendicant.
Some are renunciants of knowledge, others are renunciants of the Vedas, and some are renunciants of action; such is the threefold renunciation pertaining to the supreme state.
The yogin is to be known as threefold: the materialist, the warrior, and the third is declared to be the one in the final stage of life, who has fully established himself in the form of yoga.
The first cultivation pertains to the former [state], while the cultivation of non-difficulty pertains to liberation; the third is said to be the final cultivation, which belongs to the Supreme Lord.
From dharma liberation is born; from wealth desire is produced. Vedic action is twofold: that of worldly engagement and that of renunciation.
Knowledge was first withdrawn, and then it was set in motion by Agni and the gods; likewise, forgiveness, self-restraint, compassion, generosity, non-greed, and practice [were restored].
Straightforwardness, freedom from envy, as well as visiting sacred fords; truthfulness, contentment, faith, and likewise restraint of the senses.
Worship of the deities, especially the honoring of Brahmins; non-violence, speaking kindly, absence of backbiting, and lack of harshness.
I shall now declare these duties pertaining to the stages of life for the four castes: the station of Prajāpati is ordained for Brāhmaṇas who perform their prescribed rites.
The station of Indra belongs to Kṣatriyas who do not flee in battles; the station of the Maruts belongs to Vaiśyas who follow their own dharma.
The Gāndharva [marriage] is for those of the Śūdra caste who are engaged in service, as well as for the eighty-eight thousand sages of perpetual celibacy.

The very abode that is remembered for them is indeed the abode of those dwelling in the forest (the *guruvāsins*); and that which is the abode of the Seven Sages (*saptarṣis*) is truly the abode of the forest-dwellers (*vanaukasas*).
For ascetics who have controlled their minds, for renunciants whose vital energy is drawn upward, that state is Brahman-bliss, from which the sage does not return.
The abode of the nectar of the yogis, known as the void, is the supreme syllable; it is the bliss of the Lord, from which a man who is liberated does not return.
Listen briefly to how liberation arises from the knowledge of the eight limbs: the five restraints (yamas) begin with non-violence; non-violence is the non-injury of living beings.

Truthful speech that is beneficial to living beings, non-stealing which is supreme non-attachment to one's own property, celibacy which is freedom from sexual intercourse, and non-possession which is the renunciation of everything.
The five observances (niyamas) begin with truthfulness and are twofold: external and internal. They are purity, contentment, austerity, and restraint of the senses.
Recitation is the chanting of mantras; resolve is the worship of Hari; the posture is said to be the lotus posture and others; breath control is the mastery over the vital air.

Meditation on the mantra is the *sagarbha* [type], while the opposite is indeed the *agarbhaka*. Thus it is described as being twofold or even threefold; and that which fills [the breath] is the *pūraka*.

Kumbhaka is so called because of its immobility, and recaka is so called because of the act of exhaling; thus, breath control is threefold. The light [breath] consists of twelve mātrās, while the next is twenty-four.
The best Pratyāhāra consists of thirty-six measures, as does Rodhana; Dhyāna is the contemplation of Brahman as the Self, while Dhāraṇā is the steadying of the mind.
The state of abiding in the thought "I am Brahman" is samādhi; it is the dwelling in Brahman. I am the Self, the Supreme Brahman, which is truth, knowledge, and infinite.
Brahman is consciousness and bliss; that alone is your true self. "I am Brahman," "I am Brahman"—bodiless and devoid of senses.

It is devoid of the ego, mind, intellect, the great principle (mahat), the I-maker (ahaṅkāra), and so forth; it is that very light which is associated with the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the rest.

"Constantly pure, awakened, liberated, true, blissful, and non-dual—He who is that Person in the Sun, He am I, indivisible. Meditating thus, a Brahmin shall be released from the bondage of worldly existence.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Duties of the Social Orders and Stages of Life," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: He who performs his daily rites day after day shall attain knowledge. Having risen during the Brāhma-muhūrta, he should contemplate dharma and artha.
When the time of dawn has arrived, the wise man, having performed his necessary duties, should meditate in his heart upon Hari, the imperishable bliss seated within a lotus.
One should bathe in pure rivers after performing purification according to the prescribed rule; by bathing in the morning, even those people who are doers of evil are purified.
Therefore, one should perform the morning bath with every effort; for they praise the morning bath, as it indeed brings about both visible and invisible benefits.
For saliva and other secretions constantly flow from one who has slept comfortably; therefore, one should not perform rituals without first bathing.
Misfortune, ill-fortune, bad dreams, and evil thoughts—all these sins are shaken off by bathing at dawn; of this there is no doubt.

It is traditionally taught that no ritual action for men is considered meritorious without bathing, especially in the case of fire offerings and the recitation of mantras; therefore, one should perform the bath.
In case of inability, however, a headless bath (without immersion) is prescribed for him; or else, wiping the body with a wet cloth is recorded as the bodily purification.
One should perform the six-limbed bath (ṣaḍaṅgasnāna), which is prescribed as consisting of the Brahma, Āgneya, Vāyavya, Divya, Vāruṇa, and Yaugika baths.
The *brāhma* purification consists of sprinkling water drops with *kuśa* grass while reciting mantras; the *āgneya* purification consists of shaking the body from head to foot while using ashes.
Indeed, bathing with the dust raised by cows is declared to be the supreme Vāyavya bath; that which is performed during rain accompanied by sunshine is called Divya.
The Vāruṇa bath consists of immersion in water; the Mānasa bath is the realization of the Self; and the Yaugika bath is declared to be the contemplation of Hari through yoga.
Known as the "Self-tirtha," it is frequented by those who discourse on Brahman; it is auspicious, produced from milk-bearing trees and originating from *mālatī* flowers.
For the purpose of cleaning the teeth, one should consume the tooth-stick made of *apāmārga*, *vilva*, or *karavīra* while facing either north or east.
Having washed and eaten, he should discard that [leavings] in a clean place with a concentrated mind; then, having bathed, he should gratify the gods, the sages, and the hosts of ancestors.

Having sipped water according to the rule, and having sipped water again while remaining silent, he should purify himself with *kuśa* grass blades moistened with drops of water, using the appropriate mantras.
With the *āpo hi ṣṭhā* verses, the *vyāhṛtis*, the *sāvitrī*, and the auspicious hymns to Varuṇa, as well as the *gāyatrī*—the mother of the Vedas—joined with the *oṃkāra* and the *vyāhṛtis*.

Having recited [the mantra], one should offer a handful of water toward the sun with the mind fixed on it; then, remaining well-composed, one should stand upon *darbha* grass whose tips point eastward.

"Having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should then meditate upon Sandhyā; such is the Vedic revelation. That which is Sandhyā is the source of the universe, transcending illusion (māyā) and indeed partless (niṣkalā)."
The wise man, having meditated upon the sovereign, absolute Śakti who arises from the three principles—red, white, and black—should indeed recite the Gāyatrī.
A Brahmin should always perform the twilight worship (sandhyopāsana) facing the east; one who neglects the twilight worship is perpetually impure and unfit for all ritual acts.
Whatever else one may do, one shall not partake of its fruit; for the virtuous Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas are those whose minds are focused on nothing else.
O best of the twice-born, those who have duly worshipped at the twilight devotions attain the supreme goal; yet if such a person exerts effort elsewhere in matters of religious duty, he fails.
Having abandoned the salutation at the twilight, he goes to ten thousand hells; therefore, one should perform the twilight worship with every effort.
By him, the supreme deity whose body is yoga should be worshipped constantly for a period of no more than a thousand [days], with a hundred as the medium, and ten as the minimum.
A wise man, being self-restrained and pure, should recite the Gāyatrī facing the east; then, with a concentrated mind, he should worship the sun as it rises.
Having performed worship with various solar mantras known as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, he approached the Great Yoga, the Sun, the God of gods.
Having been consecrated with the mantra, one should prostrate upon the ground with the head, [reciting]: "Oṃ, to Khakholka, the peaceful one, the cause of the three causes."
I offer myself to you; salutations to you whose form is knowledge! You alone are the supreme Brahman, water, light, essence, and the immortal.
"Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, you are the syllable Om, the All, the eternal Rudra. Having indeed recited this supreme hymn, the Heart of the Sun.
In the morning and at midday, one should pay homage to the Sun; then, having returned home, the Brahmin should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the prescribed rule.
Having kindled the fire according to the prescribed rules, one should offer oblations into Jātavedas; the officiating priest, the son, the wife, the disciple, or even a uterine brother may do so.
Having obtained specific permission, one should perform the oblation according to the rules; for any rite performed without the mantra yields no fruit, neither in this world nor in the next.
One should pay homage to the deities and present offerings; one should also attend upon the guru and practice what is beneficial for him.

Thereafter, the twice-born should diligently engage in the study of the Vedas according to his capacity; he should recite them, teach them to disciples, retain them in memory, and indeed reflect upon them.
And the best of the twice-born should study the treatises on dharma and other subjects, as well as the Vedic expositions and all the auxiliary sciences of the Vedas in their entirety.
Then, for the sake of his family's welfare, the twice-born man should employ the Lord through various means to accomplish diverse goals and ensure the attainment of security and well-being.
Then, at the time of midday, one should fetch earth for the purpose of bathing, as well as flowers, unbroken grains of rice, sesame seeds, kusha grass, and pure cow dung.
One should perform one's bath in rivers, natural pools, tanks, and lakes, but never at all in those belonging to others.
Without having removed five lumps of earth, one always defiles the bath; the head should be washed with one lump of earth, and likewise the area above the navel with two.
The lower part [of the feet] should be washed with three [applications of clay], and the feet likewise with six; the clay prescribed should be the size of a large myrobalan fruit.

Having applied cow dung to his limbs according to the prescribed measure, he should then wash himself, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to rule, and subsequently bathe with a concentrated mind.

Having smeared [the ground] while standing on the bank, he should consecrate the water with mantras using those very same insignia (liṅgas), or with auspicious Varuṇa-mantras corresponding to those insignia.
At the time of bathing, one should remember Viṣṇu, for water is Nārāyaṇa; having looked at the sun while reciting the syllable Om, one should immerse oneself three times in the body of water.
Having sipped water once, the knower of mantras should sip again with this mantra: "You move within all beings, dwelling in the secret cave, facing in every direction."

"You are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ*-call, you are the waters, light, essence, and immortality. Or, one may recite the *drupadā* verse three times, accompanied by the *vyāhṛtis* and the *praṇava*.
A wise man should either recite the Sāvitrī or likewise the Aghamarṣaṇa; thereafter, he should perform the sprinkling with the verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ."
Then, with the *vyāhṛtis*, one should likewise cause these waters to flow; thereafter, the consecrated water [should be offered] with the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
Submerged underwater and facing downward, one should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, or the Drupadā verse, or the Sāvitrī, or the verse beginning with "tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam."
Or one may repeat the Praṇava, the God of gods, and meditate upon Hari; having taken water in the hand and performed the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) after reciting [the mantra].
Having sprinkled that water upon his head, he is liberated from all sins; having performed the twilight devotions and sipped water for purification, he should constantly remember the Lord.

Then, one should stand facing the sun with hands joined in añjali and filled with upward-pointing flowers; having cast them [toward the sun], one should gaze at the deity as he rises, for it is not possible [to look directly].
One should [worship] with the mantras "ud u tyam," "citram," "taccakṣuḥ," and especially with the verse "haṃsaḥ śuciṣad" and the Sāvitrī.
Then one should recite the Gāyatrī with other solar and Vedic mantras, and subsequently various other mantras while seated on a grass mat with the tips pointing eastward.
Standing and gazing at the sun, one should perform the recitation with a concentrated mind, using beads made of crystal, lotus seeds, rudrākṣa, or those produced from the putrajīva tree.
However, it is traditionally taught that an inner garment (antarakṣālā) should be worn there; if one is indeed wearing wet clothes, one should perform the rite while standing in the midst of water.
Otherwise, being composed on pure ground upon *darbha* grass, having circumambulated clockwise and then bowed down to the earth;

Having sipped water according to the scriptures, one should perform the private recitation (svādhyāya) according to one's ability; thereafter, one should satiate the gods, the sages, and the hosts of ancestors.
Having uttered the syllable *Oṃ* at the beginning and "I satiate" (*tarpayāmi*) at the end, one should satisfy the gods and the brahminical seers with water and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
One should worship the ancestors, the gods, and the sages with devotion, according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Sūtra.

The wise man should satisfy the celestial sages and the ancestors with handfuls of water; he should wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder for the gods, and around the neck for the libation to the sages.

But for the ancestral rite, O Bhārata, he should wear the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) and use that same part of the hand as the tīrtha; having wrung out his bathing garment and sipped water, he should remain silent.
One should worship the gods with their own respective mantras using flowers, leaves, and likewise water—namely Brahmā, Śaṅkara, Sūrya, and likewise Madhusūdana.
O Hara, being free from anger, one should also offer flowers and other oblations with devotion to whatever other deities one desires, using the Puruṣa Sūkta.
Indeed, all the deities are water; by him they have been properly worshipped when he, concentrated on the water, meditates upon the Deity preceded by the syllable Om (praṇava).
One should indeed place the sacrificial ladles individually with a salutation; for no Vedic ritual action exists that is devoid of worship.
Therefore, one should hold Hari in the mind there—at the beginning, middle, and end—by means of the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ" and the Puruṣa Sūkta.
And with his mind fixed on the supreme self, being tranquil, he should offer himself to Viṣṇu of stainless luster by means of the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ".

Having bathed with his head uncovered and having worshipped Hari in the Puṣpaka chariot, he should perform the five sacrifices: the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice to humans, and likewise the sacrifice to Brahman.

If it were performed before the libation (tarpaṇa), how could the sacrifice to humans (manuṣyayajña) take place? Having indeed performed the sacrifice to humans, one should then practice the private recitation of the Vedas (svādhyāya).

The Vaiśvadeva sacrifice must be performed; that is traditionally known as the devayajña (sacrifice to the gods). That which is this offering (bali) to all beings is to be understood as the bhūtayajña (sacrifice to the spirits).
The best of the twice-born should give food upon the ground outside for dogs, for those who cook dogs (outcastes), for those who have fallen from their caste, and likewise for birds.

O best of men, one should feed even a single Brahmin with the ancestors in mind; that daily śrāddha, intended for the ancestors, is a sacrifice to the manes (pitṛyajña) that bestows a favorable rebirth.
Or, having set aside some food according to his ability, being composed in mind, he should present it to a twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Vedas.
One should always honor the guest, bow down to, and worship the twice-born who is tranquil with one's mind, speech, and actions, welcoming them into one's own home.
They say that "bhikṣā" (alms) is a mouthful of food; four times that is a "puṣkala"; and four times a puṣkala is called an "hantakāra."
A guest should indeed be waited upon personally for as long as it takes to milk a cow; furthermore, one should honor guests who have arrived according to one's ability.
One should indeed give alms according to the rule to a mendicant who is a student of sacred knowledge; free from greed, one should give food to those in need according to one's ability.

Restrained in speech and without disparaging the food, he eats together with his kinsmen; yet, O best of the twice-born, a twice-born man who has not performed the five great sacrifices [is not truly so].

If that deluded soul eats [forbidden food], he goes to the womb of an animal; therefore, one should daily practice the study of the Vedas according to one's ability and be capable of performing the great sacrifices.
Likewise, the worship of the gods quickly destroys sins; yet he who, out of delusion or laziness, fails to perform the worship of the deities [incurs sin].
He who eats [thus] goes to the hells and is born indeed among swine; I shall now fully declare impurity—he who is thus impure is always a sinner.
Impurity arises from association, and purification comes from avoiding such association; all wise Brahmins declare that impurity lasts for ten days.
O best of the twice-born, among Brahmins, in the event of deaths or births, purification is immediate until the eruption of teeth; until the tonsure ceremony, it lasts for one night.
For three nights following the initiation ceremony, and ten nights thereafter; for a Kṣatriya, it is twelve days, and for a Vaiśya, ten or five days.
A Śūdra shall indeed be purified in one month; for ascetics (yatins), there is no sin. In cases of miscarriage, purification is achieved in as many nights as there are months [of gestation].
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "Description of Daily Duties and Impurity," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the unsurpassed dharma of giving (dāna), which is the bestowal of wealth with faith upon a worthy recipient.

Generosity, as taught by those who know it, bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; one should acquire wealth through righteous means, for that is the source of the fruits of giving and enjoyment.

They say that teaching and officiating at sacrifices are the livelihood [of a Brahmin], as is the acceptance of gifts; however, one following the livelihood of a Kshatriya should avoid usury, agriculture, and trade.
That which is given to worthy recipients is proclaimed as "giving" (dāna). Giving is said to be of four types: constant, occasional, for a specific desire, and pure.
Whatever is given day after day to a non-benefactor—a Brāhmaṇa, moreover—constantly, without aiming for any fruit; |||
That which is given into the hands of the learned for the pacification of sin is designated as occasional (naimittika) giving, as practiced by the virtuous.
That gift which is given for the sake of offspring, victory, sovereignty, or heaven is declared as "kāmya" (desire-based) by the sages who contemplate dharma.
When a gift is bestowed upon those who know Brahman for the sake of pleasing the Lord, with a mind endowed with goodness, that gift is stainless and auspicious.
He who gives land covered with sugarcane, barley, wheat, and rice to one learned in the Vedas is not born again.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to the gift of land; by giving knowledge to a Brahmin, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
One should give alms every day with faith to a celibate student; being liberated from all sins, one shall attain the abode of Brahman.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, a wise man, having fasted, should honor seven or five Brahmins with honey, sesame seeds, and ghee.
Having honored [the deity] with perfumes and other offerings, one should cause [the text] to be recited or recite it oneself, saying, "May Dharmarāja be pleased," according to what is in one's mind.
Whatever sin has been committed throughout one's entire life perishes at that very moment by placing sesame seeds upon a black antelope skin, together with gold, honey, and clarified butter.
He who gives ghee, food, and water to a Brahmin, especially on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, overcomes all evil deeds.
Having instructed the King of Dharma, he is released from fear; by fasting on the twelfth day and worshipping Viṣṇu, one destroys all sin.
A man who desires to propitiate whichever deity he wishes to worship certainly becomes liberated from all sins.
One desiring progeny should always worship the Brāhmaṇas with gifts, feed women and the gods, and indeed constantly worship Purandara.
One desiring spiritual luster should worship the Brāhmaṇas through their devotion to the Veda; one desiring health, the Sun; and one desiring wealth, the Fire-god.
One who desires the success of their actions should indeed worship Vināyaka; one who desires enjoyments should worship the Moon, and one who desires strength should worship the Wind.
One desiring liberation from the entire cycle of worldly existence should worship Hari with diligent effort; whether free from desire or possessing all desires, one should indeed honor Gadādhara.
The giver of water obtains satisfaction; the giver of food, imperishable happiness; the giver of sesame seeds, desired offspring; and the giver of a lamp, excellent vision.
The giver of land obtains everything; the giver of gold, long life; the giver of a house, the finest dwellings; and the giver of silver, supreme beauty.

The giver of clothing attains the same world as the Moon; the giver of horses attains the same world as the Aśvins; the giver of a bull attains abundant prosperity; and the giver of a cow attains the realm of the Sun.
The giver of a vehicle and a bed obtains a wife; the giver of fearlessness obtains sovereignty; the giver of grain obtains eternal happiness; and the giver of the Veda obtains the eternal Brahman.
One who bestows knowledge upon those learned in the Vedas is glorified in the heavenly world; by providing fodder for cows, one is liberated from all sins.
By the provision of fuel, a man’s fire becomes kindled; likewise, medicine, oil, and food are provided for the pacification of a sick person's disease.
One who gives [food] becomes free from disease, happy, and long-lived; likewise, one avoids the path of the Forest of Sword-leaves, which is lined with razor edges.
A man who gives an umbrella and sandals crosses over even fierce heat; whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is dear to him in his home [should be given].

One who desires that very gift to become inexhaustible should give it to one endowed with those respective qualities on the solstices, at the equinoxes, and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
What is given during times such as the solstices becomes inexhaustible, especially at sacred fords like Prayāga and Gayā.
There exists no dharma superior to the dharma of giving for living beings; therefore, by one desiring heaven, long life, and prosperity, and for the pacification of evil, giving should be practiced.
But that sinful man who, out of delusion, prevents cows, Brahmins, fire, or deities from being given to them, shall go to a womb among the animals.
But he who does not provide food during a time of famine, while Brahmins are dying, is a slayer of a Brahmin and is censured.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Duties of Giving," in the section on Conduct (*Ācārakāṇḍa*), within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Brahmā said: O twice-born ones, hereafter I shall proclaim the rules for expiation (*prāyaścitta*). [The four great sins are: the killer of a Brāhmaṇa, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and the violator of the Guru’s bed.
These five are the great sinners (pātakin), and the fifth is one who associates with them; the gods have declared that minor sins (upapāpa) include the killing of a cow and so forth.
A killer of a Brahmin shall dwell in the forest for twelve years, having built a hut; or else, he may practice fasting unto death or even throw himself from a mountain precipice.
For the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow, one should either enter a blazing fire or enter the water oneself, even at the cost of completely relinquishing one's life.
By giving food to a learned man, one removes the sin of killing a Brahmin; or, by bathing at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice, a twice-born man is liberated.
Or one should cause all one's possessions to be given to a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas at the world-renowned confluence of the river Sarasvatī.
A twice-born man who has bathed at the three daily junctures, fasted for three nights, and bathed at Setubandha while pure, is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Having bathed at Kapālamocana and likewise in Vārāṇasī, the best of the twice-born who has drunk liquor—having drunk liquor that is fire-colored—[is purified].
By drinking milk, ghee, or cow urine, one is liberated from that sin; a thief of gold is released from guilt when struck with a mace by kings.
Clad in bark garments, a twice-born man who has violated his teacher's wife out of lust for her shall perform the vow for killing a Brahmin in the forest.
One who has approached the wife of his guru shall embrace a red-hot, glowing image made of black iron; and those who have approached the wives of their gurus shall perform the vow of Brahmahatyā.
Or, that twice-born man who associates with one who has fallen from his caste should perform five or four Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
To remove that evil, he should perform the very same vow for that [offense]; or else, being vigilant, he should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance for one year.
The gift of all one's possessions according to the prescribed rule purifies all sins; likewise, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance and the Atikṛcchra performed according to the rule do the same.
Traveling to sacred fields such as Gayā and other sites is destructive of sin; he who, having reached the lunar day of the new moon (amāvāsyā), propitiates Bhava [Śiva], [attains great merit].
Having fed the Brahmins, one is liberated from all sins; likewise, one who has fasted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight with a concentrated mind [is also purified].
To Yama, the King of Dharma, to Death, to the Ender, to Vaivasvata, to Time, and to the Destroyer of all beings.
Having bathed in a river during the forenoon, one should offer seven handfuls of water mixed with sesame seeds for each [deity]; thus, one is liberated from all sins.
One should practice celibacy, sleep on the ground, observe fasting, and worship the twice-born while performing these vows, remaining peaceful and with a restrained mind.
Having fasted on the sixth day of the bright fortnight, one who is composed in mind should worship the Sun-god on the seventh; he is liberated from all sins.
Having fasted on the eleventh day and worshipped Janārdana, one is liberated from great sins by fasting again on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight.
Austerity, recitation of mantras, visiting sacred fords, and the worship of gods and Brahmins at times such as solar and lunar eclipses destroy even the most grievous sins.
Even a man burdened with every sin, if he should give up his life at sacred fords according to the prescribed rules, is liberated from all transgressions.
Whether her husband be a slayer of a Brahmin, ungrateful, or defiled by a great sin, a woman shall deliver him by entering the fire together with him.
But for that woman who is devoted to her husband and eager to serve him, no sin exists either in this world or in the next.
Likewise, Rāma’s fortunate wife Sītā, the goddess renowned throughout the three worlds and daughter of the King of Daśārṇa, conquered the Lord of the Rākṣasas.
"One who has bathed at Phalgutīrtha and other such sites shall obtain the fruit of all proper conduct," so the Blessed Viṣṇu said to me in the past, O you of firm vows.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Expiations," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Having heard this, Brahmā spoke thus regarding the eight treasures of Hari: namely, Padma, Mahāpadma, Makara, and Kacchapa; [and Śaṅkha, Mukunda, Nanda, and Neela].
Mukunda, Kunda, Nīla, and Śaṅkha are the other treasures; these appear when prosperity is true. I shall now describe their essential nature.
A man marked by a lotus is born as one of the *sāttvika* type; such a person, whose essence is courtesy, engages in the accumulation of gold and other valuables.

One should fashion objects of silver and so forth and give them to ascetics, those who sacrifice to the gods, and others; one marked with the great lotus should give wealth and other gifts to a righteous person.
The two treasures, Padma and Mahāpadma, are remembered as being of the nature of *sattva*. [The former] is marked by a crocodile and is the collector of swords, arrows, spears, and other weapons.
One should give to one who is learned, cultivate friendship, and always maintain alliances with kings; for the sake of wealth, one may even go to destruction by an enemy or enter into battle.
The *makara* and the tortoise are indeed remembered as the two *nidhis* characterized by *tamas*; the female tortoise (*kacchapī*) neither trusts, nor enjoys, nor gives.
That treasure also makes a hoard upon the earth, yet it belongs to a single man; Rājyasamgrahī was recognized by Rājasena Mukunda.
Having enjoyed his pleasures, he should give to singers and to courtesans and the like; Nandin, composed of passion and darkness, shall be the support of the family.
When praised, he indeed becomes pleased; he acquires many wives, shows laxity toward former friends, and forms attachments with others.
Marked by the color blue and endowed with the splendor of *sattva*, one becomes a collector of clothing, grain, and other goods, and constructs ponds and similar works.

One should cause the construction of a triple-storeyed mansion, a treasure-chamber, and mango groves and the like; for one person, there shall be a conch-treasure, which he himself enjoys until the end of his wealth.
One who eats poor food, whose attendants do not wear fine garments, and who is intent only on nourishing himself—even if he possesses a conch shell—bestows it upon another man in vain.

Because they yield fruits of a mixed nature due to their being observed in a mixed manner, the form of the treasures has been described by Hari as well as by Hara and others; just as Hari spoke regarding the *Bhuvanakośa* and other works, so shall I speak.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Nine Treasures," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Hari said: Agnīdhra, Agnibāhu, Vapuṣmān, Dyutimān, Medhā, Medhātithi, Bhavya, Śabala, and Putra were his sons.
Jyotiṣmat was born as the tenth; these indeed were the sons of Priyavrata. Medhā, Agnibāhu, and Putra were the three who were devoted to yoga.
Those highly fortunate ones, remembering their past lives, desired to be freed from kingship; so the king divided the seven continents and bestowed them upon the seven.
The earth, extending for fifty crores of yojanas, has risen above the waters and stands like a boat upon the surface of a river.
O Hara, the islands named Jambū and Plakṣa, and another called Śālmala; then Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara is the seventh.
These continents are surrounded by seven oceans, equal [in number], consisting of salt water, sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and fresh water.
O Bull-bannered One, each continent and ocean is twice the size of the preceding one; Mount Meru is situated in Jambūdvīpa, extending for a hundred thousand yojanas.
Its height is eighty-four thousand yojanas; it enters sixteen thousand yojanas below [the surface] and is thirty-two thousand yojanas wide at its summit.
Below, extending for sixteen thousand [yojanas], it is shaped like a pericarp; to its south are the Himavat, Hemakūṭa, and Niṣadha mountains.
Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgin are the mountain ranges in the north; O Rudra, those eternal men who dwell in the regions beginning with Plakṣa reside there.
Furthermore, there was no condition of the [degenerate] ages for them at all; for nine sons were born to Agridhna, the lord of Jambūdvīpa.
Nābhi, Kimpuruṣa, Harivarṣa, Ilāvṛta, Ramya, the one called Hiraṇmaya, Kuru, and Bhadrāśva.
King Ketumāla gave those regions bearing their respective names to them; and from Nābhi and Merudevī, O Hara, a son named Ṛṣabha was born.
His son was named Bharata, who remained at Śālagrāma observing his vows; Sumati was the son of Bharata, and his son was Taijasa.
Indradyumna was his son, and from him Parameṣṭhin is remembered; Pratīhāra was his son, and Pratihartṛ was his offspring.
Suta was born from him; then Prastāra was his son, and Vibhu was the son of Prastāra. Pṛthu was his son, and Nakta was the son of Pṛthu; Gaya is recorded as the son of Nakta.
Nara was the son of Gaya; his son was Virāj Agata. From him was born the wise and highly resplendent Bhauvana, who was his son.
Tvaṣṭṛ was born from Tvaṣṭṛ, and Viraja was his son; Rajas was also his son. Śatajit was the son of Rajas, and Viṣvagjyotis is recorded as his son.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Lineage of Priyavrata Useful for the Description of the Cosmic Egg," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Hari said: O bull-bannered one, in the center is the region of Ilāvṛta; to the east is the wonderful Bhadrāśva; and to the southeast is the region of Hiraṇvān.
Beyond that, the region of Kimpuruṣa is recorded as being to the south of Meru; Bhārata is said to be to the south, and Hari is in the southwest.
In the west is Ketumāla, and Ramyaka is in the north-west; and in the north is the region of Kuru, which is filled with wish-fulfilling trees.
O Rudra, spiritual accomplishment is natural everywhere except in Bhārata; [this applies to] Indradvīpa, Kaśerumān, Tāmravarṇa, and Gabhastimān.
Nāgadvīpa, Kaṭāha, Siṃhala, and likewise Vāruṇa—this, however, is the ninth among them, an island surrounded by the ocean.
O Rudra, the Kirātas are to its east, the Yavanas are situated to its west, the Andhras are to the south, and the Turuṣkas are also to the north.
The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras dwell within it; so too do Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, and the Ṛkṣa mountain.
The Vindhya, the Pāriyātra, and seven other principal mountain ranges are here; as well as the Vedasmṛti, the Narmadā, the Varadā, the Surasā, and the Śivā.
The Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, Sarayū, Kāverī, Gomatī, as well as the Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Kṛṣṇaveṇī, and Mahānadī.
The Ketumāla, Tāmraparṇī, Candrabhāgā, Sarasvatī, Ṛṣikulyā, Kāverī, Mattagaṅgā, and Payasvinī.
The Vidarbha and Śatadrū rivers are auspicious and destroyers of sin; people from the Middle Country and other regions drink their waters.
The Pañcālas, Kurus, Matsyas, Yaudheyas along with the Paṭaccaras, the Kuntis, and the Śūrasenas are known as the people of Madhyadeśa.
O Bull-bannered One! The Pādmās, Sūtas, Māgadhas, Cedis, Kāśis, Videhas, and likewise the Kosalas are the people of the east.
The Kaliṅgas, Vaṅgas, Puṇḍras, Aṅgas, Vaidarbhas, and Mūlakas, as well as the regions situated within the Vindhyas, are recorded as being in the southeast.
The inhabitants of the kingdoms of Pulinda, Aśmaka, and Kīṃnara; the Karṇāṭas, Kambojas, and Ghaṇas, who dwell in the Deccan (Dakṣiṇāpatha).
The Ambaṣṭhas, Draviḍas, Lāṭas, Kāmbojas, Śakas with women’s faces, and those dwelling in Ānarta are to be known as being in the southwest of Yakṣiṇī.
The Strīrājyas, the Saindhavas, the Mlecchas, and likewise the Yavanas are to be known as being in the west, along with the Mathuras and the Naiṣadhas.
The Māṇḍavyas, Tuṣāras, Mūlikas, Aśvamukhas, Khaśas, Mahākeśas, and Mahānāsas are the regions in the north-west.
The Lambas, Mūṣakas, Stanapās, as well as the Madras, Gāndhāras, and Bāhlikas—the Mlecchas whose dwellings are on the Himālayas—resort to the northern direction.
The Trigartas, Nīlakolas, Ātas, Brahmaputras, along with the Taṅkaṇas, the Abhīṣāhas, and the Kāśmīras, are proclaimed as being situated to the north.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Cosmic Egg," in the section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Hari said: The seven sons of Medhātithi, the lord of Plakṣadvīpa, were as follows: the eldest was named Śāntabhava, and after him came Śiśira.
Sukhodaya, Nanda, Śiva, Kṣemaka, and Dhruva as the seventh—these indeed were the lords of Plakṣadvīpa.
Gomeda, Candra, Nārada, Dundubhi, Somaka, Sumanas, and the mountain Baibhrāja is the seventh here.
The Anutaptā, Śikhī, Vipāśā, Tridivā, Kramu, Amṛtā, and Sukṛtā—these seven rivers flow there.
The lord of Śālmaladvīpa is Vapuṣmān; his sons, who give their names to the regions, are Śveta, Harita, Jīmūta, and Rohita.
Vaidyuta, Mānasa, and Saprabha as the seventh; then Kumuda, Unnata, Droṇa, Mahiṣa, and Balāhaka.
Krauñca, Kakudmān—these indeed are the mountains; and these are the rivers: Yonitoyā, Vitṛṣṇā, Candrā, Śuklā, and Vimocanī.
Vidhṛti is remembered as the seventh among them; they are said to grant the pacification of sins. Now hear of the seven sons of Jyotiṣmān in Kuśadvīpa.
Udbhida, Veṇumān, Dvairatha, Lambana, Dhṛti, Prabhākara, and Kapila—these are the sequence of regions (varṣas) named after them.
Vidruma, Hemaśaila, Dyutimān, Puṣpavān, Kuśeśaya, Hari, and Mandarācala as the seventh.
Dhūtapāpā, Śivā, Pavitrā, Sanmati, Vidyudabhra, and Mahī—these others are all removers of every sin.
In Krauñcadvīpa, there were seven sons of the high-souled Dyutimat: Kuśala, Mandaga, Uṣṇa, Pīvara, and then Andhakāraka.
O Hara, Muni and Dundubhi were also among them; these seven were his sons: Krauñca, Vāmana, and the third was Andhakāraka.
Divāvṛt was the fifth, and another was Dundubhi Puṇḍarīkavat; Gaurī, Kumudvatī, Sandhyā, Rātri, and Manojava were also there.
Khyāti, Puṇḍarīkā, and these seven rivers of the regions [flow through Śākadvīpa]. From Bhavya, the lord of Śākadvīpa, seven sons were born.
Jalada, Kumāra, Sukumāra, Aruṇi, Baka, Kusumoda, Samodārki, and the seventh, Mahādruma.
Sukumārī, Kumārī, Nalinī, and Dhenukā; Ikṣu, Veṇukā, and Gabhastī as the seventh.
From Śabala and Puṣkareśa, Mahāvīra and Dhātaki came into being; and likewise, the Mānasottara mountain constitutes two regions.
It rises fifty thousand yojanas upward and is just as wide, being perfectly circular on all sides.
Puṣkara is surrounded by the ocean of sweet water; beyond the ocean of sweet water, the configuration of the world is seen.

Twice as large is the golden earth, devoid of all living beings; beyond that is the Lokāloka mountain, ten thousand yojanas in width; it is pervaded by darkness, and that darkness is enclosed within the shell of the cosmic egg.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Cosmic Egg," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Hari said: "O Bull-bannered Lord, the height of the earth is said to be seventy thousand [yojanas]. Each of the netherworlds (pātālas) is ten thousand [yojanas] deep."
Atala, Vitala, Nitala, Gabhastimat, the one called Mahātala, Sutala as the foremost, and Pātāla as the seventh.
It is black, white, reddish, yellow, sandy, rocky, and golden; furthermore, Daityas and serpents dwell there.
In the fierce Puṣkaradvīpa, however, there are hells; hear of them: Raurava, Sūkara, Rodha, Tāla, and likewise Vinaśana.
Mahājvāla, Taptakumbha, Lavaṇa, Vimohita, the one called Rudhira, Vaitaraṇī, Kṛmiśa, Kṛmibhojana, and Jana.
The Asipatravana, Kṛṣṇa, Nānābhakṣa, and the dreadful Dāruṇa; likewise the sinful Pūyavaha, Vahnijvāla, and Adhaḥśiras.
Saṃdaṃśa, Kṛṣṇasūtra, Tamaḥ, Avīci, Śvabhojana, Apratiṣṭha, and Uṣṇavīci are recorded as the hells.
O Rudra, those sinners who administer poison, weapons, or fire are cooked within them; indeed, the worlds of Bhūtas and others are situated one above the other.

O Rudra, that egg was enveloped by water, fire, air, and ether, as well as by the *bhūtādi* (the origin of the elements), and it was further encased by the Great Principle (*mahat*) and by *pradhāna*.
The egg is pervaded tenfold, and Nārāyaṇa resides therein.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Netherworlds and Hells within the Cosmic Egg," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Hari said: I shall describe the dimensions and configurations of the Sun and other celestial bodies; listen to me. The chariot of the Sun measures nine thousand *yojanas*.
O Bull-bannered One, its pole is likewise twice that length; it measures one and a half crores and seven additional hundred thousand [yojanas].
Its axle measures a yojana, and upon it is established a wheel with three naves, five spokes, and six rims, which is imperishable by nature.
The entire wheel of time, consisting of a year, is established upon it; the second axle of Vivasvat measures forty thousand [years].
But for the chariot of the bull-bannered god, O Lord, the measurement of the axle is five and a half cubits; this same measurement applies to both halves of the yoke.
The shorter axle of the chariot, which rests upon the support of the Pole Star (Dhruva), is equal in length to half that yoke; however, the second wheel is situated upon the axle on Mount Mānasa.
Gāyatrī, Bṛhatī, Uṣṇih, Jagatī, Triṣṭubh, Anuṣṭubh, and Paṅkti—these are said to be the meters that serve as the bay horses of the Sun.
Dhātṛ, Kratusthalā, Pulastya, Vāsuki, Rathakṛt the grāmaṇī, Heti, and Tumburu [are the presiding deities] in the month of Caitra.
Āryamā, Pulaha, Rathojas, Puñjikasthalā, Praheti, Kacchanīra, and Nārada were present in the month of Mādhava.
Mitra, Atri, Takṣaka, Rakṣas, Pauruṣeya, Menakā, Hāhā, and Rathasvana—these are stationed on the chariot of Bhānu in the Jyeṣṭhā constellation.
Varuṇa, Vasiṣṭha, Rambhā, Sahajanyā, Kuhū, Budha, Rathacitra, and Śukra dwell in the month known as Āṣāḍha.
Indra, Viśvāvasu, Srotas (Śrotra), Elāpatra, as well as Aṅgiras, Pramlocā, and Nabhas— these indeed reside in the month of Āṣāḍha, while the serpents reside in the month of Ārka (Jyeṣṭha).
Vivasvān, Ugrasena, Bhṛgu, Āpūraṇa, Anumlocā, Śaṅkhapāla, and Vyāghra were the [planets] in the month of Bhādrapada.
Pūṣan, Suruci, Dhātṛ, Gautama, Dhananjaya, Suseṇa, and another, as well as Dhṛtācī, dwell when the sun is in Āśvayuja.
Viśvāvasu, Bharadvāja, Parjanya, Airāvata, Viśvācī, Senajit,
and Āpa were the presiding deities in the month of Kārttika.
Aṃśu, Kāśyapa, Tārkṣya, Mahāpadma, Urvaśī, Citrasena, and Vidyunmārga are the presiding deities of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Kratu, Bharga, Urṇāyu, Sphūrja, Karkoṭaka, Ariṣṭanemi, and the other, Pūrvacitti—their wives are the Saras; these seven dwell in the solar orb during the month of Pauṣa.
Tvaṣṭṛ, Jamadagni, Kambala, Tilottamā, Brahmāpeta, Ṛtajit, and Dhṛtarāṣṭra as the seventh—these seven dwell in the solar orb during the month of Māgha.
In the month of Phālguna, Viṣṇu, Aśvatara, Rambhā, Sūryavarcas, Satyajit, Viśvāmitra, Rakṣas, and Yajñāpeta were indeed the presiding deities.
O Brahman, in the orb of the Sun, sages empowered by the potency of Viṣṇu praise the Sun, while Gandharvas sing before him.
The night-stalkers go along with the Apsarases dancing; the Pannagas carry [the chariot], and by the Yakṣas the reins are gathered.
Likewise, the Bālakhilyas sit surrounding him; Soma’s chariot has three wheels, and its horses have the luster of jasmine.
Joined on the left and right by ten [units], that chariot of the son of the Moon moves along, produced from the substances of mercury (*vārya*) and *yva-granthi*.
Yoked to eight tawny horses swift as the wind, he was equipped with a protective fender and a chassis, drawn by steeds born of the earth.
The great chariot of Śukra was likewise equipped with quivers and banners; the chariot of the son of Earth (Mangala) was also like molten gold.
The great chariot of Bhauma was also golden, glorious, and drawn by eight horses.
He was joined by eight horses, born from fire, as red as rubies, yoked to a golden chariot along with white steeds.
Bṛhaspati indeed remains for a year in each zodiac sign, his chariot yoked with dappled horses born from the sky.
Having mounted [his chariot], Śanaiścara, the slow-moving one, proceeds slowly; for Svarbhānu’s horses are eight in number, bee-black in hue, and they draw a grey chariot.
O Lord of Beings, O Śiva, once yoked, they carry [the chariot] without ceasing; likewise, the eight horses of Ketu’s chariot possess the speed of the wind.
Having the color of smoke from burning straw, and reddish like lac-dye, the islands, rivers, mountains, and oceans are the body of Lord Hari.

Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Cosmic Egg," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Now begins] the Jyotiḥśāstra (the Science of Astrology).
Sūta said: Having explained the measurement of the earth and the stellar sphere, Keśava, the giver of all, spoke this essence of Jyotiṣa consisting of four hundred thousand verses to Rudra.
Hari said: The Kṛttikās have Agni as their deity; the Rohiṇīs are remembered as belonging to Brahmā; the Ilvalās have Soma as their deity; and Ārdrā is declared to belong to Rudra.
Punarvasu likewise has Āditya as its deity; Tiṣya has Guru (Jupiter) as its deity; Aśleṣā has the serpents as its deities; and Maghā has the ancestors as its deities.
Bhaga and Aryaman are likewise associated with Pūrvaphalgunī and Uttaraphalgunī; Savitṛ is associated with Hastā, and Tvaṣṭṛ is proclaimed to be associated with Citrā.
The constellation Svātī is proclaimed to have Vāyu as its deity; Viśākhā, O Bull-bannered One, is said to have Indra and Agni as its deities.
Mṛgaśīrṣa is proclaimed as belonging to Maitra, Anurādhā to Śakra (Indra), and likewise, Mūla is declared by the knowers of such things to have Nirṛti as its deity.
Āṣāḍhā and Pūrvāṣāḍhā belong to the Waters; Uttarāṣāḍhā belongs to the Viśvedevas; Abhijit is declared to belong to Brahmā; and Śravaṇā is remembered as belonging to Viṣṇu.
Vāsava is likewise called Ṛkṣa by the wise; similarly, O Śiva, the constellation Śatabhiṣā is declared to belong to Varuṇa.
The constellation Āja is Pūrvabhādrapadā; likewise, Ahirbudhnya is Uttarabhādrapadā; Pauṣṇa is the asterism Revatī; and Aśvayuj is the deity of the horses.
The constellations Bharaṇī and likewise Yāmya (Ārdrā) have been declared as the deities of the lunar mansions; Brahmāṇī is established in the east on the ninth lunar day of the bright fortnight.
Māheśvarī is in the north on the second lunar day of the tenth fortnight, and Vārāhī is situated in the south on the fifth and the thirteenth lunar days.
On the sixth and the fourteenth [lunar days], Indrāṇī is situated in the west; on the seventh and the full moon day, Cāmuṇḍā is in the northwest.
On the eighth lunar day conjoined with the new moon, Mahālakṣmī resides in the northeast; on the eleventh and third lunar days, Vaiṣṇavī resides in the southeast.
On the twelfth and the fourth lunar days, as well as in the southwest, one should not undertake journeys and other activities while facing the Yoginī Kaumārī.
Aśvinī, Anurādhā, Revatī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Mūla, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Hastā, and likewise Jyeṣṭhā are said to be most auspicious for setting out on a journey.
The five constellations beginning with Hasta, as well as the three Uttaras, Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Puṣyā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Punarvasū.
The group of constellations beginning with Kṛttikā, Bharaṇī, Āśleṣā, Maghā, Mūla, and Viśākhā is traditionally held to be the most excellent for donning new garments.
Three [asterisms] are likewise proclaimed as being downward-facing; in these, one should avoid ponds, tanks, wells, land, and grass.
Digging up a temple, as well as digging for hidden treasure; the practice of astrology, the commencement of astronomical calculations, and entering into underground caverns.
O Bull-bannered One, one should perform [the rites] only when these other [asterisms] are situated below: Revatī, Aśvinī, Citrā, Svātī, Hastā, and Punarvasū.
Anurādhā, Mṛgaśirā, and Jyeṣṭhā—these are known as the side-facing [nakṣatras]. [Under them, there is] the taming of elephants, camels, horses, oxen, and buffaloes.
One may perform the sowing of seeds, as well as going and coming, and the setting in motion of wheels, machines, chariots, boats, and so forth.
One should also perform those actions that are prescribed for the [other] flanks during these [asterisms]: Rohiṇī, Ārdrā, Puṣya, Dhaniṣṭhā, and the three Uttaras.
Vāruṇa, Śravaṇa, and the nine [asterisms] facing upward are traditionally taught; under these, one should perform royal consecration and the binding of the turban.
One should cause all of these to be erected with their openings facing upwards; likewise, the fourth, sixth, eighth, and ninth [mudrās] are inauspicious.
The new moon, the full moon, the twelfth, and the fourteenth; the first day of the dark fortnight is excellent, as is the second day joined with the son of the Moon (Mercury).
The third [lunar day] is auspicious with the son of the Earth (Mars), and the fourth with Saturn; the fifth is auspicious with Jupiter, and the sixth with Mars and Venus.
The seventh [tithi] is auspicious with the son of Soma (Mercury); the eighth with Mars and the Sun; the ninth with the Moon and Venus;
and the tenth is auspicious with Jupiter.
On the eleventh day, Jupiter and Venus [are auspicious]; on the twelfth, Mercury; on the thirteenth, Venus and Mars; and the fourteenth is most excellent for Saturn.
The full moon day and the new moon day are also most auspicious when Jupiter is present; the sun burns the twelfth lunar day, and the moon burns the eleventh.
Mars shall burn the tenth period, and Mercury shall burn the ninth; Jupiter burns the eighth, and Venus shall burn the seventh.
The son of the Sun (Saturn) burns the sixth lunar day; indeed, there is no [inauspiciousness] regarding journeys and other activities on the first, ninth, fourteenth, and eighth days.
One should avoid setting out on a journey on Wednesday; likewise, one should avoid the sixth lunar day when the sun is in Aries or Cancer, and the eighth lunar day when it is in Virgo or Gemini.
The fourth lunar day is [inauspicious] in Taurus and Aquarius; the twelfth in Capricorn and Libra; the tenth in Scorpio and Leo; and the fourteenth in Sagittarius and Pisces.

These [asterisms] are burnt; indeed, men should not travel during them, as there will be suffering and other such misfortunes. The Sun is in the three Viśākhās, and the Moon is in the three Pūrvāṣāḍhās.
O Śiva, the triad of Dhaniṣṭhā is for Mars; the triad of Revatī is indeed for Mercury; the triad beginning with Rohiṇī is for Jupiter; and the triad of Puṣya is for Venus.
One should avoid the three Uttarā-phalgunī constellations on Saturdays; during these astrological conjunctions, calamities, death, disease, and the like may occur.
The Sun is in Mūla, the Moon in Śravaṇa, Mars in the latter Proṣṭhapadā, Mercury in Kṛttikā, and Jupiter in Punarvasu, O Rudra.
Pūrvaphalgunī with Venus and Svātī with Saturn—these are the Amṛta-yogas, which accomplish all undertakings.
What is the time for killing?
It is the time when the power [of the planets] is not weak; this should be known as the proper time by those expert in the science of time, starting from the lunar nodes (*parvan*) and so forth.

Having combined the letters and measures of the names of the woman and the man, if the remainder upon division by three is two, there is the destruction of the woman; if it is one or zero, it shall be for the man.
Five ghaṭikās are proclaimed for Viṣkambha, seven for Śūla, six for Gaṇḍa and Atigaṇḍa, and nine for Vyāghāta and Vajra.
On the days of Vyatīpāta, Parigha, and Vaidhṛti, one should avoid all ritual actions, for on these occasions death is indeed present.
Hasta and Ārdrā are auspicious for Jupiter; Anurādhā is auspicious for Mercury; Rohiṇī is excellent for Saturn; and Mṛgaśīrṣa is indeed auspicious for the Moon.
Revatī is most excellent when Venus is present, and Aśvinī is auspicious when Mars is present; indeed, these are the Siddhi-yogas that destroy all defects.
O bull-bannered Lord, Pūrvaphalgunī belongs to Bhārgava (Venus), Citrā to Soma (the Moon), Uttarāṣāḍhā to Bhauma (Mars), and Dhaniṣṭhā to Budha (Mercury).
O Rudra, Śatabhiṣā on Saturday, Rohiṇī on Friday, and Revatī on Saturday, O Śambhu—these are proclaimed as the Viṣa-yogas.
Puṣya, Punarvasu, Revatī together with Citrā, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, as well as Hasta, Aśvinī, and Mṛgaśiras.

A person should perform the birth rites and other ceremonies under the asterism Śatabhiṣā. O Rudra, Viśākhā, the three Uttaras, Maghā, Ārdrā, Bharaṇī, Āśleṣā, and Kṛttikā bring death upon one who sets out on a journey.

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Constellations, Their Deities, the *Dagdhayoga*, and Other Matters," in the section on Astrology (*Jyotiḥśāstra*) within the *Ācārakāṇḍa* of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Hari said: The period (*daśā*) for the Sun is known to be six years; for the Moon, it is recorded as fifteen; for Mars, it is eight; and for Mercury, it is recorded by the wise as seventeen.
Ten years are to be known for Saturn, nineteen for Jupiter, twelve years for Rāhu, and twenty-one for Venus.
The period of the Sun brings about suffering and causes agitation and the destruction of the king; likewise, the period of the Moon bestows prosperity and provides desired food and happiness.

The period (daśā) of Mars bestows suffering and brings about the destruction of kingdom and other such things; the period of Mercury bestows celestial women, grants sovereignty, and increases the treasury.
The period (daśā) of Saturn brings about the loss of kingdom and causes suffering for kinsmen; the period of Jupiter bestows sovereignty and grants happiness, dharma, and other blessings.
The period of Rāhu brings about the loss of kingdom, disease, and suffering; the period of Venus bestows elephants and horses and grants the acquisition of kingdom and women.
Aries is the domain of Mars, Taurus is proclaimed to be that of Venus, Mercury is to be known as belonging to Gemini, and the Moon belongs to Cancer.
Leo is the domain of the Sun; Virgo is the domain of Mercury; Libra is the domain of Venus; and Scorpio is the domain of Mars.
Sagittarius belongs to Jupiter, while Capricorn and Aquarius belong to Saturn; Pisces also belongs to Jupiter—this is proclaimed as the planetary domain (grahakṣetra).
If there are two full moon days (paurṇamāsī) in that month and the constellation Pūrvāṣāḍhā occurs twice, it should be known as Dvirāṣāḍha; in this [lunar year], Viṣṇu sleeps in the sign of Cancer.
Aśvinī, Revatī, Citrā, and Dhaniṣṭhā are for the purpose of adornment. Deer, snakes, monkeys, cats, dogs, pigs, and birds [are the animals associated with these].
The mongoose and the rat are auspicious on the right during a journey; likewise, a Brahmin girl, a female jackal, a conch shell, a kettledrum, and the earth are favorable.
The sight of bamboo, women, and full water-jars during a journey is auspicious; likewise, jackals, camels, donkeys, and the like on the left side during a journey are auspicious.
Cotton, medicinal herbs, oil, cooked food, charcoal, serpents, a woman with disheveled hair, red garlands, and a naked person—these and others are seen as inauspicious omens.
I shall describe the characteristics of the syllable *hakrā*: in the east it yields great fruit; in the southeast there is grief and torment; and in the south one incurs loss.
In the southwest, there is grief and distress; in the west, one obtains sweet food; in the northwest, one attains wealth; and in the north, there will be quarrels.
Death is declared in the northeast; this is the fruit and non-fruit of hiccup. Having drawn the solar wheel (ravicakra), Bhāskara appears in the likeness of a man.
In whichever constellation the sun resides, three [units] should be placed on its head; three should be given to its mouth, and one each should be assigned to its two shoulders.
One should place one [star] on each of the two arms, one on each of the two hands, five stars on the heart, and one at the navel.
One should place one constellation at the secret place (guhya) and place one on each knee; the remaining constellations should be assigned to the feet of the Sun.
If a man has a mark on his foot, he will be short-lived; if it is on his knee, he will travel to foreign lands; and if it is located on his private parts, he will be a violator of another's wife.

If it resides in the navel, one is content with little; if in the heart, one becomes a great lord (Maheśvara); if in the hand, one becomes a thief; and if displaced from its location, one becomes a banner-bearer (Dhvaja).
If the constellation is situated in the shoulders, one obtains wealth; if in the mouth, one obtains sweet food; and if it is situated on the head, there will be fine garments.

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Planetary Periods (Daśā) and Other Matters" in the section on Astrology (Jyotiḥśāstra), within the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Hari said: The Moon situated in the seventh house, or in any of the Upacaya houses (the third, sixth, eleventh, and tenth), is auspicious in all respects; likewise, it is auspicious when it is in the second, fifth, or ninth house during the bright fortnight (Śuklapakṣa).
Being honored by the world, the Moon is regarded like a preceptor; listen now to those twelve states of the Moon as well.

I shall now declare the results for each set of three asterisms beginning with Aśvinī: [the first] indicates one who was abroad and is seen again; the second indicates one in a state of death; and the third brings victory.
The state of laughter, the state of play (or sport), and indeed the state of joy; the state of despondency, the state of enjoyment, and the state of fever are thus established.
The state of trembling, the state of happiness, and that which pertains to the twelve states shall be: travel abroad, loss, death, victory, laughter, pleasure, and happiness.
Grief, enjoyment, fever, trembling, and happiness are the results in sequence; situated in the first house, it produces contentment, but in the second, there is no peace.
In the third [month], there is honor from the king; in the fourth, the arrival of quarrels; and by the fifth moon, there will indeed be the gain of a woman.
In the sixth house, there is the acquisition of abundant grain; in the seventh, pleasure and honor; in the eighth, danger to life; and in the ninth, the accumulation of a treasury.
In the tenth house, the accomplishment of one's purpose is certain; in the eleventh, victory; but with the twelfth moon, there is only death—of this there is no doubt.

One should travel toward the east during the seven constellations beginning with Kṛttikā; one should go toward the south during those beginning with Maghā; and toward the west during those beginning with Anurādhā.
A northern journey is highly commended during the seven asterisms beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā; likewise, Aśvinī, Revatī, Citrā, and Dhaniṣṭhā are well-adorned for such purposes.
Mṛgaśīrṣa, Citrā, Puṣya, Mūla, and Hasta are always auspicious for the giving away of a daughter, for journeys, and for rites such as consecrations.
For Venus and the Moon, situated in the first house, bestow auspiciousness, as do they in the second; and Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Mars likewise in each respective house in the third.
Mars, Saturn, the Moon, and the Sun [are situated] in the fourth house; Mercury is excellent in the fourth; Venus and Jupiter are in the fifth, joined with the Moon and Ketu.
Mars in the sixth house in a mandakāra yoga is auspicious; Jupiter and the Moon in the seventh; Mercury and Venus in the eighth are excellent; and Jupiter situated in the ninth house is auspicious.
The Sun, Saturn, and Moon are the planets in the tenth house; all [other] planets are in the eleventh; and Mercury as well as Venus in the twelfth shall be givers of happiness.
The crocodile is best with the lion, the ram is most excellent with the virgin; the fish is [best] with Libra, and the crab with Aquarius.
A Bull with Sagittarius, and a Scorpio with Gemini—this combination of six and eight signs leads to affection; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Auspicious and Inauspicious Positions of the Planets," in the section on Astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) within the *Ācārakāṇḍa* of the first part of the *Pūrvakhaṇḍa* in the glorious *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Measurement of the Hours of the Ascendant (*lagna*) and Other Matters," in the section on Astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) within the *Ācārakāṇḍa* of the first part of the *Pūrvakhaṇḍa* in the glorious *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
The Glorious *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*: Chapter 63.
The Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 63.
Hari said: O Śaṅkara, listen as I describe the characteristics of men and women in brief. Their feet should be free from sweat, soft on the soles, and resemble the interior of a lotus.
Indeed, the feet of an excellent king should have closely joined toes, copper-colored nails, beautiful ankles, be free of visible veins, and be as high-arched as the shell of a tortoise.
The feet are rough and pale-nailed, crooked, and sunken with visible veins; they are shaped like winnowing baskets, parched, and have widely spaced toes.
Suffering and poverty would prevail; there is no need for further deliberation on this point. A shank that has few hairs is excellent, resembling the trunk of an elephant.
For great-souled kings, there may be a single hair in each pit; for scholars and likewise for those learned in the Vedas, there are two hairs in each.
Those with three hairs on the penis are poor; one with fleshless knees is diseased; and one with few sexual organs will be wealthy but deprived of sons and other such blessings.

If the penis is thick, one will be poor; if it is crooked, one will have only one testicle; if it is uneven, one will indeed be fickle toward women; and if the testicles are symmetrical, one will become a king.
A man with pendulous testicles will have a short life and be destitute, while one with small testicles will be poor; however, a man with pale or dark-colored testicles shall be happy.

Those who are penniless have noisy urination; kings have it with a silent stream. Those rich in enjoyments have symmetrical bellies, while the penniless have bellies resembling [the narrow necks of] jars.
Those with snake-like bellies become poor; and by the lines on the forehead, one's lifespan is declared. He on whose forehead three well-aligned lines are seen [is long-lived].
That man who sees two lines lives for sixty years, endowed with happiness and sons; and a man lives for forty years upon seeing [two] lines.
One with a single line lives for twenty years, while those with lines reaching to the ears live for a hundred years.

A lifespan of seventy years is indicated by two lines, while a lifespan of sixty years occurs with three lines; with lines that are both distinct and indistinct, a man shall have a lifespan of twenty years.
