One whose lines are deficient lives for forty years; indeed, by means of broken lines, a man meets an untimely death.
He on whose forehead a trident or even a spear-head is seen shall live for a hundred autumns, endowed with wealth and sons.
O Rudra, he whose line of life is reached from the middle by the index finger and the middle finger shall live for a hundred autumns.
The first line of knowledge indeed follows from the thumb; the line reaching the base of the middle finger is the life-line (āyūrekhā) beyond that.
If the line of longevity (āyūrekhā) rests upon the little finger and is either unbroken or clearly distinct, such a person shall live for a hundred autumns.
O Rudra, he upon whose palm the lines reveal a lifespan shall live for a hundred years as an enjoyer of pleasures; of this there is no doubt.
The line of life, originating from the little finger and extending toward the middle finger, shall grant a human being a lifespan of sixty years.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "Description of Male Characteristics in Sāmudrika Astrology," within the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Hari said: A maiden whose hair is curly, whose face is perfectly round, and whose navel spirals to the right, is one who increases the prosperity of her family.
And she who possesses a golden complexion and red lotus-like hands shall also be a devoted wife among thousands of women.
A maiden who has curly hair and whose eyes are circular will certainly be a partaker of misery, and her husband will die.
A maiden with a face like the full moon, possessing a radiance equal to the rising sun, with large eyes and lips like the *bimba* fruit—that maiden attains happiness.
With many lines there is suffering; with few lines, poverty. Through red lines one attains happiness; through black lines, one goes into servitude.
In matters of business, she is a wise counselor; in ritual acts, she is a virtuous wife; in acts of affection, she is a mother; and in the bedchamber, she is a beautiful courtesan.
The woman upon whose palm there appears a goad, an earring, or a wheel shall give birth to a son and obtain a husband who is a lord of men.
But she whose sides are hairy, whose breasts are hairy, and whose lower lips are sunken, quickly causes her husband's death.
She on whose palm the lines form a wall and an archway, even if born in a family of slaves, attains the status of a queen.
She whose line of body hair is upturned and continuous, even if born in a royal family, falls into the state of a slave.
She whose ring finger and thumb do not touch the ground quickly kills her husband and conducts herself according to her own will.
Merely by her movement, an earthquake is produced; she quickly causes the death of her husband and conducts herself according to her own will.
Through the oil for the eyes one gains good fortune; through the oil for the teeth, food; through the oil for the skin, a bed; and through the oil for the feet, a vehicle.
A woman’s auspicious feet are smooth, elevated, and have copper-colored nails; they are marked with the signs of a fish, a goad, and a lotus, and are characterized by the discus and the plow.
A woman's feet are praised when they are free from sweat and have soft soles; her shanks are auspicious when hairless, and her thighs resemble the trunk of an elephant.

The secret organ is excellent, broad like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, and most sublime; the navel is praised as being deep, auspiciously spiraling to the right, and hairless; the three folds of skin on the belly belong to a noble woman, and her heart and breasts are free of hair.

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Women," in the section on Astrology (Jyotiḥśāstra) within the Section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa), in the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Hari said: I shall proclaim the auspicious characteristics of men and women as spoken by the Ocean, by the mere knowledge of which one perceives the past and the future.

His feet were free from perspiration, with soft soles resembling the interior of a lotus; his toes were joined together and his nails were copper-colored; his feet were well-formed and devoid of prominent veins.

When the ankles are elevated like the shell of a tortoise and the heels are well-formed, these are said to belong to a king; whereas feet that are shaped like a snake's hood, rough, crooked, and veiny belong to others.
His feet were withered, with pale nails and sparse toes; they were like dry, astringent wood, longing for the road as he was about to depart.

Those who cause the destruction of their lineage and those who slay Brahmins are like stakes or snakes; those who take pleasure in approaching women who should not be approached have shanks with sparse body hair.
The shanks are covered with soft hair and are symmetrical, possessing the luster of an elephant's trunk; the thighs and knees are well-proportioned and fleshy, as prescribed for a king.
Sṛgālajaṅghā was born from Niḥsva; Rauma was born from each one of the Cakūpakas; two were born to the kings and two to the learned Vedic scholars, and two to the wise for the sake of prosperity.
Those with three or more [lines] will be destitute, partakers of misery, and censured; moreover, if the hair is curly, the man dies in a foreign land.

One with fleshless knees will possess good fortune; those that are slightly depressed indicate pleasure with women; those that are protruding indicate poverty; and those that are fleshy indicate sovereignty.
A man with a small penis is said by the great sages to have a long life and be wealthy; whereas one with a large penis is devoid of offspring and destitute of riches.
If the penis is bent downwards, one will be deprived of sons and wealth; if it is curved in another way, one will have sons, but if it is bent downwards, there will be poverty.
If the linga is small, a man will be childless; if it is ridged, he will be happy; and if the linga is joined with thick knots, he will be endowed with sons and other blessings.
One with hands whose fingers are hidden in the palms, long, and curved, is devoid of wealth; yet such a person is powerful, fond of combat, and capable of acting swiftly.

One who is weak and has only one testicle, or whose testicles are uneven and unstable, will have women; one with symmetrical testicles is said to be a ruler of the earth, and one with pendulous testicles lives for a hundred years.
Through those [lines] being prominent, one has a long life; through rough jewels, one is a lord; through white jewels, one is destitute; and through dark ones, one partakes in happiness.
Men may have urine that is either noisy or silent, and they may be poor; likewise, their urine may flow in one, two, three, four, five, or six streams.
Kings are said to have urine that flows in a clockwise curve; those with scattered urine are destitute, yet they bestow primary happiness.
Women are indicated by single streams and by smooth, elevated jewels; those possessing the wealth of a woman-jewel have even [streams], while maidens have those that are depressed in the middle.
Those with dry breath and one that is parched are proclaimed to be unfortunate; those with the scent of flowers become kings, while those with the scent of honey possess great wealth.

If the semen has the smell of fish, there will be sons; if it smells of fat, daughters; if it smells of meat, one will be a man of great enjoyment; and if it smells of wine, one will be a performer of sacrifices.
One who has a pungent odor is poor; one who copulates quickly is long-lived, while one who copulates slowly is short-lived; and one with thick buttocks is devoid of wealth.

One with fleshy buttocks shall be happy, while one with buttocks like those of a lion is known as a king; a man with hips like a lion's becomes a monarch, whereas one with hips like a monkey's is destitute.

Those with bellies like a snake's will be poor; those with bellies resembling cooking pots or jars will be wealthy; those with broad sides will be affluent, while those with reddish and sunken sides will be destitute.
Those with symmetrical armpits are rich in enjoyments; those with sunken armpits are devoid of wealth; kings possess elevated armpits; and those with uneven armpits are deceitful.
Those with fish-shaped navels are said to possess great wealth; those with deep navels are considered happy; while those with broad, shallow navels are destined to share in suffering.

The navel situated in the middle of the *bali* indeed causes affliction by the trident; a counter-clockwise rotation [indicates] the person to be accomplished, while likewise, one to the right indicates intelligence.
A line extending along the side bestows long life; when seated, it makes one a lord of wealth; below that, it makes one rich in cattle; and the lotus-seed vessel (padmakarṇikā) brings about kingship.

One with a single line on the forehead lives for a hundred years; one with two lines is said to be a possessor of wealth and enjoyments; one with three lines becomes a king or a teacher; and one with straight lines is happy.
He avoids forbidden women, possesses well-proportioned limbs, and has kings as his attendants; his flanks are fleshy, soft, perfectly symmetrical, and covered with hair that curls to the right.

Men with nipples that are inverted, small, devoid of substance, and lacking in prominence become unfortunate; conversely, those with nipples that are not inverted and possess these qualities become fortunate.
Those with uneven and long [breasts] are poor; those with yellowish and thick [breasts] are kings. A heart that is even, elevated, firm, fleshy, and broad [is auspicious].

Among kings and the lowest of men, one with hair on the head as coarse as a donkey's bristles is base; a wealthy man should have a broad chest, while one who is powerful possesses a full and robust breast.
Men who are destitute have uneven chests; likewise, those who meet their end by the sword are destitute; and men with uneven collarbones are destitute, as are those whose bones are bound together.

Those with prominent [jaws] are wealthy; those with depressed [jaws] are destitute; those with full [jaws] are endowed with riches. One with a flat throat is poor, while one with a veinless and dry throat is happy.
One with a buffalo-like neck will be a hero; one with a deer-like neck will be learned in the scriptures; a king with a conch-like neck will be a ruler; and one with a long neck will be a glutton.

A fragrant [tail] with a curved back is auspicious, while the opposite is inauspicious; one whose armpits resemble the leaves of the *aśvattha* tree, which is fragrant and covered with hair like that of a deer, is most excellent.
Otherwise, however, they are the cause of being devoid of wealth and poverty; moreover, when they are contracted, crooked, small, joined together, and broad, they are auspicious.
In a lord of kings, the arms are rounded and fleshy, hanging down to the knees; in the destitute, they are hairy and short; and in the best of men, they resemble the trunk of an elephant.
The fingers of the hand itself are auspicious when provided with weapons and banners; for the wise they are slender, while for servants they are said to be flat.

Those with thick fingers will be destitute; those with bent fingers will be very emaciated. Those with hands like a monkey's will be destitute, while those with hands like a tiger's will possess strength.
And men whose palms are depressed suffer the loss of paternal wealth; those with well-concealed, closely-knit, and fragrant wrists are auspicious.
Kings who are devoid of taxes and free from clamor are destitute of wealth; those who are concealed and lowly are proclaimed to be wealthy.
Those who give with palms turned upward are givers of prosperity; those who are harsh are men of harsh deeds; and those who are lords give with hands and palms that are red like lac.

Men who are addicted to the wives of others are considered to be impoverished when their nails are yellow and rough; those with nails like chaff are impotent, as are those with crooked or cracked nails.

Likewise, those with deformed nails are indigent, while those with discolored nails are prone to suspicion of others; those with copper-colored thumbs are kings, and likewise, those with "barley-marked" (yava) thumbs are wealthy.
One born with lines originating from the base of the thumb will have a daughter; one with long finger-joints will be long-lived and fortunate, while one with widely spaced fingers will be destitute.
A king possesses thick fingers and wealth, and indeed three lines on his palm that originate from the wrist.
A man marked with a pair of yokes becomes a donor of sacrificial halls; those shaped like a thunderbolt belong to the wealthy, while those resembling the tail of a fish belong to the wise.

In the case of a king, [the marks] resemble a conch, a parasol, a palanquin, an elephant, or a lotus; in the case of a lord of treasures, they resemble a water-pot, a goad, a banner, or a lotus stalk.

The marks resembling a rope appear on those wealthy in cattle; those resembling a svastika appear on a lord of kings; and those resembling a discus, sword, javelin, bow, and spear appear on the hand of a monarch.

One who possesses a mortar is rich in sacrifices; one who possesses an altar is an Agnihotrin; one who possesses a pond or a temple tank is virtuous; and one who possesses a triangular shape is likewise righteous.
The lines at the base of the thumb indicate sons, and those that are fine indicate daughters; a line extending from the forefinger to the base of the little finger [indicates longevity].
One with a broken line on the chin attains a lifespan of a hundred years, yet faces danger from trees; those with many lines on the chin are destitute, and those with thin chins are devoid of wealth.
Those with fleshy lips are endowed with wealth; kings have lips that are slightly reddish. Those with lips resembling the bimba fruit, or those that are cracked, rough, and chapped, [are otherwise].
Teeth that are uneven and lacking in luster are inauspicious; teeth that are smooth, dense, sharp, and even are auspicious; and a tongue that is red and even is auspicious.

The palate should be known as smooth and long when there is wealth; it is characterized by loss of wealth when it is white, and when it is black, it is rough. The face should be even, gentle, and well-proportioned.
The face of kings is stainless and smooth; that of the sorrowful is the opposite; the face of the unfortunate brings great suffering; from a woman's face, one obtains a son.
The face of the wealthy is round, that of the destitute is long; the face of the cowardly evildoer is curved, while that of the rogues is square.
The beard of childless men is sunken and crooked; that of the miserly is short; that of those who enjoy pleasures is full and lovely; and a beard that is glossy, auspicious, and soft is excellent.
One with a compact head, an uncracked forehead, and red whiskers is a thief; those with red, sparse, and coarse whiskers and ears shall meet a violent death.
Those with fleshless, flattened ears will have miserable enjoyments; those with short ears will be kings, while those with spike-like ears or hairy ears will have their lifespans cut short.
Kings are proclaimed to be wealthy if they have large ears; likewise, monarchs possess smooth, well-knit, long-hanging, and fleshy ears.
One with sunken cheeks is indeed a seeker of enjoyments; one with full cheeks is a counselor. One with a parrot-like nose will be happy, while one with a dry nose lives for a very long time.
One who delights in approaching women who should not be approached will have a nose with a severed tip; one with a long nose possesses good fortune, while a thief has a crooked organ.
A flat nose indicates death; one that is deficient belongs to those of meager fortune. A nose with small nostrils, well-formed cavities, and free from curvature belongs to a lord of kings.

If a sneeze occurs from the right side during a cruel [astrological period], it belongs to those who possess strength; if it is compressed, resonant, and accompanied by a ringing sound, it is produced by Jīva.
Those with eyes that are curved at the corners, resembling lotus petals, partake in happiness; those who are wicked and sinful have eyes like those of a cat, tawny as honey.
The generals were cruel, with squinting eyes, greenish-yellow eyes, and those stained with impurity; they were brave, with crooked eyes and eyes like those of elephants.
Those with deep-set eyes will be lords; those with large eyes will be ministers; those with eyes like blue lotuses will be learned; and those with dark-brown eyes possess good fortune.
Indeed, there may be the plucking out of eyes that have black pupils; the sinful shall have eyes like [blazing] circles, and those with divine eyes shall become destitute.

One with eyes that are moist, large, and wide will possess great wealth; one with eyes that are very prominent will have a short life; one with broad and elevated eyes will be happy; and those with uneven eyebrows will be poor.

One whose eyebrows are thick, long, and closely joined will be wealthy; one with eyebrows as high as the crescent moon will be poor; and one with eyebrows that are broken or drooping in the middle will be destitute.
They may be attached to women who are forbidden, yet they remain devoid of sons; likewise, they have broad, conch-like foreheads that are uneven.
Men with eyebrows resembling the crescent moon are wealthy; those with broad, shell-like, and veiny eyebrows are doers of evil.
Those with veins appearing like the svastika sign are lords of wealth; those with sunken foreheads are fit for bondage and likewise devoted to cruel deeds.
Those with contracted foreheads are miserable, while those with prominent ones are kings; weeping that is tearless, affectionate, and not dejected brings auspiciousness to men.

Weeping that is copious with tears and piteous brings suffering, whereas weeping that is dry brings happiness; laughter that is without trembling is excellent, while laughter with eyes closed brings misfortune.
A wicked man laughs excessively and many times as if he were mad; moreover, those who live for a hundred years have three lines extending across their foreheads.
With four lines there will be kingship and a lifespan of ninety-five; with a single line, a lifespan of ninety; and with broken lines, one becomes a womanizer.
If [the lines] reach the hairline, a man shall live for eighty years; likewise, by five, seven, six, or many [lines], he shall live for fifty.
If there are forty lines that are curved, thirty that reach the eyebrows, and twenty that are curved to the left, the lifespan is short due to these minor lines.

Kings have heads shaped like umbrellas; one with a depressed head is wealthy; those with flattened heads face the death of their father; and those with perfectly rounded heads possess cattle and other riches.
He has a pot-shaped head, delights in evil, and is destitute of wealth and other possessions; his hair is black, curled, glossy, and grows one by one from each pore.
O kings, [the sacrificial posts] should not have uneven tips, nor be soft, nor be excessively thick; they should likewise have many roots, be irregular, thick at the top, and tawny in color.
Those who are destitute indeed have very ugly, thick, and black (or discolored) hair; whatever limb is exceedingly rough, veiny, and devoid of flesh [is likewise a sign].
All that would otherwise be inauspicious becomes auspicious through this; it is vast in three respects, profound, long-lasting, and subtle in five respects.
This king has six protuberances, four short [limbs], and is ruddy; he possesses seven [features]. It is said that three things—the navel, the voice, and the heart—are deep.
For a man, the forehead, face, chest, eyes, armpits, and nose—these six, along with the nape of the neck, are the broad features of a king.
The shanks, the neck, and the penis are elevated and short; the back, the four [palms and soles], the palate, the lower lip, and the nails are red.
The corners of the eyes, the feet, the tongue, the lips—these five are indeed subtle; the teeth, the finger-joints, the nails, the hair, and the skin are auspicious.
Long [limbs], the space between the breasts, the arms, teeth, eyes, and nose—these are declared to be the characteristics of men; now I shall describe the characteristics in women.
If a queen’s feet are smooth and even, her soles copper-colored, her nails likewise, her toes joined together, and their tips prominent—one who attains such a woman shall become a king.

His auspicious soles are like lotuses, with concealed ankles and well-developed heels; they are free from perspiration, soft on the surface, and adorned with the marks of a fish, an elephant goad, and a banner.
The feet of a maidservant bear the marks of a vajra, a lotus, and a plough; otherwise, her shanks are hairless, well-rounded, veinless, and auspicious.
The two knees are auspicious when they are even, without prominent joints, and smooth; the two thighs are auspicious when they are symmetrical, hairless, and shaped like the trunk of an elephant.

The secret region of women is vast and excellent, resembling the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree; their hips and foreheads are well-proportioned, and their thighs are auspiciously elevated like the shell of a tortoise.
A hidden jewel is a giver of prosperity; a heavy hip is auspicious. A navel that is broad, fleshy, well-filled, deep, and expansive is auspicious.
Her navel spirals to the right; her waist is adorned with three folds; her breasts are hairless, full, firm, symmetrical, and auspicious.
Firm and hairy thighs are praised, as is a neck that is soft and shaped like a conch shell; slightly reddish lower lips are excellent, and the face should be fleshy and round.
His teeth are like jasmine flowers; his speech is like the song of the cuckoo—polite, free from deceit, and as pleasant as the cry of a swan.
For women, a nose that is straight, with even nostrils, is beautiful and auspicious; the eyes should resemble blue lotuses, reaching down to the nose and not drooping.
The eyebrows, resembling a young crescent moon, should not be broad; likewise, the forehead should be auspicious, shaped like a half-moon, not high, and hairless.
The pair of ears is well-fleshed, symmetrical, soft, and well-proportioned; the hair on the head is glossy, dark blue, soft, and curled.

For women, the head is considered equal to the best part [of the body], as are the feet, the palms of the hands, or [marks resembling] a horse, an elephant, the śrīvṛkṣa tree, a sacrificial post, an arrow, a barley grain, or a tomara spear.
With rows of banners and yak-tail whisks, with mountain-shaped earrings and altars, with conchs, parasols, and lotuses, and with fish, svastikas, and excellent chariots.
Women who possess the marks such as the goad and others will be favorites of kings; their wrists are hidden, and their hands resemble the interior of a lotus.

The palm of auspicious women should be neither depressed nor elevated; marked with lines, it makes a woman one who does not become a widow and who enjoys sensual pleasures. A line that rises from the wrist and reaches the middle finger on the hand [indicates this].
Whether it appears on the palm of the hand or on the sole of the foot, for both women and men, such a mark leads to sovereignty and happiness.
A line originating from the base of the little finger, extending into the space between the index and middle fingers, makes one a hundred years of age.
Deficient lines at the base of the thumb cause a deficient lifespan; broad lines are proclaimed to indicate sons, while thin ones indicate daughters.

A short, deeply severed [line] indicates a short lifespan, while a long, unsevered one indicates a long lifespan; such is said to be the auspicious characteristic for women, whereas the opposite is inauspicious.
She whose little finger or ring finger does not touch the ground, or whose index finger extends beyond the thumb, is an unchaste woman.
Above, the two calves are provided with two pedestals and are exceedingly veined; they are hairy and very fleshy, and likewise the belly is shaped like a water-pot.
A secret organ that spirals to the left, is depressed, or small belongs to those who are miserable; with a short neck one is destitute, and with a long neck there is the destruction of the family.
Women will be broad-hipped and fierce; of this there is no doubt. Even when the eyes are squinting or tawny, a virtuous woman may have dark and tremulous eyes.
If it is sunken at the pits of the cheeks, she is certainly unfaithful; but if it hangs down over the forehead, that woman kills her husband's younger brother.

A woman who has hair on her belly destroys her father-in-law; one who has hair on both buttocks destroys her husband; and she who has hair on her upper lip is certainly not auspicious for her husband.
Breasts covered with hair are inauspicious, as are uneven ears; moreover, jagged and uneven teeth lead to suffering for you.
Those with long ears are prone to theft and eat black meat; they bring death to their husbands, possessing hands like those of carnivorous beasts and resembling wolves, crows, and the like.
Indeed, those with veins that are prominent, uneven, and shriveled are devoid of wealth; she whose upper lip is elevated and rough speaks harshly during quarrels.

The defects in women who are ill-formed have been described, as well as the qualities that follow from them; the characteristics of men and women have been declared, and I shall now speak of that which bestows knowledge thereof.

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Men and Women," in the section on Physiognomy (*sāmudrika*) within the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*), in the *Ācārakāṇḍa* of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Hari said: Even one devoid of auspicious marks may become auspicious by worshipping a stone marked with the discus (*cakrāṅkita*). First is the form of Sudarśana, and the supreme is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
He who possesses three wheels is Acyuta; he who possesses four wheels has four arms. He is known as Vāsudeva, then Pradyumna, and thereafter Saṅkarṣaṇa.
Puruṣottama shall be the eighth; the Navavyūha consists of ten aspects; Aniruddha shall be the eleventh; and the twelfth consists of twelve aspects.
Beyond this, in the Śakra [mandala], there should be Ananta and the others in sequence, beginning with one; they are marked by the Sudarśana [mantra], and when worshipped, they grant all desires.
Wherever there is a Śālagrāma stone and the deity born of Dvāravatī, where there is the union of these two, there is liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Śālagrāma, Dvārakā, Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, Gayā, Vārāṇasī, Prayāga, Kurukṣetra, and Sūkara.
The Gaṅgā, the Narmadā, the Candrabhāgā, the Sarasvatī, Puruṣottama, and Mahākāla—these, O Śaṅkara, are the sacred fords (tīrthas).
These indeed remove all sins and bestow liberation upon those who have partaken [of them]: Prabhava, Vibhava, Śukla, Pramoda, and Prajāpati.
Aṅgiras, Śrīmukha, Bhāva, Yuvan, Dhātṛ, as well as Īśvara, Bahudhanya, Pramāthin, Vikrama, and Viṣu.
Citrabhānu, Svabānu, Tāraṇa, Pārthiva, Vyaya, Sarvajit, Sarvadhārī, Virodhin, Vikṛti, and Khara.
Nandana, Vijaya, Jaya, Manmatha, Durmukha, Hemalamba, Vilamba, Vikāra, Śarvarī, and Plava.
Śubhakṛt, Śobhana, Krodhī, Viśvāvasu, Parābhava, Plavaṅga, Kīlaka, Saumya, Sādhāraṇa, and Virodhakṛt.
Paridhāvī, Pramādin, Ānanda, Rākṣasa, Nala, Piṅgala, Kāla, Siddhārtha, Raudri, and likewise Durmati.
Dundubhi, Rudhirodgārī, Raktākṣa, Krodhana, Akṣaya, Aśobhana, and Śobhana—indeed, these years are so named solely by their names.

O Rudra, I shall explain the time for the sake of complete accomplishment based on the rising of the five vowels: the King (Sa), the Queen (Ā), the Neutral (U), as well as Affliction (Ū) and Death (Ṛ).
One should write the vowels ā, ī, ū, ai, and au within a grid of five fire-squares (five-by-five), using lines drawn vertically and horizontally that follow the sequence of the six fires.
In the fire-cells (the third), there is one lunar day; then three, and then the king (six); these are Jaya, Udāsa, and Mṛtyu-pīḍā, belonging respectively to Mars and Mercury.
Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, the Sun, and the Moon, as they have been described; and the asterisms beginning with Revatī and ending with Mṛgaśiras—these constitute the first digit (kalā).

Elsewhere, there are five times five lunar mansions; likewise, the rising [of the breath] occurs in Caitra and the other months. Furthermore, the first syllable of the names of the two months is determined by twelve-day intervals.

If the *kalā-liṅga* should remain for five [periods], his death will indeed occur; these are the *kalā*, the lunar day (*tithi*), the day of the week (*vāra*), the asterism (*nakṣatra*), and the month itself.
And likewise, the arising of the name occurs previously and not otherwise: Oṃ Kṣaiṃ (Kṣauḥ) Śivāya Namaḥ.
O Śiva, remove the perception of poison and possession from my emaciated limbs; indeed, recite the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha, which deludes the three worlds and leads to the lotus.
The *Mṛtyuñjaya-gaṇa* and *Lakṣmī*, written with yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and other substances on birch bark (*bhūrja*), when worn around the neck or on the arm, bestow victory and other benefits.

Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Śālagrāma, the Sixty-Year Cycle, Svara, and Udaya," in the Jyotiḥśāstra section of the Ācārakāṇḍa within the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
(The Jyotiḥśāstra is hereby completed. Sūta said: Having heard this from Hari, Hara spoke to Gaurī concerning the knowledge residing within the body.
Mars is proclaimed as fire, the Sun as earth, and Saturn as water; Rāhu is situated in the station of air and illuminates the right nostril.
Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon as the fourth—these likewise cause the left channel to remain in the center for oneself.
When the moon is conjoined with Ilā, one should perform ritual actions, as well as dwell in sacred places, practice meditation, engage in trade, and have audiences with kings.
One should diligently perform other auspicious rites when the flow is in the right channel (dakṣanāḍī), but [avoid them] during the flow of Saturn, Mars, and Rāhu.
Even so, there may arise an increase of evils for these people; however, the discernment between the auspicious and the inauspicious is indeed known through the *Svarodaya*.
Within the body, the channels (nāḍīs) are manifold in form and very extensive; from the bulb (kanda) situated below the navel, they have emerged like sprouts.
Seventy-two thousand [channels] are situated in the center of the navel; they are all arranged like a wheel and are known as the carriers of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Among them, three are supreme: the left, the right, and the middle. The left is said to be of the nature of the Moon, and the right is like the Sun.
The central channel is Fire, bearing fruit and fulfilling time; the left is indeed the form of nectar, established for the nourishment of the world.
When the southern wind blows with the portion of Rudra, it constantly dries up the world; when it blows through both [paths] together, death occurs, destroying all undertakings.

In exhalation, however, it is the left [channel] that occurs; in inhalation, it is remembered as the right. Likewise, during the flow of the *iḍā*, there is the gentle [state], as well as the positions of the moon and the sun.
One should perform cruel deeds when the vital breath is situated in Piṅgalā; for journeys, all undertakings, and the removal of poison, [the breath should be in] Iḍā.
In eating, in sexual union, and in battle, Piṅgalā bestows success; in rites such as eradication and killing, it is Piṅgalā who grants success in these actions.
She bestows success in sexual union, in battle, in eating, in auspicious undertakings, in journeys, and in the practice of sorcery.

And for the sake of accomplishing peace, liberation, and one's goals, the *iḍā* [nāḍī] should be employed by kings; likewise, both [nāḍīs] should be used during the flow when avoiding the cruel and the gentle [states].
The wise man should recognize it as being like poison and should remember this when performing gentle and auspicious rites, such as those for gain, victory, or longevity.
In going and coming, Vāmā is honored everywhere; likewise in battle and the like, in eating, in killing, and in union with women.
The auspicious right channel is recommended for entry during minor rites; it determines all auspicious and inauspicious actions, as well as gain and loss, victory and defeat.
If one asks about the living and the non-living, it is not accomplished through the Middle Way; rather, it is accomplished in Vāmācāra or Dakṣiṇācāra, wherever the Leader resides.
If one who is situated in the *tanu* asks [a question], there is success therein without a doubt; likewise when Vāmadeva, whose will is at its own disposal, flows within the self.

Standing in that portion, one should inquire; success will be fruitless [if the breath remains there]. Whether on the left or on the right, wherever the auspicious breath (śivā) migrates, [therein lies the result].
When the Haṃsa has set out according to its portion, terrible deeds are performed in the terrible [state], moderate ones in the gentle, and indeed all-flowing [deeds] in both.
Then the yogin, skilled in yoga, should recognize death; wherever he may stand—whether facing left, right, or straight ahead—he should inquire.
In each respective direction, the rising of the wind should always be equal; that from the front-left is the best, while that from the back-right is auspicious.
On the left, Vāmā is proclaimed; on the right, Dakṣiṇā is auspicious. On the left, Vāmā is indeed auspicious; on the right, Dakṣiṇā is auspicious.

The living being lives by means of the life-force; whatever is devoid of that becomes insentient. Whatever task is undertaken, characterized by victory and auspiciousness, [is accomplished through it].
All of that arises within the *pūrṇanāḍī* through non-conceptualization; the three fortnights are said to extend from that up to the other channels and so forth.
Up to the sixth question, if it is full (pūrṇā), the first [alternative] wins; but if it is empty (riktā), the second shall speak without hesitation.
The wind equal to the left-hand practice arises, bestowing the accomplishment of karma; when the right-hand path is active, it is uneven and possesses uneven syllables.
Otherwise, when the flow is to the left, if the name indeed consists of an odd number of syllables, then that warrior attains victory in the midst of battle.
If, indeed, an equal number of syllables arises during the flow of the *dakṣavāta* (right-side wind), one should observe it within the central channel; of this there is no doubt.

When the vital breath has entered Piṅgalā, one should conquer the battle that is to be pacified; as long as the movement [of the breath] arises in the channel, one should cause it to reach that direction.
He is not even born to give [anything]; there is no need for deliberation on this point. However, in the midst of battle, wherever the channel (nāḍī) should always flow—
One attains victory in that direction; one should predict defeat in the empty [direction]. One should know victory when the movement is born, and one should declare death in the case of the dead.
He who understands both victory and defeat is a wise man; for wherever Śiva moves, whether on the left or on the right, there lies success.
Having performed that, one attains that state; the journey is continuously auspicious. When there is a flow of the moon and sun, one should engage in battle.
But whoever, remaining there, asks [the question], that virtuous person will certainly be victorious as far as the direction in which the wind blows.
There is no doubt that [the result] arises even if Indra stands before one; the ten nāḍīs beginning with Meṣī are situated on the right and the left.
In such and such a manner, on that firm path of discernment, they know that in successive stages one enters into emergence during emergence and into withdrawal during withdrawal.
Having heard the words of the questioner, one should discern [the answer] by means of the bell-shaped [hand gesture]; O Śivā, whether on the left or the right, it abides within the five principles.
Fire is above, water is below, and the wind is situated horizontally; the earth should be known to be in the middle, while space is everywhere at all times.

Above is death, below is peace; the wise one should effect eradication in the transverse direction. One should know that immobilization is in the center, while liberation is everywhere for the all-pervading one.

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Determination of Auspicious and Inauspicious Signs in the Svarodaya," in the section on Conduct (*Ācārakāṇḍa*) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. The venerable Sūta said: I shall now describe the examination of gems. There was an Asura named Bala who conquered Indra and the other gods; they were unable to defeat him.
At the sacrifice, when the gods requested him as a victim under the pretext of granting a boon, Bala, being of supreme courage, gave himself up as the sacrificial animal;
thus slain by the gods, he attained the state of a beast.
Like a sacrificial animal, Bala was slaughtered by them, restrained by the thunderbolt of his own words; he did so for the sake of the world's welfare and out of a desire for the benefit of the gods.
Because that being was purified and his actions were pure, all the limbs of his body became seeds of jewels.
Then, for the gods, the yakṣas, the siddhas, and the wind-eaters, there arose a very great crocodile that was born from the seeds of their own jewels.
As they were falling through the sky in their celestial chariot with great speed, whatever seed of jewels fell here and there, in any quantity whatsoever;
Whether in the great ocean, in a river, on a mountain, or even in a forest, a location attains the character of a mine for various things due to the weight of what is contained within it.
Within them appear jewels that destroy demons, poisons, serpents, and diseases, as well as those which eliminate sins; likewise, there also appear those that are defective.
Vajras, pearls, rubies along with emeralds are mentioned; furthermore, there are excellent sapphires, lapis lazuli, and topazes.
The karketana gem with its fine hair-like markings, the one called rudhira, as well as crystal and coral—these are specified with care by experts for inclusion in the collection.
The shape and color, first the qualities and defects, their results, the examination, and the value—these are to be understood by those skilled in gems as the principles of all treatises.
Those things that are born under unfavorable planetary configurations (kulagna) or on an afflicted day are joined with defects and are deprived of a wealth of virtues.
A ruler of the earth who desires prosperity should either wear or collect jewels that have been purified by examination.
Those who are learned in the treatises, skilled, and expert examiners of gems—they alone are proclaimed to be knowers of the proper measure of value.
Since this diamond (vajra) of great power has been proclaimed by the wise as the source of all examination, we shall therefore describe this examination beginning with the diamond.
In whatever regions of the earth even a fragment of his bone happened to fall, there diamonds of various forms appeared, as if produced by the desire of Indra to conquer him.
Haima, Mātaṅga, Saurāṣṭra, Pauṇḍra, Kaliṅga, Kosala, Veṇvātaṭa, and Sauvīra—these are the eight pleasure-resorts of Vajra.

Those born in the Himalayan mountains are known to be copper-colored like the moon; those from the banks of the Veṇvā are remembered as being like dark clouds. In Sauvīra, they are like black lotuses and clouds; those born in Saurāṣṭra are like dark clouds. Those from Kaliṅga have the beautiful luster of refined gold; in Kosala, they have a yellow radiance; those originating in Puṇḍra are dark; and in the region of Mataṅga, they do not possess an excessively yellow radiance.

If a diamond that is exceedingly light in color, possessed of excellent qualities, perfectly symmetrical on its sides, and free from lines, spots, stains, "crow's foot" marks, and fearsome flaws—even if such a diamond, as small as a single atom, is seen anywhere in this world—it is indeed a true abode for the gods, provided it has a sharp point and edge.
In the Vajras, the form of even the deities is said to be through the application of colors; and the differentiation [of the deities] must be made from the colors, based precisely upon those colors.
Green, white, yellow, tawny, dark, and copper-colored—these are naturally beautiful, being the respective colors of Hari, Varuṇa, Śakra, Hutavaha, Pitṛpati, and Marut.

The [complexion] of a Brahmin should be as white as a conch shell, a kumuda lily, or crystal; that of a Kshatriya should have the luster of a hare or the brownish eyes of a cat; that of a Vaishya should resemble the beautiful leaf of a plantain tree; and that of a Shudra should possess a brilliance equal to a polished sword.

Two types of diamond color for kings have been prescribed by the wise, but they are not suitable for everyone: that which is as red as a fragment of javā or coral, or that which resembles the juice of turmeric.

Because of his lordship over all castes, the king may at his pleasure wear ornaments made from the materials of all castes that possess excellent qualities; but no one else may ever wear anything other than what is prescribed for his own caste.
For the mixture of castes that occurs through the practice of the low and the high is considered less grievous than the mixture of Vajra-castes, which is held to be more painful than that.

A wise person should not practice the adoption of the Vajra [vehicle] merely by engaging in the classification of paths; for the manifestation of the excellence of virtuous qualities is the cause of prosperity, while its opposite is the cause for the arising of calamity.
If even a single horn of it is seen to be cracked or shattered, that diamond, though possessed of excellent qualities, should not be kept in the home by those seeking their own welfare.

With its points shattered by fire and its center filled with speckles of soot-colored stains, even the wielder of the thunderbolt would not quickly restore his vajra to its former splendor, for that splendor was ever eager to find a worthy support.
That which has a portion appearing like blood, or which is variegated with red colors—one should not have that carried; for it brings an end to life even for one who dies according to his own will.
With edges numbering ten million on each side, and with six, eight, or twelve facets, possessing lofty and perfectly sharp points—these are the qualities of a diamond produced from its source.

A diamond that is pure in its six facets, stainless, with a sharp and clear edge, possessed of color, light, well-proportioned, and free from defects—such a diamond, which scatters the rays of a rainbow across the atmosphere, is not easily found upon this earth.

He who, with body ever restrained, always bears a thunderbolt that is sharp-pointed, stainless, and free from all defects, shall experience an increase in women, prosperity, sons, wealth, grain, cattle, and slaves every day until the end of his life.
Fears of predatory beasts, fire, poison, tigers, thieves, and water, as well as the effects of Atharvan rites, are warded off from afar by him.
If one should possess a diamond free from all defects weighing twenty *taṇḍula* grains, those learned in the science of gems declare its highest price to be two hundred thousand *rūpaka*s.

Three parts less, half, and half of that remaining; thirteen, thirty, and half-parts thereof; then an eightieth part, a hundredth part, and a thousandth part—this is the application for small proportions.
The price that was first prescribed for a diamond made from twelve grains of rice is determined to be reduced by one unit at each subsequent step for every single decrease in weight.
Furthermore, the method for weighing diamonds is not by rice grains alone; one should calculate a rice grain as being equal to eight white mustard seeds.
However, a diamond that is endowed with all its qualities and floats upon water is desired for wearing, even among the entire category of gems.
For even if it is slightly flawed, whether the defect is visible or invisible, a person obtains a diamond worth one-tenth of its original value.
For a diamond, whether small or large, that possesses many manifest defects, not even a hundredth part of its true value is prescribed.
Although a diamond with manifest flaws may be seen as an ornament, its value will be slight for the purpose of refining gems.
When a king endowed with a wealth of virtues encounters a flaw that obstructs him, even a gem devoid of quality is no ornament for that king; it is as good as having no jewelry at all.
A woman desiring the birth of a son should not wear a diamond, even if it possesses excellent qualities, except for those that are long, flattened, triangular, and so forth.
With iron, with topaz, and likewise with hessonite, with beryl and crystal, and also with various kinds of glass.
Skilled people can produce counterfeits of diamond; therefore, they must be examined by wise and expert investigators.
Their testing should be performed with alkaline substances, abrasives, and whetstones; for whatever gems exist on earth, as well as other metallic ores.
One may scratch all things with a vajra, yet it cannot be scratched by them; the heaviness of all jewels is the cause for supporting weight.
The wise describe that [vajra] as being the opposite: birth carves out non-birth, while the diamond-crusts carve out birth.
Diamond scratches diamond; diamond is not scratched by anything else. This includes diamonds, pearls, gems, and whatever other species of jewels there may be.

For those [flames] that are obstructed, there is no upward movement; for some, if it should somehow arise, it moves crosswise because they have been pierced. For those being scraped crosswise, that [movement] is thwarted at their sides.
Even if it has chipped edges, is marked with spots or lines, or is discolored, a thunderbolt that possesses a rainbow nevertheless bestows wealth, grain, and sons.
Bearing the mace as described, which is beautiful with flashes of lightning, the king—having overwhelmed the prowess of his enemies through his own valor—enjoys the lands of all his vassals.

Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Examination of Gems, Their Varieties, Vajra, and So Forth," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Sūta said: Pearls are renowned in the world as being produced from the frontal globes of the lordly elephant, clouds, boars, conch-shells, fish, serpents, oyster shells, and bamboo; among these, those born from oyster shells are the most abundant.

In that very place, the root alone of a single *ratna* stone is ever set; however, those who know them say that among them, only those originating from mother-of-pearl are to be pierced, while the rest are said to be unpierceable.

Whether produced from bamboo, the king of serpents, or whales, or that which is born from a conch shell or a boar—though they are generally freed from their luster, they are nevertheless praised for their auspiciousness.

Of the eight origins of pearls proclaimed here by those who know the determination of gems, that which arises from conch shells and that which is produced from the frontal globes of lordly elephants are declared to be the lowest.

A conch shell arises from the middle of an elephant's frontal globes; it is of the same color as its own source, wine, or fresh skin, large and the size of a dangling fruit, yellowish-white in hue, and devoid of luster.
Those *kambavas* born from the lineage of the preeminent conch that was drunk by the touch of Śārṅga’s mouth, as well as elephants of pure breed, are declared to be the sources of pearls.

From these, a pearl is produced that is round, yellowish in color, and lacking luster; it has a hue similar to the back of a *pāṭhīna* fish, and from the fish, it is well-rounded, light, and exceedingly fine.

Fish that move in the midst of the ocean are born from the mouths of aquatic creatures; it is taught that they possess a color identical to the tips of the boar's tusks, originating from those very tusks.

Somewhere, somehow, that preeminent king of boars is born upon a region of the earth; it is described as having the luster and color of hailstones, and its origin is said to be from the joints of bamboo.

Those bamboos grow in places enjoyed by divine beings, not in common areas; they possess the gait of a bull, the pure form of a fish, and in their shape, they are resplendent with an exceedingly brilliant color.

Possessing a luster equal to the edge of a sword that has been thoroughly polished and free of all conceptual construction, one may attain great jewels of immense brilliance, or a kingdom and vast prosperity that are otherwise difficult to obtain.

Those who perform meritorious deeds become endowed with splendor; thus, those skilled in ritual procedures, being purified and diligent, strive with effort at an auspicious moment to test the gem-treasure produced from the head of a serpent, which resembles a pearl.

When that great rite of protection was performed upon the palace roof, then, amidst the deep resonance of great kettledrums and the flashing of streaks of lightning within the intervals, [the sky was filled].
The sky is covered by fresh clouds, heavy and hanging low as they press against the breasts [of the clouds]; neither serpents, nor demons, nor diseases, nor even the evils of calamities can reach it.
Those who destroy the pearl arising from the head of a serpent, which remains within its shell, do not reach the earth born from the clouds; for when it has fallen away, the gods carry it off.
His radiance enveloped the quarters of space, his solar orb discernible in the sky; he eclipsed the entire luster of fire, the moon, the planets, and the stars.
Just as it produces light by day, so too during those nights plunged in deep darkness, its waters were beautiful with the luster of various jewels and adorned with the four oceans.
It is my conviction that there would be no price for it, even if the entire earth were filled with gold; for even one who is lowly may sometimes obtain it through the ripening of great merit.

He enjoys that entire earth free from rival wives for as long as it endures; not only does this result from the merit of the king who performed those auspicious deeds, but it is also due to the fortune of his subjects.
A thousand yojanas all around, it turns away every misfortune; the row of teeth of that great demon is like a garland of stars fallen from the sky.
Among the waters of various colors, her own pure-colored milk fell into the water of her husband, who was like a preeminent jewel of great quality, radiant with a mass of rays from a full moon.

That seed, which had previously existed in other lives, attained its abode within oyster shells; in whatever region of the ocean that beautiful seed of the pearl-gem fell, there the water, scattered by clouds, remained within the shell and attained the state of a pearl.
The eight mines are those of Siṃhala, Pāralaukika, Saurāṣṭrika, Tāmraparṇa, Pāraśava, Kauvera, Pāṇḍya, Hāṭaka, and Hemaka.
Produced from oyster shells, it is not of inferior color; it arises in Vardhana, Pārasi, Pātāla, Lokāntara, and Siṃhala, distinguished by its dimensions, shape, quality, and luster.

The specific varieties of its source are inconceivable; therefore, a wise person should strive for excellence in both form and measurement. Furthermore, there is no fixed rule regarding merits and defects, for all types of forms exist everywhere.
The price of this pearl, which possesses the luster of mother-of-pearl and has been weighed against another [standard], is five thousand and three hundred rūpakas.
That which is less than half a māṣaka is of a price reduced by two-fifths; that which one might carry for three māṣakas has its maximum price prescribed as two thousand [paṇas].
Two [palas] and a half carry its price at more than a thousand with three hundred; for that which is weighed at two māṣakas less, the price is said to be eight hundred.

Experts say that for a [ruby] weighing one and a half *māṣakas*, its maximum price is two hundred [gold pieces], provided it possesses twenty-three equal qualities and six *guñjās* [of weight]. For one weighing one and a quarter [māṣakas], the price would be one hundred [gold pieces], if it is endowed with those same qualities.
If it weighs no less than sixteen [māṣas], they call that the variety known as Dārvika; it fetches a price of one hundred and ten [māṣas] more, even from the hand of a fool.
Experts declare that ten units of double [weight] constitute one *dharaṇa*; such a piece fetches seventy-nine times its own value, provided it is not devoid of excellence in its qualities.
A full *dharaṇa* of thirty [units] is proclaimed to be its scale (*śikya*); the settled determination is that its value shall be forty [units].
If she has forty teeth, she should receive thirty as her price; if Soma has fifty teeth, however, his price is twenty.
Sixty would be the *nikaraśīrṣa*; its value is fourteen. Eighty and ninety are proclaimed as *kūpya*; their values are eleven and nine respectively.

Having taken that entire vessel of food and cooked it with the addition of the juice produced from a citron, one should then rub it with the roots of soft and thin plantain fibers; thus, one may quickly produce a pearl of any desired size, pierced through.

Having placed it inside a fish-shaped vessel smeared with clay, one should subsequently bake it gently; then, by means of a *biḍālapuṭī* (cat-pouch) seal, one should cook it in milk, then in clarified butter (*sudhā*), and finally, once cooked, again in milk mixed with pure curd.

Then, through rubbing with a stainless cloth, the pearl becomes pure, endowed with vast qualities and splendor; so spoke Vyāḍi, who was of great power in the worlds, perfected, compassionate, and devoted to the welfare of the wise.
Silver, resembling white glass, when combined with a hundred parts of gold and held within the mercury, becomes pearl, an ornament for the body.
For in this way, skillful people in the land of Siṃhala act whenever there is any doubt regarding the artificiality of a pearl.
One should let it soak for a night in warm, salty oil or water; or else, having wrapped it in a dry cloth, it should be rubbed with grains of rice.
That which does not undergo discoloration should be known as unadulterated; it is white, of standard proportions, glossy, heavy, transparent, and perfectly pure.
A pearl that is brilliant, well-rounded, and possesses excellent qualities is considered virtuous.

That pearl which possesses weight proportionate to its size, is endowed with rays of light, is white, well-rounded, and has a uniform, fine perforation, brings joy even to one who does not purchase it; such a pearl is declared to be possessed of excellent qualities.
Thus, when a pearl has attained union through the arising of all these qualities, not even a single fault or any kind of misfortune shall ever come upon its owner.
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Examination of Pearls," within the section on Conduct (*Ācārakāṇḍa*) of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said: Having taken the blood of that great-souled great Asura—the seed of the finest gems—the Sun set forth to traverse the sky, which was as dark blue as a sword-blade.

Having encountered the Lord of Laṅkā on the way—whose mind was haughty with the pride of valor and who had incessantly conquered the gods in battles—he was forcibly obstructed by him, just as [the sun] is by Rāhu.

The sun released [its heat] into that most excellent river, whose deep great lake was agitated by the beautiful rounded hips of the women of Siṃhala, and whose two banks were lined with betel-nut trees.
From that time forward, that Gaṅgā, yielding equal merit and fruit, attained renown by the name Rāvaṇagaṅgā.
From that time forth, during the nights, her banks, strewn with jewels, shone as if sharpened within and without by hundreds of golden iron arrows set ablaze.

On its banks there are rubies of brilliant and lovely hue, and in its waters there are lotus-gems; those arising from Saugandhika, those born of Kuruvinda, and those produced from crystal are all of great quality.

Some possess a beauty with a color like that of the bandhūka, guñjā, indragopa insect, javā flower, fresh blood, or raw meat; others are radiant with the hue of pomegranate seeds, while still others have the luster of kiṃśuka flowers.

Having a color identical to that of the *khindura*, lotus, blue water-lily, saffron, and even lac-dye, they shine by their own radiance even when the passion is dense; clearly discernible, they possess a manifest beauty in their centers.

Having attained a connection with the piercing rays of the sun's light through a mass of beams, those produced from crystal and endowed with excellent qualities color all their sides to a great distance.

Some possess a brilliance equal to a red lotus, its hue intensely crimson and variegated with the colors of safflower and indigo; others have the luster of the flowers of the aruṣkara and kaṇṭakāri plants, while still others have the radiance of vermilion.
Some possess the brilliance of the eyes of the male cakora bird, the cuckoo, and the sārasa crane; others, moreover, have a luster equal to that of the finest blossoming red lotuses.
Possessing brilliance, hardness, and weight, and generally similar to those produced from crystal, there are gems arising from the *saugandhika* that have the lovely luster of blue and red lotuses.

Granted that passion may exist in those born of Kuruvinda gems, it is not at all like that which exists in those born of crystal; for even when all are bent down, the latter remain lusterless within despite their great power.
But those kuruvindas which are born in the Gaṅgā of Rāvaṇa bear a deep red hue like that of a ruby, yet possess the luster of crystal.
In the Māndhra country and elsewhere, none of those who follow their [proper] castes are born who would receive even a fraction of a price.
In the very same way, those originating from the region known as Tumburu are produced with similar properties; indeed, they are considered to be of little value.
Excellence of color, weight, glossiness, evenness, translucency, brilliance, and largeness—this is the collection of the qualities of jewels.
Those gems that are cracked, porous, stained with impurities, devoid of luster, rough, and discolored are not praised, even if they are equal in all respects regarding their species and qualities.
Whoever, out of ignorance, wears a jewel that has been defiled by a flaw, is beset by a multitude of defects such as grief, anxiety, death, and loss of wealth.
A wise man should diligently observe the five types of women who are the most desirable among living beings and serve as their counterparts.

Those originating from Kalaśapura, the Siṃhala country, the Tumburu region, and Muktapāṇīya, as well as those from Śrīpūrṇaka, are similar to one another and are of inferior quality compared to the Padmarāgas.

That which is called *kalaśa* originates from the husk (*tuṣa*); that which arises from *tumburu* is so named because of its coppery color; likewise, that produced in the land of Siṃhala is called *kārṣṇya* because of its blackness; and that which is called *muktā* (pearl) comes from the sky due to its natural state.

The *śrīpūrṇaka* ruby, being devoid of luster, possesses a distinction that rests solely upon its marks of caste; it nourishes a coppery hue, yet through its internal union, it is full like a lotus-gem amidst frost.
One who appears smeared with oil, or one who loses his luster when rubbed, or one whose head is pressed down by the two fingers and bears dark streaks on the sides—[these are to be avoided].

Having obtained it and having lifted it up according to its nature, he who bears all qualities exceedingly; or he who, being of equal measure and equal species, may be equal by virtue of his weight—just as a wise man, though born from a mine of jewels, would recognize [the true gem] by its weight and its quality.

If there is doubt that [the writing] will not fade, one should rub it with an emery stone; even after they have written to one another, [it should be done] with [a substance] produced from their own birth-signs.
Just as it is impossible for anyone to produce a scratch on a ruby or a sapphire by means of either a diamond or a kuruvinda gem, so too [is it impossible to describe the Buddha].

Among all gems of a given species, there are never any of a different species that possess an identical color; nevertheless, for the sake of distinguishing them, the highest degree of differentiation has been taught.

A gem of inferior birth should never be worn by one endowed with virtues, even if it is strung together with one of excellent quality; for a wise man would never wear something of a different species, even if it were fastened together with the Kaustubha jewel itself.
Just as even a single outcaste, having encountered many twice-born men, can kill them without effort, so too can one of a different caste cause the ruin of jewels endowed with manifold virtues.
Even when placed in the midst of rivals, and even while existing in a state of negligence, no calamity whatsoever touches the wearer of a great-quality ruby in this world.
And those calamities arising from the onset of defects do not assail him who, being self-restrained, wears a ruby whose beautiful luster is intensified by its excellent qualities.

The price that has been assigned to a diamond based on its number of grains of rice, once its value has been established, is the price of a highly virtuous ruby that is equal in weight to a single māṣaka.
For a precious gem is praised when it is endowed with both color and clarity; yet if it lacks even a little of these two, it falls away from its gem-like value.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Examination of Rubies," in the section on Conduct (*ācārakāṇḍa*) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said: Taking the bile of the lord of the Dānavas, Vāsuki, the king of serpents, departed swiftly as if splitting the sky in two.
Then, illuminated by the radiance of the jewel on his own head, he shone like a single great silver causeway across the ocean of the sky.
Then, as if destroying heaven and earth with the flapping of his wings, Garuḍa prepared to strike the lord of serpents.

Suddenly that lord of serpents released him upon the foothills of Mount Māṇikya, which were perfumed with the thick fragrance of flower buds and where *turuṣka* trees were anointed by the goddess Surasā.

Immediately after his fall, having passed through that same excellent abode near Ramā, he reached a place on the shore of the ocean belonging to the earth, in the valley at the foot of the excellent Māṇikya mountain.
Then, as that bile was falling away, Garuḍa approached and seized it; overcome by fainting, he suddenly released it all through the two nostrils.

In that regard, emeralds that possess the luster of the throats of soft parrots, the *śirīṣa* flower, the back of a firefly, green grass, moss, the *kalhāra* lotus, young grass, or the hoods of serpents are auspicious.

Wherever the bile of the lord of the Daityas fell, struck by the arms of the king of serpents, that region became exceedingly rich in its mineral source, yet difficult to reach due to its hardships, while being endowed with many virtues.
Whatever is produced in that emerald mine is proclaimed to be for the pacification of all poisons and diseases.
That poison produced by the fangs of a great serpent, which cannot be treated by any collection of mantras or medicinal herbs, is pacified by that [remedy].
Furthermore, whatever else is produced there in the mine that is free from defects is proclaimed to be the most excellent among purifying substances.
It appears exceedingly green in color, soft, and matted with streaks of light, as if filled within with gold dust.
Endowed with the qualities of shape and color, possessing equal passion and not lacking in gravity, it bathes the entire hermitage in radiance through the touch of the sun's rays.
Having abandoned its greenness, that within which light has been placed shines like fresh grass due to being struck by the radiance of a recent flash of lightning.
And that which bestows upon the mind an exceeding clarity when beheld—that, for those who know gems, is the mental conviction that it is a great mass of emeralds.
Because of the extreme pervasiveness of its color, its interior is enveloped in clear rays; it possesses a dense, glossy, and pure luster, with a radiance equal to that of soft peacock feathers.
With its radiant luster and brilliant color, it shines with a dense form; yet even so, it retains the very same name it had before, for it possesses those same qualities.
Variegated, harsh, dull, rough, and filled with stones and gravel; smeared with bitumen—emerald of such a kind is defective.
Any gem that has been treated at its joints other than emerald should not be worn or purchased in any way by those desiring their own welfare.
The *bhallātakī* and the *putrikā*, due to their similarity in color, should be recognized as being of different species from the emerald gem.
Polished with a linen cloth, the little statuette loses its luster; indeed, by the very lightness of glass, it is possible to bring about such a transformation.
Even for someone following an emerald with various forms and qualities of excellence, the color of the marking-nut (bhallātaka) undergoes a transformation simply by its own sound.
There are other diamonds, such as pearls and whatever else belongs to the twice-born; for these, when unstrung, their luster does not ascend upward.
And due to the straightness [of some], it arises for certain individuals in some way; yet for those who look askance at it, it perishes immediately.
While they were bestowing cows and gold, and performing the preparatory rites and the application of protective mantras during their ablutions, sipping of water, and silent recitations;
When rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests, as well as the worship of gurus, were being obstructed by various kinds of afflictions arising from poison;
The wise should wear this emerald, which is free from defects, endowed with excellent qualities, set in gold, and capable of being borne by those moving about in battle.
Whatever price is produced for a ruby when weighed on a scale, an emerald endowed with excellent qualities obtains even more than that.
And just as the value of rubies is diminished by defects, so too would there be an even greater loss in the case of emeralds due to their defects.

Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Examination of Emeralds," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. Sūta said: In that very land, where the young *lavalī* flowers and sprouts are plucked by the fingertips of the women of Siṃhala, the pair of eyes of the son of Diti (Hiraṇyakaśipu)—exceedingly beautiful and possessing the luster of a blooming lotus—fell down.

Due to that cause, the coastal region of the ocean shines forth, spreading with the luster of waves beautiful on both sides; it gleams, adorned with lines of blooming *ketaka* groves and possessing dense jewels of sapphire.

There, gems arise from flowers resembling the dark lotus, the plow-bearer (Balarāma), the one who wields the sword (Kṛṣṇa), the bee, the bow-armed one (Viṣṇu), the body of Śiva, and the saffron-colored flower of the throat; they also arise from the fresh blossoms of the *girikarṇikā* plant, possessing a similar luster.

Some were like the clear waters of the ocean, the repository of all fluids; others resembled flocks of peacocks; some had the luster of bubbles arising from indigo dye; and others possessed the hue of the throats of intoxicated cuckoos.
In that [mountain], there arise sapphires of great quality, uniform in kind, radiant with the beauty of distinct colors.

Those [gems] that are accompanied by flaws such as earth, stone, rock-cavities, gravel, or fear-inducing cracks, and those corrupted by defects in color or luster caused by mica-scales, are to be rejected.
For it is from that very source that many jewels are produced; the wise, whose intellects are awakened by the scriptures, praise them.
Whatever qualities are seen in a ruby when it is worn, a person obtains those very same qualities by wearing a sapphire.
Just as there are three types of origin for rubies, so too should it be understood without distinction for sapphires.
The very same criteria by which a ruby is examined are also observed for the sapphire.
And however much fire one might step over by means of using a ruby, one may step over a far greater distance from an indranīla gem.
Nevertheless, no gem whatsoever should ever be placed in fire for the sake of examination or for the increase of its qualities.

If the measure of the fire is not fully understood, and it is corrupted by the defects of burning, it will lead to misfortune for the master, the performer, and likewise the one who causes it to be performed.
In this world, mirrors, blue lotuses, karavīra flowers, crystal, and so forth, along with lapis lazuli, are declared by the wise to be of different species, though they resemble the indranīla gem.
Their states of being heavy toward the guru and their state of hardness should always be understood, especially as they increase progressively like glass and other such materials.
Just as a certain sapphire may possess a coppery-red hue, so too are both the Karavīra and the Utpala copper-colored for the purpose of protection.
That sapphire in whose center the blue radiance of Indra’s bow shines forth is called an *indranīla*; it is highly precious and rare upon the earth.
That [gem] which, due to the predominance of its own color, brings all milk—even a hundredfold quantity—to a state of blueness, is called Mahānīla.
Whatever may be the price of a highly precious ruby weighing one māṣa, that same amount would be the price of a highly precious sapphire weighing one suvarṇa.

Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Examination of Sapphires," in the section on Conduct within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. Sūta said: O twice-born ones, I shall now describe the examination of Vaidūrya (cat's-eye), Puṣparāga (topaz), Karketana, and Bhīṣmaka, as proclaimed by Brahmā and related by Vyāsa.

From the roar of the son of Diti, which resembled the tumultuous sound of the ocean agitated at the end of an aeon, there arose beryl—multicolored and the seed of a luster and hue beautiful with its splendor.
Not far from the mountain Vidūra with its lofty slopes, there was a mine situated along the boundary of Kāmabhūtika.
Because it originated from that sound, the mine of great qualities arose, transcending the world and serving as an ornament for the three worlds.

Resembling the roar of that very lord of the Dānavas, and displaying a beautiful form like a rain-cloud at the beginning of the monsoon, various Vaidūrya gems emitted diverse radiance from him, appearing like a multitude of sparks.
Taking as a standard the ruby, whatever jewel colors exist upon the earth, vaidūrya surpasses them all in the beauty of its hue.

Among those, the best is that which is blue like a peacock's neck or has the luster of a bamboo leaf; those gems whose beauty resembles the wing-tip of a blue jay are not praised by those learned in the science of jewels.
A virtuous vaidūrya gem provides its owner with supreme enjoyments; however, one possessed of defects brings about misfortunes. Therefore, one should examine it with great care.
Girikāca, śiśupāla, kāca, and sphaṭika that are permeated by smoke—these are of different species, yet they resemble the vaidūrya gem.
One should know *śeṣapālaka* by the absence of lines and its lightness; *sphaṭika* by its brilliance like mountain-glass and its radiant color.
Whatever is the price of a high-quality sapphire weighing one *suvarṇa*, that very same price is prescribed for a lapis lazuli gem weighing two *palas*.

Just as all those of a different species that may resemble a genuine gem in color, nevertheless possess the supreme mode of distinction that can be inferred through various differences; so it is here.
This distinction should always be examined with ease by a wise man; for the distinction of affection—lightness and softness—is indeed a universal sign of a different nature.

Being filled with wholesome and unwholesome qualities and bound by various applications of refinement, they acquire the emergence of virtues and faults; like jewels, they become distinct, possessing different values according to their respective worth.

When, in due order, the past and present [jewels] are securely bound together by a binding cord with effort, even if those jewels are free from defects, they obtain a price six times [their individual value].
The value of these gems, which have come from mines beyond the shores of the ocean, is not uniform throughout the entire earth.
That which was declared by Manu as a suvarṇa consisting of sixteen māṣakas, its seventieth part shall serve as the basis for the designation [of the māṣaka].
A *śāṇa* is measured as four *māṣas*, and a *māṣaka* consists of five *kṛṣṇalas*; the tenth part of a *pala* is proclaimed to be a *dharaṇa*.
Thus has the procedure for gems been declared for the determination of the value of jewels.

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Examination of Vaidūrya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Sūta said: From the skin of that enemy of the gods, which fell upon the Himālaya mountain, flowers began to emerge from those [scars].
Passions are great virtues.
A stone that is beautiful with a yellowish-white luster is known as Padmarāga; it is called Kaukaṇṭaka if it is reddish-yellow.

That which is blood-red yet yellow, clear, and reddish-brown (kāṣāya) is declared to be of one kind; that which is the color of pale blue and white, glossy, and smooth is possessed of excellent qualities.
That which is extremely red is indeed known as *padmarāga*; moreover, that very same stone, when being intensely blue, is called *indranīla*.
For one who knows the essence of jewels, its value is indeed declared to be like that of a lapis lazuli gem; and likewise is the fruit of wearing it, yet for women, it becomes a bestower of sons.

Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Examination of Puṣparāga," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Sūta said: Vāyu, having joyfully seized the claws of the lord of the Daityas, cast them into groves of excellent lotuses. Thereupon, the Karketana gem was produced, endowed with the power of the wind; it is the most worshipful on earth.

In its color, it shines like blood, moonlight, or honey, glowing with a reddish-yellow hue like a blazing fire; yet when it is blue, white, rough, or fractured, it appears as such due to the influence of defects such as disease and the like.
Lustrous, pure, and possessing even color, yellowish-green in hue, heavy, and variegated; free from flaws, cracks, and insect holes—those karketana gems are supremely purifying.
When it has been wrapped in a golden leaf and heated in the fire until it becomes radiant, it then destroys disease, dispels the Kali age, prolongs life, sustains the lineage, and bestows happiness.

Those men who bring such a gem of many virtues, a karketana stone, for the sake of auspicious adornment, become honored, possessed of great wealth and many kinsmen; they remain eternally radiant and are filled with joy.

Some, having cast off their [natural state], possess a distorted, agitated, and dark luster; they are withered, discolored, turbid, and deformed; lacking brilliance, intense radiance, noble lineage, and physical nourishment, they bear bodies resembling the *karketana* gem.

If a karketana gem has its color and form thoroughly examined and possesses the brilliant luster of the newly risen sun, then for that supreme jewel, when weighed, a price equal to its greatness as declared by those learned in the treatises on gems should be determined.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Examination of Karketana Gems," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: In the northern region of the Himavat mountains, the semen of that enemy of the gods fell; it became the source of origin for the most excellent Bhīṣma gems.
From that, there arise white stones resembling conchs, lotuses, and *syonāka* flowers, as well as radiant ones; then there arise young [stones] resembling diamonds and formidable rocks.
He who, with faith, wears even a pure *bhīṣmamaṇi*—set with gems such as gold—around his neck or other parts of his body, always attains great prosperity.
Indeed, even when he is nearby, the forest-dwellers—leopards, wolves, śarabhas, elephants, lions, tigers, and other such predators—flee upon seeing him.

Therefore, there is no fear for one who has been polished by the touchstone; they do not mock the Lord. A terrifying gem, endowed with excellent qualities, becomes a perfectly fitting ornament upon the finger.

Through the libation for the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa), the satisfaction of the ancestors becomes lasting for many years. Even the poisons of snakes, birds, rats, and scorpions are pacified; and fearsome dangers from water, fire, enemies, and thieves perish.
A wise person should avoid from afar a man who resembles moss or a cloud, who has a yellowish luster yet is devoid of radiance, whose brilliance is soiled, and who is discolored.
The price of these should be determined by the best of the wise through their knowledge of place and time: for things that have come from afar, it is much; for those produced nearby, it is little.

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Examination of Vaidūrya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Sūta said: On auspicious and excellent mountains, by rivers, and in other locations situated in the northern regions, [the gems] were established after the Lord of the Dānavas was worshipped with great honor in those famous places, through the power of his own claws and arms.
Those *pulaka* gems produced in Daśārṇa, Avagadara (or Avada),

Mekala, Kāla, Gādī, and other regions, which possess the color of *guñjā*, collyrium, honey, or lotus stalks, and which have a luster resembling *gandharva*, fire, or plantain— these are praised as excellent.
Those *pulaka* beads, which bear various patterns resembling conch shells, lotuses, bees, and suns;
