which are free from flaws in their threading; which are supremely pure and auspicious; and which are adorned with many beautiful divisions, bestow prosperity.

Those accompanied by crows, jackals, donkeys, jackals, wolves, and vultures of fierce appearance, with mouths wet with flesh and blood, are givers of death and must be avoided by the wise; their price is said to be five hundred *palas*.
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Examination of the Body Hairs," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said: Taking the form of the Dānava as desired, the Fire-god cast it into the Narmadā river, and a small portion into lands such as those of the low-born.

In that regard, having extracted the gem known as Rudhirākṣa— which is composed of indragopas, has the color of a parrot's beak, and in its shape is equal in size to a manifest pīlu fruit— it is indeed uniform in all respects.

If that film should be as white as the full moon, of an exceedingly pure color, and resembling sapphire on the scale, it is said to produce sovereignty and servants; and when it has ripened, it indeed becomes the color of the divine vajra.
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Examination of the Blood-Eyed Jewel," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said: In the lands of Kāverī, Vindhya, Yavana, Cīna, and Nepāla, Lāṅgalī diligently scattered the fat of the Dānava.
From that, there arises the substance called oil, pure as space, and then crystal; it is white like a lotus stalk or a conch shell, yet endowed with some slight variation in color.
Indeed, it is not equal to jewels; rather, it destroys evil. Once consecrated by a craftsman, it immediately obtains some small value from that [act].
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Examination of Sphaṭika," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Having taken the entrails of that Bala, Śeṣa cast them into the Kelā and other waters; there, corals of excellent qualities are born.

Among those, the primary [gems] are declared to be those with the luster of rabbit's blood, resembling the *guñjā* and *japā* flowers, deep blue, and those from Devakaroṃka; their origins are in these places and they possess a divine hue.

Even if it originates elsewhere, that [coral] does not possess its primary value due to the application of specific craftsmanship; for that coral is indeed translucent, soft, glossy, and of beautiful hue.

O Śaunaka, the examination of the Pulaka, Rudhirākṣa, Sphaṭika, and Vidruma gems has been declared for the sake of discerning jewels—gems that bring wealth and grain in this world and destroy the affliction of poison and fear.

Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Examination of Coral," in the *Ācārakāṇḍa* of the first part of the *Pūrvakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. (The examination of gems, pearls, and so forth is hereby completed. (Now begins the majesty of sacred fords and holy fields. Sūta said: I shall describe all the sacred fords (*tīrthas*). The Gaṅgā is the most excellent among all sacred fords. The Gaṅgā is easily accessible everywhere, yet she is difficult to attain at three specific places.
At Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean—Prayāga is the supreme sacred ford, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those who have died there.
Vārāṇasī is the supreme sacred ford (tīrtha) for men; by serving the alms gathered there, one conquers evil and obtains all desires, for it is there that Viśveśa and Keśava reside.
Kurukṣetra is a supreme sacred site that bestows worldly enjoyment and liberation through acts such as giving; Prabhāsa is also a supreme sacred site, for Somanātha resides there.
And the delightful city of Dvārakā, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; the meritorious Prācī Sarasvatī; and the supreme Saptasārasvata.
Kedāra, which destroys all sins, is the supreme Śambhalagrāma; the sacred site of Nara-Nārāyaṇa is Vadarikāśrama for the sake of liberation.
Śvetadvīpa, the city of Māyā, Naimiṣa, the supreme Puṣkara, Ayodhyā, Arghyatīrtha, Citrakūṭa, and the Gomatī.
The Vaināyaka Mahītīrtha, the supreme hermitage of Rāmagiri, Kāñcīpurī, the Tuṅgabhadrā, Śrīśaila, and Setubandhana.
Rāmeśvara is a supreme holy site, as is the excellent Kārttikeya; likewise Bhṛgutuṅga, Kāmatīrtha, and the holy site of Amarakaṇṭaka.
In Ujjayinī is Mahākāla; at Kubjaka is Śrīdhara Hari; Kubjāmraka is a great sacred ford (tīrtha), as is Kālasarpa, which grants all desires.
And Mahākeśī, Kāverī, Candrabhāgā with Vipāśā, as well as the holy site of Ekāmra, Brahmeśa, and Devakoṭaka.
Know that the beautiful city of Mathurā, the great river Śoṇa, and the great sacred ford Jambūsaras—these are indeed holy places of pilgrimage.
Wherever the Sun, Śiva, Gaṇeśa, the Goddess, or Hari reside—in these and other such places—bathing, giving gifts, recitation, and austerity [yield great fruit].
Worship, ancestral rites, and the offering of funeral cakes—all these become inexhaustible; the Śālagrāma bestows everything and is the supreme sacred site of Paśupati.
Kokāmukha, Vārāha, Bhūṇḍīra, and the one named Svāmī; Mahāviṣṇu is at Mohadaṇḍa, and Madhusūdana is at Mandāra.
Kāmarūpa is a great pilgrimage site where Kāmākhyā resides; and there is the Puṇḍravardhana pilgrimage site, where Kārtikeya dwells.
Viraja is a great sacred ford (tīrtha), as is the sacred ford of Śrī Puruṣottama; Mahendra Mountain is a sacred ford, and the Kāverī river is another supreme sacred ford.
The Godāvarī is a great sacred ford; the Payoṣṇī is a river that grants boons; the Vindhya is a sin-removing sacred ford; and the Bheda of the Narmadā is supreme.
Gokarṇa is a supreme sacred site, as is the city of Māhiṣmatī; Kālañjara is a great sacred site on earth, and Śuklatīrtha is unsurpassed.
When purification has been performed, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow resides nearby; there is the Viraja-tīrtha which grants everything, and the Svarṇākṣa-tīrtha, the most excellent of holy sites.
Nanditīrtha, which bestows liberation and grants the fruit of ten million holy places; then the great Nāsikya Tīrtha, and beyond that, Govardhana.
The Kṛṣṇaveṇī, Bhīmarathī, Gaṇḍakī, and Irāvatī; the meritorious Bindusaras Tīrtha, and the supreme Viṣṇupādodaka.
Meditation on Brahman is the supreme sacred ford; restraint of the senses is a sacred ford; self-control is indeed the highest sacred ford, and likewise, purity of being is the supreme one.
He who bathes in the mental sacred ford—the lake of knowledge with meditation as its water, which removes the impurities of passion and hatred—attains the supreme goal.
For those people who perceive duality, thinking "this is a sacred ford" and "this is not," going to a sacred ford and whatever fruit it yields are prescribed for them.
For one who knows that "all is Brahman," there is no place that is not a sacred ford; in these [waters], bathing, giving gifts, ancestral rites, and the offering of rice-balls become inexhaustible.
All rivers, all mountains, the sacred ford (tīrtha) frequented by gods and others, Śrīraṅga—the sacred ford of Hari—and the Tāpī, the most excellent great river.
The Saptagodāvara is a sacred ford, and Koṇagiri is a supreme sacred ford; there dwells the goddess Mahālakṣmī, and the Praṇītā is a supreme river.
On the Sahya mountain, O Lord of the gods, you are Ekavīra; at Gaṅgādvāra, Kuśāvarta, Vindhya, and the Nīla mountain, you are Sureśvarī.
Having bathed at the Kanakhala tīrtha, he shall not be born again. Sūta said: These and other tīrthas are indeed givers of all things through bathing and other rites.

Having heard this from Hari, Brahmā spoke to Vyāsa, who was accompanied by Dakṣa and the others. After mentioning these holy places, he further spoke of the most excellent of all holy places called Gayā, which is imperishable for all and bestows the world of Brahmā.
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of All Holy Places," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

**The Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 82.** *Salutations to the auspicious Gaṇeśa.* (Now begins the Greatness of Gayā. Brahmā said: O Vyāsa, I shall proclaim in brief the supreme greatness of Gayā, which is the essence of all essences and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Listen.
Formerly, there was a most powerful and supreme asura named Gaya, who performed a most terrible penance that caused distress to all living beings.
The gods, tormented by that penance, went to Hari for the sake of his destruction; Hari said to them, "It must come to pass through those whose essence is Śiva."
"His great body shall be cast down; so be it," the gods said to Hari. And once, for the sake of worshipping Śiva, they [took] lotuses from the Ocean of Milk.
Having brought him to the land of Kīkaṭa, the powerful one made him his bed; deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, he was slain by Viṣṇu with his mace.
Therefore, Viṣṇu, as Gadādhara, remains at Gayā as the bestower of liberation; his body exists there in the form of a liṅga, while the Grandfather (Brahmā) resides in Śuddha.
Janārdana, Kāleśa, and another, Prapitāmaha—Viṣṇu then declared: "This shall become a sacred field (puṇyakṣetra) established by divine ordinance."
The man who performs sacrifices, ancestral rites, the offering of funeral cakes, bathing, and other such acts, shall go to heaven and the world of Brahmā; that man shall not go to hell.
Recognizing Gayātīrtha as supreme, the Grandfather (Brahmā) performed a sacrifice and honored the Brahmins who had arrived for the purpose of officiating as priests.
Having created great rivers carrying flavorful waters, as well as ponds and the like, he likewise created edible and consumable fruits and the wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu).
The Lord gave the Gayā-kṣetra, extending five krośas, to the Brāhmaṇas; however, out of greed for wealth and other gifts at the Dharma-sacrifices, they accepted them.
Then those Brahmins, having been cursed at Gayā, remained there; it was decreed that their learning should not continue for three generations, nor should their wealth continue for three generations.
"May there be for you a river carrying water and a mountain of stone"; when they had thus petitioned him, the Lord Brahmā granted them his favor.
For those meritorious people who perform śrāddha at Gayā go to the world of Brahmā; by those who honor you, I am always honored.
Knowledge of Brahman, performing a śrāddha at Gayā, dying in the house of a cow, and residing at Kurukṣetra—these are the fourfold means of liberation for men.
O Vyāsa, all the oceans, rivers, as well as ponds, wells, and lakes, go to the sacred ford of Gayā desiring to bathe; of this there is no doubt.
The killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and violating the teacher’s wife—all sins arising from association with such persons are destroyed by performing a śrāddha at Gayā.
Those who died by natural causes, those killed by animals or thieves, and those bitten by snakes—all go to heaven through the śrāddha performed at Gayā.
The fruit that a man obtains by offering funeral cakes at Gayā cannot be described by me even in hundreds of millions of years.
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gayā," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Brahmā said: In the Kīkaṭa region, Gayā is meritorious; the Rājagṛha forest is meritorious; the district of Cāraṇa is meritorious; and among rivers, the Punarpunā is meritorious.
Muṇḍapṛṣṭha is in the east; Gayā is proclaimed to have a measurement of two and a half krośas in the west, south, and north.
The sacred field of Gayā extends for five krośas, and Gayāśiras for one krośa; by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) there, eternal satisfaction is attained.
From Nagā, Janārdana, the well, and Uttaramānasa—this is declared to be Gayāśiras, and it is called Phalgutīrtha.
In that regard, by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), the ancestors attain the supreme goal; merely by going to Gayā, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
At Gayā, Janārdana, the God of gods, exists in the form of the ancestors; by beholding that lotus-eyed one, one is indeed liberated from the three debts.
Having seen the chariot-path at Gayātīrtha, as well as Rudrapada and the others, Kāleśvara, and Kedāra, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
Having seen the god Pitāmaha, one is liberated from all sins; and having seen the Prapitāmaha, one goes to the world free from affliction.
Likewise, by bowing with great effort to that god Gadādhara, Mādhava, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), a man is not born again.
O brahmin sage, by beholding the high-souled Maunāditya, and especially Kanakārka, with silence, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
Having worshipped Brahmā, one shall attain the world of Brahmā; that man who, having risen at dawn, beholds the Gāyatrī.
By performing the twilight devotion (sandhyā) with diligence, one obtains the fruit of all the Vedas; and by beholding the Sāvitrī at midday, one obtains the fruit of sacrifice.
By beholding Sarasvatī in the evening, one obtains the fruit of giving; by beholding Īśvara situated on the mountain, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
Having seen Dharmāraṇya and the Lord Dharma, one's debt is destroyed; having seen the god Gṛdhreśvara, who would not be liberated from bondage?
Having seen Dhenu in Dhenuvana, one leads one's ancestors to the world of Brahmā; and having seen Prabhāseśa at Prabhāsa, one attains the supreme goal.
By seeing Koṭīśvara and Aśvamedha, one's debt shall be destroyed; by seeing Svargadvāreśvara, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
By beholding Rāmeśvara and Gadālola, one shall attain heaven; likewise, by beholding Brahmeśvara, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.
Having seen Mahācaṇḍī at Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, one shall obtain all desires; and having seen Phalgvīśa, Phalgucaṇḍī, Gaurī, and Maṅgalā.
One becomes free from debt to the ancestors by visiting Gomaka, the divine Gopati, Aṅgāreśa, Siddheśa, Gayāditya, and likewise Gaja.
Having seen Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors; having bathed at Phalgutīrtha and seen the god Gadādhara, a man [attains the same].
What is not sufficient for men who perform good deeds? Here, twenty-one generations of men go to the world of Brahmā.
Whatever sacred fords exist on earth, whatever oceans and lakes there may be, they shall all go to Phalgutīrtha once every single day.
On earth, Gayā is meritorious; within Gayā, Gayāśiras is meritorious; and likewise, Phalgutīrtha is the most excellent, for it is indeed the mouth of the gods.
To the north of the Kanakā river is the Nābhi-tīrtha in the center; the meritorious Brahma-sadas tīrtha bestows the world of Brahmā through bathing.

By offering funeral cakes and other oblations at the well, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors; likewise, by performing a śrāddha at the Akṣaya-vaṭa, the performer leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā.
Having bathed at Haṃsatīrtha, a person is liberated from all sins; likewise at Koṭitīrtha, Gayālole, Vaitaraṇī, and Gomaka.
A person faithful in performing śrāddha at Brahmatīrtha, Rāmatīrtha, Āgneyatīrtha, and Somatīrtha leads twenty-one generations of men to the world of Brahmā.
One who performs a śrāddha at Rāmahrada leads his ancestral lineage to the world of Brahmā; one who performs a śrāddha at Uttaramānasa is not born again as a human being.

At Dakṣiṇamānasa, a performer of śrāddha shall lead his ancestors to the world of Brahmā. At Svargadvāra, a man performing śrāddha shall likewise lead his ancestors to the world of Brahmā. One who performs the libation for Bhīṣma at its peak (kūṭa) delivers his ancestors. Likewise, by performing śrāddha at Gṛdhreśvara, one becomes free from debt to one's ancestors.

One who is faithful to the ancestral rites (śrāddha) leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā by means of a cow in the forest; one who gives a sesame-cow, having bathed and beheld the cow, attains this without doubt.
Having performed the śrāddha at Aindra, Naratīrtha, Vāsava, or Vaiṣṇava, as well as at a great river, one leads one's ancestors to the world of Brahmā.
Having performed bathing, the *saṃdhyā* rites, libations (*tarpaṇa*), and *śrāddha* at the Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī tīrthas, one attains [the merit of] one hundred and one [offerings].
Such a man leads his ancestral lineage to the world of Brahmā; restrained and with his mind fixed on the ancestors, he shall emerge from the womb of Brahman.

Having gratified the ancestors and the gods, one does not enter the confinement of rebirth; through libations offered with the *kākajaṅghā* plant, the satisfaction of the ancestors becomes inexhaustible.
By performing a *śrāddha* at the pond of Mataṅga in the Dharmāraṇya forest, one goes to heaven; and by doing so at the Dharmayūpa well, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
"May the gods be my authority and the world-protectors be my witnesses; having come here, I have performed this atonement for my ancestors upon this Matanga."
Having bathed at Rāmatīrtha and performed the Śrāddha ceremony at Prabhāsaka, it is said that the groups of ancestors are indeed liberated from their state as ghosts upon the stone slab.

One who performs the *śrāddha* rite on a cow nourished by itself shall uplift seven generations of its lineage three times over; one who performs the *śrāddha* on a *muṇḍapṛṣṭha* bull and others leads the ancestors to the world of Brahmā.
Indeed, there is no place in Gayā where a sacred ford (tīrtha) does not exist; throughout the five-krośa Gayā field, wherever one may be, one should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
A man obtains inexhaustible fruit and leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā; he should offer his own funeral cake (piṇḍa) into the hand of Janārdana.
O Janārdana, this funeral cake (piṇḍa) has been placed by me in your hand; may it attend upon him who has gone to the other world, providing inexhaustible liberation.
One certainly attains the world of Brahmā together with one's ancestors by performing rites at Gayā, at Dharmapṛṣṭha, and likewise at the lake of Brahmā.
What is given to the ancestors at Gayāśīrṣa and at the Akṣayavaṭa tree becomes inexhaustible; so too at Dharmāraṇya, Dharmapṛṣṭha, and Dhenukāraṇya.
Having seen these, one should deliver twenty ancestors belonging to a noble lineage; this is called Brahmāraṇya, the western region of the great river.
The eastern portion is Brahmasada; Nāgādri is Bharata’s hermitage. One who performs a śrāddha at Bharata’s hermitage shall attain the state of Mataṅga.
To the south of Gayāśīrṣa and to the west of the Mahānadī river is that which is known as Campakavana; for there indeed lies the Pāṇḍuśilā.
One who performs a *śrāddha* there on the third lunar day at the confluence of the Niścirā, at the Mahāhrada, and at the Kauśikī, shall obtain inexhaustible fruit.
To the north of the Vaitaraṇī is a reservoir known as the Third; there are the footprints of Krauñca, where one who performs the Śrāddha rite leads his ancestors to heaven.
To the north of Krauñcapāda is a body of water called Niścīra; there, a single visit and a single offering of a funeral cake [to one's ancestors] [yields great merit].
How much more difficult is it to remain permanently established in this very state? Having touched the waters of the Mahānadī, one should offer libations to the ancestors and the deities.
One shall attain inexhaustible worlds and uplift one's lineage; when the Sandhyā prayer is recited with the Sāvitrī mantra, it becomes equivalent to twelve years of practice.
The man who dwells at Gayā during both the bright and dark fortnights purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation; of this there is no doubt.
Having seen Muṇḍapṛṣṭha at Gayā, the mountain Aravinda, and thirdly Krauñcapāda, one is liberated from sins.
And when a lunar or solar eclipse occurs while the moon is in Capricorn, the offering of funeral cakes at Gayā is difficult to obtain even throughout the three worlds.
A śrāddha offered at Mahāhrada, at the Kauśikī river, especially at Mūlakṣetra, and in the cave of Gṛdhrakūṭa, yields great fruit for seven [generations].
Where there is the Māheśvarī stream, one who performs the śrāddha rite shall become free from debt; having reached the meritorious river Viśālā, renowned throughout the three worlds.
The man who performs the *śrāddha* attains the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice and ascends to heaven; by bathing at Māsapada, the performer of the *śrāddha* obtains the fruit of the *vājapeya*.
By offering a funeral ball (piṇḍa) at Ravipāda, the elevation of the fallen occurs; he who, staying at Gayā, gives food, by him his ancestors become possessed of a son.
The ancestors, terrified by the fear of hell, long for sons, thinking: "Whoever shall go to Gayā will deliver us."
Seeing his son arrived at Gayā, there shall be a festival for the ancestors; indeed, by merely touching the water with his feet, he will surely offer it to us.
Whether it be one's own son or another person, whenever one causes a funeral cake (piṇḍa) to be offered at Gayākūpa under someone's name, that person shall be led to eternal Brahman.
One who visits ten million sacred fords (tīrthas) shall attain Puṇḍarīka, the world of Viṣṇu; that river which is renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Vaitaraṇī.

She has indeed descended into the field of Gayā for the sake of delivering the ancestors; whoever performs the Śrāddha rite, offers funeral cakes (piṇḍas), or makes a gift of a cow there, [attains the highest goal].
If a son should ever go to Gayā at the turn of time, he would deliver twenty-one generations of his lineage; of this there is no doubt.
One should feed those very Brahmins who have been designated by the priest; for them is the place of the Brahma-seat, and likewise the drinking of Soma.
The Brahmins occupy the station ordained by Brahmā; they themselves are ordained by Brahmā. When they are honored, all the deities together with the ancestors are likewise honored.

One should satisfy the Brahmins at Gayā with offerings to the gods and ancestors (havya-kavya) according to the prescribed rites; for it is ordained that Gayā is the place for the abandonment of the body.
Whoever performs the rite of releasing a bull in the unsurpassed sacred field of Gayā obtains the merit of a hundred Agniṣṭoma sacrifices; of this there is no doubt.
A man of great intelligence, even for his own sake—and indeed for others as well—should perform the offering of the funeral cakes at Gayā, even without sesame seeds.
To as many paternal kinsmen, relatives, and friends as there may be, a funeral cake (piṇḍa) should be offered according to the prescribed rite on the Vyāsa-Gayā ground.
Having bathed at Rāmatīrtha, a man obtains the fruit of [giving] a hundred cows; and having bathed in the Mataṅgavāpī, he shall obtain the fruit of a thousand cows.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Niścirā, one leads one's ancestors to the world of Brahmā; having bathed at the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, one obtains the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
By dwelling at Mahākauśī, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice; it flows forth from the lake of Pitāmaha and purifies the world.
In its vicinity is the famous Kapilā, known as Agnidhārā; by bathing here, one who performs a śrāddha rite attains the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and achieves fulfillment of purpose.
One who performs a *śrāddha* at Kumāradhārā shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice; furthermore, by approaching and bowing to Kumāra, one shall attain liberation.
Having bathed in the Somakuṇḍa, a man goes to the world of Soma; by offering funeral cakes at the Saṃvarta pond, a man shall become fortunate.
A man who has washed away his sins goes to Pretakuṇḍa, as does one who offers funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Devanadī, Lelihāna, Mathana, and Jānugartaka.
At such sacred sites as these, one who offers funeral cakes (piṇḍa) shall deliver his ancestors; and by bowing to the gods, beginning with Vasiṣṭheśa, he shall achieve the destruction of his debts.
Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gayā," in the section on Conduct (*ācārakāṇḍa*) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Brahmā said: One who is about to go to Gayā should perform the *śrāddha* ceremony according to the prescribed rules, don the garb of a pilgrim (*kārpaṭī*), and perform the circumambulation of the village.
Then, having gone to another village and partaken of food remaining from a *śrāddha* ceremony, he should proceed on his way after performing a circumambulation, avoiding the acceptance of gifts.
For one who has merely set out from home toward Gayā, every step is indeed a stairway for the ancestors to ascend to heaven.
Shaving the head and fasting—this is the rule for all sacred fords, with the exception of Kurukṣetra, Viśālā, Virajā, and Gayā.
One should perform the śrāddha at Gayā every day, both by day and night; likewise, a śrāddha performed at Vārāṇasī or at the Śoṇanada tīrtha yields great merit.
By performing śrāddha again and again at Mahānadī, one leads the ancestors to heaven; having gone to Uttaramānasa, one attains unsurpassed perfection.
One should perform the śrāddha rite at that place and likewise perform the ritual bath; he obtains all divine desires as well as the means to liberation in every respect.
Having gone to Dakṣiṇamānasa, one should observe silence and perform the offering of rice-balls and other rites; at Dakṣiṇamānasa, one obtains the clearing away of the three debts.
With the most excellent serpents, who inspire joy in the perfected ones (siddhas), yet cause terror to the wicked; who are licking their lips, most formidable, and invincible.
The sacred ford named Kanakhala is renowned throughout the three worlds; it lies to the north of Muṇḍapṛṣṭha and is frequented by hosts of celestial sages.

Having bathed there, one goes to heaven; furthermore, a *śrāddha* offered there becomes inexhaustible. Having performed the proper rites such as offering the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), one should then bow to the Sun and perform this [following] act.
Kavyavāha, Soma, Yama, and Aryaman, as well as the Agniṣvātta, Barhiṣad, and Somapa Pitṛ-deities.
"May my highly fortunate ancestors come here, protected by you all—those who were born in my lineage and those who are my own kinsmen."
I have come to this Gayā for the purpose of offering the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) to them; having offered the cakes at Phalgutīrtha, behold the god Pitāmaha.
Then, having bathed at Phalgutīrtha and beheld the god Gadādhara, a man becomes free from debt to his ancestors. He shall then behold Gadādhara and become free from debt to his forefathers.
One shall immediately deliver oneself, as well as ten ancestors and ten descendants; this is declared to be the rite for the first day, and on the second day one should proceed.
One who offers funeral cakes and other oblations at the pond of Mataṅga in Dharmāraṇya shall obtain the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice upon reaching Dharmāraṇya.

The fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices shall be obtained at Brahma-tīrtha; one should perform the Śrāddha and offer the rice-balls and water-libations in the space between the well and the sacrificial post.
That rite for the ancestors performed with well-water becomes inexhaustible; having gone to the abode of Brahmā on the third day after the new moon, one should bathe and then perform the libation.

Having performed the ancestral rites (śrāddha) and so forth, they should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) between the sacrificial post (yūpa) and the well; situated near the pasture for cows, these [ancestors] were established by Brahmā, reaching up to Brahmā himself.
Merely by serving them, the ancestors attain liberation; by circumambulating the sacrificial post, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Having bathed at Phalgutīrtha on the fourth day and performed the libations for the gods and others, one should perform the Śrāddha ceremony at Gayāśīrṣa and at the Rudrapadas and other sites.
A śrāddha performed at Piṇḍāraka, at Dehimukha, at Vyāsa, at Pañcāgni, at Padatraya, and before the Sun, the Moon, and Kārttikeya, is likewise inexhaustible.
One should perform the Śrāddha for nine deities, or for twelve deities, on the Anvaṣṭakā days, at the rite of prosperity (Vṛddhi), at Gayā, and on the anniversary of a death.

In this place, the śrāddha for the mother is performed separately, whereas elsewhere it is performed together with the husband; however, having bathed at Daśāśvamedha and beheld the god Pitāmaha (Brahmā), [one attains the highest state].
Having touched the foot of Rudra, a man does not return here again; he obtains that fruit which one would attain by giving away the earth filled with wealth three times over.
Having performed a śrāddha at Gayāśiras, he obtains that fruit; one should offer a funeral ball (piṇḍa) at Gayāśiras even if it is only the size of a śamī leaf.
The ancestors attain divinity; there is no need for deliberation on this point. The wise Mahādeva has set his foot upon Muṇḍapṛṣṭha.
By performing austerities there at the head of Gayā (Gayāśīrṣa), one obtains great merit; and for those whose funeral cakes (piṇḍas) he offers by name, [he secures their liberation].
Those dwelling in hell go to heaven, and those dwelling in heaven attain liberation, after bathing on the fifth day at Gandālole at the foot of a banyan tree.
Having approached the foot of a banyan tree, one should offer rice-balls to the ancestors; by doing so with either leafy vegetables or warm water, one shall deliver the entire lineage.
When a single Brahmin is fed at the Akṣayavaṭa after performing a Śrāddha and beholding his great-grandfather, it is as if ten million have been fed.
One obtains inexhaustible worlds and uplifts a hundred generations of one's lineage; many sons are to be desired, so that even if only one among them goes to Gayā.
"One should either perform the horse sacrifice or release a dark-colored bull, dedicating it to a certain deceased person. Having said this, a certain ghost spoke to a merchant.
Perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Gayāśīrṣa in my name; thus I shall be liberated from the state of a preta, and it shall grant heaven to the giver as well.
Having heard this, the merchant Gayāśīrṣa offered a ball of rice (piṇḍaka) to the King of the Pretas together with his younger brothers, and thereafter he gave it to his own ancestors.
All were liberated; Viśāla also became a provider of funeral cakes along with his son. In Viśālā, Viśāla became the prince and spoke to the twice-born:
"How can I have sons and the like? Viśālaka asked the brahmins; they replied, "Everything will be yours through the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Gayā."
Then Viśāla, having offered the funeral cakes at Gayāśīrṣa, obtained sons; seeing three men—white, red, and black—in the sky, he spoke to them.
"Who are you? he asked, and one among them, who was white, replied to Viśālaka: "I am your father, the white one; I have gone to the auspicious world of Indra."
"My son's father was a murderer of a Brahmin and a supreme evildoer; this grandfather, O Kṛṣṇa, has slain sages."
O giver of funeral cakes, we had reached the Avīci hell, but having been liberated, we were reborn; thus, all of us have been set free and are now proceeding to the supreme heaven.

Having fulfilled his duties and ruled the kingdom, Viśāla went to heaven; yet those ancestors in my lineage for whom the rites of the funeral cake and water-libations have been omitted—[may they be satisfied].
And those whose tonsure ceremony has not been performed, those who have just emerged from the womb, those for whom no cremation rite was performed, and likewise others who were not consumed by fire;

May [the ancestors] who were given [this offering] upon the ground be satisfied; being satisfied, may they go to the supreme state—namely, the father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather.
The mother, the paternal grandmother, and likewise the paternal great-grandmother; as well as the maternal grandfather and the maternal great-grandfather.
The great-grandfather on the mother's side, as well as the maternal grandmother, the maternal grandfather, and likewise the great-grandmother on the mother's side.
And may this ball of rice reach others as well, remaining inexhaustible.

Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gayā," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. Brahmā said: Having bathed at the Pretaśilā and other sites with the water of the Varuṇā river, one should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) with these mantras, having first invoked the supreme ancestors.
"Those who have died in our family and for whom no destination is known—I shall summon them all here with water and sesame seeds upon the surface of the *darbha* grass."
For the sake of the deliverance of those who have died in my paternal lineage and those who have died in my maternal lineage, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa).
And for those in my maternal grandfather’s family whose destination is unknown, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa) for the sake of their deliverance.
For the sake of delivering all those who have not yet cut their teeth and those who were afflicted while in the womb, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa).

And for those members of my kin who are bereft of name and lineage—whether in my own family or another’s family—for whom no destination is known, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa) for the sake of their deliverance.
To those who died by hanging, those killed by poison or weapons, and those who committed suicide—to them I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa).
I offer this funeral cake for those who died in a fire, and for those killed by lions or tigers, or even by fanged or horned beasts.
To those who were cremated by fire, as well as others who were not cremated, and to those killed by lightning or thieves—to them I offer this funeral cake.
For the sake of uplifting those who have gone to the Raurava, Andhatāmisra, and Kālasūtra hells, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa).
For the sake of the deliverance of those who have gone to the terrible Asipatravana and the Kumbhīpāka hells, I offer this rice-ball.
For the sake of delivering those others who dwell in the world of pretas and in places of torment, I offer this rice-ball.
And those who have entered the womb of an animal—birds, insects, or reptiles—or those who dwell in the womb of a tree, to them I give this funeral cake (piṇḍa).
To those who have been led by the commands of Yama to abide in incalculable hells, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa) for the sake of their deliverance.
To those who wander through thousands of different births by their own karma, for whom a human birth is difficult to obtain—to them I offer this funeral cake.
May all those who were kinsmen or non-kinsmen, and those who were kinsmen in another birth, always attain satisfaction through this offering of rice balls.
Whatever ancestors of mine exist in the form of hungry ghosts (preta), may they all forever attain satisfaction through this offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
Those who were born in my father’s lineage, as well as in my mother’s lineage, those of my gurus, fathers-in-law, and kinsmen, and whoever else among my relatives has died;
Those in my family for whom the ancestral offerings have ceased, those deprived of sons and wives, those whose rites have been neglected, as well as those born blind and the lame;
May the funeral offering given by me reach those of my family who were deformed or born from unripened wombs, whether they were known or unknown; may it abide for them inexhaustibly.
May the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Īśāna, be my witnesses; having reached Gayā, I have performed the rite of deliverance for my ancestors.
O Lord Gadādhara, I have come to Gayā for the sake of my ancestral rites; may you be my witness today that I am freed from the three debts.
The Great River, the Lake of Brahmā, the inexhaustible banyan tree, Prabhāsa, the rising sun, Gayāśiras, the Sarasvatī, Dharmaka, Dhenupṛṣṭha—these are located at Kurukṣetra and in Gayā.
Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Majesty of Gayā," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Brahmā said: This stone known as Pretaśilā at Gayā exists in three locations: at Prabhāsa, at Pretakuṇḍa, and also upon the head of the demon Gayāsura.

This stone, composed of all the gods, is maintained according to dharma for the sake of prosperity; it [liberates] those among men who have fallen into the state of pretas, such as friends, kinsmen, and others.
Since the auspicious Pretaśilā exists for the sake of uplifting them, therefore sages, kings, queens, and others always [resort] to this place.
Those who perform ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and other ceremonies on that stone go to the world of Brahmā; for the stone is situated upon the back of the head of the demon Gayāsura.
Therefore, this mountain is called Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, for it consists of all the gods; and because at the feet of Muṇḍapṛṣṭha are the sources of the Brahma-lakes and other waters.
Among them was a lotus grove, and for that reason he was designated as Aravinda; he was called the mountain Aravinda because it was marked by the footprints of Krauñca.
Therefore, Mount Krauñcapāda bestows the world of Brahmā upon the ancestors; and the primordial deities, beginning with Gadādhara, were established at the very beginning.
Because they remain unmanifest in the form of stone, the stone is composed of the gods; having covered Gayāśiras, the stone remains there due to its great weight.
After some time, Hari—the primordial wielder of the mace, who is without beginning or end—manifested and remained present along with Mahārudra and the other gods.

For the sake of protecting the Dharma, for the destruction of unrighteousness and the like, and for the purpose of annihilating the Daityas and Rākṣasas, he formerly became a fish, just as he did in the past.
The Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-lion, the Dwarf, the Mighty Rāma, as well as Rāma the son of Daśaratha, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Kalki.
Thus, the manifest Gadādhara existed in an unmanifest form; for he was worshipped here at the very beginning by the gods, beginning with Brahmā.
Therefore, he who goes to the primordial Gadādhara together with the gods and offers him water for the feet, perfumes, flowers, and other such offerings, [attains the highest state].
The water for the guest-offering (arghya), the vessel, the water for the feet (pādya), fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, excellent food offerings (naivedya), and various kinds of garlands.
Garments, crowns, bells, fly-whisks, spectacles, ornaments and the like, as well as alms-food such as gifts of grain and so forth.
For them, wealth, grain, longevity, the perfection of health, progeny such as sons, spiritual welfare, knowledge, and desired objects of pleasure are [the fruits].
A wife, residence in heaven and other realms, a kingdom returned from heaven, noble birth, endowment with courage, and the crushing of enemies in battle.

Freed from slaughter and bondage, one shall attain liberation in the end; those who perform the ancestral rites, the offering of rice balls, and so forth, go to the world of Brahmā along with their ancestors.
Those who worship Jagannātha, Subhadrā, and Balabhadra, having attained knowledge and prosperity along with sons, go to Puruṣottama.
There, in the presence of Puruṣottamarāja, Sūrya, and Gaṇa, the offering of rice-balls and other gifts for the ancestors bestows the world of Brahmā.
By bowing to Kapardin Vighneśa, one is liberated from all obstacles; by worshipping Kārtikeya, one shall attain the world of Brahmā.
By worshipping the twelve Ādityas, one is liberated from all diseases; by thoroughly worshipping Vaiśvānara, one attains supreme radiance.
Having worshipped Revanta, one obtains unsurpassed horses; by honoring Indra, one attains great sovereignty, and by worshipping Gaurī, one shall obtain good fortune.
Having worshipped the knowledge-goddess Sarasvatī, having fully honored Lakṣmī and Śrī, and having propitiated Garuḍa, one is liberated from the multitude of obstacles.
By worshipping Kṣetrapāla, one is liberated from the host of planetary afflictions; by worshipping Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, one shall obtain all desires.
By properly worshipping the eight Nāgas, one bitten by a serpent is liberated; and by honoring Brahmā, one attains the world of Brahmā.
By worshipping Balabhadra, one shall obtain strength and health; and by honoring Subhadrā, one shall attain supreme good fortune.
By worshipping Puruṣottama, one attains all desires; by worshipping Nārāyaṇa, one becomes the lord of men.
By touching and bowing to Nārasiṃha, one shall be victorious in battle; by worshipping Varāha, one shall obtain sovereignty over the earth.
By touching the Mālā and Vidyādhara [mantras], one attains the station of a Vidyādhara; by worshipping Ādigadādhara, one obtains all desires.
Having worshipped Somanātha, one shall attain the world of Śiva; having paid homage to Rudreśvara, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
By bowing to Rāmeśvara, a man becomes as beloved as Rāma; by praising Brahmeśvara, a man is destined for the world of Brahmā.
By worshipping Kāleśvara, a man becomes a conqueror of death; and by honoring Kedāra, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Having fully worshipped Siddheśvara, one becomes a perfected being (siddha) and shall go to Brahmapura; indeed, having seen the primordial Gadādhara together with the original Rudras and others.
Having uplifted a hundred families, a man shall lead them to the City of Brahmā; one seeking dharma shall obtain dharma, and one seeking wealth shall obtain wealth.
One who desires pleasures shall obtain pleasures; one whose aim is liberation shall obtain liberation; one who seeks a kingdom shall obtain a kingdom; and one who seeks peace shall obtain peace.
Having fully worshipped the primordial Gadādhara, one attains all goals; a woman desiring sons obtains sons, and one desiring good fortune obtains it.
And she who desires progeny, having obtained sons, should worship Ādigadādhara with śrāddha, the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas), the gift of food, and the giving of water.
By worshipping the primordial Gadādhara, one attains the world of Brahmā; for among all the sacred pilgrimage sites on earth, the city of Gayā is the most excellent.
Likewise, he who has the form of stone and so forth is indeed the supreme Gadādhara; for when he is seen, the stone is seen, since everything is Gadādhara.

Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gayā," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa (hereby concludes the Greatness of Gayā). In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 87, Hari said: "I shall describe the fourteen Manus and their sons, beginning with Suka. First was Svāyambhuva Manu, and Agnidhra and others were his sons."
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and the greatly effulgent Vasiṣṭha—these are proclaimed as the seven sages (ṛṣis).
The Jayākhyas, the Amitākhyas, the Śukras, and likewise the Yāmas—these four groups of twelve each are the drinkers of Soma.
Viśvabhuj was Vāmadeva-Indra, and Bāṣkali was his enemy; that Daitya was slain by Viṣṇu with his great-souled discus.
Then there was Manu Svārociṣa, and his son Maṇḍaleśvara; also Citraka, Vinata, Karṇānta, Vidyuta, and Ravi.
Bṛhadguṇa, Nabhas, Mahābalaparākrama, Ūrjastambha, Prāṇa, Ṛṣabha, and Niścara;
Datta, Ambha, Liṣṭha, Avarīvan, and Ṛṣya—these seven are proclaimed; the Tuṣitas are said to be twelve, as are those who are the Pārāvatas.
The wise Indra, the enemy of the gods, was slain by the Lord Madhusūdana, the performer of many deeds and the ocean of compassion, who took the form of an elephant.
The sons of Auttama Manu were Āja, Paraśu, Vinīta, Suketu, Sumitra, Subala, and Śuci.
Deva, Devāvṛdha, Rudra, Mahotsāha, Ujjita, Rathaujas, Ūrdhvabāhu, Śaraṇa, Anagha, and Muni; Please perform the translation.
Sutapās, Śaṅku—these are proclaimed as the seven sages (ṛṣis). They are the Vaśavartins, Svadhāmans, Śivas, Satyas, and Pratardanas.
Five groups of deities are proclaimed, and each of them consists of twelve; Indra, Svaśānti, his Śukra, and the Dānava named Pralamba.
Hari Viṣṇu, in the form of a fish, slew that Dānava; and the sons of Tāmasa Manu were Jānujaṅgha and Nirbhaya.
Navakhyāti, Naya, Priyabhṛtya, Vivikṣipa, Dṛḍheṣudhi, Prastalākṣa, Kṛbandhu, and likewise Kṛta.
Jyotirdhāmā, Pṛthu, Dhṛṣṭa, Kāvya, Caitra, Cetāgni, and Hemaka— these seven sages are celebrated as the wise ones who possess divine luster.
The Haris, the Devatās, and four groups of twenty-seven each; Indra, Śibi, his enemy, and the Bhaumarathas are recorded [as the lords of these nakṣatras].
By Hari, in the form of a tortoise, the asura Bhīmaratha was slain, as well as Mahāprāṇa, the son of Raivata Manu and a practitioner of spiritual power.
He is the kinsman of the forest, devoid of enemies, the inner limb, the supreme slayer, and pure; he is firm in his vows, the banner, and the peak—thus are the sages described as his attributes.
Vedaśrī, Vedabāhu, and likewise Ūrdhvabāhu; Hiraṇyaroman, Parjanya, Satyanetra, and Svadhāman.
The Abhūtarajasas, the Devāśvamedhas, the Vaikuṇṭhas, and the Amṛtas—
these are the four classes of deities.
In this group there are fourteen deities: the powerful Lord Indra, the peaceful Śatru, and the Daitya who was slain by Viṣṇu in the form of a swan.
The sons of Cākṣuṣa Manu were Uru, Puru, Mahābala, Śatadyumna, Tapasvin, Satyabāhu,
and Kṛti.
Agniṣṇura, Atirātra, Sudyumna, and likewise Nara; Haviṣmān, Uttama, Śrīmān, Sudhāmā, and Virajas.
Abhimāna, Sahiṣṇu, Madhuśrī, and the Ṛṣis are recorded; as well as the Āryas, the Prabhūtas, the Bhāvyas, the Lekhas, and the Pṛthukas.
It is likewise declared that there are five hosts of the gods belonging to Aṣṭaka: Indra, Manojava, Śatru, Mahākāla, and Mahābhaja.
He was slain by Hari, who assumed the form of a horse; these sons of Vaivasvata Manu were devoted to Viṣṇu.
Ikṣvāku, Nābhāga, Dhṛṣṭa, Śaryāti, Nariṣyanta, Pāṃsu, Nabhas, and Nediṣṭha.
Karūṣa, Pṛṣadhra, and Sudyumna were the sons of Manu; and Atri, Vasiṣṭha, the venerable Jamadagni, and Kaśyapa [were the sages].
Gautama, Bharadvāja, and Viśvāmitra as the seventh; likewise, the forty-nine Maruts have been proclaimed.
The Ādityas, Vasus, and Sādhyas are three groups of twelve; likewise, the Rudras are proclaimed to be eleven and the Vasus eight.
Two are designated as the Aśvins, and likewise ten as the Viśvedevas; ten are the Āṅgirasa gods, and thus there are nine groups of gods.
Śakra was indeed named Tejasvin, and his enemy was known as Hiraṇyākṣa; then that one called Hariṇya was slain by Viṣṇu in the form of a boar.
I shall now declare the sons of the future Manu named Sāvarṇya: Vijaya, Cārvavīra, Nirmoha, Satyavāk, and Kṛti.
Varishtha, Garishtha, and Samgati; then Ashvatthaman, Kripa, Vyasa, Galava, and Diptiman.
Likewise, Rāma and Ṛṣyaśṛṅga are proclaimed as the seven sages (ṛṣis); and there are also the Sutapas, the Amṛtābhās, and the principal gods (suras).
The host of those gods is recorded as consisting of twenty members each; among them, Bali, the son of Virocana, shall become Indra.
Having given these three paces to Viṣṇu when he was begging for them, one who abandons prosperity and the station of Indra will thereafter attain perfection.
Hear now of the sons of Vāruṇi Dakṣasāvarṇi, the ninth [Manu]: Dhṛtaketu, Dīptiketu, Pañcahasta, Nirāmaya, Pṛthuśravas, Bṛhadudyumna, Ṛcīka, and Bṛhatguṇa.
Medhātithi, Dyuti, Savasa, Vasu, Jyotiṣmat, Havya, Kavya, the Rishi Vibhu, and Īśvara.
Para, Marīci, Garbha, and those three who possess excellent qualities; Deśa, Śatru, Kālakākṣa, and their slayer, Padmanābha.
At that time, there will be twelve hosts of gods, each consisting of one; their Indra will be the exceedingly heroic and marvelous Hara.
Now hear of the ten sons of Dhamaputra, the son of Manu Vaivasvata: Sukṣetra, Uttamaujas, and the valiant Bhūriśreṇya.
Śatānīka, Niramitra, Vṛṣasena, Jayadratha, Bhūridyumna, Suvarcas, Śānti, and the powerful Indra.
Ayo, Mūrti, Haviṣmān, Sukṛti, Avyaya, Nābhāga, Apratimaujas, Saurabha, and likewise the Ṛṣis.

At that time, there will be a host of deities numbering one hundred, known as the Prāṇas; their Indra will be the very powerful one named Śānti. Bali shall be his enemy, and Hari will cause him to be slain with a mace.
I shall now declare the sons of you, Rudra, who have eleven sons: Sarvatraga, Suśarman, Devānīka, Puru, and Guru.
Kṣetravarṇa, Dṛḍheṣu, Ārdraka, Putraka, Haviṣmān, Haviṣya, Varuṇa, and Viśvavistara.
Viṣṇu, Agnitejas, and the seven sages are proclaimed; likewise, the Vihagaṅgamas, the Kāmagas, and the Nirmāṇarucis.
Each of their hosts consists of thirty-three members, and Indra is indeed their leader; his enemy Dhasagrīva, appearing in the form of Śrī, shall cause him to be slain.
Now hear of the sons of Manu, the twelfth son of Dakṣa: Devavān, Upadeva, Devaśreṣṭha, and Vidūratha.
Mitravan, Mitradeva, the heroic Mitrabindu, Mitravāha, and Pravāha were the sons of Manu, the son of Dakṣa.
Tapasvī, Sutapas, Tapomūrti, Taporati, Tapodhṛti, Dyuti, and another, Tapodhana, were the seven [sages].
The Svadharmas, the Sutapas, the Haritas, and likewise the Hahitas, as well as these groups of Surāris—each of these is a group of ten.
And there, O auspicious lady, Indra shall be named Ṛtadhāman, while his enemy shall be named Tāraka; Śaṅkara, having become Hari in the neuter form, will slay him.
Learn from me the sons of Trayodaśa Manu, Raucya: Citrasena, Vicitra, Tapas, Dharmarata, and Dhṛti.
Sunetra, Kṣetravṛtti, Sunaya, Dharmapa, Dṛḍha, Dhṛtimat, Avyaya, Niśārūpa, and Nirutsuka.
The seven seers are proclaimed to be free from delusion and perceivers of reality: Svaromāṇa, Sudharmā,
Sukarmā, and likewise Amara.
There, indeed, were thirty-three distinct hosts of gods; Indra was the lord of heaven, and the enemy of the gods was a Dānava named Tviṣṭibha.
And Mādhava will cause his death by assuming the form of a peacock. Now hear from me, my son, about the sons of Manu Bhautya, the fourteenth.
Uru, Gabhīra, Dhṛṣṭa, Tarasvin, Grāha, Abhimānin, Pravīra, Jiṣṇu, Saṃkrandana, Tejasvin, and Durlabha—these were the sons of Manu Bhautya.
Agnīdhra, Agnibāhu, Māgadha, Śuci, Ajita, Mukta, and Śukra are proclaimed as the seven sages (ṛṣis).
The Cākṣuṣas, the Karmaniṣṭhas, the Pavitras, the Bhrājinas, and the Vacovṛddhas—these five groups of seven gods have been proclaimed.
The pure Indra is the great Daitya; Hari himself is the slayer of enemies. The one God, however, exists in four ways through Viṣṇu in the form of Vyāsa.
Then he composed the Purāṇas and the eighteen branches of knowledge (vidyās), as well as the six auxiliary limbs (aṅgas), the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, and the extensive treatise on Nyāya.
The Purāṇas, the Dharmaśāstra, Āyurveda, Arthaśāstra, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda—these indeed are the eighteen branches of knowledge.
Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Manu and His Lineage," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said: Hari described the Manvantaras to Brahmā and others, and to Hara; Mārkaṇḍeya spoke the hymn to the Pitṛs to Krauñcuki—listen to that.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: In former times, Ruci, the Prajāpati, free from possessiveness and egoism, fearless and possessed of immeasurable power, wandered over this earth.
Seeing that sage—who was without fire, without a dwelling, who ate but once a day, who had no fixed hermitage, and who was liberated from all attachments—his ancestors spoke to him.

The ancestors said: "O child, why have you not performed the meritorious act of taking a wife—a source of heaven and liberation, and a constant companion in this world that is otherwise without a friend?"
A householder who performs the proper worship of all the gods, the ancestors, the sages, and those in need, shall attain the worlds.
By uttering "svāhā," he distributes [the offering] to the gods; by uttering "svadhā," to the ancestors; and by the giving of food, he provides for his servants and even for guests.
Therefore, O sage among men, you have by fate incurred this bond of debt both to us and to all living beings, day after day.
Without having procreated sons, without having satisfied the ancestors, and without having performed the Māṇḍya rite, how do you wish to attain the heavenly realm?
O son, let there be for you only the awakening to afflictions through right means; having abandoned hell upon death, there will be only affliction in another birth.
Ruci said: "Possession leads to extreme suffering, to sin, and likewise to a downward rebirth; therefore, I did not previously take a wife."
A means for resolving one's own doubt is undertaken through momentary consultation; yet even this does not become a cause for one's own liberation because of attachment to it.

It is better indeed that this self of mine, though smeared with the mud of worldly existence, be washed daily by the waters of knowledge, rather than that self which is free from attachments yet remains unwashed.
The self, marked by the mire of karma accumulated through many births, should be washed by the wise with the waters of knowledge of reality, while their senses remain restrained.

The ancestors said: "It is indeed proper for one with restrained senses to perform purification even for oneself; however, this is not the path of means by which you, my son, are currently proceeding."

As you dispel your impurity through the five sacrifices, austerities, and gifts performed without attachment to their fruits, so too shall your previous actions, both auspicious and inauspicious, be exhausted.
Thus, for one who acts with the nature of a causal agent, bondage does not occur; nor does that action lead to bondage if it is not closely associated [with the ego].
For in this way, O child, the karma performed in previous lives—consisting of merit and demerit for human beings—is incessantly exhausted through experiences composed of pleasure and pain.
In this way, the wise wash away the self and protect it from bondage; guarded by their own discernment, they are not consumed by the mire of evil.
Ruci said: "O Grandfathers, ignorance is cooked away in the Veda through the path of ritual action; why then do you enjoin me to the path of action?"
The Pitṛs said: "All this is ignorance; this speech regarding action is false. Nevertheless, there is no doubt that action is the cause for the attainment of knowledge."

That which is performed by the virtuous for the sake of avoiding the non-performance of what is enjoined is indeed self-restraint leading to liberation; whereas any other form of restraint, on the contrary, leads to a downward rebirth.
If you consider it best that I should wash [this], you too will be consumed by the sins arising from the non-performance of what was ordained.
Even ignorance becomes beneficial for people, like poison, through the means of its practice; for it does not lead to bondage when [properly] undertaken.
Therefore, my child, perform the marriage ceremony according to the prescribed rites; otherwise, let your life from birth be fruitless, having failed to attain that which is beyond the world.
Ruci said: "I am now old; who will give me a wife? For a poor man, the taking of a wife is difficult."
The ancestors said: "O child, our downfall and your own descent into the lower realms will surely come to pass; yet you do not welcome our words."
Having spoken thus, O best of sages, his ancestors suddenly became invisible while he was looking on, like lamps extinguished by the wind.
The sage Mārkaṇḍeya, of great asceticism, related to Kraiñcukya the entire account of Ruci, characterized by his conversation with his father.
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "Knowledge of Ritual Action," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Being questioned again by Kraiñcikīnva, Mārkaṇḍeya spoke to him once more; his mind was deeply distressed by those words of his father.
Desiring a maiden, the brahmin-sage wandered the earth; failing to find a maiden and inflamed by his father’s command, he fell into deep anxiety, his mind exceedingly distressed.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? How may my marriage come about quickly, so as to bring prosperity to my ancestors?"
As that high-souled one was reflecting thus, the thought arose in his mind: "I shall propitiate this Brahmā, born from the lotus, through ascetic penance."

Then that high-minded one performed divine austerities for a hundred years; remaining there for a long time in the forests, established in his observances, he then undertook a supreme discipline for the sake of propitiation.
Then Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, revealed himself and said, "I am pleased; tell me what you desire."
Then, having prostrated before Brahmā, the refuge of the world, he spoke of that which he desired to do at the word of the ancestors.
Brahmā said: "You shall become a Prajāpati; you must create subjects. O Brahmin, having created subjects and begotten sons, you must likewise establish the ritual acts."
Having fulfilled your duties, you shall thereafter attain perfection; therefore, as instructed by your ancestors, do you take a wife.

"By all means, meditate upon this and perform the worship of the ancestors; for when they are satisfied, those very ancestors will grant you your desire. When the grandfathers are content, what would they not give—wives and sons?"
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having heard these words of the Ṛṣi Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, he performed the libation for the ancestors on a secluded sandy bank of the river.
Then the brahmin, becoming single-mindedly disciplined and with his neck bowed low in devotion, respectfully praised the ancestors with these hymns.

Ruci said: "With devotion I pay homage to the ancestors who dwell as presiding deities, for they are gratified even by the gods during the śrāddha rites with offerings preceded by the utterance of svadhā."
I pay homage here to the ancestors in heaven who are gratified by the great seers with devotion through mental śrāddhas, by those desiring both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
I pay homage to the ancestors in heaven, whom the perfected ones gratify at the ancestral rites with all kinds of divine and unsurpassed offerings.
With devotion I pay homage to the ancestors who are worshipped in heaven by the Guhyakas, who, through identification with them, attain supreme and ultimate prosperity.
I pay homage to the ancestors who are always worshipped by mortals on earth with faith during śrāddha rites, and who bestow the nourishment of desired worlds.
I pay homage here to the ancestors who are always worshipped by the learned on earth; they grant the progeny of Prajāpati and bestow the attainment of all desired objects.

I pay homage to those ancestors who are indeed gratified by forest-dwellers—those whose sins are washed away by austerity, who are restrained in diet, and who perform ancestral rites with forest-grown offerings.
I pay homage to the ancestors who are constantly gratified by Brahmins who are lifelong celibates practicing dharma, with self-restrained minds through their meditative absorptions.
I pay homage to the ancestors whom the Kṣatriyas satisfy with śrāddha offerings; through the complete ritual of ancestral oblations (kavya), they bestow the fruits of both worlds.
I pay homage to the ancestors who are always worshipped on earth by Vaiśyas, who are constantly devoted to their own duties with flowers, incense, food, and water.
I pay homage to the ancestors at the śrāddha ceremony with devotion even by Śūdras; known by the name Sukālins, they satisfy the entire world.
I pay homage to the ancestors in the Śrāddha ceremony who, subsisting on nectar, are always gratified by great asuras in Pātāla, having abandoned deceit and pride.

I pay homage to the ancestors who are worshipped with śrāddha offerings in the netherworld (rasātala) by the nāgas, who desire all objects of their wish, according to the prescribed rites and with every enjoyment.

I pay homage here to the ancestors, who are always fully gratified by the ancestral offerings (śrāddha), as well as by the serpents there, according to the prescribed rites and endowed with the abundance of mantra-enjoyments.

I pay homage to the ancestors who dwell visibly in the world of the gods, or upon the surface of the earth, as well as in the intermediate space; may they, who are worthy of worship by the enemies of the gods, accept what is offered by me.
I pay homage to the ancestors who are the supreme reality, who dwell in formless celestial chariots, whom the lords of yogis worship with stainless minds as the cause for liberation from afflictions.

I bow to the ancestors who exist in the celestial realm as embodied beings, partaking of the *svadhā* offering when there is an intention for desired fruits; they are capable of bestowing all things one might wish for, yet they grant liberation when no such desires are entertained.

May all those ancestors of yours be satisfied in this rite—those who grant the desires of those who wish for them: the state of a celestial being, the rank of Indra, or even more than that, as well as elephants, horses, jewels, and great mansions.

May those ancestors who always dwell in the rays of the moon, in the orb of the sun, and in the white celestial chariot, be satisfied in this rite with food and water; may they attain nourishment through perfumes and other offerings.

May those ancestors who find satisfaction in the oblation poured into the fire, who eat while residing within the bodies of Brahmins, and who attain joy through the offering of funeral cakes—may they be satisfied by this food and water.

May those who were fully gratified by the gods with rhinoceros meat, by the great sages with desirable black sesame seeds and divine, charming offerings, and by others with kāla vegetables, attain joy here.
And may all those poetic compositions that are most dear to you, which have been honored by me, be present here in these flowers, scents, water, and food offerings prepared by me.

May those ancestors of mine who are worshipped day by day with oblations, those who are honored on earth during the Ashtaka rites at the end of the month, and those who are worshipped at the end of the year and on festive occasions—may they attain satisfaction here.

Worthy of worship are those among the twice-born who shine like the moon and white water-lilies; those among the kṣatriyas who possess the hue of fire and the sun; likewise, those among the vaiśyas who are bright as gold, and those among the śūdra folk who have the luster of indigo.

All of them together find satisfaction in this world through my offering of flowers, perfumes, incense, water, food, and the like, as well as through the fire-oblation; I am forever prostrate before those ancestors.

May those who, having been gods in former lives, eat the auspicious *kavya* offerings brought for the sake of their satisfaction, and who, being satisfied, become the creators of prosperity—may they be satisfied; I bow down to them.

May the Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and fierce Asuras destroy whatever is inauspicious for living beings; may those primordial ones, worshipped by the Lord of the Immortals, be satisfied in this [rite], for I bow down before them.
May the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs, the Barhiṣad Pitṛs, the Ājyapa Pitṛs, and likewise the Somapa Pitṛs—these ancestors, gratified by me at this Śrāddha—attain complete satisfaction.

May the Agniṣvātta groups of ancestors protect my eastern quarter; likewise, may the Barhiṣad ancestors always guard my southern quarter. Similarly, may the Ājyapa protect the western, and the Somapa the northern.
May the ancestors always provide protection for me from all sides—from Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and Piśācas, as well as from the malice of Asuras.
Viśva, Viśvabhuj, Ārādhya, Dharma, Dhanya, Śubhānana, Bhūtida, Bhūtikṛt, and Bhūti—these are the nine hosts of the ancestors.
The Auspicious One, the Giver of the Auspicious, the Maker, the Healthy One, the Refuge of those more healthy, and the Cause of Healthiness—these six are remembered as the Gaṇas.
Vara, Vareṇya, Varada, Tuṣṭida, Puṣṭida, Viśvapātṛ, and Dhātṛ—these seven are remembered as the Gaṇas.
The Great One, the High-Souled, the Honored, the Possessor of Majesty, and the One of Great Strength—these five groups of ancestors likewise destroy all evil.
The fourfold group of ancestors is described as follows: one who bestows happiness, another who bestows wealth, another who bestows dharma, and one who bestows prosperity.
May those thirty-one classes of ancestors, by whom the entire world is pervaded, be satisfied here by what is offered by me.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: As he was thus offering praise, a towering mass of splendor suddenly appeared, pervading the entire sky.
Seeing that immense splendor standing there, having completely enveloped the world, Ruci knelt upon the earth and sang this hymn of praise.
Ruci said: I always pay homage to those ancestors who are honored, formless, of radiant splendor, meditative, and possessed of divine vision.
I bow to those bestowers of desires, who are the leaders of Indra and the other gods, as well as of Dakṣa and Mārīci, and likewise of the seven ṛṣis and others.
I bow to all those leaders of Manu and the others, as well as the sun and the moon, and to my ancestors even within the ocean.
With palms joined in reverence, I pay homage to the constellations and the planets, to wind and fire, to the sky, and likewise to heaven and earth.
With palms joined in reverence, I perpetually pay homage to Prajāpati, Kaśyapa, Soma, Varuṇa, and the Lords of Yoga.
Homage to the seven Gaṇas likewise in the seven worlds; I pay homage to Brahmā, the self-born, who possesses the eye of yoga.
I likewise bow down to the hosts of Pitṛs who have Soma as their support and who bear forms of Yoga, as well as to Soma, the father of the worlds.
Likewise, I pay homage to those other ancestors who have the form of fire, since this entire universe consists entirely of fire and moon.
Those who are in fire, and those who are the embodiments of Soma, Sūrya, and Agni, as well as those whose nature is the world and likewise whose nature is Brahman.
To all those yogis who are my ancestors, with a restrained mind, I offer salutation after salutation; may you, the consumers of the *svadhā* offering, be gracious.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus praised by him, those best of sages, the Pitṛs, then emerged, illuminating the ten directions with their splendor.
And he saw them standing before him, adorned with the offerings of flowers, perfumes, and ointments that had been presented to him.
Having prostrated with radiant devotion, Ruci once again joined his palms in reverence and, showing distinct respect, said: "Salutations to you! Salutations to you!"
Then the gratified ancestors said to that best of sages, "Choose a boon," and he, with his neck bowed, spoke to them.
Ruci said: "The Creator has commanded me to be the progenitor of creatures; therefore, I desire a blessed, divine wife who shall bear offspring."
The ancestors said: "Right here, let your most enchanting wife appear instantly; and from her, O best of sages, a son shall be born to you."
O Ruci, this wise lord of the manvantara, distinguished by your very name, shall attain renown throughout the three worlds as Raucya.
He too shall have many sons of great strength and prowess, high-souled protectors of the earth.
And you, having become Prajāpati and created the fourfold progeny, shall—once your office has expired and you are a knower of dharma—then attain perfection.
And for that man who shall please us with devotion by means of this hymn, we, being satisfied, shall grant him enjoyments and supreme meditation upon the Self.
Therefore, those who desire long life, health, wealth, as well as sons, grandsons, and so forth, should indeed constantly praise [the deities] with this hymn.
Whoever, standing before the foremost of the twice-born while they are eating at a śrāddha ceremony, shall recite with devotion this hymn that brings us pleasure;
When our supreme presence has been established through the joy of hearing this hymn, that śrāddha will undoubtedly become inexhaustible by us.
Even if a Śrāddha is performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas, or if it should be defiled, or if it is performed with wealth acquired through unjust means, or otherwise improperly;
Even if offerings are presented by those unworthy of faith, or are prepared in such a manner, or offered at an improper time or place, or even if they are devoid of the prescribed ritual rules;
Even if a śrāddha is performed by men out of lack of faith or relying on hypocrisy, it nevertheless serves for our satisfaction through its mere recitation.
Wherever this hymn, which brings happiness, is recited at a śrāddha, our satisfaction there lasts for twelve years.
This auspicious hymn bestows satisfaction for twelve years during the winter season, and for twice that number of years during the cool season.
In the spring, sixteen [offerings] are for the sake of satisfaction in the rite of Śrāddha; and in the summer, these same sixteen are likewise recited as effecting satisfaction.
O Ruci, even when the śrāddha is performed incompletely, if it is perfected by means of this hymn, our satisfaction becomes inexhaustible during the rainy season.
Even that which was recited during the autumn season, when offered at the time of a funeral feast (śrāddha), provides us with satisfaction lasting for fifteen years through these men.
In whichever house this remains written at all times, our presence shall be there whenever a śrāddha has been performed.
Therefore, O highly fortunate one, this should be recited by you before the Brahmins while they are eating at the śrāddha; it brings about our nourishment.
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Hymn to the Ancestors Composed by Ruci," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 90. Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, from the midst of that river, there arose a beautiful woman named Pramlocā, a slender-limbed and excellent Apsaras, standing near him.
And that excellent Apsaras, Pramlocā, spoke to the high-souled Ruci with very sweet syllables, propitiating him once again.
A maiden of exceeding beauty, a woman blessed by my grace, was born from the high-souled Puṣkara, the son of Varuṇa.
"Accept this woman of excellent complexion, given by me to be your wife; from her, O high-minded one, a son shall be born to you who will be a Manu."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having been told "So be it" by him, she then drew forth from that water a beautiful maiden, Māninī by name.
And on that riverbank, O best of sages, that great sage, having brought her there, took her hand according to the prescribed rites.

From her was born his son, possessed of great heroism and great splendor. Sūta said: The sages, beginning with Svāyambhuva, meditate upon Hari through their actions, being devoted to vows, conduct, worship, meditation, praise, and the chanting of prayers.
It is devoid of body, senses, mind, intellect, vital breath, and ego; it is indeed bereft of space and entirely free from fire.
Indeed, it is devoid of water, abandoned by the Dharma, deprived of earth, and deserted by all living beings.
The presiding lord of the elements, likewise the bound controller, the sovereign, the all-pervading, whose form is the nature of consciousness, the overseer of all, and the stainless one.
He is the Great Lord, free from attachment, worshipped by all the gods; he is the embodiment of splendor, yet devoid of substantiality, and transcends all ascetic toil.
It is eternally free from passion (rajas), distinct from the three qualities (guṇas), devoid of all forms, and indeed bereft of agency and other such attributes.
It is free from latent impressions, pure, devoid of all defects, exempt from thirst, and free from that very sorrow and delusion.
Indeed, it is devoid of old age and death, immovable, free from delusion, without origin, and likewise exempt from dissolution.
Truth is the Supreme Lord, devoid of all conduct, partless, free from the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, and beyond names.
The Lord of the gods, whose nature is peace, is the presiding witness over the states of waking and the rest; he eternally abides in waking and the other states, yet is devoid of cause and effect.
Thus, it is seen by all, possessed of form, subtle, more subtle than the subtle, supreme; it is the vision of knowledge, the consciousness of hearing, and has the nature of supreme bliss.
Devoid of the Viśva, likewise free from the Taijasa, and indeed devoid of the Prājña, it is the Fourth (Turiya), the supreme imperishable.
The all-protector, the destroyer of all, whose form is the self of all beings, indeed devoid of the qualities of intellect, supportless, Śiva, and Hari.
It is indeed devoid of modification and is that which is to be known through the Vedāntas; it is the supreme being in the form of the Veda, beyond the senses and auspicious.
The God is devoid of sound and free from taste; He is bereft of touch and devoid of mere form.
Devoid of form and entirely free from fragrance, beginningless Brahman extending to the end of the cranial aperture—I am that absolute Brahman alone.
Having understood this, one who has conquered the senses should practice meditation upon Mahādeva; for that person who practices meditation in this manner shall become a human being who is Brahman.
Thus has the meditation of Aśvinī been fully explained by me to you; now I shall speak of something else—tell me what it is, O Bull-bannered One!

Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "Meditation on Hari," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Rudra said: O wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, speak again of the meditation upon Viṣṇu, by the mere knowledge of which a man becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done.

Hari said: I shall explain the meditation on Hari, which destroys the web of illusion (māyā). O Hara, that meditation is of two kinds, distinguished by the formal (mūrta) and the formless (amūrta), and so forth.
O Rudra, the formless has been described; now, alas, I shall speak of the formed: [He who is] like ten million suns, victorious, radiant, and singular.
Hari, white as a jasmine flower or cow’s milk, should be meditated upon by those seeking liberation; he is endowed with a large and very beautiful conch shell.
Endowed with a discus possessing a fierce garland of flames equal to a thousand suns, he is peaceful, holding a mace in his hand, and has a beautiful countenance.
Adorned with a highly precious crown blazing with jewels, the omnipresent God likewise held a weapon and bore a lotus.
Wearing a forest garland, radiant, with symmetrical shoulders and golden ornaments, well-clothed, pure of body, with beautiful ears, he is seated upon a lotus.
His body was golden, adorned with beautiful necklaces and auspicious armlets; he was equipped with bracelets and endowed with a forest garland.

Endowed with the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, accompanied by Lakṣmī and the eyes of the one worthy of her worship, he possesses qualities such as the power to diminish and so forth, and is the agent of both creation and dissolution.
He is the object of meditation for sages, for asuras, and for gods; he is exceedingly beautiful; he dwells within the hearts of all beings born from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
The eternal, imperishable, and pure Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Great God who bestows grace upon all, was shimmering with crocodile-shaped earrings.
The destroyer of suffering, worthy of worship, auspicious, the destroyer of the wicked; the self of all, possessing all forms, omnipresent, and the destroyer of the malevolent planets.
Adorned with beautiful finger-rings and possessing brilliantly shining nails, the Great Lord (Maheśvara) is a refuge, a bringer of happiness, and one of gentle form.
Adorned with every ornament and anointed with beautiful sandalwood paste, he is accompanied by all the gods and brings joy to all the gods.
He desires the welfare of all worlds, he is the Lord of all, and the creator of all; he is established in the solar orb, situated in fire, or abiding in water.
Vāsudeva, the sustainer of the world, Viṣṇu, is to be meditated upon by those seeking liberation; one should meditate on Hari, the Lord, as the Self, thinking, "I am Vāsudeva."
And those who meditate thus upon Viṣṇu attain the supreme goal; for in ancient times, Yājñavalkya likewise meditated upon Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Gods.
Having attained the state of being a teacher of the Dharma, he went to the supreme station; therefore, O Śaṅkara, Lord of Gods, you too should meditate upon Viṣṇu.
Whoever recites this meditation on Viṣṇu attains the supreme goal.
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "Meditation on Viṣṇu," in the section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa) within the first part of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 93.
Maheśvara said: O Hari, O Keśighna, O Mādhava, please tell me in truth how that Dharma which was previously proclaimed by Yājñavalkya was practiced.

Hari said: Having approached Yājñavalkya, who was residing in Mithilā, the sages paid him homage and questioned him regarding the duties of the social classes (varṇadharma) and other matters in their entirety. With his senses subdued, he meditated upon Viṣṇu and explained them to them.
Yājñavalkya said: "In that land where the black antelope roams, learn the laws (dharma) which are blended with the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, the Dharmaśāstras, and the auxiliary sciences."
The Vedas are the fourteen sources of the sciences and of Dharma; the expounders of the Dharmaśāstras are Manu, Viṣṇu, Yama, and Aṅgiras.
Vasiṣṭha, Dakṣa, Saṃvarta, Śātātapa, Parāśara, Āpastamba, Uśanas, Vyāsa, Kātyāyana, and Bṛhaspati.
Gautama, Śaṅkha-Likhita, Hārīta, Atri, and likewise I—these, having propitiated Viṣṇu, became teachers of Dharma.
Whatever substance, endowed with faith, is given to a worthy recipient at the proper place and time through the right means—that possesses the complete characteristics of Dharma.
Sacrificial rites, conduct, self-restraint, non-violence, charity, and the practice of Vedic study—this is the supreme dharma: the perception of the Self through yoga.

A council of four who know the Vedic dharma, or even one consisting of those learned in the three Vedas, declares what constitutes one's own duty; or else, a single person who is the most excellent among those who know the inner self.

The castes are the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra; however, the first three are the twice-born. For them, the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony and ending with those at the cremation ground are indeed performed with sacred mantras.

The *garbhādhāna* (conception rite) occurs during the fertile period; the *pumsavana* (male-making rite) before the fetus moves; the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair) in the sixth or eighth month; and the *jātakarman* (birth rite) upon delivery.

On the eleventh day the naming ceremony is performed; in the fourth month, the first outing; in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food; and one should perform the tonsure according to family custom.
