In this way, the sin arising from the seed and the womb is pacified; these rites for women are to be performed silently, except for the marriage ceremony, which is accompanied by mantras.

Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "Description of the Duties of the Social Orders as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Yājñavalkya said: The initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) for a Brāhmaṇa should take place in the eighth year from conception or the eighth year from birth; for a Kṣatriya, in the eleventh year; and for a Vaiśya, in the twelfth year—or according to the custom of their respective families.
Having initiated his pupil with the Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛti) first, Kuru should teach him the Veda and instruct him in the rules of purity and conduct.
During the day and at the twilights, one should void urine and feces facing north with the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) worn over the ear; however, if it is at night, one should face south.
Having held his penis and risen, the observer of the great vow should perform purification with earth and drawn-up water to remove both odor and residue.
With his hands between his knees, seated in a clean place facing north or east, a twice-born man should always perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) using the Brāhma-tīrtha.
The bases of the little finger, the forefinger, and the thumb, as well as the tips of the hand, are respectively the *prājāpatya*, *pitṛ*, *brahma*, and *daiva* tīrthas.
Having sipped water three times and wiped the mouth twice, one should touch the sense-orifices with water—water that is natural, free from impurities, and devoid of foam or bubbles.
The twice-born are purified by water reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate respectively; women and Śūdras are purified when it merely touches the lips once.
Bathing with mantras dedicated to the water-deities, sprinkling [the body], restraint of the breath, worship of the sun, and the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra with full conviction.
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with its Śiras, preceded by the Vyāhṛtis and joined with each Praṇava; this is the threefold regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma).
Having restrained the breaths and sprinkled himself with water while reciting the three verses addressed to the waters, he should sit reciting the Sāvitrī until the stars appear in the west.
One should thus remain standing during the morning twilight until the sun is seen; then one should perform the fire-rite (agnikārya) at both twilights.
Then he should salute the elders, saying, "I am so-and-so," and he should also attend upon his teacher with a concentrated mind for the sake of Vedic study.
When summoned, he should study and report everything to him; he should always act for his benefit through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
He should carry a staff, a deerskin, a sacred thread, and a girdle; he should go about begging alms from blameless Brahmins for his own sustenance.
The practice of begging for alms by Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas should be characterized by desire at the beginning, middle, and end, respectively.
Having performed his fire-rites, he should eat, being humble and with the permission of his guru, after first performing the *āpośāna* rite, honoring the food and not disparaging it.

Established in the life of a student, a Brahmin shall not eat food from a single person except in times of distress; however, he may eat at a *śrāddha* feast as much as he desires, provided he does not violate his vow.
One should avoid honey, meat, fermented foods, and so forth; that is a guru who, having performed the rites, imparts the Veda to him.
He who initiates [the student] and bestows [the Veda] upon him is proclaimed as the Ācārya; he who teaches a single portion is the Upādhyāya, and he who performs the sacrifice is called the Ṛtvij.
These are to be honored according to their seniority; among them, the mother is the most venerable. For each Veda, the period of studentship (brahmacarya) shall be twelve years or five.

Some say it lasts until the time of formal initiation; others say until the tonsure ceremony in the sixteenth year; and [the periods for the respective castes] extend up to the sixteenth, twenty-second, and twenty-fourth years.

The ultimate time limit for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) for Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas is as follows: beyond this, these individuals fall [from their caste], being deprived of all religious duties (*dharma*).
Those who have fallen from the Sāvitrī are Vrātyas; except through the Vrātyastoma sacrifice, they are born a second time from their mother at the binding of the girdle of Muñja grass.
Therefore, the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are the twice-born; they [are entitled] to sacrifices, to austerities, and indeed to auspicious deeds.
The Veda alone is the supreme means for attaining the highest good for the twice-born; with honey and milk, the twice-born man should satisfy the gods.
He should daily recite the Ṛgveda verses for the ancestors with honey and ghee; likewise, the twice-born should recite the Yajus, the Sāman, and the Atharvāṅgirasa.
For he daily satisfies the ancestors and the gods with clarified butter and nectar, as well as with dialogues, Purāṇas, Nārāśaṃsī verses, and Gāthās.
He who studies the Itihāsas and the sciences daily according to his ability satisfies the ancestors and the gods with meat, milk, rice, and other offerings.
Being satisfied themselves, they satisfy him with the auspicious fruits of all his desires; whatever sacrifice he studies, he shall obtain its fruit.
A twice-born man who has completed his studies partakes in the fruit of the gift of land and of ascetic penance; however, a lifelong celibate student shall dwell in the presence of his teacher.

In the absence of these, one who has conquered his senses should accomplish [the rite] in the body of his son, his wife, or even in the sacred fire, according to this procedure; he attains the world of Brahmā and is not born here again.
Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Duties of the Social Orders as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
In the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, Chapter 95:
Yājñavalkya said: "O sages of firm vows, listen to the duties of the householder. Having given wealth to his teacher and having bathed with his permission,"

Having completed the student life of celibacy, he should marry a woman endowed with auspicious marks—one who has not belonged to another before, who is pleasing, who is not a sapinda relative, and who is younger than himself.

One should marry a woman who is healthy, has brothers, and does not belong to the same *ṛṣi* lineage or *gotra*, and who is beyond the fifth degree on the mother’s side as well as the seventh degree on the father’s side.
A bridegroom of equal caste, learned in the Vedas, wise, and free from defects, should be chosen from a great family of Vedic scholars renowned for ten generations.
As for what is said regarding the taking of a Śūdra wife by those of the twice-born castes—that is not my opinion, because in that case, he himself is born [as a Śūdra].
Three wives in the order of the castes, two likewise, and one respectively, are the lawful wives for the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya; for one born of the Śūdra caste, she alone is his own.
The Brāhma marriage consists of giving away a girl, adorned according to one's means, after inviting her; the son born of that union purifies twenty-one persons on both sides.

Having received the *daiva* [form of marriage] from the officiating priest at a sacrifice, and the *ārṣa* [form] for a pair of cows; the first-born son purifies fourteen generations, and the one born later purifies six.
Having said this, that body which is given by one practicing dharma to a seeker shall purify, along with its progenitor, six generations of ancestors and oneself.
The Āsura [form] arises from the taking of wealth; the Gāndharva, from mutual agreement; the Rākṣasa, from abduction by force; and the Paiśāca, from the deception of the maiden.
The first four [forms of marriage] belong to the Brāhmaṇa, as do the Gāndharva and Rākṣasa forms for the Kṣatriya; the Āsura form belongs to the Vaiśya, while the last one is censured for the Śūdra.

The hand should be taken in marriage from women of the same caste; a Kṣatriya bride should take hold of an arrow, and a Vaiśya bride should take up a goad, at the wedding of a man of the first-born caste.

The father, the grandfather, the brother, a kinsman, and likewise the mother—each subsequent one among these gives the daughter in marriage upon the failure of the preceding, provided they are of sound mind.
By not giving her away at the proper time, he incurs the guilt of killing an embryo. In the absence of such givers, the maiden may choose a husband for herself.

A maiden is given only once; one who abducts her shall be subject to the punishment for a thief. Indeed, he who abandons an unblemished wife is punishable, but he may abandon one who is extremely corrupt.

If a woman is childless, her husband’s younger brother, a kinsman (sapiṇḍa), or one of the same lineage (samānodaka) shall, after being consecrated with clarified butter, approach her during her fertile period at the command of the Guru.
One should proceed until conception occurs; otherwise, one would become fallen. By this rite, once born, he shall be the son of the owner of the field.
One should cause an unfaithful wife to dwell deprived of her authority, soiled, subsisting on mere alms, humiliated, and sleeping on the ground.
Soma gave them purity, and the Gandharva gave them beautiful speech; Agni gave them the state of being fit for all sacrifices, since women are indeed sacrificially pure.

If there is infidelity during the fertile period, purification occurs through menstruation; however, they must undergo abandonment if there is abortion, or if they commit the murder of the fetus or their husband, or likewise any other great sin.

A wife who drinks liquor, is diseased, hostile, barren, wasteful of wealth, or speaks unpleasantly, as well as one who has been superseded by a second marriage, must be maintained; otherwise, there would be a great loss of merit.
Where there is harmony between husband and wife, there the three aims of life flourish; she who, whether her husband is dead or living, does not approach another man [is a virtuous wife].
He attains fame in this world and rejoices with Umā in the next; however, abandoning a pure wife, he should provide her with a third share of his property until her death.
The word of her husband must be carried out by women; this is the supreme duty of a woman. Of the sixteen nights of a woman's fertile period, she should approach him on the even nights.

A celibate student (*brahmacārī*) should avoid the sacred days (*parvan*), as well as the first three nights [of the lunar fortnight]. Approaching a woman in this manner, he should also avoid her when she is emaciated, and on the days of the asterisms Maghā and Mūla.
He shall surely produce a son endowed with auspicious marks and free from disease; or he may act according to his desire toward women, recollecting his own power.
One should be devoted solely to one's own wife, for women must be protected from all sides by the husband, brothers, father, kinsmen, mother-in-law, father-in-law, and brothers-in-law.
Women should be honored by their kinsmen with ornaments, clothing, and food; they should keep the household utensils in order, be skillful, cheerful, and averse to wasteful expenditure.
She should always perform prostration at the feet of her mother-in-law and father-in-law; she should avoid playfulness, bodily adornment, social gatherings, festivals, and looking [at herself].
A woman whose husband has gone abroad should abandon laughter and visiting the houses of others; her father should protect her in childhood, and her husband alone in youth.
In old age, the son indeed protects her, and otherwise, her kinsmen do so; she should not remain without her husband, whether by day or by night.
In the performance of religious rites, one should employ the eldest wife and never the youngest; a husband should cremate a virtuous wife with the Agnihotra fire.

She should take a husband according to the prescribed rites and establish the sacred fire without delay; thus, having attained fame in this world, she shall go to heaven for the welfare of her husband.

Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Duties of Householders as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Pūrvakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Āgama-Ṛg-Āruḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Yājñavalkya said: I shall now declare the supreme rules concerning those born of mixed castes (*saṅkara-jāti*) and others, such as householders. From a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother is born a Mūrdhāvasikta; from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Vaiśya woman is born a [Māhiṣya].
One born from a Śūdra woman by an Ambaṣṭha is a Niṣāda or a Parvata; one born from a Vaiśya woman by a Kṣatriya is a Māhiṣya, who is designated as a Mleccha.

From a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother, a Karaṇa is born; this same rule is recorded for other [lower] castes. From a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇī mother, a Sūta is born, and likewise from a Vaiśya father, a Vaidehaka.
From a Śūdra, however, is born the Cāṇḍāla, who is despised by all castes; from a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya woman bears a Māgadha, and from a Śūdra, she bears a Kṣattṛ.
A Vaiśya woman indeed gave birth to a son, the Āyogava, by a Śūdra; and from a Māhiṣya man and a Karaṇī woman, a Rathakāra is born.

Those born in the inverse (pratiloma) and direct (anuloma) orders should indeed be known as non-existent and existent [respectively]. Through excellence of birth, one is to be known as a twice-born (dvija) in the seventh or even the fifth generation.
Upon the reversal of actions, there is equality as before between the higher and the lower; the householder should perform the rites prescribed by the Smṛti every day in the nuptial fire.

Or, even apart from the time of giving [the gift], once the twice-born has performed the rites for the body in the Vedic fires used for the *vaitānika* sacrifices and completed the rules for purification;

One should perform the morning twilight devotion preceded by the cleansing of the teeth; having offered oblations into the fire, one should, with a concentrated mind, recite the mantras dedicated to all the deities.
A householder should master the meaning of the Vedas and various treatises, and he should approach the Lord for the sake of attaining success in yoga, protection, and other such goals.
Having bathed, one should likewise satiate and worship the gods and the ancestors, as well as the Vedas, the Purāṇas, and the Itihāsas, according to one's ability.

For the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice of recitation, one should mutter the knowledge pertaining to the self; [one should also perform] the offering of bali, the svadhā-rite, burnt offerings, Vedic study, and hospitality toward guests.

One should perform the great sacrifices for the spirits, ancestors, gods, Brahmā, and humans; one should cast what has been offered into the fire for the gods and present the bali-offering to the spirits.
One should scatter food on the ground for dogs, outcasts, and crows; food should be given daily to the ancestors and to men, as well as water.

One should perform one's daily private recitation every day and should not cook food for oneself alone; [one should rather provide for] children, female dependents, the elderly, pregnant women, the sick, and young maidens.
Having fed his guests and dependents, he should eat the remnants of the meal with his wife according to the ritual of the Prāṇāgnihotra, consuming the food without disparaging it.
One should eat food that is measured, ripened, wholesome, and prepared with the meat of young animals and so forth; it should be consumed both before and after with the *āpośāna* ritual.
The twice-born should prepare food that is both unblemished and immortal; it should be given to guests and according to the [social] orders, to the best of one's ability and in due order.
A guest must not be turned away even in the evening; there is no doubt about this. Alms should be given with respect to the mendicant who observes virtuous vows.
One should feed all those who have arrived, and a large bull to a Śrotriya; however, a Snātaka, a teacher, and a king are to be honored every year.
Likewise, a beloved friend, one to whom one is married, and the officiating priests at a sacrifice; furthermore, a traveler is declared to be a guest, as is a Śrotriya who has mastered the Vedas.
These two are worthy of honor for a householder who desires the world of Brahmā; he should not take pleasure in food prepared by others, except when invited by those beyond reproach.
He should avoid restlessness of speech, hands, and feet, as well as overeating; and he should follow a learned guest who has been satisfied as far as the boundary of his domain.
He should spend the remainder of the day with learned, beloved, and kinsmen; then, having performed the evening twilight devotions and offered oblations into the fire, he may take his meal.
One should act together with devoted servants and contemplate one's own welfare; having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, a Brahmin should be honored with wealth and other gifts.
The path must indeed be yielded to the elderly, the afflicted, and those carrying burdens; sacrifice, study, and giving are the duties of the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya.
Receiving gifts is the additional duty for a Brāhmaṇa, as are officiating at sacrifices and teaching; for a Kṣatriya, however, the primary duty is the protection of the subjects.
Agriculture, trade, commerce, and cattle-rearing are prescribed for the Vaiśya; service to the twice-born is prescribed for the Śūdra. A twice-born man should not neglect his sacrifices.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, restraint of the senses, self-control, forbearance, straightforwardness, and charity are the means for the practice of dharma for all.
One should practice a livelihood that is consistent, straightforward, and free from deceit; he who possesses more than a three-year supply of food is worthy to drink the Soma.

One for whom there is food sufficient for a year may perform the rites pertaining to the Prajāpati sacrifice; likewise, the Soma sacrifice should be performed every year, and the animal sacrifice at each solstice.
The *Agrayaneṣṭi* and the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices must be performed with diligence; in the absence of these, a twice-born man should perform the *Vaiśvānarī* sacrifice.
One should not perform a deficient rite when the necessary materials are available, for it yields no fruit; by performing a sacrifice through begging from a Śūdra, one is born as a Caṇḍāla.

One should not take what is obtained for the sake of sacrifice; otherwise, one might become a vulture or even a crow. One may instead be a possessor of grain in a granary or a jar, or one who gathers for three days, or even one who provides only for tomorrow.
Or he may live by gleaning ears of grain; each of these modes is superior to the one preceding it. He should not strive for wealth that conflicts with his Vedic study, nor from any source whatsoever.

If suffering from hunger, he may seek wealth from kings, pupils, or those for whom he performs sacrifices; however, he should avoid those who are hypocritical, motivated by selfish motives, heretics, and those who act like crows.
Wearing white garments, with hair, beard, and nails kept short, and being pure, he should not eat while looking at his wife, nor while wearing only one garment, nor while standing.
One who has mastered the Veda should never speak what is unpleasant, remaining disciplined; carrying his staff and water-pot, he should perform circumambulation of the gods.

But one should not urinate in a river, in the shade, on ashes, in a cow-pen, in water, or on a path; nor should one face the fire, the sun, a cow, the moon, the twilight, water, a woman, or a twice-born man.
One should not look at fire, the sun, or a naked woman, nor at one engaged in sexual intercourse; nor should one void urine or feces, nor sleep with the head toward the west.
One should not throw spittle, blood, feces, urine, or poison into water; one should not warm one's feet over a fire, nor should one step over it.

One should not drink water from one's cupped hands; one should not wake a sleeping person; one should not play with dice against gamblers; and one should not lie down to sleep with those who are diseased.
One should avoid forbidden actions, the smoke from a funeral pyre, crossing a river [by swimming], and staying upon hair, ashes, chaff, embers, or skulls.

One should not point out a cow suckling her calf, nor should one ever enter through any opening other than the gate; one should not accept gifts from a king who is greedy and acts contrary to the scriptures.

The commencement of the study of the chapters (of the Veda) takes place on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, or under the asterism Śravaṇā, or under the asterism Hasta when the medicinal herbs have appeared, or on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
On the Rohiṇī day of the month of Pauṣa, or likewise on the Aṣṭakā, one should perform the formal dismissal of the Vedic texts (chandasām utsarga) according to the rules outside, near water.

There is a three-day suspension of Vedic study upon the death of a pupil, an officiating priest, a teacher, or a relative; likewise upon the performance of the Upākarma and Utsarga ceremonies, and when a person learned in one's own Vedic branch has died.
Upon the occurrence of thunder at twilight, a lightning strike, an earthquake, or the fall of a meteor, one should complete the Veda and recite the Āraṇyaka for a day and a night.
On the fifteenth day, the fourteenth day, the eighth day, during an eclipse, at the junctions of the seasons, after eating, or after receiving gifts related to a funeral rite (śrāddha).
When the interval is filled by cattle, frogs, mongooses, dogs, snakes, cats, and pigs, it constitutes a day and night; likewise for the fall and the rise of Śakra.

In the presence of the barking of dogs, the howling of jackals, the braying of donkeys, the hooting of owls, the sound of *sāman* chants, the cry of an arrow-wound, or near impurity, a corpse, a *śūdra*, an outcaste, a cemetery, or one who has fallen [from his caste].

In an impure place, or when one is oneself impure; during a downpour of lightning and thunder; after eating while the hands are still wet; inside water; at midnight; or during an excessively strong wind.
When there is a conflagration of the quarters, during dust-storms, at the terrifying twilights, when running, when there is a foul odor, and when a learned man has arrived at one's house.
Traveling in a donkey-cart, a camel-cart, or on an elephant, horse, or boat; climbing a tree or a mountain—these thirty-seven occasions are known as temporary interruptions for study (*anadhyāya*).
One should not step over the Veda as taught, nor a teacher, nor the shadow of a king, nor another's wife, nor blood, feces, urine, spittle, or the remnants of anointing ointments.
Brahmins and those whose nature is that of Kṣatriyas should never be treated with contempt; one should cast away remnants of food, excrement, urine, and water from the feet from a distance.

One should practice the conduct prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti; one should not touch another's vital spot, nor should one engage in censure or beating. However, one may strike a son or a disciple [for the sake of correction].
A householder should always practice righteousness and never act contrary to it; he should not engage in disputes with his mother, father, guests, or kinsmen.
One should not bathe in the waters of others without first removing five lumps [of earth]; however, one may bathe in rivers, springs, natural reservoirs, and lakes.

One should avoid the beds and other belongings of others, and one should not partake of food from them except in times of distress— specifically from a miser, a prisoner, an enemy, or one who does not maintain a sacred fire.
[One should not accept gifts] from those accused of theft, usurers, courtesans, those initiated for a communal sacrifice, physicians, the sick, the angry, eunuchs, and those who live by the stage.

[One should avoid the food] of those who are cruel, fierce, fallen, or outcaste; of those who are hypocritical or eat the leavings of others; of those who sell the scriptures, and of those who are ruled by women or perform sacrifices for an entire village.
[One should not accept gifts] from a cruel man, a king, a dyer, an ungrateful person, one who lives by slaughter, a slanderer, a liar, and likewise a seller of Soma.
One should never eat the food of bards or goldsmiths, nor meat that is prepared in vain, or that which is infested with hair and insects.
One should avoid food that is stale, leftover, touched by a dog, defiled by an outcaste, touched by a woman in her menses, publicly proclaimed [as unfit], or insufficient.

Food smelled by a cow, the leavings of birds, or that which has been intentionally touched by the foot; and among Śūdras, those who are slaves, cowherds, family friends, or sharecroppers [are to be considered as equals].
Food may be eaten from a barber and from one who offers himself [as a servant]; food that has stood overnight may be eaten if it is mixed with oil or has been kept for a long time.
One should also avoid preparations of wheat, barley, and cow's milk that are not oily, as well as the milk of camels, one-hoofed animals, and women.
One should avoid the flesh of carnivorous birds, the dātyūha, and the parrot; as well as cranes, single-hoofed animals, swans, balākās, cranes, and lapwings.
One should avoid eating kṛsara, saṃyāva, milk-rice, cakes, and fried pastries in vain, as well as the kurara, web-footed birds, the khañjarīṭa, and wild animals and birds.
Having intentionally eaten a blue jay, a fish, or a blood-footed bird, or having intentionally eaten dried meat, a man shall observe a fast for three days.
Having eaten onions, garlic, and the like, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; however, eating meat after having worshipped the gods and ancestors at a Śrāddha ceremony, one incurs no fault.

That person of wicked conduct who kills animals contrary to the prescribed rules shall dwell in a terrible hell for as many days as there are hairs on the animal's body; having abandoned meat and attained his desires through prayer, he then goes to Hari.
Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "Description of Śrāddha as Taught by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part (Pūrvakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 97.

Yājñavalkya said: O virtuous ones, I shall now proclaim the purification of substances; listen to that. [I shall describe the purification] of gold, silver, lotuses, conch-shells, ropes, leather, and so forth.
The purification of vessels and seats is desired by means of water; that of the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles by hot water, and that of grain and other such items by sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
Woollen and silken cloth is purified by scraping, by scrubbing wooden vessels such as those used in sacrifices, and by washing with warm water and cow urine.
One who looks at the face of a woman while eating alms-food, or food that has been cooked again, or food made of earth, or food defiled by hair, flies, or insects, must likewise bathe.

Purification occurs by casting [impurities] into fire; the purification of the ground is by sweeping and so forth; and that of tin, lead, and copper is by means of alkaline substances, acids, and water.

Iron and bronze are always pure when their impurity is unknown; they are purified by ashes and water. When smeared with impure substances, they are cleansed by removing the odor and the stain with earth and water.
Water on the ground that is naturally pure, which quenches the thirst of cows, is likewise pure; so too is meat fallen from the jaws of dogs, cāṇḍālas, carnivorous beasts, and the like.
A ray of light, fire, dust, shadow, a bull, a horse, the earth, and the winds; the droplets from a horse, a goat, or a cow, as well as drops from sipping water—these are pure.
Having bathed, drunk, sneezed, slept, eaten, or walked upon a road, and after putting on another garment, one who has already sipped water (ācamana) should sip water again.

After sneezing, spitting, sleeping, putting on a garment, or shedding tears—in these five instances—one should not sip water for purification; instead, one should touch the right ear. For the gods, beginning with Agni, reside in the right ear of the Brahmin.
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Purification of Substances as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Yājñavalkya said: Now I shall declare the rules for giving gifts; listen to that from me, O you of excellent vows. Brāhmaṇas are superior to others, and among them, those devoted to ritual action are the best.

One should know that even among those endowed with austerity, the knower of Brahman is the most worthy recipient; to such a worthy recipient, cows, land, grain, gold, and other gifts should be given with due honor.
A gift should not be accepted by one who is deficient in both knowledge and austerity; for by accepting it, he leads both the giver and himself to a lower state.
One should give daily to a worthy recipient, especially on auspicious occasions; even when requested, one should give according to one's ability, purified by faith.
A milch cow with golden horns and silver hooves, well-behaved, covered with cloth, accompanied by a bronze vessel, and given along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), should be bestowed.
The horn [of the calf] is made of ten suvarṇas, and the hoof is made of seven palas; the bronze vessel for the calf is declared to weigh fifty palas.
Either a male calf or even a female calf, with a golden pippala-leaf vessel, should be given to her as well, so that she may have offspring free from disease.
The donor attains heaven for as many years as there are hairs [on the gift], and if it be a *kaṣilā* stone, he further delivers his lineage up to the seventh generation.
As long as two feet and the face of the calf are visible at the birth canal, for that long the cow should be known as the Earth, as long as she does not release the fetus.
Having given a cow, whether with her calf or without her calf, in whatever manner possible—provided she is healthy and not afflicted—the donor is glorified in heaven.
Massaging those who are fatigued, attending to the sick, worshiping the gods, washing the feet of others, and clearing away the remnants of food from twice-born men are equal to the gift of a cow.
By giving whatever is desired to a twice-born man, one attains heaven; by giving land, islands, food, clothing, and clarified butter, one shall go to the abode of Śrī.
By giving a house, grain, an umbrella, a garland, a tree, a vehicle, clarified butter, water, a bed, and ointment, one is glorified in the heavenly world.

The giver of the Veda attains the world of Brahmā, which is difficult even for the gods to reach; for indeed, [he gives] the meanings of the Vedas, the sacrificial treatises, and the scriptures on Dharma.
Even by writing it down for a price, one may attain the world of Brahmā; for the Lord created this as the root of the universe in the beginning.
Therefore, with every effort, one should compile a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas; or, having written down the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, he who bestows them [upon others].

One obtains merit equal to the gift of the Veda and attains double the exaltation; [but one who studies] Lokāyata, fallacious reasoning, and the speech of commoners and barbarians [attains the opposite].
A twice-born man must not listen to this, for it leads that twice-born man downward; he who is capable but does not accept [this teaching] shall attain the worlds of the giver.
Kuśa grass, vegetables, milk, perfumes, and water should not be refused; even from one of evil deeds, that which is brought unasked may be accepted.

Except from unchaste women, eunuchs, and outcasts, as well as from enemies; however, for the sake of honoring gods and guests, for the purpose of satisfying the ancestors, and for his own subsistence, he may accept gifts from anyone at all.

Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Duties of Giving as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Yājñavalkya said: Now I shall describe the procedure for the Śrāddha, which destroys all sins: [the rites performed on] the new moon day (Amāvasyā), the Aṣṭakās, the Vṛddhi [ceremonies], the dark fortnight (Kṛṣṇapakṣa), and the two solstices (Ayana).

The substance [of the gift], the excellence of the Brahmin recipient, the equinoxes, the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign, the Vyatīpāta yoga, the Gajacchāyā conjunction, and the eclipses of the moon and the sun.

A person who has a personal inclination for the *śrāddha* is proclaimed as one fit for the *śrāddha*-times; likewise, one who maintains the sacred fires among all gods, a *śrotriya*, and a youth learned in the Vedas.

One who knows the meaning of the Vedas, one who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāman, one who knows the Trimadhu, one who knows the Trisuparṇa, a sister's son, an officiating priest, a son-in-law, a person for whom one sacrifices, a father-in-law, and a maternal uncle.

Those who have performed the Triṇāciketa rite, daughters' sons, disciples, relatives, and kinsmen; those devoted to ritual action, those devoted to austerity, those who maintain the five fires, and lifelong celibates.

Furthermore, Brahmins who are devoted to their fathers and mothers are the deities of the śrāddha; likewise, one who is diseased, one with deficient or redundant limbs, one who is one-eyed, and one born of a remarried woman [are excluded].
Those who have broken their vows of celibacy, those who are devoid of proper conduct, and those who are not devotees of Viṣṇu—all of them are never worthy of the śrāddha.
One should issue the invitation on the previous day; the twice-born guests should remain self-restrained, and having had their teeth cleaned, one should seat them upon their seats in the forenoon.

In rites for the gods and likewise for the ancestors, one should place the vessels according to one's ability in their respective places: two in the eastern part for the gods, three in the northern part for the ancestors, and one each separately for both.

The same applies to the maternal grandfathers; or one may perform the Vaiśvadeva rite for them. Then, having given water for washing the hands, one should also provide *kuśa* grass for the purpose of seats.
Having invoked them and being permitted by them, he should scatter barley over the food with the verse "viśve devāsaḥ," and then [place it] in a vessel containing a strainer.
Having poured milk with the mantra "śanno devīḥ," and likewise barley grains with the mantra "yavo 'si," he should pour them into their hands with the mantra "yā divyāḥ."

Then, having likewise offered scented water, lamps, garlands, and wreaths, one should perform the rite with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) and circumambulate the ancestors counter-clockwise (apradakṣiṇa).
Having offered double-folded *kuśa* grass and having invoked the ancestors with the verse "uśantas tvā," the knower [of the ritual] should then recite the mantra "āyantu naḥ."

If the purpose is barley, it should be performed with sesame seeds; one should perform the offering of water (arghya) and so forth as before. Having offered the arghya, one should place the remnants of those offerings into their vessel according to the prescribed rule.
With the words, "Thou art the place for the ancestors," he places the vessel face down below; then, taking food soaked in ghee, he asks, "I shall perform the offering in the fire."

Being thus addressed with the words "Do so," he should, having offered oblations into the fire according to the ritual for the ancestors (pitṛyajña), present the remnants of the offering into the vessels with a concentrated mind.
Having given food into whatever vessels are available, especially those made of silver, one should consecrate the vessel with the mantra: "The earth is the vessel."

Having performed [the ritual], he should place his thumb upon the twice-born [guest] with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," as well as the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis and the verses beginning with "madhu vātā."

Having recited [the mantra] as desired, one should speak to them, and they too should eat while remaining silent; one who is free from anger and haste should offer the desired food, which should be sacrificial (haviṣya).
Having recited purificatory mantras until satisfied, as well as the previously mentioned prayers, one should take food and say, "Are you satisfied?", and then consecrate the remainder with a mantra.
He should scatter that food on the ground and offer water once for each [deity]; taking all the food together with sesame seeds, he should face the south.

One should offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) near the remnants of the meal, as in the Pitṛyajña; likewise, one should offer them for the maternal grandfathers, and thereafter provide water for sipping (ācamana).

Then, having caused the benediction to be recited, he should offer the water for imperishability (akṣayyodaka); and having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to his ability, he should utter the word "svadhā."
Having been authorized by the recitation of *vācyatām*, let the *svadhā* be uttered for the ancestors; when the Brahmins have said, "Let there be *svadhā*," he should then pour water upon the ground.
Saying "May they be pleased," he thus offers water for the Viśvedevas, [reciting]: "May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny."
"May our faith not depart, and may we have much to give"—uttering such dear words with a cheerful voice, one should bow down and bid them farewell.
With the words "vāje-vāje," the dismissal is performed with affection, preceded by the ancestors, into that vessel where the remnants of the offerings were previously poured.
Having turned that paternal vessel face upwards, he should dismiss the Brahmins; having followed them clockwise, he should eat what was served to the ancestors.
He should remain celibate for that night together with his wife; having thus performed the circumambulation, he should also honor the elders and the Nāndīmukha ancestors.

One should offer cakes mixed with large jujube fruits (karkandhu) placed upon a vessel; the Ekoddiṣṭa rite is devoid of the invocation to the gods, consists of a single portion of food, and has a single purifying blade of grass (pavitraka).

Devoid of the *āvāhana* and *agnaukaraṇa* rites, and performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), one should dismiss the Brahmins with the words "May they be present" (*upatiṣṭhatām*) in place of the rite for imperishability (*akṣayya*).
One should say, "Be pleased," and they should reply, "We are indeed pleased. One should prepare four vessels mixed with scents, water, and sesame seeds.

For the sake of the *arghya* offering, one should pour the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessels of the ancestors with the two verses beginning "ye samānāḥ"; the remainder of the rite should be performed as before.
This Sapindikarana rite for a woman is also performed as an Ekoddista; however, for one whose Sapindikarana occurs before the completion of a year, [the following applies].
A twice-born man should also give food along with a water-pot for a year; and he should offer rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) to cows, goats, Brahmins, or into fire or water.
Indeed, by means of sacrificial food (haviṣya) one satisfies [the ancestors] for a month, but by milk-rice (pāyasa) for a year; likewise by fish, deer, ram, bird, goat, and spotted antelope meat.
The ancestors here are satisfied by the offerings of the meat of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, the boar, and the hare, respectively, for each successive month as they increase in duration.

One should undoubtedly give [the śrāddha] on the thirteenth day of the rainy season and under the Maghā asterism; by giving śrāddha in this manner starting from the first day [of the lunar fortnight], one obtains daughters and other blessings.
To those slain by the sword, however, offerings are given on the fourteenth day; for [this bestows] heaven, progeny, vigor, valor, land, and likewise strength.
He obtains preeminence among sons, good fortune, prosperity, leadership, auspiciousness, the power of a rolling wheel, as well as success in trade and other such matters.
Health, fame, freedom from sorrow, the supreme goal, wealth, knowledge, success in speech, base metals, as well as cattle, goats, and sheep.
He who duly offers a śrāddha with horses and long life during the period beginning with Kṛttikā and ending with Bharaṇī shall obtain these desires.
O twice-born ones, garments and other such items certainly gratify the man who performs a śrāddha, as do longevity, progeny, wealth, knowledge, and the pleasures of heaven and liberation.
Just as the Grandfather always bestows sovereignty out of affection.

Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Rules for Śrāddha as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Pūrvakhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The glorious *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*, Chapter 100:
Yājñavalkya said: "Learn now the characteristics of one who is afflicted by Vināyaka: in dreams, he plunges excessively into water and sees shaven-headed men."
The assembly was dejected and its undertakings fruitless due to this omen; likewise, the king lost his kingdom, and the pregnant princess lost her husband and her son.

On an auspicious day, one should perform the ceremonial bathing for him according to the prescribed rites, after his body has been rubbed with a paste of white mustard seeds mixed with clarified butter.
With his head anointed with all medicinal herbs and all fragrant substances, and seated upon an auspicious throne, he should cause auspicious Brahmins to recite benedictions.
One should throw earth, yellow pigment (rocanā), perfumes, and guggulu into the waters that have been drawn from a lake by four people of the same caste using water-pots.
Likewise, it should be placed upon a red seat made of an ox-hide; it is remembered by the sages as a purifier, possessing a thousand eyes and a hundred streams.
With that I consecrate you; may the purifying waters cleanse you. May King Varuṇa grant you fortune, and may Sūrya and Bṛhaspati grant you fortune.
Indra and Vāyu have granted you fortune, and the Seven Sages have granted you fortune; whatever misfortune is in your hair, at your parting, or upon your head—[may it depart].
May the waters on your forehead, ears, and eyes always destroy that [evil]; likewise, for one who has bathed, [may they destroy it] with mustard oil using a ladle made of udumbara wood.
One should offer oblations at the head, grasping the *kuśa* grass with the left hand; namely, *mita*, *samita*, as well as *śālakaṭaṅkaṭa*.
And at the end, having spread *kuśa* grass everywhere upon the ground at a crossroads, one should offer [oblations] to Kuṣmāṇḍa and the Prince (Rājaputra), accompanied by the word *svāhā*.
Rice that has been husked and rice that has not, as well as meat-rice, variegated and fragrant flowers, and the three kinds of liquor;
Radish, fried cakes, and likewise garlands of *uṇḍeraka* flowers; curd, milk-rice, boiled rice, and molasses-flour mixed with *modakas*.
Having brought all these together and placed them on the ground with his head toward them, he should worship Ambikā and offer the arghya with palms joined in reverence.
Having performed the rite for averting evil with dūrvā grass, mustard seeds, flowers, and those born at the birth of a son, he should pray to the virtuous Ambikā.
Grant me form, grant me fame, O Blessed One; grant me fortune. Grant me sons, grant me prosperity, and grant me all my desires.

Afterwards, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas with white garments and ointments; one should give a pair of garments to the preceptor and likewise worship the planets. One who is devoted to the worship of the Sun will thus obtain the auspicious fruit of his actions.
Thus ends the one hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for Gaṇapati as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Yājñavalkya said: One who desires prosperity, or one who desires peace, or one afflicted by the malevolent gaze of the planets or by sorcery, should perform the planetary sacrifice (*grahayañña*) according to the rules; and these are the planets as remembered by the wise.
Sūrya, Soma, Maṅgala, Budha, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and Ketu are remembered as the host of planets (graha).
Learn of the colors from copper, crystal, red sandalwood, gold, silver, iron, lead, and bell-metal.
Red, white, and likewise red; yellow, yellow, white, and black; black, black—these are the colors in sequence, and from them arise the substances and the sages.

One should place the colors for the planets and draw them upon a cloth for the purpose of the fire offering (*homa*). One should bathe and offer oblations with the substances prescribed for the planets according to the ritual rules. Gold should be given as gifts, along with garments of excellent quality.
Fragrances, offerings, and guggulu incense should be presented; there, oblations (caru) must be prepared for each respective deity with the appropriate mantras.

One should offer oblations with these very verses in their proper sequence: "With the black path," "O gods," "Agni is the head, the summit of heaven," and "Awake! (RV 10.8.1; 7.45.1; 8.44.16; 10.189.1).
"Bṛhaspate paridīya," "sarve annātparisutam," "śanno devī," "kayā naśca," and "ketuṃ kr̥ṇvan"—these [verses] are used in sequence.
Arka, palāśa, khadira, apāmārga, then pippala, audumbara, śamī, dūrvā, and kuśa are the sacrificial fuels (samidh) in sequence.
It should be offered as an oblation accompanied by honey, clarified butter, and curd; likewise, jaggery-rice, milk-rice, sacrificial food (haviṣya), and milk-porridge made with ṣaṣṭika rice.
One should offer curd-rice, sacrificial oblation, cakes, meat, and various kinds of food to the planets according to their sequence; thereafter, one should present vessels to the planets.

A cow, a conch, a bull, gold, a garment, a horse, a black cow, iron, and a goat—these are indeed the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) in order. Since the planets should always be worshipped, the fruit of sovereignty and other such rewards is obtained.

Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "Description of the Pacification of Planets as Taught by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 102.

Yājñavalkya said: I shall describe the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha); let the great sages listen to that. Having entrusted his wife to his sons, or else going to the forest together with her, he should depart for the woods.

The forest-dweller shall remain celibate, maintaining the sacred fires and the domestic fire, being patient; he shall serve the fires, the ancestors, the gods, and guests with food not produced by the plow.

But the self-possessed one, wearing a beard, matted hair, and body hair, being self-controlled, bathing at the three periods of the day, and abstaining from accepting gifts, should satisfy his dependents.
Devoted to sacred study, habituated to meditation, and delighting in the welfare of all beings, he may take possession of wealth either once a day or once a month.

In the month of Āśvayuja, one should abandon what has been prepared; one should employ the time with vows and other observances, or eat once every fortnight or month, and become one who uses his teeth as a mortar.

One who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa penance should sleep on the ground and subsist on fruits and the like; in the summer he should stand amidst five fires, and during the rainy season he should lie upon the bare ground.

In the winter, one should spend the day practicing yoga while wearing wet clothes. He who pricks himself with thorns and he who anoints himself with sandalwood paste—toward both of them, as well as toward everyone else, he remains free from anger and fully content.

Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "Description of the Duties of a Forest-Dweller as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 103.

Yājñavalkya said: "O best of beings, listen as I proclaim the duty of the mendicant (bhikṣu). Having performed the sacrifice in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee (sarvavedasadakṣiṇā), whether from the forest or from the home..."

Even at the end of the Prājāpatya vow, having consigned the sacred fires into himself, he—intent on the welfare of all beings, tranquil, bearing the triple staff and the water-pot—[should live as a forest-dweller].
Having renounced all pleasure gardens, one should resort to a village for the sake of alms; one should wander for alms with vigilance, not at evening and not being conspicuous.

In the village of Rohita, a mendicant who is free from greed and takes only what is necessary for sustenance may become a Paramahaṃsa or a single-staffed ascetic (ekadaṇḍī), beginning with the observance of the Yamas.
A perfected yogi, casting off the body, attains immortality even here; a householder who is a donor, fond of guests, and possessed of knowledge is liberated even through the ancestral śrāddha rite.

Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "Description of the Duties of Forest-Dwellers and Renunciants as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the glorious *Āgama-Ṛg-Āruḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*.
The glorious *Āgama-Ṛg-Āruḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, 104.

Yājñavalkya said: A killer of a Brāhmaṇa shall become a dog, a donkey, or a camel; a drinker of liquor shall become a frog or a yak, once they have fallen from hell due to the exhaustion of their sinful karma.

A thief of gold becomes a worm or an insect; one who violates the teacher’s bed becomes grass and the like; one who has contracted consumption becomes a man with black teeth, deformed nails, or the disease known as *śipiviṣṭa*.
All these [sins] may arise from the sequence of killing a Brahmin, or they may all belong to the child; one who steals food becomes deceitful, and one who steals speech becomes mute.
One who steals grain becomes one with an extra limb; a slanderer has a putrid nose; one who consumes oil becomes an oil-drinker; and a backbiter has a foul-smelling mouth.
By purchasing a Brahmin’s daughter, one becomes a Rākṣasa in the forest; by stealing jewels, one is born as a low-caste man; and by stealing leaf-vegetables, one becomes a peacock.
Having stolen a cluster of flowers, one becomes a musk-rat; having stolen grain, a mouse; having stolen fruit, a monkey; and likewise, having stolen livestock or milk, one becomes a goat or a crow.
The flesh-eater becomes a vulture, the leper a dog, and the stealer of salt a cricket; having obtained the fruit according to their karma, they reach the state of animals through the passage of time.
Those lowest of men, fallen from their auspicious marks and impoverished, are born; thereafter, having become stainless, they arise as yogis in a great family.
They are born endowed with auspicious marks and possessed of wealth and grain.
Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Ripening of Karma as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
By failing to perform what is prescribed, by engaging in what is censured, and by not restraining the senses, a man falls [into a lower state].
Therefore, one must diligently perform expiation for the sake of purification; in this way, both his inner self and the world will become serene.
The world would be at peace if one were thus [to act]; through expiations, there is the destruction of sin. Those who do not perform expiation and are devoid of remorse [fall].
Indeed, those who commit evil go to the hells of Mahāraurava and Raurava, as well as Tāmisra and Lohaśaṅku, which is filled with a foul stench.
The Haṃsābha, the Lohitoda, the Sañjīvana, the river-path, the Mahānilaya, the Kākola, the Andhatāmisra, and the Vāpana.
Indeed, due to their lack of merit, evildoers go to Avīci and Kumbhīpāka; namely, the killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief, the adulterer, and the violator of the Guru’s bed.
Censuring one's guru and censuring the Vedas—these two are indeed equal to the killing of a Brahmin—as is eating forbidden food and the performance of crooked actions.
Licking the mouth of a menstruating woman is equal to drinking liquor; stealing a horse, a gem, or similar valuables is equated with the theft of gold.

Sexual intercourse with the wives of friends, with virgins, with women of one's own kin, with women of the lowest castes, and likewise with women of the same lineage (sagotra), is declared to be equal to violating the bed of one's guru.
The father’s sister, the mother’s sister, the maternal uncle’s wife, the daughter-in-law, the mother’s co-wife, the sister, and likewise the teacher’s daughter;

One who approaches the wife of his teacher or his own daughter is a violator of the guru's bed; his punishment is the cutting off of the penis and death, as is the case for the woman if she was willing.
Killing a cow, being a *vrātya*, theft, the non-payment of debts, failing to maintain the sacred fires, selling forbidden goods, and superseding a younger brother in marriage;
Teaching for a fee, receiving instruction from a paid teacher, adultery, causing a younger brother to marry before the elder, usury, and the manufacture of salt;
For one born of a true Śūdra, Vaiśya, or Kṣatriya, living off censured wealth, atheism, the breaking of vows, and the sale of a bull or a cow are [grounds for loss of caste].
Abandoning one's father, mother, or friends; selling a pond or a grove; defiling a maiden; and officiating at the marriage of a younger brother whose elder brother is unmarried.
Giving away one's daughter to that very person, crookedness, the breaking of a vow, undertaking actions for one's own sake, and consorting with women who drink liquor.
Abandoning one's Vedic study, the sacred fire, and one's sons; likewise, abandoning one's kinsmen; engaging with improper scriptures; and the sale of one's wife or oneself.
Minor sins have also been declared; now learn the expiation for them: carrying a skull as his banner, subsisting on alms, and making his past deeds known.
A killer of a Brahmin shall attain purification after twelve years by eating sparingly; or else, he may offer his own body, beginning with the hair, while reciting "Svāhā to the hairs."

Or one may offer oblations ending with the marrow, using their respective mantras in due order; through the protection of a Brāhmaṇa, purification shall occur, and by performing it in this manner, there is indeed purification.
Or, having protected a bird, a cow, or a Brahmin from danger—even if he himself is killed for their sake—he shall remain self-controlled in the forest and recite the Vedic Saṃhitā three times.

Or, having resorted to the Sarasvatī river, he should bestow his wealth upon a worthy recipient; one who kills a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice shall perform the penance prescribed for a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa.

Or, like one who kills an embryo according to its caste, so too should one perform the vow for slaying an Ātreyī woman—even if she has not been killed—should he have approached her with the intent to kill.

If a Brāhmaṇa engaged in a Soma sacrifice drinks [forbidden liquor], he should observe a vow of twice the duration; one who has drunk *surā* is purified by drinking *surā*, water, clarified butter, and cow urine.
Or, wearing rags and matted hair, he should consume ghee that has the color of fire; the slayer of a Brahmin should perform this vow and then undergo the purificatory rites once more.
Likewise, a Brāhmaṇa woman who drinks liquor by drinking blood, feces, or urine is fallen from the world of her husband and becomes a vulture, a sow, or a dog.
A twice-born man who has stolen gold, having given a pestle to the king and having made his deed known, shall become pure by being killed by him.
Or, by giving gold equal to his own weight, the twice-born man shall attain purification; or he should lie down secretly upon an iron bed with an iron woman.
Having cut off his penis and testicles, he should cast them away in the south-western direction; then, one who has violated the Guru’s bed must perform the Prājāpatya penance for a year.

Or, for three months, he should practice the Cāndrāyaṇa penance while reciting the Vedic Saṃhitā; a killer of a cow should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and remain self-restrained for one month.
One who sleeps in a cow-pen and follows the cows is purified by the gift of a cow; furthermore, purification for minor offenses (upapātaka) may be achieved through the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
For the killing of a Kṣatriya, a man should again give a thousand cows with a single bull as the eleventh, either subsisting on milk for a month or performing a Parāka penance.
Or he may perform the vow for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa for three years; for a killer of a Vaiśya, he should perform this for one year, or else give one hundred and one cows.
A killer of a Śūdra shall do this for six months, or else give ten cows; having killed an uncorrupted woman, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra.
For killing a cat, an iguana, a mongoose, a domestic animal, or a frog, the sinner should drink milk for three days or perform the Kṛcchra penance or even more.
For an elephant, five blue bulls should be given; for a parrot, a two-year-old calf; for donkeys, goats, and rams, a bull; and for a crane, a three-year-old bull.

For cutting down trees, shrubs, creepers, or climbing plants, one hundred ṛc-verses should be recited; and a student observing celibacy becomes an *avakīrṇin* by having sexual intercourse with a woman.
By sacrificing a donkey to Nirṛti as an animal victim, one is purified; for eating honey and meat, the Kṛcchra penance and the remaining vows must be performed.

If one who has been sent on a mission should die, the preceptor shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances; having acted contrary to the will of the preceptor, he becomes pure only after propitiating him.
One may win over enemies by the gift of grain and other such means, or even through acts of affection; if a Brahmin dies while such assistance is being rendered, there is no sin.
One who has been falsely accused of a great sin or a minor sin by another should subsist on water for a month, reciting [mantras] with his senses restrained.

One who approaches his brother's wife without being authorized should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; having approached a woman in her courses, he becomes pure after consuming clarified butter at the end of three nights.
Dwelling in a cow-pen for one month as a celibate student, subsisting on milk and devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī, one is liberated from the sin of accepting improper gifts.

One who performs sacrifices for those who have fallen from their caste (vrātya) should perform the kṛcchra penance three times; likewise one who causes the Veda to be forgotten, one who eats barley for a year, and one who abandons those who have sought refuge.

One who has traveled in a donkey-cart or a camel-cart, or who has bathed naked, slept naked, or had sexual intercourse with a woman during the day, should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
Having addressed a Brahmin with "thou," having uttered "huṃ" at him, or having defeated him in debate, the sages should propitiate him and then fast for one day.

If a Brahmin raises a staff [to strike], the penance is a *kṛcchra*; if he actually strikes him down, it is an *atikṛcchra*, after carefully considering the place, the time, the age, the capacity, and the nature of the offense.
A penance must be prescribed in cases where no expiation has been specifically mentioned; for women, the abandonment of the fetus and the reviling of the husband are causes of falling [from caste].
This is the fault when near a planet; therefore, one should avoid her from afar. One who is aware of this fault should perform the vow with the permission of his preceptor.
But one whose sin has not been publicly proclaimed should perform the secret vow; having fasted for three nights, a killer of a Brahmin should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn.
Having offered a milch cow into the pure water, he should subsist on air for a day while reciting the verse, "To the body hairs, svāhā! (lomabhyaḥ svāhā).
Having recited [the mantra] over water, one should offer forty oblations of clarified butter; having fasted for three nights and offered clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍī verses, one becomes pure.
The drinker of spirituous liquor, the stealer of gold, and the violator of the Guru’s bed are liberated by standing in water and reciting the Rudra-hymn and the Sahasra-śīrṣa hymn.
One should perform a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) for the removal of all sins; one becomes pure by drinking the water of the moon while joined with the syllable Oṃ.

Having observed a fast, a twice-born man who has consumed semen, feces, or urine is purified from the sin committed through ignorance once the three daily twilight prayers (sandhyā) have been performed.

Indeed, through the recitation of the Rudra-ekādaśa, the destruction of sin occurs for the twice-born; [he becomes] devoted to the study of the Vedas, peaceful, and intent upon the performance of the five great sacrifices.
Alas, sins do not touch one who has quickly remembered [the Lord] and cast them away; by reciting the Gāyatrī a thousand times, one becomes pure, except in the case of killing a Brahmin.
Celibacy, compassion, patience, meditation, truthfulness, sincerity, non-violence, non-stealing, gentleness, and self-control—these are remembered as the *yamas*.

Bathing, silence, fasting, sacrifice, study of the Vedas, restraint of the generative organ, austerity, freedom from anger, devotion to the teacher, and purity are recorded as the observances (niyamas).
Having consumed the five products of the cow—cow’s milk, curd, urine, dung, and ghee—one should fast on the following day; thus one performs the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance.
With each of the *sāntapana* substances taken separately over six days, followed by a day of fasting, this seven-day rite is known as the *mahāsāntapana* penance.
The *parṇakṛcchra* is declared to consist of the daily practice, performed individually, of water infused with *parṇa*, *udumbara*, *rājīva*, *bilva* leaves, and *kuśa* grass.
One should drink each of these—boiled milk, ghee, and water—daily for one day each; followed by a fast for one night, this is the purifying Taptakṛcchra penance.
Eating once a day, eating only at night, likewise eating only what is unasked for, and fasting—this is declared to be the Pādakṛcchra penance.
In whatever manner it may be performed, this threefold *prājāpatya* is so called; this very same penance becomes an *atikṛcchra* by subsisting on only as much water as fills the palms of one's hands.
The *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* consists of subsisting on milk for twenty-one days, while the *parāka* is declared to consist of twelve days of fasting.
Taking one of each—oil-cake, water from boiled rice, buttermilk, water, and barley meal—daily, along with one day of fasting, is called the *saumya-kṛcchra*.
Through the practice of these for three nights each, one should perform them in sequence; this is known as the "Tulāpuruṣa" rite, which lasts for fifteen days.

One should eat morsels of food in increasing amounts during the bright fortnight, equal in size to a peacock's egg; one should decrease them by one each day during the dark fortnight—this is the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
Alternatively, one may consume exactly two hundred and forty morsels of food in a single month; this is another form of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

Having bathed at the three sessions of the day, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance consisting of morsels of food; one should recite purificatory mantras and consecrate the morsels with the *gāyatrī*.
For sins not specifically prescribed, purification is achieved through the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; he who performs this for the sake of dharma attains the same world as the Moon.
But one who performs the Kṛcchra penance while desiring righteousness attains great prosperity.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of Atonements as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Yājñavalkya said: I shall now proclaim the purification rites for the deceased; listen to this, O you who are firm in your vows. One who has not yet reached two years of age should be buried, and no water libations should be offered thereafter.
Having followed [the body] as far as the cremation ground accompanied by other kinsmen, they should recite the Yama-sūkta while chanting it with the common fire.

If he has maintained the sacred fires, he should be cremated according to the ritual procedure for those who have established the fires; otherwise, the kinsmen approach the waters from the seventh or the tenth day.

Facing the direction of the ancestors (the south), they should perform the water-libation rites for themselves with the mantra "Apanaḥ śośucad agham"; the same applies to the water-libation rites for maternal grandfathers, teachers, and the wives of teachers.

The paternal kinsmen, the maternal uncles, the sons, friends, the sister's sons, the father-in-law, and the officiating priests—restrained in speech, they pour water once, pronouncing the name and the lineage.

But they shall not perform water-libations for heretics or those who have fallen from their caste, nor for those who have violated their vows of celibacy, for *vrātyas*, nor for women who follow their lusts.
Women who drink liquor and those who commit suicide do not participate in the impurity rites or the water libations; therefore, one should not weep, for the stability of life is transitory.
One should perform the rite according to one's ability, and then, having chewed neem leaves, go toward one's home while remaining self-controlled at the door of the house.
Having sipped water, they should then touch fire, water, cow dung, and white mustard seeds; then, having touched them, they should enter [the house] by placing their feet slowly upon a stone.

Regarding the rites such as entering [the funeral ground], even from touching a deceased person, purification for those who merely look upon it occurs instantly; for others, it comes through bathing and self-restraint.
Eating food that has been purchased or obtained, they should sleep separately on the ground; for three days, food should be offered to the deceased by means of the Piṇḍayajña rite.
Water should be kept for one day in the open air, and milk in an earthen vessel; the Vaitāna and Āvasathya sacrifices, as well as the rites enjoined by the Vedas, must be performed.
Immediate purification is prescribed from birth until the tonsure ceremony; until the initiation into vows, it is considered one night; and beyond that, it is ten nights.

Impurity due to death is declared to last for three nights or ten nights; however, in the case of a child less than two years old, the impurity of birth (sūtaka) belongs to both parents, while that of death belongs to the mother alone.
In the interval between birth and death, one is purified by the remaining days: ten for the [lowest] caste, twelve for the [next], and likewise fifteen for the [highest] castes.
Likewise, there is a period of impurity for thirty days in the case of a *preta*; however, for unmarried girls and young children, purification occurs immediately after the day [of death].

And [the same applies] toward the teacher's resident pupil, a fellow student, a maternal uncle, and a learned brahmin; as well as toward sons other than those born of one's own body, and toward wives who have gone to another man.
Likewise, on the day of death, there is purification for those killed by kings, cows, or Brahmins, as well as for those who commit suicide, provided it occurs immediately thereafter.

O Lord of the Earth, there is no period of impurity for kings who have been killed by poison and the like, nor for those engaged in sacrificial sessions, those observing vows, celibate students, donors, and knowers of Brahman.
Immediate purification is prescribed in cases of giving gifts, marriage, sacrifice, battle, national calamity, and even in times of dire distress.
Time, fire, action, earth, wind, mind, knowledge, austerity, recitation, repentance, and fasting are the causes of purification for all.

For those who have committed improper acts, the giving of gifts is the means of purification, just as the current of a river purifies; furthermore, a twice-born man may live by the occupation of a Kshatriya or even that of a Vaishya in times of distress.
Fruit, soma, linen, creepers, curd, milk, ghee, water, sesame, boiled rice, meat broth, alkali, honey, lac, and cooked oblation;
Clothing, stones, liquor, flowers, vegetables, clay, leather, sandals, the skin of the black antelope, silk, salt, and meat as well.
A man following the livelihood of a Vaiśya shall not sell oil-cakes, roots, or perfumes; however, for the sake of dharma, he may sell sesame seeds in exchange for an equal amount of grain.
A twice-born man, even when fallen into distress, should not sell salt and such items; and a Brahmin, by accepting gifts from a low person, is not defiled, just as the sun is not.

In that same way, one should engage in agriculture and other such activities; likewise, horses are not to be sold. Having seen those who are hungry, standing [in distress], and deprived of a livelihood, the king should provide a righteous means of subsistence for the Brahmins and others.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Impurity and its Removal as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Sūta said: Parāśara spoke to Vyāsa concerning the duties of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama-dharma): "In every Kalpa, through the process of destruction and creation, beings and other entities are indeed diminished."

Revelation (śruti), tradition (smṛti), and the conduct of the virtuous—whatever has been composed by the twice-born—are the Vedas; and the duties (dharmas) among the Brāhmaṇas and other classes have always been recorded by Manu and others.
In the Kali age, charity is the dharma; and in the Kali age, one should abandon the doer [of the deed]. However, an evil act performed therein bears fruit within a year, even as a curse.
Through right conduct, one shall obtain everything: the six duties day after day—namely, the twilight prayers, bathing, recitation, fire-offerings, and the worship of the gods, guests, and others.
At that time, there will indeed be unprecedented Brahmins of excellent vows and unprecedented ascetics; and a Kshatriya, having conquered the armies of his enemies, shall protect the earth.

Trade, agriculture, and so forth belong to the Vaiśya, while devotion to the twice-born belongs to the Śūdra. One falls [from one's status] through eating forbidden food, theft, and approaching those who should not be approached.
A twice-born man practicing agriculture should not yoke an ox when it is exhausted; he should bathe for half the day, perform yoga and other such practices, and feed the Brahmins.
One should perform the five sacrifices, cause the cruel [deed] to be censured, and one who is possessed by sin should not sell sesame or clarified butter; such is the sacrifice at the slaughterhouse.
Having given one-sixth to the king, one-twentieth to the gods, and one-thirty-third to the Brahmins, the cultivator is not defiled by sin.

Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are farmers become thieves if they do not give [the grain] from the threshing floor; however, a Brāhmaṇa is purified in three days from the birth or death impurity of a deceased person.
A Kṣatriya [is purified] after ten days, a Vaiśya after twelve days, and a Śūdra after a month; a Brāhmaṇa reaches purification after ten days, while a Kṣatriya does so after twelve days.
A Vaiśya is purified in fifteen days, while a Śūdra is purified in a month; those who share a single funeral rice-ball (paṇḍa) but have separate doors and dwellings are considered heirs.
Upon birth and upon death, there shall be *sūtaka* (impurity) for them; it lasts ten nights in the fourth generation, six nights in the fifth, and three nights in the male line.

In the sixth [month], purification occurs after four days; in the seventh, after three days. When a child dies in another country, purification is immediate, because [the child] has already died [there].
For those children who have not yet cut their teeth and for those who have just emerged from the womb, there is no cremation with fire, no offering of funeral cakes, and no water libations.
If a woman’s fetus miscarries or is lost, the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) lasts for as many days as the number of months the fetus had remained.

From the time of naming until the end of the tonsure ceremony, impurity lasts for a day and night; from the commencement of the vows (initiation) until they are completed, it lasts for three nights; and beyond that, it lasts for ten days.

The flow [of menses] may last up to the fourth day; the cessation occurs on the fifth or sixth. There is no impurity resulting from celibacy, the Agnihotra sacrifice, or the avoidance of social contact.
Artisans, craftsmen, physicians, female and male slaves, servants, one who maintains the sacred fire, a Vedic scholar, and a king are proclaimed to be immediately pure.
The mother is purified after ten days; the father becomes pure by bathing upon birth. Impurity due to birth occurs through contact; having performed ritual ablution, the father becomes pure.
In the midst of a wedding, a festival, or a sacrifice, if a death or birth-impurity occurs, it is ordained that one must abstain from anything other than what was previously intended.

Birth-impurity is purified by death; for one born when another has died, it is like the impurity of death. However, for those who perish in cattle-rustling raids and similar calamities, the birth-impurity lasts for one night.
One is purified by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma) for carrying a destitute or deceased person; however, from carrying a deceased Śūdra, one shall remain impure for three nights.

There is no funeral consecration for one who commits suicide, one killed by poison, one strangled, or one bitten by a worm; having touched a cow-killed person or one bitten by a worm, one is purified by performing a *kṛcchra* penance.
She who abandons a blameless and non-degraded husband during his youth shall remain a woman for seven births and experience widowhood again and again.

By having sexual intercourse with a woman during her menstrual period, one incurs the sin of killing a child; however, a sow-like woman is one who approaches a forbidden man, those who have broken their vows, and those from whom the rites of food and water have been withdrawn.

The legitimate son of the body and the son born of the wife are both born of the father and are givers of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to the father; however, for one who has superseded his elder brother in marriage, there shall be a Kṛcchra penance, and for the girl [who was given away], likewise a Kṛcchra.

The giver should perform an *atikṛcchra* penance, and the officiating priest (*hotṛ*) should perform a *cāndrāyaṇa* penance, [if the recipient is] among those who are humpbacked, dwarfs, eunuchs, those with stammering speech, or the mentally dull.
There is no fault in marrying again if the husband is born blind, deaf, mute, lost, dead, has renounced the world, is impotent, or has fallen from his caste.
In five calamities, another husband is ordained for women; a woman who dies together with her husband shall dwell in heaven for as many years as there are hairs on her body.

A man bitten by a dog or similar animal becomes pure through the recitation of the Gāyatrī; however, a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires and has been killed by Cāṇḍālas or others should be cremated with the common fire of the world.

Having washed its bone with milk, one should burn it with one's own fire while reciting the mantra; however, if death occurs while away from home, one should again fashion an effigy out of kuśa grass and burn it.

Having spread out six hundred palāśa sticks upon a black antelope skin, and having placed a śamī stick at the head [of the skin], one should place the fire-drill (araṇi) at the "testicles" [the tail-end].
One should place the *kaṇḍa* in the right hand and the *upabhṛt* in the left hand; one should place the mortar on the side and the pestle on the back.

Having cast the grinding stone upon his chest, he should place the rice, clarified butter, and sesame seeds in his mouth; the *prokṣaṇī* vessel in his ear, and the *ājyasthālī* (clarified butter pot) in his two eyes.
One should place pieces of gold in the ears, eyes, mouth, and nostrils; by means of the implements for the Agnihotra sacrifice, one shall attain the world of Brahmā.
With the words "To this world of heaven, svāhā!", he offers a single oblation of clarified butter; [he should avoid] the swan, the crane, the curlew, the ruddy goose, and the cock.
One who kills a deer or a ram is purified by a day and night; having killed all kinds of birds, one is purified by a day and night.

Having killed all four-footed animals, one should recite [the mantra] while fasting for a day and night. Having killed a Śūdra, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; having killed a Vaiśya, the Atikṛcchra; for killing a Kṣatriya, the Cāndrāyaṇa; and for killing a Brāhmaṇa, one should undergo the Dvāviṃśatimāsika and Triṃśanmāsika penances.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Dharma as Spoken by Parāśara," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 108.

Sūta said: I shall proclaim the essence of political ethics (nītisāra), which is based upon the treatises on statecraft (arthaśāstra) and other sciences; it is beneficial for kings and others, meritorious, and bestows longevity, heaven, and other rewards.
A man desiring success should always cultivate association with the virtuous; there is no benefit from the wicked, neither for this world nor for the next.
