One should avoid conversation with the base, yet one may look upon the non-crooked; one should avoid conflict with a friend and intimacy with one who serves an enemy.
Even a wise man comes to ruin through instructing foolish disciples, supporting wicked women, and associating with the corrupt.
One should avoid from afar a foolish Brāhmaṇa, a warrior (Kṣatriya) who does not fight, a dull-witted Vaiśya, and a Śūdra who is well-versed in the syllables of the Veda.
An alliance with an enemy at the right time, and war with a friend at the right time—the wise man, relying on cause and effect, lets the proper time pass.
Time ripens all beings; Time destroys all creatures; Time remains awake while others sleep; for Time is indeed insurmountable.
Time takes away vitality; in time the embryo develops; Time brings forth creation, and Time again shall withdraw it.
Time is eternally subtle in its movement, and it is conceived here as being twofold: by way of gross synthesis and by way of subtle internal movement.
Bṛhaspati, the omniscient, spoke this Essence of Ethics to the Lord of the Gods, by means of which Indra became all-knowing, slew the Daityas, and attained heaven.
Royal sages and brahmins should perform the worship of gods, brahmins, and others; they must sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha), which destroys even the greatest sins.
One who maintains association with the excellent, engages in noble discourse with the learned, and cultivates friendship with those free from greed, does not come to ruin.
One should never engage in slander, nor for the sake of another, nor in jesting, nor with another's wife, nor in dwelling in another's house.
Even a stranger who brings benefit is a kinsman, while a kinsman who brings harm is a stranger; a disease born of one's own body is harmful, whereas medicine from the forest is beneficial.
He is a kinsman who is intent on one's welfare; he is a father who provides nourishment; he is a friend in whom there is trust; and that is a country where one can live.
He is a servant who is obedient; that is a seed which sprouts; she is a wife who speaks kindly; he is a son who lives.
He lives who possesses virtues; he lives who possesses dharma. For him who is devoid of virtue and dharma, his life is fruitless.
She is a wife who is skillful in the home; she is a wife who speaks kindly; she is a wife whose life is her husband; she is a wife who is devoted to her husband.
She was constantly bathed and fragrant, always speaking kindly, eating little, speaking little, and perpetually endowed with auspiciousness.
She is constantly devoted to dharma, always dear to her husband, always pleasant of speech, and always desirous of him during the fertile season.
Endowed with these primary rites, she increases all good fortune; he who possesses such a wife is not a mere mortal, but a lord of the gods.
He whose wife is misshapen-eyed, dejected, fond of quarreling, and always speaking in opposition—she is old age; old age is not merely the passing of years.
He whose wife has taken refuge with another and longs for the house of another, being of evil conduct and devoid of shame—this is true old age; it is not mere aging that is old age.
She whose wife is discerning of virtues, follows her husband, and is content with even the smallest thing—she is truly beloved; any other is not beloved, though she may claim to be so.
A wicked wife, a deceitful friend, a servant who speaks back, and living in a house with snakes—these are nothing but death; of this there is no doubt.
Abandon association with the wicked; cultivate the company of the virtuous. Perform meritorious deeds day and night; constantly remember impermanence.

A woman who has the region of her neck like a serpent, whose speech is like that of a hooded snake, who is fierce, dark, agitated in song, and whose eyes are overwhelmed with blood; who resembles a tiger, whose face is terrible in anger, and who is as formidable as a crow’s tongue with flickering flames of fire—such a woman, though clever, should not be courted, for she wanders into the houses of others, her mind is distracted, and she is devoid of affection.

Attachment arises by the power of fate sometimes for a son, for one who has done good, and for a fire that consumes its fuel; it may even arise for a goldsmith who steals the gold of Sītā. But passion for courtesans never truly comes to pass.

When a serpent is seen in one's home, when a disease has been diagnosed by a physician, and when the body is beset by the stages of life such as childhood and so forth—who, surrounded by these times, can attain composure?

Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Essence of Ethics Spoken by Bṛhaspati," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: One should save wealth for times of distress; one should protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth; but one should always protect oneself, even at the cost of both wife and wealth.

One should abandon an individual for the sake of a family; one should abandon a family for the sake of a village; one should abandon a village for the sake of a country; and one should abandon the entire earth for the sake of the self.
Indeed, dwelling in hell is better than living in a home of evil conduct; for from hell one's sin is exhausted, but from a wretched home one does not turn back.
The wise man moves with one foot while standing firm on the other; he should not abandon his former abode until he has examined his future destination.

One should abandon a country of wicked conduct; one should abandon a residence that is fraught with calamities; one should abandon a miserly king; and one should abandon a friend who is full of deceit.

What is the use of wealth that has fallen into the hands of a miser? What is the use of knowledge that is crowded with many deceitful grasping? What is the use of beauty devoid of virtue and prowess? What is the use of a friend who turns his back at the time of misfortune?

Many companions never seen before become friends to one who stands firm in his position; but for one deprived of wealth and fallen from his station, even his own kin become enemies at an improper time.
One should recognize a friend in times of adversity, a hero in battle, one who is pure in private, a wife when wealth has been exhausted, and a guest who is dear even during a famine.

Birds abandon a tree whose fruit is exhausted; cranes leave a dried-up lake; courtesans forsake a man devoid of wealth; ministers desert a fallen king; bees abandon a withered flower; and deer flee from a forest consumed by fire. Indeed, every person acts out of self-interest; for who is truly dear to anyone?
Win over the greedy by giving wealth, the praiseworthy with a gesture of salutation, the fool by complying with his whims, and the wise man with truthfulness.
For the gods, virtuous men, and the twice-born are pleased by sincerity; others [are pleased] by food and drink, while the wise are pleased by the gift of honor.
One should win over the superior by prostration, the deceitful by sowing dissension, the base by giving small gifts, and an equal by means of equal prowess.
For whatever a person's disposition may be, a wise man, speaking what is beneficial for each of them and entering into their company, should quickly bring them under his own influence.
One should never place trust in rivers, clawed beasts, horned animals, those with weapons in hand, women, or royal households.
A wise person should not disclose the loss of wealth, mental anguish, misconduct within the home, deception, or insults.
Association with base and wicked people, a total lack of respect, affection for others' homes, and residing in another's house are the destroyers of a woman's virtuous conduct.
In whose family is there no fault? Who has not been afflicted by disease? Who has not encountered calamity? And whose prosperity has been uninterrupted?

What man on earth has not become arrogant upon attaining wealth? Whose misfortunes have not arrived? Whose mind on earth has not been shattered by women? Who indeed is beloved by kings? Who has not come within the range of Time (Death)? What wealth has attained lasting dignity? Or what man, having fallen into the snare of the wicked, has escaped in safety?

How could a wise person perform that action in which one finds no friends, kin, or relatives, nor even a sense of self, where the emergence of results is not seen even when the deed is accomplished, and where there is great suffering in the event of failure?
One should avoid that country where there is no honor, no affection, no kinsmen, and no acquisition of knowledge whatsoever.
Amass that wealth which brings no fear from kings or thieves, and which one does not have to abandon at death.

The heirs indeed divide that which was acquired through life-threatening labors once the person has died; but whatever evil deed was committed out of a desire for wealth, that alone becomes the inheritance of the one who is struck down by his own fault.
Wealth that is accumulated and stored away, which a miser touches again and again like a rat, leads only to suffering.
Naked, wretched, and harsh, with begging bowls marked upon their hands, they demonstrate here in this world such a fruit for one who does not give.
Miserable people instruct others and beg, saying "Give!"—such is the state of one who does not give; may you never become like that.
That wealth which is not matched by hundreds of sacrifices, nor given to the virtuous when requested, but is guarded by a miser—that wealth is eventually spent in the houses of thieves or kings.
The wealth of a miser goes neither to the gods, nor to the brahmins, nor to his kinsmen, nor even to himself; rather, it goes to fire, thieves, and the king.
May you never obtain those objects which are gained through excessive hardship, by transgressing the Dharma, or by bowing down before an enemy.

Lack of practice is the destruction of knowledge; wearing poor clothing is the destruction of women; eating when food is digested is the destruction of diseases; and prolixity is the destruction of an enemy.
The punishment for a thief is death; for a bad friend, it is silence; for women, it is sleeping separately; and for a Brahmin, it is not being invited [to a feast].
Wicked people, artisans, servants, malicious individuals, drums, and women become gentle when struck; they are not vessels for respectful treatment.
One should know that servants are tested in being sent on errands, kinsmen when misfortune arrives, a friend in times of calamity, and a wife when wealth is exhausted.
It is traditionally taught that for women, the appetite is twofold, wisdom fourfold, resolve sixfold, and desire eightfold.
One should not conquer sleep with dreams, nor should one conquer a woman with desire; one should not conquer fire with fuel, nor should one conquer thirst with wine.
Desire for women flourishes through meals containing meat, unctuous foods, wines, fragrant ointments, delightful garments, and garlands.
Even regarding celibacy, it must be said that the stirrings of passion arise; for upon seeing a pleasing man, a woman's womb becomes moistened.
Upon seeing a well-dressed man, whether he be a brother or a son, the womb of women becomes moist; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Śaunaka.

Rivers and women are of a similar nature; in their independence regarding movement and other such acts, rivers cause banks to collapse with their waters, and women cause noble families to fall through their faults.
A river causes the bank to fall; a woman causes the family to fall. The course of women and of rivers is independent and playful.
Fire is never satiated with wood, nor the great ocean with rivers; Death is never satiated with all living beings, nor are beautiful-eyed women with men.
There is no satiety for the learned, for those who are beloved, for those who speak kindly, for pleasures, for sons, for life, and for excellence.

A king is never satiated by the accumulation of wealth, nor does the ocean reach satiety with water; a wise man is not satiated by what he has spoken, and the eye is never satiated by the sight of a king.

For those supreme men who live by their own labor earned through righteousness, who always delight in their wives according to the scriptures, who have conquered their senses, and who are fond of guests—for them, liberation is found even in the home.
For one of virtuous deeds, heaven shall consist of women who are pleasing to the mind, beautiful in form, and well-adorned, as he dwells upon the rooftops of palaces.
Neither by gifts, nor by honor, nor by straightforwardness, nor by self-control; neither by weapons nor by scriptures—in every way, women are difficult to manage.
Slowly one should acquire knowledge, slowly wealth, and slowly one should ascend a mountain; slowly one should pursue pleasure and virtue—these five things, step by step.
Worship of the gods and the like is eternal; the giving of gifts to Brahmins is eternal; knowledge endowed with virtue is eternal; and a true friend is eternal.

Those who do not study the sciences in their childhood, and those who, established in youth, are destitute of wealth and wives—they are to be pitied in this world of living beings; they wander about in human form like wild beasts.
A student of the scriptures should not set his mind on recitation or eating; for the sake of knowledge, he should travel even to the farthest distance with the speed of Garuḍa.
Those who, being afflicted by desire, do not study the sciences in their youth, and whose wealth is lost in their prime, are humiliated in old age and burn like a lotus in the cold season.

Reasoning is unstable, the scriptural traditions are diverse, and there is no sage whose view is not divided; the truth of Dharma is hidden in a cave, and the path is that which has been trodden by the great multitude.
The internal mind is discerned through facial expressions, gestures, gait, movements, speech, and the changes in the eyes and face.

A wise person infers even what has not been spoken, for the fruit of intelligence is the knowledge of another's gestures; a meaning expressed is grasped even by a beast, and horses and elephants carry out what is shown to them.

One fallen from wealth should go on a pilgrimage; one fallen from truth shall indeed go to the Raurava hell; one fallen from yoga should resort to truth and fortitude; and one fallen from his kingdom should resort to hunting.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Great Essence of Ethics," in the Section on Conduct within the First Part of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: He who abandons certainties and pursues uncertainties loses his certainties; indeed, that which is uncertain is already lost.

Knowledge in the hands of a man devoid of the instrument of speech is like a weapon in the hands of a coward; it produces no satisfaction in the body, just as beautiful wives bring no joy to a blind man.

The power to enjoy food when there is food, the power for pleasure with excellent women when there is wealth, and the power to give charity when there is abundance—these are not the fruits of meager austerity.

The Vedas have the Agnihotra sacrifice as their fruit; virtuous conduct has auspicious character as its fruit; wives have pleasure and sons as their fruit; and wealth has giving and enjoyment as its fruit.
A wise man should choose a girl born of a noble family even if she is ugly, but he should never choose one who is not of noble birth, even if she is beautiful and possesses shapely hips.
For what is the use of that wealth which is associated with misfortune? Who indeed would take the jewel from the crest of a serpent?
One should accept an oblation even from a family that is corrupt, a well-spoken word even from a child, gold even from impurity, and a jewel of a woman even from a base family.
Nectar should be taken even from poison, gold even from filth, the highest knowledge even from a low person, and a jewel of a woman even from a base family.
There is no friendship with a king, nor is there ever a snake without venom; there is no family that remains stainless where women are born.
One should employ a devoted person in the family, engage a son in the sciences, involve an enemy in calamities, and direct a beloved one toward dharma.
Servants and ornaments should be employed only in their proper places; for a crest-jewel never indeed looks beautiful upon the foot.
The crest-jewel, the ocean, fire, the bell, and the unbroken sky—or else the protector of the earth—[are situated] from the head down to the feet by way of [their respective] positions.
For a high-minded man, there are only two destinies, like those of a cluster of blossoms: either to be borne upon the heads of all people, or to fall at the summit of the forest.
If a gem fit for a collection of golden ornaments is set in lead, it neither cries out nor does it shine; rather, the blame falls upon the one who joined them.
Between horses, elephants, and iron; between wood, stone, and cloth; and between women, men, and water—there is a vast difference.
For even when one whose conduct is firm is humiliated, the destruction of all his virtues cannot be achieved; even when fire is cast downward by a villain, its flame never goes below.
A noble steed does not endure the stroke of the whip; a lion does not tolerate the trumpeting of elephants; nor does a hero endure the terrifying roar directed at him by an enemy.

If, by fate, one is deprived of wealth or suddenly fallen from fortune, one should never desire the service of the wicked or the base; for even when tormented by intense hunger, a lion does not eat grass for the sake of food, but generally drinks the warm blood of elephants.
He who desires to reunite with a friend who has once proved treacherous embraces death itself, just as a female mule conceives a fetus.
The offspring of an enemy, even if they speak sweet words, must not be overlooked by wise men; for at certain times, they bring about calamity, being as terrible as vessels of poison.
One should eliminate an enemy by means of an enemy who has been won over by favors, just as one extracts a thorn embedded in the foot with another thorn held in the hand.
One should never think of those who are constantly intent on doing harm; they will fall by themselves, like trees growing on a riverbank.
For indeed, misfortunes disguised as benefits and benefits disguised as misfortunes always arise for the destruction of one who is dependent on fate.
Indeed, when destiny is favorable, a virtuous intellect arises that is appropriate for the occasion; thus, all is well for a person in every respect.
In matters of investing wealth, as well as in the pursuit of knowledge, in eating and in worldly dealings, one should always be free from shame.
A wealthy man, a Vedic scholar, a king, a river, and a physician as the fifth—if these five are not found in a place, one should not establish a residence there.
Where the five—worldly conduct, fear, shame, courtesy, and a disposition for generosity—are not found, one should not dwell there even for a single day.
A king who knows the divisions of time, a river, and a virtuous person as the fifth—wherever these are not found, one should not make one's dwelling.
"O Śaunaka, it is said that there is no final perfection of knowledge in any single place; everyone knows only a portion, and an omniscient being does not exist anywhere."

There is no one here in this world who is all-knowing, nor is there anyone on earth who is utterly ignorant; rather, he who understands by means of knowledge—whether inferior, superior, or middling—is a wise man by virtue of that.
Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Great Essence of Ethics," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: I shall now describe the characteristics of the king and his servants; for the protector of the earth must always properly examine all of them.
Devoted to truth and righteousness, he should constantly protect the kingdom; having conquered the enemy armies, he should rule the earth according to dharma.
One should pluck flower after flower, but one should not cut the root; like a garland-maker in the forest, and not like a charcoal-burner.
Milk-drinkers who milk the earth do not consume its products in a distorted manner; kings should enjoy another's kingdom without causing it harm.
Just as one who seeks milk from a cow should not cut off its udders, so too a kingdom, when oppressed by excessive application [of taxes], does not prosper.
Therefore, one should protect the earth with every effort; for the protector, the land shall bring fame, long life, glory, and strength.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu, a righteous king who is devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins and has conquered his senses is capable of protecting his subjects.
Having attained unstable sovereignty, a king should direct his mind toward Dharma; for in an instant wealth may perish, and riches and such are not under one's own control.
Truly, sensual pleasures are enchanting; truly, worldly prosperities are delightful; yet life itself is as fickle as the flickering glance from the corner of a woman's eye.
Old age stands threatening like a tigress, and diseases break out upon the body like enemies; life flows away like water from a broken jar, yet no one here practices what is beneficial for the self.

O humans, why do you act without hesitation? Perform what is beneficial for others and what is conducive to your own welfare; for you rejoice while struck by the arrows of Madana through the slow, lingering glances of passionate women. Do not commit sin; remain ever devoted to the twice-born and Hari. Life passes away completely, slipping away under the guise of Death, which has become like a water-clock.
He who looks upon the wives of others as his own mother, upon the wealth of others as a clod of earth, and upon all beings as himself—he is a wise man.
For this very purpose, O best of Brahmins, kings desire sovereignty: that their word may not be obstructed in any of their undertakings.
For this very purpose kings accumulate wealth; having protected themselves, they bestow that wealth upon the twice-born.
The sound of the syllable *oṃ* causes the kingdom of the brahmins to flourish; by that practice, the king prospers and is not afflicted by diseases.
Even sages, though they are incapable [of worldly accumulation], gather stores of material goods; how much more so, then, a protector of the earth who nurtures his subjects like his own children?
He who has wealth has friends; he who has wealth has kinsmen. He who has wealth is honored in this world; he who has wealth is a wise man.
Friends, sons, wives, and well-wishers abandon one who is destitute of wealth; yet they resort to him once again when he possesses riches, for in this world, wealth is indeed a person's kinsman.
For a king who is devoid of the treatises is indeed blind; one who is blind sees by means of his spies, but one bereft of the treatises does not see at all.
He whose sons, servants, ministers, and priests have their senses dormant will not possess his kingdom for long.
He by whom these three—sons, servants, and kinsmen—are won, has conquered the earth with its four oceans along with all other kings.
He who transgresses those things enjoined by the scriptures and those supported by reason—that king indeed perishes both in this world and in the next.
Upon encountering adversity, a king should not give way to mental anguish; with an even mind and a serene soul, he should remain equanimous toward both pleasure and pain.
The steadfast, having encountered hardship, do not become despondent; does the moon not rise again after entering the mouth of Rāhu?

"Fie, fie upon those men who pamper themselves with the pleasures of the body! Do not distress this very body which is already emaciated by poverty. For it is heard that the sons of Pāṇḍu, though deprived of their noble wives and wealth, abandoned their suffering and attained happiness once again."
Having mastered the science of the Gandharvas, instrumental music, and the arts of courtesans, as well as the science of archery and the treatises on statecraft, the king should protect the world.
That king who becomes angry with a servant without cause takes upon himself the madness of poison released by a black serpent.
One should always restrain the gaze from fickleness and refrain from false speech, both toward a learned Brahmin and toward one's own circle of servants.
A king who acts with negligence and is arrogant toward his servants and kinsmen will always be swiftly overcome by his enemies within his own realm.
A king should never frown while uttering the sound "huṃ. That lowest of kings who punishes his servants without fault shall lose all the pleasures and enjoyments of this world.
Enemies are overcome by those who act with ease while remaining firm in conflict.
Exertion, daring, fortitude, intelligence, power, and valor—when one possesses this sixfold enthusiasm, even a god fears him.
When an action has been performed with diligence yet success is not found, destiny is indeed the cause; nevertheless, human effort must always be exerted.
Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Great Essence of Ethics," in the Section on Conduct within the First Part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said: Servants are to be known as being of many kinds—superior, inferior, and middling—and they should be appointed to the three types of tasks according to their respective fitness.
I shall now describe the examination of servants; for whatever quality belongs to each particular servant, that I will fully explain exactly as it has been taught.
Just as gold is tested by four means—by rubbing, cutting, heating, and striking—so too should a servant be tested by four means: by speech, by conduct, by appearance, and by work.
One endowed with noble birth, good conduct, and virtue, devoted to truth and righteousness, handsome and very serene, is appointed as the superintendent of the treasury.
One who examines the value and form becomes a gemologist; one who thoroughly understands strengths and weaknesses is appointed as a commander-in-chief.
One who knows the truth of gestures and outward appearances, who is strong, pleasant to behold, vigilant, and capable of subduing others, is called a *pratīhāra*.
Intelligent, eloquent, wise, truthful, and with senses subdued—he who has thoroughly examined all the scriptures is indeed a virtuous scribe.
One who is intelligent, wise, capable of discerning the minds of others, firm, and who speaks exactly as instructed—such a person is appointed as a messenger.
One who knows all the treatises on law (smṛti), is learned, has conquered his senses, and is endowed with the qualities of heroism and valor, is appointed as the superintendent of dharma.
One who is skilled through ancestral lineage, learned in the scriptures, truthful in speech, pure, and firm—such a person is called a cook.
One who has practiced Āyurveda, who is pleasing to behold by all, and who is endowed with longevity, virtuous conduct, and good qualities—such a person alone is ordained as a physician.

One who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, is devoted to the practice of recitation and sacrifice, and is constantly intent on bestowing blessings—such a person is the royal chaplain.
The king should always avoid employing as officials one who is a mere scribe, a reciter, an accountant, an opponent, or one who is possessed by laziness.
The mouth of the wicked man, like that of a serpent—twisted-tongued, causing agitation, cruel, and utterly terrible—is intended solely for doing harm.
A wicked person should be avoided even if he is adorned with learning; is a serpent not terrifying, even when decorated with a jewel?

Who indeed does not feel fear toward a wicked person who displays anger without cause? For the poison of a great serpent and the unbearable, harsh speech of the wicked always lie together in his mouth.
He who would slay a servant who pursues the same goal, possesses equal capability, knows his vital points, is industrious, and has seized half the kingdom, is himself not slain.

Those who possess valor, speak with gentle and measured words, have conquered their senses, and are true in their prowess—even if they act contrary to these qualities at first and later—are servants who are not beneficial.
Free from laziness, well-contented, and ever-alert; equanimous in pleasure and pain—such steadfast servants are rare to find in the world.

One who lacks patience and self-control, who is cruel-minded and a reviler, who is hypocritical, deceitful, treacherous, and full of longing, who is incompetent and terrified by fear—he must indeed be abandoned by the king.
Well-maintained missiles and various types of weapons should be brought into the fort; then one shall strike down the enemy.
Then, for six months or a year, the lord of men should maintain peace while observing his own accumulation of resources; thereafter, he should strike down the enemy once again.
O Lord of the Earth, he who appoints fools [to office] suffers these three consequences: infamy, loss of wealth, and even a fall into hell.
Whatever action he performs, whether auspicious or inauspicious, by that the king increases through the subtle effects of his servants' deeds.
Therefore, a lord of the earth should constantly employ a wise man for the accomplishment of dharma, kama, and artha, indeed for the welfare of cows and brahmins.
Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Science of Ethics Spoken by Bṛhaspati," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: One should employ those who possess virtues and avoid those devoid of them; for all virtues reside in the wise, while faults exist solely in the foolish.

One should always sit with the virtuous, one should form associations with the virtuous, and engage in debate and friendship with the virtuous; one should not perform any action whatsoever with the wicked.
One should remain even while imprisoned with those who are wise, discerning, knowers of the Dharma, and speakers of truth; but one should never dwell in a kingdom together with the wicked.
One who leaves tasks unfinished is joined with misfortune; therefore, one should cause all tasks to be completed without remainder.
Just as one who extracts honey should milk the essence from the flower without destroying it, so should the king milk the earth and the cow while having regard for their calves.
Just as the six-legged bee gathers honey from flowers in due order, so should a king, having acquired wealth, make a store.
An anthill, a honeycomb, and the moon in the bright fortnight; likewise, royal property and alms—each grows by accumulating little by little.
Having observed the depletion of what has been earned and the accumulation of what has been given away, one should make each day fruitful through acts of giving, study, and righteous deeds.

Faults arise for the passionate even in the forest; the restraint of the five senses is asceticism even in the home. For one who engages in blameless action and whose passion has ceased, the home is a grove of penance.
Dharma is protected by truth; knowledge is protected by yoga; the alms-bowl is protected by cleaning; and a family is protected by modesty.

Better is dwelling in the Vindhya forest, better is death from hunger, better is lying upon a bed infested with snakes or falling into a well, and better is entering the midst of fearful waters swirling in eddies than to say to one's own kin, "Give me even a small amount of wealth."
Wealth does not diminish through enjoyment when one's fortune is exhausted; for as long as previously acquired merit remains, riches never perish.
Knowledge is the ornament of Brahmins, a king is the ornament of the earth, the moon is the ornament of the sky, and good character is the ornament of everyone.

These sons of kings, Bhīmasena, Arjuna, and the others—heroes equal to the moon, true to their vows, possessing bodies like the sun, and protected by Keśava—are now situated among malevolent planets, fallen under the power of the wretched, and have gone forth to live on alms. For who is capable of what? By the power of destiny, the lines of karma cause one to wander.

Salutations to that Ear, by whom Brahmā was confined within the vessel of the cosmic egg like a potter’s wheel; by whom Viṣṇu was cast into the great peril of the thicket of his ten incarnations; by whom Rudra was made to wander for alms with a skull held in the hollow of his hands; and by whom the Sun is made to revolve eternally in the sky.

The donor was Bali, the beggar was Murāri, and the gift was the earth in the presence of the Brahmins; having given it, only imprisonment as the fruit was obtained. Salutations to you, O Fate, who acts according to your own will!
Even if Lakṣmī were one’s mother and Janārdana himself were one’s father, punishment would always fall upon that person whose conduct is rooted in evil intellect.

Wherever, in whatever manner, and in whatever way one’s well-determined karma was performed in the past, that very same result one has deposited within oneself must be experienced by oneself in the interim.
Suffering is ordained by oneself; happiness is ordained by oneself. Indeed, from the time one enters the bed of the womb, one experiences the results of previous lives.

For a man is not able to escape the consequences of a deed he has committed, whether by entering the atmosphere, nor by going into the midst of the ocean, nor by entering a cave among the mountains, nor even by being held upon his mother’s head or in her lap.

With Dugastrikūṭa as its rampart, the ocean as its moat, the Rākṣasas as its warriors, and the supreme livelihood provided by the science taught by Uśanas—Rāvaṇa, despite all this, was destroyed by the power of Time.
In whatever age, at whatever time, whether by day or by night, and in whatever muhūrta or even instant—that is exactly so, and not otherwise.
They travel through the atmosphere or enter into the surface of the earth; they sustain all the directions, and nothing is perceived that has not been given.
Knowledge previously studied, wealth previously given, and actions performed in the past—these indeed run ahead of one who runs.

In this world, actions are paramount; even though Janaki was born under an auspicious asterism and a favorable planet, and at a time when Vashistha had fixed the auspicious moment for her birth, she became a vessel for suffering.
When Rāma has thick calves, Lakṣmaṇa moves with a sound, and Sītā has thick hair—these three are vessels of suffering.
A son does not go [to hell] by the karma of the father, nor does a father by the karma of the son; they go by what they themselves have done, bound by their own karma.
In these bodies born of karma, physical and mental diseases fall like arrows released here by firm archers.

Otherwise, a wise person seeks the goal with an intellect pregnant with the teachings of the scriptures; like a master, he performs his actions differently than what was previously conditioned by past karma.
Whether a child, a youth, or an old man, whoever performs good or evil deeds, he experiences the results in that very state of existence, birth after birth.
Even a man who does not look ahead, even one living in a foreign land, is carried by the wind of the ripening of his own karma to wherever that fruit awaits.

A person obtains the wealth that is destined to be obtained; even a god is not able to prevent it. Therefore, I do not grieve, nor do I feel astonishment, for the line upon my forehead does not change: "What is ours is not that of others."
A snake in a well, an elephant on one's shoulder, and a rat running in its hole—what man can escape from karma, which is even swifter than these?
True knowledge does not become small even when it is being given; like water in a well, it only becomes more abundant.

Those who have attained prosperity through righteousness are truly virtuous, whereas those who have attained it through unrighteousness are not; for in this world, both dharma and artha are great, and one should remember this for the sake of achieving one's purpose.
If those very same sufferings that a wretched person undergoes for the sake of food were instead undergone for the sake of Dharma, one would no longer be a vessel for affliction.
Of all forms of purity, purity regarding food is preeminent; he who is pure by means of the objects of food is truly pure, whereas one is not made pure by earth and water alone.
Truthfulness is purity, purity of mind is purity, restraint of the senses is purity, compassion toward all beings is purity, and bathing in water is the fifth kind of purity.
For one who possesses truth and purity, heaven is not difficult to attain; indeed, he whose speech is truthful excels even the horse sacrifice.
Indeed, even with a thousand applications of clay and a hundred washings with water, one of evil conduct whose consciousness is corrupted by inner disposition is not purified.
He whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained, and who possesses knowledge, austerity, and fame—he enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.
He does not rejoice in honors nor does he become angry at insults; being free from anger, he would not speak harshly—this is the characteristic of a virtuous person.
When a wise and pleasant man who is poor hears beneficial words at the proper time, no one is satisfied with him.
That which cannot be obtained by mortals through the power of mantras, through heroism, through wisdom, or through human effort—what cause for lamentation is there in that?
He was obtained by me without being asked, and he has departed again at my command; he has gone back to where he came from—what cause for lamentation is there in that?
On a single tree, various birds always gather at night; at dawn they depart for other directions—what cause for lamentation is there in that?
When all those traveling together as a single caravan are bound for the same destination, what cause for lamentation is there if one among them travels more quickly?
O Śaunaka, beings have an unmanifest beginning, a manifest middle, and an unmanifest end; what cause for lamentation is there in this?
One whose time has not yet come does not die, even if pierced by hundreds of arrows; but one whose time has arrived does not live on, even if merely touched by the tip of a blade of kusha grass.
One obtains only what is to be obtained; one goes only where it is to be gone; and one experiences only those sorrows and joys that are destined to be experienced.

Whatever a person attains through those [causes], what will mere lamentations accomplish? Just as flowers and fruits, even without being prompted, do not bypass their own appointed time, so too does previously performed karma.

Neither moral conduct, nor noble birth, nor learning, nor wisdom, nor virtues, nor purity of seed [bring success]; rather, the fortunes previously acquired through austerity bear fruit for one in due time, just as trees do.
There where death is the slayer, there where prosperity and riches reside—in each of those places he goes of his own accord, impelled by his own past actions.
Action performed in the past follows its doer, just as among thousands of cows, a calf finds its mother.
Thus, previously committed karma follows its doer; enjoy your own well-performed deeds, O fool, why do you lament?
Just as an action previously performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious, so indeed does the doer follow it in another birth.
A base person sees the faults of others even when they are as small as mustard seeds, yet he does not see his own, even when they are as large as bilva fruits, despite seeing them.
O twice-born one, for those possessed of passion, hatred, and the like, there is no happiness anywhere; indeed, upon reflection, I see that true happiness exists only where there is peace.
Where there is attachment, there is fear; attachment is a vessel for suffering. Sufferings have their root in attachment; when it is abandoned, there is great happiness.
The body alone is the abode of both suffering and happiness; both life and the body are born together with birth itself.
Everything dependent on another is suffering; everything dependent on oneself is happiness. One should know this, in brief, to be the defining characteristic of happiness and suffering.
After happiness comes suffering, and after suffering comes happiness; for human beings, happiness and suffering revolve like a wheel.
That which has passed away is already gone; if one remains far removed from it, one dwells in the present and is not afflicted by grief.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter in the *Bṛhannītisāra*, within the *Ācārakāṇḍa* of the first part of the *Pūrvakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said: No one is anyone’s friend, and no one is anyone’s enemy; friends and enemies alike arise solely due to specific causes.
By whom was this jewel-mine created: the two syllables "mitra" (friend), which are a protection from sorrow, a protection from fear, and a vessel for affection and trust?
By whomsoever the two syllables "Ha-ri" are uttered even once, the girdle has been fastened by him for the journey toward liberation.
Men do not place such trust in their mother, nor in their wives, nor in a uterine brother, nor even in their own son, as they do in a friend born of their own nature.
If one desires eternal happiness, one should completely avoid three faults: gambling, the investment of wealth, and looking at another's wife in his absence.
One should not sit in a secluded place even with one's mother, sister, or daughter; for the powerful collection of the senses drags away even a learned man.
Lust, which finds perverse pleasure, does not exist among those who are self-controlled; for just as there is a means of slaughter, so too does punishment follow.

It is possible to perceive the course of the wind at the end of an eon, or even that of the horse of the great ocean, but it is not possible to perceive the movement of one who is not attached to the four [elements].
There is no opportune moment, there is no privacy, and there is no man who does not desire them; therefore, O Śaunaka, it is only through these circumstances that the chastity of women arises.
Indeed, one woman may always serve another, even if she is pleasing to her, due to the lack of available men; yet such a woman remains truly devoted to her husband.
Whatever secrets a mother, afflicted by passion, may commit, they should not be scrutinized by her sons through the lens of moral transgressions.

Sleep dependent on others, following the whimsical deeds of others' hearts, constant derision and laughter—even when free from sorrow; the body staked as a wager, the throat torn by the hooves of lecherous men, and a livelihood sustained by intense longing: such is the life of a courtesan, highly esteemed in this world.
Fire, water, women, fools, serpents, and royal households—these six must always be approached with caution; they can take one's life instantly.

What is surprising if a brahmin, skilled in the Vedas and the sciences of grammar, should be a scholar? What is surprising if a king, skilled in the science of governance, should be righteous? What is surprising if a woman, endowed with beauty and youth, should be virtuous? But it is truly a marvel if a man, even though he be destitute, should never commit an evil deed.
One should not reveal one's own vulnerabilities to others, but should discern the vulnerabilities of others; one should conceal one's own limbs like a tortoise and observe the dispositions of others.
Dwelling in the depths of Pātāla, situated behind high walls, by whom indeed are women not obtained, even if they are hidden from view by the growth of their hair?
For one who knows the vital points, who is sharp, and who is like a thorn to his own kin, being equal in nature to them, does not cause such pain as an external enemy who has established enmity.
He is truly wise who wins over a fool with sweets, a disciplined man with what is beneficial, a woman with wealth, the gods with austerity, and all the worlds through excellent conciliation.

Those who desire a friend through deceit, righteousness through impurity, the cultivation of prosperity through the torment of others, knowledge through ease, or a woman through the use of a man, are indeed not wise.
If a foolish man cuts down a fruit-bearing tree for the sake of its fruit, his undertaking shall indeed be fruitless, and he will incur a great fault.
O Brahmin, I do not believe that a woman who drinks liquor can truly be chaste, even if she is an ascetic who possesses spiritual power and has exerted great effort from afar.
One should not trust the untrustworthy, nor should one even trust a friend; for a friend, when provoked to anger, might reveal all one's secrets.
Trusting in all beings and being virtuous toward all beings—one should conceal one's own nature within oneself; this indeed is the characteristic of a holy man.
Whatever action has been performed, it follows the doer; therefore, even while engaged in any activity whatsoever, one should maintain a resolute mind.
An intelligent man should avoid these six things: elderly women, fresh liquor, dried meat, the three roots, curd at night, and sleeping during the day.
For a poor man, socializing is poison; for an old man, a young woman is poison; poorly learned knowledge is poison; and food eaten during indigestion is poison.
Song is dear to the unskilled; a high seat is dear to the lowly; giving is dear to the poor; and a young woman is dear to the aged.

Excessive drinking of water, eating hard food, suppression of natural urges, exhaustion of the bodily constituents, sleeping during the day, and staying awake at night—by these six factors, diseases dwell within men.

Indeed, early morning sunlight, excessive sexual intercourse, smoke from cremation grounds, warming the palms over a fire, and looking at a menstruating woman while she is naked—all these surely diminish one's very long lifespan.
Dried meat, old women, the morning sun, fresh curd, sexual intercourse at dawn, and sleep immediately after eating—these six are instant destroyers of life.
Freshly clarified butter, grapes, a young woman, a meal of milk, warm water, and the shade of a tree—these six are instantly life-taking.
Water from a well, the shade of a banyan tree, and the breasts of women—these are warm during the cold season and cool during the hot season.
Three things immediately increase strength: an oil massage for the head, wholesome food, and sleep; three things immediately take away strength: traveling on foot, sexual intercourse, and fever.
One should never eat dried meat or drink milk together with one's wife or friends, nor with kings; such actions cause separation in an instant.
Fortune abandons even the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu) if he wears tattered clothes, bears stains on his teeth, eats excessively, speaks harsh words, and sleeps at sunrise or sunset.

Constant cutting of grass, scratching the earth, rubbing the feet, impurity of the teeth, wearing soiled garments, and roughness of the hair; sleeping during the two twilights, sleeping naked, excessive eating and laughing, and playing musical instruments upon one's own body or a seat—these would bring about the loss of even Keśava’s own fortune.
A well-washed head, well-massaged feet, attendance upon beautiful women, eating little, not sleeping naked, and avoiding sexual intercourse on forbidden days—these six bring back long-lost fortune.
Indeed, by wearing any flower—especially the *pāṇāḍara*—upon one's head, misfortune (*alakṣmī*) is dispelled.
The western shadow of a lamp, the shadow of a bed or a seat, and whatever auspiciousness resides at the bathing place of a washerman—therein Fortune herself abides.
One who desires long life should not indulge in the morning sun, the smoke from a funeral pyre, an old woman, fresh curd, nor the dust raised by a broom.
One should know that the dust raised by elephants, horses, chariots, grain, and cattle is auspicious, whereas that raised by donkeys, camels, goats, and sheep is inauspicious.
The dust of cows, the dust of grain, and the dust arising from the body of one's son—this dust is highly auspicious and the destroyer of great sins.
The dust of goats, the dust of donkeys, and the dust from brooms—this dust is a great evil and a cause of great sin.
The wind from a winnowing basket, water from the tips of fingernails, water used for wiping after bathing, water from hair, and dust from a broom destroy merit previously acquired.
One should not pass between two Brahmins, nor between a Brahmin and fire, nor between a husband and wife, nor between two masters, nor between a horse and a bull.
What wise person would place their trust in women, kings, fire, serpents, Vedic study, service to enemies, or the savoring of sensual enjoyments?
One should not trust the untrustworthy; one should not over-trust even the trustworthy. Danger arising from misplaced trust cuts down even the very roots.
If one remains trusting after making peace with an enemy, he is like one who falls asleep at the top of a tree and only awakens when he has fallen.
One should not be excessively mild, nor should one be excessively harsh in action; for the mild subdues the mild, and the fierce subdues the fierce.
One should not be excessively straight, nor likewise excessively soft; for there, the straight trees are cut down, while the crooked ones remain standing.
Fruit-bearing trees bend, and virtuous people bow; but dry trees and fools break rather than bend.
Just as unwanted sorrows come and go, so should a man deal with those who seek him out; he should brush them aside like a cat brushing away dust.
The noble always move forward and backward with abundant success, whereas the ignoble act in the opposite manner; therefore, conduct yourself as you wish.
A secret counsel is betrayed when it has six ears, and it is compromised when it has four; but even Brahmā himself cannot fathom a counsel that has only two ears.
What is the use of that cow which neither gives milk nor bears calves? What is the purpose of a son who is born but is neither learned nor righteous?
By even a single good son—wise, endowed with learning, and a lion among men—the family is illuminated, just as the sky is by the moon.
Even by a single fine tree, when it is in bloom and fragrant, the entire forest is made to smell sweet, just as a family is by a good son.
For one virtuous son is better than a hundred devoid of merit; the moon alone dispels the darkness, not even a thousand stars.
One should fondle [the son] for five years, and strike him for ten years; but when the sixteenth year has arrived, one should treat the son like a friend.
Being born, he takes away the wife; growing up, he takes away the wealth; dying, he takes away the life-breaths—there is no enemy equal to a son.
Some are tigers with the faces of deer, and some are deer with the faces of tigers; for if one does not truly know their actual nature, there will be distrust at every step.
There is one fault among the patient, and a second does not exist: that people consider one who is endowed with patience to be weak.
One should approve of this alone, for enjoyments are indeed subject to momentary destruction; and the thoughts of one who is discerning toward those he holds dear are truly undisturbed.
O Śaunaka, when the father has died, the eldest brother is equal to a father; for he becomes the father of them all and the protector of them all.
He conducts himself with impartiality toward all his younger brothers, as well as toward those who share the same enjoyments and livelihood, just as he does toward his own sons.
Indeed, the combination of many things of little substance is formidable; a rope woven from blades of grass can even bind an elephant.
For he who, having stolen the property of another, bestows it as a gift, that donor goes to hell; the fruit of that act belongs to the owner of the wealth.
Through the destruction of the property of the gods, through the seizure of a Brahmin’s own property, and through the transgression against Brahmins, families fall into a state of being non-noble.

For the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and likewise for one who has broken his vow, atonement has been prescribed by the virtuous; but for the ungrateful person, there is no atonement.
The ancestors and the gods do not eat the offerings of a mean man who is the husband of a low-caste woman, nor of one conquered by his wife, nor of one in whose house lives a paramour.
Know that the ungrateful, the ignoble, the long-simmering in anger, and the crooked—these four are Cāṇḍālas; the fifth is one who is so by birth.
A foolish enemy, though small, must not be neglected through contempt; even a tiny fire, if not extinguished, reduces the entire world to ashes.
It is my conviction that he alone is truly at peace who is peaceful while still in the prime of life; for when the bodily constituents are wasting away, in whom would tranquility not arise?
O best of Brahmins, since prosperity is common to all like public roads, one should not become filled with joy thinking, "This is mine."

The body is dependent on the mind and subject to the elements; when the mind perishes, the elements go to destruction. Therefore, the mind must always be protected; when the mind is healthy, the elements flourish.
Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Great Essence of Ethics," in the section on Conduct within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said: One should avoid from afar a bad wife, a bad friend, a bad king, a bad son, a bad daughter, and a bad country.

Dharma has gone forth into exile, asceticism has wavered, and truth has departed far away; the earth yields fruitless results, men are deceitful, and the Brahmins are consumed by greed. Mortals are enslaved by women, women are fickle, and base people have risen to high positions. Alas, what a misery is life indeed in the Kali Age! Blessed are those people who are already dead.
Blessed are those who do not witness the ruin of their country, the destruction of their family, the wives of others, or a son mired in evil vices.
There is no peace with a bad son; how can there be delight in a bad wife? There is no trust in a false friend; there is no security of life in a wicked kingdom.
Another's food, another's property, another's bed, another's wife, and dwelling in another's house—even from Indra, these will take away one's prosperity.
Sin is transmitted among men through conversation, the touching of bodies, social association, eating together, and sharing seats, beds, and vehicles.
Women are ruined by beauty; asceticism is destroyed by anger; cattle perish by wandering through doors; and the best of the twice-born is ruined by the food of a Śūdra.
From sharing a seat, from sharing a bed, and from mixing in a row at a meal, sin is transmitted from one person to another like water passing from one jar to another.
There are many faults in pampering and many virtues in striking; therefore, one should strike both a disciple and a son, but not pamper them.
For embodied beings, old age is the passage of time; for mountains, water is their decay; for women, it is the lack of enjoyment; and for garments, the sun's heat is their decay.
The base desire strife; the mediocre desire peace; the excellent desire honor, for honor is indeed the wealth of the great.
Pride is indeed the root of wealth; when pride exists, what is the use of riches? For one whose pride and arrogance have fallen away, what is the use of wealth or even of life?
The base desire wealth; those of middling quality desire both wealth and honor; the excellent desire honor alone, for honor is indeed the wealth of the great.
Even in the forest, lions do not bow to anyone, nor do they gaze at food when they are hungry; those born into noble families, even when deprived of wealth, do not undertake base occupations.
Neither consecration nor ritual refinement is performed for the lion in the forest; for one whose nature is eternally powerful, the sovereignty of the king of beasts comes of its own accord.
A negligent merchant, a deceitful person, a proud monk, a dissolute man, a poor man who lusts after desire, a beautiful woman who speaks unpleasantly—these do not undertake their respective tasks.
A generous man who is poor, a miser who is wealthy, an unruly son, service to the wicked, and death while helping others—these five are the misfortunes that befall a man.

Separation from a beloved, humiliation by one's own kin, a remainder of debt, service to a wicked person, and friends who turn their faces away due to poverty—these five burn intensely even without fire.

And among those thousands of anxieties, four are like the edge of a sword: being insulted by the low-born, a wife who is hungry, a wife who is disaffected, and the obstruction caused by one's own kin.
A submissive son, wealth-yielding knowledge, freedom from disease, association with the virtuous, and a beloved wife who remains under one's control—these five are the uprooters of suffering.
The deer, the elephant, the moth, the bee, and the fish—these five are destroyed by five [senses] alone. How can that one destroyer not be slain, who indulges in all five with all five?
One who is impatient, harsh, arrogant, poorly dressed, or who has come uninvited—these five types of Brahmins are not to be honored, even if they are equal to Bṛhaspati himself.
Lifespan, karma, wealth, knowledge, and even death—these five are distinguished for an embodied being at the very moment of birth.
In climbing mountains, in water, in a herd of cows, in subduing the wicked, and in rising from a fall— these five qualities are traditionally held to be most excellent.
The shadow of a cloud, affection for a rogue, intimacy with another's wife—these five things, as well as youth and wealth, are indeed unstable.
In this world, life is unstable; wealth and youth are unstable; sons, wives, and the like are unstable; but Dharma, fame, and glory are stable.
A hundred-year lifespan is exceedingly short; night takes away half of it, and even that remaining half is rendered fruitless by disease, grief, old age, and fatigue.

The lifespan of humans is limited to a hundred years; half of that passes in sleep, and more than half of what remains is spent in childhood. A portion is lost to the sorrow of separation from kin and death, and another is consumed in service to kings. What is the use of pride for those whose remaining life is as fickle as the heart of a water-wave?
In this world, death, consisting of day and night, moves about in the form of old age; it devours all beings just as a serpent swallows the wind.
Whether walking or standing, waking or sleeping, if one does not act for the benefit of all sentient beings, one's behavior is like that of a beast.

What difference is there between a beast and that man-beast whose intellect is devoid of discernment regarding what is beneficial and harmful, who has been subjected to many speculations during the time of his studies, yet whose mind is satisfied merely with filling his belly?
He whose fame is not celebrated for heroism, austerity, generosity, learning, or the acquisition of wealth, is merely his mother’s excrement.

That life which is lived even for a moment by men renowned for their wisdom, prowess, and fame, and whose honor remains unbroken—that alone, the knowers declare, is called true living; for even a crow lives long and eats the offerings of others.

What is the use of life devoid of wealth and honor? What is the use of a friend who is filled with fear and suspicion? Practice the vow of a lion and go; do not despair! Even a crow lives for a long time and eats the offerings.

He who here in this world shows no compassion toward himself, his teacher, his circle of servants, the destitute, or the affairs of his friends—what is the fruit of his life in the world of men? Even a crow lives long and consumes offerings.
He whose days come and go empty of the three aims of life does not truly live, even though he breathes like a blacksmith's bellows.
The fruitfulness of one's life lies in acting with self-reliance, not in being dependent on others; those whose actions are dependent on others are dead even while they live.
Base men are indeed easily satisfied; a mouse’s paws are easily filled. Yet the base man, being dissatisfied, is content with even a very little.
The shadow of a cloud, fire from grass, service to the low-born, water on the road, a courtesan’s passion, and affection for a villain—these six are like bubbles.
The world does not find happiness through speech that is devoid of substance; for life has pride as its root—when pride withers, whence can there be happiness?
The king is the strength of the weak; weeping is the strength of a child; silence is indeed the strength of a fool; and falsehood is the strength of a thief.
For in whatever measure a person masters the scripture, in that same measure his intelligence shall increase and his discernment shall shine forth.
For in whatever way a person directs his mind toward what is wholesome, in that very way he becomes universally embraced as one beloved by the world.
A person is ruined by these three: greed, negligence, and misplaced trust; therefore, one should not be greedy, nor negligent, nor should one place undue trust.
One should fear as long as the danger has not yet arrived; but once the intense danger has arisen, one should indeed remain fearless.
A remainder of debt, a remainder of fire, and likewise a remainder of disease increase again and again; therefore, one should not leave any remainder.
One should return a favor for a favor and inflict injury for an injury; I see no fault in this, for one should treat the wicked with wickedness.
One should avoid such a friend who destroys one's business behind one's back while speaking kindly to one's face; he is likewise a deceptive enemy.
Indeed, even a virtuous person is ruined by association with the wicked; even clear water is made turbid by mud.
He eats as does a virtuous twice-born; he partakes of the determination of what remains equally. Therefore, with every effort, the twice-born should be honored with diligence.

That is truly enjoyed which is the remnant of what has been eaten by the twice-born; he is wise who does not commit sin; that is true friendship which is performed in one's absence; and that is true dharma which is practiced without hypocrisy.
That is no assembly where there are no elders; they are no elders who do not speak of dharma. That is no dharma for us where truth is absent; that is no truth which is pierced by deceit.
Among men, the Brahmin is the foremost; among luminous bodies, the sun is the foremost; among all limbs, the head is the foremost; and among vows, truth is supreme.

That is auspicious where the mind is serene; that is true life which is not service to another; that is truly earned which is enjoyed by one's own kin; and that is a roar which is made against enemies in battle.
That woman does not give rise to intoxication; he is happy, being free from craving. He is a true friend in whom there is trust; he is a man who has conquered his senses.
In this world, that alone is praiseworthy where respect and affection have been abandoned and friendship has vanished, and one’s own self is made the object of praise.
One should not search for the source of rivers, of *agnihotra* sacrifices, of the *Bhārata*, or of a water-jar; for a fault is never removed by tracing it back to its source.
Rivers end at the salt ocean; sexual union ends with the exhaustion of women's desire; gossip ends with slander; and wealth ends with the threefold suffering.
The glory of sovereignty ends with a Brahmin’s curse; spiritual luster ends with sin; residence in a cowherd settlement ends with the sipping of water; and a family ends with a woman, O Lord.
All dwellings end in decay; all elevations end in a fall; all unions end in separation; for life indeed ends in death.
If he wishes for [the guest] to return, he should not follow him too far; he should turn back at the edge of the water or from a tree of glossy appearance.
One should not dwell where there is no leader, nor where there are too many leaders; one should not dwell where a woman is the leader, but one may dwell where a fool is the leader.
The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the son protects her in old age; a woman does not deserve independence.
One should abandon a barren wife in the eighth year, one whose children have died in the ninth, one who gives birth only to daughters in the eleventh, and one who speaks unpleasantly immediately.
Because men do not desire them, out of fear of their own attendants, and because they have abandoned the bounds of propriety regarding wealth, these three remain faithful to their husbands.
A wise person should avoid from afar a weary horse, an elephant in rut, cows that have recently calved, and frogs in waterless places.

For those distressed by worldly affairs, there is neither friend nor kinsman; for those distressed by desire, there is neither fear nor shame; for those distressed by anxiety, there is neither happiness nor sleep; and for those distressed by hunger, there is neither strength nor vigor.
Whence can there be sleep for the poor man, for the lowliest servant of another, for one who is addicted to another's wife, and for one who steals another's property?
The man who is free from debt and freed from disease sleeps happily; likewise, he who eats with plenty of room and is not attached to his wife sleeps happily.
A lotus rises above the water; a servant becomes arrogant when his master is powerful.
For a lotus remaining in its place, Varuṇa and Bhāskara are friends; yet for that very same lotus when displaced from its place, they cause its soaking and its withering.
Those who are friends to one established in his position become his enemies; the sun feels affection for the lotus in the water, yet it dries up and draws out the land.
Those who remain in their proper place are honored, and those who remain in their station are honored; but when they have fallen from their place, hair, teeth, nails, and men are no longer honored.
Conduct reveals one's family; speech reveals one's country; eagerness reveals one's affection; and the body reveals one's diet.
Rain upon the ocean is in vain; food for one who is already satiated is in vain; a gift given to the wealthy is in vain; and a good deed performed by a base person is likewise in vain.
Even one who stands afar is near if he dwells in another's heart; but even one standing nearby is far away if he has departed from the heart.
A distorted face, a feeble voice, perspiration on the body, and great fear—those very signs that appear at the time of death are present in a beggar.
Better is the birth of one who is hunchbacked, a killer of insects, or expelled by the wind, and who dwells upon a mountain peak, than that of one who begs.
For since Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, assumed the form of a dwarf after being entreated [by Bali], who else could be more exalted than he, such that his purpose would not suffer a loss of dignity?

The mother who does not teach her children is an enemy, and the father who does not is a foe; those boys who have not been educated do not shine in the midst of an assembly, just as cranes do not shine among swans.

Knowledge is indeed a beauty superior to that of a handsome form; knowledge is wealth most carefully guarded; knowledge is the achiever of good deeds and the maker of one beloved by the people; knowledge is the teacher of teachers. Knowledge is the destroyer of the suffering of kinsmen; knowledge is the supreme deity; knowledge is honored among kings; for a man devoid of knowledge is but a beast.
Whatever wealth and property is seen within the interior of the house must be taken away entirely; yet the vidyā is not carried off by others.
In former times, Viṣṇu recounted the *Śaunakīya*, the *Nītisāra*, and all the *Vratas*; there Śaṅkara heard them, from Śaṅkara Vyāsa heard them, and from Vyāsa they were heard by us.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Essence of Ethics Spoken by Śaunaka and Other Matters," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious *Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*.

Brahmā said: "O Vyāsa, I shall describe the vows by which Hari becomes the bestower of all things. When Hari is worshipped on every month, lunar mansion (nakṣatra), lunar day (tithi), or day of the week,"
By means of eating once a day, eating only at night, fasting, offering fruit, and so forth, one bestows wealth, grain, and the like, as well as sons, sovereignty, victory, and other such blessings.

Vaiśvānara, when worshipped on the first lunar day (pratipad), bestows wealth; Kubera, when worshipped on the first lunar day, grants prosperity; and likewise, Brahmā, when worshipped on the first lunar day, grants nourishment, as does Śrī in the Aśvinī nakṣatra.
On the second day, Yama, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, and the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada) are present here; on the third day, the three deities—Gaurī, Vighneśa, and Śaṅkara—are present.
On the fourth day, Hari is worshipped as the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha); on the fifth, Hari; on the sixth, Kārtikeya and Ravi; and on the seventh, Bhāskara, the bestower of wealth.

On the eighth and ninth days of the Durgā festival, one should worship the Mothers and the deities who bestow wealth upon the directions; on the tenth day, Yama; and on the eleventh day, the Moon and the sages.
On the twelfth day, Hari; on the thirteenth, Kāma; on the fourteenth and fifteenth, Maheśvara and Brahmā, as well as the Pitṛs, bestow wealth.
On the new moon day, the days of the week beginning with Sunday (the Sun) are to be worshipped; likewise, the lunar mansions and the astrological conjunctions, when honored, bestow all things.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of Vows for Specific Lunar Days and Others," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Brahmā said: In the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, on the thirteenth day known as Vyāsān-aṅga-trayodaśī, one should use a tooth-stick made of *mallikā* wood and worship Śiva with *dhuttūra* flowers.

One should offer the *naivedya* to Anaṅga and consume honey during the Pauṣa month; one should worship Yogeśvara with *bilva* leaves and flowers from the *kadamba* tree, using a tooth-stick made of sandalwood or the like, and offering *kṛsara* (rice and sesame) and other foods as the *naivedya*.
O Sage, having worshipped Naṭeśvara in the month of Māgha with kunda flowers and a necklace of pearls, one should use a tooth-stick from the Plakṣa tree and offer pūrikā cakes as the food offering.
In the month of Phālguna, one should worship Vīreśvara with Marūbaka flowers; sugar, leafy vegetables, and maṇḍa should be offered, and a tooth-stick made from mango wood should be used.
In the month of Caitra, one should sacrifice to Svarūpa; at night, one should consume camphor; and as an offering for cleaning the teeth, one should give a *śaṣkulī* made from *āṭa*.
In Vaiśākha, the worship of Śambhu is performed with *damanaka* and *aśoka* flowers; for the one of Great Form, the food offering consists of rice cooked with jaggery (*guḍabhakta*) and *puṭṭavara*.
One should consume a tooth-stick and likewise offer nutmeg; one should worship Pradyumna in the month of Jyeṣṭha with campaka flowers and chew a tooth-stick made of bilva wood.
Likewise, for one who has committed the sixth offense against the teaching of Umāpati, one should worship with agallochum, a tooth-stick, and apāmārga grass.

In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should offer karavīra flowers to Śambhu, the wielder of the trident; subsisting on fragrances, one performs the purification of the karavīra-born [flower] with ghee and other offerings.
One should worship Sadyojāta in Bhādrapada with bakula flowers and cakes; Gandharva in Āśvina, and the Lord of the Gods (Indra) with madanaka flowers.
In the month of Kārttika, one should worship Rudra with campaka flowers, golden vārī fish, and by offering jīmūta modakas, while using a tooth-stick made of khadira wood.
One who uses the Badarī tree as a tooth-stick and eats ten mouthfuls of Madana fruit, and provides milk and vegetables, should worship Śiva with lotuses at the end of the year.

One should offer ten thousand oblations of sesame, rice, and other grains, along with perfumes and other substances, into the fire situated upon a golden mandala, while reciting the mantras of Rati, Muktā, and Anaṅga.
Having performed a vigil with songs and musical instruments and having worshipped the Lord, one should present to a twice-born man a bed, a vessel, an umbrella, a garment, and a pair of sandals.

A man who devoutly feeds a cow and a twice-born person shall have fulfilled his purpose. This entire concluding rite (*udyāpana*) for all vows should be understood as being like this; and the fruit shall consist of prosperity, sons, health, good fortune, and heaven.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Vow of Anaṅga-Trayodaśī," in the Ācāra-kāṇḍa of the first part of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Brahmā said: I shall now describe the vow of Akhaṇḍa-Dvādaśī, which bestows the peace of liberation (kaivalya). In the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should fast and subsist on products of the cow (gavya).

On the twelfth lunar day, one should worship Viṣṇu and, for four months, give a vessel filled with five kinds of grain to a Brahmin, reciting this: [Recite this: "May the Lord of the World accept this gift of a vessel containing five grains, offered by me for the sake of the welfare of my parents and myself. Then, having honored the Brahmin with garments, ornaments, and other gifts, he should say: "O Brahmin, may you be pleased; may you grant me prosperity and long life. Having thus performed the rite of giving, he should feed the Brahmins with various foods and sweets, and himself eat what remains. By doing so, he attains the fruit of a thousand cows and is honored in the world of Viṣṇu. This is known as the *pañcavrīhi-dāna*, which destroys all sins and grants liberation from the cycle of rebirth. One who performs it on the twelfth day of the month of Vaiśākha attains the highest state. Thus ends the description of the *pañcavrīhi-dāna*.
O Viṣṇu, whatever vow has been performed by me throughout seven births, may it remain unbroken for me here through your grace, O Blessed One.
O Supreme Person, just as you alone are the entire world in its undivided state, so indeed do all these undivided portions exist for me, encompassed by you.

One who performs the vow by offering vessels of barley meal mixed with ghee at the beginning of Caitra and at the beginning of Śrāvaṇa, having fulfilled the vow, shall become a partaker of women, sons, and heaven.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Akhaṇḍa-dvādaśī Vow," in the Ācāra-kāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrva-khaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Brahmā said: I shall describe the Agastya-arghya vow, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. When the Sun has not yet entered the sign of Virgo (Kanyā), [the rite should be performed] three days before that occurs.
O Sage, having worshipped the image made of kāśa flowers in the water-jar, one should indeed offer the *arghya* to Agastya at nightfall while keeping a vigil.

Having worshipped with curd, unbroken grains (akṣata), and other offerings, and having fasted with fruits and flowers, [one should offer] that which is endowed with five colors and combined with gold and silver.

One should cause the *arghya* offering to be presented with a vessel filled with seven kinds of grain, smeared with curd and sandalwood paste, while reciting the mantra beginning with "Agastyaḥ khanamāna."
Resembling a khāsa flower, born from fire and wind, son of Mitra and Varuṇa, O pot-born one, homage be to you!

A Śūdra, a woman, or others should abandon grain, fruit, and liquids by this very [rite]; one should give a water-pot along with gold and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a twice-born man; and having performed it for a year, one should feed seven twice-born men, thereby becoming a partaker of all things.

Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Vow of the Arghya-offering to Agastya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. Brahmā said: I shall now describe the Rambhā-tṛtīyā, which bestows good fortune, prosperity, sons, and other blessings. One should fast on the third lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.

Then, with bilva leaves and holding kuśa-grass water in his hand, he should worship Gaurī; in the month of Pauṣa, he should worship the Daughter of the Mountain at the Kadamba tree and other such sites with marubaka flowers.

One who gives camphor and so forth, one who gives *kṛsara*, one who provides jasmine tooth-sticks, one who offers the *Subhadrā* [flower] in the month of Māgha with white water-lilies (*kalhāra*), and one who eats ghee while giving *maṇḍaka* cakes;

In the month of Phālguna, one should worship Gomatī with a tooth-stick made of *gītī* wood; having fashioned a tooth-stick from *kunda* flowers, the giver of *śaṣkulī* cakes should offer them while reciting the *jīvā* mantra.
In the month of Caitra, one should worship Viśālākṣī with *damanaka* flowers, offer *kṛsara*, consume curd, use *tagara* as a tooth-stick, and worship Śrīmukhī.

In Vaiśākha, one who gives a banyan tree should worship with Karṇikāra and Aśoka flowers; in Jyeṣṭha, the giver of a field should worship Nārāyaṇī with hundred-petaled lotuses; and in Āṣāḍha, the possessor of cloves should indeed worship Mādhavī.
One who eats sesame seeds with bilva leaves and offers milk-rice and *vaṭaka* cakes, and uses an udumbara tooth-stick and *tagara* [incense], attains prosperity in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
In the month of Māllika (Mārgaśīrṣa), one should worship with a tooth-stick of milk-tree wood; in Bhādrapada, one should worship with lotuses, offering horns and giving food and clothing.
In the month of Āśvayuja, one should cause the princess to consume jīraka with japā flowers at night; in Kārtika, one should worship her with offerings of kṛsara.

One who subsists on the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) should worship the goddess Padmaja with jasmine flowers; at the end of the year, one should honor Brahmins together with their wives, offering them rice cooked with ghee.

Having worshipped Umāmaheśvara, one should offer jaggery and other such items, along with garments, umbrellas, gold, and so forth; having kept a vigil at night with songs and instrumental music, one who gives cows and other gifts in the morning shall attain all perfections.
Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Rambhā-Tṛtīyā Vow," in the Ācāra-kāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrva-khaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
