Brahmā said: He spoke of the Cāturmāsya vows; one should perform them on the Ekādaśī day, or on the full moon of the month of Āṣāḍha, after worshipping Hari with all one's being.
"O Lord Keśava, since you are pleased with me, may this vow which I have undertaken before you reach fulfillment without any obstacle."
O Lord Janārdana, if I should die while this vow is still unfulfilled after having undertaken it, may it become complete for me through your grace.
Having thus worshipped, one who desires to perform the vow of Hari should undertake the observance, worship, recitation, and so forth; by doing so, all evil is destroyed.

Having bathed and performed worship, one should undertake vows, ritual worship, recitation, and so forth; he who, having bathed, worships Viṣṇu for four months while eating but one meal a day, goes to the world of Viṣṇu, which is free from all impurity.

One who has abandoned liquor, meat, and wine, who knows the Vedas, and who worships Hari, attains the world of Viṣṇu free from oil; such a person, having performed a quarter of a *kṛcchra* penance, becomes a partaker of Viṣṇu.
By fasting for one night, one becomes a celestial deity dwelling in a vimāna; by eating only every sixth mealtime and fasting for three nights, a man shall go to Śvetadvīpa.
By performing the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, one attains the abode of Hari and liberation unasked; by the Prājāpatya, the world of Viṣṇu; and by the Parāka vow, one reaches Hari.

One who subsists on barley meal and barley gruel obtained as alms, one who eats milk, curd, and ghee, one whose food consists of cow’s urine and barley gruel, one who consumes the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one who eats vegetables, roots, fruits, and the like, and one who avoids all savory juices—such a devotee belongs to Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Cāturmāsya Vow," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Brahmā said: I shall describe to you the vow known as Māsopavāsa (the month-long fast), which is the most excellent of all. A forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), an ascetic (*yati*), or a woman may perform this month-long fast.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, one should undertake this vow for a period of thirty days.
"O Viṣṇu, from this day forward, until your rising, I shall worship you without fail for exactly thirty days."
O Viṣṇu, if I should die during the interval between the twelfth days of the bright fortnights of the months of Kārttika and Āśvina, may there be no violation of my vow for me.

One who observes the vow should worship Hari while bathing at the three daily sessions and offering perfumes and other articles; however, one should avoid anointing the limbs with oil or applying perfumes within the temple of the deity.
Then, having performed worship on the twelfth day, one should provide a meal for the twice-born; thereafter, the practitioner of the month-long fast for Hari should break his fast.

One observing the vow who faints midway should consume milk and other such substances; by means of milk and the like, the vow is not destroyed, and one shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Vow of Monthly Fasting," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Brahmā said: I shall now describe the vows for the month of Kārtika. Having bathed, one should worship Viṣṇu by eating only once a day, or eating only at night, or by subsisting on food obtained unasked, throughout the month.
Whether by means of milk, vegetables, fruits, and the like, or again by fasting, one who is completely liberated from all sins and has attained his desires shall go to Hari.

The vow of Hari is always excellent; even better than that is the vow during the southern transit of the sun (dakṣiṇāyana); better than that is the Cāturmāsya; and better than that is the Bhīṣmapañcaka in the month of Kārttika.

Then, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, one should undertake the excellent vow; having bathed, one should worship Hari three times a day with barley and other offerings for the sake of the ancestors and others.

Remaining silent, one should sacrifice with clarified butter and other offerings, or with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and water; then, having bathed [the deity], one should anoint it with camphor and similar substances.
For five days, the twice-born should burn incense of guggulu resin smeared with clarified butter; he should offer milk-rice as the food offering and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Oṃ, salutation to Vāsudeva; one should offer clarified butter, rice, sesame seeds, and so forth, with the eight-syllable mantra ending in svāhā.
On the first day, one should worship the feet of Hari with lotuses; on the second, the knees with bilva leaves; and on the following day, the navel with fragrant substances.
On the fifth day, one should worship the head with *bilva* and *javā* flowers; one should sleep on the ground and consume cow dung in due order, using *mālatī* flowers.

Cow’s urine, curd, and milk—these constitute the *pañcagavya* on the fifth day; one should observe the night-vow (*nakta*) on the fifteenth day, and by becoming a practitioner of this vow, one shall partake in both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should regularly observe the Ekādaśī vow during both fortnights; it destroys the flood of sins and the hellish state, bestows everything, and grants the world of Viṣṇu.
When the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), the twelfth day (Dvādaśī), and the thirteenth day (Trayodaśī) meet at the end of the night, Hari is eternally present wherever that Ekādaśī occurs.

Where the tenth and eleventh lunar days coincide, even if one is situated among asuras and other such beings, one should perform the breaking of the fast on the twelfth day; one may do so even during a period of birth-impurity or death-impurity.

O Sage, one should observe the fast on the fourteenth day mixed with the first day of the lunar fortnight; likewise, one should observe the full moon and the new moon days when they are mixed with the first day.

One should observe the second [lunar day] mixed with the third, and likewise the third; one should always observe the fourth when it is joined with the fifth, and the fourth conjoined with the next; the fifth unassociated with the sixth, and the sixth joined with the seventh.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Bhīṣmapañcaka and Other Vows," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Brahmā said: I shall now describe the Śivarātri vow, which grants all desires, along with the narrative of how Gaurī questioned the Lord of Beings (Śiva) regarding this supreme vow.

Īśvara said: On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight between the months of Māgha and Phālguna, Rudra, when worshipped through a night vigil on that day, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Hara is to be worshipped on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) by those devoted to desire, while Keśava is to be worshipped on the twelfth (dvādaśī). When worshipped by those who have observed the fast, he likewise delivers them from hell.
In Arbuda, there was a wicked Niṣāda king named Sundarasena; accompanied by hunters, he went to the forest to kill deer.
Having failed to obtain deer and other prey, afflicted by hunger and thirst on the mountain, he remained awake at night, stationed within a bower on the banks of a lake.
There stood a linga protecting itself and casting its body aside; consequently, leaves fell upon the head of the linga itself, which remained unaware.
He threw water upon the linga to settle the dust, but by a lapse of attention, a single arrow slipped from his sprout-like hand.
Having gone to the ground on his knees, he touched the linga and took hold of it; thus there occurred bathing, touching, worship, and a vigil.
Having returned home in the morning and eaten the food provided by his wife, he died at the appointed time and was led away by the messengers of Yama, bound with nooses.
Then, having been defeated in battle by my hosts, he was set free; together with the dog, that stainless one became a member of my retinue and stayed by my side.

Thus, merit arises from ignorance, while from knowledge comes imperishable merit; having worshipped Śiva on the thirteenth lunar day, the practitioner of the vow should observe the prescribed restraint.
"O Lord, tomorrow morning on the fourteenth day, I shall keep vigil during the night; I will perform worship, charity, austerity, and fire-offerings according to my own ability."
Having remained without food on the fourteenth day, O Śambhu, I shall eat on the following day for the sake of enjoyment and liberation; O Lord of Īśvara, be my refuge.

Having bathed [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the nectars (amṛta), and having taken refuge in the Guru at that time, one should worship Hara with perfumes and other offerings, reciting: "Oṃ, salutations, salutations to Śiva."

One should offer oblations of sesame, rice, and grain, as well as a sacrificial porridge mixed with ghee; having performed the fire sacrifice and offered the final oblation, one should listen to sacred stories accompanied by song.
At midnight, at the third watch, and again at the fourth, having likewise recited the root mantra, one should ask for forgiveness at dawn.
O God, by your grace, this vow has been performed by me without obstacle. Forgive me, O Lord of the worlds, O Hara, Sovereign of the three realms!
Whatever merit I have performed today, which has been offered to Rudra—by your grace, O God, I have today completed my vow.
"O illustrious one, be gracious to me and please go toward my home; by the mere sight of you, I am purified, of this there is no doubt."
One should feed those established in meditative concentration and give gifts such as clothing and umbrellas; O God of gods, Lord of beings, you who bestow grace upon the worlds!
"May the Lord be pleased with that which has been given by me with faith"; having thus asked for forgiveness, the observer of the vow should perform the twelve-year penance.
Having obtained fame, prosperity, sons, a kingdom, and other blessings, one shall go to the city of Śiva; one should perform the vigil here during all twelve months as well.
One who observes the vow and gives lamps after feeding twelve people shall attain heaven.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Śivarātri Vow," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 125—the Grandfather (Brahmā) said: "King Māndhātā was a universal emperor (cakravartin) because he fasted on the Ekādaśī; one should not eat on the Ekādaśī of either fortnight."
The eleventh day mixed with the tenth was observed as a fast by Gāndhārī; her hundred sons were lost. Therefore, one should avoid that [mixed day].

Where the eleventh day is conjoined with the twelfth, there Hari is present; where the eleventh day is conjoined with the tenth, there the asura is present. When doubt arises due to the contradiction of many scriptural statements, [the following applies].

In that case, the twelfth day (dvādaśī) should be observed; the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the thirteenth day (trayodaśī). Even if there is but a single moment (kalā) of the eleventh day (ekādaśī), it should be fasted upon, as should the twelfth day.
The eleventh, the twelfth, and especially the thirteenth—when these three are conjoined, that lunar day is to be accepted; it is auspicious and removes all sins.

O twice-born one, having fasted on the eleventh day, or indeed on the twelfth, one should observe the conjunction of the three days; never, however, should one observe it when it is joined with the tenth day.
Keeping a vigil at night, listening to the Purāṇas, and worshipping Gadādhara while fasting on two Ekādaśīs, King Rukmāṅgada attained liberation; others as well [attain it] through the Ekādaśī vow.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Ekādaśī," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: I shall now describe that supreme mode of worship which brings about both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and by means of which the world indeed attained the highest goal.
Having arranged the general mandala, one should place Dhātṛ at the gateway, as well as Vidhātṛ, Gaṅgā, and the great river Yamunā.
One should worship Dvāraśrī and Daṇḍa, as well as Pracaṇḍa and Vāstupuruṣa; and in the center, one should worship Ādhāraśakti, Kūrma, and Ananta.
The earth, the Dharma, as well as knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty; and likewise the four beginning with Adharma, the bulbous root, the stalk, and the lotus.

The pericarp is the quality of sattva, the filaments are the quality of rajas, and the quality of tamas consists of the spheres of the Sun and the other deities, as well as the powers beginning with Vimalā.
Having worshipped Durgā, Gaṇa, Sarasvatī, and Kṣetrapāla in the corners, and having honored the seat and the form while recollecting Vāsudeva and Bala.
Then one should worship the great-souled Aniruddha, Nārāyaṇa, as well as his limbs such as the heart and so forth, and his weapons such as the conch and so forth.
The Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 127.

Brahmā said: In ancient times, on the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha, conjoined with the Sun asterism (Pūrvā-phalgunī), a certain Ekādaśī was observed as a fast by Bhīma.
Having performed this wondrous vow, he became free from his debt to the ancestors; it is renowned as Bhīmadvādaśī, which increases the merit of living beings.
Even without the [proper] lunar mansion, this destroys sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; it destroys great evil just as a wicked king destroys his realm.
Just as a bad son ruins a family, as a bad wife ruins her husband, as unrighteousness ruins righteousness, and as a bad minister ruins a king; so too does [a bad companion] ruin a man.
Just as knowledge is [subverted] by ignorance, as purity by impurity, as faith by lack of faith, and truth by falsehoods;
Just as heat may destroy snow, so the accumulation of wealth may cause harm; just as giving is ruined by boasting, and austerity is ruined by pride.
Just as through lack of training, as a son [is lost] by those who have gone afar, as peace is lost through anger, and as wealth is lost through not guarding it.
Just as knowledge leads to liberation when free from desire, and just as a fruit is obtained through effort, so too has this auspicious Dvādaśī been proclaimed for the destruction of sins.
The three Puṣkaras—namely, the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and sexual intercourse with the teacher’s wife—when committed simultaneously, destroy [all other sins].
Nor indeed are the sacred field of Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, Prabhāsa, the Kālindī, Yamunā, Gaṅgā, or even the Sarasvatī.
Indeed, all sacred fords are equal to the Ekādaśī; there is no gift, no recitation, no fire-offering, nor any other meritorious deed anywhere that can compare to it.
On one side is the gift of the entire earth, and on the other is the day of Hari; yet even greater than that is this single, most excellent Ekādaśī, which brings great merit.
Having fashioned an image of the Lord Varāha out of gold, one should place it upon a new vessel or indeed in a copper bowl set atop a water-pot.
O Brahmins, having performed worship with great effort using gold, lamps, and other offerings, [one should do so] toward that which contains all seeds and is wrapped in white cloth.
Salutation to the Boar for the feet; salutation to the one in the form of a boar for the hips; to the one with a deep resonance for the navel; to the bearer of the Śrīvatsa for the chest.
One should worship the arm with "To the Thousand-headed One," the neck with "To the Lord of All," the mouth with "To the Soul of All," and the forehead with "To the Source."
The hairs [of the head] are to be worshipped as the hundred rays of the Lord who wields the discus; having worshipped them according to the ritual, one should keep a vigil during the night.
Having heard this Purāṇa which sets forth the majesty of the God, and having given it in the morning to a virtuous Brahmin who is a petitioner, [one attains the fruit].
Having presented the retinue along with a golden boar as an offering, the practitioner of the vow, not being overly satiated, should afterwards perform the breaking of the fast.

Having done this, a man should know that he shall not become a suckling again; by fasting on the meritorious Ekādaśī, he is indeed released from the three debts, and having performed all vows and other rites, he attains his heart's desire.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of Ekādaśī," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Brahmā said: "O Vyāsa, I shall describe the vows by which Hari, the giver of all, is pleased. A vow (*vrata*) is indeed a rule ordained by the scriptures, and it is considered a form of austerity (*tapas*)."
The specific observances (niyamas) of this vow are self-restraint and the like; one should bathe daily at the three sessions of the day, sleep on the ground, and keep the senses subdued.
One should avoid conversing with women, Śūdras, and outcasts; furthermore, one should offer the five purificatory oblations according to one's ability.
A virtuous man should perform all these *kṛcchra* penances; however, for the sake of preserving his hair, he should observe double the vow.
One observing a fast should avoid bell-metal, black gram, lentils, chickpeas, millet, leafy vegetables, honey, and food belonging to others.
Flowers, ornaments, garments, incense, perfumes, and ointments—these may be spoiled by fasting; likewise, the cleansing of teeth and the application of collyrium [are spoiled].
Having used a tooth-stick and the five products of the cow, one should observe the morning vow; [one becomes pure] by drinking water repeatedly and by chewing betel.
The fast is defiled by sleeping during the day and by sexual intercourse; [the virtues are] forbearance, truthfulness, compassion, charity, purity, and restraint of the senses.
Worship of the gods, offering oblations into the fire, contentment, and non-stealing—this common duty is recorded as being tenfold in all religious observances.

Eating at night when the stars are visible is called *nakta*; eating at night when they are not visible is called *anakta*. One should consume one *pala* of cow’s urine and half a thumb’s measure of cow dung.
One should provide seven palas of milk and three palas of curd; one pala of ghee should be given, along with one pala of kuśa-water.
One should perform the Brahmakūrca vow with the Gāyatrī, the mantra beginning with "gandha," the verse "āpyāyasva," the Dadhigraha formula, and the mantra "tejo 'si" from the Devatāsūkta.
The establishment of the sacred fires, consecrations, sacrifices, gifts, and vows; the Vedic observances, the rite of releasing a bull, the tonsure ceremony, and the girdle initiation.

One should avoid auspicious rites and consecrations during the intercalary month (malamāsa). The lunar month is that which extends from new moon to new moon, while the solar month consists of thirty days.

The solar month is measured by the sun's transit [of a zodiac sign], whereas the sidereal month consists of twenty-seven [lunar days]. The solar month is for marriage and other such rites, while the civil (sāvana) month is established for sacrifices and similar ceremonies.

The pairs [of tithis] are the second and third, the fourth and fifth, the sixth and seventh, the eighth and ninth, the tenth and eleventh, the twelfth joined with the thirteenth, the fourteenth, and the full moon.
Even when the new moon occurs on two lunar days, the month yields great fruit; however, this same [conjunction] occurring in reverse order is most terrible and destroys previously performed merit.

The menstrual flow of women does not destroy a vow that has already been commenced by the practice of austerity; however, other physical acts such as giving gifts and so forth must be performed by them personally.
If a breach of the vow should occur through anger, negligence, or greed, one shall not eat for three days and the shaving of the head must take place.
If the body lacks the capacity [to perform the vow], one should have the son or others perform the vow; if a Brahmin observing the vow faints, one should cause him to drink water and other liquids.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Definitions of Vows," in the section on Conduct (*ācārakāṇḍa*), within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Brahmā said: O Vyāsa, listen now as I describe the vows beginning with the first lunar day (*pratipad*). This is known as the *Śikhivrata*; by performing it, one attains the station of Vāsava (Indra).

Having observed the practice of eating only one meal a day, he should, upon its completion, give a tawny cow as a gift; and from the beginning of Caitra, he should perform the worship of Brahmā according to the rules, with offerings of perfumes, flowers, gifts, and delightful garlands and other articles.

One should worship the God with offerings of sesame seeds and shall obtain all desires; furthermore, by offering a garland of flowers on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika, one obtains these for an entire year.

A man who gives flowers and other offerings shall possess beauty of form; by worshipping Śrīdhara with splendor on the third day of the dark fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa, he shall likewise partake in prosperity.
One should perform the sacrifice on a bed that is not empty and give fruit to a twice-born man; having given the bed, one should pray: "Obeisance to Śrīdhara and to Śrī."
On the third lunar day, one should worship Umā, Śiva, and Agni; sacrificial food (haviṣya) should be offered as the oblation, and likewise, the *damanaka* flower.
One obtains the fruit starting from the month of Caitra; this has been declared to me by Umā: he who avoids salt on the third lunar day beginning with Phālguna [attains that fruit].
Upon completion, one should give a bed and a house furnished with household utensils, having honored a Brahmin couple, saying, "May Bhavānī be pleased."
One shall dwell eternally in the world of Gaurī, which bestows supreme good fortune. Gaurī, Kālī, Umā, Bhadrā, Durgā, Kānti, and Sarasvatī—[these are her names].
Maṅgalā, Vaiṣṇavī, Lakṣmī, Śivā, and Nārāyaṇī are the [names] in sequence; beginning from the third lunar day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one shall obtain non-separation [from her].
On the fourth lunar day at the beginning of the bright fortnight of Māgha, one who observes the vow while fasting should give sesame seeds to a Brahmin and himself consume water mixed with sesame.
The completion [of the practice] occurs within two years, and one shall attain the beginning and end without obstacles. "Gaḥ svāhā" is this root mantra, joined with the *praṇava* (Oṃ).

Glaiṃ glāṃ [is for] the heart; gāṃ gīṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ [are for] the head and the crest-lock; gūṃ [is for] the armor; goṃ and gaiṃ [are for] the eyes; and goṃ [is used] in the rites of invocation and so forth.
Āgaccha ulkāya, Gaṇa ulkā, Puṣpa ulka, Dhūpa ulkaka, Dīpa ulkāya, Mahā ulkāya; and then the offering and the purification.

The Gāyatrī mantra for Sidedholka is prescribed for the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the thumb and the other fingers: "Oṃ, may we know Mahākarna; may we meditate upon Vakratuṇḍa; may that Danti inspire us."
One should worship these Gaṇas likewise with offerings and oblations of sesame seeds: "Svāhā to the Gaṇa, to Gaṇapati, and to Kūṣmāṇḍaka."

Obeisance indeed to Amogholka, the One-Tusked One, who has the form of the Destroyer of Tripura; Oṃ, obeisance to the one with dark-blue fangs, whose mouth is terrifying, and who causes trembling in battle.
At the end of "Padmadaṃṣṭāya svāhā," the mudrā is indeed dancing among the Gaṇas; with clapping of hands and laughter, there shall be the fruit of good fortune and other benefits.
Likewise, on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship Gaṇeśa; for a year, one obtains learning, prosperity, fame, long life, and a lineage of sons.
Having fasted on a Monday and on the fourth lunar day, one should worship Gaṇa; by reciting the mantra, offering oblations, and remembering the Vidyā, one shall go to heaven and attain liberation.

He who worships on the fourth day of the bright fortnight with offerings of sugar-candies, sweetmeat balls, and flour-cakes, performing the propitiation of Vighna, shall attain all his desires and good fortune.
One should worship the son and others with *damana* flowers; the fourth [day] is called *damana*. With "Āṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati," ending in the dative case, one should worship Gaṇa.
In whichever month one may offer oblations, recite mantras, or maintain mindfulness, one attains all desires and achieves the destruction of all obstacles.
One should worship Vināyaka, Mūrtika, and the others with these names; he too attains a good rebirth, as well as the happiness of heaven and liberation.
Worshipped by the hosts, Vakratuṇḍa, Ekadaṃṣṭrin, Tryambaka, Nīlagrīva, Lambodara, Vikaṭa, and Vighnarājaka.
One should worship the Gaṇa on the twelve-spoked [wheel]: the smoke-colored Bhālacandra as the tenth Vināyaka, and Gaṇapati with the face of an elephant.
Whether performed individually or collectively, one who observes the Madhavī vow shall obtain all desires on the auspicious fifth day of the months of Śrāvaṇa, Āśvina, Bhādrapada, and Kārttika.
Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Kālīya, Maṇibhadraka, Airāvata, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Karkoṭaka, and Dhanañjaya.
For these, having been bathed with clarified butter and other substances, bestow the perfections of long life and health: Ananta, Vāsuki, Śaṅkha, Padma, and Kambala.
Likewise, every month he [subdued] the nāgas Karkāṭaka, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Śaṅkhaka, Kālīya, Takṣaka, and Piṅgala.

One should worship the eight Nāgas during the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada; one shall attain liberation and go to heaven. They should be drawn on both sides of the door, and one should worship them during the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa.

On the fifth day, one should worship the Nāgas and offer oblations to Ananta and the Mahoragas. Milk and clarified butter should be presented as the food offering (*naivedya*), which removes all poisons. The Nāgas hold hands in the gesture of granting fearlessness; thus, this fifth day is for the extraction of the effects of being bitten.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Fifth Vow for the Extraction of Poison," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: In this manner, one should worship Kārttikeya in the month of Bhādrapada; all acts such as bathing and giving gifts performed on this day are said to be inexhaustible.
On the seventh day, one should also cause the Brahmins to eat the food and worship the Sun with the mantra: *Oṃ khakholkāya amṛtatvaṃ (tantvaṃ) priyasaṅgamo bhava sada svāhā*.
On the eighth day, one should break the fast after consuming black pepper; by bathing with self-restraint on the seventh day and worshipping the Sun, one becomes a partaker of heaven.

His son was Vasumanas, and Tridhanvan was his offspring; Trayyāruṇa was his son, and Satyarata was his son.
He who was known as Triśaṅku then became Hariścandra; from Hariścandra came Rohitāśva, and from Rohitāśva came Harita.
Harita’s son was Cañcu, and Cañcu’s son was Vijaya; from Vijaya was born Ruruka, and from Ruruka was born his son Vṛka.
From Vṛka was born King Bāhu, and from Bāhu, Sagara is recorded to have been born; from Sagara and Sumati, O Hari, sixty thousand sons were born.
Of Keśinī there was only one son, known by the name Asamañjasa.
His son was the learned Aṃśumat, and his son was Dilīpa; from Dilīpa came Bhagīratha, who brought the Gaṅgā to the earth.
Śruta was the son of Bhagīratha, and from Śruta, it is said, came Nābhaga; from Nābhāga was born Ambarīṣa, and from Ambarīṣa came Sindhudvīpa.
Sindhudvīpa’s son was Ayutāyu, whose son was Ṛtuparṇa; from Ṛtuparṇa came Sarvakāma, and Sudāsa was his son.
The son of Sudāsa was known by the name Mitrasaha; his son, born of Damayantī, was known as Kalmāṣapāda.
Aśvaka was his son, and from Aśvaka, Mūlaka (or Mṛcchaka) was born; after him came King Daśaratha, and his son was Ailavila.
Viśvasaha was his son, and Khaṭvāṅga was his offspring; from Khaṭvāṅga came Dīrghabāhu, and Aja was the son of Dīrghabāhu.
His son was Daśaratha, and four sons are recorded as his: Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Śatrughna, and Bharata, all of great strength.
From Rāma were born Kuśa and Lava; from Bharata, Tārkṣya and Puṣkara; and Citrāṅgada and Candraketu were born from Lakṣmaṇa.
Subāhu and Śūrasena were born from Śatrughna; Kuśa’s son was Atithi, and Niṣadha was indeed the son of Atithi.
Nala was the son of Niṣadha, and Nabha is recorded as the son of Nala; Puṇḍarīka was the son of Nabha, and Kṣemadhanvan was his offspring.
Devānīka was his son; from Devānīka came Ahīnaka; from Ahīnaka came Ruru; and Pāriyātra was the son of Ruru at the sacrifice.
From Pāriyātra came Dala at the sacrifice; Dala’s son is remembered as Chala. From Chala came Uktha, from Uktha came Vajranābha, and from him came Gaṇa.
From the Gaṇa was born Uṣitāśva, from whom Viśvasaha arose; Hiraṇyanābha was his son, and his son is known as Puṣpaka.
From Puṣpa came Dhruvasandhi; from Dhruvasandhi came Sudarśana; from Sudarśana came Agnivarṇa; and from Agnivarṇa came Padmavarṇa.
From Padmavarṇa was born Śīghra, and from Śīghra his son Maru was born; Prasuśruta was the son of Maru, and Udāvasu was his son.
From Udāvasu came Nandivardhana; from Nandivardhana came Suketu; from Suketu was born Devarāta, and from him was born his son Vṛhaduktha.
From Bṛhaduktha came Mahāvīrya, and Sudhṛti was his son; from Sudhṛti came Dhṛṣṭaketu, and from Dhṛṣṭaketu came Haryaśva.
From Haryaśva, Maru was born; from Maru came Pratīndhaka; from Pratīndhaka came Kṛtiratha, and Devamīḍha was his son.
From Devamīḍha was born Vibudha; from Vibudha came Mahādhṛti; from Mahādhṛti was born Kīrtirāta, whose son was Mahāromā.
From Mahāromṇa came Svarṇaromā, and Hrasvaromā was his son; from Hrasvaromā came Sīradhvaja, whose daughter was Sītā.
His brother was Kuśadhvaja; from Sīradhvaja came Bhānumān; from Bhānumān came Śatadyumna; and from Śatadyumna, Śuci is recorded as having been born.
Ūrja was the son of Śuci, and Sanadvāja was his son; from Sanadvāja was born Kuli, and Anañjana was the son of Kuli.
From Anañjana was born Kulajit, and his son was Adhinemika; Śrutāyu was his son, and Supārśva was his offspring.
From Supārśva was born Sṛñjaya; from Sṛñjaya was born Kṣemāri; from Kṣemāri was born Anenā, and his son is known as Rāmaratha.
From that Rāmaratha came Satyaratha; Upaguru is recorded as the successor from Satyaratha; from Upaguru came Upagupta, and Svāgata followed from Upagupta.
Svanara was born from Svāgata, and Suvarcas was his son; Supārśva was the son of Suvarcas, and Suśruta was born from Supārśva.
Jayas was born from Suśruta, and from Jayas, Vijaya arose; Ṛta was the son of Vijaya, and Sunaya was the son of Ṛta.
From Sunaya was born Vītahavya; from Vītahavya, Dhṛti is remembered [as having been born]. Bahulāśva was the son of Dhṛti, and from Bahulāśva, Kṛti is remembered [as having been born].
In both lineages of Janaka, the reliance upon yoga has been described.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Solar Lineage," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Hari said: The lineage of the Sun has been told; now hear from me the Lunar lineage. Brahmā was the son of Nārāyaṇa, and from Brahmā was born Atri.
Atri’s wife was Soma, who was the beloved of the preceptor of the gods; from Soma, Tārā gave birth to Budha, and the son of Budha was Purūravas.
Then, from Budhaputra and Urvaśī, six sons were born: Śrutātmaka, Viśvāvasu, Śatāyu, Āyu, Dhomān, and Āvasu.
The son of Amāvasu was named Bhīma, and Bhīma’s son was Kāñcana; Suhotra was the son of Kāñcana, and Jahnu was born from Suhotra.
From Jahnu was born Sumantu; from Sumantu came Apajāpaka. Balākāśva was his son, and from Balākāśva, Kuśa is recorded to have been born.
From Kuśa were born Kuśāśva, Kuśanābha, Amūrtarayas, and Vasu; from Kuśāśva was born Gādhi, and Viśvāmitra was his son.
The maiden Satyavatī was given to the twice-born Ṛcīka; from Ṛcīka was born Jamadagni, and Rāma was his son.
From Viśvāmitra were born Devarāta, Aduchandas, and other sons; from Āyu came Nahuṣa, and from him were born Anenas, Raji, and Rambhaka.
From Kṣattravṛddha was born Kṣattravṛddha, and from him came King Suhotra; from Suhotra were born three sons: Kāśya, Kāśu, and Gṛtsamada.
From Gṛtsamada was born Śaunaka; likewise, from Kāśya came Dīrghatamas. From him was born Vaidya Dhanvantari, and Ketumān was his son.
Bhīmaratha was the son of Ketumān, and Divodāsa was his son; from Divodāsa came Pratardana, who was renowned there as Śatrujit.
Ṛtadhvaja was his son, and from Ṛtadhvaja came Alarka; from Alarka Sannati was born, and Sunīta was the son of Sannati.
Satyaketu was the son of Sunīta; Vibhu was the son of Satyaketu; Suvibhu was the son of Vibhu; and Sukumāra was the son of Suvibhu.
From Sukumāra was born Dṛṣṭaketu, and Vītihotra was his son. Bharga was the son of Vītihotra, and Bhargabhūmi was his son.
These high-souled Kāśis were devotees of Viṣṇu; Rajeḥ had five hundred sons who were destroyed by Śakra.
From Kṣattravṛddha was born Pratikṣattra, and Saṃjaya was his son; Vijaya was the son of Saṃjaya, and Kṛta was the son of Vijaya.
From Kṛta was born Vṛṣadhana, and Sahadeva was his son; from Sahadeva came Adīna, and from Adīna came Jayatsena.
From Jayatsena was born Saṃkṛti, and from Saṃkṛti came Kṣattradharmā; from him were born Yati, Yayāti, Saṃyāti, Ayāti, and Vikṛti in succession.
The sons of King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, are well known; Devayānī gave birth to Yadu and Turvasu.
Druhyu, Anu, Pūru, Śarmiṣṭhā’s son Vārṣaparvaṇi, Sahasrajit, Kroṣṭuman, and Raghu were the sons of Yadu.
From Sahasrajit came Śatajit; from him indeed were born Haya and Haihaya. Anaraṇya was the son of Haya, and Dharma was born from Haihaya.
From Dharma was born Dharmnetra, and from Dharmnetra came Kunti; from Kunti was born Sāhañji, and Mahiṣmān was his son.
Bhadraśreṇya was his son; Bhadraśreṇya’s son was Durdama; from Durdama came Dhanaṃjaya, and Kṛtavīrya was the son of Dhanaṃjaya.
From Kṛtavīrya was born Arjuna, who had mastered the sacred fires, accomplished his duties, possessed vital energy, and was endowed with great strength; from Arjuna came Śūrasenaka.
Jayadhvaja, Madhu, Śūra, Vṛṣaṇa, and Pañca were the five who shared a common vow. From Jayadhvaja came Tālajaṅgha; from Tālajaṅgha came Bharata.
Madhu was the son of Vṛṣaṇa, and from Madhu came the lineage of Vṛṣṇi. Āhi was born as the son of that great-souled Kroṣṭu.
From Āhu arose Uśaṅku; from him was born Citraratha; from Citraratha came Śaśabindu, who had one hundred thousand wives.
And he had ten hundred thousand sons, the foremost of whom were Pṛthukīrti and the others: Pṛthukīrti, Pṛthujaya, Pṛthudāna, and Pṛthuśravas.
From Pṛthuśravas was born Tama; from Tama was born Uśanas. His son was named Śitagu, and from him came Śrīrukmakavaca.
Rukma, Pṛthurukma, Jyāmagha, Pālita, and Hari were the sons of Śrīrukmakavaca; likewise, Vidarbha was born from Jyāmagha.
And from his wife Śaibyā, he begot Kratha and Kauśika from Vidarbha; from Romapāda came Babhru, and from Babhru came Dhṛti.
The son of Kauśika was Ṛci, and from him, it is said, came King Caidya; Kunti was his son, and Vṛṣṇi is recorded as the son of Kunti.
Vṛṣṇi’s son was Nivṛti, and likewise Nivṛti’s son was Daśārha. Vyoma was the son of Daśārha, and Jīmūta was his offspring.
From Jīmūta was born Vikṛti; from him Bhīmaratha arose; from him Madhuratha was born, and Śakuni was his son.
Karambhi was the son of Śakuni; his son is remembered as Devavān. From Devakṣattra, who was devoted to the gods, Madhu is said to have been born.
Kuruvaṃśa was the son of Madhu, and Anu was born from the Kuru lineage; Puruhotra was the son of Anu, and Aṃśu was born from Puruhotra.
From Aṃśu was born Sattvaśruta, and from him indeed came King Sāttvata; from Sāttvata were born Bhajina and Bhajamāna, and Andhaka was the son of Sāttvata.
Mahābhoja, Vṛṣṇi, Divyāvanya, Devāvṛdha, Nimivṛṣṇi, Bhajamāna, and likewise Ayutājit were born.
Śatajit, Sahasrājit, Babhru, and the divine Bṛhaspati were born; from Mahābhoja came Bhoja, and from that Vṛṣṇi came Sumitraka.
From him [came] Svadhājitt by name, and likewise Anamitrāśinī; Anamitra’s son was Nighna, and from Nighna, Śatrājita was born.
Another famous son was Prasena, and likewise Śibi from Anamitra; Satyaka was the son of Śibi, and from Satyaka came Sātyaki.
Sañjaya was the son of Sātyaki, and Kuli was his son; Yugandhara was the son of Kuli—these are proclaimed as the descendants of Śibi.
In the lineage of Anamitra was Vṛṣṇi; his son was Śvaphalka, and Citraka was also his son. From Śvaphalka and Gāndinī, Akrūra was born, who was indeed a devotee of Viṣṇu.
From Upamadgu came Akrūra, and from him Devadyota was born; Devavān and Upadeva are recorded as the two sons of Akrūra.
Pṛthu and Vipṛthu are recorded as the sons of Citra; Śuci was the son of Andhaka; Kukura was the son of Bhajamāna; and likewise [the son] of Kambalabarhiṣ.
From Kukura was born Dhṛṣṭa, and from him came Kāpotaromaka; his son was Viloma, and Tumburu was the son of Viloma.
From him Dundubhi was born, and from him Punarvasu is remembered; his [sons] were Āhuka and Āhukī, and Āhuka had a daughter as well.
Devaka and Ugrasena [were born]; from Devaka was born Devakī, as well as Vṛkadevā, Upadevā, Sahadevā, and Surakṣitā.
Vasudeva married Śrīdevī and Śāntidevī; Devavān and Upadeva are recorded as the two sons of Sahadevā.
Kamsa and Sunāman were the sons of Ugrasena, as were Vaṭa and others. Vidūratha was born from Bhajamāna, and Śūra was born from Vidūratha.
Now, Śamī was the son of Sūra, the son of Vidūratha; Pratikṣattra was the son of Śamī, and Svayaṃbhōja was his son.
From Svayambhoja was born Hṛdika, and his son was Kṛtavarman; from Śūra, who was indeed Devamīḍhuṣa, were born Deva and Śatadhanu.
Ten sons were born to Māriṣā, beginning with Vasudeva; and [there were also] Pṛthā, Śrutadevī, Śrutakīrti, and Śrutaśravā.
Rājādhideva gave Pṛthā, the daughter of Kunti, to Śūra; she was given by Kunti to Pāṇḍu, and from her, Dharmarāja, Vāyu, and Indra [beheld offspring].
Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, Pārtha, Nakula, and Sahadeva were born to Mādrī by the two Aśvin deities; formerly, Karṇa was born to Kuntī.
From Śrutadevī was born Dantavakra, who was indeed invincible in battle; and from Kaikaya, five sons beginning with Santardana were born to Śrutakīrti.
From Rājādhidevī were born Vinda and Anuvindaka; and from Damaghoṣa, Śrutaśravas gave birth to Śiśupālaka.
Pauravī Rohiṇī was the wife of Madirānakadundubhi; Bhadrā was the foremost among his wives, including Devakī. From Rohiṇī, Balabhadra was born.
From Balabhadra and Revatī were born Sāraṇa and others, as well as Śaṭha; and from Devakī, Niśaṭha and Ulmuka were born, making six children in total.
Kīrtimān, Suṣeṇa, the noble Bhadrasena, Ṛjudāsa, and Bhadradeva—Kaṃsa indeed slew them all.
Saṃkarṣaṇa was the seventh and Kṛṣṇa himself was the eighth; furthermore, Hari had sixteen thousand wives.
Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, the sweetly smiling Lakṣmaṇā, and the excellent Jāmbavatī—these eight gave birth to many sons.
Pradyumna, Cārudeṣṇa, and Sāmba were the principal sons; from Pradyumna was born the mighty Aniruddha by Kakudminī.
From Aniruddha and Subhadrā was born a king named Vajra; Pratibāhu was the son of Vajra, and Cāru was his son.
In the lineage of Turvasu, Vahni was born; Vahni’s son was Bharga; from Bharga, Bhānu was born as a son; and the son of Bhānu was Karandhama.
Learn from me the lineage of Maru, the son of Karandhama, and that of Druhyu. The son of Druhyu was Setu, and Āraddha was his offspring.
From Āraddha was born Gāndhāra, and from Gāndhāra came Gharma; Ghṛta was the son of Gharma, and Durgama was the son of Ghṛta.
O Pracetas, listen to me regarding the lineage of Anu himself; Sabhānara was the son of Anu, and from him Kālañjaya was born.
From Kālajaya was born Sṛñjaya, and from Sṛñjaya came Puruñjaya; Janamejaya was his son, and Mahāśāla was his offspring.
Mahāmanas is remembered here as the great Śāla king of Aśvinara; from Aśvinara was born Śibi, and Vṛṣadarbha was the son of Śibi.
From Mahāmanojāt, Titikṣu had a son named Ruṣadratha; Hema was born from Ruṣadratha, and Sutapas was born from Hema.
From Bali, Sutapas was born; from him came the Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Kaliṅgas, Andhas, Paiṇḍras, Bāleyas, Anapānas, and Aṅgatas.
From Anapāna came Diviratha, and from him Dharmaratha was born; Romapāda was the son of Dharmaratha, and Caturaṅga was his son.
Pṛthulākṣa’s son was Campa; from Pṛthulākṣa came Campa’s son, Haryaṅga, and his son was Bhadraratha.
His son was Bṛhatkarman, from whom Bṛhadbhānu was born; Bṛhanmanas was the son of Bṛhadbhānu, and his son was Jayadratha.
Jayadratha’s son was Vijaya; Vijaya’s son was Dhṛti; Dhṛti’s son was Dhṛtavrata; and from Dhṛtavrata came Satyadharman.
His son was Adhiratha, and Karṇa was his son.
Now hear from me concerning Vṛṣasena and the descendants of Karṇa’s lineage.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lunar Dynasty," in the Ācārakāṇḍa, within the first part (Pūrvakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Hari said: Janamejaya was born from Puru; from Janamejaya came Namasyu; his son was Abhayada; and from Abhayada was born Sudyu.
Sudyu’s son was Bahugati, and Saṃjāti was his offspring; Vatsajāti was the son of Saṃjāti, and Raudrāśva was his son.
Ṛteyu, Sthaṇḍileyu, Kakṣeyu, Kṛteyuka, Jaleyu, and Santateyu were the excellent sons of Rodrāśva.
From Ratināra and Ṛteyu was born his son Pratiratha; his son was Medhātithi, and his son is recorded as Ainila.
Duṣyanta was the son of Aṇiṇa, and his son was Bharata; he was born of Śakuntalā, and from Bharata was born Vitatha.
Vitatha’s son was Manyu, and it is remembered that Manyu’s son was Nara. Nara’s son was Saṃkṛti, and Garga was indeed the son of Saṃkṛti.
From Garga was born the son Manyu, and from him Śini was born as a son; from that son of Manyu, who was possessed of great heroism, was born the son Urukṣaya.
From Urukṣaya was born Trayyāruṇi, and from Vyūhakṣatra, who was born of Manyu, came Suhotra; his sons were Hastin, Ajamīḍha, and Dvimīḍha.
Hastin and Purumīḍha were born, and from Ajamīḍha came Kaṇva; from Kaṇva was born Medhātithi, from whom the Kāṇvāyana twice-born ones descended.
From Ajamīḍha came Bṛhadiṣu; his son was Bṛhaddhanu; his son was Bṛhatkarman; and his son was Jayadratha.
From Jayadratha was born Viśvajit, and Senajit was his son; Rucirāśva was the son of Senajit, and Pṛthusena was his son.
Pārā was the son of Pṛthusena, and from Pārā was born the king Dvīpa; Sṛmara was the son of that king, and Sukṛti was the son of Pṛthu.
Vibhrāja was the son of Sukṛti; from Vibhrāja was born Aśvaha; from him came Kṛtyā; and Brahmadatta was his son, whose son was Viṣvaksena.
From Dvimīḍha was born Yavīnara; from Yavīnara came Dhṛtimat; from Dhṛtimat was born Satyadhṛti; and his son was Dṛḍhanemi.
Supārśva was the son of Dṛḍhanemi; likewise, Sannati was born from Supārśva. Kṛtu was the son of Sannati, and from Kṛtu, Ugrāyudha was born.
From Ugrāyudha was born Kṣemya, and his son was Sudhīra; from Sudhīra came Purañjaya, and his son was Vidūratha.
From Ajamīḍha and Nalinī was born a king named Nīla; from Nīla was born a son named Śānti, and Suśānti was his offspring.
From Suśānti was born Puru, and Arka became his son; from Arka came Haryaśva, and from Haryaśva, Mukula was born.
From Mukula were born Yavīnara, Bṛhadbhānu, Kampilla, and Sṛñjaya; and from Śaradvan was born the great Vaiṣṇava Pāñcāla.
Divodāsa was the second son of Śaradvat by Ahalyā; his son was Śatānanda, and the son of that virtuous man was Satyadhṛti.
Kṛpa and Kṛpī were born to Satyadhṛti through Urvaśī; and from the loss of his virility, Kṛpī gave birth to the preeminent Aśvatthāman as the husband of Droṇa.
From Divodāsa was born Mitrayu; from Mitrayu came Cyavana; from Cyavana was born Sudāsa, whose son was Saudāsa.
Sahadeva was his son; from Sahadeva came Somaka; Jantu was born from Somaka, as was another great son, Pṛṣata.
From Pṛṣata was born Drupada, and from him Dhṛṣṭadyumna arose; from Dhṛṣṭadyumna came Dhṛṣṭaketu, and from Ajamīḍha was born Ṛkṣa.
From Ṛkṣa, Saṃvaraṇa was born; Kuru was born from Saṃvaraṇa. Sudhanus, Pīkṣin, and Jahnu were the sons of Kuru.
From Sudhanus was born Suhotra; from Suhotra was born Cyavana; from Cyavana was born Kṛtaka, who was the Vasu Uparicara.
Bṛhadratha was the youngest, and Satya and others were the sons of Vasu; from Bṛhadratha came Kuśāgra, and from Kuśāgra, Ṛṣabha was born.
From Ṛṣabha was born Puṣpavān; from him was born King Satyahita. From Satyahita came Sudhanvan, and from Sudhanvan came Jahnu.
From Bṛhadratha was born Jarāsaṃdha; Sahadeva was his son. From Sahadeva came Somāpi, and Śrutavat was the son of Somāpi.
Bhīmasena and Ugrasena, Śrutasena, and the unconquered Janamejaya were his sons; and from Jahnu, Suratha was born.
From Suratha came Sārvabhauma; from Vidūratha [came] Jayasena; and Āvadhīta was the son of that Sārvabhauma.
Ayutāyu was his son, and Akrodhana was his son; Atithi was the son of Akrodhana, and Ṛkṣa was the son of Atithi.
From Ṛkṣa was born Bhīmasena; from Bhīmasena came Dilīpa; from Dilīpa came Pratīpa; and from Pratīpa came Devāpi.
Śaṃtanu and Bāhlīka—these three were brothers, all kings. From Bāhlīka was born Somadatta, and from him came Bhūri and Bhūriśravas.
Śala was born to Śantanu by Gaṅgā as a great and righteous Bhīṣma; Citrāṅgada and Vicitravīrya, however, were born to Śantanu by Satyavatī.
Ambikā and Ambālikā were the two wives of Vicitravīrya; from them were born Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu, and likewise Vidura was born from his maidservant.
Vyāsa begot from Dhṛtarāṣṭra a hundred sons, headed by Duryodhana, through Gāndhārī; and five were born to Pāṇḍu.
Prativindhya, Śrutasoma, Śrutakīrti, Śatānīka, and Śrutakarman—these five were born from Arjuna by Draupadī in succession.
Yaudheyī, Hiḍimbā, Kauśī, Subhadrikā, Vijayā, and Reṇumatī—these five bore sons in succession from [Pāṇḍu].
Devaka, Ghacotkaca, Abhimanyu, Sarvaga, Suhotra, Niramitra, and Parīkṣit, who was born of Abhimanyu.
Janamejaya will follow him; now hear of the kings who shall come after him.
Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lunar Dynasty," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—141.
Hari said: Śatānīka, Aśvamedhadatta, Adhisomaka, Kṛṣṇa, Aniruddha, Uṣṇa, and then King Citraratha.
Śucidrava, Vṛṣṇimat, Supeṇa, Sunīthaka, Nṛcakṣus, Mukhābāṇa, Medhāvī, and Nṛpañjaya.
Pāriplava, O sages, Medhāvī, Nṛpañjaya, Bṛhadratha, Hari, Tigma, Śatānīka, and Sudānaka.
Udāna, Ahni, Nara, Daṇḍapāṇi, Nimittaka, and Kṣemaka were the Śūdras; then the father was born first, and after him the son.
But the Bṛhadbalas declare that there were kings born of the Ikṣvāku lineage; after Bṛhadbala came Urukṣaya, and after him Vatsavyūha.
From Vatsavyūha were born Sūrya, his son Sahadeva, Bṛhadaśva, Bhānuratha, Pratīcya, Pratītaka, Manudeva, Sunakṣatra, Kinnara, and Antarikṣaka.
Suparṇa, Kṛtajit, the righteous Bṛhadbhrāja, Kṛtañjaya, Dhanañjaya, Saṃjaya, and Śākya as well.
Śuddhodana, Bāhula, Senajit, Kṣudraka, Sumitra, and Kuḍava; now hear from Sumitra about the Māgadhas.
Jarāsaṃdha, Sahadeva, Somāpi, Śrutaśravas, Ayutāyu, Niramitra, Sukṣatra, and Bahukarmaka.
Śrutañjaya, Senajit, Bhūri, and likewise Śuci; Kṣemya, Suvrata, Dharma, Śmaśrula, and Dṛḍhasenaka.
Sumati, Subala, Satyajit, Viśvajit, and Iṣuñjaya—these are remembered as the kings of the Bārhadratha lineage.
Then the kings will become unrighteous and like Śūdras; for the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself, the imperishable, is the creator of heaven and the other realms.
Dissolution is of three kinds: occasional, elemental, and absolute. In dissolution, the earth goes into the waters, the waters into fire, and fire into heat.

The wind merges into the wind, and the ether into the ether; the ego-constituent (ahaṅkāra) dissolves into the intellect (buddhi), the intellect into the individual soul (jīva), the individual soul into the unmanifest (avyakta), and that [unmanifest] into the Self (ātman).
The Self, the Supreme Lord Viṣṇu, is the one Nārāyaṇa, the Man; He alone is the supreme imperishable, for the entire world, including heaven and so forth, is indeed perishable.
Kings and others have met their destruction; therefore, one should avoid sin. One should practice Dharma steadfastly, so that by abandoning sin, one may go to Hari.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Vision of the Future Royal Dynasties," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Brahmā said: The Lord Hari, having descended, protected Viṃśa and the others for the sake of destroying the dharma of the Daityas and for the protection of the Vedic dharma and other sacred traditions.
The Unborn One assumes incarnations in the form of a fish and other beings; having become a fish, he slew the Daitya Hayagrīva, who was a thorn to the horses.
Having brought back the Vedas, Keśava protected Manu and the others; and for their welfare, he became a tortoise and supported Mount Mandara.
Indeed, during the churning of the Ocean of Milk, the divine Dhanvantari emerged, appearing while carrying a water-pot filled with nectar.
He taught the eight-limbed science of Ayurveda to Suśruta; and Hari, assuming the form of a woman, caused the gods to drink the nectar of immortality.
Then, having descended as a boar, he indeed slew Hiraṇyākṣa; he supported the earth and protected the deities.
Then Narasiṃha, having manifested, slew his enemy Hiraṇyakaśipu and the Daityas, and protected the Vedic dharma and other sacred traditions.
After that, Paraśurāma, the lord of the world born of Jamadagni, became Hari; twenty-one times he made the earth devoid of Kṣatriyas.
He slew Kārtavīrya in battle and gave the earth to Kaśyapa; having performed a sacrifice, the mighty-armed one remained on Mount Mahendra.
Then, from Daśaratha, the fourfold Madana was born as his sons: Rāma, who was destined for greatness, and his younger brothers Bharata and the others.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, Śatrughna, and Jānakī, Rāma’s wife, as well as Rāma himself, acted for the benefit of his mothers in order to fulfill his father’s word of truth.
Having arrived at Śṛṅgavera, Citrakūṭa, and the Daṇḍaka forest, he then cut off the nose of Śūrpaṇakhā and [slain] Khara and Dūṣaṇa.
Having slain the night-roaming Rākṣasa who had abducted Sītā, namely Rāvaṇa, he installed his younger brother Vibhīṣaṇa in the city of Laṅkā.
Having installed [Vibhīṣaṇa] in the kingdom of the rākṣasas, together with Sugrīva, Hanumān, and others, he ascended the Puṣpaka chariot along with Sītā, who was devoted to her husband.
Accompanied by the well-disposed Lakṣmaṇa, he indeed returned to his own city, Ayodhyā; there he ruled the kingdom and protected the subjects, including the gods and others.
She performed sacrifices such as the horse sacrifice for the protection of the Dharma; she took her pleasure with King Rāma according to her desire.
While Sītā remained in Rāvaṇa’s house, she did not resort to Rāvaṇa; in deed, thought, and speech, she was always devoted to Rāghava.
Sītā was indeed devoted to her husband, just like Anasūyā; listen as I describe the greatness of such a devoted wife.
In former times, there was a leper named Kauśika living in Pratiṣṭhāna; his wife worshipped her husband, though he was so afflicted with disease, as if he were a god.
Though rebuked, she regarded her husband as a deity; when told by her husband, that courtesan brought a prostitute, having taken an excessive fee.

Then, on the road, that twice-born man [Vasiṣṭha] saw Māṇḍavya, who was not a thief but had been impaled on a stake under the suspicion of being one, and who was tormented by extreme suffering in the darkness.
Mounted upon his wife's shoulders, Kauśika caused him to move; enraged by the touch of his feet, Māṇḍavya spoke to him.
"His death shall occur at sunrise, by him who has kicked me with his foot. Hearing that, his wife said, "The sun will not rise."
Then, due to the absence of sunrise, there was constant night for many years; consequently, the gods fell into fear.
They went for refuge to Brahmā, and the Lotus-born One said to them: "Indeed, the power of your asceticism will be pacified by this very splendor."
Due to the greatness of the devoted wife, the sun does not rise; and because of its failure to rise, there is likewise the destruction of you mortals.
Therefore, for the sake of the rising of the Sun, you must propitiate Anasūyā, the ascetic and devoted wife of Atri, who is his consort.

Having gone there, the devoted wife Anasūyā propitiated them; she brought about the rising of the sun and restored her husband to life. Indeed, Sītā was even more distinguished than the devoted wife Anasūyā.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Vision of the Ten Incarnations," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Brahmā said: Henceforth I shall recount the *Rāmāyaṇa*, which, when heard, destroys all sins. From the navel-lotus of Viṣṇu, Brahmā was born; Marīci became his son.
From Marīci came Kaśyapa; from him, Ravi; from him, Manu is remembered. From Manu came Ikṣvāku, and in his lineage, King Raghu is remembered.
From Raghu was born King Daśaratha, powerful and majestic; he had four sons of great strength and prowess.
Rāma was born of Kausalyā; Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī, [was born]; and two sons, Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna, were born of Sumitrā.
Rāma, devoted to his father and mother, obtained a collection of divine weapons from Viśvāmitra; thereafter, he indeed slew the Yakṣī Tāṭakā.
In the sacrifice of Viśvāmitra, the powerful one indeed slew Subāhu; then, having gone to Janaka’s ritual, he married Jānakī.
The heroic Lakṣmaṇa took Ūrmilā; Bharata took the daughter Māṇḍavī; and Śatrughna indeed took Kīrtimatī and both daughters of Kuśadhvaja.
Having gone to Ayodhyā with their father and others, Rāma and the rest remained there; Śatrughna and Bharata went to their maternal uncle, Yudhājit.
When the two had departed, that best of kings prepared to bestow the kingdom; he was then entreated by Kaikeyī to give it instead to her son, Rāma.
Rāma desired to dwell in the forest for fourteen years, together with Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā, for the sake of his father’s welfare.
Having abandoned his kingdom like a blade of grass, he went to Śṛṅgaverapura; leaving his chariot at Prayāga, he proceeded to the Citrakūṭa mountain.
Due to his separation from Rāma, the king ascended to heaven; having performed the funeral rites, Bharata, accompanied by his army, returned and spoke to Rāma.
"Having returned to Ayodhyā, O great-minded one, rule the kingdom! But he did not wish to do so, having instead given his sandals to Bharata for the sake of the kingdom.
Then, having been dismissed, Bharata protected the kingdom of Rāma; remaining devoted in Nandigrāma, he, observing his vow, did not enter Ayodhyā.
Rāma also departed from Citrakūṭa and went to the hermitage of Atri; having paid homage to Sutīkṣṇa and Agastya, he arrived at the Daṇḍaka forest.
There, a rākṣasī named Śūrpaṇakhā came to devour them; then, having had her ears and nose cut off by Rāma, she was driven away.
Impelled by him, Khara, Dūṣaṇa, and Triśiras likewise arrived with an army of fourteen thousand rākṣasas.
Rāma, for his part, dispatched those [demons] to the city of Yama with his arrows; meanwhile, urged by the Rākṣasī, Rāvaṇa arrived in order to carry her away.
Then, having first assumed the form of a deer while carrying his triple staff, Rāma, urged on by Sītā, struck down Mārīca.
As he was dying, he cried out, "Alas, Sītā! Lakṣmaṇa! Then Lakṣmaṇa, having been called by Sītā, arrived, and Rāma beheld him.
Having gained an opportunity and taken Jānakī onto his lap, Rāvaṇa said, "Surely Sītā has been abducted by the illusory power of a rākṣasī."
Having pierced through Jaṭāyu, the powerful one then went to Laṅkā and found her protected there in the shade of an Aśoka tree.
Having arrived, Rāma beheld the leaf-hut empty; then the Lord, having grieved for Jānaki, began to search for her.
Having performed the funeral rites for Jaṭāyus and having gone toward the southern direction as directed by him, Rāghava then formed a friendship with Sugrīva.
Having pierced seven palm trees with a straight-knotted arrow, he then pierced Vālin, the lord of monkeys, in Kiṣkindhā.
Rāma, staying himself on Ṛśyamūka, made Sugrīva his ally; Sugrīva, in turn, dispatched monkeys as large as mountains.
Having gone to the western, northern, and eastern directions—each filled with festive joy—to search for Sītā, they have now returned.
And those who, searching for Jānakī, were wandering toward the southern direction through forests, mountains, islands, and the sandy banks of rivers.
Indeed, not seeing Jānakī and having resolved upon death, Hanumān, that elephant among monkeys, learned [the truth] from the words of Sampāti.
He leaped across the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, which was a hundred yojanas wide; there he beheld Jānakī situated within the Aśoka grove.
She was being threatened by the rākṣasīs and by the rākṣasa Rāvaṇa, who said to her, "Become my wife," while she was thinking only of Rāghava.
Having given his finger-ring to Sītā, the monkey spoke words of well-being to her: "I am the messenger of that Rāma; do not grieve, O Maithilī."
"And give me a token of recognition by which Rāma will remember me. Having heard that, Sītā gave the jewel from her braid to Hanumān.
"O monkey, you must speak in such a way that Rāma may lead [the army] here quickly. Having said, "So be it," Hanumān shattered the divine grove.
Having slain Akṣa and other Rākṣasas, and having himself come to their imprisonment, he saw Rāvaṇa with all the arrows of Indrajit and spoke to him.
"I am Hanuman, the messenger of Rama; give Maithili back to Rama. Having heard this, he became enraged and set his tail ablaze.
The mighty monkey, his tail ablaze, having set Lanka on fire, returned to the side of Rama.
Having eaten fruit in Madhuvana, he reported that Sītā had been seen; he also gave the jewel from her braid to Rāma, and Rāma went to the city of Laṅkā.
Accompanied by Sugrīva, Hanumān, Aṅgada, and Lakṣmaṇa, Vibhīṣaṇa also came to seek refuge with Rāghava.
Rāma consecrated that younger brother of Rāvaṇa in the sovereignty of Laṅkā; and having constructed a bridge over the ocean with Nala, Rāma crossed it.
And standing upon Suvela, he beheld the city of Laṅkā; then those heroic monkeys, Nīla, Aṅgada, Nala, and the others, [did likewise].
Then Dhūmra, Dhūmrākṣa, Vīrendra, Jāmbavat and others, with Mainda and Dvivida as their leaders, shattered the city of Laṅkā.
Having slain the Rākṣasas of massive bodies, who resembled heaps of black collyrium, Rāma—along with Lakṣmaṇa and the monkeys—destroyed all the Rākṣasas.
And Vidyujjihva, Dhūmrākṣa, Devāntaka, Narāntaka, Mahodara, Mahāpārśva, Atikāya, and Mahābala.
Kumbha, Nikumbha, Matta, Makarākṣa, Akampana, Prahasta, Vīra, Unmatta, and the exceedingly powerful Kumbhakarṇa.
The powerful Rāghava indeed cut down the son of Rāvaṇa with various divine weapons; having severed his multitude of arms, he struck down Rāvaṇa.
Then, having taken the pure Sītā and remaining in the Puṣpaka chariot, he arrived at Ayodhyā, the most excellent city, together with the monkeys.
Thereupon he ruled the kingdom, protecting his subjects like his own children; having performed ten horse-sacrifices, he made the ritual offering of the fallen horse at Gayāśiras.
Having performed the funeral rites for the funeral cakes according to the rules and having bestowed gifts, Rāghava, upon seeing his two sons Kuśa and Lava, consecrated them both in the kingdom.
Rāma ruled the kingdom for eleven thousand years; thereafter, Śatrughna slew Lavaṇa and the actor Śailūṣa.
Having bowed to the sages beginning with Agastya and having heard the origin of the Rākṣasas, he went to heaven together with the people residing in Ayodhyā, his purpose fulfilled.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Rāmāyaṇa," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: I shall now proclaim the Harivaṃśa, the supreme majesty of Kṛṣṇa. From Vasudeva and Devakī were born Vāsudeva (Kṛṣṇa) and Balarāma.
Indeed, for the sake of protecting Dharma and the like, and for the destruction of Adharma and the like, Kṛṣṇa, having drunk deeply from her breasts, brought Pūtanā to her end.
Then the cart was overturned, and the twin *arjuna* trees were shattered; the serpent Kāliya was subdued, and Dhenuka was struck down.
Having held up Mount Govardhana and been worshipped by Indra, Hari fulfilled his burden-lifting feat and made a solemn vow.
For the protection of Arjuna and others, Ariṣṭa and his ilk were struck down; the Daitya Keśin was slain, and the cowherds and others were fully satisfied.
Cāṇūra, the wrestler Muṣṭika, and Kaṃsa were cast down from their platforms; and Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, and others—indeed, the eight supreme wives of Hari.
That great-souled one had sixteen thousand other wives; their sons, grandsons, and descendants numbered in the hundreds and thousands.
And from Rukmiṇī was born Pradyumna, who slew Śambara; his son was Aniruddha, the husband of Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa.
Wherein a great battle took place between Hari and Śakra, and Bāṇa’s thousand arms were severed, leaving him with only two.
By him Naraka was slain, by whom Pārijāta was carried away; Bala and Śiśupāla were killed, as was the monkey Dvivida.

After Hari had departed, Aniruddha gave birth to Vajra, who became king; he made Sandīpani his preceptor along with [Sandīpani’s] son, and he appointed Ugrasena as the protector of Mathurā and of the gods.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Harivaṃśa," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: I shall now fully relate the Bhārata, which was the removal of the earth's burden; Kṛṣṇa performed it by fighting on behalf of the Pāṇḍavas and others.
From the lotus of Viṣṇu’s navel was born Brahmā; Brahmā’s son was Atri, and from Atri came Soma. From him came Budha, and from him Purūravas was born of Ilā.
In that lineage, his son was Yayāti, as well as Bharata and Kuru; in his lineage was Śantanu, and the son of Śantanu by Gaṅgā was [Bhīṣma].
Bhīṣma was endowed with all virtues and had reached the further shore of the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.
Two sons were born to Śāntanu by Satyavatī; however, the Gandharva Citrāṅgada slew the son Citrāṅgada.
Another Vicitravīrya became the husband of the daughter of the King of Kāśī; when Vicitravīrya had ascended to heaven, [Pāṇḍu] was born from Vyāsa through that wife.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra was the son of Ambikā, Pāṇḍu was the son of Ambālikā, and Vidura was born to a maidservant; from Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī bore [sons].
There were hundreds of mighty warriors, headed by Duryodhana; meanwhile, five sons were born to Pāṇḍu from Kuntī and Mādrī.
Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, Arjuna, Nakula, and Sahadeva—these five possess great strength and prowess.
The enmity between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas arose indeed through the power of destiny; the Pāṇḍavas were oppressed by the fickle-minded Duryodhana.
Those heroes, though burnt in the house of lac, were liberated through their own stainless wisdom.
Then, having slain the Rākṣasa Baka, those great-souled ones entered the dwelling of a Brāhmaṇa in that city of Ekacakrā.
Then, having learned that the self-choice marriage (*svayaṃvara*) of Draupadī was taking place in the kingdom of Pañcāla, with valor as her bride-price, the Pāṇḍavas married her.
With the consent of Droṇa and Bhīṣma, Dhṛtarāṣṭra then bestowed half of the kingdom upon them; they subsequently obtained it in Indraprastha, the most excellent of cities.

Then, having constructed the assembly hall, those of firm vows performed the Rājasūya sacrifice. Meanwhile, Arjuna obtained his beloved Subhadrā in Dvāravatī—the sister of Vāsudeva—with the consent of the Slayer of Mura.
The divine chariot Nandighoṣa, the unsurpassed bow of Agni, that celestial weapon named Gāṇḍīva renowned throughout the three worlds, inexhaustible arrows, and likewise impenetrable armor.
With that bow, the heroic Pāṇḍava Bībhatsu, endowed with great prowess and accompanied by Kṛṣṇa as his second, gratified the god of fire.
Having conquered the kings in his world-conquest and taken their jewels, he joyfully gave them to his great brother Yudhiṣṭhira, who was skilled in statesmanship.

The righteous Yudhiṣṭhira, surrounded by his brothers, was defeated by the sinful Duryodhana through a game of dice involving deceit—a game played according to the counsel of Karṇa and Duḥśāsana and the will of Śakuni.
Then, for twelve years, they performed great austerities in the forest, accompanied by Dhaumya and Draupadī as the sixth, surrounded by a multitude of sages.
Having taken refuge in Virāṭa’s city in disguised forms, those highly wise ones lived there for one year, protecting it from that seizure of cattle.
Having departed for their own kingdom, those heroes respectfully requested King Duryodhana for five villages as half of his realm.
Endowed with strength and surrounded by seven divine akṣauhiṇīs, they did not reach [their goal] and waged war at Kurukṣetra.
Duryodhana and the others, joined by eleven [divisions], exerted themselves; the battle that ensued was chaotic and resembled the war between the gods and the asuras.

Bhīṣma was the commander-in-chief at the outset of Duryodhana’s army, and Śikhaṇḍin was that of the Pāṇḍavas; between them there occurred a most terrible battle, day and night, with weapons against weapons, arrow against arrow.
Covered by hundreds of arrows from Śikhaṇḍin and Arjuna, Bhīṣma, looking toward the northern solstice, meditated upon the Lord who wields the mace.
Having spoken many kinds of teachings and having gratified many ancestors, he became absorbed in the stainless state of bliss, free from all taint.
Then the valiant Droṇa went forth to fight with Dhṛṣṭadyumna; that battle lasted for five days and was exceedingly terrible.
Where those protectors of the earth were slain by Pārtha in battle, even Droṇa, having encountered an ocean of grief, attained heaven.

Then Karṇa went to fight with Arjuna, the great-souled one; after engaging in a great battle for two days, that heroic man, submerged in the ocean of Pārtha’s weapons, subsequently attained the world of the Sun.
Then Śalya went forth to fight with the wise Dharmarāja; within half a day, Śalya was slain by arrows resembling blazing fire.
Then the valiant Duryodhana, seizing his mace with speed, rushed toward Bhīma like Yama, the Destroyer at the end of time.
Then, having been struck down by the hero Bhīma with his mace, Aśvatthāman, the son of Droṇa, went to the sleeping army during that night.
Remembering the slaughter of his father, the valiant one struck with the strength of his arms; he then slew Dhṛṣṭadyumna and the sons of Draupadī.
While Draupadī was weeping, Arjuna, having conquered Aśvatthāman by means of the Aiṣika weapon, seized that supreme crest-jewel.
Yudhiṣṭhira, having comforted the women who were overwhelmed with grief, bathed and offered libations to the gods, the ancestors, and the grandfathers.
Then, comforted by Bhīṣma, he ruled over a great kingdom and performed the horse sacrifice for Viṣṇu according to the rules, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Having installed Parīkṣit on the throne, the king, having heard of the destruction of the Yādavas in the Mausala [Parvan], recited the Thousand Names.
Then Viṣṇu, accompanied by his brothers Bhīma and the others, went to heaven; Vāsudeva [remained] once more for the purpose of deluding the Buddhas, the enemies of the gods.
Furthermore, Kalki Viṣṇu will appear again in the village of Śambhala; mounted upon a horse, he will then reduce all the worlds to ashes.
Indeed, for the protection of the gods and others, for the removal of unrighteousness, and for the sake of slaying the wicked, he takes an incarnation.
Just as Dhanvantari, born from the churning of the Ocean of Milk, indeed proclaimed the Ayurveda for the sake of the life of the gods and others.
By hearing the Bhāratas and the incarnations from the high-souled Śuśruta, the son of Viśvāmitra himself, a man shall go to heaven.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Mahābhārata and Other Works," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Dhanvantari said: O Suśruta, I shall now declare the diagnosis of all diseases in accordance with their true nature, just as it was previously proclaimed by the eminent sages, beginning with Ātreya.

Disease (roga), evil (pāpmā), fever (jvara), affliction (vyādhi), morbid change (vikāra), corrupted state (duṣṭa), illness (āmaya), consumption (yakṣmā), affliction (ātaṅka), ailment (gada), and distress (bādhā) are synonymous terms.
The etiology, the premonitory symptoms, the clinical signs, the therapeutic suitability, and the pathogenesis—this fivefold knowledge of diseases is traditionally taught.

They say that the "source" (nidāna) is the precursor form by which [the disease] is characterized, using such synonyms as sign (nimitta), cause (hetu), sphere (āyatana), condition (pratyaya), arising (utthāna), and reason (kāraṇa).

A disease that is about to arise, not yet dominated by any specific pathological humor (doṣa), has unmanifest signs due to its subtlety; such are the symptoms of diseases according to their respective natures.

That very [substance] when it has attained manifestness is designated as "form" (rūpa); it is the manifestation of configurations, and is called a sign (liṅga), a characteristic (lakṣaṇa), a mark (cihna), and a shape (ākṛti).
The application of medicines, foods, and regimens—which are contrary to the cause, the disease, and the perverted [symptoms], yet which produce the opposite effect—brings about happiness.
One should recognize the alleviation of a disease as that which is known as "sātmya" (wholesome); its opposite is "anupaśaya" (non-alleviating), designated as "asātmya" (unwholesome) for the disease.
Just as a disease is produced by a specific morbid humor and its subsequent spreading, that manifestation is designated as *samprāpti* (the full onset).
It is differentiated according to the distinctions of number, type, predominance, strength, and time, just as it will be stated here that there are eight types of fever.

When the *doṣas* are combined, one should determine their relative proportions through various calculations; one should then indicate the predominance of the disease based on whether [a particular *doṣa*] acts independently or in dependence upon others.

The specific determination of strength and weakness is made through the totality of the causes and other factors, as well as by the portions of night, day, and the time since the last meal, according to the nature of the disease.
Thus has the meaning of the etiology been stated; it shall now be taught in detail: the etiology of all diseases indeed consists of the provoked humors (malas).
The provocation of these [humors] is said to result from the indulgence in various unwholesome things; the threefold unwholesome application for each of the three has been previously described.

Through the excessive use of bitter, pungent, astringent, sour, and dry [substances], as well as through insufficient intake, running, agitation, staying awake at night, and speaking in an excessively loud voice;

The wind (vāyu) becomes aggravated by physical activity, exertion, grief, anxiety, exercise, and sexual intercourse; it also flares up during the summer season, at the end of the day, at the end of the night, and after eating.

Pitta is provoked by pungent, astringent, sharp, hot, and acrid substances, by anger, and by burning sensations; it is also aggravated during autumn, at midday, during the middle watch of the night, and at times of internal heat.

By means of substances that are sweet, sour, salty, unctuous, heavy, obstructive to the channels, and cold; and by means of comforts such as pleasant sitting, sleep, indigestion, and daytime sleeping, which are nourishing; [the kapha increases].

When there is indigestion even of food that has been eaten due to the improper administration of emetics and other therapies, and when phlegm (kapha) predominates during the forenoon and the first part of the night, I shall describe the mixed types [of disorders].

Furthermore, there is *sannipāta* (the combination of all three humors) due to their mutual mixing, as well as from eating food that is contaminated, undigested, irregular, incompatible, and so forth.
With spoiled liquor and water, dried vegetables, raw radishes, oil-cake, and meat that is stale, putrid, dried, or emaciated;

Due to those various factors that produce the three humors, from the transformation of food, from the corruption of the bodily constituents, from the wind in front, and from the disturbance caused by possession by spirits;

Due to corrupted food, excessive phlegmatic humors, affliction of the birth-star (janmarkṣa), various improper conjunctions, the indulgence in sins, abnormalities in the delivery of women, and likewise through improper medical treatment;
Thus enraged, following the specific course of each disease, the humors (doṣas) quickly resort to elixirs (rasāyana) and undergo transformation within the body.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of All Diseases," in the section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Dhanvantari said: I shall now declare the diagnosis of fever for the sake of understanding all fevers. Fever is the lord of diseases, a malevolent force, the king of death, a devourer, and the end-maker. It was born from the upward-turning eye of Rudra, who became enraged at the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
That torment, consisting of delusion and characterized by suffering, arises from one's own misconduct; cruel in nature, it persists through various births under diverse names.
Pākala is the affliction in elephants, abhitāpa in horses, alarka in dogs, indramada in clouds, nīlikā in waters, jyotis in medicinal herbs, and that which is called ūṣara in the earth.
In the case of an affliction arising from phlegm (kapha), there occurs nausea, vomiting, cough, stiffness, coldness of the skin and other parts, and eruptions appearing on the limbs.

In due time, there is either the manifestation or the increase of all [symptoms] according to their respective natures; the non-alleviation of what was described as the etiology, and the alleviation by the opposite.

Loss of appetite, indigestion, stiffness, and lethargy; burning in the heart, improper digestion, drowsiness, and lassitude; and the failure of the enema to expel the doshas through massage and downward pressure.

Excessive salivation, nausea, loss of appetite, a mouth with a watery taste, clear urine, heat, heaviness of the limbs, frequent urination, lack of digestion, and absence of emaciation are the symptoms of *āma-jvara* (fever with undigested toxins).
Hunger, emaciation, lightness of the limbs, mildness of fever, and the discharge of the humors—these are the signs of a fever free from *āmaja* (undigested) toxins after eight days.

Just as in a combination [of doshas], symptoms manifest according to their own specific characteristics; even when fever arises from a combination, there may be headache, fainting, vomiting, burning of the body, dryness of the throat and mouth, loss of appetite, pain in the joints, insomnia, agitation, horripilation, yawning, and excessive talkativeness—these occur due to the wind (vāta) combined with bile (pitta).

Fever born of kapha and vāta is characterized by burning sensations, loss of appetite, pain in the joints and head, spitting, labored breathing, cough, discoloration of the skin, coldness, stiffness, blurred vision, vertigo, drowsiness, and excessive salivation.

Coldness, stiffness, perspiration, burning sensations, instability, thirst, cough, the discharge of phlegm and bile, delusion, drowsiness, a coated tongue, and a bitter taste in the mouth—these should be known as the symptoms of fever arising from phlegm and bile (śleṣmapitta-jvara).
In this [fever], there is burning with all the symptoms occurring repeatedly; it is followed by great coldness, excessive sleep during the day, and wakefulness at night.
Either constant sleep or its total absence, excessive perspiration or its total absence, singing, dancing, laughing, and so forth, as well as the cessation of natural inclinations.
The eyes are tearful, turbid, red, sunken, and have disheveled eyelashes; there is pain in the calves, sides, head, joints, and bones, as well as vertigo.
The ears are ringing and painful, or indeed become extremely cold; the tongue is scorched and rough, and the joints of the limbs feel heavy and tremble.
Spitting up blood and bile, rolling of the head, excessive thirst, and the appearance of dark-red circular patches on the abdomen.
Heartache, indigestion, diminished or excessive activity, a greasy mouth, loss of strength, weakness of voice, and delirium.

One should call that *sannipāta* "abhiṇyāsa" (prostration) when there is delayed digestion of the humors, constant drowsiness, and persistent wheezing in the throat, as well as loss of vitality (*hataujas*).

When the wind (vāyu) is obstructed in the throat, it intensely compresses the bile (pitta) within; due to its pervasive nature and its lightness, the bile then moves toward the external pathways. Consequently, in a fever arising from the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta), there occurs yellowness of the eyes.

When the doshas have increased and the digestive fire (agni) has been destroyed, the fever characterized by all symptoms is a sannipāta fever; it is incurable, whereas otherwise it is difficult to cure.

Except for that which arises from a combination [of humors], where pitta, remaining separately, produces a burning sensation either in the skin or in the internal cavity, whether before or after [the other symptoms].

Similarly, when vāta and kapha are involved, coldness occurs; however, burning sensation and other symptoms are difficult to overcome in those two conditions. In that case, during the onset of coldness and so forth, the kapha is liquefied and dried up by pitta.
When pitta is pacified, fainting, intoxication, and thirst arise; furthermore, at the end of the burning sensation and other symptoms, drowsiness, lethargy, and vomiting occur in succession.
