Sweat is produced in four ways: from external contact, from possession, from curses, and from malevolent spells; that born of injury arises from burning sensations and the like.
And due to that fatigue, the wind (vāyu), generally vitiating the blood, produces a fever accompanied by pain, sorrow, discoloration, and distress.
[It is] born from planetary possession, medicine, poison, anger, fear, grief, and desire.
In this [child], there may also be a sudden onset of seizures and weeping; from the smell of medicinal herbs, fainting, headache, vomiting, and emaciation occur.
From poison arise fainting, diarrhea, a dark complexion, burning sensations, and vertigo; from anger, trembling and headache; and from fear or grief, delirium.

From desire arise delusion, aversion, burning sensations, and the loss of shame, sleep, intellect, and fortitude; in possession by spirits and the like, these symptoms belong to the *sannipāta* (combined) type, while in the case of [affliction by] form and so forth, they belong to the *marut* (wind) type. Of these two, [the latter is characterized as follows].
The two types of severe *sannipāta* fever arising from anger within anger and from bile—those born of curses and malevolent spells—are considered the most unbearable of all.
And it is tormented and scorched by the mantras used for exorcism; first the body suffers here and there, and then [it is afflicted] by eruptions and vertigo.
In one constantly afflicted by fainting, the fever increases day by day; thus fever is seen to be of eight types, yet it is also twofold in brief.

It is bodily or mental, mild or sharp, internal or external in its location, natural (prākṛta) or modified (vaikṛta), curable or incurable, and associated with phlegm (sāma) or free from it (nirāmaka).
Previously, there was heat in the body and heat in the mind; however, due to the movement of the vital winds (pavana) through yoga, it becomes cold when associated with phlegm (śleṣman).

When fever is associated with pitta, there is a burning sensation; when it is mixed, the symptoms are mixed; furthermore, when it is localized internally, there will be excessive complications in the fever, such as internal agitation and the retention of waste products.
Furthermore, external fever with external force is established as being caused by wind and the other humors in their natural order during the rainy season, autumn, and spring respectively.

The other type is the modified (vaikṛta), which is generally difficult to cure; however, the natural (prākṛta) fever arising from vāta is common. In the rainy season, the vitiated vāta produces a fever associated with pitta and kapha.
In autumn, one should pacify the pitta, and its attendant, the kapha; because of their inherent nature and because it is the season of excretion, there is no danger from fasting in that season.
In spring, Kapha [predominates], and Vata and Pitta follow it; fever caused by strong [doshas] in those with few complications is curable.

In every respect, a fever characterized by abnormal symptoms is declared incurable from the outset; likewise are those accompanied by complications, those with intense heat, those with weak digestion, and those with excessive urination.
There is no discharge, no wasting away, and no appearance of hunger or fever; rather, there is an excessive force of fever, thirst, delirium, labored breathing, and vertigo.
The onset of impurity and internal agitation are the signs of the fever being ripened; once it has reached maturity, one should avoid contrary treatments and observe fasting for seven nights.

Fever is said to be of five types according to the strength or weakness of the humors (mala) and the season (kāla); it is generally taught that most cases arise from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta).
The continuous, the constant, the quotidian, the tertian, and the quartan fevers; the humors, urine, feces, and the pervasive impurities flow through the channels.
Scorching the entire body, increased by [the qualities of] equanimity and so forth, they are powerful, heavy, and, being dependent on the *rasas*, affect it without distinction.
They would constantly produce an unbearable fever that is without rival; then, it would quickly exhaust the impurities, the heat, and the bodily constituents.
The various modes of the tastes and so forth, whether pure or impure, [result] respectively from wind, bile, and phlegm after seventeen, twelve, and [ten] days.
"Generally, one follows the boundary for both liberation and destruction"—this is the opinion of Agniveśa, while the traditional teaching of Hārīta is as follows:
The seventh, ninth, and likewise the eleventh lunar days are each double [the duration of the others]; this is the boundary of the three defects, leading both to liberation and to destruction.
Due to purity or impurity, fever may persist here for even a long time in those who are emaciated, afflicted by disease, and consumers of improper diet and other such habits.
Even a minor fault, having acquired strength from any one of the [three] defects such as wind (duṣṭi) and so forth, becomes an adversary because it is accompanied by irregular increase and decrease.

The deranged humor (doṣa), accompanied by mental distraction and characterized by irregular decline and increase, produces fever; being powerful, it manifests at its own specific time to cause the fever.
Furthermore, when its opposing forces have been weakened and its afflictions exhausted, the fever subsides and becomes subtle, dissolving into the bodily constituents such as the rasa.
Because of its sluggishness, it brings about emaciation, discoloration, dullness, and other such states, due to the proximity of the distortions of the channels that carry the vital fluids.
The fault of pervading the entire body does not arise quickly; for the virtuous, it is constant, whereas for others, it is the opposite due to the contrary nature of their practice.
An irregular fever, characterized by an irregular onset and associated with the time of night, is generally a disorder residing in the blood that produces a continuous fever.

At the junction of day and night, one should resort to a single [dose] on another day; in that [condition], the flesh-carrying channel is involved, and in the third-day fever, the fat-carrying channel.
Grāhī arises from pitta and vāta in the head, from kapha and pitta in the trika (the sacral region), and from vāta and kapha involving the back; it is known to recur with an interval of one day.
The fourth [type of fever] resides in the impurities, fat, marrow, or bone; indeed, another [type] residing specifically in the marrow manifests its specific power.
Due to the wind (vāyu), it first enters the elbows and calves in two ways, and then the head; having reached the bones and marrow, it is the fourth-day fever in its reverse form.
It causes fever for three days in three ways, but releases it for one day; this occurs due to the relative strength or weakness of the doshas and the arising of other symptoms and activities.
Due to the non-inversion of the departed [elements], one should observe a fast for seven nights; likewise, fever may arise from the mind and from karma at various times.
Because it moves through the profound elements, because it arises from a combination [of all three humors], and because the humors reach an equal height, the quartan fever is difficult to treat.
Because in these subtle fevers, which are increasingly more remote, the *doṣa* moves slowly and in small quantities through the channels of blood and so forth over a long period of time.

Because it destroys the body without remainder and produces feverish heat and other symptoms, when its progression has been interrupted through effort, the fever is perceived as being accompanied by heat.
Irregular and characterized by irregular undertakings, it follows the course of the night; its movement becomes increasingly slow and its power diminishes accordingly.
In due time, that provoked Dosha produces fever after a long or even a very long duration, according to its similarity with the Rasa and other elements.
Just as a seed sown in the earth and moistened with water does not wait for time to sprout, so too does the seed of faults [take effect].
Just as poison, having gained momentum, carries its strength into the internal seat, so too does the poison of the humors (doṣas), when its strength is augmented by time, become provoked once again.
In this way, irregular fevers such as the *satata* (continuous) and others arise; they are characterized by nausea, heaviness, dejection, breaking pain in the limbs, and yawning.

Loss of appetite, vomiting, and dyspnea occur in all types of fever when the rasa-dhatu is affected; spitting of blood, thirst, dryness, heat, and the appearance of eruptions occur when the rakta-dhatu is affected.

When [the fever] is located in the blood, there is burning sensation, redness, giddiness, intoxication, and delirium; when it is located in the internal heat (pitta), there is thirst, exhaustion, stool that is touched [by mucus], internal burning, vertigo, and darkness [of vision].
When fat is located within the flesh, there is foul odor, twitching of the limbs, excessive sweating, extreme thirst, vomiting, a foul smell from the mouth, or an inability to endure [such symptoms].

In the stage of asthige, there is incoherent speech, exhaustion, loss of appetite, and the breaking sensation in the bones; furthermore, there is the aggravation of the humors (doṣas), awakening from sleep, labored breathing, convulsions of the limbs, and moaning.

Internal burning with external coldness, labored breathing, hiccup, indeed [pain] reaching the marrow, the vision of darkness, the cutting of the vital points (marmans), and stiffness of the penis [occur].

When semen flows toward the base of the penis, death occurs; when it remains within the semen itself, death follows. In the case of the other five [types of flow], they become increasingly difficult to cure as they progress further.
As if smearing the limbs with phlegm and heaviness, accompanied by mild fever, delirium, and coldness, such is the Pralepaka fever.

He suffers from a constant mild fever, is parched, and moves with difficulty due to cold; his limbs are stiff, he is dominated by phlegm (śleṣman), and he becomes one who consumes the strength of his own body.
One who passes urine that has the color of a variety of turmeric and resembles its paste is known as the "Hāridraka" fever; it is considered a fatal variety of fever.
In a person where phlegm and wind are equal and bile is deficient, a fever arises that is intense during the day but mild at night, or conversely, it arises at night.

When the body has had its strength taken away by the sun during the day and has been further dried up by physical exertion, a fever caused by Vata will certainly manifest in the early part of the night.
When the phlegm and bile are situated in the stomach and located below it respectively, half of the body becomes cold and half becomes hot.
When bile is deposited in the body and phlegm is situated at the extremities, the body becomes hot because of that, while the hands and feet become cold.

That [fever] which resides in the lymph-chyle and blood is curable; that which has reached the flesh and fat is difficult to cure; and that which has reached the bone and marrow is incurable, its luster destroyed by those respective parts of the body.
Unconscious and afflicted by the force of the poison, he gazes as if in a rage; he constantly voids hot and foul excrement with great force.

The body becomes light, free from fatigue, delusion, and fever; there is a burning sensation in the mouth, excellence of the sense organs, and absence of pain; there is perspiration, sneezing, a natural inclination of the mind toward yoga, a desire for food, and itching on the head—these are the symptoms of the departure of fever.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Fever and Other Diseases," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Dhanvantari said: Now, therefore, I shall proclaim the diagnosis of *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disease). It is caused by excessively hot, bitter, pungent, sour, salty, and burning substances.
When excessively consumed along with other such foods like *kodrava* and *uddālaka*, the pitta provoked by pitta-disorders causes the liquid blood to faint (become unconscious).
Having attained a state of mutual similarity with those [humors], they pervade the body due to the corruption of bile and blood, as well as from their mutual contact and affliction.
Among those that follow the variations of odor and color, it is designated as "rakta" (red); it originates from the sites of blood, namely the spleen and the liver.
Heaviness of the head, loss of appetite, desire for cold things, a sensation of fumes, sour eructations, vomiting, nausea, cough, dyspnea, giddiness, and exhaustion [are the symptoms].
Redness is not beneficial; there is a fishy odor from the mouth, and you are free from fever. There is a red, yellow, or greenish discoloration of the eyes and other parts.
In this [state], there will be an inability to distinguish between blue, red, yellow, and other colors; one will possess the nature of madness even while dreaming.
When aggravated, it flows upward through the nose, eyes, ears, and mouth; downward through the penis, womb, and anus; and through all the pores of the skin.

Since disorders arising from phlegm (kapha) and other humors located in the upper body are cured by purgation, many medicinal preparations are used for pitta; indeed, purgation is the most excellent medicine for pitta.

Where phlegm (kapha) is the persistent sequela, there too a purgative is the means of purification; for those [patients] in whom it is purified, sweet decoctions that are phlegm-increasing are beneficial.

Those substances which are pungent, bitter, or astringent, or which by their very nature increase phlegm (kapha), or those that move downward, or those that are merely palliative, do not sustain life; therefore, emesis is the means to achieve success in such cases.
Emesis is a mild medicine for pitta, yet it is not a mild remedy for one whose strength persists and who has suppressed the pitta.
For that [patient], astringent and exclusively sweet [therapies] are beneficial; however, when [the disease] is afflicted by both phlegm and wind, it is incurable and requires palliative treatment.
Because it is contrary to the natural order and because no medicine can cure it, it is unbearable; indeed, there is no purificatory treatment whatsoever for this one who moves against the grain.
In cases of raktapitta, purification (śodhana) and reverse-order therapy (pratiloma) are recommended; likewise, pacification (upaśamana) and purification are desired here.
Indeed, when the humors are combined, emesis is beneficial in every respect; for in that case, the movement of the humor is observed to be like the auspicious weapon [striking] its target.
And the complications (upadrava) result from the transformation (vikṛti) of those [doshas]; this has been established therein.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Raktapitta," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Dhanvantari said: Since cough is a disease that acts with great speed, it shall now be described. Five types of cough are recognized, arising from Vāta, Pitta, Kapha, injury (Kṣata), and wasting (Kṣaya).
All of them will be neglected until their destruction, each succeeding one being more powerful than the last; the symptom of those yet to come will be itching in the throat and loss of appetite.
There, the downward-moving wind (anila), having ascended upward and reached the chest, spreads through that throat, causing dryness of the ears, mouth, and throat.
Having filled the channels of the veins, they then cause the limbs to twitch; they seem to toss the eyes about, while the voice becomes distressed and the sides of the body are oppressed.
It proceeds with a crooked sound like that of a cracked bell-metal vessel, causing pain in the heart, sides, and head, as well as delusion, agitation, and loss of voice.
It causes a dry cough accompanied by great force, pain, and sound; with horripilation, it produces dry phlegm which, after being expelled with difficulty, diminishes in quantity.
From pitta arise yellow eyes, a bitter taste in the mouth, fever, and vertigo; there is vomiting of bile and blood, thirst, hoarseness, a sensation of fumes in the throat, and intoxication.
In Kāsavega, there is a continuous sensation like the appearance of stars; due to phlegm, there is slight pain in the chest and head, while the heart feels numb and heavy.
From the application of a paste on the neck, there arises nasal catarrh, vomiting, loss of appetite, horripilation, and the discharge of thick, oily phlegm.
When, through various rash acts such as fighting and so forth performed beyond one's strength, the wind (vāyu) is provoked and becomes afflicted, it becomes powerful and is followed by bile (pitta).
The aggravated [wind] produces cough; by that [aggravation], it causes phlegm mixed with blood, which is yellowish, dark-brown, dry, knotted, and abundant.
One should spit with a throat that is aching and as if split apart, and with a chest pierced as if by sharp needles and afflicted by piercing pain.

Afflicted by a painful sensation like a piercing spear, characterized by breaking pain, oppression, and heat, he experiences joint-splitting pain, fever, labored breathing, thirst, loss of voice, and trembling.
Then, for one suffering from pain in the sides who coos like a pigeon, there occurs vomiting of phlegm and other humors, and his digestive power, strength, and complexion decline.

In one who is emaciated, there is the presence of blood and urine, dyspnea, and stiffness of the back and waist; these are the primary symptoms of Rājayakṣman when the bodily constituents, especially the vital breaths (prāṇas), are aggravated and flee.
In the seat of consumption (yakṣma), they produce a cough and then expectorate phlegm that resembles putrid pus—thin, mixed, and greenish-red.
One sleeps excessively, the heart feels as if it were being pricked and cooked, and there is a sudden desire for heat and cold, excessive eating, and loss of strength.
The mouth becomes glossy, clear, and curved; the eyes become beautiful and radiant; thereafter, all the symptoms of wasting appear in him.

Thus, this cough born of wasting (kṣayaja) destroys the bodies of those who are already emaciated; however, it may be palliable in those who are strong. Likewise, the cough born of chest injury (kṣataja) is also palliable, provided it is of recent onset.

These two may also be established by implication; furthermore, there is a separate sequence for the "to-be-proven" (sādhya) and so forth. All those that are mixed and those requiring nourishment belong to the aged and the elderly.
Since diseases such as cough, dyspnea, consumption, vomiting, and loss of voice arise from neglect, one should therefore conquer them with haste.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Cough," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Dhanvantari said: Now, therefore, I shall proclaim the diagnosis of the disease of dyspnea (śvāsa). Dyspnea arises from the aggravation of cough or through previous provokers of the bodily humors (doṣas).
Even by dysentery, diarrhea, vomiting, poison, jaundice, and fever; by dust, smoke, wind, injury to the vital organs, or by cold water—

The five types [of tamaka-shvāsa] are the minor (kṣudraka), the intermittent (tamaka), the interrupted (chinna), the great (mahat), and the fifth, the upward-moving (ūrdhva); in these, the wind, obstructed by phlegm, moves in all directions.
Situated in the chest, it vitiates the channels that carry breath, water, and food; thus corrupted, it produces asthma originating from the stomach (āmāśaya).

Its premonitory symptoms are pain in the heart and the sides, upward movement of the vital breath (prāṇa), constipation, and a splitting sensation in the temples; in this condition, exertion and overeating [aggravate it].
Impelled by the wind, that same impure wind itself, impelling the minor [channels], moves against the grain through the vessels after the wind has provoked the phlegm.
Seizing the head and neck and pressing upon the chest and sides, it causes severe coughing, wheezing, delusion, loss of appetite, and a thick nasal discharge.
He produces a breath of intense force that afflicts the vital breath; he faints from its impulse, and finds momentary relief at the end of each spitting.
Lying down, he breathes with difficulty; when seated, he seeks relief; his eyes are wide open, his forehead is profusely perspiring, and he is in extreme pain.
With a parched mouth, frequent breathing, and trembling, the patient longs for warmth; the condition increases with clouds, rain, cold, eastern winds, and substances that increase *śleṣman*.
That astamaka fever, though generally palliable, may become curable in a strong man; however, the first type of it does not subside with cold treatments when accompanied by fever and fainting.

Afflicted by the pain of the tearing of vital organs like that of coughing and labored breathing, he suffers from perspiration, fainting, abdominal distension, and the sensation of burning and awakening in the bladder.
With his gaze cast downward, his eyes sunken, and one eye bloodshot with affection, his mouth parched, he was wailing in distress, deprived of luster and consciousness.
Gasping with a most terrible and piteous sound, he wheezes, tossing about restlessly and incessantly like a frenzied bull in rut.
His knowledge and discernment were lost; his eyes and face were bewildered; he rolled his eyes, his urine and feces were suppressed, and his speech was faltering.
With a parched throat, and with excessive pain in the ears, temples, and head, he who breathes out long and upward but cannot draw it back down;
With his mouth and ears obstructed by phlegm and afflicted by the enraged wind, he looks upward with wandering eyes, casting them about on all sides.
When the vital points (marmas) are being severed, one who laments with speech restrained will fail; these [spirits] remain unmanifest, but when manifest, they certainly take away life.
Thus ends the one hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Asthma," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Dhanvantari said: O Suśruta, I shall now declare the diagnosis of the disease of hiccough; listen to that. [I shall describe] its single cause, its premonitory symptoms, its classifications, and its various types.
Hiccough is of five types: arising from food, minor, twin, great, and deep; it is caused there by wind through improper and hurried consumption.
Afflicted by food and drink that is dry, sharp, rough, and unsoothing, the vital air (prāṇa) produces hiccups that are soft-sounding and follow upon hunger.
That [hiccup] which occurs equally with meals and drinks is born of food (sānnajā); when the vital air is provoked by exhaustion, it brings about the minor hiccup (kṣudrā hikkā).
Flowing from the base of the collarbone, it indeed possesses a slow velocity; it increases with physical exertion and becomes soft immediately after eating.
That hiccup which proceeds with slow and twin-like impulses increases in intensity at the beginning and continues to grow as it reaches its conclusion.
One should designate that as *yamala* when it causes the head and neck to tremble, and is accompanied by delirium, vomiting, diarrhea, rolling of the eyes, and yawning.
That [disease] is Yamalā, Veginī, Hikrā, and Parināmavatī; it belongs to one whose pair of eyebrows and temples are destroyed, and whose eyes have lost their hearing.
Paralyzing the body, speech, memory, and consciousness, it torments the seeker and strikes at his vital points.
Bowing down from behind, the Great Serpent-Stride proceeds with envy; it possesses great pain, great sound, great speed, and great power.
And from the heart or from the navel, it proceeds as before.
Possessing such a form, she may perform great yawning and stretching; however, one who is profound through a profound causal basis shall accomplish it well.

One should avoid the first two [types of diarrhea], as well as those with all symptoms, the acute (veginī), that which is chronic in everyone, and that of an elderly person who indulges in sexual intercourse.
For one whose body is emaciated by diseases and weakened by the cessation of food, all illnesses lead to destruction; however, they do not act with such rapidity as this.
Hiccups and dyspnea, for they indeed take up residence at the time of death.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Hiccup," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Dhanvantari said: Now, therefore, I shall proclaim the diagnosis of the disease of consumption (yakṣman), which is followed by many diseases and is the precursor of many diseases.
Rājayakṣmā, kṣaya, śoṣa, and rogarāj are its names; for in ancient times, it was the king of the stars, the twice-born, and of kings.

And because it is both a king (rājan) and consumption (yakṣman), it is therefore considered *rājayakṣmā* (kingly consumption); furthermore, it is called *kṣaya* (consumption) because it causes the wasting away of the body and the medicinal substances, and because it arises from that [wasting].

The King of Diseases is called "Drying" (śoṣa) because it dries up the bodily fluids and other constituents, just as a king [rules over his subjects]. Its cause is rashness and the suppression of natural urges, which leads to the depletion of semen, vitality, and unctuousness.
The improper abandonment of the rules for food and drink are its four causes; by these, the wind (vāyu) is provoked, which then needlessly excites the bile (pitta) throughout the entire body.
Entering the joints of the body, they afflict those vessels, either blocking the openings of the channels or likewise discharging them excessively.
It causes pain in the middle, upper, lower, and lateral parts of the heart; its future form will be severe catarrh and fever.
Excessive salivation, sweetness in the mouth, softness of the digestive fire and the heart, a state of greed for food and drink, and perceiving the pure as impure;
The falling of flies, grass, hair, and the like into food and drink generally causes nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, and a decline in strength, even after one has bathed.
Excessive whiteness of the hands, thighs, chest, feet, face, belly, and eyes; a goad on the arms; [excessive whiteness] of the tongue; and the sight of loathsomeness in the body.
A fondness for women, liquor, and meat; loathsomeness; veiling the head; the growth of nails, hair, and bones; and being overcome in a dream—these shall come to pass.
There is falling by lizards, snakes, monkeys, beasts of prey, and birds; and one mounts upon hair, bones, husks, ashes, and other such things.
Seeing deserted villages and regions, the drying up of waters, celestial lights in the sky, and forest fires blazing among the trees;
When located in the trunk (koṣṭha), it causes chronic catarrh, dyspnea, cough, pain in the voice box and head, loss of appetite, upward breathing, dryness, and downward vomiting.
When pain and awareness are located at the side and situated at the joints, fever arises; these eleven symptoms are produced by *rājayakṣman*.
One should recognize their complications as diseases that cause the destruction of the throat, along with yawning, body aches, spitting, diminished digestive fire, and foul breath.
In that condition, due to Vāta, there is pain in the head and sides, body aches, obstruction of the throat, and loss of voice; due to Pitta, [pain occurs] in the feet, shoulders, and hands.
Burning sensation, diarrhea, vomiting of blood, foul breath, fever, intoxication, anorexia, vomiting, cough, heaviness in the head and body—these arise from phlegm (kapha).

Excessive salivation, chronic rhinitis, dyspnea, hoarseness of voice, and weak digestion arise from the humors (doṣas), due to the dullness of the digestive fire and the predominance of swelling, coating, and phlegm.
When the channels are obstructed and the bodily constituents (dhātus) are diminished, a burning sensation arises in the seat of the mind, and other complications indeed ensue.
Food mixed with sour juices is digested right there in the stomach; generally, for those whose constituent elements are diminished, food does not lead to the nourishment of the body.
For its essence does not serve for blood or flesh; rather, being supported on all sides, it exists solely as that which is subject to decay.

If the signs are slight, one should avoid treating a patient whose disease is extremely emaciated and whose six functional organs have deteriorated; otherwise, one should certainly treat them even in all such cases.
Due to the individual or combined doshas, and from the depletion of all the fat, hoarseness of voice occurs; his voice becomes weak, dry, and unstable.

From vāta, there is a throat that has the appearance of a parrot's color and is pacified by unctuous and warm treatments; from pitta, there is a burning sensation in the palate and throat, and constant dryness occurs.
The throat feels as if smeared with phlegm and the mouth makes a wheezing sound; when all the symptoms are present simultaneously and mutually contradictory, it becomes *kṣaya* (wasting disease).

There is excessive smoky appearance and the emergence of symptoms characteristic of *śleṣman* (phlegm); here, wasting diseases (*kṣaya*) are difficult to cure, and one should avoid those that are slight in all respects.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Consumption," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Chapter 153] Dhanvantari said: O Suśruta, I shall now declare the diagnosis of anorexia (arocaka). Anorexia arises from the humors (doṣas) localized in the tongue and the heart.

The fifth [type of taste] arises from the combination [of all three humors] and from mental distress; the mouth becomes astringent, bitter, and sweet respectively in cases of wind and the other [humors].

The mind becomes entirely devoid of its natural flavor when afflicted by grief, anger, and the like; it is likewise corrupted by each of the individual humors (doṣas), by all of them combined, and by other factors as the fifth.

The *udāna* wind expels all the faults that have been accumulated and are ready for elimination; consequently, his afflictions quickly subside, and in due course, he experiences a distaste for worldly pleasures.
The navel and back ache quickly, and one vomits food; thereafter, one vomits frothy matter that is thin, scanty, and slightly astringent.

Accompanied by the emission of sounds, occurring with great difficulty or easily and with forceful urgency, it causes coughing and dryness of the mouth, and is associated with affliction of the voice due to Vāta.

Due to pitta, [the vomitus] resembles alkaline water, is smoky-colored, greenish-yellow, or bloody; it is sour, pungent, and bitter, and is accompanied by thirst, fainting, burning sensations, and suppuration.
From *kapha*, it is unctuous, thick, yellow, and mixed with honey-like phlegm; it is sweet, salty, copious, persistent, and causes horripilation.
Accompanied by loss of appetite, swelling, sweetness in the mouth, drowsiness, nausea, and cough—when possessed of all these symptoms, the patient should be abandoned in every respect.

Everything is loathsome to him through sight, hearing, and so forth; in diseases born of wind and the like, or those caused by worms or contaminated food, colic, trembling, and nausea occur, especially in that which is born of worms.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Anorexia," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious *Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*.

Dhanvantari said: O Suśruta, I shall now describe to you the diagnosis of heart disease and other ailments. Heart diseases are traditionally classified as fivefold, including those caused by worms (*kṛmi*) and those affecting the heart itself.
Due to wind, emptiness is excessively experienced; one weeps bitterly, the heart feels as if it is being split, parched, or paralyzed, and there is a sensation of voidness and dizziness.
Sudden dejection, grief, fear, lack of interest in sound, trembling, shaking, delusion, obstruction of breath, and sleeplessness;

From pitta arise thirst, fatigue, and a burning sensation; from kapha, there is sweating and a sequence of sour eructations. Vomiting of sour bile and a fever characterized by a smoky appearance [are also present].
Due to phlegm, the heart becomes stiff and heavy as if filled with stones; there is cough, weakness in the bones, spitting, drowsiness, lassitude, loss of appetite, and fever.
In heart disease caused by the three doshas and by worms, there is darkening of the eyes, entry into darkness (fainting), nausea, swelling, itching, and discharge of phlegm.
And here, the heart is constantly torn as if by a saw, as one attempts to treat this terrible disease that brings death so swiftly, indeed very swiftly.

Thirst arises from wind (vāta), bile (pitta), phlegm (kapha), and their combination (sannipāta); the sixth type occurs from the loss of strength (balakṣaya) and from complications (upasarga), with wind and bile being the causes.
Indeed, when provoked in all [the bodily constituents], it causes the complete drying up of the dhātus, and produces confusion, trembling, burning sensations, and delusion throughout the entire body.

Thirst arises when the vessels carrying blood to the root of the tongue, the throat, the internal membranes, the palate, and the mouth are dried up; this is the general characteristic of these [types of thirst].
Dryness of the mouth, lack of thirst for water, aversion to food, loss of voice, roughness of the throat, lips, and palate, and exhaustion upon protruding the tongue [are the symptoms].
Incoherent speech, mental derangement, excessive belching, and likewise illness; from wind (vāta), emaciation, dejection, ringing in the ears, and dizziness of the head [arise].

From pitta arise loss of the sense of smell, bad taste in the mouth, impairment of hearing, loss of sleep and strength, an increase in coldness, acidity, and froth, as well as fainting and a bitter taste in the mouth.

Constant redness of the eyes, emaciation, burning sensation, and excessive tearing occur when the phlegm is provoked from the rasa-dhatu and the wind (vāta) is provoked in the water-carrying channels.
The channel, however, being filled with phlegm, is then dried up like mud; consequently, the throat feels as if covered with bristles, there is drowsiness, and sweetness in the mouth.
Distension of the abdomen, heaviness of the head, numbness, vomiting, anorexia, lassitude, and indigestion—this is the type characterized by all symptoms.
From the suppression of blood arising from [suppressed] semen, or from the suppression of vāta and pitta, thirst occurs in one who has suddenly partaken of cold water after being overcome by heat.

That which arises from heat moves upward to the stomach and is indeed born of bile; that which arises from excessive drinking and intoxication has a sharp onset, as does that produced by the improper cooking of fats.

Thirst arising from phlegm is caused by the consumption of unctuous, pungent, sour, and salty foods; that which is of the nature of depletion is characterized by the symptoms described for the loss of rasa.
That intense thirst which arises from other long-term diseases and afflictions such as consumption, delusion, and fever is known as being characterized by secondary complications (*upasarga*).
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Acid Bile (Āmlapitta)," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Dhanvantari said: I shall declare the diagnosis of alcoholism (madātyaya) and other related conditions as spoken by the sages. [Alcohol] is sharp, sour, dry, subtle, acidic, habit-forming, difficult to digest, and light.
Wine is expansive and clear; its opposite is fat. Furthermore, qualities that arise acutely, those occurring during the day, and those that cause mental agitation [are also contrary].

Beings are brought to the end of their lives by poison acting with intensity; likewise, liquor, through its qualities such as sharpness and the like, destroys the qualities of the vital energy that is otherwise characterized by dullness and weakness.
Through ten qualities, he brings his mind to a state free from activity and free from agitation; thus he abides in the first and even the second stage of intoxication, which is the abode of joy.
Stricken by false conceptualization, the fool is deluded into thinking this is happiness; having reached the junction between the mediocre and the superior, intoxication becomes his royal throne.
Like an unrestrained serpent, one might do anything; therefore, this ground is for the unspeakable and is the abode of immorality.
This one is the supreme guide for those on the many paths of this difficult terrain; yet, remaining motionless, he lies face down, situated here in the third stage of intoxication.
Even after death, the evil-souled one goes to an even more wretched state—[judged by] dharma and adharma, pleasure and pain, honor and misfortune, and what is beneficial and what is harmful.
One who is afflicted by delusion and confusion does not know; joined with emaciation, delusion, and the like, he falls downward along with madness, wandering, and fainting, accompanied by epilepsy.

Those who are strong, have eaten well, or are great eaters do not become excessively intoxicated. The disease known as *madātyaya* (alcoholism) arises from *vāta*, *pitta*, *kapha*, or from all three combined.
Their general characteristics are profound delusion, pain in the heart, violent breaking [of the body], thirst, somnolence, exhaustion, fever, and loss of appetite.
Visual obstruction, darkness before the eyes, cough, dyspnea, insomnia, excessive perspiration, constipation, swelling, and mental confusion [arise].
He is overcome as if by a dream, and though spoken to, he does not respond; from bile (pitta) there arise burning fever, perspiration, delusion, and constant confusion.

In the case of phlegm (kapha), there is vomiting, nausea, sleepiness, and heaviness of the abdomen; in the case of all three combined (sarvaja), all symptoms are present. Having recognized this, one who drinks liquor [should be treated accordingly].
Suddenly, both [the eyes] may become beautiful yet subject to destruction and wasting; this occurs especially due to a severe wind disorder (*māruta*).
Spitting of phlegm that destroys [the voice], dryness of the throat, excessive sleepiness, intolerance of sound, distraction of the mind, and indeed wind-pain in the limbs [are the symptoms].

Heart disease, throat ailments, delusion, dyspnea, thirst, vomiting, and fever—these afflict one who does not turn away from intoxicants; however, he who has conquered his self and acts with discernment shall be free from them.
He who has abandoned passion, delusion, and unwholesome food is never afflicted by physical or mental disorders; these three would otherwise be his diseases.

Intoxication (mada), fainting (mūrchā), and prostration (apasaṃnyāsa) arise from the obstruction of the channels that carry fat, blood, and moisture; they manifest according to the increasing strength of the [doshas] involved.

In this state, intoxication arises from all defects, as well as from blood, liquor, and poisons; due to the infinity of its powers, it is a deceptive appearance, flickering, treacherous, and enveloping.
In intoxication arising from wind (vāta), the body becomes rough, dark, and reddish; through bile (pitta), one is prone to anger, has a reddish-yellow complexion, and is fond of quarreling.

In dreams, one who is dominated by phlegm (kapha) utters incoherent speech and is intent on meditation; through the combination of all [humors] (sannipāta), there occurs stiffness of the blood and corruption of the limbs.
The symptoms of bile (pitta) are present at the outset; here, there is a distorted sense of one's own authority, trembling, excessive sleep, and exhaustion greater than all others.

One should diagnose wind and the other humors among the blood and other tissues by observing the excellence of their specific characteristics: [blood affected by] wind becomes reddish, blue, or black, and the patient enters into darkness as if plunging into it.
One awakens quickly; there is pain in the heart, trembling, dizziness, coughing, a dusky-red complexion, and fainting—these are the symptoms when [the disease] is of the nature of wind (māruta).
Seeing the sky as red or yellow due to bile, one enters into darkness; and upon awakening, one is afflicted by sweat, burning heat, and thirst.
One whose appearance is like that of a broken jar, with eyes agitated by red and blue, sees the sky resembling a cloud due to phlegm; one should enter [the practice] while observing this.
After a long time, I awoke from that darkness; my heart and chest were overflowing with moisture, and my limbs were heavy and motionless, as if bound by the laws of royalty.
Possessing every hideous form, like another seizure caused by the three humors, it quickly casts one down motionless, even without loathsome movements.
When the humors (doṣas) have completed their onset in the states of intoxication and fainting in embodied beings, they subside by themselves, whether through renunciation or by means of medicines.
Exceedingly powerful, they paralyzed the activity of speech, body, and mind; having fallen into a state of total renunciation, they took refuge in the destruction of their vital breaths.
Because of that, men become like wood and resemble the dead; they would die quickly, very quickly, if medical treatment were not applied.
One should quickly turn back a man who is sinking into renunciation, which is like a fathomless ocean with its vast currents of water teeming with crocodiles.
Driven here and there by the activities of pride, anger, and passion, one applies logic equally to what is reasonable and unreasonable; this is not the case when one is intoxicated by liquor.
Having distinguished between the vessel that is the region of the heart, its natural capacity, or its age, one drinks accordingly; thereafter, one drinks the nectar.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Alcoholism and Other Disorders," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Dhanvantari said: Now, O Suśruta, I shall explain the diagnosis of hemorrhoids (ārśas), those peg-like growths which always arise upon the flesh of living beings.
Therefore they are called *arśāṃsi* because they obstruct the passage of the rectum; the humors (*doṣa*), having corrupted the skin, flesh, and fat, produce various forms [of growths].
They say that fleshy sprouts arising from food, drink, and so forth produce hemorrhoids; briefly, they are divided into two types: congenital and those arising from another [previous] birth.

The fissures at the tips of the dried [flesh], located along the region of the anus, measure four and a half finger-breadths; within that, three [fissures] are situated at a distance of two and a half finger-breadths.
The *bālyapravāhiṇī* [channel] among them is the *visarjinī* within the middle of the anus; it is for external non-restraint, located one finger-breadth outside the anus and so forth.
Beyond that, the body hairs there measure one and a half finger-breadths; the reason for this is that, although they arise simultaneously [with the body], their seeds were scorched during childhood.

The production of the seeds of hemorrhoids occurs due to the misconduct of the mother and father, from the provocation of the deities, or from another cause such as a derangement of the humors (sānnipāta).
Thus, all diseases arising from one's family lineage are declared to be incurable; those that are congenital are especially so, being harsh and unsightly.
The internal, pale, and those with severe complications should be applied separately according to the individual doshas, their combinations, and their accumulation.
The [tumors] caused by vāta and kapha are dry, while those caused by pitta are moist; the causes for the provocation of the doshas are as previously stated regarding clothing and other factors.
When the impurity is excessively accumulated in the fire [of the stomach], this [disease] arises again through sexual intercourse, from drinking, agitation, irregularity, hard food, or meager food.

From the friction caused by the breaking of the ground arising from the eyes, neck, lips, and so forth of the riding animal, and from contact with extremely cold water and continuous, excessive straining;
From the suppression of the urge to void urine or feces, or from their forced expulsion, there arise disgust, diarrhea, and indeed *grahaṇī*; this too is a complication.

Furthermore, from physical exertion, exposure to uneven ground and the like, and especially from the activities of women—such as the miscarriage of an immature fetus or the excessive pressure of a growing fetus—[the fetus may suffer].
By these and other such factors, the apāna wind becomes aggravated within the waste; it then resides in the folds of the rectum, which are moist, active, and full-bodied with a brilliant appearance.
Before they are born, these are the symptoms: weakness of the digestive fire, constipation, aching of the bones, cramps in the calves, and vertigo.
There is swelling of the eyes that are closed tight, or there may be retention of feces; furthermore, the wind (vāyu), being obstructed, generally moves below the navel.
Accompanied by blood, cutting pain, and labored contraction with labored breathing, there is rumbling in the intestines, flatulence, and an abundance of caustic eructations.
There is abundant urine, scanty feces, loss of appetite, a smoky sensation in the abdomen, pain in the head, back, and chest, lassitude, and diarrhea.

Lust for the objects of the senses, anger arising from the experience of suffering, apprehension, dysentery, swelling, and [diseases such as] jaundice, abdominal tumors, and enlargement of the abdomen.
These very [defilements] increase when those whose names have not yet been struck down are born; for pride, being turned back by them, blocks the downward path.
It agitates the other winds within all the sense organs and the body, likewise drying up the urine, feces, bile, phlegm, and wind.
Then, having stolen the digestive fire, they all generally become afflicted by hemorrhoids; the person becomes extremely emaciated, his energy destroyed, dejected, wasted away, and lusterless.
Devoid of essence and shorn of luster like a tree consumed by fire, he was seized by the agonizing, violent, and fierce maladies described by Yakṣma that afflict the vital organs.
Likewise, [it is characterized] by cough, thirst, bad taste in the mouth, dyspnea, catarrh, exhaustion, breaking pain in the limbs, vomiting, sneezing, swelling, and fever.
Afflicted by impotence, deafness, numbness, and gravel-like grit in the throat, emaciated, with a broken voice, he meditates repeatedly while spitting and suffering from loss of appetite.
One suffers from pain in all the joints, bones, heart, navel, anus, and groins, and bile flows from the rectum resembling the color of a blue crane's belly.
The stool is passed as dry, with mucus at its tip, alternating between digested and undigested matter; it is pale-yellow like turmeric, stained yellow, and slimy.
The anal papillae are characterized by an excess of wind (vāta), being dry, accompanied by a tingling sensation, swollen, reddish like glowing embers, rigid, uneven, and rough in appearance.
Mutually dissimilar, crooked, sharp, and with gaping mouths, they resemble the fruits of the *śimbī*, the date palm, the *karkandhu* jujube, and the cotton plant.
Some resemble kadamba flowers, while others are like mustard seeds; they cause excessive pain in the head, sides, shoulders, calves, thighs, groins, and other parts.
They cause sneezing, eructation, constipation, oppression in the chest, and loss of appetite; they bring about cough, dyspnea, irregularity of digestion, ringing in the ears, and vertigo.
Afflicted by these [doshas], one passes stool that is knotted, scanty, noisy, accompanied by mucus, followed by frothy blood and slimy discharge, and obstructed.

His skin becomes black, and his feces, urine, eyes, and face become bound [with darkness]; indeed, for him, there arises the occurrence of abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic enlargement (plīhodara), and prostate-like growths (aṣṭhīlā).
Those dominated by pitta have blue mouths and a reddish-yellow or blackish luster; they have thin tips, secrete fluid, are spread out, small, soft, and flaccid.
Resembling the tongue of a parrot, fragments of liver, or the mouth of a leech, they cause burning, wasting, fever, perspiration, thirst, fainting, loss of appetite, and delusion.
They possess heat, are liquid, blue, hot, yellow, red, and of pale-white complexion; they have barley-shaped middles, and their skin, nails, and other features are green, yellow, or turmeric-colored.
Those [tumors] dominated by phlegm (śleṣman) have large roots, are dense, cause mild pain, and are white; they are protruded, enlarged, unctuous, stiff, round, heavy, and firm.
They are slimy, motionless, smooth, abundant with itching, and pleasant to the touch; they resemble the seeds of the *karīra* and *panasa* fruits, as well as cow's udders.
It causes distension of the groins, suppuration of the scrotum, cutting pain in the bladder and navel, along with cough, dyspnea, nausea, excessive salivation, anorexia, and coryza.
[Excessive] use of *kṣāra* causes great suffering, heaviness of the head, coldness, debility, weakness of the digestive fire, vomiting, diarrhea, and other such disorders.
The discharges of fat, semen, phlegm, abundant feces, and blood do not flow out nor do they break through; the skin and other parts become pale and oily.

Due to the combination of symptoms and the accumulation of associated disorders, these hemorrhoids possess all the clinical characteristics; they are blood-dominant, appear like growths at the anus, and are endowed with a yellowish appearance.
Resembling the sprouts of the banyan tree and similar to guñjā berries or coral, they are exceedingly harmful, hot, and afflicted by severe constipation.
Blood flows out suddenly due to its excessive discharge, and the patient suffers from the pains arising from the depletion of blood.
With diminished complexion, strength, and enthusiasm, his vital energy destroyed and his senses clouded by the consumption of mung beans, kodrava, jambīra, karīra, chickpeas, and the like.
Vata, provoked by dry and constipating factors, becomes powerful in the seat of feces; obstructing the downward-moving channels, it dries up the lower parts.
Feces may cause severe obstruction of flatus, feces, and urine; by that, intense pain arises in the abdomen, back, heart, and sides.
There is distension of the abdomen, stool, nausea, cutting pain, and especially colic in the bladder, as well as the occurrence of swellings on the cheeks.
Due to the upward movement of the wind (vāyu), there arise vomiting, loss of appetite, fever, heart disease, disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī), urinary retention, and dysentery.
Deafness, excessive headache, dyspnea, pain in the head, cough, chronic catarrh, mental disorders, thirst, asthma, bilious disorders, abdominal tumors, abdominal diseases, and so forth.
And these extremely dreadful diseases born of wind arise; this is the supreme complication, characterized by hemorrhoids, death, and upward movement of gases.

In those whose digestive tract is overcome by wind (vāta), [the disease] arises even without those [external causes]; however, the innate defects (doṣas) which reside within the inner membrane (valī) [also cause it].

Those [diseases] that are established [in the body] are incurable; those born from the combination of two [humors], as well as those located in the second stage and supported by strength, are palliable through the power of the digestive fire and other factors.

They say that those [tumors] which have persisted for more than a year are difficult to cure; likewise, those born on the outer layer of skin (bāhyā valī) and those aggravated by a single doṣa are hard to treat.

Hemorrhoids that have not been present for long are easily curable; those occurring in the penis and other such areas will be described according to their respective locations, as will those born from the umbilical region.
The Vyāna wind, having taken up the phlegm along with the slimy and soft tissues of a mole, produces hemorrhoids on the exterior of the skin.

They know this [condition] to be like a wedge, firm and hard, and specifically as a "leather-wedge" (carmakīla). From Vāta, there is pricking pain and roughness; from Pitta, there is blackness at the edges.

The sliminess, the knottedness, and the discoloration of the phlegm [are signs]; therefore, a wise person should quickly exert effort toward the pacification of hemorrhoids, for they quickly cause the disease known as obstructed intestinal obstruction (baddhagudodara).
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Hemorrhoids," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Dhanvantari said: O Suśruta, I shall now describe the diagnosis of diarrhea (atīsāra) and dysentery (grahaṇī). These are of six types, caused by the humors (doṣas) individually, by all of them combined, and by fear and grief.
That diarrhea arises all the more intensely from drinking excessive water, as well as from dried foods, fat, oil, sesame paste, and sprouted grains.

Due to the consumption of alcohol, dry substances, or excessive quantities of food, from the disorder caused by excessive unctuousness, and from the presence of parasites or incompatible foods, the wind (vāyu) becomes aggravated in that manner.

It causes the downward wind (apānavāyu) to disperse; by striking the digestive fire with that very wind, it activates the functions of the stomach, the rectum, and the liquefaction of feces and excrement.
The symptoms of that impending diarrhea manifest as a breaking pain in the heart, anus, and abdomen, perspiration of the limbs, and retention of waste matter.
In that condition, there is distension and indigestion; due to the wind, it is free from fever, and one voids very small amounts of stool that are soundless, devoid of fecal matter, and obstructed.
The urine is rough, frothy, and clear, or it is drawn in frequent spurts; likewise, it has the appearance of burnt meat, is slimy, and causes cutting pain.
With a parched and prolapsed anus, his hair bristling and sighing deeply, he vomits what was eaten as yellowish-green, tinged with bile, resembling the color of young grass.

Accompanied by phlegm, it is reddish, extremely foul-smelling, and characterized by thirst, fainting, perspiration, and a burning sensation; it is thick and involves pain, heat, and suppuration in the anus.
In that condition, there is slimy, scanty, and continuous discharge accompanied by tenesmus; there is horripilation, distress, and heaviness in the bladder, anus, and abdomen.

Even when [the ritual] has been performed, he remains unattached; the soul of all, possessing all characteristics, he would cause that which was done to melt away when the mind is agitated by fear and laid low.

Then the wind (vāyu) should be quickly checked by means of hot, liquid, and floating substances; they say that the symptoms in cases of balanced vāta and pitta are the same as those arising from grief.

Briefly stated, diarrhea is of two types: with undigested matter (sāma) and without it (nirāmaka). When the disease of the rasa-dhatu arises along with blood, due to heaviness one voids stool in water; the feces are foul-smelling, accompanied by flatulence, distension, pain, and excessive salivation.

The opposite condition is *nirāma*; however, due to *kapha*, some do not even sink [into the disease]. Among those with diarrhea, one who is not diligent [in treatment] suffers from the disease of *grahaṇī*.

Due to his excessive accumulation of the effects of extinguishing the digestive fire, he may suffer from diarrhea—either with mucus or without mucus—caused by the digestion of food that has been improperly processed.

That diarrhea, by its very nature, is characterized by excessive flow and rapid evacuation; it occurs through undigested food when it is still raw, but when the food is digested, it does not occur at all.

Cirakṛt grahaṇī-doṣa causes the accumulation and discharge of stools; it may cause sudden diarrhea or sudden constipation, or alternating episodes of both. It arises in four ways: from each of the individual doṣas and from their combination (sannipāta).
The premonitory symptoms are a sense of heaviness in the limbs, diminished breath, excessive salivation, a bad taste in the mouth, loss of appetite, thirst, fatigue, and vertigo.
Distension of the abdomen, vomiting, a ringing sound even in the ears, emaciation, nausea, suppressed eructation, and fever are the general symptoms [of poisoning].
Fainting, headache, constipation, swelling of the hands and feet, drowsiness, dryness of the palate due to wind (vāta), darkness before the eyes, and ringing in the ears [occur].
It causes pain in the sides, thighs, groins, and neck, as well as acute cholera-like cramps; it increases all diseases when they have already manifested, and it wards off hunger and thirst.

When digested, it causes flatulence; when eaten, one attains well-being. From [excessive] wind (vāta), there arises suspicion of heart disease, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, and anemia.

After a long time, one repeatedly voids feces that is painful, liquid, dry, hard, and accompanied by sound and froth; moreover, there is discharge from the anus along with labored breathing and coughing.

Due to the yellow [dosha], one emits liquid that has a yellowish-blue luster or a yellow appearance; the patient is afflicted by foul-smelling and sour eructations, burning sensations in the heart and throat, loss of appetite, and thirst.
Due to phlegm, there is suffering in digestion, mental distress, vomiting, anorexia, burning of the mouth, spitting, coughing, nausea, and rhinitis.
The heart feels as if weighted down by torpor; the abdomen is motionless and heavy; eructations are foul and sweet; and there is a sense of exhaustion accompanied by horripilation.

In the case of the combined type (*sarvaja*), the stool is discharged mixed with mucus and bound together by heavy and sour substances; there is weakness even in one who is not emaciated, and all the symptoms of the individual types are observed.

The three impurities, thirst and the rest, which are declared in the section on the constituent parts (of the body), are also the defects of the *grahaṇī* in this [treatment]; they are the cause for all [the preceding] conditions.

Vāta diseases, urinary stones, leprosy, urinary disorders, abdominal dropsy, fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, and chronic diarrhea—these eight are the great diseases that are extremely difficult to overcome.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Urinary Disorders," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Dhanvantari said: Now, therefore, O Suśruta, listen to the diagnosis of urinary obstruction (mūtraghāta). The bladder, the head of the bladder, the penis, the waist, the scrotum, and the anus—these are the locations [affected].
The rectal bone cavities are said to have a single channel; for even though the bladder is downward-facing, it is connected by the openings of the urine-carrying channels.
They fill the lateral channels with smooth (subtle) fluids that flow incessantly; having entered through those very same [channels], they produce the twenty types of disorders.
Urinary obstruction and prameha afflict the vital organs with difficulty, causing pain in the bladder, groins, and penis, characterized by frequent voiding of urine in very small quantities.

In the Vataja type, urine is passed with difficulty; in the Pittaja type, it is yellow and accompanied by constant burning and pain; in the Kaphaja type, it is reddish, and there is heaviness and swelling of the bladder and penis.

When the wind, having turned back from the opening of the bladder and drying it up, is accompanied by all impurities and possesses their entire nature, it becomes associated with desire and obstruction.
Then, from that urine mixed with bile, phlegm, or semen, a terrible stone (aśmarī) is gradually formed, just as bile [forms] the gallstone (rocanā) in a cow.
All [types of this disease] have phlegm (śleṣman) as their substrate; furthermore, its premonitory symptom is distension of the bladder and intense pain all around its vicinity.

Obstruction of urine, difficulty in urination, fever, and loss of appetite are the general symptoms; there is pain in the navel, the perineal suture (sīvanī), the bladder, and the region above the bladder.
In that condition, the urine becomes copious, and likewise during the obstruction of the passage; having bound it firmly, one voids it with ease—clear and resembling cow-dung stones (gomedaka).
From its agitation, there arises blood and flesh on the path, and pain occurs; therein, afflicted by the onset of wind (vāta), the patient gnashes his teeth and trembles.
It seizes the penis and excessively pains the navel; accompanied by wind, it discharges feces repeatedly and passes urine drop by drop.
His urinary stone (aśmarī) will be dark and rough, as if covered with thorns; due to the pitta, the bladder feels burning and hot, as if it were being cooked.
The stone (aśmarī) formed from phlegm is shaped like the kernel of a bhallātaka fruit, red, yellow, or white; it causes the bladder to feel as if it is being pricked, and it is cold and heavy.
The stone (aśmarī) is large, smooth, honey-colored, or white; these occur in children, and most frequently in them alone.

Because the accumulation of seminal fluid is slight, one is comfortable in its retention and discharge; however, a large stone of semen (śukrāśmarī) arises from the suppression of the emission of semen.
The wind, having seized the semen that has either fallen from its place or is unexpelled within the testicles, dries it up; that semen thus becomes a stone (aśmarī).
It causes pain in the bladder, difficulty in urination, and produces white swelling; as soon as it arises, it becomes dry and dissolves away.

In this condition afflicted by fever and cough, there is gravel (śarkarā) just like a stone (aśmarī); or rather, that [stone] is broken apart by the wind, whereas this [gravel] occurs when the wind moves in its natural downward direction.
It exits together with urine; when the process is reversed, it undergoes digestion. Retention of urine causes the enraged Vāyu to become obstructed at the opening of the bladder.

In cases of urinary obstruction, pain, or itching, and sometimes when there is a discharge from the left side, one should incise the bladder after lifting it up, reaching as far as the edge of the uterus, and then excise the thickened, prolapsed portion.
When the bladder is pressed, it causes pain and burning there, as well as throbbing and cramps; furthermore, urine is discharged drop by drop.
This obstruction of the flow is also known as vātabasti; it is difficult to overcome, while the second type, involving powerful vāyu, is even more difficult to overcome.
The Vāyu, having taken refuge in the space between the rectum and the bladder, produces a firm, stone-like,
elevated nodule that is devoid of strength.
Vātāṣṭhīlā is caused by the vitiated wind, which, becoming coiled within the bladder, produces the discharge of feces and urine along with intense pain.
When urine is obstructed, one wanders about, experiences stiffness, twisting pain, and heaviness, or else voids the urine in very small quantities, repeatedly.

When urine is suppressed for a long time, it results in what is called *vātakuṇḍalikā*; the urine does not flow out, or it is obstructed, and that condition is known as *mūtrātīta*, characterized by little pain.
When the urine, obstructed by suppression and turned back from below the navel by the wind, fills the abdomen, it is then called Udara.

Due to the vitiation of the digestive fire, a perforation of the stomach, or by the wind (vāyu), one may experience intense pain, distension, weakness, and the retention of waste products, as well as urine resembling that [feces].
In one with scanty urine, the expelled [urine] remains in the bladder, at the navel, or in the rectum, and after staying there, it flows out slowly, either with pain or without pain.
If the discharge of urine is interrupted, it is harmful to the teacher and the penis; there will be thirst in the mouth and a sudden, persistent, and slight swelling within the bladder.

A glandular growth that causes pain similar to that of a urinary stone is called *mūtragranthi*. It occurs when, in one who has urinated and engaged in sexual intercourse with a woman, the semen is expelled by the *vāyu* (bodily wind).
When one urinates while displaced from the normal position, the urine flows either before or after [the act], resembling ash-water; that is called *mūtraśukra*.
When, in a person who is dry and weak, the upward movement of wind (udāvarta) causes the feces to enter the urinary tract, then the urine becomes mixed with feces.
If the urine droplets have an equal odor [to the stool], one should diagnose that as *vighāta*. It occurs due to pitta, physical exercise, pungent and sour foods, flatulence, and so forth.
When the urine is located in the bladder due to aggravated Vāyu, it causes a burning sensation; first it turns the urine turbid, then it becomes mixed with blood or even purely blood.
They call that *uṣṇavāta* which is repeatedly and painfully hot; it occurs when pitta and vāta are located in the bladder of one who is parched and whose body is exhausted.
Pitta and kapha, when both are congealed by vāta, produce a wasting of urine accompanied by pain and burning, known by that name (mūtra-śukra).
Then, with great difficulty, one voids urine that is yellow, red, white, or thick; it is accompanied by a burning sensation and may have the color of the powder of *rocanā* or a conch shell.
They say that when it is dry or possesses all colors, it is called *mūtrasāda*. Thus, the diseases originating from the urine have been described in detail.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Urinary Retention and Dysuria," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Dhanvantari said: "O Suśruta, listen; I shall now describe to you the diagnosis of urinary disorders (prameha). There are twenty types of prameha: ten arising from phlegm (kapha) and [the remaining] from bile (pitta)."

Six and four [types of urinary disorders] arise from wind (vāta), and they carry fat, marrow, and phlegm (kapha). One who suffers from *hāridramēha* passes pungent urine resembling turmeric and feces that is like turmeric.
In *mañjiṣṭhameha*, the urine is like water mixed with madder; in *raktameha*, it is warm, salty, reddish in appearance, and resembles blood.
In *vasāmeha*, one voids urine frequently that is mixed with fat (*vasā*) or resembles fat; in *majjameha*, one voids urine frequently that resembles marrow (*majjā*) or is mixed with marrow.
One suffering from hastimeha passes urine incessantly like a rutting elephant, devoid of force, accompanied by semen, and obstructed.

The patient suffering from madhumeha indeed becomes like honey; it is said to be of two types: when Vāyu is provoked by the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātu), or when its path is obstructed by the humors (doṣa).
When obstructed, it manifests the symptoms of the humors; it may appear signless, becoming depleted in one moment and full in the next, and thus becomes difficult to cure.
If neglected for a long time, every [type of] urinary disorder indeed develops into madhumeha; and because it is sweet among the urines, one generally voids urine like honey.
All of these are termed madhumeha because of the sweetness of the body; furthermore, there is indigestion, loss of appetite, vomiting, drowsiness, cough, and catarrh.
Complications arise in cases of phlegm-born urinary disorders (meha): pricking pain in the bladder and penis, tearing of the scrotum, and fever.

Burning sensation, thirst, acidity, fainting, and diarrhea are the symptoms of those born from pitta; while upward movement of wind (udāvarta), trembling, palpitations in the heart, and restlessness are those born from vāta.
Pain, sleeplessness, emaciation, dyspnea, and cough arise; [the skin diseases] śarāvikā, kacchapikā, jvālinī, vinatā, and alajī [also occur].
Masūrikā, sarṣapikā, putriṇī, savidārikā, and vidradhi—these are the ten types of pustules resulting from the neglect of prameha.
Due to the binding action of phlegm (kapha), food generally tends to move slowly therein; it is sweet, sour, salty, unctuous, heavy, slimy, and cold.
New grain, liquor, soups, meat, sugarcane, molasses, milk, and curd; sitting and reclining in the same place as others—these are to be avoided.
Corrupted by *prameha*, the *kapha* takes refuge in the bladder; having vitiated the body, it corrupts the moisture, sweat, fat, muscle-fat, and flesh.

When phlegm and the other [doshas] are excessively diminished, the pitta and blood, having taken refuge in the urine, draw the bodily element (dhātu) toward the bladder; and when that [urine] is depleted, the wind (māruta) likewise acts upon it.

The cognition of what is curable, what is incurable, and so forth, arises through that very [knowledge] and originates from it; likewise, when a fault is equal, the action performed is equal because of its supreme nature.

Their general characteristic is the production of copious and turbid urine; although there are differences in the specific doshas and dushyas involved, these arise from the particular nature of their combination.

The differentiation among the types of meha is determined by variations in the color of the urine and other characteristics. [In udakameha, the urine is] clear, very white, cold, odorless, and resembles water.
In meha-udakameha, the urine is somewhat turbid and slimy; in ikṣumeha, it is exceedingly sweet like the juice of sugarcane.
In *sāndrameha*, one voids urine that has become thick and remains turbid overnight; in *surāmeha*, the urine is like liquor—clear on the surface and thick at the bottom.
With his hair standing on end, the patient suffering from *śukrameha* passes urine that is thick, white like flour, resembling semen, or mixed with semen.
One suffering from *sikatāmeha* passes urine containing impurities in the form of sand; one suffering from *śītameha* voids very frequently urine that is sweet and extremely cold.
In Śanairmeha, the patient urinates very slowly and in small quantities; in Lālāmeha, the urine is slimy and mixed with threads of saliva.

In *kṣārameha*, one voids urine that possesses the smell, color, taste, and touch of an alkaline substance, like alkaline water; in *nīlameha*, it is blue and has a blue luster; in *kālameha*, it resembles ink.

They arise at the joints and vital points (marman), as well as in fleshy parts; they are elevated in the center with a depression at the periphery, and are characterized by a lack of discharge and intense pain.
A pustule shaped like a shallow bowl is known as *śarāvikā*; one shaped like a tortoise and accompanied by burning pain should be recognized by the wise as *kacchapikā*.
A large, blue pustule is known by the name Vinatā; it burns the skin upon its appearance, being flaming and a giver of great suffering.
Alopecia (alajī) is red or white, covered with pustules, and is severe; while masūrikā should be recognized by its shape being like that of a lentil (masūra).
A large, small, or very minute pustule shaped like a mustard seed, located on the tongue, characterized by suppuration and great pain, is known as putriṇī.
Round like the tuber of the vidārī plant and hard, it is called vidārikā; however, that which possesses the characteristics of an abscess (vidradhi) should be known as vidradhikā.
The putriṇī, vidārī, and duḥsahā types arise from an abundance of fat (medas), while other types, characterized by a predominance of pitta, arise immediately from a deficiency of fat.
These pustules may arise according to the respective aggravation of the humors (doṣas); even without urinary disorders (prameha), they are produced in one whose fat (medas) is corrupted.
And they are not perceived as long as they are devoid of color—whether yellow or red—being thus free from the premonitory symptoms of *meha*.

That which is discharged as urine is known as *raktapitta*. Perspiration, body odor, flaccidity of the limbs, addiction to lying down, eating, and sleeping, burning sensations in the heart, eyes, tongue, and ears, coarseness and severity [of temperament], and excessive growth of hair and nails [are its signs].

A fondness for cold, dryness of the throat and palate, sweetness in the mouth, burning sensations in the hands and feet, and even ants running toward one's urine—these are the signs of an impending group of urinary disorders (meha).

In urinary disorders (prameha), there is thirst and a sweet discharge; in diseases of honey-like sweetness (madhvāmaya), various types of morbid changes occur. Alternatively, due to over-saturation, it may arise from phlegm (kapha), or when the humors are depleted, it may be of the nature of wind (anila).

The complete forms of *kapha*-type and *pitta*-type urinary disorders, as well as those arising from sexual indulgence (*ratisambhava*), gradually transition into one another; however, those caused by *pitta* are palliable (*yāpya*), while a urinary disorder (*meha*) that is curable (*sādhya*) exists, provided it is not fated otherwise (*diṣṭa*).
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Prameha," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Dhanvantari said: O Śuśruta, listen as I describe the diagnosis of abscesses (vidradhi) and abdominal tumors (gulma). [They are caused] by the consumption of stale, excessively hot, dry, parched, and burning foods.
The Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 160.

Dhanvantari said: "O Śuśruta, listen as I describe the diagnosis of abscesses (vidradhi) and abdominal tumors (gulma). [They arise] from the consumption of stale, excessively hot, dry, parched, and burning foods."
Through crooked postures, various movements, and those various factors that vitiate the blood, the skin, flesh, fat, bones, and marrow become corrupted, and the disease takes refuge in the abdomen.
That swelling which occurs both externally and internally, characterized by great piercing pain and intense agony, whether it be circular or elongated, is known as the disease *vidradhi* (abscess).
Due to the humors (doṣas), whether individually or combined, and due to blood that has not flowed out, [the disease] moves here and there in the body, being hard, knotted, and non-exuding.
In the interim, there occurs a severe and deep swelling that increases the growth of tumors; it exudes fluid like an anthill, and indeed, a deficiency of digestive fire (agnimāndya) arises.
In the navel, bladder, liver, spleen, lungs, heart, abdomen, and groins; when the heart trembles, there is exceedingly intense pain in each of those respective locations.
It has a dark-red appearance at its base, develops irregularly, is asymmetrical in shape, causes loss of consciousness, vertigo, distension, discharge, creeping sensations, and sound.
From pitta, it is reddish-copper or black, accompanied by thirst, delusion, fever, and burning; from kapha, it is pale, itchy, and characterized by frequent shifting, elevation, and suppuration.

That which arises from the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta) is characterized by impurity, coldness, stiffness, yawning, loss of appetite, and heaviness; it persists for a long time, lacks proper transformation, and involves a mixture of symptoms.
By implication, the external and internal characteristics here are diarrhea and the appearance of black, cracked, dark-colored eruptions, accompanied by intense burning pain and fever.
The symptoms of bile (pitta) appear externally through blood, and likewise internally in women; furthermore, blood arising from injuries caused by weapons and the like is a cause of disease.
Blood arising from a wound, driven by the wind (vāyu) and inciting bile (pitta), produces an abscess (vidradhi) characterized by pitta and blood, accompanied by many complications.

Thus, the classification of complications is understood according to the difference in their locations: for if [the wind] is blown into the navel, it reaches the bladder and causes difficulty in urination (mūtrakṛcchra).

In the spleen, there is obstruction of inhalation and exhalation, enlargement, and excessive thirst; in the kloman, there is constriction of the throat; and in the heart, there is aching pain throughout all the limbs.
Delusion, fainting, coughing, as well as a crushing sensation in the heart, and the arising of morbid humors (doṣas) in the interior of the belly and flanks, as well as in the belly itself.
Likewise, there is pain in the hip joints, the groin, the waist, and the back, as well as in the sides; furthermore, there is obstruction of flatus in the anus.

One should determine their state of being unripe, ripening, or suppurated as one does for swellings; when suppurated, those located above the navel discharge through the mouth, while others discharge from the anus.

One should recognize that the abscess arising from the accumulation of morbid humors and fluids occurs in the anus, the chest, or the navel; that which is born from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta) causes a displacement of its own seat.

Indeed, when the *nābhi* and *vastistha* swellings have ripened, they may burst either internally or externally; furthermore, the swelling of one that has increased internally is afflicted by complications once it has become emaciated.
In that case, there will be an abscess for sinful men and sinful women; and if the fetus dies within the womb, a thick swelling will arise.
When the breast is afflicted, there is pain characterized by an external abscess; however, because their blood is subtle, this does not occur in young girls.
The enraged wind, its movement obstructed, causes the swelling of the base of the penis; reaching from the scrotum and groin, it flows into the sac that contains the testicles.
