By compressing [the scrotum], it causes enlargement of the vessels in the testicles; the morbid humors (doṣas) reside there within the fatty tissues, and that disease, known as Vṛddhi, is of seven types.

In the two [diseases] ending with *mūtra* (urinary disorders), due to *vāta*, there is likewise [swelling] either externally or internally; it is filled with wind, rough to the touch, dry, and causes burning from the *vāta*.
Resembling a ripe udumbara fruit, it is characterized by burning, heat, and suppuration due to pitta; due to kapha, it is intense, heavy, unctuous, itchy, hard, and slightly painful.
A swelling covered with black vesicles is a lymphatic enlargement; one that is red is a vascular enlargement; and an enlargement of fat, like phlegm, is soft and resembles a palmyra fruit.
For one who has the habit of retaining urine, as he goes there, the urine-born [semen]—free from lust, full of fortitude, and flowing gently—undergoes no agitation.
There is difficulty in urination, and below it, swelling of the scrotum and its coverings, caused by those who provoke the Vāta through excessive exertion and immersion in cold water.
When embodied beings are agitated by the retention of feces and urine and by the contortions of their limbs, their vital energy becomes disturbed and they become emaciated within.
The Vayu, having become disordered, may cause that blood to descend; then, situated at the joint for a moment, it produces a swelling resembling a tumor.

If it is neglected, there occurs an increase in the mass of the tumor, various pains such as flatulence, and manifold diseases; being severely compressed within, it moves with a sound, and swelling the head, it returns again to the top of the skull.
This increase of blood (raktavṛddhi) is incurable; it has a form similar to the increase of wind (vātavṛddhi), with dry, black, or reddish veins, resembling a window covered by wool.
The wind (vāta), having become accumulated through contact with the eight distinct humors and by the defect of the menstrual flow (ārtava), produces the eighth [type of disorder] in women.
One who is emaciated by fever, fainting, diarrhea, and such actions as vomiting, or one who is afflicted by cold or hungry, may still possess strength.
He who, being afflicted by these [symptoms], consumes food and drink or indulges in fasting, immersion in water, and so forth, while entertaining lowly notions, causes the disease to flare up.
Without practicing oleation and sudation, one might resort to drying treatments; or, having been purified, one might suffer a loss of purity, or experience tremors.
His humors (malas) are either dominated by wind (vāta) individually or all together; accompanied by blood due to the wind, they follow along the channels of the body.
The wind, having obstructed the upward and downward pathways, indeed causes a piercing pain; it is perceivable by touch, arises from a Gulma, is hot, and has the nature of a knot.

Due to emaciation, the destruction of phlegm and feces, or the obstruction of the channels, the wind (vāyu) takes up residence in the abdominal cavity; through dryness, it attains a state of hardness.
That which is independent is defective in its own substratum; that which is dependent is defective in another's substratum. Therefore, like a mass [of phlegm], it is indeed mixed with impurities.
It is called Gulma when it is located in the bladder, navel, heart, or sides; in the type born of Vāta, there is headache, fever, and rumbling in the spleen and intestines.
There is piercing pain as if from a needle, diarrhea, and urine is passed with difficulty; furthermore, there is swelling in the limbs, face, and feet, as well as a deficiency of digestive fire.
Due to the mobility of the wind (anila), it causes the skin and other parts to become rough and dark; lacking a fixed configuration, it produces various kinds of pain.
Like a thicket swarming with ants, it throbs and is pushed about; from pitta arise burning, sour eructations, fainting, diarrhea, perspiration, thirst, and fever.
A yellowish discoloration appears over all the limbs, and there is the manifestation of swelling from internal tumors; the phlegm (śleṣman) wanes and then flares up, as if burning its own seat.
From phlegm (kapha) arise numbness, loss of appetite, malaise, fever in the head, chronic rhinitis, lethargy, nausea, and a whitish or darkish discoloration of the skin and other parts of the body.
The Gulma is deep-seated, hard, heavy, and like a fetus situated within the womb; the Marakas (fatal factors) run about right there in their own locations.

Generally, those tumors (gulma) that arise from the combination of two doṣas have mixed characteristics; that which arises from all three doṣas is characterized by intense pain and burning, rapid suppuration, and is thick and elevated.
This incurable blood-gulma arises only in women; it occurs in one who suffers from colic during her menses, or in one who has a diseased womb.
Or if a woman indulges in excessive wind-increasing activities, her provoked wind obstructs the menstrual flow that is established every month within the womb.
She experiences nausea, longings, and the appearance of breast milk, as well as unrestrained behavior; she makes the fetus comfortable and causes the male organ to manifest within its womb.

Gradually, through contact with the wind (vāyu), pitta causes an accumulation of blood in the female reproductive organs; this produces for her the same symptoms as those described for gulma caused by vāta and pitta.
Furthermore, there is intense pain in the uterus and in the site of the blood, as well as vaginal discharge, foul odor, and frequent sensations of trickling and aching.
Sometimes a gulma appears like a pregnancy; all these arise from passion (rati). A gulma ripens after a long time, whereas an abscess (vidradhi), on the other hand, does not increase [in size].
It ripens very quickly because it is based on corrupted blood; therefore, due to its rapid burning nature, it is called *vidradhi*.
There is a burning sensation in the bladder, pain in the spleen, a loss of digestive fire, complexion, and strength, or else the onset of the natural urges.
In the opposite case, there is not much pain in the external parts of the abdomen; rather, there is discoloration, coughing, or excessive protrusion externally.
That which is accompanied by distension, extremely severe pain, and intense bloating in the abdomen due to the obstruction of flatus above and below is designated as ānāha.
Dhana is like a pebble (aṣṭhī), while a granthi is a protruding stone-like growth; pratyaṣṭhīlā is similar in shape but is associated with all the symptoms of a liṅga.

Likewise, wind arising from the receptacle of digested food (pakvaśaya), due to its association with intense pain, causes frequent eructation, constipation, a lack of satiety, and gurgling sounds in the intestines.
Flatulence, distension, and loss of digestive power are the signs of impending gulma.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Abscesses and Gulma," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Dhanvantari said: "O Suśruta, listen as I describe the diagnosis of abdominal enlargements (*udara*). Indeed, all diseases arise from weak digestion, but abdominal enlargements especially so."
Others, moreover, are born with diseases such as piles due to the accumulation of impurities; their upward and downward vital airs being obstructed, they become agitated and fail to flow properly.

Having vitiated the prāṇa and apāna breaths, they cause them to enter the joints of the flesh; having distended the abdomen, they produce abdominal enlargement (udara) through eight distinct varieties.

Afflicted by the individual humors, by all three combined, or by splenomegaly, inguinal hernia, ulcers, and edema, they suffer with dryness of the palate and lips, and swelling of the entire feet, hands, and abdomen.
Men whose physical activity, strength, and appetite have vanished, and whose bellies are distended as if blown up, become like hungry ghosts; such are the signs of what is to come.
Hunger is destroyed, everything is digested with a burning sensation as if there were a loss of appetite, and that man who does not recognize when food is digested consumes unwholesome things.
The strength of the limbs wanes; one pants even when inactive and with little exertion; the intellect turns away from its objects, and there is also emaciation due to grief and other such symptoms.

In one suffering from abdominal disease, there will be constant weakness in the limbs, back, and joints, as well as loss of strength due to digestion by old age, even when eating light and small quantities of food.
When water is produced within the *āmāśaya*, there occurs independence [of the humors], lassitude, the production of impurities, weak digestive fire, burning sensations, swelling, and flatulence.
Death occurs everywhere in the waters; lamentation therein is fruitless. Like a window, the belly gurgles through the network of veins.
If one suppresses the urge by means of mantras, it may be destroyed; however, this results in pain in the heart, waist, navel, anus, and groin when the wind (māruta) is obstructed.
The wind exits accompanied by sound, it carries away urine in small quantities, there is no excessive restlessness, and the man’s mouth becomes tasteless.

In that condition, vātodara (wind-type abdominal enlargement), there is swelling in the hands, feet, face, and abdomen, as well as pain in the flanks, sides of the abdomen, waist, back, and breaking pain in the joints.

Dry cough, aching of the limbs, heaviness in the lower body, accumulation of impurities, a dark-red discoloration of the skin and other parts, and a loss of the sense of taste in the mouth [are its signs].
His abdomen becomes painful to the touch and prone to bursting, covered with blue and black veins; it becomes distended, and he produces a strange sound within his belly.
In this condition, the Vāyu produces a painful sound and movement in every direction; in Pittaja Udara, there is fever, fainting, a burning sensation, and a bitter taste in the mouth.

There is vertigo, diarrhea, yellowness of the skin and other parts, and a greenish abdomen; the vessels and other areas appear yellowish-coppery, accompanied by perspiration, heat, and a burning sensation.
In cases of *śleṣmodara* (abdominal enlargement due to phlegm), there is smoky fuming, softness to the touch, rapid suppuration, burning pain, lassitude, perspiration, swelling, and heaviness.

Drowsiness, distress, loss of appetite, labored breathing, coughing, paleness of the skin and other parts, abdominal enlargement, and blurred vision; the abdomen is oily and covered with white and black veins.
When water increases excessively, it becomes hard, cold to the touch, heavy, and stable; it provokes the three doṣas through those various impurities that arise from the three doṣas.
Corrupted by all types of vitiating factors, the accumulated impurities, becoming excited upon reaching the digestive tract, produce symptoms accompanied by emaciation, fainting, and vertigo.
They produce a most dreadful abdominal enlargement characterized by all three types of morbid humors, which suppurates quickly; and it increases even further when exposed to cold winds.
From overeating, from agitation, from activities such as traveling or drinking, from unwholesome drinks and the like, and from emetics, diseases, and emaciation;
The spleen, situated on the left side, increases when displaced from its normal position; having grown from blood or from the nutrient fluids (*rasa*) and so forth, it produces pain.
That [fetus] is like a hard, protruding stone, elevated like the back of a tortoise; as it grows gradually, it causes distension in the abdomen.
It is accompanied by dyspnea, cough, thirst, a bad taste in the mouth, flatulence, fever, pallor, fainting, vomiting, a burning sensation in the skin, and delusion.
It has a reddish luster, a variegated luster, and is adorned with blue and yellow; it is accompanied by upward-moving wind (udāvarta), constipation, delusion, thirst, distress, and fever.

Due to heaviness, loss of appetite, and hardness, as well as from obstruction, delusion, and transference, the liver (yakṛt) may also become displaced from the right side like a splenic enlargement (plīha).
When the liver has become cooked and feces are constantly bound in the rectum, one becomes afflicted by hemorrhoids, upward-moving wind (udāvarta), or other such ailments.
The provoked *apāna* wind causes feces, bile, and phlegm to become obstructed; thus confined within the abdomen, it produces fever and pain.
Cough, dyspnea, heaviness in the thighs, headache, pain in the navel and flanks, retention of waste, loss of appetite, vomiting, and the accumulation of impurities and wind in the abdomen.
The abdomen is covered with a network of firm, blue, and reddish veins; and from above the navel, it generally takes on the shape of a cow's tail.
When the abdomen is pierced by bone fragments, other foreign bodies, or the like, the liver and other organs undergo suppuration, and [the pus] flows outward through those perforations.
If there is pain in the rectum while the stool is still undigested, then there will be a very small amount of fecal matter; it may have an abnormal odor and be slimy, yellowish, or reddish.
Then, having filled the belly, the remainder begins its terrible expansion; it grows rapidly below the navel and quickly attains the nature of water.
When the form of the *doṣa* is aggravated and pervaded by dyspnea, thirst, and vertigo, they call this *chidrodara*; others, however, call it *paristrāvin*.

[This occurs] in one who has begun drinking unwholesome liquids and the like, who suddenly indulges in unwholesome food, who drinks excessive water, whose digestive fire is weak, and who is emaciated and extremely thin.

The wind (anila) is obstructed from its own path, and the phlegm (kapha), congealed by water, increases; that very water increases further from the accumulation of even a single drop of its own measure.
Due to that [wind's] provocation, the abdomen becomes afflicted with thirst, pain in the anus and the flanks, cough, dyspnea, and anorexia; it is covered with veins of various colors.
From that which is filled with water, soft to the touch, and characterized by similar agitation and trembling, the *bakodara* (water-born) arises, stable and unctuous, enveloping the channel.
And when all [the humors] have been displaced from their own locations during equanimity, they become ripe and liquefied, causing even the joints, channels, and orifices to become moistened.
When the sweat is indeed obstructed, those [humors] remaining within become faint; filling that very abdomen, they cause the disease of the abdomen (udara).
A thunderbolt situated in the belly of a guru, whether stationary or struck, does not produce sound; likewise, one that is weak, terrible, or touched by a nāḍī causes death.
The disappearance of the veins within the abdomen is said to be the general characteristic [of abdominal diseases]: wind, bile, phlegm, spleen, combined humors, and water-ascites.

An abdominal enlargement (udara) that has produced fluid within a fortnight and is accompanied by complications such as obstruction is considered, by its very nature, to be almost entirely the most difficult to treat.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-first chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Dhanvantari said: O Suśruta, listen as I describe to you the diagnosis of jaundice (pāṇḍu) and edema (śotha). When the humors (malas), with pitta predominating, are provoked by the aforementioned causes of provocation, [they produce these conditions].
If, being cast up and down by the powerful wind, it remains stationary after reaching the ten vessels, it pervades the entire body.
Vitiating the skin, blood, phlegm, and flesh while residing in the nutrient fluid (rasa), it produces various types of discolorations on the skin within the layers of the skin and flesh.
Turmeric itself is yellow, and among those [humors], this severe disease has reached an excess of paleness; therefore, it causes heaviness.

There is a loosening of the contact between the elements and a decay of qualities arising from the immature state; consequently, blood, fat, and bone become deficient in essence, and the sense faculties become flaccid.
With limbs as if dissolving, with a heart melting away, and with a face like the peak of a mountain of arrows, one should cultivate a state of numbness there by means of the tongue.
One who has diminished thirst, an aversion to cold, decayed greed, and extinguished digestive fire; one with weak strength, suffering from fever, dyspnea, earache, and likewise dizziness.

It is of five kinds, according to whether it is caused by the humors individually, by all of them combined, or by eating clay; its premonitory symptoms are palpitations of the heart and dryness of the skin.

Loss of appetite, yellowish urine, absence of perspiration, and scanty urination occur there due to the aggravation of fat and wind; in that condition, there is intense pain and a sense of moisture within the body.
Darkness of the eyes, blackness of the head, nails, feces, urine, and eyes; swelling, bad taste in the nose and mouth, dryness of the stool, and fainting with pain in the flanks.

In the case of pitta, there is a greenish-yellow appearance in the veins and other parts, fever, darkness of vision, thirst, emaciation, fainting, foul odor, a desire for cold, and a bitter taste in the mouth.
Diarrhea, acidity, burning sensations, moisture in the heart due to *kapha*, drowsiness, salivation, horripilation, and loss of voice [result from this].
Cough and vomiting arise from the accumulation [of humors]; when the signs are lost, it is extremely difficult to endure. When provoked by vāyu and pitta, kapha becomes bitter or sweet.

Having corrupted the fat and other tissues, and due to its dryness causing the discharge of blood, it brings about the depletion of the bodily channels, following the same procedure as previously described.

When anemia arises from consumption (wasting), there is discharge from the navel, feet, mouth, and penis; one passes stool that is broken, mixed with blood, accompanied by phlegm, and containing worms.

If one who suffers from a bile disease consumes substances that increase bile, it causes jaundice; the bile, having risen from the stomach and intestines, burns the blood and flesh and carries them away.

The urine, eyes, and face become yellow, while the mouth and excrement are red; there is a burning sensation, indigestion, and thirst; the patient resembles a frog in appearance and has weakened sense organs.
In one afflicted by *pāṇḍuroga*, there may arise a swelling accompanied by *pitta*; and through neglect, swellings and other such conditions lead to the difficult-to-cure *kumbhakāmalā*.
When jaundice occurs with a greenish-blackish bile, there is anemia; when wind and bile are involved, there is vertigo, thirst, desire for women, and mild fever.
Drowsiness, or loss of digestive fire—these they call *halīmaka*; excessive laziness also occurs as a premonitory symptom (*upadrava*) of these conditions.

Swelling (śotha) is declared to be the primary [symptom]; therefore, it is described here: the vitiated Vāyu, along with Pitta, blood, and Kapha, leads the corrupted humors outward through the vessels.

For when their movement is obstructed by those [doshas], they take refuge in the skin and flesh, producing a raised, compact swelling; therefore, they call that a *śotha* (swelling) due to its accumulation (*nicaya*).

Due to the specificities of all causes, it consists of nine types according to the variations in form; [it arises] from various distinct humors, from all [combined] humors, from trauma, and even from poison.

When that very [breast] is being led upward, it may arise from desire in all its parts; the wise know it to be of three kinds by means of specific characteristics, such as being broad, elevated at the tips, and knotted.
The general cause of swellings is the derangement of the humors (doṣas); specifically, such a disease occurs rapidly in one who is emaciated by labor, fasting, and similar depletions.
When one consumes in excess what is extremely cold for the guru, or salt, alkaline, pungent, sour substances, leafy vegetables, water, sleep, or staying awake;

Obstructing the flow of bodily impulses, dried meat, indigestion, fatigue, sexual intercourse, walking long distances, or even traveling in a jolting vehicle—all these lead to the digestion of undigested food.
Dyspnea, cough, diarrhea, hemorrhoids, abdominal enlargement, menorrhagia, fever, constipation, lassitude, vomiting, hiccup, anemia, and erysipelas;

Those [doshas] located in the upper part cause swelling in the upper body; those in the bladder cause it in the lower part; those in the middle cause it in the middle; those moving through all parts cause it throughout the whole body; and that which follows its specific substrate moves in that particular direction.
Its premonitory symptoms are sneezing, distension of the vessels, and heaviness of the limbs; due to Vāta, the swelling is mobile, dry, with rough hair, and reddish or dark in color.

There is a sensation like that of a conch-shell, distension of the bladder, intestinal swelling, piercing pain in the thighs and fat, numbness, upward movement of Vāta, exhaustion, and the body quickly rises when pressed down.
The ointment should be pacified by massages; it is mild at night and intense during the day. When that area is smeared with a paste of bark and mustard seeds, it experiences a tingling sensation.
Appearing yellow, red, or blackish, and born from the derangement of bile (pitta), it causes emaciation; it either subsides quickly or first burns the body in its middle part.
Thirst, burning fever, perspiration, vertigo, exhaustion, intoxication, and delusion; a desire for food, diarrhea, a foul odor, intolerance to touch, and softness [of the body].
It is characterized by itching, pale hair, hard skin, coldness, heaviness, oiliness, smoothness, and stability; it causes pain, drowsiness, vomiting, and impairment of the digestive fire.
And by means of malice, through cutting, piercing, and wounding with weapons and the like, and by cold winds, sour winds, and those arising from *bhallātaka* and *pikaccha* plants.
From contact with juices that have dried, there occurs a swelling accompanied by spreading (visarpa), characterized by intense heat, a reddish appearance, and generally the symptoms of Pitta.
Poisoning arises from the crawling over or urination by venomous creatures, as well as from the bites of fangs, teeth, or claws—even by those creatures that are not inherently poisonous.
Due to contact with substances defiled by feces, urine, semen, or impure things; from the touch of the wind from a poisonous tree; and from being sprinkled with a mixture of poisons.
A swelling that is soft, mobile, pendulous, rapid in onset, and causes burning pain and distress is curable when recent; it is incurable if accompanied by complications, as previously stated.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Pāṇḍuroga and Sōtha," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Dhanvantari said: O Suśruta, I shall now describe the diagnosis of Visarpa (erysipelas) and other diseases; listen to that. Visarpa occurs due to the obstruction [of channels] by the vitiated Doṣas, appearing like a swelling (śotha).
They say that the external [support] therein is due to fear or fatigue; furthermore, as one proceeds further, the fault becomes increasingly difficult to remedy, according to the circumstances.
Aggravated by provocative factors, especially those that cause a burning sensation, they quickly enter the body here; for though they reside within, they manifest externally.
Due to the excessive application of thirst, the irregular movement of the bodily urges, and the rapid loss of digestive fire and strength, the poison spreads externally.
Among these, the Vata-type visarpa is characterized by pain identical to that of Vata-fever, and is accompanied by swelling, throbbing, pricking, piercing, exhaustion, distress, and horripilation.
From pitta, it moves rapidly, exhibits the symptoms of pitta-fever, and is excessively red; from kapha, it is accompanied by itching, is unctuous, and has a pain similar to that of kapha-fever.

Those arising from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta), endowed with all their symptoms, and neglected, are covered with eruptions (sphoṭa) possessing the characteristics of all [the humors] and exhibit the features of an ulcer; they also discharge sweat while bearing the marks of a wound.
Accompanied by fever, vomiting, fainting, diarrhea, thirst, and vertigo arising from wind and bile, as well as glandular swellings, loss of digestive fire, darkness before the eyes, and anorexia.
It causes all the limbs to become as if strewn with glowing embers; whatever region the erysipelas (visarpa) spreads to, that very place becomes thus.
It appears black like extinguished embers, blue, or red, and it is covered with eruptions as if burnt by fire; because of its rapid movement, it quickly subsides.

When Vāta is exceedingly strong, it causes a spreading erysipelas (visarpa) that follows the vital points (marman); it causes pain in the limbs, robs one of consciousness and sleep, and excites labored breathing.
And having reached such a state, that man suffers from hiccuping; at times, seized by pain in his vital organs, he lies upon the ground or sits upon a bed or seat.
Then, struggling, afflicted, and with delusion of mind and body, he experiences a sleep from which it is difficult to awaken; this is called agnivisarpa.
The wind (vāyu), obstructed by phlegm (kapha), pierces that phlegm in many ways; or, in one with increased blood, it pierces the blood located in the skin, vessels, ligaments, and flesh.
Having corrupted [the blood], it becomes long-lasting, thick, and coarse in nature, forming a chain of nodules accompanied by reddish discoloration at the edges, intense pain, and fever.

Accompanied by dyspnea, cough, diarrhea, dryness of the mouth, hiccup, vomiting, giddiness, delusion, discoloration, fainting, breaking pain in the limbs, and loss of digestive fire—this is Granthivisarpa, arising from the provocation of Kapha and Vāta.
From the combination of kapha and pitta arise fever, stiffness, drowsiness, lethargy, headache, exhaustion of the limbs, convulsions, delirium, anorexia, and vertigo.

Fainting, loss of digestive fire, cracking of the bones, thirst, heaviness of the sense organs, evacuation of undigested matter (āma), and a coating of the channels—these symptoms spread throughout the body.
Generally, it affects the stomach region without causing excessive pain, and it is covered with eruptions that are excessively yellow, red, or pale.
It is glossy, black, dark-colored, dirty, swollen, and heavy; it suppurates deeply, generally becomes hot to the touch, becomes moist, and then bursts open.

When the flesh has become cooked and sloughed away, the network of tendons and veins is clearly visible, it spreads everywhere with all the aforementioned symptoms, involves the entire skin, and emits the odor of a corpse—this erysipelas is called Kardama.
Provoked by injury from an external cause and impelling the blood along with pitta, the wind (vāyu) produces visarpa, which is covered with eruptions resembling kulattha beans.

[The disease] characterized by eruptions (sphoṭa), swelling, fever, pain, and burning, with dark-red blood, is caused by the doshas individually; these three types are curable, as are those born from two doshas provided they are without complications.

Those who have undergone all possible treatments yet remain incurable, whose vital organs (marmans) are all afflicted, whose sinews, vessels, and flesh are withered, who are moist and emit the stench of a corpse—[these are incurable].

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Vīsarpa," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Instantly impelled by past sinful actions, those pure [winds], having entered the channels, become joined with them and [enter] the skin, fat, blood, and flesh.
Corrupting and drying up [the tissues], they emerge from there and cause discoloration of the skin; the experts designate this as Kuṣṭha.
If that which is neglected over time remains so, it enters all the internal cavities of the body, moistens all the internal and external tissues (dhātus), and brings about their dissolution.
It successively invades the worms accompanied by sweat, moisture, and contraction, as well as the subtle and dreadful [worms], and finally the body hair, skin, sinews, and vessels.

That which appears as if covered with ashes is described as external leprosy (bāhyakuṣṭha). Leprosies are of seven types, arising from the humors (doṣas) individually, in pairs, or when combined together.

Although all [types of kuṣṭha] involve the three doṣas, they are designated according to whichever one predominates: the kāpāla type arises from vāta, the audumbara from pitta, and [the maṇḍala type] from kapha.
One should also examine those known as maṇḍala and ṛṣya, which arise from vāta and pitta; as well as carma-kuṣṭha, ekakuṣṭha, kiṭima, sidhma, alasa, and vipādikā.
Diseases arising from vāta and śleṣman include dadru and śatāruṣī; those from śleṣma and pitta include puṇḍarīka along with visphoṭa, as well as pāmā and carmadala.

A *kākaṇa* is for all [other skin diseases]; the first triad [of *kākaṇas*] is for *dadru*; with a *kākaṇa* added, it is for *puṇḍarīka* and *arya-jihva*; thus, there are seven [units] for the great leprosies (*mahā-kuṣṭha*).

Excessive smoothness or roughness of touch, perspiration or lack thereof, discoloration of the skin, burning sensation, itching, numbness, pricking pain, horripilation, elevation, and darkness [of vision] occur in the skin.
Excessive pain in wounds, rapid formation and long duration, dryness even in those that have healed, and excessive irritation at the slightest cause [are signs of vitiated blood].
Horripilation and blackness of the blood are the primary symptoms of leprosy (kuṣṭha); that which resembles a blackish-red skull, being dry, rough, and thin, [is also indicative].
Covered with hair that is discolored and spread over a wide area, accompanied by intense pricking pain—that is known as the uneven (viṣama) type of kāpāla kuṣṭha.
One should call the *kuṣṭha* that has the appearance of an udumbara fruit "audumbara"; it is described as being circular, very thick, and characterized by excessive burning pain.
The udumbara fruit that is unscarred, without pits, and free of worms—firm, true, heavy, oily, white or reddish, yet possessed of impurities—is [of inferior quality].
A circular patch (maṇḍala) is described as being characterized by mutual adhesion, swelling, excessive itching, discharge, and parasites, and as being smooth with a yellowish luster.
Vicarcikā is characterized by itching, eruptions, a dark-brown color, and moisture; it is rough at the edges, red at the margins, dark-brown in the center, and elevated.

That which is described as having the appearance of a deer's tongue is called ṛṣyajihva; it is infested with many worms. That which has the touch of an elephant's hide or a donkey's skin is said to be the leprosy known as carma.
Furthermore, *kiṭima* is painless, resembling the scales of a fish, dry, the color of fire, painful to the touch, itchy, and rough-black.

That which is rough on the surface but smooth within, and sheds dust when rubbed inside; that which is smooth to the touch, thin, glossy, clear, and free from sweat or floral exudations—[these are the characteristics of a good gem].

Generally, it causes emaciation of the upper body, is covered with pustules and itching, and produces *vipādikā* (cracking of the feet) on the hands and feet characterized by redness and excessive shedding of skin.
It is characterized by intense pain and deep itching, covered with reddish pustules, and possesses the hue of long-stretching durvā grass or the atasi flower.

That which is called *ucchūnamaṇḍala* is characterized by itching and is known as *dadru*; it has thick roots, is accompanied by burning and pain, involves the discharge of blood, and consists of many ulcers.
It generally causes burning, moistening, and pain throughout all stages of its development; the circular patch is reddish, pale, and accompanied by itching, a burning sensation, and pain.
When covered with raised eruptions red like lotus petals by water, that indeed becomes a *puṇḍarīka*, being strewn with white and reddish pustules.
Visphoṭa eruptions, pustules, scabies, itching, and exudative pain—these are characterized by being small, dark, reddish, and dry, occurring mostly on the buttocks, hands, and elbows.

Accompanied by cracking sensations and tolerance to touch, characterized by itching, redness, and intense burning, it is called *raktadala*, *carmadala*, or *kākaṇa*, and is marked by severe burning pain.
That which is reddish-brown and black, resembling a *kākaṇī* coin or the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), arises from its respective causes when possessed of all the black characteristics.

One should prescribe treatments according to the specific signs and actions for each distinct humor; however, one should abandon a case of leprosy that follows its own predominant humor or involves all the humors.

That which is described among the types of leprosy (kuṣṭha), as well as that which resides in the bones, marrow, and semen, and that which involves the fat (medas)—these are difficult to cure; however, that which has reached the skin, bones, and flesh is manageable with palliative treatment.

That which arises from phlegm and wind, is located in the skin, and is stainless, is easy to treat; however, when it is situated in the skin and becomes severe, there is discoloration and roughness of the body.
In the blood and the flesh, there is perspiration, heat, and swelling; moreover, there are eruptions localized in the hands and feet, and excessive distress in the joints.
Through constant application, there is the breaking down of the fat; however, there is no excessive awareness regarding the marrow, bones, eyes, urges, and voice.
When the semen is infested with worms, there is injury to one's own wife and offspring; all the other symptoms, as previously described, occur in the case of the deer and other [animals].

White leprosy (śvitra), also known as kilāsa, arises solely from the vitiation of the bodily tissues; it is a severe condition, characterized by a lack of discharge, and is dependent on the origin of all three humors (dhātus).
From Vāta it is dry and reddish; from Pitta it is copper-colored like a lotus petal, accompanied by burning, and causes the loss of body hair; from Kapha it is white, thick, and heavy.

One should indicate that it is accompanied by itching and, in sequence, involves blood, flesh, and fat; both types are difficult to treat by their very color, and each subsequent one is more severe than the last.
Leucoderma that is not white-haired, abundant, or confluent, which is new, produced by causes other than fire, and curable; otherwise, it is to be rejected.
One who desires accomplishment should especially avoid vitiligo (kilāsa), even if it has arisen very recently on the private parts, the palms of the hands, or the lips.
Diseases generally arise from indulgence in contact, the same food, and similar things, as well as from sharing the same bed or seat, and from the use of the same clothes, garlands, and ointments.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Kuṣṭha Disease," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Dhanvantari said: Worms are said to be of two kinds, distinguished by being external or internal. They are further classified as fourfold based on their origin from external impurities, phlegm (kapha), blood, or feces.
Therein, twenty kinds of external [demons] arise from impurities; they are the size of sesame seeds, possessing specific shapes and colors, and they take refuge in hair and clothing.
Those known by the names *yūkā* (lice) and *likṣā* (nits) have many legs and are minute; they are of two kinds, causing pustules in the abdomen and producing itching and swellings.
The internal causes of leprosy arise from phlegm, while those originating externally are caused by sweet foods, molasses, milk, curd, fish, and newly harvested rice.
Arising from phlegm in the stomach and having increased, they spread in all directions; some resemble broad leather straps, while others are like earthworms.
Resembling the sprouts of mature grain, they are slender, long, and minute; white and with a coppery luster—these are the seven types by name.
The entrail-eaters, the belly-twisters, the heart-seizers, the great anus-devourers, the cyuravas, the darbha-flowers, and the fragrant ones—they all cause [these afflictions].
Nausea, salivation, indigestion, loss of appetite, fainting, vomiting, fever, abdominal distension, emaciation, sneezing, and chronic rhinitis;
Minute creatures born from blood reside in the locations of the blood-carrying vessels; they are footless, circular, and copper-colored, and some are invisible due to their extreme subtlety.
Keśādā, Romavidhvaṃsā, Romadvīpā, and Udumbarā—these six, together with Saurasamātṛ, share the same function as Kuṣṭha.
Arising from feces in the large intestine, they spread upward; when increased, they may become directed toward the stomach.
Then, his eructations and breaths will follow the odor of excrement; they will be broad, circular, thin, or thick, and dark-brown, yellow, white, or black.
These five types of worms—namely the kakerukas, makerukas, sausurādās, those called śūlas, and the lelihās—indeed produce [these ailments].
Cracking of the anus, colic, constipation, emaciation, roughness, pallor, horripilation, loss of digestive fire, and itching of the rectum—these occur when [the doshas] move into the wrong channels.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Worms," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Dhanvantari said: O Suśruta, I shall declare to you the diagnosis of wind-diseases (vātavyādhi); listen to that. In every way, the narration of what is harmful is indeed an obstacle [to well-being].
He whose body is not seen by the wicked wind, who is without distinction, he is Viśvakarman, the soul of the universe, the universal form, the Lord of Creatures.
He is the creator, the sustainer, the all-pervading Viṣṇu, the destroyer, death, and the end-maker; since it has been declared thus, one should always strive with diligence for this purpose.

Once the knowledge of the defects has been stated for him, and having ascertained the natural and modified actions according to the brief and detailed classifications of the specific types of defects;
Each of these fivefold types of heroism involves a distinct transformative activity; their classification, along with their causes and characteristics, is now described.
When the wind is provoked by factors that deplete the bodily constituents (dhātu), it is not properly pacified; it fills those very same channels of the fourfold network even more.
Then, having concealed the opening from those [channels] filled with defects, your wind, becoming enraged once, produces colic, constipation, and rumbling in the intestines.
It certainly causes obstruction of the menses, loss of voice, stiffness of the eyes, back, and waist, as well as other various afflictions difficult to endure within the body.
Vomiting arising from the stomach, dyspnea, cough, cholera, itching, obstruction, perspiration, and other such diseases located above the navel [are treated by upward-moving vāyu].
It causes impairment of the sense organs such as hearing, cracking and roughness of the skin, intense pain, labored breathing, affliction by poison, and discoloration.
It causes obstruction within the intestines, loss of appetite, emaciation, and vertigo; it produces a nodular growth in the flesh and fat, and a roughness upon the skin and other tissues.
The vital points of the body are excessively pierced, as if struck by a staff or a fist; one perceives sharp pain located in the bones and joints of the thighs and the pelvic region.

When located in the marrow, it causes instability in the bones; when in the bone, it causes insomnia and pain; and when in the semen, it causes either premature ejaculation or its disordered alteration.

Residing within the respective fetal membranes or the semen, or located in the head, it causes distension and emptiness; situated there, when provoked, it produces swelling and difficulty in movement.

Vata located in the joints causes a sensation like touching a water-filled leather bag and dryness; when it pervades the entire body, it produces pricking, piercing, throbbing, and breaking sensations.

Stiffening, convulsing, sleepiness, breaking of the joints, and trembling—when the provoked [wind] repeatedly enters all the channels (dhamanīs), it then seizes the limbs; this disease is known as ākṣepaṇa.
When the wind, having been repelled below, moves upward once again, then, seizing the heart, it causes pain in the head and the temples.
One should contract the limbs all around, or bend the jaw of the victim; one should also cause him to breathe with great difficulty while closing both eyes.
Free from attachment and accompanied by *upatantraka*, one should coo like a pigeon; that very same [wind], when joined with the wind in the heart, resides in the nose of a dwarf.
It frequently attains a state of health and frequently becomes afflicted with ill-health; that which arises from trauma is considered the most difficult to treat.
Then there is the suppression of perspiration when the wind, its continuity severed, pervades the entire body and it is further stretched out.
It causes the disappearance of vision, paralysis of the eyes, yawning, exhaustion, and the loosening of the teeth, rendering one's efforts futile.
It causes external pain in the sides, stiffness of the jaw, back, and head, extension of the body outward, and a drawing sensation from the back toward the heart and head.
In that state, the chest is heaved up or the shoulder is bent down; there is discoloration of the teeth and the mouth, and indeed an absence of perspiration from the body.
They call the patient suffering from wind-disorder *hanustambha* (lockjaw) when the bodily winds, having reached the feces, urine, and blood, cause external extension [of the jaw].
The defects of the body extend from head to foot; even for one who remains as mere pallor, the extension of the wound is greatly increased.
Health may be restored during a paroxysm of the limbs by means of shaking all the limbs; likewise, it may be restored by scraping the tongue, eating hot food, or through excessive pride.
When the Vāyu, located at the root of the jaw, becomes aggravated, it causes stiffness of the jaw and produces either the state of having the mouth wide open or the state of having the mouth closed.
By that [wind], there occurs a paralysis of the jaw, with chewing and speaking occurring only with great difficulty; when the wind paralyzes the tongue, it is called *vāgvādinī* or *śirāstambha*.

Stiffness of the tongue arises from that [karma], resulting in an inability to consume food, drink, or speak; it also results from carrying heavy loads on the head or from speaking excessively in jest.
From uneven pillows and from chewing hard foods, the wind increases; and by those wind-disorders, it becomes established in the upward direction.
She distorts his face, and he laughs and stares loudly; thereafter, she renders his power of speech weak and causes his eyes to become fixed.
Loosening of the teeth, loss of voice, loss of hearing, inability to perceive objects, lack of sense of smell, destruction of memory, terror, and labored breathing arise.
Spitting, pain in the sides, the closing of one eye, intense pains above the collarbone, or even the paralysis of one half of the body;
Some call this condition *ardita*, while others call it *ekāṅga*; it occurs by affecting the blood in the vessels that support the head. What [remedy] should one apply to those vessels of the head?
That seizing of the head which is rough, painful, and black is incurable; likewise, when the wind (vāyu) seizes the body as well as the tendons (snāyu).
It destroys one side of the body; that is called *pakṣāghāta*. One half of the entire body becomes incapable of action and devoid of sensation.
Some know [this condition] as disease of a single limb, while others recognize it as pain in the armpits; when the *vāyu* resides in the entire body, there is obstruction of all limbs and stiffness.

A hemiplegia caused by pure vāta is considered most difficult to cure; it is difficult to treat when associated with another [dosha], and it is incurable when aggravated by the cause of wasting (kṣaya).

One whose channels are obstructed by undigested matter (āmabaddha) and whose limbs are stiffened due to the presence of phlegm (kapha) will suffer from Daṇḍāpatānaka; indeed, this condition is entirely incurable.
The wind arising from the base of the shoulder, having contracted the vessels located there, produces *bāhuka* by causing a throbbing sensation externally.
That which is at the base of the fingers, the tendons on the back of the arms, and that which causes the loss of function in the arms is called the *vipūcī*.
When the Vāyu residing in the waist displaces the tendons (kaṇḍarā) of the thigh, then the person becomes lame; he becomes a cripple (paṅgu) through the destruction of both thighs.
One should know that a person who trembles at the start of movement and walks as if limping is "limping like a pea" (kalāyakhañja), being one whose connections and bonds have been severed.
Through the consumption of cold, hot, liquid, dry, heavy, and unctuous substances; likewise through indigestion, physical exertion, agitation, unctuousness, and staying awake at night.
At the appropriate time, phlegm that has become excessively accumulated overcomes the other humors and takes possession of the body.
Then, having filled the interior of the thigh bones with congealed phlegm, that bone bathes the thigh with that [phlegm] and likewise with cold wind.
One characterized by a dark-complexioned body and by stiffness, lassitude, fainting, aversion to food, and fever is called *urustambha*; others, however, call it *bāhyavāta*.
A swelling of the wind-blood (vātaśoṇita) in the middle of the knee, accompanied by great pain and resembling the head of a large jackal, is to be known as kroṣṭukaśīrṣa.
When, due to stepping on uneven ground with the feet or from exhaustion, the wind (vāta) seizes the ankle, that condition is called vātakaṇṭaka.
When the wind (vāyu) afflicts the heels, the fingers, the navel, or the throat, and one suppresses it with forceful tossing [of the body], that is called gṛdhrasī.
If both feet become numb and experience a tingling sensation, that should be recognized as *pādaharṣa*, arising from the provocation of *kapha* and *vāta*.
When the wind (vāyu), conjoined with bile (pitta) and blood (asṛj), causes a burning sensation in the feet—especially while walking—one should designate that condition as *pādadāha*.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Vātavyādhi," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Dhanvantari said: O Suśruta, I shall describe the diagnosis of Vātarakta (gout/rheumatism) to you; listen to that. [It is caused] by incompatible foods, eating before the previous meal is digested, anger, sleeping during the day, and staying awake at night.
Vāta-śoṇita (blood-bile disorder) generally arises in those who are delicate, those who follow improper diet and lifestyle, and those who are corpulent or indulgent.
Due to the suppression of fire and impurity, when the blood of men is vitiated, the wind—increased by Vata-aggravating factors and cold things—becomes enraged and moves along an improper path.
Obstructed by such blood, it causes affliction at that very moment; likewise, the wind (vāta) produces pain in the anus, as well as phlegm (balāsa) and vāta-śoṇita (blood disorders caused by wind).
Having first stabilized it, one should generate [the breath]; afterwards, it flows everywhere. Specifically, its characteristic is that it hangs down due to vomiting and other such actions.
Likewise, there will be a disease equal to leprosy known as *sāmbuda*, occurring in the knees, calves, thighs, hips, shoulders, hands, feet, and the joints of the limbs.
Itching, throbbing, piercing pain, splitting sensations, heaviness, and numbness—having arisen, they subside, and having subsided, they manifest again and again.
Sometimes taking its stand at the base of the feet and sometimes even at the hands, it runs through the entire body like an enraged rat through its hole.
First, the self supported by skin and flesh arises; thereafter, after some time, it becomes deep-seated and invades all the bodily constituents (dhātus).

In the regions of the waist and other such restrained areas, there is swelling that is coppery, dark, or reddish, knotted, and suppurating; that [disease] as well as the wind [afflicts] the bones and marrow.
Moving with great speed, it acts as if cutting through the interior, making everything circular; moving everywhere throughout the body, it renders one lame or crippled.
When wind (vāta) is predominant, there is excessive pain, throbbing, and breaking sensations; the swelling is dry, blackish, or dark-brown, and it fluctuates in size.
Contraction of the vessels, fingers, and joints, stiffness of the limbs, and intense pain; aversion to cold, lack of relief from [cold], rigidity, tremors, and numbness [are the symptoms].

In the blood-type [ulcer], there is swelling with excessive pain and piercing sensations; it becomes copper-colored and tingling, and it does not subside with either unctuous or dry treatments, being accompanied by itching and discharge.

In the case of pitta, there is burning sensation, confusion, sweet taste in the mouth, fainting, intoxication, thirst, intolerance to touch, pain, crying out, emaciation, suppuration, and excessive heat.
In cases of kapha, there is numbness, heaviness, numbness, oiliness, and coldness; itching and mild pain occur, and from the combination [of doshas], all the symptoms appear together.

One should treat blood-bile (raktapitta) arising from a single doṣa as curable, and that born of two doṣas as manageable; however, one should quickly abandon that most dreadful form arising from all three doṣas.
The wind (māruta), having quickly struck the blood in the limbs and entered the joints of the extremities, obstructs one another and, by means of agonizing pains, takes away the vital breaths.

In the fivefold vital air (prāṇa), which is of the nature of wind, [diseases arise] from dryness, restlessness, and leaping; from overeating, injury, and the forceful provocation or suppression of natural urges.
When aggravated, it may cause impairment of the eyes and other sense organs; furthermore, chronic catarrh, burning sensations, thirst, cough, dyspnea, and so forth arise.
Residing in the throat, clavicles, and head, it causes constriction of the throat, loss of impurities, vomiting, anorexia, chronic rhinitis, goiter, and other such disorders.

The *vyāna* [vital air] is vitiated by excessive walking, bathing, sporting, and activities involving the sense objects, as well as by incompatible foods, dry substances, fear, joy, despair, and so forth.
The loss of virility, enthusiasm, and strength; grief, mental agitation, and fever; complete exhaustion in every way, horripilation, and a state of deep sleep.
The Samāna [vāyu], through irregular, undigested, cold, or mixed foods, causes leprosy, erysipelas, and other diseases, as well as a general exhaustion of all the limbs.

Corrupted by sleeping and staying awake at improper times and other such factors, the *akṛt* produces diseases such as colic (*śūla*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and chronic diarrhea (*grahaṇī*), which have their seat in the desire-organ (*kāma*).
The *apāna* [vital air] is provoked by dry and heavy food, suppression of natural urges, excessive straining, and by the over-indulgence in riding in vehicles, sitting, rising, and walking.
When aggravated, it produces all diseases localized in the colon (pakvāśaya), as well as many others such as disorders of urine and semen, hemorrhoids, and prolapse of the rectum.

Due to the pervasive nature of the *sāma* stage, all parts of the body are affected by drowsiness, numbness, and heaviness; because of its unctuousness, there is awakening at the proper time, as well as coldness, swelling, and loss of digestive fire.

One should recognize that state as free from *āma* and liberated when itching and dryness have been eliminated and there is a corresponding pacification; conversely, it is characterized by the absence of drowsiness and other such symptoms.
The obstruction of wind by wind is said to have many varieties; when obstructed by pitta, there is burning, thirst, colic, giddiness, and darkness.

From pungent, hot, sour, and salty [foods], there is a burning sensation and a desire for cold; from cold, heavy, and painful [foods], and from pungent substances, ghee, and milk, [these symptoms] increase.

When [the fever] is covered by phlegm (kapha), there is a desire for jumping, exertion, dryness, and heat; when covered by phlegm, there is aching of the limbs, nausea, heaviness, and loss of appetite.

In the stage of blood involvement (raktāvasthā), there is always a burning sensation and intense pain arising from the skin and flesh; the swelling becomes intensely red, and circular patches (maṇḍalas) appear.

The swelling becomes hard with flesh, accompanied by nausea and pustules; there arises a tingling sensation as if ants are crawling over it. The swelling on the limbs is mobile, soft, cold, and causes loss of appetite.

That [vāta] obstructed by fat should be known as difficult to treat, like "rich vāta" (āḍhyavāta). When the skin is covered, there is a sensation of touch that is both hot and cold; when the marrow is covered, however, there is irregular yawning and a sense of being constricted.
When the swelling is covered by semen, one experiences pain and pressure, yet finds relief through manual manipulation; furthermore, in such a case, there is no excessive discharge.

When the food has been digested, there is certainly pain in the abdomen; when it has been fully digested, a cutting sensation occurs. When the bladder is obstructed by urine, there is non-emission of urine and distension.
When the openings are obstructed, there is a blockage; then, cutting through its own location, the man, overcome by fever, quickly falls down and suffers fainting.

When the vitiated semen has been pressed once by another [person], it may be discharged after a long time; or, when the bodily wind (vāyu) is obstructed by all the tissues (dhātus), there is pain in the hips, groins, and back.
When the wind moves in reverse, the heart is oppressed; when the vital breath (prāṇa) is enveloped by bile (pitta), there is vertigo, fainting, pain, and a burning sensation.

In the case of Vyāna, however, there is pain, lassitude, loss of voice, and a burning sensation throughout the entire body; furthermore, there is a gradual loss of movement and activity, along with a fever accompanied by piercing pain.

In the case of the Samāna [vāyu], there is impairment of heat, cessation of perspiration, excessive thirst, and a burning sensation; in the case of the Apāna [vāyu], however, there is a yellowish coloration of the excrement.

When the vital breath (prāṇa) is obstructed by phlegm (śleṣman), there occurs an increase of mucus, a burning sensation, as well as constipation and dysuria; furthermore, there is a resonant sound and the obstruction of the channels (srotas).
Spitting, perspiration, and the obstruction of inhalation and exhalation; in the udāna [vital breath], there is heaviness of the limbs, loss of appetite, and impairment of speech and voice.
In the drinking of [poisoned] water, there is a loss of strength and complexion, a seizing together of the joints and bones, heaviness in all limbs, and an extreme increase in bulk.

When the *samāna* [vāyu] is obstructed, there is ignorance regarding actions, absence of perspiration, and weak digestion; when the *apāna* is obstructed, there is the retention of all urine and the cessation of the passage of feces.
Thus, they know the disease of vātarakta to be of twenty-two types, wherein the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the others likewise mutually invade one another in their proper order.
All these, as well as the twentyfold obscuration of knowledge—namely, nausea, suppression of breath, catarrh, and stiffness of the head.
When the apāna is obstructed by the prāṇa, there occurs heart disease and dryness of the mouth; when the prāṇa is obstructed by the udāna, there will indeed be a loss of strength.

By means of careful investigation, the physician should differentiate all coverings (obstructive humors), taking into account the locations of the *vātas* and the increase or decrease of their functions.

Pitta is the mutual covering for the five [vital breaths] beginning with prāṇa; and there is the abiding of pitta and the others when they are mixed, as well as by those [breaths] when they are combined.
Likewise, one should carefully observe those mixed [disorders] caused by pitta and the others, which are manifold in their combinations, according to the emergence of their respective symptoms.

One should repeatedly observe even firm symptoms that appear gradually. Specifically, *prāṇa* is said to be life and *udāna* is said to be strength; from the affliction of these two, there occurs the loss of both lifespan and strength.
Whether the winds are obstructed, unknown, known, or displaced from their positions, they would be difficult to overcome even with great effort, though they may be free from immediate harm.
Abscesses, splenic disorders, heart disease, abdominal tumors, loss of digestive fire, and other such conditions arise as complications when those [doshas] are obstructed and neglected.
O Suśruta, this introduction has been uttered by me as spoken by Ātreya, for the sake of discerning all diseases and for the increase of the lifespan of men and others.

Having thus understood [the nature of] diseases and so forth, one should indeed perform medical treatment; the three myrobalans (triphalā), combined with honey, clarified butter, and jaggery, destroy all diseases.
Alternatively, triphalā combined with the three pungents (savyoṣā) is a destroyer of all diseases; or else, it may be combined with śatāvarī, guḍūcī, agni, and viḍaṅga.
Śatāvarī, guḍūcī, agni, śuṇṭhī, mūṣalī, balā, punarnavā, bṛhatī, nirguṇḍī, and nimba leaves.
Or, Triphalā, processed seven times with the juice of Bhṛṅgarāja, Āmalaka, and Vāsaka, or even just once, [should be consumed].

As previously stated, powders, boluses (modaka), pills (vaṭikā), clarified butter (ghṛta), oil, or decoctions (kaṣāya) prepared with the aforementioned ingredients according to their availability cure wasting diseases (śoṣaroga). These should be administered in a dose of one pala, half a pala, one karṣa, or even half a karṣa.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Vatarakta," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 168: The Diagnosis is completed. Dhanvantari said: "O Suśruta, listen as I briefly describe the essence of proven formulations that cure all diseases, for the sake of preserving the lives of living beings."
From the consumption of foods that are astringent, pungent, bitter, sour, and dry, and from anxiety, sexual intercourse, physical exercise, fear, grief, and staying awake at night;
The wind becomes disturbed due to loud speaking, excessive burden, and the over-exertion of physical labor; it is also provoked during rain, after food has been digested, and at the end of the day.

From the consumption of hot, sour, salty, alkaline, and pungent foods, from eating when indigestion is present, and from exposure to intense heat and fire, as well as the indulgence in alcohol and anger;
The bile of a person becomes aggravated at the time of digestion, at midday, at the end of the rainy season, during the summer months, and also at midnight.
From the excessive consumption of sweet, sour, salty, unctuous, heavy, and cold foods, and also from the habitual use of fresh grain, slimy substances, and the meat of marshy animals;
The derangement of phlegm (kapha) arises from a lack of physical exercise, daytime sleep, and the comforts of beds and seats; it also becomes aggravated after eating and during the spring season.
Roughness of the body, contraction, piercing pain, and stiffness, as well as numbness, horripilation, rigidity, and emaciation; these are the effects [of vāyu].
Darkness of the limbs, looseness of the joints, and an increase in fatigue and exhaustion are the signs of Vāyu; one should declare a disease endowed with these to be of the nature of Vāta.
Burning heat, perspiration, moisture, agitation, passion, exhaustion, pungency, acidity, the foul odor of a corpse, sweat, fainting, excessive thirst, and vertigo.
A person with symptoms of pitta [experiences] a yellowish or greenish complexion; whereas in the body, there is oiliness, sweetness, slowness of action, and firmness.
Stiffness, lack of satiety, a sense of congestion, swelling, itching, heaviness, and an excessive preoccupation with itching and sleep are the characteristics arising from kapha.

One should recognize a disease arising from two doṣas through the combination of their respective causes and symptoms; that which arises from all causes and possesses all three sets of symptoms is of the sannipātika type.

The body of embodied beings is said to be the substratum of the humors (doṣa), the constituent elements (dhātu), and the waste products (mala). Their equilibrium is health; their imbalance, resulting from decrease or increase, is the opposite.

Fat, blood, flesh, fat-tissue, bone, marrow, and semen are known as the constituents (dhātus); wind, bile, and phlegm are the humors (doṣas); and feces, urine, and so forth are the impurities (malas).
Wind is cold, light, subtle, destructive to the voice, stable, and powerful; bile is sour, pungent, and hot, and when undigested, it is a cause of disease.

Sweet, salty, unctuous, heavy, and excessively slimy is the phlegm (śleṣman); the wind (vāyu) resides in the rectum and hips, while the bile (pitta) is situated in the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya).
The seat of kapha is the stomach, the throat, or the joints of the head; pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes provoke the wind (vāta).

Bitter, sour, and salty tastes increase *pitta*; sweet, hot, and salty tastes increase *kapha*. These same tastes, when applied in their opposite forms, serve to pacify them; they lead to the alleviation of the diseased and become causes of happiness in those who abide in health.

It should be known as beneficial for the eyes, sweet, and an increaser of the rasa-dhatu and blood; it is predominantly sour, pleasing to the mind, and likewise a stimulant of digestion and a promoter of assimilation.

Bitter (tikta) is a digestive stimulant, a destroyer of fever and thirst, a purifier, and a desiccant; it increases pitta, is scraping, astringent, and constipating, while being both absorbent and drying.

Substance is the supreme substratum of taste, potency, and post-digestive transformation; it persists between the stages of taste and transformation, and it swiftly serves as the basis for all substances.

Cold, hot, and salty are considered the potencies (vīrya) of tastes, or alternatively, their power (śakti); furthermore, the post-digestive transformation (pāka) of tastes is of two kinds, being either pungent or otherwise.
The excellence of the physician, the medicine, the patient afflicted by disease, and the attendant—these are the four factors of medical treatment; their opposites lead to failure.

Having understood the place, time, age, digestive fire, similarity [of constitution], natural temperament, medicine, body, mental state, strength, and the disease, one should perform the medical treatment.

A region with abundant water and trees is marshy (anūpa) and causes the provocation of phlegm and wind; another, characterized by sparse trees, is arid (jāṅgala) and is dominated by diseases of blood and bile.
A location endowed with mixed characteristics is known as common. One up to sixteen years of age is called a child; one up to seventy is called middle-aged; and beyond that is called old.
Generally, as previously described, treatments involving alkali, fire, or surgery are avoided for those whose *kapha*, *pitta*, and *vāyu* have been diminished, or for those who are advanced in age.

Nourishment should be administered to the emaciated, reduction to those with a corpulent body, and preservation to those of moderate build; these are considered the three types of bodily constitutions.
One's strength should be diligently assessed through stability, exertion, and contentment; such a person is unwavering, possesses great energy, and is a man of great courage.
When drinks, food, and so forth, even if they are contrary to one's own nature, are prepared for the sake of one's immediate well-being, that is called "concordance" (*sāmya*).

From the consumption of phlegm-inducing foods by a pregnant woman, a man with a phlegmatic constitution is born; likewise, from wind-inducing or bile-inducing foods, one of those respective constitutions is born, while a person of balanced constitution results from wholesome eating.
A man who is emaciated, rough-skinned, and has sparse hair, who remains fickle-minded, delights in much speech, and is prone to sleep, is of a windy (vāta) constitution.
One who has premature gray hair, is fair-complexioned, perspires easily, is irritable yet intelligent, and perceives luminous objects even in dreams, is said to have a pitta constitution.
A man of phlegmatic constitution (śleṣmaprakṛti) has a steady mind, a clear voice, subtle features, and glossy hair; in his dreams, he beholds water and rocks.

A person who possesses a combination of two or three doshas is to be known by their mixed characteristics; even when other doshas are present, that which is predominant is considered the primary constitution (prakṛti).
The digestive fire (jāṭharāgni) is of four types—dull, sharp, irregular, and balanced—arising from a predominance of phlegm, bile, and wind, respectively, or from their equilibrium.
In a balanced state, one should maintain it; in an aggravated state, suppress the wind (vāta); in a sharp state, counteract the bile (pitta); and in a dull state, purify the phlegm (śleṣman).
It is the source of all diseases, causes indigestion, and destroys the digestive fire; its symptoms are fourfold, consisting of undigested matter (āma), sourness, flatulence, and constipation.
From undigested food (āmadoṣa), cholera (viṣūcikā), and likewise heart-ache, lethargy, and so forth, one should induce vomiting there with water containing vacā and salt.
From sourness (amlāt), there arise the absence of semen, vertigo, fainting, and thirst; in that case, drinking cold water and resorting to [medicines] for wind (vāta) are indicated.
Body aches, heaviness of the head, and diseases such as indigestion occur; therefore, one should sleep during the day and avoid fasting.

In cases of *śūla* (colic) and *gulma* (abdominal tumors), which indicate the obstruction of the passages of feces and urine, sudation therapy should be administered, along with the drinking of salt water.

Undigested food, sourness, and flatulence caused respectively by kapha, pitta, and vāyu—having smeared the abdomen with asafoetida, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), and rock salt, the wise physician [should treat them].
One should practice sleeping during the day, for it destroys all forms of indigestion; since a mass of diseases arises from unwholesome food, one should therefore abandon such food.
Or, if taken with warm water as an after-drink along with honey, it becomes a digestive aid; however, milk is generally incompatible with *karīra* fruit, curd, and fish.
Bilva, śoṇā, gambhārī, pāṭalā, and gaṇikārikā constitute this great five roots (mahat-pañcamūla), which stimulates digestion and subdues kapha and vāta.
Śālaparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, the two types of bṛhatī, and gokṣura constitute the minor pañcamūla; it removes vāta and pitta and is aphrodisiac.

Both [these formulations] consist of ten roots and alleviate fevers caused by the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta); they are recommended for cough, dyspnea, drowsiness, and pain in the flanks.

With these, one may conquer gray hair through the application of oils, ghees, or medicinal pastes. Water should be four times the quantity of the [medicinal] ingredients for a decoction, and the resulting decoction should likewise be four times the quantity [of the oil or paste].

The oil and milk should be equal in quantity, and the paste should be one-fourth the amount of the oil. When cooked with these combined medicinal ingredients, the preparation is suitable for enemas (basti) and internal consumption (pāna). One should likewise prepare the cooking process so that it is "rough" for massage (abhyaṅga) and "mild" for nasal administration (nasya).
One should know that health is the state of the gross body and senses, along with the underlying nature (prakṛti) upon which they depend; one should treat such a person as possessing longevity.
He who perceives objects through his senses in a distorted manner is subject to death; as is he who hates his physician, friends, and teachers, and who treats his loved ones as enemies.
He whose ankle, knee, forehead, jaw, or cheek has fallen away or shifted from its place will soon give up his life.
One should abandon that person whose left eye sinks, whose tongue is dark, whose nose is deformed, whose lips are black and displaced from their position, and whose mouth is black.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "Technical Terminology of the Medical Science," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Dhanvantari said: I shall now describe the rules for after-drinks (anupāna) for the sake of distinguishing between what is beneficial and what is harmful. Red rice (raktaśāli) destroys the three doṣas and wards off thirst and obesity.
Mahāśāli rice is highly aphrodisiac; kalama rice alleviates phlegm and bile; and white ṣaṣṭika rice is generally cooling, heavy, and a destroyer of the three doṣas.
Śyāmāka is drying, parching, dry, increases vāta, and subdues kapha and pitta; priyaṅgu, nīvāra, and koradūṣa are proclaimed to be like it.
Barley, when soaked many times, is cooling and removes phlegm and bile; wheat is aphrodisiac, cooling, heavy, sweet, and destroys wind.
Mudga (green gram) conquers kapha, pitta, and blood; it is astringent, sweet, and light. Māṣa (black gram) provides great strength, is aphrodisiac, removes pitta and kapha, and is heavy.
Rājamāṣa is non-aphrodisiac, it destroys kapha and pitta, and relieves afflictions caused by vāta. Kulattha removes asthma, hiccups, heart disease, kapha, abdominal tumors (gulma), and vāta.
Makuṣṭhaka is cooling, constipating, and destroys fever caused by blood and bile; caṇaka is known to destroy virility, blood, phlegm, and bile, while increasing wind (vāta).
Masūra is sweet, cooling, constipating, and subdues kapha and pitta; likewise, kalāya is rich in all these qualities and is extremely wind-increasing.
Āgkī is known to destroy kapha and pitta and is likewise considered aphrodisiac; atasī should be known as increasing pitta, while siddhārtha conquers kapha and vāta.
Sesame is salty, sweet, unctuous, strengthening, hot, and increases pitta; various types of grain are strength-depleting, dry, and cold.
Citraka, iṅgudī, nālīka, pippalī, madhuśigru, cavya, caraṇa, nirguṇḍī, tarkārī, and kāśamardaka;
The bilva fruits destroy kapha and pitta, kill worms, and are light and digestive stimulants. Varṣābhū and mārkaṇḍa destroy vāta and kapha and eliminate the [other] doṣas.
The castor plant (eraṇḍa) has a bitter taste; black nightshade (kākamācī) removes the three doṣas; cāṅgerī destroys phlegm and wind; and mustard (sarṣapa) gives rise to all the doṣas.
In the same way, *kausumbha* and *rājikā* increase wind and bile; *nāḍīca* destroys phlegm and bile; and *cucu* is sweet and cooling.
The lotus leaf destroys the [three] humors, while the *tripuṭa* greatly increases wind; the *vāstuka*, containing alkali, destroys all humors and is an excellent appetizer.
The taṇḍukīya, vipahara, and likewise others such as pālaṅkya; radish causes the aggravation of the humors (doṣas) when raw, but when steamed, it alleviates wind and phlegm.
Indeed, that which is beneficial for the throat is considered best when cooked; it removes all defects. This applies to karkoṭaka, vārtāka, padola, and kāravellaka.
Kūṣmāṇḍa removes leprosy, urinary disorders, fever, dyspnea, cough, pitta, and kapha; it alleviates all the doṣas, is beneficial for the heart, and cleanses the bladder.
Kaliṅga and alābu destroy pitta but generate vāta; trapuṣa and urvāruka increase vāta and kapha while warding off pitta.
Vṛkṣāmla destroys kapha and vāta; jambīra alleviates kapha and vāta. Pomegranate destroys vāta and is constipating; the nāgaraṅga fruit is heavy.
Keśara and mātuluṅga are digestive stimulants and alleviate kapha and vāta; māṣa removes vāta and pitta, while its skin is unctuous, hot, and dispels wind.

The *sāramāmalaka* is aphrodisiac, sweet, pleasing to the heart, and slightly sour; it stimulates the appetite after a meal, is meritorious, and is like nectar. The *harītakī* is comparable to ambrosia.
The emblic myrobalan (*āmalaka*) is laxative and subdues phlegm and wind; likewise, the *akṣa* fruit conquers the three humors. The tamarind fruit is sour, removes wind and phlegm, and is laxative.
The lakuca fruit is unwholesome; the bakula is sweet and conquers kapha and vāta; the bījapūraka destroys abdominal tumors, vāta, kapha, dyspnea, and cough.

The wood-apple (kapittha) is constipating, destroys the [three] humors, and when ripe, is heavy and removes poison; it increases phlegm and bile, while the immature fruit, when fully grown, increases bile.
Ripe mango increases wind and bestows muscle, semen, complexion, and strength; jambu fruit destroys wind, destroys phlegm and bile, is constipating, and causes flatulence.
Tinduka destroys kapha and vata; Badara removes vata and pitta. Bilva causes constipation and increases vata, while Priyala dispels vata.
They say that the rājādana fruit, the moca, the panasa, and that which comes from the coconut increase semen and flesh, and are sweet, unctuous, and heavy.
Grapes, madhūka, dates, and saffron conquer vāta-rakta (gout); māgadhī (long pepper) is sweet when ripe and is excellent for removing asthma and pitta.
Fresh ginger is appetizing, aphrodisiac, digestive-stimulant, and removes phlegm and wind; dried ginger, black pepper, and long pepper are considered conquerors of phlegm and wind.
It is the consensus of medical authorities that black pepper (marica) is non-aphrodisiac; asafoetida (hiṅgu), however, destroys abdominal tumors, colic, and constipation, and removes wind and phlegm.
Yavānī, dhanyaka, and ajājī are excellent for removing vāta and kapha; rock salt (saindhava) is known to be beneficial for the eyes, aphrodisiac, and a pacifier of the three doṣas.
Sauvarcala salt destroys constipation, is hot, and cures heart pain; viḍaṅga is hot, relieves colic, is sharp, and subdues vāta.
Romaka salt increases vāta, is sweet, appetizing, moistening, and heavy; yavakṣāra (barley alkali) cures heart disease, anemia, and throat diseases, and stimulates the digestive fire.
Sajji-kshara is burning, illuminating, and sharp; it is a digestive solvent that destroys the humors (doshas). Atmospheric water (nabhasa-vāri) is light, beneficial for the heart, and removes poison.
Water from rivers is not easily digestible, increases wind, and is dry; water from lakes is sweet and light; water from ponds removes wind and phlegm; and water from tanks is known to increase wind.

Water from mountain springs (nairjhara) is heating, digestive-stimulating, dry, light, and destroys phlegm. Water from wells (kaupa) stimulates digestion but increases pitta, whereas water from pits dug in the earth (audbhida) subdues pitta.
That which is touched by the rays of the sun during the day and by the rays of the moon at night, being entirely free from all defects, is equal to the water of the sky.
Warm water removes fever, dyspnea, fat, wind, and phlegm; boiled and cooled water destroys the three doṣas; and that which has been left overnight increases the doṣas.
Cow’s milk subdues wind and bile, is unctuous, heavy, and a rejuvenative; that of the buffalo is even heavier and more unctuous than cow’s milk, and it extinguishes the digestive fire.

Goat's meat cures bloody diarrhea, removes cough, dyspnea, and phlegm; it is beneficial for the eyes, life-sustaining, and serves as a nasal therapy for women suffering from internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta).
Curd is an excellent subduer of wind, aphrodisiac, and a producer of pitta and kapha; however, whey produced from churning destroys the doshas and cleanses the channels.

Freshly extracted butter (navanīta) destroys the afflictions of malabsorption syndrome, hemorrhoids, and facial paralysis; whereas curd-solids (kilāṭa) and similar products are heavy and causes of skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
But buttermilk, as described by the ancient sages, cures malabsorption syndrome, edema, hemorrhoids, anemia, diarrhea, and abdominal tumors; it pacifies the three doṣas.
Cow's ghee is aphrodisiac, sweet, and alleviates vāta, pitta, and kapha; it promotes intelligence and vision, and when processed with medicinal herbs, it conquers all three doṣas.

Clarified butter (ghṛta) processed [with these ingredients] destroys epilepsy, insanity, and fainting; one should know that the ghee of goats and other animals possesses qualities similar to cow’s milk; and urine removes phlegm and wind, as well as all worms and poisons.

Oil produced from sesame seeds removes paleness, abdominal diseases, skin disorders, hemorrhoids, swelling, abdominal tumors, and urinary disorders; it alleviates wind and phlegm, is strengthening, and promotes hair growth.
Mustard oil destroys worms and jaundice, and removes phlegm, fat, and wind; linseed oil is harmful to the eyes, yet it removes bile and destroys wind.

Honey produced from trees (akṣaja) is said to destroy kapha and pitta, benefit the hair, and nourish the skin and ears; it is declared to alleviate the three doṣas and is also proclaimed to increase vāta.
