Sugarcane cures hiccup, dyspnea, worms, vomiting, urinary disorders, thirst, and poison; it destroys blood-bile (raktapitta), is strengthening, aphrodisiac, and increases phlegm (kapha).

Phāṇita (unrefined molasses) is bilious and parching; *tavara* is light; *surā* (rum) is light; *matsyaṇḍikā* (crystallized sugar) is aphrodisiac, unctuous, sweet, and conquers blood disorders, pitta, and vāta.
Fresh jaggery (guḍa) alleviates wind and bile, is parching, subdues wind, and increases phlegm; however, old jaggery is highly beneficial, pacifies bile, and clarifies the blood.
Gaḍa-śarkarā removes blood-bile (raktapitta) and is aphrodisiac when combined with fats; wine produces all types of pitta, yet it conquers kapha and vāta due to its acidity.
Those varieties produced from *sauvīra* are sharp and cause *rakta-pitta*. Gruel made from fried rice (*maṇḍa*) is digestive, appetizing, and wholesome.
This light gruel, containing curd, pomegranate, and the three pungents (vyoṣa), along with jaggery, honey, and long pepper, facilitates the downward movement of wind and cleanses the bladder.
This rice gruel, well-prepared, cures cough, dyspnea, and dysentery; milk-rice (pāyasa) generates phlegm and is strengthening; and kṛśarā destroys wind (vāta).
Well-washed, strained, unctuous, pleasantly warm, light, and appetizing; prepared with bulbs, roots, fruits, and grains, it is nourishing and heavy.
Soup that is well-prepared, light, and served lukewarm is beneficial; likewise, steamed and squeezed vegetables, seasoned with fats and other ingredients, are wholesome.
A soup made with pomegranate and āmalaka stimulates the digestive fire and alleviates vāta and pitta; when prepared with āmalakas alone, it destroys dyspnea, cough, coryza, and kapha.
Soup made from barley, jujube, and horse-gram is beneficial for the throat and subdues Vāta; that made from mung bean and āmalaka is constipating and destroys Kapha and Pitta.
Curd with jaggery subdues wind; roasted flour (saktu) is parching and increases wind. A cake filled with ghee stimulates the digestive fire, while *śaṣkulī* is aphrodisiac and heavy.
Edible flour-balls (piṣṭaka) mixed with meat are known to be nourishing; those prepared with oil are harmful to the eyesight, and those steamed in water are difficult to digest.
Mandakas are considered wholesome when very hot, whereas gukhas are considered wholesome when cold; water as a post-drink destroys fatigue, thirst, and other such ailments.
Protection is provided by means of food, drink, and so forth; one becomes entirely free from disease. [The poison] is not hot, resembles the color of a peacock's neck, and causes discoloration.

The odors, touch, and tastes will be intense, and the consumer will suffer mental anguish; upon smelling it, there will be eye disease that is incurable even by the best of physicians; trembling, yawning, and so forth—this is the characteristic of poison.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Rules for Subsequent Drinks and Other Remedies," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Dhanvantari said: Fever is known to be of eight types: those arising from the humors individually, from combinations of two, from all three combined, and from external causes. To alleviate thirst and fever, one should administer water cooled after being boiled with musta, parpaṭaka, uśīra, candana, udīcya, and nāgara.
One should first administer this digestive medicine, which removes fever, to the patient suffering from fever: *nāgara*, *devadāru*, coriander, and the two types of *bṛhatī*.
A decoction prepared from āragvadha, abhayā, mustā, tiktā, and granthika is digestive and beneficial for fever accompanied by undigested toxins (āma) and colic.
Equal parts of *madhūka* pith, rock salt, *vaca*, black pepper, and long pepper should be finely ground with water and administered as a nasal drop (*nasya*) to restore consciousness.
A decoction prepared from trivṛt, viśālā, triphalā, kaṭukā, and āragvadha, combined with alkali (kṣāra), is a purgative that should be drunk; it removes all types of fever.
A decoction of mahauṣadha, amṛtā, musta, candana, uśīra, and dhānyaka, combined with sugar and honey, destroys tertian fever.
Having tied it with seven red threads around the waist at the root of the Apāmārga plant on a Sunday, one certainly destroys tertian fever.
On the northern bank of the Gaṅgā, a childless ascetic has died; one should offer him water with sesame seeds, and the fever lasting for one day will be released.
Oils prepared with the decoction and paste of *guḍūcī*, as well as those of *triphalā*, *vāsaka*, *mṛdvīkā*, and *balā*, are effective destroyers of fever.
A decoction of *dhātrī*, *śivā*, *kaṇā*, and *vahni* is the ender of all fevers; now I shall describe the medicine that removes fever accompanied by diarrhea.

Decoctions prepared from *pṛśniparṇī*, *balā*, *bilva*, ginger, blue lotus, coriander, *pāṭhā*, *indrayava*, *bhūnimba*, *musta*, and *parpaṭaka*, along with *mahauṣadha* (ginger), cure acute diarrhea accompanied by fever.
A decoction made from nāgara, ativiṣā, musta, bhūnimba, amṛtā, and vatsaka removes all fevers and destroys all types of diarrhea.
Milk boiled with musta, parpaṭaka, divya, and śṛṅgavera, along with śālaparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, bṛhatī, and kaṇṭakārikā [is beneficial].
Balā, aśvadaṃṣṭrā, bilva, and so forth, along with pāṭhā, nāgara, and dhānyaka—this [group] is beneficial when combined in food for all those suffering from diarrhea.
A decoction of bilva and mango stones, along with sugar and honey, cures diarrhea; likewise, kuṭaja bark combined with pippalī is beneficial in cases of diarrhea.
A decoction of vatsaka, ativiṣā, viśva, kaṇā, and kanda, when administered, is effective for diarrhea accompanied by blood and characterized by colic due to undigested matter (āma).

Now, the treatment for *grahaṇī*: since *grahaṇī* destroys the digestive fire (*agni*), clarified butter (*havis*) boiled with the decoction and paste of *citraka* is a destroyer of *grahaṇī*. It cures abdominal tumors (*gulma*), edema (*śotha*), abdominal enlargement (*udara*), splenic disorders (*plīha*), colic (*śūla*), and hemorrhoids (*arśas*), and it stimulates the digestive fire.
One should add here five salts: sauvarcala, saindhava, viḍaṅga, audbhida, and samudra.
Know that medicine for hemorrhoids is threefold: indeed, it consists of surgery, caustic alkali, and fire; yet that which truly destroys hemorrhoids is fresh, recently extracted buttermilk.
For the destruction of hemorrhoids, one should consume gudūcī combined with pippalī, along with abhayā fried in ghee and amlaloṇikā.
The combination of sesame, sugarcane juice, and linseed destroys hemorrhoids and skin diseases; likewise, pañcakola with black pepper and the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa) stimulates the digestive fire.
Harītakī, when eaten with ginger, jaggery, or even combined with rock salt, constantly stimulates the digestive fire.
A decoction made from Triphalā, Amṛtā, Sārivā, Tiktā, Bhūnimba, and Nimba, combined with honey, destroys anemia (pāṇḍuroga) along with jaundice (kāmalā).

A bolus (*modaka*) composed of *trivṛt*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *śyāmā*, long pepper (*pippalī*), sugar, and honey, brings an end to *sannipāta* disorders and cures hemorrhagic fever (*raktapitta*).
While there is clothing, hope, and life itself, why does one suffering from blood-bile, consumption, or coughing fall into despair?
A decoction of *āṭarūpaka*, grapes, and *pathyā*, mixed with sugar and enriched with honey, cures cough, dyspnea, and hemorrhagic disorders (*raktapitta*).

Vāsā juice mixed with sugar and honey, when drunk, conquers blood-born [fevers]. Sallakī, badarī, jambu, priyāla, āmra, arjuna, and dhava—these, or milk enriched with honey, each separately used, are warders-off of blood.
Having drunk ghee prepared with the fresh juices of *nirguṇḍī*—including its roots, fruits, and leaves—one who was wasted by consumption shines like a god, free from all disease.
Harītakī, pippalī, śuṇṭhī, and marica, combined with jaggery, are declared to be a modaka that cures cough and destroys thirst and loss of appetite.
One *prastha* of ghee, prepared with thirty *palas* each of the juices of *kaṇṭakārī* and *guḍūcī*, cures cough and kindles the digestive fire.
Black *dhātrī* (myrobalan) cooled with ginger and combined with honey cures hiccup; one suffering from hiccup and asthma should drink *bhārgī* with ginger and warm water.
Or, in the case of a disorder of the voice, one should hold a piece of khadira wood smeared with oil in the mouth; or one may take a pathyā fruit combined with pippalī, or combined with nāgara.
One should take the powder of viḍaṅga and the three myrobalans with honey to cure vomiting; or one may drink a decoction of āmra and jambū mixed with honey.
Triphalā dispels all vomiting and draws away thirst; when drunk with honey, it also cures vertigo, fainting, and heart disease.

The five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are beneficial when drunk for dispelling epilepsy, planetary afflictions, and the like; likewise, the juice of the kūṣmāṇḍa gourd mixed with ghee and liquorice serves that same purpose.
Ghee prepared with the juice of *brāhmī*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *śaṅkhapuṣpī* should be consumed as an ancient remedy that destroys insanity, possession by spirits, and epilepsy.
Ghee cooked with a decoction and paste of *aśvagandhā*, along with four times the amount of milk, destroys wind, acts as an aphrodisiac, promotes flesh, and produces offspring.
One who drinks the powder of *nīlī* and *muṇḍīrikā* combined with honey and clarified butter, along with a decoction of *chinnā*, overcomes even the most difficult cases of *vātarakta*.
Five *pathyā* fruits with jaggery cure leprosy, hemorrhoids, and wind disorders; likewise, the fresh juice, paste, powder, or decoction of *gaḍacī*.
Ghee boiled with milk and the decoction and paste of black *guḍūcī* is an ender of vātarakta and a pacifier of skin diseases, ulcers, and the like.
Guggulu combined with Triphalā removes vātarakta and fainting; likewise, Guggulu taken with cow’s urine destroys ūrustambha.

A decoction of ginger and gokṣura relieves the pain and colic of vāta associated with āma; likewise, [a decoction] of the ten roots (daśamūla), amṛtā, eraṇḍa, rāsnā, ginger, and devadāru [is effective].
The decoction, combined with black pepper and jaggery, destroys swelling of the heart; it is declared to be a bolus (modaka) that cures cough and destroys thirst and loss of appetite.
In thirty palas of juice each from kaṇṭakārī and guḍūcī, one prastha of ghee is prepared; this indeed cures cough and heart disease and stimulates the digestive fire.
A decoction combined with black dhātrī, sugar, ginger, black pepper, and rock salt, when taken with castor oil, destroys heavy vāta accompanied by āma.
Balā, punarnavā, eraṇḍa, the two types of bṛhatī, and gokṣura, along with hiṅgu and lavaṇa, when drunk as a yellow decoction, alleviate vāta-śūla.
One should cause [the patient] to drink a decoction prepared with triphalā, nimba, yaṣṭīmadhu, kaṭukā, and āragvadha, mixed with honey, for the alleviation of burning sensations and pain.

Water boiled with triphalā and yaṣṭīkā destroys the pain of indigestion (pariṇāma). Iron rust (maṇḍūra) purified with cow’s urine and combined with the powder of triphalā, when licked with honey and ghee, cures colic born of the three doṣas.
Trivṛt and black harītakī taken in parts of two, four, and five [respectively] are made into pills equal in weight to treacle; these remove diseases caused by the obstruction of feces.
This powder, consisting of *harītakī*, alkali of barley (*yavakṣāra*), *pippalī*, and *trivṛt*, should be drunk with ghee; it is the destroyer of *udāvarta*.
Pills made from Trivṛt, Harītakī, and Śyāmā, processed with the milky sap of Snuhī and drunk with urine, are excellent for breaking up abdominal distension (ānāha).
Ghee prepared with a paste of trikaṭu, triphalā, dhānyaka, viḍaṅga, cavya, and citraka, when properly processed, cures vāta-gulma.
Long pepper root brought with milk removes heart pain; one should drink half that amount of Sauvacala along with clarified butter and Śivā.
Or by means of *kaṇā*, stone-rupturing drugs (*pāṣāṇabheda*), powdered *śilājatu*, rice-gruel, or even molasses, one who suffers from dysuria survives.
One afflicted by disorders of Vāta, accompanied by pain and difficulty in urination (mūtrakṛcchra), should drink a decoction of amṛtā, nāgarī, dhātrī, vājigandhā, and trikaṇṭaka.
Yava-kṣāra (barley-alkali) equal in measure to white sugar removes all types of urinary distress; likewise, the juice of Nidigdhikā mixed with honey destroys urinary distress.
Salt mixed with the paste of the three myrobalans (triphalā) is known to cure urinary retention; when the urine is obstructed, one should introduce camphor powder into the penis.

A decoction derived from the root of *śigru* is pungent and hot, and it causes the falling of stones. The juice of *dhātrī* combined with honey and *niśā* removes all types of *meha*. A decoction of *triphalā*, *dāru*, *dārvī*, and *aṣṭa*, taken with honey, destroys *meha*.
One who desires to increase corpulence should gradually and progressively abandon sleeplessness, sexual intercourse, physical exercise, and anxious thoughts.
One who eats barley or śyāmāka grain with honeyed water will become stout; conversely, by drinking hot food or rice-gruel with its scum, one becomes lean of body.
Sacā, vyajīraka, vyoṣa, hiṅgu, sauvarcala, and āmalaka, when drunk with honey, destroy blood disorders, eliminate phlegm, and stimulate all the digestive fires.
One suffering from abdominal enlargement (jaṭhara) should drink one *prastha* of ghee prepared with four parts water, two parts cow’s urine, and a paste of *citraka*, along with milk.
One should increase the ten-day periods by one day each for ten days, adding a day of the *paippalika* [practice] along with milk; likewise, one should decrease it again in the same manner.
One should eat sixty-grain rice with milk; thus, [this regimen] for one thousand recitations of the Kṛṣṇa-mantra is nourishing, promotes longevity, and destroys enlargement of the spleen.

Ghee prepared with the decoction and paste of *punarnavā* removes swelling; it should be consumed with cow’s urine, or *pippalī* taken with milk, or *abhayā* in equal parts with jaggery, or *viśva* (ginger) should be used by one suffering from swelling.
By drinking castor oil produced from the *eraṇḍa* plant, combined with milk prepared with *balā*, a man shall conquer intestinal hernia (*antravṛddhi*) accompanied by flatulence and colic.
A paste made from *pathyā* (chebulic myrobalan) combined with black salt and oil extracted from *bhraṣṭorucaka*, is a supreme remedy for curing hemorrhoids.
Glandular swellings (gaṇḍamālā) are destroyed by using the root of nirguṇḍī as a nasal drop; furthermore, fomentation with smuhī and gaṇḍīrī destroys tumors (arbuda).
By applying a paste of *hastikarṇapalāśa*, along with *dhattūra*, castor oil plant (*eraṇḍa*), *nirguṇḍī*, *varṣābhū*, *śigru*, and mustard seeds, one cures goiter (*galagaṇḍa*).

This ointment destroys elephantiasis (ślīpada), even that which is long-standing and extremely severe; it also destroys abscesses (vidradhi) using śobhāñjana, rock salt (sindhūttha), and asafoetida (hiṅgu).
Śarapuṅkhā mixed with honey is a healer of all wounds; likewise, an application of Nimba leaves heals swelling and wounds.
Triphalā, khadira, dāru, and nyagrodha purify wounds; a physician should sprinkle these over a fresh wound that is accompanied by pain.
Having recognized traumatic wounds (āgantuvraṇa), the physician should apply a medicated ghee mixed with yaṣṭīmadhuka and slightly warmed, combined with ghee and honey.
One should employ cooling treatments that destroy the heat of pitta and rakta; a decoction made from bamboo bark, eraṇḍa, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and vanidā [is recommended].
Asafoetida and rock salt, when drunk, cause the blood located in the visceral cavity to flow out; or alternatively, one may use the unsalted broth of barley, jujube, and horse gram.
One should eat food or drink gruel mixed with rock salt; the juice of karañja, ariṣṭa, and nirguṇḍī destroys worms in ulcers.
Guggulu combined with the powder of triphalā and formed into pills is a free-acting remedy that destroys constipation and heals wounds.
Alternatively, oil prepared with the fresh juice of dūrvā grass, or with kampillaka, or with a paste of dārvī bark, is a preeminent healer of wounds.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "Description of the Treatment for Fever and Other Diseases," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Dhanvantari said: "O Suśruta, listen to the treatment for diseases such as sinus ulcers (nāḍīvraṇa). Having opened the sinus with a surgical instrument, the procedure for sinus ulcers should be performed just like that for ordinary wounds."

One should conquer fistula-in-ano, malignant ulcers, pain, and hemorrhoids by using equal parts of guggulu, the three myrobalans (triphalā), and the three acrids (vyōpa) combined with clarified butter.
Oil prepared from the juice of nirguṇḍī removes sinus ulcers and malignant wounds; it is beneficial for skin diseases such as pāmā when used for drinking, massage, and nasal drops.

Guggulu combined with one part each of triphalā, kṛṣṇā, and three, five, and one [parts of other ingredients] respectively, forms a pill (ghuṭikā) that is beneficial for those suffering from swelling, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and fistula-in-ano.

In the case of venesection in the middle of the *dhvaja* (penis), there is suppuration in syphilis (*upadaṃśaka*); therefore, that [infection] must be guarded against with great effort, for it causes the destruction of the *śiśna*.
One should drink a decoction of paṭola, nimba, triphalā, and guḍūcī, along with guggulu and khadira; thus the secondary ulcer (upadaṃśa) is destroyed.
One should burn *triphalā* along with *sāmasī* and honey in an iron cauldron; this ointment applied to venereal sores heals the ulcer instantly.
Ghee cooked with the pastes and decoctions of triphalā, nimba, bhūnimba, karañja, khadira, and other such [herbs] is the supreme remedy for upadaṃśa.
Having first recognized that it is broken, one should sprinkle it with cold water; once it has healed, an ointment should be applied and it should be bound with kuśa grass.
Black gram, meat, as well as clarified butter, milk, vegetable broth, and pure water—these nourishing foods and drinks should be administered to a patient suffering from a fracture.
One who consumes a paste of garlic, honey, ghee, and sugar in equal proportions will experience the rejoining of bones that have been severed, shattered, or fallen out in no time at all.
Aśvattha, triphalā, vyoṣa, and varā, taken in equal parts and combined with an equal amount of guggulu, is a restorer for broken joints.
In all types of kuṣṭha, emesis, purgation, and bloodletting [are indicated], as well as [the use of] vacā, vāsā, paṭola, nimba, and the bark of kaliṅgī.
A decoction drunk with honey, combined with Madana fruit, removes Vata; a purgative should be administered using Trivṛt, Karṇaphala, and Triphalā.
Oil prepared with realgar and black pepper destroys leprosy; this ointment is effective for all types of leprosy, as is rice cooked with *śivā* (myrobalan) and five kinds of molasses.
Kustha applied as an ointment with the milky sap of karañja and gaja, along with an unguent of karavīra after the body has been anointed with oil, removes skin diseases.
Turmeric, sandalwood, rāsnā, guḍūcī, iḍagaja, āragvadha, and karañja—this ointment is supreme for removing skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
Realgar, viḍaṅga, vākucī, and mustard seeds, ground with urine along with karañja, constitute this ointment which destroys skin diseases like the sun.
This ointment, prepared by grinding viḍaṅga, eḍagaja, vacā, kuṣṭha, niśā, saindhava salt, and sarṣapa with urine and sour gruel, destroys ringworm and skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
Seeds of *prapunnāṭa*, *dhātrī*, resin of *sarja*, and *snuhī* ground with *sauvīra*—this is the supreme ointment for ringworm.
One should grind the leaves of *āragvadha* with sour gruel; this destroys ringworm, skin exudations, leprosy, and even vitiligo.

Vāgujī taken warm with milk conquers leprosy for one who subsists on a milk diet. Sesame, ghee, triphalā, honey, vyōṣa, bhallātaka, and sugar—these seven taken in equal parts are aphrodisiacs, purifying, destroyers of disease, and grant freedom of action.
The powder of viḍaṅga, triphalā, and kṛṣṇā, licked with honey, destroys skin diseases, worms, urinary disorders, sinus ulcers, and fistula-in-ano.
He who should consume abhayāriṣṭa—consisting of harītakī, āmalaka, and niśā—shall conquer all types of skin diseases after one month; of this there is no doubt.
A decoction of ten thousand *khadira* sprouts burnt in a pot, combined with the juice of *sākṣadhātrī*, honey, and *mūla* [ghee], is a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*) that destroys leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).
Having drunk a decoction of *dhātrī* and *khadira* combined with *vāgajī*, one quickly destroys vitiligo as white as a conch or the moon; of this there is no doubt.
By drinking bhallātaka oil for a month, a person shall conquer disease; likewise, khadira water, when consumed through drinking and other means, becomes a conqueror of leprosy.

One should eat a large quantity of *somarājī* fruit that has been infused with a decoction of *malapūka*, specifically one *karṣa* in weight; then, while abstaining from salt, one should drink a decoction of *akṣa* and *phalgu*.
Apamārga (Euphorbia) applied as a paste cures even incurable vitiligo; likewise, vāsā, śuddhā, triphalā, paṭola, and karañjaka may be employed.
If ghee is processed with the decoction and paste of nimba and black vetra, it becomes "vajraka"; by its use, one conquers leprosy and lives for a hundred years.
One should cook oil with four times as much of the natural juice of dūrvā grass; by mere anointing, scabies, eczema, and ringworm are destroyed.
Oil prepared with the bark of *druma*, *arka*, and *kuṣṭha*, the salts, cow’s urine, *gambhārikā*, and *citraka* cures skin diseases, ulcers, and other such ailments.

(Now, the treatment for *amlapitta*): Likewise, *dhātrī*, *nimba* fruit, and *citraka* with cow’s urine; or a decoction of *vāsā*, *amṛtā*, *parpaṭikā*, *nimba*, *bhūnimba*, *mārkarai*, *triphalā*, and *kulattha*, taken with honey, destroys *amlapitta*.
A decoction of the three myrobalans (triphalā), patola, and bitter herbs, when drunk with sugar and yaṣṭīmadhu, conquers fever, vomiting, and acid bile (amlapitta).
Vāsā-ghṛta, Tikta-ghṛta, and Pippalī-ghṛta should be administered in cases of amlapitta, as should Guḍakūṣmāṇḍaka.
Pippalī combined with honey destroys amlapitta; a bolus (modaka) made of pathyā, pippalī, and jaggery cures kapha and weak digestion.
Having ground ajājī together with dhanvyāka, one should cook it with one prastha of ghee; this removes phlegm, bile, and anorexia, and cures weak digestion and vomiting.
(Thus ends the treatment for acid bile.
A decoction made from long pepper (*pippalī*), amṛtā, bhūnimba, vāsaka, ariṣṭa, parpaṭa, khadira, and ariṣṭaka removes the pain of eruptive boils (*visphoṭa*) and fever.
Ghee combined with the juice of triphalā and trivṛt should be administered for the purpose of purgation to pacify visarpa and fever.
The decoction known as Aṣṭaka, prepared from Khadira, Triphalā, Ariṣṭa, Paṭola, Amṛta, and Vāsaka, conquers Romāntika and Masūrikā.
Rubbing with the powder of garlic destroys skin diseases such as leprosy, erysipelas, boils, and itching, and it also eliminates mosquitoes.
Having excised with a surgical instrument skin-warts, moles, freckles, and dark spots, one should cauterize them completely with alkali or fire.
An ointment of *paṭola* and *nīlī* destroys *jālagardabha* disease. Oil boiled with *guñjā* fruits and the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* destroys itching, *dāruṇaka*, leprosy, and wind-related disorders.
The marrow of *arka* seeds, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *nālīcchā*, and *bhṛṅgarāja*, along with iron powder and fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*), when digested and cooked, produce black hair.
Two *prasthas* of milk with sugar, one *pala* of *madhuka*, and one *kuḍava* of oil, when cooked together, form an errhine (*nasya*) that removes gray hair.
In diseases of the mouth, however, one should hold a gargle (gaṇḍūṣa) of triphalā; likewise, house-soot, barley-alkali (yavakṣāra), pāṭhā, vyopa, and rasāñjana [are used].
One should hold in the mouth a powder consisting of *tejovatī*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *lodhra*, and *citraka*, mixed with honey; this cures diseases of the neck, teeth, and mouth.
The tender sprouts of *paṭola*, *nimba*, *jambu*, and *mālatī* constitute the excellent "five sprouts" (*pañcapallava*) decoction for cleansing the mouth.
The lukewarm juice of garlic, ginger, śigru, pāṭalī, radish, and rudantī is excellent for filling the ear.
In a case where the ear is afflicted with severe pain, accompanied by noise and discharge, one should pour lukewarm goat's urine mixed with powdered rock salt (saindhava) into it.
Oil cooked with the juice of *jātī* leaves overcomes ear infections (*pūtikakarṇa*). Mustard oil mixed with ginger, when applied warm, removes earache.

Milk boiled with the five roots (pañcamūla), citraka and harītakī, ghee-jaggery confection (sarpirguḍa), the six-ingredient preparation (ṣaḍaṅga), and vegetable soup (yūṣa) are for the alleviation of chronic rhinitis (pīnasa).
Diseases arising in the eyes and abdomen, as well as catarrh, ulcers, and fever—these five are pacified by fasting for five nights.
The filling of the eyes with the juice of *dhātrī* removes inflammation; likewise, rock salt with honey, or the juice of *śigru* and *dāru* combined with *añjana*, [achieve the same].
An external plaster applied from turmeric, deodar, rock salt, chebulic myrobalan, wild barley, and white clay, ground together, cures eye diseases.

By applying a paste of *abhayā* mixed with milk from a cow that has recently lost its calf, or by holding warm, finely ground leaves of *śuṇṭhī* and *nimba* with a small amount of rock salt over the eye, swelling, itching, and pain are briefly relieved.
Abhayā, akṣa, and amṛta, combined in parts of one, two, and four respectively, taken with honey and ghee as a linctus, or as a decoction, destroys all eye diseases.
This collyrium, prepared with sandalwood, the three myrobalans, betel nut, and the roots of the palāśa tree ground with water, removes all darkness [of ignorance].
Black pepper ground with curd is an ointment that removes night-blindness; likewise, ghee boiled with milk and the decoction and paste of triphalā [is effective].
This, when drunk at the onset of night, quickly destroys cataracts: long pepper, the three myrobalans, grapes, iron powder, and rock salt.
A pill-collyrium ground with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* is recommended; it destroys blindness, cataracts, and other eye diseases.
The three pungents, the three myrobalans, black salt, rock salt, realgar, rucaka salt, conch-shell navel, jasmine flowers, and neem.
Rasāñjana, bhṛṅgarāja, ghee, honey, and milk—having ground these together, a pill is made that destroys all eye diseases.
The root of burnt *eraṇḍa* ground with *kākī*, or the flower of *mucukunda*, when applied as a paste, quickly destroys headache.

Oil boiled with one hundred palas each of castor root, *cakrā*, and *vyāghrī* is used as a nasal drop (*nasya*) to remove diseases of wind and phlegm, cataracts (*timira*), and those located in the upper part of the body.
Nācanam (or lavana) with jaggery, or viśva with long pepper and rock salt, [is used] in all diseases such as arm-stiffness and other upward-moving disorders.

In the case of Sūryāvarta, medicinal treatments such as nasal therapy (nasya) should be administered. A decoction of the ten roots (daśamūlī) combined with ghee and rock salt, used as a nasal drop, destroys the piercing pain in the limbs and relieves the headache of Sūryāvarta.
A woman afflicted by vāta and asṛgdara should drink a mixture of sauvarcala salt, cumin, madhūka, and blue lotus (nīlotpala) combined with curd and honey.
In cases of Pitta-type fever, one should administer the fresh juice of Vāsaka, or the juice of Guḍūcī, or the paste of Āmalakī seeds with water, along with sugar and honey.
For the pacification of *pāṇḍu* and *pradara*, one should drink the sweet juice of the root of *āmalakī* or that of *kārpāsa* with rice-water.

The root of *taṇḍulīyaka* together with *rasāñjana* and honey, when drunk with rice-water, conquers all types of menorrhagia (*asṛgdara*). Likewise, the root of *kuśa* drunk with rice-water conquers menorrhagia.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "Description of the Treatment for Nāḍīvraṇa and Other Diseases," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Dhanvantari said: O Suśruta, listen as I describe the treatment for diseases of women and others; in cases of disorders of the female reproductive tract (yoni-vyāpad), treatments that conquer Vāta are most highly recommended.
Vacā, upakuñcikā, jātī, kṛṣṇā, vāsaka, saindhava, ajamodā, yavakṣāra, citraka, combined with sugar.

Having ground [the ingredients] and stirred them with water and other liquids, one should eat it fried in ghee; this cures pain in the vagina and flanks, heart disease, abdominal tumors, and hemorrhoids.
By applying an ointment of jujube leaves, the dilation of the womb is pacified; and by applying an ointment of *lodhra* and gourd fruit, it brings about firmness to the womb.
Ghee cooked with the five tender leaves, piṣṭāhva, and mālatī flowers, and heated by the sun, stops the flow of blood and destroys foul odors from the vagina.
Having consumed sour gruel, a *japā* flower, a leaf of *jyotiṣmatī*, ground *dūrvā* grass, and *citraka* mixed with sugar;
The powder of dhātrī, añjana, and abhayā, when drunk with water, removes [uterine] dust; likewise, lakṣmaṇā taken with milk, or used as a nasal drop during the fertile period, bestows a son.
Half an *āḍhaka* of milk, clarified butter, and *aśvagandhā* bestow sons; even a barren woman shall obtain a son by drinking [milk] with clarified butter, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), and *kesara*.
Milk boiled with the roots of *kuśa*, *kāśa*, *urubūka*, and *gokṣuraka*, combined with sugar, is an excellent remedy for the colic of a pregnant woman.
By applying a paste of pāṭhā, aṅgali, siṃhī, āmalaka, and kūṭaja—either individually or combined—to the navel, the bladder, and the vulva, a woman gives birth easily.
In the case of a Sūta woman, there occurs pain in the heart, head, and bladder known as Arkanda (or Kvalla); in that condition, she should drink Yava-kṣāra with whey or lukewarm water.
A decoction prepared from the ten roots (daśamūlī), taken with clarified butter, removes diseases of the urinary tract; furthermore, powdered śāli rice taken with milk acts as a galactagogue.
For the purification of breast milk, she should consume the fresh juice of the vidārī tuber and likewise the root of cotton, while subsisting on a diet of green gram soup.
One should administer this electuary—consisting of kuṣṭha, vacā, abhayā, and brāhmī, sweetened with honey and ghee—to a child to produce a fine complexion, longevity, and luster.

In the absence of breast milk, one should drink goat’s milk or cow’s milk possessing similar qualities. For one suffering from inflammation caused by fire, fomentation should be performed with earth heated by fire.
One should drink *leha* (electuary) made from *mustā*, *viṣā*, and *āragvadha* in cases of vomiting and fever; a preparation of *mustā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *viṣā*, *bilva*, and *kūṭaja* cures diarrhea.
Honey, trikaṭu, and citron prevent hiccup and vomiting; kuṣṭha, indrayava, siddhārtha, niśā, and dūrvā overcome skin diseases.
A bath with a decoction of mahāmuñjī, tikta, and uśīra removes the afflictions of the planets; likewise, an ointment made from saptacchada, turmeric, and sandalwood [is recommended].

The wearing of conch, lotus, seed-pearls, rudrākṣas, coral, iron, and so forth [is prescribed]. With the mantra "Oṃ kaṃ ṭaṃ yaṃ gaṃ to Vainateya, obeisance," and with the mantra "Oṃ hoṃ hāṃ haḥ," peace for children is attained through sprinkling and the offering of oblations (bali). [The mantra is: "Oṃ hrīṃ! O Bālamahārāja, accept this oblation; release the child! Svāhā!"
One pala of Śirīṣa taken with rice-water destroys poison; likewise, white Varṣābhū taken with rice-water cures the bite of a snake.
Curd and clarified butter, Taṇḍulīya, soot from a house, and Niśā likewise; ground together with honey and rock salt, this is a destroyer of poison.
A decoction of the root of *aṅkoṭa* drunk with clarified butter is an ender of poison; that medicine which destroys old age and disease is an elixir (*rasāyana*).

Abhayā (chebulic myrobalan) should be consumed sequentially with sindūra, honey, ghee, sugar, long pepper, dry ginger, pippalī, honey, and jaggery during the rainy season and the other seasons respectively by one desiring the qualities of a rejuvenative elixir.

At the end of a fever, one should consume one *abhayā* and two *vibhītaka* fruits; having eaten these along with four parts each of honey, clarified butter, and *dhātrī*, it bestows a lifespan of a hundred years.
Yellow Ashwagandha taken with milk and ghee cures all diseases; the fresh juice of Mandukaparni and Vidari is like nectar.
By eating sesame, dhātrī, and bhṛṅgarāja, one shall live for a hundred years; likewise by consuming trikaṭu, triphalā, citraka, guḍūcī, and śatāvarī.
The powder of *viḍaṅga* and iron, taken with honey, destroys disease; so too do *triphalā*, *kaṇā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *guḍūcī*, and *śatāvarī*.

Powdered *vidanga* and *bhṛṅgarāja*, and so forth, when processed with [appropriate substances], removes all diseases; having licked this powder mixed with honey and ghee along with *vidārī*, one may approach ten women.
One should cook ghee with the paste of śatāvarī and ten times its amount of milk; when combined with sugar, long pepper, and honey, it is known as *jāraka*.
Pratimarṣa, avapīḍa, nasya, pravapana, and śirovirecana—these are called the fivefold therapy (pañcakarma).
The six seasons are traditionally reckoned in order by pairs of months beginning with Māgha; one should practice the service of fire and consume preparations of honey and milk.

Likewise, one should not sleep during the day in the spring when accompanied by a woman; during the rainy season, one should abandon sleeping and other such activities, as well as exposure to the rays of the autumnal moon.
Śāli rice, muddā beans, rainwater, boiled milk, and likewise the leaves of nimba, atasī, kusumbha, śigru, and sarṣapa are wholesome.
Oils extracted from the roots of *jyotiṣmatī* indeed cure worms, skin diseases, urinary disorders, as well as ailments of wind and phlegm and headaches.
Pomegranate, emblic myrobalan, jujube, karamarda, priyāla, citron, nāgagra, āmrātaka, and kapittha.
Pittala is a subduer of Vāta and an agitator of Kapha; likewise are Jīmūtaka, Ikṣvāku, Kuṭaja, and Akṛtabandhana. Water [is also such].
These—dhāmārgava, madana, indrayava, and vacā—should always be combined for emetic purposes; they are administered for emesis in the forenoon.

The digestive tract is soft due to pitta, harsh due to the predominance of vāta and kapha, and moderate when the doṣas are in equilibrium; in these three conditions, Trivṛt is the appropriate purgative.
Saindhava salt combined with sugar and honey, nagara, and trivṛt; or harītakī and vihaṅga taken with cow’s urine—these are purgatives.
Castor oil and a decoction of triphalā in double the quantity should be administered; once the patient has been fed, one should then induce emesis in cases where vāta is predominant among the doṣas.

One should prepare a nozzle from bamboo or similar material, measuring six, eight, or twelve finger-breadths in length; its aperture should be like that of a jujube fruit, and it is used as a bladder for a patient lying on his back.
This same procedure is declared for the administration of a non-unctuous enema (nirūha); the dosage is respectively half, three, and six palas for the mild, medium, and superior types.
Pathyā, akṣa, vātryoka, and dvicaturbhāga, which destroy diseases when processed with a decoction of śatavārī, bhṛṅgarāja, sindhuvāra, and other such herbs.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Treatment for Women's Diseases and Other Matters," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Dhanvantari said: I shall now describe the substances beginning with the sweet group which remove morbid passions (or discolorations): Śāli rice, Ṣaṣṭika rice, wheat, milk, ghee, meat-broth, and honey.
Marrow, śṛṅgāṭaka, yavaka, ervāru, gīkṣura, gambhārī, lotus seeds, grapes, dates, and balā.
Nārikela, ikṣu, ātma-guptā, vidārī, priyālaka, madhuka, tāla, and kṣmāṇḍa—this is the primary sweet group (madhura-gaṇa).
When consumed excessively on its own, it pacifies fainting and burning sensations, clarifies the six sense faculties, yet produces worms and increases phlegm.
One should apply a plaster of jaggery (guḍa) and other substances for conditions such as dyspnea, cough, loss of voice, sweetness in the mouth, throat lesions, goiter, and elephantiasis.
Pomegranate, emblic myrobalan, mango, wood-apple, karamarda, citron, hog-plum, jujube, and tamarind fruit.
Curd, buttermilk, fermented rice-gruel, lakuca fruit, and sour vetasa—this sour-salty flavor combined with ginger is digestive and promotes digestion.
Sour [taste] is moistening, generates wind, is exhilarating, causes a burning sensation, and is carminative; however, when consumed in excess, it certainly causes the hypersensitivity of the teeth.
It causes coldness of the body and burns the voice, throat, mouth, and heart; having ripened wounds that are cut or split, it is activated by the digestive fire.
The saline group consists of salts such as yavakṣāra, sarjikā, and others; it is purifying, digestive, moistening, and it causes disintegration and spreading.

That single rasa which obstructs the channels and produces softness, when excessively consumed, may cause itching of the limbs, swelling of the abdomen, discoloration, as well as blood-wind disorders (raktavāta), hemorrhagic fevers (pittarakta), and pain in the generative organs and so forth.
Vyoṣa, śigru root, mūlaka, devadāru, kuṣṭha, garlic, valguja fruit, mustā, guggulu, and lāṅgalī.

Kaṭuka (the bitter group) is digestive, purifying, and a destroyer of leprosy, itching, and phlegm; it removes obesity, lethargy, and worms, and counteracts semen and fat. However, when consumed excessively on its own, it causes vertigo, burning sensations, and other such ailments.
Kṛtamāla, kīra, haridrā, indrayava, as well as svādukaṇṭaka, vetra, the two types of bṛhatī, and śaṅkhinī.
Guḍūcī, candravantī, trivṛt, maṇḍūkaparṇī, kāravellaka, vārtāku, karavīraka, and vāsaka;
Rohiṇī, conch powder, karkoṭa, jayantikā, jātī, vāruṇaka, nimba, jyotiṣmatī, and punarnavā.
The bitter taste is astringent, appetizing, and digestive; it is purifying, destroys fever and thirst, and overcomes fainting, throat ailments, and the like.
For that [excessive practice] causes the complete drying up of feces, urine, and moisture; when indulged in to excess, it produces lockjaw, convulsions, pain, headaches, ulcers, and other ailments.
Triphalā, sallakī, jambu, āmrātaka, vacā and so forth; tinduka, vakula, śāla, pālaṅkī, mudga, and cillaka.

Astringent (kaṣāya) is grasping, healing, firming, moistening, and drying; when consumed excessively by itself, it causes pain in the heart, as well as dryness of the mouth, fever, flatulence, stiffness of the neck, and so forth.
Turmeric, kuṣṭha, salt, meṣaśṛṅgī, the two types of balā, kacchurā, sallakī, pāṭhā, punarnavā, and śatāvarī.

Agnimantha, brahmadaṇḍī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, eraṇḍaka, as well as barley, jujube, horse-gram, and so forth—consuming one karṣa of each or of the entire group known as daśamūla removes wind and excessive bile.
Śatāvarī, vidārī, bālaka, uśīra, candana, dūrvā, vaṭa, pippalī, badarī, and likewise sallakī.
Plantain, blue lotus, lotus, udumbara, and patolaka; furthermore, this is the group that removes phlegm, consisting of turmeric, jaggery, and kuṣṭha.
Śatapuṣpī, Jātī, Vyoṣa, Āragvadha, and Lāṅgalī, along with ghee, oil, muscle fat, and marrow, are considered the foremost among unctuous substances (snehas).

Likewise, ghee is recommended for those desiring wisdom, memory, intelligence, and digestive fire; however, in cases of Pitta disorders, plain ghee is used, while in Vata disorders, it should be combined with salt.

It should also be administered when there is an excess of phlegm, combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and alkali, for those suffering from tumors, sinus ulcers, worms, phlegm disorders, fat-related diseases, and wind disorders.

Oil should be administered for the sake of lightness and firmness to those individuals with hard bowels, as well as to those whose bodily constituents (dhātus) have been depleted by exposure to wind and sun, carrying heavy loads, sexual indulgence, or physical exercise.

In cases where the pathways are obstructed by dryness, afflictions, wasting, excessive fire, or wind, one should perform the treatment for the female reproductive tract after first cauterizing the network of vessels in the case of headache.
The dose for the best [patient] is one pala; for the middling, three akṣas; and for the lowest, half a pala, in the case of fats, decoctions, and medicinal herbs.
Warm water should be given with ghee, whereas it is recommended separately for oil; however, in cases of thirst associated with kapha, pitta, or unctuous substances, a person should drink warm water.

The downward movement of wind, bright and firm stools, and unctuousness are considered the signs of one who has been properly oleated; for one who is dry, oleation should be administered, and for one who is excessively oleated, drying therapy should be performed.

Sudation is desired for disorders of wind and phlegm, whether the wind or the phlegm predominates, using *śyāmāka* grain, *koradūṣa*, *anna*, buttermilk, oil-cake, or parched grain flour. One should not administer sudation to those who are excessively obese, dry, weak, or fainting.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "Description of Yoga-samādhi and Other States," in the Ācāra-kāṇḍa of the first part of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Dhanvantari said: "O Suśruta, listen as I describe ghee, oil, and other substances that cure diseases: Śaṅkhapuṣpī, Vacā, Somā, Brāhmī, and Brahmasuvarcalā."
One should cook one prastha of ghee with equal parts (one akṣa each) of abhayā, guḍūcī, aṭarūpaka, and vāgujī.
One *prastha* of the juice of *kaṇṭakārī* combined with one *prastha* of milk—this is known as *Brāhmī-ghṛta*, which is supreme for producing learning and memory.
Triphalā, citraka, balā, nirguṇḍī, nimba, vāsaka, punarnavā, guḍūcī, bṛhatī, and śatāvarī.

With these [substances], ghee should be cooked according to availability to subdue all diseases. One should cook half an āḍhaka of oil in a decoction of one hundred parts of *balā*, using the pastes (*kalka*) of *madhūka*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *candana*, *utpala*, and *padmaka*.

With small cardamom, long pepper, kuṣṭha, cinnamon, cardamom, agallochum, and saffron, along with aromatic substances, aśvagandhā, and the jīvanīya group, [this mixture] is prepared by being infused in one āḍhaka of milk.
This, cooked over a mild fire, should be placed in a beautiful silver vessel; it cures all disorders of wind (vāta) that reside within all the constituent elements (dhātu) of the body.
This oil, known as Rājavallabha, which is strengthening and beneficial for the voice, should be prepared by adding one prastha of śatāvarī juice and likewise one prastha of milk.
Śatapuṣpā, devadāru, māṃsī, śaileyaka, balā, candana, tagara, kuṣṭha, manaḥśilā, and jyotiṣmatī.

One should cook one prastha of ghee with these pastes, each weighing one karṣa; it is for those who are humpbacked, dwarfs, or lame, as well as for the deaf, those with facial freckles, and those afflicted by leprosy.
For those whose limbs have been broken by wind, those who fail in sexual union, those whose bodies are worn out by old age, and those with bloated faces and parched mouths;
This oil, which brings an end to the families of diseases, quickly destroys all those vātas located in the skin, as well as those situated in the vessels and the tendons.
This Nārāyaṇa oil, spoken by Viṣṇu, is a destroyer of diseases; one may prepare it separately as an oil or a ghee using each of the medicinal herbs individually.
A plaster may be prepared from śatāvarī or guḍūcī combined with citraka and gocarana; or it may be made from nirguṇḍī or kaṇṭakārī along with their juices and other ingredients.
Or with the dwelling of a frog, or with vāsaka, the three fruits (triphalā), brāhmī, eraṇḍa, bhṛṅgarāja, and kuṣṭha.
A bolus, a pill, or even a powder made from *musalī*, the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *khadira*, and the *vaṭa* group [of trees] destroys all diseases.
Combined with ghee, honey, or even water, sugar, jaggery, and so forth, as well as salts and pungent spices, it removes wind according to what is available.
Or else, one may use citraka, arka, trivṛt, yavānī, hayamāraka, sudhā, bālā, gaṇikā, saptaparṇa, and suvarcikā.
A wise person should cook oil with *jyotiṣmatī*; this "exudation" oil (*niṣyandana-taila*) should be administered copiously for fistula-in-ano.
This great oil, beginning with *citraka*, is supreme for cleansing and healing, it imparts all complexions, and it shatters all diseases.
Ajamodā with vermilion, yellow orpiment, the two types of turmeric, the two alkalis, together with sea-foam, ginger, and resin from the *sara* tree;
Sesame oil combined with Indravāruṇī, Apāmārga, Kadalī, and Syandana, along with goat’s urine, [should be prepared].
One should cook this Ajamoda-taila over a gentle fire, combined with cow’s milk; it removes scrofula (gaṇḍamālā).
One who is skilled should cook it until it is cooked and then purify it; one should effect healing and softening with this oil.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "Description of Brāhmī Ghee and Other Remedies," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 175.
Rudra said: In this manner, Dhanvantari, who is Viṣṇu, spoke to Suśruta and others. Hari, in turn, spoke to Hara (Śiva) regarding various medicinal formulations that destroy diseases.
Hari said: O Śaṅkara, in all fevers, fasting must first be performed; likewise, one should drink boiled water and remain in a windless place.
O Lord, fevers indeed go to destruction through the application of fire and fomentation; likewise, a decoction of *guḍūcī* and *mustaka* removes fever caused by *vāta*.
Listen now to [the preparation] with *durālabhā* and ghee, which removes fever caused by *pitta*: it is made with *śuṇṭhī*, *parpaṭa*, *mustā*, *bālaka*, *uśīra*, and *candana*.
A decoction with ghee cures fever born of phlegm; likewise, one with dry ginger and durālabhā, or with vālaka, or with dry ginger and parpaṭa, cures all types of fever.
A decoction of kirātatikta, nāgaramothā, guḍūcī, dry ginger, and musta will alleviate fever caused by pitta; now hear another excellent formulation.
A decoction made from bālaka, uśīra, pāṭhā, kaṇṭakārī, mustaka, and likewise suradāru, is a fever-destroyer.
O Śaṅkara, that [mixture] of dhanyāka, nimba, and mustā with honey, combined with paṭola leaves, guḍūcī, and triphalā, [is likewise beneficial].
This yellow powder, derived from *harītakī*, *pippalī*, *āmalaka*, and *citraka*, removes all fevers, stimulates hunger, and subdues *vāta*.
A powder or a decoction made from dhānyaka, uśīra, parpaṭa, āmalakī, and guḍūcī, combined with candana and honey, [removes] fever.
It shall be a subduer of all fevers; now hear [the remedy] that removes *sannipāta* fever: with turmeric, nimba, triphalā, mustaka, and devadāru.
Water boiled with the decoction of kaṭurohiṇī, paṭola, and patra, when drunk, subdues fever born of the three doṣas.
By consuming the powder of *nāgabalā* along with *kaṇṭakārī*, *nāgara*, *guḍūcī*, and *puṣkara*, one will overcome asthma, cough, and other such ailments.
In fever caused by kapha and vāta, hot water prepared with viśva, parpaṭaka, uśīra, musta, and candana should be given to the thirsty patient.

One should give very cold water, which cures thirst, vomiting, fever, and burning sensations; a decoction of the five roots beginning with Bilva (bilvādi-pañcamūla) should be used in fever caused by Vāta.
Pippalīmūla, guḍūcī, and viśvabheṣaja are digestive; this decoction, when administered in vāta-fever, is supremely pacifying.

A decoction of *parpaṭa* and *nimba*, taken with honey, destroys fever born of bile (*pitta*). Even when this treatment is being administered, if consciousness does not return to the patient, [further measures must be taken].

One should cauterize either the feet or the forehead with an iron probe. A decoction of *tikta*, *pāṭhā*, *parpaṭa*, *viśālā*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *trivṛt*, taken with milk, is a purgative that cleanses all fevers.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "Description of Various Formulas for Removing Fever," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Blessed Lord said: Beautiful hair grows upon a bald man within seven nights from the application of burnt elephant tusks mixed with goat’s milk and *rasāñjana*.
Oil prepared with one-fourth part of the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* combined with the powder of *guñjā* promotes the growth of hair.
Anointing with a mixture of ela, māṃsī, kuṣṭha, and murā is auspicious; likewise, taking the fruit of guñjā as an ointment cures *candralupta* (alopecia).
Indeed, by applying a paste of powdered mango seeds, the hairs become fine; and an application of a paste made from *karañja*, *āmalaka*, *elā*, and lac removes redness.
By applying a paste of mango stone marrow and *āmalaka*, the hair indeed becomes firmly rooted, thick, long, glossy, and does not fall out.
The excellent oil prepared with viḍaṅga and gandhapāṣāṇa, along with four times its quantity of cow’s urine, or indeed with manaḥśilā alone, [is highly effective].

By massaging the head, one may bring about the destruction of hair-whorls and lines appearing on the scalp. Freshly burnt conch-shell powder, when rubbed and applied as a paste over lead, [achieves the same].
O Bull-bannered Lord, the hair becomes smooth and deep black; [one should take] *bhṛṅgarāja*, iron powder, *triphalā*, and *bījapūraka*.
Indigo, oleander, and jaggery—cooked together with these in equal parts, this great medicine, when applied as an ointment, turns gray hairs black in this world.
The marrow of the mango stone, the three myrobalans,
blue vitriol, and *bhṛṅgarāja*, along with aged, processed iron powder and sour gruel, produce black hair.
Having ground the seeds of *cakramarda*, *kuṣṭha*, the root of *eraṇḍa*, and very sour *kāñjika* together, this ointment removes diseases of the head.
Saindhava salt, vacā, hiṅgu, kuṣṭha, nāgeśvara, śatapuṣpā, and devadāru—with these, oil is prepared.
Combined with one-fourth part of cow-dung juice, it brings an end to severe earache through the filling of the ear-canal with that [mixture].
O Śiva, by filling the ears with sheep's urine and rock salt, the destruction of foul odors, worms, discharges, and other ailments of the ears shall occur.
By applying a paste made from the petals of *mālatī* flowers with their juice as an ointment, and by filling [the area] with cow's urine, the discharge of pus is destroyed.
Kaṣṭha, māṣa, marica, tagara, honey, pippalī, apāmārga, aśvagandhā, bṛhatī, and white mustard seeds.

Barley, sesame seeds, and rock salt, used as a foot-powder (udvartana), are auspicious; they cause the growth of the penis, arms, breasts, and ears. Likewise, mustard oil, *bhallātaka*, *bṛhatī*, and pomegranate fruit [produce similar effects].
Anointed with the processed bark-fibers, the linga increases by means of that.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Growth of Hair and Other Matters," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Hari said: Indeed, the juice of *Sobhāñjana* leaves mixed with honey, when applied to the eyes, removes diseases from the feet; of this there is no doubt.
Eighty sesame flowers, jasmine blossoms, uśīra, nimba, āmalaka, ginger, long pepper, and taṇḍulīyaka.
One should make a pill from this, dried in the shade and ground with rice-water; when suddenly applied as a collyrium to the eyes with honey, it removes timira and other such disorders.
One should grind the marrow of the *bibhītaka* seed, conch-shell navel, realgar, neem leaf, and black pepper with goat's urine.
Puṣpa destroys night-blindness, as well as timira and paṭala; [one should take] four parts of conch-shell and half that amount of realgar.
Having ground together rock salt and half that amount [of the other ingredient] with water, one should make a pill, dry it in the shade, and apply it as an ointment to the eyes.
The great medicine consisting of the three pungents (trikaṭu), the three myrobalans (triphalā), and the fruits of karañja destroys cataracts, film over the eye, and piciṭa.
Having ground rock salt and the two types of turmeric with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, the mere application of that collyrium destroys cataracts and other such ailments.
The root of the *āṭarūṣaka* (castor plant), ground with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), should be applied as a plaster over the eyes and eyelids; by this, eye pain is destroyed.
Satakratu (sour gruel) drunk with the root of badarī removes pain in the eyes; likewise, rock salt, pungent oil, and the root of apāmārga [are effective].
O Śaṅkara, by rubbing [the ointment] with milk and sour gruel in a copper vessel and applying it as collyrium, even Piñjaṭa himself will be destroyed.
Oṃ dadru sara kroṃ hrīṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ, dadru sara hrīṃ hrīṃ oṃ uṃ ū sara krīṃ krīṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ. By this mantra, when applied as an ointment, women indeed come under one's control.
The root of *bilvaka-nīlikā* ground and used as an ointment—by merely applying this as an eye-salve, cataracts (timira) are indeed destroyed.
Kaṭuka (long pepper),
tagara, haridrā, āmalaka, vacā, and khadira ground together with clarified butter constitute a collyrium that cures eye diseases.
He who performs *dhauti* with his mouth full of water and washes his eyes with a large measure is daily liberated from all eye diseases by dawn.
A preparation made from the root or even the leaf of white *eraṇḍa*, when applied as a wash after being heated over a goat-dung fire, cures the throbbing pain in the eyes caused by Vāta.
An ointment made of sandalwood, rock salt, old palāśa leaves, harītakī, a layer of flower-petals, indigo,
and *vakrikā* removes [cataracts].
The root of the guñjā plant, rubbed in goat’s urine, destroys cataracts; it should be applied with a probe made of silver, copper, or gold, rubbed by hand.
O Rudra, ground *udvartana* [ointment] destroys the disease of jaundice (*kāmalā*); likewise, the fruit of *ghoṣā*, when smelled after being inhaled, destroys jaundice that has been ingested.
Dūrvā grass, pomegranate flowers, lac, and harītakī—these, when used as a juice, indeed destroy nasal polyps and vātarakta.
O Bull-bannered One, O Blue-and-Red One, by grinding the root-fiber of *jāṅgalī* with its own juice and administering it as a nasal drop (*nasya*), hemorrhoids are destroyed in an instant.

O Rudra, with cow’s ghee, resin of the *sarja* tree, *dhanyāka*, rock salt, *dhuttūraka*, and red ochre—sealing wax prepared with these [substances]— Please provide the final answer in the following format: The final answer is: $final_answer$. The final answer is: O Rudra, with cow's ghee, resin of the sarja tree, dhanyāka, rock salt, dhuttūraka, and red ochre—sealing wax prepared with these [substances]—
With oil, it cures wounds on the lips that have cracked or split; likewise, chewing and holding a *jātī* leaf in the mouth removes oral diseases.
By consuming the seeds of kesara, loose teeth become firm. [The following is also used: muṣṭaka, kuṣṭha, elā, yaṣṭika, honey, and vālaka.
By eating this coriander, remove the foul odor from the mouth, whether it arises from astringent or pungent tastes or from the consumption of bitter vegetables.
For one who practices this regularly, the foul odor of the mouth shall cease, and all dental wounds will likewise come to an end.
The practice of holding gargles and mouthfuls of sour gruel mixed with oil removes diseases of the mouth caused by burning from betel leaf and lime.
And for one who has expelled the phlegm through the chewing of ginger, [the following are beneficial]: slices of citron, cardamom, licorice, and long pepper.
Furthermore, having licked the powder of these along with jasmine petals, and likewise by chewing the root of *śephālikā* and *jaṭā*, one overcomes throat-pain (*galashuṇṭhi*).
By drawing blood from the vessels of the nose, the disease *śaṃśakara-jihvikā* is destroyed; [this is done by] the juice of *śirīṣa* seeds mixed with four times as much *haridrā*.

O Lord of Beings, when that is cooked, it serves as a nasal medication (nasya) that cures diseases of the head; by the mere application of this nasal medication, diseases of the throat are destroyed instantly.
The destruction of dental worms occurs by chewing the root of *guñjā*; likewise, a decoction of *kākajaṅghā*, *snuhī*, and *nīlī* mixed with honey [achieves the same].
O Śiva, a ghee prepared with *karkaṭapāda* mixed with milk destroys worms that have infested the teeth or originated from them.
And by that, having been softened, the teeth should not produce a grating sound; or else, having smeared them with only the *karkaṭapāda* [herb] or with *aśiva*, one should proceed.
Indeed, by grinding the fruits of *jyotiṣmatī* with water for three weeks and applying a paste of white *abhayā* to the teeth, one removes stains and discolorations.
Lodhra, saffron, mañjiṣṭhā, loha, kāleyaka, barley, and rice—these, combined with liquorice and honey, [should be used].
An application of the face with [substances] ground with water makes the faces of women beautiful. Furthermore, one *prastha* of oil prepared with two parts of goat’s milk [is likewise beneficial].
Alternatively, using one karṣa each of red sandalwood, mañjiṣṭhā, and lac, together with liquorice and saffron, produces a radiant complexion of the face within seven days.
The powder of ginger and long pepper, along with *guḍūcī* and *kaṇṭakārikā*—water boiled with these, when drunk, indeed stimulates the digestive fire.
O Lord of the First, it indeed destroys wind-pain and consumption; [the herbs] karañja, parpaṭa, uśīra, bṛhatī, and kaṭurohiṇī [are used].
Gokṣura boiled with water and drunk removes fatigue; it brings about the destruction of burning sensations, bile, fever, wasting, and even fainting.
Honey, ghee, and powdered long pepper, boiled and mixed with milk, when drunk, will cure heart disease, cough, and irregular fever.

O Bull-bannered One, for all medicinal herbs used as decoctions, one should take exactly half a karṣa; however, O Lord whose banner is the bull, the specific dosage should be understood according to the patient's age.
Milk drunk in combination with the juice of cow dung, as well as the juice of *kākajaṅghā*, will destroy irregular fever (*viṣamajvara*).

Milk boiled with ginger (maśuṇṭhi) will cure the fever of a woman who has recently given birth; likewise, liquorice (yaṣṭīmadhuka), musta, rock salt (saindhava), and the fruit of bṛhatī [are effective].
O Śiva, by giving these things, as well as by the gift of a horse, a man shall obtain sleep; likewise, O Śiva, sleep shall come through the gift of pepper, a broken horse, and a halter.
The root of *kākajaṅghā*, when placed on the head, induces sleep; likewise, oil prepared with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) and resin (*sarjarasa*) has the same effect.
Combined with cold water, it destroys fever through its application as an ointment; likewise, it removes the heat born from blood-fever and burning sensations.
Śṛka-śaivāla-mantha, śuṇṭhī, pāpāṇabheda, śauvāñjana, gokṣura, or indeed varuṇacchanna;

Having given water boiled with the root of *Saubhāñjana* and these [other ingredients], along with asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) and barley-alkali (*yavakṣāra*), when drunk, it destroys wind disorders (*vāta*).
O Śiva, long pepper, the root of long pepper, and likewise marking-nut—water boiled with these and drunk is an excellent remover of colic.
Ant-hill earth prepared with the roots of *aśvagandhā* and *mūlaka*; O Rudra, by rubbing [the limbs] with this, *ūrustambha* (stiffness of the thighs) is pacified.
Indeed, the root of *bṛhatī* ground with water and drunk acts as a certain means for breaking up obstructed wind (*saṃghātavāta*).
The root of fresh *tagara* taken with buttermilk will indeed destroy *jhiñjinīvāta*,
just as Indra’s thunderbolt destroys a tree.
The *asthisaṃhāra* powder, taken with a single meal, or even with meat broth, cures wind disorders and heals fractured bones.
Coated with ghee, dried, and combined with goat’s milk—by the removal of that [substance], one should destroy the pain in the feet; there is no doubt regarding this procedure.

Honey, clarified butter, rock salt, beeswax, jaggery, red ochre, guggulu, and resin of the sarja tree, when applied as a plaster, cause the bursting of fissures and the purification of the *kloman* (the pleura).
O Bull-bannered Lord, when a foot is smeared with pungent oil and heated over a smokeless fire, it becomes as level as if it had been ground with earth.
Sal resin, beeswax, cumin, and myrobalan—when used as an ointment after an application of medicated ghee, they indeed alleviate the pain of burns from fire.
Sesame oil burnt by fire, combined with barley ash, destroys wounds burnt by fire when applied as an ointment many times.
Buffalo butter, burnt ground sesame seeds, and bhallātaka, when applied as an ointment or used as a nasal drop, destroy wounds and pain in the heart.

O Hara, O Śaṅkara, O Bull-bannered One, the wound caused by the weapon has been filled with camphor, cow’s milk, and ghee, and it has been bound with a white-colored cloth; yet it still touches upon inflammation and pain.
The wound from the sword-strike was filled with the very sap from the root of that mango tree; healed of the wound by the application of the sap, it became as if filled with clarified butter.
The roots of śarapuṅkhā, lajjālukā, and pāṭhā, ground with water and applied as a paste, cause the injury from a weapon to subside.
The root of *kākajaṅghā*, dried for exactly three nights, indeed destroys suppuration, putrefaction, and pain in a wound when applied with *rohita*.
Sesame oil mixed with water and the root of the *apāmārga* plant—by the application of that sprinkling, the pain arising from a blow shall be destroyed.
O Śaṅkara, by grinding together harītakī, rock salt, and ginger with water and consuming it, indigestion is indeed destroyed.
The root of the *nimba* tree tied around the waist will cure pain in the eyes; the root of *śaṇa* burnt together with betel leaf removes [excessive] seminal flow.
Haridrā steamed with rice, the root of white mustard, and the seeds of *mātuluṅga*—an ointment made from these in equal parts, when applied for seven nights, will produce a beautiful body.

O Bull-bannered Lord, by administering a nasal drop (*nasya*) made from the leaf of white *aparājitā* with the juice of *nimba* leaves, or with the essence of honey, there shall be liberation from *ḍākinīs*, the Mothers, and *brahmarākṣasas*.

The root of white jayantī, collected under the asterism of Puṣya, along with the roots of white aparājitā, arka, and citraka—having made a pill from these, a woman becomes submissive by means of a tilaka mark.
O Rudra, one should know that equal parts of long pepper, iron powder, ginger, and emblic myrobalan, along with rock salt and honey-sugar, [form this preparation].

By consuming [it] for seven days in portions the size of an udumbara fruit, a man shall become strong and live for two hundred years. "Oṃ ṭha ṭha ṭha"—when employed in all rites for subjugation, it fulfills all desires.
Having collected it, O Śaṅkara, the wise man should burn that dwelling of the crow; when those ashes are placed upon the head of the enemy in a funeral pyre fire, [the result follows].
O Rudra, listen to that supreme yoga which causes him to be eradicated: indeed, one's excrement should be cast upon the skin of a wild rat.

One should indeed cause the suppression of the excrement of [the victim] by tying it with a thread from a cat's tail, having smeared the name of the person [to be targeted] with the blood of a black crow.
Then, O Hara, having been cast into the very center of a withered leaf, that woman or indeed that man is devoured by flocks of crows.
Sugar, honey, jaggery, milk, sesame, and gokṣuraka in equal parts—O Rudra, he shall destroy the enemy; O Hara, this is the rite of eradication.

If one offers oblations into the fire with the blood of an owl, a black crow, and a hundred sticks of *bilva* wood, while uttering the names of two individuals, a great enmity will arise between them; of this there is no doubt.

The flesh of a Rohita fish prepared with bear’s milk and the oil refined from it, when used for massage, cures the disease; furthermore, by administering sandalwood water as a nasal drop (nasya), the growth of hair occurs once again.
When the root of the *lāṅgalikā* plant is held in the hand and smeared upon the body by that man, he dispels the pride of old age.
O Śiva, by means of peacock blood alone one seizes the life-force; O Lord, this applies even to blazing serpents dwelling in their holes.
Indeed, the body of a serpent or a python, when burnt in a funeral pyre, has its ashes cast before enemies, which will cause them to break and flee.
When thrown with this mantra, it causes the great destruction of the enemy: *oṃ ṭha ṭha ṭha cāhīhi cāhīhi svāhā | oṃ udaraṃ pāhihi pāhihi svāhā*.
If the impurity of Sudarśanā is collected under the Puṣya asterism and cast into the middle of the house, serpents will avoid it.
O Śiva, a wick made from the root of the arka plant, ignited by the sun-fire (arka-agni) and combined with mustard oil, destroys the snakes of the path.
Cat flesh, excrement, and yellow orpiment, processed with goat's urine—when smeared with this, a mouse will drive away other mice.
O Rudra, one who has been liberated in the temple [is truly free]; there is no need for further deliberation on this point. [One should offer] fruitless *arjuna* flowers, *bhallātaka*, and *śirīṣa*.
Lac, resin of the Sarja tree, Viḍaṅga, and Guggulu—incense made from these destroys flies and mosquitoes.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "Description of Eye-salve and Other Remedies," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Hari said: One should give *brahmadaṇḍī*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, *priyaṅgu*, and *nāgakeśara* mixed with betel leaf (*tāmbūla*) while reciting the mantra; by this, women come under one's control. The mantra is: *Oṃ nārāyaṇyai svāhā*.
He to whom betel is given shall become submissive through this excellent mantra: Oṃ hariḥ hariḥ svāhā.

Godanta and yellow orpiment, combined with *kākajihvā* and reduced to powder, should be applied to the head of anyone; that person will become submissive. White mustard seeds and the remains of an offering (*nirmālya*) cause the destruction of whatever house they enter.
If the root of the *vaibhītaka* or the *śākhoṭaka*, joined with its leaf, is placed at the door of a house, there will certainly be quarreling there.
One should grind the flesh of a wagtail together with honey; by smearing it upon the womb during the period of menstruation, a man shall become a slave.
Having fumigated with agallochum, guggulu, and blue lotus, together with jaggery, one will become beloved at the king's gate.
The root of the *śvetāparājitā* ground together with *rocanā*, when used as a forehead mark (*tilaka*), will bring whoever one looks upon under one's control even within the royal palace.
A person becomes submissive by using kāka-jaṅghā, vacā, kuṣṭha, nimba leaves, and saffron, combined with one's own blood.

Having taken the pure blood of a wild cat, one should steep it in *karañja* oil; then, over the fire of Rudra, one should cause soot to fall using a lotus leaf. From that collyrium, one shall become invisible.

Oṃ, homage to Khaḍgavajrapāṇi, the great general of the yakṣa army, svāhā! Oṃ rudraṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ, the swift vidyā of the excellent spear! Oṃ, O Mothers, paralyze [him], svāhā! One should recite this vidyā, which wards off thieves, one thousand times. By means of the root of the *mahāsugandhika* plant placed upon the waist, semen is paralyzed.

Oṃ, homage to all sentient beings! Homage! Accomplish, accomplish success, svāhā! Having consecrated a karavīra flower seven times with this mantra, one should wave it before women; in an instant, she will indeed come under one's control.
One should grind brahmadaṇḍī, vacā, and leaves together with honey; by anointing the limbs with this, a woman desires no other husband.
The crest of the *brahmadaṇḍī* plant, when thrown into the mouth, causes the immobilization of semen; the root of *jayantī*, held in the mouth, bestows victory in legal disputes.
The root of *bhṛṅgarāja* ground and combined with semen, having applied it as collyrium to the eyes, indeed makes a man submissive.
One should offer the Aparājitā flower together with a blue lotus along with betel leaf; this is the supreme means of subjugation.
On the big toe, the foot, the ankle, the knee, and likewise the hip; on the navel, the chest, the belly, the armpit, the throat, and the cheek.

The digits of the moon reside on the lips, the eyes, the forehead, and the head; in women they are situated from top to bottom during the bright fortnight, and from bottom to top during the dark fortnight, whereas in men they are situated from bottom to top during the bright fortnight and from top to bottom during the dark fortnight.

O Rudra, on the left and right limbs respectively, the sixty-four arts (kalās) that produce melting and other effects are proclaimed in the Kāmaśāstra as means of subjugation; beginning with embracing, they bring women and maidens under control.
With a forehead mark (*tilaka*) made of *rocanā*, *gandhapuṣpa*, *nimba* flowers, *priyaṅgu*, saffron (*kuṅkuma*), and sandalwood (*candana*), one shall bring the world under one's control.
Oṃ hrīṃ! O Goddess Gaurī, grant me good fortune, sons, and mastery over others. Oṃ hrīṃ! O Goddess Lakṣmī, [grant] all good fortune that enchants the three worlds.
O Rudra, by the application of fragrant turmeric and saffron, as well as incense and sweet-smelling flowers, one shall bring others under control.
A man becomes submissive by applying a paste of *durālabhā*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, *kuṅkuma*, and *śatāvarī* mixed with sesame oil to the female organ.
O Rudra, if a woman fumigates her vulva with the smoke of neem wood, she shall become fortunate; her husband will become her slave.
Buffalo butter, lac, and licorice—by smearing these on the vulva, good fortune shall arise, and likewise, the husband shall become a servant.
Licorice, cow’s milk, and thorny milkweed—these should be taken in equal parts with warm water; when reduced to one-fourth, this brings about the excellent conception of a fetus.
One should soak the seeds of the mātuluṅga with milk; having drunk that, one obtains a fetus—of this there is no need for doubt.
One desiring a son should cause [the woman] to drink the seeds of the *mātuluṅga* and the roots of the *eraṇḍaka* combined with clarified butter.

Paśvagandhā boiled in the milk of a dead animal produces urine. One should grind the seeds of the palāśa tree with honey; by drinking this during her menstrual period, a woman shall become free from menstruation and pregnancy.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-eighth chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—179. Hari said: Having boiled yellow orpiment, alkali of barley, *patrāṅga*, red sandalwood, nutmeg, vermilion, and lac, one should smear it upon the teeth.
Having cleansed the teeth with a decoction of *harītakī*, one should apply an ointment; O Rudra, there is no doubt that a man's teeth will become red or white.
One should boil radish over a mild fire and fill the ears with its juice; by filling the ears with this, ear discharge is destroyed.
Having taken an arka leaf, one should warm it slowly over a mild fire; having squeezed it, one should fill the ears with its juice, and the earache will be destroyed.

One should cook oil with priyaṅgu, madhuka, dhātakī, and rows of utpala flowers, along with mañjiṣṭhā, lodhra, lākṣā, and the fresh juice of kapittha; by filling [the vagina] with this, the discharge of women will be destroyed.
The alkali of dried radish and ginger, asafoetida, great medicinal root (musta), costus, vacha, kuṣṭha, devadāru, śigru, and rasāñjana;
Sauvarcala salt, yavakṣāra, as well as sarjaka and saindhava; likewise, granthi, viḍa, and musta, mixed with honey in a fourfold proportion.
Likewise, the juice of *mātuluṅga* and the juice of *kadalī*, along with those [other ingredients], when cooked in oil, will quickly remove discharges and the like; of this there is no doubt.
By filling the ears with pungent oil (kaṭutaila), the destruction of worms in the ears occurs; likewise, [the use of] turmeric, nimba leaves, long pepper (pippalī), and black pepper [is recommended].
O Hara, grind together viḍaṅga, bhadramusta, and the seventh ingredient, viśvabheṣaja (ginger), with cow’s urine and form them into pills. One pill cures indigestion, and two remove cholera.
Patola taken with honey, or likewise with cow’s urine, destroys eye disease; this "Śaṅkarī" wick-candle is a remover of all eye ailments.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Hari said: One should powder together equal parts of vacā, māṃsī, bilva, tagara, padmakesara, nāgapuṣpa, and priyaṅgu. A mortal who is fumigated with this may roam the earth like a god of love (Kāmadeva).
One should combine camphor and *devadāru* with honey; by applying that very mixture as an ointment to the penis, one can indeed subjugate a woman.

During sexual intercourse, a man should restrain his own organ; he should smear the left hand of the woman with the [substance] from his left hand. Once smeared, the woman comes under his control and desires no other man.

Oṃ, O Raktacāmuṇḍā, bring such-and-such a person under my control, bring them! Oṃ hrīṃ hraiṃ hraḥ phaṭ. Having recited this mantra ten thousand times, O Śaṅkara, one will become a subduer by means of a tilaka made with gorocana mixed with one's own blood.
Rock salt, black salt, *sauvīra* salt, fish gall, honey, clarified butter, and sugar—by applying this to the vulva of women, [the desired effect is achieved].
The man who engages in sexual intercourse with his own wife and will not go to another woman [should take] śaṅkhapuṣpī, vacā, māṃsī, somarājī, and phalguka.
Having made buffalo butter into a paste, the best of physicians should grind it together with the roots and leaves [of the aforementioned herbs] using milk and clarified butter.
Having purified a pill, one should insert it into a woman's womb; even if she has given birth ten times, she will become a virgin again.
Mustard seeds, vacā, fruits of the madana tree, cat dung, and dhattūra, combined with a woman's hair;
This incense removes quartan fever and destroys the fevers of ḍākinīs; it consists of the flowers of the arjuna tree, along with bhallātaka and viḍaṅga.
A fumigation made from *balā*, resin (*sarjarasa*), *sauvīra* salt, and mustard seeds destroys mosquitoes, as well as snakes, lice, and flies.
From the powder of *bhūtalā*, there shall be a paralysis [of the female organ] by filling the womb; furthermore, by smearing it upon the womb, the paralysis of the vulva (*bhaga*) arises.
Thus ends the one hundred and eightieth chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—181. Hari said: Betel leaf, ghee, honey, and salt, when placed in a copper vessel and combined with milk, are a supreme remedy for eye pain.
One should lick a paste of harītakī, vacā, kuṣṭha, vyoṣa, hiṅgu, and manaḥśilā, soaked in honey and ghee, for cough, dyspnea, and hiccups.
A person should lick the powder of pippalī and triphalā with honey; thereby chronic rhinitis, cough, and even severe dyspnea are destroyed.
O Vṛṣadhvaja, one should lick the ash of Citraka with its roots mixed with powdered Pippalī, combined with honey, to cure asthma, cough, and hiccup.
Blue lotus, sugar, licorice, and padmaka in equal parts, mixed with rice-water, will pacify blood disorders.
Ginger, sugar, and honey combined together form a pill that, upon mere consumption, results in a voice as melodious as a cuckoo's.
Having rubbed with this substance—yellow orpiment, conch powder, and the ashes of plantain leaves—it is the best means for removing body hair.
Salt, yellow orpiment, and the fruits of the *tumbinī* plant, combined with lac juice, constitute an excellent means for removing body hair.
One should grind together lime, yellow orpiment, conch-shell ash, realgar, and rock salt with goat's urine.
From its application at that very moment, there is the excellent removal of body hair; [the ingredients are] conch-shell, *āmalaka*, *patra*, and the flowers of *dhātakī*.
Having ground that [substance] together with milk, one should hold it in the mouth for seven days; then the teeth become glossy, white, and possess a stainless luster.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-first chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. The Lord Hari said: Curd is generally forbidden during the autumn, summer, and spring seasons; however, curd is recommended during the winter, the cool season, and the rainy season.

If sugar is drunk with fresh butter after a meal, it produces intelligence. O Hara, a man who should eat one *pala* of old jaggery shall become endowed with strength and be able to unite with a thousand women.
Having powdered kuṣṭha and mixed it with ghee and honey, one should consume it at the time of sleep; this destroys wrinkles and graying hair.
O Śaṅkara, having made a powder of Atasī, Māṣa, and Godhūma, a wise man should smear his body with Pippalī mixed with ghee and honey; thus, O Śaṅkara, a mortal becomes eternally like Kandarpa.
Having eaten a preparation made from barley, sesame, ashwagandha, musali, sarala, and jaggery, a young man shall become strong.
By drinking asafoetida, black salt, and dry ginger with boiled water, the pain known as *pariṇāma-śūla* and indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) are indeed destroyed.
One should grind dhātakī and somarājī together with milk; by this, even a weak person will become stout—of this there is no doubt.
