In the east, one should invoke Asitāṅga Bhairava for Kāmarūpa, with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmāṇī"; and in the south, one should invoke Ruru Bhairava for Koṅkaṇa, with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to Māheśvarī."
Likewise, in the west, "Homage indeed to Caṇḍa"; in the north, "Homage to Kaumārī, to Ulkā, and to Krodha," [and] to Vaiṣṇavī.
In the southeast corner, [offer] to Aghora and Unmattabhairava, and to Vārāhī; in the southwest corner, to Sāra, Kapālī, Bhairava, and Māhendrī.
In the northwest corner, one should worship Jālandhara, Bhīṣaṇa, Bhairava, and Cāmuṇḍā; and in the northeast corner, one should worship Vaṭuka, Saṃhāra, and Caṇḍikā.
Then one should worship Rati, Prīti, Kāmadeva, and the five-arrowed god; through meditation, worship, recitation, and fire-offerings, the Goddess becomes eternally perfected.
The eternal Tripurā shall destroy disease through the sequence of Jvālāmukhī; I shall now describe the sequence of Jvālāmukhī—she, the auspicious one, is to be worshipped in the center.
Nityāruṇā, Madanāturā, Mahāmohā by her very nature, Mahendrāṇī, Kalanākarṣiṇī, and likewise Bhāratī.
Brahmāṇī, Māheśī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Aparājitā.

Vijayā, Ajitā, Mohinī, Tvaritā, Stambhinī, Jṛmbhiṇī, and Kālikā are to be worshipped outside the lotus; one should also worship the sequence of Jvālāmukhī, which brings about the removal of poison and other afflictions.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-eighth chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—199.

Bhairava said: Now I shall describe the Cūḍāmaṇi for the sake of purifying [the results of] auspicious and inauspicious [omens]; having remembered the Sun, the Goddess, Gaṇeśa, and the Moon, a person should draw it.

One should count the banners and other [signs] in sequence—whether they appear as three lines resembling the color of cow-urine, or according to the statements of the inquiry, or as produced from the directions and positions.
The banner, smoke, lion, dog, bull, donkey, elephant, and the crow should be known as the eighth; one should assign them by means of their names and mantras.

Seeing a banner in the place of the banner, there is thought of sovereignty, wealth, and so forth; when Dhūmra is situated in the place of the banner, there is thought of minerals and it brings profit.

When a lion is situated in the position of the banner (dhvaja), there shall be gain of wealth and so forth; when a dog is situated in the position of the banner, there shall be concern for female servants, pleasure, and the like.

Seeing a bull in the position of the flag (dhvajasthāna) indicates anxiety regarding one's status and brings gain; seeing a donkey in the position of the flag results in suffering, affliction, and the like.

Seeing an elephant at the position of the banner (dhvaja), there will be anxiety regarding one's station, victory, and so forth; likewise, seeing a crow at the position of the banner, there will be anxiety regarding afflictions and the loss of wealth.
Having seen a banner in the place of smoke, there is first suffering and then wealth; likewise, having seen smoke in the place of smoke, there will be strife, suffering, and so forth.

When a lion is situated in the smoky (dhūmra) position, there will be mental anxiety, loss of wealth, and so forth; when a dog is situated in the smoky position, there will be victory, gain, and the like.
Seeing a bull in the place of smoke, one obtains women, cattle, horses, wealth, and so forth; seeing a donkey in the place of smoke, there is disease as well as the loss of wealth.

If an elephant is seen in the position of the smoke-colored [deity], there is the attainment of a kingdom, victory, and so forth; if a crow is situated in the position of the smoke-colored [deity], there is the destruction of wealth and kingdom.

Seeing a banner in the position of Leo, one should predict the attainment of a kingdom and so forth; when Dhūmra is situated in the position of Leo, there is the acquisition of a daughter, wealth, and the like.

When the lion is situated in the place of the lion, there is victory and meeting with friends; when the dog has gone to the place of the lion, there is anxiety regarding women and the acquisition of a village.
Seeing a bull in the position of the lion indicates the gain of houses, fields, and wealth; seeing an elephant in the position of the lion likewise indicates lordship over a village.
Seeing an elephant in the place of the lion, there is health, long life, happiness, and so forth; when a crow is situated in the place of the lion, there is a daughter, grain, virtues, and the like.

Seeing a banner in the place of the dog indicates anxiety regarding one's position, as well as happiness and other such matters; when Dhūmra is situated in the place of the dog, there is quarrel and the destruction of one's undertakings.
If the lion is situated in the position of the dog, there will be failure in one's undertakings; if the dog is situated in the position of the dog, there will be loss of wealth.
Seeing a bull in the place of a dog, a sick person is freed from disease; seeing a donkey in the place of a dog, there will be fear of strife.

If an elephant is seen in the place of a dog, there will be a reunion with one's son and wife; however, if a crow is situated in the place of a dog, there will be suffering and the destruction of the family.
Seeing a banner in the position of Taurus, there is royal honor, happiness, and so forth; when Dhūmra is situated in the position of Taurus, there is royal honor, happiness, and so forth.

When Leo is situated in the house of Taurus, there is good fortune, wealth, and so forth; when Canis Major (the Dog) is situated in the house of Taurus, strength, prosperity, and desire are said to arise.
Seeing a bull in the house of Taurus brings fame, contentment, happiness, and so forth; seeing a donkey in the house of Taurus will result in great gain and other benefits.
Seeing an elephant in the position of Taurus, there will be union with women, elephants, and the like; if a crow is situated in the position of Taurus, there will be acquisition of a place and honor.

Seeing a banner (dhvaja) in the position of the donkey (khara), there will be illness, grief, and so forth; when smoke (dhūmra) is situated in the position of the donkey, there will be fear of thieves and the like.

When the lion is situated in the place of the donkey, there is honor, prosperity, victory, and so forth; when it is situated in the place of the dog or the donkey, there is suffering and the loss of wealth.
Seeing a bull in the place of the donkey indicates happiness and union with loved ones; seeing a donkey in the place of the donkey, one should predict suffering, affliction, and the like.
If an elephant is seen in the place of the donkey, there will be happiness, sons, and so forth; if a crow is situated in the place of the donkey, there will be quarrel as well as disease.

Seeing a banner in the position of the elephant, one obtains women, victory, prosperity, happiness, and so forth; when Dhūmra is situated in the position of the elephant, there is an acquisition of wealth and grain.
When a lion is situated in the place of an elephant, there is the attainment of victory and success; when a dog is situated in the place of an elephant, there is health, happiness, and prosperity.
Seeing a bull in the place of the elephant indicates wealth, honor, and so forth; seeing a donkey in the place of the elephant indicates suffering first, followed by happiness.

Seeing an elephant in the position of the elephant indicates fields, grain, happiness, and so forth; when a crow is situated in the position of the elephant, there is the acquisition of wealth and grain.
Seeing a banner in the place of the crow, there will be the destruction of the undertaking; when Dhūmra is situated in the place of the crow, one shall go to the suffering of the Kali age.
When a lion is situated in the place of a crow, there is conflict and indeed suffering; when a dog is situated in the place of a crow, there is fear of the destruction of the home and so forth.
Seeing a bull in the place of the crow portends fear of displacement from one's position and similar misfortunes; seeing a donkey in the place of the crow portends the loss of wealth and defeat.
If an elephant is seen in the place of the crow, there will be wealth, fame, and so forth; if a crow is situated in the place of the crow, there will be departure to foreign lands and the like.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-ninth chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 200.

Bhairava said: O Goddess, I shall declare the conquest of the vital breaths (*vāyujaya*), which brings victory and knowledge of the quarters; it consists of a fourfold set of auspicious practices known as Vāyu, Agni, Jala, and Śakra.
The wind should be present on both the left and the right and should be abundant; fire should flow upwards, while Varuṇa should be below.
Mahendra is situated in the middle; during the bright fortnight he moves to the left, and during the dark fortnight he moves to the right, for three days each at the time of sunrise.

If the rising occurs on the path of the sun and the setting occurs by way of the moon, then there will be prosperity starting from the first lunar day; however, if it is the reverse, there will be decline.
The collections of qualities increase; otherwise, an obstacle is appropriate. O fair-faced one, sixteen transitions are proclaimed for both day and night.
And when the wind shifts, having remained for half of a half-watch (one hour and a half), then a loss of health is to be known; the wind thus wanders within embodied beings.
When the wind is situated in the right nostril during eating and sexual intercourse, one who holds a sword in hand and is filled with desire shall conquer his enemies in battle.
Traveling toward the left is auspicious and adorned with success in all undertakings; when the wind blows from that direction, it is a favorable omen for a living being.
In the Māhendra, Vāruṇa, or Vāta [wind], no calamity whatsoever arises; there is drought when the wind blows to the right, and rain when it blows to the left.
Thus ends the two-hundredth chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—201.

Dhanvantari said: I shall now declare the Ayurveda of horses, which defines all the characteristics of a horse. One with a crow-like beak, a black tongue, a tree-like face, and a hot palate [is to be avoided].

One with protruding teeth, one with missing teeth, one with horns, one with gaps between the teeth, one with a single testicle, one whose testicles have not developed, one covered in a sheath, one with cloven hooves, and one with breasts.
Mārjārapāda, Vyāghrābha, Kuṣṭhavidradhisannibha, Yamaja, Vāmana, and Mārjāra with tawny eyes.
A horse of this defect should be abandoned; the best horse is born in Turaṣka, the middling is five cubits long, and the lowest is three cubits.
Those steeds that are not cramped, as well as those with short ears, which have a variegated luster, are not lacking in power, long-lived, and do not become dejected.

Through the worship of Revanta, through fire-oblations, and by providing portions for the twice-born, one is protected; [one should offer] *sarala* wood, neem leaves, *guggulu*, mustard seeds, and clarified butter.
One should tie a mixture of sesame seeds, vacā, and hiṅgu around the neck of the horse. Wounds are said to be of two kinds: those of extrinsic origin and those arising from internal humors.
That born from Vāta ripens slowly; that born from Kapha ripens quickly. That born from Pitta is characterized by burning in the throat, while that born from blood is mildly painful.

For the purification of malignant wounds caused by external factors such as insects, weapons, and the like, one should use castor root, the two types of *niśā* (turmeric and *daruharidrā*), *citraka*, and ginger.
Garlic or rock salt, nourished with buttermilk or sour gruel; or a bolus of sesame flour mixed with curd and rock salt; or a bolus combined with nimba leaves—these serve to cleanse and heal wounds.
One should prepare a powder by combining patola, nimba leaves, vacā, citraka, pippalī, and śṛṅgavera together in one place.
The drinking of this destroys worms, phlegm, and sluggish wind. Likewise, neem leaves, *paṭola*, *lañca*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *khadira* [are used].
Then, having boiled the horse's blood until it has been strained, the wise physician should administer it for three days alone for the alleviation of the horse's skin disease.

In cases of leprosy with open sores, mustard oil is beneficial; likewise, a decoction of garlic and other ingredients is for the purpose of pacifying [the disease] through drinking and as a food additive.
In cases associated with other types of Vāta, one should immediately administer a nasal drop (nasya) there, combined with the juice of mātuluṅga or the juice of māṃsī.
On the first day, two *pala* [of medicine] are taken, increasing by one *pala* each day until eighteen *pala* are reached on the final day.
In the lowest [quality], there should be eight palas; in the middle, there should be fourteen. During autumn and the heat of summer, [the tax] should neither be given nor caused to be given.

In diseases caused by Vāta, [one should use] oil combined with sugar, ghee, and milk; in Kapha disorders, pungent oils combined with the three acrids (vyoṣa); and in Pitta disorders, [oil] with the decoction of the three myrobalans (triphalā).
A horse that eats rice, sixty-day rice, and milk is not to be despised; a horse resembling a ripe jambu fruit in color, with a golden hue, is not to be despised.
At the half-watch, one should feed the draft horse guggulu; one should quickly feed it milk-rice and milk so that the horse becomes well-steadied.

In disorders of digestion, one should give milk and śāli rice for vāta-type conditions; for pitta-type conditions, one should administer them with meat broth weighing one karṣa, along with honey, mung bean soup, and ghee.

In cases of phlegm (kapha), one should administer mung beans or kulattha, which are pungent and bitter; for deafness, for those afflicted by disease, for poor appetite, and in disorders of the three doṣas, guggulu is indicated.
For all diseases, one should give one pala of dūrvā grass as fodder on the first day; thereafter, one should increase it by one karṣa per day until it reaches five palas.
In the case of both drinks and food, eighty palas is the maximum; sixty for those of middling capacity, and forty for those who enjoy [the lower grade].
It is combined with a decoction of triphalā for ulcers, leprosy, and lameness; and it is joined with cow’s urine for weak digestion and swelling diseases.

In cases of wounds involving wind and bile, or in such diseases, cow’s milk mixed with ghee should be administered; and for those who are emaciated, food combined with meat should be given for the purpose of nourishment.
Five palas of well-ground *guḍūcī* mixed with ghee should be given to horses in the morning during the autumn and summer seasons.
That very [medicine], which destroys disease, bestows nourishment, and increases strength and vigor, should be given to the horse, either mixed with milk or otherwise.

By means of the pharmaceutical preparations of *guḍūcī*, one should take four, three, or two *palas* respectively for those of middling and inferior capacity, following the same method as that for *śatāvarī* and *aśvagandhā*.
Where the behavior of the mounts suddenly becomes uniform, and they die quickly, one should declare that to be an *upasarga* (an affliction).

Through fire offerings and other rites, protection, feeding of Brahmins, the performance of bali-offerings, and pacification rituals, as well as by means of the medicinal preparations of harītakī and other drugs, there shall be the pacification of calamities.
Harītakī, combined with cow’s urine, oil, and salt—starting with five at first, then increasing by five until reaching a full hundred—is the best; however, the dosage may also be eighty or sixty.

I shall now declare the Ayurveda of elephants; the pharmaceutical preparations (kalpas) mentioned are beneficial for the elephant. For the elephant, the dosage is fourfold, and by means of these, one destroys the diseases of the elephant.
The pacification of planetary portents and diseases, as well as rites for peace, are accomplished by honoring the gods and brahmins with jewels and giving a tawny cow.
Having fasted, one should have a garland tied to the two tusks of an elephant by physicians who have consecrated vacā, white mustard seeds, and other substances with the mantra.
One should protect the elephant by worshipping the Sun and others, as well as Śiva, Durgā, Śrī, and Viṣṇu; one should offer oblations to the spirits and bathe it with four jars of water.
One should give consecrated food and sprinkle the elephant with ashes; this auspicious and pure protection against spirits will always guard the elephant.
Triphalā, pañcakola, daśamūla, viḍaṅga, śatāvarī, guḍūcī, nimba, vāsaka, and kiṃśuka.
Beneficial for destroying diseases of elephants, it is dry and astringent; thus has been stated the essential summary of what is taught in the two systems of Āyurveda.

Thus ends the two hundred and first chapter, titled "Description of the Ayurveda of Elephants and Horses," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Hari said: O Śiva, furthermore, the fresh root of *punarnavā* or *apāmārga*, when inserted into the vagina while still moist, removes the pain of the female organ and relieves the labor pains and distress of young women.
Either the root of the *bhūmikūṣmāṇḍa* plant or rice powder, when drunk with milk for seven days, will cause women to have abundant milk.
The pain in a woman's breasts is destroyed by an ointment made from the roots of *rudra*, *indra*, and *vāruṇī*; furthermore, a *polikā* (cake) cooked in ghee must certainly be prepared.
O Maheśāna, when it is eaten, it destroys the pain of the womb; when applied as a paste with the root of *kāravella*, it emerges [from the body].
The female organ enters [the male organ]; no deliberation is required here. [One should apply] roots of indigo and paṭola with clarified butter and sesame water.
O Rudra, a paste made from these ground together indeed cures the discoloration of Jvālāgardabha; likewise, Pāṭhā root ground with rice-water and drunk cures it.
Likewise, drinking *kuṣṭha* will remove evil diseases; and indeed, water from a bellows drunk with honey will [remove] that which has entered within.
O Śiva, O Rudra, lac, which is like clarified butter, when drunk together with milk, effects the cessation of the torment of malignant diseases.
It removes the disease of menorrhagia; there is no need for hesitation in this matter. O Śiva, a powder of dvijayaṣṭī and trikaṭuka, when drunk, removes [the ailment].
O Maheśvara, by means of a decoction of sesame seeds, remove the blood-tumor (raktagulma) of women; and when tied with a flower, O Great Lord, it removes that of young maidens.
The bulb of the red lotus, mixed with sugar and sesame seeds, when drunk along with sugar by women, causes the miscarriage of the fetus.
The flow of blood will cease by the use of cold water; O Rudra, [blood] that has been drunk, however, [is cured] by boiled *kāñjika* with *śarapuṅkhā*.
Asafoetida combined with rock salt quickly brings about childbirth for women; likewise, the root of the citron tied around the waist brings about childbirth.
At the root of an *apāmārga* plant, according to the name of a pregnant woman, when it is entirely uprooted, a son shall be born; otherwise, a daughter.
When the root of the Apāmārga plant is placed upon the head of women, the labor pains of childbirth will perish; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
O Śiva, O Hara, when filled with camphor, madanaphala, and madhuka, the womb of even an old woman becomes beautiful; how much more so, then, that of a young woman?

The child upon whose forehead a tilaka made with gorocanā is applied, and to whom sugar and kuṣṭha are given to drink, shall be free from fear—O Śiva—the child shall be safe from poisons, spirits, seizing demons, and other diseases.
O Rudra, the constant wearing of conch, nābhi, vacā, kuṣṭha, and iron shall provide protection for children against afflictions.
The powder of *palāśa* leaves, mixed with honey, cow's ghee, *āmalaka*, and *viḍaṅga*, when drunk immediately, makes a man highly intelligent.
Within one month, O Mahādeva, one becomes free from old age and death.
O Rudra, if the seeds of the Palāśa tree, taken in equal parts with ghee, sesame, and honey, are consumed for seven days, they bring old age to complete destruction.
Having consumed the powder of *rudrāmalaka* mixed with honey, oil, and ghee for one month, a man shall become youthful and attain mastery over speech.
O Śiva, the powder of auspicious *āmalaka* taken at dawn with honey or water will strengthen the nose. O Śiva, it should be consumed at daybreak.
Having consumed the powder of kuṣṭha with clarified butter and honey in the morning, a man will indeed possess a body fragrant like that of a celestial being and shall live for a thousand years.
O Maheśvara, these are split mung beans, dehusked, soaked in ghee, dried, and indeed cooked with milk.
O Mahādeva, having consumed [the substance] with honey, clarified butter, and milk, one may desire a hundred women; this occurs at that very moment—of this there is no doubt.
And mercury becomes auspicious when treated with castor oil and sulphur; sprinkled with water from the three times of day, it bestows strength through its consumption.
Milk prepared with dehusked mung beans and seeds of *śimbā*, when drunk with the oil of *apāmārga*, enables one to satisfy the desires of a hundred women.

Thus ends the two hundred and second chapter, titled "Description of Various Applications of Medicinal Herbs," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 203.
Hari said: If a cow hates her own calf, one should give her own milk mixed with salt; then the calf will become dear to her.
Indeed, a dog's bone tied around the neck, as well as that of a buffalo or a cow, causes the entire mass of worms to fall away; of this there is no doubt.
The falling of a cow's hoof-print occurs from eating the root of the guñjā plant.
O Śiva, the juice of the *varuṇa* fruit, when churned with the hand, causes the swarm of worms belonging to quadrupeds and bipeds to fall away.
O Rudra, one should thus heal the wound by filling it with *jayā*; furthermore, drinking elephant urine indeed cures afflictions caused by cows and buffaloes.
Lentils and *śāli* rice seeds, ground with buttermilk and drunk with the milk of a cow, a buffalo, or a bull, will be beneficial for a man.
O Śiva, the leaf of the *śarapuṅkhā* plant given with salt destroys the bursting of water and the destruction of horses' manes.
O Hara, if even a single leaf of *ghṛtakumārī* endowed with its characteristic marks is given, the itching of the horse's mane will undoubtedly cease.

Thus ends the two hundred and third chapter, titled "Description of the Application of Various Medicinal Herbs," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 204 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Thus did Dhanvantari expound the science of medicine to Suśruta; now, therefore, I shall state the names of the medicinal herbs in brief.
Sthirā, vidārigandhā, śālaparṇī, and aśumatī; lāṅgalī and kalasī are considered synonyms for kroṣṭupucchā and guhā.
Furthermore, *punarnavā* is known as *parṣābhū*, *kaṭhillī*, and *kāruṇā*. *Eraṇḍa* is *urvūka*, while *āmarda* is *vardhamānaka*.
Jhaṣā is known as nāgabalā; śvadaṃṣṭrā is considered to be gokṣura. Śatāvarī is called varā, bhīru, pīvarī, indīvarī, and varī.
Vyāghrī, bṛhatī, kṛṣṇā, haṃsapādī, and madhusravā are synonyms for dhāmanī; kaṇṭakārī, kṣudrā, siṃhī, and nidigdhikā are synonyms for the same.
Vṛścikā, tryamṛtā, kālī, viṣaghnī, sarpadaṃṣṭrikā, markaṭī, ātmaguptā, ārṣeyī, and kapikacchukā are synonyms.

*Mudgaparṇī*, *kṣudrasahā*, *māṣaparṇī*, *mahāsahā*, *tyajā*, and *parā* are known as the great [plants]; they are designated by the names *daṇḍa*, *yonī*, and *aṅka*. *Nyagrodha* should be known as *vaṭa*, while *aśvattha* is considered to be *kapila*.
Plakṣa, gardabhāṇḍa, parkaṭī, and kapītana are synonyms for the fig tree. Pārtha, kakubha, and dhanvin are to be known as names for the arjuna tree.
The *nandīvṛkṣa* is a sprouting tree and is said to be nourishing; the *vañjula* is known as the *vetasa*, and the *bhallātaka* is also called *aruṣkara*.
Lodhra is also known as sāravaka, dhṛṣṭa, and tirīṭa; furthermore, the bṛhatphala is the mahājambū, while the other is known as the bālaphalā.
The third is *jalajaṃbū*, which is also known as *nādeyī*; it is also called *kaṇā*, *kṛṣṇā*, *upakuñcī*, *śauṇḍī*, and *māgadhikā*.
Pippalī has been described by those who know it; its root is known as granthika. Ūṣaṇa is to be understood as marica, while śuṇṭhī is called viśva and mahauṣadha.
One should know that *vyoṣa* is the "three pungents" (*kaṭutraya*), and it is also called *tryūṣaṇa*. *Lāṅgalī*, *halinī*, *śreyasī*, and *gajapippalī* are synonyms for the same plant.
Trāyantī is known as Trāyamāṇā, and Utsā is remembered as Suvahā; Citraka is called by the names Śikhī, Vahni, and Agni.
*Ṣaḍgranthā*, *ugrā*, *vacā*, *śvetā*, and *haimavatī* are known as synonyms for *vacā*. *Kuṭaja*, *vṛkṣaka*, *śakra*, *vatsaka*, and *girimallikā* are synonyms for *kuṭaja*.
One should recognize the seeds of Kaliṅgendrayava-ariṣṭa; mustaka is known by the name megha, and kauntī should be understood as hareṇukā.
Elā is said to be bahulā, as well as sūkṣmailā and truṭi; likewise, padmā, bhārṅgī, and kāñjī are to be known as brāhmaṇayaṣṭikā.
Mūrvā is known as madhurasā, tejanī, and tiktavallikā; mahānimba and bṛhannimba are synonyms for dīpyaka, which is yavānikā.
Viḍaṅga is the enemy of worms (krimiśatru); rāmaṭha is indeed called hiṅgu. Ajājī is known as jīraka, and kāravī is upakuñcikā.
Kaṭukā and kaṭukarohiṇī are to be known as pungent and bitter; tagara is nata and vakra; and coca is tvaca and varāṅgaka.
Udīcya is called bālaka, and hrībera is known by names meaning "water"; patraka is designated by terms for "leaf," while cāraka is named after a "thief."
That which has a golden luster and is known by the names of "nāga" is called nāgakeśara; likewise, asṛk, kuṅkuma, kāśmīra, and bāhlika are declared to be synonyms for it.
Iron is designated as *ayo* and *loha* by those who know its technical names; one should know that *pura*, *kuṭanaṭa*, *mahiṣākṣa*, and *palaṅkaṣā* [are synonyms for it].
Kāśmarī is known as kaṭphalā and is also celebrated as śrīparṇī; śallakī is called gajabhakṣyā, patrī, surabhī, and strava.
One should know that *dhātrī* is *āmalakī*, and *akṣa* is *vibhītaka*; *pathyā* and *abhayā* are to be understood as *pūtanā*, and *harītakī*.
Triphalā is said to be simply the three fruits, and that is to be known as phalatrika; udakīrya, dīrghavṛnta, and karañja are thus proclaimed [as its constituents].
Yaṣṭī is declared to be yaṣṭyāhvaya; maduka is madhuyaṣṭikā. Dhātakī is tāmraparṇī, and samaṅgā is considered to be kuñjarā.
One should know that white sandalwood is cool, as are *gośīrṣa* and white sandalwood (*sita-candana*); and red sandalwood is the second type, known as *rakta-candana*.
Kākoli is recorded, as well as Vīrā, Vayasyā, and Arkapuṣpikā; Śṛṅgī, Karkaṭaśṛṅgī, and Mahāghoṣā are also proclaimed.
Tugākṣīrī is auspicious; it is known as vāṃśī and vaṃśalocanā. Mṛdvikā is remembered as drākṣā, and it is likewise considered to be gostanikā.
Uśīra, mṛṇāla, sevya, and likewise lāmajjaka; as well as sāra, gopavallī, gopī, and bhadrā are so described.
Dantī and kaṭaṅkaṭerī are known as dāruniśā; haridrā is called rajanī, pītikā, and rātrināmikā.
Vṛkṣādanī, chinnaruhā, nīlavallī, rasā, and amṛtā are synonyms; vasuka and koṭa are to be known as vāśira, while kāmpilla is considered [another name for] the same.
Pāṣāṇabheda, Ariṣṭa, Asmabhit, Kuṭṭabhedaka, Ghaṇṭāka, Śuṣkaka, Vaca, and Sūcaka are known as synonyms for the plant vacā.
Surasa and bījaka are indeed called pītaśāla; vajravṛkṣa, mahāvṛkṣa, snuhī, snuk, sudhā, and guḍā [are synonyms].
One should know Tulasī as Surasā, and it is also called Upasthā; Kuṭheraka, Arjunaka, Parṇa, and Saugandhiparṇika are synonyms for it.
Nīla, sindhuvāra, nirguṇḍī, sugandhikā, sugandhiparṇī, vāsantī, and kulajā are to be known as synonyms.
Kālīyaka is known as pītakāṣṭha; furthermore, that which is called kataka is known as gāyatrī and khadira, while its variety is considered to be kandara.
The *indīvara*, *kuvalaya*, *padma*, and *nīlotpala* are considered synonyms; likewise, *saugandhika*, *śatadala*, *abja*, and *kamala* are said to be names for the lotus.
Ajavarṇa, ūrja, vājikarṇa, aśvakarṇaka, śleṣmāntaka, as well as śelu, and bahuvāra are thus described.
Sunandaka, Kakudbhadra, Chatrākī, and she known as Chatrasaṃjñakā; Kabarī, Kumbhaka, Dhṛṣṭa, Kṣudvidha, and likewise Dhanakṛt.
Kṛṣṇārjaka is proclaimed as Karāla and Kālamāna; Prācī, Balā, Nadīkrāntā, Kākajaṅghā, and Vāyasī [are synonyms].
Mūṣikaparṇī is to be known as Bhramantī and Ākhuparṇikā; Viṣamuṣṭi, Drāvaṇa, and Keśamuṣṭi are also declared [to be synonyms].
One should know that *kiṃlihī* is *kaṭukī*, and *dantaka* is *amlavetasa*; *aśvatthā* is *bahupatrā*, and *āmalakī* should also be understood [by its synonyms].
Arūṣakaraṃ, patraśūka, kṣīrī, and rājādana are considered synonyms; likewise, one should call mahāpatra, dāḍima, and karaka names for the same fruit.
Masūrī, Vidālī, Śaṣpā, and Kālindī are its synonyms; it is called Kaṇṭakā, Mahāśyāmā, and will also be referred to as Vṛkṣapādī.
Vidyā, Kuntī, Nikumbhā, Tribhaṅgī, Tripuṭī, Trivṛt, Saptalā, Yavatiktā, Carmā, and Carmakasa.
Śaṅkhinī, sukumārī, tiktākṣī, akṣipīluka, gavākṣī, amṛtā, śvetā, girikarṇī, and gavādinī.
Kāmpillaka, raktāṅga, guṇḍā, and rocanikā are synonyms; likewise, hemakṣīrī is known as pītā, while gaurī is indeed kāladugdhikā.
Gāṅgerukī, nāgabalā, viśālā, and indravāruṇī; tārkṣya, śaila, blue-colored añjana, and rasāñjana.
The exudation of the *śālmali* tree is known by the name *mocarasa*; *pratyakpuṣpī* and *kharī* are to be understood as synonyms for *apāmārga*, which is also called *mayūraka*.
One should designate *siṃhāsya*, *vṛṣavāsāka*, and *māṭarūṣaka* [as synonyms]. The wise know *jīvaka*, *jīvaśāka*, *karbura*, and *śaṭī* [to be synonymous].
Kaṭphala is somavṛkṣa; agnigandhā is sugandhikā; śatāṅga is śatapuṣpā; and miṃsi is considered to be madhurikā.
Puṣkaramūla, puṣkara, and puṣkarāhvaya are synonyms for jñeya; likewise, yāsa, dhanvayāsa, duṣparśa, and durālabhā are synonyms.
Vākucī and somarājī are celebrated as somavallī; mārkaṇḍa and keśarāja are called bhṛṅgarāja.
That which is known by the experts as eḍagaja is called cakramarda; it is also termed suraṅgī, tagara, and snāyu. Kālānāśā, however, is vāyasī.
Mahākāla is known as belastaṇḍulīya and ghanastana; ikṣvāku is tiktatumbī, and it is called tiktālabu.
Dhāmārgava, koṣātakī, and yāminī—one should know these as varieties of kośātakī, which is also designated by the name kṛtabhedana.
Likewise, jīmūtaka is known as kākāhvā; khuḍḍāka is devatāḍaka; gṛdhranakhī is considered to be hiṅgu and kākādanī.
Aśvāri should also be understood as such; karavīra is the horse-killer (aśvamāraka). Sindhu, saindhava, sindhūttha, maṇi, and mantha are declared to be synonyms for rock salt.
Alkali derived from the tips of barley is called *yavakṣāra*; *sarjikā* and *sarjikākṣāra* are proclaimed as the second type.
Kāśīśa and puṣpakāśīśa should be known as a medicine for the eyes; it is also designated by the names dhātukāśīśa and kāśī.
One should know that *saurāṣṭrī*, *mṛttikākṣāra*, *kākṣī*, and *paṅkaparpaṭī* are synonyms; likewise, *samākṣika*, *dhātu*, *tāpya*, and *tāpyutthasaṃbhava* are synonyms for the mineral pyrites.
Śilā should be known as manaḥśilā, nepālī, and kulaṭī; āla is designated as manastālaka or haritāla.
Gandhaka is called sulphur; rasa is said to be mercury; tāmraka, audumbaram, śulbam, and likewise mlecchamukham, should be known as copper.
Adrisāra, tvakṣya, and tīkṣṇa are said to be iron, as is lohaka; mākṣika, madhu, and kṣaudra are known as honey, which is the nectar of flowers.
That which has water remaining is called *jyeṣṭha*; *kāñjika* is indeed *suvīraka*. *Sītā* and *sitopalā* are both known as *matsyaṇḍī* and *śarkarā* (sugar).
Equal parts of cinnamon bark (*tvak*), cardamom (*elā*), and cinnamon leaves (*patraka*) constitute the *trisugandhi*; when combined with *nāgakeśara*, it is known as *caturjātaka*.
Pippalī, pippalīmūla, cavya, citraka, and nāgara constitute the *pañcakola*; it is also known as *kolaka* by the name *kola*.
Priyaṅgu is known as kaṅguka; koradūṣa is kodrava; tripuṭa is designated as puṭa; and kalāpa is considered to be laṅgaka.
The *satīna*, the round (*vartula*), and the bamboo (*veṇu*) are also proclaimed [as types of dice]; likewise the *picuka*, the *pitala*, the *akṣa*, and the *biḍālapadaka*.
One should know that a karṣa is likewise a mouthful of gold; they maintain that half a pala is a śukti, as well as eight māṣakas.
One *pala* is a *bilva*, which is a *muṣṭi*; two *palas* one should call a *prasṛti*. One should know that four *palas* constitute an *añjali* and a *kuḍava*.
Eight palas constitute one māna; that is recorded as the measure. Four kuḍavas make one prastha, and four prasthas make one āḍhaka.
A *kāśapātra* is said to be equal to a *droṇa* of four *āḍhakas*; a *tulā* is said to be one hundred *palas*, and a *bhāga* is recorded as twenty *palas*.
This type of measurement has been declared by the learned for solid substances; however, for liquid substances, it is proclaimed that the measure is double.
Bhadradāru is devakāṣṭha; it may also be called dāru or devadāruka. Kuṣṭha is declared to be āmaya, as well as māṃsī and nalada.
Śaṅkha is śuktinakha; vyāghra is known as vyāghranakha; one should know pura to be palaṅkaṣa, and mahiṣākṣa is guggulu.
Rasa, gandharasa, and bola are synonyms; sarja is considered to be sarjarasa. Priyaṅgu is called phalinī, śyāmā, gaurī, and kāntā.
Karañja is called naktamāla, pūtika, and cirabilvaka; śigru is known by the name śobhāñjana and is also celebrated as jñānamāna.
Jayā, jayantī, śaraṇī, nirguṇḍī, and sindhuvāraka; morāṭā and pīluparṇa; and tuṇḍī would be the same as tuṇḍikerikā.
Madana, gālava, and bodha are said to be synonyms for ghoṭā and ghoṭī; caturaṅgula is known as sampāka and by the name vyādhighāta.
One should know that *āragvadha* is called *rājavṛkṣa* and *raivata*; *dantī* is *kākendu* and *tiktā*; and *kaṇṭakī* is *vikaṅkata*.
Nimba is well-known as Ariṣṭa; they know Paṭola as Kolaka; Vayasthā, Viśalyā, Chinnā, and Chinnaruhā are considered synonyms.
Vaśā, dantī, and amṛtā constitute the collection of names for guḍūcī; likewise, kirātatiktaka, bhūnimba, and kāṇḍatiktaka [are synonyms].
Sūta said: O Śaunaka, these are the names of Hari as well as those of forest herbs; therefore, I shall now declare the grammatical analysis (vyākaraṇa) as spoken by Kumāra.
Thus ends the two hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Section on Conduct," in the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, the *Pūrvakhaṇḍa*.
In the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, Chapter 205:
Kumāra said: "Now, O Kātyāyana, I shall explain grammar in brief for the purpose of discerning established words and as a means for the intellectual development of children."

A word (pada) is defined as that which ends in a nominal suffix (suP) or a verbal suffix (tiṅ). There are seven case-inflections (vibhakti) of the nominal suffixes; those beginning with su, au, and jas are called the nominative (prathamā), and they apply to the base consisting of the nominal stem (prātipadika).

In the case of address, when the gender and so forth are expressed, as well as in the object and the agent, that which is meaningful and devoid of verbal roots and suffixes is a nominal stem (prātipadika).

The second case (dvitīyā) occurs after the words *am*, *u*, and *śas*, as well as for that which is the object (*karman*) of an action; the second case is prescribed for the object, and also when used in conjunction with *antarā* and *antareṇa*.
The third case ending (*ṭā*, *bhyām*, *bhis*) is prescribed for the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the agent (*kartṛ*); that by which something is done is the instrument, and he who does it is the agent.

The fourth case ending occurs after words ending in *ṅe*, *bhyām*, and *bhyas* when the grammatical factor is the recipient (*sampradāna*). That for which one has the desire to give, or which one holds back, or which is pleasing, is the recipient (*sampradāna*).
The fifth case ending (pañcamī) occurs after [a word] in the sense of the ablative (apādāna) kāraka; that from which one departs, takes, or receives danger.

The sixth case (ṣaṣṭhī) occurs after the suffixes ṅasi and ṅas when the primary meaning is the relationship of ownership; the seventh case (saptamī) occurs after the suffixes ṅi and sup, and that [seventh case] pertains to the locus (adhikaraṇa).

The locus (*ādhāra*) and the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) [are termed *kāraka*] through the employment of verbs meaning "to protect"; that which is intended or not intended [as the object] is traditionally held to be the *apādāna*.

The fifth case ending occurs in connection with *pary-upa*, as well as with *itarat*, *ṛte*, and words expressing direction other than "east"; the second case ending occurs when used with *ena* and with those [words] designated as *karmapravacanīya*.

The prefixes *pari*, *prati*, and *anu* are used with the sense of desire (*vīpsā*), state (*itthambhāva*), and characteristic (*cihna*) respectively; *anu* is also said to be used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*), inferiority (*hīna*), and proximity (*anupa*).
The second and fourth case endings are used for the action of moving or going; indeed, two case endings are used for an inanimate object when expressing disregard toward the object of the verb *man*.

The use of *namaḥ*, *svasti*, *svadhā*, *svāhā*, *alam*, and *vaṣaṭ* is prescribed [with the dative]; likewise, the fourth case is used in the sense of "for the sake of" (*tādarthya*), as well as after words expressing an action (*bhāvavācin*) that have the sense of the infinitive suffix *-tum*.

The third case (instrumental) occurs in connection with "saha" (with); the seventh case (locative) occurs when denoting time or state; and the sixth case (genitive) also occurs in connection with these [previously mentioned words], as well as with words expressing contempt or bodily defects and qualifying attributes.

The two [words] *svāmī* and *īśvara* are used with the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) when expressing selection from a group (*nirdhāraṇe*), and the word *adhipati* is used with the genitive when accompanied by the word *sākṣin*, *dāyāda*, or *prasūta*; furthermore, both [the first two] are used with the genitive when employed with a word denoting a cause (*hetu*).

Likewise, when *smṛ* has the sense of "remembering," with *kṛ*, when there is a "preparatory effort" (*pratiyatnaka*), and when verbs meaning "injury" (*hiṃsā*) are employed, the agent (*kartṛ*) is designated as the object (*karman*) in relation to the action (*kṛti*).

The genitive case is not used for the agent or the object when they are expressed by a word ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix; furthermore, a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is of two kinds: namely, the verbal root (*dhātu*) and likewise [the nominal base].

From the roots *bhū*, *as*, and *ad*, the suffix *la* becomes *tiṅ*; indeed, ten types of *lakāras* are traditionally taught. *Ti*, *tas*, and *jhi* constitute the first person; *si*, *thas*, and *tha* the middle person; and *mi*, *vas*, and *mas* the last person.

The *parasmaipada* endings are *ti*, *tas*, *anti*; *si*, *thas*, *tha*; *mi*, *vas*, *mas*. The *ātmanepada* endings are *ta*, *ātām*, *jha*; *thās*, *āthām*, *dhvam*; and *i*, *vahi*, *mahi* for the first, middle, and last persons respectively.

The substitutes for *iḍ*, *bahis*, and *mahi* are derived from the verbal root, as well as those beginning with *ṇic*; even when a noun is employed [as the subject], the first person [of the verb] shall occur.
The second person is prescribed for the word *yuṣmad* (you), and the first person for *asmad* (I/we); the roots are said to begin with *bhū*, and likewise those ending in *san* and so forth.

The suffix *laṭ* is prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*) for the present tense, and *sma* with *laṭ* for the past; *laṅ* optionally for the remote past (*bhūte 'nadyatane*), and *loṭ* and the others for the benedictive (*āśiṣi*).
The optative suffix (*loṭ*) denoted as permitted in the case of injunctions and so forth may also occur in the sense of counsel, as well as in invitation, entreaty, inquiry, request, and benediction.

The *liṅ* occurs for the past that is not witnessed; the *liṭ* occurs for the past; the *lṛṭ* occurs for the future. That same [future tense marker] occurs for the non-contemporary future, derived from the verbal root.

The *leṭ* suffix is prescribed for the sense of the *liṅ* (optative) when there is the non-occurrence of the action (*kriyātipatti*) following a word ending in the agentive suffix *dātṛ*; it occurs in all three tenses and in the senses of the abstract state (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), and the agent (*kartṛ*).
The suffixes *tavya*, *anīya*, and those beginning with *tṛc* are similar [to the kṛt suffixes] and are used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*).
Thus ends the two hundred and fifth chapter, titled "Description of Grammar," in the section on Conduct (*Ācārakāṇḍa*) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Sūta said: O Brahmins, I shall now explain the examples of grammatical formations (*siddha-udāharaṇa*), preceded by the rules for euphonic combination (*saṃhitā*) and so forth: *svasāgatā vīdam*, *suttamaṃ syāt*, and *pitṛṣabhaḥ*.
The letter *ḷ* is renowned as *seva*; by means of wisdom, it is the plow-pole (*lāṅgalīṣā*). The letter *tav* is the water of the Gaṅgā; it is also *ṛṇa*, *arṇa*, and *prārṇa*.

One who is afflicted by cold, a goldsmith, a follower of Indra, a butcher, one who sits with his wife, and one who performs ancestral rites—these, when associated with the letter *la*, will be victorious in policy.
The leader, salt, and cows—these are not lords; rather, know that the goddess’s house is here, and these two are clever.
"These horses are his six"—that is not speech; "and the six petals"—that is its movement; "it does not cross over that"—that is the water; "that cremation ground"—that is it.
"O Sugata, you cook here; O Bhagavan, you cover [the fire]; from you comes the 'jhanat' sound; and it is remembered that you cross over [the world]."
You write upon that wheel; you lie down, yet you are unlike others; you fly within the cosmic egg, and you always perform worship.
Who acts with difficulty? Who does what? Who is established in the fruit? Who sleeps? Who is impotent? And who attains dignity?
"Who is here? Who indeed? "The gods say so. And they said, "O, go! Viṣṇu, who is self-born, goes, as does Bṛhaspati, the lord of speech and the leader of the host."
This [world] would go toward us as its *ṛk* and *sāman*, and it likewise goes toward him; the shadow of a hut is like a shadow, and other junctures (*sandhi*) are of such a nature.
Six types of compounds have been enumerated: that [compound] consisting of two words is the *karmadhāraya*; the *dvigu* is the three Vedas; and the village is considered this *tatpuruṣa*.

That which is made for its sake, that which has that as its purpose, and wealth [obtained] from fear of a wolf—knowing these, one who is skilled in knowledge understands the *bahuvrīhi* and the *avyayībhāva* compounds.

The suffix *bhāva* is used in the sense of the feminine as previously stated; however, *dvandva* refers to gods, sages, and humans. The suffixes *taddhita* include *pāṇḍavaḥ*, *śaivaḥ*, *brāhmaṃ*, and those beginning with *brahmatā*.

The words *deva*, *agni*, *sakhi*, *pati*, *aṃśu*, *kroṣṭṛ*, and *svāyambhuva* are masculine; likewise, the words *nā*, *praśasta*, *cara*, *gaura*, and *glau*, as well as those ending in *-abja*, are also masculine.
The words *aśvayuj*, *kṣmābhuj*, *marut*, *kravyād*, *mṛgāvidh*, *ātman*, *rājan*, *yuvan*, *pathin*, *pūṣan*, *brahmahan*, and *halin* end in a consonant (*halanta*).
Viḍve, dhā, uśanā, anaḍvān, madhuliṭ, kāṣṭhataṭ, likewise vanavāri, asthi, vastu, jagatsāma, and ahanī.

The words *karman*, *sarpiḥ*, *vapūḥ*, and *tejaḥ* are neuter; likewise, those ending in short vowels (*a*, *i*, *u*) are neuter. Furthermore, *jāyā*, *jarā*, *nadī*, *lakṣmīḥ*, *śrīḥ*, *strī*, *bhūmiḥ*, and *vadhūḥ* [are feminine].
Furthermore, *bhrū*, *punarbhū*, *dhenu*, *svasṛ*, and *mātṛ* are feminine; likewise, *vāk*, *sraj*, *diś*, *utkruddh*, *yuvati*, and *kukubh* are generally feminine.

Dyu and divau refer to heaven, while prāvṛṣ refers to the rainy season; sumāna and uṣṇih are feminine. Now I shall describe to you those words which, through association with qualities, substances, or actions, take on feminine gender.
Śuklakīlāpa, Śuci, Grāmaṇī, Sudhī, Paṭu, Kamalabhū, Kartṛ, Sumata, Bahavaḥ, and Sunau.

The truths are not [attained] by those who do not maintain the sacred fires, nor likewise by men who eat long-stalked [vegetables]; both the "all-seeing" and the "both" [are attained], as well as one or the other.
The suffixes -tara and -tama, nema, tva, sama, as well as sima and its derivatives, and likewise pūrva, adhara, dakṣiṇa, uttara, and avara.

Furthermore, this [distinction] between "other" (para) and "proximate" (antara) applies to whatever is expressed by the pronouns *adas* and *idam*; for the former (*adas*) is used for the first person (*yuṣmad*) and the latter (*idam*) for the second person (*asmad*), according to their respective degrees of remoteness and proximity.
Likewise, "katipaya," "dvau," and so forth—all such words as well as "śṛṇoti" and the rest, along with "juhoti," "jahāti," and also "dadhāti"—[are similarly used].

*dīpyati* (he shines), *stūyati* (he praises), *puttrīyati* (he treats as a son), *dhanīyati* (he treats as wealth); *truṭyati* (it breaks), *mriyate* (he dies), *cicīṣati* (he wishes to collect), and *ninīṣati* (he wishes to lead).
All abide in all, for all; from all, they have gone everywhere. They belong to all and exist in all; thus it is with the Viśvādya deities.

The term *pūrva* is declared to mean "eastern," "prior," "from the east," "in the east," or "the first. Sūta said: Having heard from Kumāra the forms of nouns and verbs established in their complete forms, Kātyāyana explained them in detail.
Thus ends the two hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The First [Section] on Conduct," in the first part of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
In the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, Chapter 207:
Sūta said: Having bowed to Vāsudeva, the Guru, Gaṇeśa, Śambhu, and Sarasvatī, I shall explain prosody according to the distinctions of *mātrā* and *varṇa* for those of limited intellect.

The groups (gaṇas) consisting of three morae (trikā) are: m, n, b, y, j, r, s, and t, which occur at the beginning, middle, and end [of the line]. In the Āryā meter, there are four groups of four morae (caturgaṇāḥ) at the beginning, end, and throughout the middle.

A syllable ending in a consonant, those ending in a visarga, a long vowel followed by a conjunct consonant, and one at the end of a quarter-verse (pāda)—whether accompanied by an anusvāra or not—are said to be heavy (guru) and consist of two mātrās.
When there is no sequence in the yoga, even if there is lightness in some places for a heavy syllable, it shall be designated as *śloka*, *cāryā*, and so forth; and *yati* is the term for a pause.
A quarter is to be known as a *pāda*, and a fourth part as a *yati*; even is even, while uneven is odd. A meter is even, half-even, or uneven; the third type is the uneven.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventh chapter, titled "Definition of Technical Terms for Prosody," in the section on Conduct (*ācārakāṇḍa*) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. Sūta said: The definition of the Āryā meter consists of eight groups (*gaṇas*). There is never a *ja* group in the odd positions. In the sixth position, there may be a *ja*, *na*, or *la* group; the foot [ends] from the second syllable of the sixth group.

In the first half, there are seven short syllables; then in the second half, five [short syllables], followed by three gaṇas and a quarter (four short syllables). This is Pathyā; Vipulā occurs when there is a deviation from the fire (three) and the leap (one).

In the middle of the [verse], when there are two *j* syllables followed by a *turya* (four-mātrā) and a *ja*, it is *capalā*; when the first half begins with *capalā* and the second half has a *sa* followed by a *jaghana*, this is the characteristic of the *āryājāti* class.

If the characteristics of the first half of an Āryā are found in both halves, it is called Gīti; Upagīti arises from the second half [having those characteristics], and Udgīti occurs by the reversal [of that].

The Āryāgīti has a heavy syllable at the end; this is the characteristic of the *gotijāti* class. If there are six *kalās* in the odd quarters and eight in the even quarters, provided they are not contiguous; and in the *vaitālīya*, the even quarter should not depend on the following one, nor should it have the *ra* and *la* gaṇas followed by a heavy syllable.
The two preceding [feet] being as before, this is considered to be the *aupacchandasika* meter.
Bhagauga shall be known as Āpātalikā, and then Dakṣiṇāntikā; in all its feet, the second syllable is a long (la) dependent on the following.
When the *udīcyavṛtti* occurs in the odd [pādas] and the *prācyavṛtti* in the even [pādas], with the fifth syllable occurring in the fourth quarter of both simultaneously, it is called *pravṛttaka*.

The *cāruhāsinī* is formed by the union of the first quarter of the *vaitālīya* with the second quarter of the *udīcī*; it consists of two even quarters and one odd quarter. This is the summary of the *vaitālīya*.

One should not eat [the syllables] *va* and *ktra*; these two would not exist if the fourth and subsequent gaṇas were present. *Pathyāvaktra* occurs when there is *ja* in the even [pādas], while it is otherwise if it begins with the reverse.

In that [meter], there are *na*, *sa*, *ca*, *pa*, *la*, *vi*, *pu*, and *la* with a seventh light syllable; or, according to Saitava, it consists of *ma*, *ra*, *u*, *ta*, *u* throughout, or *ma*, *ra*, *na*, *ta*, *u* preceded by the ocean (four *ga*s).
That which has sixteen syllables and possesses immovable stability is called *mātrāsamaka*.

Likewise, when there is a *ma* at the ninth position, a *ga* at the end, and *ja*, *na*, and *la* following, it is the *viśloka* meter; or, when there are two sets of four *ga*s, it is the *dvānavāsikā*.

In the [syllables] numbering five, eight, and nine, there shall be the *la* [laghu]; *citrā* consists of sixteen [mātrās]. That which is taught as having equal mātrās and so forth is called *padākulaka*.

In the *dala* meter, it is determined as a fixed rule that there are always long syllables (*la*) without short vowels (*vṛtta*), short vowels without heavy syllables (*varṇa*), and heavy syllables without short vowels.
In the first half, the *gantu* consists of twenty-eight *tīlas*; in the second, thirty. In this [meter], the *śikhā* is the *gantu*, and from the inversion of that, it becomes the *khañja*.

In the first two feet there are sixteen *gaṇas* of *anaṅgakrīḍā*, thirty-two *caras*, and twenty-seven *tilas*; in the last two feet, there are *lās*, twenty-seven *tilas*, and *gantas*, which is the *rucirā* meter.
The meters measured by morae (*mātrāvṛtta*) have been explained; now I shall indeed speak of the meters measured by syllables (*varṇavṛtta*).

Thus ends the two hundred and eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Āryā and Other Meters," in the section on Prosody within the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. Sūta said: That [meter] is known as Śrīrukthā; Utyukthā consists of two heavy syllables (gurus); Mo is Nārī; Ro is Mṛgī; Magau in the middle is Kanyā; and by Pratiṣṭhā [is defined]. *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*—209. Sūta said: [The meters] are to be known as Śrīrukthā; Utyukthā is a female [meter] consisting of two heavy syllables; Mo is Nārī; Ro is Mṛgī; Magau in the middle is Kanyā; and by Pratiṣṭhā [is defined]. *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*—209. Sūta
O cowherd, *paṅkti* is well-established; *tanumadhyā* is known as *tayau*. With two *na*s and two *ya*s, it is *bālalalitā*; indeed, these are the *gāyatrī* meters.

If the feet consist of *ma*, *sa*, *ga*, and *ra*, it is *madalekhā*; the meter *uṣṇik* is thus remembered by the wise. If the feet are *bha*, *bha*, *ga*, and *ga*, it is known as *citrapadā*; and *vidyunmālā* consists of *ma*, *ma*, *ga*, and *ga*.

The *māṇavaka* consists of the sequence bha, ta, la, ga; *haṃsaruta* is known as ma, na, u, ga; *samānikā* is ra, ja, ga, la; *jaralā* is ja, ra, la, ga; and *pramāṇikā* is [the same as] *jaralā*. Any other [meter] besides these two is *vitāna*; this is declared to be the *anuṣṭubh* meter.

With *ra*, *na*, *sa*, and *ma* [syllables], there is the *halamukhī*; with *na*, *u*, and *ma*, it becomes the *śiśubhṛtā*. This is declared to be the *bṛhatī* meter; when *sa*, *ma*, *ja*, and *ga* occur, it is called *virājitam*.
The *paṇava* consists of *ma-na-ya-ga*; the *mayūrasāriṇī* consists of *ma-ra-bha-ya-ga*. The *rukmavatī* consists of *ra-jā-ra-ga*, followed by *bha-ma-sa-ga*.

The *manoramā* is composed of *ma*, *ta*, *bha*, *sa*, and *ga*; the *narajā* consists of *na*, *ra*, *ja*, *ga*. That which is known as the *paṅkti* meter has *ja*, *sa*, *ta*, *ga*, and *ga*. The *upasthita* consists of *ja*, *sa*, *ta*, *ga*, and *ga*.
That which consists of the gaṇas ja, ta, ja, and two gas, preceded by a guru, is the Indravajrā.

Upajātis consist of other [varieties] beginning and ending with these; Sumukhī has the gaṇas na, ja, ja, followed by a la and a ga; Dodhaka consists of bha, bha, bha, followed by two gas; and Śālinī consists of ma, ta, ta, followed by a ga and a ga.
The *Abdhiloka* consists of *viccheda*, *vāta*, *ūrma*, *mamatā*, and *gaga*; *Śrī* is said to consist of *bhata*, *nana*, and *ga*, with five and six [syllables] respectively.
The *maganā* is said to have the playful grace of a bee; *rathoddhatā* consists of *na*, *ra*, *la*, and *ga*; and *svāgatā* consists of *ra*, *na*, *bha*, *ga*, and *ga*.

*Vṛttā* consists of *na*, *na*, *sa*, *ga*, and *ga*; *Samadrikā* consists of *na*, *na*, *ra*, *la*, and *ga*. *Śyenikā* consists of *ra*, *ja*, *ra*, *la*, and *ga*; *Śikhaṇḍita* consists of *ja*, *sa*, *ta*, *ga*, and *ga*. Thus has the *triṣṭubh* meter been fully described by the great-souled Piṅgala.

*Vaṃśastha* consists of *ra-na-au-bha-sau*; *vaṃśasthavila* consists of *ja-tau-ja-rau*. Following that, *indravaṃśā* consists of *ja-ra-au*. With four *ta*s, it is known as *toṭaka*. *Drutavilambita* consists of *na-bhau-bhra-u*; *puṭa* consists of *na-nau-ma-yau*.
This Muditavadanā [mudrā] is formed by the Vasus (8) and the Vedas (4); it is described as having nine fingers and two eyes (2), and one should form it accordingly.

That *stragviṇī* is considered to have the syllables *ja*, *sa*, *ja*, and *sa* in its feet, with a caesura after four syllables; it is variegated with flowers and possesses a gait tossed by water through its aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*).
The *bhujaṅgaprayāta* meter is proclaimed to consist of four *ya*s; *prayaṃvadā* consists of *na*, *bha*, *ja*, and *ra*s, while *maṇimālā* consists of *ta*, *ya*, *ta*, and *ya*s.

*Lalitā* consists of *ta*, *bha*, *ja*, and *ra*, with a caesura at the sixth and twelfth syllables; *Pramitākṣarā* consists of *sa*, *ja*, *sa*, and *sa*; while *Ujjvalā* consists of *na*, *na*, *bha*, and *ra*.

The Vaiśvadevī meter consists of the gaṇas ma, ma, and bha; it has five syllables per foot and a pause (yati) after the fifth. The Jaladharamālā meter consists of the gaṇas sa and ma; it has four syllables per foot and a pause at the end of each quarter-verse (pāda).

The *praharṣiṇī* metre consists of nine *ta*s, one *ga*, and a *kṣamā* (12) syllable count; its caesura occurs at the fifth and sixth syllables (*rasaiḥ*). The *manajaragāḥ* (ma-na-ja-ra-ga) with a caesura at the third, fourth, and tenth syllables (*vahnibhiḥ daśabhiḥ*) [constitute another variety].

The *rucirā* metre consists of the gaṇas ja, bha, sa, ja, and ga, with a caesura after the fourth and seventh syllables; the *mattamayūra* consists of ma, ta, ya, sa, and ga, with a caesura after the seventh and tenth syllables.
Mañjubhāṣiṇī consists of sa, ja, sa, ja, ga, u; Sunandinī consists of sa, ja, sa, ma, ga, u; Candrikā consists of na, na, ta, ta, and ga, with a pause (yati) at the seventh and sixth syllables.

The *Aparājitā* meter is said to consist of seven syllables with no restriction (*asambādhā*), followed by a *matana-sa* (ma, ta, na, sa) gaṇa, with a caesura after the fifth syllable (*bāṇagrahaiḥ*), and then *na*, *na*, *ra*, *sa*, a light syllable, and a heavy syllable (*ladhuguruḥ*). It is defined by its seven *svaras* (syllables).

This *praharaṇakalikā* consists of *na*, *na*, *bha*, and *na*; likewise, *vasantatilakā* consists of *la* and *ga*. *Siṃhonnatā* consists of *ta*, *bha*, *ja*, *ja*, *ga*, and a heavy syllable (*guru*).
The Śarkarī metre is established as having *sa*, *na*, *ga*, *ga*, *vi*, *da*, *nu*, *a*, *tha*, *su*, *ke*, *sa*, *ra*, *ma* in its feet, with *na*, *ra*, *na*, *ra*, *la*, *ga* in each quarter.

The *Śreṣṭhā* consists of fourteen short syllables and ends with a long syllable (*ga*). It has a pause at the sixth and seventh syllables, and likewise pauses at the eighth and seventh syllables, forming a *sraj* [metre].

The *mālinī* consists of a cluster of eight *ma* syllables followed by *na*, *na*, *ma*, and *ya*. The *prabhadraka* consists of *va*, *sa*, *su*, *ra*, *ya*, *ti*, and *ra*, with *na*, *ja*, *ra*, and *ja* as the final feet.
That which consists of *elā*, *sayau*, *nanau*, and *yaḥ* with eight *citralekhā* syllables, and where *marau* and *mayau* occur, is called this *atiśarkarī*.
From *svarā* comes *kha*; *vṛṣabhagajajṛmbhita* consists of *bha*, *na*, *na*, *ga*, and *na-ga*; *bhranā* consists of *na-jabha-jara*; *vāṇinī* consists of *ga*; and *piṅgala* has declared *aṣṭi*.

The *śikhariṇī* consists of six, eleven, and seven syllables; its gaṇas are *ya*, *ma*, *na*, *sa*, *bha*, *la*, and a heavy syllable (*guru*). The *pṛthvī* has eight, five, and seven syllables; its gaṇas are *ja*, *sa*, *ja*, *sa*, *ya*, *la*, and a heavy syllable.

*Vaṃśapatrapatita* consists of ten syllables per foot with *bha*, *ra*, *na*, *bha*, *la*, and *ga*; *Hariṇī* consists of six, four, and seven syllables, with *na*, *sa*, *ma*, *ra*, *sa*, and a heavy syllable (*guru*).

The *mandākrāntā* consists of six syllables, four syllables, seven syllables, with the *ma*, *bha*, *na*, *ta*, *ta*, *ga*, and a heavy syllable (*guru*). The *nardataka* consists of *na*, *ja*, *bha*, *ja*, *la*, *u*, *ga*, and a pause (*yati*).

*Kokilaka* consists of seven *ṛtu*s (six) and four (*abdhi*) syllables; *Atyaṣṭi* is as before. *Kusumitalatā* has *ma*, *ta*, *na*, and *ya*, with *ya* and *ya* [as the final two], by *bhūta* (five), *ṛtu* (six), and *aśva* (seven); *Dhṛti* is the same.

The *Meghavisphūrjita* consists of *ra*, *ga*, *vi*, *sphū*, *rji*, *tā*, *ra*, and *ga*; the *Śārdūlavikrīḍita* consists of *ma*, *sa*, *ja*, *sa*, *ta*, *ta*, *ga*, and *ga*, with twelve and seven syllables respectively.

Chanda is said to be Atidhṛti; after that, Kṛti occurs. [The definition of Kṛti is: seven horses (seven gaṇas), six seasons (six mātrās), a beautiful-faced one (a long syllable), [the gaṇas] bha, ra, ma, na, ya, bha, la, and a heavy syllable (guru).

In the *vṛtta* meter, when there are two *ra* gaṇas and a *ja* gaṇa in each quarter, followed by a *ga*, *la*, and *ga*, it is called *kṛti*. When there are three *sa* gaṇas and seven *na* gaṇas, it is *snagdharā*; when there are *ma*, *na*, *bha*, *na*, *sa*, and three *ya* gaṇas, it is *prakṛti*.
Bhadraka consists of ten *ga*s; *Bhrau*, *Nrau*, *Naranā* constitute Yathākṛti; *Najau* and *Bhaśva* are Aśvalalita; and *Jabhau* and *Jabhalagā* shall be [the next two meters].
When the *mattākrīḍa* consists of eight *gaṇas* of two syllables (*mau*), followed by *na*, *na*, *la*, *la*, and a heavy syllable (*guru*), it is called *vikṛti* when the *saṃkṛti* is divided.

In the *krauñcapadā* meter, there are five, seven, and twelve syllables in the first two feet; the third foot consists of the ganas na, sa, bha, and na, followed by ya; and the fourth foot consists of the ganas bha, ma, sa, and bha, with pauses at five, five, eight, and seven syllables respectively.
Nine [syllables] in each [quarter] is declared *atikṛti*; indeed, *utkṛti* is said to have eight [syllables]. With eight, eleven, seven, and ten [syllables], there is the *bhujaṅgavijṛmbhita*.

The *yati* (caesura) known as *apavāha* occurs at nine, six, six, and five syllables; the *gaṇas* consist of six *sa*s, one *ga*, and two *g*s. *nanarasair lagayuktaiś ca apavāhākhyakaṃ yatiḥ |* *guhaiḥ ṣaḍbhiḥ rasair bāṇair monāḥ ṣaṭsagagā gaṇāḥ ||*
This Daṇḍaka is a precipice of fierce conduct; therefore, we have not descended from it. From this [Daṇḍaka] ending in the vowel *r* augmented by *v*, there arise the Vyāla, Jīmūta, and others.

Thus ends the two hundred and ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Even Meters and Others," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Sūta said: If there are *sa*, *sa*, *sa*, *la*, and *ga* in the odd feet, it is Upacitraka; if there are *bha*, *bha*, *ga*, and *ga* in the even feet, it is Drutamadhyā; and if there are *bha*, *bha*, *ga*, and *ga* [in both], it is [Drutavilambita]. The Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—210. Sūta said: [If] *sa*, *sa*, *sa*, *la*, and *ga* are in the odd foot, it is Upacitraka; if *bha*, *bha*, *ga*, and *ga* are in the even foot, it is Drutamadhyā; and *bha*, *bha*, *ga*, and *ga* [are the rule for Drutavilambita].
In the odd quarter, the ganas are known to be *na*, *ja*, and *ja*; in the other [even quarter], they are *ga* and *ga*.

In the *viṣama* (odd) feet, there are the gaṇas *ga*, *sa*, *ga*; in the *sama* (even) feet, *bha*, *bha*, *ga*, *ga*, *ga*. In the odd feet, *ta*, *ja*, *ra*, *ga*; in the even feet, *ma*, *sa*, *ja*, *ga*, *ga*, *guru*. This is *Bhadravirāṭ*; however, in *Ketumatī*, there are *sa* and *ja* in the odd feet.

In the *sagau* meter, when the feet are equal, *bhrau*, *na*, *ga*, and *ga* constitute the *ākhyānakī*; however, when the feet are unequal, *tau*, *ja*, *ga*, and *ga* [constitute it] in the even foot, while *ja*, *ta*, *ja*, and two *gurus* [constitute it] in the odd foot.

Viparītākhyānaka consists of the syllables ja, ta, ja, ga, and ga in the odd positions; likewise, ta, ta, ja, ga, and ga in the even positions, with a 'ga' at the end—thus it has been illustrated by Piṅgala.

In the uneven feet, *puṣpitāgrā* consists of *na*, *na*, *ra*, and *ya*; in the even feet, they say *vaitālīya* consists of *na*, *ja*, *ja*, *ra*, and *ga*. The other meter called *aparavaktra* is *aupacchandasika*.
Vāṅmatī consists of the gaṇas ra, ja, ra, and ja, occurring in an odd-numbered foot.

Thus ends the two hundred and tenth chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of the Ardhasamavṛtta and Other Meters," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Sūta said: The first quarter consists of eight syllables, the second of twelve syllables, the third of sixteen syllables, and the fourth of twenty syllables. The Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 211.
Sūta said: The first quarter consists of eight syllables, the second of twelve syllables, the third of sixteen syllables, and the fourth of twenty syllables.
For the general characteristic of the lower part is indeed established by means of the *padacaturūrdhva* meters.
The *āpīḍa* is declared to consist of all *sarva* [syllables], with two [syllables] occurring at the end of each preceding quarter-verse.

In the second [verse], when the first foot consists of eight syllables, it is a *kalikā*; in the third, it is a *lavalī*. Furthermore, when there are four feet each of eight syllables, this is called the *amṛtadhārā*, as previously described.

(Thus ends the section on *padacaturūrdhva*. In the first quarter, there are *sa*, *ja*, *sa*, and *la*; in the second, *na*, *sa*, *ja*, and *ga*; in the third, *bha*, *na*, *bha*, and *ga*; and in the fourth, *sa*, *ja*, *sa*, *ja*, and two *g*s.
Saurabhaka would be like the previous [Viyoginī] in the third foot, with ra, na, bha, and ga; Lalita would be like Adgatā, with na, na, sa, and sa in the third foot.

(Thus ends the section on Udgatā. In the Upasthitapracupita meter, there are *ma*, *sa*, *ja*, and *bha* in the first foot; *sa*, *na*, *ja*, *ra*, *ga*, and *sa* in the second; *na*, *na*, and *sa* in the third; and *na*, *na*, *ja*, *ya*, and *ya* in the fourth; while the remaining feet are as before.
In the third foot, there is a specific rule: the meter would be *nau sanau nasau*.
In the third foot, *ta*, *ja*, and *ra* [occur], and the rest is as before; in the first foot it is as before, and in the remaining [feet] *ta*, *ja*, and *ra* [occur]—this becomes the Śuddhavirāj.

(Thus ends the section on Upasthitapracupita. Alternatively, a verse with uneven syllables per quarter, such as five or six, is called *yāvakam*. In this context, it is not termed *gāthā*; it would be like the *daśadharmā* and other such [verses].

Thus ends the two hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Irregular Meters and Other Topics," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Sūta said: In the process of constructing the table (prastāra), the first letter is 'l'. Then, for the subsequent positions, the letter is equal to the preceding one. In the middle of the "naṣṭa" (finding a specific meter) calculation, if the position number is even, the letter is 'l'; if it is even when halved, it is 'l', and if it is odd, it is 'g' (a long syllable).
The quality is reversed; it is delightful when stated twice and removes [the fault] when stated once.
In the case of two, it is "half-form" (dvirardha-rūpa); in the case of zero, "zero" (śūnya) is uttered twice. Up to that point, it is multiplied by half; finally, it is diminished by two times two.
In the other [direction], it is full; in the other, it is full; thus Meru would be level when spread out.

The number of fingers and the number of syllables in the meter are determined by the first finger and then upward; this essence of prosody is declared to be the count itself doubled and diminished by one.
Thus ends the two hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Definition of Prosody," in the first section (Pūrvakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 213 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa].
Sūta said: O Śaunaka, just as Brahmā spoke to Vyāsa after hearing from Hari, I shall likewise describe to you the conduct of Brāhmaṇas and others, which bestows all blessings.
Having understood both the Śruti and the Smṛti, one should perform the rites prescribed by Śruti; if a Śrauta rite is not prescribed, then one should perform a Smārta rite.
If one is unable even to perform that, the wise person should practice the conduct of the virtuous; for the Śruti and Smṛti are the eyes of the Brahmins for perceiving their duties.

The supreme dharma is that declared in the Śruti; the secondary is that contained in the Smṛti scriptures; and that which is attained through the conduct of the virtuous—these are the three eternal dharmas.
Truthfulness, charity, compassion, freedom from greed, knowledge, sacrifice, worship, and self-restraint—these eight are the purifiers and the characteristics of the conduct of the virtuous.
The bodies and sense organs of those ancestors were composed of light; they were not defiled by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
The primary dwellings of the social classes and their religious practices have been proclaimed; truth, sacrifice, austerity, and charity—this is the defining characteristic of dharma.
Non-appropriation of what is not given, generosity, study, silent recitation, knowledge, wealth, austerity, purity, noble birth, and freedom from disease.
And the cause for the cessation of saṃsāra proceeds from dharma alone; from dharma come happiness and knowledge, and from knowledge liberation is attained.
Sacrificing, studying, and giving according to the scriptures are declared to be the eternal common duty of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
Sacrificing for others, teaching, and receiving gifts from a pure person—these three modes of livelihood, the sages say, belong to those of the highest caste.
Living by the sword, protecting living beings, and tending cattle, agriculture, and trade are recorded as the means of livelihood for the king and the Vaiśya respectively.

For a Śūdra, service to the twice-born; for the twice-born, service according to their respective order; for a student (brahmacārin), dwelling with a teacher, tending the sacred fires, and the private study of the Veda.

Having bathed three times [daily], he should offer himself for bathing and provide alms-food to his guru; he remains with him until the end of his life, wearing a girdle, or having matted hair, carrying a staff, or being shaven-headed, while taking refuge in his guru.

He should perform the Agnihotra rites and maintain his livelihood through his own duties; he may engage in sexual intercourse with his lawful wife on days other than the sacred festival days (parvan).
The performance of worship and other rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests, as well as the observance of the meaning of the Śruti and Smṛti—this is the duty of the householder.

The wearing of matted hair, the performance of the agnihotra sacrifice, sleeping on the ground, the wearing of animal skins, dwelling in the forest, and subsisting on milk, roots, wild rice, and fruits.
Abstaining from forbidden food, bathing three times a day, observing vows, and honoring the deities and guests—this is the dharma of the forest-dweller.
The renunciation of all undertakings, subsisting on alms-food, dwelling at the foot of a tree, freedom from possessiveness, absence of malice, and equanimity toward all living beings.
The capacity for experiencing pleasure and pain through contact with the pleasant and unpleasant; internal and external purity; restraint of speech; and the practice of meditation.
The withdrawal of all the senses, constancy in concentration and meditation, and the complete purification of one's being—this is called the dharma of the wandering mendicant.

Non-violence, speech that is pleasant and true, truthfulness, purity, forbearance, and compassion are said to be the common duty for those belonging to the social orders (varṇas) as well as those bearing the marks of religious stages (liṅgins).
All those who act according to what has been taught attain the supreme goal. From the time of awakening until sleep, I shall describe to you the dharma of the householder.
One should wake up during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and reflect upon dharma and artha, as well as the physical austerities rooted therein and the true meaning of the Vedas.
Having risen at the end of the night, having performed purification and being composed, one should, remaining vigilant at all times, bathe and perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā).
One should perform the morning twilight devotion preceded by the cleansing of the teeth; and during the day, one should void both urine and feces facing the north.
And at night, he should perform [the rites] facing south, and during both twilights as during the day; whether in shade or in darkness, by night or by day, the twice-born man should act thus.

However, one should perform it facing the east, except in cases where there is danger to life; and it should be done on auspicious ground that is smeared with cow dung, free of charcoal, not an anthill, and not recently ploughed.
One should not void urine or feces on paths frequented by those who live off the shade [of trees], nor within water, nor in a temple, nor at an anthill, nor on a spot where mice dwell.

One should discard earth from the dwellings of others, from what has been left over after purification, and from a cremation ground. One should apply one application of earth to the penis, and two applications of earth to the left hand.

Two applications of earth should be given for both [the penis and the left hand]; this is declared to be the purification by urine. One application is for the penis, three for the anus, and likewise ten for the left hand.
Five [handfuls] for the feet, ten for each hand, and seven handfuls of earth; the first application of earth is prescribed to be the measure of half a prasṛti.
The second and third [periods] are proclaimed to be half of that; however, one who is seated and yet unable to void excrement or urine [is exempt].
He should always perform half of his own prescribed purification; for daytime purification, half of that at night, or alternatively, a quarter is ordained.

However, while these are prescribed for one who is healthy, a person in distress should perform them according to their strength. Fat, semen, blood, marrow, saliva, feces, urine, earwax, and excrement—these are the substances used.
Phlegm, tears, rheum of the eyes, and sweat—these twelve are the impurities of men; one should perform purification to such an extent as one considers sufficient for purity.
There is no fixed limit for the number of purifications required when not specifically prescribed; indeed, purification is said to be of two kinds: external and internal.

External purification is said to be by means of earth and water, while internal purification is the purity of one's disposition. First, one should sip water three times; then, one should wipe the mouth twice.
Having wiped [the mouth] with the base of the thumb, one should touch the mouth three times; thereafter, immediately after, one should touch the nose with the thumb and the forefinger.
Again and again, one should touch the eyes and ears with the thumb and ring finger; the navel with the little finger and thumb; and the heart with the palm.
One should then touch the head with all [the fingers] and the two arms with the tips; by reciting the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman verses three times in succession, one shall gratify them.
First, he wipes twice over the Atharvāṅgirases; then that [portion] is comfortable. Then, in due order, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, and the Vedāṅgas, and the Vedāṅgas.
One should touch the ether in the mouth, the wind in the nostrils, the sun in the eyes, the quarters of space in the ears, the knot of the vital breaths at the navel, and Brahmā in the heart.
Having touched the head with the Rudra mantra, one gratifies [Rudra]; then the crest-lock with the Ṛṣis; and the arms with Yama, Indra, Varuṇa, Kubera, Vāsava, and Agni.
Having sprinkled water on his feet, he should meditate on Viṣṇu and Indra; on his two hands, Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, Candra, and the Mountains; and on the joints of his fingers [the same].
Regarding the rivers such as the Gaṅgā and others, those lines which are situated in the middle of the hand—when the time of dawn has arrived, having performed purification according to the rules.
Thereafter, one should perform the bath preceded by the cleansing of the teeth; for when the mouth is stale, a man is always considered impure.
Therefore, one should indeed perform the cleansing of the teeth with every effort, using the *kadamba*, *bilva*, *khadira*, *karavīra*, *vaṭa*, or *arjuna* trees.
The *yūthī*, *bṛhatī*, *jātī*, *karañja*, *arka*, and *atimuktaka*; the *jambū*, *madhūka*, *pāmārga*, *śirīṣa*, *udumbara*, and *asana*.
Trees such as the milk-exuding *kaṇṭakī* are recommended for cleaning the teeth; those that are pungent, bitter, or astringent bestow wealth, health, and happiness.

Having washed and eaten, one should discard [the remains] in a clean place and then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana); likewise on the new moon day, the sixth, the ninth, and also on the first day of the lunar fortnight.
One should avoid using a tooth-stick on the day of the sun (Sunday), as well as when a tooth-stick is unavailable or on a prohibited lunar day.
One should perform the cleansing of the mouth with twelve mouthfuls of these; they praise the morning bath as beneficial, producing both visible and invisible results.
One whose self is purified by bathing at dawn destroys all sin through the recitation of mantras and other rites; yet the body is exceedingly impure, being endowed with nine apertures.
This [impurity] flows out day and night; therefore, the morning bath is a means of purification, generating clarity of mind and increasing physical beauty and good fortune.
One should perform that which pacifies grief and suffering, like a bath in the Gaṅgā, today on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, under the Nakṣatra Hasta.
And regarding the removal of the ten sins: without giving away the impurity of one's gifts, there is indeed contrary conduct, namely violence and the pursuit of another's wife.
Harsh speech, falsehood, slander, incoherent talk, speaking of the property of others, and thinking of what is undesirable with the mind.
For the purpose of destroying the afflictions of this [present] state, I perform this bath in the Gaṅgā; for forest-dwellers and householders, the morning bath is performed briefly.
A renunciant should bathe three times a day, while a student of sacred knowledge bathes once; having sipped water and invoked the sacred ford, he should bathe while remembering the imperishable Hari.
It should be known that there are thirty million Rākṣasas named Mandehas; these evil-minded beings desire to devour the rising sun.
He who does not perform the twilight worship slays the sun; [the ancestors] consume him with water purified by mantras, which takes the form of fire.
The junction of day and night is indeed called *saṃdhyā*; that *saṃdhyā* lasts for two *nāḍikās*, as long as visibility remains.

At the conclusion of the Gandhyā rite, however, the fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed to be performed by oneself; for the fruit that comes from performing the oblation oneself is not produced by anyone else.
What is offered by a sacrificial priest, a son, a teacher, a brother, a sister’s son, or a husband, that indeed becomes an offering made by oneself.
Brahmā is indeed the Gārhapatya fire; the three-eyed Lord is the Dakṣiṇāgni; Viṣṇu is the Āhavanīya fire; and Kumāra is called Satya.
Having performed the fire-oblation at the proper time, he should then recite the solar mantras with a concentrated mind, as well as the Sāvitrī and the Praṇava, according to the prescribed rule.
