For one who is constantly disciplined in the Praṇava, in the seven Vyāhṛtis, and in the three-footed Sāvitrī, no fear exists anywhere.
The person who, having risen at dawn, constantly recites the Gāyatrī, is not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
The goddess is described as being white in color, likewise clothed in silken garments; she holds a rosary, is auspicious, and is seated upon a lotus throne.
Having invoked according to the rule with this Yajus mantra, "Thou art splendor," this Yajus was formerly seen by the gods who desired the vision of the divine sight.
Having invoked her who resides within the solar disc and also abides in the world of Brahmā, one should recite the mantra and then dismiss her with a salutation.
One should perform the worship of the deities precisely in the forenoon; since there is no god higher than Viṣṇu, one should therefore always worship him.
A wise person should not conceive of the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva as being separate. In this world, there are eight auspicious things: a Brāhmaṇa, a cow, and fire; [and five others].
Gold, clarified butter, the sun, water, and likewise the king as the eighth—these one should constantly behold and worship by circumambulating them.
First, the study of the Veda; then reflection, practice, recitation, and its impartation to disciples—thus the study of the Veda is fivefold.
He who, having had the meaning of the Vedas, the sacrificial treatises, and the codes of law transcribed for a price, gives them away, goes to the world of the Vedas.
He who, having written the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, bestows them as gifts, obtains merit equal to the gift of the Veda, doubled.

And likewise, in the third part [of one's life], one should accomplish the welfare of those who are to be supported: mother, father, teacher, brother, offspring, the destitute, and those who have sought refuge.
The guest who has arrived, the fire, and the group of those to be supported have been declared [as such]. Supporting this group of dependents is praised as a means for attaining heaven.
One should therefore make every effort to provide for the group of dependents; it is better that one person lives who supports many than that many live who are supported by one.
Other men, though living, are as good as dead, for they merely fill their own bellies; yet even a dog possesses the capacity to fill its own belly.
From objects that have increased and arisen from here and there, all activities proceed, like rivers from mountains.
The earth containing all mines of jewels, grains, livestock, and women—because of their utility for wealth, they are designated as "wealth" (artha).
A Brahmin should live in times of non-distress by adopting a mode of livelihood that involves no harm to living beings, or at least very little harm.
Wealth should be known to be of three kinds: white, variegated, and black; its classification should be understood as sevenfold, distinct for each.

Wealth acquired through inheritance, that given out of affection, and what is obtained together with one's wife—these three kinds of property belong to all social classes (varṇas) without distinction.
The specific wealth of a Brāhmaṇa is seen to have three characteristics: officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the constant acceptance of gifts from pure persons.

They say that for a Kṣatriya as well, there are three specific kinds of wealth: that obtained for the sake of purification, that received from taxes, and likewise that acquired through fines and that born of victory.
The specific wealth seen for a Vaiśya is also distinct: agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade; while that of a Śūdra arises from serving these [higher castes].
A twice-born man may personally engage in the activities of a lazy man, such as agriculture and trade, for himself or for another; by doing so himself during times of distress, he incurs no sin.
Many means of livelihood have been proclaimed by the sages; yet among all of these, they consider usury to be the most effective.
Through drought, fear of kings, or afflictions such as rats, there may be obstacles to agriculture and similar pursuits; however, such [obstacles] do not exist in usury.
Whether in the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight, by night or even by day, in heat, rain, or cold, the growth does not cease.

The prosperity that accrues to those who have gone abroad, who subsist on various kinds of merchandise and engage properly in lending at interest, arises precisely for one who is well-established [in his own business].
Having obtained his gain, he should worship the ancestors, the gods, and the Brahmins; when they are satisfied, they undoubtedly pacify that fault of his.
One who practices trade and usury should give clothing, gold from the Ganges, and so forth; a farmer should give food, drink, vehicles, beds, and seats.
Having given twenty [cows] and a hundred [units] of livestock, gold, and so forth to kings, the self-possessed man should make a store of barley-gruel by means of one-fourth [of his income].
With one half [of the income], one should maintain oneself along with the performance of obligatory and occasional rites; and one quarter should be used to increase the fundamental capital.
Knowledge, craftsmanship, prosperity, service, cattle-rearing, trade, agriculture, living by alms, and usury—these are the ten means of livelihood.

Wealth acquired through receiving gifts belongs to the Brāhmaṇa; that acquired by conquest with weapons belongs to the Kṣatriya; wealth acquired by righteous means belongs to the Vaiśya; and wealth acquired through service belongs to the Śūdra.
A river with abundant water, vegetables, clay, leaves, sacrificial fuel, and *kuśa* grass, as well as the Vedic chanting of Brahmins—the sound of the sacred fire—is the supreme wealth of the wise.
But when something is obtained unasked, there is no fault in accepting it; the gods know that to be nectar, therefore one should never reject it.
Desiring to offer precious substances to his teacher, and intending to honor the gods and guests, he may accept gifts from anyone; however, he should not satisfy himself with them.
A twice-born man may accept [gifts] from a virtuous person or even from one who is not virtuous; for one who possesses good qualities has few faults, whereas one devoid of qualities sinks down.
Thus, having supported himself by means of manual labor or other such activities, the best of the twice-born should perform purification through penance before others.
And in the fourth part [of the day], one should collect earth for the purpose of bathing, as well as sesame seeds, flowers, kuśa grass, and so forth; the bath should be performed in natural water.

Daily, occasional, optional, that which is an auxiliary to ritual acts, and that which removes impurities; along with cleansing, sipping water, and immersion—these are proclaimed as the eight types of bathing.
A man who has not bathed is unfit for recitation, fire-offerings, and other such rites; therefore, the morning bath is proclaimed as the obligatory daily bath (nityasnāna) for that purpose.

Having touched a Cāṇḍāla, a corpse, excrement, and so forth, or having touched a woman in her menses, one must bathe; when one who is already fit for bathing bathes, that is indeed an occasional (naimittika) bath.
Bathing such as the Puṣya-bath and others, as prescribed by the rules of the astrologers, is designated as optional (kāmya); one should not perform it without a specific desire.
One who desires to recite purificatory mantras, or wishes to honor the deities and guests, should perform a bath; that is proclaimed as the bath that is an integral part of the ritual action.
The practice there is for the purpose of removing impurities, and not otherwise; [it is performed] at lakes, at bathing-places dug by the gods, at sacred fords, and at rivers.
Since bathing itself is the ritual action, it is therefore called *kriyā-snāna*; the limbs are purified by water, and one obtains the fruit of bathing at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*).
Through cleansing, bathing, and mantras, sin is swiftly destroyed; this includes daily rites, occasional rites, and the removal of impurities that forms part of ritual action.

In the absence of a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), however, one should perform the rite with warm water or water drawn from others; water drawn from the ground is meritorious, and more so than that is water from a spring.

The merit from that [lake] is more essential than that; therefore, it is said that [the merit of] water from a sacred ford (tīrtha) is greater than that, and the merit of the Ganges is greater than all.
The water of the Gaṅgā quickly purifies sin committed until the end of one's life; so too does the water present at Gayā and Kurukṣetra.

Therefore, one should know that other water from the Gaṅgā is supreme; [it is especially so] on the occasion of the birth of a son, during auspicious conjunctions, and likewise at the sun's passage into a new zodiacal sign.
Bathing at night upon the sighting of Rāhu is commended, but not otherwise; as is bathing at every dawn, during the twilight, and when the sun has risen.
That which is equal to the Prājāpatya penance destroys great sins; whatever fruit would accrue from performing the Prājāpatya for twelve years [is obtained by this].
One who bathes at dawn, endowed with faith for a year, obtains those vast enjoyments comparable to the eclipses of the moon and sun, if he so desires.

One should always bathe in the morning during the two months of Māgha and Phālguna; indeed, he who, having reached the month of Māgha, bathes in the morning and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya), [attains great merit].
In this way, one dispels even the most terrible sin within a mere month—whether it be [the murder of] one's mother, father, brother, friend, or teacher.
Whoever immerses himself [in the water] for the sake of another shall receive a twelfth part [of the merit]; Viṣṇu is especially pleased by *āmalaka* fruits on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*).
A man desiring prosperity should always perform his bath with *āmalaka* fruits; [otherwise, he may encounter] distress, infamy, short life, wealth, or even death.
Health and the attainment of all desires result from anointing oneself with the sun and other [planets]; likewise for one who has fasted, observed a vow, and had his hair and beard shaved by barbers.
Fortune remains pleased for as long as she does not touch the oil; having bathed in this manner, a man should satisfy the ancestors, the gods, and human beings with libations.
Standing in water reaching to the navel, one should contemplate with a focused mind: "May my ancestors come; may they accept this handful of water."
One should likewise offer three handfuls of water at a time toward the southern sky; having put on dry clothing, those standing on dry ground should do so upon strewn *barhis* grass.
Those who know the ritual rules should perform the libation, but never in a vessel; for whatever in water is harsh as flesh, or whatever is impure, [is avoided].
"May all that which is unpeaceful and defiled depart; having taken water with this mantra using the left hand."

One should cast that in the southwest direction for the destruction of demons; [it removes] whatever sin arises from eating forbidden food and so forth, as well as from the acceptance of improper gifts.
Whatever evil deed I have committed through speech, mind, or bodily actions—may Indra, Varuṇa, and Bṛhaspati together purify that for me.
Saying, "May Savitṛ, Bhaga, and the sages beginning with Sanaka, as well as the entire world from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, be satisfied," [he offers].
Performing a concise libation, he should cast three handfuls of water; then, free from envy, he should perform the worship of the gods, beginning with Brahmā.
One should worship all the gods with mantras pertaining to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Savitṛ, Mitra, and Varuṇa—using those specific mantras—and pay homage to them.
One should place the flowers individually with the *namaskāra* mantra; then one should worship Viṣṇu, who consists of all the gods, as well as Bhāskara.
Whoever offers flowers or even water with the Puruṣasūkta, by him this entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, becomes worshipped.
And one should worship Janārdana with other Tantric mantras as well; first the arghya offering should be presented, and after that, the unguent.
Then [one should perform] the offering of a handful of flowers, incense, and sacrificial fruits; likewise, bathing within the water, as well as sprinkling and sipping water for purification.
One should consecrate the water intended for the sacred bathing place (tīrtha) by reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa Sūkta three times, doing so constantly.
This is declared by the great-souled ones to be the procedure for bathing; for the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas, the bath is prescribed to be performed with mantras.

For a Śūdra, however, it is traditionally held that he should simply remain silent while showing reverence; teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña), while the libation of water is the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña).

The offering to the gods is human, that to the spirits is elemental; the honoring of guests is not a sacrifice. [An offering] in a cow-pen yields tenfold merit, while in a fire-sanctuary it is more than a hundredfold.
In sacred fields of accomplishment, at holy fords, and in temples of the deities, [the merit] is infinite in the presence of Viṣṇu, numbering hundreds of thousands of millions.
And likewise, in the fifth portion, a distribution according to the truth is prescribed for the ten million ancestors, gods, and humans.
He who, having first given to the brahmins, eats together with his friends, attains heaven after death by practicing the gift of food.
One should first eat what is sweet, salt and sour in the middle, and pungent, bitter, and astringent, as well as milk, at the end.
One should completely avoid eating leafy vegetables grown in the ground at night, and one should never be addicted to the consumption of a single taste.
The food of a Brāhmaṇa is declared to be nectar; the food of a Kṣatriya is declared to be milk; the food of a Vaiśya is indeed just food; and the food of a Śūdra is declared to be blood.
One should dwell here for a new moon day, or even for just one year.
Therein both Śrī and Lakṣmī dwell; of this there is no doubt. In the belly is the Gārhapatya fire, and in the region of the back is the Dakṣiṇa fire.
The Āhavanīya fire is in the mouth, and the Satya fire is on the head; he who knows these five fires is called one who has established the sacred fires (āhitāgni).
The body, water, Soma, and various kinds of food are said to be the objects of enjoyment; for Prāṇa, Agni, and Āditya are indeed one and the same enjoyer.
May this food be for my strength from earth, water, fire, and air; may it result in unimpeded happiness for me as well upon its transformation.
Then, having wiped his hands, he should consume betel; thereafter, with a well-composed mind, he should listen to the Itihāsa.
With the study of the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth, during the sixth and seventh parts [of the day], a man should then perform his ablutions and worship the evening twilight.

O twice-born one, this practice has been declared by me for the day; the wise man who reads or hears this code of conduct shall go to heaven. For it is remembered, O twice-born one, that Keśava is the performer of dharma through right conduct.
Thus ends the two hundred and fifth chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Now I shall describe the rules for bathing, since all religious rites have their root in bathing. One should procure earth, cow dung, sesame seeds, darbha grass, and fragrant flowers.
At the time of bathing, one who is restrained and pure, seeking to bathe, should bring these [substances] and place them upon the ground in a secluded spot, ending with scented water.
Having divided that clay and the cow dung into three parts, the wise man should then wash his feet and likewise his hands with water and clay.

Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, with his topknot tied, having sipped water properly and remaining silent, he should worship the water while circumambulating it clockwise with the verse "uruṃ rāja."
One should cause that water to swirl with the three-verse hymn beginning, "Those hundred of yours."

Oṃ. For King Varuṇa has made a wide path for Sūrya to follow. May the speakers be established as those whose hearts are wise. Homage to Agni-Aruṇa; may the noose of Varuṇa be praised away. Homage to Varuṇa!

Oṃ, those hundred and those thousand great sacrificial nooses of yours, O Varuṇa, which are spread abroad—may Savitṛ, Viṣṇu, all the gods, and the Maruts of beautiful praise release us from them today. Svāhā! Having formed the *sumitriyāṇa* gesture with the palms joined, one should pour water out over the north and then cast it behind. Oṃ, may the waters and the plants be friendly to us; may they be unfriendly to him who hates us and whom we hate.
Having first washed his feet and hips with three portions of earth each, and having rinsed his hands and sipped water, he should then pay homage to the water.

Oṃ, Viṣṇu strode across this; he established his foot in three places, and it is gathered in his dust. Afterwards, even though one is already pure, one should sip water while reciting the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
One should indeed cleanse one's limbs with clay while reciting the verse "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," and one should immerse oneself facing the sun while reciting the verse "āpo asmān."
Oṃ! May the Waters, our mothers, purify us; may those rich in clarity cleanse us with their clarity. For they, the goddesses, carry away every impurity; from them, purified and cleansed, I emerge.
Then, having submerged and emerged slowly from the vessels without becoming agitated, and having smeared them with cow dung while reciting the verse "mānastoke," one should proceed.

Oṃ! Do not harm us in our honor, nor in our children, nor in our life-span, nor in our cattle, nor in our horses. O Rudra, do not slay our heroic men who are full of wrath; we, bearing oblations, invoke you forever.
Then one should consecrate [the disciple] with the Varuṇa mantras in their proper order: with the two verses beginning "imaṃ me varuṇa," and also with "tvanno" and "satvanno."
"O Waters, you are the end of suffering," and "May they release me at the purificatory bath"; and "Om, O Varuṇa, hear this my call today and be gracious; seeking your protection, I pray to you."

Oṃ. I approach you with a prayer, honoring you; the sacrificer seeks this through oblations. O Varuṇa, be gracious here; do not steal away our life, but grant us wide space and long life. Oṃ. O Agni, you who know, may you appease the wrath of the divine Varuṇa for us. Being the best of sacrificers, the greatest bearer of oblations, and most radiant, release us from all hatreds, Svāhā! Oṃ. O Agni, be a protector to us, most near to us at the dawning of this morning. Appeasing Varuṇa for us, being generous, grant us mercy; be easy for us to invoke. Oṃ. O Waters, O Herbs, do not harm us. O King Varuṇa, release us from that [sin] for which we have cursed, saying "O Varuṇa, O slayer of cows!"—release us from that, O Varuṇa! Oṃ. O Varuṇa, loosen the highest bond from us, untie the lowest, and release the middle one. Then, O Āditya, in your service, may we be sinless before Aditi. May they release me from the bond of Varuṇa. Having crossed over the wife of Yama, I am freed from every evil. You are the purifying bath (Avabhṛtha); you move again and again toward us. Through the gods, you go to the mind-made [state]; protect us from the flower-like [impurity] created by the gods. May the intellect be small [in its faults].

Having thus consecrated himself, and having immersed himself and sipped water again, he should cause [the deity] to drink with these purifying mantras that do not contain gender-specific marks, using a blade of darbha grass.
With the three verses beginning with "āpohiṣṭhā," with this [verse] "idamāpo haviṣmatīḥ," with the two verses beginning with "devīrāpaḥ," and with the three-verse hymn beginning with "āpodevāḥ."
"drupadādiva," "śanno devīḥ," and "apām rasaḥ"; these nine verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" are the purificatory (pāvamānī) hymns.
The Lord of Consciousness (Citpati) moves slowly, having submerged himself in meditative absorption; [he recites] "Hiraṇyavarṇāḥ" and other purificatory (pāvamānī) verses.
One should, according to one's ability, employ the *Taratsamā*, the *Śuddhavatī* verses, the *Pavitra* hymns, and many meritorious *Vāruṇī* verses, as far as one is capable.
Accompanied by the syllable *oṃ*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *gāyatrī*, one should perform the consecration at the beginning and at the end according to the proper sequence.
The cleansing rite is prescribed for one who is actually standing in the midst of water; having recited the mantra three times while submerged within the water, one should perform the Aghamarṣaṇa.
One should recite three times the verses beginning with "drupadād" and the three-verse hymn beginning with "ayaṃ gauḥ," or other mantras prescribed by tradition, while remaining composed in mind.
The wise man should mutter the Gāyatrī together with the Vyahṛtis and the Praṇava; or he may repeat the Praṇava, or meditate upon the imperishable Viṣṇu.
The waters are the abode of Viṣṇu, and he alone is called the Lord of Waters (Appati); these [elements] are his very bodies, therefore one should indeed meditate upon him within the waters.
Having immersed oneself repeatedly in the waters with the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ," one should indeed recite this Gāyatrī dedicated to Viṣṇu for the purpose of constant remembrance of Viṣṇu.
Oṃ! Let this water carry away its own impurity, washing away the blood; let it be as the immortal nectar for the Hotṛ priest, and as a non-terrifying remedy for the swelling.

May the purifying waters release me from that sin. May the waters rich in oblation, the measurers, come forth; may he who possesses the oblation appear. May the divine Asura possess the oblation; may Sūrya possess the oblation. O divine waters, that wave of yours which is fit for the oblation, endowed with power, and sweet as the Ādityas—O deities, grant that to the bright and pure gods. Of those [waters], you are the sharer of the portion, the one who draws the ploughshare of the ocean, the first-arriving guest, the waters most fierce and free from sorrow.

May the divine waters, rich in sweetness, full of food, and possessing royal power, take up the sesame seeds; those by which one sprinkles for Mitra and Varuṇa, and by which one leads Indra to food. May the divine waters, who are the source of the two-fold blood and who abide in the sun, grant us well-being. Of the essence of the waters, may you take that which is the most excellent.

The divine waters, rich in sweetness, have risen up toward the sun for the friendship of all creatures. From their place, let the plants with their seeds spring forth. May the gentle Fathers purify me; may the Waters, the Father, and the powerful one purify me with the filter that extends through life. May my grandfathers purify me, and may my great-grandfathers purify me with the filter that extends through life, so that I may attain a full span of years. O Agni, grant us long lives, food, strength, and skin; O you who possess the skin, protect our skins. May the divine folk purify me; may they purify me with mind and intellect. May all beings purify me, O Jātavedas; purify me! Purify me, O shining God, with the bright filter, O Agni, according to your wisdom and your powers. That filter of yours which is spread within the flame, O Agni—by that may Brahmā purify me. May Pavamāna, the dweller in light, the observer of men, purify me with his filter. May he who is the Purifier purify me. O God Savitṛ, by both means—the filter and the impulse—we purify this prayer. The divine Waters, purifying and belonging to all gods, take hold of these [offerings]; may they, being worthy of worship, lead them to us. Through her, rejoicing in the communal feasts, may we be masters of riches. May the Lord of Thought purify me with the flawless filter, with the rays of the Sun. Whatever desire I have for you, who are purified by that filter, may I be able to fulfill it. May the divine Savitṛ, the Lord of Speech, purify me with the flawless filter, with the rays of the Sun. O Lord of the Filter, whatever desire I have for you, who are purified by the filter, may I be able to fulfill it. O Lord of Heaven, may I be able to fulfill it. This spotted cow has stepped forth; she purifies the hundredfold mother and the father. May the divine Savitṛ purify me with the flawless filter, with the rays of the Sun. O Lord of the Filter, whatever desire I have for you, who are purified by the filter, may I be able to fulfill it. Om! The wise ever behold that highest step of Viṣṇu, like an eye fixed in the sky.
Having bathed in this manner and put on two clean, unwashed garments, he should then wash his hands with earth and water, thoroughly rinsing them.
If one has already sipped water, one should sip again with the mantra during bathing or eating; likewise, one should repeat the Drupadā verse three times and also the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn.
Having sipped water and sprinkled himself, and having sipped water three times, he should then worship the Sun with his joined palms containing flowers placed upon his head.
Having thrown water and stirred it, [he recites] "ud u tyam," "citram," "taccakṣur devahitam," and also "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat."
With arms raised and mind concentrated, looking at the sun, he should recite these [mantras] and likewise the Gāyatrī according to his ability, having thus worshipped the Maker of Day.
With the *anuvāka* beginning with "vibhrāṭ," with the *sūkta* of Puruṣa, with the *śivasaṅkalpa*, and likewise with the *maṇḍala-brāhmaṇa*.
Furthermore, the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) should be performed according to one's ability with the Divākīrti hymns and other solar mantras proclaimed by all the gods.

Or, for the sake of accomplishing the recitation, one should recite the Adhyātmavidyā according to the prescribed rule; having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder and having sipped water three times, [one should worship] Śrī, Medhā, Dhṛti, and Kṣiti.
One should fully satisfy Vāc, the Mistress of Speech, as well as Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Umā, Arundhatī, Śacī, and Mātṛ.
Jayā and Vijayā, Sāvitrī and Śānti, Svāhā, Svadhā, Dhṛti, and likewise the supreme Aditi.

One should offer libations to the wives of the sages and to the maidens, as well as to the deities associated with specific desires; however, one who desires all auspiciousness should offer libations to Sarvamaṅgalā.
Saying, "May this world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, be satisfied," one should cast three handfuls of water and perform the libation (tarpaṇa).
Thus ends the two hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rules for Bathing," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: I shall now fully describe the libation (tarpaṇa), which grants satisfaction to the gods and the ancestors.

Oṃ, let the Modas be satiated. Oṃ, let the Pramodas be satiated. Oṃ, let the Sumukhas be satiated. Oṃ, let the Durmukhas be satiated. Oṃ, let the Vighnas be satiated. Oṃ, let the makers of obstacles be satiated. Oṃ, let the Vedas (Chandās) be satiated. Oṃ, let the Vedas be satiated. Oṃ, let the medicinal herbs be satiated. Oṃ, let the eternal one (Sanātana) be satiated. Oṃ, let the other teachers be satiated. Oṃ, let the year with its divisions be satiated. Oṃ, let the gods be satiated. Oṃ, let the Apsarases be satiated. Oṃ, let the Devāndhakas be satiated. Oṃ, let the oceans be satiated. Oṃ, let the Nāgas be satiated. Oṃ, let the mountains be satiated. Oṃ, let the rivers, humans, and Yakṣas be satiated. Oṃ, let the Rākṣasas be satiated. Oṃ, let the Piśācas be satiated. Oṃ, let the Suparṇas be satiated. Oṃ, let all beings be satiated. Oṃ, let the fourfold classes of beings be satiated. Oṃ, let Dakṣa be satiated. Oṃ, let Pracetas be satiated. Oṃ, let Marīci be satiated. Oṃ, let Atri be satiated. Oṃ, let Aṅgiras be satiated. Oṃ, let Pulastya be satiated. Oṃ, let Pulaha be satiated. Oṃ, let Kratu be satiated. Oṃ, let Nārada be satiated. Oṃ, let Bhṛgu be satiated. Oṃ, let Viśvāmitra be satiated. Oṃ, let Raivata be satiated. Oṃ, let Cākṣuṣa be satiated. Oṃ, let Mahātejas be satiated. Oṃ, let Vaivasvata be satiated. Oṃ, let Dhruva be satiated. Oṃ, let Dhava be satiated. Oṃ, let Anila be satiated. Oṃ, let Prabhāsa be satiated.

Wearing the sacred thread around the neck (*nīvītī*): Oṃ, may Sanaka be satiated. Oṃ, may Sanandana be satiated. Oṃ, may Sanātana be satiated. Oṃ, may Kapila be satiated. Oṃ, may Āsuri be satiated. Oṃ, may Voḍhu be satiated. Oṃ, may Pañcaśikha be satiated. Oṃ, may Kavyavāha, the carrier of offerings for humans, be satiated. Oṃ, may Anala be satiated. Oṃ, may Soma be satiated. Oṃ, may Yama be satiated. Oṃ, may Aryaman be satiated.

Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*): *Oṃ*, may the *agniṣvātta* ancestors be satisfied. *Oṃ*, may the *somapa* ancestors be satisfied. *Oṃ*, may the *barhiṣad* ancestors be satisfied. Salutation to Yama; salutation to Dharmarāja; salutation to Mṛtyu; salutation to Antaka; salutation to Vaivasvata; salutation to Kāla; salutation to Sarvabhūtakṣaya; salutation to Audumbara;
salutation to Dadhna; salutation to Nīla; salutation to Parameṣṭhin; salutation to Vṛkodara; salutation to Citra; salutation to Citragupta.

May the world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, be satisfied. *Oṃ*, svadhā and obeisance to the fathers. *Oṃ*, svadhā and obeisance to the grandfathers. *Oṃ*, svadhā and obeisance to the great-grandfathers. *Oṃ*, svadhā and obeisance to the mothers. *Oṃ*, svadhā and obeisance to the grandmothers. *Oṃ*, svadhā and obeisance to the great-grandmothers. *Oṃ*, svadhā and obeisance to the maternal grandfathers. *Oṃ*, svadhā and obeisance to the maternal grandfathers' fathers. *Oṃ*, svadhā and obeisance to the maternal grandfathers' grandfathers. May they be satisfied. "May the lower, the higher, and the middle ancestors, the Soma-loving ones, arise. Those who have gone to this life, the non-cruel knowers of Truth—may those ancestors protect us in our invocations. By pronouncing the [paternal] lineage, one offers the first handful of water to the father: *Oṃ*, may the Aṅgiras, our fathers, arise; the Atharvans and the Bhṛgus, arise. May we abide in the good-will and the auspicious favor of those worthy of sacrifice. *Oṃ*, may our Soma-loving fathers, the Agniṣvāttas, come by the paths traveled by the gods. Rejoicing with the *svadhā* offering at this sacrifice, may they speak for us and protect us.

Oṃ, you who carry strength, nectar, clarified butter, milk, and sweet juice, overflowing with nourishment—you are the *svadhā*; satisfy my ancestors! Oṃ, *svadhā* and obeisance to the fathers (*pitṛ*). Oṃ, *svadhā* and obeisance to the grandfathers (*pitāmaha*). Oṃ, *svadhā* and obeisance to the great-grandfathers (*prapitāmaha*). Oṃ, *svadhā* and obeisance to the maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*). Oṃ, *svadhā* and obeisance to the maternal great-grandfathers (*pramātāmaha*). Oṃ, *svadhā* and obeisance to the maternal great-great-grandfathers (*vṛddhapramātāmaha*). [The portion for] the grandfather’s [lineage]: Oṃ, the fathers have eaten; the fathers have rejoiced; the fathers, being satisfied, [have attained bliss]. *Śuṃ* (or *Sva*).

Come hither, O Pitṛs, and drink; partake of the three worlds and the celestial realms, for you are the purifiers of the abode. O Jātavedas, Lord of the chariot, accept this well-performed sacrifice with the *svadhā* offerings. Om! For the one who follows the cosmic order (*ṛta*), the winds blow sweetly and the rivers flow with honey. May the plants be sweet for us; may the nights and the dawns be full of sweetness. May the earthly realm be honeyed; may the sky, our father, be honeyed. May the lord of the forest (the tree) be full of honey for us, and may the sun be honeyed. May the cows be sweet for us.

The offering of the *añjali* for the great-grandfather: *Oṃ, homage to you, O fathers, for the sap; homage to you, O fathers, for the vigor; homage to you, O fathers, for the life-force; homage to you, O fathers, for the *svadhā*; homage to you, O fathers, for the terrible; homage to you, O fathers, for the wrath. Homage to you, O fathers, give us houses, O fathers! Homage to you, O fathers, I offer this garment to you, O fathers!* Three times the *añjali* is offered for the maternal grandfathers; then [the *añjali*] for the mothers and the others.
And those born in our family who have died childless or without heirs—may they be satisfied by this water squeezed from my garment which I have offered.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Libation to the Devas and Others," in the Ācārakāṇḍa, within the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
(Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇa—216)

Brahmā said: I shall now proclaim the supreme characteristics of the *vaiśvadeva* fire-oblation (*homa*). Having kindled the fire and sprinkled water around it, one should recite: "Oṃ! I drive away that fire which devours raw flesh; let it go far away to the kingdom of Yama, carrying off all impurities. Let this other Jātavedas remain right here; may he, knowing the way, carry the oblation to the gods. "Oṃ! O Purifier Vaiśvānara, this is your seat. O Great Brahman, whose form is the splendor refined within the womb of the two fire-sticks (*araṇī*), I awaken you, Vaiśvānara, for three moments. "Oṃ! May both [fires] come to us from afar. May Agni, whose back is radiant with his own light, be established in heaven."
He has ascended the ridges of the earth; Vaiśvānara Agni, whose back is radiant with power, has entered the plants. Homage to the divine one; he has entered the sixth [region] by night.

Oṃ, svāhā to Prajāpati! Oṃ, svāhā to Soma! Oṃ, svāhā to Bṛhaspati! Oṃ, svāhā to Agni and Soma! Oṃ, svāhā to Indra and Agni! Oṃ, svāhā to Heaven and Earth! Oṃ, svāhā to Indra! Oṃ, svāhā to the Viśvedevas! Oṃ, svāhā to Brahmā! Oṃ, svāhā to the Waters! Oṃ, svāhā to the herbs and trees! Oṃ, svāhā to the Grahas! Oṃ, svāhā to the divine deities! Oṃ, svāhā to Indra! Oṃ, svāhā to the attendants of Indra! Oṃ, svāhā to Yama! Oṃ, svāhā to the attendants of Yama! Oṃ, svāhā to all beings who roam during the day! Oṃ, svāhā to the Vasus, the Dhātṛs, and the Pitṛs! Oṃ, I, desiring prosperity, offer this bali-oblation to those beings who roam about, wretched and blinking in the midst of the world; may the Lord of Prosperity grant me prosperity! Oṃ, may the Lord of Prosperity grant it down to the outcastes, the fallen, and the crows!
Thus ends the two hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Vaiśvadeva," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Brahmā said: Now I shall describe briefly the rules for the Sandhyā (twilight worship) for the twice-born. Whether one is impure or pure, or even if one has fallen into any state whatsoever;
Whoever remembers the lotus-eyed one is pure both externally and internally.

The *gāyatrī* metre; Viśvāmitra the seer; three-footed. The oceans are its belly; the moon and sun are its eyes; fire is its mouth; Viṣṇu is its heart; Brahmā and Rudra are its head; Rudra is its crest-lock. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). *Oṃ bhūḥ*—at the feet. *Bhuvaḥ*—at the knees. *Svaḥ*—at the heart. *Mahaḥ*—at the head. *Janaḥ*—at the crest-lock. *Tapaḥ*—at the throat. *Satyam*—at the forehead. *Oṃ*—salutation to the heart. *Oṃ bhūḥ*—*svāhā* to the head. *Oṃ bhuvaḥ*—*vauṣaṭ* to the crest-lock. *Oṃ svaḥ*—*huṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*). *Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ*—*phaṭ* to the weapon (*astra*).

Oṃ bhūḥ, Oṃ bhuvaḥ, Oṃ svaḥ, Oṃ mahaḥ, Oṃ janaḥ, Oṃ tapaḥ, Oṃ satyaṃ; that is the three-footed [Gāyatrī]. Oṃ āpo jyotī raso 'mṛtaṃ brahma bhūrbhuvaḥ svarom. Oṃ sūryaśca, etc. Oṃ āpaḥ punantu, etc. Oṃ agniśca, etc.

Oṃ! May the boon-granting goddess come; she who is the deity Brahmā in the forenoon, the Sandhyā named Gāyatrī, with a red body and red garments, mounted upon a noble swan, seated upon a glorious lotus.
Holding a water-pot, peaceful, and wearing a rosary of beads, may the boon-granting goddess, white in form, arrive at midday.
And Māheśvarī Sāvitrī is adorned with white garments and other ornaments; she is mounted upon the shoulders of a bull and holds a trident and the gesture of granting boons.
May the boon-granting goddess Sarasvatī come in the afternoon—she who resembles the flax flower, belongs to Viṣṇu, and has Garuḍa as her vehicle.
Clad in yellow garments and endowed with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, she is described as white in color and seated within a solar mandala.
Seated upon a white lotus throne, adorned with white flowers: Oṃ āpo hiṣṭhā mayo bhuvaḥ, tā na ūrje dadhātana.

For the sake of great battle, for the sake of sight: *Oṃ*, that most auspicious essence which is yours, may you cause us to partake of it here, like mother cows seeking their calves. *Oṃ*, we come to you with longing, O Waters, for whose abode you quicken us; grant us progeny. *Oṃ*, may the waters and plants be friendly to us; *Oṃ*, may they be unfriendly to him who hates us and whom we hate. *Oṃ*, as one released from a wooden stake, as one bathed and cleansed of impurity, as clarified butter purified by a strainer—may the waters cleanse me from sin. *Oṃ*, from the kindled heat of austerity, Order (*ṛta*) and Truth (*satya*) were born; from that, Night was born; from that, the ocean and the waves; from the ocean and the waves, the year was born, ordaining days and nights, the ruler over all that blinks. The Ordainer fashioned the sun and moon as before, as well as heaven, earth, the intermediate space, and the sky.

For the Gāyatrī [mantra], Viśvāmitra is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ), Savitṛ is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for silent recitation (japa). Oṃ. His rays bear aloft that god, the knower of all beings (jātavedas), the Sun, so that everyone may behold him. Oṃ. The brilliant array of the gods has risen—the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni. Sūrya, the soul of all that moves and stands, has filled the heaven, the earth, and the mid-region. Oṃ. That divine eye, placed for our benefit, rises bright in the east. May we see for a hundred autumns; may we live for a hundred autumns; may we hear for a hundred autumns. Oṃ. He who has eyes on every side, faces on every side, arms on every side, and feet on every side—he, the one God, generating heaven and earth, fans them together with his arms and wings. The gods who know the way, who know the path, whose minds are focused—O Lord of the mind, place this sacrifice to the gods in the wind; Svāhā! Thus one should recite.
"O Goddess who dwells upon the mountain, since a peak has arisen on the northern part of the earth, go as you please, permitted by Brahmā."
Thus ends the two hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Sandhyā Ritual," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Brahmā said: O Vyāsa, I shall now describe the Śrāddha ceremony, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men. First, one should invite Brahmins, especially those who are celibate students (brahmacārins).

One should invite the gods with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (pradakṣiṇopavīta) and the ancestors with it over the left shoulder (vāmopavīta); one should wash their feet while reciting the appropriate mantras.

"Oṃ, welcome to you"—this is the question. When they have replied, "Oṃ, a very warm welcome," [the host says]: "Oṃ, svāhā! This water for washing the feet and this arghya offering is for all the Viśvedevas. With these words, he offers water along with unbroken kuśa grass at the feet of the divine brāhmaṇas using the *devatīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the gods).

Then, facing south with the sacred thread over the left shoulder, one should offer water along with bent *kuśa* grass and flowers to the feet of the Brahmins representing the ancestors, using the *pitṛ-tīrtha*, saying: "Obeisance to our father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such name and *śarman*; this water for washing the feet and this *arghya* is *svadhā*.
This is the offering of water accompanied by *kuśa* grass and flowers.

In the same manner, [the offering] is made for the maternal grandfather and others. Saying "This is the water for sipping, svāhā, svadhā," [he pours it] into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa; saying "This is your arghya," he places flowers into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa.

Saying "Oṃ, this seat is established; here it is established," one should first seat the Brahmins representing the gods facing east with the seven *vyāhṛtis*: "Oṃ bhūḥ, Oṃ bhuvaḥ, Oṃ svaḥ, Oṃ mahaḥ, Oṃ janaḥ, Oṃ tapaḥ, Oṃ satyam.

Then, one should seat the Brahmins representing the ancestors facing north. One should then recite three times: "Oṃ, to the deities, to the ancestors, and to the great yogis; salutation to Svadhā and Svāhā; may they be ever-present."

Oṃ. Today, in this place, in such-and-such month, when the sun has entered such-and-such zodiac sign, on such-and-such lunar day, I shall perform the *dṛśrāddha* preceded by the Viśvedevas for my father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, belonging to such-and-such lineage and named such-and-such Śarman.

Oṃ, svāhā to all the Viśvedevas! Oṃ, I shall invoke the Viśvedevas. When it is said, "Invoke them," [one recites]: Oṃ, O Viśvedevas, come hither; hear this invocation. Sit down upon this sacred grass (barhis). Oṃ, O Viśvedevas, hear this my call—those who are in the intermediate space, those who are in heaven, those whose tongue is Agni, and those who are worthy of sacrifice—having sat down upon this sacred grass, rejoice! Oṃ, the plants hold a consultation with Soma, the king: "O King, we shall protect that man for whom a Brāhmaṇa performs [this rite]. Oṃ, may the highly fortunate Viśvedevas of great power come here. May they, who are appointed to this Śrāddha, remain attentive. Oṃ, the Asuras and Rākṣasas are driven away from the sacrificial ground (vedi)!—[reciting this] three times while scattering barley grains.
"Oṃ, I shall prepare the vessel. Being authorized with "Oṃ, do so," he prepares the purification within the vessel.

*Oṃ śanno devīr abhiṣṭaya āpo bhavantu pītaye / śaṃyor abhi sravantu naḥ.* Thus is the offering of water into the vessel. *Oṃ yavo 'si yavayāsmad dveṣo yavayārātīḥ.* Thus is the offering of barley. *Gandhadvārāṃ durādharṣāṃ nityapuṣṭāṃ karīṣiṇīm / īśvarīṃ sarvabhūtānāṃ tvām...* [I worship you, who are the gateway of fragrance, invincible, eternally nourishing, abundant, and the sovereign of all beings.]

"I invoke Śrī with a smile"—with these words, one offers the fragrance. Then, having poured water into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa with the mantra: "Oṃ! Those divine waters which have arisen from the milk, those which are in the atmosphere and those on earth—those waters, golden-hued and worthy of sacrifice, may they be auspicious, propitious, pleasant, and favorable to us; here is the *argha*, salutations! one takes the purification-strainer (*pavitra*) with that very vessel and places the residual water (*saṃsrava*) and the strainer beside the Brāhmaṇa. Then, having set the residual water in the first vessel, one should place it face upwards upon the *kuśa* grass. Upon that, one should offer *kuśa* grass.

To all the gods, these offerings of fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, a pair of garments, and a sacrificial thread—salutation! May the offering of fragrance and the rest be flawless. "Let it be so," is the response of the Brāhmaṇas.

Then, the formula for seeking permission is: "I shall perform the Śrāddha for my father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, along with their wives, and for my maternal grandfather, maternal great-grandfather, and maternal great-great-grandfather, along with their wives. When the Brāhmaṇas have said, "Do so," one should mutter three times: "Oṃ, to the deities and to the ancestors... (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.37).

"Oṃ, to our fathers and grandfathers of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so Śarman, together with their wives—this seat, Svadhā! Thus one gives the seat on the left side of the Brāhmaṇas. "Oṃ, I shall invoke the Pitṛs. When [the Brāhmaṇas] say, "Oṃ, invoke them," [he recites]: "Oṃ, desiring you we set you down; desiring you we kindle you. Desiring it, O Pitṛs, come hither for the sake of the oblation to eat. Oṃ, may our gentle Pitṛs, those consumed by the fire (Agniṣvātta), come by the paths traveled by the gods. Rejoicing in this sacrifice with the Svadhā offering, may they speak in our favor and protect us. This is the invocation. "Oṃ, driven away are the demons and the Rākṣasas who sit upon the altar! With these words, he scatters sesame seeds. He pours water into the vessels placed according to the order of the east-facing seats. "Oṃ, you are sesame, having Soma as your deity, produced by the gods at the Gosava sacrifice; mixed with ancient waters and the Svadhā offering, satisfy the worlds of our Pitṛs, Svāhā! With this, he offers the sesame seeds.

Having placed fragrant flowers in both hands and lifted the vessel for the ancestors, one recites the verse *yā divyā* and says: "O our father of such-and-such lineage, named Devaśarman, together with your wife, this is your *arghya*; *svadhā*! Taking the vessel containing the impure water, one places it face down upon *kuśa* grass to the right of the left side, saying: *oṃ pitṛbhyaḥ sthānam asi* ("O ancestors, this is your place").

Oṃ, may the worlds, the abodes of the ancestors, be purified; you are the abode of the ancestors. (Touching the vessel turned face down. To our father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, of such-and-such lineage, together with their wives: these perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, fragrant powders, upper garments, and sacred threads are for you—svadhā! (The offering of the perfumes and other items via the *pitṛ-tīrtha*.)

"May the gift of fragrance and so forth be inexhaustible; may there be the fulfillment of intentions. This is the declaration of the Brahmins. Such is the ritual for obtaining permission from the maternal grandfather and others. *Oṃ yā divyā...* (with these words) the sweeping of the ground is performed. Then, taking food smeared with clarified butter while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*dakṣiṇopavītī*), one says to the Brahmin representing the ancestors: "Oṃ, I shall perform the *agnaukaraṇa* rite. When he replies, "Oṃ, do so," one offers two oblations (*āhuti*) into the hands of the Brahmin representing the gods, saying: "Oṃ, svāhā to Agni Kavyavāhana. Having set aside the remaining food for the sake of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), one places the other half into the vessel for the father and others, and into the vessel for the maternal grandfather and others.
And one should cast it out.

Having placed the vessel, the mudrās, and so forth, and having offered *kuśa* grass, one should take hold of the vessel with both hands turned downward and recite for the consecration of the vessel: *oṃ pṛthivī te pātraṃ dyaurapidhānaṃ brāhmaṇasya mukhe amṛte amṛtaṃ juhomi svāhā*. Then, with the mantra: *idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame tredhā nidadhe padaṃ | samūḍhamasya pāṃsure | viṣṇo havyaṃ rakṣasva*, one should place the thumb of the twice-born (the Brāhmaṇa) face-downward into the middle of the food.

"Apahatā" (is recited) three times while scattering barley. "Oṃ, I destroy everything that is impure; all the Asuras and Dānavas have been slain by me; the Rakṣasas, Yakṣas, along with the hosts of Piśācas, and all the Yātudhānas have been slain by me"—with these words, one scatters white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*).

Then, for the ancestors known as the Dhūrilocanas, one should perform the mental dedication with water, kuśa grass, and so forth, saying: "Svāhā! May this food, together with ghee, drink, and side dishes, [be offered]. Then: "Oṃ, may this food be inexhaustible; Oṃ, may there be the fulfillment of the intention."

Then, having placed food with its condiments and clarified butter into the brahmin’s vessel for the ancestors and others using the sacred thread over the left shoulder (the *viparīta-upavīta* fashion), and having laid a blade of *kuśa* grass touching the ground upon it, he should take hold of the vessel with both hands turned upward while reciting the mantra: "Oṃ, the earth is your vessel."

With *oṃ idaṃ viṣṇuḥ*, he should place the thumb of a twice-born man face-upward upon the food. With *oṃ apahatāḥ*, he scatters sesame seeds. Kneeling with his left knee on the ground, having resolved the food—consisting of this food along with ghee, water, and side-dishes, excluding forbidden items—as *svadhā* for our ancestors and grandfathers together with their wives belonging to such-and-such lineage (*amukagotra*), he says: *oṃ ūrjaṃ vahantīramṛtaṃ ghṛtaṃ payaḥ kīlālaṃ paristrutaṃ svadhāstu tarpayata me pitaraḥ*. Then follows the offering of a continuous stream of water while facing south.

"Oṃ, may this *śrāddha* be free from defects; Oṃ, may there be the fulfillment of the resolve. Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, we meditate upon that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he impel our intellects.

Having thus dismissed [the ancestors], one should mutter: "Oṃ, the winds blow sweetly for the one who follows the cosmic order; let the rivers flow with sweetness. May our plants be full of honey; may the nights and the dawns be sweet.

May the earthly realm be sweet; may the sky, our father, be sweet. May our lord of the forest be full of honey; may the sun be full of honey; may our cows be full of honey. Honey, honey, honey! Thus is the recitation.

He should say, "Enjoy [the food] at your pleasure, remaining restrained in speech. When they have finished eating, he should recite the *Pitṛstotra* beginning with "The Seven Hunters" (*saptavyādha*). And that is: "The seven hunters among the Daśārṇas, the deer on Mount Kālañjara, the cakravāka birds on Śarādvīpa, and the swans in Lake Mānasa."
Those high-born brahmins of Kurukṣetra, who have mastered the Vedas, have set out on a long journey; why do you despair?

Then, facing south with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*vāmapravītī*), one should satisfy [the ancestors] while that [food] is being offered before them: "Oṃ! May those beings in my lineage who have been cremated by fire and those who have not been cremated be satisfied by what is given upon the earth; being satisfied, may they go to the supreme state. With these words, one should scatter food mixed with ghee and saturated with water upon *kuśa* grass on the ground.

Then, having offered a mouthful of water (*jalagaṇḍūṣa*) according to the procedure for Brahmins, and having recited the *Sāvitrī* with the *Vyāhṛtis* as before, along with the three verses beginning with "madhu vātā," he asks the Brahmins representing the gods, "Oṃ, is it pleasing to you? When they reply, "It is very pleasing," he asks, "Oṃ, what shall be done with the remaining food? He then eats together with his loved ones. To the Brahmin representing the ancestors (*pitṛ*), wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavīta*), he asks, "Oṃ, are you satisfied? When he replies, "Oṃ, we are satisfied," he sprinkles the ground and scatters rice grains in four triangular circles.

*Oṃ*, [Name], of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*), our father, [Name] Devadarśana, together with your wife: this is your seat for the *piṇḍa*; *svadhā*. In this manner, in the middle of the line, having recited the *Gāyatrī* with the *Vyāhṛtis* and the verse "madhu vātā" three times, and having formed a *piṇḍa* of food with clarified butter, he places it upon *kuśa* grass, saying: "[Name], of such-and-such lineage, our father, [Name] Śarman, together with your wife: this *piṇḍa* is for you; *svadhā*. In this manner, [he offers] to the grandfather in the middle of the line. Then, reciting the *Gāyatrī* with the *Vyāhṛtis* and the verse "madhu vātā" three times, he scatters the remains of the *piṇḍas* near the *piṇḍas*. Saying "Oṃ, may those who eat the smears be pleased," he performs the hand-cleansing upon the scattered *kuśa* grass with the water used for washing the *piṇḍas*. He sprinkles the *pitṛ-piṇḍas* with the formula: "[Name], of such-and-such lineage, our father, [Name] Śarman, together with your wife: may you accept this water; and those who follow you here, and those who follow after you—for them, *svadhā*. Having turned the vessel for the *piṇḍas* face down and joined his palms in reverence, he should mutter: "O fathers, rejoice; partake according to your portions. Having touched water and turned back to the left, facing north, he restrains his breath three times and mutters: "Salutation to the six seasons (*ṛtus*)."

Turning only with the left hand, one offers flowers, saying: "May there be for me unbrokenness, freedom from misfortune, merit, peace, and prosperity. Facing south, one mutters: "May these rejoicing ancestors satisfy themselves according to their respective portions. Having loosened his garment and joined his palms, he mutters: "Oṃ, homage to you, O ancestors; homage to you. He gazes at the house, saying: "O ancestors, grant us houses. Then, having looked at them and said, "O ancestors, we always love you," and having uttered, "This is your garment, O ancestors," he gives the thread, saying: "O [Name] of such-and-such gotra, this is your garment; Svadhā! Taking a water vessel with the left hand, he pours a stream of water over the *piṇḍas*, reciting: "Carrying strength, nectar, clarified butter, milk," and so forth.

One should sprinkle each *piṇḍa* with the water remaining in the vessel previously set aside; then, having invoked the *piṇḍa*, offer perfumes (*gandha*) and other articles, and place a blade of *kuśa* grass upon the *piṇḍa*. Then, one should recite three times the mantra: "Oṃ, they have eaten and rejoiced; they have been satisfied; the beloved ones have shouted for joy; the wise ones, possessing their own splendor, have praised you with their newest hymn—O Indra, those who know your two bay steeds."

Oṃ. Thus is the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) for the Brahmins representing the maternal grandfather and others. Having sprinkled the ground with water while reciting, "Oṃ, may it be well-sprinkled," he offers water into the hands of the Brahmins, saying: "Oṃ, the gods reside in the midst of the waters; everything is established in the waters. May the waters placed in the hand of the Brahmin be auspicious for us. [Then he says: "May the waters be auspicious. This is the offering of water. "Lakṣmī dwells in flowers; Lakṣmī dwells in the lotus; Lakṣmī dwells in cow-pens. May there always be joy for you. [Then he says: "May there be joy. This is the offering of flowers. "May my merit be unbroken; may there be peace, nourishment, and fortitude for me. Whatever brings about welfare in the world, may that always be mine. [Then he says: "Oṃ, may there be unbrokenness and freedom from misfortune. This is the offering of barley and rice grains.

"May this food, drink, and so forth be inexhaustible for our father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, of such-and-such lineage, together with their wives"—with these words, one offers sesame seeds and water into the hands of the Brahmins representing the ancestors. The Brahmin should say, "So be it. This is the inexhaustibility and blessing for the maternal grandfathers and others. "Oṃ! May the ancestors be free from wrath; may our lineage increase; may our donors prosper, as well as the Vedas and our progeny. May faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give. May our food be abundant and may we receive guests. May there be those who ask of us, and may we never have to ask anyone. May these blessings be realized in truth."

"May there be joy. When [the Brahmins] have said, "So be it," he releases the *pavitra* (sacrificial grass ring) intended for the *arghya* water at the place where the rice balls (*piṇḍa*) were offered. Taking a blade of *kuśa* grass as a *pavitra*, he touches the Brahmin representing the father and others with that *kuśa* and says, "I shall cause the *svadhā* to be uttered. [The Brahmin replies], "Om, let it be uttered. [He continues], "Om, may *svadhā* be pronounced for the fathers and grandfathers, by name and clan-name (*śarman*), together with their wives. When [they reply], "Let there be *svadhā*," he should pour a stream of water over the rice balls while reciting: "Carrying strength, nectar, and clarified butter..."

Then, [one should say]: "Oṃ, may the Viśvedevas be pleased at this sacrifice"—and the offering of barley-water is made into the hands of the Brahmins representing the gods. When he has said, "May they be pleased," one should mutter "Oṃ, to the deities" three times.

Having turned the alms-bowls upside down and performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*dakṣiṇopavītī*), facing east, he should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) with the words: "Oṃ, this silver, as a fee for the establishment of the *śrāddha*, I bestow upon you, O Brāhmaṇa named Devaśarman of such-and-such a lineage (*gotra*), together with your wife. Thus is the giving of the sacrificial fee to the Brāhmaṇa representing the gods.

Then, regarding the Brahmins representing the ancestors, the question is asked: "Are the *piṇḍas* well-prepared? [The response is: "They are well-prepared. Having offered a stream of milk upon the *piṇḍas*, one moves the *piṇḍas*. Regarding the Brahmin representing the guest (*atithi*), having turned the *piṇḍa*-plate face upwards, [one recites]: "Oṃ, O Vājins, come to us for food in our contests;

O wise ones, immortal, knowers of Truth, drink of this honeyed draught, rejoice, and being satisfied, depart by the paths traveled by the gods. This is the dismissal of the *piṇḍas* toward the sky—[the mantra] beginning with "āmā vāja-sya."

"May there be procreation; may these two, Heaven and Earth, of all forms, come hither; may the ancestors come hither, and may Soma come with immortality. This is the dismissal of the deities. "Oṃ, please return," is the dismissal of the Brahmins who represent the ancestors. The Brahmins should turn back before they have departed. The remaining ritual involves the offering of the *piṇḍas* (rice balls) to cows and other animals. This is the conclusion.
This procedure for the śrāddha has been declared; when recited, it destroys sin. Indeed, wherever this rite is performed according to this method, [it yields its fruit].
"The attainment of heaven by the ancestors shall likewise be inexhaustible and certain. Thus has been described the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha, which bestows the world of Brahmā upon the ancestors.
Thus ends the two hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Brahmā said: I shall now describe the daily *śrāddha* (nityaśrāddha), which is similar to the previous [rites] but with its specific distinctions. [The formula is: "Oṃ! I shall perform today for you the *śrāddha* of my ancestors—my father, grandfather, and so forth, belonging to the [such-and-such] gotra and named [such-and-such] Śarman, together with their wives—using prepared food. In this rite, there should be the offering of seats and other such items, excluding the Viśvedevas.

I shall now describe the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, which is performed in the same manner as the previous [rites] with its specific distinctions. On occasions such as seeing the face of a newborn son, the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* should be performed facing east, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), using barley, jujube fruits (*badara*), and *kuśa* grass, with the *devatīrtha* (the part of the hand between the thumb and forefinger), ending with salutations (*namaskāra*), and following the ritual procedure of the south. Holding the right knee, one should say: "Today, on this occasion of our prosperity (*vṛddhi*) named so-and-so, while the *śrāddha* for our great-grandmother, grandmother, and mother—named so-and-so, belonging to such-and-such lineage (*gotra*) and known by the names of the Vasus and Satyas among the Viśvedevas—is being performed, [this *śrāddha*] with prepared food is offered unto you."
"I must perform [this]" is the invitation to the gods and Brahmins; "Oṃ, you shall do so," said by him, is likewise the invitation to the other gods and Brahmins.

Then, having been addressed by him thus: "On the occasion of the increase [of prosperity] for such-and-such a person, I shall perform the *nāndīmukha* śrāddha with prepared food (*siddhānna*) for you on behalf of my great-grandmother, belonging to the such-and-such lineage and named such-and-such Devī," the invitation of the Brahmins representing the great-grandmother is completed; in this very same manner follows the invitation of the Brahmins representing the paternal great-grandmother and the others.

The request for permission to perform the *śrāddha* for the gods, the ancestors, all the deities, and the Brahmins. On the seat: *Oṃ viśvedevāsa āgata śṛṇutāma imaṃ havam / taṃ barhir niṣīdata*. *Oṃ viśvedevāḥ śṛṇutemaṃ havam ye me antarikṣe ya udyaviṣṭha / ye agnijihvā uta vā yatrāsa āsadyāsmin barhiṣi mādayadhvam*. *Oṃ āgacchantu*—thus is the invocation of the Viśvedevas and the offering of perfumes (*gandha*) and other items. The recitation for the determination of the absence of defects (*acchidrāvadhāraṇavācana*).

Then follows the request for permission for the great-grandmothers (*prapitāmahī*) and others, the offering of seats, the offering of scents (*gandha*) and other items, and the recitation for the determination of the rite’s flawlessness (*acchidra*). In this same manner, [the rites] are performed for the grandmother (*pitāmahī*) and the mother. Then, the request for permission for the great-grandfathers (*prapitāmaha*) and others; the offering of seats, the invocation (*āvāhana*), the offering of scents and other items; and the performance of the request for permission and so forth for the maternal great-grandfather (*vṛddhapramātāmaha*) and others. The formal declaration of the food (*annasaṅkalpa*) is as follows: "Oṃ! To the gods known as Vasus and Satyas, this food—accompanied by ghee, water, side-dishes, *badara* fruits, and curd, and excluding forbidden items—is offered with salutation (*namaḥ*). "Oṃ! O [Name] of such-and-such lineage, O [Name] Devī, my paternal great-grandmother, you who are of the *nāndīmukha* type! This food, together with *badara* fruits and curd, is offered with salutation. In this same way, [the offerings are made] to the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) and the maternal great-grandfather (*pramātāmaha*).

Listen as I describe the specific details of the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, which must necessarily be performed first. First is the invitation, then the washing of the feet, and the offering of a seat. [The formula is: "Today, for my father, of such-and-such lineage and named Amukadevaśarman, I shall perform the annual *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha with prepared food (*siddhānna*) among you. Then follows the request for permission to perform the śrāddha, the offering of a seat, the giving of perfumes and other items, and the preparation of the food. One should recite the prayers while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*nivītī*). Having turned to face the north, one should perform the śrāddha for the guest.

Then, knowing that [the ancestors] are satisfied, facing south with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*vāmaupavītī*), one should scatter food near the remains with the mantra "agnidagdhāḥ" (RV 10.15.14). Then, over the line, one should pour a stream of water with the formula: "O Father, so-and-so Devaśarman of such-and-such lineage, this water for rinsing the mouth is for you; and for those who follow you here and those who follow you there, to them be *svadhā*. The remainder is as before.
Thus ends the two hundred and nineteenth chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Brahmā said: I shall now describe the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, which, when performed correctly at the proper time—at the end of the full year on the anniversary of the death—bestows the world of the ancestors upon the deceased and others.

One should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* in the afternoon as previously described. [This includes] the invitation of the Brahmins representing the grandfather and the others. [The mantra for the seat is: "Oṃ, to the gods known as Purūravas and Ārdrava, this seat; obeisance. The offering of the seat is made on the left side. Then follows the invocation (*āvāhana*). Thereafter, one seeks permission by saying: "I shall perform the Śrāddha for the grandfather, great-grandfather, and great-great-grandfather, together with their wives. Then, having prepared three vessels, placed *kuśa* grass upon the vessels, and covered them with another vessel, one completes the rite up to the sealing of the integrity of the offerings (*acchidrāvadhāraṇa*). One proceeds in the same manner for the father as well.

The request for permission to perform the *śrāddha* ceremony by addressing the deceased by name, ending with the word "preta," together with his wife; and the inspection of the vessel of the gods for any defects.

Having completed that, one should slightly move the vessels in the order of the grandfather, great-grandfather, and great-great-grandfather. Having uncovered them, one recites these two mantras: "Oṃ! Those ancestors who are equal and of one mind in the realm of Yama—for them [is] the world; Svadhā! Homage! May the sacrifice be effective among the gods. Oṃ! Those living ones of mine who are equal and of one mind among the living—for them may prosperity be effective in me in this world for a hundred years. With these two mantras, having poured the water from the vessel of the father into the vessels of the grandfather and great-grandfather, and having set aside the vessel of the great-great-grandfather, one pours the water and the *pavitra* grass from the vessels of the grandfather and great-grandfather into the vessel of the father.
One should cast [it].

Then, the offering of the *pavitra* (sacred grass ring) contained in the vessel is placed into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa representing the father. With a flower from the vessel, one worships the head, hands, and feet [of the Brāhmaṇa]; then, giving water into the Brāhmaṇa’s hand while lifting the vessel with both hands and reciting "oṃ yā divyā," one says: "oṃ, O [Name] of such-and-such lineage, my grandfather [Name] Devaśarman, together with your wife, this is your *arghya*; svadhā! Taking a small amount of the *arghya* water along with the *pavitra* from the vessel of the ancestors into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa representing the grandfather, and taking a small amount of water...

Having covered [the vessel] with another vessel for the purpose of pouring the rice-balls, one places the vessel face down upon kuśa grass with its tips pointing south on the left side of the Brahmins invited for the ancestors, saying: "Thou art the seat for the ancestors."

The offering of scents and other items, as well as the *agnaukaraṇa* (placing food in the fire), is performed for the grandfather, the great-grandfather, and the great-great-grandfather. One should place the remaining food into the vessel of the great-great-grandfather and the others. Even after completing the sequence up to the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of the grandfather’s vessel, one performs the consecration of the Brāhmaṇas’ vessels. Having performed the insertion of the thumb and the scattering of sesame seeds, one says: "O [Name], of such-and-such lineage, this food—accompanied by ghee, water, and side-dishes, excluding forbidden items—is for you; and for those who follow you here, and those whom you follow, to them be *svadhā*!"

Then one should offer *apośāna* water to the gods and others. Upon the arrival of a guest, one should perform a *atithi-śrāddha*. At this juncture, the scattering of food (*vikiraṇa*) takes place. Having asked the question regarding the paternal and maternal grandfathers, one asks the Brahmin representing the father: "Oṃ, has it been well-savored by you? The response is: "Oṃ, may the vessel for the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) be free from defects. Then, with the formula: "Oṃ, [Name] of such-and-such lineage, my father [Name], together with your wife; this is your rice-ball, and for those who follow you here, and those whom you follow—to them, *svadhā*! Thereafter, having completed the declaration of the fulfillment of the resolve (*saṅkalpa-siddhi-vācana*), one divides the rice-ball into two parts. Reciting the two mantras beginning with "ye samānāḥ" and "sumanasaḥ," one should cast [the portions] into the vessels of the grandfather and the great-grandfather.

Having offered scents and other articles upon the *piṇḍas*, the shifting of the *piṇḍas* [to the ground] is performed. The guest Brahmin is asked whether he has eaten well (*svadita*). The Brahmins perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). Betel nuts are offered according to the order in which they ate. Water is poured into the hands of the Brahmins in the order of the great-grandfather and so forth, with the words: "May it be well-sprinkled; may the waters be auspicious. Water is also poured into the hand of the Brahmin representing the ancestors with the words: "May there be inexhaustibility for the lineage; may it attend [upon you]."

"May the ancestors be non-terrible (aghora)," [he says]; when "so be it" has been said, he requests permission from the Brahmins beginning with those representing the grandfather by saying, "Please pronounce the *svadhā*."

When it is said, "Oṃ, let it be spoken," [the response is] "Oṃ, let the *svadhā* be spoken for the Grandfather (Brahmā) and the others. When it is said, "Let there be *svadhā*," [the officiant says] "O Brāhmaṇa of the ancestors, let the *svadhā* be spoken for the ancestors. When it is said, "Let there be *svadhā*," [he performs] the pouring of a stream of water toward the south with the mantra "Oṃ, carrying strength (*ūrja*). Into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa representing the Viśvedevas, he gives barley-water with "Oṃ, may the Viśvedevas be pleased in this sacrifice. Then, he mutters three times: "Oṃ, to the deities..."

Having moved the alms-bowls and sipped water (ācamana), he gives a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the ancestors beginning with the grandfather; then, he requests a blessing from the Brahmin representing the father, saying, "May blessings be granted to me. When [the Brahmin] says, "May it be accepted," the giver makes the bowl face upward, saying, "May our donors increase," and performs the dismissal with the verse, "In strength after strength... The dismissal of the Brahmin representing the father is performed with the words, "May you be pleased."
I have related to you the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa Śrāddha as proclaimed by Vyāsa; Viṣṇu is the Śrāddha, Hari is the performer of the Śrāddha, and Hari is the fruit of the Śrāddha and other rites.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Performance of Śrāddha," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part (Pūrvakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Brahmā said: O Śaṅkara, listen as I shall speak in brief the essence of Dharma, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is subtle, and destroys all sins.
Sorrow indeed carries away men's learning, righteousness, strength, fortitude, happiness, and even their energy; therefore, one should abandon sorrow.
Karma is one's wife, karma is one's world, and karma is one's kinsman; it is karma that impels a person here toward happiness and suffering.
Giving is the supreme dharma; through giving, everything is obtained. Through giving, one attains heaven and sovereignty; therefore, a person should practice giving.
On one side, they say, is a gift accompanied by all excellent offerings; on the other side is the protection of the life of a living being who is terrified by fear.
Those who, despite austerity, celibacy, sacrifices, or ritual bathing, are destroyers of dharma, indeed go to hell.
And those men who are devoted to fire-offerings, silent recitation, ritual bathing, and the worship of deities, and who are endowed with truthfulness, forbearance, and compassion, go to heaven.
There is no one who bestows happiness or suffering, nor is there anyone who takes them away; beings experience only the happiness and suffering that they themselves have created.
Those for whom life is for the sake of Dharma cross over all hardships; who, being contented, would not be able to subsist on fruits and roots?
For everyone indeed plunges into difficulties out of a desire for happiness; this alone would be the most difficult task to accomplish, namely, the work of greed.
From greed arises anger; from greed proceeds malice; and from greed come delusion, deceit, pride, and envy as well.
He who has abandoned passion, hatred, falsehood, anger, greed, delusion, and pride, being peaceful and free from evil, goes to the supreme world.
O Hara, the gods, sages, nāgas, gandharvas, and guhyakas worship here one who is righteous, not one who is merely wealthy nor one who is lustful.
If a mortal obtains through infinite strength, heroism, wisdom, or manly effort that which was unobtainable, what cause for lamentation is there in that?
Compassion for all sentient beings, restraint of all the sense faculties, and the perception of impermanence everywhere—this is remembered as the supreme good.
The life of that man who does not practice the Dharma while looking as if Death were right before his eyes is as useless as the fleshy protuberance on the neck of a goat.

An embryo-killer, a slayer of a Brahmin, a killer of a cow, a patricide, or one who violates the teacher’s bed—by giving land endowed with all excellent qualities, such a person is liberated from these sins.
It is my conviction that there is no gift superior to the gift of a cow; a cow acquired by righteous means, when given away, delivers the entire family.
O Bull-bannered One, there is no gift superior to the gift of food; by food this entire world, both moving and unmoving, is sustained.
The gift of a maiden, the ritual release of a bull, visiting sacred fords, as well as sacred learning, the gifting of elephants, horses, and chariots, and jewels, gems, and the earth.
All other gifts do not equal even a sixteenth part of the gift of food. From food come the vital breaths, strength, and luster; from food come vigor, fortitude, and memory.
One should cause wells, step-wells, tanks, and groves to be constructed; having delivered twenty-one generations of one's kin, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
The sight of the virtuous is meritorious and excels even visiting sacred pilgrimage sites; a pilgrimage site bears fruit in time, whereas meeting the virtuous yields fruit immediately.
Truthfulness, self-restraint, austerity, purity, contentment, forgiveness, straightforwardness, knowledge, tranquility, compassion, and charity—this is the eternal Dharma.
Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Essence of Dharma," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious *Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*.

Brahmā said: I shall now describe the expiations (*prāyaścitta*) and other rites that destroy the multitude of hells. A fly, a drop of saliva, a woman, the earth, water, fire, a cat, and a mongoose—these are always pure.

If a twice-born man should, through negligence, consume food touched by the leavings of a Śūdra, he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If a Brahmin is ever touched by another Brahmin who is impure from eating, he must perform a bath, recite prayers, and take his meal only at the end of the day.
Food containing flies or hair becomes pure instantly by being vomited; likewise for one who eats from the palm of the hand, or with the fingers, or with the forearm.
If he does not drink water, he shall be purified in a day and night; however, the water remaining after being drunk that was taken with the left hand is like liquor.

Water contained within a leather vessel would be impure; one should not drink it. Furthermore, if a person of the lowest caste (antyajātī) should dwell in one's house without being recognized, [the water becomes unfit].
For the twice-born, the Cāndrāyaṇa or Parāka penance is the means of purification; however, for a Śūdra, it is the Prājāpatya, according to others when the offense is later discovered.
Whoever eats cooked food there, one should cause him to perform half a *kṛcchra* penance; and for whoever eats of those [remnants] as well, a quarter-*kṛcchra* is prescribed.
A twice-born man who eats the food of washermen, actors, or those who subsist on bamboo and leather, shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
If a Brahmin should drink water from the wells or vessels of a Cāṇḍāla out of ignorance, he must perform the Sāntapana penance; for a Vaiśya, half of that is prescribed.

If one unknowingly eats at the house of an outcaste Śūdra, one quarter of the penance must be given; the penance shall be three *kṛcchras* for eating at the home of an outcaste (*antyaja*), and a *parāka* for going to the home of an outcaste.
A twice-born man who eats the leavings of an outcaste is purified by the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; when he eats the food of a Caṇḍāla through negligence, he should perform the Aindava (Cāndrāyaṇa) penance.

For the Kṣatriya caste, the Sāntapana penance lasts for six nights; others say it is likewise for twelve nights. If a Brāhmaṇa, through negligence, eats fruit from a single tree belonging to a Caṇḍāla, he becomes pure after one day and night.

If one who has eaten and is seated, but has not yet sipped water for purification (ācamana), should touch a Caṇḍāla, he should mutter the Gāyatrī eight thousand times or the Drupadā verse one hundred times.

O twice-born ones, if excrement or urine is deposited by Cāṇḍālas or Śvapacas, the penance shall be three nights; however, if it occurs in the presence of those born of the lowest castes (antyajas), it is a Parāka.
If one has approached women unintentionally, the expiation there is the *parāka* penance; however, for one born of the lowest castes (*antyajāti*), no expiation is prescribed.

If a twice-born man drinks water from vessels defiled by liquor and other such substances, he shall be purified by one-quarter of the Kṛcchra penance and by the rite of re-consecration (punaḥsaṃskāra).

Those Brahmins who have retired from their vows and, having gathered food, drink, and other provisions, desire to enter another household—whether it be among those devoted to the thunderbolt, fire, wind, or other deities.
One should indeed perform three *kṛcchra* penances and three *cāndrāyaṇa* observances; the sage Vasiṣṭha declared that the sacraments beginning with the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) must be performed.
