A woman becomes pure by performing the Prājāpatya and other penances after eating twice [on two consecutive days]; likewise, a twice-born man who has been touched by one who is impure from food remnants, or by a dog, or by a Śūdra, [is purified in the same manner].
Having fasted for one night, he is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); however, if he has been touched by one outside the [four] castes, he is purified after five nights.
Continuous streams that are not defiled, dust raised by the wind, women, children, and the elderly—these are never considered impure.
The mouth of women is always pure; fruit fallen by birds is pure; a calf is pure when discharging milk; and a dog is pure in the act of seizing game.
Water that stands in water is pure, and that which grows on dry land is pure on dry land; one should place one's feet right there, and having sipped water (ācamana), one attains purity.
Bell-metal that has not been smeared by liquor is purified by ashes; however, that which is mixed with urine or liquor is indeed purified by repeated heating in the sun.
Bell-metal vessels that have been smelled by a cow, those containing the remnants of food from a Śūdra, and those struck by crows or dogs, are purified by ten applications of ash.

A Brahmin who eats from the vessel of a Śūdra should fast for three days and consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); likewise, a dog or a Śūdra who touches the leavings of such a person commits an offense.
Having touched a woman in her menses, one who has fasted shall be purified by consuming the five products of the cow; likewise when on paths in waterless regions infested with thieves and tigers.
If one has urine or feces while holding an object in the hand, one is not defiled; having placed that object on the ground and performed purification with a concentrated mind, one is purified.
Barley-gruel, curd, milk, buttermilk, and rice-and-pulse porridge—these may be accepted even from a Śūdra; likewise, meat and honey may be accepted even from an outcaste.
If a Brahmin or any other twice-born man drinks liquor made from molasses, flour, or honey, he shall become pure by drinking liquor that is red-hot like fire.

A Brahmin should recite the Gāyatrī five hundred times, and a Kṣatriya one hundred times; and a Brahmin who has eaten food from a drinking vessel during a period of birth-impurity [should likewise recite it].
A pure Brahmin is purified in ten days, a Kṣatriya in twelve days, a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified in a month.

Immediate purification is prescribed for kings in the midst of battles, at sacrifices and the like, when they have gone to another country, upon the death of a child, and during monthly ancestral rites.

Likewise, an unmarried girl, a twice-born man who has not yet received the girdle of muñja grass, a child whose teeth have not yet emerged, and a girl of three years of age [are exempt from impurity].

Their purification occurs after three nights; in the case of a miscarriage, it is after three nights; for a woman who has given birth, it is equal to the number of months [of pregnancy]; and for a menstruating woman, it is on the fourth day.
During a famine, the ruin of a kingdom, or at the birth or death of a person, religious observances are not considered faulty for those who are devoted to the duty of giving.

At the time of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), at a wedding and similar occasions, when gods or twice-born brahmins have been invited, or even when [the rite] has been previously resolved upon, there is no impurity (*āśauca*) due to death or birth.

Likewise, a twice-born man becomes impure by touching a woman who has recently given birth; however, he is not so in a place where the sacred fires are offered oblations or where the Veda is being recited.
For those who constantly perform the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, no birth-impurity (sūtaka) shall occur; yet if one eats in an impure house, a twice-born man becomes pure after three nights.
If a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, a Vaiśyā, or a Śūdrā woman who is in her menses should touch one another, the Brāhmaṇī becomes pure after three nights.

A Kṣatriya woman becomes pure after two nights, a Vaiśya woman by fasting, and a Śūdra woman by bathing; however, one should not dismiss [the ritual] for the sake of a single Droṇa measure [of grain].
If food has been brought by a crow or a dog, one should cast it outside; having sprinkled it with water mixed with gold and earth, one should heat it over a fire.

Having seen a dog, a jackal, and a monkey fallen into a well, and having drunk the water of that well, a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure in three days; a Kṣatriya in two days alone; and a Vaiśya after one day at most.
If one draws out a bone, skin, filth, or even a mouse from a well, the water becomes pure once it has been strained and purified with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

Likewise, one should throw ashes and other substances into a pond, lotus-pool, or similar body of water; having drawn out six jars of water, it becomes pure through the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

If menstrual blood falls into the midst [of the water], one should remove thirty jars; likewise for having sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached, or for consuming liquor and beef.
A Brahmin is purified by the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, a Kṣatriya by the Prājāpatya, a Vaiśya by the Sāntapana, and a Śūdra becomes pure in five days.
When the expiation has been performed, one should give cows and a feast for Brahmins; in cases of play, sleeping, and so forth, the wearing of indigo-dyed cloth does not cause defilement.
One should not touch indigo-dyed cloth, for by touching indigo one goes to hell; even so do the killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and the violator of the guru’s bed.
Having seen a bear, they are purified, as is the fifth person associated with them; thereafter, one should give a hundred cows and provide a meal for Brahmins.
A killer of a Brahmin shall dwell in the forest for twelve years, having constructed a hut; or the drinker of spirituous liquor shall cast himself into a well-kindled fire.
A thief of gold should bestow all his property upon a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas; and one who has violated the Guru’s bed should give a thousand cows and a bull.

One who has committed a sin by obstructing a watering place should perform two *kṛcchra* penances; likewise for one who binds two legs of an animal, or for one who sets fire to a house in the wilderness.

If a cow dies due to the fault of a neck-ornament, one must perform a penance for a quarter of a Kṛcchra; likewise, having caused a fracture of the bones or even a breakage of the horns of cows, the same applies.

In the event of a wound to the skin or the loss of the tail, one should drink barley-gruel for half a month; however, for all injuries caused by elephants, horses, weapons, and the like, the penance is certainly a *kṛcchra*.
Having unintentionally swallowed feces, urine, or anything touched by liquor, the three twice-born castes must undergo the rite of re-initiation.

Shaving the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the religious observances—all these are discontinued for the twice-born upon the performance of the purificatory rite (punaḥsaṃskāra).
Raw meat, ghee, honey, and oils produced in their proper season—all these are considered pure once they have been removed from a vessel belonging to a person of the lowest caste.

Oil and the like, clarified butter, honey-wine, merchandise, and liquids; likewise, eating once a day, eating at night, eating only what is unasked for each for one day, and fasting—this constitutes the *pādakṛcchra* (quarter-penance), which is indeed twice the amount of a half-*kṛcchra*.
That shall be a Prājāpatya penance, which destroys all sins; a Kṛcchra consisting of seven fasts is known as the Mahāsāntapana.
For three days one should drink hot water, for three days one should drink hot milk, and for three days one should drink hot clarified butter; this Taptakṛcchra penance destroys all sins.

Fasting for twelve days constitutes the Parāka penance, which destroys all sins; one should increase the morsels of food by one each day during the bright fortnight and decrease them during the dark fortnight.
The milk of the golden-colored cow, the white-colored cow dung, the urine of the copper-colored cow, and the ghee produced from the blue-colored cow.
For a cow of black color, there should be curd mixed with darbha-water; eight māṣas of cow urine and four of cow dung.
Twelve māṣakas of milk are prescribed, ten of curd are said [to be used], and five māṣakas of ghee; this *pañcagavya* is the remover of impurities.
Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Expiations," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Brahmā said: O Vyāsa, I have declared with devotion those duties practiced by the sages, by which Viṣṇu is indeed pleased, as well as through the service rendered to the Sun and other deities.
By means of libations, burnt offerings, and the worship of the twilight devotions, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu—the bestower of dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation—is attained.
For Dharma is indeed the Blessed Viṣṇu; the worship of Viṣṇu, the libation, the fire-oblation, as well as the twilight prayers, meditation, and concentration—all of these are Hari.

Sūta said: O Śaunaka, listen as I describe the dissolution of the universe in its entirety. A thousand cycles of the four yugas is known as one day of the single lotus-born Brahmā, which constitutes a kalpa.
Understand from me the conditions of the ages beginning with Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara: in the Kṛta age, Dharma has four feet—truth, generosity, austerity, and compassion.
At that time, men who are wise and contented will be protectors of the Dharma and takers of it; indeed, those men shall live for four thousand years.

At the end of the age, the Kṣatriyas were conquered by the Brahmins, and the Vaiśyas and Śūdras were likewise conquered by the twice-born; furthermore, Viṣṇu slew the exceedingly powerful Śūra and the Rākṣasas.
In the Tretā Yuga, Dharma stands on three feet, consisting of truth, charity, and compassion; in that age, men are devoted to sacrifice, and likewise the world is born of the Kṣatriya order.
The red Hari is worshipped by men, and men have a lifespan of one thousand years; there Viṣṇu is Bhaumaratha, and the Kṣatriyas slew the Rākṣasas.
When the yellow-complexioned Acyuta has departed, Dharma will be deprived of its two feet; the lifespan of people will be four hundred years, and the progeny will consist of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas.
Having seen there those of small intellect, Viṣṇu, assuming the form of Vyāsa, again divided that single Yajurveda into four parts.
He taught all his disciples; learn from me their names: Paila for the Ṛgveda and Jaimini for the Sāmaveda.
Atharvaṇa, Sumantu, the great sage Yajurveda, Vaiśampāyana, Aṅga, and Sūta himself—the eighteen Purāṇas by whom Hari alone is indeed known.
Primary creation, secondary creation, genealogy, the periods of the Manvantaras, and the history of the dynasties—thus the Purāṇa has five characteristics.
The Brāhma, the Pādma, the Vaiṣṇava, the Śaiva, the Bhāgavata, as well as the Bhaviṣya, the Nāradīya, the Skānda, the Liṅga, and the Varāha.
The Mārkaṇḍeya, the Āgneya, the Brahmavaivarta, the Kaurma, the Mātsya, the Gāruḍa, and immediately after that the Vāyavīya—these eighteen are designated as those known by the name Brahmāṇḍa.
Other minor Purāṇas have indeed been narrated by sages; the first is that spoken by Sanatkumāra, and another is the Nārasiṃha.
The third is designated as the Skānda, spoken by Kumāra; the fourth is known as the Śivadharmākhya, spoken by Nandīśvara.
The wonderful account spoken by Durvāsas, that which was spoken by Nārada thereafter, as well as the Kāpila and Vāmana, and likewise that narrated by Uśanas.
The Brahmāṇḍa, the Vāruṇa, and that which is called the Kālikā; likewise the Māheśvara, the Sāmba, and the Sarvārthasañcaya; furthermore, the Parāśarokta, the Mārīca, and that called the Bhārgava.

O Sage Śaunaka, the Purāṇas, the Dharmaśāstras, the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs (aṅgas), Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Āyurveda, Arthaśāstra, Gāndharvaveda, and Dhanurveda—these are indeed remembered as the eighteen branches of knowledge (vidyās).
And at the end of the Dvāpara age, Hari removed the heavy burden [of the earth]; when Dharma stood on only one foot and Acyuta had departed, he became Kṛṣṇa.
At that time, people will become ill-behaved and merciless. The qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are seen within the person; impelled by time, these too revolve within the self.
When beings, the mind, intelligence, and the senses are abundant, one should know that it is the Kṛta Yuga, in which there is delight in knowledge and austerity.
O Śaunaka, know that when embodied beings possess the power for optional rites and for fame, then it is the Tretā age, born of the quality of passion (rajas).
When greed, discontent, pride, hypocrisy, and envy prevail, as well as the performance of rites for desired fruits, that is the Dvāpara age, characterized by rajas and tamas.

When falsehood is constant, when sleep is the means for [committing] violence and other evils, and when sorrow, delusion, fear, and wretchedness prevail—that is remembered as Kali in the quality of darkness (tamas).
In that [place] people will be lustful and constantly speaking harshly; the regions will be overrun by bandits, the Vedas will be corrupted, and [the land] will be defiled by heretics.
Kings will subsist on the alms of their subjects, overcome by their bellies and genitals; they will be devoid of vows, like mere children, impure, and householders while claiming to be mendicants.

Those who practice austerities while living in villages, those who have renounced worldly ties yet are greedy for wealth, those who are short-statured yet consume vast amounts of food—they are considered thieves, though they are called holy men.
Servants will abandon their masters, ascetics will abandon their vows, Śūdras will accept gifts, and Vaiśyas will be devoted to religious observances.
The people are anxious, and the subjects are like *piśāca* demons; through unrighteous consumption, the worship of the fire-god and the honoring of guests [are neglected].
When the Kali age has arrived, O Śaunaka, all people will become devoted to women, resembling Śūdras, and they will not perform the ancestral rites or the water-libations for their forefathers.
In the Kali age, women will have many offspring yet possess little fortune; intent on scratching their heads, they will disobey commands when rebuked.
O Brahmins, people afflicted by heresy will not worship Viṣṇu; yet there is indeed one great merit in this Kali age, which is a storehouse of vices.
By the mere chanting of Kṛṣṇa’s names, one should abandon great bondage; the fruit that is obtained by meditating on Viṣṇu in the Kṛta age is attained by chanting in the Tretā age.

In the Dvāpara age, [liberation comes] through service; in the Kali age, it comes from the chanting of Hari's names. Therefore, O Śaunaka, Hari should always be meditated upon, sung of, and worshipped.
Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of the Yugas," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 224] Sūta said: At the end of a thousand cycles of the four yugas, there occurs the occasional (naimittika) dissolution of Brahmā; and at the end of the Kalpa, a hundred-year drought arises.
Then seven fierce suns arise in the sky; having drunk all the water, they dry up the three worlds.
Having become Viṣṇu and Rudra, he burns the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvas, Svar, and Mahas, along with the mobile and immobile beings of Jana, as well as the nether regions below.
Viṣṇu may burn the three worlds, yet he creates clouds from his mouth; indeed, great clouds of various colors rain down for a hundred years.

The powerful wind, having the form of Viṣṇu, blows for a hundred years; when the world has become a single ocean, Viṣṇu, assuming the nature of Brahmā, lies upon the seat of Ananta during that year in which all things mobile and immobile have perished.
Having slept for a thousand years, that Lord Hari created the world once again; now, O Śaunaka, listen as I describe the elemental dissolution (prākṛtika-pralaya).
When a full hundred years have passed, having withdrawn the entire universe and having placed Brahmā within his own body, Hari is liberated through the powers of yoga.

Those who have gone to the abode of Brahmā also go to the supreme state. O twice-born one, there were clouds endowed with the brilliance of the sun during a drought; then, as those clouds rained for a hundred years, the cosmic egg was filled.
With its internal waters, the shell of the Lord of the World is split; when a full lifespan of Brahmā has passed, it breaks apart and dissolves into the water.
Thus that support of the world dissolves into water and earth; the waters dissolve into fire, and fire dissolves into air.

Then the wind enters into space, and space enters into the origin of the elements (bhūtādi); the Great One (mahat) enters into the unmanifest (avyakta), and that primordial nature (prakṛti) enters into the Supreme Puruṣa.
Hari sleeps for a hundred years, and then, at the end of the day, he emits the world of moving and non-moving beings, which has become manifest through the sequence beginning with the unmanifest.
Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Occasional Dissolution," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Sūta said: Having understood the three types of suffering—ādhyātmika (internal) and the rest—and being an expert in the wheel of transmigration, one who has attained knowledge and dispassion reaches the ultimate dissolution.
I shall first describe the wheel of saṃsāra, starting from the time of the departure [of the breath], without which the human goal would not become absorbed in the Supreme Self.
A man who dwells above, having abandoned his body, attains another; he is led by the servants of Yama to the realm of Yama within twelve days.
In that regard, whatever water the kinsmen offer along with sesame seeds, and whatever funeral cake (piṇḍa) they offer, he partakes of that in the world of Yama.
One goes to hell because of evil and goes to heaven because of one's own merit; the doer of evil goes to hell, while the doer of merit indeed goes to the celestial realm.
Released from both heaven and hell, he is even born in the womb of women; yet that dual seed of his does not become overwhelmed by that [womb].
From that, there is the *kalala*, consisting of a bubble, and then blood; from the *peśī* comes the *aṇḍa*, which is equal to a *pala* in weight, and from that, it is called the sprout (*aṅkura*).
The secondary limbs—the fingers, eyes, nose, mouth, and ears—depart from the major limbs; beyond those, however, are the nails and so forth.
From that, the skin, body hairs, and head hairs arise; thereafter, the person remains with his face turned downward, and in the tenth month, he is born.
Then the deluding power of Viṣṇu (vaiṣṇavī māyā), which causes extreme bewilderment, envelops him in childhood, youth, adolescence, and even old age.
And thereafter, upon death, a human being attains those respective states; thus one wanders in this wheel of saṃsāra like a waterwheel.
Though released from hell, he is born among sinful wombs; moreover, by accepting gifts from the fallen, even a wise man would go to a lower birth.
Once released from hell, he becomes a beggar worm; but by committing an offense against his preceptor, O twice-born one, he becomes a dog.
A creature who, having insulted a friend, mentally covets that friend's wife or even his wealth, is undoubtedly reborn as a donkey.
Having caused suffering to one's parents, one is born as a tortoise; likewise, he who, having relied upon his master for sustenance, deceives that very master.
He too, having fallen into delusion, is born as a monkey after death; one who misappropriates a deposit, released from hell, is born as a worm.
The envious person, even when released from hell, becomes a rākṣasa; and the man who betrays trust is born in the womb of a fish.
Having died after amassing grains, one is born as a mouse; but from violating another's wife, one is born as a terrible wolf.
Through attachment to the wife of a brother, a man is born as a cuckoo; by approaching the wife of a teacher or others, a man is born as a pig.
One who creates obstacles for sacrifices, gifts, or marriages shall become a worm; likewise, he who eats food without first offering it to the gods, the ancestors, and the Brahmins.
Even if released from hell, he is born as a crow; and due to insulting an elder brother, he is born in the womb of a crane.
But a Śūdra who has approached a Brāhmaṇa woman is born in the womb of a worm; having produced offspring from her, he becomes a wood-worm within timber.
One who is ungrateful is born as a worm, an insect, a moth, or a scorpion; likewise, a man who seizes the property of one unarmed is reborn as a donkey.
One who kills a woman becomes a worm, and one who kills a child is born as such; moreover, a man who steals food is born as a fly.
By stealing clarified butter one becomes a cat; by stealing sesame seeds, a mouse; by stealing ghee, a mongoose; and by stealing meat, a crow.
Having stolen honey, a man is born as a gadfly; having stolen a cake, he becomes an ant; and having stolen water, that evil-souled one is born as a crow.
If one steals wood, one is born as a Hārīta bird or a pigeon; but having stolen a vessel of gold, one is born from a worm-womb.
If cotton is stolen, one is born as a curlew; likewise, a fire-thief becomes a crane. Having stolen cosmetic pigments or a leaf of potherb, one is born as a peacock.
A man who steals red cloth becomes a jīvañjīvaka bird; one who steals auspicious perfumes becomes a muskrat, and one who steals a rabbit becomes a rabbit.

One who steals a bundle [of grass] becomes a eunuch; one who steals wood becomes a wood-carrier; one who steals grass becomes an insect; by stealing flowers one becomes poor; and a man who steals what is carried [as a load] becomes a lame beggar.
The stealer of vegetables becomes a green pigeon, and the stealer of water becomes a cātaka bird; having gone to the most dreadful hells such as Raurava, the stealer of houses likewise suffers there.
One who steals grass, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, or bark shall become a tree; this very same sequence is observed for those who steal cows, gold, and other such items.
One who steals knowledge shall become mute after having gone through many hells; indeed, one who offers oblations into a fire that lacks fuel becomes weak of digestion.
Slandering others, ingratitude, encroaching upon another’s boundaries, cruelty, mercilessness, and consorting with the wives of others;

One should recognize from these indications that those who steal the property of others, revile the deities, practice deceit, bind men, exhibit miserliness, and commit the slaughter of humans, have not been liberated from hell.
Compassion toward living beings, discourse regarding the next world, ritual action, truthfulness, speech for the sake of benefit, and the recognition of the authority of the Vedas.

Service to gurus, gods, sages, and perfected beings; self-restraint like that of the virtuous; performing sacred rites; right conduct; and friendliness—these they know to be the characteristics of heaven. Through the realization of the eightfold yoga, one attains the ultimate fruit.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Ripening of Karma and Other Matters," in the section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said: I shall describe the supreme Great Yoga with its constituent limbs, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and which pacifies all sins. Listen as it is recited with devotion.
"‘It is mine’ is the root of suffering; ‘it is not mine’ is its cessation. Indeed, the high-minded Dattātreya spoke this to Alarka."
The sprout "I" has arisen; the great trunk consists of the aggregates of "mine," while houses and fields are its branches and wives its tender shoots.

With wealth and grain as its great leaves, rooted in evil, and exceedingly difficult to traverse, the great tree of ignorance has grown according to the prescribed rule for the sake of pleasure and peace.
Severed by the axe of knowledge, they have gone to dissolution in the Lord; having attained it, the stainless and thornless essence of Brahman has been drunk.
The supreme wise ones attain both happiness and liberation; indeed, O King, neither you nor I have yet reached the dissolution of the body and the senses.
Neither the subtle elements and so forth, nor speech, nor likewise the internal organ [is this]; O Indra among kings, whom do you see as being the primary principle between us two?

"O King, though he has died today and is born again as a knower of the field (kṣetrajña) composed of the qualities (guṇas) on the following day, there is nevertheless a state of distinctness within that unity; such is the case for the field and the self."
This separation preceded by knowledge occurs for the yogin when [dualistic] knowledge has perished; that is liberation: unity with Brahman and non-unity with the material qualities (guṇas).
That is his home where he dwells; that is his food by which he lives; and that alone is said to be for liberation—whether through knowledge or ignorance, it is not otherwise.
O King, through the enjoyment of meritorious and non-meritorious deeds, as well as through the non-performance of obligatory duties, there occurs their exhaustion.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the five *yamas*. Then there are the *niyamas*, among which purity is said to be of two kinds.
Contentment, austerity, tranquility, worship of Vāsudeva, self-restraint, the lotus posture and others, and breath control which is the mastery over the vital winds; these constitute yoga.

Each of these is also threefold by means of inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka). That which lasts ten mātras is the mild [breath], while that which is double that duration is the middling.

That which is endowed with three times the measure of qualities is declared to be the highest; when joined with recitation and meditation it is the "embryonic" (garbha), while the opposite is the "infant" (arbha).
One should first conquer sleep, then trembling with the middle [dose], and finally the digestion [of the medicine] with the third; thus the arisen defects are overcome in succession.
Seated upon his seat, having placed the *praṇava* within his heart, he should practice yoga with a one-pointed mind, touching the penis and the scrotum with his two heels.
Having suppressed the activity of *tamas* by means of *rajas*, and likewise that of *rajas* by means of *sattva*, the knower of yoga, becoming motionless, should remain steady while practicing yoga.
Having restrained the senses from their objects, as well as the vital breaths and so forth, one should undertake pratyāhāra through complete withdrawal.
Eighteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) are prescribed as one concentration (dhāraṇā); two concentrations are known as yoga by the yogis who perceive reality.
In the eastern channel, in the heart, and here the third [channel] likewise in the chest; in the throat, the mouth, the tip of the nose, the eyes, between the eyebrows, and on the crown of the head.

Furthermore, concentration (*dhāraṇā*) upon that [object] and upon what is beyond it is taught to be tenfold; having attained these ten concentrations, one attains the nature of the imperishable (*akṣara*).

Just as fire cast into fire [is extinguished], so too is the self merged into the Supreme Self; one should mutter the single-syllable "Om," which is of the nature of Brahman and possesses great merit.
The letter A, the letter U, and the letter M are the three syllables; from these arise the three measures (mātrās), characterized by the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas.

The primordial half-mora, devoid of qualities, accessible to yogis, and situated as the supreme (parā), is to be known as Gāndhārī, resting upon the Gāndhāra note; this is the imperishable Brahman designated as the supreme Oṃkāra.
I am Brahman, the supreme light, devoid of the gross body; I am Brahman, the supreme light, devoid of old age and death.
I am Brahman, the supreme light, free from the impurity of the earth; I am Brahman, the supreme light, devoid of air and space.
I am Brahman, the supreme light, devoid of the subtle body; I am Brahman, the supreme light, devoid of place and non-place.
I am Brahman, the supreme light, devoid of even the subtlest trace of smell; I am Brahman, the supreme light, entirely devoid of hearing and touch.
I am Brahman, the supreme light, devoid of tongue and nose; I am Brahman, the supreme light, devoid of prāṇa and apāna.
I am Brahman, the supreme light, devoid of vyāna and udāna breaths; I am Brahman, the supreme light, entirely free from ignorance.
I am Brahman, the supreme light, the fourth state, the highest goal, devoid of body, senses, mind, intellect, vital breath, and ego.
I am Brahman—the supreme light, whose nature is knowledge, eternally pure, enlightened, liberated, great bliss, and non-dual—for the sake of liberation.

Sūta said: Thus, O Śaunaka, I have described to you the eight-limbed yoga that grants liberation; by performing the obligatory and occasional rites, those bound by material nature attain dissolution [into the source].
For in saṃsāra, many [beings] arise; having gone through various states, one is liberated. Once liberated, he who was deluded by ignorance is freed through knowledge.
Then that yogi dies without suffering, neither as a sick man nor as one bereft of kinsmen; he is not joined with sins, nor does he undergo maturation in hell.
May he not suffer while dwelling in the womb; may he be the imperishable Nārāyaṇa. The Blessed One, the bestower of enjoyment and liberation, is attainable through exclusive devotion.
Through meditation, worship, recitations, proper hymns of praise, observance of vows, sacrifices, and gifts, the purification of the mind is attained; and through that, knowledge is obtained.
By means of mantras beginning with the *praṇava* and through recitation, the twice-born attained liberation; even Indra reached the supreme station, as did the excellent Gandharvas and Apsarases.
The gods have attained godhood, the sages have reached the state of sages, the gandharvas have attained the state of gandharvas, and kings and others have attained the status of royalty.
Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Eight-Limbed Yoga," in the section on Conduct within the first part of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said: I shall now proclaim devotion to Viṣṇu, by which everything is attained; for Hari is pleased by devotion alone, and not by anything else.
The remembrance of Hari is certainly the root of great welfare, the source of a continuous stream of merit, and the sweet fruit of life.
Therefore, service has been declared by the wise to be the primary means for accomplishing devotion; those who chant the names, deeds, and other qualities of the Lord of the World are truly devoted.
Shedding tears out of great joy, with their hair standing on end, they said: "We are the executors of the divine command of Maheśa, the Creator of the World."
Those Vaiṣṇavas who are indeed affectionate should perform their daily rites here, even while not hearing the imperishable Brahman uttered by the Blessed One.
He who speaks with devotion preceded by prostration is indeed a Vaiṣṇava; likewise, affection for his devotees, honoring them, and rejoicing in their merit [are the marks of a Vaiṣṇava].
Upon hearing his stories, there is joy, tears, and physical transformations; by him, with his whole being, devotion has been directed toward Viṣṇu through bhakti.

Because he has perfected his soul through the Brahmins, he is indeed a great devotee of the Lord; he constantly provides for the welfare of all beings, renounces attachment for their sake, personally worships Viṣṇu, and lives entirely dependent upon Him.
Indeed, this eightfold devotion exists even in a barbarian; he is a lord of Brahmins, a venerable sage, and he attains the supreme goal.

To him gifts should be given and from him they should be received; he is to be honored like Hari. For a devotee of the Blessed One, even if he be a Caṇḍāla, purifies by his mere memory, conversation, or worship, O best of the twice-born, according to his own nature.
"Show compassion to one who has sought refuge and says, 'I am yours'; grant fearlessness to all beings—this is the vow of Hari."
One who has mastered all the Upanishads is superior to thousands of mantra-reciters; and a devotee of Viṣṇu is superior to ten million such masters of all the Upanishads.
Those who are single-mindedly devoted go to the supreme state by means of their own bodies; for Viṣṇu is equal to them through that single-mindedness, and therefore he is their ultimate refuge.
Because those whose minds are devoted to the Lord are declared to be single-mindedly dedicated, they are most dear to the God of gods, even more so than all other beloved ones.
Even in times of adversity, his devotion is always unwavering; that love for Viṣṇu is superior and remains constant even amidst worldly objects.
As I constantly remember Viṣṇu, she does not depart from my heart; for though I am a firm devotee who has mastered the meaning of all the scriptures, beginning with the Vedas, she remains.

One should know that he who is not devoted to the Lord of All is the lowest of men; even if one has not studied the Vedas and Shastras, nor performed the rites of sacrifice, everything is accomplished by him who bears devotion to Vishnu.

Even those who have performed sacrifices, who preside over principal rituals, and who have reached the further shore of the Vedas, do not attain that goal which the best of sages, the devotees, attain.
Any Vaiṣṇava in this world, even if he follows false conduct or belongs to no stage of life, purifies all the worlds like the risen thousand-rayed sun.
Even those who are cruel, evil-minded, and devoted to sinful conduct go to the supreme abode if they are solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
When firm and unwavering devotion to Janārdana arises, then what need is there for the happiness of heaven? That devotion alone is the cause of nirvāṇa.

For men wandering there in this saṃsāra, which is as difficult to traverse as a desert, there is indeed but one hand to hold: that by which Janārdana may be pleased. He who does not hear the divine qualities of the Discus-wielding God of gods should be known as a desert-dweller, deaf, and excluded from all dharma.
If, when the name of Viṣṇu is proclaimed, the body of a person does not bristle with horripilation, that body shall be like a corpse.
O best of the twice-born, for those men whose minds are fixed upon Him, devotion leads to liberation before long, and there is the complete destruction of all sin.

Beholding his own messenger with noose in hand, Yama indeed whispers into his ear: "Avoid him who has taken refuge in Madhusūdana; I am the lord over other men, but certainly not over the devotees of Viṣṇu."
Moreover, even if one of very wicked conduct worships Me with undivided devotion, he is to be regarded as righteous indeed, for he has rightly resolved.
He quickly becomes righteous in nature and attains eternal peace; O best of Brahmins, know this for certain: a devotee of Viṣṇu never perishes.
What need has he for virtue, wealth, or pleasure? Liberation stands in his very hand, he whose devotion to Hari is firm—the root of all the worlds.
For this divine illusion of Hari, composed of the gunas, is difficult to overcome; those who take refuge in Him alone cross over this illusion.

What remains for men to accomplish through the performance of sacrifice to propitiate those whose intellect is fixed on Hari? Viṣṇu is propitiated by devotion alone; nothing else is of assistance therein.
That Great-Souled One, Janārdana, does not attain such satisfaction through various gifts given, nor through flowers, nor even through ointments, as he does through devotion.
Of the poisonous tree of saṃsāra, there are indeed two fruits comparable to nectar: devotion to Keśava at some time, or meeting with his devotees.

While leaves, flowers, fruits, and water—attainable without hardship—are always available, one should instead exert effort toward the Ancient Person, who is attainable through devotion alone and is the singular attainment of liberation.
The ancestors clap their hands and the grandfathers dance, saying: "A Vaiṣṇava has been born in our family; he will deliver us."

Since even sinful men such as Śiśupāla and Suyodhana—who, being ignorant, cast insults at the Lord of Bliss—have attained liberation, their sins having been shaken off by mere remembrance, what doubt can there be regarding those people who possess supreme devotion?
Those who have taken refuge in that Śaraṇa, even if they are devoid of the yoga of meditation, transcend death and go to that very abode of Viṣṇu.

O Mādhava, let this horse of my mind—which is struck by hundreds of afflictions arising from worldly existence and which wanders about unrestrained through the openings of the senses—be tethered to the hitching post of Your feet with the firm bond of devotion.
Viṣṇu alone is the supreme Brahman, though he is described here as having three divisions; those who are deluded do not know this within the paths of the Vedantic tenets.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of Devotion to the Blessed Lord," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: That man who bows down to Him—the cause of liberation, without beginning or end, unborn, immutable, and imperishable—becomes worthy of being saluted by all the world.
I always bow with devotion, with my mind, to Viṣṇu, who is bliss, non-dual, pure consciousness, all-pervading, the Lord, and the one whose abode is the heart.
I bow to that Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, the witness of all, who, dwelling within, beholds the auspicious and inauspicious of the entire universe.
Even when uttered by one who is powerless, a salutation directed toward the wielder of the discus (Cakrapāṇi) indeed causes trembling among the multitudes of grass-like beings in saṃsāra.

In Kṛṣṇa—whose beautiful dark body resembles the belly of a shimmering rain-cloud, who is the Supreme Person presiding over the worlds, and the ultimate object of knowledge—a single firm prostration made with the sole intent of devotion is indeed capable of instantly purifying even an outcaste.
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground, he who worships with a salutation attains that destination which cannot be reached even by hundreds of sacrifices.
Even for those rushing through the shoreless wilderness of the difficult saṃsāra, a single prostration to Kṛṣṇa will deliver them by means of liberation.
Whether sitting, lying down, or standing, or wherever one may be, one should take sole refuge in this mantra: "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa."
The word "Nārāyaṇa" exists, and speech is under one's control; yet that fools still fall into hell—what is more wonderful than this?

Even if some person of pure mind were to have four faces, or even ten million faces, he might indeed speak of but a single ten-thousandth part of the qualities of Viṣṇu, the best of gods—or perhaps not at all.
All the sages, beginning with Vyāsa, though praising Madhusūdana, turn back due to the exhaustion of their intellects, not because of an exhaustion of Govinda’s qualities.

When his name is uttered, even by one who is unwilling, a person is instantly liberated from all sins, just as deer are terrified by a lion; he has thus girded his loins for the journey toward liberation.
Even in a dream, the mere touch of this name destroys the inexhaustible heap of sins of a person; how much more so, then, when the name of Janārdana is proclaimed by a man before his very eyes?
O Brahmin, those who, permeated by true devotion, have uttered the names "Kṛṣṇa," "Acyuta," "Ananta," and "Vāsudeva," have not gone to the city of Yama.
Just as the destruction of fire occurs upon the rising of the sun, even so is the destruction of the flood of impurities through the chanting of the names of Hari.
Where is the ascent to the vault of heaven, which never returns to decay, for those whose minds are darkened by delusion as they travel the long road?

The proclamation of the names of Hari, the lotus-eyed one, is the provision for the journey; it is the sole remedy for the effects of the poison when bitten by the serpent of saṃsāra. By reciting the Vaiṣṇava name "Kṛṣṇa" with patience, a person becomes liberated.
What one obtains by meditating in the Kṛta age, by reciting mantras in the Tretā, and by performing worship in the Dvāpara, that same thing one obtains in the Kali age by simply remembering Keśava.
He on whose tongue-tip reside these two syllables, "Ha-ri," shall cross the ocean of saṃsāra and go to the abode of Viṣṇu.

Even if surrounded by thousands of known misdeeds, a person who desires supreme excellence and seeks complete purification will not see existence again in a dream, provided that human being is devoted solely to the narrative of the praise of Nārāyaṇa.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Devotion to Viṣṇu," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Sūta said: May he who offers flowers and even water with the Puruṣasūkta to Hari—the essence of the worship of the Lord of all worlds—attain [the highest goal].
