By him who does not worship Viṣṇu, this entire world of moving and unmoving beings would remain unhonored; one should know such a person to be a slayer of Brahman.
He who does not meditate upon Viṣṇu—from whom the activity of all beings proceeds and by whom all this is pervaded—shall become a worm in excrement.
Being cooked in hell and rebuked by Yama, he was told: "But why was the god Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, not worshipped by you?"
The Lord, who bestows his own world upon those who worship him even with water or the mere absence of material things—has he not been worshipped by you?
Neither mother, nor father, nor even kinsmen do that which Hṛṣīkeśa does when he is satisfied and worshipped with faith.
By a person who observes the conduct prescribed for their caste and stage of life, the Supreme Person Viṣṇu is propitiated; there is no other path that causes him satisfaction.
That Great-Souled Janārdana is not so pleased by various gifts given, nor by flowers, nor by ointments, as he is by devotion.

Neither through wealth, sovereignty, or greatness, nor through progeny or ritual action, nor even through those who are liberated can oneness with Hari be attained; the root is the propitiation of Hari.
Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of Viṣṇu," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Having examined all the scriptures and having reflected upon them again and again, this one conclusion is well-established: Nārāyaṇa is to be meditated upon at all times.

What is the use of gifts for him, what use are sacred pilgrimage sites, what use are austerities, or what use are sacrifices—for he who constantly meditates upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa with undivided mind?
Sixty thousand and sixty hundred sacred fords do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of a single prostration to Nārāyaṇa.
Know that among all possible penances and ascetic acts without exception, the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa is the supreme.
For that man in whom attachment arises even toward committed sin, the one supreme expiation is the constant remembrance of Hari.
Even he who meditates on Nārāyaṇa for a single moment without sloth attains the state of heaven; how much more so one who is devoted to Him as his supreme goal?
For the yogi established in yoga, whatever mental modification arises during the states of waking, dreaming, or deep sleep, that becomes based upon Acyuta.
Whether rising or falling, speaking or entering, eating or waking—whoever should remember Govinda, Mādhava; ||| 12.308 ||
Devoted to one's own respective duty, one should fix the mind upon Janārdana; this is the teaching according to the scriptures—what is the use of many other words?
Meditation alone is the supreme dharma; meditation alone is the supreme austerity; meditation alone is the supreme purity; therefore, one should be devoted to meditation.
There is no higher object of meditation than Viṣṇu, and no austerity greater than fasting; therefore, the contemplation of Vāsudeva is declared here to be the most essential.
Even that which is difficult to obtain, supreme, attainable, and beyond the range of the mind—Madhusūdana grants that as well, even when not requested, to one who meditates upon him.
Whatever ritual act may fail among the sacrifices performed through negligence, that becomes complete simply by the remembrance of Viṣṇu; such is the Vedic revelation.
There is no purifier of evil deeds equal to meditative absorption; it is the fire of yoga that burns away the causes for future bodies.
But the yogi who has perfected samādhi and whose karma has been burnt away by the fire of yoga attains liberation in this very birth without delay.
Just as a fire with rising flames or the wind burns dry grass, so too, when Viṣṇu is established in the mind, all the yogi’s sins are consumed.
Just as gold becomes pure through contact with fire, so too is the impurity of human beings eternally consumed by Vāsudeva.
Whatever sin remains after a thousand baths in the Gaṅgā and ten million baths at Puṣkara, that is destroyed when Hari is remembered.
Whatever sin is certainly destroyed by thousands of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), that same sin is destroyed in a mere moment through meditation on Hari.
Neither the wicked speech arising from the influence of the Kali age nor the doctrines of heretics shall affect the mind of that person in whose heart Keśava resides.
That lunar day, that day and night, that conjunction, and that moon, as well as that very astrological sign, are renowned as auspicious whenever Hari is remembered therein.
That is a loss, that is a great flaw, and that is the mute dullness of one devoid of purpose, if for even a moment or an instant Vāsudeva is not meditated upon.
For him in whom Govinda is not in the heart, and Acyuta is not in the mind, there is the Kṛta Age in the Kali Age, and the Kali Age in the Kṛta Age.
He whose mind is constantly fixed upon Govinda, whether he is walking before Him, behind Him, or even while standing still, is always one who has accomplished his purpose.
O Maitreya, for one whose mind is fixed on Vāsudeva during the practices of chanting, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth, even the fruit of the sovereignty of Indra constitutes an obstacle.
Without abandoning the life of a householder, and having performed great austerity, he—whose mind is offered to Keśava—cuts through the illusion of human existence.
Men show forgiveness toward the angry, compassion toward the foolish, and joy toward those of virtuous character, when Govinda dwells within their hearts.
One should meditate upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa during acts such as ritual bathing and giving of gifts, and especially during all rites of expiation for misdeeds.
Blessed are they, victorious are they; how could there be defeat for those in whose hearts dwells Janārdana, dark as a blue lotus?
Even for swarms of insects and birds whose minds are surrendered to Hari, there is indeed an upward destiny; how much more so for wise human beings?
Why is the shade of the tree that is Vāsudeva not resorted to—a shade that is neither too cold nor causes excessive heat, and which quiets the gates of hell?
O friend, neither the curse of Durvāsas nor even the kingdom of the Lord of Śacī is capable of harming one who has placed Madhusūdana within his heart.
Whether one is speaking, standing, or performing other actions according to one's will, when the thought does not depart, one should consider the dhāraṇā accomplished.

Nārāyaṇa, who resides in the center of the solar disc, seated upon a lotus throne, adorned with armlets, crocodile-shaped earrings, a crown, and necklaces, possessing a golden body and bearing the conch and the discus—He is to be meditated upon at all times.
Indeed, there is no purifier found here equal to meditative absorption; even one who eats the food of an outcaste, though sinful, is not defiled by it.
If the mind of a living being is always so attached to the sphere of sense objects that it is not even thus [attached] to Nārāyaṇa, who would not be liberated from bondage?
Sūta said: Whosever mind possesses devotion to Viṣṇu, whom else would that living being ever bow to? He at once delivers himself from the ocean of evil.
That is true knowledge where Govinda is; that is true discourse where Kāśyapa is; that is true action which is for his sake—what is the use of much other talk?
That is a true tongue which praises Hari; that is a true mind which is offered to Him; those alone are praiseworthy hands which perform His worship.

The gods know that bowing to the Lord is the fruit of the head; worshipping Him is the fruit of the hands; reflecting upon His qualities and deeds is the fruit of the mind; and praising the virtues of Govinda is the fruit of speech.
Even a heap of sinful karma as large as Mount Meru or Mandara is entirely destroyed by the mere remembrance of Keśava.
Whatever action a person performs, whether good or evil, by dedicating it all to Nārāyaṇa, he is not defiled even while acting.
The fourfold collection of beings, from grass up to the four-faced Brahmā—the entire world of moving and unmoving things—is fast asleep through your māyā.

When the mind is fixed upon Him, one does not go to hell; even heaven is a hindrance when He is being contemplated; and even the world of Brahmā is insignificant compared to Him, in whom liberation dwells within the heart and grants itself even to men of dull intellect—what wonder is it that this [world] goes to its dissolution when Acyuta is glorified?
Those who perform fire rituals, recitation, bathing, meditation on Viṣṇu, and worship there, will cross over the ocean of suffering.
The king is the refuge of the kingdom, and parents are the refuge of the child; Dharma is the refuge of all mortals, and Hari is the refuge of everything.
O best of sages, for those who bow to Vāsudeva, the eternal source of the world, there exists no sacred ford superior to them.
One should perform worship with priceless jewels and likewise engage in the private recitation of sacred texts, constantly meditating upon that very Govinda without weariness.
A man who regards even a Śūdra, a devotee of the Blessed One, a Niṣāda, or a Śvapaca as equal to those of the twice-born castes does not go to hell.
Just as one always praises a wealthy person with devotion out of a desire for wealth, who would not be liberated from bondage by praising the Creator of the universe?
Just as fire that has reached its source burns even moist fuel, so does Viṣṇu, abiding in such a manner, burn away all the sins of yogins.
Just as deer and other wild animals do not resort to a mountain that is ablaze with fire, so too do all evils avoid the man who is devoted to the practice of yoga.
To whatever extent one has faith, to that same extent is one's accomplishment; by this alone is the power of Kṛṣṇa measured.
Even out of enmity, Śiśupāla, the son of Damaghoṣa, attained the ultimate reality by remembering Govinda; how much more so one who is devoted to him?
Thus ends the two hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Viṣṇu," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Sūta said: O Śaunaka, I shall now recite the hymn to Nṛsiṃha as spoken by Śiva. Formerly, all the hosts of Mothers addressed these words to Śaṅkara:
"O Blessed One, we shall devour the entire world, including its gods, asuras, and humans; it behoves you to grant us permission for this through your grace."
Śaṅkara said: "All subjects must be protected by you without a doubt; therefore, let your minds, which are mostly inclined toward cruelty, be quickly turned away."
Thus disregarding those words spoken by Śaṅkara, they undisturbedly devoured the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile.
While the three worlds were indeed being devoured by the host of Mothers, the Blessed Lord Śiva meditated upon the God in the form of Nṛsiṃha.
The god who is without beginning or end, the source of the existence of all beings, with lightning-like tongue, great fangs, and a garland of quivering manes.
Adorned with jeweled armlets and a crown, decorated with golden filaments, and resplendent with a great golden waistband.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, adorned with jeweled anklets, his splendor pervades the entire pavilion-like interior of the universe.
His body hairs were joined together in shapes resembling whirlpools, and he wore a great garland composed of all kinds of flowers.
As soon as he was meditated upon, the Blessed One granted him a vision in whatever form Rudra had been meditated upon with devotion.
In that very form, which was difficult even for the gods to behold, Śaṅkara prostrated before the Lord of Gods and then offered praise.
Śaṅkara said: Homage be to you, O Lord of the World, who assume the form of Narasiṃha; you who are resplendent with the shells of the claws that destroy the lords of the Daityas.

Homage be to the Lotus-navelled One, the beautiful Teacher of the World, whose golden-hued body is marked by the circles of his nails; who possesses a voice like the roar of the ocean at the end of an aeon, and a radiance equal to ten million suns.
O you who possess the fearlessness of a thousand Yamas, the prowess of a thousand Indras, the vastness of a thousand Dhanadas, and whose nature consists of a thousand feet!
O you who resemble a thousand moons, whose stride is like that of the thousand-rayed sun and Hari, possessing the splendor of a thousand Rudras, and praised by a thousand Brahmās.
Chanted over by a thousand Rudras, beheld by the thousand-eyed one, crusher of a thousand births, liberator from a thousand bonds.

O you whose eyes possess the speed of a thousand winds, O you who show compassion through a thousand commands! Having thus praised Hari, the Lord of the gods of gods, who has the form of Nṛsiṃha, Śiva, bowing low with humility, addressed him once more.
"The Mothers who were created by me for the destruction of Andhaka, disregarding my word, shall instead devour these wondrous creatures."
Having created them, even though I am unconquered, I am not able to withdraw them; having first brought them into being, how could I take pleasure in their destruction?
Thus addressed by Rudra, Hari, who possesses the form of Narasiṃha, then became the Lord of Speech (Vāgīśvara), with a thousand tongues at the tips of which were the goddesses of speech.
Likewise, the omnipresent Hari, having withdrawn all the hosts of gods and the fierce groups of Mothers, and having brought peace to the world, vanished from sight.
Whoever, with senses restrained, recites this Nārasiṃha hymn, for him it grants all desires, just as Rudra does; of this there is no doubt.

One should meditate upon Nṛsiṃha, whose eyes are like the rising sun, who emerges from a blooming lotus, and who blazes like a flaming fire; he is without beginning, middle, or end, unborn, ancient, the Lord of both the transcendent and the immanent, and the repository of all worlds.
One who recites this abandons the continuous web of suffering, just as the sun sheds its frost; when he manifests the form of the assembly of mothers, he then remains in their presence.

May he who brought about the destruction of Tripura, having propitiated that best of gods and obtained [his favor] to perform the worship of the Lord of Gods in the form of Narasimha, protect [us] and likewise the hosts of Mothers of the World.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Hymn to Nṛsiṃha," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Sūta said: I shall proclaim the Kulāmṛta hymn which Hara spoke when questioned by Śrī Nārada; likewise, listen as it was told to Nārada.

Nārada said: He who is always bound by pairs of opposites—by desire and anger, by the auspicious and the inauspicious, and by objects of the senses such as sound—is a person of wicked intellect, being tormented by them.
A living being is liberated for a moment from the ocean of death and saṃsāra. O Blessed One, O Destroyer of Tripura, I indeed wish to hear this from you.
Having heard those words of Nārada, the three-eyed Śambhu, Hara, with a gracious countenance, spoke to that ṛṣi.
Maheśvara said: O best of sages, I shall speak of the supreme nectar of knowledge, the ultimate secret, the mystery that destroys suffering and removes the fear of the bonds of existence; listen.
By whose illusory power the entire world—the fourfold collection of beings from blades of grass up to the four-faced Brahmā, including all that is moving and unmoving—is plunged into deep sleep.
If anyone awakens through the grace of that Viṣṇu, he crosses over saṃsāra, which is difficult even for the gods to cross.
Intoxicated by the pride of wealth and power, and turning their backs on the knowledge of reality, living beings—infatuated with their children, wives, and families—perish.
All are submerged in a single ocean like aged wild elephants; whoever binds himself to you is a fool, like a silkworm.
I do not see his liberation even in hundreds of millions of births; therefore, O Nārada, one should always properly worship Viṣṇu, the imperishable God of all gods, and meditate upon him with joy.
But he who always meditates upon Viṣṇu—the omniscient, immovable one, unborn, without beginning or end, and established within the self—is completely liberated.

One who constantly meditates on Viṣṇu, the God worthy of being conceived in the womb, is liberated; one who constantly meditates on Viṣṇu—the bodiless Creator, whose delight is in all knowledge, the immovable yet omnipresent—is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon Vāsudeva—Viṣṇu, the Guru—who is free from conceptual construction, free from appearance, free from proliferation, and free from affliction, one is liberated.
One who constantly meditates upon Viṣṇu—the auspicious single syllable, who is the self of all and whose nature is the consciousness of the Self—is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu—who transcends speech, knows the three periods of time, is the Lord of the universe, the witness of the world, and superior to all—one is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu, who is served by Brahmā and the other gods, Gandharvas, sages, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and yogis, one is liberated.
For the entire world, desiring liberation from the bonds of saṃsāra, is indeed released by constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu, the giver of boons, after having praised him in this way.

Anyone who, desiring liberation from the bonds of saṃsāra, remains composed and constantly meditates upon the infinite and imperishable Lord Viṣṇu, who is established in the universe, the unborn Lord of all, is liberated.
Sūta said: Thus was he, whose banner bears the bull, questioned by Nārada in the past; that which was explained to him by him has been related by me to you.
Constantly meditating upon that very same immutable, partless Brahman, you will surely attain, my dear, the eternal and imperishable state.
Thousands of horse sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of one whose mind is focused for a single moment.
Having heard this preeminence of Viṣṇu from the Lord, the divine sage, having properly propitiated Viṣṇu, attained perfection and reached the supreme state.
Whoever should recite or even hear this supreme hymn constantly, even the sin committed by them throughout ten million lifetimes shall be utterly destroyed.
Whoever recites with diligence this divine hymn of Viṣṇu, proclaimed by Mahādeva, daily attains immortality.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Hymn to Kulāmṛta," in the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. [Chapter 233 of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*] Sūta said: I shall now fully proclaim that hymn spoken by Mārkaṇḍeya: "I have taken refuge in Dāmodara; what can Death do to me?"
I have taken refuge in the imperishable God, who bears the conch and the discus, whose form is manifest, and who is born from below; what can death do to me?
I have taken refuge in Varāha, Vāmana, Viṣṇu, Nārasiṃha, Janārdana, and Mādhava; what can death do to me?
I have taken refuge in the Puruṣa, the seed of the Puṣkara field, the merit of the world, the Lord of the universe, and the Protector of the world; what can death do to me?
I have taken refuge in the thousand-headed God, the eternal, who is both manifest and unmanifest, the Great Yoga; what can death do to me?
I have taken refuge in the Great Self, the soul of all beings, the source of sacrifice, unborn yet born of no womb, whose form is the universe; what can death do to me?
Having heard this hymn uttered by that high-souled one, Death then fled away, pursued and tormented by the messengers of Viṣṇu.
Thus was Death conquered by the wise Mārkaṇḍeya; when the lotus-eyed Nṛsiṃha is propitiated, nothing is difficult to attain.
This meritorious and auspicious *Mṛtyvaṣṭaka*, which pacifies death, was spoken by Viṣṇu himself for the benefit of Mārkaṇḍeya.
Whoever, being pure and self-restrained, recites this with devotion three times a day, for that man whose mind is fixed on Acyuta, there shall be no untimely death.
Having meditated upon the ancient Puruṣa, Nārāyaṇa—the eternal and immeasurable—who shines more brilliantly than the sun within the center of the heart-lotus, that yogi likewise conquered death.
Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Mṛtyvaṣṭaka Stotra composed by Mārkaṇḍeya," in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: O Śaunaka, listen as I shall proclaim the hymn to Acyuta, which bestows all things; it is the supreme [teaching] that Brahmā, when questioned, spoke to Nārada.
Nārada said: "You should tell me how Viṣṇu—the inexhaustible and immutable granter of boons—is to be praised by me every day at the time of worship."
They are blessed, they are of noble birth, for they bestow all happiness; their life is fruitful who always praise the Imperishable One.
Brahmā said: O sage, I shall proclaim the hymn of Vāsudeva that bestows liberation; listen, for when he is properly praised with this at the time of worship, he becomes gracious.
Oṃ, homage! Homage to the Blessed One Vāsudeva; homage to the remover of all [sins]; homage to the one of pure body; homage to the one whose very nature is knowledge.
Homage to the Lord of all gods; homage to the bearer of the Śrīvatsa; homage to the one who holds a shield and sword in hand; homage to the one garlanded with lotuses.
Salutation to the foundation of the universe, and salutation to the one clad in yellow garments; salutation to the one in the form of Nṛsiṃha, and repeated salutations to Vaikuṇṭha.
Homage to the one whose navel is a lotus; homage to the one who reclines upon the ocean of milk; homage to the one with a thousand heads; homage to the one who reclines upon the body of the serpent.
Homage to him who holds the axe in his hand; homage to the one who brings an end to the kṣatriyas; homage to the one whose vow is true; indeed, repeated homage to the unconquered one.
Homage to the Lord of the three worlds, and homage to the wielder of the discus; homage to Śiva, the subtle, the ancient—homage again and again!
Homage to the one in the form of Vāmana, who took away King Bali’s kingdom; homage to Yajñavarāha, to Govinda—homage again and again!
Homage to you, supreme bliss; homage to you, supreme syllable. Homage to you, the true essence of gnosis; homage to you, the bestower of gnosis.
Salutations to you, O Supreme Non-duality; salutations to you, O Supreme Person. Salutations to you, O God who creates the universe; salutations to you, O Originator of the universe.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the Universe; salutations to you, O Cause of the Universe. Salutations to you, O slayer of the demon Madhu; salutations to you, O destroyer of Rāvaṇa.
Salutations to you, O slayer of Kaṃsa and Keśin; salutations to you, O destroyer of Kaiṭabha. Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, whose banner bears Garuḍa.
Salutations to you, O slayer of Kālanemi; salutations to you, whose seat is Garuḍa. Salutations to you, son of Devakī; salutations to you, joy of the Vṛṣṇis.
Salutations to you, O beloved of Rukmiṇī; salutations to you, O son of Aditi; salutations to you, whose abode is Gokula; salutations to you, who are dear to Gokula.
Victory to you, Kṛṣṇa, who assumed the form of a cowherd! Victory to you, beloved of the gopīs! Victory to you, the upholder of Govardhana! Victory to you, the increaser of Gokula!
Victory to you, O slayer of the hero Rāvaṇa! Victory to you, O destroyer of Cāṇūra! Victory to you, O light of the Vṛṣṇi clan! Victory to you, O subduer of Kālīya!
Victory to you, O Truth, witness of the world! Victory to you, accomplisher of all aims! Victory to you, known by the knowers of Vedānta! Victory to you, O Mādhava, giver of all!
Victory to you, the unmanifest refuge of all! Victory to you, O omnipresent Mādhava! Victory to you, the subtle essence of consciousness! Victory to you, the stainless mind!
Victory be unto you, O Supportless One! Victory, O Peaceful and Eternal One! Victory, O Lord, nourisher of the world!
Victory, O Viṣṇu; homage be unto you!

You are the Guru, O Hari, and you are the disciple; you are the initiation, the mantra, and the maṇḍala; you are the ritual placement (nyāsa), the mudrās, and the commitments (samaya); and you are the means of accomplishment, such as the flowers and other offerings.
You are the support; you indeed are the infinite; you are the tortoise; you are the earth-lotus; for you are dharma, knowledge, and the rest—the powers of the altar and the mandala.
O Lord, you are Rāma, the wearer of the disguise; you again are the slayer of Khara; you are the divine Brahman-sage, and you are Viṣṇu of true prowess.
You are Nṛsiṃha, the supreme bliss; you are Varāha, the upholder of the earth; you are Suparṇa, as well as the discus, the mace, and the conch.
O Lord, you are Śrī; you are Muṣṭisattva; O God, you are the eternal Mālā; for you are indeed Śrīvatsa, the Kaustubha, the Śārṅga bow, and likewise the quiver.
You are together with the sword and shield; you are the guardians of the directions, O Lord; you are the piercer and the ordainer; you are Yama and you are the consumer of oblations.
You are the Lord of Wealth, you are Īśāna, you are Indra, and you are the Lord of the Waters; you are the sovereign of the Rakṣasas, you are a Sādhya, you are Vāyu, and you are the Maker of Night.
You are the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and the two Aśvins; you are the hosts of Maruts; you are the Daityas, Dānavas, and Nāgas; you are the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and birds.
You are the Gandharvas, the Apsarases, the Siddhas, the Pitṛs, and the great gods; you are indeed the elements and the objects of the senses, as well as the unmanifest and the sense organs.

You are the mind, the intellect, and the ego; you are the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the Lord within the heart. You are the sacrifice, you are the exclamation vaṣaṭ, you are the syllable oṃ, and you are the sacrificial fuel and the kuśa grass.

You are the altar, O Hari; you are the initiation, you are the sacrificial post, and you are the fire. You are the wife, you are the sacrificial cake, you are the hall, and you are both the offering-spoon and the ladle.

You are indeed the pressing-stones and the entire assembly; you are the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and the winnowing-basket and other implements; and you are certainly the Brahman priest, the pestle, and the mortar.
You are the Hotṛ priest, you are the sacrificer, you are the grain, and you are the animal-sacrificer; you are the Adhvaryu, you are the Udgātṛ, and you are the sacrifice, O Puruṣottama.
You are the quarters, the netherworld, the earth, and the sky; you are the creator of the stars, and among gods, animals, and humans, you are this entire world of the moving and the unmoving.
O Lord, whatever is seen—the entire universe and all that exists—is all this Your form, manifested for the purpose of being perceived.
They take refuge in the Supreme Brahman, which is difficult even for the gods to attain; who knows that stainless one, accessible through yoga and beyond the reach of the senses?
The Lord is the imperishable, eternal Person, unmanifest, unborn, and undecaying; He is devoid of dissolution or origination and is all-pervading.
Omniscient, devoid of qualities, pure, blissful, undecaying, supreme, consisting of consciousness, eternal, peaceful, full, non-dual, and imperishable.
O Lord, those inhabitants of heaven who do not know your supreme nature worship you as that form which is seen at a distance during your incarnations.
O Supreme Person, O Lord, how can I possibly propitiate you, who are so subtle, who are accessible only to the mind, and who are beyond the reach of the senses?
O Lord, whatever is worshipped here in this maṇḍala according to the ritual procedures with flowers, incense, and so forth—in that very place all prosperities reside.
Whatever has been worshipped by me through the distinctions of Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others, you should forgive all of that—both what was done and what was left undone by me.
O Lord, O Supreme Person, I am unable to perform the worship correctly as prescribed; whatever recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth have been performed are rendered ineffective.
Therefore, out of devotion, I seek your forgiveness for my actions during the day, at night, at the twilights, and in all circumstances.
O Hari, my devotion to the pair of your feet is indeed unshakable; I have no such affection for my own body, nor for dharma and other such things.
O Lord of the World, since my love for you is absolute, what deed has not been performed by me that serves as a means to attain heaven, liberation, and the like?
O Acyuta, for one who possesses firm devotion to Viṣṇu, the bestower of the fruits of all desires—who indeed is capable of performing your worship or offering you praise?

"Today my praise has been offered and honored; forgive me, for salutations be unto you! Thus has the hymn to Cakradhara been correctly recited by me. O Sage, if you desire the supreme state, praise Viṣṇu with devotion."
Whoever praises the Teacher of the World with this hymn at the time of worship, [attains...]
Having severed the bonds of saṃsāra, he shall soon attain liberation; so too shall any other who, being self-controlled and pure, recites [this] with devotion at the three junctions of the day.
O Sage, by this hymn of praise, even he shall obtain all his desires; one seeking a son obtains sons, and one who is bound is released from bondage.
One possessed by passion is freed from disease; the poor man obtains wealth; one seeking knowledge acquires learning; and he attains fortune and fame.
Possessing the memory of past births and endowed with intelligence, whatever he desires with his mind, he is blessed, all-knowing, wise, virtuous, and the performer of all deeds.
He who praises the Supreme Person is truthful in speech, pure, and a giver; for all those others are unworthy of conversation, as they are excluded from all righteous dharma.
For those who do not perform virtuous deeds dedicated to Hari when they arise, the mind of that evil-souled person is not pure, and his speech is likewise defiled.
He whose devotion to Viṣṇu, the bestower of all goals, is unwavering, having duly propitiated Lord Hari, the giver of all happiness;

A person who possesses faith, O best of gods, attains exactly whatever fruit they rightly desire—whether it be action, desire, or anything else—for there is no interval between him and the Siddhas who bestow the bodies of Asuras and other beings.

I bow to that unborn, immortal Lord Vāsudeva, who is of the nature of eternal bliss, free from fear and death, who is contemplated by all sages as the primordial, pure one; who is seated within the hearts of all, and who, as the witness of everything, knows all.

I worship with the flowers of my own being the Lord of all worlds—the eternal, well-pleased, exceedingly pure and stainless, devoid of qualities, and in whom all things rejoice in happiness; may that All-Witness, the conscious Self, enter the lotus of my heart.
Thus have I described the supreme power of the highest Viṣṇu, who is without beginning or end; therefore, that Supreme Lord should be properly contemplated by a man desiring liberation.

Having meditated upon Viṣṇu—the ancient Puruṣa whose nature is pure consciousness, who is effulgent like the sun, stainless, and utterly pure, the supreme non-dual—what yogi would not attain liberation therein?
That person who constantly recites this hymn, being likewise restrained and tranquil, with his sins shaken off and his power expanded, goes to the vast realm of Murāri.
He who desires wealth, complete happiness, as well as virtue, pleasure, and likewise liberation—having renounced everything, he goes for refuge to Viṣṇu, the supreme, ancient, and most excellent one.

He who has taken refuge in Vāsudeva—the all-pervading Lord, the sustainer of the universe, the pure one, and the cause of the destruction of the entire cycle of existence—who is stainless and free from attachment, attains liberation.
Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Hymn to Acyuta," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: I shall now declare the knowledge of Brahman, the established conclusion of Vedānta and Sāṅkhya; meditating thus: "I am Brahman, the supreme light, Viṣṇu."
The single light is situated threefold in the sun, in the sky of the heart, and in fire; just as the ghee residing within the bodies of cows does not produce strength for them.
Having emerged and joined with their karma, that great power was bestowed upon them; likewise, Viṣṇu, though residing within their bodies, does not act for the benefit of men.
Without worship, the omnipresent Supreme Lord [is not attained]; however, for those whose minds desire to ascend, both ritual action and knowledge have been proclaimed.
For those who have ascended the tree of yoga, knowledge is considered the supreme renunciation; yet when one desires to know sound and other objects of sense, attachment and aversion arise.
A man joined with greed, delusion, and anger would commit evil; the hands, the genitals, the stomach, and speech as the fourth—this is the fourfold [set].
He whose [mind] is thus well-restrained is called a Brahmin by the wise; he does not take the wealth of others, nor does he commit violence.
The hands of one who does not delight in gambling with dice are well-restrained; the genitals of one who delights in avoiding the wives of others are well-restrained.
He eats this food without greed, for his belly is restrained; he speaks what is true, beneficial, and measured, because his speech is restrained.
For one whose senses are thus restrained, what need is there for asceticism or sacrifices? It is the perpetual unification of the intellect, the mind, and the senses.
This meditation is proclaimed to be both "with seed" (sabīja) and "without seed" (nirbīja). It is that which joins the intellect, situated between the eyebrows, with its objects.
When the senses have ceased their activity, yet the mind remains unsettled;
This living being perceives external and internal dreams; thus do the wise say of the living being in the waking state.
When he, situated in the heart, being deluded by darkness, does not even remember—let alone know anything else—that state is called deep sleep (suṣupti).
He who, while awake, experiences neither lethargy, nor delusion, nor confusion, and who, being self-controlled, does not perceive objects consisting of words and their meanings; [he is liberated].
Having withdrawn the senses from their objects, as well as the mind, and having likewise withdrawn the intellect, the ego, primordial nature, and even the intellect itself;

Having restrained even his own nature (prakṛti) by means of the power of consciousness (cicchakti), he abides in the absolute; he beholds within himself the Self, which is the illuminator of the self, by means of the self.
He is established in the fourth state (turiya), which is of the nature of consciousness, immortal, pure, actionless, all-pervading, and auspicious; of this there is no doubt.
The five qualities beginning with sound and the three qualities beginning with *sattva*—these indeed constitute the eight petals of the lotus of the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*).
The state of equilibrium produced by the *guṇas* is *prakṛti*, and therein lies the pericarp; the embodied deity, whose nature is indeed consciousness, resides within that pericarp.
When the individual soul departs, having abandoned the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) and primordial nature consisting of the qualities (guṇas), then it attains liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Breath control, recitation, withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation, and absorption—these six are the means for accomplishing yoga.

The destruction of evil, the gratification of the deities, restraint of the senses, and being joined with recitation and meditation constitute the "embryonic" (garbha) rite; that which is the opposite is the "non-embryonic" (agarbhaka).
The best consists of thirty-six measures, the middling of twenty-four measures, and the lowest of twelve measures; one should constantly recite the syllable Oṃ.
When the *praṇava*, which is the designator, is known, the designated Brahman becomes gracious. One should mutter the six-syllabled mantra (*oṃ namo viṣṇave*) and the twelve-syllabled *gāyatrī*.
The engagement of all the senses with their respective objects and the withdrawal of the mind from that [engagement] is proclaimed as *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal).
Having withdrawn the senses from the objects of the senses, he is indeed beneficial; for he stands firm in the practices of withdrawal, together with his intellect, acting with promptness.
For as long a period as is occupied by twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), for that duration one should fix the mind upon Brahman.

The meditation (dhyāna) taught by Brahmā for that very [state] consists of twelve concentrations (dhāraṇās). When one is self-controlled and disciplined, one becomes satisfied; that is designated as meditative absorption (samādhi).
The mind of one who meditates intensely does not waver while he is thus contemplating.
Having reached the prescribed duration of time, that is known as *dhāraṇā* (concentration), wherein the mind, attached to the object of meditation, perceives only the object of meditation.
When one knows no other object, this is proclaimed as meditation; contemplating the object of meditation, the mind attains immobility within that which is to be meditated upon.
That meditation which is declared supreme by the sages who contemplate meditation is indeed the object of meditation itself; for the meditator has become one with it in every respect.
When one perceives that which is free from duality, that is called samādhi; the mind, devoid of conceptual construction, should not contemplate the objects of the senses.
When the mind of that yogi who meditates on the Supreme Self as abiding within himself is completely absorbed in Brahman, he is then said to be established in samādhi.

The mind attains identity with that [object]; he who remains thus is proclaimed to be established in samādhi. The steadiness of the mind, as well as delusion, dejection, and negligence, [are obstacles].
The faults described for yogins are those that give rise to obstacles to yoga; for the sake of stabilizing the mind, one should contemplate everything in its gross form.
That vow, having become motionless, shall attain stability when situated in the sun; for nothing whatsoever exists in the world apart from the Supreme Self.

Having realized that very one who possesses universal form as the single reality, one is liberated; one should meditate upon the Omkara, the supreme Brahman, the all-pervading Lord seated upon a lotus.
One should recite [the mantra] devoid of the field and the knower of the field, accompanied by three measures; first, one should contemplate Pradhāna within the heart, and above that—
Tamas, rajas, and likewise sattva are the three circles in sequence; they are black, red, and white, and within them is the Puruṣa known as the individual soul (jīva).
Above that is an eight-petalled lotus of qualities and sovereignty; knowledge is its pericarp, and discernment is remembered as its filaments.
The stalk of this lotus is dispassion, and its root is the supreme Vaiṣṇava dharma; situated there upon the pericarp is the all-pervading Lord, as motionless as the individual soul.

One should meditate upon the syllable Om, the means to liberation, joined within the heart; if one should give up the vital breaths while thus meditating, one goes to Brahman, which is its own presence.
Having established Hari within the lotus of the body, one who meditates with devotion and chanting—some, through the eye of meditation, perceive the Self by means of the self.
Likewise, others [attain it] through Sāṃkhya-intellection, while other yogins do so through Yoga; this is the knowledge that reveals Brahman and shatters the bonds of worldly existence.
In this regard, the yoga of one-pointedness of mind bestows liberation; of this there is no doubt. For he who has conquered his senses and faculties and is exalted by knowledge [attains it].
That yogi who is established in the Supreme Self is said to be liberated; the rules regarding postures and locations are not the means for accomplishing yoga.
All extensive elaborations are proclaimed to cause delay; Śiśupāla attained perfection through the weight of his practice in constant remembrance.
Practicing yoga, they perceive the Self by means of the self, and cultivate compassion toward all beings and aversion toward sense objects.
A yogi who keeps his ears, belly, and other organs guarded is liberated; when a man does not perceive the objects of the senses through the senses, he is freed.
Like a piece of wood, the yogi who is absorbed in Brahman then becomes liberated; having reduced all castes, all fortunes, and all sins to ashes.
And by the fire of meditation, the wise one attains the supreme goal; for just as fire is seen through friction, so indeed is Hari perceived through meditation.
The oneness of Brahman and the Self is Yoga, and it is the highest of the high; liberation does not come through external forms, but rather through internal practices such as *yama* and the rest.

Indeed, that direct realization of the Self through the knowledge of Sāṅkhya, through Yoga, and through the hearing of Vedānta is designated as liberation; it is the perception of the nature of the Self in what is not the Self, and the perception of the nature of the existent in what is non-existent.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Knowledge of Brahman," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

The Blessed Lord said: O Nārada, listen as I shall explain the knowledge of the Self according to its true nature. They call non-duality (advaita) Sāṅkhya, while Yoga therein is the state of one-pointedness of mind.
Those perfected in the yoga of non-duality are liberated from the great bondage; through awakening, past, present, and future karma are destroyed.
One whose tree of saṃsāra has been cut down by the axe of right reflection attains the state of Viṣṇu through the sacred ford of knowledge and dispassion.
Waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are called the triple city of Māyā; everything is contained within this very eternal, non-dual state.
That supreme state is entirely devoid of the activity of name-and-form; having created the infinite world, the Lord himself entered into it.
"I know this Person, whose nature is consciousness, beyond darkness; 'I am He'—this is for liberation, for there is no other path to freedom."
Hearing, reflection, and meditation are indeed the means for attaining true knowledge; liberation is not obtained through sacrifice, charity, austerity, pilgrimage, or the Vedas.
Just as by means of renunciation, meditation, worship, ritual action, and so forth, the Vedic word is twofold: "Perform action" and "Renounce [action]."
Some have stated here that sacrifices and other rites for those who are liberated and free from desire serve only for the sake of purifying the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) toward liberation.
Liberation through knowledge in a single lifetime does not belong to those who perceive duality; such are the Brahmins born into families of yogis who have fallen from yoga or practice flawed yoga.
A living being is bound by action; through knowledge, one becomes liberated from existence. One should indeed take refuge in self-knowledge, for ignorance is that which is otherwise.
When all desires that reside within one's heart are liberated, then one attains immortality even while living; of this there is no doubt.
Since it is all-pervasive, how does it go; who goes, and where does it go? Since it is infinite, no location exists; since it is formless, whence can there be movement?

Because it is non-dual, no one exists; because it is consciousness, how could there be insentience? That which is designated as "other" is merely the state of the movement of another's thought and speech.
How can there be coming, going, or staying for one who is like space? Waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are merely imagined through illusion.
O wise one, that which is the radiant reality is the merit that is indivisible; just as you are dear to yourself, so too are you dear to us all.
O Great Sage, just as the mind is on the path of awakening for all, so it is held to be for all beings at all times and for everything.

I do not perceive here any self-consciousness; therefore, it is full and uninterrupted—the waking state, the dreaming state, as well as the conduct of the dreamless sleep and even the bliss of deep slumber.
If there is no recollection of a forgotten object, for whom would it arise? Let it be true that the atom (*aṇu*) is likewise bodiless (*aśarīra*) and supreme (*para*).
If there were no experience of all pleasures and pains, how could the Omniscient One always and everywhere know the heart of every being?
Relying upon Him as the witness, who can know His activity? That which is distinct from Truth, Knowledge, and Infinity would not be separate from Truth and Knowledge.
Bliss is not separate from infinity, nor is infinity separate from bliss; you alone are the supreme Brahman, characterized by existence, knowledge, and the rest.
Having realized that "I am Brahman," the supreme reality, one becomes all-knowing; just as when a single object made of clay is known, all this world of moving and non-moving things is understood.
Just as everything becomes golden by means of a single golden gem, so too does the entire world become [golden] through the knowledge of the Lord, who is himself possessed of knowledge.
Just as a rope is not clearly seen due to the defect of darkness, so too the self is not clearly seen due to the defect of delusion.
The nature of a thing is conceptualized otherwise through distinctions such as the coils of a serpent; likewise, the self is conceptualized otherwise through attributes such as being like space.

Even that substance which is directly perceived is said to be difficult to see, just as space and so forth are [said to be such] by means of qualities like form and so on, which are otherwise imagined.
For just as a snake is [imagined] in a rope, silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, or water in a mirage, O Viṣṇu, so too is the world [imagined]. It is only a thirst for satisfaction.
Just as a certain twice-born man, crying out "Alas! Alas! O Brahmin! I am ruined!", might think he has regained his Brahminhood upon the disappearance of the eclipse; so it is with this.
Similarly, possessed by māyā, the individual soul (jīva) thinks, "I am the body"; yet, through the destruction of māyā, it again realizes its own true nature, thinking, "I am Brahman."

Just as one who has been freed from an eclipse is no longer looked upon with hostility by respectable people, so too this [world] ceases through the manifestation of its true nature, and not without that [manifestation].
Both are equal in being beginningless, yet their natures are distinct from one another; through investigation, it is seen that one is truly real while the other is ultimately false.
For even though I am unborn, I manifest once again after passing away through my own *māyā*; by the will of *māyā*, I become twofold as husband and wife for the happiness of the world.
The three qualities (traiguṇya) exist separately in twenty-eight distinct forms; and eighty-four thousand varieties are observed, consisting of the forms of men and women.
The entire universe arises from these through illusion, like that which is born from a fragment; in the beginning and at the end, these—name, form, action, and so forth—do not exist.
The conceptualization of existence at any time does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality; just as chariots and the like in a dream appear to exist but do not exist in truth.
Likewise, in the waking state, beings do not exist in their true presence; through *māyā*, they assume a dual form in the two states known as waking and dreaming.
Thus, this supreme Brahman, in the two states of dream and waking, is called the non-dual state whose form is the unmoving deep sleep.
Established through the investigation of illusion, it dissolves by that very investigation; even that conceptualization, though existing in time, is devoid of any ultimate reality.
Thus, for her, the Sun is established as the one born of truth; from the existence of that which is real, there follows the unreality of non-existence.

Even beyond that knowledge is our infinite Self, Śuka, who is full within by his own nature. Because I am not born from any eternal entity and because I have performed no action, I am immortal. Like a lamp, I am the light within the heart; I am Brahman for the sake of liberation.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Nature of Self-Knowledge," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. The Blessed Lord said: I shall proclaim the essence of the Gītā as it was spoken of old to Arjuna; [he who is] whose self is united with the eightfold yoga and who has reached the further shore of all Vedānta.

The supreme attainment of the Self is none other than that which is devoid of the body and so forth; it is not the eye consisting of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and the rest, which ends with the body characterized by inferior forms and qualities.

For in deep sleep, the vital breath (prāṇa) is perceived as devoid of consciousness; nor is the "I" the Self, because it is associated with suffering and the like, as well as with the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra).
Like a smokeless fire with blazing flames,
like the radiant sun, or like the fire of lightning in the sky, [he dwells] within the heart-center, in the Self by the Self.
The ear and the other senses do not perceive their own respective selves by means of themselves; it is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who is omniscient and all-seeing, that perceives them.
For when the Self shines forth like a lamp burning within a cloth, knowledge arises for men through the destruction of sinful karma.
Just as one sees one's own self within oneself in that which resembles the surface of a mirror, so too does one perceive the senses, the objects of the senses, and the five great elements.
Having thoroughly discerned the mind, the intellect, the ego, the unmanifest, and likewise the Puruṣa, one who is pervaded by the Supreme becomes liberated from all bonds.
Having withdrawn the entire collection of senses into the mind, O Pāṇḍava, and having established the mind itself within the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra);
Having established the ego-sense in the intellect, the intellect in primordial nature (prakṛti), primordial nature in the Puruṣa, and the Puruṣa in Brahman, one should rest there.
Having fully realized "I am Brahman, the supreme light," one is liberated. This house has nine doors; it is the witness of three and five.

The wise one who knows that [the field] is presided over by the Knower of the Field is the excellent sage. Thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of knowledge.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Essence of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā," in the Ācāra-kāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrva-khaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. The Blessed Lord said: O Pārtha, Yama and Niyama, Āsana, Prāṇāyāma, Pratyāhāra, as well as Dhyāna and Dhāraṇā as the seventh, O Arjuna. *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—238* The Blessed Lord said: O Pārtha, [the eight limbs are] Yama, Niyama, Āsana, Prāṇasaṃyama (Prāṇāyāma), Pratyāhāra, as well as Dhyāna, and Dhāraṇā as the seventh, O Arjuna.
And what is called "concentration" is said to be the eightfold yoga for the sake of liberation: [the restraint] of action, mind, and speech toward all beings at all times.

The dharma that consists in refraining from violence is indeed non-violence, which is the supreme happiness; for that act of violence which is performed according to the prescribed rule is proclaimed as non-violence itself.
One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak an unpleasant truth, nor should one speak a pleasant falsehood—this is the eternal dharma.
The theft of property, whether by stealth or by force, is *steya* (theft); the non-practice of that is *asteya*, a means for achieving dharma.
The renunciation of sexual intercourse at all times, in all circumstances, and in every way—whether by deed, mind, or speech—is declared to be *brahmacarya*.
The non-acceptance of material things even in times of distress, according to one's will, is called "non-possession" (aparigraha); one should avoid it with great effort.

Purity is twofold: external, consisting of earth and water, and internal, arising from one's disposition; contentment is satisfaction with whatever is obtained by chance, which is the hallmark of happiness.
The one-pointed concentration of the mind and the senses is the supreme austerity; so too is the emaciation of the body through such practices as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances.
The wise declare that the recitation of the Vedānta, the Śatarudrīya, the Praṇava, and so forth, constitutes *svādhyāya* for men, which brings about the purification of the inner being (*sattva*).

Unwavering devotion toward Hari through the actions of speech, mind, and body—such as praise, remembrance, and worship—is this contemplation of the Lord. The postures known as Svastika, Padma, and Ardhasana are likewise prescribed.
Prāṇa is the wind born of one's own body; āyāma is its restraint, [applied] to the senses as they wander among objects that are as if non-existent.
The Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 239.

Brahmā said: I shall proclaim the Brahmagītā, by knowing which one is liberated from worldly existence; through the knowledge arising from the realization "I am Brahman," liberation occurs for all people.

From the knowledge of the meanings of the two words "I" and "Brahman," the knowledge of the sentence arises. The wise consider the meanings of these two words to be twofold: the expressed (vācya) and the indicated (lakṣya).

The variegated (śabala) is proclaimed as that which is expressed by the sentence, while the pure (śuddha) is the indicated meaning; it consists of the vital breath, the body, and the self, which is incomparable to the minds of those who have restrained their senses.
Thus, by the word "I," the form that is not the foremost (the unmanifest) is served by the Vedas; however, the immediate, non-dual form is realized by the word "I."
That which consists of immutable bliss and consciousness, together with the transcendent, and which is composed of the vital breath and the physical body, is the second division.

For here, the aspect that perceives what is beyond the senses would be indicated by the word "I" (*vāham*); likewise, by the word "Brahman" itself, the cause consisting of the vital breath and the physical body [is indicated].
By abandoning the notions of finality and mediacy, non-dual bliss-consciousness will be described by means of the term "the inner Brahman" (*pratyag-brahma*).
And for one who remains having characterized non-dual bliss-consciousness as "I am Brahman" and "Brahman am I," regarding the two referents of the word "Brahman":

Furthermore, from the statement "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*), which aims at the fruit of one's own direct experience, the knowledge of oneness (*aikyajñāna*) certainly arises far more readily from the Vedānta.
Liberation results from the cessation of the effects of ignorance through knowledge, by virtue of their identity.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Essence of the Brahmagītā," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Blessed Lord said: From that, although it is Brahman, space (kha) arises; from space, air (marut); and from air, fire (anala).

From fire comes water, and from that, the earth, which gives birth to the form of the phenomenal world; from that arises the seventeenth principle, the subtle body (liṅga), as well as the five organs of action.
The organs of speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ; then the organs of cognition: the ear, skin, eyes, tongue, and the nose; and there are the five vital airs.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, vyāna, and udāna; the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) consists of the mind (manas) and the intellect (dhī); and the mind is characterized by doubt.
But the intellect (*buddhi*), which consists of determination, has this subtle nature; it is the *sūtra* of Hiraṇyagarbha, characterized by its own effects as its mark.
The fivefold-composed elements indeed arise from the non-fivefold-composed elements; from those fivefold-composed elements, the cosmic egg was produced.

The body known as the gross (sthūla), which is well-known in the world and possesses feet and other limbs, consists of the fivefold-combined elements (pañcīkṛta-bhūta) and their effects, and is situated therein.
All that is produced from the body of living beings is said by the wise to be gross; however, the body situated within the Supreme Self is declared to be threefold.

Furthermore, you, the individual soul (jīva), who enters the two bodies, are in reality none other than Brahman itself, which has entered the two bodies according to the scriptural statements concerning its own differentiation.

Like water and the sun, and like the jujube fruit, the individual soul (jīva) sustains the vital breaths and other functions; it is traditionally remembered as the witness of the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
He is distinct from those states known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; He is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), without parts, unattached, and eternally pure by nature.
The Supreme Self alone is that which is considered threefold through the states of waking, dreaming, and so forth; it is the internal organ situated within the aggregate of internal organs.
For one who perceives waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, there is always modification regarding the fruit, the action, and the agent; I shall now describe waking and the other states.
Now, consciousness through the sense faculties is declared to be the waking state; it is the cognition arising from the impressions of the waking state for one who seeks objects.
Dreaming and deep sleep are the states of the intellect when the collection of instruments [is withdrawn]; its abiding in the causal state of Brahman is by way of the nature of time.

The living being perceives the states of waking and so forth through both gradual and non-gradual processes; however, at the time of commencing meditative absorption (samādhi), one should first bring them under control.
Then, when the desire for liberation has arisen and the internal organ has become isolated, one should dissolve the collection of fields and leave only that field remaining.
Just as a jar is not distinct from the clay because it is its effect, so too, objects such as vessels are not distinct from the fivefold-composed elements.

The learned authorities declare that the subtle body (sūkṣmaśarīra) is distinct from the quintuplicated elements (pañcīkṛtāni bhūtāni) and consists of the non-quintuplicated elements (apañcīkṛtabhūta).
The subtle body (liṅga) is not distinct from the unevolved elements; it does not exist without the earth as its support, nor does that [earth] exist without it.
Fire does not exist without wind, nor indeed does wind exist without space; and space does not exist without Brahman, for there is no pure space apart from Brahman.

Then, being of pure nature, there is the non-occurrence of waking, dreaming, and so forth; it is devoid of the state of being a living soul (jīvatva), having attained conformity with its own intrinsic consciousness.
Eternal, pure, awakened, liberated, true, and non-dual is Brahman; the suffixes "-tattvam" and "-padam" remain [as case endings], and the word "tat" (that) denotes Brahman.
The letter *u*, the letter *a*, and the letter *m*—this is the pair of Ṛks. "I am Brahman; I am Brahman, the knowledge that increases the destruction of ignorance."
This Self is the supreme light, whose nature is consciousness and bliss; it is indeed Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite, as proclaimed by the Śruti in the words, "Thou art That."

"I am Brahman, untainted; I am Brahman, all-pervading. That Person who is in the sun, I am He, the beginningless one. This essence of the Gītā was taught to Arjuna, by which indeed there is absorption into Brahman.
Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Essence of the Brahma-Gītā," in the Ācāra-kāṇḍa of the first part of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, Chapter 240, Hari said: "O Rudra, this essence of the Purāṇa known as the Gāruḍa has been proclaimed by me to you, while Brahmā and others were listening; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
O Rudra, he who reads or hears this, which brings about knowledge, fame, splendor, fortune, victory, health, and so forth, shall become all-knowing and go to heaven.
Brahmā said: "O Vyāsa, thus have I heard this ancient Purāṇa of Viṣṇu, which bestows liberation. Vyāsa said: "Having heard this meritorious Gāruḍa Purāṇa, Brahmā spoke thus to us."
Dakṣa, Nārada, and others, having meditated upon Brahman, attained Hari; and by me, Sūta, this supreme Purāṇa has been narrated to you.
Having heard which, one who has attained all desires shall obtain the fruit of Brahman; therefore, Viṣṇu spoke this most essential Gāruḍa [Purāṇa] to Garuḍa.
It possesses great essence and bestows the wealth of the Dharma, desire, liberation, and so forth. Sūta said: "O Śaunaka, the preeminent Gāruḍa Purāṇa has been declared to you."

That which Vyāsa formerly spoke to me as the essence uttered by Garuḍa—having heard the auspicious Gāruḍa Purāṇa from Brahmā, Hari, while meditating on the Lord, divided that single Veda into four parts.
"Śuka indeed told me those eighteen Purāṇas; however, this most excellent Gāruḍa has been narrated by me to you, O Śaunaka."
In the midst of the sages who were listening, he asked about the teacher of all things; whoever should read it, or listen to it, or cause it to be heard with a concentrated mind.
One who writes it oneself, causes it to be written, or indeed maintains it in a book, shall surely attain the purpose of the Dharma; and one who seeks the purpose of wealth shall attain wealth.
One who desires pleasures shall obtain those pleasures; one whose aim is liberation shall obtain liberation. Whatever one desires, all that one shall obtain from hearing the *Garuḍa*.
A Brāhmaṇa shall become one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas; of this there is no doubt. And a Kṣatriya here on earth becomes the protector of a Kṣatriya as well.
Indeed, no one else may hear this Purāṇa which is equal to the Vedas; if that foolish-minded person should speak it [to others], he shall suffer the loss of his fame.
If a learned Brāhmaṇa who has been initiated recites this to anyone else, this Gāruḍa [Purāṇa] must be heard by all those who have been initiated by Brāhmaṇas.
Just as Viṣṇu is, so is Tārkṣya; by praising Tārkṣya, Hari is praised. Having heard the Gāruḍa and the Vasurāja, King Vasu indeed obtained everything.
Varuṇa said: I pay homage to the mighty-armed one, the lord of birds, whose vehicle is the tawny horse; he who dwells above Viṣṇu and who has terrified the great asuras.
Salutations to you, O destroyer of the pride of the Nāgas, the increaser of Vinatā’s joy, you who are impartial yet favor the virtuous, and who are gazed upon by the wretched Daityas.
By their mutual curse, Supratīka and Vibhāvasu became an elephant and a tortoise, and the two brothers remained joined together.
When it is raised up, it is one *yojana* in height; it is twice that length [two *yojanas*] and three *yojanas* in thickness, with a circumference of one hundred *yojanas*.
O bird, those two base ones, though possessing four arms, must not be eaten by you; they have been liberated from the fault of the curse they inflicted upon one another.
"By tasting the land of the Niṣādas, why did you speak ill of the Lord? Therefore, the Lord of Despair has been released; even there, a Brahmin was [harmed] by you."

All the gods, led by Śakra, were defeated by you in battle; long ago, O descendant of Kaśyapa, you brought back that Soma after extinguishing the fire.
Having made the two Nāgas sight-poisonous and blinded them with dust, did he not strike them with his sharp-pointed [weapon], while they were devoid of agitation and their minds were struck down?

"What is the color of Uccaiḥśravas? "He is white," he replied; but he said, "I consider him to be black in color, as I saw him previously."

By mere meditation, poison—whether stationary or mobile—is destroyed; and whoever recites or hears this shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Sūta said: Having heard the Gāruḍa Purāṇa, Vasurāja indeed attained everything; the blessed Garuḍa, meditating upon Viṣṇu, attained everything.
The man who recites this meritorious Gāruḍa Purāṇa shall attain all his desires and thereafter reach the supreme goal.
By reciting even a single quarter-verse of this hymn, all evil shall be destroyed; and for whomever this exists in their home, everything auspicious shall come to pass here in this world.
The wisdom that resides in the hand of one who holds the Gāruḍa [Purāṇa] is within his grasp; whoever reads or hears this shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Through hearing [this] and so forth, one shall attain dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; one seeking sons obtains sons, and one seeking desires attains desire.
One seeking knowledge obtains knowledge; one seeking victory obtains victory; even a sinner guilty of such acts as the killing of a Brahmin attains purification from that sin.
Even a barren woman obtains a son, and a maiden finds a virtuous husband; one seeking security attains security, and one seeking enjoyment shall obtain enjoyment.

One who seeks auspiciousness shall obtain auspiciousness; one who seeks virtues shall obtain virtue; one who seeks the meaning of poetry shall obtain the state of being a poet; and one who seeks the essence shall obtain the essence.
One who seeks knowledge attains that wisdom which crushes all saṃsāra; this is the auspicious, blessed Gāruḍa [tantra], proclaimed by Garuḍa.
There shall be no untimely death for one who recites even a single verse; by reciting even half a verse of this, the destruction of wicked enemies is certain.
Having heard this from Sūta at the sacrifice of Śaunaka, I, while contemplating "I am Brahman" along with the sages, became liberated through the grace of the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
Thus ends the two hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Garuḍa Purāṇa," in the Ācāra-kāṇḍa (Section on Conduct) of the first part of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
May there be auspiciousness! Thus concludes the Ācāra-kāṇḍa in the first part of the Śrī Garuḍa Purāṇa. The Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Now begins the second part of the first section, the *Pretakāṇḍa*, known as the *Dharmakāṇḍa*. Om! Salutations to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva. Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa, and to Nara, the best of men, and to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then proclaim the *Jaya*.

Having seen the variety of their faults and even their falling within the domain of death, who would be cheerful in mind? How can there be any wonder in death?

Whether it occurs immediately or after a delay, does he attain another body? For one being led along the path of Yama for a year, what purpose would there be in the act of dying?
What atonement is there for one of evil mind who has died during the five-day period? Grant me grace; you ought to sever my delusion entirely.
I have asked about everything; please speak for the benefit of the world.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Elaboration of Questions," in the Pretakhaṇḍa of the Dharmakāṇḍa, within the second part of the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 2.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "Well asked by you, O auspicious one, for the benefit of mankind indeed! Listen with an attentive mind to everything concerning the rites for the deceased."
It is free from any correct differentiation, extracted from the Śruti and Smṛti, and that which has not been seen even by the gods led by Indra, nor by yogis who contemplate yoga.

O Tārkṣya, these sesame seeds produced from my sweat are purifying; by means of these sesame seeds, the asuras, dānavas, and daityas flee in all directions.
White sesame seeds, black sesame seeds, and sesame seeds resembling cow’s urine—may they indeed burn away the sins committed by me with my body.
A single sesame seed given is equal to a droṇa of gold; when given during libations, gifts, or fire-offerings, it becomes inexhaustible.
Darbha grasses arise from body hair, and sesame seeds from sweat; it is not otherwise. Through the śrāddha rite, both the deities and the dānavas are satisfied, as are the ancestors.

According to the rule of application, Brahmā is the universe and also its source of sustenance; starting from the left with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), Brahmā, the ancestors, and the gods of the gods [are worshipped].

By that, those ancestors are satisfied when the rite is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder; Brahmā stands at the root of the darbha grass, and the Lord Janārdana stands in the middle.

One should know Śaṅkara to be at the tip of the darbha grass; the three gods are said to reside in the kuśa. O Lord of Birds, the brāhmaṇas, the mantras, the káśa grass, the fire, and the tulasī are likewise [sacred].
O bird, these do not become like withered offerings even when performed again and again: Tulasī, Brāhmaṇas, cows, Viṣṇu, and Ekādaśī.
For men sinking in the ocean of worldly existence, there are five means of transport: Viṣṇu, Ekādaśī, the Gītā, Tulasī, and Brahmin-cows.
In this essence-less and difficult saṃsāra, the six-footed [Tulasī] bestows liberation; likewise, sesame seeds are incomparable purifiers, as are darbha grass and tulasī.
And these [rites] ward off the miserable destinies for one who is suffering and heading toward them; one should pick up the darbha grass with both hands and sprinkle it upon the ground with water.
At the time of death, one should cast *darbha* grasses into the hands of the patient; for he who is cast away by the *darbhas* is indeed enveloped by the *darbhas*.
Even a man devoid of mantras goes indeed to the world of Viṣṇu, having made a tuft of hair on his head and standing with his feet placed upon the surface of the earth.
As an expiation for this worthless ocean of saṃsāra, one should smear a pure fire-pit with cow dung and establish it upon a bed of darbha grass.
By giving a gift of a vehicle, one dispels all evil; it is like divine salt-flavor, which grants all desires to men.
Since all food-flavors are not intense without salt, and since that which is pleasing to the ancestors is auspicious, it shall therefore bestow heaven.
Since this salty flavor originated from the body of Viṣṇu, yogis therefore praise this gift as being "with salt" (salavaṇa).
When the life-breaths of women of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes, as well as of the Śūdra people and of the sick person, do not depart from the surface of the earth;
Then salt should be given for the opening of the door to heaven; hear further, O Lord of Birds, the detailed description of the form of Death.
For whom there would not be a separation of life and body by time, and for living beings, death at its appointed hour would be a total oblivion.
Just as the wind drags the clouds hither and thither, even so, O Tārkṣya, like those clouds, all beings follow the power of Time alone.
Whether they be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), or darkness (tāmasa), all states of being, which are essentially temporal in nature, indeed manifest within living beings.
The Sun, the Moon, Śambhu, Water, Vāyu, Śatakratu, Fire, Space, Earth, Mitra, the Herbs, and likewise the Vasus.
O slayer of serpents, rivers and oceans, as well as existence and non-existence—all these are created by Time and withdrawn by it once again.
When death has arrived, O bird, men are withdrawn by Time; then, through the conjunction of fate, some disease arises.
There would be a deficiency of the sense faculties and a loss of strength and vigor if one were simultaneously bitten by ten million scorpions and ten million lice.
Then, O bird, suffering born of death is inferred by that [sign]; thereafter, in an instant, consciousness becomes impaired and sinks into insensibility.
Then the vital breaths are drawn forth by the messengers of Yama who stand nearby; at that time, a loathsome form arises as the breaths reach the throat.
Then he vomits foam and his mouth becomes covered with saliva; then, from that body, a person the size of a thumb emerges, crying out "Alas! Alas! (hā hā).
At that very moment, O dear one, he is led away by the messengers of Yama toward his own house, once again facing this state of death at its appointed time.
The earth element, provoked within the body and impelled by a fierce wind, blazes like a fire without fuel and shatters the vital points (marmas).
The vital air named udāna moves upward from there; it prevents the downward movement of food and those who have no desire to eat.
He who has not spoken falsehoods, nor caused a breach of affection, and who is a believer and full of faith, attains a happy death.
He who would not abandon the Dharma out of desire, nor out of passion, nor out of hatred; who acts according to what has been taught and is gentle—he attains death with ease.
Those who impart false knowledge attain the greatest darkness, as do false witnesses, liars, and those who betray trust.
Those who revile the Vedas likewise fall into delusion and death; they are terrifying, foul-smelling, and carry staffs and clubs in their hands.
Then the evil-minded messengers of Yama arrive; when such a terrible path is reached, trembling arises within him.
He too cries out incessantly for his father, mother, and children; yet that speech of his, though indistinct, manifests with effort as a single syllable.
His vision indeed wanders due to terror, and his face withers from gasping; then, overcome by that agony, he abandons that body.
It becomes untouchable and contemptible at that very moment. Thus has the true nature of death been described; now, something else will also be mentioned in this context.
I shall now answer for you the second question regarding diversity: it is due to the non-existence of former karmas, O Blessed One.
There would be a diversity of enjoyments for the wandering living beings here in this world, such as the state of a god, a demon, or a yakṣa, which bestows happiness.
O Lord of Birds, human existence, animal existence, and that of birds and so forth—which bring extreme suffering—occur here according to the gradations of one's karmas.
In this regard, I shall proclaim to you the ripening of karmas, through the diversity of which this living being wanders in saṃsāra, so that its manifold nature may become clear.
Having reached the terrible and dreadful hells born of great sins (mahāpātaka), those who have committed great sins are reborn on earth once their karma is exhausted.
Listen to me, O best of beings, regarding those characteristics by which they are defined: a slayer of a Brahmin enters the wombs of deer, horses, pigs, and camels.
A stealer of gold shall attain the state of worms, insects, and moths; and one who violates the Guru’s bed shall gradually become grass and shrubs.
A killer of a Brahmin shall suffer from consumption; a drinker of spirituous liquor, black teeth; a stealer of gold, deformed nails; and one who violates the teacher’s bed, a skin disease.
Whosoever dwells with any of these acquires their characteristics; by associating with one who has fallen from his status for a year, he himself becomes an outcast.
Sin is transmitted among men through conversation, touch, shared breath, traveling together, eating together, sitting together, officiating at sacrifices for them, teaching them, and sexual union.
Having gone to the wives of others and having stolen the property of a Brahmin, one is born as a Brahma-rākṣasa in a desolate region of the forest.
One who steals jewels will be born into a low caste; and having taken the leaves or branches of a tree, a man becomes a musk-shrew.
By stealing grain one becomes a mouse; by stealing a vehicle, a camel; by stealing fruit, a monkey; by eating food without [offering] mantras, a crow; and by stealing household utensils, a vulture.

One who steals honey becomes bitten by bees; one who steals fruit becomes a vulture; one who steals a cow becomes an iguana; likewise, one who steals fire becomes a crane. One who steals a woman's garment becomes afflicted with white leprosy, and one who steals flavorful food suffers from a loss of appetite.

One who steals bell-metal becomes a swan; one who steals the property of another becomes afflicted with epilepsy; a killer of his guru becomes a person suffering from chronic convulsions; and one who commits cruel deeds becomes a dwarf.
One who abandons his lawful wife becomes a creature on earth that pierces with sound; one who steals the property of gods or Brahmins becomes a pale-skinned eater of human flesh.

One who steals consecrated offerings is born with a goiter and suffers from a major disease; one who misappropriates what has been deposited becomes one-eyed, and one who lives off women becomes lame.

One who abandons his wife while she is still in her youth becomes unfortunate; furthermore, one who eats the food of a prostitute or one who approaches the wife of a Brahmin becomes a jackal, suffering from abdominal tumors caused by wind.
The stealer of a bed becomes a mendicant ascetic; the stealer of clothing becomes a moth; from envy one becomes blind from birth; and the stealer of a lamp becomes a skull-bearer.

One who is a Kausika, a betrayer of friends, one who suffers decay, a reviler of his father and others, one whose speech falters, a speaker of falsehood, and a false witness—all these become those with dropsy.
Then that gnat, with its lips cut off, shall become an obstacle at the wedding; or else he shall become a low-born outcaste who voids excrement and urine in the public square.

One who causes difficulty in urination becomes a defiler of a maiden, and one who sells the Vedas incurs impotence; a seller of the Vedas becomes a leopard, and one who officiates at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice becomes a boar.
From that [state], one becomes a cat; from there, a firefly; from there, a consumer of what is being carried; a worm that eats putrid things; and one who is envious becomes a bee.
