One who extinguishes a fire shall become afflicted with leprosy; one who takes what is not given shall become a eunuch; a stealer of cows shall become a serpent; and a stealer of food shall suffer from indigestion.
One who gives water becomes a fish; one who gives milk becomes a crane; and by giving stale food to a Brahmin, one shall incur hunchbackedness.
O bird, he who steals fruits sees his lineage die out; indeed, the man who eats food without having given it away shall be childless.
O King, by stealing a book, one becomes a formless piśāca after departing for the religious life; one who steals water becomes a cātaka bird, and one who steals a man becomes blind from birth.
Having promised wealth to the twice-born, if one does not give it, he becomes a jackal; by slandering those of noble birth, one obtains the body of a tortoise.

One who sells fruit becomes unfortunate; one who is the husband of a low-caste woman becomes a wolf; one who touches fire with his foot becomes a cat; and one who eats the flesh of others becomes afflicted by disease.
A man who breaks a water conduit shall become a fish; likewise those who do not listen to the stories of Hari nor offer praise to virtuous people.
O Hari, let this [mantra] reach those men at the root of their ears and no other people—those dull-witted ones who seize the morsel of food situated in the mouth of another.
If one seeks divine implements for this Gaṇḍamālin, yet practices dharma through deceit, he shall become Gajacarma.

Diseases such as headaches afflict the betrayer of trust; likewise, one who causes pain to the *liṅga*, misappropriates the property of Śiva, or consumes the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*) to Śiva [is similarly afflicted].
Women also, by abducting [men] through this same path, incur guilt; they become wives of these very same creatures.

"Understand that all this belongs to hell at the end of enjoyment. O Khagha, I have told you this in brief as it is being shown to you; for the varieties of living beings are exactly like the varieties of material objects."

Thus, the diversity of human beings' pleasures, pains, and even their births has been described as resulting from their own various karmas; they declare that from wholesome action comes the wholesome, and likewise from unwholesome action comes the unwholesome.
All this that I was asked by you here has been fully explained.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Description of the Rituals for the Deceased and the Ripening of Karma," in the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa*, within the *Pratākhaṇḍa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
*Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*— 3.
Sūta said: Thus encouraged, the bird, having heard of the hells, asked about the various infernal realms with his inner self agitated.
Garuḍa said: Tell me the true nature of the hells into which those who perform evil deeds are cast, abounding as they do in suffering; and proclaim their various divisions.
The Blessed One said: "O younger brother of Aruṇa, thousands of hells indeed exist; it is not possible to describe them in detail, so I shall speak of them according to their principal ones."
Now learn from me about that primary hell named Raurava; indeed, it is there that the man who gives false testimony and the man who is untruthful go.
Raurava is indeed two thousand yojanas in extent; there, moreover, is a pit of knee-deep depth that is extremely difficult to cross.
There, a mass of burning coals was made level with the earth; there, the ground of coals was heated by an extremely fierce fire.
In the midst of that, the followers of Yama release the evildoer; burning with intense fire, he runs about.
At every step, his foot bursts and is shattered again; he proceeds by taking steps that are extracted [from the ground] within a single day and night.
In this way, he is released after a thousand vast leagues; thereafter, for the sake of purifying other sins, he goes to a similar hell.
Raurava has been described by me as the first hell; now hear, O bird, about the hell named Mahāraurava.
It extends for five thousand yojanas all around; there the ground is made of copper, and beneath it is fire.
Scorching with that [radiance], she, possessing a brilliance like a flashing lightning bolt, appears as exceedingly fierce to sinners upon the mere sight of her.
And there, with his hands and feet bound by the followers of Yama, the evildoer is released and goes along, wallowing in the midst [of the river].
Being devoured by crows, cranes, wolves, owls, mosquitoes, and scorpions, as well as by other fierce creatures, he is dragged along on the path.
Burning with grief, his mind lost and wandering, he cries out repeatedly in agitation, "O Father!", and being overwhelmed by distress, he finds no peace.
Thus, liberation is attained by those men who have transcended [worldly existence], even if tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of years of evil have been committed by them with corrupt minds.
Likewise, another named Atiśīta (Exceeding Cold) is there by its very nature; it is as long as Mahāraurava and is likewise enveloped in blinding darkness.
Afflicted by cold, men are bound there in that terrible darkness; having encountered one another, they embrace and seek refuge in each other.
Their teeth break as they tremble from the affliction of cold; moreover, O bird, there are calamities there consisting of the extreme power of hunger and thirst.
A cruel wind, carrying fragments of snow, shatters their bones; there, possessed by hunger, they incessantly devour the marrow, blood, and bone-fluids that have oozed out.
Being embraced as they wander together in union, even so there is likewise great suffering for men in that darkness.
O best of birds, one who has accumulated many [evil deeds] reaches that which is known as Nikṛntana; beyond that is another, the most excellent of hells.
O bird, there the potter's wheels revolve incessantly; upon them, men are dragged along by the Kālasūtra cord.
O best of birds, by means of the Yāmānuja-mark situated on their fingers, [they protect] from the soles of their feet to the crown of their heads; yet no loss of life occurs for them.
Their bodies, cut into hundreds of pieces, indeed become whole again; in this manner, those who have committed evil deeds wander for thousands of years.
Listen as I speak until that evil has been entirely exhausted and he no longer falls into hell.
There, the hell-beings dwelling therein experience unbearable suffering; those very wheels and water-wheels [operate] there from another direction.
Certain men who have committed evil deeds and have become the cause of their own suffering are mounted upon wheels and made to whirl there.
For as many as thousands of years there is no cessation of their existence, like those bound in water-wheels or like those tied in a water-bag.
Men wander about, vomiting blood again and again, with entrails protruding from their mouths and eyes hanging down by the entrails.
Listen now to another hell called Asipatravana, where beings experience sufferings that are unbearable in this world.
There, upon a ground of glowing embers, seven fires with fierce rays blaze for a thousand yojanas in that intense and most dreadful place.
There, the beings dwelling in hell are constantly scorched; yet in their midst, a foot with cool and glossy leaves is said to appear.
O best of birds, where there are fragments of fruits upon the leaves, there very powerful dogs roam about, feeding on meat.
With large mouths and great fangs, they possessed the immense strength of tigers; then, they beheld before them a forest providing cool shade.
There, living beings go, tormented by hunger and heat, crying out in great misery, "O mother! O brother! O father!"
For those who had gone there, their pair of feet was being scorched by the fire situated on the earth, yet even there, the breeze was exceedingly cool.
By that wind they are blown, and thus their swords fall upon them; severed, they fall to the ground into a mass of blazing fire.
And while another part of the entire scorched earth is being licked, those dogs swiftly tear at his body.
O dear one, I have described this extremely terrifying Forest of Sword-leaves (Asipatravana), where many fragments of those [beings] are found as they weep.
Beyond this, learn from me of the even more terrifying Taptakumbha hell; there, heated cauldrons are situated on all sides, filled with flames of fire.
Filled with heaps of blazing fire, heated oil, and iron dust, those of evil deeds are indeed cast head-first into these by the servants of Yama.
They are boiled there, their limbs bursting open and their marrow and fluids flowing out, while their skulls split asunder and their bones are hacked by terrifying beings.
Torn apart by vultures, they are released again only to be seized by them with even greater speed; once more they are scorched with a crackling sound and reduced to a single mass of oil.
Then, with their heads, limbs, sinews, flesh, skin, and bones liquefied, they are quickly struck by the staffs of the Yama-men.
In the Kṛtāvarta hell, where there is great boiling oil, those who have committed evil deeds are boiled. Thus, O bird, has this Tapta-kumbha hell been described by me in detail to you.
The first is said to be Raurava, the next is Mahāraurava; the third is Atiśīta, and the fourth is indeed Nikṛntana.
The fifth is Apratiṣṭha, and another is Asipatravana; the seventh is Taptakumbha—these seven are considered to be the hells.
Other hells as well are likewise heard of, O lowest of men; for indeed, they fall into those various hells according to the gradations of their actions.
For they are as follows: Naraka, Rodha, Śūkara, and Tāla; Tapta-kumbha, Mahājvāla, Śabala, and Vimohana.
Krimi, Krimabhakṣa, Lālābhakṣa, Viṣañjana, Adhaḥśiras, Pūyavaha, Rudhirāndha, and Viḍrabhuja.
Likewise Vaitaraṇī, Sūcīmukha, Asipatravana, the most terrible Agnijvāla, Sandaṃśa, and Abhojana.
Tama, Kālasūtra, Loha, Abhida, Apratiṣṭha, Avīci, and other such hells.
All the hells situated within the domain of Yama are characterized by darkness; indeed, those who have performed evil deeds fall into them individually.
All those [hells] beginning with Raurava are proclaimed to be beneath the earth; a man who is a killer of a cow, a killer of a bull, a destroyer of an embryo, or a giver of fire shall fall there.

A killer of a Brahmin shall immerse himself in a boar; a drinker of liquor and a thief of gold [shall do likewise]; a slayer of a Kṣatriya shall fall from a palm tree; and having killed a Vaiśya, one goes to a miserable state.

He who commits the murder of a Brahmin, he who violates the bed of his guru, he who approaches his own sister, one who is in a heated cauldron, as well as a king's soldier and a liar—[these all fall into this hell].
The seller of molten metals, likewise the guard of a prison, the one who sells *mādhvī* liquor, and he who abandons his dependents;
He who approaches his daughter or his daughter-in-law, he by whom the Veda is sold, and he who defiles the Veda—these are known as Mahājvālins.
Those who despise their guru and strike him with the arrows of speech, and the man who approaches a woman who should not be approached, shall go to the Śabala hell.
The hero who violates the established order falls into delusion; and he who performs a wicked deed goes to the realm of those who feed on worms.
One who hates gods and Brahmins falls into the Lālābhakṣa hell; likewise do the maker of sacrificial vessels, the potter, the embezzler of deposits, and the physician.

One who sets fire to groves and one who administers poison go to Viṣañjana; likewise, he who accepts gifts from the unworthy and he who performs sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice.
That man who lives by means of Kṣatriyas shall go head-first downward; [so too shall he who sells] milk, liquor, meat, lac, perfumes, liquids, and sesame seeds.
One who sells such things as these shall fall into the terrible hell Pūyavaha; likewise, he who binds chickens, cats, pigs, birds, deer, or goats shall go to that same hell.
A keeper of goats, a keeper of buffaloes, one who lives by a water-wheel, a banner-seller, a Brahmin who subsists on the stage, a bird-catcher, and a village priest;
One who sets fire to a house, a poisoner, one who eats from a sacrificial vessel, a seller of Soma, a drinker of liquor, an eater of meat, and likewise a slaughterer of animals;
"These fall into the Rudhirāndha hell; these indeed fall," so say the wise of those who, while seated in a single row, serve poisoned food.
They fall into the terrible hell Viḍbhuj; of this there is no doubt. The one who seizes honey falls into Vaitaraṇī, and the one who reviles falls into that called Mūtra.
In the Asipatravana hell, there are those who are impure and wrathful; even there, the deer-hunter is made to eat flames of fire by crows.
Due to a lapse in his vow during a sacrifice, he shall fall into the Sandaṃśa hell; likewise, if ascetics or celibate students discharge their semen during sleep.
Those who are taught by their sons, and those who are commanded by their sons—all of them go to hell, to a place of torment, and to a state of hunger.
But those who, filled with anger and joy, perform actions contrary to the duties of their caste and stage of life—all of them are inhabitants of hell.
Situated above is the great, terrible Raurava, which is hot by nature; below it is known as Sudāruṇa, which is dark and cold by nature.
In this very sequence, all [the hells] are situated one below the other; and the intensity of suffering in all of them increases according to the causes of their respective karmas.
And there is an increase in happiness everywhere here through the cause of the Dharma; for the gods see the most dreadful hells with their faces turned downward.
Those hell-beings also see all the gods situated above; these and other hundreds of hells are located in the sky.
Day after day he is cooked in hell; elsewhere he is burned; in another place he withers and is split apart; in yet another place he is ground to powder and dissolved.
In one place they are boiled, in another they are set ablaze, and likewise in another they are struck by winds; for a single day in hell, it may be as long as a hundred years.
Then, having emerged from all those states, the sinner experiences the condition of an animal among worms, insects, moths, stationary beings, and single-hoofed creatures.
Having gone to those places abounding in wild elephants, as well as to the cow-pens, there were asses, horses, mules, oxen, śarabhas, and yaks.
These six are the single-hoofed animals; now hear of the five-clawed ones. As for those born of other wombs, which are full of great sin and yield only suffering—
One may obtain human birth as a hunchback, a despicable person, or even a dwarf; or one is born among the wombs of humans such as Caṇḍālas, Pukkasas, and others.
They dwell in the womb for a moment and die again and again, accompanied by whatever remainder of merit and demerit they possess.
Thereafter, he may ascend to the womb of a Rohiṇī, or become a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, a king, and so forth; and at other times, he even attains the state of a Brāhmaṇa or a lord of gods.
Thus do those of evil deeds fall downward into the hells; now listen as I describe how those who perform meritorious acts proceed.
Those men, directed by Yama to a meritorious state of rebirth, dwell among throngs of Gandharvas who sing and are filled with the joy of dancing festivals.
Adorned with the sweetness of necklaces and anklets, the stainless celestial chariots, radiant with divine perfumes and garlands, move swiftly along.
And having fallen from there, they are born in the households of other high-souled kings as those who protect the livelihoods and wealth of the people, free from disease.
They obtain intense enjoyments, and from there they go upward; otherwise, having reached the downward path, those men descend as before.
For every living being born in the world of death, death is certain; for the most sinful, the soul certainly departs by way of the lower path.
Earth dissolves into earth, and likewise water into water; fire dissolves into fire, and wind into wind.
And in space there is likewise space, all-pervading as in the moon; therein are desire and anger, as well as the five sense-faculties within the body.
O Tārkṣya, these have been described as the thieves residing within the body; desire, anger, ego, and the mind are the leaders therein.
And that Time is indeed the dissolution, joined with merit and demerit, endowed with the five senses, and together with all the gods.
He enters the new body just as a thief enters a secure house; all those seven constituent elements (dhātus) that reside within the body [are likewise entered].
For this body consists of six sheaths; all the winds within embodied beings, as well as urine, feces, and whatever other diseases arise from their conjunction.
Bile, phlegm, marrow, flesh, fat, bone, semen, and sinew—all these, together with the body, are consumed by fire.
O Tārkṣya, this destruction of all embodied beings has been told to you; now I shall further describe to you how their bodies come to be.
The body is a single pillar bound together by sinews, adorned with three beams, joined with the sense organs, and possessing nine gates.
It is assailed by sense objects, agitated by desire and anger, filled with passion and hatred, and infested by the thief of craving, which is difficult to traverse.
This city is partitioned by the net of greed, enveloped in the cloth of delusion, firmly bound by illusion, and presided over by greed.
Those men who do not recognize the Self within this body of all embodied beings, which is permeated by these qualities, are considered to be mere beasts.
In this very way, the fourfold body has been fully explained to you; eighty-four hundred thousand species were fashioned in the past.
Those born from sprouts, those born from sweat, those born from eggs, and those born from a womb—all this has been explained to you in detail regarding hell.
Or perhaps there is a desire to ask that which has come in due order.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Description of Hell and the Process of Entering and Exiting It," in the Pretakalpa, within the second part (Dharmakāṇḍa) of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Whether committed knowingly or unknowingly, whatever impurity has been created by men—for the purification of that sin, an expiation must be performed by men.

A wise person should first perform the ten-fold ablution with ashes and other substances; furthermore, according to his capacity, he should also practice the substitutes for the six-year vow and so forth.
Or half of that, or half of that again, or even half of that; then, according to one's ability, one should perform the ten gifts—listen indeed.
Cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, clarified butter, clothing, grain, molasses, silver, and salt—these indeed are known as the ten gifts.
A man should give ten [cows] to those who have arrived for the sake of expiation; thereafter, on the path to the gate of Yama, which is thick with pus and blood, [he proceeds].
To cross the Vaitaraṇī river, one should give a Vaitaraṇī cow; she who has black udders and black limbs is indeed known as the Vaitaraṇī.
Sesame seeds, iron, gold, cotton, salt, as well as the seven grains, land, and cows—each one of these is traditionally held to be purifying.
These eight great gifts should be given to an excellent twice-born man by one who is afflicted; hear from me their forms and locations.
An umbrella, sandals, garments, a signet ring, a water-pot, a seat, a vessel, and a footstool—these are remembered as the eightfold [requisites].
A vessel of sesame seeds, a vessel of clarified butter, and a bed with its furnishings—all these should be given, as well as whatever is dear to oneself.
A horse, a chariot, a queen, an ornament, and even a garment should be given to the Brahmins by him himself, preceded by the sacred Veda.
O bird, one should offer other gifts as well according to one's own capacity; for him by whom atonement has been performed, even ten gifts [are required] on this earth.
The gift of a cow, the gift of the Vaitaraṇī river, and likewise the eight other gifts; as well as the gift of a vessel of sesame seeds, a vessel of clarified butter, and the gift of a bed.
And by giving land according to the prescribed rite, one does not enter the womb of hell; moreover, the wise desire the gift of salt even as an independent act.
Since this salty taste has arisen from the body of Viṣṇu, when the life-breaths of a sick person do not depart from the surface of the earth, [it is because of this].
Then salt should be given, as well as the opening of the gate of heaven; and whatever gifts have been personally bestowed by men [shall likewise be granted].
And all those things stand before him; O bird, he alone is truly a man by whom penance has been performed along with its constituent parts.
Having reduced sins to ashes, one is glorified in the heavenly world; for the milk of cows, O best of birds, is indeed nectar.
Therefore, he who gives a cow attains immortality; indeed, by giving the eight gifts, one shall dwell in the abode of the Gandharvas.
For in that fierce [hell], the abode where a person is burned, by the gift of an umbrella, a beautiful shade arises on the road, bestowing satisfaction.
If one gives sandals, one easily crosses the forest of sword-leaves with its sharp edges and proceeds mounted upon a horse.
By giving food and a seat, one indeed enjoys happiness on the road; by giving a water-pot, the donor shall indeed be happy in a waterless region.
The messengers of Yama, though extremely fierce, terrifying, and dark-brown in hue, do not cause suffering out of courtesy because of the gift of clothing and ornaments.
O bird, a sesame vessel given to a brahmin will certainly destroy the threefold evil arising from speech, mind, and body.
By the gift of a vessel of clarified butter, a man shall dwell in the world of Rudra; likewise, by giving a bed equipped with all its furnishings to a twice-born man.
Crowded with various apsarases, he ascends a celestial palace; having sported for sixty thousand years in the abode of Śakra.
Falling from the world of Indra, he shall become a king in this world—youthful, free from defects, and endowed with all necessary implements.
O Lord of Birds, he who gives a horse to a Brahmin dwells in the heavenly world for as many years as there are hairs upon that horse.
Indeed, they attain as many abundant, radiant worlds, [as well as a chariot] yoked with four horses and equipped with all necessary implements.
Having given a chariot to a twice-born man, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.

Having given to an eminent brahmin a buffalo that yields abundant milk, which has the hue of a fresh cloud, whose calves are well-satisfied with mouthfuls of grass, and whose hindquarters are beautiful, adorned with a golden tilaka—what wonder is there in this that he conquers the world?
By the gift of a palm-leaf fan, one is fanned by the wind on the road; by the gift of a garment, one becomes endowed with beauty, fortunate, and glorious.
He who bestows a house equipped with flavorful food and household utensils upon a Brahmin, his lineage does not perish and he attains unsurpassed heaven.
In this matter, O best of birds, there exists the lightness or heaviness of the fruit, depending on the distinction between faith and lack of faith, and the gravity or insignificance of the gift.
Then, O bird, one experiences that same joy as when one bestowed gifts of water and likewise provided flavorful drinks here in times of distress.
He by whom food has been given with a mind purified by faith attains satisfaction even then, even without food.
If one should perform renunciation according to the prescribed rule when death is near, he shall not return again; he is fit for becoming one with Brahman.

If a dying person is led toward a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), liberation shall occur upon reaching that tīrtha, even if he dies while on the way; for him, there is no doubt that at every step it is equal to performing a sacrifice.
O twice-born one, if he should undertake the vow of fasting unto death according to the prescribed rule when death has arrived, he too does not wander further in saṃsāra.
The answer to the fourth question, "What is charity? has been stated; now hear the answer to the question, "What is between burning and death?"
Then, having ascertained that the life-force has departed, the son or other relative should quickly bathe and wash that corpse with pure water without hesitation.

Having clothed [the deceased] in new, unwashed garments, one should sprinkle his body with sandalwood water; then, indeed, one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite at the place where the deceased lies.
Just as the fitness for burning and so forth occurs prior to the actual application, there would likewise be seating and sprinkling; yet these four [actions] would not exist [in that manner].
There should be the invocation, worship, the touching of the vessel, immersion, the formal resolve regarding the gift of food, and the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) should always take place.
The five ritual items would not exist; the line and the water-offering for washing would not exist; and furthermore, the three-fold offering of inexhaustible water would not exist.

O best of birds, one should perform the recitation of the *svadhā* formula, the pronouncement of blessings, and the application of the *tilaka*; one should offer a water-pot, give food with black gram (*māṣa*), and provide a gift of iron as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
The moving of the *piṇḍas* has been declared, but this triad has not been declared: namely, the concealing, the dismissal, and likewise the recitation of the *svasti-vācana*.
This procedure has been declared for you regarding these six types of impure śrāddhas: those performed at the place of death, at the door, and likewise at the crossroads; these are indeed the six.
O bird, when there is rest, a pile of wood, or a collection [of materials], at the place of death, the deity known as Śava is pleased with the earth.

By this, the traveler at the door shall be [satisfied], and the deity of the site (vāstudevatā) shall be pleased; by this, the sky-farer (khecara) at the crossroads and the deities beginning with the Bhṛtas shall be gratified.
At rest, this one is known as a *bhūta*; being satisfied by that, he is called a *sādhaka* on the funeral pyre; and when gathered together, he is called a *preta*.
Taking sesame seeds, darbha grass, clarified butter, and other offerings, the sons and others indeed proceed while reciting verses addressed to Yama or the Yama-sūkta.
Day after day, even as he is presented with cattle, horses, men, and bulls, Vaivasvata is not satiated, like a wicked man with liquor.
Having recited this verse, or having recited a well-spoken hymn on the road, all the kinsmen should proceed toward the forest in the southern direction.
O bird, one should perform two *śrāddhas* on the way according to the previously mentioned procedure; thereafter, one should slowly place the corpse upon the ground with its head facing south.

Having placed [the body] on the cremation ground, one should perform the previously mentioned *śrāddha* ceremony; the sons and other relatives should themselves carry the grass, wood, sesame seeds, clarified butter, and other necessary materials.
Any rite performed with items brought by a Śūdra becomes entirely fruitless; one should wear the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) and face the south.
O Bird, an altar should then be constructed there according to the scriptures; having divided the cloth into two parts, one should cover it with half of that.

One should cast half [of the portion] directly onto the ground for the purpose of dwelling in the cremation ground; then, according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should place the *piṇḍa* into the hand of the deceased (*preta*).
Anointing with clarified butter (ājya) should be performed on all the limbs of the corpse; now hear the rule for the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) during the interval between death and cremation.

The corpse becomes fit for the offering through the five funeral cakes (piṇḍa) previously mentioned; otherwise, due to its defilement, it indeed becomes a source of harm for rākṣasas and other such beings.
Having swept the ground, smeared it with cow-dung, scraped it, and removed the debris from the altar, he should sprinkle it with water and kindle the fire there according to the prescribed ritual.
Having worshipped the deity known as Kravyāda with flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata), the wise man should cremate one who maintained the sacred fires according to the Vedic injunctions.

One should avoid the fire of a Caṇḍāla, the fire of a funeral pyre, and the fire of one who has fallen from caste; for you are the creator of beings, the source of the world, and the protector of the worlds.
"Therefore, bestow upon him this nectar that leads to heaven. Having thus honored the flesh-eating spirit, one should perform the oblation of the body.
When the body is thus half-burnt, one should then offer an oblation of clarified butter with the mantra: "From this you were born; from you may he be born again."
Having spoken thus by name, "To this world of heaven, svāhā!", he should likewise offer an oblation of clarified butter mixed with sesame seeds accompanied by the mantra.
Then one should weep intensely; in this way, he will find happiness there after performing the cremation and the funeral rites immediately following the burning.

O Bird, one should offer a funeral ball (piṇḍa) for the deceased to pacify the pain of cremation; then, having performed a circumambulation, those who were watching the departure of the pyre [should depart].
Those who have recited the *sūktas* should go for the sake of bathing, preceded by the youngest; then, having gone near the water-sieve and washed their garments, they should proceed.
Having put that [garment] on again, they should then say to that man: "O men, we shall now perform the water libation with our clothes on."
If [the deceased] has died at least ten years ago, the sons and other relatives, led by the eldest, should say "Do so," while wearing a single garment and with their topknots untied.
All, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītin), should enter the water silently while facing the direction of the ancestors, reciting the mantra: "Apanaḥ śośucadagham."
Those who perform the bath should not splash the water; instead, having come to the bank and tied their topknots, they should take straight *kuśa* grass.
Then, having placed water mixed with sesame seeds in his two right hands and taking it up in his joined palms, the grieving man [should offer it] toward the south from the *paitṛka-tīrtha*.
O bird, all of them, restrained in speech, should throw [the seed] upon the ground or upon a stone, either once, three times, or even ten times.

"May they be satisfied," or "Let them be satisfied," or "I satisfy them," or "May they attend"—one should utter these [mantras] in this manner when the words "O deceased one, belonging to such-and-such gotra" have been spoken.
After the water-offering with joined palms has been performed, the cleaning of the teeth should be carried out; all kinsmen, O Kāśyapa, abandon [these rites] for nine days.
Then, having emerged from the water and put on [fresh] garments, they should wring out their bathing cloth once and enter upon a clean spot of ground.
One should not shed tears after offering the funeral libation of water for cremation; for the deceased, being powerless, must consume the phlegm and tears shed by the kinsmen.

Therefore, one should not weep; rather, rites should be performed according to one's own ability. Then, when they had all sat down, a certain well-versed performer of rituals, an expert in the Purāṇas, [proceeded].
One should dispel sorrow by proclaiming the impermanence of cyclic existence; for in this human state, which is as pithless as the trunk of a plantain tree, one must seek out its essential core.
He who acts [with attachment] is utterly deluded regarding that body which resembles a bubble on water; for this body, composed of five elements, has returned to its fivefold state.
What cause for lamentation is there in that matter, since one's own body arises from one's own actions? Even the earth, the ocean, and the gods must go to their destruction.
"How can the world of mortals, which resembles foam, not go to destruction?"—thus one should cause those seated upon the soft grass to hear.
Having heard this, they should go home preceded by children; having bitten off the tips of their fingernails, they should remain restrained at the door of the house.
Having sipped water, one should [touch] fire, water, cow dung, white mustard seeds, young dūrvā shoots, a bull, and other auspicious objects.

Having touched [the body] and having slowly placed their foot upon a stone, they should enter; however, for one who has maintained the sacred fires, the destruction of the body is performed according to the Vedic injunction.
One should not bury a child less than two years old, nor should one perform the water libation for it; however, this does not apply to a devoted wife who follows her husband in death.

Having first performed the ritual application and paid homage to her husband, she should ascend the funeral pyre; but she who, through delusion, falls from the pyre, must perform the Prājāpatya penance.
As many as there are thirty-five million hairs on a human being, for so long a time shall she who follows her husband dwell in heaven.
Just as a snake-catcher forcibly draws a serpent from its hole, even so that woman, having been drawn out, rejoices together with him alone.
There, devoted to her husband and praised by hosts of apsarases, she sports with him for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras endure.
Whether her husband be a slayer of a Brahmin, a thief, or a betrayer of friends, an unwidowed woman purifies him by following him in death.
That woman who, upon the death of her husband, ascends the funeral fire, being equal in conduct to Arundhatī, is glorified in the heavenly world.
As long as a woman does not cause herself to be cremated when her husband has died in the fire, she is by no means released from that female body.
She who follows her husband purifies three lineages: that of her mother, that of her father, and that of the one to whom she is given.

She who is distressed when her husband is distressed, joyful when he is joyful, dejected and emaciated when he is away on a journey, and who dies when he dies—she is to be known as a devoted wife (*pativratā*).
A beloved wife ought not to ascend a separate funeral pyre; however, those of the Kṣatriya and other castes who are of the same varṇa may indeed ascend it here.
Starting from a Cāṇḍālī woman up to a Brāhmaṇī woman, the rule is the same for all of them, provided they are not pregnant and are neither very young nor very old.
O bird, I have explained the procedure for cremation in general; do you wish to hear some specific details regarding it as well?
Garuḍa said: "O Lord of the World, tell me how the cremation should be performed when the master has gone abroad, or is dead, or his bones have perished."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: If the bones of a man who has gone abroad cannot be found, I shall describe to you their destination, location, and the prescribed rite.
Listen, O Tārkṣya, to that which is supremely secret regarding the difficult deaths of husbands: those who have died from excessive fasting or have been struck down by fanged beasts.

Those who cling to the neck during an embrace, those who are emaciated, those who strike with the beak, those killed by poison, fire, bulls, or Brahmins, and those who commit suicide by cholera—[these do not attain heaven].
Listen to the state of those who have died by falling, by hanging, or by water; or by serpents, tigers, horned beasts, calamities, stones, or floods.
By Brahmins, by beasts of prey, by falls, by [death from] trees or lightning, by claws, by iron, by falling from mountains, by the collapse of walls, and likewise by leaping from cliffs;
In the Kaṭvā forest and in the intermediate space (antarikṣa), as well as from thieves, Cāṇḍālas, menstruating women, female dogs, Śūdras, washermen, and others who are thus adorned [with impurity].

Those who have died leaving remnants of food above, those who have died leaving remnants of food below, and those who have died leaving remnants of food on both; as well as those who have died by the stroke of weapons and those likewise touched by the breath of a dog.
That should be known as a miserable death, occurring without the prescribed rites; by that sin, having experienced the hells, they partake in the state of hungry ghosts (preta).

One should not cause their cremation; there shall be no birth-impurity (sūtaka) nor water-libations (udakakriyā). One should not perform the ritual for the dead, nor should one perform the funeral rites (aurdhvadaihika).
One should not offer the funeral rice-ball; for if one offers it out of negligence, all of that fails to reach [the ancestors] and perishes in mid-air.
Therefore, O bird, his sons, grandsons, and sapindas who desire their own welfare must perform the Narayana-bali out of fear of public reproach.
Yama declared that their purification shall occur in this manner and not otherwise; once the Nārāyaṇa-bali rite has been performed, they become fit for the funeral ceremonies.
The rite that purifies him shall not be otherwise; one should duly perform the entire Nārāyaṇa-bali at a sacred ford.
O Brahmin, one should have the rite performed before Kṛṣṇa by which a man becomes purified; first, however, a libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed by Brahmins learned in the Purāṇas and the Vedas.
One should offer libations intended for Viṣṇu with all medicinal herbs mixed with unbroken grains (akṣata), using either the Puruṣasūkta or Vaiṣṇava mantras.
Facing the south and recollecting the deceased as Viṣṇu—one who is the beginningless and endless God, the bearer of the conch, the discus, and the mace—[one should proceed].
O inexhaustible one, lotus-eyed one, be the bestower of liberation upon the departed; at the conclusion of the libation, may you be free from passion and devoid of envy.
Having become one whose senses and mind are conquered, pure, and devoted to dharma, he should perform exactly eleven śrāddhas there with devotion.
In the performance of all rites, being one-pointed and composed, one should offer water, rice, barley, wheat, and millet.

One should cause auspicious sacrificial food (haviṣyānna), ritual hand-gestures (mudrā), an umbrella, and a turban to be offered; one should cause all types of offerings to be given, including milk mixed with honey.
One should give the eightfold gift accompanied by clothing and sandals; one should liberate [the recipient] from all sins and must not practice deception regarding the row [of diners].

When the rice balls have been placed upon the ground, everything accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains should be given to all the Brahmins according to the injunctions of the Vedas and Shastras.
In a conch shell, a sword, or a copper vessel, one should perform the libations separately, while remaining joined in meditation and concentration and resting upon the ground with both knees.
One should indeed cause the arghya to be offered with a Ṛg-verse, specifying the arghya separately for each: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Yama, and the deceased as the fifth.
Then, they should be placed in separate jars together with the five jewels, along with garments, sacred threads, mung beans, and footprints.
One should perform the five offerings to the deities according to the prescribed rule; thereafter, one should offer a stream of water for each individual rice-ball separately.
In a conch shell, or a copper vessel, or if those are unavailable, even in one made of clay, having taken water with sesame seeds mixed with all medicinal herbs;
One should give a copper vessel filled with sesame seeds, together with gold and a ritual fee (dakṣiṇā), to a preeminent Brāhmaṇa; likewise, one should perform the gift of the foot.
Then one should offer sesame seeds dedicated to Yama and an iron vessel as a sacrificial fee; having thus offered the Viṣṇu-bali according to the rules and according to one's capacity.
It swiftly rescues [the victim]; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. Now hear from me the specific [procedure] regarding one who has died from a snakebite.
Having fashioned an elephant out of a bhāra of gold and likewise a cow, and having given them to a Brahmin according to the prescribed rite, one shall attain freedom from debt to one's father.

Having thus offered the serpent-oblation (sarpabali), one is liberated from the affliction caused by serpents; thereafter, an effigy (puttalaka) should be fashioned, provided with all medicinal herbs.
And hear, O Kāśyapa, the method for the distribution of the Palāśa stalks: having spread out a black antelope skin and, with Kuśa grass, fashioned a human figure.
The collection of bones is said to consist of three hundred and sixty stalks; having placed those stalks individually upon these respective limbs.
One should place forty [syllables] on the head, ten on the neck; one should apply twenty on the region of the chest, and likewise twenty on the abdomen.
One should place one hundred [units] on the two arms, twenty on the region of the hips, one hundred on the two thighs, and thirty on the two shanks.
One should place four [bones] on the penis, six on the two testicles, and ten on the parts of the toes; in this manner, one should arrange the bones.
One should place a coconut in the position of the head and a gourd in the palate; one should place the five jewels in the mouth and a plantain fruit on the tongue.
One should apply *nālika* to the intestines, and likewise *vālukā* to the nose; one should apply *mṛttikā*, *haritāla*, and *manaḥśilā* to the fat.
Mercury is placed in the place of semen, and likewise, yellow orpiment in the feces; realgar is applied to the limbs, and sesame oil is placed in the joints.
Just as barley flour is in meat, honey in blood, a mass of matted hair in the head-hair, and deer-skin in skin;
A palm-leaf ornament on the ears, guñjikā berries on the breasts, a śatapatra lotus on the nose, and a lotus on the region of the navel.

A pair of eggplants should be placed upon the testicles, while a gṛñjana root is auspicious for the penis; clarified butter should be applied to the navel, and a trapusa fruit is prescribed for the two buttocks.
With pearls upon her breasts, as if with saffron unguent on her head, and with auspicious incense of camphor and agallochum, and with fragrant garlands;
One should place the lower garment and the silken thread at the heart; prosperity and growth on the two arms; and a cowrie shell upon the two eyes.
Pomegranate seeds upon her teeth, campaka flowers upon her fingers, vermilion at the corners of her eyes, and offerings such as betel—[all these she bears].
Having prepared the deceased with all medicinal herbs and performed the worship as prescribed, one should also place the sacrificial vessels in sequence according to the rite involving fire.
"May women purify my head; may this [head] of mine be purified by Varuṇa as well. Having performed the purification of the deceased with the water from a Śālagrāma stone, [one should proceed].
A well-behaved, milch cow, sesame seeds, iron, gold, cotton, and likewise salt, should be given with Viṣṇu in mind.
The seven grains, land, and cows—each one is remembered as purifying; therefore, one should give a vessel of sesame seeds and likewise the gift of a footstep.
One should indeed perform a Vaiṣṇava Śrāddha for the sake of one's own liberation of the deceased; then, having envisioned Viṣṇu within the heart, one should effect the release of the deceased.

Having thus fashioned an effigy, one should cremate it according to the prescribed ritual; for its purification, however, the performer of the rite, such as a son or other relative, should perform an expiation.
Three, six, twelve, and likewise fifteen *kṛcchra* penances are prescribed for him according to the specific cause requiring expiation, just as they are for a Brahmin.

If one is unable [to perform the penance], one may instead perform a substitute offering (pratyāmnāya) such as a cow, gold, or other items; likewise, if one lacks the qualification to perform it oneself, a kinsman should perform the purification in this manner.
But that which is given by an impure person, or intended for an impure person, does not reach its destination; it all perishes in mid-air.

Having accomplished purification, the post-mortem rites such as cremation must be performed; he who performs cremation and the other rites without having first completed the expiation (niṣkṛti) [is at fault].

Listen now to the expiation for those acts, performed either intentionally or unintentionally, in their respective order: having touched fire, water, a ritual bath, [a corpse], carrying [it], or conversing [with it].
One who carries the corpse of any of these deceased persons, or burns it, is purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance, as well as by cutting the ropes [of the bier] and shedding tears.

Having performed the water-libation rite with the sacred grass, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance; for a minor cause, the penance should be slight, and for a major cause, it should be great.
Garuḍa said: "O Lord, O observer of noble vows, tell me the characteristics of all three: the Kṛcchra, the Taptakṛcchra, and likewise the Sāntapana."

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Eating in the morning for three days, in the evening for three days, and eating food obtained unasked for three days, followed by three days of fasting—this is declared to be the *kṛcchra* penance.
One should drink each of these—boiled milk, ghee, and water—daily for one day each; followed by a fast for one night: this is declared to be the *taptakṛcchra*.
Having consumed cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass, one should fast on the following day while performing the *sāntapana-kṛcchra*.
O bird, I have fully explained this procedure for one who has died a bad death; then one should recognize the deceased as having attained the extinction of the lamp.

Then one should perform the cremation with fire and observe impurity for three days; for ten days, the ritual of the pit and the *piṇḍa* offerings must be performed, beginning with those for the deceased.

One should then perform the ritual in this manner; thereafter, the deceased becomes a partaker of liberation, provided that the cremation was performed upon a substitute image due to the delusion that [the person] was dead.
Therefore, he should come and perform an immersion in a pit of clarified butter; furthermore, the purificatory rites such as the birth ceremony (jātakarman) and others must be performed once again.
A man should wed his own married wife according to the prescribed rites when the fifteenth year has passed, O Bird, or else when the twelfth year has elapsed.

For one who is unknown to have died or who has gone abroad, one should perform a funeral rite using an effigy. Listen now to the specific rule regarding the death of a woman in her menses or one who has recently given birth.
When the woman who has given birth has died, the performers of the sacrifice act in this manner: taking water in a jar, as well as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

Then, having first bathed [the person] according to the prescribed rite with water from a hundred winnowing baskets, one obtains purity through speech by consecrating the waters with meritorious mantras.
O Lord of the Self, having bathed her with that very [water], one should perform the cremation; having bathed the deceased woman who was in her menses with the five products of the cow.

Having fashioned an image out of cloth, one should perform the cremation according to the prescribed rite. Listen as I describe the cremation procedure for one who has died during the *pañcaka* period.
Beginning with half of Dhaniṣṭhā and ending with Revatī, this group of five constellations is always defiled and shall always be inauspicious.
No cremation should be performed there, nor should one feel despondency toward any living beings; water should not be offered to them, for it would always result in inauspiciousness.
After the five [days], all the funeral rites must be performed; otherwise, suffering arises for his sons and kinsmen.
In these lunar mansions, loss certainly occurs for one who has died; or else, if the cremation is performed according to the prescribed rites on the current lunar mansion, [the loss is averted].
That [rite] for human beings is indeed preceded by oblations; therefore, the brahmins should perform the ritual according to the rules, with mantras and in accordance with the prescribed injunctions.
Then, four effigies fashioned from darbha grass and consecrated with the Ṛkṣa-mantras should be thrown near the place where the corpse is situated.
Then a cremation should be performed together with those effigies; at the end of the period of birth-impurity, the sons should then perform rites for pacification and nourishment.
For that man who has died among the five [categories of sinners] and does not obtain a funeral rite (sati), one should offer sesame seeds, a cow, gold, and clarified butter on his behalf.
One should cause gifts to be given to the Brahmins, which destroy all obstacles: food, sandals, an umbrella, a gold coin, and two garments.

A sacrificial fee is given to the Brahmin as a means of liberation from sin. Thus has this procedure, which removes the five [sins], been fully described by me; as well as the journey to Saṃyaminī, the duration of the year, and the funeral rites.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rites for Cremation, Characteristics of Difficult Cremations, the Return of the Deceased, the Death of a Woman in Her Menstrual Period, and Expiatory Rites for the Five Kinds of Death," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa. —
The Glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, Chapter 5.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Having thus cremated the deceased man and having bathed and offered water with sesame seeds, the women should go in front, while the men should follow behind.
One should cause [the child] to eat neem leaves while weeping, addressing him by name; and the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) should be performed once he has been placed upon a stone.
O Bird, having entered the house, all of them—the sons and others, along with the sapindas—shall indeed remain in a state of impurity for ten nights.

All of them, eating food that has been purchased or obtained, should sleep separately; they should eat food free from pungent condiments and salt, and they should immerse themselves in water for three days.
They should abstain from eating meat, sleep on the ground, remain celibate, not touch one another, and refrain from giving gifts or studying.
Stained, with downcast faces, wretched, and deprived of enjoyments, they avoid the massaging of their limbs and the combing of their hair.
They should eat from vessels made of clay or leaves; they should reside there for one day or perhaps for three days.
Garuḍa said: O Lord, regarding that which is called "impurity" (āśauca), what is its definition, for how long must it be maintained, and by what kind of men is it to be observed?

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "This [obstacle] must be quickly dispelled by means of time and other factors, for it acts as a prohibitor of the funeral cakes, Vedic study, giving, and so forth; indeed, that obstacle is a great impediment to the man."
Impurity on account of death is ordained for ten days among the sapinda relatives; it shall be exactly the same in the case of a birth for those who desire complete purification.
For those who offer water for a birth, purification is held to occur after three nights; those who offer water for a death become pure after the remainder of the three-day period.

Until the eruption of teeth, impurity is declared to last for one day; until the tonsure ceremony (*caula*), it lasts for one night; until the initiation into Vedic study (*vratādeśa*), it lasts for three nights; and beyond that, for ten nights.
Impurity has been fully explained to you; now I shall speak of the subject at hand in brief: water should be placed in the third heaven and milk in a vessel made of clay.
"O Kāśyapa, with this mantra, 'Bathe here! Drink here!', one should [place] three pieces of wood bound together by cords at a crossroads at night for the sake of prosperity."
On the first day, or the third, or likewise the seventh or ninth, the collection of the bones should be performed by those belonging to that same lineage on that day.
After that period, the touching of the limbs of the sapinda relatives is prescribed; likewise, those who share the same water (samānasalila) become eligible for all ritual acts.
Having bathed with a restrained mind, one should prepare the sacrificial porridge (caru) in the northeast and offer the piṇḍa for the pretas outside, omitting only the darbha grass.
On the ground for the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and on kusha grass for the conditioned (saṃskṛta), one should, with a concentrated mind, offer nine balls of rice over nine days.

Having offered the tenth funeral ball (piṇḍa), one becomes pure during the remainder of the night, whether the person is of a different lineage or the same lineage, a woman or a man, or even an ascetic.
He who makes an offering on the first day should complete it on the tenth day; he may offer cooked rice, or groats, or even vegetables.

Whatever substance is used on the first day shall continue for the ten-day period; it is prescribed that the offering be made with one handful [of water] throughout the entire duration of the impurity.
Alternatively, on the day the gift is given, one may offer that same number of handfuls for each day; thus, over ten days there are ten handfuls, over a fortnight fifty, and at the end, fifty.
Or, O bird, it may be a hundred añjalis increased by two; for when the period of impurity lasts three days, then there are ten añjalis.
On that first day, there were three handfuls; on the second day, four; and likewise, on the third day, there were three.
O bird Śatāñjali, when there were thirty [years] in the first day, there were forty in the second day, and thirty in the third day.
In this manner, the handfuls of water are to be distributed for both sides; in all ancestral rites, the son is the primary person possessing the authority.

The scattering of rice balls should be performed silently, as well as the offering of flowers, incense, and so forth; when the tenth day arrives, one should perform the ritual bath outside the village.
In that case, the clothes, hair, beard, and nails must be discarded; a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure by touching water, and likewise a Kṣatriya by touching his mount.

A Vaiśya [should carry] a goad or reins, and a Śūdra who has performed his duties [should carry] a staff; the shaving of the hair is performed by the sapinda relatives who are younger than the deceased.

The ritual duty, however, consists of sixteen [funeral rites] performed with six and ten funeral cakes (piṇḍas) respectively; for by these, the first period of impurity (mala) lasts until the tenth day after death.
O best of birds, for ten days the sons and others there prepare rice-balls; these are divided into four portions every day.
With two parts the body is sustained; with the third, the followers of Yama are satisfied; and with the fourth, one sustains oneself as well.
Within nine days and nights, the body shall attain completion; likewise, the head of the deceased is fashioned by the first lump of clay.
But with the second [mantra], one should [touch] the ears, eyes, and nose in brief; and with the third, likewise in sequence, the throat, shoulders, arms, and chest.
With the fourth morsel, one should likewise [satisfy] the navel, the genitals, and the anus; with the fifth, however, the knees, the shanks, and the feet at all times.
All the vital points [are struck] by the sixth [syllable], while the channels are struck by the seventh; the teeth and body hair by the eighth, and virility by the ninth.
By the tenth, however, there is fullness, a state of satiety, and the reversal of hunger; O Vainateya, listen to me as I describe the sixteenth, the middle one.
O Bird, there are eleven [Śrāddhas] beginning with Viṣṇu and ending with Viṣṇu, as well as five Śrāddhas for the gods; among these, the sixteenth is the Madhyamāṣṭamī.
If the foolish Bali-Nārāyaṇa rite is performed on the eleventh day, the ritual release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga) must indeed also be performed there.
If a bull is not released on the eleventh day for a deceased person, his state as a preta remains firmly fixed, even by hundreds of performed śrāddhas.

If the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) has not been performed when the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍapātana*) is made, one should know that everything is fruitless; it will not reach the deceased.

Apart from the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga), there is nothing else on the surface of the earth [that can save one]; neither a son, nor a wife, nor a daughter's son, nor a father, nor a daughter.
Immediately after his death, the bull festival must certainly be performed for him, involving four heifers, or else a bull should be released.
If, when the eleventh day has arrived, the acquisition of a bull occurs, he who has been adorned according to the prescribed rite shall not remain in the state of a preta.
Having fashioned that bull out of *darbha* grass and flour, the wise man should release it at the time of the bull's consecration (*vṛṣotsarga*), should he somehow fail to obtain an actual bull.
Having fashioned a bull out of either clay or darbha grass, one should release it; on the eleventh day, one should give whatever was desired by that person while they were alive.
One should give a bed, a cow, and other such gifts on behalf of the deceased; likewise, one should feed many Brahmins for the sake of pacifying the hunger of the departed spirit.
I shall speak of the third, the sixteenth [chapter]; O Vainateya, listen to it: there are twelve monthly [rites], as well as the first six-monthly one.
The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is considered the third of the sixteen [rites]: on the twelfth day, at the three-fortnight mark, at six months, monthly, and at the end of the year.
Due to differences of opinion, they speak of this sixteenth [offering] as the third; for one by whom these sixteen *śrāddhas* for the deceased have not been offered.
His state as a piśāca remains firm even by the offering of hundreds of śrāddhas; the first [offering] is prescribed on either the eleventh or the twelfth day.
O Bird, son of Vinatā, at the beginning of each month and on the anniversary of death, one should perform the purification for those who are deficient [in years] by either one day or three days.
For indeed, Śrāddha rites are performed at the end of a month, six months, a year, and three fortnights; likewise, the Sapiṇḍana rite occurs when a full year has passed or half a year.
For men, [the rite] may be performed after three fortnights, or on an auspicious occasion, or even on the twelfth day; for family customs are infinite, and the lifespan of men is subject to decay.
Because the body is unstable, the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite is recommended on the twelfth day; O Lord of Birds, hear from me the procedure for these Sapiṇḍīkaraṇas.
O Kāśyapa, that too should be performed according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite; one should prepare four vessels provided with sesame seeds, perfumes, and water.
There is one vessel for the preta and likewise three vessels for the ancestors; O bird, one should pour the contents of the preta-vessel into the three ancestral vessels.
One should offer four balls of rice and complete them at the eastern ends; from that point on, the deceased indeed partakes in the commonality of the ancestors.
Then, O Lord of Birds, once that deceased one has attained the status of a progenitor (pitṛ), one should worship his ancestors with all the rites of the śrāddha ceremony.
In the case of ascending the same funeral pyre and likewise in death on the same day, there is no *sāpiṇḍya* for the woman; rather, upon the death of her husband, the woman's [lineage] becomes his.

O bird, there is no doubt that for a husband and wife, there is unity of the funeral rite, unity of time, and unity of the performer in the case of a śrāddha and other rites, as well as when they are cremated together.

Or she may ascend the funeral pyre on a day other than the anniversary of her husband's death; however, when that anniversary of his death arrives, she should be joined with him by means of a separate *piṇḍa*.
And one should complete [the rites] every year simultaneously.
For one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite occurs before the completion of a year, the monthly offerings and the water-pot (*udakumbha*) must also be given for that entire year.
The *navaśrāddha*, the rite of *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, and the sixteen *śrāddhas* must be performed by a single person alone, even among those who have divided their wealth.
Sapiṇḍya with the paternal grandmothers and likewise with the maternal grandfathers has been stated; sapiṇḍya with the husband is also declared for a woman, according to the distinction of her dress.
I shall tell you the time for the *navaśrāddha*; listen, O Kāśyapa! On the day of death, at the place of death, one should perform the *śrāddha*, O bird.
And then, on the way, a second rest was made; thereafter, at the place of collection, the third Śrāddha is declared.
O bird, there are indeed nine śrāddhas: on the fifth, the seventh, likewise on the eighth, the ninth, and also on the tenth and eleventh.
These nine types of ancestral rites (śrāddha) are traditionally known as the "third" and the "sixteenth"; they should be performed by men according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.
The *navaśrāddha* (the rite for the newly deceased) is proclaimed to be performed on the first, third, fifth, seventh, ninth, and likewise on the eleventh day.
These six are spoken of here, or they may become nine through sacrifice; I have explained them to you according to the differing opinions of the sages.
The conventional view is my preferred position, though some here maintain that it is yoga; likewise, in both the first and second cases, a single purifying thread (pavitraka) should be given.
When the twice-born have finished eating, a ball of rice (piṇḍa) should be offered to the deceased; then the sacrificer and the twice-born should recite the prayer, "May it be pleasing to him."
"May it be inexhaustible for [Name]"—thus it should be said at the conclusion; likewise, understand that the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is prescribed in this manner throughout the year.
After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, one should perform those sixteen *śrāddhas* according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa*, with the exception of the *pārvaṇa*.
Whatever one performs each year, he shall perform those [rites] accordingly; on the eleventh and twelfth days, the deceased partakes for two days.

One should offer the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) for both a woman and a man, addressing it as "O deceased one" (preta). Once the rite of sapinda-ship (sāpiṇḍya) has been performed, the designation "deceased one" ceases for him.
The offering of lamps should be performed outside the house throughout the rainy season; food, a lamp, water, clothing, or whatever else may be given.
O son of Vinatā, I have briefly described to you the annual rites, which provide satisfaction to the deceased through the term "preta" until the completion of the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa ceremony.
Listen now to how his journey to the abode of Vaivasvata took place: on the thirteenth day, immediately following the Śravaṇā-rite.
O Tārkṣya, seized by the servants of Yama like a snake caught in its skin, one person travels along that path as if he were a captured monkey.
The body assumes another form that flows like the foremost of winds; one is born from a physical mass for the purpose of falling, while the other is derived from the ancestors.
Just as there is a predominance of their respective dimensions, ages, stages, and shapes, so too, in terms of measurement, it is eighty-four thousand yojanas.
The intervening path between the world of Yama and the world of humans should be known as two hundred yojanas plus half a krośa.
He travels there every day for forty-seven days, and thus in forty-eight and thirty days [he reaches his destination].
Thus, while traveling along a path that must be traversed in this sequence, those devoted to evil are dragged toward the city of Vaivasvata by the followers of Yama.
Listen, O younger brother of Aruṇa, to how that world with its manifold expansion arises: on the thirteenth day, he was bound by extremely terrible nooses.
Yama, indeed with a goad in his hand and a face contorted by a frown, agitated by the stroke of his staff, drags [the deceased] toward the southern direction.
In places rough with kusha grass, thorns, anthills, stakes, and stones, as well as in some places filled with blazing fires and hundreds of fierce chasms;
Scorched by the blazing heat of the sun and being burned amidst gadflies, he is dragged away by the messengers of Yama, who are as terrifying as the howling of jackals.
The doer of evil deeds proceeds along the terrible path to the abode of Yama; while his body is being consumed by fire, he undergoes great destruction.
Likewise, while its limb is being devoured, torn apart, and cut for a very long time, the living being experiences terrible suffering.
Even though one has entered another body due to the ripening of one's own karma, there are sixteen cities on this path; hear them from me.

The city of Yama, the city of Saturn, the abode of the two mountains, Gandharva, Śailāgama, Krauñca, the city of Cruelty, the city of Wonders, the city of Many Calamities which bestows suffering, the city of Various Laments, the abode of Intense Heat, the fierce city of Rainfall, and the city Abounding in Cold—these sixteen cities of great terror were never seen by you.
There, going toward the city of Yama while crying out, "Son! Son! he constantly wails, "Alas! Alas!", remembering his own misdeeds committed.
On the eighteenth day, O Tārkṣya, he will reach that city, where there is the river Puṣpabhadrā and a beautiful banyan tree.
He desires rest here, yet those soldiers do not allow him to rest; nor has anything been given to his son on this earth by them out of affection or compassion.
He eats a morsel of food once a month and then proceeds to Sauripura; as he travels, he laments, oppressed by the blows of hammers.

O body, cross over! At that time, neither a reservoir was made by me for the satisfaction of humans, nor for the satisfaction of beasts and birds, nor was a pasture created for the sake of satisfying cattle—what you have done, [the consequence] of that must now be borne by you.
There, that king, known by name as Jaṅgama, who could assume any form at will, ate the funeral cake with apprehension, having become fearful upon seeing him.
After three fortnights, having been joined with water and offered upon the ground, he then departs; departing thus, he laments, tormented by the blows of swords.

O body, you have not practiced constant charity, nor have you provided daily fodder for cows; you have not indeed given gifts of sacred manuscripts, nor have you followed the path seen in the Purāṇas and the Vedas—so now, cross over by whatever has been done by you!
Having gone to the city of the Lord of Nagas and having eaten such food as was provided, he should then depart from there on the second lunar day, which had been designated by his kinsmen.
Even as he was walking, struck by the blade of a sword, he lamented: "Everything has turned out to be the ruin of another for me, the crest-jewel of fools."
Through a great accumulation of merit, I have obtained this human birth; now that the third month has arrived, [I shall go] to the auspicious city of the Gandharvas.
Having eaten the third monthly funeral cake there, he departs; as he goes along, being struck by that [cake] on the path, he laments thus:

O body, nothing was given by me in charity, nor was an oblation offered into the fire; no penance was performed in the caves of the snowy mountains, nor was the great water of the Ganges resorted to—so cross over [the ocean of existence] for that which has been done by you!
In the fourth month, during the arrival of the rains, one may encounter rain there; above that, there would be birds and stones in close proximity.
Having eaten at the fourth-month ancestral rite (śrāddha), he crawls there; even as he falls, lamenting and severely oppressed by stones and the like.

I have not followed the path of knowledge, nor the path of yoga, nor the path of action, nor the path of devotion; nor have I gained anything from the company of the virtuous or from sacred learning. O body, cross over [the ocean of existence] by means of that which you have performed.
Then, O Kāśyapa, in the fifth month, when one goes to Krūrapura, having consumed the funeral cakes and water offered on earth, one proceeds to Krūrapura.
While thus lamenting as he went along, he was struck down on the path with sharp-edged spears, crying out: "Alas, mother! Alas, father! Brother! O children! Alas, alas, my wives!"
"I was not instructed by you when I reached such a state as this. To him lamenting thus, the messengers of Yama speak:
O fool, where is the mother, where is the father, where is the wife, and where is the son or friend? O witless one, enjoy what is earned by your own karma; they have long since departed on the path.

"You know that provisions are the strength of travelers; one who lacks provisions cannot strive for the journey to the next world. You must certainly go by that path upon which there is not even buying or selling."

Having eaten the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) along with water at the Krauñca mountain during the period of less than six months, and having rested for the duration of a ghaṭī, one shall proceed to the city of Vicitra.
Thus lamenting as he goes, he is pierced by the tip of the stake.
"Where shall I go? For life does not depart; alas, for one who is dead, there is no further death! Lamenting thus, that husband, bearing a body fit for torment, departs.
In that city of Vicitra, there was a king named Vicitra; being satisfied by a single morsel of food every six months, he would travel about the city.
Thus lamenting as he went along, he was struck by the tip of a palace turret.
Is there anyone—mother, brother, father, or son—who exists for me, who might rescue me from this sin as I fall into the ocean of suffering?
As they were traveling on that path, there lay the auspicious Vaitaraṇī river, a hundred yojanas wide and filled with pus and blood.
There, sailors, fishermen, and others appear; they say: "If the Vaitaraṇī has been given by you, then board this boat and cross the river with ease."
In that situation, he by whom the cow was given shall cross it with ease; however, the one who did not give it shall be seized by the boatmen and made to pay a toll.
O bird, one is pecked at by crows, ravens, cranes, and owls with sharp beaks; in the end, for those who have not given gifts beneficial to humanity, there is the Vaitaraṇī river.
Once given, she shall burn away all my sin and lead me to the world [of the gods]; when the seventh month has arrived, he who dies shall go to the city of many calamities.
Having consumed the seventh-month funeral cake (piṇḍa), he indeed goes toward the water; while going thus, tormented by the blow of the iron bar (parigha), he laments.

Nothing was given, no oblation offered, no austerity practiced, no ritual bath taken, and no beneficial deed performed; O deluded soul, experience the consequences of whatever kind of action you have carried out.
O Tārkṣya, having eaten there in that other place which causes suffering for eight months and then having consumed water, he proceeds with the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to the city of Nānākranda.
And as he departs, tormented by the blows of the pestle, he cries out: "Where are my wife’s clever and artful words of endearment?"
Where is there food, and where is the killing with spears, javelins, and clubs? For in the ninth month, one is indeed cast into the city of various wails.
He eats the funeral ball (piṇḍa) with compassion and even utters various cries; indeed, that which is given in the tenth month then becomes his well-heated abode.
While he was thus lamenting on the road, struck by the blow of the plowshare, [the king thought]: "Where now is that massaging of my feet with the tender hands of my son?"
Where is there the dragging of my feet by those who resemble messengers of Vajra? Having eaten the funeral cakes and other offerings there during the tenth month, he moves forward.
When the eleventh month is complete, he goes to the city of Raudra; even as he goes, he laments like one whose back is being tormented.
Where am I now, tossing from moment to moment upon a bed with cotton quilts; and where, again, was I when my back was dragged by a staff fallen from the hand of a soldier?
O Bird-born One, having eaten the funeral cakes and other offerings given upon the earth, one should then depart from that place; this city is named Payovarṣaṇa.
Thus lamenting as he goes, he is struck on the head with axes; where, alas, was the sprinkling of scented oil by the tender hands of servants?
Where is the pain inflicted on the head by axes out of anger by the followers of the miser? And there, he eats the food of the *ūnābdika* śrāddha while suffering great misery.
When the year is thus complete, he should go to the city of Śītāḍhya; while going there, his tongue will be cut by a knife and he will weep.
On one hand, there is the description of sweetness through pleasant speech; on the other hand, as soon as it is uttered, there is the cutting off of the tongue with sword-leaves and the like.
Having consumed the annual offerings of rice-balls and the like, he moves about there, presiding over various deities born of those *piṇḍas*, who cause great terror.
She reveals her sin and reproaches herself; even so does a woman lament upon this path.
From there he goes to the city of Yāmya, which is not very far away; it is forty yojanas in length and breadth, and four times that in circumference.
There are indeed thirteen gatekeepers there named Śravaṇas; they are pleased by the performance of the Śravaṇā rite, but otherwise they would become enraged.
Then, he quickly beholds Yama there in the midst of Death, Time, the Ender, and the others—red-eyed and resembling a mass of crushed collyrium.
The Lord has a face made terrifying by his fangs and a form formidable with its frown; he is surrounded by hundreds of diseases and by hideous, frightening mouths.
With great arms grasping a staff and a noose in hand, he is most terrifying; then, directed by him, the living being goes to a state of existence that is either auspicious or inauspicious.
The sinner goes to a sinful destination, as was told to you previously; so too for those who give umbrellas and sandals, and those who provide dwellings.
But those who have performed meritorious deeds then see Yama there, appearing with a gentle form, wearing earrings and a crown, and endowed with majesty.
Indeed, on the eleventh and twelfth days, after six months, and likewise at the end of the year, one should feed many Brahmins there, for their hunger is great.
O bird, he who, while still living, does not accomplish his own purpose by means of what has been provided by others—such as sons, wife, and so forth—suffers greatly later on.
All this has been told to you regarding the course of events in Saṃyaminī; the duties for the rainy season have been explained to you—what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Description of Annual Duties, the Path to the World of Yama, and Torments," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part (*uttarakhanda*) of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
[Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 6]

Garuḍa said: Even for one who is engaged in spiritual practices and devoted to sacred fords and charity, there is truly no passage to the next world if the rite of releasing a bull has not been performed.
Therefore, O Kṛṣṇa, I have heard that the release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga) must be performed. What is the fruit of the bull-sacrifice, and by whom was it performed in ancient times, O Hari?
What kind of ox is said to be suitable, and at what specific time? What procedure has been prescribed for it? Please tell me all this out of compassion.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Lord of Birds, I shall relate a highly meritorious history which was told by the son of Brahmā to King Vīravāhana.
In the city of Virāṭhana, there was a king named Vīravāhana; he was righteous, true to his word, generous, and a source of satisfaction to the Brahmins.
Once, O Tārkṣya, that heroic and high-souled one went to the forest for hunting; desiring to ask something, he went to the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha.
Having paid homage to the sage there and taken his seat, the king, bowing low with devotion, questioned him in the assembly of seers.
The king said: "O Sage, I have practiced dharma according to my ability and with great effort; yet, having heard the decree of Yama, I am exceedingly afraid in my heart."
O illustrious one, O treasury of compassion, tell me how it is that I do not see Yama, nor the messengers of Yama, nor the hells of terrifying appearance.
Vasiṣṭha said: O King, many kinds of dharma are described by those learned in the scriptures; yet, because of its subtlety, people do not understand it, being deluded regarding the path of action.
Among the religious duties being undertaken—charity, sacred fords, austerity, sacrifice, renunciation, and the ancestral rites—the release of a bull is distinguished as preeminent.
One should desire many sons, so that even if only one among them goes to Gayā, or performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice, or sets free a dark-colored bull.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, whether committed intentionally or unintentionally, are purified by marrying a blue woman or by swimming across the ocean.
O Indra among kings, for him whose bull is not released on the eleventh day, his state as a *preta* remains fixed; what then would be the use of the *śrāddha* rites performed for him?
It must be performed somehow or other, whether at a sacred site or in a city; one is liberated by means of bull-sacrifices, O bird, and not otherwise through other practices.
A bull of five auspicious marks, young, with a black blanket [on its back], wandering thoroughly in the midst of the herd of cows according to the prescribed rite.
O Bird, having performed the marriage ceremony with four heifers, two, and one, using auspicious materials accompanied by mantras, one should release him.
