One should fashion a golden image of the Fire-god with the six verses beginning with "iha ratiḥ" on the full moon of Kārttika, Māgha, or Vaiśākha, at the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti), or on the days of the eclipses.
At a sacred ford (tīrtha) and especially on the anniversary of an ancestor's death (pitryekṣayāha), it is highly praised [to give] one that is red in color, yet white at the face and the tail.
That bull which is yellow in its hooves and horns but blue elsewhere is so described; one that is white in color is a Brahmin, while the red one is said to be a Kṣatriya.
The Vaiśya is of yellow complexion, and the Śūdra is recorded by the wise as being black; thus they are designated according to their respective colors among the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
Alternatively, the red color is indeed recommended for all of them—the father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather.
They pray for a son who, once born, will perform the rite of releasing a bull; for you, O Dharma, are the giver of joy to the world in the form of a bull.
Therefore, you who are the abode of the eightfold form, grant me peace; drink from the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, and graze upon the grass within the sacred altar-ground.
"O Bull, my good deed must be recounted before the King of Dharma: the mark of the trident on my right shoulder and the sign of the discus on my left thigh."
Having thus made this prayer and having worshipped the bull, together with its heifer, with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and other offerings, one should release them.
Therefore, O King, perform the rite of releasing a bull according to the prescribed injunctions; for one who possesses many means of merit, there is no other way to attain a happy state.
O King, formerly in the Tretā Yuga, there lived in the city of Videha a wise Brahmin named Dharmavatsa, who was devoted to his own duties.
A devotee of Viṣṇu, exceedingly radiant and finding contentment with whatever he obtained, the noble Kuśa went to the forest when the festival of the ancestors arrived.
While he was wandering here and there, gathering *kuśa* grass and *palāśa* leaves, four men of handsome appearance suddenly approached him.
Seizing him while his mind was bewildered, they returned through the air to a place thick with many trees and terrifying with its mountain fastnesses.
They led him from one forest to another, filled with rivers and streams; there, O King, he beheld a city of great extent.
It was adorned with gate-towers and decorated with palaces and mansions; it was crowded with men and women at its courtyards, marketplaces, and stalls.
It resounded with the combined blasts of trumpets and the music of lutes and drums; meanwhile, some were wretched, afflicted by hunger, soiled, and devoid of vitality.
Then he saw those who were previously dejected, soiled, and clad in rags, now standing before him joyful and well-nourished, adorned with garments of gold.
Seeing those who resembled gods even more than that, he was struck with wonder: "Is this a dream, or is it an illusion, or perhaps a mental delusion of my own?"
The men led the doubting brahmin into the presence of the king; there the brahmin beheld him in a palace made of gold.
There sat the king upon a great, divine lion-throne, fanned by parasols and chowries, resplendent with a crown of gold.
And seeing that brahmin endowed with great splendor and being praised by excellent bards, the king also rose up and joined his palms in reverence.
He worshipped the god according to the prescribed rites with offerings such as madhuparka, and with a satisfied mind, he praised the deity with supreme joy.
O Lord, today my birth has become fruitful and my lineage purified, since you have come within the range of my vision, O Dharma, who are a devotee of Viṣṇu.
Having bowed and praised him in many ways, the king, remaining prostrate, said: "O Lord, let him by whom you have been brought here be led back to that very place."
Having heard these words of the king, the bull among the twice-born inquired. The Brahmin said: "Who is this country? From where do the superior, middling, and inferior worlds come?"
By what merit are you adorned with the sovereignty of Brahmā? For what purpose have I been brought here, and why am I being led back to that very same place?
"I see everything as if it were unprecedented, like one who has entered a dream. The King said: "But he who is devoted to his own duty and always intent on devotion to Hari..."

He who is detached from the objects of the senses is worthy of my worship, of this there is no doubt; he who is constantly devoted to pilgrimages and is particularly skilled in the ritual of releasing a bull.
He who is devoted to truth and charity is worthy of homage even by the dwellers of heaven; O scorcher of foes, he has been brought here for you to behold, and is indeed deserving of worship.
"O Lord, favor me; forgive my rashness. Having spoken thus, he signaled to his ministers with a movement of his eyebrows.
He will explain it all to you; it is not yet appropriate for him to speak himself, as he is a neighboring king who knows all the Vedas and understands the heart's desire of the monarch.
Vipaścit said: "O Brahmin, in a previous birth, this man was known as Vaiśya Viśvambhara, living in the city of Virādha, which was adorned by twice-born men and gods."
Always living by the occupation of a Vaiśya, he should protect his family, constantly attend to the cows, and honor the Brāhmaṇas.
Constantly devoted to the giving of alms, hospitable, and tending the sacred fire, he duly fulfilled the duties of a householder together with his wife, Satyamedhā.
By means of the Smārta rites he conquered the worlds, and by the Śrauta rites, the fire-eaters; once, having visited numerous sacred fords together with his kinsmen.
As soon as he saw him approaching his residence with his hair standing on end along the path, he quickly prostrated himself like a staff and stood with palms joined in reverence.
The ocean of the waters of compassion questioned him who was endowed with discipline. The seer said: "O virtuous one, from where have you come, accompanied by these brahmins and kinsmen?"
"Having seen you, the abode of Dharma, my mind is deeply moved. Viśvambhara said: "Indeed, knowing that the body is wasting away and that death stands before me,"
Having set out on a pilgrimage to sacred fords with his lawful wife, he visited the holy sites according to the prescribed rites and distributed abundant wealth as gifts.
"As long as you have come within the range of my sight, I shall go to my own home. Lomaśa said: "In this auspicious land of Bhārata, there are many sacred fords (tīrthas)."
"Tell me all those [deeds] which were indeed performed by you. The Vaiśya said: "The Gaṅgā, the daughter of the Sun, and the highly meritorious Sarasvatī—"
Where Brahmā, the lord of the gods, performed ten horse-sacrifices, there is Kāśī, the king of holy places, where Mahādeva, the treasure-house of compassion, resides.
Where he whispers the Tāraka mantra into the ears of deceased beings, there is the meritorious hermitage of Pulaha, as well as the Phalgutīrtha and the Gaṇḍakī river.
Cakratīrtha, Naimiṣa, and the infinite Śivatīrtha; Gopratāra, Nāgeśa, Ayodhyā, and that known as Bindu.
There, the lotus-eyed Rāma himself, the bestower of liberation, resides; furthermore, there are the fires of Agni, Vāyu, Kubera, and Kumāra, as well as the fires of trees.
Saukara, Mathurā where Hari is eternally present, Puṣkara, Satyatīrtha, Jvālatīrtha, and Dineśvara.
Indratīrtha, Kurukṣetra, where the Sarasvatī flows eastward, the Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, Nirvindhyā, Malaya, and the Kṛṣṇaveṇikā.
Having beheld Godāvarī, Daṇḍaka, Tāmracūḍa, Sadodaka, Dyāvābhūmīśvara, and Śrīśaila, the lord of mountains;
O Sage, on that Veṅkaṭa mountain where there are always innumerable liṅga-tīrthas, Hari himself, possessed of great splendor, dwells under the name of Śrīraṅga.
Right there is the goddess named Veṅkaṭī, the slayer of Mahiṣa; also Candratīrtha, Bhadravaṭa, Kāverī, and Kuṭilācala.
The Avaṭodā, the Tāmraparṇī, the Trikūṭa, the Kollaka mountain, the Vāsiṣṭha Brahmatīrtha, the Jñānatīrtha, and the great ocean.
Hṛṣīkeśa, Virāja, Viśāla, Nīlaparvata, Bhīmakūṭa, Śvetagiri, Rudratīrtha, and Umāvana.
It was there that the goddess Girijā attained Śaṅkara through her ascetic penance; and there also are Vāruṇa-tīrtha, Sūrya-tīrtha, and the highly auspicious Haṃsa-tīrtha.
Where, by immersing themselves, crows attained the state of royal swans, and where an asura obtained divinity merely through bathing.
Having beheld Viśvarūpa, Vanditīrtha, Ratneśa, Kuhakācala, and Nara-Nārāyaṇa, one is liberated from tens of millions of sins.
The Sarasvatī and Dṛṣadvatī rivers, the Narmadā which bestows happiness upon men, and the meritorious Nīlakaṇṭha, Mahākāla, and Amarakaṇṭaka.
The Candrabhāgā, the Vetravatī, the lord of the Gaṇas Vīrabhadra, Gokarṇa, Bilvatīrtha, Karmakuṇḍa, and Satāraka.
By merely bathing there, one is quickly liberated from the bondage of karma; other sacred fords as well were established by you out of compassion.
A pure understanding arises that the favor of the virtuous is paramount; on one side are all the sacred fords, and on the other are compassionate holy men.
Those who have fulfilled their vows move about for the sake of favoring living beings; you are the preceptor of all castes, superior in both knowledge and age.
Therefore, O Sage, I ask you something concerning the ancient primordial being: what should I do, whom indeed should I question, for my mind is exceedingly restless?
It is devoid of desire for the realm of Brahman, yet excessively longing for sense objects; it cannot endure separation even for a moment, speaking as if it were darkness.
O Brahmin, just as one who has prospered attains peace, so too does this supreme field of actions, which is deluded by various states of being, attain tranquility.

"Out of compassion, please tell me how the mind may become pure and inclined toward discernment. The sage replied: "The mind is indeed powerful and eternally subject to modification by its very nature."
Just as elephant-keepers bring even a rutting elephant under their control, so too, through association with the virtuous and by means of spiritual practices, one remains unwearied.
One should bring [the mind] under control through intense yoga of devotion and inquiry; I shall relate to you a historical account that will provide conviction.
Nārada told me of his own birth as it occurred within his life story. Nārada said: "O Sage, in former times, there was the son of a maidservant belonging to a certain preeminent brahmin."
Even in my childhood, I was thoroughly instructed and educated; there too, I came into contact with great beings of meritorious deeds.
During the rainy season, while we were staying in my house, by the power of our good fortune, through our service, obedience, humility, and self-restraint—
Having attained supreme contentment, they spoke these words out of compassion: "By this, my pure intellect has become inclined toward what is auspicious."
"By means of which he beheld everything as consisting of Viṣṇu within his very self. The sages said: "Listen, child; we shall explain it for your benefit, O boy."
Indeed, by that which is maintained, there shall be happiness both here and in the hereafter for the various beings in saṃsāra—gods, animals, humans, and all other kinds of people.
Bound by the snares of karma, they experience various kinds of enjoyments; through the quality of *sattva* one attains divinity, and through *rajas*, the state of humanity.

Driven by ignorance and following the impressions of his latent tendencies, the living being falls into the state of an animal due to darkness; having obtained rebirth from a mother, he dies again and again.
Having thus passed through countless wombs, even those lands of karma, one may at some point, by the turn of fate, obtain the human state which is so difficult to find.
By the great grace of the Great Ones, having known Hari, one is liberated from the crocodile of disease, the net of delusion, and the shoreless ocean of existence.
I see nothing else for one desiring to cross over [this world] than the remembrance of Rāma, just as butter is not found in curd, nor light anywhere within wood.
By means of such churning practices and spiritual disciplines, one should know the Supreme and become happy; for the Self is eternal, immutable, true, all-pervading, the sustainer of all, and great.
He is immeasurable, self-luminous, and ungraspable even by the mind; he whose nature is being, consciousness, and bliss abides in the heart of all living beings.
Even when all things perish, space never perishes; it abides within all beings, as well as in fire and water.
The Self is everywhere untainted, like the wind among earthly objects; the Blessed One is compassionate toward his devotees and acts for the protection of the virtuous.
Just as a horse appears in the worlds and is perceived by those who know it, so too should you cultivate within your heart that which is characterized by such discernment through the intellect.
Satisfied by the yoga of devotion, the Unborn One reveals Himself; thereupon, one becomes fulfilled and forever free from desire for anything anywhere.

Therefore, having abandoned the ego-sense toward the body along with its attachments, one should move through the worlds—worlds that are like dreams—without clinging and free from the sense of "mine."
Where is constancy in a dream, and where is truth in a magical illusion? Where is permanence in an autumn cloud, or where is reality in the physical body?
Having understood that all things moving and unmoving which appear are born of ignorance and karma, the yogi who has mastery over his conduct will thereby attain perfection.
Having spoken thus, all those virtuous ones, who are compassionate toward the distressed, departed; and I, following the path they described, practiced accordingly every day.
Then, before long, I beheld within myself this marvel: consisting of light, eternally blissful, and as pure as the autumnal moon.
Having drenched me with floods of bliss and made me full of longing, that great splendor vanished like lightning in the sky.
Meditating with devotion upon that very same wonder in my mind, I cast off my body in due time and went to the imperishable Hari.
O Brahman, by his will, my birth as Brahmā occurred again through the grace of the Blessed One, though I was free from desire for the three worlds.
"Pressing the lute repeatedly, I wander about singing," having said this and shared his own experience with me, the wandering sage departed.
For me, too, there arose supreme wonder and great satisfaction; therefore, through association with the virtuous and through devotion to the Supreme Self.
The mind, purified, stainless, and tranquil, shall attain nirvāṇa; even the sin generated over many lifetimes [is destroyed] through association with the virtuous.
"O knower of dharma, it perishes quickly, like autumn waters. The Vaiśya said: "Having drunk the nectar of your words, my heart has attained peace."
"By the sight of you, the fruit of all sacred fords has been produced within me. Having heard these words of his, the best of sages spoke:

Lomaśa said: O Indra among kings, for your own benefit and because you desire the fruits of the three goals of life, that which was well-performed by you has been accomplished even without the release of many bulls.
I consider everything to be as ineffective as water from a mist; there is no means on the surface of the earth that is even equal to the ritual release of a bull.
They proceed with ease to the destination of those who perform meritorious deeds—those by whom the release of a bull has been performed and those who have acted as officiants for the horse sacrifice.
"I have seen both of them as equal and divine in the presence of Śakra; therefore, having gone to Puṣkara and performed the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga), you [shall attain your goal]."
"Therefore, O virtuous one, go home so that everything may be accomplished. Vipaścit said: "Then he returned once more on the full moon day of Kārttika to the excellent Puṣkara."
Where the Blessed One, in the form of a boar and the fulfiller of the sacrifice, resides, he performed everything according to the rules together with the best of sages.
Many sacred fords were visited, and thereafter there was an encounter with Lomaśa; yet the merit born from the marriage of Nīla became even greater than that.
Having enjoyed divine sense-objects and having ascended an excellent celestial chariot, he was born by virtue of that merit into the royal family of Vīrasena.
For those who perform the rite of releasing a bull—which is proclaimed by Vīrapañcānana as the sole means for accomplishing the four aims of human life—and for those who serve therein:
Touched by the spray of water from the cow's tail, they became divine in form; standing at a distance, they beheld themselves with beautiful features and well-nourished bodies.
Furthermore, those people who appear even further away—unfortunate, soiled, coarse, emaciated, and destitute of clothing—[are also seen].
Those who, not seeing the bull-sacrifice, harbor resentment—all this conduct of the king from his previous birth was reported.
"I have heard from Parāśara this wonderful narrative concerning the Dharma; therefore, out of compassion for me, please go to your own home."
Having heard the words of Vipaścit, that brahmin was filled with supreme wonder; escorted by the king’s servants, he went to his home.
Vasiṣṭha said: Therefore, O King, if you are afraid even of Yama, perform the release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga), which is the most excellent of all rites, according to the prescribed injunctions.
O best of kings, there is no means of spiritual practice superior to the release of a bull; thus have I told you the secret of Dharma.
If a woman who has sons dies before her husband, she should not perform the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga), but she should give a milch cow as a gift.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O bird, having heard the words of Vasiṣṭha, the king went to Madhupurī and performed the entire rite of vṛṣotsarga according to the prescribed rules.
Having returned home, he considered himself to have accomplished his purpose; in due time, he met his end and was led away by the followers of Vaivasvata.
Having left Kālanagara, he traveled a great distance along the road and asked his messengers, "Where is the city of Śrāddhadeva?"
Wherein the sinners are cast down by the agents of Yama for the purification of their sins, there dwells that god who discerns between dharma and adharma.
"That city of sin has departed; it must not be beheld by those such as you. Having seen Dharmarāja before them, they spoke with the utmost reverence.
Then the god, possessing a divine form and accompanied by gods and gandharvas, revealed himself to that high-souled king.
Having prostrated himself like a staff, the king stood before him with palms joined in reverence; his mind filled with joy, he praised the god in many ways.
The King of Dharma also, having praised the king, spoke these words: "Let him be led to the world of the gods, where enjoyments are most abundant."
Having heard that, Vīravāhana questioned Yama: "O Lord, I do not know by what merit you are leading me to heaven."
The King of Dharma said: "Meritorious deeds were performed by you—generosity and sacrifices in full detail; indeed, at the word of Vasiṣṭha, the release of a bull was carried out in Mathurā."
O King, even a very small amount of Dharma, if practiced correctly, expands into great abundance through the grace of the twice-born and the gods.
Having spoken thus, the brother of Yamunā vanished in an instant; Vīrabāhu went to heaven and rejoiced together with the gods.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O bird, I have described to you in great detail the sacrifice of the bull; by hearing of how it effects the removal of the karma of living beings, one is liberated from sins.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Release of a Bull," in the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, within the *Uttarakhaṇḍa*, in the section concerning the two-eyed ghost (*Dvidṛd-dṛpreta-kalpa*), during the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
Garuḍa said: "O Hari, I have heard this great narrative regarding the fruit of releasing a bull. Now, tell me another story wherein your own wondrous majesty is revealed."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Today I shall relate to you a most wonderful dialogue between Santaptaka and the pretas, intended indeed to make known his true nature.
A certain Brahmin, intensely heated by his asceticism and with his sins burnt away by penance, having realized the worthlessness of cyclic existence, wandered only in the forests.
Once, that twice-born man set out on a pilgrimage, his eyes fixed upon the prostrations made by throngs of Vaikhānasa sages.
And because his senses were withdrawn, he became one who suppressed outward activity; moving by means of latent impressions alone, he indeed fell away from the path.
While walking thus at the time of midday bathing, he who was desirous of water opened his eyes and gazed toward all directions.
Then he beheld that dense forest, filled with thickets and hundreds of shrubs and trees, crowded with bark-covered reeds and the branches of spreading trees.
There were *tāla* and *tamāla* trees, as well as *priyāla* and *panasa*; likewise, *śrīparṇa*, *śāla*, *śākhoṭa*, *syandana*, and *tinduka* trees.
Sarja, arjuna, āmrātaka, śleṣmātaka, abhītakas, picumarda, ciñciṇī, karkandhū, and karṇikāras;
These and many other trees are there, yet no path is seen even for birds; how much less, then, for a human being?
In that most terrible forest, crowded with lions and tigers, and inhabited by hyenas, gavayas, bears, and buffaloes.
It was surrounded by hyenas, wild boars, elephants, monkeys, and likewise deer, as well as by beasts of prey, and others such as piśācas and rākṣasas.
The twice-born Santaptaka, his mind somewhat terrified with fear and fleeing in all directions, returned once more to Yadbhavishya.
Even amidst the humming of crickets and the hooting of owls, Kunīlāṅga, lending his ear, moved forward five steps.
There he saw a corpse bound with sinews at the top of that banyan tree, and likewise five most dreadful *preta*s upon its branches.

O bird, their limbs were reduced to mere sinews, bones, and skin, with their bellies clinging to their backs, as if they had abandoned their noses out of fear of falling into the hollows of their own eyes.
[They were] those whose bones had been struck down by swarms of needles, hooks, and saws, and who held constant great festivals for tasting marrow, fat, and fresh brains.
Seeing them with their great tusks clashing at their tips and their bones grinding against one another, his heart was terrified; he contracted his stride and came to a halt.
Seeing that a brahmin had arrived in the desolate forest, they ran forward, each saying, "I will go first! I will go first!"
Two of them seized his two hands, while others seized his two feet; a fifth seized his head.
Intent on plowing, they spoke with words appropriate to their own kind and clearly articulated syllables, saying, "I am eating," and "I am devouring."
Suddenly, they seized him together and departed; they did not consider how much meat remained on the boy or what was to be done with it.
They beheld this corpse, its intestines torn open by their own fangs; then, descending from the sky, they seized it with their feet.
With their bodies mangled, they returned once more to the sky; that bird, seeing himself being carried away through the atmosphere, [reflected].
Overwhelmed by fear, he went to me in his mind for refuge; with his heart, he mentally offered salutations to the Discus-bearer, who is equally composed of pure consciousness.

May Mukunda—who, by the stroke of his discus, drove the crooked crocodile far away and removed its suffering, thereby liberating the elephant from the crocodile’s jaws—cut asunder the bonds of my karma.

May that Discus of mine—the enemy of Mura, who, having caused Bhīma the king of Magadha to slay these pure kings imprisoned by him, was himself released after binding others for the sake of Bharga’s sacrifice—cut asunder this noose of karma.
In this world, he praised me with his mind alone; being thus praised, I arose and went suddenly to that place where he was being led by the *pretas*.
O bird, seeing us being led away by them, curiosity arose within me; I asked: "For how long did I follow behind them?"
O slayer of serpents, by my mere presence, that twice-born man was instantly endowed with the bliss of a king sleeping upon a palanquin.
Then, as Maṇibhadra was going toward Meru, he was seen by me on the road; having winked his eye, he was indeed led to his own side by me, the king of the Yakṣas.
I said to that great yakṣa: "Be indeed my opponent; destroy those hungry ghosts once more and carry away the corpse located there."
Thus addressed, he gave way to a most terrible and unbearable rage, and assumed that form of a *preta*, which causes suffering even to other *pretas*.
Stretching out his two arms and licking the corners of his mouth, he advanced toward those hungry ghosts, driving them back with a powerful wind from his broad chest.
With his two arms he seized two by two, and with his feet one from the head; then he suddenly struck the pretas with a firm fist.
With all their faces pale, they each seized that twice-born man and the corpse by the hands and feet, and began to fight.
With their claws, blows from their palms, likewise blows from their feet, and bites from their fangs, they all tore that single preta apart.
Having rendered their blows fruitless, he then seized them alive—not as corpses—just as Death seizes the vital breath.
As soon as the corpse was taken away, those most cruel ones, having released the single brahmin on Mount Pāriyātra, were exceedingly delighted.
That preta, traveling with the speed of the wind, arrived in a mere instant; he then became invisible, and they returned, their hopes shattered, to the brahmin.
As soon as the Brahmin began to recite there on that mountain, at that very moment, it was as if by the majesty of my abode and of the Brahmin himself.
Immediately, the memory of their former birth arose within them; having circumambulated that brahmin, the bull among the twice-born, they then spoke.
Having said, "Today you ought to forgive us," those hypocritical gods—[an act] as impossible as the overturning of a mountain or the drying up of the ocean—[departed].
Having heard those words of theirs, he then asked: "Who are you? Is this an illusion, or a dream, or perhaps a delusion of the mind?"
The pretas said: "Understand this very truth: we pretas are indeed born of our own karma. The brahmin asked: "What are your names, what is your conduct, and how have you come to this state?"
"How were those who were previously undisciplined disciplined now? The pretas said: "Listen, O chief of brahmins; we shall answer your questions in due order."
"O Great Yogi, through the sight of you, our sins have been removed. I am Paryuṣita by name, and this one is known as Sūcīmukha."
The third is Śīghraga, the fourth is Rodhaka, and the other is Lekhaka. The Brāhmaṇa said: "How indeed can there be such a thing as 'uselessness' for the pretas born of their own karma?"
"O preta-s, tell me without delay the etymological derivation of these names. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "Having been thus addressed by the brahmin, they each spoke their respective answers."
Paryuṣita said: "Once, at the time of a śrāddha ceremony, I indeed invited a brahmin."
Having delayed, that old man arrived at my house; since I had not yet performed the śrāddha rite, I ate that cooked food out of hunger.
Having drawn out and given even a small amount of stale food to a brahmin, that sinner, upon death, went indeed to a contemptible womb because of that sin.
"Because it was given as something stale, it is therefore remembered as 'paryuṣita' (stale). Sūcīmukha said: "Once upon a time, a certain Brahmin woman went to the holy site of Bhadravaṭa."
An old woman whose five-year-old son was her sole source of life—I, a kṣatriya heir, placed her under restraint.
In that desolate forest, having encountered a band of wicked travelers, he [robbed] her provisions along with her clothing, as well as the garments of her son.
O Brahmin, I took them, pressing them to my head with my fist; at that moment, the boy, afflicted by thirst, was drinking the water contained in the vessel.
In that place where there was only so much water, I warded him off with a roar of "hum"; then, like one parched with thirst, I drank all the water from the vessel.
Terrified by fear and parched with thirst, the boy fell down lifeless; his mother, having died from grief for her son, threw her own body into the well.
O Brahmin, because of this sin, I have attained the state of a preta; my mouth has an opening as small as the point of a needle, while my body is the size of a mountain.
Although I might obtain food, it cannot be eaten; even as the fire of my hunger blazes, my mouth remains clenched shut.
Therefore, O Brahmin, because I have an opening in my mouth equal in size to the point of a needle, I am known by the name Sūcīmukha (Needle-mouth).
Śīghraga said: "Formerly, belonging to the Vaiśya caste and possessing great wealth, I went with a certain friend to another land to engage in trade."
I had a friend with great wealth, and from him arose a great greed in me; yet, because I turned my back on what was unseen, even my very root has perished.
Then, having departed from there by boat upon that river flowing along our path, we began to cross it as the sun was turning red.
And that friend of mine, distressed by the fatigue of the journey, fell asleep upon my lap; at that moment, an exceedingly cruel thought arose within me, who am a great sinner.
When the hero had perished, I then cast him, who was in my lap, into the flood; while I was performing this deed, it was not even known by the people on the boat.
Taking all the goods he had there—jewels, pearls, gold, and so forth—he returned quickly from that place to his own home.
Leaving all of that in my own house, I informed his wife: "My brother was indeed slain by bandits on the road after they plundered his wealth."
"O mother of children, I have fled; do not weep," I said to her. At that moment, she, afflicted by grief, felt a sense of possessiveness toward her home and kinsmen.
Having sacrificed even his most beloved life according to the prescribed rite, he offered it into the fire; then, seeing that the region was indeed free of thorns, he went home filled with joy.
Having come here, I have consumed all that wealth throughout my life; for I quickly returned after having deposited it with my friend Pūra.
"For this reason, I am a preta known by the name Śīghraga. Rodhaka said: "O Lord of Sages, I was formerly of the Śūdra caste."
By the king's favor, I held the office of a great hundred-village steward; my parents were both advanced in age, and I had one younger uterine brother.
And that brother of mine was quickly separated from me by a single hunter; deprived of his clothes and ornaments, he experienced supreme suffering.
His parents secretly gave him various things that had not been given [to him], and I have heard from his parents what they gave to him through their trusted friends.
Having understood all that in its true nature, I caused my parents to be imprisoned; having bound them with firm shackles in a solitary, empty temple.
Then, afflicted with grief, the two of them gave up their lives by drinking poison; and that boy, O twice-born one, wandered about, deprived of his parents.
O Brahmin, having died of hunger while previously destroying towns, cities, villages, and hamlets, I have, because of this sin, passed away and entered the state of a preta.
"Since my parents were imprisoned, I am therefore called Rodhaka. The scribe said: "O Brahmin, in former times I was a most excellent twice-born man in Avantī."
"For I was appointed by King Bhadra to the worship of the gods; however, there were many images there belonging to many different names."
Then, as I performed worship for them, there appeared upon their limbs many kinds of jewels; yet, while doing so, a sinful thought arose within me.
Having shattered all their limbs with sharp iron, I also performed the extraction of the jewels from their eyes and other parts.
And having observed the statues with their limbs fashioned otherwise than they should be, and their eyes devoid of jewels, the king raged like a fire.
Thereafter, that bull among Brahmins, the king, made this vow: "Whosoever shall have stolen these jewels and gold..."
"For once he is known by me, he will undoubtedly be put to death; having learned all of that, I shall go to his house at night bearing a sword."
Having entered the king's palace, I killed the king like a sacrificial animal; then, taking the jewels and gold, I departed elsewhere in the middle of the night.
In the great forest, by a tiger, I was carved with the claws as if with chisels, because of the image that had been fashioned by me out of metal.
"O twice-born one, because of this sin, I am a preta by name; after the exhaustion of my experience in hell, I have attained this state of a preta."
The Brāhmaṇa said: "Such names have been declared by you for these ten states; let them describe to me their conduct alone, as well as their food."
The pretas said: "Where there is no following of the Vedic path, no modesty, no righteousness, no self-control, no forbearance, no fortitude, and no knowledge—there we dwell."
We shall inflict suffering upon him who, in his house, [eats] meat and blood derived from that [creature's] body, in due order—neither performing the *śrāddha* nor the *tarpaṇa*.
"We eat and we drink; this is our declared conduct. Now hear of our food, which is despised by all the world."
"O sinless one, have you indeed seen anything? Tell us what has been known by you: vomit, feces, rheum of the eyes, phlegm, urine, and tears?"
"O twice-born one, do not ask us further about this food and drink; O Master, shame arises in us when speaking of our own sustenance."
O Lord, we are ignorant, dull-witted, and overcome by darkness; yet, O Brahmin, we have suddenly regained the memory of our former births.
"O Lord, we do not know at all whether they have been disciplined or undisciplined. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "While the deceased were speaking thus, and while the twice-born man was listening accordingly..."
Then I showed him this very same form, O Tārkṣya; and that best of the twice-born, having seen the Person standing before him within his own heart, was struck with wonder.
The lord of birds praised me with hymns and prostrated like a staff; those hungry ghosts also performed penance thereafter, their eyes wide with wonder.

O bird, those whose speech falters through affection did not say anything at all; yet, salutations be to you who, out of compassion, truly effect the deliverance of those whose minds are stained by passion (rajas), whose hearts are distracted by worldly objects (go-racitta), and whose intellects are deluded by ignorance (tamas).

While the twice-born was speaking thus, that mountain shone brilliantly on all sides from six celestial chariots, possessing immense splendor, adorned with excellent garments, and produced by my own will.

Thus, having traveled to my world by means of a celestial chariot, that best of brahmins ascended to the fifth realm; then, through the power of association with the virtuous, those hungry ghosts went to heaven, a place of immeasurable merit, like unto the abode of Garuḍa.

The pretas descended to heaven through the power of their association; among my group was a Brahmin named Viṣvaksena, known as Taptaka, who possessed great wealth. All this has been recounted by me to you; indeed, that man who proclaims this or hears it shall not fall into the state of a preta.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Five Pretas," in the *Pretakalpa* section of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
Garuḍa said: "O Lord, who has the authority here regarding all post-mortem rites (*aurdhvadehika*)? How many kinds of rituals are prescribed? Tell me all of this."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O bird, the son, the grandson, the great-grandson, his brother, the brother’s offspring, or even the lineage of a sapinda—these kinsmen are eligible to perform the funeral rites.
In the absence of all those, O Bird, the rites should be performed by the *samānodaka* descendants; and when both lineages have been extinguished, the rites should be performed by women.
And the king, having severed his bonds by his own will, should perform the preliminary rites, the intermediate ones, and likewise the subsequent rites.
Every year, a bird, according to the rules for the ekoddiṣṭa rite, should perform a śrāddha there; hear from me the fruit thereof.
Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, the Nāsatyas, Sūrya, Agni, Vasu, and Marut; the Viśvedevas, the hosts of ancestors, birds, humans, and animals.
By performing a śrāddha endowed with faith, one gratifies the entire world—including the crawling creatures, the hosts of mothers, and whatever else is designated as a living being.
Being themselves satisfied, they satisfy him with sons, wives, and wealth; thus, the distinction between qualification and ritual action has been briefly described.
Garuḍa said: O best of gods, O Viṣṇu, if not even one among those mentioned should be eligible, what then ought to be done by a wise man?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: When there is no entitlement and no certainty [of the recipient's identity], a man himself should offer the śrāddha for the sake of the living being while that being is still alive.
Having observed the fast, well-bathed, united with Kṛṣṇa, and composed in mind, one should worship Viṣṇu, the Lord of All, who is both the agent and the enjoyer.
Accompanied by sacrificial fees and sesame seeds, one should, with a well-composed mind, offer three water-cows to the ancestors, saying "Svadhā."
Recalling [the mantra], "To Agni Kavyavāhana, svadhā! Homage! and recalling [the mantra], "To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, svadhā! Homage!"
To the south, however, one should offer the third oblation accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), while recollecting: "Svadhā! Obeisance to Yama Aṅgiras!"
Having placed the Brahmins between those two and consulted with them, he should feed them; having set the first [line] in the north, he should set the second in the south.
Having placed the third [offering] in the middle, one should thereafter perform the invocation (āvāhana) and so forth; having first worshipped the Viśvedevas with the invocation and other rites.
"O Brahmin, I feed you for the sake of the Vasus; O Brahmin, I feed you for the sake of the Rudras; O Brahmin, I feed you for the sake of the Sūryas"—thus he should say to them.
One should perform the remaining rites, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), as in the Śrāddha for the ancestors; then, one should give a cow to a Brahmin dedicated to the Vasus.
Then, one should offer a vessel of sesame seeds to Agni in the southeast, to Rudra in the south, to Sūrya and the twice-born in the southwest, and to the Viśvedevas in the west.
Having thus given the inexhaustible water while saying "Svasti," he should then dismiss those twice-born men while recollecting the eight-syllabled Lord Viṣṇu.
Then one should meditate upon Kāmeśvarī, the Mistress of the Family, Śiva, and Nārāyaṇa; thereafter, on the fourteenth day, one should go to whichever excellent river may be available.
Muttering the mantra "Victory to you! while holding garments and pieces of iron, he himself should kindle the fire there, facing the south.

Having fashioned an image of Brāhmī with fifty blades of *kuśa* grass, one should burn it after performing the cremation-ground fire-oblation (*śmāśānika-homa*) up to the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Or else, one should meditate upon Niragni, Bhūmi, Yama, and Rudra; having offered oblations in the primary place, one should subsequently invoke him.
Then, one should cook another *caru* mixed with mung beans in the fire, and a second one mixed with sesame seeds and rice, along with a *pavitraka*.
One should offer the first with "Oṃ, salutation to you, Pṛthivī," and immediately thereafter, the second with "Oṃ, salutation to Yama."
"Oṃ, salutations! Now, salutations to Rudra, the lord of the cremation grounds. Then, [he offered oblations] into the blazing, kindled fire upon the ground that was naturally formidable."
One should offer seven handfuls of water to the seven known as the Yamas: to Yama, Dharmarāja, Mṛtyu, and Antaka; [and to Vaivasvata and Kāla].
To Vaivasvata Kāla, the taker of all life-breaths, [one should offer oblations] seven times along with the utterances of *svadhā*, *namas*, and the *praṇava*.
"O [Name], of the [Gotra] lineage, may this water with sesame seeds be for you. One should then offer ten funeral cakes (piṇḍas) accompanied by water-offerings (argha) and flowers.
May incense, lamps, offerings, and perfumes be inexhaustible for all; having offered ten rice-balls (piṇḍas), one should meditate upon the gentle face of Viṣṇu.
And one should perform the monthly *māsika* rites every month; thereafter, at the end of the period of impurity (*āśauca*), one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for oneself or for the deceased.
Knowing that power, health, wealth, and lifespan are unstable, one should perform [the rite] according to one's ability. O bird, I have thus explained all this to you regarding the *jīva-śrāddha*.

Thus, in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the second part, the Dharma-kāṇḍa, in the Preta-kalpa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, is the eighth chapter titled "The Description of the Performer of the Śrāddha and the Self-Śrāddha. Garuḍa said: O sinless one, you have described up to the first rite (the Ādyā-kriyā), saying that even a king [performs it]. By whom was that first rite performed for someone by some king in ancient times?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Suparṇa, listen; I shall tell you how the rite was performed by the king. In the Kṛta Yuga, there was a king of the Vāṅgas named Babhruvāhana.
O Lord of Birds, that sovereign of the earth, as the protector of the earth bounded by the four oceans according to dharma, enjoys the entire land divided into four quarters.
While he was ruling that kingdom, there was no one who committed evil; O Tārkṣya, there was neither fear of thieves nor indeed any fear of the lowly.
There was no fear of disease even when he was the lord of that realm; his subjects delighted in their own duties, and he was like the sun in his splendor.
In his imperturbability he was like Mount Meru, and in his endurance he was like the earth; that mighty-armed one, possessing abundant forces and vehicles, at one time—
Surrounded by hundreds of horses, he went into the dense forest amidst the lion-roars of the warriors and the sounds of conchs and kettledrums.
As that king proceeded, there arose a sound of "kila-kila" everywhere, while he was being praised on all sides by the foremost of brahmins.
He went forth with great joy to the forest, desiring to hunt deer; as he was going, the wise man beheld a forest resembling the Nandana grove.
It was thickly covered with Bilva, Arka, and Khadira trees, joined by the banners of Kapittha trees, and surrounded on all sides by rugged mountains.
It was devoid of water and human beings, extending for many yojanas, and filled with extremely fierce deer, lions, and other forest-dwelling creatures.
That tiger among men, together with his servants, forces, and vehicles, sportively agitated that forest, slaughtering various wild animals.
Then the king pierced the belly of a certain deer; following the trail of that deer, the monarch entered the forest.
Alone, his strength stolen away and afflicted by hunger and thirst, he reached the edge of the forest and entered a vast wilderness.
Overcome by intense thirst, he searched for water here and there; from afar, he saw a lake resounding with the cries of swans and cranes.
Having arrived at the lake as indicated, he plunged in together with his horse, amidst the pollen of lotuses and the dust of blue water-lilies.
Having drunk water that was fragrant, pure, and cool, he emerged from the lake and went to a pavilion on the bank of the pond, exhausted by the fatigue of the journey.
Seeing a banyan tree, he quickly tied his horse to its roots; having spread out a mat there and placed his shield as a pillow, he lay down.
Then, fanned by the wind, he slept there for a moment; while the king was sleeping there for a moment, the preta indeed appeared with his vehicle of ghosts.
Then someone arrived there, accompanied by a hundred pretas, his body consisting of nothing but bones, skin, and sinews, wandering about in distress.
Seeking food and drink, he found no stability anywhere; seeing this unprecedented being, the king fixed an arrow upon his bow.
Having seen the king, he too stood before him for a long time like a pillar; observing him standing there, the king was seized with curiosity.
And he asked him, "Who are you, or why have you come to this transformation? The preta replied: "I have abandoned my state as a preta; I have attained a supreme destination."
"O mighty-armed one, through union with you, there is no one more fortunate than I. Babhruvāhana said: "What is this [you are doing] in this terrible forest, so exceedingly fearsome on all sides?"
O Koṇapa, as it was being violently shaken by the wind in the form of a whirlwind, moths, mosquitoes, small insects, headless trunks, and heads [were scattered].
Fish, tortoises, lizards, scorpions, bees, and snakes—with their heads downward and feet upward—were crying out most piteously.
Harsh winds blow, and lightning-fires blaze; like a mass of grass tossed here and there by the wind, all things seem to whirl about.
Various living beings are seen, as well as serpents and swarms of locusts; their cries are heard in many ways, yet they are not seen here or there.
"Seeing all this transformed, my heart trembles. He replied to him: "Those for whom there is neither the consecration with fire, nor the *śrāddha*, nor the water-offering rituals..."
There are six funeral cakes and ten body parts, but no sapindīkaraṇa rite for those who are betrayers of trust, drinkers of liquor, or stealers of gold.
Those who have died by an unnatural death, those people who are intent on malice, those who are devoid of expiatory rites, and those who delight in approaching women who should not be approached;
Driven here by their own past actions, those living beings are seen to be severely afflicted, finding food and drink difficult to obtain.
O King, out of compassion for these, perform their funeral rites—for those who have neither mother nor father, neither son nor kinsmen.
The king himself should perform their duties, for the monarch must also perform auspicious deeds for his own sake pertaining to the world beyond.
Liberated from all sufferings, by which one may cross over the miserable states—whose brothers are they, whose sons, and even whose wives, when they are experts only in their own self-interest?
You should place no trust in them, because one must enjoy the fruits of one's own actions; for wealth remains behind in the house, and kinsmen likewise at the cremation ground.
The body takes on wood [as fuel], while both sin and merit go along with it; therefore, you who desire the true welfare of yourself should act quickly and correctly.
"One must perform the rites for the hereafter with this unstable body. The king said: "You appear like a ghost, emaciated in form and with terrifying eyes."
"O King of the Pretas, out of affection for me, tell me everything exactly as it is. Thus questioned by the king, he indeed related his entire story.
The preta said: "O best of kings, I shall tell you everything from the beginning regarding the cause of my state as a preta; having heard it, you ought to show compassion here."
There was a city named Vaidiśa, which brought all prosperity and happiness; it was crowded with people from various regions and filled with diverse kinds of jewels.
O King, I lived there, which was filled with various flowering groves and inhabited by various meritorious people, always devoted to the worship of the gods.
"I am of the Vaiśya caste, Sudeva by name; let this be known to you. By me, the gods have been gratified with sacrificial offerings (havya), and the ancestors with ancestral oblations (kavya)."
The brahmins have been fully gratified by me through various modes of giving; indeed, both their food and their recreation have been well-provided for by me.
Whatever I have given many times to the poor, the helpless, and the distinguished has all become fruitless for me due to the arrival of fate.
"I have no lineage, dear father, nor friends, nor kinsmen; nor do I have such a well-wishing friend who would perform the funeral rites for me."

"O best of kings, because of that, my state as a preta has become firmly established; [the rites for] the eleventh day, the three fortnights, the six months, and the annual anniversary have been neglected."
O King, there are indeed other monthly *śrāddhas*, making sixteen in total; for him to whom these *preta-śrāddhas* are not offered, [the ancestors remain as hungry ghosts].
"Her state as a preta remains firmly fixed even by hundreds of funeral offerings (śrāddha). Knowing this, O Great King, deliver me from the condition of a preta."
"The king is said here to be the kinsman of all the social classes; therefore, O Indra among kings, deliver me, and I shall give you this precious jewel."
O best of excellent kings, O lord of the earth, O master, having shown compassion toward me, you should act in such a way that I may attain auspiciousness.

"Since the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga) was not performed for me by my sapindas or even my gotra-kinsmen out of cruelty during this cold season, I have consequently attained this wretched state of being a preta."
With my body overcome by hunger and thirst, I shall obtain neither food nor drink; therefore, this transformation—emaciation and so forth, resulting in the loss of flesh—is indeed occurring.
I experience again and again the great suffering born of hunger and thirst; indeed, this inauspicious state of being a preta was brought about because the rite of releasing a bull was not performed.
"Therefore, O King, ocean of compassion, I entreat you before you. The King said: "How is it to be known by men that a *preta* exists in my family?"
"Therefore, tell me this: how indeed is one released from the state of a *preta*? The *preta* said: "A *preta* should always be inferred by men through their physical marks and their suffering."
I shall describe those afflictions on earth caused by spirits among the royalty: when women’s fertile seasons become fruitless and the lineage does not increase.
Even those of tender age die; that is the suffering born of the deceased. There is also the sudden loss of livelihood and indeed a lack of standing among people.
There may be a sudden fire in the house; that suffering arises from the spirits of the departed. There will be constant quarreling in one's own home, as well as false accusations.
The occurrence of elephantiasis and other such ailments, as well as suffering arising from ghosts, may even occur when one has personally released wealth with great effort onto the open road.

That suffering arising from the state of a preta would not be obtained at all, nor would it perish; yet, even with good rain, there would be loss of agriculture, and from trade, the destruction of one's livelihood.
The wife may become hostile, and that suffering arises from the departed spirits; thus, O King, through such suffering, men obtain knowledge of the deceased.
If the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga) is performed, then one is liberated from the state of being a preta; therefore, O King, you too, O Lord, should likewise perform the vṛṣotsarga.
Out of great compassion, even though the king was present, he granted me authority here; therefore, I myself have obtained this slain prince.
O King, having taken that wealth from me, perform the bull-sacrifice festival (vṛṣotsava) on the full moon of Kārttika, or on the full moon of Āśvayuja, or at some time during the month of Āśvina.
On a day conjoined with the Revatī asterism, you should perform my bull festival; having summoned meritorious Brahmins and established the sacred fire according to the prescribed rite.

O King, gold should likewise be prepared according to the ritual with the six mantras; you should feed many Brahmins with the wealth obtained from those jewels. When this has been done, O protector of the earth, my liberation will come to pass.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "So be it," and then, O bird, the king accepted the jewel.
The right to perform the rites belongs only to him who is the receiver of the wealth; such is the discourse between those two—the deceased king and the performer—regarding their respective duties.
Then, with the clanging of bells and the booming of kettledrums, the fourfold royal army fell upon them.
As soon as she had arrived there, the preta vanished; having departed from that forest, the king also returned to the city.

On the full moon day of the month of Kārttika, he performed the ritual release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga) in honor of the deceased, according to the prescribed rules, using the wealth obtained from that jewel.

Even though he was a ghost, having instantly obtained a body of gold, he bowed to the king, saying, "O King, this is your majesty's power. Praising him thus, that grateful being departed for heaven as Garuḍa, by the king who recognized his debt.
All this has been related to you, how he was indeed raised from the state of a ghost by the king; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus, in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa, in the second part, the Dharmakāṇḍa, in the Pretakalpa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, is the ninth chapter titled "Description of the Rituals for the Release of a Bull Performed by Kings.
Garuḍa said: Upon the performance of the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite and the annual anniversary (Ābdika), men may attain the state of a god, a human, or a bird through their own past actions.
How can a *śrāddha* ceremony truly grant satisfaction to those whose food is distinct, whether it be that which is eaten by other twice-born ones or that which is offered into the fire?

How can that which is given be enjoyed by a *preta*, who consists of both the auspicious and the inauspicious? Furthermore, the necessity of performing the *śrāddha* on the new moon day (*āmāvāsya*) and other such occasions is declared in the *Śruti*.

The Blessed One said: "O Lord of Birds, hear how the *śrāddha* ceremony grants satisfaction to the departed spirits (*preta*s). Even though this deity has become a human being through the application of karma,"
His food, having become nectar, follows him even in the state of a god; in the state of a gandharva, it takes the form of enjoyments, and in the state of an animal, it becomes grass.
For the ancestral offering (śrāddha) follows even in the state of a serpent by way of the form of wind; it becomes fruit in the state of a bird, and likewise, meat among the Rākṣasas.
Likewise, in the state of a Dānava there is flesh; in the state of a Preta, blood; in the state of a human, food, drink, and so forth; and in childhood, there is the flavor of sensual enjoyment.

Garuḍa said: How do the funeral offerings (kavya) and sacrificial offerings (havya) given here by people reach the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka), and who is said to be the one that conveys them there?
If the *śrāddha* ceremony were to provide nourishment even for deceased beings, it would be like adding oil to increase the flame of an extinguished lamp.
And once men have died, O Master, as they enter the state produced by their own karma, who could possibly bring about the welfare of their son, and how?
The Blessed Lord said: O Tārkṣya, the authority of direct perception is stronger than that of scripture; however, an object revealed by scripture possesses the nature of nectar and the like.
The name and lineage of the ancestors indeed convey the offerings to the gods and the ancestors; likewise, the mantras of the śrāddha rite convey them through devotion.
"How can these insentient things bring about attainment?"—this is not to be understood as a fault, O Suparṇa; I shall tell you another [factor] that brings about attainment.
Agniṣvātta and the others are established as their presiding deities; [the offering] given according to rule at the proper time to a worthy recipient is what they receive.
These lead the food to that place where the living being resides; name, lineage, and mantras—they lead the food that has been given.
Even when they have attained hundreds of wombs, satisfaction attends them—those dwelling in other worlds under various names and lineages.

Three rice-balls (piṇḍas) are indeed offered upon darbha grass on the ground with the sacred thread over the right shoulder; thus they go to and satisfy the ancestors residing in the state of the departed (pretas).

Those who have not reached the places of torment are the five kinds of superior beings on earth; they are those born in various forms within the classes of birth such as the animal realm and so forth.
Whatever food these ancestors have in their various wombs, that very food remains present in the *śrāddha* offerings for them at those times.
Just as a calf finds its mother when the cows have been lost, so does food lead the Brahmin to the place where the living being resides.
The Pitṛs, who are the recipients of the Śrāddha, are always together with the Viśvedevas; having always partaken of this Śrāddha, they in turn satisfy the Pitṛs.
The Vasus, Rudras, and sons of Aditi are the ancestors who are the deities of the śrāddha; when they are gratified in the śrāddhas, they satisfy the ancestors of human beings.

Just as a pregnant woman truly nourishes both herself and her fetus through the fulfillment of her pregnancy-longings, so too do the gods nourish themselves and the ancestral manes of men through the śrāddha offerings.
Upon hearing that the time for the śrāddha has arrived, the ancestors rejoice; having meditated upon one another in their minds, they descend with the speed of thought.
For the ancestors dwelling in the intermediate space eat together with the Brahmins; they remain there in the form of wind, and having eaten, they proceed to the supreme goal.
O Bird, those Brahmins who have been invited on the day preceding the Śrāddha—having entered as their ancestors and partaken of the meal—depart for their own abode.
If, however, only one Brahmin has been invited to a *śrāddha* by the performer of the rite, his father resides in his stomach and his grandfather on his left side.
The great-grandfather sits to the south, while the consumer of the rice-balls remains behind; at the time of the Śrāddha, Yama brings the deceased ancestors from the abode of Yama.
Kāśyapa, they release those dwelling in hell from their human state, as they cry out, tormented by hunger, while confessing the evil deeds they themselves have committed.
They desire milk-rice mixed with honey for their sons and grandsons; therefore, one should satisfy them there according to the prescribed rite with that milk-rice.
Garuḍa said: "O twice-born one, O giver of honor, has anyone seen your ancestors who have come from that world and are eating on this earth?"
The Blessed One said: "O Garuḍa, listen; I shall tell you how Sītā indeed beheld her ancestors within the body of the Brahmin, as well as her father-in-law and the other three at one time."
Having indeed received his father’s command, Rāma departed for the forest; thereafter, Rāma set out with Sītā for the purpose of the Puṣkara pilgrimage.
Having arrived at the sacred ford, he began the śrāddha ceremony; meanwhile, Jānakī prepared ripe fruit and offered it to Rāma.
Having bathed at the word spoken by her beloved, she protected him when the sun had reached the middle of the sky and the time of *kutu-pa* had arrived.
All the sages who had been invited by Rāma arrived; seeing those munis come, Vaidehī, the daughter of Janaka, [was filled with joy].
Having taken the food by Rāma’s command, she approached to serve it; then, she stepped back a great distance and stood among the brahmins.
Then, having concealed herself by covering herself with shrubs, she remained hidden; and at that time, the joy of the Raghus, knowing Sītā to be in a secluded spot, [approached].
Having reflected for a very long time on what this might be, that virtuous woman quickly went a little way off for the sake of modesty.
"Or rather, why should I not seek out that woman while feeding the Brahmins? Reflecting thus, he himself proceeded to feed the Brahmins.
When the foremost of the twice-born had departed, Rāma said this to his beloved: "How was it that you remained hidden under your palms upon seeing the lords of the sages arrive?"
"O slender-limbed one, tell me the reason for all this; do not delay. Thus addressed by her husband, Sītā stood with her face cast down, shedding a flood of tears, and spoke these words to Rāghava:
Sītā said: "Listen, O Lord, to what kind of wonder has been seen by me here."
"O Raghava, your father was seen by me before the Brahmins, adorned with all his ornaments, along with two others who were likewise adorned."
Having seen your father, O Lord, I departed from your presence; how could I, clad in bark and deerskin, stand before the king?
O slayer of enemy heroes, this which has been uttered is the truth: how could food be given by me with my own hand to the king?
How indeed could we possibly give food to him in a grass bowl, he who is even the servant of servants and never enjoys anything for himself?

"How shall I go before the king with limbs smeared with sweat and filth, I who was formerly seen by the king adorned with all ornaments? O descendant of Raghu, I have been cast aside by him out of shame. Śrī Bhagavān said:
Having heard these words of his beloved, Rāma was struck with wonder in his mind.
Realizing that it was a marvel, she then returned to her own place; how Sītā beheld her ancestors has thus been reported to you.
Furthermore, hear briefly something more regarding the greatness of the śrāddha: when the new moon day has arrived, [the ancestors] stand waiting at the door of the house.
Becoming like the wind, the hosts of ancestors, distressed by hunger and thirst, long for the ancestral offering of men until the setting of the sun.
Then, when the sun had set, hopeless and filled with sorrow, they departed after sighing deeply for a long time and reproaching their own lineage.
Therefore, one ought to perform the śrāddha with great effort on the new moon day; if his kinsmen, such as sons and others, perform the śrāddha for him, [he attains the highest state].
Those who are uplifted by the śrāddha performed at Gayā attain the world of Brahmā along with him; for them, hunger or thirst never arises anywhere.

Therefore, a wise person should perform the śrāddha rite with great effort and correctly; therefore, one should perform the śrāddha with devotion according to the rules, even if using only vegetables.
One should perform the ancestral rite at the proper time; in such a family, no one suffers. [The performer gains] long life, sons, fame, heaven, renown, nourishment, strength, and prosperity.
Through the worship of the ancestors, one obtains cattle, wealth, and grain; indeed, the rite for the ancestors always excels even the rite for the gods.
For the nourishment of the ancestors is auspicious even before that of the deities; those who worship the ancestors, the gods, the Brahmins, and the sacrificial fire [attain this].
For they worship me alone, the inner self of all beings, having performed the ancestral rite (śrāddha) according to the Smṛti injunctions in accordance with their own means.
A human being gratifies the entire world, from Brahma down to a blade of grass, by the scattering of food that is performed on the earth by men.
O sky-walker, even those who have fallen into the state of a piśāca attain satisfaction through that [water], as well as by whatever water falls upon the ground from their bathing garments.
By that [water], satisfaction arises for those who have attained the state of crossing over; and whatever fragrant waters fall upon the surface of the earth, [they likewise bring satisfaction].
By that [offering], there is nourishment for those who have attained the state of gods, as well as for those who are outside their own family, who are fit for ritual action, yet remain unconsecrated.
But those who have failed [in their duties] subsist on scattered food, sweepings, and water; and they consume the water used for rinsing after meals and that which has been used during the day.
In the same way, others who have attained the state of *piśācas* or even the state of worms and insects find satisfaction through that [offering] to the Brahmins.
When the morsels of food have been lifted up, those who remain on the ground longing for food—by that very act, there is nourishment for them who have returned to the state of humanity.
While those twice-born men were performing their duties in this manner, some scattering of water or food occurred, whether pure or indeed impure from remnants.
Through that food, when the śrāddha has been properly performed, those in their families who have indeed passed into another birth receive nourishment.
The Caṇḍālas and those born of such base wombs as the Pukkasa and others partake of that śrāddha which is performed by men with wealth acquired through unjust means.
Thus it is attained, O bird: that which is given here by kinsmen performing the śrāddha—whether food, water, or vegetables—indeed brings about satisfaction.
All this that you have asked me has been explained to you: the immediate attainment of another body upon the surface of the earth, without delay.
I shall explain to you in brief that which you have asked: how the body [perishes] both immediately and with delay.
Hear from me how a mortal attains that distinction: thereafter, he becomes a person the size of a thumb, like smokeless light.
He immediately attains a single body composed of air, just as a water-louse, when about to die, withdraws its hind leg.
When the stability of the supreme foot has become firm, then the embodied soul completely casts off that former body.
At first, for the sake of enjoyment, a body composed of air appears; it is like the sense organ of one who is dying, which continues to grasp its objects.
That [self] is devoid of activity; it moves through the body by means of the vital air alone. Whatever body it attains, that too it departs from of its own accord.
Having grasped its own [nature], the living being emerges as if from the interior of a womb; whether it is departing, stationary, or engaged in enjoyment, it is endowed with the qualities (guṇas).
The deluded do not perceive it; those with the eye of knowledge see it. For they say that the *ātivāhika* body is composed of air.
Thus they indeed speak of that very same thing as belonging to the Yātudhānas; such is the body of men born from a physical embryo, which is called Suparṇa.
If the ten funeral cakes (piṇḍas) prescribed for the ten-day period are offered by sons and others, then the one born of wind (vāyuja) shall attain oneness with the body born of the funeral cakes.

If one born from a physical body were not to suffer the torments of wind, O Lord of Birds, then consider this: just as the embodied being in this very body passes through childhood, youth, and old age, so too does it attain another body; understand this to be certain.
Just as a person, having cast off worn-out garments, takes others that are new, so the embodied soul, casting off worn-out bodies, enters into others that are new.
Weapons do not cut this, nor does fire burn it; water does not moisten it, nor does the wind dry it.
It has already been told to you that one attains a body made of air immediately; now hear from me indeed concerning that body which is attained after a delay.
Sometimes, while lingering, he may obtain a body born of a physical aggregate; or else, he may go to the world of Yama in accordance with his own karma.
By the word of Citragupta, he experiences the hells; having undergone the torments, he then assumes the body of a beast, a bird, or the like.
That which a person grasps becomes a locus of "mine-ness" through delusion; having experienced the fruit of both auspicious and inauspicious karma, the human being is liberated.
Garuḍa said: "O ocean of compassion, tell me how even one burdened with many sins might reach you after having crossed the ocean of the existence of suffering."
O Lord of Ramā, tell me, who am listening and inquiring, how a person may no longer experience further contact with suffering.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: A man attains perfection by being devoted to his own respective duty; hear how one who is intent on his own work finds that perfection.
With the impurity caused by the failure of his karma removed through constant meditation on Vāsudeva, he is endowed with a purified intellect and, having restrained himself with fortitude;
Having abandoned sense objects such as sound and having cast aside passion and aversion, one who frequents solitude, eats moderately, and has restrained speech, body, and mind;
Constantly devoted to the yoga of meditation and firmly established in detachment, [he abandons] egoism, power, pride, desire, anger, and possessiveness.
Being liberated, free from the sense of "mine," and peaceful, one is fit for becoming Brahman; beyond this, O son of Kaśyapa, there is no further duty for men.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Satisfaction-bestowing Nature of Śrāddha," in the *Śrīgaruḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, within the second section on Dharma, the *Pretakalpa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
In the *Śrīgaruḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, Chapter Eleven:
Garuḍa said: From what cause does one obtain human birth? How does one meet with death? O best of gods, who dies, and having resorted to a body, where does it perish?
Whence do the sense faculties depart? How indeed can one become untouchable? Where are the actions performed here, and how does one experience them as they proceed?
"Be gracious to me; you ought to sever my delusion entirely. O best of gods, I am Kāśyapa, born from the womb of Vinatā. How do human beings go to the realm of Yama and to the realm of Viṣṇu?"
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Having abducted another's wife and having stolen the property of a Brahmin, [one falls].
One who steals jewels will be born as a Brahmarākṣasa in a desolate forest region or will be born into a low caste.
Whatever desire one contemplates, one is born with that as one's characteristic mark; weapons do not cut this, nor does fire burn it.
Neither do the waters moisten it, nor does the wind dry it; [therein are] the mouth, the eyes, the nose, the two ears, the anus, and the passage for urine.

For all creatures, such as those born from eggs and so forth, these apertures exist everywhere; specifically, there are eight upward-facing apertures extending from the navel up to the crown of the head.
O bird, virtuous mortals indeed ascend through the aperture above on their death anniversary, continuing until the annual rites are completed according to the prescribed injunctions.
Indeed, even a man who is destitute can perform all actions; for wherever a living being dwells within the body, there he experiences the fruits of both the auspicious and the inauspicious.

O Lord of Birds, he likewise consumes the defects born of mind, speech, and body; once dead, he attains happiness and is not bound by the snares of illusion. But that man who is bound by the snares and devoted to improper action—

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Gateways of Departure Indicating the Upward and Downward Courses," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O Tārkṣya, thus has the classification of the life of human beings been told to you for their benefit and for the sake of their liberation from the state of being a *preta*."
There are eighty-four lakhs of living beings, divided into four categories: those born from eggs, those born from sweat, those born from sprouts, and those born from a womb.
Twenty-one lakhs are proclaimed as egg-born (aṇḍaja); likewise, those born from sweat (svedaja) and those born from sprouts (udbhijja) are stated in due order.
Likewise, humans and others are said to be born from a womb; indeed, among all living beings, human status is difficult to attain.
The state of possessing the treasure of the five faculties is attained through great merit by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of other castes.
The washerman, the leather-worker, the actor, the basket-maker, the fisherman, the Meda, and the Bhilla—these seven are indeed remembered as the lowest-born (antyaja).
Due to the distinctions between Mlecchas and Tumbas, there are numerous divisions of castes; indeed, for all living beings, there are thousands of such caste divisions.
Indeed, for all living beings, there are thousands of varieties; yet their food, sexual union, sleep, fear, and likewise anger are the same.
For all living beings, supreme discernment is exceedingly difficult to attain; indeed, there are manifold distinctions of bodies in the form of one-footed creatures and others.
Where the black-spotted deer roams, that place is called Dharmadaśa; there all the deities, beginning with Brahmā, reside in every way.

Among beings, those with breath are the best; among those with breath, those who live by their intelligence; among the intelligent, humans are the best; and among humans, the brahmins are traditionally held to be the best.
Having attained this human birth, which is the sole means for achieving heaven, he who does not accomplish one of these two goals has certainly deceived himself.

One who possesses a hundred desires a thousand; one who possesses a thousand strives to acquire a hundred thousand; a lord of a hundred thousand seeks a kingdom; and even a king wishes to obtain the entire earth.

Even as a wheel-turning monarch he attained the state of a god; even as a god he became the sovereign of all the gods; and even as the lord of the gods he attained the higher realms—nevertheless, craving does not turn back.
But one who is overcome by craving falls into hell; however, those who are liberated from craving attain residence in heaven.
In this world, a person who is self-dependent certainly becomes happy; sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are its qualities.
And thus, one who is dependent on sense objects certainly becomes miserable.

The deer, the elephant, the moth, the bee, and the fish—these five have been destroyed by the five [senses] alone. How is it that the one who is heedless, who indulges in all five with all five, is not destroyed?
In childhood, the fool consists of his father and mother; in youth, he consists of his beloved; and in old age, he consists of his sons and grandsons; at no time does he consist of himself.
A man bound by fetters made of iron or wood may be released; but one bound by the fetters consisting of son and wife is never released.
One person commits the evil deeds, while the multitude enjoys the fruit; those who enjoy the fruit are separated from the act, yet the doer alone is stained by the fault.
No one—whether a child, an old man, or even a youth—conquers death; likewise, pleasure, pain, and the like come again and go away.
While all are looking on, the deceased abandons everything; a living being is born alone, and alone indeed does it perish.
Even alone one experiences the fruit of good deeds, and alone that of evil deeds; having cast off the dead body, which is like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, the two [body and soul] depart.
Relatives turn away and depart, but Dharma follows him; wealth remains in the house, while friends and kinsmen turn back at the cemetery.
The fire consumes the body, while merit and demerit depart; though the body is burnt by the fire, merit and sin remain together [with the self].
A human being experiences everywhere either merit or evil, according to whatever wealth was not given to supplicants while the sun had not yet set.
I do not know whose wealth that will belong to tomorrow morning; his riches cry out, "Who shall be my master?"
Neither was it given to the foremost of the twice-born for the sake of helping others; rather, whatever was obtained—be it much or little—was due to merit performed in a previous birth.
Having understood this, wealth is given for the sake of the Dharma; by means of that wealth—purified by a mind of faith—the Dharma is sustained.
Dharma devoid of faith yields no fruit either in this world or the next; for from dharma arises wealth, and from dharma desire also arises.
Dharma alone leads to liberation; therefore, one should practice dharma. Dharma is accomplished through faith, not by vast heaps of wealth.

For the sages, possessing nothing yet endowed with faith, have gone to heaven. O bird, whatever is offered in sacrifice, given as a gift, or performed as austerity without faith is said to be non-existent; it yields no fruit either here or after death.

Thus, in the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the second part of the Uttarakhaṇḍa, in the section concerning the Pretas of Dharmaka, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, is the twelfth chapter titled "The Description of the Deceased Following Only Dharma.
Garuḍa said: "O Lord of Gods, by what action is the state of a *preta* not produced? O Supreme Lord, tell me that regarding all living beings on earth."

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Now I shall describe, in brief, the funeral rites for the anniversary of death (kṣayāha-aurdhvadaihika), which must be performed by men desiring liberation using only the hand of clay (kvahasta).

Especially for women, when a child has passed five years, there is no rite on this earth other than the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) for the purpose of ending the state of being a ghost (*pretatva*). Apart from the release of a bull, nothing else exists.
Whether he is alive or dead, for one who performs the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga), the state of being a preta shall not occur, even without [other] gifts, sacrifices, or vows.
Garuḍa said: "O best among the foremost of gods, O Madhusūdana, tell me: at what time should one perform the rite of releasing a bull—whether while living or even after death?"
But what fruit would there be at the end from the sixteen śrāddhas performed?

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: If one performs the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍapātana) without having performed the release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga), that spiritual merit does not accrue to the giver; it is fruitless for the deceased.
If for a deceased person the bull is not released on the eleventh day, his state as a preta remains firmly established, even by hundreds of performed śrāddhas.
