Garuḍa said: For those whose death has been brought about by a serpent, there is no ritual such as cremation with fire; this applies even if one dies by water, a horned animal, or by weapons and the like.
O Lord, how can there be purification for those who have died an unnatural death? O God, you ought to sever this doubt of mine completely.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: A Brāhmaṇa becomes pure in six months; a Bāhuja (Kṣatriya) in six months and a half; a Vaiśya in one and a half months; and a Śūdra becomes pure in one month.
If, having given all kinds of gifts at a sacred ford, one dies while remaining pure and observant of celibacy, such a person does not go to a miserable rebirth in this world.

Having performed the rite of releasing a bull and other such acts, one should practice the dharma of an ascetic; if one meets death while in the state of an ascetic, he shall go to the eternal abode of Brahman.
He who performs forbidden acts while devoid of the conduct of the virtuous may not go to the punishment of Yama, provided he has performed rites such as the release of a bull.
A son, or a brother, or likewise a grandson, a kinsman, a member of the same lineage, or one who inherits the property, should perform the Vṛṣotsarga rite upon the death [of the deceased].
In the absence of sons, the wife, the daughter's son, or even the daughter herself shall perform the rite; while sons exist, one should not cause the *vṛṣotsarga* to be performed by anyone else.
Garuḍa said: "O Lord of the Gods, those men and women who have no sons—O God, you ought to sever this doubt of mine completely."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "There is no destination for one who is childless, nor indeed is there heaven; therefore, by whatever means possible, one should bring about the birth of a son."
Whatever gifts have been given by men themselves, all of those indeed stand before him.
Whatever various condiments, foods, and edibles are given with one's own hand, at the end of life, the fruit thereof is inexhaustible.
Cows, land, gold, garments, food, and footwear—wherever a living being dwells, these things attend him there.
As long as the body is healthy, one should practice dharma; for when it is unwell and driven by others, one is unable to accomplish anything.
For one who is alive yet dead in this world, no funeral rites for the deceased are performed; having become like the wind and overcome by hunger, he wanders day and night.
He is born again and dies as a worm, an insect, or a moth; he may even enter an inauspicious womb, and having been born, he perishes immediately.

As long as this body is healthy and free from disease, as long as old age is far off, as long as the power of the senses is unimpaired, and as long as there is no exhaustion of the life-span—during that very time, a wise person should exert great effort toward their own spiritual welfare. For when the house is already ablaze, what kind of endeavor is it to dig a well?

Thus, in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the second part, the Dharma-kāṇḍa, in the Preta-kalpa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, is the thirteenth chapter titled "The Praise of the Vṛṣotsarga, the Gift of Dharma, Sons, and Others.
Garuḍa said: O Lord, tell me the fruit of that which is given by one who is afflicted or dying; or of that which is given by one in a state of health, even if it is devoid of ritual injunctions.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: A single cow given by one whose mind is at ease is equal to a hundred cows given by one who is ill, and a thousand cows given by one who is dying; these are considered gifts of wealth when no other riches are available.

Even for one who has died, a hundred thousand [cows] purified by ritual are equal to that; through the conjunction of a sacred ford and a worthy recipient, a single cow bestows the merit of a hundred thousand.
O best of birds, when given into a worthy vessel, the gift of a donor increases day by day for the sake of merit, as does the acceptance of gifts by the wise.
Is the fire of mantras, which removes poison and cold, a vessel for faults? One should give daily to a worthy recipient, especially on auspicious occasions.
A wise person desiring their own welfare should never give anything to an unworthy recipient; for a cow given to an unworthy recipient may lead the donor to hell.
It shall cause the downfall of the recipient along with twenty-one generations of their kin; for whatever has been done with one's own hand, its fruit is obtained after reaching another body.
Just as wealth placed in the ground with one's own hand, so too does one obtain its fruit; this I declare, O Lord of Birds.
Even one who is childless, and especially one who desires liberation, as well as one who is destitute, should particularly perform the ancestral rites for his mother and paternal grandmother.
For whatever is performed with even a very small amount of wealth by one's own hand becomes inexhaustible, just as clarified butter poured into the sacrificial fire.
A single milch-cow should be given as a dowry for one son; if she is sold, she burns the family down to the seventh generation.
Therefore, while life is flickering, one should perform all [virtuous deeds]; having taken the provisions of generosity, one travels happily upon the great path.
Otherwise, a living being suffers on the road like one who is without provisions for the journey; knowing this, O best of birds, one should perform the sacrifice of the bull.
He who dies without having performed [this rite] and remains childless does not partake of liberation; yet even one who is childless attains happiness on the Great Path if he should perform it.
One does not attain through sacrifices such as the Agnihotra, nor even through various kinds of gifts, that same goal which is attained by the ritual release of a bull.
And among all sacrifices, the bull-sacrifice is likewise the most excellent; therefore, one should perform the bull-sacrifice with every effort.
Garuḍa said: "Out of favor, please tell me about the anniversary of death and the funeral rites: at what time, on which lunar day, and by what procedure should they be performed?"
What fruit does one obtain by performing this? Tell me that now; by your grace, O Govinda, a human being becomes liberated.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: During the months beginning with Kārttika, when the sun has entered the southern solstice, in the bright fortnight, on auspicious lunar days such as the twelfth (dvādaśī), O King of Birds.
At an auspicious lunar mansion or moment, in a pure place, being composed, he should summon a Brāhmaṇa who is knowledgeable in the ritual rules and possesses auspicious characteristics.
One should perform the purification of the house through recitations, burnt offerings, and gifts; on an auspicious day under the constellation Abhijit, one should worship the planets and the gods.
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to one's ability with various mantras, and first of all, O Lord of Birds, one should perform the installation of the planetary deities (grahas).
One should perform the worship of the Mothers and cause the stream of wealth (vasordhārā) to fall; having established the fire right there, one should indeed perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having established a Śālagrāma stone, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava Śrāddha; and having worshipped a bull right there with garments, ornaments, and decorations.
One should first consecrate four yearling heifers; then one should perform a circumambulation, and at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa), perform the ritual dismissal (visarjana).
Having recited this mantra while standing facing north: "O Dharma, you were created in the form of a bull by Brahmā in ancient times."
By the power of your renunciation, deliver me from the ocean of existence, having consecrated me with auspicious and purifying mantras according to the prescribed ritual.
One should perform the ritual release of the bull (vṛṣotsarga) with the *tanakrīḍanti* mantra; thereafter, one should consecrate Nīla with the water from the Rudra-pitcher.
Having established that water at the base of the navel, one should place it upon the head; then one should perform the *ātma-śrāddha* and give gifts to the best of the twice-born.
If one must travel by water, one should cause water to be offered there; and whatever was dear to the person while they were alive, that one should give according to one's ability.

When the rite of bull-liberation (vṛṣotsarga) has been performed, what is deficient attains completeness; one who dies while well-satisfied on a difficult path goes [to heaven], of this there is no doubt.
Men who are always devoted to giving do not see the world of Yama, provided that the *śrāddha* offering for the eleventh day is given to the deceased being.
Whether given by oneself or given by another, [the gift] does not remain secure here or in the next world for thirteen, seven, five, or three [generations] respectively.
Endowed with faith and devotion, one should perform the offerings of land; one should prepare seven or five vessels of sesame seeds in due order.
Thereafter, one should feed the Brahmins and cause a single cow to be given; then, according to the Vedic injunction, one should offer a bull with the mantra "śanno devīḥ."
One should perform the marriage ceremony with four young heifers; a discus should be placed on the left side, and likewise a trident on the right.
The wise man should give the price for the bull and release that bull, performing the rite according to the rules for a single ancestor (ekoddiṣṭa) with the utterance of "svāhā."
One should diligently perform the rites on the eleventh day and the twelfth day; prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, one should perform the sixteen *śrāddhas*.
Having fed the Brahmins, one should cause gifts of footprints to be given; having placed [the image] upon cotton, one should likewise place Acyuta upon a copper vessel.
Having covered that which stands there with a cloth, one should offer the *argha* with auspicious fruits; having fashioned a boat made of sugarcane, one should wrap it with silk thread.
Having placed clarified butter in a bronze vessel for the sake of the Vaitaraṇī river, one should perform the rite of boarding a boat and worship the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
And that gift, according to one's own realization of the Self, is infinite for those submerged in the ocean of existence and afflicted by grief, heat, pain, and suffering.
For those who are destitute of the boat of Dharma, Janārdana is indeed their savior; likewise, sesame, iron, gold, cotton, and salt [are to be given].
The seven types of grain, land, and cows—each one is remembered as purifying; one should prepare vessels of sesame seeds and cause the gift of a bed to be given.
One should give gifts according to one's ability to the poor, the helpless, and the distinguished; O Tārkṣya, he who acts in this manner shall have sons, even if he was previously sonless.
He attains success just like those celibate students; a person should perform the obligatory and occasional rites as long as he lives.
Whatever dharma is performed, its fruit shall be inexhaustible; for the Śrāddha of the year includes the merit of pilgrimages, vows, and other such rites.
O bird, merit should be diligently bestowed upon the deities, the gurus, and likewise upon one's mother and father; it increases day by day.
For whatever abundant gift anyone bestows at this sacrifice, all of that becomes inexhaustible for them, just as it is said to be on the sacrificial altar.
Just as ascetics who observe the vow of celibacy are most worthy of honor in the world, so too are they always honored by everyone in the world.
I am always the granter of boons to him, as are the four-faced Brahmā and Hara; they go to the supreme worlds—this is my true word.
Wherever the bull, having been released, drinks water from a reservoir, or constantly digs at the earth with his horns in great joy;
Abundant food and drink shall be presented to the ancestors; on the full moon day or the new moon day, one should cause vessels of sesame seeds to be given.
Whatever fruit one obtains by giving gifts during thousands of solar transits and hundreds of solar festivals, that very fruit is indeed obtained in the rite of releasing the blue bull.
Young heifers should be given to the Brahmins, as well as plots of land; and vessels of sesame seeds should be given to the twice-born who are devotees of Śiva.
And having clothed Umāmaheśvara alone, one should cause him to be given [offerings]; he who resembles an Atasī flower, is clad in yellow garments, and is the infallible Acyuta.
For those who pay homage to Govinda, no fear exists; those who desire liberation from the state of a preta will perform acts of veneration.
"They shall go to the higher worlds"—this is my true word. All this regarding your funeral rites has been told to you by me.

Having heard this, one is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt about this. Having heard its incomparable majesty, Garuḍa was filled with joy and, for the benefit of human beings, questioned Keśava once again.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Gift of Cows, the Release of Bulls, the Ten Gifts, the Abundant Gifts, and Other Rituals," in the *Pretakalpa* (Section on the Departed) within the *Dharmakāṇḍa* (Section on Dharma), the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* (Latter Section) of the *Śrī-Gāruḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa. —
*Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, Chapter 15.
Garuḍa said: "O Blessed One, tell me everything regarding the determination of the world of Yama—the majesty and the detailed path of a living being, beginning from the moment of its departure."
The Blessed One said: Listen, O Tārkṣya, I shall declare the determination of the path of Yama—namely, all the stages of departure and the sixteen cities.
The distance between the realm of Yama and that of humans is, by measurement, eighty-six thousand yojanas.
O bird, when some disease arises through the application of karma after one has experienced in this world the fruits of evil deeds or misdeeds as they were acquired, [then...]
For all beings, there is merely a sign according to their performed karma; whoever has death ordained for them will certainly encounter it.
When the embodied soul, through the yoga of action, leaves its own body here, one should then prepare the ground by smearing it with cow dung.
Then, having scattered sesame seeds and *darbha* grass, one should place gold in the mouth; likewise, one should place a *tulasī* plant and a *śālagrāma* stone in close proximity.

In this way, through the *sāmādisūkta* hymns, death [occurring] at a bridge bestows liberation; likewise, [death occurs] by means of casting gold needles into the houses of living beings who have been heated.
One [drop] should be placed on the face, and likewise on the pair of nostrils; two each should be applied in due order to the eyes and the ears.
Then, one should likewise place one [leaf] upon the linga and one within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa); one should also cause tulasī to be offered upon both hands and at the throat.
A pair of garments should be given, and one should worship with unbroken grains (*akṣata*) mixed with saffron; one should provide it with a flower garland and lead the other through the door.

The son, together with his kinsmen, and the Brahmin, together with the city-dwellers, [prepared for the rite]; the son himself, having placed the deceased father upon his shoulder along with his kinsmen, [proceeded].
Having gone to a cemetery site, facing either east or north, one should have the funeral pyre constructed right there on ground that has not been burned before.
When the collection of impaired senses has reached a state of insentience within consciousness, [one should offer] fuel-sticks of *śrīkhaṇḍa*, *tulasī* wood, and *pālāśa*.
Then the vital breaths, drawn near by the messengers of Yama, begin to move; one perceives the world as a single unity, and the divine vision arises.
A certain person may exhibit a loathsome and dreadful form, with life-breaths clinging to the throat, vomiting foam, and having a mouth covered in saliva.
The wicked-souled are beaten there by the servants with bonds of nooses, while the virtuous are led away with ease by the leaders of heaven.
The sinners go with great suffering along the difficult path of Yama; and Yama, having become four-armed and bearing the conch, discus, mace, and other weapons, [waits for them].
One should properly treat those devoted to meritorious deeds and virtuous ones like friends; having summoned all evildoers, Yama should subdue them with punishment.

With a roar like the clouds at the time of universal dissolution, possessing a luster equal to a mountain of collyrium, mounted upon a buffalo, difficult to propitiate, and having a brilliance like the flash of lightning.
His body was three yojanas in extent, fierce and extremely terrifying; he was formidable, holding an iron staff, with a noose in his hand, and possessed a hideous form.
With crooked eyes and inspiring extreme terror, a person the size of a thumb emerges from the corpse of sinners, crying out "Alas! Alas! as he departs.
At that very moment, his own body—motionless, devoid of life-breaths, and loathsome—is led away by the messengers of Yama while he gazes upon it from afar.
It quickly becomes untouchable, foul-smelling, and universally despised; for the body indeed passes through three stages, known as worm, excrement, and ashes.
O Tārkṣya, what pride should be felt by men who are destroyed in an instant? For from wealth comes charity, from speech come truth and eloquence, and likewise from life come fame and merit.
Benefiting others is the essence extracted from this worthless body; indeed, as it is being led away in this manner, the messengers of death threaten it.
Displaying intense terror again and again for the sake of hell, move quickly, you evil-souled one! You have gone to the abode of Yama.
"We shall lead you without delay to the Kumbhīpāka and other hells," he heard such words from his kinsmen, as well as their lamentations.
Lamenting "Alas! Alas! loudly, he is led away by the servants of Yama; therefore, one should perform the *śrāddha* rite at the proper time and likewise on the eleventh day.

At the time of the deceased's departure, one should offer six morsels of food in succession: at the place of death, at the door, and at the crossroads, O Tārkṣya, for the sake of the causal principle.
There are six [impurities] regarding resting, piling wood, and likewise gathering; hear their cause, O Tārkṣya, as well as the six regarding the preparation of the funeral cakes.
In the place of the deceased, that which is called a "corpse" (śava) is offered by that name; by that being given, the presiding deities of the house and the site are satisfied.
By that [offering], the ground becomes satisfied, as does its presiding deity; at the gateway, however, a *piṇḍa* should be offered, having addressed it by the name "Traveler."
By that gift, the household deities stationed at the doorway are gratified; one should cause it to be given with reference to the deity named Khecara at the crossroads.
Furthermore, beings and other divine classes do not cause harm; therefore, one should have this known as the "resting of beings" performed there during the break.
The Piśācas, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, and whoever else dwells in the various directions, shall not cause any impediment to his body being offered as an oblation.
O Lord of Birds, one is born as a preta from the funeral pyre, the funeral mound, and so forth; some say that the "accomplisher" (sādhaka) resides within the funeral pyre.
Some wise ones who know the cosmic cycles say that it is indeed a preta; from that time onward, it is offered in various places under the name of "preta."
Thus, by means of these five lumps, the corpse becomes fit for the offering; otherwise, they indeed become as previously described, leading to harm.
One should offer the first ball of rice at the moment of departure, likewise one at the half-way point, and the third on the funeral pyre; thus three balls of rice are prescribed.
Vidhātṛ [is worshipped] on the first piṇḍa, Garuḍadhvaja on the second, and the messengers of Yama on the third; thus the ritual application is proclaimed.
When this third funeral ball (piṇḍa) is offered, he is liberated from the defects of the body; and the soul, having become the substratum, should cause the funeral pyre to blaze with flames.
Having swept and smeared [the ground], then having scraped and removed [the debris] from the altar, and having sprinkled it and established the fire there according to the prescribed rule;
Having worshipped the deity known as Kravyāda with flowers and unbroken rice grains: "O Creator of beings, O Source of the world! You are the protector of the worlds."
"Therefore, O gatherer, lead this deceased one to heaven. Having thus honored the flesh-eater, one should perform the oblation of the body.
When the body is thus half-burnt, one should then offer an oblation of clarified butter; with the mantra "To the body hairs, svāhā," one should perform the homa according to the prescribed rule.
Having placed that deceased person upon the funeral pyre, one should then offer oblations of clarified butter to Yama, to Antaka, to Mṛtyu, and likewise to Brahmā.

One [oblation] should be offered into the mouth of Jātavedas, and likewise one into the mouth of the deceased; thereafter, one should ignite the fire on the eastern side of the funeral pyre once again.
From this you were born; from you may he be born again. For that world of heaven, svāhā! The purifier blazes.
Having thus offered an oblation of clarified butter mixed with sesame seeds accompanied by mantras, the cremation must then certainly be performed by the son.
Then one should weep intensely; in this way, he will find happiness there after the cremation, once the rite of piling the funeral pyre has been performed.
O Bird, one should offer a funeral ball (piṇḍa) for the deceased to pacify the pain of cremation; for spirits wait upon that deceased person who seeks his kinsmen.

Immediately after the cremation, the sons should perform a bath along with their clothing; thereafter, they should offer water with sesame seeds, pronouncing the name and lineage [of the deceased], saying, "May it remain."
Then all the people of the countryside should clap their hands and say, "Viṣṇu! Viṣṇu! and they should praise the deceased by reciting his virtues.
All the people, having come from every direction to his house, [placed] cow dung and white mustard seeds on the southern side of the door.
Having placed the god Varuṇa within his own dwelling and concealed him, one should eat neem leaves; having consumed clarified butter, one may then go home.
O Lord of Birds, some sprinkle the cremation site with milk; one should not shed tears, but should offer handfuls of water to him.
Since the deceased helplessly consumes the phlegm and tears shed by his kinsmen, one should certainly not weep; rather, funeral rites should be performed according to one's own ability.
And one should offer milk and water in an earthen vessel for three days, O Tārkṣya, when the sun has set, either at Valabhī or at a crossroads.
Bound, with his heart utterly bewildered, and driven by his past deeds, he longs for a body while being led away by the messengers of Yama, gazing at cremation grounds, crossroads, and houses.
Pindas should be offered into the pit for ten days, day after day, and water-offerings (añjali) should be presented daily, always with the deceased in mind.
The increase [of the offerings] should be performed until the tenth-day piṇḍa; for the rite must be performed by the son, and in his absence, by the wife.
In his absence, the disciple should do so; in his absence, a uterine brother should cause water and the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to be offered at the cremation ground or at another sacred site.
Whatever one might give on the first day—whether boiled rice, parched grain flour, or vegetables, roots, fruits, and so forth—one should give that same thing on the following day.
"O Lord of Birds, for ten days the sons and others provide funeral cakes (piṇḍas) here; these are divided into four portions every day."
Two parts are for the sake of the body, providing pleasure to the five elements; the third belongs to the messengers of Yama, and the fourth is that upon which others subsist.
Within nine days and nights, the deceased attains completion; for the being whose body is thus completed, intense hunger arises on the tenth day.
There is no ritual injunction, nor even a mantra, nor the invocation with *svadhā*, nor blessings; whatever is given after pronouncing the name and lineage, that pertains to the ten-day period.
O bird, when the body is burnt, a new body is produced in this manner: on the first day, the head is generated from that primary mass.
The neck and shoulders are in the second [section], and the heart is in the third; by the fourth, the back is formed, and by the fifth, the navel.
On the seventh day, the six [limbs]—the hips, the private parts, and the thighs—are formed; likewise on the eighth, the palate and the feet; and on the ninth and tenth days, hunger arises.
Having obtained a body and overcome by hunger, he stands at the door of the house; on the tenth day, one should offer him that funeral ball (piṇḍa) together with meat.
Since a preta, once a body has arisen, is possessed of extreme hunger, his hunger is not extinguished by anything other than flesh.
On the eleventh day and the twelfth day, the deceased enjoys [the offerings] for two days; one should apply the term "preta" (deceased) to both women and men.
Whatever substance is given—be it a lamp, food, water, clothing, or anything else—it should be offered with the word "preta," for it grants joy even after death.
On the thirteenth day, that preta is led along the great path; relying upon a body born of funeral offerings, it remains hungry by day and by night.

The path of cold, heat, spikes, carnivorous beasts, and fire belongs to the sinners; however, hunger and thirst exist only for those who have performed evil deeds, while everything is pleasant for those of purified self.
And on the path filled with forests of sword-leaves, these sufferings exist: he is constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, and tormented by the servants of Yama.
Day after day, the deceased indeed travels two hundred and forty-seven yojanas in a single day and night.
Bound by the nooses of Yama and crying out "Alas! Alas!", he abandons his own home and proceeds toward the city of Yama.
That preta proceeds in due order toward the city of Yama, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious, passing along the way through various such excellent cities.
The regions of Yama, Sauripura, Nagendrabhavana, Gandharva, Shailagama, Krouncha, Krurapura, and Vicitrabhavana bring many calamities and bestow suffering.
Before him were the city of Nānākranda, the birthplace of Suta, the fierce Payovarṣaṇa, the city of Śītāḍhya, and the city of Yāmya, where many are terrified by the heat.
On the thirteenth day, that preta was seized by the servants of Yama; as he traveled along that path, he was like a captured monkey.
Likewise, as he travels along the road, crying out "O son! O son! and constantly wailing "Alas! Alas!", what kind of deed have I committed?
When it spreads forth, it asks, "Why is human birth obtained? [The answer is: Human birth is obtained through the application of great merit.
Having obtained that [wealth], he indeed does not give his own money to beggars; rather, with a faltering voice, he says, "That has become dependent on another."
He is tormented excessively by the servants of Yama and remembers his previous existence.

No one is the giver of pleasure or pain; the notion that another gives them is a false delusion. One always experiences the very karma performed by oneself in the past; O embodied being, atone for whatever you have done.

I have not given gifts, nor have I offered oblations into the fire; I have not practiced austerities in the caves of the snowy mountains, nor have I resorted to the great waters of the Ganges. O embodied one, cross over somehow by means of that which you have done!

No constant charity was given, no daily provision for cows was made, no gift of the Vedas was offered, nor were books of the Shastras; never before has such a path been seen, nor has it ever been traveled—O embodied one, cross over that which you have now brought upon yourself!

Indeed, no reservoir was ever constructed for the sake of humans in this waterless land, nor for the sake of beasts and birds; nor was a pasture made for the satisfaction of cattle. O embodied one, you have done nothing at all that is beneficial.
I have not enjoyed the pleasure of my husband's company, nor did I enter the fire when he died; since he is dead, I shall observe his vow. O body, deliver me from whatever you have done!

This female body, a vessel for manifold sufferings, has been obtained by me through misdeeds committed in the past; it has not been withered away by month-long fasts, nor by *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, nor by the observance of combined restraints.
I have spoken what was to be said regarding men; therefore, O bird, listen attentively. Having obtained a female body, the embodied soul proclaims the deeds performed in the past.

Thus, in the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the second part, in the *Dharmadṛpta-pretakalpa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, this is the fifteenth chapter titled "The Description of the Extent of the Realm of Yama, its Majesty, and the Journey Therein.
The Blessed Lord said: "O Lord of Birds, while that preta was thus lamenting, crying out intensely, and being tormented by the servants (kiṅkaras),"
For seventeen days he is dragged along the path of the wind; but on the eighteenth day and night, he first goes to the city of Yama.
In that delightful, excellent city, there was a great multitude of pretas; there also flowed the Puṣpabhadrā river, and there stood a banyan tree of pleasing appearance.
There, that person is made to rest by the servants of Yama; being deeply afflicted there, he will remember the happiness of his wife, children, and others.
Afflicted by thirst and oppressed by exhaustion, he weeps with piteous words for his own wealth, his wives, his home, his sons, and his pleasures.
Then he indeed grieves for his servants, friends, and everything else; while he is afflicted by hunger in that city, it is said to him by his own attendants:

The servants said: "Where is wealth? Where are sons and wife? Where is the home? Where are you, such as you are? Enjoy what has been acquired by your own karma; go forth for a long time upon the great path."

O traveler to the next world, you know that the strength of wayfarers depends upon provisions; yet you exert yourself for provisions, though you must certainly travel by that path where there is neither buying nor selling.
"O bird, you have not heard the words uttered by the messengers of Yama. Thus addressed, he was then struck by all of them with mallets.
If a monthly funeral ball (piṇḍa) is offered here by sons to a worthy recipient out of affection or compassion, he partakes of it and thereafter proceeds to the city of Sauri.
There, indeed, was a king named Jaṅgama, who bore the form of Death; seeing him, [the king] became terrified by fear and set his mind on taking rest.
Having gone to that city, he eats water mixed with food; then, having passed through that city, he proceeds to where that which was given at the three-fortnightly rite is located.
In the beautiful city of Nagendra, a hungry ghost wanders day and night; as he travels through the terrifying forests, he cries out upon seeing them.
Tormented by terrifying beings, he weeps again and again; then, at the end of two months, he passes beyond that city.
Having eaten food and drunk water, and whatever was given here by his kinsmen, he is then led away by the servants of Yama while being tormented by nooses.
When the third month has arrived, having enjoyed the auspicious city of the Gandharvas for that third month, he goes forward there.
In the fourth month, he indeed reaches the city of Śailāgama; there, stones rain down upon the one who stands as a preta.
If one partakes of the śrāddha offered on the fourth month, one shall become happy therein.

Then, in the fifth month, the deceased spirit goes to the city of Krūra; staying in that city, the spirit indeed enjoys what was given here by his sons. Thereafter, in the sixth month, the spirit goes to the city named Krauñca.
There, nourished by the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and the ancestral offering (śrāddha) given previously, he rested for half a muhūrta, trembling and deeply distressed.
Having passed through that city while being threatened by the servants of Yama, he proceeds to the City of Paintings (Citranagara), where King Vicitra resides.
Indeed, where the son of Sūrya, the younger brother of Yama, rules as king, five and a half months constitute what is known as a half-yearly period.
Struck by the messengers of Yama, he eats there for less than six months; furthermore, on the path, hunger afflicts him excessively again and again.
Some son or kinsman of mine remains alive, who brings me joy as I am falling into an ocean of grief.
While he was thus lamenting on the path and being restrained by the servants, thousands of fishermen arrived there before him.
We [are here] for you, who desire to cross the great Vaitaraṇī river, which is a hundred yojanas wide and filled with pus and blood.
"Filled with various fish and surrounded by flocks of various birds, we shall carry you across in comfort," they said to her.

"O traveler, grant me passage if you have the inclination. Thereupon, she gave him a cow, and by means of that boat she was able to cross over. It is taught that the gift of a cow is for the welfare of men and serves as the Vaitaraṇī river at the end.
It burns away all the sins of others and leads them to the world of Viṣṇu; O best of birds, if it is not given, one suffers by associating with such a person.
While the body is in a healthy state, one who desires to cross that river should observe the Vaitaraṇī vow and give a cow to a learned man.
But as he was being consumed, he reproached himself, saying: "I did not give even a little to the twice-born for the sake of provisions on my journey."
"O fool, you have not given gifts, nor offered oblations, nor recited mantras, nor bathed, nor performed worship; experience the exact result of whatever kind of action you have committed."
At that very moment, utterly bewildered in his heart and struck by the soldiers, he speaks; on the far bank of the Vaitaraṇī, he consumes what was given to him in jars and other vessels.
O Tārkṣya, having eaten at a śrāddha ceremony performed within six months [of death], one goes ahead; therefore, in that case especially, one should feed auspicious brahmins.
Tārkṣya travels two hundred and forty-seven yojanas every day and night, even when he is exhausted.
When the seventh month arrives, one should go to a city that is free from many calamities; there, one should partake of the śrāddha offered in the seventh month.
When the eighth month has arrived, one goes to the city of Nānākranda; having seen the hosts of Nānākranda wailing most piteously.
And he himself, empty-hearted and afflicted by suffering, cries out; yet, having partaken of that monthly *śrāddha* offering, he becomes happy there.

Leaving that city, the deceased goes toward Tapta-pura; having reached Sutapta-nagara, in the ninth month he enjoys the feeding of Brahmins, the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), and the Śrāddha performed by his son.
When the tenth month has arrived, he goes to the realm of Rudra; having consumed what was given during that tenth month, he departs.
Having eaten for ten months and one day, one encounters a rain of water; there, clouds pour down rain that brings suffering to the pretas.
Then the ship set sail, its crew afflicted by great hunger and thirst; in the twelfth month, he ate the śrāddha offering there, feeling extremely cold.
When the year is somewhat less than that, or at the eleventh and a half years, he goes to Śītapura, where the cold is extremely painful.
Then, afflicted by cold and hungry, he indeed looked toward the ten directions, thinking: "Is there some kinsman who might remain and dispel my suffering?"
The servants speak thus to him: "Where indeed is such merit of yours? Having heard their words, he exclaims, "Alas, O Fate!"
"For destiny is indeed one's prior merit, and that has not been accumulated by me"; reflecting thus many times, he again takes recourse in fortitude.
Then, extending forty-four yojanas, lies the delightful city of Dharmarāja, teeming with gandharvas and apsarases.
It is presided over by eighty-four hundred thousand [deities] in both embodied and unembodied forms; thirteen gatekeepers reside in the city of Dharmarāja.

Having repeatedly deliberated upon what actions are auspicious and what are inauspicious, as well as the conduct of humans, the sons of Brahmā, the Śravaṇas, then speak of them in the world, being themselves honored by those who honor [the teachings].
Whatever was spoken and whatever was done by men who were contented and prosperous—all that they reported to Citragupta and Yama.
Possessing the power of hearing from afar and the range of vision from afar, these eight indeed move through the sky, the earth, and the netherworld (pātāla), performing such deeds.
Their wives were likewise formidable, each having a distinct name; such was their power that they held authority over mortals.
Whosoever among men worships me here through vows, gifts, and ascetic practices, for him those [planets] become gentle, bestowing a peaceful death.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Procession for the Departed and Other Rites," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part (*dvitīyāṃśa*) of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī-Gāruḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
The Glorious *Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*: Chapter Seventeen.
Garuḍa said: "O Lord, a single doubt oppresses my heart: Whose sons are the *śramaṇas*, and how do they reside in the city of Yama?"
O Lord, why do they know the actions performed by humans? How do they all hear them, and from where has this knowledge come?
"O Lord of the Gods, tell me by your grace where they eat. Having heard the words of the king of birds, the Blessed One spoke these words:
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen to these true words that bestow happiness upon all; I shall relate to you the activities of those who hear them.
When the entire world, both stationary and moving, had become one, while I, the Lord of the World, was formerly asleep in the Ocean of Milk;
Standing at his navel, he performed austerities for very many years; the fourfold collection of beings that had been created as a single mass was brought forth.
It was first created by Brahmā and then protected by Viṣṇu; thereafter, Rudra, the embodiment of dissolution, was created by Brahmā.
The all-pervading wind was created; then the sun, possessing an increase of splendor, was created; thereafter Dharmarāja was created together with Citragupta.
Having created all this and more, the Lotus-born One performed austerities; many years passed while he remained within the lotus-navel of Brahmā.
Whosoever was previously created [as a specific being] should perform that particular action; at a certain time there, Brahmā, accompanied by the world, [appeared].
Rudra, Viṣṇu, and likewise Dharma govern the earth; we do not know anything [of this], so let what is to be done here in the world be told.
Thus all the gods, intent on reflection, deliberated at that time; having considered the counsel of Brahmā, they were then urged by the wise ones.
Taking up flowers and leaves, he emitted twelve sons at the word of Brahmā; they were masses of splendor with large eyes.
Whatever one speaks in this world, whether auspicious or inauspicious, they quickly bring it to the range of Brahmā’s hearing.
The knowledge of hearing from afar and the range of vision from afar—all birds hear [the sound] from that very distance; therefore, they are known as "hearers" (*śravaṇa*).
Having thus remained in space and understood the activities of living beings, they speak before the King of Dharma at the time of death.
They discourse upon virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation; for there is indeed one path of virtue and a second path of wealth.
There is another path of desire, and the fourth is the path of liberation; indeed, O Vainateya, those who are supreme proceed by means of the path of Dharma.
The giver of wealth travels by means of celestial chariots; the giver of desired objects, by means of horses; and he who longs for liberation moves forth in celestial chariots yoked with swans.
But the other goes on foot through forests of sword-leaves, afflicted by stones and thorns, and indeed proceeds while bound by nooses.
Whoever in this world of men should worship the Śravaṇa [constellation] here with a vardhanī vessel and a water-pot filled with cooked food;
O Lord of Birds, one should worship the ears there along with me; I shall grant him that which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Having devoutly fed eleven auspicious and pure Brahmins, he should worship a twelfth, together with his wife, for my pleasure.
Having been honored by all the gods, they go to heaven out of a desire for happiness; when they have been thus honored, the King of Dharma is pleased with them through Citragupta.
When they are satisfied, those people who are devoted to righteousness go to my city; [I shall describe] the greatness of the Śravaṇas, their origin, and their auspicious deeds.
O tiger among birds, he who hears this is not defiled by sins; having enjoyed happiness in this world, he is glorified in the heavenly realm.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Śravaṇa" in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Having heard the words of the Śravaṇas and having meditated for a moment, [he spoke] again regarding that which has been done by men—both merit and sin—day and night.
Having fully understood all of that, Citragupta shall report it; then Citragupta tells him all his deeds.

Whatever action has been performed by speech alone, as well as that which was performed by the body, and likewise mental action—whether auspicious or inauspicious—one experiences the results of what has been done.
Thus, O Tārkṣya, the determination of the path of the departed has been told to you; now all the places where rest is found have been described to you.
Intending him as the recipient, one gives food; he travels happily on the great path. By day or by night, one should be a giver of lamps in that place, intending him as the recipient.
And those men by whom a lamp has been given travel upon a path that is pitch-black, most terrible, filled with dogs, devoid of landmarks, and ablaze.
Indeed, the offering of lamps on the fourteenth day of the month of Kārttika leads to happiness. Now, I shall briefly describe the expiation for the path of Yama.
By the merit of the rite of releasing a bull, he goes to the world of the ancestors; thereafter, by means of the rice-ball offering on the eleventh day, his body becomes purified.
By the gift of a water-pot, the servants shall obtain satisfaction.
By the gift of a bed, a person dwells in celestial palaces and goes to the heavens; on that very day all [gifts] are given, especially on the twelfth day.

In the thirteenth [chapter], those who, while still living, give footprints—that is, all things whatsoever—the most excellent, here for the sake of the deceased and for their own sake; [for them there is no end to their merit].
Relying upon that, O Vainateya, he travels on the great path; O Lord of Birds, there is but one single conventional designation everywhere.
There shall be the attraction of those who are superior, inferior, or middling; according to one's fortune, so much will be exceeded on the path.
Whatever is given by oneself through one's own property, that pertains to him alone; but having relied on what is given by kinsmen after he has died, one may become happy.
Garuḍa said: "O Lord of Gods, why are thirteen steps to be given, and of what nature are they? To whom are they given? Tell me that exactly as it is."
The Blessed One said: An umbrella, sandals, garments, a finger-ring, a water-pot, a seat, and a vessel—this is known as the sevenfold insignia.
The fierce heat that exists there, by which a human being is scorched, becomes a beautiful shade through the gift of an umbrella, providing satisfaction to the departed spirits.
He who gives a pair of sandals certainly crosses over the terrible Forest of Sword-leaves, where those mounted on horses travel.
If a seat, a welcome,
and food are given to that twice-born man, that preta eats with ease as he travels slowly along the path.
In a place crowded with many people, yet free from wind and water, one certainly becomes happy by the gift of a water-pot.
Whoever should offer a copper water-vessel for the sake of the deceased certainly attains the fruit of a thousand gifts of drinking-water stations.
The messengers of Yama, though extremely fierce, formidable, and dark-brown in hue, do not cause suffering out of courtesy because of the gift of clothing and ornaments.
Even though they run along with their weapons, those messengers of Yama do not come within the range of sight on the path, due to the granting of the seal-ring.
By the gift of vessels and seats, by the offering of raw grain and cooked food, and by the offering of clarified butter and the sacred thread, one shall attain the state of perfection.
Thus, while traveling on the road, one who is afflicted by thirst and oppressed by fatigue will certainly become happy by giving the milk of a buffalo-cow.
Garuḍa said: O Lord, whatever is given in one's own home for the sake of the deceased goes along the great path; by whom is that which has been given received?
The Blessed One said: Varuṇa accepts the gift; he delivers it into my hand; and I, in turn, bestow it upon the divine Bhāskara; from Bhāskara, he enjoys happiness.
Due to the power of their forbidden actions, when their lineage is severed here on earth, they all go to hell until the exhaustion of their sin.
At a certain time, when [the period] was complete, the righteous one, seated upon his buffalo throne, beheld the hells filled with various cries of lamentation.
He is the lord of eighty-four hundred thousand hells; among them, the most excellent and terrible are those twenty-one.
Tāmisra, Lohaśaṅku, Mahāraurava, Śālmalī, Raurava, Kuḍmala, Kālasūtraka, and Pūtimṛtikā.
The Crushing Hell, the Iron Goad, the Poisonous, and the Intense Heating; the Great Hell with its turbulent waves, and the Great Path of Revival.
Avīci, Andhatāmisra, Kumbhīpāka, likewise Asipatravana, and Patana—these are the twenty-one [hells].
But those who have indeed spent many years in the terrible hell, for whom there is no progeny at all, they go [after death] as messengers.
Sent indeed by Yama for the sake of a deceased human, they seize day after day the food, drink, and other offerings that have been given.
Hungry, they indeed plunder the preta right there in the middle of the path; at the end of the month, some people offer a meal, a funeral ball (piṇḍa), to them there.
They all attain satisfaction every day for an entire year; through such meritorious acts as these, one shall gradually go to the city of the Sun.
Then, at the end of a year, when the abode of Yama is drawing near and causing great terror, the preta shall emit a hand-sized [flame].
Seeing that body born in ten days from ten funeral cakes, his splendor surged forth like that of Rāma, the son of Jamadagni.
Relying upon a body born of karma, one should cast off the previous body; like the wind no larger than a thumb, one ascends the leaf of a *śamī* tree.

Just as one who walks stands with only one foot while moving with the other, so too the embodied soul, helpless and driven by its karma, moves like a caterpillar from blade of grass to blade of grass.
Just as a person, casting off worn-out garments, takes up others that are new, so the embodied soul, casting off worn-out bodies, enters into other new ones.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Various Gifts through the Release of a Bull, the Journey to the Realm of Yama, and the Attainment of a Body Born of Karma," in the second part of the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa concerning the Dharma-dṛg Preta-dṛg.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 19.
The Blessed One said: Having become like the wind and overcome by hunger, he takes recourse in a body born of karma; having reached that body, he goes along with Yama.
There, the city of Citragupta extends for twenty yojanas; there, the scribes behold all sins and merits in their entirety.
When great gifts have been bestowed, one who has gone there shall become happy; the auspicious city of Vaivasvata extends for twenty-four yojanas.
Those men by whom iron, salt, cotton, and a vessel of sesame seeds have been given—by that very act, the attendants of Yama are satisfied.
Having gone there, they all spoke to the doorkeeper: "The doorkeeper Dharmadhvaja always remains stationed there."
By the gift of the seven grains, one becomes Dharmadhvaja, filled with joy; having gone there, the gatekeeper announces his auspicious and inauspicious fortune.
The virtuous and righteous people behold the form of Dharmarāja as it truly is, whereas the evil-minded perceive the form of Yama as most terrifying.
Seeing it, people cry out "Alas! Alas! in terror; yet for those mortals who have practiced the giving of gifts, there is no fear anywhere.
Seeing the virtuous man who has attained [this state], the son of the Sun rises from his place and thinks: "This one shall pierce my mandala and proceed to the world of Brahmā."

Through generosity, the Dharma is easily attained, and the path of Yama brings happiness. This path is vast, yet it is not followed by anyone here; without the merit of giving, my child, one cannot go to the temple of Dharma.
On that fierce path, indeed, terrifying servants of Yama stand before each individual city, a thousand strong.
Having seized the sinner, the executors of torment cook him in water; they seize him month after month until only a quarter of him remains.

O Kāśyapa, those by whom funeral offerings have not been given go with great suffering; therefore, they should be given according to one's ability. Without having given them, they go like cattle, seized by bonds and fetters.
By performing such deeds, that man shall perceive his destiny as a divine, ancestral, human, or even hellish rebirth.
Or, by the word of the King of Dharma, liberation may arise from that; having truly attained human birth, that son shall attain the status of a son.
In whatever manner a person has performed an action, he shall go to that very womb; experiencing the results exactly as they were done, he wanders through all the worlds.

Having fully understood that all things are impermanent, one should practice the Dharma while human existence still prevails, for that is the time for attaining the bliss that transcends the entire world.
The nature of bodies is always either worms, ashes, or excrement; one should indeed cast [the body] like a man with a lamp in hand into a great and terrible blind well.
Through the power of great merit, a human birth is obtained; he who, having attained it, practices the Dharma, shall go to the supreme goal.
Even knowing [this], one undergoes suffering in vain through the practice of dharma, and departs [from it].

It is said that through hundreds of births one attains human status; even there, O bird, the state of the twice-born is more difficult to obtain. For him who observes and cherishes the vows therein, immortality comes into his very hand by grace.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Entering the Abode of Yama and the Attainment of Another Body, such as that of a Human, by One Who Has Received His Permission," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
[Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 20]
Garuḍa said: "Where do those who exist in the form of *preta*s take up residence? Once they are liberated from the world of *preta*s, how and where do they go?"
They are attended by eighty-four million hells, guarded there by Yama and by thousands of spirits.
"How do they wander in the world, having emerged from hell? Having heard what was uttered by Garuḍa, Lakṣmīnātha spoke this.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O King of Birds, listen to where the ghosts (pretas) indeed roam: those who have taken another's wife for their own sake, and those who have committed violence out of force; these become night-stalkers.
In that very same way, those most sinful beings, intent on searching for their own offspring, wander about bodiless and are severely afflicted by hunger and thirst.
Those hungry ghosts (pretas) from whom living beings escape as if released from a prison, nevertheless devise means for their own destruction among their kinsmen.
They block the doors to the ancestors and likewise sever their path; they seize the ancestral shares like thieves from travelers.
Having returned again to their own abode, they enter the place of Mitra; staying there, they behold the bonds of disease, sorrow, and the like.
They afflict [the body] by becoming feverish under the pretext of occurring every other day, or by becoming tertian fevers through the torment of cold, wind, and so forth.
Furthermore, those who remain in places such as where food scraps have been left constantly contemplate various other diseases, headaches, and cholera for them.
Deceived by their own offspring, they drink water mixed with the leftovers of food, while the worlds are protected by hosts of spirits.
In this way, those who have performed improper actions are reborn as pretas due to various defects.
Garuḍa said: How do those pretas act? In what form? Whose [are they], and what [is their nature]? By what method are they known? Do they speak or do they not speak?
Cut through this delusion of the mind if you wish for my welfare; O Hṛṣīkeśa, in this age of Kali, the state of a preta arises frequently.
The illustrious Viṣṇu said: A ghost torments his own family and torments others by finding their flaws; while alive he appears affectionate, but once dead, he attains a state of wickedness.
One who recites the Rudra-mantra, is devoted to dharma, worships deities and guests, speaks the truth, and is pleasant in speech—such a person is indeed not tormented by pretas.

One who has fallen away from all ritual duties, an atheist, a reviler of the Dharma, and a man devoted to speaking untruths is tormented by pretas; in the Kali age, one who is intent on impure actions becomes a preta, O Tārkṣya.
In the Kṛta age and up to the end of the Dvāpara age, there is neither a ghost nor any affliction; among many born of the same parents, only one enjoys happiness.
One has performed evil deeds, while another possesses a virtuous lineage; one is tormented by spirits, while another is endowed with sons and wealth.
O Kāśyapa, due to the fault of a deceased ancestor, one son may suffer loss while another becomes the father of a daughter, and there shall be discord with one's kinsmen.
A continuity is never seen; that which has arisen perishes. The destruction of the sacrificial animal and its substance—that is the suffering arising from the state of a preta.
A reversal of one's natural disposition, enmity with kinsmen, and the sudden onset of misfortune—such suffering arises from the influence of a *preta*.
Atheism, loss of livelihood, and likewise great greed, as well as constant quarreling—such is the suffering arising from the state of a preta.
A slayer of father or mother, and a reviler of gods and Brahmins—such a person incurs these faults; that suffering arises from the state of being a preta.
One who is devoid of daily obligatory rites, abandoned by recitation and fire-offerings, and a stealer of others' property—such is the suffering arising from the state of a preta.
Even with good rain, there is destruction of crops and commerce perishes; it causes strife in the world, and that affliction arises from the pretas.
If a whirlwind should afflict him while he is walking on the road, that should be known as the affliction of a preta; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Lord of Birds.
Connection with a low birth, performing base actions, and constantly delighting in unrighteousness—this is the suffering born of the state of a preta.
Through calamities, there shall be loss of wealth; whatever is undertaken perishes; there is ruin from thieves, fire, and kings; that suffering arises from the departed spirit.
The occurrence of a great disease, the affliction of children, and whatever suffering the wife endures—all that suffering arises from a preta.
When there is an absence of righteousness arising from the Vedas, the Smṛtis, the Purāṇas, and the treatises on Dharma, that suffering arises which originates from the state of being a preta.
If a man utters censure against deities, sacred fords, or twice-born brahmins—whether in their presence or behind their backs—that suffering arises from the state of a preta.
The seizure of one's own livelihood, as well as the destruction of one's own standing and the extinction of one's lineage—these cannot occur otherwise than through the fault of becoming a *preta*.
Where there is miscarriage among women, where menses are not seen, and where children die, that affliction arises from pretas.
If, due to impurity of heart, she does not perform the annual *śrāddha* and other rites, she herself shall not perform them; that suffering arises from the state of being a *preta*.
Having gone to a sacred ford (tīrtha), if one becomes attached to others and abandons his own duty, there will be no success in his religious acts; that suffering arises from the state of a preta.
There will be quarrels between husband and wife, anger during meals, and a mind intent on harming others; such suffering arises from the influence of a preta.
Where neither flower nor fruit is seen, and where there is separation from one's wife—that is the suffering born of the realm of the departed spirits.
For those men in whom the sign of one intent on constant eradication arises, their own vital energy becomes fruitless in its own field; that affliction originates from a *preta*.
Furthermore, like one who destroys his own kin, he slays even his own son as if he were an enemy; there is neither joy nor happiness, for that is the torment arising from the state of a preta.
One who does not obey the words of one's father, does not attend to one's own wife, and is always distracted by a cruel disposition—that is the suffering arising from being a preta.

Likewise, one who performs improper rites becomes a *preta* due to actions contrary to the prescribed rules; this also occurs through association with those who are corrupt at that time, except in the case of the ritual release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*).
Or else, O Tārkṣya, due to the power of their attachment to what they have seen, those whose bodies have not been consumed by fire are born as pretas, by which living beings are tormented.

Knowing this, O best of birds, one should perform the rite for the liberation of the deceased; for he who does not acknowledge the existence of pretas will, upon death, himself fall into the state of a preta.
In the family where there is the fault of a hungry ghost (preta), happiness is not found; there is the destruction of five things: intellect, joy, delight, wisdom, and fortune.
In the third or fifth generation, there will indeed be a severing of the lineage; moreover, he will be poor, destitute, and a doer of evil deeds in birth after birth.

Whosoever among the forms of *pretas* have distorted faces and fierce, terrifying appearances, who do not recognize their own kin—sons, daughters, fathers, brothers, wives, or daughters-in-law—and who, having assumed a desirable form, speak as they please while devoid of a happy rebirth, alas, these wretched ones, fallen by the power of fate and desiring to eat, remember their own past misdeeds.

Thus, in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the second part, the Dharma-kāṇḍa, in the Prata-kalpa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, this is the twentieth chapter titled "The Description of the Abode of Pretas and the Manner of Their Affliction. Garuḍa said: I am eager to ask how the pretas attain liberation, so that once liberated, no further suffering arises for human beings.
"O Lord, you have described these symptoms as being caused by affliction from a *preta*; when will their liberation occur, and how may they no longer remain in the state of a *preta*?"

What is the authoritative proof for the state of being a preta, and for how many years in number does one remain in that state? Having fallen into this long-lasting condition of a preta, how may one attain liberation?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Those spirits attain liberation; I shall tell you how that occurs: as soon as a human being realizes, "This suffering has indeed been caused by me," [they are liberated].
One who desires welfare for the sake of inquiry should report to the Vajrācārya: "In my dream, I saw an auspicious tree, a mango or a campaka tree, laden with fruit."
If a brahmin, a bull, or a deity is seen wandering while visiting sacred fords, or if such a dream is seen when some deceased person born of one's own lineage [is present];
Having recognized the truth in dreams through the power of pretas, wondrous things are seen; these are certainly due to the affliction of pretas.
As long as the mind is intent on bathing at sacred fords and devoted to dharma, yet causes the decline of dharma, then the affliction of a preta shall descend.
Then, she brings about a breakdown of his mind for the sake of his destruction; for auspicious things are beset by many obstacles at every step.
O Bird, they repeatedly incite one toward what is not beneficial, as well as all forms of exorcism and cruelty; these are all wrought by the *pretas*.
He who abandons all obstacles and practices the means to liberation gains the excellent fruit of his actions and attains the eternal state of a preta.
He shall indeed be liberated by that; it is the supreme bestower of welfare. O bird, he himself is satisfied when that which is given is offered for his sake.
Listen to this truth, O Tārkṣya: he who gives and he who enjoys [the gift] should unite himself with spiritual welfare; as a deceased being, he shall attain long-lasting satisfaction.
Being satisfied, they always desire the welfare of their own kinsmen; however, those wicked strangers who are unknown afflict those born of their own lineage.

Satisfied and compassionate toward those who are being born, they restrain them; later, when the time has come, they attain liberation through their own sons. O Lord of Birds, they always bestow prosperity and growth upon their kinsmen.
That deluded soul who, through seeing, speaking, gestures, or by causing harm, does not enable [the deceased] to attain their destination, becomes tainted by the curses of the departed spirits.
He shall be childless and without cattle, poor and likewise diseased, deprived of livelihood and lowly in birth after birth.
Thus do those hungry ghosts speak, depending upon whom they have come to be; for those situated there, liberation will occur in due time when their karma is exhausted.
Garuḍa said: "Neither name nor lineage is seen, and no recognition whatsoever arises; some astrologers say that this is suffering originating from a *preta*."
There is neither dreaming nor activity, nor indeed any seeing at any time. O best of gods, tell me for certain what must be done in that state.
The Blessed One said: Whether they speak truth or falsehood, the gods of the earth say this; therefore, having reflected in your heart, consider this as the truth uttered by the twice-born.
Placing devotion to the Lord foremost, being entirely devoted to devotion toward his father, and having performed the *kṛṣṇabali* offering preceded by the *puraścaraṇa* rite;
One should perform the purification of the body through recitation, fire-offerings, and gifts; by doing so, O Lord of Birds, all obstacles are destroyed.

If he is afflicted by *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, or others, he should then perform the *Nārāyaṇa-bali* dedicated to the ancestors; "he shall be liberated from all afflictions"—this is my truthful word.
Where there is suffering for one's ancestors that cannot be dispelled by other rites, one should therefore, with every effort, be devoted to the service of the ancestors.
In the ninth or tenth year, a man, for the sake of destroying the Piśācas, should mutter ten thousand Gāyatrīs and perform a fire-oblation with a tenth part of that number.

Having first performed the *kṛṣṇabali* sacrifice, one should carry out the rites such as the release of the bull (*vṛṣotsarga*). Thus, freed from all calamities, one shall obtain every happiness, attain the highest world, and achieve preeminence among one's kinsmen.
In this world, there is no other supreme deity equal to one's father and mother; therefore, one should always worship them with every possible effort.
For the father who instructs one in what is beneficial is a manifest divinity; whatever other divinities exist in the world, they do not originate from the body.
The very body is the sole means for living beings to attain heaven and liberation; since the body has been given in this way, who else could be more worthy of worship than that?
Having thus reflected in his heart, whatever a bird offers today, it eats all that itself; those who know the Vedas understand this as a gift.
Because a son protects his father from the hell named Punnāma and other such realms, he is called "putta" both in this world and in the next.
O bird, if the parents of anyone should die of an untimely death, one should abandon the performance of vows, pilgrimages, marriages, and ancestral rites for one year.
Whoever reads or even hears this chapter on dreams, which indicates the signs of the departed, shall not see the marks of a ghost.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Chapter on Dreams," in the second part of the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, within the Dharmakāṇḍa Pretakalpa, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 22.
Garuḍa said: "How do the pretas come into being? By what means is their destination reached? What would be their form, O Lord, and what would be their food?"
O Lord of the Gods, how are those hungry ghosts so well-pleased, and where do they dwell? O God, being gracious out of compassion, please answer this question of mine.
The Blessed One said: "Those who are indeed devoted to evil deeds and follow the influence of their past karma, they are born as *preta*s after death; listen to them as I describe them."
He established step-wells, wells, and tanks, as well as groves, temples of the gods, water-stations, dwellings, fine trees, and likewise dining halls.
He who sells the dharma inherited from his father and grandfather is a partaker of sin; upon death, he attains the state of a preta until the dissolution of all beings.
Those who, out of greed, encroach upon the grazing grounds, village boundaries, ponds, gardens, or forest thickets, indeed become pretas.
Death for evildoers comes from a Caṇḍāla, from water, from a serpent, from a Brāhmaṇa, from lightning-fire, and from fanged beasts.
Those who died by hanging, those killed by poison or weapons, those who committed suicide, and likewise those killed by cholera and other such diseases;
Those who have died from great diseases, from malignant diseases, or by bandits; those who have passed away without the funeral rites being performed, and those who were devoid of prescribed conduct.
He whose fire a Śūdra maintains—by which the rites such as the release of a bull are omitted, and by which the monthly rice-balls (piṇḍas) are neglected—is that very person [who has lost his status].
Those who have died from the falling of mountains, by the collapse of walls, through the defects of menstruation and the like, or those who have not been properly buried in the earth;
Those who died in the intermediate space (antarikṣa) without remembering Viṣṇu, and those here on earth who have become ghosts due to birth-impurities or contact with dogs and the like;
Those who have fallen under the power of such and other premature deaths—all of them, dwelling in the realm of hungry ghosts, wander through the desert wastes.
He who abandons his mother, sister, wife, daughter-in-law, or daughter when no fault has been seen in them will certainly be reborn as a preta.

O Tārkṣya, one who betrays his brother, a slayer of a Brahmin, a killer of a cow, a drinker of liquor, one who violates the teacher’s bed, or a stealer of gold and silk—such a person indeed attains the state of a preta.
One who steals deposits, betrays friends, is devoted to the wives of others, is treacherous, and is cruel will certainly be born as a preta.
Having abandoned the path of his own family and likewise delighting in the dharma of others, and being devoid of both learning and virtuous conduct, he will certainly be born as a preta.
In this very context, O observer of noble vows, they cite this ancient history: the dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Bhīṣma. I shall relate that, by hearing which one may attain happiness.

Yudhiṣṭhira said: "By what ripening of karma does the state of a preta arise? Or by what is one released from it? Tell me that, O Grandfather; having heard which, O observer of noble vows, I shall not again fall into such delusion."

Bhīṣma said: By that very same [action] by which one becomes a ghost (preta), and by that very same [action] by which one is liberated, one falls into a terrible hell difficult to cross even for the gods.
By the constant hearing of this, which is meritorious to hear and recite, men who have fallen into the wombs of hungry ghosts are completely liberated.
For it is heard, O child, that in former times there was a brahmin of celebrated vows, renowned by the name Santaptaka, who had retired to the forest for the sake of ascetic penance.

One who is devoted to the private recitation of scripture, engaged in burnt offerings, intent on sacrifice, and endowed with compassion— performing all sacrifices through proper method and not wasting time.
Devoted to the holy life, disciplined in austerity and gentleness, possessed of fear regarding the next world, and stainless through truth and purity;
For he is disciplined by the words of his guru, devoted to honoring guests, ever-exerting himself in the yoga of the Self, and free from all dualities.
Always engaged in the practice of yoga with the desire to conquer saṃsāra—one who is thus disposed, of virtuous conduct, longing for liberation, and having conquered the senses—[should proceed].
Many years indeed passed for him in the lonely forest; then, a thought arose in him regarding the visiting of sacred fords (tīrthas).

"I shall wither my body with the very waters of sacred fords. Having bathed quickly at that holy site at the rising of the sun, the ascetic, having performed his prayers and salutations, set out upon the road.
One day, a brahmin of great asceticism, having lost his way while traveling on the road, beheld five most dreadful ghosts.

In a lonely forest region, a place devoid of trees and beset by danger, he beheld these five beings of distorted form and terrible appearance; with his heart slightly trembling, he stood there with eyes wide open.
Then, summoning his courage and casting fear far away, he who spoke with sweet words asked: "Who are you, you of such deformed countenances?"
What impure karma was performed by which you have reached this state of transformation? Or how did you set out together in one direction, and where is it certain that you will end up?

The King of the Pretas said: "O best of the twice-born, this state of being a preta has indeed been attained by each through his own respective actions; all of us were devoted to harming others and fell under the power of a sinful death."

Constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, they have entered the state of hungry ghosts (preta); their speech is lost, their splendor is destroyed, their consciousness is ruined, and they are devoid of awareness.
"O father, being exceedingly distressed, we do not know the direction or the intermediate points; where indeed shall we go, deluded as we are, for we are piśācas born of our own karma?"
Neither mother nor father are there for us; having suddenly attained this state of being a preta through our own karmas, we are overwhelmed by the agitation of newly arisen suffering.
O Brahmin, by the sight of you we have been gladdened and refreshed; stay for a moment while I shall relate the entire account from the beginning.
I am named Paryuṣita, and this one is Sūcīmukha; Śīghraga and Raudhaka are likewise known as the fifth scribe.

"In this way, we have all indeed attained the state of pretas by virtue of our names. The Brahmin said: "How does the occurrence of names come about for pretas born of their own karma? Is there some specific cause by which you speak of yourselves by your own names?"
The King of the Pretas said: "O twice-born one, I have always eaten what was delicious, while I have given away what was stale."
Because I was indeed asked by a hungry brahmin who was traveling quickly, for this reason my name is Paryuṣita.
"O best of the twice-born, he travels swiftly because he was entreated by a hungry brahmin; it is for this reason that he is so fast."
"Many were indicated by him, O Brahmins, out of a desire for more food; with this as the cause, he is known as Sūcimukha (the Needle-mouthed)."
He always eats delicious food alone, excluding those whom he ought to support; because of his lack of respect for the Brahmins, he is called Rodhaka.
In the past, having observed silence, he would scratch the ground when entreated; by the ripening of that karma, he is called a scribe.
O twice-born one, they attained the state of a preta through the power of their karma; these were their names: Meṣānana, Lekhaka, Rodhaka, and Parvatānana.
Moving swiftly, with a face like that of a beast, indicative, and possessing a needle-like mouth; look at this reversal of form, O Master, for she is exceedingly miserable!
Having assumed forms composed of illusion, we roam upon the surface of the earth; all of us with deformed shapes, hanging lips, and distorted faces.
These fierce beings with massive bodies were born through their own karma; I have thus explained to you all the causes for their state as pretas.
"Through the sight of you, we have all become wise; ask whatever you have faith in hearing, and I shall tell it to you."
The Brāhmaṇa said: All living beings who live upon this earth are rooted in food; I wish to hear from you, moreover, the truth regarding your own food.
The pretas said: "O best of the twice-born, O illustrious one, if you have faith in hearing about our foods, then listen with a well-composed mind."
The Brāhmaṇa said: "O great pretas, tell me each your respective food. Thus addressed by the Brāhmaṇa, the pretas spoke as follows, one by one.
The pretas said: "Listen to our food, which is despised by all beings; having heard it, O Brahmin, you will despise it again and again."
The food of the pretas consists of phlegm, urine, and excrement, along with the impurities of bodies, as well as other kinds of leftovers.
Indeed, the hungry ghosts (pretas) feast there in houses that are impure, with household utensils scattered about, soiled, and where a birth has occurred.
In that house where there is no truth, no purity, and no self-restraint, and where there is association with outcasts and thieves, the ancestors indeed consume [the offerings].
Indeed, in those [offerings] that are devoid of the *bali* mantras, lacking the *homa*, and deficient in Vedic study and vows, the *preta*s partake.
When a householder is conquered by women, there is neither shame nor moral restraint; where the elders are not honored, the ancestors truly do not eat there.
Where there is greed as well as anger, sleep, sorrow, fear, and intoxication; where there is constant indolence and strife—there indeed do the pretas feast.
When a woman deprived of her husband resorts to the seed of another, the *pretas* indeed consume that seed, which is mixed with urine.
O father, shame arises in me as I speak of my own food: that which is the menstrual blood from the womb, the preta-s indeed consume that.

Disgusted with my state as a preta, I ask you, O one of firm vows: tell me how I may not become a preta again, O rich in asceticism. Constant death is better for a living being than to ever become a preta.
The Brāhmaṇa said: A man who is constantly devoted to fasting, intent upon the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances, and purified by various vows, is not born as a *preta*.
A man who performs the vow on the eleventh day, accompanied by a night vigil and purified by other meritorious deeds, is neither a *preta* nor is he born as a *preta*.
That man who, having indeed performed sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha and others, gives gifts, and is the builder of parks, gardens, ponds, and the like, as well as of water-stations (prapās).
He who, according to his ability, causes a maiden to marry a Brāhmaṇa, and who bestows knowledge and fearlessness, is not born as a preta.
A man who dies while the food of a Śūdra remains undigested in his stomach, or one who dies by an unnatural death, is reborn as a preta.
A man who performs sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, who abandons those worthy to sacrifice, and who is constantly devoted to craftsmen, is born as a preta.
Having associated with those who drink liquor and having consorted with women who drink liquor, a man who eats meat out of ignorance is born as a preta.
A man who gives away a daughter for a bride-price, as well as property belonging to the gods, the property of a Brahmin, or likewise the property of a guru, is born as a preta.
He abandons his mother, sister, wife, daughter-in-law, and likewise his daughter; such a one who abandons those with whom no fault has been seen is a *preta*, like a fool.
One who steals deposits, betrays friends, is constantly devoted to the wives of others, is a betrayer of trust, and is deceitful—he shall see that [hell].

One who betrays his brother, a slayer of a Brahmin, a killer of a cow, a drinker of liquor, one who violates the teacher’s bed, one who abandons the family tradition, one who is always devoted to speaking falsehoods, and a thief of gold and land—he indeed sees that [vision].
Bhīṣma said: While the brahmin was speaking thus, the sound of a drum arose in the sky, and a rain of flowers released by the gods fell upon the twice-born man.
Five celestial palaces belonging to the pretas indeed arrived; having gone to heaven in those divine palaces, they questioned that sage.
