Through conversation with a wise man and by the proclamation of meritorious deeds, the deceased, liberated from their sins, shall attain the supreme state.
Sūta said: Having heard this narrative, Garuḍa trembled like a leaf of the holy fig tree; for the benefit of mankind, he questioned him once again.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of the Five Pretas Concerning the Origin of the State of a Preta and Liberation Therefrom," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
(Chapter 23 of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*).
Garuḍa said: "What indeed do the pretas do when established in the state of piśācas? Or do they ever speak anything? Tell me that, O Lord of the Gods."
The Blessed One said: I shall describe their true nature, their signs, and their dreams exactly as they are. Afflicted by hunger and thirst, they indeed enter their own homes.
O Lord of Birds, they establish themselves within the bodies of the Vāyus; while their own kinsmen lie there, they bestow upon them the signs and reveal them.
There he goes with his own sons, his own wives, and his own kinsmen; there a horse, an elephant, a bull, or a mortal is seen with a distorted face.
But he who, having risen, sees himself lying down in a distorted manner and perceives this inversion, should know that to be a creation of a preta.
For if, in a dream, two men are bound in various ways with fetters, and a deceased ancestor appears in poor raiment begging for food in that dream;
In a dream, one whose food is being eaten may see someone—either oneself or another—running away after seizing it; or, afflicted by thirst, one may drink water.
In a dream, one mounts a bull and travels together with bulls; one flies up into the sky, and, afflicted by hunger, goes to a sacred ford.
He who speaks with his own voice regarding a bull, a brahmin, a horse, a phallus, an elephant, a deity, a spirit, a ghost, or a night-stalker;

O Lord of Birds, in the midst of a dream, one will certainly see various signs of a *preta* due to the affliction of a *preta*: one's own wife, kinsman, son, or lordly husband, seeing them as either living or dead.

He who, overwhelmed by hunger and thirst, begs from another even in a dream, shall go to the sacred ford (tīrtha) and burn funeral cakes (piṇḍas); there is no doubt that he is afflicted by the defects of the deceased.
Or else, in a dream, he sees his son, a domestic animal, father, brother, or wife departing from the house; such visions arise from the defects of the deceased.
O Lord of Birds, these are the signs; one should announce the expiation. Having performed a bath at home or at a sacred ford, one should perform libations with water at the Śrīvṛkṣa tree.
One should offer black grains and worship to a master of the Vedas; the wise person should perform a fire sacrifice according to his ability and have the scriptures recited in their entirety.
For whoever, with faith, reads or even hears this description of the signs of a preta, the marks of a preta shall perish.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the State of the Preta, its Characteristics, its Signs, and the Means of Liberation Therefrom," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part (*dvitīyāṃśa*) of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
— *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*: 24.
Garuḍa said: "No one dies before their time; such is the teaching of the Vedas. Why then does death overtake even a king or a learned Vedic scholar?"
That which was previously stated by the Brahmins as false is indeed seen; for the statement spoken in the Vedas says that a human lives for a hundred years.
In the world of men, all the social classes, the twice-born, and even the lowest castes and mlecchas live together in this region known as Bhārata.
That is not seen in the Kali age; why is this, O Lord? Please instruct us. From the moment of conception, whether a child, an old man, or a youth, one meets with death.
Whether possessing wealth or destitute, delicate or handsome, unlearned or learned—a Brahmin, indeed, or any other person.

That man who is devoted to austerity, whose nature is yoga, and who is a possessor of great knowledge; who delights in all forms of knowledge, is illustrious, righteous-souled, and of incomparable prowess.
All this arises without exception upon the surface of the earth; why, then, does even a king or a learned Vedic scholar meet with death?
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! Since you are my devotee and dear to me, listen to these secret words which destroy various lands."
Death, ordained by the Creator, comes swiftly and carries one away; therefore, O Lord of Birds, son of Kaśyapa, you of great splendor, I shall speak further.
It was declared in the Vedas of old that a human being lives for a hundred years; yet, through the power of improper action, one perishes even quickly.
By the mere non-study of the Vedas, one does not follow family tradition; through laziness there is abandonment of duties, and constant devotion to what is forbidden.
Eating at various houses, as well as being intent upon the fields of others—through these and other such great faults, the destruction of one's lifespan occurs.
One should not enter the abode of a brahmin who lacks faith, is impure, is an atheist, has abandoned auspicious rites, and delights in malice toward others and falsehood.

A king who does not protect, who is constantly devoid of dharma, cruel, addicted to vices, foolish, and excluded from the teachings of the Vedas—a king who oppresses his subjects is subject to the decree of Yama.
They bring one under the power of death, and from that state, one undergoes torment, having abandoned one's own actions and those which are the primary modes of livelihood.
He who is constantly devoted to the work of others goes to the realm of Yama; such is the case for a Śūdra who performs any task whatsoever without serving the twice-born.

Whether among the highest, the lowest, or the middling, he is cooked in the world of Yama; [there,] bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, self-study of scripture, and worship of the gods [are of no avail].
That day of men is in vain on which these [virtues] are not practiced; for the body is impermanent, unstable, without support, and born of the fluids [of the parents].
In this body composed of food and water, I shall now describe these qualities: that food which is prepared in the morning certainly perishes by evening.
O Lord of Birds, what permanence can there be for a body nourished by such flavors, once one realizes that half of the body has already departed through its own past actions?
A person should take the supreme medicine for the destruction of evil: Is the body more [dear] to the one who provides food, or rather to the mother who conceived it?

Whether it be for both [the Lord and the individual], or for the Lord alone, or even for a child, a fire, or a dog—what supreme sacrifice is there in that which is designated as worms, excrement, and ashes?
One must exert the supreme effort toward the destruction of sin; for the sin accumulated over many lifetimes is indeed threefold.
When he attains human birth, then he suffers for everything; recollecting all his previous births, his mind becomes despondent.
Having observed the dwellings in the womb and likewise the destinies born of karma, if one then dwells in a human womb, one becomes a sinner.
Wherever among beings—whether born from eggs or otherwise—one moves about, there mental anxieties, physical diseases, afflictions, old age, and the transformation of form prevail.
O best of birds, though liberated from dwelling in the womb, one who is shrouded by the darkness of ignorance does not realize this while still relying on childhood.
He who, even in youth, perceives while blinded by darkness is a partaker of liberation; whether a child, an old man, or a youth, he attains death through the [proper] foundation.
Whether wealthy or destitute, delicate or ill-favored, unlearned or learned—O Brahmins, such is every other person as well.

The man who is devoted to austerity, disciplined in yoga, possessed of great wisdom, delighting in great charity, illustrious, righteous in soul, and of incomparable prowess—without a human body, he experiences neither pleasure nor pain.
Through the bonds of natural karma, a human being meets with death; for five years after conception, one undergoes maturation through very slight sins.
Having become more than five years old, one ripens through great sins; because one fills the womb, even after death one comes and goes.
"By the power of that gift, though dead, he shall live as a mortal on earth for a long time. Sūta said: Having heard these words of Kṛṣṇa, Garuḍa spoke this speech.

Garuḍa said: "How should one perform the rites such as the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) when a child has died, or when those who perished in the womb, up until the rite of tonsure (cūḍākaraṇa) for the infant?"
"How, what, and by whom should it be given? What ritual is prescribed for the end of life? Having heard this speech uttered by Garuḍa, Viṣṇu then replied.
Śrī Viṣṇu said: If the fetus of a woman perishes or is miscarried, the period of impurity lasts for as many days as the number of months the fetus had remained.

One who desires his own welfare should not perform any [funeral rites] for him; therefore, once he has been born, until the tonsure ceremony of the child has taken place, [if he dies, no rites are required].
Milk food is given to children according to their capacity until the tonsure ceremony; however, the cremation of the body is prescribed at five years of age.
Milk should be offered as the auspicious food for children; however, for one who has died at an age exceeding five years, the rites prescribed for their own caste should be performed.
One should perform all the rites, such as the offering of water-pots and milk-rice; O best of birds, that [deceased] is indeed connected by the bond of debt.
"For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain. O tiger among birds, that which must be done leads indeed to the destruction of the body once again."
If one gives what pleases him to that person while remaining in a destitute family, he will become short-lived and poor, devoid of pleasure and devotion.
A mortal may undergo rebirth; therefore, [the debt] should be paid except for a child. A verse is sung in the Purāṇa, which appears to me in every respect as follows:

Sweet food should be given as an offering, for the capacity to give is rare; likewise, the capacity to enjoy the meal is found in the meal itself, and the capacity for pleasure is found in an excellent woman.

The power to give arises from spiritual development; it is not the fruit of meager austerity. Through giving one obtains enjoyments, and through service to sacred fords one obtains happiness. He who dies having spoken well is a wise man, the best among those who know the Dharma.
From taking what is not given one becomes poor; from the state of poverty one commits evil deeds; through the power of evil one goes to hell, becoming poor once more and again an evildoer.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Causes of Short Life and Death, and the Last Rites for Children," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī-Gāruḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
— *Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*: 25.
Śrī Viṣṇu said: Hereafter I shall proclaim the determination regarding men and women, whether they are living or dead, or even those more than five years of age.
But when the fifth year is complete, the male being becomes firmly established; he perceives all the sense faculties as well as the distinctions between form and formlessness.
Through the ripening of past karma, the killing and binding of living beings—whether they be Brahmins and others or even those of the lowest castes—is certainly a sinful act that leads to death.
If the fetus is lost, no ritual is required; if the infant dies, milk should be given. Furthermore, one should give milk mixed with rice porridge due to the failure of strength.
On the eleventh or twelfth day, one should prescribe the rites for a boy, even without the bull-sacrifice or the ritual for the bull, and without the great gift-offering.
Food, clothing, and ornaments for children and infants; whether for a child, a youth, or an elder—once dead, one indeed becomes a jar.
One should cast a child who is two months short of two years old upon the ground; beyond that age, O best of birds, cremation of the body is prescribed.

According to all the scriptures, one is called a *śiśu* (infant) until the eruption of teeth, a *bāla* (child) until the tonsure ceremony (*āśikha*), and a *kumāra* (youth) from the tying of the girdle of muñja grass (*mauñjībandhana*).

How should one act regarding Śūdras and others? There is doubt because of the exclusion of the girdle ceremony; having omitted the ninth month from conception, [the period for initiation] lasts until the sixteenth month from birth.
Furthermore, one up to twenty-five years is a child (bāla), who is to be known as "other" (para); up to five years is childhood (kaumāra), and up to nine years is youth (paugaṇḍa).

One who is sixteen years old is a youth (kiśora); beyond that, one should designate him as being in his prime (yauvana). Even if he dies in the fifth year, whether he was initiated (vṛta) or not initiated (avṛta), [he attains the goal].
One should perform exactly what was previously described, including the ten piṇḍas; this is because of the engagement in very few actions and due to the slight bondage of sense objects.
As long as a living being is subject to increase and remains entangled in sense objects, they desire even the slightest action regarding their own body and clothing.
Whatever may be the means of subsistence for someone, that very thing one desires to give here; such are the sons born from the seed of Brahmā, who are beloved by the celestial sages.
O bird, whether a child, an old man, or even a youth, embodied beings certainly face punishment by Yama and his messengers; all embodied beings desire a pot [of water].
The embodied soul, being all-pervading here, always experiences pleasure and pain; then, it casts off that body just as a snake sheds its worn-out skin.
The person [within] is the size of a thumb, sustained by vital air and possessed of hunger; therefore, gifts should certainly be given when a child has died.
One enjoys for five years from birth that which was given [as a gift] but not consecrated; if death occurs to a child over five years old, [the donor suffers the consequence].
One should perform rites such as the release of a bull, excluding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, and when the twelfth day has arrived, one should perform the sixteen *śrāddhas*.
One should offer rice-balls with milk-rice and jaggery in the proper sequence, as well as the offering of a water-pot and whatever other supplementary gifts there may be.

One should give food to a twice-born man, as well as great gifts and so forth according to one's ability; and whatever gifts such as lamps may be given, these should always be done when [the child] is more than five years old.
O best of birds, before the vow begins, one must perform everything necessary for the satisfaction of the deceased; if all this is not done, he falls into the state of a Mudgala.
Indeed, before the vow itself, one should first offer to the group of ancestors; one should perform the sixteen *ekoddiṣṭa* rites with the utterance of *svāhā*.

With straight darbha grass and white sesame seeds, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīti), and performing the rites with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (apasavya)—when this is done, [the ancestors] attain the supreme goal.
Furthermore, having become long-lived, they are surely born again into their own family; such a son bestows all happiness and increases the joy of his parents.
Just as space is indeed one, and just as the moon and sun appear as one [reflected] in various places, so too see all forms within jars and other objects as being distinct, yet equal to that [space].
In the same way, the self always behaves toward all sons according to whatever was their respective nature at the prior union of semen and blood.
Through that application of his being, he takes on the form of a father and is born as the son of someone whose sons perform that same action.
"From his father's side, he is someone exceptionally rich in beauty, a connoisseur of virtue, and devoted to charity; there has never been, nor will there ever be, anyone like him in this world."

One blind person does not become blind from another; one mute is not born from a mute; nor indeed does one deaf come from a deaf person, nor a learned man from a learned man. Those who are suitable [for this task] are not to be seen; listen to my words.

Garuḍa said: "The ten kinds of sons are traditionally recorded as the legitimate (aurasa), the son of the wife (kṣetraja), and so forth; what then of the son who is taken in adoption, and the son of a female slave?"
Having fallen under the power of birth and death, what destiny does one attain who has neither a daughter, nor a grandson, nor a son?

"How should his funeral rite (śrāddha) be performed, and by what procedure should it be done? The Blessed One replied: "Upon seeing the face of a son, one is liberated from the debt owed to the ancestors."
By the sight of a grandson, a person is released from the three debts; through sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, one attains the infinity of worlds and reaches heaven.
A son born in another's field and others who grant only worldly enjoyment—such a son should perform the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha according to the prescribed rule.

Other sons perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha, not the *pārvaṇa*. However, one born of a Brāhma-marriage elevates [the deceased], whereas one who has been "taken" (an adopted son) leads him downward. Indeed, by performing the annual śrāddha, he is born into hell.
O Bird, indeed all gifts should be given, except for the gift of food; a son who has been formally adopted should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, not the *pārvaṇa*.
Having offered the annual śrāddha for both his father and mother, he is not defiled; provided that, setting aside the ekoddiṣṭa rite, he performs the pārvaṇa rite.
He who has taken possession of anyone—whether it be himself, his ancestors, or even those such as the sons of female slaves—shall lead them to the abode of Yama.
At a sacred ford, they should perform the ancestral śrāddha rite and give gifts to a twice-born man; likewise, he who, having taken a son as a dependent, provides cooked food for him.

One should know that a śrāddha performed with the food of a śūdra is in vain, just as for a twice-born man; that śrāddha does not gratify the ancestors headed by the Grandfather (Brahmā). Knowing this, O best of those who go to heaven, one should abandon sons of low birth.
One born to a Brāhmaṇa woman from a Brāhmaṇa is considered the lowest, like a Caṇḍāla; likewise, so is he who is born to a Brāhmaṇa woman from a Śūdra or from one who has renounced the world.

Know these two to be outcastes (caṇḍāla), O Lord of Birds: he who is born of a woman of the same lineage, and the son who, having fathered a child by a woman permitted for cohabitation with the gods, dies before her.
Happiness is to be attained through good conduct; through bad conduct one goes to hell. Even those born of low birth prosper in happiness if they possess good conduct.

Freed from the impurities of the Kali age, honored by hosts of Siddhas, and fanned by celestial damsels with chowries of immortality, he alone shall uplift even his hundred ancestors, as well as his kinsmen—sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons—even if they are submerged in hell.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Funeral Rites for a Deceased Child and the Funeral Rites Performed by Sons— Whether Legitimate or Adopted," in the *Pretakalpa* section of the *Dharma-kāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttara-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī-Gāruḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
[Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa— 26]
Garuḍa said: "Tell the truth, O best of gods; having shown compassion toward me, O Lord, at what time should the *sapiṇḍana* rite be performed for deceased beings?"
If they are sapinda, from where do they go; if they are not sapinda, what is their destination? By what means indeed does sapindatva exist between a man and a woman? You should explain this.
How do a woman and a man attain supreme oneness together? While the husband lives, how can women perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite?

O Lord of the Gods, how do women go to the world of their husbands or to the heavenly world? How is the funeral rite (śrāddha) performed for one who ascends the funeral pyre, and how does the ritual release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga) take place?
O Lord, for the benefit of the worlds, please graciously explain how the offering of the water-pot (ghaṭadāna) should be performed once the sapindikarana rite has been completed.
The Blessed One said: "O bird, I shall explain the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite exactly as it is, O best of birds, regarding that which a human being performs for the duration of a year."
Once the sapindikarana has been performed, he goes to the world of the ancestors; therefore, the son must perform the sapindikarana for his father.

When the year is complete, one should perform the introduction of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa-praveśana); by means of this rite for the introduction of the cakes, his annual death-day ceremony (mṛtāhnika) becomes perpetual.

O tiger among birds, it is certain that at the end of the year there is a reunion with the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*). Once the *sahapiṇḍa* rite has been performed, the deceased then attains the supreme goal; having completely relinquished that name, he thereafter becomes part of the assembly of ancestors (*pitṛgaṇa*).

Or else, after three fortnights or six months, one should reunite with the great-grandfathers, having ascertained the auspicious occasions such as births and marriages, as well as those rites prescribed for one's own lineage.
One should not perform a marriage while the householder is deceased; nor should a mendicant accept alms until the sapindikarana rite has been performed.
"O Lord of Birds, one remains impure even within one's own lineage as long as one has not offered the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa); once the offering is made, the designation 'preta' ceases."
Because family customs are infinite, because the lifespan of men is subject to exhaustion, and because the body is unstable, the twelve-day period is recommended.
Whether he is without the sacred fires or with them, one should perform the sapindikarana rite on the twelfth day.
The Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite has been declared by the seers who perceive reality as taking place on the twelfth day, or after three fortnights, or six months, or even a year.
For one who has a son, an ekoddiṣṭa rite should never be performed; rather, after the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, it should be offered wherever [the śrāddha] is prescribed.

In each of those cases, the triad must be performed; otherwise, one becomes a killer of the ancestors. If one is unable to perform all three, one should perform the Pārvaṇa rite as prescribed by the Sage.
Therefore, one should perform it on that very day, following the instruction from the mouth of Pitāmaha; because [the specific days and months] may be unknown, the pārvaṇa rite is thus prescribed.
For one whose body has not yet been produced, there is no giving together with the ancestors; by these sixteen *śrāddhas*, the deceased is liberated and reborn.

One should not perform the sapinda-relationship for a woman who is childless; nor, as long as she lives with her virtuous husband, should one perform the offering of rice balls (sapiṇḍatā) together with him.

In the case of a bride who has been consecrated here through marriages such as the Brāhma and others, the offerings of rice-balls and water must be performed for her by means of her husband’s lineage name.

In the case of marriages such as the Āsura and others, whatever maiden may have been wedded, one should perform the rites of offering rice-balls (piṇḍa) and water for her according to the gotra of her father.
The son must always perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for his father; in the absence of a son, it shall be the wife; and in the absence of a wife, a uterine brother.
A brother, or a brother’s son, or a sapinda, or even a disciple, having performed the sapindikarana rite, should thereafter perform the nāndīmukha ceremony.
O Bird, the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite must be performed for an elder brother who is childless by his younger brother’s son or by his wife.
Manu has declared that if among brothers born of the same father one should have a son, they all become possessed of sons through that son.
In the case of all those who are childless, the wife should perform the sapindikarana rite; or she may have it performed by a sacrificial priest (rtvij) or even by a family priest (purohita).
Having had his tonsure and initiation performed, he should perform the ancestral śrāddha for his father; he may utter the word *svadhā*, but he must not pronounce the syllables of the Veda.
The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for a woman should be performed by three [relatives]: her husband and the others; or by her paternal uncle, her brother’s son, or her younger uterine brother.

Whether before a year has passed, at the juncture [of the year], or even when a full year has elapsed—for those deceased ancestors who have been made *sapiṇḍa*, there shall be no separate ritual performance for them.
O child, once the sapindikarana has been performed, separate status is indeed censured; he who offers a separate funeral cake (pinda) becomes a slayer of his father.
Once the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa has been performed, separate status is no longer possible; if a separate Piṇḍa has been offered, one must perform the Sapiṇḍana again.
He who performs the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite after having already performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* shall lead both himself and the deceased to the realm of Yama.

For one year, the wise man should perform the offering of barley-gruel (yāvaka) by means of the name and lineage; the water-pot and other items, as well as the daily food and whatever gifts of land are prescribed, should be offered to only one [deceased] once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has been completed.

Having calculated the number of years since the anniversary of the death, food together with water should be given to a Brahmin, as well as a jar filled with water for the birds and other such offerings.

At the end of that alms-gathering, his entire livelihood for the year is provided according to his own capacity; possessing a divine body and seated in a celestial chariot, he goes happily to the abode of Yama.
Indeed, while the father is alive, there is no sapinda relationship with the son; likewise, for women, there is no sapindana as long as the husband is living.
For that devoted wife who ascends the funeral fire on the fourth day, the rites such as the release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga) and others should be performed on the anniversary of her husband's death.
Before the birth of a son, the daughter shall belong to her husband’s lineage; after the birth of a son, she shall again go to her father’s lineage.
When the two wives ascend the funeral pyre together, they remain eternally one; however, on the anniversary of his death, the son must perform the *śrāddha* for each separately.

If two childless persons should die on the same day, one should perform separate *śrāddha* rites for them on a single funeral pyre; however, their *sapiṇḍana* rite should be performed together with that of the husband.
Whether individually, collectively, or as a couple together with the husband, they are not tainted by great evils; this word of mine is the truth.
When a husband and wife have both died while ascending the same funeral pyre, one should perform a single offering of cooked food, but offer the rice-balls separately.

In the eleventh month, one should perform the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*), the sixteen *śrāddhas* for the deceased, the gift of water-pots and other items, and whatever great gifts (*mahādāna*) there may be; one should perform these separately for as long as a year, so that the deceased may attain lasting satisfaction.
But for those who have died within the same lineage, whether they be women or men, one should prepare a single sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), yet perform the oblation (homa) separately for each.

On the eleventh day, the śrāddha rite, the separate offering of rice balls (piṇḍas), and the feeding [of Brahmins] must be performed with a single cooking; it is censured for husbands and wives to have separate rites, as well as for others.

A son should perform the Śrāddha rites with a single cooking; he should offer only one scattering of food (vikiro), though he may offer many funeral cakes (piṇḍas). This applies at a sacred ford, during the dark fortnight, or even during an eclipse of the moon or sun.
When a woman, having approached her husband who is like a corpse, burns him, the fire consumes his limbs but does not afflict her own self.
Just as the impurity of metals being smelted is consumed by fire, so too does a woman consume the body in a fire that is like nectar.
In the divine and other realms, a person with a divine body becomes pure; he is not burned at all by heated oil, iron, or fire.
Likewise, she who is united with her husband is never burned; even when he has died, the inner self, having attained oneness, is also dead.
If she dies elsewhere after abandoning union with her husband, she does not go to the world of her husband until the dissolution of all beings.
Having abandoned her mother and father, even though they were endowed with wealth, she prospers in happiness for a long time by following her deceased husband.
Measured by divine years, for three and a half crores of years, he shall dwell forever in heaven together with the stars.
At the end of that [life], she moves through the world and is born into a family of those who possess enjoyments; for that devoted wife, having attained great joy with her husband, remains faithful.
A woman who does not thus unite with her husband in accordance with dharma will, in birth after birth, be afflicted by suffering, ill-behaved, and unpleasant in speech.
A *valgulī*, a house-lizard, or a two-faced *godhā* indicates a woman who, having abandoned her own husband, follows after another man.
Therefore, with every effort, a woman should serve her own husband—whether he be dead or living—with her mind, her actions, and her speech.
Whether he is living or even dead, she who commits an offense against him shall become unfortunate and attain widowhood in birth after birth.
Whatever is offered with faith to the gods and to the ancestors, the fruit of that is obtained from the worship of the husband; therefore, one should perform the honoring of the husband.
When this has been done, O best of birds, one shall dwell in the world of the ancestors for a long time; as long as the sun and moon endure, so long shall one remain in heaven like a god.
Furthermore, having become long-lived, they are born into a noble family; just as a woman devoted to her husband does not experience the suffering caused by her husband.
All of this has indeed been told by me to you, O Lord of Birds; I shall now describe the specific [rite] that bestows happiness upon the deceased.
Whatever has been performed on the twelfth day should all be repeated until the *sapiṇḍana*; one should always and constantly perform the monthly offerings of water-pots and food.
O bird, there is no performing of what has already been done, except for funeral rites; if any man performs such a rite, his previously performed merit perishes.
One should perform [the rite] again for one who has died; thus the deceased shall attain inexhaustible merit. Every month, jars filled with water and containing boiled rice should be offered.

O Tārkṣya, even if a son performs the *sapiṇḍana* rite before the completion of the year or before the performance of the funeral rites, he must nevertheless offer one ball of rice (*piṇḍa*) and a jar of water every month for a year.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Sapindikarana in the Pretakalpa," in the Dharma-kanda, the second part of the Uttara-khanda, in the glorious Garuda Mahapurana, within the dialogue between Sri Krishna and Garuda.

In the glorious Garuda Mahapurana—Chapter 27—Tarkshya said: "O Lord, how do the pretas dwell here, and what is their form? By which specific fruits of their actions do they become great pretas or pishachas? For the sake of compassion for all beings, tell me this, O Madhusudana."
"O Lord of Gods, if you wish to do what is pleasing to me, tell me that gift by which one is released from the state of a preta, and by which it is not [repeated], O auspicious one."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "Well asked by you, O Tārkṣya, for the benefit of human beings indeed! Listen with an attentive mind to the characteristics of the departed that I shall speak."
For this is most secret of secrets and must not be told to just anyone; yet, O mighty-armed one, because you are devoted, I shall tell it to you.
Long ago in the Tretā Yuga, O dear one, there was a king named Babhruvāhana in the beautiful city of Mahodaya; he was devoted to righteousness and possessed great strength.

He was a performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, illustrious, devoted to Brahmins, and esteemed by the virtuous; he was endowed with the qualities of good character and conduct, and possessed of compassion and courtesy.
Constantly devoted to the duty of a Kshatriya, that mighty king always protected his subjects like his own sons, meting out punishment to those who deserved it.
Once, that mighty-armed one, having gone out on a hunt with his army, entered a dense forest filled with various kinds of trees.
Then, in the middle of the forest, the king saw from afar a deer in a place frequented by hundreds of tigers and resounding with the cries of various birds.
Struck by that very firm arrow, the deer took the shaft from him and vanished from sight in the forest.
With that blood flowing from his armpit, the king followed him; then, following the trail of the deer, he entered another forest.
With his throat parched by hunger and fainting from the heat of exhaustion, the king reached a body of water and plunged in along with his horse.
Having drunk that cool water, scented with the fragrance of lotuses, Babhruvāhana then emerged from the pure water.
Having reached a banyan tree—cool in its shade, enchanting, with great spreading branches, heart-pleasing, and resounding with the songs of flocks of birds.
Having reached that great tree, which stood like a raised banner for that entire forest, the lord of the earth sat down.
Then he saw a hungry ghost (preta), whose senses were agitated by hunger and thirst, with hair standing on end, filthy, hunchbacked, emaciated,
fleshless, and terrifying to behold.
Its feet were composed of bones bound together by sinews as it ran hither and thither, surrounded on all sides by many other hungry ghosts.
Seeing that hideous and terrible sight, Babhruvahana was struck with amazement; and the ghost, seeing the king who had come to that dreadful forest, was likewise amazed.
Then, with a joyful heart, he approached him; at that time, O King, the Lord of the Dead spoke these words to Tārkṣya.
I have abandoned the state of a preta and have attained the supreme goal; through union with you, O mighty-armed one, there is no one more fortunate than I.
The king said: "You are black-complexioned with a gaping mouth; you appear like a ghost. Out of affection for me, tell me truly how it is that you are thus."
Thus questioned by the king, he indeed related his entire story.
The preta said: "O best of kings, I shall tell you everything from the very beginning; having heard the cause of my state as a preta, you ought to show me compassion."

There was a city named Vaidiśa, endowed with every prosperity; it was crowded with people from various regions, filled with diverse jewels, possessed of manifold merits, and thick with various kinds of trees.
There I dwelt for a long time, always devoted to the worship of the gods; know that I am a Vaiśya by birth, Sudeva by name.

The gods have been gratified by the sacrificial offerings (havya), and likewise the ancestors by the ancestral offerings (kavya); and the Brahmins have been fully satisfied by me through various modes of giving.
I have indeed properly arranged marriages and alliances, and I have bestowed gifts in many ways upon the poor, the helpless, and the distinguished.
All of that, O dear one, has become fruitless due to my fate; I shall tell you how my meritorious deeds have likewise turned to naught.
"I have no lineage, dear father, nor friend, nor kinsman; indeed, I have no such friend who might perform the funeral rites for me."

"O best of kings, because of that, my state as a preta became firmly established. There are the eleventh-day rite, the three-fortnightly rite, the six-monthly rite, the annual rite, and other monthly rites; thus there are sixteen śrāddhas."

O King, for one to whom these funeral rites (śrāddhas) for the deceased are not offered, the state of being a ghost remains firmly established, even though hundreds of other śrāddhas have been performed.
Knowing this, O Great King, deliver me from the state of a preta; for it is said here that the king is the kinsman of all the social classes.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, deliver me; I give this jewel-gem to you, so that I may attain auspiciousness, O most excellent of monarchs.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, if you desire compassion for me, quickly perform for yourself all the rites pertaining to the afterlife and this world.
The king said: "How do people become *preta*s here even when the funeral rites (*aurdhvadaihika*) have been performed? And by what actions do they become *piśāca*s here? Tell me that."
The preta said: "O best of kings, those who seize the property of the gods, the wealth of a Brahmin, or the accumulated riches of women and children, go to the womb of a preta."
Those who indeed consort with female ascetics, those of the same lineage, or women who are forbidden, become great pretas who carry off lotuses.
Those who steal coral and diamonds, those who carry off garments, as well as those who steal gold, when encountered face-to-face in battle—[these are the ones to be slain].
Those men who are ungrateful, atheistic, cruel, and likewise reckless; those who are devoid of the five sacrifices, yet devoted to great acts of giving.

O King, those who commit treachery against their master, those who commit treachery against friends or Brahmins, and those who commit sins at sacred fords, are born into the womb of a preta; O Great King, it is through such deeds as these that one is born into the womb of a preta.

The king said: "How do you and they become liberated from the state of a preta in this world? And how should I perform the funeral rites for my own self? By what procedure should that be done? Tell me all of this."
The preta said: "Listen, O Indra among kings, to the summary of the discipline centered on Nārāyaṇa: listening to the true scriptures, the worship of Viṣṇu, and association with virtuous people."
I have heard that these lead to the destruction of the preta-realm; therefore, I shall describe to you the worship of Viṣṇu, which destroys the state of being a preta.
O King, having procured two measures of gold, one should fashion an image of the divine Nārāyaṇa, adorned with all ornaments.

One should bathe her, who is covered with a pair of yellow garments and anointed with sandalwood and aloe-wood paste, with various kinds of water; having performed the consecration (adhivāsa), one should then worship her.
To the east, one should worship the god Śrīdhara; to the south, Madhusūdana; to the west, the god Vāmana; and to the north, Gadādhara.
Having worshipped Pitāmaha in the center, one should likewise worship the god Maheśvara separately according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Then, having circumambulated the fire and gratified the deities with ghee, curd, and milk, O King, he likewise offered oblations to the Viśvedevas.
Then, having bathed, with a disciplined mind and composed spirit, the sacrificer performed his own funeral rites according to the rules in the presence of Nārāyaṇa.
One who has disciplined his self and is free from anger and greed should undertake all the śrāddha rites, as well as the ritual release of a bull.
To thirteen brahmins he gave garments, umbrellas, sandals, rings, and pearls, along with vessels, seats, and food.
Water-pots containing both food and water should indeed be given for the benefit of the deceased; furthermore, having given a gift of a bed, one should offer a water-pot for the deceased.

One should worship the name "Nārāyaṇa" placed within a *saṃpuṭa* (enclosure); having done this according to the prescribed rule, one shall obtain the fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious actions.

The King said: How should one prepare the *pretaghaṭa* (the vessel for the deceased), and by what ritual procedure should it be offered? Speak for the sake of compassion for all, [explaining] the vessel that grants liberation from the state of a *preta*.
The preta said: "Well asked, O Great King! I shall tell you; listen to me regarding that firm gift by which the state of being a preta may no longer exist."
The gift known as the "Vessel for the Pretas" destroys all that is inauspicious; it is difficult for all the worlds to obtain and brings about the end of miserable rebirths.

Having fashioned a vessel of refined gold, adorned with Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu along with the world-protectors, and containing cavities filled with milk and clarified butter, bow down with devotion and give it to a Brahmin; what need have you for any other hundreds of gifts?
Brahmā is in the center, as well as Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara, the imperishable Śaṅkara; and on his neck, one should place the world-protectors (lokapālas) in order, starting from the east.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rites, O King, with incense, flowers, and sandalwood, one should then offer a golden jar containing milk and clarified butter.
This act, which surpasses all other gifts and destroys great sins, O King, should be performed with faith for the sake of averting the state of being a preta.

The venerable one said: While he, whose mind was thus restrained, was speaking in this manner with the deceased, his army—crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots—arrived following closely behind him.
Then, when Bala had arrived, the ghost gave the great jewel to the king, paid his respects, made further entreaties, and vanished from sight.
Departing from that forest, the king also went to his own city; having reached his city, he related all that had been spoken by the preta.
O bird, he performed the funeral rites and other ceremonies according to the rules; by the gift of that merit, the deceased was liberated and went to heaven.

"Even a deceased ancestor attains a good rebirth through a funeral rite (śrāddha) performed by another; how much more so, then, does a father go [to heaven] when the rite is performed by his own son—this is truly marvelous!"
Whoever hears this meritorious history or causes it to be heard shall not fall into the state of a preta, even if they are possessed of sinful conduct.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Causes of the State of a Preta and the Means for its Cessation," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, specifically the conversation between Babhruvāhana and the Preta.
— *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*: 28.
Garuḍa said: For the sake of compassion for all beings, tell me, O Madhusūdana, by what gift or by what meritorious deed one may be released from the state of a preta.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, I shall proclaim a gift that quickly destroys all suffering. Having fashioned a jar made of refined gold, joined with Brahmā, Īśa, and Keśava, along with the world-protectors (Lokapālas), and filled to the brim with milk and clarified butter, bow down with devotion and give it to a Brahmin. What need have you for any other hundreds of gifts?
Garuḍa said: "O Lord, what has this been told? Tell it to me in detail, O Lord—the ritual for the next world following the time of the soul's departure."
O Lord, O Janārdana, tell me what is beneficial for me in this saṃsāra; explain how men should properly perform the rites pertaining to the afterlife.
O Best of Gods, how do the pretas come to have such massive bodies, fierce forms, and terrifying appearances? By what auspicious or inauspicious karmic actions do they become so?
"Pishachas arise here; of what karma is this the fruit? Tell me that, O Lord of Gods, for I wish to know it."
Why is the fivefold jewel cast upon the ground? Why are they placed in the mouth? And why are sesame seeds and *darbha* grasses positioned below the feet toward the south?
For what purpose is the mandala smeared upon the ground with cow dung? For what purpose is Viṣṇu remembered and the Viṣṇusūkta recited?
For what purpose do his sons and grandsons stand before him? For what purpose is the offering of lamps, and for what purpose is the worship of Viṣṇu?
For what purpose does a person in distress give gifts to the best of the twice-born? And why does he ask forgiveness from his kinsmen, friends, and even enemies?
For what reason are sesame seeds, iron, gold, cotton, salt, the seven grains, land, and cows given away?
And how does a living being die, and from where does one who has died go? And how does the *ativāha* body then come to rest?

The son should carry the *śaṃva* on his shoulder, and the grandson is the giver of fire. For what purpose, O God, Lord of Gods, is there an anointing with clarified butter (*ājya*), and from where does it come?
For what purpose should one recite the Yama-sūkta while carrying water toward the northern direction, using a single garment and gazing at the solar disc?
One should place barley, mustard seeds, dūrvā grass, and stones; chew nimba leaves; and arrange the cloth, the man, and the woman in an inverted order.
Having come to the house, food should be eaten together with those of the same lineage; for what purpose should the son offer the nine rice-balls?
For what purpose is milk placed at a crossroads in a baked earthen vessel, having tied three pieces of wood together with a cord and positioned them at a four-way junction during the night?
A lamp is offered every day throughout the year during the night; for what purpose is the offering of water for cremation, and why is there conversation with one's own kinsmen?

"O Blessed One, what occurs through the nine rice-balls of the *ativāha*? How is there an invocation for the gods and ancestors, and how is the invocation of the *vāha* performed? O Lord, why is this done, and why should one cause the rice-balls to be offered?"
What is that which is given to him immediately after the offering of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa)? And what is the purpose of the collection of the bones and the gift of the bed?

On the second day, how can there be a bath for a twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires? On the fourth day, why should a bath to remove impurity be performed by all people together on the tenth day?
Why should one bring shoulder-carriers home with oil and ointments? They should also provide them with massages while they are resting on land or in water.
On the tenth day, one should offer that rice-ball (piṇḍa) with meat; but why is there a rice-ball on the eleventh day, and how does the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga) take place?
Tell me, from where do these sixteen *śrāddhas* come that last for a year? By means of the injunction regarding food and so forth, there are three hundred and sixty [rites].
And every day, food from a jar should be given for the satisfaction of the preta; for at the appointed time, O Lord, a human being dies, being impermanent.
I do not see any opening at all; how then did that living soul depart? Whence do the elements—earth, water, and likewise mind—depart?
O Protector, speak to me of fire, as well as wind and space; and how do these five winds proceed toward attainment?
Lust, delusion, and the other five thieves reside within the body; O Janārdana, from where do thirst, desire, and egoism depart?
Whether it be merit or demerit, whatever good deed has been performed—when the body has perished, where do the various acts of giving go?
For what purpose is the *sapiṇḍana* performed, whether at the completion of a year or otherwise? With whom is the merging of the deceased carried out, and what is the ritual procedure therein?
For those who have been cremated, those not yet cremated, those men fallen upon the earth, and whatever other beings there may be—what shall become of them at the end?
Those who are sinners, those of wicked conduct, and those who have attained the state of a mudga-bean; the self-killer, the slayer of a Brahmin, the thief, and the betrayer of trust.
O Mādhava, what is the destiny of that Śūdra who drinks from a tawny cow, who recites a syllable of the Veda, or who wears the sacred thread?
"When a Brahmin’s wife has been taken hold of by another, I am afraid of that sin; tell me that, O Lord of the World! Since I have asked all this of you, speak for the welfare of the world."

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled “The Description of the Questions Regarding the Fruits of Various Gifts and Rites Performed at the Time of Death in the Post-Mortem Rituals,” in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
[Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 29]
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "Well asked by you, O blessed one, for the benefit of mankind indeed! Listen with an attentive mind to everything concerning the rites after death."
Free from the distinctions of desire, extracted from the Śruti and Smṛti, that which has not been seen even by the gods led by Indra, nor by yogis who contemplate yoga.
O child, this is more secret than the secret; it has never been told to anyone anywhere. Since you are indeed devoted, O fortunate one, I shall tell it all to you.
There is no destination for one who has no son, nor indeed is there heaven for him; by whatever means possible, the birth of a son must be accomplished.
If liberation is not attained, the son shall deliver [the ancestor] from hell; the cremation must be performed by the son, and the offering of fire by the grandson.
With sesame seeds and darbha grass upon the ground, the hut shall indeed be made of the elements; and five jewels are placed in the mouth, by which the life-force (jīva) sprouts forth.
One should smear the ground with cow dung and scatter sesame seeds and darbha grass upon it; on that very ground, the afflicted person, being liberated, burns away all sin.
One who offers *darbha* roots leads [the deceased] to heaven; there is no doubt about this. For those *darbha* grasses on the ground that are mixed with sesame seeds, there is indeed no doubt.
Everywhere the ground is pure where no smear exists; where a smear persists, it is purified by further smearing.
Yātudhānas, piśācas, and rākṣasas who perform cruel deeds—these enter the patient who is unstained [by sin] and liberated; of this there is no doubt.
The daily fire-sacrifice, as well as the ancestral rite (śrāddha) and the purification of the feet of Brahmins performed upon the ground without a mandala—this too is fruitless.
On this earth, a sick person is never liberated without a maṇḍala; for Brahmā, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Śrī, and Hutāśana (Agni) themselves abide within the maṇḍala—therefore, one should construct a maṇḍala.
But he who dies otherwise—whether a child, an old man, or even a youth—he indeed goes to another womb and sports with the vital air.

Just as iron mixed with copper gives rise to a distinct birth [as brass], so it is for one who has thus become like the wind; for such a person, there is neither the śrāddha rite nor the water libation.
O Tārkṣya, these sesame seeds produced from my sweat are purifying; through the gift of sesame, the Asuras, Dānavas, and Daityas are satisfied.
May white sesame seeds, black sesame seeds, and sesame seeds resembling cow’s urine burn away the sins committed by me with my body.
A single droṇa of sesame seeds is equal to a droṇa of gold; when given for the purpose of libation, charity, or fire-offering, it becomes inexhaustible.

Darbha grass is produced from hair, and sesame seeds arise from sweat; the deities are satisfied by gifts, and likewise the ancestors by the *śrāddha* rite; and Brahmā and the universe subsist upon the performance of ritual application.

With the sacred thread worn over the left shoulder (savya), those beginning with Brahmā attain satisfaction; with it worn over the right shoulder (apasavya), the ancestors and the deities of heaven are satisfied.
One should know that Brahmā is at the base of the kuśa grass, Keśava is in the middle of the darbha, and Śaṅkara is at the tip of the darbha; thus, the three gods reside within the kuśa.
O Lord of Birds, Brahmins, sacred mantras, kusha grass, fire, and tulasī do not become "worn-out offerings" (nirmālya), even when they are employed again and again.

The kuśa grass in the funeral cakes, the flower offerings at the rite for the deceased, the brahmins at a feeding for the dead, the mantras among śūdras, outcasts, and the fire upon the funeral pyre [are all impure].
Tulasī, Brāhmaṇas, cows, Viṣṇu, and Ekādaśī, O bird—these five are indeed the vessels for virtuous people sinking in the ocean of worldly existence.
Viṣṇu, Ekādaśī, the Gītā, Tulasī, the brāhmaṇa, and the cow—this sixfold path bestows liberation upon the boundless and difficult wilderness of saṃsāra.
Sesame seeds, the three kinds of purifiers, darbha grass, and tulasī leaves—these ward off the miserable rebirth of a dying person.
One should sprinkle the ground with water using *darbha* grass held in both hands; at the time of death, one should place the *darbha* blades into both hands of the patient.
That man who is cast upon the darbha grass, even if he is without the sacred mantras, goes indeed to the world of Viṣṇu when he is enveloped by that darbha.
He who dies on the ground at the root of *darbha* grass, with *darbha* grass in hand, purified by penance, [is liberated] from the shoreless ocean of *saṃsāra*.
Standing upon a layer of *darbha* grass on ground smeared with cow dung, one dispels all evil through the gift bestowed there.
Salt is that divine essence which grants all desires to men, because without salt, all other food flavors are not intense.
Since this salt flavor has originated from the body of Viṣṇu, it is dear to the ancestors, auspicious, and therefore bestows heaven.
Yogins especially praise the gift of salt for Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, and those of Śūdra birth.
When the life-breaths of the afflicted depart upon the surface of the earth, salt should then be given; it is the opening of the door to heaven.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Necessity of Giving Sons, Darbha Grass, Sesame, Tulasī, Cows, Land, Gold, Copper Vessels, and Other Items in the Rites for the Deceased," within the Dharmakāṇḍa of the Pretakalpa, in the second part of the Uttarakhanda of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
The Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 30.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Tārkṣya, to the supreme secret, the most excellent of all gifts; the highest among all charities, and the most closely guarded even by the dwellers of heaven.
This one great gift, the most excellent of all, is cotton; by giving it, the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svar are pleased in succession.
All the deities, beginning with Brahmā, shall obtain satisfaction from this act; this great gift should be bestowed for the sake of the liberation of the deceased.

He shall dwell for a long time in the world of Rudra, and thereafter he shall become a king here on earth—handsome, fortunate, eloquent, illustrious, and of incomparable valor. Having completely conquered the realm of Yama, O Tārkṣya, he goes to heaven.
For one who gives a cow, sesame seeds, land, or gold to a twice-born man, the sin accumulated over that person's lifetime perishes at that very moment.
Sesame seeds and cows are a great gift that destroys even the most heinous sins; these two are to be given to a Brahmin, never to anyone of another caste.
A gift consisting of sesame seeds, cows, or land may be given by one who has made a formal resolve; however, it should never be given to other castes, nor to those among one's own dependents.

Likewise, one should give unreserved gifts to those who depend on one for support and to women; when one is afflicted by illness or during an eclipse, these two types of giving are especially distinguished. A gift given to the afflicted takes effect at that very moment.
But that which is given again to one who is still living reaches him unrefined; truly, truly, truly, this applies to what is given to one with impaired faculties.

Whatever gift the son rejoices in, that gift becomes infinite; therefore, as long as he lives for a long time, that son should give it, since by doing so the deceased—whether in the state of an *ativāha* or a *preta*—obtains enjoyments.

When one is unwell at the time of death, or when the body has fallen and remains upon the earth, the satisfaction [of the deceased] occurs through the subsequent performance of the *ativāha* rite for the body.
When a gift is given to a cripple, a blind man, or one with a squint whose eyes are only half-open, and when *darbha* grass is spread over sesame seeds, that gift is said to be inexhaustible.
Sesame seeds, iron, gold, cotton, salt, as well as the seven grains, land, and cows—each one of these is traditionally held to be purifying.
The King of Dharma is pleased by the gift of iron and other metals; by the offering of sesame seeds, he is satisfied; and when salt is given, there is no fear of Yama.
By the gift of cotton, one shall have no fear of living beings; cows rescue a person from the three kinds of sin.
From the gift of gold one attains happiness in heaven; from the gift of land one becomes a king; and by the gift of both gold and land, there shall be no suffering in hell.
All the messengers of Yama, who are as terrifying as Yama himself, all become bestowers of boons and depart, gratified by the seven kinds of grain.
By the mere remembrance of Viṣṇu, the supreme goal is attained. All this has been told to you—namely, the goal which is reached by mortals.
Therefore, they praise a son who, by his father’s command, gives [the inheritance] while seeing his father standing on the ground with eyes only half-open.
At that time, the son who causes all manner of gifts to be given would excel even the performance of a śrāddha at Gayā; such a son is the delighter of his lineage.
When he has fallen from his own position, his sons must then exert effort for the sake of their father who is bereft of strength; they are the ones who deliver their father.
What is the use of giving many gifts? One should perform the funeral rites for one's father; the great horse-sacrifice is not worth even a sixteenth part of it.
That righteous son is indeed highly honored even by the gods, he who causes gifts to be given on behalf of his afflicted father on this earth.
One should give a gift of iron with the hand joined to the ground; one shall not encounter the terrible Yama, nor go to his abode.
The axe, the pestle, the staff, the sword, and likewise the dagger—these are seen in the hands of Yama for those who have committed evil deeds.
Therefore, one who is afflicted by disease should give iron to a Brāhmaṇa; this gift is declared for the satisfaction of Yama’s weapons.
Those who are in the womb, infants, youths, and likewise the elderly—by these specific gifts, they may burn away their own sins.
The Churiṇas, Śyāma and Śabala, the Ṣaṇḍas, the Markas, the Udumbaras, and the Śabalas and Śyāmadūtas—these are pleased by the gift of iron.
Sons, grandsons, kinsmen, those of the same lineage, and friends likewise do not give gifts for one who is afflicted by disease; for they are indeed equal to killers of Brahmins.

Listen now to the destination of one who has reached the state of the five elements and is joined with the earth; moreover, the *ativāha* spirit, being a *preta*, shall obtain the merit for the year beyond.
The triad of fires, the three worlds, the three Vedas, the three immortals, the three times, the three twilights, the three castes, and the three powers.
From the feet upward to the hips, Brahmā presides; from the navel to the neck, Hari resides in the body of the human being.
Īśāna, the Great Lord, both manifest and unmanifest, resides in the head; he is the single form whose three parts are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara.

I am the vital breath residing within the body among the fourfold collection of beings; I bestow upon them righteousness and unrighteousness, the inclination toward action, pleasure and pain, and what has been done or left undone.

Having established the growth of a living being, which was previously infused with its own latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), I alone thus impel the souls toward their actions; and so, living beings certainly go to heaven, hell, or liberation.
Whether one is situated in heaven or in hell, there shall be nourishment through the śrāddha; therefore, a wise person should perform the three kinds of śrāddhas.
The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-Lion, the Dwarf, Rāma [Dāśarathi], Rāma [Bhārgava], Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Kalki—these ten names should always be remembered by the wise.

Living beings go to heaven in happiness; and when humans fall from heaven, having obtained happiness and wealth, being endowed with compassion and courtesy, and enriched by sons, grandsons, and riches, they shall live for a hundred autumns.
One should give gifts to the sick and have the worship of Viṣṇu performed; likewise, one should mutter the eight-syllable mantra or the twelve-syllable mantra.
One should worship with white flowers, with food offerings cooked in ghee, and likewise with perfumes and incenses prescribed by the Śruti, Smṛti, and Mantras.
Viṣṇu is the mother, Viṣṇu is the father, and Viṣṇu is my kinsmen and relatives; what use have I for that dwelling where I do not behold Viṣṇu?
Viṣṇu is in the water, Viṣṇu is on the land, and Viṣṇu is on the peak of the mountain; Viṣṇu is even amidst the mass of blazing flames—the entire world is permeated by Viṣṇu.
We are the waters, we are the earth, we are the darbha grass, we are the sesame seeds; we are the cows, we are the king, we are the wind, and we are all living beings.
We are gold, we are grain, we are honey, we are clarified butter; we are the Brahmins, we are the gods, and we are Śambhu, Bhūr, and Bhuvaḥ.
I am the giver, I am the receiver, I am the sacrificer, I am the sacrifice; I am the taker, I am righteousness, I am indeed the earth, and I am the water.

O bird, one should apply the mind to righteousness and unrighteousness through auspicious and inauspicious actions; whatever action is performed anywhere is the result of what was earned in a previous birth.
I alone shall bestow my mind upon Dharma, and I alone upon Adharma; he who inflicts torment even for the sake of Dharma, to him I grant liberation.
O Tārkṣya, at the end [of his life], the Vaitaraṇī is said to be for the benefit of human beings; by overcoming the flood of sins with that river, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Whatever sin was committed in childhood, in youth, and in old age—whatever sin was done in all stages of life, even in other births.
Whatever action has been performed by deed, mind, or speech during the night, likewise at dawn, at midday and afternoon, or during the two twilights;
Having given even once an excellent Kapila cow that fulfills all desires, one shall deliver oneself from the accumulation of sins at the time of death.
May cows be before me, behind me, and likewise at my sides; may cows be in my heart; I dwell in the midst of cows.
May that Goddess Lakṣmī, who resides in all beings and who is established in the gods, dispel my sin in the form of this cow.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of Various Gifts," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
Śrī Viṣṇu said: Those men who are joined with sin go to the abode of Yama; however, for men, that which is given with me as witness becomes the bestower of infinite fruit.
The giver of land dwells in heaven for as many years as there are atoms in that land; and those who give sandals go forth mounted upon horses.
Due to the merit of giving an umbrella, the hungry ghosts (pretas) are never burned by the heat of the sun through the exertion of fatigue; indeed, they wander happily on the road.
For whomsoever one gives food, by that [act] he shall be nourished.
In darkness that is most terrible, formless, and devoid of any visible mark, men proceed by means of illumination alone through the gift of a lamp.
Whether in the month of Āśvina, Kārttika, or Māgha, or even on the anniversary of one's death, the offering of a lamp should indeed be given on the fourteenth lunar day for the sake of happiness.
And men should offer [this] daily on a very difficult path for as long as a year, out of a desire for the happiness of the deceased.
The pure-souled person shines within his family and attains radiance; that man who provides the gift of a lamp becomes composed of light and is worthy of worship.

In a temple or for a twice-born person, one should place the lamp facing east or north; for a deceased ancestor, it should be made very steady, facing south, after consecrating it with water and making a formal resolve (saṅkalpa).

In this world, whoever—whether living or even for the sake of one who has died—bestows these thirteen verses accompanied by all manner of offerings, shall travel upon the Great Path, freed from all great suffering.
Whatever seat, vessel, or food is given to a twice-born man, if he does not eat it with pleasure, he will not travel far on the path by means of that gift.
By the gift of a water-pot, one who is thirsty drinks water.
A vessel, a gift of clothing, a flower, and a finger-ring—these eleven should be given for the sake of delivering the deceased from the realm of hungry ghosts.
Thirteen pindas should thus be offered according to one's ability by one desiring the welfare of the deceased; in this way, that deceased person becomes satisfied.
By giving food, sesame seeds, thirteen water-pots, a ring, and a pair of garments, she goes to the supreme state.
Whoever bestows a horse, a boat, or even an elephant upon a Brāhmaṇa, enjoys the corresponding happiness in accordance with its greatness.
He who gives a buffalo wanders through various worlds; the mother of Yama’s son is a buffalo that bestows a happy rebirth.
Betel and flowers should be offered to the servants of Yama, for they increase their joy; being thus gratified, they all cause no suffering in that place.
They say that gifts of cows, land, sesame seeds, and gold should be given according to one's own capacity.
Whatever person should offer a water vessel made of clay for the sake of the deceased, that man obtains the fruit of offering a thousand vessels of water.
The messengers of Yama—extremely fierce, terrifying, and dark-brown—do not frighten that person once the gift of clothing has been bestowed.
Indeed, one who is traveling on a path, afflicted by thirst and oppressed by fatigue, will certainly become happy through the practice of giving water from a jar.

A bed provided with a southern-facing orientation, equipped with weapons and garments, and accompanied by a golden image of the Lord of Fortune (Śrīpati), should be given to a Brahmin for his well-being; thus, liberated from the state of a ghost, he rejoices together with the gods.
This, O Tārkṣya, has been told to you regarding the gift arising from the funeral rites; now I shall describe another matter: the entry into another body.
For a living being born in the world of death, death is indeed certain; O scorcher of foes, one who dies shall proceed according to one's own dharma.
O Lord of Birds, for living beings who have died in former times, that wind, having become subtle, exits from the circle of the mouth.
Through the nine gates, the hairs, and the cavity of the palate of people, the life-force certainly departs through the anus in the case of the most sinful.
And after the Lord of Winds has departed, the body falls; struck by the wind, it falls indeed like a tree that is without support.
Earth dissolves into earth, and likewise water into water; fire dissolves into fire, and wind into wind; and space dissolves into space within Śaṅkara, who is all-pervading.
In that regard, O Tārkṣya, desire, as well as anger and the five sense organs—these are declared to be the thieves who dwell within the body.
Desire, anger, egoism, and the mind are indeed the leaders therein; and this Time, accompanied by merit and demerit, is the destroyer.
The nature of the world is indeed fashioned by one's own karma; furthermore, a person goes to another body on account of their good and evil deeds.
Endowed with the five sense-faculties and together with all objects of perception, he enters a new body, just as a person enters another house when his former one has been burnt down.
Those elements which reside within the body and give rise to all its constituents—this body consists of six sheaths and the elements of both mother and father.
O Tārkṣya, in that same way, all the bodily winds of living beings, as well as urine, feces, and whatever other diseases arise through their conjunction, would come into being.
Bone, semen, and likewise sinew are burned along with the body; this, O Tārkṣya, has been described to you as the destruction of all embodied beings.
Furthermore, I shall describe their body as it is: having a single pillar, bound with tendons, and supported by two columns.
The tiny body is endowed with the sense-faculties, possesses nine gates, is assailed by sense-objects, and is agitated by desire and anger.
This city known as "the person" is filled with passion and hatred, is extremely difficult to cross due to the fortress of craving, and is ensnared by the net of greed.
Endowed with these qualities is the body of all embodied beings; within it abide all the deities and the fourteen worlds.
Those men who do not know the self are considered to be like beasts; thus have I explained to you this fourfold body.
In the past, eighty-four lakhs of birth-origins were created: those born from sprouts, those born from sweat, those born from eggs, and those born from a womb.
O sinless one, all this that I was asked by you has been explained.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Giving and the Entry into Another Body," in the Pretakalpa of the second part of the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 32.
Tārkṣya said: How is a living being produced within the fourfold collection of elements? [How do] skin, blood, flesh, fat, marrow, bone, and life arise?
The feet, the hands, as well as the private parts, the tongue, the hair, the nails, the head, the joints, the channels, and likewise many various kinds of lines.
Desire, anger, fear, shame, the mind, joy, pleasure, and pain—[this world] is variegated, perforated, and enveloped by a manifold net.
I consider this world-ocean of existence to be a magical illusion; O Hṛṣīkeśa, who here in this world crowded with suffering could be its creator?
The illustrious Viṣṇu said: I shall declare the supreme, most secret determination of this treasury, by the mere knowledge of which omniscience is attained.
Well asked by you, O Vainateya, regarding the cause of life in this world with compassion; listen with a one-pointed mind.
And among women during their fertile period, four days should be avoided; for it was during that time that in ancient times the sin of killing a Brahmin arising from Vṛtra [was incurred].
Brahmā, having extracted it from Śakra, gave it away with a fourth part; for as long as the body remains, the face of the sinner is not seen [in its true form].
On the first day she is a Cāṇḍālī; on the second, a slayer of a Brahmin; on the third, she is to be known as a washerwoman; on the fourth day, she becomes pure.
Within seven days, through the performance of worship, she becomes fit for the ancestors and the gods; the embryo that exists within those seven days arises from that [impurity] like a thief.
At the time of conception, whatever kind of mental conceptualization arises in the minds of the parents, such is the nature of the birth of the embryo; of this there is no doubt.
Sons are born on even nights, and daughters on uneven nights; therefore, avoiding the first seven nights, one should approach his wife on the even nights.
It is generally declared that women have sixteen nights during their fertile season; if the embryo remains within her on the fourteenth night, [it will be a male].
A virtuous son, a treasure-house of merit and fortune, shall be born there; O Lord of Birds, that night cannot be obtained by ordinary people.
Generally, conception occurs here within eight days; on the fifth day, women should be given sweet food to eat.
One should avoid from afar that field which is pungent, alkaline, sharp, and hot; for it is a vessel for medicinal herbs, yet its seed is like nectar.
Having sown [seeds] therein, a person who is a master shall obtain the fruit perfectly; moreover, one should avoid the sun's heat upon it and practice only what is cool.
Having taken betel, flowers, and sandalwood paste, and wearing clean garments, a man, having fixed his mind on righteousness, should lie down upon a comfortable bed.
Whatever kind of mental conceptualization a person has at the time of conception, a being enters the womb with the arising of a nature corresponding to that.
Through the union of semen and blood, the formation of a physical mass occurs; the living being grows within the womb like the lord of the stars in the sky.
For consciousness, in the form of a seed, is eternally established within the semen; when desire, the mind, and the semen attain oneness, [then conception occurs].
Then the man attains a state of liquefaction within the womb of the woman; with a predominance of blood, a female is born, and with a predominance of semen, a male is born.
When the semen and blood are in equilibrium, the embryos attain the state of being neuter (ṣaṇḍatva). Within a day and night it becomes a *kalala*, and after five days it becomes a *budbuda*.
On the fourteenth day, flesh arises, accompanied by mixed elements; on the twentieth day, the flesh becomes solid, and the embryo grows gradually.
On the twenty-fifth day, strength and nourishment arise; likewise, when the month is complete, one should maintain the five principles.
When two months have passed, the skin and fat are produced; marrow and bones arise in three months, and hair and fingernails in the fourth month.
In the fifth month, the ears, nostrils, and chest are formed; in the sixth, the throat-passage and the abdomen; and in the seventh month, the private parts and so forth.

After eight months, the embryo is complete with all its major and minor limbs; in the eighth month, the living soul moves repeatedly within the womb of the nurse; when the ninth month has arrived, the strength of the one dwelling in the womb becomes firm.
Upon the exhaustion of that residence in the womb, medical treatment arises for him; he is then born as either a woman, a man, or a neuter.
It possesses the three powers, has large eyes, is endowed with the six sheaths, is equipped with the five sense organs, and is adorned with ten channels.
He who knows that which is endowed with the ten qualities of the vital breath (prāṇa) is a knower of yoga: marrow, bone, semen, flesh, hair, blood, and likewise strength.
This body of a living being consists of the six sheaths and is composed of the five elements; in the ninth or tenth month, it is born as one composed of the five elements.
Drawn forth by the winds of birth, overwhelmed by agony, and nourished by the *suṣumṇā* channel, he remains in the womb of the woman, hurrying.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—afflicted by these elements and bound by the ligatures of sinews, [the self remains].
These seven, which are situated within the channels (nāḍī), are declared to be the fundamental constituents: skin, bone, channels, body hair, and flesh as the fifth.
These five qualities of the earth have been declared by me, O Lord of Birds; now listen, O Kāśyapa, to how water likewise possesses five qualities.
Saliva, urine, semen, marrow, and blood as the fifth—these are declared to be the five qualities of water; they should be understood with diligent effort.
Hunger, thirst, sleep, laziness, and lust—these, O Tārkṣya, are declared by all yogis to be the five qualities of fire (tejas).
Passion, hatred, as well as shame, fear, and likewise delusion—this, O Tārkṣya, is said to be the fivefold set of qualities born of wind.
Contraction, running, leaping, extension, and suppression as the fifth—these are declared to be the five qualities of the wind (vāyu).
Sound, thought, profundity, hearing, and the transition into truth—these five qualities of space should be diligently understood, O Tārkṣya.
The ear, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose are the organs of perception; and the two hands, the two feet, the anus, and the organ of generation are the organs of action.
Iḍā and Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā as the third; Gāndhārī, Gajajihvā, Pūṣā, and likewise Yasā.
Alambuṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī is recorded as the tenth; these ten principal channels are situated within the center of the body.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna; as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.
Thus these ten vital airs (vāyu) have been described, well-established within bodies; they alone provide nourishment for all embodied beings from the food that has been consumed.
The vitalizing wind (prāṇa) leads [the breath] through all the joints of the body; as soon as food is eaten, it is divided into two parts by the wind.
Having entered the cave properly, he placed the water above the fire and that food upon the water, each with its own separate portion of food and water.
One should blow gently upon that fire with one's own breath from below; thus fanned by the wind, the fire separates the waste matter from the essence.
The waste, separated from the body by twelve impurities, becomes distinct: the ears, eyes, nose, tongue, teeth, navel, skin, and anus.
