For these nails are indeed seats of impurity, as are feces, urine, and so forth; this body of six sheaths is said to arise from the union of semen and blood.
O son of Vinatā, it is said that there are thirty-two teeth and three and a half crores of body hairs in common for all [beings].
There are seven hundred thousand hairs, and the nails are said to be twenty; one thousand palas of flesh are generally situated within the body.
One hundred palas of blood and ten palas of fat, along with skin of equal measure, are indeed prescribed by the ancients for *tārkṣya*.
The marrow is twelve palas; the great blood (mahārakta) is three palas; the semen should be known as two kuḍavas, and the blood is recorded as one kuḍava.
The phlegm is six [palas], as are the feces and urine; however, the bones are said to exceed three hundred and sixty [palas].
Thus the summary has been fully explained; now we shall describe its expansion: indeed, pleasure, pain, fear, and security are obtained solely through karma.
The wind draws [the fetus] out from the womb with its face downward and feet upward; having placed the palms of the hands against the sides of the knees, it grows.
The two thumbs are placed above, the fingers of the hands are at the knees, the eyes are on the back of the knees, and the nose is between the knees.
In this way, the being situated within the mother’s womb undergoes gradual growth; the bones attain solidity, and it lives by means of what has been eaten and drunk.
The channel named Āpyāyinī is fixed there at the navel; in women, it becomes attached to the cavity of the intestines.
The food and drink consumed by women thus pass into the womb; nourished by them, that living being attains growth.
Many memories of his former births in the cycle of existence arise there for him; then, being tormented here and there, he attains a sense of world-weariness.
"I shall not do so again; as soon as it has been consumed here from my belly, I will strive in such a way that I may never conceive a fetus."
Thinking thus, the living being indeed remembered hundreds of births that had been previously experienced, whether as gods or as human offspring.
Then, in the course of time, as the creature turns over with its face downward, it is born thereafter in the ninth or even the tenth month.
As it is being expelled, it is afflicted by the wind pertaining to Prajāpati; then, oppressed by suffering, it emerges while wailing.
Emerging from the belly, he experiences unbearable fainting; then, accompanied by the pleasure of the touch of air, he regains consciousness.
Then the deluding Māyā of Viṣṇu seizes him; with his mind deluded by her, he suffers the loss of knowledge.
Then, having lost its knowledge while in the state of a child, the living being subsequently attains the stage of childhood, youth, and also old age.
Furthermore, in that same way, a human being undergoes death and birth; consequently, he wanders in this wheel of saṃsāra like a waterwheel.
At times a man attains heaven, and at times he goes to hell; he experiences both heaven and hell as the fruit of his own actions.
O best of the twice-born, when one has experienced [the fruits of] karma, one goes to the earth with little effort; likewise, when it is nearly exhausted in heaven or even in hell.
This is the great suffering in the hells that those dwelling in heaven perceive: they do not rejoice here, but are being cast down by the denizens of hell.
Even in heaven there is incomparable suffering, for from the very moment of ascent, the thought persists in the mind: "I am about to fall."
Beholding even those who have gone to hell, one experiences great suffering; thus, night and day, I am restless with the thought, "I too shall go to such a fate."

There is great suffering in dwelling in the womb; for one being born, there is the pain of passing through the birth canal; and once born, there is only suffering during childhood as well as in old age.
The connection with desire, envy, anger, and the like is difficult to endure even in youth; old age is a bad dream, and at death there is intense suffering.
Dragged by the messengers of Yama, he goes downward even into hell; then there shall be birth from a womb again, and likewise the suffering of death.
Thus, in this wheel of saṃsāra, living beings are whirled around like a water-wheel; bound by their former fetters, they are pierced again and again.
There is no happiness whatsoever for a bird in a field crowded with hundreds of sufferings; therefore, O son of Vinatā, men must strive for liberation.
All this has been explained regarding how the formation of the embryo occurs; I shall now speak concerning the sequence of questions asked, or whatever you desire to know.
Garuḍa said: "I have received the answer to the two great questions posed in the middle; let the answer to the third question also be provided."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: You have asked what must be done by one who is dying; listen, I shall tell you the answer that has been spoken there in brief.
Having recognized that a person's death is imminent, one should then bathe them with cow urine, cow dung, excellent earth, water from sacred fords, and water infused with *kuśa* grass.
Then, having put on two clean, pure, and beautiful washed garments, one should first spread out darbha grass and scatter it with the tips pointing toward the south.
One should place sesame seeds there upon ground smeared with cow dung.
Or, O Lord of Birds, one should place gold in the mouth [of the image] with its head facing either east or north; there, O Lord of Birds, should be the Śālagrāma stone and the Tulasī plant.
Furthermore, with a composed mind, one should light a ghee lamp in his presence and likewise perform the recitation of the mantra: "Namo bhagavate vāsudevāya."
First, having uttered the *praṇava*, the performance of worship and the giving [of gifts] are prescribed; then, one should duly honor Hṛṣīkeśa with flowers, incense, and other offerings.
One should worship with prostrations, praises, meritorious acts, and through the yoga of meditation; and one should give gifts to the brahmins as well as to the poor and the helpless.
One should relinquish the sense of "mine" regarding sons, friends, wife, fields, grain, wealth, and so forth, while remembering the feet of Viṣṇu within one's heart.
If one is in a state of extreme distress, then when one's own person is dying, the sons and others should recite the Puruṣasūkta aloud.
All this has been told to you regarding the duty when death is imminent; now I shall tell you, in brief, the entire fruit of all this.
Through bathing, purity is attained; from that, the removal of impurity occurs; from that, the remembrance of Viṣṇu arises; and from the knowledge of Him, all fruits are bestowed.
A bed of *darbha* grass leads the afflicted person to heaven, without a doubt; by scattering sesame seeds and *darbha* grass, one's bath becomes equivalent to a sacrificial rite.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Śrī, and likewise Agni attend upon one in the maṇḍala; therefore, one should construct a maṇḍala.
O bird, if a man’s evil be slight, he goes to the highest world with his head turned either toward the east or the north in this body.
When the five jewels are placed in the mouth, knowledge sprouts within the living being: Tulasī, Brāhmaṇas, cows, Viṣṇu, Ekādaśī, and the bird (Garuḍa).
For men sinking in the ocean of worldly existence, there are these five very rafts: Viṣṇu, Ekādaśī, the Gītā, Tulasī, and the Brahmin-cow.
In this essence-less and difficult saṃsāra, the six-word mantra that bestows devotion—“Namo bhagavate vāsudevāya”—is what a person should recite.
Preceded by the syllable Oṃ, one shall attain union [with the deity]; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, through worship, one attains my world and shall go from here to heaven.
In the absence of bondage yet in the presence of the sense of "mine-ness," knowledge arises from the Puruṣasūkta; for whichever of these means is predominant, O Kāśyapa.
Understand that the respective fruits will also be proportionally greater; one should give according to one's ability so that he may always be pleased.
All this fruit of bathing and other rites has been declared by me to you; whatever qualities exist in the Cosmic Egg (Brahmāṇḍa), those are established within the body.
The netherworlds, the mountains, the worlds, as well as other continents and oceans, and all the planets beginning with the Sun, are situated within the body.
One should know that the region beneath the feet is Tala, while the region above the feet is Vitala; know that Sūtala is at the knees, and Mahātala is in the region of the thighs.
Likewise, the wise one should perceive Talātala in the two thighs, Rasātala in the region of the genitals, and Pātāla situated in the hips, starting from the feet.
One should know Bhūrloka in the middle of the navel, Bhuvarloka above that, Svargaloka in the heart, and likewise Maharloka in the region of the throat.
One should place Janaloka on the region of the face, Tapoloka on the forehead, and Satyaloka in the great aperture; thus are the fourteen worlds.
Mount Meru is situated in the triangle; Mandara is in the lower corner; Kailāsa is in the south, and Himācala is on the left side.
Niṣadha is in the upper portion, Gandhamādana is in the south, and Malaya (or Ramaṇa) is on the left line; these seven are the principal mountain ranges.
Jambūdvīpa is situated in the place of the bones; Śākadvīpa is established in the marrow; Kuśadvīpa is situated in the flesh; and Krauñcadvīpa is located in the veins.
Śālmalidvīpa is located in the skin, Plakṣa in the collection of body hair, and Puṣkaradvīpa resides in the nails; following these are the oceans.

Likewise, the ocean of salt water (Kṣāroda) is in the urine; the ocean of milk (Kṣīroda) is in the alkaline secretions; the ocean of wine (Surodadhi) resides in the phlegm; and the ocean of clarified butter (Ghṛtasāgara) is in the marrow.

One should know the ocean of taste (Rasodadhi) to be in the sense of taste, and the ocean of curd (Dadhisagara) in the blood; the sweet ocean (Svādūda) is located in the region of the uvula, and the ocean of the womb (Garbhoda) is situated in the semen.
The Sun resides in the nāda-cakra, and the Moon in the bindu-cakra; Mars is to be known as residing in the eyes, and Mercury is remembered as being in the heart.
One should know that Jupiter resides in the place of Viṣṇu; Venus is situated in [the place of] Śukra; Saturn is stationed in the place of the navel; and Rāhu is always situated in the mouth.
Ketu is situated in the region of the anus; thus the mandala of the planets within the body is declared to be distributed from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
For those who have arisen in saṃsāra certainly die; there is no doubt that they suffer from fierce hunger and thirst, as well as burning sensations and fainting spells.
Where these fierce afflictions arise, they are indeed born from the sting of scorpions; and at the time of fullness, destruction occurs for all embodied beings.
For those who have gone to the world of Yama, they indeed run on and on through the midst of heated sand and into the midst of blazing fire.
Seized by the hair, O Tārkṣya, the most wicked and base beings, who are utterly devoid of compassion and righteousness, are led away by the servants of Yama.
These dwell in the world of Yama within a hut; no [physical] birth exists there. Thus, O Tārkṣya, a living being is born in the mortal realm through its own karmas.
Those who are born in this cycle of existence certainly die; for there is no doubt regarding lifespan, karma, wealth, knowledge, and even death itself.
For these five are created while the embodied being is still in the womb; by karma a creature is born, and by karma alone it perishes.
Happiness, suffering, fear, and security are all attained through action alone; and the wind draws the fetus out from the womb with its face downward and feet upward.
From birth, the illusory power of Viṣṇu swiftly deludes [beings]; a living being undergoes rebirth through the connection formed by its own past actions.
From good deeds one becomes superior, possessing enjoyments and being born into a noble family; according to the degree of evil deeds, one is born into a lowly family.
O Lord of Birds, he is poor, diseased, foolish, a doer of evil, and a vessel for suffering; what more than this need I tell you?

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Origin of Living Beings, the Division of their Constituent Elements, and the Division of the Worlds," in the second section (Uttara-khaṇḍa) of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa concerning the vision of Dharma and the vision of the deceased. The Glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*— Chapter 33.

Garuḍa said: "The origin and characteristics of a living being have been told to me, your son. But how large is the realm of Yama within the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile? Tell me its extent in detail, and how long is the path said to be?"
O Lord, by what sins committed, or by what auspicious deed, do human beings go there? Please tell me this in detail.
The Blessed One said: "The distance between the world of humans and the realm of Yama is eighty-six thousand yojanas in measure."
Like heated, molten copper, the great path is a blazing fortress; there the most sinful men of deluded minds go.
There were indeed thorns of many kinds, extremely sharp and terrible to behold; by them the ground was covered, and likewise the fire was fierce.
There is no shade of trees there where a man may rest, for he is seized by the nooses of Time through his own fierce deeds.
On that path there was no food by which one might nourish one's life, nor was water seen there by which thirst might be quenched.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, he travels along the great path; somewhere on that most difficult road of Yama, he trembles from the cold.
Whatever kind of evil belongs to a person, such is the path for him; miserable, wretched, and deluded, they cross over it, overwhelmed by sufferings.
Some weep bitterly, and some utter cries of betrayal, as they are repeatedly tormented by the defects produced by their own past actions.
O bird, such indeed is that path to be known as dreadful; those men in the world who are free from craving travel easily upon it.
Whatever gifts have been given by men on earth, those very same gifts appear before them on the path in the world of Yama.
The water-offering and funeral rites for the cremation do not reach the wicked; those base evildoers wander about like the wind itself.
Such is that terrible path described to you, O observer of noble vows; I shall further describe the condition of the road of Yama.
Between the southern and southwestern directions lies the city of Vaivasvata; it is entirely composed of diamond, divine, and impenetrable even by gods and asuras.
It is square, with four gates, seven walls, and archways; Yama himself dwells therein, accompanied by his messengers.
Its measurement is said to be exactly one thousand yojanas; it is divine, composed of all kinds of jewels, and possesses the brilliance of lightning-flames and the sun.
That cave of the King of Dharma was vast, with a golden luster, and rose to a height of five hundred yojanas.
It was surrounded by thousands of pillars adorned with lapis lazuli gems, featuring latticed windows of pearl nets and decorated with hundreds of banners.
It was rich with the resonance of hundreds of bells, surrounded by hundreds of archways, and always adorned with these and other such ornaments.
There, the Blessed One sat upon a level and auspicious Dharma-seat, ten *yojanas* in extent and resembling a dark blue cloud.
He knows the Dharma, is of virtuous character, and is endowed with righteousness; he is Yama, the benefactor who strikes fear into those joined with evil and bestows happiness upon the righteous.
It was filled with gentle breezes, various festivals, diverse expositions, and the sounds of conchs and musical instruments.
Upon entering the middle of the city, there is indeed the house of Citragupta, which is twenty-five yojanas in extent.
It was ten stories high, magnificent and divine, encircled by an iron wall, with hundreds of thoroughfares and adorned with hundreds of banners fluttering in the sky.
The residence of Citragupta was crowded with hundreds of lamps and filled with the sound of singing, adorned by those skilled in various paintings.
Seated there upon a divine and most wonderful throne made of jewels and pearls, he calculates the lifespan among humans and among other beings.
He is never deluded regarding either good or evil deeds; whatever has been acquired by anyone, he knows that exactly as it is.
He records the performed actions, free from the eighteen defects; to the east of Citragupta’s abode lies the great house of Jvara.
Furthermore, on the south [is the seat] of Śūla and Latāvisphoṭaka; on the west, of Kālapāśa, as well as Ajīrṇa and Aruci.
To the north of the central seat, one should know there is likewise another, Viṣacikā; in the northeast is indeed Śiro-rti (headache), and in the southeast is Mṛkatā (dumbness).
Atisāra is in the southwest, and the one called Dāha is in the northwest; Citragupta always stands there, surrounded by these.

O Tārkṣya, whatever action anyone performs, he must scratch out all of it at the gate of the palace of Dharmarāja; thus, at night, the messengers stand there with those lowest of men who have committed evil deeds and are being tormented.
Beaten by the messengers of Yama with great nooses and mallets, men are slaughtered for their various sins committed through their past actions.
Furthermore, those of evil deeds are cut in two like pieces of wood with various excellent weapons, as well as with various machines and saws.
Others, intensely surrounded on all sides by blazing coals, are scorched like lumps of iron due to the ripening of their past karma.
Others, having been thrown upon the surface of the earth and hacked with axes, are seen crying out due to the ripening of their past karma.
Some most wicked men are tormented intensely by the messengers of Yama with boiling concoctions made of molasses, and others likewise with boiling oils.
On that very day, I saw others in the world of Yama begging by the millions, "Give! Give!"—they for whom my own possessions had been devoured by you.

Thus, O Tārkṣya, the hells for sinners have been described many times through the various deeds mentioned and spoken of in all the scriptures. Now I shall describe the benefit of giving, so that there may be happiness therein.

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Detailed Description of the Extent of the World of Yama," in the Dharma-kāṇḍa of the second part of the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Tārkṣya, to the characteristics of righteousness and unrighteousness according to the proper method; for men who run forward, their good and evil deeds run ahead of them.
In the Kṛta age they praise austerity; in the Tretā age, the means of knowledge; in the Dvāpara age, sacrifice and giving; but in the Kali age, giving alone.
The wise have declared this to be the supreme duty of householders: for those who perform sacrifices and works of public utility according to their ability, there is no sin.
For one who has planted trees, or dug wells, pits, and reservoirs, there will be great happiness as they travel along the path of Yama.
Those who provide fire and heat for a brahmin afflicted by cold go to a state of bliss, being fully satisfied with all their desires.
Gold, jewels, pearls, and so forth, as well as garments and ornaments—all this has been given by him by whom the earth itself was given.
Whatever gifts have been bestowed upon the earth by men remain in the vicinity of those [deceased] on the path to the realm of Yama.
O son, whatever various condiments, foods, and edibles one gives according to the prescribed rite, that reaches the deceased.
The self indeed has the name "son"; a son is a savior in the abode of Yama. Because he delivers his father from the terrible [realm], he is therefore called a "son" (putra).
Therefore, the son must offer the śrāddha until the end of his life; for by that means, the deceased indeed obtains enjoyments during the period of transition.
The handful of water that is offered by kinsmen for the deceased who is being cremated—taking on the form of the departed—it goes to the abode of Yama, bringing satisfaction.
For three days, milk was placed in an unbaked earthen vessel; then, having bound three pieces of wood together with cords, it was set at a crossroads at night for the sake of propitiation.
O bird, on the first day, the second, and likewise the third, the deceased, assuming a body of wind, drinks milk situated in the sky.

On the fourth day, the collection [of bones] should be performed; or even on the fourth day for one who maintains the sacred fires. The gathering of the bones should be done, and thereafter one should offer handfuls of water.
Neither in the forenoon, nor at midday, nor in the afternoon, nor during the twilights; but when the first watch has passed, one should offer handfuls of water for the deceased.
When the son has offered [the water], all those kinsmen and well-wishers—both of his own caste and of other castes—must offer a handful of water into the river.
A Brahmin should not go too far to quickly offer the handful of water; he should do so once the women have returned, for that is the constant custom of the world.
When a Śūdra has passed away and a Brāhmaṇa carries his wood to the funeral pyre or follows him, he shall remain impure for three nights.
Then, when three nights have passed, one should go to a river that flows to the ocean; by performing a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and consuming clarified butter, one becomes purified.

A Śūdra may go everywhere; a Vaiśya, to three [castes]; and the one following him (the Kṣatriya), to two; each may approach women of their own respective castes to offer the funeral libation of water when [a relative] has died.
After offering the funeral libation (jalāñjali), one should thereafter perform the cleaning of the teeth; O Kāśyapa, all kinsmen of the same lineage should abstain from these for nine days.

The best of the twice-born go to offer the funeral libation (jalāñjali) at that very place where one has died—whether on the road or in the house—for the wise have ordained that there is no displacement from that location whatsoever.
Women should walk in front, and the new stores of provisions behind; those standing upon stones should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
One should look at barley, mustard seeds, and dūrvā grass in a full vessel; one should cause [the patient] to consume neem leaves and perform an oil bath.
One should not perform [the rite] with those of low caste, nor should one feed them at home; one should eat from an earthen vessel and avoid using one that is turned face-upward.
One should grasp the virtues of the deceased and recite the verses of Yama; one should contemplate both the auspicious and inauspicious deeds accumulated through previous karma.
With that very body he has obtained, he experiences the fruits of his good and evil deeds; moving in the form of wind, he indeed wanders, and as wind he ascends upwards.
A hut is certainly constructed through the performance of the ten-day rites; indeed, by means of the sixteen *navaka-śrāddhas*, a person enters that hut.
The hut on the ground should indeed be made of earth with sesame seeds and darbha grass; and five jewels should be placed in the mouth, by which the life-force (jīva) flourishes.
When the flower has indeed perished, then one should not conceive a fetus; therefore, with care, one should scatter sesame seeds and darbha grass upon the ground.
Whether he is born as an animal or as an immobile being, wherever that creature may be born, the śrāddha offering reaches him right there.
Just as an arrow released by an archer toward a target reaches it, so too does a śrāddha performed for a specific person accrue to that very person.
As long as the body has not been produced, the faithful do not perform the propitiation; having fallen into the delusion of hunger, he was satisfied after ten days.

He for whom the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍadāna*) has not been performed wanders in the sky; dwelling in the water for three days, and likewise in fire for three days, he dwells in the sky for three days, but for one day in a dwelling.

When the body and the fire have been consumed, he is satiated with water alone; likewise, an oil-bath is performed with water, and in the house, [the rite is completed] with cakes and *kṛsara* porridge.
On the first day, the third, the fifth, or even the seventh, as well as on the ninth and the eleventh, the Śrāddha is called "the ninefold" (navaka).

Whether at the door of one's house, in a cremation ground, at a sacred ford, or even in a temple—at that very place where the first rice-ball (piṇḍa) is offered, there one should complete all [the offerings].
The śrāddha performed on the eleventh day is declared to be common to all; bathing is prescribed for the sake of purification for the four castes.
Having performed the eleventh-day rite and having bathed again, one should become pure; he who gives a bed to a Brahmin as prescribed grants liberation to the deceased.
It would not come to pass even if someone of another lineage were to perform the rite, or if some man, being satisfied, were to perform it for women.
Whatever rice-ball (piṇḍa) is offered on the first day according to the prescribed rite, one should perform all subsequent śrāddhas with that very same food.

One should perform the funeral rites (śrāddha) for ten days without mantras, according to the name and lineage. Having discarded the garments in which the śrāddha was performed, one should enter the house.
Whether of a different lineage or the same lineage, whether a woman or a man, whoever performs [the rite] on the first day shall complete it for ten days.
The body of the living being is certainly produced from ten lumps, and its growth within the womb occurs over the course of ten months.
For as long as the period of impurity lasts for him, so long shall the rites of offering rice-balls and water be performed; this indeed is the rule prescribed for all four castes.
Where the period of impurity lasts for three nights, one should cause three [pindas] to be offered on the first day, four on the second day, and likewise three on the third day.
One should offer milk and water separately in two bowls for one day; indeed, one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha on the fourth day.
By the funeral cake (piṇḍa) offered on the first day, the head is produced; the eyes, ears, and nose are produced on the second day.
On the third day, the cheeks, the face, and likewise the neck are produced; on the fourth day, the heart, the flanks, and the abdomen arise in exactly the same manner.
On the fifth day, the hips, the back, and the anus are produced; on the sixth, the two thighs are to be known [as formed]; and on the seventh, the emergence of the ankles occurs.
When the eighth day arrives, O bird, the two shanks appear; the two feet are to be known [as appearing] on the ninth, and on the tenth, there is powerful hunger.

On the eleventh day, one should offer that rice-ball (piṇḍa) with meat; cooked food should be given to him, as well as kṛśara, cakes, and milk. Having washed the Brahmin’s feet, one should offer the arghya, incense, and a lamp.
There are twelve monthly śrāddhas, as well as one on the eleventh day; there is also the three-fortnightly rite, and two at the sixth month—these constitute the sixteen śrāddhas.

Those who know the Vedas understand that the month in which the lunar day (tithi) on which one dies occurs is to be known as the first [month] for the monthly offering to be given on the anniversary of death.
The śrāddha performed with the corpse in hand, at the place of death, or upon the seat of a brahmin—that indeed is the first śrāddha; it should take place on the eleventh day.

That lunar day on which a man died is the one to be observed for the monthly *śrāddha*; however, in the case of the three fortnights (*tripakṣa*), one should certainly not observe a lunar day that is empty (*rikta*).
For one who dies on the full moon day, the *unakā* is the fourth; for one who dies on the fourth, the *unakā* is the ninth.
One who dies on the ninth day, as well as on the fourteenth which is a *riktā*—these should be known as *riktā* days by one skilled in the funeral rites.
The śrāddha performed on the eleventh day is proclaimed as the "Navaka"; one should discard the food at a crossroads and perform a bath once again.
Starting from the eleventh day, food accompanied by water for the jar should be offered day after day to the best of the twice-born for the duration of a year.
In the human body, there is indeed a collection of bones; that same number exists in all bodies—three hundred and sixty.
For those bones indeed become nourished by the water-pot; therefore, the pot is given, and satisfaction arises for the deceased.
On whichever day a living being dies, whether in a forest or on difficult terrain, at that very time the cremation shall take place, and the period of impurity (sūtaka) begins from the day of death.
A vessel of sesame seeds, as well as food, perfumes, incense, and so forth, should be given on the eleventh day; by that, the twice-born becomes purified.
A Kṣatriya becomes pure after twelve days, and likewise a Vaiśya after fifteen; for a Śūdra, purification occurs after one month in the case of both birth and death impurity.

For three months, there shall be impurity for three nights; for six months, however, it is for a "pakṣiṇī" period; and for less than a year, it is for one day. Having offered water libations when the full period has elapsed, one becomes pure. According to this very principle, purification shall apply to all castes.
Starting from the eleventh day, every year thereafter, one should worship the Viśvedevas and offer a single pinda.
Just as all the hosts of stars are eclipsed by the rays of the sun, so too is everything eclipsed; a preta never exists anywhere.
The best of the twice-born always praise the gift of a bed; since life is impermanent, who indeed will provide it after one has passed away?
A man is a kinsman and a father only so long as he lives; once he is dead, realizing "he is dead," affection ceases in an instant.
For the self alone is the friend of the self; knowing this again and again, and reflecting that "even while living," one should pursue one's own welfare.
"Who among the deceased would have a son give a bed for a brahmin together with a cotton mattress? Knowing all this to be so, one should cause [the gift] to be given by one's own hand.

Therefore, having obtained a bed made of strong wood, firm, beautiful with ivory and other ornaments, lovely, and adorned with bands of gold; and having placed upon it a golden image of Hari accompanied by Lakṣmī—
One should fashion a pitcher filled with clarified butter; it should be understood by the wise as the "sleep-pitcher" for the pleasure of Garuḍa.
Betel, saffron powder, camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood; a lamp, sandals, an umbrella, a fly-whisk, a seat, and a vessel.
One should place seven kinds of grain according to one's ability at the sides, as well as whatever else may be useful for one who is lying on the bed.
Having prepared a bed equipped with a golden pitcher, a water-jar, a mirror, a five-colored canopy, and such bedding, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having worshipped her together with her husband—who bestows the happiness of the heavenly realm—and having honored her with most beautiful garments, one should cause her to put on a new cloth.
The house was furnished with ornaments for the ears, neck, fingers, and arms, with various other decorations, and equipped with household utensils and provided with a cow.
Then the arghya offering should be presented with the five jewels, fruits, and unbroken grains of rice.
Just as the bed of Kṛṣṇa is never empty of the daughter of the ocean, so may my own bed likewise never be empty in birth after birth.
Having thus provided a pure bed and asked for forgiveness, one should dismiss [the officiant]; this is the procedure proclaimed for the eleventh day as well.
For he who gives for the sake of dharma when a kinsman has died is indeed a true kinsman; listen now as I describe the specific distinction regarding this point.

Whatever he had previously possessed in his own home that was useful—whatever clothing, vessels, or vehicles were attached to his body, and whatever else was dear to him—all of that he should provide for him.
The wise man should place an auspicious golden figure upon the bed; having worshipped it, the death-bed should be given away as prescribed.
By the power of the gift of a bed, all comforts shall attend a living being in the abode of Purandara as well as in the residence of the Son of the Sun (Yama).
The terrifying-faced messengers of Yama do not torment him; that man is never afflicted by heat or cold anywhere.
By the power of the gift of a bed, a preta is released from bondage; even one joined with evil deeds goes to the heavenly world.
Mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot and attended by hosts of apsarases, he shall remain there, freed from all sins, until the dissolution of all beings.
The woman who performs the *navaka*, the *ṣoḍaśa-śrāddha*, the *śayyā*, and likewise the annual rite for her husband, attains indeed infinite merit.
She was of benefit to her husband while she lived; she did not do so when dead. As a virtuous and truthful woman, she rescued her beloved while she was alive.
For the woman, one should indeed cause all of this to be given: curd-rice, a bed, gold, saffron, collyrium, clothing, ornaments, and likewise a couch.
Whatever here in this world may be beneficial to women—be it an ornament attached to the body or any object of enjoyment and the like—[is subject to decay].
Having gathered all that together, one should assign each to its respective place; one should worship the world-protectors, the planets, the Goddess, and Vināyaka.
Then, wearing white garments and holding a handful of flowers, the wise man should recite this mantra in the presence of the Brahmin.
This is indeed an image of a preta, provided with all requisites and endowed with every kind of jewel; it has been offered to you, O Brahmin.
The Self is Śambhu; Śivā is Gaurī; and Śakra is with the hosts of gods. Therefore, by this gift of a bed, may that very Self be propitiated.
It should be given to a teacher who is a Brahmin with a family; once it has been accepted, the recipient should proclaim there, "Who gave this?"
Then, having circumambulated and prostrated, one should dismiss [the recipient] according to this rite; O bird, one should cause the gift to be given to a single person.
A cow, a house, a bed, and women should not be given to many; for these, when divided as sacrificial fees, cause the donor to fall.
O Tārkṣya, hear now what the fruit is for one who bestows it in this manner: he is honored in the heavenly world for more than a hundred divine years.

Whatever merit is gained during the Vyatīpāta yoga, on the full moon day of Kārttika, during the two solstices, or whatever merit is gained at Dvārakā during an eclipse of the moon or sun; [all that is attained by this].
Whatever merit is found at Prayāga, Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, and Arbuda; at the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean.
The gift that is given to them is indeed superior even to that; it does not equal even a sixteenth part of this gift of a bed.
Wherever that living being is born, there alone he experiences the fruit of his actions; when his karma is exhausted, he returns to earth as a human of auspicious appearance.
Possessing great wealth, knowing the Dharma, and proficient in all the scriptures, that bull among men, upon death, goes once again to Vaikuṇṭha.
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot and surrounded by apsarases, oh, he rejoices together with the ancestors in the offerings to gods and manes!

The Śrāddha performed on the Aṣṭakās, as well as on the day of the new moon (Amāvāsyā), during the Maghā asterisms, and on whatever other festivals for the ancestors (pitṛ-parvan) there may be—on all these occasions [one should offer].
Listen, O Tārkṣya, according to the rule: if the ancestors remain in the state of a preta, the śrāddha offerings do not reach them unless the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa has been performed.
The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be performed when the year is complete, without a doubt; having first performed the rite for the purification of the corpse and the sixteenth *akṣayya-śrāddha*.
One should join the purification of the paternal line with fifty [verses]; however, having reached a festive occasion (vṛddhi), one may perform it for a Śūdra according to one's own will alone.

Now, the *sapiṇḍana* rite on the twelfth day is to be performed for one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*). As long as he does not perform it, he remains a *preta* even though he possesses the fire. Therefore, the *sapiṇḍana* must be performed by the one maintaining the fires on the twelfth day.
One should not perform the Gayā-śrāddha or the fortnightly (aparapakṣika) śrāddha within the year following the cremation, except for the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite.
If there should be many co-wives, yet only one should have a son, then all of them shall be considered mothers of sons by virtue of that single offspring.

A son who is not a *sapiṇḍa* relative and does not maintain the sacred fire should not perform the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*). By performing it, he becomes a sinner and is even born as a slayer of his ancestors.
When her husband has died, the woman who likewise renounces her life—his *sapiṇḍana* rite should indeed be performed for her together with that of her husband alone.
Even for those who were not formally married—whether they be Vaiśyas or Kṣatriyas—a son may perform the *sapiṇḍana* rite for any of his father’s wives.
When a Śūdra woman is married by a Brāhmaṇa through negligence, that Ekoddiṣṭa Śrāddha is performed for her by him alone, and she is united with him.
But as for the other ten sons born within the four castes, they should always be joined with their respective mothers during the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite.

On the Anvaṣṭakā days, at the Śrāddha performed for the sake of prosperity (vṛddhi), and at the Sapiṇḍana rite, the offering to the woman should be made separately from that of the father, including her own Piṇḍa.
O Tārkṣya, it is my opinion that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite should be performed for the mother together with her maternal grandmother, and for the father together with his paternal grandfathers.
But when she dies without a son, the husband should perform the *sapiṇḍana* rite; he should thus unite her with the three [ancestors] beginning with his mother, in accordance with the sacred law.
O Tārkṣya, for women who have neither a son nor a husband, the sapindikarana rite should be performed at a time of prosperity by their brothers, heirs, or brothers-in-law.
For those who are bereft of sons and grandsons, there is neither a kinsman nor a brother-in-law; the offering should be given by others together with the brothers through the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.
If the Sapindikarana rite has not been performed due to ignorance or some obstacle, one should then perform the nine rites, the sixteen Sraddhas, and the annual anniversary rite.

If there is no burning, it should not be performed; if there is burning, the wise man should have it done. Having fashioned an effigy of *darbha* grass, he should cause the corpse to be cremated with fire.
The son should perform [the rites] for the father, but the father should not perform them for the son; out of excessive affection, one should not perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for a virtuous [son].
Even when there are many sons, one alone may perform the rites: the *navaśrāddha*, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, and the other sixteen *śrāddhas*.
However, even among those whose wealth has not been divided, one alone may perform the funeral rites; this has indeed been declared by the sages.
Once divided, the annual rites and other such duties should be performed separately; each son must perform them individually for himself.
For him to whom these sixteen *śrāddhas* for the deceased have not been offered, the state of being a *piśāca* remains fixed, even by hundreds of other *śrāddhas* performed.
O Lord of Birds, in the absence of a son, a brother, a brother’s son, a sapinda, or even a disciple shall perform the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite.
For all those who are childless, a daughter-in-law should perform the sapindikarana rite; or else, one should have a sacrificial priest (ṛtvij) or even a family priest (purohita) perform it.
If an eclipse occurs within the year after the father has died, the sons should not perform the pārvaṇa śrāddha, nor the nāndīmukha śrāddha.
One should not perform a *tīrtha-śrāddha*, a *gayā-śrāddha*, or any other ancestral *śrāddha* during the year following the death of one's primary guru.
On the Yamaka days, on the Gajacchāyā, on the Anvaṣṭakās, and on the Yugādis, the ancestral pinda should not be offered except for the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite.
Some say that the gift for the Sacrificial Person (Yajñapuruṣa) and likewise that for the gods and others must be performed even if the year is incomplete or even during its middle.
For that which is offered even to the ancestors, excluding the water-offering (argha) and the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa), all of that must indeed be performed; this is recorded as the very rule.
The ancestors are gods to the gods, and likewise the sages are gods to the ancestors; the ancestors are gods to the sages, and therefore the Father indeed triumphs.
He becomes the lord of sacrifice for the ancestors, gods, and humans; whatever is given to the lord of sacrifice is given to all embodied beings.
If a son performs a śrāddha within a year after his father has died, he is deprived of the merit acquired over seven lifetimes; of this there is no doubt.
But those who have become pretas, their rites of offering rice-balls and water having been neglected, all wander about driven by the wind, tormented by hunger and thirst.
When the father has passed away, the paternal rites are suspended; however, should there be the death of the mother, the paternal rites are not suspended.
If the mother has died while the father remains alive and the paternal grandmother is also living, the *sapiṇḍana* must nevertheless be performed together with the paternal grandmother alone.
"Truth, truth, and again the truth—listen to my words: for those men on earth whose funeral rice-balls have not been gathered together,"

One should certainly not attend to those for whom food has been given by their sons in various ways; neither the *hantakāra* offering nor the *śrāddha* rite nor even a handful of water should be offered on their behalf.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Post-Mortem Rites and Other Matters," in the *Pretakalpa* section of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī-Gāruḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
Tārksya said: O Janārdana, tell me of another doubt of mine: suppose the wife of some man has met her death. What is the procedure? Please explain this to me.
The paternal grandmother lives, as do the paternal great-grandmother and the paternal great-great-grandmother; likewise, the father is devoted to his mother.
The maternal grandfather, as well as the great-grandfather on the mother's side—by whom is the mother united with these? Tell this to me, O Lord.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O bird, I shall speak again regarding the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite; one should certainly unite [the deceased] with Umā, Lakṣmī, and Sāvitrī.

Three are known as eaters of the rice-ball (piṇḍa), and three are remembered as those who abandon it; three are those who smear the rice-balls with ointment, and the tenth is the one present at the line (paṅkti).
These men are renowned in both the paternal and maternal lineages; by performing this sacrifice, the patron shall deliver ten ancestors and ten descendants.
He becomes a sapinda at the beginning once the sapindikarana rite has been performed; however, the most remote one who is to be excluded is known as the great-great-grandfather (vṛddhaprapitāmaha).
The last should be known as the renouncer (tyājaka), while the first would be the smearer (lepaka). But he who is the last smearer would be one who stays near the row (paṅktisannidha).
"The sacrificer shall be one; ten are the ancestors of the remote past, and ten are those of the recent past. Thus, these ancestors are to be known as numbering twenty-one.
He who performs the supreme śrāddha in this world according to the prescribed rule—there is no doubt that he is born [in a higher state]; hear now what the fruit of that is as well.
O bird, if one's lineage is severed, it is the father who indeed gives sons; even he who is his great-grandfather may become the giver of the oblation.
When the Śrāddha has been performed, these indeed are remembered as the benefits for the ancestors; the aged great-grandfather (prapitāmaha) shall receive abundant food and other offerings.
O bird, that man whose lineage is indeed severed in this mortal world shall dwell in a terrible hell, like an elephant sunk in the mud.
He is born in other wombs where trees and reptiles dwell; without a continuous lineage, he is certainly not liberated from hell in this world.
Whether it be his teacher or his disciple, anyone who is a son of his body—even if far away—should perform the Nārāyaṇabali out of devotion on his behalf.
Purified and freed from all sins, he will certainly dwell in the world of the gods, having escaped from hell; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
Beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā and ending with Revatī, this group of five constellations is always to be avoided; it is inauspicious at all times.

No cremation (or *bali* offering) should be performed there for Brahmins or any other caste; no water should be offered there, for it will certainly result in misfortune. Even if one's own kin are afflicted by suffering, the funeral rites (*lokayātrā*) must not be carried out.
Everything else for him must be performed immediately after the *pañcaka*; otherwise, suffering arises even for his sons and kinsmen.
There will be loss in his household during these asterisms for one who has died; or else, even in the midst of those asterisms, cremation is prescribed for him.
For human beings, however, it is performed immediately due to the offering of oblations; the merit from making an immediate offering at a sacred ford is supreme even compared to cremation.
The brahmins must perform [the rite] according to rule, accompanied by mantras and following the prescribed procedure; thereafter, effigies are thrown near the corpse.
Then, four brahmins made of darbha grass and consecrated with mantras should perform the cremation together with those effigies.
Then, at the end of the period of birth-impurity, the son should perform the most excellent rite of pacification.
For that man who has died among the Pañcaka group and finds no destination, one should offer sesame seeds, cows, gold, and clarified butter on his behalf.
A gift is given to the Brahmins, which destroys all calamities; at the end of the period of impurity, that deceased person attains a [favorable] state through virtuous sons.
O Brahmin, a vessel, sandals, an umbrella, a golden seal, and two garments are given as a sacrificial fee; this liberates one from all sins.
Indeed, for children, the elderly, and the sick who have died among the five [classes], if one does not perform the prescribed rite, obstacles arise for that person.
In a śrāddha for pretas, one should avoid these eighteen items: blessings, double-folded darbha grass, the syllable Om, and the practice of offering a single piṇḍa.

One should not utter the word "svadhā" or the term "pitṛ" in reference to the offering into the fire, the remnants of the śrāddha, the Vaiśvadeva portion, the scattered food (vikiro), or the ritual exclamation.
One should not utter the word "anu," nor perform the invocation (āvāhana), nor carry a firebrand; one should not perform the circumambulation or the formal dismissal (visarjana) beyond the boundary.
A twice-born man should not perform the sesame oblation nor likewise the full-offering; if he does not perform the Vaiśvadeva rite, the performer goes to a downward state.
The sixteen [rites] previously mentioned are likewise known as the "impure śrāddha": performed at the site, at the gate, on the half-way path, at the funeral pyre, and when the corpse is in hand.

The fifth [piṇḍa] is for the spirits dwelling in the cremation ground; the sixth is declared to be for those who have gathered [the remains]. These ten piṇḍas offered during the ten days constitute what is proclaimed as the first set of sixteen śrāddhas.
Furthermore, O Tārkṣya, hear from me the sixteenth [chapter], the second in the middle [section]: here, according to the prescribed rule, exactly eleven śrāddhas are to be performed.
Those who know the reality have declared that there are sixteen [shrines], including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others, as well as the fivefold śrāddha.
There are twelve monthly *śrāddhas*, as well as one on the eleventh day; that which occurs every three fortnights, and the two *rikta* days—these, O Bird, make sixteen.

Having first performed the rite for the purification of the corpse, one should perform the other [rites] numbering three times sixteen; however, for the purification of the lineage of ancestors, one should not employ even half of a hundred.
He who is deprived of half of a hundred and is not included in the row does not partake; likewise, forty-eight śrāddhas destroy the state of being a preta.
One who has fallen short by fifty times may become a member of the assembly; in truth, such a person should be reconciled with the half of a hundred through a sincere act of faith.

(Now, the procedure for the corpse: The binding of the hands and feet of the corpse onto the bier must be performed there. If this procedure is not carried out in this manner, it will result in the corpse being seized by piśācas.
If the corpse is expelled during the night, the kingdom becomes free from fear; if the corpse is not released, or if it is released with difficulty, there will be misfortune.
If one eats at will when it is heard that a corpse is situated in the middle of the village, that food should be known as being like meat, and its water like blood.
While a deceased person remains within the village, one should avoid betel, tooth-sticks, eating, sexual intercourse, and the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa).

Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, fire-offerings, libations, and worship of the gods are performed by the kinsmen according to their duty for the sake of purification when a deceased person remains within the village.
O Lord of Birds, such is the conduct of kinsmen and relatives; by violating the duty toward kin, one becomes stained by the sin of a ghost.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sapiṇḍana and the Rite for the Corpse," in the second section (Dvitīyadṛdhadṛpretakalpa) of the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
Tārkṣya said: Why is fasting meritorious and a giver of imperishable states? And why does one who dies at a sacred ford (tīrtha), having abandoned his own home, attain such merit?
If one who has become a *kuṭīcara* dies at home or dies while still at home without having reached a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), what destination does he attain?
If one who has performed renunciation (saṃnyāsa), whether in a sacred place or even at home, dies before reaching his appointed end, how should his funeral rites be performed?
O Lord, if a restrictive rule is established, a failure of the mind surely arises; by what means could there be accomplishment for such a person—whether through performance or non-performance?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "If anyone indeed meets death after practicing fasting, having cast off the human body, he shines forth equal to me."
As many days as one lives while maintaining a vow of fasting, those days are equal to sacrifices accompanied by complete sacrificial fees.
If one undergoes renunciation at a sacred ford or in one's home and then dies there, he too obtains every day double the previously mentioned fruit.
And when one has taken up the fast upon the onset of a great disease, that disease shall not arise again, and one shall shine like a god.
If a person, being afflicted by illness, takes up renunciation, he is not born again on this earth in the ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra.
Day after day, food should be given to Brāhmaṇas; likewise, one should offer vessels of sesame seeds according to one's ability, as well as gifts of lamps and worship of the gods.
For one who conducts himself in this manner, various sins—both great and small—are consumed; upon death, he attains liberation, just as all the great seers have done.
Therefore, fasting grants men the state of Vaikuṇṭha; for that reason, whether one is healthy or in the final stage of life, one should practice that which has liberation as its characteristic.

For that man who, having renounced his sons, wealth, and other possessions, goes to a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha), the deities beginning with Brahmā shall become bestowers of satisfaction and nourishment upon him.
If one who has set out facing a sacred ford (tīrtha) should die even midway while engaged in the vow of fasting, he shall dwell in the assembly of the ṛṣis.
If one has observed the vow of fasting and dies even at home, he shall leave behind his own kin and wander alone in heaven.
If a person renounces both food and likewise water, having drunk the water from my feet, he is not born again on this earth.
The forest deities protect that person who has gone to such a sacred ford and sits with his work completed; however, the messengers of Yama specifically do not remain by his side.
The man who frequents sacred fords (tīrtha), being freed from all sins, shall partake in the fruit of that sacred ford if he dies there or is cremated there.
Even if one dies elsewhere while constantly practicing [the path], that wise person shall become a twice-born knower of the Vedas in an auspicious land and family.
O Tārkṣya, a man who, having undertaken a fast unto death, survives, should summon the Brāhmaṇas and renounce all his possessions to them.
Having been authorized by those twice-born men, he should perform the entire Cāndrāyaṇa penance; he should not speak untruth thereafter, but should practice only dharma.
And whoever, having gone to a sacred ford, returns home again, being permitted by the Brahmins, should then perform an expiatory rite.
Having given gifts of gold, cows, land, elephants, and horses, he who reaches a sacred ford at the time of death is truly fortunate.
When death is imminent, one who has set out from home for a sacred ford (tīrtha) gains the merit of a gift of a cow at every step, provided that no violence occurs.
Whatever sin is committed in the home is purified by bathing at a sacred ford; however, if one commits sin there [at the ford], it is indeed like adamantine cement.
He shall suffer there for as long as the moon, sun, and stars exist; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, whatever gifts are given there truly become inexhaustible.
When someone is afflicted by illness, gifts should be given even by men who are destitute; specifically, cows, sesame seeds, gold, and the seven types of grain.
Upon seeing a man who is generous, all the inhabitants of heaven, together with the ṛṣis, Citragupta, and Dharma, are always delighted.
As long as wealth remains under one's own control, one should bestow it upon a Brahmin; for when one has died, who will compassionately give away all that is dependent on another?
The wealth which was placed in the hands of a Brahmin by sons on behalf of their father, he used that to provide for himself along with his sons and grandsons.
A gift given to one's father is said to be a hundredfold; to one's mother, a thousandfold; to a sister, a hundred-thousandfold; and what is given to a uterine brother is inexhaustible.
If, out of greed, negligence, or even delusion, they do not give, then all those stingy sinners grieve when they have died.
Wealth acquired through excessive hardship and which is by nature fickle has but one destination: giving; all other uses lead to misfortune.
Death laughs at the protector of the body who guards his wealth, just as an unfaithful wife laughs at her own husband who is devoted to his son.
O Tārkṣya, even upon acquiring vast wealth, that righteous and gentle man remains indifferent; he regards both himself and his riches as if they were mere blades of grass.
He shall have no afflictions, nor indeed any web of delusion; at the time of death, he shall have no fear arising from the messengers of Yama.
O Kāśyapa, for seven thousand years one dwells in water, eleven in fire, sixteen in wind, sixty in great battle, and eighty in a cow-pen; but through fasting, there is an inexhaustible state.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Destination of One Who Dies by Fasting," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
**Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 37** Tārkṣya said: O Janārdana, tell me truly about the offering of the water-pot (*udakumbha*). By what ritual procedure is this rite to be performed?

O Janārdana, what are their characteristics, by whom are they fulfilled, and to whom should they be given? At what time should those offerings that accomplish the satisfaction of the deceased be bestowed?

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: I shall speak again concerning the gift of water-pots. They should be given with reference to the deceased, provided with food and drink; especially for great birds, they grant liberation to the departed spirit.
On the twelfth day, or in the sixth month, or after three fortnights, or even at the end of a year, water-pots should indeed be offered on his path for his own happiness.
Day after day, water-pots filled with sesame seeds, cooked food, and water should be offered upon a well-smeared patch of ground.
A vessel should be given there to the preta according to one's inclination; being well-pleased by that gift, the preta departs with the messengers of Yama.
On the twelfth day, one should especially cause water-pots to be given; there, according to the prescribed rule, one should formally resolve to provide twelve jars.
There, one vardhanī vessel filled with cooked food and fruit should be given to an auspicious brahmin after making a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) dedicated to Viṣṇu.
One [offering] indeed for Dharmarāja; by him being pleased, one becomes a partaker of liberation. And one for Citragupta; having gone there, one shall become happy.
The first sixteen [vessels] should be offered, filled with water and black gram (māṣa) food.
Starting from the *uktrānti-śrāddha*, for each of the sixteen *śrāddhas*, one should designate one Brāhmaṇa for each of the sixteen [offerings].
Starting from the eleventh day, that which is called the "Dṛḍha" should be given daily for as long as a year, consisting of cooked food and water-filled vessels.
Large water vessels were provided, along with small jars; there was indeed one *vardhanī* vessel among them, and within it was a bowl made of bamboo.
Having worshipped her with fragrant scents, one should cover her with a garment and especially cause water-filled vessels to be given to the Brahmins.
O Lord of Birds, having formed this resolve day after day according to the prescribed rite, [one should give it] to a noble-born Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with Vedic knowledge and virtuous conduct.

It should be given to one who possesses both learning and virtuous conduct, but never to a fool; for one who is endowed with Vedic knowledge and good conduct is capable of rescuing and crossing over [the ocean of existence].
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Śrāddha with a Water-Pot," in the Dharma-kāṇḍa of the Preta-kalpa, within the second part of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Tārkṣya said: O Lord, tell me of liberation and heaven as sought through charity and pilgrimage; by what means does one attain liberation, and by what means does one dwell in heaven for a long time?
By what does the vital heat (tejas) depart from the world of light (svarloka) and from the world of truth (satyaloka)? By what does one obtain human birth, and by what does one sink into the hells?
O bestower of liberation upon devotees, tell me this after having ascertained it for certain: when which [being] has died is there no rebirth in heaven?
The illustrious Viṣṇu said: Human birth occurs in the land of Bhārata among the thirteen castes.
Having reached that sacred field, one dies and is not subject to rebirth: Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā, Kāśī, Kāñcī, and Avantikā.
The city of Dvāravatī is to be known as one of these seven that bestow liberation; he who, even when his life-breaths have reached his throat, should say "I have renounced," [attains it].
One who has died goes to the city of Viṣṇu and is not born again on earth—by whomsoever the two syllables "Ha-ri" have been uttered even once.
He has girded his loins for the journey toward liberation—he who constantly remembers me, saying, "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa."
Just as a lotus pierces through the water, so do I lift [the soul] out of hell; wherever there is a Śālagrāma stone or a Dvāravatī stone.
Where there is a conjunction of these two, there is liberation without a doubt; wherever the Śālagrāma stone is present, it brings about the destruction of the taints of sin.

Liberation for a living being is certain upon death in its proximity. By planting, protecting, watering, meditating upon, touching, or praising it, O bird, the *tulasī* burns away the sins of men accumulated over lifetimes.
He who has bathed in the mental sacred ford—the lake of wisdom with truth for its water, which removes the impurities of passion and hatred—is not smeared by sins.
The deity is not found in wood, nor ever in stone; the deity is found in the internal disposition (bhāva). Therefore, one should cultivate that disposition.
Every morning, the fishermen behold the Narmadā; yet they do not go to the city of Śiva, for the activity of their minds is too heavy with worldly attachment.
Whatever the perception of the mind may be, such is the fruit of karma for human beings; such is their passage to the next world, as subtle as the investigation of a thread through a needle's eye.
He who is intent on sacrificing his life for the sake of a Brahmin, for the sake of a cow, or for the protection of women from violent assault, shall indeed attain liberation.
He who dies by fasting shall indeed attain liberation; he who dies by fasting is released from all bonds.
Having given gifts to the Brahmins, one may thereafter attain liberation; these indeed are the paths to liberation as well as the paths to heaven.

During a cattle-raid, the destruction of a country, or at the deathbed, in battle, or at a sacred pilgrimage site—when a living being who is superior, inferior, or middling is being oppressed, by renouncing his life there, he shall obtain a long residence in heaven.
A wise person should learn two things: life and death; life through giving and enjoyment, and death on the battlefield or at a sacred ford.
In Harikṣetra, Kurukṣetra, and likewise in Bhṛgukṣetra; in Prabhāsa, Śrīsthala, Arbuda, and Tripuṣkara.
The man who dies at Bhūteśvara dwells in heaven for the duration of a day of Brahmā; thereafter, he falls back to the surface of the earth.
He who gives the means of subsistence for a year to a Brāhmaṇa free from faults, having extracted all impurity, is glorified in the heavenly world.
He who marries off a maiden to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas shall dwell in the world of Indra, surrounded by his own kinsmen.
And by giving great gifts, a person shall obtain their fruit.

One who undertakes the restoration of dilapidated step-wells, wells, tanks, groves, and temples shall obtain the same fruit as the original builder; or, by restoring them when they have fallen into ruin, one's merit becomes double that amount.
Having constructed a leaf-hut that wards off both cold and heat, he gives it to a learned brahmin who has a family.
A person is honored in heaven for thirty-five million years.
A woman of the same caste who, being virtuous, follows her deceased husband in death, attains heaven upon dying for as many years as there are hairs on her body.
She who, having abandoned her sons, grandsons, and others, follows her own husband, shall attain heaven; both of them, adorned by celestial women, shall enjoy that realm.
She who, having always harbored thoughts of treachery toward her husband and committed many sins, follows after her own husband, washes away them all.
If her husband should be a doer of evil, practicing great sins, even a woman who follows his will incurs no sin at all.
He who constantly gives a gift of at least one morsel of food as a rule attains a celestial chariot yoked with four chowries.
Whatever sin has been committed by a person until the end of life, all that goes to destruction through the granting of a means of livelihood for a year.
The sin accumulated over three lifetimes—past, present, and future—is entirely washed away by the marriage ceremony of a Brahmin girl.
A large pond is equal to ten wells; a lake is equal to ten ponds; and a water-station in a waterless forest is equal to ten lakes.
He who constructs a pond in a waterless region, he who gives a gift to a destitute brahmin, and he who maintains compassion for all living beings—he shall become the leader of the heavens.
Through these and other such meritorious deeds, one becomes a partaker of heaven; having obtained all that fruit, he shall attain supreme stability.
Abandoning worthless actions, one should always be devoted to righteousness; for charity, self-restraint, and compassion—these three are the essence on this earth.
Giving to a virtuous person who is poor, honoring one who bears the marks of an ascetic, and performing funeral rites for a destitute deceased person bestow the fruit of ten million sacrifices.

Thus, in the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the second part, the Dharma-kāṇḍa, in the section on the Pretas (*Pretakalpa*), within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, is the description of the causes for the attainment of the highest worlds, for rebirth, and for liberation, as well as for human existence—this being the thirty-ninth chapter of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Tārkṣya said: O Lord, having shown compassion toward me, please explain the rules regarding periods of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*), for the sake of the discernment of the minds of men and for their welfare.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Lord of Birds, upon death and birth there is a fourfold impurity (sūtaka) which is generally avoided by all four castes alike.
In both cases, one should avoid the food of the family for ten days; giving, receiving, burnt offerings, and Vedic study are suspended.
Having understood the place, the time, as well as oneself, the substance, the purpose of the substance, the logical justification, and the specific circumstance, one should perform the ritual action.
In the case of entering a cave or fire, and for those who have died in a foreign land, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on; immediate purification is prescribed.
For those living beings who are still in the womb and those who have emerged from the womb, there is no cremation with fire, no period of impurity, and no water libations.
Artisans, craftsmen, physicians, as well as male and female slaves, kings, and those learned in the Vedas are proclaimed to be immediately pure.
A sacrificer, one observing a vow,
one purified by mantras, a maintainer of the sacred fires, and likewise a king— for these there is no birth-impurity, as well as for whomsoever kings so desire.
Upon a birth, a twice-born man should not cause confusion among his sapinda relatives; the mother becomes pure after ten days, while the father is purified by bathing.

Manu has declared that in the case of death or birth-impurity occurring during a marriage, a festival, or a sacrifice, the food intended for those occasions may be eaten if the wealth was previously earmarked for them.

For all [relatives], the impurity is thus; however, for the mother and father, there is birth-impurity (sūtaka). Birth-impurity belongs to the mother alone; the father becomes pure by performing ritual sipping (upaspṛśya).
If death or birth should occur again within ten days, the Brahmin shall remain impure for as long as that [second period] has not yet reached its tenth day.
When the rule has been established, one should offer gifts to a distressed Brahmin; likewise, as declared by the sages, it does not incur fault if performed at the proper time.
However, by bathing with a clay vessel containing water mixed with sesame seeds and likewise with earth at the end, a person shall become pure.
One should give gold and a bull to a member of the assembly, and to a twice-born man, a Kṣatriya should likewise give double that amount, while a Vaiśya should give three times as much.
A Śūdra must give four times as much wealth to a Brāhmaṇa; in this very sequence, the four castes are purified.
If [the body] has decayed within seven or eight days and lacks the sacraments of the household stage, his impurity (sūtaka) lasts for as many days as the number of years [he would have lived].
For those who have perished for the sake of Brahmins, or in the course of rescuing women or cows, or those who have perished in battles, there is impurity for only one night.
For those brahmins who perform the funeral rites for a destitute deceased person, O best of men, there is no inauspiciousness whatsoever regarding their own meritorious deeds.
No impurity whatsoever remains for them when they have a Brahmin as their companion; it is declared that they are immediately purified by plunging into water.
When the Śūdras have turned back and have reached the water's edge, then they should not be looked upon by a Brāhmaṇa; so say those who know the Vedas.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Period of Impurity and Other Matters," in the second part of the Pretakalpa, within the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
Tārkṣya said: O Blessed One, some Brāhmaṇas have fallen under the power of untimely death (apamṛtyu). What is their path? What is their place? And what will be their destination?
Furthermore, what would be appropriate for them, or of what nature would their ritual injunctions be? I desire to hear that; tell it to me, O Madhusūdana.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Since the transformation into death has occurred for the twice-born who have become *pretas*, I shall now describe their path, destination, and the prescribed rites.
Listen, O Tārkṣya, to this supreme secret: when a death has occurred that is difficult to overcome—such as that of Brahmins who have died from fasting or have been struck down by fanged beasts.

Those who have drowned while clutching at a neck, those who are emaciated, those killed by a beak, those killed by poison, fire, bulls, or Brahmins, and those who commit suicide through cholera—[these do not attain the merit of the gift].
Listen to the state of those who have died by falling, by hanging, or by water; they go to a terrible hell, as do those who have been killed by barbarians and the like.
Those touched by dogs, jackals, and the like; those not cremated; those swarming with worms; those who died after having been transgressed [by others]; and those afflicted by great diseases.
Those who have been falsely accused, as well as those who are physically unimpaired yet nourished by sinful food, [are purified] from a Caṇḍāla, water, a serpent, a Brāhmaṇa, and from lightning-fire.

Those who have died from fanged beasts, from falling from trees and the like, or those defiled by contact with a woman in her courses, a woman who has recently given birth, a Śūdra woman, or a washerwoman;

Released from hell by that sin, they partake of the state of hungry ghosts (pretas); one should not perform their cremation, nor the period of ritual impurity (sūtaka), nor the water-libation rites (udakakriyā).

One should not perform the funeral rites for them, nor the offerings of food on the anniversary of death, nor any post-mortem ceremonies; O Tārkṣya, for them one should instead perform the Nārāyaṇa-bali sacrifice.
For the sake of the welfare of the entire world, listen to that which removes the fear of sin: burning [the image] for six months is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa, and for three months for a Kṣatriya.
For a Vaiśya, it is prescribed for one and a half months; for a Śūdra, it is ordained immediately. This applies at the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, Naimiṣa, and Puṣkara.
In a pond full of water, or in a lake of pure water, in a large reservoir, a well, a cow-pen, a house, or a temple;
O Brahmin, one should perform an offering named for Nārāyaṇa before the image of Kṛṣṇa; the libation for the deceased should be performed with Purāṇic and Vedic mantras.
One should offer libations to Viṣṇu with all kinds of medicinal herbs mixed with unbroken grains (akṣata), using either the Puruṣasūkta or Vaiṣṇava mantras.
Facing the south, one should remember the deceased as Viṣṇu—the god who is without beginning or end, and who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
The imperishable, lotus-eyed Lord shall become the bestower of liberation upon the deceased; and at the conclusion of the libation, he is free from passion and devoid of envy.
Having become one whose senses and mind are conquered, pure, devoted to the Dharma, delighting in the virtue of generosity, peaceful, restrained in speech, and purified, he should bow down.
The sacrificer there should be pure and accompanied by his kinsmen; with devotion, he should perform exactly eleven śrāddhas there.
Through the ripening of all his past actions, he was concentrated one-pointedly on each [grain]: sixty grains of water-rice, barley, wheat, and millet.
One should cause auspicious sacrificial food (haviṣyānna), a seal (mudrā), an umbrella, a turban, and a single garment to be offered, as well as all kinds of grain mixed with milk and honey.
One should give the eightfold gift consisting of garments and sandals; one should cause this to be given to all the Brahmins and should not form a restrictive seating arrangement.

While the rice-balls remain on the ground, one should separately perform the libation (tarpaṇa) using a conch vessel or a copper vessel, accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Endowed with meditative concentration and mental retention, and having knelt upon the ground, one should give [the gift] to all the Brahmins according to the injunctions of the Vedic scriptures.

In a rite for a single deceased person (ekoddiṣṭa), one should cause the arghya water to be offered separately with a Rigvedic verse; the water, made sweet and placed upon the prepared seat, is [offered] with the mantra "āpo devīr madhumatīḥ."
"Thou art taken with a support"—with this [formula] he should offer the second oblation; and with "By that eye which is purifying," he should offer what has been prepared for the third.
The gods are in the fourth; go to the ocean in the fifth; Agni-jyotis in the sixth; and Hiraṇyagarbha in the seventh.
On the eighth day, one should know the verse "yamāya tvā"; likewise, on the ninth, "yajjagran"; on the tenth, "yāḥ phalinī"; and then, on the eleventh, [one offers] the rice-ball (piṇḍa).
One should perform the dismissal of the rice-balls with the mantra "bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ," and having performed the Śrāddha for the eleven deities, one should perform it again on the following day.

One should invite five Brahmins who are experts in the four Vedas, endowed with learning, virtuous conduct, and good qualities, who are of one's own kin and preeminent in character; they should be physically unimpaired and highly praised, and never those who are to be avoided.
Viṣṇu should be made of gold, and Rudra likewise of copper; Brahmā should be made of silver, and Yama should be made of iron.
One should place a lead image, or else one made of darbha grass, representing the preta; then, with the mantra "śanno devī," one should install Govinda in the western direction.
One should place Rudra to the north with the mantra "O Agni, come hither" (agna āyāhi), and Prajāpati to the east with the mantra "I praise Agni" (agnim īḷe).
With the mantra "iṣetvorje," one should place Yama on the right; having prepared a mandala in the center, a man made of darbha grass should be placed there.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Yama, and the fifth, Preta, should then be placed in separate jars, accompanied by the five jewels.

One should perform the recitation separately with garments and sacred threads (yajñopavīta), each accompanied by its own specific mudrā; there, the recitation for Brahmā and the other deities should likewise be performed separately.
One should perform the five offerings (śrāddha) for the deities according to the prescribed rule; thereafter, one should offer a stream of water separately upon each pedestal.
In a conch shell, or a copper vessel, or if those are unavailable, even in an earthenware one, one should take water with sesame seeds combined with all medicinal herbs.
A seat, sandals, an umbrella, a signet ring, a water-pot, a bowl, a bowl-rest, and garments—this is the eightfold set.
O Lord of Birds, one should give a copper vessel filled with sesame seeds, along with gold and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), to a preeminent Brāhmaṇa in accordance with the prescribed rite.
One should give land upon which crops have grown to a Brahmin who has mastered the Ṛgveda, and one should give a milch cow to a Brahmin whose essence is the Yajurveda.
For the singer of the *sāman*, one should give gold dedicated to Śiva; for Yama, sesame seeds and iron; and thereafter, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Afterwards, a doll should be made, provided with all medicinal herbs; now hear, O Kāśyapa, the procedure for the arrangement of the stalks of the Palāśa tree.
Having spread out a black antelope skin and fashioned a human figure with kuśa grass, the collection of bones is said to consist of three hundred and sixty stalks.
Having placed those stalks individually upon these limbs, one should place forty in the region of the head and ten in the neck.
One should apply twenty [strokes] on the chest, twenty on the abdomen as well, one hundred on the pair of arms, and twenty on the region of the hips.

One should place one hundred bones on the two thighs and thirty on each of the two shanks; one should place four at the penis and six on the two testicles; ten on the toes of the feet—in this manner, one should distribute the bones.
