One should place a coconut in the position of the head and a gourd in the palate; one should place the five jewels in the mouth and a plantain fruit on the tongue.
One should place a tube in the intestines, and likewise for the child and the vital breath; one should apply fat and marrow, and for urine, one should use cow's urine.
Sulfur and the metallic ores should be given, as well as yellow orpiment and realgar; mercury should be placed in the place of semen, and likewise brass in the place of feces.
Likewise, apply realgar to the body, sesame paste to the joints, barley flour to the flesh, and indeed honey as well.
One should apply the roots of the *vaṭa* tree to the hair, deer-skin to the skin, palm leaves to the ears, and *guñjā* seeds to the breasts.
A hundred-petaled lotus should be placed on the nose, a lotus in the region of the navel, an eggplant on the pair of testicles, and auspicious gṛñjana on the penis.
Clarified butter should be applied to the navel, and tin is prescribed for the loincloth; pearls should be placed on the breasts, and the head should be anointed with saffron.
With incense of camphor and agalloch, auspicious garlands, and fragrant perfumes, one should place a silk thread as a garment and a golden ornament upon the heart.
The two arms represent supernatural power and prosperity, the two eyes are marked with cowrie shells, and vermilion is applied to the corners of the eyes, along with offerings such as betel leaf.

Having prepared the deceased with all medicinal herbs, one should perform the worship as prescribed; and according to the ritual involving fire, one should place the sacrificial vessels in their proper sequence.
Having performed the purification of the deceased with the *ṛc* "śirome śrīḥ" and "punantu varuṇa," using water from the Śāliśāla stone, one should proceed.
A well-behaved, milch cow should be given in honor of Viṣṇu.
Sesame seeds, iron, gold, cotton, salt, the seven types of grain, land, and cows—each one of these is declared to be an equivalent ransom.
Then, having given a vessel of sesame seeds, one should likewise give the gift of one's feet.
Great gifts should be given, as well as a vessel of sesame seeds; thereafter, the Vaitaraṇī [cow] adorned with all ornaments should be given.

A self-possessed person should indeed perform a Vaiṣṇava Śrāddha for the sake of the liberation of the deceased; then, having envisioned Viṣṇu within his heart, he should effect the release of the deceased.
Having recollected "Oṃ Viṣṇu" with reference to the deceased, his death, and the cremation by fire, one should then observe the period of ritual impurity (sūtaka) for three days.
The performer of the ten-day rites must offer rice balls for the enjoyment of the deceased; one should perform the entire annual ritual in this manner, and thus the deceased partakes in liberation.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Determination of Happiness, Suffering, Gain, and Loss in the Case of Untimely Death," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī-Gāruḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
[End of] the Glorious *Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*: 41.

The illustrious Viṣṇu said: O Lord of Birds, one should perform the rite of releasing a bull according to the prescribed rules during the months beginning with Kārttika, on the auspicious day of the full moon.

One should commence the *nāndīmukha* śrāddha for the conclusion of the marriage; one should perform the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of the ground as well as the installation of the sacred fire (*agnisthāpana*).
Then, having established the fire according to the rules in a pond, a well, or a cow-pen, one should perform everything according to the marriage rite, including the recitation by the Brahmins.

The placing of the sacrificial vessels, the cooking of the oblation, the gathering of the *upayamana* grass and other materials, and the sprinkling with water—after these, the twice-born should perform the *homa* together with a Brāhmaṇa priest.
One should offer the two Āghāra libations and the two Ājyabhāga portions as the two eyes; furthermore, six oblations (three each) should be offered with the mantra beginning "prathame 'hni."

The two libations (āghāra) and the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) are performed with milk-rice (pāyasa); likewise for the deities of the limbs: to Agni, Rudra, Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Śiva, Bhava, Mahādeva, Īśāna, and Yama.

One should perform a single oblation with flour paste using the mantra "pūṣā gā anvetu," and for both [the bride and groom], a *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation should be made with the *caru* and the milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
First, one should perform the oblation of the *vyāhṛtis* as an expiation for Prajāpati; then, one should perform the consumption of the remnants and the release of the *praṇītā* water.
Then, having performed the purification rite and offered a sacrificial fee to a Brāhmaṇa, one who is purified by the recitation of the Rudra-mantra with its six ancillaries shall attain liberation.
O Bird, having bathed a single-colored bull and a single heifer, one should then adorn them with all types of ornaments.

Having established that pair [of images], the deceased shall attain liberation. Afterward, an offering of water (tarpaṇa) should be performed with uplifted [hands] preceded by mantras; then one should feed the Brāhmaṇas and satisfy them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Then, the ekoddiṣṭa śrāddha should be performed according to the prescribed rules; likewise, water and food should be offered for the sake of the liberation of the deceased.
Then, on the twelfth day, one should perform [the rites] separately month after month; for when joined with this procedure, it indeed effects the liberation of the deceased.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Release of a Bull," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
The glorious Viṣṇu said: Just as a calf finds its mother among thousands of cows, so does the karma performed in the past follow after its doer.
Āditya, Varuṇa, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Soma, Hutāśana, and the Lord who wields the trident—all rejoice in the giver of land.
There is no gift equal to the earth; there is no treasure equal to the earth; there is no teaching equal to truth; and there is no sin greater than falsehood.
Gold is the first offspring of Agni; the earth belongs to Viṣṇu, and cows are the daughters of the Sun. He who gives gold, a cow, and land has thereby bestowed the three worlds.
They say there are three supreme gifts: cows, land, and Sarasvatī; these rescue one from hell through recitation, worship, and fire-offerings.
Even after having committed many fierce and extensive evils, one is purified by the gift of land, even if it is only the size of a cow-hide.
Even if it carries away [the mind] through greed, one should restrain and ward it off; he who does not protect it goes to a terrible hell.
That which ought not to be done must not be done, even if one's life-breaths have reached the throat; that which ought to be done must indeed be done—thus do those who know the Dharma understand.
In causing a change in one's livelihood, the sin is equal to that of killing a thousand cows; likewise, in cutting off a livelihood, the penance is the gift of a hundred thousand cows.
A single cow taken away is better than a hundred cows given; even by giving a hundred after taking one, equality with that act is not achieved.
But he who, having given it himself, himself obstructs [the recipient], that sinner goes to hell until the dissolution of all beings.
And not even by means of a horse sacrifice duly performed with ritual fees is there such [merit] as there is when a wretched Brahmin, emaciated by lack of livelihood, has been rescued.
That merit which is gained when a weak and terrified Brāhmaṇa is protected is not attained even through the Vedas or at a sacrifice accompanied by very large sacrificial fees.
Vehicles and forces, though well-nourished by the wealth of Brahmins, crumble at the time of battle like sandcastles.
He who seizes land, whether given by himself or given by another, is born as a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years.

The property of a Brahmin, when consumed out of friendship, burns the family unto the seventh generation; that same property, when taken in the form of theft, burns it as long as the moon and stars endure.
A man might perhaps digest iron filings or stone powder; but what man in the three worlds could ever digest the sound of the Veda?
By the destruction of the property of the gods, by the seizure of the property of Brahmins, and by the transgression against Brahmins, entire families fall from their noble status.
There is no sequence of respect for a Brahmin who is devoid of learning; for one does not offer oblations into ashes after setting aside a blazing fire.

Whatever gifts, whether offerings to the gods (havya) or offerings to the ancestors (kavya), are given at the time of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), the Sun bestows them again and again until the end of seven kalpas.

Among receiving gifts, teaching, and officiating at sacrifices, they say that receiving gifts is the most desirable; one is purified from receiving gifts by recitation and burnt offerings, but the Vedas do not purify the act of officiating at sacrifices.
Always reciting mantras, always performing fire offerings, and avoiding food cooked by others, he is not defiled even if he accepts the earth filled with jewels.

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Gift of Land and Other Matters," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa. The glorious Viṣṇu said: Those who have perished by water, fire, or hanging, those who have fallen from the life of a wandering mendicant (*pravrajyā*), and those who have died by fasting unto death (*anāśaka*)—they are purified by the *Aindava* penance after giving a cow and likewise a bull.
For one who is less than twelve years of age but more than four years old, the mother, the father, or another relative shall perform the penance.
Therefore, even for an ignorant person, there is neither offense nor sin; he incurs no royal punishment, nor is there any need for expiation.
If a woman who has been bitten is seen with blood [flowing from the wound], she becomes afflicted; on the fourth day, having bathed and discarded her shoes and other such items, she becomes pure.
When an impurity arises due to a sick person, one who is not sick should bathe ten times; by bathing repeatedly and then touching him, that sick person shall become pure.

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Purification," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.

The glorious Viṣṇu said: "O Tārkṣya, death by one's own will [is of various kinds]: that of horned animals, fanged beasts, and reptiles; likewise, death caused by Cāṇḍālas and others, by self-inflicted violence, or by means of poison and the like."
Those whose death occurs through falling into water or fire, by wind, or likewise by fasting and other such means, are declared to be evildoers.

Those belonging to heretical sects and those outside the stages of life, as well as those who have committed great sins, women who are unchaste, and likewise those who have fallen after having ascended [to a higher status].
For them, there shall be no *navāśrāddha*, nor the *saṃskāra* of *sapiṇḍana*; furthermore, even the sixteen *śrāddhas* that have been prescribed do not apply to them.

If one should cast wages into the water, or if the domestic fire at a crossroads should be extinguished, or if one should burn the sacrificial vessels in the fire—these [are the punishments] for a person of evil deeds who maintains the sacred fires.
When a full year has passed for them, O Kāśyapa, compassionate persons should perform this rite, having reached the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) in the bright fortnight.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu and Yama with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and other offerings, one should place ten rice-balls, smeared with ghee and mixed with honey, upon blades of darbha grass.
Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, meditating upon Viṣṇu and Yama, he should silently offer each of those [portions] while facing south.
Having extracted and mixed them, he should afterwards cast them well into the sacred water (tīrtha); while casting them, he should proclaim the name and the lineage (gotra) of the deceased.
Furthermore, one should again worship Viṣṇu and Yama with flowers and sandalwood paste, along with incense, lamps, and food offerings consisting of various kinds of eatables and delicacies.
On that day of fasting, one should invite Brahmins who are endowed with noble lineage, learning, and austerity, and who are possessed of virtuous conduct.
Nine, seven, or five [offerings], according to one's own capacity; on the following day at midday, one should likewise worship Yama and Viṣṇu.
He should properly seat those Brahmins facing north; at the beginning of the invocation, the offering of water (argha), and so forth, he should invoke Viṣṇu together with Yama.
Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, one should perform the rite and proclaim the name of the deceased; remembering the deceased, Yama, and Viṣṇu, one should complete the śrāddha.
One should set aside [rice] from all other portions for the purpose of offering the rice-balls (piṇḍas); or alternatively, one should offer ten separate rice-balls, or five, in due order.
First, one should offer [the food] to Viṣṇu, to Brahmā, and to Śiva; then to Śiva together with his attendants, and fifthly, also to the deceased.
One should remember his name and lineage and proclaim the word "Viṣṇu"; one should offer the fifth piṇḍa preceded by a salutation.

Remembering that deceased person according to his capacity, one should offer gifts of cattle, land, lumps of food, and so forth; and with sesame seeds, one should [offer] sesame seeds into the hands of the Brahmins which are joined with *darbha* grass.
One should give food to the twice-born, as well as betel-leaf and a sacrificial fee; in this manner, one should worship the most eminent Brahmin with a golden coin.

Recalling the name and lineage [of the deceased], he should give [the gift] while saying, "May there be pleasure for Viṣṇu"; then, having followed behind the twice-born, he should turn away from the water, facing south.

Reciting the name and lineage [of the deceased], one should cast [the remainder] on the ground with the words, "May there be satisfaction. Together with friends and kinsmen, one should eat the remainder while remaining restrained in speech. This annual rite and others should be performed according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* (single-offering) ceremony.
When this is done, even those who have committed evil deeds will go to the heavenly world; and once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and other rites have been performed, they truly attain it.

Now, if someone should die through negligence by means of water or other causes, one should perform for him everything according to the prescribed rule, beginning with the rites for the cycle of existence.
Out of negligence or by choice, a mortal should not go face-to-face with a serpent; one should worship the Naga on both fortnights, specifically on the fifth lunar days.
One should fashion an image of the Nāgas out of flour on the ground; one should worship it with white flowers, fragrant scents, and sandalwood paste.
One should offer incense and lamps, scatter white rice grains, and likewise present food made of raw flour as well as milk.
Having approached him, one should speak thus while casting off one's garments and ornaments; on that day, one should eat sweet food and conclude the *deva-śrāddha*.
Then, according to one's means, one should give a golden serpent to an excellent brahmin; having given a cow, one should then say: "May the King of Nagas be pleased."

One should perform the other rites as previously described according to one's capacity; one should carry them out exactly as prescribed by the rules of one’s own Vedic branch. Thus, one should liberate those beings from the state of a preta and lead them onto the path to heaven.

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of What Should and Should Not Be Done, and Ritual Actions, Regarding Death by Unnatural Causes," in the *Pretakalpa* (Section on the Departed) of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa. —
*Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa* 45.

The illustrious Viṣṇu said: "O Lord of Birds, I shall thus describe to you the annual Śrāddha; every year, both the legitimate son and the son born of the wife should perform it according to the Pārvaṇa rite."
The Ekoddiṣṭa rite is performed according to this procedure and by these same [prescribed] rules; it is not the Pārvaṇa rite.

The two sons of a man who died without a sacred fire—the legitimate son and the son born of the wife—shall themselves remain without a sacred fire; they shall not perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite annually, but rather the *pārvaṇa* rite.
But when either the son or the father possesses the sacred fires, the *kṣetraja* and *aurasa* sons should perform the *pārvaṇa* rite there every year.

Whether they are without sacred fires or possess them, whether they be sons or even fathers, some maintain that the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite should be performed by sons on the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*).

For one whose [ancestral] share undergoes depletion at the time of the new moon, or again during the fortnight of the departed (pretapakṣa), the Pārvaṇa rite must be performed every year by all his sons as well.

The *ekoddiṣṭa* rite should be performed for men who have no sons, and likewise for women. In the *ekoddiṣṭa*, as well as in sacrificial rites, *kuśa* grass with roots should be taken; however, at a *śrāddha* for prosperity (*vṛddhi-śrāddha*) or at death, it should always be cut once and stripped of its outer parts.
If impurity (āśauca) should arise when the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha is to be performed, one should indeed perform that Śrāddha immediately upon the cessation of the impurity.
If an obstacle should arise when the Ekoddiṣṭa has arrived, one should indeed perform that Śrāddha on the same lunar day of the following month.

The Śrāddha for a Śūdra, for his wife, for his son, for his daughter, for the twice-born who have not yet undergone initiation, and for a twice-born man who has not yet been initiated, should be performed silently.

If one goes to the slaughterhouse at the same time for many or even for two, one may perform the cooking by way of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*), but one should perform the *śrāddha* offering separately for each.
One should first give [the offering] for the one who died first, then again for the second, and then for the third; this is the rule (the sequence) when there is a concurrence [of deaths].
He who performs this every year in whatever manner possible, remaining unwearied, shall deliver all his ancestors and attain the supreme goal.
If the day of death is not known, as well as the day of departure, but the month is known, then the anniversary of the death should be observed on the new moon day (darśa) of that month.
When the month is not known but the day alone is known, then that day should fall in either the month of Mārgaśīrṣa or Māgha.
When the day and month of death are unknown, however, I have declared that for the purpose of the *śrāddha*, the day and month of departure [from home] should be taken.
Furthermore, when neither the day nor the month of departure is known, the news of death should be accepted according to the previously stated sequence.

Even in the absence of travel, if those two [the anniversary of death and the anniversary of birth] are forgotten, they should still be observed at that time, just as in the case of the monthly death-anniversary rite.
If someone dies in the house while the householder is away on a journey, then at the conclusion of the period of impurity, when the performance of the *śrāddha* rite has commenced;
If the householder returns and learns of what occurred there, then the period of impurity (āśauca) applies to those householders, but it does not apply to the property and such at that time.

A Śrāddha ceremony that has been commenced by a son or others must be completed in its entirety according to the true rule; even in that case, one should avoid accepting a gift during the Śrāddha from afar.
Neither the giver nor the eater is aware of birth-impurity or death-impurity; he never attributes that fault to either of them.
But when either a birth-impurity (sūtaka) or a death-impurity (mṛtaka) is known only to one [party], then the fault belongs solely to the eater; the other, the giver, is not defiled.
He who performs the anniversary of the death day in the manner thus described, even if the day of death is unknown, constantly delivers [the deceased].
Now, in the daily *śrāddha*, having reverently honored the twice-born with perfumes and other offerings, one should properly join them together while designating all the hosts of ancestors.

The invocation, the utterance of *svadhā*, the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*), the ritual of placing food in the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), and so forth; likewise, the observances such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and the Viśvedevas.

In the daily *śrāddha*, one should exclude these [unworthy persons] and prepare food fit for consumption; having given a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, one should dismiss them with salutations.
Whatever food one should give to Brahmins for the sake of the Viśvedevas and other deities, that should be performed like a *nitya-śrāddha*; it is called a *deva-śrāddha*.

The *śrāddha* for the mother should be performed to the east at the beginning of the rite; likewise, the *śrāddha* for the paternal ancestors should be performed similarly. On the following day, during a *vṛddhi* ceremony, the *śrāddha* for the group of maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*) should take place.
One should perform the three types of śrāddha, as well as the Vaiśvadeva according to the Tantric tradition.
One should first prepare for the mothers, immediately after that for the fathers, and likewise offer for the maternal grandfathers; thus indeed is the sequence.
But in the *śrāddha* for one's mother, in the absence of Brahmins, one should invite eight virtuous women of noble birth who are accompanied by their husbands and sons.

One should perform the *iṣṭāpūrta* rites, the *śrāddha*, and likewise the *ābhyudayika* rite; however, on occasions such as portents and the like, one should perform it exactly like the *nitya-śrāddha*.

"By performing the daily (nitya), ancestral (daiva), prosperity-seeking (vṛddhi), optional (kāmya), and occasional (naimittika) śrāddhas according to the prescribed method, one shall attain perfection. Thus has it been told to you, O Tārkṣya; what else do you wish to ask?"

Thus, in the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the second part, the Dharma-kāṇḍa, in the section on the Pretas, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, this is the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Annual and Other Śrāddhas. Tārkṣya said: "By the power of their well-performed deeds, various kinds of heavens belong to men; as do enjoyments, exquisite beauty, strength, intelligence, and prowess."
O Lord, truth indeed arises for the meritorious both in this world and the next; truth, truth, and again truth—this is the word of the Vedas, and it is not otherwise.
Dharma triumphs, not adharma; truth triumphs, not falsehood; patience triumphs, not anger; Viṣṇu triumphs, not the asura.
In the same way, truth has been known by me: from good deeds, excellence arises; for where merit is most excellent, there the person is likewise more excellent.
In this way, I wish to hear how sinners are born, by what ripening of karma, and how they come to be subject to their respective destinies.
O best of gods, tell me in brief, as I desire to know, whatever womb one enters and in what form one is born.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O Tārkṣya, men in this world, having experienced the enjoyments resulting from their auspicious and inauspicious deeds, are born with certain characteristics; hear those from me, O Kāśyapa."
The teacher is the ruler of those who possess self-control; the king is the ruler of the wicked; but for those who commit secret sins in this world, Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is the ruler.
Those who have not performed the prescribed penances and are thus released from the various torments of the world of Yama proceed to the continuum of individual existence.
Having returned to human existence, they bear the marks of their evil deeds; O best of birds, I shall describe those marks to you.
Having endured all the torments and gone to the abode of Vaivasvata, those who have crossed over the torments return to the world marked by their signs.
One who speaks falsely becomes stammering; one who lies regarding a cow becomes mute; a killer of a Brahmin is born with leprosy, and a drinker of liquor has black teeth.

One who steals gold becomes one with deformed nails; one who violates the teacher’s bed becomes one with a skin disease; one who associates with the low-born becomes born of a base womb; and one who fails to give gifts becomes poor.

A twice-born man who officiates at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice goes to the state of a crocodile or a pig; one who performs many sacrifices becomes a donkey, and from eating without sacred mantras, he becomes a crow.
Those who consume without investigation are like tigers in the lonely forest; a cat is a constant threatener, a firefly is a burner of the undergrowth.
He who gives knowledge for the sake of a bowl shall become a bullock; he who gives stale food to a Brahmin shall become a dog.
One who steals a book out of stinginess will be born blind from birth; for one who steals fruits, a child dies—of this there is no doubt.
Upon death, he goes to the state of a monkey; his face becomes like a cheek with a goitre. If he eats food without having given it away, he shall be childless.
One who steals clothing becomes a lizard; one who administers poison becomes a wind-eater (a snake); and by abandoning the life of a wandering mendicant, O King, one becomes a desert-dwelling piśāca.
By stealing water one becomes a cātaka bird; by stealing grain, a mouse; and by consorting with a girl who has not reached puberty, one becomes a serpent—so says the sacred tradition.
One who lusts after the wife of his guru will certainly become a chameleon; and a man who breaks a flowing spring of water shall become a fish.
By selling what should not be sold, a man becomes a crane or a vulture; by approaching women through improper channels, he becomes a wolf, and by cheating in trade, an owl.
One who eats at the eleventh-day rite for the deceased is reborn as a crow; one who, having promised wealth to the twice-born, does not give it, becomes a jackal.
One who goes to the king's enemy becomes a fanged beast; a thief becomes a dog; a seller of *śārivā* fruit becomes a boar; and one who is the husband of a low-caste woman becomes a bull.
A cat that touches fire with its paw becomes diseased and a consumer of the flesh of others; from approaching a woman in her courses, one becomes impotent, foul-smelling, and a thief of fragrances.
Whether it be this or that, whether little or much, whoever steals what belongs to another will, having stolen it, certainly enter the womb of an animal; of this there is no doubt.
O Lord of Birds, these and other such signs, which are indeed the expansions of one's own karma,
are seen by those human beings.
Thus, having experienced the hells in succession for their evil deeds, one is born by the remainder of that karma into these aforementioned wombs.
Then, O Kāśyapa, for a hundred births among all beings in the mortal world, one is born; of this there is no doubt when the wholesome and the unwholesome have been equalized.
When the semen and blood of a woman and a man have conjoined, the being composed of the five elements is born, endowed with the five gross elements.
The sense organs, the mind, the vital breaths, knowledge, lifespan, happiness, fortitude, retention, impulse, suffering, and indeed false egoism—these are [the effects].
But for that self, which is beginningless and yet desires a beginning for itself, this entire world—consisting of form, color, passion, hatred, existence, and non-existence—is [the result].
Then, for one bound by their own karma, there shall be growth within the womb; indeed, this is the characteristic of a living being as previously described by me to you.
O Tārkṣya, when the wheel has thus been set in motion within the fourfold collection of beings, the birth and destruction of embodied beings come to pass.
O bird, for all castes, upward movement occurs through one's own duty alone, while downward movement occurs through unrighteousness; this arises from deviating from one's own duty.
O Vainateya, whatever actions such as giving and enjoying are seen in the states of divinity and humanity, all that is the fruit born of karma.
One will surely fall again into a terrible, inauspicious hell, earned through desire and anger and not ordained by one's karma; for that person, no crossing back out exists.

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Auspicious and Inauspicious Destinies of the Soul," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
In the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, Chapter 47:
Garuḍa said: "O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, please speak out of your supreme compassion regarding the gift, the greatness of giving, and the dimensions of the Vaitaraṇī river."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: That great river named Vaitaraṇī on the path of Yama is bottomless and difficult for sinners to cross; it is terrifying as soon as it is seen.
Abounding with water of pus and blood, and filled with the mud of flesh, it is overwhelmed by various terrors upon seeing the sinners who have arrived there.
The water boils quickly within the vessel like clarified butter; it is filled with pus teeming with worms and covered by those with adamantine beaks.
And with crocodiles and sea-monsters equipped with diamond-like saws, as well as other predatory aquatic creatures capable of tearing through flesh.
For at the end of the dissolution, those twelve suns indeed rise up; there, mortals who are evildoers suffer while crying out.
Crying out repeatedly, "Alas, brother! Son! Father!", living beings wander about, sink down, and fall into exhaustion.
The great river is seen to be filled with four kinds of living beings; those who give gifts of cows cross over it, while others fall into it.
Those fools who despise me, as well as their teachers, gurus, elders, and others—their dwelling shall indeed be there.
Those fools who abandon a devoted wife of virtuous character, who is wedded to them and steadfast in her duties—their dwelling shall be eternal [in hell].

Indeed, having committed the murder of those who have placed their trust in them—such as masters, friends, ascetics, women, children, the infirm, and others—the sinners fall there and are cooked in its midst while crying out in agony.
He who approaches to obstruct a peaceful Brahmin who is hungry shall be devoured by worms there until the dissolution of all beings.
If one has promised wealth to a Brahmin and does not give it, yet, when summoned, says "it does not exist," his residence shall indeed be there [in hell].
The arsonist, the poisoner, the false witness, the drinker of intoxicants, the destroyer of sacrifices, the one who approaches the king's wife, and the slanderer;
One who interrupts a conversation, one who seizes what has been given by oneself, one who destroys the boundaries of fields, and one who violates another's wife;
A Brāhmaṇa who sells liquids, as well as one who is the husband of a Vṛṣalī, and he who causes the breach of a pond for thirsty cattle;
A girl who defiles herself, one who regrets having given a gift, a Śūdra who drinks the milk of a Kapilā cow, and a Brāhmaṇa who eats meat; [these five are equal to those who drink liquor].
These dwell there constantly; do not entertain any doubt about this anywhere. O bird, only a miserable, atheistic, and base person would dwell in that place.
One who is always resentful, always angry, who treats his own words as the ultimate authority, and who constantly destroys the speech of others, shall dwell for a long time in the Vaitaraṇī hell.
But he who possesses egoism, the sinful one who engages in self-glorification, the ungrateful, and the one who causes distress to the fetus—he sinks into the Vaitaraṇī river.
If, by some stroke of fortune, a desire to cross over should ever arise in you, listen, O Kāśyapa, to that which would make it favorable.
During the solstices, the equinoxes, auspicious conjunctions (vyatīpāta), at the break of day, during lunar or solar eclipses, at the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), or on the new moon day.
On other auspicious occasions, the highest gift is bestowed; at those times, the faithful are indeed constant in their practice of giving.
That indeed should be the time for giving, since prosperity is unstable; bodies are impermanent, and wealth is by no means eternal.
Death is ever-present; therefore, one should practice the accumulation of dharma. One should also prepare the auspicious Vaitaraṇī river, either black or pale-red in color.
[One should give] a cow with golden horns and silver hooves, accompanied by a bronze milking vessel, covered with a pair of black cloths, and provided with the seven types of grain.

One should fashion a golden image of Yama seated upon a heap of one *droṇa* of cotton, holding a copper vessel and equipped with an iron staff; having constructed a raft made of sugarcane stalks, it should be fastened with very firm bonds.
Having placed that cow, born from the body of the Sun, upon a raft, the Brahmin should provide it with an umbrella and sandals.
One should present the ring and garments to a Brāhmaṇa; having taken up kuśa grass with water, one should recite this mantra:
Having heard of that Vaitaraṇī at the most terrible gate of Yama, and desiring to cross it, I give this to you; homage to Vaitaraṇī!
May cows be before me; may cows be at my side; may cows be in my heart; I dwell in the midst of cows.
O Viṣṇu-form, best of the twice-born, O protector of the earth, deliver me! This dakṣiṇā has been given by me to you; salutations to Vaitaraṇī.
Having circumambulated Dharmarāja, the Lord of All, and the cow named Vaitaraṇī, one should present everything to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having grasped the tail of the cow and placed the brahmin at its head, [one should say]: "O little cow, wait for me at the gate of Yama, which is full of great terror."
O Goddess of gods, salutations to you, Vaitaraṇī, for the sake of deliverance! One should follow him as he goes and lead him entirely to his home.
O Vainateya, when this is done, that river becomes "Sutara" (Easy to Cross); and whatever man on earth should give [this gift], he shall obtain all his desires.
By the power of well-performed deeds, there is happiness both here and in the next world; it is a thousandfold when one is healthy, and a hundredfold when one is afflicted.

But that gift which is given for one who has already died is considered equal to giving in their absence; therefore, it should be given with one's own hand, for when one is dead, who will give to whom?
Those devoid of the virtue of generosity live as miserable wretches; therefore, with this unstable body, one should perform stable deeds.
The vital breaths will certainly depart, like wandering guests.

Thus, O King of Birds, this entire mockery of the multitude of living beings has been described to you. Therefore, for the sake of the liberation of the deceased and for the welfare and auspiciousness of the world, one should perform the funeral rites and live for the benefit of others.
Sūta said: Thus instructed by the powerful Viṣṇu, O Brahmins, Garuḍa attained great satisfaction upon hearing the account of the deceased man's conduct.
Having meditated in his mind upon the Lord of All, the cause of all causes, he again questioned Keśava regarding everything, including vows, sacred fords, and other such matters.
The sages [know] all this regarding living beings—their origin and so forth, as well as death, birth, the state of being a preta, and the funeral rites for the deceased.

I have indeed declared the cause for liberation in its entirety: "Blessed are they, victorious are they; whence can there be defeat for those in whose hearts Janārdana, dark as a blue lotus, resides?"
Dharma triumphs, not adharma; truth triumphs, not falsehood; forbearance triumphs, not anger; Viṣṇu triumphs, not the asuras.
Viṣṇu is the mother, Viṣṇu is the father, and Viṣṇu is one's own kinsmen and relatives; for those whose intellect is firmly fixed upon Him, there shall be no miserable rebirth.
Auspicious is the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu; auspicious is he whose banner bears Garuḍa; auspicious is the lotus-eyed one; Hari is the abode of auspiciousness.
Hari is the Bhāgīrathī, O brahmins; the Bhāgīrathī is Hari; the Bhāgīrathī, Hari, and the brahmins—this is the essence within the three worlds.
Having drunk this nectar of speech belonging to Viṣṇu, which issued from the mouth of the Sūta and was adorned with the meaning of all the scriptures, the sages attained great satisfaction.
Thus the sages, headed by Śaunaka, praised one another and the charioteer who perceives all matters; they attained incomparable joy.
Whether impure or pure, or even having reached every possible state of existence, whoever remembers the lotus-eyed Lord becomes pure both externally and internally.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Ripening of Karma and Other Matters," in the second section (Uttarakhaṇḍa) of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa concerning the vision of the deceased and the nature of dharma.
In the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*—Chapter 48:

Tārkṣya said: "Those mortals who dwell in the world of men all go to their death in every caste at their own appointed time, according to the measure of their own merit. Tell me, O Lord, how this is so."

They travel along a path most difficult to traverse, established upon a track fashioned by the Creator; by what merit alone do they attain joy, and by what alone do they maintain their lineage, strength, and vitality?

Sūta said: Then, having heard this, the Lord remembered his own form and the terrifying nature of his deeds, and spoke to Garuḍa: "He by whom the earth was created, along with the world of moving and unmoving beings; he by whom the all-pervading Yama was ordained as the punisher."

The Blessed One said: Having entered that other second path leading to Yama, which consists of the long-term accumulation of dharma, artha, kāma, and liberation, and having reached his own body there—[which is] indeed like the size of a thumb—is he [then] in his own abode?

O twice-born one, having taken up the noose and being established in a body within this most meritorious region, he weeps again and again; yet, due to delusion, he does not perform the worship of the Lord of Gods nor the satiation of the ancestors and deities, nor does he seek the continuity of his lineage through sons.

I have no kinsman who travels the path of Yama, nor do I have any need for the acquisition of a Brahmin’s body. Having attained the state of a Brahmin, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain, I have not studied the Vedas, Purāṇas, or Saṃhitās. A precious jewel has been lost from my hand; rescue it from wherever it has gone, for you must fulfill what was done by you.

That Kṣatriya who, in battle, drank blood from his own forehead with his own arms—that indeed constitutes the drinking of Soma at the great sacrifice; though he is as good as dead, he goes to liberation while still alive.
Many positions have been taken and many drinks have been consumed, both of which are censured; yet he who, taking up a weapon, goes face-to-face against his enemies in battle, is liberated from sin.

Whether one belongs to the lineage of the Kṣatriyas, the Vaiśyas, or even the low-caste Śūdras; whether one is a slayer of those engaged in battle, of gods, of brahmins, or of children; or a killer of women, the elderly, or of the wretched and ascetics.

If one turns his back when these are in distress, all the gods turn their backs upon him; his ancestors do not drink the water with sesame seeds, nor does the consumer of oblations accept that which was offered.

O Lord of Birds, when battle has arrived, he who takes up a weapon and faces the enemy army out of hatred or fear, yet does not advance—his kṣatriya strength has likewise departed; whereas he who gives this earth and gold to a brahmin becomes great once again in this world.

He gave gifts during eclipses, always performed ritual bathing at excellent holy sites, and having gone to Gayā, he constantly offered funeral cakes (piṇḍas) for his ancestors; such a person who dies in battle [attains liberation].

I, who lament upon the field of battle when abandoning the body of a Kṣatriya, or at the slaughter of my master, or during the seizure of cattle, or at the killing of women and children, or for the sake of a caravan on the road—by me neither my own treasury has been struck nor has it been cast down.

Then the Vaiśya lamented over his own duties: "Bound by the noose, I have not even accumulated [wealth]; out of delusion and for the sake of my family, I did not speak the truth in buying and selling."

Having attained a Śūdra body, you never performed glorious acts such as giving gifts to the twice-born or honoring the twice-born; you never constructed a reservoir of water upon the earth, nor did you consecrate an eminent Brāhmaṇa who had not yet been consecrated.

Abandoning my own duties due to intoxication, I remained complacent; I did not cast off my body at a sacred ford, nor was dharma strengthened by me, nor was worship of the gods performed for the sake of liberation.

Having likewise attained a body born of a physical aggregate, they enter bodies composed of air—whether belonging to those known as the castes or the outcaste barbarians—desiring these while on the path crowded with dharma.
While traveling on the path, each having achieved his own goal that cuts through the dharma of others, listen to those words of the Lord of Birds which he speaks so charmingly.

For the three worlds are indeed the essence among all worlds; Jambudvīpa is the essence among all continents; the land of the gods is the essence among all lands; and the human being alone is the essence among all living beings.

In this world, the four castes are praised, and among the castes, those men who are most righteous are praised; by means of dharma one attains all happiness, and standing upon the great path, one acquires knowledge.
When my life has ended and I have abandoned this body, O bird, I shall exist as a worm or an insect; I shall be fashioned as a reptile, a mosquito, a quadruped, or a wild boar.

For while still situated in the womb, one knows everything; yet once born, one may immediately forget both this and that which was thought while in the womb, as one passes from infancy through youth to old age.

If that which was conceived in the womb is lost through delusion, and is remembered again once the body has passed away; when that [body] has perished, what was conceived in the heart is gone, yet it is remembered again once the body has entered the womb.

When that [thought] had vanished from my heart, I reflected again: "I have practiced deception against others in my own treasury; I have protected my body by transgressing righteousness through gambling, trickery, and even the practice of theft."

Wealth was acquired by me with great hardship, yet I did not personally enjoy the riches I desired; instead, I gave betel, food, sweets, and products of the cow to the fire-god, the deities, guests, and my circle of kinsmen.

O embodied one, even during an eclipse of the moon or at the conjunction of the sun, you have never visited this most excellent and supreme sacred ford; now, rescue your own treasury which has been filled with filth and urine—whatever was done by you!

I have neither seen, nor bowed to, nor worshipped the form of the Three-Strider standing here upon this earth; nor has Prabhāsanātha been praised with devotion anywhere, O embodied one—consider what you have done!

Having gone to the most excellent places on earth near sacred fords, I did not place wealth in the hands of the learned; nor, having bathed my body according to the rules before a brahmin preceptor, have I ever offered even a morsel of food—so cross over whatever you have done.

There is no worship of the Mother, nor Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara, nor Gaṇeśa and Caṇḍī, nor even the Sun; yet, by means of services, offerings, and sandalwood paste, you somehow cross over that which was done by you.

O King, out of delusion I have lost all this which was like the status of a god among men; that person of utterly deluded intellect does not perceive his destination. O embodied one, cross over wherever you have been led by your own actions.
Having reflected in their minds upon these words, which bring about dharma, wealth, and fame, those who dwell in a noble land and delight in dharma attain liberation in the world of men.

While being struck by the hosts of Yama’s messengers who speak thus and by mallets made of Time itself, he indeed remembers, "Alas, Fate! Alas, Fate!", that wealth which he himself earned but never gave away.

Neither the gift of land, nor the gift of cows, nor the gift of water, nor the gift of clothing; not even the fruit, betel, or ointment—none of these were given by you on this earth. Why, then, do you grieve?
Your father is dead, as is your grandfather—he who once held you within his own womb; all those kinsmen are dead as well, yet you have seen all of this while still alive.

Your treasury has been consumed by fire, and the accumulation of wealth and grain has been seized by your sons; only that which was done—the collection of well-spoken words and the Dharma—will follow after you.

No one at all is seen who has returned from death—neither a king, nor an ascetic, nor even a preeminent brahmin; for whatever mortal on this earth was reckless enough to die, he has met his destruction.

Thus those hosts, including the kinnaras, spoke, having summoned their courage though filled with grief; and hearing the most wonderful words of the hosts, he who had attained human form replied, O Lord of Birds:

By the power of generosity, Dharma is established as his celestial chariot; his father is compassion for his mother; his wife is Speech, who speaks words of sweet meaning; his bath is at a sacred ford; and his circle of kinsmen is excellent.

Whatever merit has been offered by the hand, all that shall then become heaven for you; he who possesses dharma will attain supreme happiness, while the sinner shall experience every kind of manifold suffering.

That man who is virtuous in conduct, who has conquered pride and anger, who is disciplined by knowledge, who does not harm others, who is content with his own wife and stays far from the wives of others—he indeed is not merely worthy of veneration on earth.

The giver of sweet food, one who has maintained the agnihotra sacrifice, a knower of Vedānta, one who lives for a thousand moons, one who fasts for a month, and a devoted wife—these six are worthy of my salutation in the world of the living.

A man endowed with such conduct likewise constructs a well with a water-wheel, a reservoir filled with water, a charitable water-station, or a temple for the heart-god; indeed, that man has performed the highest dharma.

A year’s worth of food was given to one learned in the Vedas, and the marriage of a daughter was performed for a twice-born man to release him from debt; even well-tilled land was given to alleviate his thirst—thus, all this constitutes my accumulated merit.

He who hears or even sings this chapter, which is the essence of meritorious deeds, with purity of heart—he is indeed of noble birth, he is endowed with dharma, and he shall surely go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Dharma and Adharma that Bring about Happiness and Suffering for Human Beings," in the *Pretakalpa* section of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī-Gāruḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa. —
*Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa* 49.
Garuḍa said: "O ocean of compassion, I have heard from you how the cycle of worldly existence for living beings arises from ignorance; now I wish to hear the eternal means for liberation."
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, compassionate toward those who have come for refuge, [I am lost] in this essence-less, terrible saṃsāra, defiled by all manner of suffering.
Infinite multitudes of living beings, residing in various kinds of bodies, are born and die; there is no end to them.
They are always afflicted by suffering; no friend is found anywhere. O Lord of Liberation, tell me, O Master, by what means are they liberated?
The Blessed Lord said: Listen, O Tārkṣya, I shall declare that which you ask me of; by the mere hearing of which a person is liberated from saṃsāra.
There exists the Lord Śiva, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman; he is partless, omniscient, the creator of all, the sovereign of all, stainless, and non-dual.

Self-luminous, without beginning or end, changeless, higher than the highest, devoid of qualities, and consisting of existence-consciousness-bliss—His portions are known as the individual souls (jīvas).
Afflicted by beginningless ignorance, like sparks in a fire, they are divided from their source by the limiting adjuncts of the body and so forth, through beginningless karmas.
Restrained by merits and demerits which bestow pleasure and pain, they obtain a body, lifespan, and experience born of karma, endowed with various corresponding species.
O bird, even for them, that supreme [state] along with the subtle liṅga-body persists through every birth until liberation, being imperishable.
Immovable beings, worms, goats, birds, cattle, trees, the righteous gods, and likewise those seeking liberation, follow this sequence respectively.
Having assumed and cast off thousands of fourfold bodies, if one becomes wise after being born anew from good deeds, one shall attain liberation.
Among the eighty-four hundred thousand bodies of embodied beings, the knowledge of reality is not obtained elsewhere except in a human body.
In this world, even after thousands or tens of millions of births, a living being may at some point obtain a human birth through the accumulation of merit.
Having attained this human birth, which is difficult to find and serves as a staircase to liberation, who in this world is more sinful than he who does not deliver himself?
That man who, having obtained this birth and having acquired the excellence of the senses, does not know what is beneficial for the self—he would be a slayer of Brahman.
No human goal exists for anyone without a body; therefore, one should protect the body and wealth and accomplish meritorious deeds.
One should always protect oneself, for the self is the vessel of everything; one should apply effort toward its protection, for while living, one beholds auspicious things.
Again there is a village, again a field, again wealth, again a house; again there is wholesome and unwholesome karma, but the body is not [reborn] again and again.
The wise always employ means for the protection of the body; moreover, even those afflicted by leprosy and other diseases do not desire its abandonment.
That [wealth] should be protected for the sake of Dharma; Dharma is for the sake of knowledge alone; and knowledge is for the sake of the yoga of meditation, through which one is swiftly liberated.
If the self itself does not restrain itself from harmful things, what other benefactor is there who will bring happiness to the self?
He who does not seek treatment for the disease of hell while still here—once he has gone to that place where there is no medicine, what will he do when afflicted by disease?
Old age approaches like a tigress, life passes away like water from a broken jar, and diseases strike like enemies; therefore, one should practice what is truly beneficial.
As long as one does not experience suffering, as long as calamities do not arrive, and as long as there is no impairment of the senses, so long should one practice for the highest good.
As long as this body remains, one should practice the reality; it is like a fool digging a well while his house is already ablaze.
Time is not perceived due to the various activities arising from saṃsāra; alas, people do not understand pleasure, pain, or what is truly beneficial for themselves.
Seeing those born afflicted, those dead, and those fallen into calamity—all suffering—the world, having drunk the wine of delusion, never feels fear.
Prosperity is like a dream, youth is like a flower, and life is as flickering as lightning; for one who understands this, how could there be any steadfastness?

A hundred-year lifespan is exceedingly short; half of that is spent in sleep and laziness. What remains is diminished by the sufferings of childhood, illness, and old age—and even that which is left is fruitless.
Alas, what man is not destroyed—he who is devoid of effort when he ought to begin a task, who is fast asleep when he ought to be awake, and who is full of confidence in a place of danger?
When the body, which resembles the foam of water, is occupied by the life-force and remains as a transient abode of suffering, how can one dwell therein without fear?

He who perceives what is harmful as beneficial, who perceives the unstable as stable, and who perceives what is disadvantageous as advantageous—he is one who does not understand his own true interest.
Though seeing, one stumbles; though hearing, one does not understand; though reciting, one does not know—deluded by the illusion of the gods.
As this world sinks into the deep ocean of time, no one at all perceives it being seized by the crocodiles of death, disease, and old age.
Time, which brings fear at every moment, is not perceived as it wanes; like a raw clay pot submerged in water, it is not noticed until it has shattered.
It is as reasonable to attempt to wrap the wind or to break the sky, as it is to tie together waves or to place one's trust in life.
By that [fire] by which the earth is consumed and even Mount Meru is shattered, and the waters of the ocean are dried up—what need is there to speak of the body?
"Offspring are mine, my wife is mine, wealth is mine, and my kinsmen are mine"—while the mortal-born one prattles thus, the wolf of Time forcibly slays him.
"This has been done, this is to be done, and this other is half-done"—thus, joined with such striving, Kṛtānta brings one under his control.
One should do tomorrow's work today, and the afternoon's work in the forenoon; for death does not wait to see whether a task has been done or left undone.
Why does he not see a savior—one who has been shown the path by old age, whose soldiers are fierce diseases, and who is presided over by the enemy Death?
Pierced by the needle of craving, sprinkled with the ghee of sense objects, and cooked in the fire of passion and hatred, Death devours the human being.
Death enters all—those who are children, those established in youth, the elderly, and even those still in the womb; such is the nature of this world.
This living being goes even to the abode of Yama, leaving behind its own body; for what reason, then, should there be attachment to relationships such as wife, mother, father, or son?
For cyclic existence is the root of suffering; whoever possesses it is miserable. He by whom its abandonment has been accomplished is happy, and no one else anywhere.
One should abandon saṃsāra in an instant—it is the source of all sufferings, the abode of all calamities, and the refuge of all evils.
A man bound by fetters made of iron or wood may be released; but one bound by the fetters consisting of son and wife is never released.
As many dear relationships as a living being forms with the mind, so many spikes of sorrow are driven into his heart.
The world has been constantly ruined by those who have stolen all its wealth—the thieves of the senses dwelling within the body that feast upon the objects of the senses; alas, what a tragedy!
Just as a fish greedy for flesh does not see the iron hook, so too the embodied being greedy for pleasure does not see the affliction of Yama.
O Bird, those men who do not distinguish between the beneficial and the harmful, who constantly follow the wrong path, and whose sole purpose is the filling of their bellies, are destined for hell.
Sleep, fear, sexual intercourse, and food are common to all living beings; the human being who possesses knowledge is so called, while one devoid of knowledge is considered a beast.
At dawn, foolish men are afflicted by excrement and urine; at midday, by hunger and thirst; and at night, by lust and sleep.
All living beings are intent upon their own bodies, wealth, wives, and so forth; they are born and they die—alas, woe! deluded by ignorance.
Therefore, attachment should always be abandoned; if it cannot be abandoned, one should associate with the great, for the virtuous are the remedy for attachment.
He who possesses neither the company of the virtuous nor discernment—those two stainless eyes—is blind; how could such a man not stray from the path?
All human beings devoted solely to the conduct of their own respective castes and stages of life do not know the supreme Dharma; these hypocrites perish in vain.
Why do some people, devoted to exertion and engaged in the practice of vows and other observances, wander about as itinerant teachers while their very selves are shrouded in ignorance?
Men who are satisfied with mere names and devoted to the ritualistic section (karmakāṇḍa) are deluded by the recitation of mantras, fire offerings (homa), and the extensive performance of sacrifices.
Deluded and bewildered by my māyā, fools desire that which is beyond perception through restrictive practices such as eating once a day or fasting, which merely wither the body.
What liberation can there be for the undiscriminating merely through the punishment of the body? Does a great serpent die simply from being struck by an anthill?
Bearing masses of matted hair and deer skins, these hypocrites merely wearing outward appearances wander through the world like men of wisdom, leading others astray as well.
One should abandon like an outcaste that person who is attached to the pleasures born of saṃsāra, who claims "I am a knower of Brahman," and who has fallen away from both ritual action and Brahman.
In this world, donkeys and other such animals roam about naked and devoid of shame, treating their homes as if they were forests; do they therefore become dispassionate?
If human beings were liberated merely by smearing themselves with clay and ashes, then would a dog that constantly dwells in clay and ashes ever become liberated?
Subsisting on grass, leaves, and water, constantly dwelling in the forest—do jackals, rats, deer, and the like become ascetics by such means?
From birth until the end of death, do those dwelling on the banks of rivers such as the Gaṅgā—beginning with frogs and fish—become yogins?
Pigeons that feed on stones and even cātakas never drink water from the earth; do they, therefore, become observers of religious vows?
Therefore, O Lord of Birds, obligatory and other such rituals merely serve to please the world; the direct cause of liberation is the knowledge of reality.
O Bird, like animals fallen into a vast well of ignorance, those bound by the fetters of the individual soul do not know the ultimate reality.
Carried hither and thither by the deep oceans of the Vedic scriptures, the false logicians remain indeed swallowed by the suppression of the six waves.
He who knows the Vedas, Agamas, and Puranas, yet does not know the ultimate truth—for such a person, all that is merely the cawing of a crow, a mere mockery.
Agitated by the thought, "This is knowledge, this is the object of knowledge," they study the scriptures day and night, while turning their backs on the supreme reality.
Bound by the composition of sentences and meters, adorned with poetic ornaments, these deluded ones remain with their senses agitated, suffering through their anxieties.
People suffer because they conceive of the supreme reality in one way, while the true nature of the scriptures is otherwise; and they provide explanations in yet another way.
Some speak of the state of being a young sage, yet they do not experience it themselves; they are devoid of self-awareness, as if lacking any instruction.
They recite the Vedas and Shastras and instruct one another, yet they do not know the supreme reality, just as a ladle does not know the flavor of the food it stirs.
The head bears flowers; the nose perceives fragrance; people recite the Vedas and Shastras; but one who awakens the true nature of reality is rare to find.
Not knowing the Reality that resides within oneself, the fool is deluded by the scriptures; like a dull-witted cowherd who, while a goat is right in his armpit, looks for it in a well.
Verbal cognition is indeed not capable of destroying the delusion of saṃsāra; for darkness can never be dispelled by the mere mention of a lamp.
The recitation of one devoid of wisdom is like a mirror for the blind; therefore, the scripture of those possessed of wisdom is the defining characteristic of the knowledge of reality.
"This is knowledge, this is the object of knowledge"—desiring to hear all of this, one does not reach the end of the treatise even after a thousand divine years.
There are many treatises and millions of obstacles to a short life; therefore, one should discern the essence from them, just as a swan extracts milk from water.
Having studied the Vedic scriptures and understood their essential truth, the wise man should discard all the scriptures, just as one seeking grain discards the straw.
Just as one who is satiated by nectar has no need for food, so too, O Tārkṣya, one who knows reality has no need for scripture.
Liberation does not come from the study of the Vedas, nor even from the recitation of the Shastras; for absolute isolation comes only from knowledge, and not otherwise, O son of Vinata.
The stage of life is not the cause of liberation, nor are the philosophical systems the cause; likewise, all ritual actions are not the cause—knowledge alone is indeed the cause.
The singular word of the Guru bestows liberation; all other sciences are mere mockery. Indeed, amidst thousands of burdensome treatises, this alone is the supreme life-giver.
For non-duality is declared to be auspicious and devoid of ritual action; it is obtained through the mouth of the Guru, not by those who have studied millions of scriptures.

They declare that knowledge is twofold: that which arises from scripture and that which arises from discernment. The Brahman of sound consists of scripture; the Supreme Brahman is born of discernment.
Some desire non-duality, while others desire duality; they do not know the reality that is equal and devoid of both duality and non-duality.
There are two words for bondage and liberation: "mine" and "not mine. By "mine" a living being is bound; by "not mine" one is liberated.
That action which does not lead to bondage is ignorance, while that which bestows liberation is knowledge; other action leads to weariness, whereas other knowledge is skill in the arts.
As long as karmas burn, as long as the latent impressions of saṃsāra persist, and as long as the senses remain restless, how can there be talk of reality?

As long as there is identification with the body, as long as there is the sense of "mine," as long as there is the momentum of effort, and as long as there is the conceptualization of mental constructs;
As long as there is no steadiness of mind, as long as there is no reflection upon the scriptures, and as long as there is no compassion from the guru, how can there be discourse on reality?

Austerity, vows, pilgrimage, recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth, as well as the discourses of the Vedas, Shastras, and Agamas—all these persist only so long as one does not find the ultimate reality.
Therefore, O Tārkṣya, if one desires liberation for oneself, one should at all times and in all circumstances remain devoted to reality with every effort.

One who is scorched by the three types of suffering and other afflictions should take refuge in the shade of the tree of liberation, which bears the flowers of knowledge of the Dharma and the fruits of heaven and liberation.
Therefore, the reality of the Self should be understood through knowledge from the mouth of a venerable guru; by this, a living being is easily liberated from the terrible bondage of saṃsāra.
Listen now as I shall tell you the final duty of one who knows reality, by which one attains liberation known as Brahman-nirvāṇa.
But when the end of life has arrived, a man who is free from fear should sever with the weapon of non-attachment both his longing for the body and whatever desire he has for that [body].
The wise man, having gone forth from the home and bathed in the waters of sacred fords, sits in a pure and secluded place upon a seat prepared according to the rules.
One should practice with the mind the pure, threefold, supreme, imperishable Brahman; having conquered the breath, one should restrain the mind while not forgetting the seed-syllable of Brahman.

The charioteer, which is the intellect (buddhi), should restrain the senses from their objects by means of the mind; and one should indeed hold the mind—which has been drawn away by actions—toward the auspicious goal by means of discernment (dhī).
"I am Brahman, the supreme abode; I am Brahman, the highest state. Having thus perceived the Self, one should establish it within the Self, which is partless.
Uttering the single syllable "Om," which is Brahman, and remembering Me, he who departs, casting off the body, attains the supreme goal.
I shall describe to you that destination which those of pure intellect attain—a destination where hypocrites, devoid of knowledge and dispassion, do not go.

Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, ever established in the inner self, with desires turned away, and liberated from the dualities known as pleasure and pain, the undeluded go to that imperishable state.
He who bathes in the mental sacred ford—the lake of knowledge with truth as its water, which removes the impurities of passion and hatred—shall indeed attain liberation.
Resorting to mature dispassion and devoted to me alone, with a perfected vision and a tranquil soul, he indeed shall attain liberation.
Having abandoned his home, he who dwells at a sacred ford (tīrtha) with a longing for death shall attain liberation if he dies in those fields of liberation.
Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā, Kāśī, Kāñcī, Avantikā, and the city of Dvāravatī—these seven are to be known as the bestowers of liberation.
Thus, O Tārkṣya, I have declared to you the eternal dharma of liberation; by hearing this, which is accompanied by knowledge and dispassion, one may attain liberation.
Those who know reality and are righteous go to liberation; men [who are virtuous] go to the heavenly realm; sinners go to miserable states; and birds and other creatures transmigrate.
Sūta said: Having thus heard from the mouth of the Blessed One the final conclusion regarding his own question, Tārkṣya, his body thrilled with joy, bowed down to the Lord of the World.
"My great doubt has been dispelled by the illumination of your words. Having said this and taken leave of Viṣṇu, he went to the hermitage of Kaśyapa.
Just as one goes to another body immediately, or as one goes with delay—there is likewise no contradiction for you between these two cases.
O dear one, he related everything exactly as it was heard from the Blessed One; even Mārīca attained joy upon hearing the words of the Lord of Ramā.
O Brahmins, your doubt has been dispelled by me; I have related this most wonderful Purāṇa known as Suparṇa.
Hari received this from Tārkṣya, Tārkṣya from him, and from him Bhṛgu; Vasiṣṭha obtained it from Bhṛgu, and from him again Vāmadeva.
From him Parāśara Muni obtained it, from him Vyāsa, and from him indeed I have received it; by me, however, this supreme secret of Hari has been proclaimed to you.
Whatever mortal hears this, or whoever recites it, shall attain happiness everywhere, both in this world and in the next.
Whatever suffering has been described here regarding one traveling to Saṃyamanī, by hearing this, merit arises, and from that, one becomes liberated.
Furthermore, because hearing about the ripening of karma and other such matters described herein brings about dispassion in men, it is indeed to be heard.

Worship this Kṛṣṇa, the lord of sages, who has conquered his senses; from whom, alas, there has arisen a stream of the essence of nectar—speech, by drinking even a single drop of whose color and form with the ladle of the ears, one may attain identity with the Self.
Vyāsa said: Having drunk this nectar of speech pertaining to Viṣṇu, which issued from the mouth of Sūta and was adorned with the meaning of all the scriptures, the sages attained great satisfaction.
Thus the sages, headed by Śaunaka, praised one another and the charioteer who perceives all matters; they attained incomparable joy.
Having heard these words of Hari spoken through the voice of the Sūta, which dispelled the doubts of the Lord of Birds, that sage, Śaunaka, considered himself even more highly honored.
Then those sages repeatedly honored the Sūta with shouts of joy, exclaiming, "O Sūta, you are blessed here! And when the sacrifice had concluded, they sent him on his way.
The Gāruḍa Purāṇa is meritorious, purifying, and destructive of sins.
For those who listen, that which is worthy of being heard always fulfills their desires.
Having heard [the scripture], all gifts, including the previously mentioned bedding and so forth, should be given to the reciter; otherwise, it will not be fruitful.
One should first worship the Purāṇa, and immediately thereafter the reciter with due respect, by means of gifts of clothing, ornaments, cows, and sacrificial fees.
One should worship the reciter with devotion through abundant gifts of food, gold, and land, for the sake of attaining the fruit of great merit.
Whatever mortal should hear this, or likewise proclaim it, shall abandon terrible torment and, with sins shaken off, go to heaven.

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Means to Liberation," in the *Pretakalpa* section of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
Thus concludes the second *Dharmakāṇḍa* of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
The *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Salutations to Śrī Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha. Salutations to Śrī Dattātreya. Salutations to Śrī Vedavyāsa. Salutations to Śrī Hayagrīva. Now begins the third section, the Brahmakāṇḍa, in the Gāruḍa Purāṇa. Om. He who is a thunderbolt to the wrestlers, the best of men to men, the embodied God of Love to women, a kinsman to the cowherds, a punisher of the wicked, and a child to his own parents; he who is death to the Lord of the Bhojas, the supreme reality ordained by the Creator for yogis, and the Lord of the Vṛṣṇis—Acyuta, together with his elder brother, shone eternally upon the arena.
Having paid homage to that very one who possesses the primordial form with the words "Namo Nārāyaṇāya," I shall proclaim this narrative of Nārāyaṇa.
The high-souled ṛṣis, beginning with Śaunaka, who were exponents of the Veda, performed most intense austerities at the highly meritorious place called Naimiṣa.
Having conquered their senses and subdued their appetites, those virtuous ones devoted to truth worshiped Viṣṇu, the primordial teacher of the world, with supreme devotion.
Proclaiming the supreme Brahman, the eye of the world, and possessed of great luster, those who knew the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures dwelt in the Naimiṣa forest.
Some worshipped the Lord of Sacrifice with sacrifices; some, the Supreme One whose nature is knowledge, with forms of knowledge; and others worshipped Nārāyaṇa with supreme devotion.
Once, those great-souled and most excellent ones held a council, desiring to know the means for attaining virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
There were twenty-six thousand sages who had drawn up their vital energy; it is impossible to state the number of their disciples and grand-disciples.
Those sages of great luster, who had cultivated their souls, met together; they were benefactors of the world, free from passion, and devoid of envy.
How may the devotion of human beings toward Hari be unswerving? By what means may all the threefold action of the self be perfected?
Seeing them thus prepared to ask this very question, the wise Śaunaka, bowing with humility and joining his palms in reverence, spoke these words.
Śaunaka said: "The Sūta, the best of Paurāṇikas, resides at the holy Siddhāśrama; that lord of ascetics and disciple of Vyāsa knows all of this."
"Therefore, let us ask him alone"—thus thought the sage Śaunaka; and then those seers departed for the holy Siddhāśrama.
The residents of the Naimiṣa forest questioned him as he sat at ease; the sages said: "We have arrived as guests, O observer of noble vows; you are our host."
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with the services of bathing and giving gifts, by what means does Viṣṇu become pleased, and how is he to be worshipped by men?
And tell us the definitive determination of reality, which serves as the means for liberation. Sūta said: Listen, all you sages, to Hari’s definitive determination of reality.
Having bowed to Viṣṇu, Śrī, Vāyu, Bhāratī, and the one named Śeṣa, as well as my preceptor Dvaipāyana-Kṛṣṇa, I shall speak according to my understanding.
There has been none equal to Nārāyaṇa, nor shall there ever be; by this word of truth, I accomplish all my aims.
Śaunaka said: O best of sages, for what reason must salutation to Viṣṇu be performed at the beginning of a book? Tell me, O Brahmin of noble vows, out of compassion for me.
Then why did you pay homage to Śrī, then to Vāyu, then to Bhāratī, and finally to Vyāsa? O Sūta, O highly fortunate Sūta, tell me the reason for this.

Sūta said: In the beginning, He who is to be saluted, who is the sole object of knowledge in all the Vedas, and who shines as the sole reality in the Veda, the Śāstra, the Itihāsas, and the Purāṇas—therefore Hari alone is indeed the one to be bowed to.

He alone is the primary and supreme authority everywhere; he alone is to be saluted, and not Śaṅkara and the others. Those who, out of lack of discipline, bow down to Śaṅkara, Vināyaka, Caṇḍikā, and Reṇukā [fall].
Likewise, Sūrya, Bhairava, the Mātṛs, as well as Vāṇī, Girijā, and Śrī—all of them are indeed Vaiṣṇavas; neither they nor their devotees exist apart from him, so say the Āryas.

One should certainly not perform prostration for the sake of worldly gain, for these deities are not pleased by mere worship; rather, all the deities, having accepted the worship, grant the fruit [of their favor] by giving something in return.

Having satisfied them, and having likewise performed the optional worship (kāmyapūjā) as desired by those who were pleased and acted according to their own inclinations, he offered it all to the Supreme Deity, Viṣṇu, Hari, who is worshipped as Śrī Puruṣa and other forms.

O best of the twice-born, these [gods] will grant pleasures and their opposites both here and in the next world, and ultimately lead to lower states and even darkness; therefore, those who desire liberation, such as the Brāhmaṇas and others, should neither worship nor bow down to them.

In the same way, O best of brahmins, even in times of great calamity, all those belonging to the various stages of life who constantly desire prosperity should always worship the primordial deities—Śrī, Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and Yama.

Those who bow down to non-Vaiṣṇavas who take the forms of Brahmā, Rudra, or Vāyu experience great suffering and great calamities, such as leprosy, fistula, and other ailments; they are certainly not devotees of Viṣṇu.

O lords of sages, I shall now state the underlying intention here, which is indeed highly secret and must be held within the heart; for in this world, O brahmins, it is the symbol of Vāyu alone that is to be worshipped, and not the symbols of Brahmā, Rudra, or others.
At the time of worshiping the God of gods, having placed the image of Vāyu in its proper place and having properly worshiped Hari, the Lord of Lakṣmī, who resides within that Vāyu; indeed.

Afterwards, one should properly worship Vāyu and Supratīka with the remains of Hari’s offerings; those fools who perform the worship of garlands, incense, ointments, and so forth separately [from the Lord] are deluded.

For them, suffering shall arise in this world and the next; there is no need for deliberation on this point. O Brahmins, perform some means of atonement for their well-being—namely, the remembrance of Viṣṇu.

Those deluded ones who, with the notion that they are seeking rewards, bow down to the images of Hari, Vāyu, or Śaṅkara installed by heretics such as the Rudras—their fruit is nothing but eternal suffering.

If the image of Vāyu has been consecrated by the best of sages, then it must indeed be bowed to; however, if the worship of Hari Viṣṇu has been performed with the remnants of the food offering (naivedya), there is not even a trace of fault.
For Hanuman is the great preceptor, ever devoted to the feet of Rama; knowing him thus, as well as the supreme Hari, who is the son of the chief god Vayu.

O best of Brahmins, let this secret be held in your hearts; there is no other way to pay homage. Those who are truly Vaiṣṇavas, the servants of the assembly of Viṣṇu—they all always worship Viṣṇu alone.

Those who indeed bow down and likewise perform meritorious and virtuous deeds, and those who bow down to Vāsudeva and Hari and properly worship them according to their own ability—[they attain the highest state].

Those who, by way of the path of worldly activity, do not worship the Supreme Divinity or another [deity] during times of distress—they alone are the Vaiṣṇavas, the servants and attendants of Viṣṇu; all others are considered merely non-Vaiṣṇavas.
