Indeed, by means of the introductory and concluding indicators, people reach Hari, the Guru, even without [directly] encountering Him; the Brahmins call those very works the true Purāṇas, for in the Kali age, no one harbors malice toward them.
Since they establish beneficial active dharmas corresponding to their respective castes, the deluded always feel envy toward them; for in the Kali age, such Brahmins are indeed very numerous.
There is no deity equal to Viṣṇu, nor is there a teacher equal to Vāyu; there is no sacred ford equal to Viṣṇupadī, and there is no devotee equal to a devotee of Viṣṇu.
They say that all other works that establish Viṣṇu are characterized by goodness (sāttvika); they alone are to be heard in the world of men, and no others, for others bring only suffering.

In the Kali age, among all the Purāṇas, there are only three that are preeminent and dear to Hari; indeed, the Bhāgavata Purāṇa is the foremost of the Purāṇas and brings about the highest good for men in the Kali age.
For creation is first expounded here; therefore, this Bhāgavata is remembered as supreme—that Purāṇa in which they describe at the outset the creation of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Rudra, and the others.

O Brahmin, the great ones speak thus of various purposes; they say that knowledge exists in both low and high forms. They declare that everything is accomplished by that very [knowledge]; for beyond this is the Bhāgavata Purāṇa.

After that, they say there is the Viṣṇupurāṇa, and after that, the one known as the Gāruḍa; these three alone are the primary ones for men in the Kali age, and furthermore, there is a certain special distinction within the Gāruḍa.
Listen, O Brahmins, to that specific distinction: the Purāṇa known as the Gāruḍa is composed of three parts. They say the first part is the Karmakāṇḍa, and they call the second part the Dharmakāṇḍa.

They say that the third part is the Brahmakāṇḍa; among those, this [Bhāgavata] is the most excellent. O Brahmins, they declare that the merit from hearing the third part is equal to the merit of the Bhāgavata.

When the third part is recited, the fruit shall be equal to that of the Vedas; there is no need for deliberation on this point. O Brahmins, the fruit has been declared to arise from merely hearing the third part, and likewise for one who recites it with understanding.
Because a third part is heard, they say that the merit for one who recites it is indeed tenfold; better than that, they say, is the Matsya Purāṇa, and better than that, they say, is the Kūrma Purāṇa.

In the same way, they say that the Vāyu Purāṇa consists of exactly three [sections] which are characterized by *sattva* in this world; furthermore, O lords of sages, something further should be understood regarding those six Purāṇas whose nature is *sattva*.

The noble ones say that the Matsya and Kūrma Purāṇas belong to the lowest quality (tāmasa), while they call the Vāyu Purāṇa and the Bhāgavata Purāṇa of middle quality (sāttvika); and they say that the Viṣṇu Purāṇa and the Gāruḍa Purāṇa are of the highest quality (sattvottama).
The wise say that the Skānda, Pādma, Vāmana, Varāha, Āgneya, and Bhaviṣya Purāṇas are rājasa in nature regarding their creation of the sections; therein, one part is sāttvika and another is tāmasa.

Because of the predominance of *rajas*, these are called "rajasic," and they should not be constantly heard by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). Yet, among them there are portions that are *sattvic*; for hearing those, the fruit is like that of the *Garuḍa* Purāṇa.
The Brahmāṇḍa, Liṅga, Brahmavaivarta, Mārkaṇḍeya, Brāhma, and Ādityaka—these, O Brahmins, are said to be tāmasa; among them, some portions are sāttvika and others are rājasa.

For these [other scriptures] are not to be heard in the world of men by those desiring the truth, as they are characterized by darkness (tāmasa); therefore, the great sages who abide in their sattvic portions regard the hearing of them as equal to touching but a single foot of Garuḍa.
They speak of the minor Purāṇas as being eighteen in number, as well as the Viṣṇudharmottara and the Bhāgavata Tantra.
The Tattvasāra, the Nārasiṃha, and likewise that which was proclaimed by Vāyu, as well as the Haṃsapurāṇa—these six, O lords of sages, [are the Purāṇas].
Know these to be purely sattvic; there is generally no doubt in this matter. Merely by hearing these, it is said that half the fruit of the Garuḍa Purāṇa is attained.
The one named Bhaviṣyottara, the Bṛhannārada, the Yama-Nārada-saṃvāda, and the Laghu-nārada as well.
The Vināyaka Purāṇa and the Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa—these they call Rājasa; by hearing them, one attains the highest worldly enjoyment.
The wise have stated that the fruit of reciting the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, the Śaiva Purāṇa, and likewise the Nandiprokta Purāṇa, is equal to one quarter of that of the Gāruḍa Purāṇa.
Those who know the true meaning of the principle of Hari declare that the Pāśupata, the Raiṇuka, and likewise the Bhairava [systems] are characterized by tamas.
O Brahmin, from hearing these [qualities], the Bhāgavata is remembered as the most excellent among all the Purāṇas, just like the foot of Garuḍa among the limbs of the body.
The merit from reciting or hearing it in a manner equal to the Vedas is the same; however, the merit from hearing its meaning is remembered as being ten times greater.

The merit of the speaker shall be twofold, and that of the expounder even greater; the great ones say it is equal to the infinite Vedas, and the Brahmins also [call it so] because of the greatness of the burden of the *Bhārata*.
Those who know the secret of Viṣṇu indeed declare that this [Purāṇa] is superior to the Vedas both in its subject matter and its essence.

In that regard, the noble ones say that the Śreṣṭhā Gītikā and likewise the Thousand Names of Viṣṇu are supreme; the great ones declare that from hearing those two within the Mahābhārata, one obtains a fruit ten times greater.

In the Kṛta Yuga, during the six-thousand-year period of the Bhārata [Manvantara], all the Daityas, having taken birth in the families of Brahmins, will constantly expel some of the newly established [inhabitants] and take up residence there themselves.
Having recognized Hari, the Lord Vyāsa in that form then composed the Bhāgavata Purāṇa; having likewise proclaimed the Vaiṣṇava [Purāṇa], he thereafter composed the one known as the Gāruḍa.
Therefore, this Gāruḍa Purāṇa is indeed preeminent and is honored by the scriptures; there is nothing equal to the Gāruḍa for the revelation of the dharma of Viṣṇu.

Just as Janārdana is the foremost among the gods, as the Sudarśana is the foremost among weapons, and as the Aśvamedha is the foremost among sacrifices, so too is Rudra when devotees have been cut down.

Just as the Gaṅgā is foremost among rivers, the lotus among water-born flowers, and the wind likewise among those whose devotion is unbroken, so too do they say that the Gāruḍa Purāṇa is preeminent among the Purāṇas for perceiving the true nature of Hari.
In the Purāṇa known as the Gāruḍa, Hari is declared to be the subject taught; therefore, Hari is remembered as the one to be saluted, the one to be approached, and the one who is worthy.

Because Śrī Devī is the very essence of fortune, her salutation is prescribed immediately thereafter; she is also remembered as the Supreme One, the Best of Men, and the Lord of Accomplished Practitioners (Sādhakeśa).
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, Vāyu also is to be saluted in the Purāṇas and other texts; and since Bhāratī consists of the form of speech, she is to be saluted immediately after Vāyu.
The person is called an *upasādhaka* because of that; therefore, immediately after that, he is always designated as *namya* by the wise according to the gradation [of stages].
Therefore, one should pay homage to Vyāsa because he is the author of this work. Śaunaka said: "Why indeed should homage be paid at the end to the high-souled Vyāsa?"
"O observer of noble vows, tell me the reason for saluting him first. Sūta said: "Indeed, the mind of Vyāsa is the primary [object of veneration] immediately following that of Viṣṇu."
Since Hari alone is Vyāsa, whose very nature is the wheel of the objects to be expressed, Vyāsa is not declared to be equal to the Blessed Lord Hari.
In this regard also, O lords of sages, I shall state the reason with due respect: Vyāsa is remembered in the Tāmasa Purāṇa as being a certain particular ṛṣi.
Thus, by relying on knowledge, the Daityas, together with their followers, enter into blinding darkness; therefore, you are saluted at the end.
This which is the supreme secret must be held in the heart without doubt; for it is said that this alone is to be bowed to by the highest, as it is indeed what is to be established here.
For that [reality] of the supreme ones is understood through both concise and detailed exposition; yet they would not know it as it truly is, since Hari is their very source of sustenance.
Hari and Vyāsa are indeed one and the same; Vyāsa is remembered as being like Hari. There is no doubt that these two alone possess the status of being the source of livelihood and the Lord.

Because she has entered into the millions of lords, her status as a sovereign (svāmitva) is proclaimed; because she is the source of subsistence for the three and because she is to be served, her sovereignty is traditionally remembered.
Because the triad beginning with Vāyu is to be served, their serviceability is traditionally taught; for Māruti is indeed the primary limb of Viṣṇu in the removal of the earth's burden.
Speech in the form of sentences is indeed remembered as the second limb; Śeṣa is the third limb of Hari, and he is not to be bowed to because of his equality with Hari.

Those who are primarily to be propitiated are declared to be the ones to whom homage is due; whereas those such as Vāyu and others, being secondary, are not to be saluted, and thus they are so remembered.
Since the names Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and others primarily denote Bhīma and the rest eternally, those lords of sages are worthy of salutation.
Indeed, it is only the state of being bowed to and the state of being the object of exposition that belong to others; all this has been explained by me—what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Subject Matter Concerning the Division of Purāṇas into Sāttvika and Others, and the Classification of Deities to be Worshipped and Not Worshipped," in the Brahmakāṇḍa, the third part of the Uttarakhaṇḍa, within the glorious *Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. —
Śrī Śaunaka said: O sage, how did the Blessed One create those presiding deities of the respective principles? I do not know the sequence of creation nor the internal distinctions among the gods.
Thus addressed by Śaunaka, Sūta spoke these words: Sūta said, "O best of Brahman-sages, your intellect is perfectly resolved."

In this very manner, the question was indeed posed to Hari by Garuḍa; O sinless one, I shall relate to you that which Hari spoke to him. Garuḍa said: "O illustrious one, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, please describe the creation."
Once the creation is known, your preeminence will be almost as well known; I shall come to possess knowledge of the gradations among Brahmā and the others.
That which was declared as the means to liberation is said to be its further accomplishment; having been liberated by Garuḍa, Kṛṣṇa spoke these words.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Therefore, because he is Viṣṇu even in his primary form, the imperishable Viṣṇu is to be known [as such].
O observer of noble vows, this incarnation is proclaimed as being due to fullness itself; for indeed, the manifold, having attained oneness, rests for the sake of dissolution.
And even therein there is a distinction; that very reality is what must be known.

Whether by perceiving [the distinction] through differentiation, or by perceiving it through both difference and non-difference—of Viṣṇu’s qualities, forms, limbs, and attributes such as bliss—or even by perceiving them within that very [reality], one shall swiftly go to the darkness [of liberation].
O best of the twice-born, those who are conceived as beginning from another person should be known as having the form of Hari, for they have indeed become one with him.
When the frost has arrived, those living beings belonging to me depart; O Virāj-rūpa, at that time they exist as Hari in many forms.
O twice-born one, at the time of dissolution they attain unity with the Root; but if Viṣṇu himself were to attain unity with the image (biṃba), [then that would be different].
How can the individual soul (jīva) be a reflection of Nārāyaṇa? There is no doubt that the jīva is subordinate to Hari and resembles him.
For this meaning of the word "reflection" has been explained in this way; therefore, one should not contemplate the unification of the forms of the original objects with that reflection.
Just as in the case of Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and others, it is their oneness that is intended to be expressed; here, no distinction between the reflected images and the original form is intended.
Moreover, even in that regard, a distinction must be understood by those who desire reality: through a single aspect, they attain oneness with the images.
They are established in the state of being living beings in one respect; there is no doubt about this. Yet, those people do not know the root of the *bimba*; indeed, they are considered asuras.
Hari, who was indeed one alone in the beginning, becomes many through the power of ignorance himself, like a reflection in a mirror from afar.
Those fools who speak thus also go to the lowest darkness. The limiting adjunct (upādhi) is said to be of two kinds: that which is of its own nature and that which is external.

The external adjunct dissolves at the time of absorption (laya), while at liberation (mukti) there remains the persistence of something else; for when all adjuncts have perished, how could a reflection exist?

For those who are qualified for liberation, the limiting adjunct (upādhi) is indeed called the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa); but for those who are qualified for [the state of] darkness (tamas), the limiting adjunct is indeed the nature of suffering (duḥkha).
For the adjunct (upādhi) of those who are eternally transmigratory is considered to be of a mixed nature; the external adjunct for all is the subtle body (liṅgadeha)—of this there is no doubt.
Because the Daityas cause suffering, Hari himself is "Duḥkhin" (the Sufferer); because he takes on the very form of their various sufferings, he appears in the form of their reflection.
One should not contemplate any mutual difference or distinction between the images situated as Daityas and the Lord in his original form.
Between the forms of Śrī, Bhū, Durgā, and others, as well as those such as Sītā and the rest, there is not even an atom’s worth of difference between them, whether externally or internally.

Having somehow understood that darkness moves toward the lower lip, one should reflect upon it; for the original object always exists in the form of a woman, situated as a reflection within the mirror.
O best of birds, when the dissolution has arrived, those who remain established with their reflections do not attain oneness with Lakṣmī.
O son of Vinatā, one should not suspect even the slightest difference in any respect between the beauty of the forms situated within the *biṃba* and that of Lakṣmī herself.

For when the Lord lies upon the ocean of dissolution, having placed within his belly all living beings—whether liberated ones such as Brahmā, Indra, and the hosts of Maruts, or those bound by karma—and even those situated in the states of heaven or hell; |||

[He sees] all living beings who have fallen into dark wells and the like, as well as others who are to be encountered in the Kali age; likewise, he sees people eternally situated in the cycle of rebirth, including insentient beings such as those in the form of bears and other creatures.

Thus, having gathered all people within his belly, he indeed sleeps perfectly within the waters during that kalpa; and Lakṣmī, who is the essence of all the Vedas, though eternally nourished by devotion toward Hari, [remains there].

Though her devotion had already increased, she seemed to show even greater reverence as she praised Viṣṇu; at that time, in every aspect of her movement and conduct, there was nothing whatsoever apart from Viṣṇu and Śrī.
The Goddess appeared in the form of Paryaṅkā, and Ramā shone forth in the form of Vāsā; at that very moment, Ramā herself was everything, yet that single Goddess manifested in many forms and spoke.
You are supreme because you are the highest among all gods; there is no god equal to you or superior to you. You are the one Brahmā—not the four-faced one, nor am I Rudra, nor Bṛhaspati.
For the word "Brahman" is primary only with respect to Viṣṇu, while it is secondary in relation to others such as Brahmā and Rudra; Hari is called "Brahman" because He is full of infinite qualities.

Because they lack the state of being complete with qualities and so forth, others are not designated as Brahman; for there is no infinity—whether by way of space, quality, or time—in any place or at any time.

Since there is no end to this, what more need be said? There is no such infinity of qualities even among those beginning with Brahmā; for I am always, in every place and at all times, together with Vāsudeva.

Nevertheless, my qualities are not infinite; therefore, the dharmas are infinite by virtue of their qualities. They exist in accordance with what has been heard and are not contradictory; for they are to be contemplated by the gods, indeed inconceivable, manifold, and infinite.

Therefore, we are never able to praise the qualities of you, Lord Viṣṇu, nor those of Hari at any time; neither I, nor Keśin, nor Speech, nor Rudra, nor the daughter of Dakṣa, nor the daughter of Menakā can do so.
Neither indeed Indra, nor Pulomajā, nor Agni, nor Yama, nor anyone else; neither Nārada, nor Bhṛgu, nor Vasiṣṭha, nor the Lord of Obstacles, nor Bali and the others.
Neither Virāṭa, nor Bhīma, nor Śani, nor Puṣkara, nor Kaśeru likewise; neither the Kinnaras, nor the Pitṛs, nor the Devas, nor even the Gandharva chiefs known as Tuṣitas.
Neither the lords of the earth nor other humans know anything of Viṣṇu; who else here could be inferior to me in merit? For Brahmā is indeed equal to him, O Mātariśvan.

In detachment, in the state of devotion to Hari, in fortitude, in the vital breaths, in yoga, in the intellect, in worldly existence, and at the time of liberation, those two were indeed equal and mutually supportive of one another.

The great ones say that Brahmā is the ego of food (anna), while they call Vāyu the Great One, the ego of the individual soul (jīva). That god Brahmā is not able to exist even for a moment in this cycle of worldly existence without Vāyu.

Without him, neither could Mātariśvan exist; there was mutual dependence and a deficiency in time, when the Great-Souled One became the regulator of the Mahat-tattva during the gross creation within the cosmic egg.

At that time, the high-souled Vāyu was indeed unable [to manifest]; he exists in the external creation according to the divisions of time. Sarasvatī and Bhāratī, however, came into being from Brahmā after the passing of a year.

When ten years had passed, O Great-souled One, Vāyu became honored by the world; yet there was only a slight deficiency in his creation of gross forms, O Great-souled One, and not even by this much was there a loss of gentleness in him.

Sarasvatī was indeed born after one year from Brahmā, at the time following his own birth; since there is a temporal deficiency in her speech compared to Vāyu, what harm is there in her being inferior?
Immediately after the wind, speech indeed came into being after a year; as long as there was birth, so long did the destruction of the previous body occur.

The remaining one is Indra, and Rudra—these three are indeed equal in terms of the power of knowledge and so forth; nevertheless, there is a deficiency in them regarding time, for their lifespan is two thousand years.

Just as Ananta, Rudra, Brahmā, and Vāyu are to be understood, so too [the time] in one's own nature (svarūpa) involves no deficiency; O Great-Souled One, in the creation of the gross and the external creation, I should not at all contemplate any deficiency in time.
O high-souled one, from them were born these three daughters—Vāruṇī, Pārvatī, and she named Sauparṇī; it should be understood that they appeared ten years after Sarasvatī and Bhāratī.

O Indra, O Varuṇa, O wife of Rudra, and so forth, grant this knowledge always without fail. He in whom such knowledge exists in this world is indeed a man of wisdom; he alone is the one to be known through the Vedas.
He who does not know the distinction "the knower is indeed not [the body]" is neither a proponent of the Vedas nor a reciter of the Vedas.
As many syllables of the Vedas as have been recited by the twice-born, so many names of Hari are always dear to Hari.
Lord Hari is my master eternally, and I am forever the servant of Hari; all the deities, beginning with Brahmā, are my gurus in their proper order.
And Hari is everywhere celebrated in the Veda as the Lord of these; he who studies the Vedas while knowing this is the best of the twice-born.
He should be known as a reciter of the Vedas; others are merely proponents of the Vedas. One who is overwhelmed by the burden of the Vedas is indeed a donkey among Brahmins.

Both the one who prided himself on his knowledge and the one who prided himself on the Veda spoke to each other at all times: "The water where Murāri resides is the Veda; it is due to the fault of associating with teachers that the twice-born have come to this state."
O Great-Souled One, there are thousands, hundreds, and millions of great offenders in the world; yet Hari, the protector, always forgives them all simply through the remembrance of His three names.

Seeing him free from all offenses, always endowed with gifts and honors, and yet deficient due to gradation, the high-souled Viṣṇu, perceiving that offense, utters a cry of "Hā Hā" with a mind of wrath.

Arise, O Govinda, you whose true nature is well known; O you who are called Kṛta, be perfectly gracious toward me! O Keśava, arise, you whose very form is bliss, you who are capable of sustaining the creation and its dissolution.

Having created Brahmā, He should impel him toward the creation of what is to be worshipped; and having created Rudra, He should impel him toward dissolution. Having observed the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Śeṣa, who are worthy of their respective attainments, grant liberation perfectly.

O Hare, O Murāri! Today you remain without sleep; O you who possess infinite knowledge [and intellect] spanning many kalpas, having correctly perceived through the vision of karma that great-souled one has attained a darkness whose nature is suffering, burn it away.

Since you, whose nature is consciousness, always cause the Daityas and others who possess a miserable intellect to fall into blinding darkness, therefore they say that you, Hari, are of a miserable nature; and because of that miserable nature, O Hari, you are the sufferer.
Arise, Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva! Arise, Kṛṣṇa, Acyuta, Mādhava! Arise, Vaikuṇṭha, O you whose form is moist with compassion! Arise, Lord of Lakṣmī; salutations, salutations to you!

Arise, O Lord of Madhu, Lord of Sarasvatī! Arise, O Lord of Rudra, as well as Lord of Ambikā! Arise, O Lord of Candra, as well as Lord of Śacī, Lord of Brahmins, Lord of Devotees, and eternal Lord of Cows!

O Murāri, you who delight in the Śāstras, arise! You who delight in the Ṛgveda, arise, O embodiment of the Nidāna! You who delight in the Sāmaveda, and likewise, you who always delight in the Atharvaveda!
O Ancient One, you are fond of prose; O You of wondrous form, arise, for you are fond of hymns of praise! You alone bring delight to the sweet singers; arise quickly, for you are the Lord of Kamalā.
Thus praised, Viṣṇu—the unborn, ancient one, eternally bound—arose with great haste.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Sequence of the Taraka-mantras of the Deities beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara," in the Brahma-kāṇḍa, the third part of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: A desire arose in me, the Lord Viṣṇu, to create those things to be created and to liberate those fit for liberation. Although the power of will (icchā-śakti) exists in Viṣṇu at all times, nevertheless, that manifestation [of the will] is a worldly phenomenon.
Then Hari assumed the worldly nature of darkness and, in that form, performed the drinking; they call that form indeed "Prakṛta," for all those who are ignorant enter into blinding darkness.
All the incarnations of Mahāviṣṇu are proclaimed to be complete; that supreme form is complete, and from the complete [form], the complete ones have emerged.
Their status as prior or posterior, however, arises solely from the distinction of their manifestation; it is by no means a matter of priority or posteriority due to the power of space or time.
The prior form and the full [form], the full one that leads to the crossing of the state of the word—having taken that form into oneself, only the Full remains.
This worldly transaction, such as the removal of the earth's burden and so forth, has no dissolution other than through his vision; it never occurs through Kṛṣṇa or anyone else.
One must not cause pain to the *tattva*; through that, one experiences sufferings. From excessive affliction of it, disease arises for him; of this there is no doubt.
But when there is suffering regarding that which is to be known, it must be undertaken together with the teacher; him they call a disciple, and he alone is remembered as the teacher.
Those who engage in a mutual inquiry into the true nature of Hari are indeed the teacher and the disciple, O you who are filled with joy for Vinatā.
Even with the guru, one should engage in laughter that is free from deceit; a disciple who is possessed of joy or resentment, or a guru who is possessed of crookedness, [should avoid such laughter].

Both of them went to hell for as long as the moon and stars endure; yet the Great-Souled Lord Hari himself, the tawny-eyed Puruṣa, the Blessed and Powerful One, by his own auspicious manly prowess, exerted his valor within his own Māyā composed of the qualities (guṇas).

Garuḍa said: O Vāsudeva, tell me the true nature of power; a doubt appears to me regarding your power. Is power the very essence of the Lord, or is it distinct from him? Speak clearly, for you know well.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O son of Vinatā, the wise who perceive the determined truth declare that the potency which Hari, the Lord himself, deposited in her called Māyā is the very nature of Nṛhari.

They say that [the universe] is divided, and they also say it is merely primordial matter (prakṛti); this should be understood as being like the lotus from his own navel and so forth. One should not think, however, that by this much there is any loss of power in Viṣṇu, whose nature is consciousness.

O Lord of Birds, if the Blessed One, who is the very embodiment of vigor, or Sudeva, were not the possessor of all goals in every place and at every time, then he would certainly not be the Supreme Lord or the Puruṣa.

With inconceivable vigor and conceivable vigor, she is of two forms: one in the form of a woman and the other likewise as a man. O Lord of Birds, both forms possess vigor; indeed, their non-duality should be correctly contemplated.
If he did not possess a female form, how could he be the very reflection of the women in heaven?

This female form born of Brahman (which is not unreal) is to be meditated upon as one's own true nature; it is not to be meditated upon otherwise. One should not contemplate it as anything other than a female form; know that a neuter being is indeed produced from it.

The neuter is indeed ninefold as its very nature; therefore, there is nothing further to be contemplated regarding Hari. O King of Birds, it should be contemplated that within the form of Hari which has become the female image, the form of Śrī exists.
Garuḍa said: The wise say that the union of woman with woman is useless; yet, within the very form of a woman, there are always those who possess the nature of women.
O Lord Kṛṣṇa, tell me the cause for my remaining there.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Lord of Birds, how could Lakṣmī not exist in the form of a woman who is the very image of the Supreme Soul? How could the Goddess, who is eternally inseparable from Him, not be present?
O Lord of Birds, she is eternally devoted to serving the infinite forms of Hari in female form, by means of her own infinitely manifold forms.

Therefore, separation from Lakṣmī is to be feared in every way. O Tārkṣya, Hari named Nārāyaṇa is independent; he never exists without Śrī. She serves the lotus-feet of Mukunda, Hari, with the utmost reverence.

Even Śrī does not exist at any place or time without Hari; this must be understood by those who desire liberation. She, in whom he deposits his power moment by moment, is mine and consists of illusion (indrajāla).
Those deluded asuras who speak thus all enter into unrighteousness; they claim that this "māyā" is indeed their primordial nature (*prakṛti*), subtle in form, and not the work of a magician.

One should know that his pride is Śrī; therein lies the instigation of vigor and their union. The Noble Ones say that union is directed toward the task to be accomplished; they do not say that this form belongs to Viṣṇu.

O Lord of Birds, how could that [form] of Viṣṇu, which is eternal and of the nature of truth, be false? That body of Prakṛti is concealed within it; they say its reality is of the nature of conventional usage.

If truth were by its very nature of the form of worldly convention, then how could it be beginningless? O Lord of Birds, if it were not eternally beginningless, it would not exist as the cause in its most subtle form.
If it is the cause by way of a subtle form, then tell me what is the cause of the phenomenal world? By the power of ignorance, Viṣṇu alone is perceived in various forms; it is Viṣṇu alone.

"Indeed, through the knowledge of the scriptures, ignorance is destroyed—of this there is no doubt—and one attains oneness with Hari. If you speak thus, O King of Birds, listen as I explain the reasoning behind it to you."

For how could ignorance possibly belong to me, Hari, the enemy of Mura, who is omniscient? Just as there is no darkness in the sun, so too there is no ignorance in Nārāyaṇa, in Hari. O king of birds, how then can you speak of such a truth? Ah!

Therefore, I am not a Brahmin from the beginningless past if I am ignorant due to the influence of association with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Where, O Lord of Birds, is that omniscient Viṣṇu, and where is the individual soul (*jīva*) of limited knowledge, devoid of true wisdom?

And how could the Vedas ever reconcile the unity of these two contradictory [positions]: that the Creator of the world is eternally free from suffering, and that he is always possessed of perfect power? At all times and in every place, [the two claims remain] opposed.

The individual soul is always a limited agent, while the Full One is eternally of the nature of suffering within the form of saṃsāra; yet they say that there is an identity between these two opposites through the power of the Māyā of the Lord and the one possessed of Māyā.

He who always harbors malice toward those Vaiṣṇavas who are under the control of the servants of Viṣṇu will never attain love for Hari, nor will he ever experience an increase in bliss, nor will he attain liberation.

The master of illusion is always accompanied by his illusory servants; nevertheless, due to their perception of duality, they are censured and made to work. By that [perception], there arises for them an increase in suffering, as well as the darkness of hell from which there is no return.

From the Lord of Birds [Viṣṇu], that subtle form is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*); it is eternal, it is always truly existent. In this way, the atoms of time, wind, and so forth, are themselves of a truly real nature.

The characteristic of the ultimate atoms (paramāṇu) should be understood by those desiring knowledge, and not otherwise; O Lord of Birds, for the particular substances composed of earth, the final [momentary] distinction is called "ultimate" (viśeṣa).
O best of the twice-born, that very thing which is the ultimate remainder is traditionally known as the atom (*paramāṇu*).
Garuḍa said: O Kṛṣṇa, O Mādhava, O Lord of the Sāttvatas, you are the ultimate atom, the final part of all things.

Thus it has been stated; however, I have a doubt regarding that which is the final particularity (*viśeṣa*), for that is not possessed of parts. Indeed, that which is possessed of parts cannot be the final particularity—this is how my words appear to be true.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Those human beings in this world who are endowed with the power to perceive specific distinctions—even they are not at all capable of perceiving the specific distinction that consists in His being the possessor of those parts.

Those sages who speak thus, as well as others such as the followers of Kaṇāda and Gautama, O Lord of Birds, declare that very same thing to be the final part, the particularity, and they call it the partless atom.
Although it is endowed with infinite parts, they describe those parts as partless due to a deluded vision;
therefore, O son of Vinatā’s womb, the state of being an atom belongs to the atom itself, not to its parts.

O Lord of Birds, within a single part of a subtle atom there exist multitudes of living beings; and within each of those beings, the forms of Hari exist individually; therefore, He is subtler than even that subtle atom.

Whether it be that which is subtler than the supreme Viṣṇu, or that which is greater than the great, there is no distinction whatsoever between them; for that which is inconceivable in form, it is yet to be contemplated.
The wise know that the absence of any limit of time is the infinity of time; the wise know that the absence of any limit of space is the infinity of space.
The wise know that when qualities are immeasurable, they constitute infinity; this threefold eternity belongs to Hari alone, and to no one else.
Although its infinity is characterized by three aspects in all its forms, nevertheless, its limitation by space is also logical.
Likewise, delimitation and pervasion are applicable even to that which is of a single nature; its inconceivable and wondrous sovereignty exists solely for the sake of conventional discourse.
There is no limitation whatsoever in terms of qualities or time; for although it is indeed all-pervasive spatially among all beings.
Nor is any division of it possible, even by a single atom; nevertheless, atomicity exists [in Him] due to the possession of sovereign power.
Therefore, know that his all-pervasiveness is also spoken of for the sake of his descent; that which is his pervasive form, they know as the supreme Nārāyaṇa.
Therefore, for those who maintain that there are infinite earth-atoms, their mutual distinction must be understood, as well as that of the Great-Souled Lord.

There is an eternal distinction between the insentient and the Lord, among the various insentient things, among the individual souls, as well as between the insentient and the souls, and likewise between the insentient and the Lord.
These five divisions are always present in every state and in every respect; yet, within such an illusion, the heroic one exerts his vigor.
From that [unmanifest], the Lord Hari, known as Puruṣa, created the three qualities.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Creation of the Three Qualities through the Door of the Bestowal of the Nature of the Lord’s Potency, and the Distinction between the Insentient and the Lord," in the Brahma-kāṇḍa, the third part of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: At that time, when the Blessed One created the three qualities from Prakṛti, Lakṣmī manifested in three forms, known by the names Śrī, Bhū, and Durgā.
The wise say that Śrī is the personification of sattva, Bhūdevī is the personification of rajas, and Durgā is indeed the personification of tamas.
O Lord of Birds, one should not perceive any distinction between forms themselves, nor between the qualities, due to their connection with the citadels and other such structures.
Those who perceive a difference go to the highest blinding darkness; for the Person has become threefold—he is Viṣṇu, he is Brahmā, and he is Bhava.

To cause the worlds to flourish through the quality of goodness (sattva), Viṣṇu himself, Hari in person, entered into Brahmā through the quality of passion (rajas) in order to carry out the act of creation.
He should be known as the primordial Brahmā, but not Hari himself; for Hari entered into Rudra in order to strike down even Tamas.
Abiding in Rudra, he is designated as Rudra, yet Hari himself is not Rudra; Viṣṇu alone is Hari manifest, and both of them are remembered as Haris.
These two manifested forms should be understood as denoting Brahmā and Rudra; by knowing this, one attains liberation, and not otherwise by any means whatsoever.
Those twice-born who perceive the identity of the forms of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the others, go to a terrible hell from which there is no return.
Having entered the three qualities (guṇas), the imperishable Puruṣa Hari indeed agitated them so that they would become oriented toward the task of creation.
From the agitation of the Blessed One’s three qualities, a great [result] arose; there is no doubt that it proceeded solely from the portions existing within those three qualities.
From Mahat were born Brahmā and Vāyu, who possess the ego-sense of space; after a year had passed for him, they were born as twins.
That reality in which rajas is predominant is called the principle of Mahat; one should understand this creation to be characterized by the inequality of the guṇas.

Garuḍa said: O Son of Devakī, for the sake of knowing the true nature of the Great Principle (mahattattva), you have described the supreme creation known as the differentiation of the qualities (guṇavaiṣamya).

"O Great Lord, tell me the meaning of the term 'guṇavaiṣamya' (the inequality of the qualities). Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O Lord of Birds, for the purpose of making known the meaning of the term 'guṇavaiṣamya'..."

Furthermore, O Lord of Heaven, in order to correctly explain that state where the qualities are in equilibrium, there is no doubt that it must first be shown therein, starting with space and so forth.
O son of Vinatā, I shall indeed show you the collection of qualities and their state as they have been gathered together from that source.
That dust which has formed into a heap should be known as double [in weight], and not otherwise; O son of Vinatā, it is so in comparison to dust that has not yet formed a heap.

Likewise, when these principles have become aggregated, they are said to be twofold; for these are born from the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti), but the root-nature itself is not considered to be born [from anything].
Since there is no discernment of the forms of primordial nature (prakṛti), therefore, O Lord of Birds, they should be known as born of nature, not as fundamental roots.
Thus, O Lord of Birds, the measure of your qualities has been declared; and their true nature has been correctly explained to you, O Lord of Birds.
In that regard, O Garuḍa, within those three groups, sattva alone is proclaimed to be unmixed with rajas and tamas; therefore, it is so called.
O Lord, it is said to be "pure" (kevala) sattva, but not because of its superiority; for at the time of creation it may be pure, but at the time of dissolution it becomes mixed.
O Lord of Birds, the multitude of beings is always unmixed; O best of the twice-born, the multitude of beings is also always mixed.
All those who perceive these enter indeed into the lower darkness; O Indra, the qualities of rajas and tamas are mixed with the other two.

O Lord of Birds, even at the time of dissolution during the process of creation, they remain indeed mixed; even when the quality of passion has become a solid mass, it contains more than a hundredfold the portion of passion.
And sattva should be known as mixed [with rajas], not otherwise, O best of birds; indeed, O son of Vinatā, it exists within a hundredth part of rajas.
That portion which was designated as one part is proclaimed to be darkness of that same measure, even when it is mixed with dust gathered into a heap.

O dear one, the state of the mass of dust is thus pervaded by the qualities of darkness (tamas); even when darkness has become a mass, O son of Vinatā, the quality of goodness (sattva) is also present.
It should be understood without any doubt that [the element] becomes mixed with darkness by an amount exceeding ten parts; such is the case regarding Garuḍa.
O son of Vinatā, among the ten parts of tamas, that one part which has been specified is equal in measure to rajas.
Even when darkness has become a mass, it certainly remains mixed [with light]; O best of birds, the persistence of the mass of darkness should be understood in this way.
Garuḍa said: "O sinless one, I have stated that even when passion has become a mass and even when darkness has become a mass, the portions of goodness are indeed predominant."
In this regard, I have a doubt; listen, O Lord of the Sāttvatas: as for how many parts of the Rāśi and how many additional portions of the Rāśis there are.
"O Lord, by that much alone there would be worldly convention, like milk and water. Having heard what was said by Garuḍa, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, [replied].
Hari, praising Garuḍa with supreme affection, spoke; Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "She who always abounds in the mass of *sattva* is superior to the mass of *rajas* and the mass of *tamas*."
O Lord of Birds, even when mixed, it is not called *sattva*; the wise know it thus as a mass of *rajas* and a mass of *tamas*.
Just as poison residing in sacrificial porridge or milk is still called "poison," so too, O Garuḍa, have I described the inherent nature of the qualities.
Now hear, O Lord of Birds, about the state of equilibrium of the guṇas, and that which is produced from the accumulated rajas, O Lord of Birds.
And that which is proclaimed as *rajas* has entered into the principle of *mahat*; when the dissolution (*pralaya*) has arrived, the *rajas* remains situated within the principle of *mahat*.
O Lord, it is clearly divided into twelve parts; indeed, when the essence has become a constellation, it is mixed with a tenth part.
O Lord of Birds, O Bird-born One, it becomes perfectly so in one part; likewise, it is indeed mixed with a mass of darkness—of this there is no doubt.
O Lord of Birds, it should be understood that it becomes mixed with a single portion of the mass of dust; it is never otherwise.

O bird-born one, the dissolution of the Blessed One within the three qualities and within the principle of Mahat should likewise be understood in the heart by those who have awakened to the meaning of reality.
Thus, O Lord of Birds, because the three qualities are mixed together, they call it the equilibrium of the qualities; know this indeed, O Bird.
"Otherwise, those who perceive [them] otherwise indeed go to the lower darkness. Garuḍa said: "O Supreme Lord, regarding these three qualities that have been gathered into a heap..."
O Brahman, O highly fortunate one, tell me briefly this truth: how is it that for the Viśālas there is an equilibrium of the qualities (guṇasāmyatā) at the time of dissolution? Please explain.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O best of men, the wise know that when the three qualities have become heaped together, they then exist in a state of complete intermingling.
Now listen properly, O my dear one, to the inequality of the qualities (guṇas), O bird, regarding what occurred previously at the time of creation when the period of dissolution had arrived.
Furthermore, that *rajas* which is mixed with *sattva* in ten parts, and which has entered into *tamas* by even a single part—that indeed is *rajas*.
That *rajas* which has entered even by a single part into *rajas*, in this way, all *rajas* has entered by twelve parts in every respect.
O twice-born one, by those ten parts of sattva, and likewise by the single part that possesses rajas, and thus by these eleven parts together with the portion of tamas—so it is indeed.
Indeed, when it is truly mixed, that is then remembered as the Mahat-tattva; O son of Vinatā, this other distinction should also be reflected upon.
One part should be known as tāmasa within the principle of mahat; there is no doubt about this, O best of men, and it is thus mixed with thirteen portions.
"One should understand it thus and not otherwise in any way. Garuḍa said: "O Blessed One, Lord of the Sāttvatas, this was previously heard by me from the Four-faced One."
"O Lord, the Great Principle (mahattattva) arises from four parts; among them, one part is said to be darkness (tamas), and three parts are indeed passion (rajas)."

Regarding this, they say that the form of Brahmā, known as the inequality of the qualities (guṇavaiṣamya), is declared to consist of four parts; this is what I have heard called the principle of Mahat.
"O sinless one, you have stated that it is produced from thirteen parts; O compassionate one, who are kind to your devotees, please sever this doubt of mine."

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: There is no dispute whatsoever between what was spoken by Brahmā and what has been spoken by me; for the quality of rajas is mixed with the fundamental essence (mūlasattva) in a proportion of one-tenth.
O Lord of Birds, all of that combined together is declared to be one part; this is what was called the "part of rajas" in the root *rajas*.
In the second part, that rajas is to be known; of this there is no doubt. And likewise, that which was mentioned as the portion of rajas in the root-tamas is also [to be understood] in the same way.
The third part is to be understood as darkness; there is no need for further deliberation on this point. Likewise, at the root in the darkness, one part is traditionally held to be darkness itself.
Thus, three parts of rajas and one part of tamas are traditionally taught; that, they say, is the body of Brahmā, known by the name "the inequality of the qualities."
Garuḍa said: "O Garuḍadhvaja, you have stated that the principle of Mahat has four parts, three of which are rajas and only one is tamas."
"O Mādhava, O Brahmin, it is understood from your words that the body of the supreme Brahmā Parameṣṭhin consists of a portion of *rajas*."
"The body of the supreme Brahmā Parameṣṭhin consists of pure sattva; for thus it is heard, O Kṛṣṇa, and this doubt afflicts me."
"Cut through this very doubt, for it is indeed worthy to be heard. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "When the *rajas* has become threefold, and likewise twelvefold..."
O bird, O twice-born one, listen to this: it should be understood that sattva has entered [the system] with ten parts more than rajas, which is in a state of indifference.
O bird, it must be stated without any doubt that, in comparison to tamas, sattva has indeed entered [into the being] as being ten parts greater.

In that regard, by comparison with darkness (tamas), darkness is said to be the eleventh part; one portion is to be known as rajas—thus say the wise. And so, O high-minded one, listen as I shall describe the parts when combined.
O Lord of Birds, upon the arising of the principle of Mahat, the material cause (upādāna) is to be known as having thirteen parts; the part consisting of rajas is said to have twelve parts.
One part is to be known as darkness; hear, O twice-born ones, the divisions therein. First, among the twelve parts, I shall declare the divisions; listen to that.
One part of it is to be known as *tamas*; *rajas* exceeds that by ten parts; and *sattva* exceeds that by a hundred parts—thus have the wise declared.
O best of beings, listen now to the divisions within that which consists entirely of darkness: one part is to be known as rajas, while tamas is ten parts plus one.
O Lord of Birds, in the Mahat-tattva, the portion of tamas should be known as ten parts, and the portion of sattva is recorded as being one part more than that.
Since the portion of *sattva* is predominant, the four-faced one is called *Śuddhasattva*; and thus, O son of Vinatā, the birth of Mahat has been described.
Through the knowledge of that, one attains liberation; but not otherwise, by any means whatsoever.

Thus, in the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Uttarakhaṇḍa*, in the dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, in the third part (*Tṛtīyāṃśa*), in the *Brahmakāṇḍa*, the fourth chapter titled "The Description of the Nature of the Body of Brahmā and the Equilibrium of Qualities through the Distinction of the Imbalance of Guṇas. O highly fortunate one, Hari himself entered into such a Great Principle (*Mahattattva*) together with Lakṣmī; indeed, Hari caused it to be agitated.

From that, the principle of *ahaṃtattva* (the I-principle) arose, consisting of knowledge (*jñāna*), substance (*dravya*), and activity (*kriyā*). At the time of the emergence of *ahaṅkāra*, one part is said to reside in *tamas*.

O Lord, that which exceeds its own tenth part by [the same] tenth part is called *rajas*; likewise, that which exceeds [its own tenth part] by a tenth part is called *sattva* by the wise; and this very Self is remembered as "I."
O twice-born one, at first Śeṣa alone was the one who identified with the principle of ego (ahaṃtattva); a thousand years later, those two, Khaga and Hara, were born.
O bird, having entered into these principles of ego (ahaṃtattva), the immutable Lord Hari himself, together with Lakṣmī, caused them to tremble.
I am threefold—as Vaikārika, Tāmasa, and Taijasa—and Rudra likewise became threefold, since he is the controller of them.
Rudra, abiding in the *vaikārika* [sattva], is remembered as *vaikārika*; Rudra, abiding in the *tāmasa* [tamas], is indeed designated as *tāmasa*.
Rudra, abiding in the Taijasa [state], is indeed remembered as the Taijasa in the world; and Hari himself, together with Lakṣmī, resides in the Taijasa principle of Ahaṃtattva.
Having entered [the body], it then caused agitation and became tenfold: namely, the ear, the eye, touch, taste, and smell.

Speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ—these ten are recorded [as the faculties]. Hari, having entered the principle of ego (ahaṃtattva) which is indeed of the nature of transformation (vaikārika), agitates it.
O Lord of Birds, at the beginning, these deities of the senses—beginning with the principle of Mahat—were elevenfold in their respective order.
At first, O Manobhimānin, Vāruṇī came into being; immediately after her, Sauparṇī and likewise Gaurī were born.
O Lord of Birds, it should be understood that from the remainder [of the lifespan], the arising of those [beings] occurs immediately thereafter; specifically, after ten years, in successive order.
Two others, Manobhimānin and Indrakāma, were born; they are to be known as Tārkṣya and Anantara, who were liberated even while still within saṃsāra.
Then he became the self of the skin, who is called Ahaṃkārika; thereafter, O best of birds, those whose nature is the hands were born.
Śacī, Rati, Aniruddha, Svāyambhuva Manu, Bṛhaspati, and Dakṣa—these are remembered as being of the nature of the hands.
Immediately after Dakṣa was born a bird named Pravāha; he is called Ativāha as well, and impelled by his own nature, he carries [the breath] along.
He should be known as immediately following the hands, but he is not remembered as being like Śacī and the others; from that, O highly fortunate one, the sense-organ of sight arose from his self.
Śatarūpā was the wife of Svāyambhuva Manu, as was Yama; furthermore, the Moon and the Sun are the four who take pride in their faculty of sight.
O Lord of Birds, it should be known that Candra is the presiding deity of the ear; Varuṇa, the self of the tongue-faculty, appeared immediately after Sūrya.
For those presiding over the organ of speech arose after Varuṇa; likewise, Prasūti became the wife of Dakṣa, and Bhṛgu, Agni, and Tvaṣṭṛ [arose].

In that regard, those very beings who were mentioned as the eaters of raw flesh and so forth are indeed great-souled ones who exercise control over the faculty of speech; by them, the infinite principles are governed.
Because of their state of equanimity, they spoke in that same manner, yet not out of pride regarding reality; O Indra of the twice-born, immediately thereafter, they became manifest.
Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Marīci, Pulaha, Kratu, Pulastya, Aṅgiras, and likewise Vaivasvata Manu.
Manu and others, infinite in number, are said to have arisen from Upastha; and immediately after that, the proud Vīndra was born from Pāyu.
Among the twelve Suns, one is Mitra; Tārā is the beloved of Guru (Jupiter); Nirṛti is the lord of the corner (southwest), and Pravahā is his beloved.
O best of the twice-born, these four lords of birds, all of whom were conceited regarding the principle of air (vāyu-tattva), were born as those conceited regarding the sense of smell (ghrāṇa).
Viṣvavasu, the two Aśvins who are the sons of Vāyu, Gaṇapa, Vittapa—the seven Vasus have been mentioned—and Agni is said to be the eighth.
Listen to the names of the Satyas: Droṇa, Prāṇa, Dhruva, Arka, Doṣa, Vaska, and Vibhāvasu as the seventh.
Likewise, the ten Rudras are to be known, and Bhava is remembered as the Root Rudra; O best of the twice-born, hear the names of the ten Rudras.
Likewise Raivata, Bhīma, Vāmadeva, Vṛṣākapi, Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Bahurūpa, and Mahat.
The ten Rudras have been declared; now hear, O twice-born one, of the six Ādityas: Urukrama, Śakra, Vivasvat, and Varuṇa.
O best of the twice-born, Parjanya has been mentioned as the sixth; however, those distinct from Parjanya have been stated to be exactly five, without a doubt.
"O Lord of Birds, it has been said that Parjanya is equal to the Gaṅgā; likewise are Savitṛ, Aryaman, Dhātṛ, Pūṣan, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Bhaga."
Forty-seven are proclaimed as the great [channels]; it should be understood that two are mentioned, namely Pravaha and Ativaha.
Likewise, O Lord of Birds, the Viśvedevas are to be known as tenfold; hear their names: Purūravas and Ārdrava are the first two.
Two were known as Dhūri and Locana; two were named Kratu and Dakṣa; two were named Satya and Vasu; and two were named Kāma and Kālaka.
Thus, the Viśvedevas are proclaimed to be known as tenfold; likewise, the group of Ṛbhus is mentioned, as well as the three types of ancestors (pitṛs).
Heaven and Earth are to be understood as these eighty-six [deities]; all the gods were born from them, being fashioned from the nostrils.
The lord of space (ākāśa), however, is well-proclaimed as Gaṇapa; those who know the meaning of reality should understand that he is the presiding deity (abhimānin) in both cases.
Except for Viṣvaksena, all the attendants of Viṣṇu, beginning with Jaya, became equal to him and were no longer inferior to Viṣvaksena thereafter.
These too are intermediate regulators of the nose; therefore, they are proclaimed as inferior to those who possess the realization of reality.
O Lord, he who was the conceited ego of the principle of touch was declared to be Apāna; and he who was the conceited ego of form was born as the great Vyāna.
Udāna is of the nature of taste, and Samāna is named after smell; these four Maruts are proclaimed as the lords of the waters.
O Lord of Birds, I shall now describe those who arose immediately after Jaya and the others; among them, Pāvaka is declared to be the first-born at the forefront of Pradhāna.
And the son of the great seer Bhṛgu is declared to be Cyavana; and the son of Bṛhaspati is celebrated as Utathya.
Raivata and Cākṣuṣa, as well as Svārociṣa, are recorded; likewise Uttama, Brahmasāvarṇi, and Rudrasāvarṇi.
Devasāvarṇi, Sāvarṇi, Indrasāvarṇi, as well as Dakṣasāvarṇi, and Dharmasāvarṇi.
"Thus, O bird, eleven types of Manus have been proclaimed; and the seven [groups] of Pitṛs, and so forth, were likewise born."
O twice-born one, listen to those who were born immediately after them, who were inferior to them: Gaṅgā, the wife of Varuṇa, and the sun-god named Parjanya.
Yamabhāryā is Śyāmalā, the beloved of Aniruddha and Virāṭ; she alone, who considers herself the vessel of the universe, is well-known by the name Uṣā.
Rohiṇī is said to be the wife of the Moon, while Saṃjñā is the wife of the Sun; these six, beginning with Gaṅgā, were born from the son of Vinatā.
Immediately after Gaṅgā and the others was born Svāhā, the deity of the mantra; she is called Svāhā, the wife of Agni, and is heard to be inferior to Gaṅgā and the rest.
Svāhā’s younger brother is to be known as Jñānātman, named Budha; this Budha, the son of Candra, is remembered as being inferior to Svāhā.
O bird, after Budha, one named Uṣā was likewise born; she who is called Uṣā is celebrated as the proud wife of the Aśvins.
She should be known as the lowest of the wise; there is no need for further deliberation on this point. From her was born Śanaiścara, renowned as the soul of the earth.
Uṣadhamas is to be known; from him Puṣkara was born. He is to be known as Karmābhimānin, who is called Śanaiścara.
Having thus created the gods who take pride in the principles (tattvas), Hari himself, the Lord of Gods, entered into those principles together with Ramā.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Deities Presiding over the Principles and Their Relative Hierarchy," in the Brahma-kāṇḍa, the third part of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Lord of Birds, those presiding deities over their respective principles remain in each of those principles, within their own abodes and their own limbs, for that purpose.
They began to properly praise Hari Nārāyaṇa; for in Viṣṇu, whose qualities are both conceivable and inconceivable, all virtues exist even where they appear contradictory.
"Indeed, each one of those [qualities] is infinite; where is my power to praise their virtues? Thinking thus, she spoke while bowing her head in modesty.
Śrī said: "O Lord, I bow at Your lotus feet; I know nothing other than Your feet. O God of gods, all qualities—whether heard or unspoken—reside in You, the Sovereign."

O Govinda, O Dāmodara, having properly created [this world] and granted me my own abode, protect me; for there is no beloved person other than you who is so full of happiness as I am through this hymn of praise.

Brahmā said: O Lord of Lakṣmī, abode of the entire universe, you are an ocean of knowledge; where, O you whose form is the universe, am I, ignorant as I am? Indeed, you possess power, whereas I am truly ignorant and my power is indeed meager.
O Abode of the World, by Your grace, Lakṣmī indeed possesses knowledge, dispassion, and devotion toward me at all times; yet, O Viṣṇu, she never possesses lordship over me.

O Murāri, grant me this forever: that I may attain only this much—the realization that "I" and "mine" are merely objects to be known; O Lord of Ramā, in those of worthy virtue there is neither negligence nor non-existence today, but only eternity.

Therefore, let my senses always fall at Your lotus feet rather than upon the path of the unrighteous; for I am destitute of even a ten-millionth part of Lakṣmī’s qualities—I have no capacity to praise You, so be graciously pleased with me.

Thus, standing before him with palms joined in reverence, the Creator, seated upon Tārkṣya, offered this hymn of praise for Viṣṇu’s qualities; and then the high-souled Vāyu, the god of gods, his heart overflowing with devotion, beheld Viṣṇu.

With a voice choked with affection, his syllables faltering as he shed tears, Vāyu spoke with palms joined in reverence: "For these gods have become your servants; [they seek] your supreme lotus-feet, which are so difficult to attain."

O Lord of the Universe, I constantly pray for the fourfold aims of human life; and having seen this, O God, it is indeed the Māyā of Hari that is the cause of them, and there is nothing else whatsoever.

Therefore, O Infinite One, though I am not even a donor, I am eager to hear the lotus feet of Your Honor, for I am one who has turned away from Kṛṣṇa, whose conduct is devoid of merit, and who is deeply distressed by his own actions.

O Lord, your descent is for the sake of bestowing grace upon you; there is no other human purpose for you whatsoever, except through these preeminent incarnations for the benefit of cows, brahmins, trees, and likewise the gods.

O Vāsudeva, while performing your sports, you provide security and assistance and nothing else; yet our minds are not satiated even as we recite the nectar-like deeds of you, the crown jewel of those who perform auspicious acts.

O Mukunda, grant me constant devotion at your lotus feet, for my devotion to you is never severed. O God of gods, may there be nothing else for me anywhere except that very [devotion] wherein You abide as the Supreme Person.
And by your grace, O Great Lord, I am where you are; this deception has occurred within my very body, as has the four-faced one, and not by others.
O Lord, my sleep shall be your salutation; my walking about shall be circumambulation; and my speaking shall be praise—knowing this, I offer myself.
And seeing that all objects worthy of my veneration are indeed images of Hari, I shall always worship those who reside there as forms of Hari, O God of gods, having reflected thus.

Whatever sandalwood, whatever flowers, incense, clothing, and whatever food, both solid and soft, there may be—all this shall indeed always be performed as a vow solely for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu.

O Murāri, I shall always revile those who are not Vaiṣṇavas and protect the true Vaiṣṇavas; I shall cut out the tongues of those who hate Viṣṇu, and for those who hear that, I shall fill their ears with molten lead.

O Lord Viṣṇu, by Your grace I possess such power as this, even though I am but a brahmin; nevertheless, I am not capable of praising You, for I am indeed destitute of even a ten-millionth part of Lakṣmī’s qualities.
Indeed, one should pray for this hymn, so that there may always be for me inexhaustible joy therein. Those who recite this hymn here in the world are truly Vaiṣṇavas and dear to Hari.
Those who constantly perform this recitation and always offer it to Hari—to them Hari is pleased; for when Keśava is fully satisfied, what is there that cannot be obtained?

Having praised him thus, the high-souled Baladeva stood silent before Hari with palms joined in reverence. Sarasvatī said: "O Blessed One, O Murāri, O Hari, who indeed is a connoisseur of aesthetic flavor [rasajña] other than through the praising or chanting of Your qualities?"

O God of gods, who are eternally praised by Brahmā and the other deities, may one attain the realization of sufficiency—that which, having entered the channel of a person's ear, cuts through the craving for the body that leads to worldly existence.

It does not merely sever the pleasure of the body; it constantly severs the affection for false houses, fields, wives, and sons, as well as for cattle and other forms of wealth, and even for priceless jewels.
Even though Lakṣmī was bestowed by you, she does not know your true nature; neither does the four-faced Brahmā know it, nor does this Vāyu; what is there to be surprised at in that?
O Lord, where is my power to offer praise for one such as You? Compared to Brahmā and Vāyu, I am always inferior by hundreds of qualities; therefore, O Hari, protect me out of compassion.
Having thus praised Hari, O lord of birds, she became silent; then Bhāratī began to praise Hari.

Bhāratī said: O Brahmā, Lord of Śiva, Lord of Lakṣmī, Hari, Murāri! For one who has constant faith in your qualities, as they thus praise you, their mind—which was previously ever-increasingly attached to unreal objects—[becomes transformed].
O God of gods, they first cultivate detachment from that world, and thereafter likewise develop firm devotion; and after that, O Lord, they constantly bring about the grace of Hari.

Therefore, that [realization] becomes direct for him; hence, my delight lies in praising the virtues. Once that [delight] has been produced in a person, it constantly cuts through the suffering of saṃsāra.

It bestows upon its qualified practitioner the fruit known as the nature of bliss once suffering has been severed; and for those who praise the qualities of Hari, it likewise destroys their sins as well as their merits.

Having understood this, the Supreme Guru, the compassionate Vāyu, who is dear to me, [revealed] the qualities of Hari—the expansion of all virtues—which are suitable for me alone and consist primarily of bliss.
Like a kinsman to the distressed, Śiva has rescued our auspicious fame as if from merits; and by your grace, by the grace of Śrī, and by the grace of Vāyu, it remains eternally ours.
Whatever the wind always does, that very thing the god always and eternally does; the god does not create opposition to the wind, yet he creates opposition to that [opposition] eternally.
The wind does not oppose Hari, nor does Viṣṇu oppose the wind; by the grace of the wind, nothing adverse exists for me, and by your grace, there is freedom from fear for you as well.

Just as there is no suffering and so forth in the root, so too there is none in the descent [of the Lord]; the wind and the others, as well as Mukunda—both of these are not of the nature of suffering during their descents.

The divine Vāyu appears as if powerless while protecting the worldly dharmas according to the requirements of the ages; however, it should not be thought that there is any lack of power in the Lord Murāri when he has descended as a human.

O God of gods, those possessed of wisdom should not contemplate the suffering of Yama and the like during an incarnation; once, I went to a place where happiness was destroyed in order to slay the Daityas.

It should not be thought that, because of this, there is no constant destruction of my suffering by Vāyu; for what power is there in me, Madhusūdana, Lord, to praise such qualities? O God, I am inferior to Vāyu in quality, whether in the form of worldly existence or in the state of liberation.
Having praised him thus, O Lord of Birds, Bhāratī became silent; immediately thereafter, Śeṣa, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to Keśava.

Śeṣa said: "Neither do I know the soles of your feet, nor does Rudra know them, nor does Garuḍa know them. I am deficient by a hundredfold part of Vāṇī's [merit]; having offered this abode, protect me, O Vāsudeva!"
Having praised him thus, O Lord of Birds, Viśa, who was born immediately after him, remained silent for a moment and then began to offer praise.

Garuḍa said: What praise can I offer to your feet, when my mind is already fixed upon your lotus-feet? How can I, born from the womb of a bird, be capable of praising you who possess such qualities? How indeed am I able to extol you?
Having praised him thus, Garuḍa became silent, filled with devotion; immediately thereafter, Rudra began to offer praise.

Rudra said: "O Lord, O Blessed One, O Infinite One, we truly do not know that devotion of yours; may it be mine at the root of the auspicious lotus-feet of Śiva. Yet, O God, even though it is ever present, it does not manifest for me; therefore, out of ignorance, I have acted against you."

O Hari, O Murāri, what power do I have—a person of dull intellect—to speak before You who are endowed with all-encompassing wisdom? O Lord, protect me, who am forever devoid of speech even by a hundredfold measure; grant me my abode and Yourself as well.
Having praised him in this way, that Rudra, the best of the twice-born, became silent; then the goddess Śeṣānantarajā Vāruṇī spoke these words.
Vāruṇī said: O Lord of Lakṣmī, Lord of Brahmā, Lord of Manu, Lord of Speech, Lord of Rudra, Lord of men! Neither Pārvatī nor the consort of Suparṇa is capable of praising your virtues.
I am ten times inferior even to Śeṣa; O Lord of the worlds, protect me eternally!
Having praised her thus, O Lord of Birds, Vāruṇī became silent; thereupon Brāhmī, born after her, began to speak to Suparṇī.

Saugandhī said: O Hari, Lord of the Universe, my voice is not capable of praising Your qualities, nor is my hearing capable of listening to Your stories, O Hari. O God, who indeed on this earth knows that Supreme Reality, Your own true nature, which even he who meditates upon it cannot fully comprehend?
Therefore, there is no power in praising your virtues; I am always inferior by ten qualities, O Lord of Sages.
Having praised him thus, O Lord of Birds, Sauparṇī became silent; then Girijā, who was born after Rudra, began to offer praise.
Pārvatī said: "O Govinda, Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, indeed I have no need whatsoever for you, O Lord; nor even by name, for he who possesses the form of good fortune is always one and only."

O Nārāyaṇa, your single name alone is supremely capable in the power of dispassion and devotion; it is sufficient for the destruction of the countless slayings of Brahmās and the like, and even for the destruction of ten million wives of gurus.
O Great Lord, I am merely the presiding deity over names and qualities; I have no power in praising You, for I am inferior to Rudra by tenfold.
"And I am always inferior; there is no need for further deliberation on this point. Having praised him thus, O Lord of Birds, that daughter of the Mountain became silent.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Hierarchy of Deities and the Praise of Viṣṇu Performed by the Various Deities Who Preside over the Principles," in the Brahma-kāṇḍa, within the third part (Uttara-bhāga) of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 7.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Immediately after Pārvatī, Indra spoke these words. Indra said: "O God of gods, O wielder of the discus, they say that for one who knows Your true nature in his heart yet remains eager only to offer praise because he is deluded—that very act of praising one who does not truly know You is called an insult."
Nevertheless, it would have been meritorious for you to have used that [name] first; since there was no power to praise Rudra and the others at that time, should one not rather say, "I have none"?
In terms of his share of qualities, Kāmadeva is always ten times inferior to Rudra; yet he is equal to me in knowledge and strength, and likewise, Kāma is always my messenger.
Having thus praised Hari, the God of gods, Brahmā—the son born immediately after him, who is of the nature of ego—stood silent with palms joined and head bowed, and then spoke.
Ahaṅkārika said: Homage to you, who are full of all the hosts; homage to you, whose form is knowledge; homage to you, who are far removed from ignorance, the Brahman whose form is the eternal truth.

"O Immeasurable One, it has been said that I am always ten times inferior to Indra; indeed, I have never been born as your equal. Nevertheless, O Teacher of the World, protect me, O Viṣṇu, by granting me a divine abode."
Having thus praised the one born of ego (Ahaṅkāra), he became silent; immediately thereafter, Śacī, born after him, spoke these words to offer praise.

Śacī said: I meditate incessantly upon your lotus feet, enriched with the emblems of the thunderbolt, the goad, the banner, and the lotus. O Lord, I remember the dust of your feet, which cannot be grasped even by the masters of speech through their minds at all times.
O compassionate one, you who are kind to your devotees, protect me who am always deficient in the ten qualities derived from the ego-sense and the vital breaths.
Having praised him thus, the divine lady Śacī became silent; immediately thereafter, Rati began to offer praise.

Rati said: I meditate upon the lotus-face of Nṛhari, who assumed a physical form out of a mind compassionate toward his servants—a face which is the abode of Śrī, which is cherished by the undecaying Rudra, Ramā, and others, and which is graced by a mass of curling locks of hair.

"O Blessed One, even Śacī herself has no power to praise your face such as this; protect me always! Having offered this praise with supreme devotion, Rati remained silent right there in the presence of the Blessed One."
Dakṣa, born immediately after Rati, began to offer praise.

Dakṣa said: I meditate with devotion upon the sacred ford (tīrtha) originating from the feet of the Blessed One, which was sprinkled by the Unborn (Aja) and is worthy of worship by the Unborn and others; from the purification of which issued the incarnation of the foremost of the Unborn, that sacred ford named Gaṅgā, which became the most excellent among rivers.

Even Rudra, by the dust of Your feet—purified by that very mass of matted locks which he bore upon his head—became auspicious from being inauspicious. O Lord of Compassion, Viṣṇu, incarnation of grace, I have no power to praise such a foot of Yours. Though I have heard of it as equal to Rati, I have not attained liberation; therefore, protect me, O embodiment of the primordial cause!
Having praised him thus, Dakṣa became silent; immediately thereafter, Bṛhaspati began to offer praise.
Bṛhaspati said: "I constantly meditate upon your lotus-like face; O Lord, grant me detachment from the objects of the senses."
If indeed the soul (jīva) possesses power over these—being the agent, the enjoyer, and always the giver—then wives, sons, friends, and cattle will all likewise perish; therefore, cut it off quickly.

O Lord, it is precisely by wandering through the wheel of saṃsāra that I have experienced the suffering of existence and have come here; I have no power to create anew, O God of gods, so protect me always, eternally, and with truth.
Having heard this, the Sage remained in supreme silence; immediately thereafter, Aniruddha began to offer praise.

Aniruddha said: Thus, having abandoned the delightful stories of Hari, you are constantly deluded by the vulva and the mouth of women; indeed, with a perverted intellect, you remain forever a sensualist dwelling like a boar within a hole filled with excrement and entrails.

O Murāri, O Lord, when I fell into and drank that which was filled with marrow, bones, bile, phlegm, feces, and so forth, its mouth being wrapped in skin and entrails—the fact that I did not experience [the resulting] state of sin is due to Your supreme power of illusion (māyā), O All-pervading One.

Mounted upon this body—which perpetually revolves in the wheel of saṃsāra, which is of the nature of intense suffering and devoid of even a trace of happiness, and which vomits impurity through its nine gates—the one of utterly deluded intellect [remains].

O Lord, I perpetually bow to you, abandoning that nectar of your discourse which destroys the very root of the Vedas—while constantly supporting my family, making no offerings and the like, and dwelling in my home.
Keep this impurity of saṃsāra far away and always bestow upon me this divine nectar of your discourse; for even as Śacī’s equal, I am not capable of praising the flood of your excellent qualities.
Having praised him in this way, O Lord of Birds, Aniruddha became silent; thereafter, his son, the mind-born Svāyambhuva, uttered a hymn of praise.
Svāyambhuva said: "Even for one who has entered into praise, there is no suffering of the womb; therefore, I have attained your most worshipful state."

Manu’s wife was Mānavī; Yama is the lord of Saṃyaminī; the moon is the presiding deity of the quarters, while the sun is the eye that governs them. Indeed, these are equal to one another, having transcended worldly existence itself.
"Know this, O bird: he is twice the size of the current [of the river]. Immediately after the Sun, Varuṇa began to offer praise."

Varuṇa said: "In the body-house fashioned by your own will—toward son, wife, wealth, and the various kinds of possessions—all people, being deluded by the meager intellect that thinks 'this is mine' and 'I am this,' sink down into the suffering of saṃsāra."

Therefore, O Hari, destroy such evil-mindedness in me and grant me the state of being Your servant at Your feet; for I am forever devoid of even half the qualities found in the foot of Manu, O Murāri.
Having thus offered praise, Varuṇa stood before him with palms joined in reverence; and Nārada, who was born immediately after Varuṇa, likewise praised Hari.

Nārada said: O Viṣṇu, by hearing and chanting Your name, there remains for me no other reality that is sweet; therefore, purify me so that Your name, which is higher than the highest, may dwell upon the tip of my tongue.
He on whose tip of the tongue the name of Hari does not exist is no Brahmin at all; he is indeed like an ox or a donkey. I do not know your true nature, for I am always inferior even to Varuṇa.
Having thus praised the God of gods, Nārada, the lord of birds, became silent; then the high-souled Bhṛgu, who appeared immediately after Nārada, proceeded to offer praise.

Bhṛgu said: What seat can there be for you who possess the Garuḍa-throne? What ornament for you who are adorned by the Kaustubha gem? What gift can there be for you whose wife is Lakṣmī? O Lord of Speech, what is there left for you to say? Therefore, I do not know your true virtues, for I am eternally lame compared to Varuṇa.
Having thus praised the god Hari, Bhṛgu became silent; immediately thereafter, Agni indeed praised Puruṣottama.
Agni said: "By your splendor, my own brilliance being fully kindled, I carry the oblation sprinkled with clarified butter to the sacrifice."
Having entered your belly by means of my own brilliance, I always digest food with full power; therefore, I do not know your excellent qualities, O Bhṛgu, for I am always equal to you in this regard.
Immediately after that, the offspring began to offer praise.

Prasūti said: Even the sages are always bewildered in their investigation of the meaning of Your names; even the gods, though terrified of You, remain constantly in the company of women; and Māndhātṛ, Dhruva, Nārada, the Bhṛgus, Vaivasvata, and all others—out of love, I bow to Him, the benefactor Viṣṇu; salutations to Him!
Therefore, I do not know your excellent qualities; what power do I always possess to describe them? Having thus offered praise, O Lord of Birds, Prasūti remained silent.
Agni is the son of Brahmā whose essence is speech, as is the sage Bhṛgu; and their wife is Prasūti—these three are remembered as being equal.
Those from Varuṇa are deficient by one-quarter; those from Pravaha are twice as inferior; those from Dakṣa are known to be less than a hundred; but those from Mitra are twice as superior.
Immediately after his birth, Vasiṣṭha, the delighter of Brahmā, bowed down with humility and began to offer praise.

Vasiṣṭha said: Homage be to that Puruṣa, the Creator; homage, homage to the cutter away of the wicked and the thorns of existence. Homage, homage to Him who is born from His own limbs; O Lord, I am eternally bowed before Your lotus feet.
"O Blessed One Vāsudeva, protect me always; for I am forever inferior to Agni, and I am always somewhat inferior to Mitra. Having thus praised the god, he remained silent there.
