Marīci, the son of Brahmā who was born immediately after Vasiṣṭha, praised his preceptor Nārāyaṇa with supreme devotion.

Marīci said: "My intellect has been struck down by Your Majesty through attachment to worldly existence, and my senses have become averse to the departure from all that is inauspicious. Yet, by speaking of even a tiny fragment of a mere trace of pleasure, I constantly direct my mind toward You; thus, I shall continue to perform inauspicious deeds."
Such am I, the Lord Ananta, always exactly equal to Vasiṣṭha.
Having praised him thus, O bird, Marīci then became silent; in that interval, Atri, with palms joined in reverence, praised Hari while suppressing his internal passion.

Your essential nature, which has descended for the sake of protecting the world that manifests from you, is likewise faultless and immutable; it is rooted in the reality of the ultimate truth, unchanging, and its very essence is bliss, and for that reason alone, it is devoid of transformation.

O Blessed One, that which is devoid of the three qualities (traiguṇya) and yet pervades all things—having entered into that, one truly does not see anything. Therefore, like a mere spark (marīci), I am unable to praise your excellent qualities, O Enemy of Mura.
Having praised him thus, O bird, Atri then became silent; immediately thereafter, his son Angiras spoke these words in order to offer praise.

Aṅgiras said: "I am indeed unable to behold your true form, with its infinite arms, bellies, and heads; adorned with thousands of infinite crowns and beautified by various costly ornaments. Being thus incapable of praising such a boundless form, I am utterly exhausted here."
O Lord of Birds, having thus offered praise, Aṅgiras became silent; immediately thereafter, Pulastya spoke these words in order to offer praise.

Pulastya said: That Blessed Lord Hari reveals to his devotees the world which is the most auspicious of all auspicious things; salutations to you, the Blessed Puruṣa, who is the protector when there is the risk of falling into the realms of hell.
I am unable to praise such virtues of yours; protect me, O Blessed One, for you are indeed equal to Aṅgiras.
Having praised him in this way, Pulastya became silent; immediately thereafter, his younger brother Pulaha spoke these words in order to offer praise.

Pulaha said: "The great-souled ones declare that for one who has abandoned the form of desire, the bathing with excellent water, the offering of fruits, flowers, and food, the worship of the Blessed One, and the performance of virtuous rites—all these would become fruitless."

I perpetually bow down to that Blessed One with a constant mind free from desire, possessing only the thought of offering myself to You. O Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, O Blessed One, I have no power for Your praise; I am like a mere blade of grass—of this there is no doubt.
Having thus offered praise, O bird, Pulaha then became silent; immediately thereafter, Kratu began to offer praise.

Kratu said: O Blessed One, at the time of the departure of the vital breath, it is Your names alone that destroy the worldly suffering of transmigration; I take refuge in Him by whom, having suddenly cast off the impurity of a single birth, one attains stainless liberation.
Even those who, overcome by devotion to Viṣṇu, utter His name alone as their sole refuge, quickly attain liberation; how much more so those who constantly meditate upon Him?
O Lord of Birds, having praised him in this way, Kratu became silent; immediately thereafter, Vaivasvata Manu spoke to offer praise.

Vaivasvata said: "Indeed, I was always devoted to the performance of ritual acts, intent upon the enjoyment of women, and intoxicated by my own anus; I was devoted to the organ of taste and to beholding you, yet now I am perfectly possessed of dispassion through supreme fear."

O Blessed One, may I always maintain devotion toward this body composed of flesh, bone, marrow, and blood, as well as toward thieves; and toward my guru, fire, the submarine fire, and the sun, may I attain perfect detachment from them through suffering—please endure this eternally.

I have supreme power in hearing the worldly rumors concerning Nārāyaṇa, yet I have no power at all in bowing down to him; I have supreme power in following after the people of the world, yet I have indeed supreme incapacity in traveling the paths to sacred fields and the like.
O Murāri, there is supreme power even among wealthy Vaiśyas and others, yet alas, there is no power even among virtuous Brāhmaṇas!
Having praised the god Vaivasvata Manu, he became silent; thereupon Viśvāmitra, his immediate successor, began to offer praise.

Viśvāmitra said: The lotus-feet of the Blessed One were not meditated upon, nor was the twilight prayer performed; even that Dharma capable of splitting open the door-panel of ignorance was not acquired. Your story, which is skillful in destroying the afflictions within, has been heard by me; O Lord, protect me always with your hearing, for I am like a child.
Having praised Viśvāmitra in this manner, the Ṛṣi became silent; indeed, the sons of Brahmā departed, leaving behind Bhṛgu, Nārada, and Dakṣa.
The seven in number beginning with Vasiṣṭha, as well as Viśvāmitra—these are recorded as being equal to Manu Vaivasvata himself.
Even those who are eternally inferior to fire, yet superior in virtues to their friends—O Lord of Birds, listen as I shall recite the hymn to that Infinite One.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Relative Hierarchy in the Praise of the Gods and Others," in the *Brahmakāṇḍa*, the third part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī-Gāruḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
In the *Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*:
After the sacrifice (*kratu*), Mitra was born.
O Lord of Birds, he began to praise Nārāyaṇa, the source of the universe.

Mitra said: "I, ignorant as I am, bow at your lotus feet, which sever worldly existence and grant auspiciousness for the cessation of existence. The Blessed Lord Vāsudeva himself knows [this]; neither I, nor Agni, nor the three gods, nor the lords of sages know it."

Furthermore, when even other foremost devotees do not know [the truth], how much less others? O Lord, who is higher than all, protect me eternally; for I am always indeed inferior to Viśvāmitra. I am always only twice the strength of Parjanya; therefore, I have no power to offer praise to You.
Having thus praised Hari, Mitra then became silent, O bird; immediately thereafter, Tārā began to offer praise.
Tārā said:
"But those who practice firm devotion with undivided intent, having abandoned all ritual actions for your sake and having renounced their own kin and relatives,"
O Viṣṇu, having heard (or seen) this discourse centered upon you, these virtuous ones listen and speak [of it], being entirely free from all attachments.
"O Lord, protect her who has fallen into their midst, for she is always like a friend. Then Anantaja and Nirṛti spoke to the Lord of Birds.

Nirṛti said: "By means of yoga, and by devotion offered to you, people attain the supreme goal; likewise, O Lord, through the service of those preeminent in all virtues, and through knowledge joined with dispassion."

"By the very restraint of the mind, people go to the supreme state of Viṣṇu; therefore, O Lord, protect me always with compassion, you who are equal to Tārā. Immediately after that, she began to praise him.

Pravāhi said: "O son, by your prowess and through your grace, supreme prosperities come as a matter of course; for those who serve the discourses which are the elixir of the Lord of Excellent Fame shall indeed be established on the path to liberation."
O God of gods, may there always be devotion; yet I am ever equal to Nirṛti. Those who recite [this] along with the Bhāṣya and Koma are proclaimed as the speakers.
Koṇādhipa, Nirṛti, Prāvahī, and Pravahapriyā—these four are proclaimed to be three times more powerful than Parjanya.

Immediately after him, O Lord of Birds, I shall describe those born in succession; listen to them. Viṣvaksena, the son born after Pravāha’s wife, a highly fortunate attendant of Hari and son of Vāyu, proceeded to praise Hari.
Viṣvaksena said: If Lord Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of liberation, is indeed eternal perfect bliss, and if there exists supreme devotion that serves as the means for attaining direct perception of Him;
Likewise, if there is sincere devotion toward one's own guru and toward all holy beings up to the level of Brahmā, in accordance with their respective worthiness;
O bird, if you should feel affection and mindfulness toward living beings such as the tulasī plant, then you will certainly become immortal; of this there is no doubt.

Having thus praised Viṣvaksena, the greatly powerful and illustrious one, Garuḍa became silent with palms joined and neck bowed; "I am indeed inferior to Mitra—there is no need for further deliberation on this point."
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Praise of Viṣṇu by Gālava, Mātaṅga, Tṛṇabindu, and Dhruva," concerning the deities and their origins, in the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa said: O Kṛṣṇa of great intellect, tell me of the nature of the Unborn (Ajā) and her offspring; O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to explain those others as well in due order.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: The deities known as the *aja* are those born within the various lineages of the gods; for those *aja* deities are indeed superior to the *karman*-deities.
Virādha, Cārudeṣṇa, as well as Citraratha, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Kiśora, Hūhū, and likewise Hāhā.
Vidyādhara, Ugrasena, Viśvāvasu, Parāvasu, Citrasena, Gopāla, and Bala are recorded as the fifteen.
O Lord of Birds, these and other Gandharvas, numbering in the hundreds, should be known as being equal to the Ajānajas both in liberation and in saṃsāra.
But those gods born of my ignorance are a hundred times inferior to those born of my karma: Ghṛtācī, Menakā, Rambhā, Urvaśī, and Tilottamā.
Suketu, Śabarī, Mañjughoṣā, Piṅgalā, and others—these are proclaimed together as the jewels among yakṣas.
For these—Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, and Cyavana—are indeed born from non-birth; they are inferior by a hundredfold to those born of karma.
O Lord of Birds, after Utathya and the sage had consecrated these [princes], the high-souled rishis declared them to be equal to the unborn Brahmā.
Śatarcin is to be known as Kaśyapa, Madhyama as Parāśara, Pāvamānya as Pragātha, and Devala as Kṣudrasūkta.
Gṛtsamada, Āsuri, Bharadvāja, and Mudgala; Uddālaka, Ṛśyaśṛṅga, Śaṅkha, and likewise Satyavrata.
Suyajña Bābhravya, Māṇḍūka Bāṣkala, the teacher of dharma Agastya, as well as Dālbhya and Dārḍhyacyuta.
Kavaṣa, Harita, Kaṇva, Virūpa, Musala, as well as Viṣṇuvṛddha Ātreya, Śrīvatsa, and Vatsala.
Bhārgava, Āpnavāna, and likewise Māṇḍūkeya; Maṇḍka, Jābācali, and Vītihavya as well.
Gṛtsamada, Śaunaka, and others are remembered as the sages (ṛṣis); by the mere hearing of their names, Hari is always pleased.
And I speak of eighteen thousand; listen, O Tārkṣya, regarding my wives. As for those eighteen thousand who are the sons of Agni and my wives, they are indeed equal to the unborn;
there should be no doubt about this.
Among them, Tvaṣṭṛ’s daughter Kaśerū was the most distinguished in her qualities; I shall now describe those born after her—listen well, O Lord of Birds.
The Pitṛs other than these seven Ājānas are fewer by a hundred; for it is the opinion of those who know the Veda that the Pitṛs are indeed superior.
Immediately after that, O best of the twice-born, listen as I describe the kings: from the eight [classes], there were one hundred and eight divine Gandharvas.
The attendants of the gods, however, possess a hundredfold greater bliss than them; indeed, these hosts are always to be commanded by the gods through their own mouths as if with their own faces.
The gods and gandharvas are declared [to be superior], and they are a hundred times inferior to those; from them, the rulers of the earth are to be known as inferior by hundreds of degrees.

From them, the supreme hosts among humans should be known as a hundredfold greater. Having thus spoken incidentally, I shall now follow the main subject: in this way, the gods beginning with Brahmā, and even those beginning with Lakṣmī, are entirely [subject to this].
Having offered praise, O twice-born one, they all stood silent with their palms joined in reverence.
Thus praised, the Lord of Gods, the imperishable Blessed Hari, reflected in his mind upon granting them a dwelling place.
This is purifying, health-giving, meritorious, and the destroyer of sin; it generates grace from Hari and is the means for attaining the bliss of one's true nature.
But those men here, O brahmins, who do not recite this hymn and do not constantly hear it—they are all indeed practitioners of illusion.
Those lowest of men who constantly eat without remembering [the deity] within always consume excrement that is perpetually infested with hundreds of worms.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Hierarchy of Deities and the Praise of Viṣṇu by the Gods," in the Brahma-kāṇḍa of the third (Uttara) section of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, Chapter Ten:
Garuḍa said: When the Lord Viṣṇu, the Blessed One and Master of the Sāttvatas, was thus praised by the gods, what kind of refuge did the Great Lord provide before entering into them?
I wish to know this, O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Great Lord; tell me correctly, O Compassionate One, if it is worthy of my ears.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Into those principles the Blessed One, the Great Lord, entered; the Blessed Hari, who is beyond all worldly ties, caused them to tremble.
In the beginning, the Blessed One created the golden cosmic egg, which extends fifty crores of yojanas in every direction.
Above that, there exists a golden image of the same size as the minute atom; beyond that, however, lies the ground of fifty crores [of yojanas].
Thus, its parts are proclaimed to be one hundred koṭis; and it is encircled on all sides by seven coverings.
The first enclosure of the great-souled Pāvaka consists of ten thousand koṭis; the second enclosure is likewise to be known.
The third enclosure of the great-souled Hara is to be known as that which is surrounded on all sides by the waters multiplied tenfold.
Surrounded on all sides by ten more than that [number] of fires, this fourth enclosure should be known, O Great Lord, as being even greater than the sky.
Thus, surrounded on all sides by those who are ten times the size of Hara, the fifth enclosure is to be known as that which is called the Ego (ahaṅkāra).
O Lord of Birds, that which surrounds the sky on all sides with a tenfold increase is declared to be the sixth enclosure, the Great Principle (mahat-tattva).
O Lord, the seventh enclosure, which is ten times the size of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) and surrounds it on all sides, is said to be the enclosure of the three qualities (triguṇa).
It is proclaimed to be ten times greater than the principle of Mahat; and immediately following the principle of Mahat, Tamas is indeed remembered as the veil.
It is proclaimed to be superior to the principle of Mahat by five qualities; and from that, Rajas is known to be twofold, for it is remembered as the veil.
And from that, the supreme obscuration of the *sattva* should be known as twofold; thus, these three combined together are declared to be a single obscuration.
Immediately after that, space (ākāśa) is described as being called "unmanifest" (avyākṛta); and within that, the imperishable Hari dwells, devoid of all boundaries.
The eighth enclosure is the Virajā river, situated between the two voids; it is five yojanas wide and encircles [the center] on all sides.
"There exists that which is to be known as most meritorious, the destroyer of worldly saṃsāra; thus, O bird, the Four-faced One was then filled with joy."
Having all bathed thoroughly in the Virajā river and cast off their subtle bodies (liṅgadeha), they thereafter attain liberation from Hari.
O son of Vinatā, know that the crossing of the Virajā river belongs only to those who possess direct perception and who go together with Brahman; it does not belong to others.
O Lord of Birds, O Brahman, for Vyāsa and others who possess direct perception, there is no crossing over the Virajā river, because their karma must still be experienced.
In this kalpa, however, for those who hold office together with Viriñca himself, there is, as a matter of rule, the complete exhaustion of all their *prārabdha* karma.
This is indeed so, there is no doubt; for others, there is no total destruction [of defilements]. Therefore, the cloth of those very ones who have crossed over passion shall become stainless.
For those who are attached to them, there is no crossing over the passionless state;
likewise, O Lord of Birds, because they possess such attachments, there is no destruction of all their undertakings.
Therefore, O Lord, there is no crossing of the Virajā river by any means; O Lord of Birds, at the time of dissolution, there is no merging into the Virajā river.
She should be known as being of the nature of Lakṣmī, the shatterer of the subtle body (liṅgadeha); she is fit for the state of Brahman. These are proclaimed as the gods named Ṛjus.
O Lord of Birds, each of those [beings] indeed exists as infinite and distinct groups; and with each of them individually, there are those worthy of liberation.
For there are indeed many living beings who, in every kalpa, create [beings] perfectly endowed with the thirty-two marks and fit for the state of Vāyu.
Those endowed with twenty-eight marks are the lords of the mountains (Śivas); those from twenty-four down to sixteen are known as the gods.
The Aṣṭakas are declared to be the sages (ṛṣis), and those fewer than them are the universal monarchs (cakravartins); this begins from the hundredth birth of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin.
It is declared to be direct perception; likewise, there is the exhaustion of what has been commenced. O twice-born one, by means of a single hundred kalpas, one attains the state of Vāyu.
After attaining the status of Brahmā over a hundred lifetimes, O Lord of Birds, he subsequently reaches the abode of Hari, beginning from forty Brahma-kalpas.

O observer of noble vows, even for Rudra, there shall be direct realization as well as the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma; after forty-one kalpas, he attains the state of being the Residue (*śeṣatva*).
He attains liberation together with Brahmā correctly and not otherwise; this begins from twenty kalpas of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin.
Even for Indra, there shall be direct realization, and likewise the exhaustion of his *prārabdha* karma; together with Brahmā himself, he goes to Hari Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme.
Garuḍa said: O Great Lord, beginning from the eighty-fifth Brahmakalpa, there shall be direct realization for Rudra as well, and likewise the exhaustion of his prārabdha karma.
"Thus have I heard, O Brahmin, as spoken by Brahmā to the beloved of Hari; yet what you have thus related, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, causes doubt to afflict me."
"Therefore, sever my doubt so that it may not arise again. Having heard those words of his, Kṛṣṇa spoke these words:

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: There is no contradiction whatsoever between what was spoken by Brahmā and what has been spoken by me; doubt exists for those with the vision of the ignorant, but for the wise, it does not exist at all.
O Lord of Birds, eighty-eight [sub-periods] are declared; and fifty-eight [others], O Lord of Birds; and forty [make up] a Brahmakalpa—thus spoke the Four-faced One.
Because the principles (tattvas) must be kept strictly secret, it was spoken thus by Brahmā in the past; this is indeed the intended meaning, and there is no doubt in this matter.
O twice-born one, those who understand the five hundred Brahmakalpas enter into blinding darkness; this truth, the absolute truth, has been spoken by me.
Immediately after Viraja was the Brahmin Ambaram, who was likewise prophesied; he too was boundless and shoreless, and Lakṣmī was his presiding deity.
O Great Lord, for one who lacks the counting of numbers, there is never any gift proclaimed by birth; of this there is no doubt.
Then Brahmā, who identifies with the cosmic egg, became known as Virāṭ; having thus fashioned this conception, the Lord, renowned as Hari, [proceeded].
In that place, O Garuḍa, Hari always remains, having ascended both below and above, distinguished by the gods who preside over the principles (tattvas).
Thus has the account of the primary creation been told; now hear, O King of Birds, about the secondary creation.
Garuḍa said: "O Hari, the creation was previously described by you, and it has been heard correctly by me."
O Lord, what indeed is to be known as the *prākṛta* (primary), and likewise, what is the *vaikṛta* (secondary)? Explain this to me in detail, for I have a great curiosity to hear it.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: From the unmanifest (avyakta) down to the earth, all those things that arise outside of the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) are declared to be material (prākṛta); by knowledge of them, one is liberated.
O Lord of Birds, the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is to be known as "modified" (vikṛta); that which is called "creation" by the wise is itself said to be the "modification."
Creation and dissolution, as well as worldly existence and devotion; the deities and the foremost of sages, and likewise the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ.
Extending through time without beginning or end, this flow of the world is always of one and the same nature; it is real and is by no means false in any way whatsoever.
But if they were to speak otherwise than this, they would indeed be destroyers of all; for this continuous flow of the world is real, and service to Hari is its purpose.
Truth, truth, and again truth—I raise my arm and declare: there is no scripture superior to the Vedas, and no deity higher than Keśava.
Those who abandon Keśava, the most excellent of all, and worship another, should be known as being in blind darkness—even if they are fathers or teachers.
Now listen, O Lord of Birds, to this supreme account of the secondary creation; he who understands it correctly in this world attains the highest state.

Thus, in the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, in the second part (*Dvitīyāṃśa*), in the section on Dharma (*Dharmakāṇḍa*), in the *Pretakalpa*, the tenth chapter titled "Description of the Primordial Creation and Certain Anomalies of the Cosmic Egg" concludes. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: The Lord known as Puruṣa, Hari himself, the Supreme Person (*Puruṣottama*), Viṣṇu, lay within the waters of the cosmic egg for a thousand years of men. Lakṣmī, in the form of water, was his bed, O son of Vinatā.
O Bhōṇḍaja, knowledge exists in the form of waves and in the form of wind.
In the form of darkness she alone existed; nothing else existed in any way whatsoever. And she existed within the waters of the cosmic egg; nothing else existed in any way whatsoever.
And in the ocean of the womb, O best of birds, Lakṣmī praised Hari; likewise, Prakṛti, along with Lakṣmī and Dhara, praised Hari in their respective forms.
Lying within the waters of the cosmic egg (garbhodaka) in the form of the Veda, he praises Hari: "O Nārāyaṇa, salutations be unto you; hear my petition."
"O illustrious one, slay the Unborn (ajā); bring liberation to those who are worthy. For the Unborn is declared to be Prakṛti, the lower nature, while there is also a higher nature."
Śatatarā is Brahmāṇī, the wife of Brahmā, who has a beautiful face; Umā is Śacī’s inferior, and those [others] are proclaimed to be even lower than her.
"O Hari, we never desire the slaughter of these women; for among men there exists the Brahman, and two natures (prakṛti) are established."
One [meaning] is eternally transmigrating and is denoted by the word "unborn" (aja); the second, however, is that which has dispelled darkness and is also denoted by the word "unborn."
Therefore, although she is proclaimed in the world as "Aje Jyeṣṭhā" (the Unborn Eldest), she bestows both pleasure and pain, while the other [form] bestows only suffering.
The attributes such as knowledge and sovereignty belong only to those who are qualified for liberation; that which veils them is proclaimed as the limb of darkness (tamaḥ).

O Lord, that which protects and covers Mahāviṣṇu with respect to the individual soul (jīva) should be known as the Supreme Nature (parā prakṛti); she is remembered as the Supreme Veiler (paramācchādikā).
Thus, that supreme wicked one is proclaimed as Ekā Tamoṅgā; O Bird, she exists only among the classes of living beings, and she is not found anywhere in Brahmā or the other [deities].

The two [energies] are designated as being like Piśācas for the sake of the individual soul (jīva), who is the qualified subject; however, I, the primordial goddess whose nature is bliss, am the impeller of those two.
In that regard, O illustrious Viṣṇu, you who are beneficial are the concealer of the one with attributes; O Great Lord, having indeed released yourself from the wicked supreme concealer.
O Great God, O Great Lord, grant liberation to Your devotees, for the Supreme Veil constantly obscures us who are perpetually wandering in saṃsāra.
Therefore, O illustrious Lord, let it be understood as my request: "For this very reason, because of its permanence, please remove that [obstacle]."
Thus praised, Hari Kṛṣṇa, though always perfectly awakened, appeared as if awakened, O Great One, for the sake of testing the ignorant.
From his navel there arose a golden lotus, the support of the worlds; it should be known as primordial (prākṛta), and the Earth-goddess is its presiding deity (abhimāninī).
And like the infinite sun, he is said to be the source of illumination; Viṣṇu consists of consciousness and bliss, and therefore he is not different from that—of this there is no doubt.
Those men who recognize [the world] as being the very nature of Viṣṇu go indeed to the lower world, as do those who associate with such people.
O Lord of Birds, the crown and other ornaments should be understood in this same way; there is no doubt that even the crowns and other such items belonging to Hari exist in two forms.

O Lord of Birds, both those that possess their own nature and those that do not are to be understood as being grasped when their respective natures are perceived; they are not [merely] their own nature.
For he created the cosmic egg there, which ordains all the worlds; and at the time of dissolution, being devoid of liberation, the wise one is said to be asleep.
O Lord of Birds, O highly fortunate one, the equality or inequality of those two should not be known; for indeed, even the dissolution of Brahmā and Vāyu does not exist.

Supreme knowledge, which is of the nature of the functional state [of the mind], is the water for the feet and the water for the guest-offering; of this there is no doubt. The cessation of the senses is called "sleep" by the wise.
O Lord of Birds, if Brahmā and Vāyu were indeed subject to the noose of Agni, how then can their state of being "unfallen" (avilīnatva) be spoken of?
Therefore, O Lord of Birds, that [distinction] between Brahman and the wind does not exist in reality; for the state known as deep sleep is indeed similar to the state of dreaming.
Understand from me that Brahman exists only in a figurative sense; therefore, O Lord of Birds, this [notion of existence] must not be accepted as real.
For those who understand reality, austerity is their eternal wealth. Śrī Garuḍa said: Since sleep is the effect of ignorance, it is declared that for them there is no sleep.
"O Lord, if you were to resolve this with the underlying intention that 'when there is a cause, then there is an effect,'" [it would not be so].
In that case, O illustrious one, tell me how fear and the like could arise for him; for even if fear and such were to exist, what loss would there be for us?
Thus addressed, Govinda spoke there as well regarding the cause: "Fear would be the product of ignorance; for here, indeed, the effect is without a cause."
Because one rejoices by realizing Brahman, deep sleep occurs therein; for if Brahman were ignorance and the like, it could never belong to that [state].
How might one appear happy? How will he act? Or how, up to the limit of liberation, is there the manifestation of knowledge? Tell me this.
O Great Lord, O Brahman, tell me: if that ignorance were not real, why would one listen to it with such great reverence?
Having heard these words of his, Kṛṣṇa spoke this speech: "O high-minded one, do not perceive his fear as being real."
Fear of me is seen in him, and it is solely for the sake of pleasing Hari; thus, his bowing has been described as being like that of one who possesses both fear and desire.
O Lord of Birds, since even a mere fraction of that [merit] has been attained by him, how could there be any suffering, ignorance, or the like in him? It cannot exist.
In accordance with Viṣṇu’s command, he imitates fear; by that, Hari is pleased—of this there is no doubt.
Brahmā hears [the sound] constantly; he is not ignorant merely because it is inconceivable. O Lord of Birds, Brahmā is never seen to be subject to suffering.
Even Brahmā, who might not know [the truth] and who acts solely for the sake of pleasing Hari, appears as if suffering; this is for the purpose of deluding those lacking knowledge.
As long as knowledge remains without exceeding its capacity, so long does Brahman exist; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.

The manifestation of knowledge is defined as the respectful cultivation of that which already exists, as well as the attainment of knowledge; this is what is traditionally known as the manifestation of knowledge.
Therefore, the supreme lord Brahmā possesses no primordial knowledge or other such qualities; rather, the four-faced Brahmā was born from the golden lotus.
Always engaged in contemplation, he performed that self-contemplation for the purpose of deluding the ignorant and solely for the sake of pleasing Hari.
Even his volition exists in that very same way, for it was not produced by ignorance; rather, having reflected, "Who indeed created me here?", that Lord [arose].
To investigate that, Brahmā entered the lotus-stalk.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Determination of the Cause of Ignorance," in the Dharma-kāṇḍa of the second part of the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Then the noble-souled devotee of Śrī Viṣṇu, stationed at Puṣkara, entered the channel and contemplated his own root-guru, Nārāyaṇa, who is beyond all qualities (nirguṇa) and without a second (advitīya).

O Lord of the Lords of Birds, at the time of reflection, one must consider that even for the four-faced Brahmā, who is a devotee of Hari with uninterrupted devotion, there remains a trace of ignorance.
Just as Viṣṇu possesses the mental resolve, so too does he constantly act; O Infinite One, his perception is always in accordance with his own capacity and never exceeds it.

Just as there is knowledge of Hari’s own nature and likewise of the phenomenal world within that very nature, so too, though it is eternally present and ever-attending, it appears as if unknown even to Viṣṇu himself.

O Indra among the twice-born, even when one performs [an act] for the sake of Hari’s pleasure, there is still a certain distinction therein; listen attentively with a restrained mind to how that God spoke and how He understands it.
Those who have realized the Vedas always perceive that which is faultless and enter into it; likewise, the Creator knows the true nature of Hari eternally, without exceeding his own capacity.

He does not perceive the true form of Hari; rather, he always perceives everything as being of a form suitable to himself. O best of the twice-born, there is no ignorance whatsoever regarding that, nor likewise regarding the true form of Lakṣmī.

The Creator does not know [it]; how then could others know it? He does not fully understand the true nature of those two; nevertheless, through a portion of the Vedas, he knows as much as Lakṣmī and the form of Hari.
O Lord of Birds, as long as the Creator does not know that which is within the scope of his own knowledge, therefore, not even a trace of ignorance can be conceived in Viriñca at any place or time.

Then, having entered the channel, Viriñca did not perceive Nārāyaṇa as being one with himself; at that time, the Lord heard the lotus-seated one say with devotion: "Perform penance upon the two-syllabled [mantra]."

Having correctly understood his intention, he said, "Perform penance solely for the sake of pleasing Hari. With his sole devotion fixed on the feet of Hari, he performed penance for a thousand divine years for the sake of Hari's pleasure.
Then Hari appeared, divine, to grant a boon to his most excellent devotee; the God of gods beheld that four-armed Viṣṇu, whose eyes were as long as lotus petals.

Beholding Hari—the Brahman Nārāyaṇa—standing before him, marked with the Śrīvatsa, adorned with the Kaustubha jewel shining upon his neck, compassionate, subject to the power of devotion, and gazing with a most gracious and moist glance.
He worshipped with great magnificence and, out of devotion, held the water from the feet of Hari; that foremost of great devotees, his soul increased by devotion, praised Hari, his own guru.

Brahmā said: "O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Lord of the worlds, O Abode of the universe, the Goddess does not know your true nature; by your grace, O Indra among gods, the Goddess shall always come to fully understand all the qualities proclaimed in the Vedas."

Nevertheless, that queen does not fully comprehend his virtuous qualities in their entirety; for even if something is not explicitly stated in the five Vedas, there nevertheless remains a distinction regarding this deity.

Those who desire the truth always discern all the hymns in the Veda, both those explicitly stated and those not stated anywhere; they first know that here, O Murāri, there are precisely four Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda.

O God, these Vedas indeed cause one to know; likewise, having first reflected upon the Purāṇa, the Mahābhārata, and the Pañcarātra in due order, the goddess Ramā herself always understands the qualities of Viṣṇu according to her own capacity.

For the Goddess specifically recognizes the aforementioned qualities as they exist in Nṛga and others according to their own fitness; she recognizes the qualities of Hari in a general way, and not eternally in their specific details.

I always recognize your qualities through the grace of Ramā and through your own grace; yet no one else recognizes even some of those qualities of Hari that are appropriate for Him and declared in the Vedas.

And by your grace and my own favor, Śeṣa shall, in the course of time, recognize those [beings], as well as their minute traces of evil karma—which are not concealed—as well as their many qualities previously known, which are suitable for them.

Having known those very qualities and having attained them, the remaining one is then remembered as "one who has acquired qualities"; and by your grace, O Lord of Umā, he shall also always [know] the qualities of Hari that are appropriate for himself.

O Hare, O Murāri, when one realizes that what was previously unattained has been obtained, then one is called "Hara. And when, O Murāri, one realizes both my world and his own, then one realizes your true nature.

O Govinda, eternally immutable, perfectly full consciousness! By your grace, there is nothing for me to attain; for even the gods who bear bodies are devoid of knowledge and remain fixed in the objects of the senses.

Those gods who are established in sense-objects are gods whose nature consists of external objects; those gods whose nature consists of external objects are always merely prattling about liberation, which is something else entirely.

O Viṣṇu, in Your own essential nature as well as in the nature of the universe, there is nothing ever equal to You; for You possess no material body, and since You have no [limited] knowledge, You are eternally without it.

Although Your body consists of perfect bliss and knowledge, You are always spoken of as "embodied" by those possessed of devotion; yet because You possess no material body, You are likewise remembered as eternally "disembodied."
I am born always devoid of the conceit of "I" and "mine" regarding this body; likewise, I am eternally bodiless and similarly always devoid of external objects.

The enjoyment of one's own wealth and wife, the enjoyment of the Satyaloka and other realms, and the enjoyment of appropriate objects such as garments and garlands—all these are indeed designated as external objects; O Viṣṇu, they are my natural desires at all times.

Nevertheless, O bird, I am eternally devoid of desire, whereas Rudra and the others possess desire; they are embodied beings, oriented toward external objects, and are likewise remembered as being possessed of ignorance.

Thus, I always maintain exclusive delight in the enjoyment of my own wife, and likewise for Hari; I shall always bear the staff, weapons, and so forth solely for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu, and never for the sake of my own body.

I have no desire for anything other than eternal bliss; therefore, I am always devoid of external objects. My wife, too, is devoid of external objects, yet she appears as if deluded, though her nature is undeluded.
To the wise, it always appears as the undeluded reality; likewise, to those lacking knowledge, it appears as ignorance. As long as knowledge exists in me, so long does knowledge exist in Vāsudeva.

As much knowledge as Vāsudeva possesses, so much knowledge is possessed by those who are upright and wise; however, for those who are ignorant or not upright, the distinction within their knowledge remains indistinct, appearing only gradually.
Just as there is perception in the light of the sun, so too is my specific knowledge; and just as there is perception in the light of a lamp, such is the knowledge possessed by Vāsudeva.

Indeed, there is a deficiency in the air consisting of its indistinct form; likewise, one should not even contemplate [it as] knowledge. Such a power of knowledge belongs to Murāri and others, extending even until their liberation.

But for the upright ones at the time of liberation, there is knowledge; for those such as Pipaṅca and Vāyu, there is no [knowledge] due to dissolution. At the dissolution of Vāyu, and likewise at the time of creation for me and Gāyatrī, there is simply no delusion.
O God of gods, those who know the reality of Hari should understand that Bhāratī is like Gāyatrī; wherever my ignorance is seen, it is always for the purpose of deluding the Daityas and others.

"By this, the pleasure of Viṣṇu, the God of gods, will be secured"—having thus resolved his mind, he thought: "I shall always perform the propitiatory rites and other ceremonies like an ignorant man, solely for the purpose of deluding the base."

Just as there is no darkness at the rising of the sun, so too, O Lord, ignorance does not exist—it simply does not exist. For the sake of pleasing Hari, I shall always listen to the definitive meaning for the benefit of the virtuous.
But for those crooked ones who have undergone hundreds of births, ignorance is indeed declared to be the very absence of direct perception from the very beginning.
But immediately after direct realization, there is neither ignorance nor doubt; O Lord of Gods, through direct realization, this remains forever throughout hundreds of births.
I indeed possess full knowledge; there is no need for deliberation on this point, O Lord, though previously, throughout a hundred births, it was beyond my direct perception.
"O Great Lord, the great seers have said that perfect knowledge exists eternally, even for Sarasvatī who has entered into the cycle of birth and perception."
O God, ignorance should indeed not be contemplated regarding Brahman and Viṣṇu; however, some distinction exists here that must be understood by those who desire the truth.
In the incarnations of Bhāratī, she is sometimes preceded by knowledge; she is always of the nature of knowledge and is entirely devoid of suffering.

For the purpose of deluding the Daityas, she appears as if suffering through her partial incarnation; yet she possesses not even the slightest suffering or the like—this is absolutely certain in every respect.
A temporary disappearance from direct perception is observed for a short duration; it is not on account of that alone that ignorance is attributed to her.
In her fundamental form, however, there is no forgetting of knowledge for Bhāratī; if it does not exist for Bhāratī, how much less so for Sarasvatī?
There has never been an incarnation of Sarasvatī in part, nor is there an incarnation of me in part, O Madhusūdana.
In the very same way, knowledge exists in Hari, Nārāyaṇa, and Vāyu—the partial incarnation—just as it exists in the original source.
All qualities such as strength and knowledge should undoubtedly be considered [as present]; nevertheless, manifestations of strength, knowledge, and so forth are observed in the wind.
In the incarnations of Vāyu, there indeed exists, through his essential power, both direct manifestation and concealment; this is true even in the cases of partial incarnations.
From power, knowledge, and so forth, up to the fundamental form, all are clearly seen; yet in the nature of the Tretā Yuga, He does not manifest such things.

O Lord, whatever form he displayed when in the nature of the Tretā Yuga, and whatever form he displays when situated in the nature of the Dvāpara Yuga—whatever form he displayed when in the nature of the Tretā Yuga, O Lord, that very same [form] he displays.
Just as the Lord manifests in whatever form he chooses when Vāyu exists in the Dvāpara age, so too does Vāyu manifest in such a form in the Kali age.
Likewise, O Lord, Vāyu manifests himself for the purpose of deluding the Daityas; those who know the internal nature of Vāyu’s incarnations [attain liberation].
They enter into half-darkness; they are Daityas, not Suras. There is no difference even in the wind regarding the definitive determination of the reality of Hari.
"I shall cut out the tongues of those who revile Viṣṇu; for that very purpose, I am always an incarnation on earth, even as Vāyu."
The contemplation of Viṣṇu, who is full of attributes, as being devoid of attributes; and the contemplation such as "I am He," which consists of the limbs of bliss and the rest that have arisen.
To contemplate birth and so forth in a body whose essence is consciousness and bliss; to contemplate cutting and piercing in limbs that are neither cuttable nor pierceable.

To contemplate separation and the like regarding the Goddess who is eternally inseparable [from Him] is like contemplating affliction, sorrow, and the like regarding Hari, who is devoid of affliction, grief, and so forth.
One should contemplate the non-sage and non-brahmin nature within forms such as Vyāsa and Rāma; one should contemplate the inner Self within forms such as Kṛṣṇa and Rāma.
The contemplation of the Inner One within the forms of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others; and the contemplation of the Supreme Victory within the forms of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others.
O Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of progeny, there was no thought of worshiping Śiva; rather, the installation of the Liṅga was performed by Rāma while he was beset by grief.

In a black [liṅga] composed of the five elements, one should contemplate the form of Hari; likewise, even in a manifest (svayambhū) place, one should conceive of it as being of the nature of consciousness and bliss.
One should contemplate one's father, mother, and the twice-born as being of the nature of Hari; likewise, one should contemplate the oneness of Rudra—who is not independent—with Hari.
One should contemplate the non-difference of Viṣṇu with Sūrya; Sūrya alone is the supreme among all, while Viṣṇu and the others are his servants.
Such reflections are considered a fault and are called "reviling Hari"; this applies even when the specific gendered forms of the words *aśvattha* and *tulasī* are not used.
Those who offer salutations while setting aside the Śālagrāma are indeed unchanging offenders against the censure of Hari.
O Lord, those who are entitled to liberation, yet through ignorance treat the Supreme Lord as separate from themselves, or whenever they do so;
Therefore, for them, suffering indeed departs during those times; of this there is no doubt. Hence, those who always perform the invocation of these [deities] in these [times] [attain their goal].
All those who perform prostrations before lingas that are not self-manifested should be known as ignorant; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
All those who, having abandoned the empty Aśvattha tree, perform prostrations [to something else] should indeed be known as Asuras; it cannot be otherwise under any circumstances.
A Tulasī plant less than two months old and a new cow that has not yet calved—all these should be known as Asuras; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
Those beginning with the *gulmas* and ending with humans are to be known as the arms of Brahmā; from our [human] lifespan up to a hundred years, this is remembered as the single *kali* age.
In the Kali age they exist as the very measure of the Kali, and at the end of the Kali they also exist; on that day, in the form of Brahman, they go to the presence of the Darkness.
Staying there, they await the path of the world without doubt, having been tormented by the practitioners of Viṣṇu’s rites who have cast aside their breath-control.
And after a hundred years, for all of them, the destruction of the linga will occur along with Kali by means of Vāyu’s blow from his mace.
They all enter into darkness to varying degrees; there is no need for further deliberation here regarding this blind darkness of saṃsāra.
Among all [vices], Kali alone is the most extreme at the end; there is no doubt that for one who reviles the devotees of Viṣṇu, there is nothing equal to that at any time.
In the blinding darkness of saṃsāra, he is everywhere a defiler of the Dharma; he possesses the notion of knowledge regarding false gifts, and the notion of happiness regarding suffering.
Therefore, there is no devotee of Śiva in the world equal to Kali; he alone is called Duryodhana, whose very nature consists of infinite suffering.
Therefore, with a hundredth part of that [power], the wife of Kali was always known in the world as Alakṣmī, and she is remembered as Mantharā.
Therefore, Vipracitti was always ten times inferior; he himself is called Jarāsandha, and after him came Kālanemi.
Therefore, that which is deficient by one hundredth part is known as *kaṃsa*; from that, those called *madhuka* and *aiṭabha* are deficient by five parts.
Those two, Haṃsa and Hiḍaṃbaka, should be known as such, O Janārdana; and Bhauma is remembered on this earth as being equal to Vipracitti.
Therefore, Hiraṇyakaśipu is remembered as being inferior by eight qualities; and from him, the great asura Hiraṇyākṣa was inferior by three qualities.
Maṇimān should be known as equal to him; Baka is remembered as slightly inferior to him; and the great asura named Tāraka is twenty times less than that.
Therefore, Śambara, that thorn of the world, was inferior in six qualities; Śālva, the lowest among the Daityas, should be known as equal to Śambara.
Hiḍimba is said to be inferior to Śambara by a factor of two; Bāṇa is to be known as lower than him, and he [is surpassed] by the one named Kīcaka.
The one known as Dvāpara is remembered as a great laughter, equal to the asura Bāṇa; Namuci, the best of daityas, is ten times inferior to him.
Both Pāka and Ilvala should be known as equal to Namuci; Vātāpi, the lowest of Dānavas, was inferior to them by four times that degree.
Therefore, the king of the Daityas named Dhenuka was inferior by half those qualities; and the Daitya Keśin was even lower than Dhenuka by half those qualities.
The great asura Tṛṇāvarta should be known as equal to the Daitya Keśin; O Lord of Ramā, Haṃsa was ten times inferior to him.
But he who is equal in three respects should be known as *tatsama*; he is remembered by the wise as *pauruṣa*. O best of men, he alone is to be understood as *veta* in his previous birth.
Therefore, O Lord, Kuṃbhāṇḍaka and Kuparṇaka are inferior by one quality each; Duḥśāsana, however, should be known as equal to Jarāsaṃdha.
Vikarṇa, the best of the Daityas, should be known as equal to Kaṃsa; he is renowned as being inferior to Kumbhakarṇa by a factor of one hundred.
Therefore, the great asura Śatadhanvan is inferior by a factor of one hundred; the enemy of Karmāri, the best of the Daityas, should be known as equal to him.
The Kālakeya, however, should be known as always considered equal to Vena; indeed, the equality of the lowest Daityas with the highest is thus described.
And because of their absorption therein, they should be known as gods; there is no doubt about this. Therefore, the great divine being of mind and consciousness is a hundred times inferior to that.
But one who identifies with that body is a hundred times superior to him; and a great deity the size of a cubit is a hundred times inferior to that.
Therefore, the great deity presiding over the foot is a hundred times inferior; however, the deity presiding over the sense of sight is superior to him by a hundredfold.
But one who takes pride in the faculty of sight is a hundred times inferior to that; and one who takes pride in touch is a hundred times greater than him.
The great Caṇḍamānasura is a hundred times inferior to that; the great Śiśramānasura is a hundred times inferior to him.
Therefore, the Karmamānasura is said to be a hundred times inferior [to him]. All the presiding deities, beginning with Rudra, are impelled by the Kalpas and other such factors.
O best of beings, they may at times act in total opposition to you; but I and the wind, O sir, shall never act in opposition to you.
O Great Lord, because the intellect of Rudra and the others perishes regarding the primary emanations and partial incarnations, they are therefore entirely severed from them.

O Lord of the Earth, because my intellect is directed toward you, I am called "Uninterrupted" (Acchinnasaṃjñika). Even though I am such as this, O God, I do not possess the power to grant you [your desire].
"O Great Lord, have compassion for me, whose devotion is unbroken. Having thus praised Hari, Brahmā stood before Him with palms joined in reverence.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Praise of Brahmā," in the second part (Dharmakāṇḍa) of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Having been thus praised by his own son with words as deep as a thundercloud, the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana, the ocean of compassion, spoke.
O Brahmā, by my grace, create these gods in due order; O Great Lord, create everything just as it was previously at that very moment.
"There is no need for that; create it for my pleasure. Thus addressed by Hari, Brahmā, having praised Hari, the Supreme, [proceeded].
Gladdening Mādhava, Brahmā, whose nature is the principle of Mahat, set his mind upon performing creation, [addressing] Vāyu, who presides over the individual soul (jīva).
In the beginning, he who is the soul of all beings created Garuḍa; and from his right hand, he likewise created Brahmāṇī, who bears the burden [of the world].
O highly fortunate one, the controller of the unmanifest, from her left hand was born the fire whose essence is the principle of Mahat, the son of Satya.
From the right hand of Brahmā, Hara, whose essence is the ego (ahaṅkāra), was born; first Śeṣa, and after him Garuḍa.
Immediately after that, the Lord Rudra was born; having been created in this manner, the great lord Brahmā remained for ten years following his own birth.
After a year, the Lord brought forth Vāyu; immediately after the birth of Vāyu, he generated Gāyatrī.
After one year, the Lord emitted Bhāratī; after Bhāratī, he emitted Śrī after ten thousand divine years.
Immediately thereafter, Garuḍa came into being; after that, following one thousand divine years, he likewise created Rudra.
Immediately after Śeṣa, the great lord, the lotus-seated one, created the goddess Vāruṇī ten years later.
Immediately after Garuḍa, the Lord created the goddess Sauparṇī; and ten years later, he likewise created Pārvatī.
After Pārvatī, he created Candra, the controller of the principle of the mind; and after ten years, he then created Vāsava.
From the right arm of Parameṣṭhin, Abhimānin was born; ten years later, the lord Śacī gave birth to him.
Immediately after Indra, and thirty years thereafter, he created Kāma from his left arm as the presiding deity of the mind-tattva.
Immediately after her, the great lord begot Rati, the wife of Kāma, as a goddess born ten years later.
He alone is proclaimed to be the presiding deity even of desire; immediately after the production of his effects, Brahmā [assumes] the vital breath consisting of ego-consciousness.
Ten years later, he then created Nāsika; and five years after that, he created the wife of that Nāsika.
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, fashioned his left nostril; and after the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra), Brahmā created Bṛhaspati along with consciousness (saṃjñāna).
And he created Nirmamā after two years, and after five years, he created Tārā as his wife.
After the Guru and after the twenty-fifth principle, the omnipresent Lord Brahmā fashioned Svāyambhuva Manu by means of his mind.
After five years, he created Śatarūpā; after Śatarūpā, however, at the end of twenty years and days.
Dakṣa, who was like a disciple, was born from the right thumb of the Lord; five years later, however, the four-faced one was born from the left thumb.
Brahmā created Prasūti with great reverence for the purpose of creation, immediately after Dakṣa and twenty-five generations thereafter.
Indeed, from the middle finger-joint, Aniruddha was fashioned; and after five years had passed, the unborn Lord created him.
From the middle phalanx of the finger [was born] his wife named Virāj; this occurred one hundred years after Aniruddha.
From the joint of his little finger, the Lord fashioned the Pravaha wind; ten years later, the Master fashioned the Pravāhin wind.
And from the joint of the little finger is Vāmadeva, without a doubt; after Pravaha, that Brahmā [is reached] after one hundred years.
Immediately after eight years had passed, the Great Lord fashioned Yama from his back, and from that very same [back], he created his wife, the goddess Śāmalā.
Immediately after Yama, and thirty years thereafter, he created Candra from his right ear, the controller of the principle of the ear.
After nine years, however, the Lord created Garuḍa from his left ear—the one who presides over the left ear—from Rohiṇī.
Immediately after the moon, and twenty years thereafter, Brahmā perfectly fashioned the sun and the deity of the right eye.
After six years, the Lord Brahmā created Saṃjñā from his left eye; she appeared immediately after Sūrya, at the end of a hundred years.
From the sense-organ of taste, the Lord created Varuṇa and his wife Māninī; twenty years later, from that very same organ, he [created others].
Brahmā created Gaṅgā as the presiding deity of the sense organ of taste, immediately after Varuṇa and ten yugas thereafter.
From his lap, Brahmā created Nārada, who is dear to the Blessed One; immediately after Nārada, however, after a period of sixty years.
The Lord Brahmā created Agni from the sense-organ of the skin; therefore, he became the presiding deity of speech immediately after five years.
Brahmā created Svāhā; they call her the deity of mantras. O Indra, after Agni, he created Bhṛgu, the most excellent of Brahman-sages.
After ten years, however, he brought forth [Atri] from the middle of his eyebrows; after another year, he created Bhṛgu’s wife.
Immediately after Bhṛgu, the Lord Brahmā himself, after a hundred years had passed, mentally begot Kaśyapa.
After one year, the Lord created Aditi; after Kaśyapa, he created Atri ten years later.
Immediately after Atri, Brahmā, ten years later, begot Bharadvāja; and after that, Vasiṣṭha.
Ten years later, however, the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā) created their wives in succession, at intervals of one year.
Immediately after Vasiṣṭha, the Lord indeed created Gautama; ten years later, he then created Jamadagni.
Ten years after that, Vaivasvata Manu came into being; immediately after Manu, [the next one] was born ten hundred years later.
The highly fortunate Viṣvaksena, the son of Vāyu and possessor of great strength, became a leader of the Gaṇas for the Lord in the fourteenth year from that time.
Immediately after him, Vīndra became the lord of wealth (Kubera) there at the age of eight; his wife became so in the following year.
Immediately after Viṣvaksena, and ten years thereafter, the lotus-seated Brahmā created Jayā and the others who are devotees of the Lord.
Immediately after Jayā and the others, Brahmā created the Vallā and other deities of action; then, after a hundred years, he created the vehicle of Śiva.
Immediately after the Karma-devas, and thirty years thereafter, Brahmā created Parjanya, who presides over the mantras and yantras.
After Parjanya, Brahmā, ten years later, begot Puṣkara, who presides over the principle of action (karma).
Thus Brahmā created [the world] through my grace, O Lord of Birds; knowing this, one attains liberation, but not otherwise by any means whatsoever.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Origin of the Devas," in the Brahma-kāṇḍa, the third part of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
Śrī Garuḍa said: O Hari, tell me of the incarnations of Lakṣmī and the gods; likewise, O observer of vows, explain to me, your disciple, the distinctions between the qualities (guṇas).

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O hero, there has never been anyone like Him—the Lord who is the primordial form, the infinite, possessed of perfect qualities by Brahmā and the other gods, independent, ancient, whose body is complete, and whose very self am I."

The feet were full, the soles of the feet were full, the nails were full, and the hips and neck were full; the thighs were full, the belly was full, and even having obtained these fullnesses, he likewise grasped the full chest.
The shoulders are fully developed and the arms are complete; the hair, beard, and teeth are full; the body hairs are full, as are the pores of the skin, and likewise the penis is full.

The testicles are full, as are the hairs of the body, the armpits, the eyes, and the ears—all these are complete. How can I describe the primal form of Hari, in which strength is entirely full throughout his entire body?

Indeed, Brahman exists even within those things that have but a single hair; for it is He who is complete. He alone is the creator of all, He alone is the destroyer, and He alone is the enjoyer of the essential essence.

Hari does not eat the essenceless parts; O Lord of Birds, listen well as I describe the essences: the essence of grapes, the essence of sugarcane, the essence of the coconut, the essence of the mango, and also the essence of the jackfruit.

The compassionate Nārāyaṇa, the best among devotees, constantly takes the essence of the orange, the essence of the areca nut, the essence of the date palm, the essence of the plantain fruit, and the essence of the seed-form.

The essence of betel, the essence of khadira wood, the essence of flowers, and the essence of sandalwood; the essence of wheat, the essence of barley, the essence of black gram, and the essence of hareṇu beans.
Likewise, pure rice, the essence of nīvāra, the essence of śyāmāka, and the essence of pure grain;

Viṣṇu accepts with supreme reverence the essence of all forbidden leafy vegetables, as well as the essence of forbidden salts, the essence of food, and the essence of all that is to be chewed or swallowed.

Viṣṇu takes the essence of soup, the essence of fine rice, the essence of milk, the essence of curd and buttermilk, the essence of ghee, the essence of asafoetida, and even the essence of mustard seed.

The essence of black pepper, the essence of cumin, likewise the essence of sacrificial oblation cooked in ghee, the essence of that which is fried in oils, the essence of roasted jaggery, and the essence of fresh butter.
Vāsudeva, the Lord of Lakṣmī and the dweller of all the worlds, eats the essence of cloves, the essence of sugar, and other such essences; and by his command, Vāsudeva also eats them constantly.

O best of disciples, hear also of the portions of the Great-Souled One that remain as the essence of those [others]; for when even these are thus deluded regarding Vāsudeva, what more need be said of the devotees of Viṣṇu in this world?

Blessed are those who consume only the essence; for them, there shall be no increase in suffering. Know that those who eat the *vaiśvadeva* offering while bypassing the wicked are indeed those whose thoughts are fixed on mere gratification.

O Lord of Birds, I shall declare the specific details regarding the Vaiśvadeva offering; a wise man should not speak of this secret elsewhere. Furthermore, when making offerings to the Sun and the other deities, one should offer them while excluding Vāyu and Hari, who resides within.

They should indeed always be known as consumers of the essence alone; therefore, Viṣṇu is the one Great Soul. He is the consumer of the essential portion, not the consumer of everything; yet, possessing unopposed power, he enjoys everything.

O Lord of Birds, listen with supreme reverence as I shall further declare other essential points that are secret: all things such as grapes and the like are indeed insubstantial, as are those objects corrupted by time and the like, or corrupted in their inherent nature.
But after the stage of over-ripeness, for four days thereafter, the jambū fruit is known to be pithless and turbid; thus it is remembered.
O Lord of Sages, after one month, the panasa fruit is considered to be sapless; O Lord of Sages, after six months, the kharjūra fruit is considered to be bitter.
O Lord, a coconut that is fresh and pure is [beneficial] immediately after being cracked open; however, after a day and night has passed, it is proclaimed to be devoid of essence.
Just as a coconut or a date becomes dry, so too is the mango described as being without essence immediately after its outer skin.
O Lord of Heroes, betel nut is prescribed after a year; O Lord of Heroes, betel leaf is proclaimed to be used after a ghaṭikā.
O Lord of the Twice-born, immediately following that, food consisting of rice with soup, milk-rice, and boiled delicacies is proclaimed to be without essence.
It is likewise recorded that after three fortnights, it is cooked in oil; and after four watches, it is cooked in ghee and becomes essence-less.
After three nights, leafy vegetables are proclaimed to be sapless; likewise are the citron, ginger, the emblic myrobalan, camphor, and the mango.
O Vīndra, after a year it is proclaimed to be sapless; after merely a fortnight, the *parpaṭa* is proclaimed to be sapless.
O twice-born one, Tulasī is always the essence, even on the Ekādaśī day; whether it be fresh or dry, when fresh it is remembered as being full of essence.
On the eleventh day, however, the wise should take the essence of the *tulasī* with their sense of touch, but not with their sense of smell nor with their sense of taste.
On the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), the food of Hari is proclaimed to be essence-less; on the eleventh day, O Lord of Birds, the sacred ford of Hari belongs to human beings.
O highly fortunate one, on the eleventh day, the sacred site should be prepared with sandalwood paste and other fragrant substances; it should be applied once, and even better if twice.
That which is mixed with sour gruel is declared to be essence-less; however, on the eleventh day [of the lunar fortnight], milk, clarified butter, honey, and water are the essence of Hari.
"It is the opinion of those who know the Vedas that there is no essence in the lords of men; O Garuḍa, in the month of Āṣāḍha, even a Śāka tree is said to be without essence."
O Lord of the Gods, in the month of Bhādrapada, curd is said to be essence-less; indeed, in the month of Āśvina, milk is proclaimed to be without essence.
Those who lack the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and the mace (gadā) are sung of as "non-Āryas"; for those who are devoid of devotion to Hari are proclaimed to be demons (asuras).
A mouth devoid of the names of Hari is said to be essence-less; food cooked without the offering to Hari is said to be essence-less.
The *atasī* flower is proclaimed to be sapless for three days; the *mallikā* is sapful for one watch (three hours), while the *jātī* is sapful for half a watch.
The *śatapatra* lasts for three watches (*yāmas*), the *karavīra* for day and night, and the *pārijāta*, O Lord of Birds, has its essence [active] for the duration of one *ghaṭikā*.
The wise say that *kesara* is called *phalgu-sāra* after three years; *kastūrī* [is so called] after ten years, while *karpūra* [is so called] after merely one year.
Sandalwood is always declared to possess essence; now listen, O Lord of Birds, as I describe those that are pure and devoid of essence.
Tuṣā, medhyā, āranāla, puṇyaka, bhiḥ, saṭā, likewise upodvrajī, alābū, and bṛhatkośātakī.
O twice-born ones, eggplant, sorrel, bilva, udumbara, fried grain, garlic, stalks, and kalanja are likewise [forbidden].
This is proclaimed to be fruitless at all times, except on the eleventh day [of the lunar fortnight], when the Vaiśvadeva rite, the Śrāddha, and the libation (tarpaṇa) are performed.
The cremation of a preta by means of a mantra is proclaimed to be worthless; for the deity Nārāyaṇa does not accept these impure oblations.
Hari himself does not take [the fruit of actions], he does not take, he does not take; nevertheless, he knows everything regarding the sinful deeds of living beings.
Hari causes the tasting [of experience] to occur, yet He Himself does not taste; and the fruit born of the karma of living beings is indeed food devoid of essence.
Living beings eat what is secondary, while Kuntī and others eat what is primary; Viṣṇu drinks only what is auspicious, for the All-pervading Lord does not drink what is inauspicious.
Who could describe His activities? Hari Himself is full bliss; there is no one equal to Him anywhere in space or time. O best of the lords of birds, I shall now speak of His incarnations; listen.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Discernment of Essential and Non-Essential Matters for the Vaiśvadeva," in the Brahmakāṇḍa, the third part of the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

In the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 15—Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Then, while the Great-Souled Lord Hari, known as Puruṣa, had gone to perform meditation, He who is the ocean of all excellent qualities, Viṣṇu Himself, appeared; He is indeed the primordial seed.

He who was Viṣṇu, called Puruṣa, existing as the seed, became that very same high-souled Vāsudeva; he existed as the primordial form within the Māyā of the wind called Puruṣa, in order to perform creation.

He who is Vāsudeva is indeed born as he who is named Saṃkarṣaṇa, whose nature consists of all excellent qualities; the Supreme Self of perfect consciousness, for the sake of Jayā, [manifests] as the wind known as Sūtrātman in order to effect creation.
He who is known by the name Saṃkarṣaṇa is indeed the same one celebrated as Pradyumna; for the purpose of producing Sarasvatī and Bhāratī, he himself became the primordial form of the Goddess.

Having created the Great Principle (mahattattva) in its subtle form, endowed with sixteen parts, that very God sported with it along with the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra); listen now indeed to what those sixteen parts are called.

The elements, the five organs of action, the organs of knowledge, and likewise the mind—having gathered these along with the individual souls (jīvas), he who possesses perfect power became known as Aniruddha.
Thus, O Lord of Sages, this Lord created all the gods, beginning with Viriñci, by means of a gross body; likewise, that Viṣṇu, designated as Puruṣa, attained the state of Sanatkumāra.

In order to practice celibacy that cannot be achieved by any other means and for the perpetual drying up of the ten sense organs, Kumāra was recited at the beginning [of the list] alongside Sanandana and others; therefore, there is no one else, and there is no need for further deliberation on this point.

That very Viṣṇu indeed assumed the form of a boar to lift up the earth and to slay the Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa; likewise, O Lord of Birds, the God took that form for the sake of protecting the virtuous and for the stabilization of the earth.

Then Hari, that Great Soul who attained the state of being my servant through the wife of the Rishi Yāminī, was not able to bestow the complete Pañcarātra in its entirety during that incarnation, for he was independent [in his choice].

That very Viṣṇu became known as Nārāyaṇa upon the Badarī mountain, the remover of impurities; he did so to perform austerities, to instruct the sages, and indeed to humble a thousand celestial nymphs.
Then the Great-Souled Hari, having assumed the form of Kapila, taught the twenty-four principles to Āsuri—which had been concealed by the power of time—and instructed him so as to uproot all doubt.

That very Supreme Self, the Giver, became Atri in the form of Atri through Rameśa and Sūyā; that Great-Souled One bestowed upon the one named Alarka the science of logic, known as Ānvīkṣikī, which consists of the knowledge of sound reasoning.

He alone, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, was born in the lineage of Vaṃśa and Draviṇa through Ākūti; O Lord of Heroes, he protected the Svāyambhuva Manvantara together with the gods.

O Indra among heroes, that very Viṣṇu became Urukrama through Merudevī, the daughter of Āgnīdhra and wife of Nābhi; and he did so to display, for all time, a source of great wonder to those who are proud and devoted to their learning.

Then Hari assumed the form of a tortoise; that great-souled one was capable of supporting Mount Mandara on his back as the gods and demons churned the ocean, or even of supporting the entire cosmic egg.

Then the Great-Souled Hari appeared, named Dhanvantari, with the luster of an emerald, holding in his hand a full vessel of nectar, solely for the purpose of warding off the defects of unwholesome food.
Then the Great-Souled Hari assumed that form of Śrī which they call Mohinī in the world, in order to completely deceive the power of those arrogant sons of Diti.
Then the great-souled Lord Hari appeared, the infinite Blessed One named Nṛsiṃha; and the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was likewise placed upon his lap and torn apart by his claws.

Then the Blessed Lord Hari, the god of gods, became a dwarf through Kaśyapa and Aditi; O King of Birds, he did so desiring to give this [earth] to Indra, and for the sake of purifying and protecting it.
Then Hari became the son of Jamadagni, whom everyone in the world calls Paraśurāma; O Lord of Heroes, the Great Lord desired to rid the earth of the Kṣatriyas who were hostile to the Brāhmaṇas.
Then that Viṣṇu, who was complete even as Rāghava, became Vyāsa four times from Parāśara and Satyavatī in order to divide the portions of the Vedas among Paila and the others.

Then, like the sun descending upon the ocean, Rāghava—the lord of monkeys, born in the solar dynasty from Kausalyā—was capable of waging war against the earth and slaying Rāvaṇa and the other leaders of the demons.
Then, in the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age, Hari became Vyāsa in the form of knowledge; the Great-Souled God himself appeared from Parāśara and Satyavatī in order to divide the Vedas.
Then Hari, that Lord Viṣṇu, desiring to utterly destroy Kaṃsa and the others, and wishing to fully protect the Pāṇḍavas, O best of heroes, became manifest as Kṛṣṇa from Vasudeva upon Devakī.
Then, O Lord of Birds, when the Kali age had fully set in, Hari was born in Kīkaṭa by the name of Buddha for the purpose of deluding the asuras, solely in order to reject the authority of the Vedas.
Then, at the junction between the two ages, Hari, the lord of heroes known as Kalki, will be born in the house of Viṣṇugupta by the name of Hari, in order to slay those kings who are mostly robbers.
The twenty-four beginning with Keśava, the [twenty-four] beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa, the thousand beginning with Viśva, and those beginning with Para are recorded as being infinite.
For the incarnations of Viṣṇu and Nārāyaṇa are indeed innumerable; they are themselves Nārāyaṇas, and there is not even an atom's worth of difference between them.
In terms of strength, form, and qualities as well, Viṣṇu is infinite and full because of his infinite attributes; it is not otherwise.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Incarnations of Viṣṇu," in the Brahmakāṇḍa, the third part of the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

The glorious Kṛṣṇa said: O Lord of Birds, O highly fortunate one, listen properly to the true nature and incarnations of Mahālakṣmī, along with the definitive conclusion regarding the knowledge thereof.
For the eye itself is indeed the self of the world other than Īśa; that which makes it its object is proclaimed to be the knowledge of Lakṣmī.
The Goddess who is never separated [from Him], whose sole refuge is the foot of Hari, eternally liberated and eternally awakened, is proclaimed as Mahālakṣmī.
And Lakṣmī is proclaimed as the wife of Hari, the Root; for the wife of the Puruṣa is Prakṛti, and she is the presiding deity of Prakṛti.
O Lord Indra, in order to perform the act of creation along with the Puruṣa and the Guṇas, she who was then called Prakṛti likewise began to consume the Tamas.
The wife of Vāsudeva is celebrated by the name Māyā, while the wife of Saṃkarṣaṇa is proclaimed as Jayā.
The wife of Aniruddha was celebrated by the name Śāntā; Kṛti, the wife of Pradyumna, became intent upon creating progeny.

The goddess Śrī is celebrated as the consort of Viṣṇu; she who identifies with the quality of purity (sattva) is Durgā, and she who identifies with the quality of darkness (tamas) is proclaimed as Kanyā.
In the Kṛṣṇa incarnation, she was indeed the younger sister of Nanda’s son, appearing as a maiden; yet, as the goddess of the earth possessed by passion, she became the wife of the boar.
Vīndra is proclaimed as the presiding deity of the Vedas, while Annapūrṇā is known as the unborn wife of Nārāyaṇa in the form of Lakṣmī.
The wife of Hari, who is known as Sacrifice (Yajña), is proclaimed to be Dakṣiṇā.
Jayantī is celebrated as the wife of Vṛṣabha; Sītā, the daughter of Videha, is proclaimed as the wife of Rāma.
Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā are celebrated as the two wives of Kṛṣṇa; indeed, his incarnations are infinite and of various kinds.
O best of Brahmins, they exist as mutually non-different from Ramā; yet they are proclaimed to be inferior to Viṣṇu, who possesses infinite and infinite qualities.
Now, Brahmā and Vāyu are inferior by ten million times to Śrī; and I shall describe the form of Brahmā—listen, O best of the lords of birds.
O Lord of Birds, he who was born from Vāsudeva through Māyā is that very one named Puruṣa, celebrated as Viriñca.
From Aniruddha, however, when Śāntā was [united], the body of the Mahat-tattva came into being; then, O Lord of Birds, it received the name Mahān Virañci.
O best of birds, he who was born here from Vāsudeva through Māyā and the quality of passion (rajas), and who is known as Vidhi, is to be understood as Viriñca.
O best of birds, he who was born within the cosmic egg as Padmanābha, seated upon a lotus, also obtained the name Caturmukha.
Thus, the four forms of Brahmā have been proclaimed; now I shall speak the names of Vāyu—listen, O best of the lords of birds.
And he who was born from Saṃkarṣaṇa in Jayā is to be known as the first Vāyu, celebrated as Pradhāna.
Because he bestows worldly activity, he is celebrated by the name of the Sūtra; and for the sake of praising Viṣṇu while He resides at Badarī, he is [so named] because of his steadfastness.
Vāyu assumed the form of fortitude (dhṛti); therefore, he is remembered as Dhṛti. He abides in the form of fortitude for those who are fit and devoted to Hari.
Since the wind resides in the heart, it is indeed known as *dhṛti* (steadfastness); and by abiding in the hearts of all, it always remembers Hari.
Therefore, O best of birds, he came to be known as Vāyu-sthiti; or rather, Vāyu alone [is he who] went to Hari in Śvetadvīpa.
O Lord of Sages, he is indeed always remembered; therefore, he is known as Smṛti. And because he is perceived by Viṣṇu through his proclamation [of the Vedas], he dwells within the hearts of all.
Therefore, by my command, the wind itself became known to me as "Liberation" (Mukti), without a doubt; through the gateway of knowledge, it bestows liberation upon devotees.
For that very wind alone, named Mukti, having become the sustainer of the earth and residing within the hearts of devotees, increases their devotion toward Viṣṇu.
Therefore, he is celebrated as a devotee of Viṣṇu; there is no doubt about this. He is indeed the very consciousness within the minds of all living beings.
Since the wind is of the nature of mind, it is therefore remembered as "mind"; it is the lord of all lords and the brother of Garuḍa in every respect.
Therefore, O best of beings, Vāyu alone is remembered as the great lord; dwelling within the hearts of all, he beholds their strength.
Therefore, O son of Vinatā, you have obtained the name "Bala" (Strength), for you abide in the hearts of all people through your sons, grandsons, and descendants.
Because he constantly performs sacrifices, he is designated as the "Sacrificer" (Yaṣṭṛ), beginning from infinite kalpas and extending even unto Vāyu.

There is no crookedness in yoga; it is remembered as being "straight. What is called crookedness in yoga is the desire for personal gain in the worship of Hari, or the worship of Hari out of a desire for the status of Īśa, Rudra, and other such deities.
But for some, O Lord of Birds, they are therefore remembered as being crooked.

Even among sages and others, there is the worship of Hari performed for the sake of specific desires; therefore, they should not be considered straightforward, so what need is there to mention ordinary men?
As long as that best of men does not abandon his optional worship, so too do the sages and others [abandon] that which is an obstacle to liberation.
Since beginningless time, there has been the latent impression (vāsanā) produced by karma; who is it that all those entitled to liberation worship?
And all that [knowledge] which was nearly lost is obtained from a Guru who awakens true understanding; having attained yoga and practiced it thoroughly, one shall attain liberation at the end.
Worship of Viṣṇu performed with a desire for worldly gain bestows power, yet it results in perverted knowledge; by that, one goes to the lower darkness.
If that very same thing is proclaimed as the opposite for the sake of knowledge—just as the perception of Viṣṇu in a stone is likewise the perception of Viṣṇu in a twice-born brahmin.
