O Lord of Birds, one may likewise have the notion of a sacred ford (tīrtha) toward water, or even toward a blade of grass; and one may have the notion of Viṣṇu toward Śiva, the Sun, or the six-faced Kārttikeya.
All such primordial knowledge is traditionally held to be erroneous; rather, one should contemplate all things, beginning with stone and so forth, as being one with [the Self].
It is said that this is the "perception of Viṣṇu," but it is not the cognition residing therein; for even throughout beginningless and endless time, the worship of Hari may be performed with desire.
Because it does not exist [in other directions], the wind in that direction is proclaimed to be straight; for others, it never exists, and therefore they are remembered as not being straight.
Or rather, it always reveals Hari directly to those who are qualified for liberation at the proper time; therefore, it is called "wisdom" (prajñā).
Even when out of sight, he always causes Hari to be seen by all; therefore, O Lord of the Vidyādharas, Vāyu is eternally celebrated as Knowledge itself.
Because he instructs his devotees on what is beneficial and what is harmful, that Wind-god dwells within their hearts; for that reason, he also received the designation "Guru."
Abiding in the hearts of yogis, he meditates upon the supreme Hari; even while meditating upon him as distinct, he is remembered as Mahādhyāta.
According to his capacity, he recognizes the supreme Hari and always knows the qualities present in Rudra and the others.
Therefore, O best of birds, this is indeed declared to be discernment; and it is traditionally remembered as dispassion resulting from the renunciation of actions performed for the sake of desire.
Alternatively, that wind, by constantly abiding in the hearts of yogis, generates dispassion; therefore, it is known as Virāga.
For the gods, happiness increases further and further according to their merit and demerit; that happiness extends upward through the higher realms as far as the world of Vāyu.
Because Vāyu produces a portion of happiness for the gods, the sages, and likewise for the highest of men, he is therefore known as Sukha (Happiness).
O Lord, the wind is the primary element there that always consumes the poison; however, the gods experience some degree of suffering, grief, and so forth.

Know that this is due to the influence of the possession by an asura; of this there is no doubt. That [possession] may affect the individual soul (jīva) to some extent, and it will gradually affect the daityas as well.
Since Kali is predominant, he is therefore remembered as "the Sorrowful" (duḥkhin); due to the merit and demerit of the Daityas, there is only increasing misery from one stage to the next.
O Lord of Sages, he always experiences that suffering and that of the subsequent ages until the end of the Kali; therefore, it is known as Kali.
O Lord, if even a slight amount of happiness, joy, or the like occurs to the Daityas, it must be understood as the possession of a deity; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
O son of Vinatā, there is no hell for the gods, nor is there any such thing as the nature of happiness arising from sense objects even for the Daityas, O twice-born one.
Whatever darkness arises from sense objects is merely uttered due to possession by a deity; for the gods, there is no darkness at all, nor is there suffering by their very nature.
The great suffering arising from sense objects never exists for the gods; nor does any suffering, grief, or the like ever occur to them due to possession by asuras.
Therefore, O Lord of Birds, Kali is always miserable, while Vāyu is always happy; such is the happiness and misery of both humans and sages.
Through that merit and demerit, Māruta becomes a consumer of merit; there is no need for deliberation here regarding the destruction of suffering and the dissolution of the impurity.
O Lord of Birds, nineteen parts, beginning with *prāṇa* and ending with *sukha*, have entered into the worlds and exist there separately.
And hear now, O best of bird-lords, concerning the Marutas and the Revatās: among the fourteen moons, the second was Virocana.
O Lord of Birds, he is proclaimed as Vāyu among Indra and the other gods; within all the elements of fire, he is the one whose gaze extends everywhere.

Therefore, that portion of the Maruts known as Rocana is proclaimed to have been Hanumān during the incarnation of Rāma, accomplishing the purpose of Rāma; he himself was born on earth as the exceedingly powerful Bhīmasena.
In the Kṛṣṇa incarnation, he is to be known as the celebrated portion of Marut.
There will be a Daitya named Maṇimān, who is known as Saṃrākṣya; he will undoubtedly cause the intermixture of all [castes].
Therefore, O Lord of Birds, he shall be known by the name Saṃkara; he will utterly destroy all the Bhāgavata doctrines in every way.
Then Vāsudeva will appear on earth, of this there is no doubt; he whose equal for the sake of sacrifice does not exist in the fourteen worlds.
Therefore, he will undoubtedly become full of wisdom; the three incarnations of Vāyu are known as those designated by the name Bhāgavata.
Establishment and the subduing of the wicked—these two alone are the purposes; there is no other purpose for the wind [element] in the nature of Vairocana.
O Lord of Sages, in the three incarnations, there is suffering arising from the womb and so forth; however, such suffering does not exist at all for Vāyu, nor likewise for Vairocana and the others.

For in the four modes of descent (avatāra), there is indeed no connection with semen and blood; it truly does not exist, O Lord of Birds, and because that [connection] does not exist, there is nothing impure therein.
Having first dried up the womb at the time of manifestation, the Goddess of Gods indeed appears during the fourfold descent.
O Lord of Birds, there are twenty-three forms of Vāyu, and through these forms—which possess straight natures—there are likewise the forms of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin.
This is indeed true, there is no doubt, regarding eternal bliss, happiness, and so forth; one should understand it exactly thus and not otherwise in any way whatsoever.
By merely hearing this, they attain liberation; of this there is no doubt. O best of the lords of birds, I shall now describe those born immediately after them; listen.
O Lord of Birds, when Kṛta was born from Pradyumna, there were two twin women, and between them was Yādavī.
O Lord of Sages, they know her who is named Vāṇī as Brahmāṇī; she is considered to be Sāvitrī, the wife of Viriñci known as Puruṣa, and she is celebrated as Sarasvatī, the wife of the four-faced one.
Thus, O best of birds, the threefold nature of speech should be understood; I shall now describe the incarnations of Bhāratī—listen with a concentrated mind.
Because she possesses the conceit of being all the Vedas, she is remembered as being composed of all the Vedas; and she is proclaimed to be the wife of the great meditator Vāyu.
She is proclaimed to be the wife of Vāyu, who is of the nature of knowledge; and because she is eternally of the nature of bliss, Bhāratī is essentially blissful.
She is proclaimed as the wife of Vāyu, whose nature is bliss; Vāyu himself is said to be her preceptor, and she remains devoted to him with faith.
Then there is the eternal Bhāratī, known as Gurubhakti; she is indeed proclaimed to be the wife of the great preceptor Vāyu.

Because it contains oil (sneha), it is remembered as "Harī" (the remover of distress) and is known as the beloved of Hari; she is also proclaimed to be the wife of Vāyu, whose form is steadfastness (dhṛti).
Because she takes pride in all mantras, she is remembered as being of the nature of all mantras; she is indeed proclaimed to be the wife of the great lord Vāyu.
All enjoyments are indeed experienced solely for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu; therefore, the goddess of speech (Bhāratī) is to be known as being celebrated by the name "Bhujinī."
She is proclaimed as the wife of Vāyu, who is of variegated form; and she who is called Śraddhā is proclaimed as the wife of Indra.
And then, O best of birds, during the Tretā age, Hanumān was born; at that time, she who is known as Bhāratī was born from the brahmin named Śiva.
Not only Bhāratī, but all the others born from him, including Āśā and the rest, attained union with their respective husbands.
And she is to be known as Anyageti, the maiden named Tanmatī; at the end of the Tretā age, O Lord of Birds, she herself shall be united with Śacī and the others.
Damayantī was born from the fire and is called Indrasenā; because she brings joy to Nala, she is also known as Nalanandinī.
In that state, O Lord of Birds, she does not attain union with her own husband; rather, it should be understood that she goes to another man by means of the wind residing within the person.
Having remained in that state for some time, she died as a maiden; she herself was then born to the high-souled Drupada along with Śacī and the others.
Born from the center of the sacrificial altar specifically for the sake of Bhīmasena, she has no connection whatsoever with others, nor is there any union between her and other husbands.
The daughter of the King of Kāśī should be known as the sole Bhāratī; she is to be known by the name Kālī, the eternal beloved of Bhīmasena.
Endowed with speech and other faculties, Draupadī, the daughter of Drupada, having cast off her body, entered [the body] known as that of the one from Kāraṭī village.
O Indra among sages, in the Kali age she will be born in the house of Saṃkara; for the sake of the third form of Vāyu, that maiden indeed met her death.
O best of sages, O lord of birds, these wives of Vāyu and the wives of Brahmā are indeed inferior to their own husbands by a hundredfold in their qualities.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Incarnation of Mahālakṣmī and Others," in the Brahmakāṇḍa, the third part of the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa said: O Kṛṣṇa, you have stated that during her four births, Bhāratī (Sarasvatī) was indeed born on earth with Śacī and the others, possessing a single body.
"O Brahmin of noble vows, tell me the reason for this, for I am your disciple. Thus addressed by Garuḍa, Madhusūdana spoke to him.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O best of birds, O lord of birds, I shall explain the cause for Bhāratī’s attainment of this distinguished body; listen with an attentive mind.
O Lord of Heroes, in former times during the Kṛta Yuga, Pārvatī was the wife of Rudra, Śacī the goddess was the wife of Indra, and Śāmalā was the wife of Yama.
O bird, the goddess Uṣas, the wife of the Aśvins, went together with her husbands to the world of Brahmā; there they then beheld Brahmā.
O best of birds, seeing them acting so insolently, Brahmā immediately displayed gestures, expressions, and amorous dalliances, and then cursed them.
And because you were arrogant, you shall obtain human birth; there, O Lord of Birds, you shall obtain union with your own husbands.
Having been thus cursed, they all went to Mount Meru; there, they easily deceived Brahmā as he sat upon it.
O Indra among heroes, while he remained silent, they stood there again, deceiving him; then, as he continued to remain silent, O Indra among heroes, they deceived him outright.
After three times [this had occurred], the great lord Brahmā cursed them: "Because you have deceived me three times and shown yourself only once."
Furthermore, after not hearing this, in four subsequent births on the surface of the earth, he will undoubtedly attain human form within a single body.
In your second birth, you will likewise attain another state of existence; in your third birth, you will likewise obtain union with a husband.
"In your first birth and in the fourth, you shall not attain the state of going to another [husband], nor shall you obtain union with your own husbands in any way."
O best of birds, having been thus cursed by Brahmā, they all then gathered on the summit of Mount Meru and deliberated together.
The curse of a Brahmin cannot be extinguished even by hundreds of means; likewise, association with the base is censurable and brings about calamity.
And through union with the supreme deity, one may become a bestower of wealth; Vāyu is the highest among the gods, so one should practice union for his sake.
Having reflected thus, Umā and the others performed service to Bhāratī; at the end of a thousand years, that Bhāratī, being gratified, spoke.
"And for what purpose indeed will those of excellent vows practice service to me? And how will those goddesses, devoted to her, act? To him, they declared their intended course of action.
"Long ago, O beautiful women, we were cursed by Brahmā in his wrathful form: 'You shall attain human status from a single body.'"
"O Lord, even in your fourth birth, and likewise in your second birth, you shall attain another state"—thus was she cursed, O beautiful lady.
"O Goddess, it was not our fault that we were led astray by the god Vāyu; therefore, O Goddess, we desire to share one body with you throughout all our births."
O best of the twice-born, having been addressed thus by them and having replied "So be it," that Bhāratī, joined by Pārvatī and the others, became manifest upon the earth.
In the house of the twice-born Śivanāman, that maiden performed austerities for the sake of the unity of action between Viṣṇu and the one known as Śiva.
O women, at this third birth as Kṛṣṇa, the great lord Viṣṇu, known as Śiva, being gratified by your ascetic penance, granted you a boon.
A union with the husband who is Righteousness (Samyaktva) will come about without worldly existence, since she and Pārvatī have been impelled in every way.
She displayed the splendor of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin; therefore, Pārvatī is superior within the body of Brahmā, without a doubt.
Even with Kṛṣṇa’s body, there will be no union for her; in this second [body], she will undoubtedly attain union with another.
The glorious Lord Hari, who dwells within Rudra, having bestowed his seed upon the woman, vanished from sight and returned to his own world.
Having cast off that body, they became the daughters of Nala; and having received the name Indrasenā, they went to the forest of asceticism.
Wandering there, they saw the sage Mudgala; by the mere sight of him, they became infatuated with desire.
Having destroyed Mudgala’s pride, the Wind-god delighted the excellent women there, such as Bhāratī and others.
Released from his body, she became known as Draupadī; because she was born from Drupada, she is remembered as Draupadī.
Since she was born from the center of the sacrificial altar, she is remembered as being womb-born (yonija); and because she is black in color, she is known on earth as Kṛṣṇā.

It is traditionally held that Bhāratī always maintains the conceit (abhimāna) of being Kṛṣṇa and others, whereas Śacī and others maintain the conceit of being in those very bodies only at certain times.
O best of birds, it is only for her whose pride arises at the very moment of union with her own husband, and not otherwise.
O best of birds, at the time for dalliance with these women, Umā has no pride at all; she is always devoted solely to sleep.
At the time of Pārtha’s delight and during the lifetime of Draupadī, it is recorded that there were two types of pride belonging respectively to Bhāratī and Śacī.
At that time, there shall be a destruction of the pride of Umā and others, as well as Śyāmā and her peers; all of them shall indeed fall into sleep—of this there is no need for further deliberation.
Vāyu himself entered Arjuna in the form of a hero, while Yudhiṣṭhira constantly delights in Bhāratī and Śāmalā.
And with his beautiful form, the Wind entered Nakula; O bird, the son of Bharata (Nakula) always delights in Uṣā.
And the Marut entered Sahadeva in the form of Nīti; O bird, he constantly delights in Draupadī, who dwells with Sahadeva.
Śacī and the others did not attain union with the body of Draupadī, nor did Māruta; therefore, one should not consider their transition to another [body] as applicable to the body of Kṛṣṇā.
One should not at all contemplate a union with Bhāratī and the others as having bodies such as those of Dharma; rather, one should contemplate their union with the body of a human being.
But for those women who possess direct perception [of the truth], there is no application of ointment whatsoever; or else, O Lord of Birds, it is like that of Mudgala at the time of sexual union.
Thus they took their pleasure; therefore, O Lord of the Gods, no fault is found in them. On one day, both Dharma and Vāyu [did so].
O giver of honor, they both sported perfectly even upon the body of Kṛṣṇa; nevertheless, there is no doubt that one must contemplate her state of being devoted to no other.
The deities know the enjoyment that belongs to the gods and is fit for their enjoyment; however, they do not at all know those mortals who exist within those very bodies.

Only the swan, and no other, knows how to distinguish milk from water; therefore, O Lord of Birds, one should contemplate union with one's own master through the body of Kṛṣṇa, and one must never contemplate the body of Kṛṣṇa as belonging to another.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Causes for the Attainment of a Distinguished Body by Bhāratī," in the Brahmakāṇḍa, the third part of the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Now, O best of the lords of birds, I shall describe those born immediately thereafter; listen with attention and, having heard them, retain them in your mind.
The immensely powerful Śeṣa was born as the younger brother of Viriñca, who is known as Puruṣa; he is the one upon whom Hari and Ramā rest when they sleep within his own body.
This was for the purpose of providing a bed, and not because of any need on the part of Hari; "I am always a servant of Hari, and I am always a worshiper of Hari."
"O Hari, I always bow to you in birth after birth. Having awakened thus, Garuḍa indeed became the bed for Hari.
O son of Vinatā, this son of Vāyu, named Kāla, has always been the Garuḍa who serves as the vehicle for Hari according to the name of the Sūtra.
Then, O Lord of Birds, from Viriñca, whose body is the principle of Mahat, I was born as Rudra, consisting of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), in order to protect Hari.
O illustrious one, these three are considered equal to one another; yet those three are a hundred times superior to both the Gāyatrī and the Bhāratī.
He alone should be known as the remainder, the devotee of Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, Vāyu, and Ananta, who is always endowed with three portions.
O bird, that Lakṣmaṇa who was born from Daśaratha as a portion of Sumitrā should also be known as Śeṣa, endowed with portions of Vāyu and Ananta.
O Lord of Birds, that Sītā was born from the Earth to perform service for Rāma; and Balabhadra, O Bird, was born from Vasudeva and Rohiṇī.
But this very one, the son of Rohiṇī, should be known as being endowed with two portions, pervaded by Hari through both his white and black aspects.
These three illustrious serpents are known as incarnations; there is no incarnation of the Lord of Serpents on earth, nor is there such a command from Hari.
I shall now describe the incarnations of Rudra; listen to them with a concentrated mind. O Lord of Birds, he who is Rudra, whose essence is the *ahaṃkāra*, became that very one.
That destroyer obtained the name Sadāśiva; he should be known as the one who presides over darkness (tamas), and because of his non-Śiva nature, he is called Sadāśiva.
Since he always wears an inauspicious garland of skulls, he should be known as a Sadāśaiva, and Śiva is not a Bhāgavata.
Since Hara wears the elephant hide as his sacred thread, he always removes all inauspicious things from the worlds.
Because, by the command of Hari, he always turns those whose minds are attached to sense-objects away from them, Viṣṇu is therefore called Sadāśiva.
Sometimes, due to the influence of the asuras, Hara acts in opposition; therefore, he should be known as Sadāśiva, and not Śiva who is devoted to the Lord (Bhāgavata).
Since this Hara desired to dwell in a cremation ground, he should be known as Sadāśiva, and not Śiva the devotee of the Lord (Bhāgavata).
O best of birds, Rudra entered the salt waters to perform penance for ten years; therefore, he obtained the name "Tapa" (the One who Performs Penance).
Śuka, the son of Vyāsa, is said to be possessed by the entry of Vāyu; he should be known as an incarnation of Rudra who appeared on earth for the sake of knowledge.
From Anasūyā, the wife of Atri, was born Rudra of great asceticism; he is to be known as Durvāsas, for the purpose of humbling the pride of kings.
Born from Droṇa and known as Drauṇi, he is proclaimed to be Rudra himself; desiring to experience his *prārabdha* karma, he manifests as the adversary.
The Rudra who is stationed in the northeast corner indeed obtained the name Vāmadeva; and Vāyu always serves him, who is situated on his own left side, as a worthy devotee.
Therefore, Rudra obtained the names Vāmadeva, as well as the status of being cultured and supreme; he attained the nature of Time and the nature of Power, but not because of physical beauty.
The great-souled Rudra, desiring to slay the Daityas dwelling in Tripura who were enemies of Viṣṇu, assumed a non-terrible form; therefore, Rudra himself obtained the name "Aghora."
To those hosts of Daityas who desired to perform service but were being afflicted by penance for some time, he was born at that very moment to grant boons; thus he obtained the name Sadyojāta.
The son of Uru was Aurva, who is proclaimed to be Rudra himself; thus, because he does not grow, he is called "Rudra," which signifies one who does not weep.
For this reason, Rudra is called "Urū" (the Wide), and his son is named Aurva; in order to leave Rudra as the remainder, Aurva became Rudra himself.
Garuḍa said: "O Hari, why does Hara, who is known as the Great One (Uru-saṃjña), weep? And why does he, who takes the form of Aurva, weep with such persistence?"
"O you of noble vows, explain this in detail to me, your grandson. Thus addressed by him, Hari, that ocean of compassion, spoke.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Having beheld his own form named Saṃkarṣaṇa, which is full of excellent qualities and whose lotus feet are bowed to by Śrī, Brahmā, Śeṣa, Jiṣṇu, Kāma, others, Bhāratī, and the Svastikas, [he remains] eternally.

Upon seeing Hari, Rudra’s body was covered in horripilation; his eyes filled with tears, his throat choked with emotion, and he was filled with joy—joy that he had never before experienced through remembrance throughout the beginningless and endless cycles of Brahmā.
"O Lord, by what merit was my lotus-foot, adorned with beautiful anklets, seen by me? Having seen and then not seeing the lotus-foot of Murāri again and again, my throat became choked."
Rudra wept, his limbs trembling with fear: "O Lord, how shall I see you again? O Mukunda, Nārāyaṇa, Universal Form, how shall my faculty of speech perform your praise?"
My sight is always associated with sin, and likewise my speech is always associated with sin; my sight has always been attached to women, whereas your sight toward me was indeed unattached.
There is no capacity for Viṣṇu to praise his own sons, wives, and so forth; there is no room for words in the praise of Viṣṇu. By what merit, O Lord, have I been seen by you?
O Lord Anantakarṇeśa, known as Sucandra, you have never heard my story with your ears; yet I have heard many worldly rumors. By what merit, O God, have I beheld you?
Having seen and looked again and again at the footstool of Hari, Kaṭha became obstructed; Rudra wept with his limbs trembling from fear, wondering how he might ever hear the story again.

O Lord Vaikuṇṭha, you are known as the excellent wind; and that which is offered to you, such as perfumes and flowers, is never defiled by the hands, nor by the mud and water consisting of urine, excrement, and the like.

O Mukunda, by what merit have I been seen by You with the water from the breasts, hair, and armpits of women, with the water from their limbs, and with unoffered garments, perfumes, and the like? O Lord!

Having smelled the fragrance of the Lord’s floral offerings again and again, Rudra’s throat became choked; with his limbs trembling from fear, he wept, wondering how he might always be able to touch them once more.

O Nṛsiṃha, O Lord of the Nose residing in the nose, by my own nose the fragrance of beautiful lotuses has never been smelled anywhere; yet thus, perfumes, flowers, and the like that have not been offered are indeed smelled again and again.
O Lord, Murāri, by what merit was Your face—with its beautiful nose and excellent teeth—seen? Having smelled again and again the fragrance of Viṣṇu’s remains, his throat became choked with emotion.
Rudra wept, his limbs trembling with fear: "How can I smell this *nirmālya* of yours? O Murāri, you who possess consciousness through the tongue, it was likewise offered by the organ of taste."

He who daily bathes before Murāri with the remains of the food offering mixed with Tulasī, especially sprinkled with the water from [the Lord's] feet, obtains the merit of ten million times ten thousand sacrifices.
O Mukunda, such remnants of your sacrificial offering—which are indeed the form of the Sun itself—have never been eaten by me; yet, O God Viṣṇu, I have eaten what was not offered to you many times.

O Lord, by what merit was it seen by me that edible and consumable food was not offered at Your lotus feet? Having repeatedly enjoyed the various offerings made to Hari, I experienced Your bliss, cherished by Ramā.

They say your head, adorned with a crown and curly locks, rests upon heaven and earth; yet it was seen by me through the accumulation of merit earned over many births and through the company of the virtuous.

"O God of gods, due to the accumulation of sins gathered over many births, you will become invisible. Thus Rudra wept with great devotion upon seeing Hari, who is replete with all auspicious qualities.
"O Vāsudeva, whose form is the universe, your lotus feet are held within the hearts of the lords of yogis; yet they were seen by me through your compassion. How shall I see them again? Thus he wept.

"O Lord, I have seen the enemy's host filled with the inexhaustible conch, discus, and other weapons, as well as the three worlds themselves; yet how shall I behold such a belly of yours again and again, O Lord of Rama? Thus he wept.

O Lord, may your broad chest be filled with bliss, filled with beautiful nails, filled with fine hair, filled with body hair, filled with virtues, and filled with a lovely neck; may it be adorned with true ornaments and graced by the stainless Kaustubha gem along with Lakṣmī.
I have beheld your chest with eyes of compassion—so very delicate, adorned with the blossoming flowers of the sacred *tulasī*, and likewise anointed with sandalwood paste.
"How might I behold him again and again? Thus Rudra wept with devotion; therefore, having obtained the name Tūru, that very Rudra became his son known as Daurvasa.

Because he made the remainder (*rudra*) of the earth (*urvi*), he became known by the name Aurva; and Aurva, seeing that the worlds were fit for liberation yet remained utterly addicted to sense objects, [acted accordingly].

And Stūdaiva, repeatedly remembering the lotus-foot of Viṣṇu, became choked with emotion; while those most wicked ones, day by day, indulged in sinful forms and evil sense-objects through their base senses.

"I do not know when I shall abandon these with the thought that they are to be discarded," he wept truly; for these fools exert themselves with the utmost care to acquire sense-objects for the sake of profit.

For all those who are devoted to sense objects abandon even their wealth and other possessions for the sake of a mere trifle; when, O Viśvamūrti, will you release these people whose intellects are ruined and who are deluded by your māyā?

Remembering again and again the illusory power of Vāsudeva, Akrūra wept with his limbs trembling from fear; abandoning his own duty and resorting to a state of wretchedness through the most difficult worldly conduct, he lamented.
Having acquired wealth and such with extreme wretchedness, all those of very sinful character squander their hard-earned money and possessions entirely in vain, like mere beasts.

"Out of the illusory power of Murāri, they never abandon those who have become worthy recipients [of gifts], perceiving them as Viṣṇu himself. The great ones say that the lives of those who ask 'How have they been lost? are in vain. Thus she wept properly.

The lifespan of these has thus passed in vain, and having seen that their youth is indeed transient, O Kṛṣṇa, O Viṣṇu, Death laughs as it rests upon their shoulders; yet those of deluded mind do not perceive this.
May my house endure for a hundred years; may my sons likewise live for a hundred years; and may I live happily for a hundred years, as does my wife of auspicious marks.

I possess cows filled with excellent milk, and my friends are indeed endowed with joy; I shall give a son for the purpose of protection, and I give my daughter to the bridegroom for the sake of marriage.
"I shall give my daughter to the virtuous, and I shall always give wealth to the wealthy; yet the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, seeing those who have never seen emptiness, laughs at them constantly."
"I shall not listen to the discourse, thinking that there will be the destruction of my fortune; I shall never worship Hari, thinking that there will be the destruction of my sons and others."
"From time to time, Hari, known by various names, is indeed the bestower of fruits for all; yet, seeing such foolish people, Akrūra, who was solely devoted to Vāsudeva, wept."

Therefore, O Lord of Birds, know that Aurva is eternally Rudra in form, having been well-instructed by Kṛṣṇa; for when Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, O Lord of Birds, cast off her own body at Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Then Rudra was born again from Menakā of Himavat; he received the name Aurva, and having been told, "Become one whose seed is drawn upward," he indeed became Ūrdhvaretas.
When the high-souled Rudradeva took the hand of the daughter of the Himālaya mountain, he became intensely infatuated with her; therefore, Rudra acquired the name "Para."

The ten Rudra-brothers beginning with Sadāśiva, the son of Sumitrā (Lakṣmaṇa), and the son of Huhū (Arjuna)—these three are equal at the time of liberation and at the time of creation; yet they are inferior to those two [Rāma and Kṛṣṇa] by hundreds of qualities.
Garuḍa said: O Kṛṣṇa, ocean of perfect compassion, please declare the definitive determination of bliss, so that it may be understood by the wise and likewise for my own sake.
Speak out of compassion for your disciple, so that you may always uplift me; O Lord Kṛṣṇa, what desire can there be for You whose every wish is already fulfilled?
Thus addressed by the high-souled Lord of Birds, the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa, being pleased, spoke out of compassion.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Śatānanda, Ekānanda is the son of Vedhas; such a Śatānanda is proclaimed to be the son of Brahmā.
O best of birds, son of Vinatā, Śatānanda is known as the son of Sarasvatī, while Ekānanda is to be understood as the son of Bhāratī.
Thus, O bird, this is to be known as the definitive conclusion regarding bliss. Everything has been told by me; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Gradations of Infinite Bliss and the Cause of Rudra’s Weeping," in the Brahma-kāṇḍa, the third part of the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 19.
Garuḍa said: "O Kṛṣṇa, O Govinda, O best of gods, you have stated that both Brahmāṇī and Bhāratī are superior even to Rudra by a hundredfold."
O Lord of the Gods, I have heard that Viriñca himself declared, up to the point of Umā, that they were devoid of infinite portions.
"O Kṛṣṇa, O Mādhava, O Lord Hari, you have stated that [the power] of all those ancestors was diminished by a thousandfold, having taken this into consideration."
O Maheśvara, from knowledge, bliss, power, and so forth, down to the vital air itself, there is a diminution of knowledge and the other qualities by a thousandfold.
"O Govinda, speak a definitive conclusion; you are omniscient, of this there is no doubt. Thus addressed by Garuḍa, Vāsudeva spoke with certainty.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Lord of Birds, it is clearly evident that for each successive one among those higher [beings], this state arises precisely through yoga, with reference to their being devoid of portions of bliss.
When bliss reaches a hundredfold measure, due to its manifest clarity, it is declared by Brahmā to possess infinite qualities.
And the state of being multiplied a thousandfold has been proclaimed by Vāyu: as it is with bliss, so it is with knowledge, with Viṣṇu, and with devotion when their power is superior.

All these qualities have been described to you in their entirety, each increasing a hundredfold in succession; and the knowledge and bliss of Bhāratī are a hundred times greater than the power of devotion.
In this way, the knowledge of the strength and other attributes of Māruta is easily understood; thus, one hundred types of knowledge regarding Māruta are to be known—of this there is no doubt.
The knowledge and power of Bhāratī are declared to be one hundred; and likewise, the knowledge of Vāyu is clearly stated to be the same.
Just as the flame of a fire, even if a hundred times greater than a lamp, does not become like the lamp; and just as fire, however abundant it may be, does not become like the sun.
Just as the moon, though twice the size of the sun, does not appear clearly, so too has the gradation of bliss been described by me to you.
Know it to be exactly so, O bird, and not otherwise in any way; I recognize the qualities residing within me, endowed with all their specific distinctions, O lord of birds.
O Lord of Birds, there is nothing whatsoever that has not been seen by me, even those forms that are exceedingly subtle.
Even in all his incarnations, the goddess Ramā knows Hari to be present.

That goddess understands all the qualities of Hari, endowed with every excellence and of undivided form; that goddess understands them in their most subtle forms, and by my grace, she knows more than even Brahmā and the other gods.

The Goddess thoroughly knows her own essential nature, which is extremely subtle and endowed with excellent distinctions; likewise, Lakṣmī thoroughly knows her own manifold expansion, which is likewise endowed with all its excellent distinctions.

Even Brahmā perceives Vāsudeva as all-pervading and His excellent qualities as superior to those of air and the other elements; yet the ear does not know the qualities of Hari, which are extremely subtle in form and endowed with specific distinctions.

Just as the gods know [the self] in its manifest form, those who are not yet liberated do not know it so; for both Brahmā and Vāyu always perceive themselves and other things as being endowed with distinctions.

Speech knows the qualities of Hari, yet even the Self-born Brahmā does not know His specific distinctions; O Lord of Birds, one should always behold Viṣṇu in the form of Kṛṣṇa as eternally beyond the nature of the three guṇas.

Śeṣa, Rudra, and Vīndra—all these perceive the state established within the mere darkness (tamas). They know the qualities as they are perceived by speech and as distinguished [from it]; O dear one, what I have spoken is indeed the truth.
Umā, Suparṇā, and Vāruṇī—these three together recognize him as well-established. O King of Birds, they do not recognize these particular forms of Hari seen by Rudra anywhere, at any time or place.

Indra and the others clearly recognize Hari, whose form pervades the ego (ahaṅkāra); and Dakṣa and the rest, as well as Soma, Sūrya, and the others, indeed know Him as abiding in the principle of the intellect (buddhitattva).

O Lord of Birds, those who constantly and thoroughly recognize Viṣṇu as Hari abiding in the true essence of all beings, and others who perceive the form of Hari within the cosmic egg according to their own capacity—[all these attain Him].

Some perceive the form of Hari residing within your heart, while others perceive it always within their own hearts; know this to be the manner of it, O Lord of Birds, and now hear from me that these six are my wives.

O Lord of Birds, my six queens beginning with Rukmiṇī, as well as my wife Śrī and Nīlā—who was the daughter of the Fire-god in a previous creation—I shall immediately embrace all of them without distinction.
O King of Birds, that maiden, who was the wife of Kṛṣṇa, would enjoy whatever desires she mentally conceived; O Lord of Birds, her father indeed always exerted extreme effort for her sake.
In that very way, she did not obtain a husband, because her mind was solely fixed on Kṛṣṇa.

Then Kavyavāha said, "O son, O dull-witted one, why do you not desire Hari as your husband? Then the daughter said to Kavyavāha, "O Lord, in this birth there can be no other husband for me than Hari, since Hari alone is the husband endowed with all virtues."

Therefore, all women in the world should always be known as widows; for they are eternally without beginning, the singular essence of the universe, most beautiful, and the bestower of liberation and desire.

All those women who do not recognize such a one as this are indeed widows for all time; they fail to perceive the husband's form as the instrumental cause, the living soul endowed with destiny, yet bereft of devotion to Hari.

O father, there is no purpose in looking at this body—which is full of impurity, leaking from the nine apertures, perpetually foul-smelling, and always loathsome—once one has abandoned Kṛṣṇa, even while the husband still lives.

The celestial women, having abandoned their own husbands, constantly delight him who dwells there; therefore, they are always considered married women and are to be revered by all people—of this there is no doubt.

If the husbands of these women were devotees of Hari, then alone would the birth of these women be fruitful; through the accumulation of merit earned over many lifetimes, their husbands may become devotees of Hari.

If their husbands are not devotees of Hari, they must certainly renounce their own bodies; for if they should properly renounce their bodies while remembering their own husbands as Kṛṣṇa and Hari in form, [they will attain liberation].

In that case, indeed, there are no such faults as self-destruction for women; this is the definitive conclusion in the scripture. However, one should never have any association with those women whose husbands do not know Viṣṇu.

Through the accumulation of merit acquired over many lifetimes, their husbands may become devotees of Viṣṇu; for in the Kali age, devotees of Viṣṇu are rare, and devotion to Hari is always difficult to attain.

Discourse on Hari is difficult to find in the mortal world; initiation into Hari is difficult to find, and indeed, the definitive realization of Hari’s true nature is difficult to find, as is association with the servants of Hari.

Circumambulation of Murāri is indeed difficult to obtain, and salutation to Him is difficult to obtain in the Kali age; likewise, the protection of His devotees is difficult to find, and the gift of food to true Vaiṣṇavas is indeed rare.

The worship prescribed in the Tantras is indeed difficult to obtain, and the utterance of the name of Murāri is difficult to obtain; the honoring of true Vaiṣṇavas is difficult to obtain, and the conversation with true Vaiṣṇavas is also difficult to obtain.

Touching a Śālagrāma stone is difficult to obtain, and the sight of true Vaiṣṇavas is indeed rare; touching a cow is difficult to obtain in the mortal world, and a true singer as well as a true Guru are rare.

A virtuous wife and virtuous sons are indeed difficult to find, as is the sight of Hari residing on Śeṣācala; yet even more difficult to obtain is the sight of Viṣṇupadī on the banks of the Kāverī at Raṅganātha.

In the sacred field of Kāñcī, service to Varadarāja and even the sight of him are extremely difficult to obtain in this world; the sight of Rāmasetu is very difficult to obtain, and the capacity for the Madhva-śāstra is likewise very difficult to attain.

The noble ones say that even for Viṣṇu residing on the banks of the Bhīmā, a vision [of him] is very difficult to obtain; and likewise for Viṣṇu residing on the banks of the Revā, and for Viṣṇupāda within the sacred field of Gayā.

Likewise, even for Viṣṇu who is established on Badarī, it is extremely difficult to attain for those dwelling in the mortal world; and ascetics like those at Śeṣācala and the hermitage of Śrīnivāsa are rare in the mortal world.
Indeed, even for Mādhava at the place called Prayāga, the constant vision [of the Lord] is difficult for men to obtain.
"Therefore, I do not desire any husband other than Kṛṣṇa at any time. Having spoken thus to her father, she departed for Śeṣācala.
At the great pilgrimage site named Kapila, the great virtuous woman ascended the mighty mountain; having seen Śrīnivāsa residing there, she bowed down to him.
Having fasted for three days and then gone to Pāpavināśana, he bathed there and subsequently departed for a secluded place for the purpose of marriage.
Two *krośas* to the north of that place, on a great plateau situated in a secluded hollow, he performed supreme austerity.
Having meditated upon the god Nārāyaṇa, the maiden remained there, and at the end of a thousand divine years, she began to offer praise.

The maiden said: "You alone are my mother and you alone are my father; you alone are my husband and you alone are my friend. You alone are my son and my most venerable teacher; you are my friend, my sister, and my beloved."

O Lord, even though we reflect upon it throughout beginningless and endless births, neither I nor all these others—such as my father and so forth—will ever truly know You; for they exist merely as instrumental causes, whereas You exist as the causeless reality itself.

Therefore, O giver of boons, my vow at that time was simply this: "May I become the wife of Murāri and of you alone"; it was not that perfection could be attained through union with Duḥsaṃgamātra and the others.

O God, best of servants, cut off the sight of those who revile you and those who mock you; O Viṣṇu, cut off the sight of those who betray their gurus; O Kṛṣṇa, cut off the friendship of those who betray your devotees.

O Lord, sever my speech with those words of betrayal; grant me union with Your lotus feet. Salutations again and again to You who dwell on Śrīśaila; salutations again and again to You, the Abode of Śrī.

O Lord, O Supreme and Lower One, O Ruler of Lakṣmī, O Embodiment of the Primordial Cause! A great length of time has passed while you have been our witness; yet it is only through the means accumulated over infinite births that the vision of You, the Four-Armed One, may be attained.
O Lord, how may I, who am thoroughly possessed of all faults and am the servant of a servant, obtain a vision of you? Be gracious, O Lord of Gods, O Abode of the World!
Thus praised, Viṣṇu, the abode of Śrī, the ocean of compassion, and Janārdana, the bestower of boons, appeared before her through her devotion.
"Choose a boon; may it be well with you; I have come here as a giver of boons. Having heard these words spoken by Hariṇa, she, with a smiling face, replied:
With supreme devotion, she spoke to Śrīnivāsa, the Lord of the universe: "O Mādhava, O handsome one, may I indeed become your wife."
Having heard these words of hers, Śrīnivāsa spoke these words. The Blessed Lord said: "O fortunate maiden, I shall be born as Kṛṣṇa upon the earth."
"I shall become your husband; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. Thus addressed, the maiden daughter spoke to Hari, the supreme heap of merit.
Extremely pleased, she spoke with a voice faltering with joy. The maiden said: "May I become the wife of Kṛṣṇa on his first day of birth."
"From my very first impression, I have chosen you above all women. Having been addressed with "Om," Madhusūdana spoke these words again.
The Blessed One said: "O beautiful lady, because they have been chosen by the maiden and because of my granting of them, their heart's desire shall be fulfilled; of this there is no doubt."
Having thus granted her a boon, he vanished on that very spot; and the maiden, having cast off her body right there, became a daughter.
She was born in the house of Kumbhaka and is known by the name Nīlā; O fortunate one, Kumbhaka was the brother-in-law of Nandaśobha.

He is to be known as Kalpavāha, remembered as the foremost of the ancestors. O best of birds, having gone to the home of that Śiva who dwells on Vṛṣabhācala, you shall be invincible by his boon alone.
O Lord of Birds, having slain the sons of Diti, Nīlā was obtained; thereafter, she was born as a maiden in the house of King Agnijit.
Agni’s son was Kavyavāha, and his daughter was named Nīlā; at her svayaṃvara, I [presented] seven bulls.
O great bird, having bound and conquered the kings who were like bulls—though they were incapable of being slain by gods or men due to the boon of Śiva—you have obtained Nīlā.
Nīlā, the daughter of Kumbhaka, entered deeply into his body through a single limb; because she entered through one part, she remained right there.
Born upon the earth in two ways, she is indeed like a young maiden; O best of bird-lords, listen as I describe her auspicious birth.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of Nīla’s Marriage," in the Brahma-kāṇḍa, the third part of the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. The glorious Kṛṣṇa said: In a previous creation, she who was the daughter of Vīndra, named Nalā, became the wife of Viṣṇu with desire; having performed circumambulation, by virtue of her merit she became known as Bhadrā. She became known as Bhadrā because of her excellence.
Seeing her established in maidenhood and named Bhadrā, her father Nala said to her: "O Bhadrā, for what reason do you cause pain to your body? Tell me its cause, O daughter."
Bhadrā said: "Listen to me, dear father; who indeed would be capable of describing the fruit of prostrations and the like?"

"Nevertheless, O father, I shall speak to you according to my ability; listen well for your own welfare. Hari is always the protector of the heart, I am His compassionate one, and I am the servant of servants to You. 'Protect me! I bow at Your feet, O Viṣṇu!'—having said this, he prostrated himself like a staff."

The wise say that a prostration to Hari made without [reciting] these [names] is empty and useless; listen to that from me: one should bow down to the god Viṣṇu while saying, "O Lord of Ramā, O Lord of Madhu, O Lord of Sarasvatī."

O God of gods, as you are pleased by salutation, you are not so satisfied by worship or ritual action; as you would restrain one from sin through the recollection of your name or through salutation, you cannot do so by other means.

O dear one, those who nourish only the body—which, though sustained by prostrations to Hari, remains devoid of devotion—say that such nourishment is indeed useless; O dear one, it is said that for those who nourish it thus, there is suffering in hell.
Yama, too, having placed him there upon that mortar, grinds him with pestles; or else, O dear one, he does not even cause him to perform the circumambulation of Viṣṇu, the God of gods.
Placing their very feet upon a foot-pressing machine, Yama constantly grinds them; because these people do not constantly utter the name "Hari-Kṛṣṇa," he declares their tongues to be useless.
In the world of Yama, Yama constantly pulls out their tongues and grinds them; O dear one, what need is there for residing in Kāśī, or what purpose is served by dying at Prayāga?

What happiness is there in dying at the front of an elephant? What is gained by performing sacrifices and the like? What is gained by wandering to all the sacred fords, or by having studied the scriptures with a very sharp intellect?

The great ones declare that everything is in vain for those on the tips of whose tongues the name of Hari does not reside, who do not bow to Viṣṇu with their bodies, and who do not perform circumambulation of Hari with their feet.

Why do they say that circumambulation, prostration, and the offering of *arghya* are performed with the name [of Hari] dedicated to Hari? Therefore, O dear one, prostration to Viṣṇu must certainly be performed, and the remembrance of Hari’s name must be practiced.

For this birth is indeed difficult to obtain yet perishable, just like a bubble upon the water; therefore, O dear one, do not place your trust in your own body, nor even in your life, thinking "this is mine" or "that is another's."

A prostration made this very moment is not truly yours; a remembrance made this very moment is not truly yours. When I shall attain death, I do not know; therefore, O Great-Souled One, place no trust in this body.
Having heard these pure words of his daughter, Nala, O lord of heroes, offered salutations and performed a circumambulation according to his ability.
She too performed circumambulations and prostrations to Hari constantly; having done this for many days, she meditated upon Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme.
And at the time of death, O bird, he abandoned his body while meditating upon Hari, in the womb of my father Vasudeva’s sister.
She was known by the name Kaikeyī, yet she was also called Bhadrā; because she was endowed with auspicious qualities, she was named Bhadrā.
O best of birds, you have recovered this auspicious lady who had been carried off by her five Kaikeya sons, O best of birds.
I shall tell you the reason for the marriage of Mitravindā; listen with an attentive mind, O best of birds.

Mitravindā said: "In a previous creation, Mitravindā by name chose Agni and Soma not out of desire; desiring always to attain Hari as her friend, the goddess there constantly contemplated the means to that end."
The Goddess reflected upon which among those means for attaining Hari was the most principal; she concluded that, even always, listening to the sattvic Purāṇas is said to be the best among them.

Wherein the excellence of Viṣṇu exists, therein likewise exists the excellence of Vāyu and of the virtuous in the Purāṇa; one should always perform the Śrāddha with the thought that it is for Viṣṇu, and no other means should ever be proclaimed there.

They say that the birth of those on a day when there is no hearing of Viṣṇu’s narrative is in vain; [so too are] bathing, chanting, the five great sacrifices, religious observances, meritorious works and charities, penances such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa, and giving of gifts.

All the initiation rites of the Vaiṣṇavas, even when properly performed, are indeed in vain for those by whom the Bhāgavata Purāṇa has not been heard from gurus who are endowed with the authentic lineage.

Those by whom the Bhāgavata Purāṇa has not been heard, and those by whom the ancient Brahmakāṇḍa has not been heard—the great ones say their birth is in vain; therefore, the discourse concerning Hari should always be heard.

One should not dwell for even a single moment, under any circumstances, in a place where there is no great river of the stories of Govinda, where there is no taking refuge at the feet of Nārāyaṇa, and where the name of Viṣṇu is never spoken.

In whatever village the scripture of the Bhāgavata does not exist, nor do those who know its essence; in whatever house the essential meaning of the Gītā is not found; or in whatever village the Thousand Names [of Viṣṇu] are not recited.

One should not dwell for even a moment, under any circumstances, where these three knowers of the essence are not present. For that person on whose day there is no discourse concerning the divine Viṣṇu, their life is indeed in vain.

Once he has entered the womb, there is no need for further deliberation; that [birth] is considered rare in the world of mortals. Though his ear be adorned with earrings and beautiful, those noble connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor say it is not truly beautiful.

The noble ones say that the ear is truly beautiful when adorned with the ornaments of the narrations of Viṣṇu; therefore, those who constantly listen to and perpetually recite the essence of the meaning of the Bhāgavata [attain that beauty].

The great ones declare that their birth is auspicious and that they likewise possess great fruit—those mortals who always listen to or indeed recite the stories of Hari while wearing turbans and bodices.

Indeed, all those people in the world are worthy of honor who do not cling to their genitals or bellies, but always speak of the Purāṇa—the essence of the Blessed One’s true reality—out of courtesy or for the sake of profit.

But for those who conceal the secrets that must be hidden regarding the truth, their destination is always the son of the Sun (Yama); whereas those who always generate a constant and sincere devotion toward the section on Dharma and the section on ritual action, they [attain the highest state].

The destiny of those who recite the Purāṇa for a fee is always like that of the son of the Sun; likewise, the destiny of those who listen to the Bhāgavata Purāṇa for a fee is like that of one who listens to the true meaning of Hari’s scriptures for a fee.

The destiny of those who perform the study of the Vedas for a fee is always that of the son of the Sun (Saturn); however, those who are content with wealth obtained by chance are always fit for this [higher path].

Those who are possessed by excessive greed for the acquisition of wealth have no qualification whatsoever for the Bhāgavata [path]. Having realized that in this world Hari alone is eternally the inner controller, and that there is no other Lord besides Him;

Thus, for those who always contemplate in this way, Viṣṇu shall provide security and well-being; for the true devotees of Viṣṇu, there is no inauspiciousness, nor is any seen arising from the nature of doubtful knowledge.

Hari bestows the fruit of both auspicious and inauspicious actions according to one's karma; therefore, one should not exert effort for that purpose, but rather for the sake of wealth and for the true nature of Hari.

Therefore, having bathed, recited the divine mantra, and offered the fragrance of Viṣṇu’s remains (nirmālya), one should become pure and constantly cause the Bhāgavata Purāṇa to be heard, even if one is already all-knowing.

According to his past karma, he will acquire wealth, Vedic knowledge, and mastery of the scriptures; he will also hear of Viṣṇu, yet hearing [of Him] with such intense devotion will be difficult to achieve.

Out of great reverence, one should savor the essence of the Bhāgavata, which is difficult to encounter in the world of mortals; and having savored that Bhāgavata Purāṇa, it is likewise difficult to remain filled with tears of bliss.

The Noble Ones have said that hearing the determination of the principles and retaining them all is extremely difficult; and having heard the principles and retained them, it is likewise difficult to dissolve desire and anger thereafter.
Having heard that crossing over by means of the retention of the principles, as well as its difficult accomplishment and its application in yoga;

Having heard the principles and immediately thereafter retaining them, one finds it difficult to dissolve desire and anger; these defects always cause even those purified by knowledge to remain possessed of doubt in this world.

Therefore, I shall always listen to the sacred discourse; there is no doubt about this. Having thus resolved my mind upon the desire for the name of Hari, I indeed applied myself to listening. Having practiced such listening until the end of my life, I have now been born upon the surface of the earth after casting off my body.
O bird, you were to dwell in the womb of Vasudeva’s sister named Sumitrā, and there you were born as Mitravindikā.
By hearing [the name] of Hari as her friend, she attained Mitravindā; therefore, she became known by the name Mitravindā.
O Lord of Birds, at the svayaṃvara, that beautiful woman placed the garland upon my shoulder amidst the kings; having taken it and shaken off all the monarchs, O Lord of Birds, we reached the city.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "Description of the Austerities and Other Deeds of Bhadrā that Secured for Her the Status of Being the Consort of the Lord," in the Brahma-kāṇḍa, the third part of the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 21.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Lord of Birds, I shall also describe the origin of Kālindī. A daughter was born to the Sun-god named Vivasvān.
O Lord of Sages, she who is known as Kālindī and remembered as the younger sister of Yamunā performed supreme austerity out of a desire to become the wife of Kṛṣṇa.
Austerity is said to be self-examination and the definitive discernment of the principles; remorse for sins previously accumulated is also recorded as austerity.
Prāya is said to be austerity, and it is called the restraint of the mind; it is declared to be expiation (prāyaścitta), O Lord of Birds, and not merely the shaving of the head.
O Lord of Birds, listen to this true account joined with remorse: O Mukunda, in the past you did not chant the divine mantra, for you were always scorched by the forest fire of afflictions.

Indeed, the nectar of Hari’s name was not remembered, while the faults and such of Hari were constantly remembered; the nectar of the reality of Hari was not remembered, while idle gossip and the like were properly heard.
The lotus feet of Hari were not worshipped, though sons, friends, and others were well-honored; the lotus feet of Hari were not saluted, though the most terrible feet of a friend were well-saluted.
O Mukunda, O Murāri, I have never seen Your face—covered with curls and wreathed in the smoke of incense—being cherished as I have cherished my sons and other kin.
My son, who was adorned with ornaments, was not cherished; nor was that which removes all sins. Indeed, nothing remained uneaten by Hari, yet food of six flavors was eaten in the house of a friend.

O Murāri, these excellent flowers and perfumes were not offered by me to you; rather, they were offered to my sons, friends, and others. I am tormented by my sons, friends, and the like; O Mukunda, when shall I behold your face?

O Mukunda, when will my tongue—which has been scorched by the food of non-Vaiṣṇavas, by vegetables such as *śigru*, by food not offered [to You], by that which is improperly prepared, and likewise by forbidden foods—behold Your face?

O Murāri, my body has never been purified by the worship of the eight-syllable mantra, nor by the divine holy waters of Viṣṇu, nor by the conch-water sanctified in ancient times; O Mukunda, when shall I behold Your face?
O Mukunda, when shall I purify my body—which has been scorched by the foul odors and defects of non-Vaiṣṇavas—with unoffered perfumes, flowers, ornaments, and various garments?
O Vāsudeva, my two feet have been burnt because they did not go upon the path to the field of Hari; and my eyes, though always burning, have never beheld your form, O Lord.
O Vāsudeva, my hands are burnt because I have not worshipped your emblem of Viṣṇu; O Murāri, I have committed a multitude of sins—O Mukunda, when shall I behold your face?
O Mukunda, do not count my faults, but extend your full compassion through pure servitude; O Lord, who are far removed from all defects, as many as the hairs that exist upon my body.
O Mukunda, when shall I behold your face upon my body, which is burdened by so many evils—by endless bodies, husbands, sons, homes, friends, wealth, cattle, servants, and the like?

Indeed, no happiness has been attained that is not measured by service to you, the divine Lord Viṣṇu, Mukunda; beyond this, I shall go neither after son, friend, nor others, for I have become your maidservant.
I know that those who might say that perfect happiness arises in the mortal world through sons, friends, and the like—urine, excrement, and so forth, always fall perfectly from their mouths.

Whatever collection of wealth has been acquired through friends and others may go to waste and turn into a form of impurity; however, whatever collection of wealth is acquired for the sake of true Vaiṣṇavas shall always be a cause for attaining Hari.

Such indeed has this become, O Mukunda; enough, truly enough of that, for through it suffering was experienced. You are always [found] by giving company to the virtuous, and you are [found] without [the company of] the wicked.
O Murāri, my body has always been scorched by association with the wicked, not joined with dispassion; O Mukunda, I do not know what state such as I shall go to—protect me with compassion!
For such is true remorse, O Lord of Birds, and not the shaving of hair and other rites; for Kanyā, having performed remorse toward the Sun, contemplated the true reality of Hari.
Hari alone is the supreme among all, because He is eternally complete with all attributes; and since the entire universe is born from Him during creation, therefore Hari is full of all attributes.

He who is the primordial *A* among the gods, from whom Brahmā and all others are not at all complete—by virtue of Lakṣmī’s grace and his long-accumulated merit, Viriñca was born endowed with perfect qualities according to his fitness.
Viriñca is not full of virtues like Lakṣmī; nor is Ramā full of virtues like Viṣṇu; nor is Bhāratī full like Vāyu; nor is Vāruṇī full like Śeṣa.
Indeed, Pārvatī is not equal to Rudra in her full form; likewise, others are never at all complete. Having reflected thus, she performed penance on the bank of the Yamunā.
Then, O bird, I went with Pārtha to the bank of the Yamunā for the sake of hunting; and seeing her there performing austerities, I spoke then to my friend Pārtha.
"O Pārtha, go quickly to the maiden and ask her, 'For what reason do you perform penance here? Having been addressed thus, he went to her side, asked this reason, and [returned] very swiftly.
Having arrived, Phālguna told me the entire account in my presence; then, at an auspicious moment, I duly performed her marriage ceremony there.

O Lord of Birds, because of her constant suffering and my continuous contemplation, I am ever-pleased and perpetually serene; since she always delights in perfect bliss, what happiness could there be for me?

O Lord of Heroes, I have indeed accepted this marriage for her sake as a favor, and not for my own pleasure; likewise, O Lord of Heroes, I shall describe Lakṣmaṇā’s beauty and the reason for taking her hand in marriage.
Listen, I shall tell you that truth; for there is nothing to be hidden from a good disciple, nor anything to be hidden from a guru.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Determination of the Reason for the Marriage of the Blessed One with Kālindī," in the Brahma-kāṇḍa, the third part of the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Lord of Birds, she who was Lakṣmaṇā in a previous creation, the daughter of Vahniveda the knower, became known as Sulakṣmaṇā because she was endowed with auspicious marks (sulakṣaṇa). O Lord of Birds!

Just as Lakṣmī is perfectly complete with her characteristics, and just as Hari is indeed perfectly complete with his characteristics; just as Vāyu is likewise full of his characteristics, so too is that Gāyatrī perfectly complete with her characteristics.

Just as Rudra and others are indeed complete with their characteristics, and [his] wife Rudrāṇī is likewise complete with her characteristics, so too, by virtue of his qualities and according to the nature of things, he is designated by a name through such a slight correspondence.
Therefore, they all call him Lakṣmaṇa; O King of Birds, first hear those auspicious marks. In Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Ramā who is full of all qualities, there are thirty-two auspicious marks.

"O Lord of Birds, they truly do exist; I shall describe them to you in due order. Having heard this from me, one attains eternal liberation. That person who has seven feet, ninety-six finger-breadths in stature, four arms, and sharp teeth—"

The noble ones say that all this combined together constitutes the single characteristic of Hari Viṣṇu; the noble ones also say that a second characteristic of Him is a face that is smooth, round, and well-proportioned.
O Indra among heroes, the noble ones declare that the third mark is when one's jaw is not protruding; and the noble ones declare that the fourth mark is when one's teeth are indeed sharp and fine.
O Lord of Birds, the noble ones say that the fifth mark is the presence of redness upon the lower lip; and the noble ones declare the sixth mark to be hands that are exceedingly red.

The noble ones say that the seventh characteristic is that in which the nails are red and very beautiful; O Lord of Men, the noble ones say that the eighth characteristic is indeed that in which there is redness upon the cheek.

The noble ones say that the hand upon which lines such as the conch and the discus appear is the ninth; while the chest of one who is well-nourished, marked with three folds, and beautiful, is like a woven thread.
The noble ones say that the tenth mark is tallness; they say the eleventh is a deep navel; and the noble ones say that the twelfth mark is indeed well-fleshed thighs.
The noble ones say that for one whose hips are long and broad, that is the thirteenth mark; the noble ones say that for one whose testicles are well-situated above, that is the fourteenth mark.
O Lord of Birds, they say that the fifteenth mark is a prominent crest; the noble ones declare the sixteenth mark to be soles of the feet that are beautifully copper-colored.
The two ankles are the seventeenth; they say the form of the neck is the eighteenth; the very red lotus-eye is said to be the nineteenth; and likewise, the arm and the knee are the twentieth.
They say that the twenty-first is broad-chested, the twenty-second has lion-like shoulders, the twenty-third has a subtle mouth, and the twenty-fourth has very serene eyes.

O Lord of the Twice-born, they say that a short penis and softness are the characteristics of the twenty-fifth [tattva]; and they say that even feet, hips, knees, and thighs, as well as even shanks, constitute the twenty-sixth.

The noble ones declare that the thirty-two marks are those where the hands are equal and the ears are equal when joined together; indeed, the thirty-two marks reside in Mukunda, and indeed, the thirty-two marks reside in Ramā.

They indeed declare that even Brahmā possesses the thirty-two marks, and that this is true of his consort Bhāratī as well; likewise, there is doubt regarding the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu) being equal [to them]. Thus, O Sadāmā, I speak—make a firm determination.
Indeed, Lakṣmī could never fully reach the end of even a single characteristic of Viṣṇu; therefore, those who know his characteristics always declare Hari to be endowed with infinite characteristics.

O Lord of Birds, Lakṣmī knows the characteristic of Vāyu’s form to be indeed superior to her own; yet Sarasvatī, in comparison to her own characteristic, is superior even to Brahmā by hundreds of qualities.

Therefore, O Lord of Birds, do not ever maintain a mind of equality toward Viṣṇu and the others regarding their physical characteristics; for they have been declared to be deficient by twenty-eight [units] in the characteristics of the eyebrows and eyes compared to Rudra and the rest.

That which he considers to be without characteristics is indeed not a bad characteristic for him; it is not to be contemplated. O Lord of Birds, the twenty-eight characteristics of Hara are certainly not to be contemplated as if they were mere words.

Therefore, Hara, in his form of wrath, is eternally present due to the absence of those two; thus it has been truly said. Consequently, O Lord of Birds, these two do not exist in Rudra, nor is there any excess whatsoever in the head or the belly.
Lakṣmaṇā and the other wives of his are endowed with twenty-seven marks; Vāruṇī and the others are likewise possessed of twenty-six marks, and Candra possesses twenty-five.
Artha is endowed with twenty-four [qualities], and Āyu with twenty-two; Śacī is undoubtedly endowed with twenty-one characteristics.
Pravāha is joined with twenty [Yamas], Yama with nineteen; Pāśa is joined with eighteen, and Anala is joined with seventeen.
Vaivasvata was joined by sixteen, Mitra by fifteen, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) by twenty-four, and Pāvaka by thirteen.
Gaṅgā is joined with twelve, Budha is joined with eleven; Śani is numbered at ten, and Puṣkara is joined with nine.
Then there were sixteen thousand wives, my beloveds; likewise, they were joined with eight [classes] and seven ancestors.
The gods and gandharvas are said to possess six [qualities], those immediately following them five; the rulers of the earth are declared to have four, and others are endowed with three.
O Brahmin, when there is some protuberance on the belly, shortness of the feet and ears, and an excess of the topknot, it pertains to the wife of Śiva.
In the Lakṣmaṇā [vein], there are five defects, excluding the head and the ankles; when the navel is excessive, there are eight defects together in the Ativāhikā [vein].
When there is an excess of the shanks, eight defects are always recorded for Śacī; in this very same way, O Lord of Birds, the defects should also be inferred.
O Lord of Sages, one who is always heard to possess ill-omened marks becomes a knower of reality; he has a large belly, a protruding navel, and fearsome fangs as long as a plow-shaft.
With eyes as deep as blind wells, with hanging ears, lips, and nose, with pendulous ankles and crooked feet, he had deformed nails and blackened teeth.
He is described as having long shanks, a long penis, a single leg, and a single nose; his beard is red, his body hair is red, and his face is crooked.
Kali is known to resemble a burnt log, with a red back; he is hairless on his body and hairless on his head, and has red cheeks and jaws.
O bird, there is constant paleness on the forehead, on the left shoulder, and on the hand; likewise, there is a cruel gaze, a gaze fixed on the feet, and a gurgling voice.
Excessive eating and excessive drinking [are indicated by] breasts resembling dry fruits; likewise, new hair grows upon the thighs, the back, and the head.
On the forehead, three [lines] are long; two are proclaimed to be equal. That fish which is shaped like a serpent is proclaimed to be at its tail.
The fish described as being at the tip of the tongue is said to be like a sandal; the fish shaped like the penis is praised for its location in the anus.
A fish shaped like a scorpion is praised for its feet, and a fish shaped like a dog is indeed proclaimed for its mouth.
There should be many lines on the hand, and hair is said to be present on the nostrils; furthermore, the thumb and the little finger should be excessively long.
"Indeed, O Lord of Birds, such ill-omens as these exist in many ways during the Kali age; however, O Lord of Birds, many auspicious marks reside within me."
O Lord, those thirty-two marks of Viṣṇu were spoken by Brahmā to you with an underlying intention, specifically in relation to Brahmā and the others.
O best of beings, there is no contradiction between what was spoken by Brahmā and what has been spoken by me; that very one described by me as having a conch-like neck is shown here, O Vyāsa.
I have stated that the red lips and the red palate are one; therefore, there is no contradiction at all, for it is perceived through such knowledge.
Those women, such as Lakṣmaṇā and others, who are endowed with twenty-seven auspicious marks;
In her private parts, eyes, hands, breasts, and likewise in her belly, she possesses five fewer marks than Bhāratī.
O Lord of Birds, it does not possess the characteristics of Rudra nor any others; it is endowed with twenty-six characteristics and is indeed devoid of the six characteristics of Vāruṇī.

There is a slight excess in the ears, the belly, the mass of hair on the head, the ankles, and the genitals; O Lord of Birds, Indra is always joined with twenty-five [features], yet he is deficient in seven characteristics.
One who possesses twenty-four marks on the hands, feet, abdomen, ears, penis, ankles, lower lip, and additionally [on other parts], as well as one with eight marks, is likewise a Nāstikavāyu.

At the navel, the ankles, the jaw, the two feet, the shoulders, the two arms, the eyes, and the lower lip—endowed with these twenty-three auspicious marks, as well as being free from the nine defects, Śacī was thus possessed of excellence.

O best of birds, know this: there is a slight excess [of hair] on the vulva, the hair, the lower lip, the ear, the shanks, the cheek, the chest, the two ankles, and likewise on the upper lip. Thus you should understand it.
The wind named Pravaha is endowed with twenty-two characteristics and ten defects; likewise, in the thumb there is a slight excess, and the Sun possesses twenty-one defects.
Then, the Fire is endowed with twenty characteristics and joined with twelve defects; it is also endowed with nineteen characteristics and joined with thirteen absences thereof.
O Khaga, Vaivasvata was endowed with eighteen marks, while he [Yama] lacked fourteen; Mitra, however, was endowed with seventeen marks.
One joined with these fifteen [planets] along with Rāhu is undoubtedly [a king]; and one joined with those sixteen [planets] is undoubtedly a lord of wealth.
He is proclaimed as being joined with those sixteen absences; and he who is joined with fifteen of them is known as the eldest son of Agni.
One joined with these seventeen defects is beyond doubt; likewise, Gaṅgā herself is proclaimed to possess those fourteen.
Likewise, there is no doubt that [the Moon] is joined with eighteen defects; however, Mercury alone is joined with thirteen of them.
There is no doubt that [the person] is joined with nineteen defects; Saturn is joined with twenty defects and twelve characteristics.
Puṣkara is proclaimed to possess eleven characteristics, and he is described as having twenty-one non-existent states.
O Bird, those ancestors who possess ten characteristics and are endowed with twenty-three defects are long-lived; of this there is no doubt.
The most excellent among gods and gandharvas are said to be endowed with eight characteristics and possessed of twenty-four defects.
The Gandharvas, who resemble humans, are endowed with seven characteristics; they are proclaimed to be possessed of twenty-five defects.
Kings are endowed with the six virtues and twenty-six faults; others besides them are endowed with five, and some indeed with only four.
O best of birds, there are none who lack these three; O lord of birds, whatever excellence of marks is seen in that man or in a king, [it is due to these].
They are not merely men, nor indeed are they lords of the earth; for none of them are ever truly supreme. O Lord of Birds, it is the same with all the gods and all the Daityas as well.
They have indeed been described in sequence by means of both characteristics and non-characteristics; O bird, they are endowed with twenty-seven characteristics and non-characteristics.

Therefore, she should not be known as possessing the [thirty-two] marks by means of those thirty-two marks; for, O Lord of Birds, while growing up in her father's house, she always sought to exalt her own family.

She said to her father: "Food and other such things should always be given by you to friends and others who are engaged in constant pursuit [of virtue], whether they are situated within or elsewhere."

The virtuous say that food, drink, and other offerings given to one who is ignorant are indeed in vain; therefore, listen today with reverence to my constant description of Hari, who resides everywhere.

The child Hari, Kṛṣṇa, in the form of a boy, constantly takes milk and the like, fresh butter, and clarified butter; he likewise takes ornaments and various kinds of clothing—one should always give these for the satisfaction of Viṣṇu.

Hari, known as Keśava and Mukunda, eats the food, drink, and other offerings given by friends; therefore, a householder should always give first—otherwise, it would indeed be in vain. Thus he becomes blessed.

Knowing that the one called Mādhava is indeed Hari who eternally accepts [the offering], one should give food and other gifts; knowing this, Viṣṇu is eternally pleased by what is given, and not otherwise, for otherwise it is indeed in vain.
O Suparṇa, Hari Vāsudeva always delights in staying there in the home; knowing this, one should always adorn one's own house with the forms of the deities at all times.

The one named Govinda resides among the Vṛṣṇis; Vāsudeva resides together with his sons; Mukunda is with his friend, and Aniruddha is with his maternal cousin; Nārāyaṇa is always present with the best of the twice-born.

Viṣṇu, in the form of Hari, always resides in the cow-pen; the one named Vāmana always dwells in the horse; Saṃkarṣaṇa is ever present among the Śūdra caste, and Pradyumna always abides among the Vaiśyas.
Janārdana always exists within the kṣatriya caste; Hari is eternally among the fishermen (dāśas). Indeed, the one Hari known as Upendra always and forever abides upon the earth, O Suparṇa.

The wielder of the discus always dwells in the elephant; the one of universal form always dwells within the ant; the creator of beings eternally dwells in the dog, and indeed at all times even in the termite.

Hari as Trivikrama exists in the intermediate space; Hari possesses infinite forms within every species. For Hari, the Lord of diverse forms who is all things, there is no color, no lineage, and no birth.
Knowing this, the goddess Lakṣmaṇā always gratified Hari with constant service, thinking, "May Hari indeed become my husband."

Desiring the status of being Viṣṇu’s wife, she indeed cast off her body among the Madras and was born as the daughter of Vīndra; and at her svayaṃvara, having pierced the target and surpassed the lords of kings, I won Lakṣmaṇā.
Having performed the marriage ceremony with Lakṣmaṇā and returned to the city, I delighted the queen; in that same manner, I shall tell you the reason why I married Jāmbavatī as my wife.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Cause of Lakṣmaṇā’s Marriage," in the Brahmakāṇḍa, the third part of the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: In a previous creation, there was a daughter of Soma who became my wife, Jāmbavatī, who is dear to me. O Lord of Birds, among them she is indeed superior, yet she is slightly deficient in five qualities compared to Rudra and the others.

When the possession by Ramā is powerful, then Keśava is held in subordination to her; when, in the course of time, he undergoes diminution due to that possession, the great ones say there is equality between them.
There is indeed always a certain degree of possession by Lakṣmī; therefore, there is a slight superiority over them.
Garuḍa said: O Kṛṣṇa, among them, what kind of worship did Jāmbavatī perform? Tell me that out of compassion, O Viśvamūrti; for what indeed was the reason for her superiority over the others?
Thus addressed by Garuḍa, the Blessed One, the son of Devakī, spoke to the son of Vinatā in a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
