Garuḍa said: Vāruṇī, the fair-browed daughter of Revata, attained the state of being Rāma’s wife so that she might always sport with him. Thus Vāruṇī exists in three forms; Pārvatī, the wife of Rudra, exists in two forms.
O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord, it is heard by me that there is some similarity between the low-born Jāmbavatī and Śeṣa; tell me the reason for this.
"And likewise, O Lord Rudra, you are always superior to Umā by many qualities; thus have you spoken, O Blessed One, for the sake of my certain understanding, O Master."
Revatī, Śrīyutā, Śrī, Śeṣarūpā, Vāruṇī, Sauparṇī, and Pārvatī—these three are the most excellent among the hundred of Śeṣa.
"O Kṛṣṇa, Madhusūdana, it is heard that such things have occurred somewhere; O Kṛṣṇa of noble vows, tell the cause of this to me, your disciple."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Lord of Birds, having understood that Jāmbavatī and the others are equal to me in their supreme state through the descent of the Supreme Being, you should know this.

Indeed, even for the qualities of those who are inferior, there exists a dependence upon those who are superior; it is precisely to illuminate this fact that [the former] is said to exceed [the latter] by a hundredfold.
O Lord of the Sages, understand what I say exactly as it is and not otherwise; I shall now speak of those born immediately after him—listen, O best of the sons of Kaśyapa.
Among the fourteen Indras, he who is the seventh is Purandara; for the wise declare that the bodies of Vṛtra and others are called "fortresses" (pura).
Because he shatters that [fortress] with his thunderbolt, he is therefore called Purandara; among the fourteen Indras, Mantradyumna was the sixth.
Since the great lord of mantras, the god Mantrānanda, shines forth, therefore Mantradyumna is also in the world; yet both are truly one and the same.
O best of birds, Arjuna, the son of Kuntī, was an incarnation on earth of Mantradyumna, Viṣṇu, Vāyu, Ananta, and Indra.
Pārtha, endowed with four [qualities], is proclaimed as Indra himself; O Arjuna, there is even a distinction regarding Vāyu in the fourth [quality].
The monkey named Vālin is known as Purandara; the wise King Gādhi was born in the Lunar dynasty (Candravaṃśa).
He is remembered as Mantradyumna, the incarnation who was the father of Viśvāmitra; for he sustained with his intellect the "cows" (gāḥ), which are the mantras declared in the Vedas.
Therefore, O Lord of Men, he was called Gādhi; for that purpose, there appeared on the earth a son of Ikṣvāku renowned as Vikukṣi.
He himself became an incarnation of Indra for the very purpose of serving Hari; moreover, because he knew Hari especially within his own womb, he was always [regarded as] Hari.
Therefore, this son of Rāma named Kuśa was always renowned in the world of mortals as Vikukṣi; he was proclaimed to be none other than Indra himself.
Because he was fashioned by the sage Vālmīki from a blade of *kuśa* grass, the lord who brings joy to Jānakī is therefore called Kuśa.
Indradyumna, Pūru, Udra, Gādhi, Vālī, Arjuna, and Vikukṣi—these seven, together with Kuśa, are proclaimed as the Indras.
He who is the son of Kṛṣṇa, Pradyumna, is proclaimed as Kāma himself; he bears the name Pradyumna because his form is of preeminent light.
Bharata, the brother of Rāma, became like the god Kāma on earth; because he carried out the command of Rāma, he was named Bharata.
Kāma, who presides over the discus, is remembered as Sudarśana; Brahmā himself is Kṛṣṇa’s son Sāṃba, the offspring of Jāmbavatī.
The descent of desire should be understood; there is no doubt about this. That Skanda, who is the son of Rudra, is proclaimed to be desire itself.

Because he constantly leaps upon his enemies, he is known as Skanda; or rather, he who is Sanatkumāra, the son of Brahmā and lord of birds, should be understood as an incarnation of Kāma—of this there is no need for doubt.
Sudarśana, Parama, Pradyumna, Sāmba, Sanatkumāra, and Sāmba—these six are the Kāmarūpakas.
Furthermore, even among Indra and Kāma, there are ten others beginning with Umā; between those two, however, Garuḍa is considered the lowest of desires, while Kāma is the lowest of Indras.
The vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed the ego (ahaṅkāra), known by the name Ahaṅkāra; it should be understood as a portion of Garuḍa, inferior to Kāma and Indra by ten degrees.
Immediately after that, O Lord of Sages, listen with a concentrated mind as I describe those born thereafter; by hearing this, one attains liberation and is freed from great sin.
Niruddha, the son of Kāma, though proclaimed as distinct from Hari, became on earth as Rāma’s younger brother in order to perform service to Hari.
He is renowned as Śatrughna because he utterly destroys his enemies; and from Pradyumna was born Aniruddha, the son of Kṛṣṇa.
He is indeed pervaded by the three forms beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa; thus the high-minded Aniruddha is to be understood as having two forms.
Rati, who is proclaimed to have two forms, is the wife of Kāma; she is known as the daughter of Rukma, Rukmavatī, the wife of Kāma.
Because she was endowed with excessive radiance, she is remembered as Rugmavatī; that daughter of Duryodhana who was Lakṣaṇā is remembered as Rati.
Kāṣṭhā was the wife of Sāmba; she endowed him with auspicious marks (lakṣaṇa), and for this reason he became known on earth by the name Lakṣaṇa, even though he was born from corrupted seed.

Thus, Rati, the wife of Kāma, is known to be of two forms. Svāyambhuva Manu, the son of Brahmā, who is equal to his preceptor, was born from Viṣṇu through the duty of kingship in order to please Hari.

Bṛhaspati, the high-souled preceptor of the gods, had three incarnations, O Lord of Birds. During the incarnation of Rāma, Bṛhaspati became the one named Bharata, joined by the entry of the Lotus-born One (Brahmā).

Having caused those monkeys, who were incarnations of the gods, to cross over, he recounted the divine deeds of Śrī Rāma; for this reason, he became known by the name Nārada, having attained the status of an *aṅga* (limb/minister) of Lord Rāma upon the earth.

In the Kṛṣṇa incarnation, Bṛhaspati became one named Droṇa, imbued with the entrance of the Lotus-born (Brahmā). Because he was born from Droṇa and because he was a teacher (guru), he came to be known by the name Droṇa.

Indeed, for the purpose of assisting Viṣṇu in the removal of those who had become a burden to the earth, Bṛhaspati descended to the earth to perform service; joined by an infusion of the Wind-god, he received the name Uddhava.
Because Hari has come here perfectly, he is indeed superior; for he, like Budha, obtained the name Āpa. This high-minded one was a constant friend of Kṛṣṇadeva and is honored in all the worlds.

Born from the right thumb was Dakṣa, the son of Brahmā, possessed of great intelligence. Having created a daughter to please Hari, that Prajāpati became known as Bhūman. From him, Dakṣa procreated sons; therefore, he is remembered as Dakṣa.
Know her to be Śacī, the wife of the King of the Gods; hear now correctly, O Lord of Birds, of her incarnation: in the Rāmāvatāra, she became Tārā, the wife of Vālin, who was equal to Śacī.

When her husband, known as Vālin, died at the hands of Rāma, Tārā then took up a union with Sugrīva; therefore, Tārā did not go to the heavenly realm—where else could that wicked woman go, for she was not even in the intermediate space?
O Lord of Sages, in the Kṛṣṇa incarnation, she herself became Tārā on earth as the wife of Vijaya; her name was Piśaṅgadevī, and her proximity to him was just like that of Arjuna.

Having begotten Babhruvāhana as his son upon her, the high-souled Arjuna indeed abandoned her; therefore, both of them—Vāra and Citrāṅgadā—are of the form of Śacī, and there is no doubt to be had in this matter.
Pulomajā was the wife of Mantradyumna; she who was Kāśikā was the wife of King Gādhi; Sumati was the name of Vikukṣi’s wife; and Kāntimatī was the name of Kuśa’s consort.

Know indeed that these seven are the lowest by their power; there is no doubt in this matter. Śacī, Rati, Aniruddha, Manu, Dakṣa, and Bṛhaspati—these six are said to be equal to one another, yet they are ten times inferior to Ahaṅkāra.
Now, that Pravaha wind, the powerful son of the primary wind (Mukhyavāyu), is the greatest among winds; he is likewise the presiding deity of the intermediate direction (Koṇādhipa).

In the nostrils, that same [wind] is called the elemental (bhautika), and it is indeed the same; it is also called the "conveyor" (ativāha), since it is the one to be reached by those seeking liberation.
"He is proclaimed as inferior even to Dakṣa and the others by five qualities. Garuḍa said: "Tell me, for what reason did he receive the name Pravaha?"
"What is the meaning of that name as it is understood? Tell me that. Thus addressed by Garuḍa, the Blessed One, the son of Devakī, Hari, being highly pleased, spoke after praising Garuḍa.
Kṛṣṇa said: "O best of birds, because he always carries those who are equal to Hari with great joy, he is therefore celebrated by the name Pravaha."
"Viṣṇu alone is the supreme among all; by name, Brahmā and the others are always subordinate to him. What I have spoken is the truth and not false; I would grasp even an angry serpent with my hand."
"If all this be true, and if it should prove false, then let that lord of serpents bite me! Speaking thus, he seized the enraged snake; yet even that serpent did not bite him.

O Lord of the Sages, it is precisely because of his sustaining this [power] that the son of Vāyu acquired the name Pravaha; whereas in the world, those such as Reṇukā who, having abandoned the form of Viṣṇu, possess the nature of Daityas are false gods.
The worship of them, as well as that of my ancestors, is thus rendered fruitless; I speak this truth, the very truth. If all of this should prove false, then let that Lord of Serpents bite me!

"I shall lead away those who perform [the rite] solely with the ancestors in mind, having completely abandoned the ancestral [rite]; that sinful soul indeed goes to the hells—this statement I speak as the truth."

Fortune is not independent, nor is the Creator; neither Vāyu nor Śiva is independent. As for others besides them—such as Gaurī, Puloman, and the rest—it goes without saying that none of them are independent in this world.
I speak the truth; Viṣṇu alone is truly the Supreme Person. Raising my right arm, I speak this truth: if all this should prove false, then let that Lord of Serpents bite me!

The individual soul (*jīva*) is real and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is real; the distinction between these two is eternally real. The insentient (*jaḍa*) is real, and the distinction between the individual soul and the insentient is real; moreover, the distinction between the insentient and the Supreme Self is real.
The distinction among all living beings is eternally real, and the distinctions between insentient things are likewise always real; if all this were false, then let that Lord of Serpents bite me!
Speaking thus, he seized the serpent who was filled with rage; the snake bit him, yet from the mere act of holding it fast, the son of Vāyu became so terrified that he lost consciousness.

Having first understood the nature of the duality, you should always accept that very duality; yet he who, though performing daily rites such as bathing, remains a sinner, that self never attains liberation.
Therefore, having thoroughly investigated these two, one should always be happy; there is nothing further to be deliberated here. If all this were false, then let that Lord of Serpents bite me!

Garuḍa said: O Lord of the gods, what is that duality, and what is its cause; tell me what it is like. Tell me what the abandonment of the two is like, and tell me what kind of happiness results from that abandonment.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: They say that two among the senses are the most powerful in this body—namely, the ears and the eyes, when they are well-formed. O King of Birds, I shall now describe the nature of those two intermediate ones, the ears and the eyes, as they are said to be.

The nature of the ear is indeed excessive delight in hearing worldly gossip through its attentive relishing; whereas in hearing the news of Hari, the nature of the ear is the cessation of the web of suffering, as well as dullness and self-restraint.

Indeed, for men and women, the very nature of the eyes during sight is such that due to excessive devotion there is no sleep or the like; likewise, for the devotees of Hari, the sight of Viṣṇu’s worship is a mass of suffering in the form of pain.
Having previously understood the true nature of those two, the fool nevertheless takes them up again and again; out of sheer ignorance, he always inserts his penis with great care into some womb.

O Lord of Sages, neither fear nor shame exists for brides, men, women, or ascetics; for they do not recognize their own sister even on the same day, and through sacrifice they consume her as if she were their own nature.

Indeed, the essential nature of Viṣṇu is always present in the consumption of food that has not been offered, as well as in the consumption of sacrificial offerings; likewise, his essential nature is present even in the consumption of things that are normally unfit for eating.

The nature of that which is to be licked belongs to what is not to be licked, and the nature of that which is to be drunk belongs to what is not to be drunk; having abandoned the true nature of both, the fool repeatedly and constantly takes them up again and again.
They say that his bathing is useless; therefore, it should be abandoned, for neither of these two [rites] should be performed. O Lord of Birds, understand this very intention, always with a smile.

Indeed, not knowing the true nature of his two wives, and having accepted one while abandoning the other, the man of deluded intellect performs his ablutions and other rites; they say that for him both liberation and worldly enjoyment are utterly in vain. If all this should prove false, then let that Lord of Serpents bite me!

Garuḍa said: "O Murāri, tell me why there are two wives; tell me also their true nature to me. Between those two, tell me which wife is to be accepted and which wife is not to be accepted; tell me this correctly."

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O King of Birds, intellect (buddhi) is my wife, and she is of two forms: one is wicked and the other is of beautiful form. Between these two, the one of wicked form is the younger, while the elder is that whose nature is beautiful intellect.

When the little finger is lost, the life-force perishes; when it remains well-established, one attains proper stability. Listen as I describe the true nature of the little finger; having heard it, form the resolve to abandon it.

Indeed, that youngest [power] which impels the individual soul always performs only desirable worldly dharma; where are the Brahmins, where is the Great-Souled Viṣṇu, where indeed are sacred discourses, where are the sacrifices, and where are the cows?
Where is the holy fig tree, where is the ritual bath, and where is this so-called purity? It destroys everything! O fool, worship your husband; honor Reṇukā and offer a lamp to the goddess Māyā.

O fool, O blind one, worship Subhairava and the others; you should always wear saffron powder. On the eighth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, worship the goddess Jyeṣṭhā with devotion and tie a thread around your neck.

On the eighth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, worship Mārgaṇandha; likewise, wear this thread around your neck. On an auspicious day, worship the lamp-pillar and wear that very same thread around your neck.

"Perform the proper worship of Mahālakṣmī and Ādyalakṣmī with devotion; then indeed live! Wear the Lakṣmīsūtra upon your neck, and you shall become possessed of great fortune (Mahālakṣmīvān)," as stated later on.

Having left [your home] on the day of the Mauñjī ceremony, you who desire good fortune, wear excellent guggulu incense with great devotion; quickly honor the married women with devotion, pleasing them with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps.

Having placed the excellent offering of ghee in a bronze vessel, perform the waving of lights for the deities of the deities; then, having spread neem leaves upon the ground, bow down and say, "May you forgive me."
Worship Mahādevī today with devotion; do not give food even to true Vaiṣṇavas. If you give food to true Vaiṣṇavas, the good fortune of one who witnesses it will go to ruin.
Having placed the lamp in a bamboo vessel in your left hand, O husband, hold it while you stand up with your right hand; rise, sir, and go for alms at five houses, completely casting aside all shame.

First, having prepared food of six flavors in your home, you should take your meal while keeping it hidden from the world; O husband, having fed them with the remnants of that food, you must indeed become their refuge.
Placing their hands upon the book, make them recite from their mouths, "Save us! Today, you must worship Lord Khaḍga, and today you must properly worship his servants as well.
Together with them, you should make the sound of a dog; always wear turmeric powder. Perform worship for Bhīmasena with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the sixteen types of offerings.
Having had that loincloth made of silver and having offered it, arrange a garland of lamps; feed those excellent servants today with devotion, and roar out well, "Bhīma! Bhīma! with great force.
Always delight those excellent servants with your own garments, wines, and a multitude of meat offerings; today, worship Mahādeva properly with the Mahārudras and the Atirudras in the correct manner.

Having said, "Take it," worship those born of the Śūdra caste who are experts in the Śaiva Āgamas; and you, O Śākaṃbhari, having had all kinds of vegetables cooked, distribute them from house to house.

Give [it] with devotion and supreme respect, having adorned it well and praising its qualities; thus, from this day forward, worship the family deity with devotion, and on that specific day, indeed look upon it with both eyes as if it were Śambhu himself.

Today, worship those foremost among his devotees properly; offer salutations at the base of his feet. On the auspicious fifth lunar day, perform the worship of an earthen image of Śeṣa with milk, parched grain, and other offerings.
O friend, having tied a snake-noose around his neck, you should feed him the remainder of that food; on the fourth day, feed him with devotion, and today, eat the offering-food well.

Having thus incited her husband, she constantly makes him lost to his own life-force (jīva). Through association with her, your husband, who is of the nature of the life-force, will truly perceive you in this world and the next.
Having abandoned attachment to her from afar and having performed every duty, you should always act with perfect wisdom; thus she spoke, urging you on: "Worship Viṣṇu with the highest reverence."

"O King of Birds, you must never worship anyone other than Hari; otherwise, that Reṇukā will not protect you, for she is like Hari, whose name is unseen, if she were not herself the constant bestower of fruits."

Having served that goddess who is loathsome, not mentioned in the Vedas, and ever treacherous toward her husband, you shall experience suffering through leprosy, fistula, and other ailments by her grace, and then go to Saṃyaminī.

Then, tell me, where has Kudavī gone? O husband, do not worship the Goddess; O husband, rather worship the Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas, who are of beautiful form and who deliver one from the suffering of saṃsāra.

Tell me, what can be said of the pure worship of the goddess Māyā, which leads even to the attainment of service and other benefits? For on the eighth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should properly worship the goddess Jyeṣṭhā, who is indeed Alakṣmī, with the perception that she is Lakṣmī.
Having tied a thread around her neck, you shall indeed experience various sufferings and fall; when you fall, you will be bound with nooses by the messengers of Yama and thoroughly beaten with whips.
For then, where would that Alakṣmī flee? Therefore, worship the root, the foot of Viṣṇu. O fool, you should always worship the principle of Vāyu, and you must not take refuge in the subtle Skanda.

O husband, having eaten that ghee and fresh butter with devotion, you shall indeed eat her leftovers; and having tied her thread around your neck, you shall experience sufferings right here, O husband.
When you fall, bound by the nooses of Yama’s messengers and being thoroughly beaten with whips, where then will Skanda flee? Therefore, take refuge in the root, the foot of Viṣṇu.

Having caused a lamp-pillar to be given and having tied a thread around your own neck with devotion, you will then be properly bound by the messengers of Yama with nooses and beaten with lamp-pillars.
Where has the lamp-pillar fled? Therefore, take refuge in the root, the foot of Viṣṇu. Having worshipped Lakṣmī on her auspicious day, you should wear her sacred thread around your own neck.
When you fall, bound by the nooses of Yama’s messengers and being thoroughly beaten with whips, where then can that Lakṣmī flee? Therefore, take refuge in the root, the feet of Viṣṇu.

On the day of the marriage thread ceremony, O dull-witted one, having devoutly worn those loathsome things and having placed the bridegroom’s *ārārtika* offering in a bronze vessel, he makes the sound "udaudaiti" while performing the waving of lights.

In that very manner, having bitten a leaf of the *picumanda* tree and having performed a dance with supreme devotion, whenever he is then bound again and again with nooses by the messengers of Yama, he is thoroughly beaten.
"O Great-Souled Lord, tell me where my family deity has fled; for I have properly worshipped it with my own limbs and with the neck-ornaments and hair of those who were distressed."
While she was being struck with clubs and slings by the most powerful messengers of Yama, where could she have fled at that time—she who was shorn of her hair and had her ears made long?

Placing a bamboo vessel in his left hand and holding a lamp in his right hand, the fool remained thus; and having performed the practice of begging for alms from house to house, he returned to his own home, O Goddess.
Whenever that happens, O fool, you will be thoroughly burned by thousands of lamps by the messengers of Yama; then, O dull-witted one, tell me: where has that noseless Reṇukā fled?
Having always properly worshipped the foolish Khaḍgadeva with devotion like a servant, you shall remain constantly in your own home, barking like a dog along with them.
Whenever he was being thoroughly beaten there by the messengers of Yama, crying out in pain, and while that excellent meal remained before him, where did the god flee at such a time?
Having separately and properly worshipped the image of Bhīmasena with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and having given him well-prepared food and a loincloth, that fool remained in his own house.
Whenever the fool is being thoroughly beaten by the messengers of Yama on the path of Yama, where indeed can he flee? Take refuge in the root, the foot of Viṣṇu.
After worshipping Mahādeva properly and saying, "Take [this] to your own home," when the house was indeed consumed by fire, where did Hara flee?

"O Great-souled One, on the day of Śākaṃbhari, all that was Śākaṃbhari—that goddess—has fled. Tell me, where has she gone? And having worshipped the god Kulāla with devotion, [tell me] where you are."

Indeed, having taken the cotton that was given by him while he stood there, he was being thoroughly crushed by the messengers of Yama with sharp-edged axes; where did he flee after abandoning Kulāladeva—who has beautiful tusks and eyes—and it is not known by whom he was sought out?

When, on the fifth day, one has devoutly worshipped the earthen image of Śeṣa in one's own home while it is present there, then the messengers of Yama shall bind him, having thoroughly girded themselves and bound him with serpent-nooses.

"Tell me, where indeed has that elephant fled, having abandoned his own excellent devotee? [He fled] after having worshipped Vināyaka with sprouts of *dūrvā* grass, sweetmeats (*modaka*), and likewise with the five kinds of edible foods."
While I was standing there, O fool, being thoroughly beaten by the messengers of Yama with heated rods, the King of Obstacles fled, leaving his tusk behind; tell me, where did he go?

Even at the time of marriage, if that fool has worshipped the goddess Piṣṭadevī with great devotion while residing in his own home, he will nevertheless be bound by the messengers of Yama and tormented on the path of Yama.
Where has Viṣṭhādevī fled, having abandoned her devotee who was being tormented? Having gone to the washerman’s house at the time of his wedding and having entreated him earnestly, the fool—

Whoever, while residing in their own home, has performed worship by wrapping the pillar-thread around the water-pot—at that very time, the messenger of Yama shall properly place that pillar-thread into his mouth.

When [the drum] was being struck, the goddess residing in the *saṃtabhasūtra* fled; tell me, where has she gone? At the time of marriage, having properly worshipped the Caṇḍālī goddess, one gains mastery over her through devotion.

When he is being served by the best of his devotees in the midst of a winnowing basket or on the riverbank, yet remains present within his own homes, then he is bound by the messengers of Yama and severely beaten upon the path of Yama by great beings.

O you of utterly deluded intellect, where has Cūḍālā fled? Worship the feet of Viṣṇu! And when your own son is tormented by fevers and other ailments, [worship] the god Brahmā who resides in the home.

Having performed worship with incense sticks, lamps, various foods and edibles, and flowers, whenever he is present in his home, he is then bound by the messengers of Yama and beaten with bamboo poles, nooses, and other instruments.
O you of utterly deluded intellect, where could that Brahmā-deva have fled? Worship the feet of Viṣṇu! For the sake of progeny, worship Bṛhatī, and indeed bind Bṛhatī and her fruit around your neck.
While you were being bound by the messengers of Yama and beaten with large thorns, O dull-witted one, where did the goddess Bṛhatī flee? Tell me that!
O fool, worship Nārāyaṇa, the supreme deity and the deliverer from all suffering; do not set your mind on insignificant deities, and likewise, do not listen to trivial speech.

O Great-souled One, having cast aside the petty gods like small slingshots and sent them far away, you must uphold the dharma of your own family’s tradition, which serves as the cause for falling into hell.

O you of deluded intellect, always purify your body at this sacred bathing-place of birth with the eight mantras; having abandoned the Māra-mudrā residing in your heart, adorn yourself with the supreme Viṣṇu-mudrās.

O you who are always deluded, devote yourself to the discourse of Hari; for your life has passed away in vain through such evil intellect. Indeed, the company of true Vaiṣṇavas is difficult to attain, and knowledge of the nature of the gradations [of souls] is easily disturbed.

O fool, by following Hari alone as your Guru, you shall know your own true goal through Him; having thus burned away your wicked intellect, O fool, always resort to that which is the form of perfect wisdom.

Having obtained a true guru together with me, and having understood the pure reality preceded by perfect dispassion, we shall attain liberation through that alone—not by mere straightforwardness, nor even by the grace of Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī.
Keeping this intention in mind, my foremost devotee spoke thus; therefore, O Lord of Birds, that devotee received the name Pravaha. Listen now to what concerns him.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Meaning that Viṣṇu Alone is the Object of Worship by Way of Defining the Hierarchy [of Beings]," in the Brahmakāṇḍa, the third part of the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 29:
"O best of birds, I shall hereafter describe the Pravaha wind; listen! He who is the son of Brahmā, born from his skin at the time of the first creation, is indeed Dharma."

Because he sustains virtuous people through his gentle form, he is named Dharma; he became the son of Sūrya and acquired the name Yama. Because he is the punisher of sinners, he is called Yama by the wise.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: After Prahlāda comes Gaṅgā, the wife of Varuṇa; she should be known as inferior to Prahlāda, yet superior to Varuṇa in greatness.
They should be known as inferior to His own essential nature; no further deliberation is required here. Yama always knows Viṣṇu as the bestower of the very nature of knowledge.
Therefore, she should always be known as Gaṅgā, the purifier of the world; through devotion, she is likewise celebrated as Viṣṇupadī—of this there is no doubt.

O Lord of Birds, in former times, when Viṣṇu, the manifest Hari, was performing his strides, [the earth] was split by the tip of the nail of his left foot, breaking open the shell of the upper cosmic egg.

Having entered with great speed that river which flows from the lotus-pollen of the feet of the Destroyer of the world’s sins—pure, the destroyer of all impurities through sight or touch, bestowing devotion at the feet of Viṣṇu even by a single immersion, white as the rays of the moon, fish-eyed, and most worthy of worship—one who remembers her, born from the foot of Hari, attains liberation in due course.

Even Indra, having consumed a drop from the Vāyukūṭa mountain ground by the wind, felt it unbearable upon his head; yet, knowing the Bhāgīrathī to be marked with the foot of Hari, he—being the foremost among the great and supreme devotees, his heart distressed by devotion and holding her upon his own head with the highest reverence—became truly auspicious, though previously most inauspicious.
O Lord of Birds, there were four forms of Bhāgīrathī; Abhiṣecanī was indeed the wife of the great physician Janendra.
In her second form, Gaṅgā became the wife of Śantanu; she was known as Suṣeṇā, the wife of Suṣeṇa, and was considered a vānarī.
Gaṅgā as the wife of Maṇḍūka is indeed remembered as Maṇḍūkinī; thus, these four forms of Gaṅgā are proclaimed.
From the Sun and from the Gaṅgā, Parjanya is said to arise; for he rains down excellent detachment, and thus he is named Parjanya.

Having abandoned the five from Śarvara and Pañcajanya, and having consumed Garvaka through the sixfold sequence, one should never practice devotion toward one's own arrow situated within one's own heart, nor toward poison.

The *liṅga* should never be nourished; rather, the *liṅga* should always be kept in a state of emaciation. One should never have attachment to the *yoni*; for when one is liberated from the *yoni*, being free from all attachments, one attains liberation.
Thus, O best of birds, detachment always takes this very form; therefore, Parjanya is Antaka. To this extent, the great-souled one named Śarabha is internal, yet he is indeed Parjanya himself.

O Lord of Birds, he whose body is adorned with perpetual hair shall be known as the bird named Śarabha; O Lord of Birds, his wife shall be Śyāmalā, who is also the wife of Yama and the eternal consort of Kali.

She who performs this mental rite with perfect understanding has therefore become known by the name Śyāmalā. I shall now describe the impurity that is antagonistic to devotion for Hari, as well as its presence in a vessel made of fine iron.
Therefore, Vaiṣṇavas should always avoid clothing that is burnt, produced from a seam, or obtained from a wedding.
O Lord of Birds, the suffering of others must always be remedied; thus should it be abandoned [only through action] by those devoted to You.
Nor should one associate even at any time with those who are devoid of devotion to Hari; they are not elevated. One should avoid contact with old [books], old musical instruments, and old clothing.

He wears a well-worn patched garment, a deerskin, and a girdle; he bears the sacred thread yet is fond of strife; he loves his home, yet it is filled with woolen blankets, sacrificial fuel, and kuśa grass—despite being utterly wretched.

If all that is dear to the wife of Kali is never at any time dear to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow—namely, well-cooked barley meal in bell-metal, husks, oil-cake, the gourd, the bilva fruit, and onions—[then how could such things be pleasing to Him]?

Long buttermilk, lack of sweetness, and bitter herbs—all these are dear to the wife of the Kali age; likewise, she delights in harsh speech, the censuring of noble-born ones, and the forceful disparagement of her own sons.

He is always excessively oppressive toward his circle of masters due to stealing rice, clothing, and other items kept in the house; he gathers with his hands his disheveled hair and is fond of gambling with the gods.
All such things, which were dear to Kali’s wife, she made perfectly pure; therefore, she received the name Śyāmalā for herself and became Devakī.
And there, Devakī was honored as the wife of Yudhiṣṭhira; she was indeed Rohiṇī, the wife of the Moon, who is always superior to Aśvinī and the other lunar mansions.

Having been held by Rohiṇī, she grew at a suitable place; therefore, she became renowned as Rohiṇī. O Lord of Birds, she who was known as the wife of Āditya should be understood as Saṃjñā, who is the very form of Nārāyaṇa.

O Lord of Birds, because she perceives, she received the name *saṃjñā*; thus, O Sun, she became known in the world as Sūrya’s wife. Furthermore, the deity who presides over the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) received the designation *Virāj*.

The group of six beginning with the Gaṅgā is always equal; they are neither superior nor inferior to one another. Among them, the Gaṅgā is eternally auspicious as the purifier of the primary fire; there is no need for deliberation on this point.

One who knows these [mantras] constantly attains merit, and Hari Keśava is eternally and perfectly pleased. Indeed, Svāhā—known as the daughter of Agni—is superior to the Gaṅgā and other rivers; she possesses manifold virtues and is by no means inferior.

O Indra among the wise, Svāhākāra, who possessed the conceit of being the form of the mantra, always obtained the name "Svāhā. From the wife of Agni, the intelligent one was born as Brahmābhimānin, and Budha, the son of Candra, was also born.

Indeed, he brought forth the entire collection of kingdoms with his intellect, and because it was supported by him, he obtained the name Budha; likewise, the high-souled Abhimanyu was born from Arjuna in the womb of Subhadrā.
Joined with portions of Kṛṣṇa, Candra, Yama, the two Aśvins, and Hara, Budha—the son of Candra and the youngest of those born from Svāhā—is a devotee at the lotus feet of Lord Viṣṇu.
The wife of Aśvin, named Uṣas, is proclaimed to be inferior in nature; she is to be known as inferior to Budha, and Svāhā is ten times more inferior than her.

The daughter of the Magadha king is Nakula’s wife, and Śalya’s daughter is Sahadeva’s wife; both of these, as well as Uṣā—the wife of the Aśvins—worship Viṣṇu, the primordial one, with sixfold devotion. Therefore, O Lord of Birds, she is known by the name Uṣā. Listen now to what follows, O Great-souled One, for I shall speak.
Then the power (śakti), whose essence is the earth, always moves slowly; therefore it is named Śanaiścara, and these are the ten lowest states of Uṣā.

Puṣkara is to be known as the self of karma; Śani is considered the charioteer and Yama is the one who conceives of himself as the leader. Puruṣa is the one who is slightly bowed, having ten [fingers] as his limit.
Because he always delights Hari and sports in Puṣkara, he is therefore celebrated in the world by the name Puṣkala.
O Lord of Birds, listen as I shall describe the dharmas that bring pleasure to Hari: having risen at the time of dawn, one should remember Nārāyaṇa, Hari.
O Bird, one should perform the salutation of Tulasī and remember Śrī Viṣṇu; and at the time of voiding feces and urine, one should remember Keśava, whose nature is the lower breath (apāna).
At the time of purification, one should meditate on Hari as Trivikrama, who drinks from the Gaṅgā; but at the time of brushing the teeth, one should meditate on Hari as the indweller within the moon.
O bird, at the time of washing one's face, one should remember Mādhava; and likewise, while scratching the cows, one should remember Hari as Govardhana.

O best of birds, one should always remember the Beloved of the Cowherds at the time of milking the cows, and at the time when the fruits of the actions performed throughout births acquired through infinite merit have reached full ripeness.

Indeed, for men there is always auspiciousness from touching cows; therefore, there is no need for further deliberation on this point. In that house where there is never an excellent cow, nor the sacred Tulasī in the courtyard—[that house is devoid of merit].

In that house where there is a great festival for the gods, yet where there is no hearing of Viṣṇu’s glories, one encounters suffering and the like due to association with it; therefore, one should never even touch such a place.
They say that the birth of one who is devoid of the touch of cows, who does not know the milking of cows, and who is devoid of the tending of cows, is meaningless.
For one who does not give even a mouthful of fodder to the cows and who fails to nourish them, there is indeed no higher destination; he is remembered as being like an outcaste of the village.
While Vatsa was drinking from his breast, he should remember Bālakṛṣṇa; and during the churning of the curd, he should remember Hari as the support of the churning-stick.

At the time of bathing with clay, one should meditate upon Hari in the form of Varāha; and likewise, when applying the sectarian marks (puṇḍras), one should meditate upon the twelve [forms] beginning with Keśava.
While holding the mudrās, one should likewise visualize the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, as well as the lotus, the Nārāyaṇī mudrā, the Kruddholkā, and the others.
O best of birds, one should remember Śrī Rāma at the time of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), and one should remember Acyuta, Ananta, and Govinda at the time of the ancestral rites (śrāddha).
During the five oblations beginning with *prāṇa*, one should meditate upon Aniruddha and the others; however, at the time of offering food and other items, one should meditate upon Vāsudeva.
At the time of the *apośana* rite, one should remember Hari who has entered within the wind; at the time of putting on the garment, one should remember Upendra, who is Hari.

Furthermore, when wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), one should remember Nārāyaṇa known as Vāmana; and likewise, at the time of waving the lamp (*ārārtika*), one should properly remember Viṣṇu known as Paraśurāma.

At the time of the *apośana* rite for the *vaiśvadeva* offering, during other fire-oblations and the like, and when applying sacred ash (*bhasma*), one should remember with devotion and supreme reverence Nārāyaṇa, the Rāma known as Jāmadagnya.

At the time of taking the water from the sacred site three times, one should remember Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Vyāsadeva in succession; and at the time of drawing up the water from the conch, one should always remember the form of Mukunda.

At every single mouthful, O Lord of Birds, one should practice the recollection of Him known as Govinda; at the time of taking each individual morsel of pure food, one should indeed properly remember Acyuta.
While eating vegetables and the like, one should always remember Dhanvantari at the proper time; likewise, while enjoying the food of others, one should properly remember Viṣṇu as Pāṇḍuraṅga.
Upon eating *haiyaṅgavīna* (fresh butter), one should indeed properly remember Kṛṣṇa known as Tāṇḍava; and when eating curd-rice, one should always remember the supreme, ancient Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa.
Likewise, at the time of consuming milk and rice, one should properly remember Hari, the Abode of Śrī; and when eating food cooked with excellent oil or ghee, one should remember Vyaṅkaṭeśa.

One should indeed remember Bālakṛṣṇa amidst the beautiful fruits of grapes, *sujambū*, plantain, mango, orange, and pomegranate, and in the exquisite abundance of excellent plantains, coconuts, and *dhātrī* fruits.

At the time of drinking a beverage, one should properly remember Viṣṇu known as Nārasiṃha; and at the time of drinking the nectar of the Gaṅgā, one should likewise remember Viṣṇu alone as the father of the Gaṅgā.

At the time of departure, one should remember Nārāyaṇa, whose vehicle is Tārkṣya, who is beyond all qualities (nirguṇa), and whose form is the universe; and at the time of kissing one's children and others, one should remember Kṛṣṇa himself, holding a beautiful flute in his hand.

At the time of sexual pleasure, one should always remember Hari, who delights in the pair of breasts of his own wife, O Gopī; and at the time of chewing betel, one should always remember Vāsudeva, known as Pradyumna.

At the time of lying down to sleep, one should constantly remember Hari in the form of Viṣṇu known as Saṃkarṣaṇa; at the time of sleep, one should remember the lotus-named one (Padmanābha); and at the time of storytelling, one should remember Hari in the form of Vyāsa.

At the time of eating, one should remember Hari who sings the flute; at all times, one should utter "Hari, Hari. And at the time of plucking the auspicious *tulasī*, one should indeed remember "Śrī Rāma, Rāma."

When cutting flowers and the like, one should properly remember Hari known as Kapila; and during circumambulation, O Lord of Birds, one should always remember Hari situated within the Gāruḍa [Purāṇa].

At the time of bowing to Viṣṇu, the God of gods, one should remember Viṣṇu as residing within Śeṣa; at the time of seeking good counsel, one should remember Nṛsiṃha; and one should always remember Nārāyaṇa.
When the fulfillment of one's actions is performed, one should properly remember Vāsudeva and Hari; thus performed, these actions become pleasing to Hari.
Puṣkara, the beloved of Hari, performed these rites correctly.

O Lord of Birds, from this very [account] that has been proclaimed, he who hears the incomparable narrative called Puṣkara endowed with faith will always be filled with devotion for the dharma that pleases Hari.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Secret of Reality," in the Brahma-kāṇḍa, the third part of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
This glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa is hereby completed. Thus the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa is finished.
